content:
Michelle Landry announces she will not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia at the next election
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
Matt Canavan could attempt a switch to the House of Representatives after a colleague announced her looming retirement, as a leading pollster said the Nationals leader had a “zero per cent” chance of holding his Senate seat if the One Nation polling surge remains unchanged.
Veteran National MP Michelle Landry on Friday announced she would not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia, around Rockhampton, at the next election.
Responding to speculation that Pauline Hanson could attempt her own switch to run in that seat, Landry said One Nation was “not very pleasant” and criticised the party’s “obnoxious” cartoon videos .
“I think they need to pull their heads in,” Landry said of One Nation .
There has been heavy speculation Canavan will run in Capricornia . Canavan earlier this month said he would do “whatever it takes” to hold Capricornia, telling Sky News: “if I’m required, if it is required to keep a seat, to hold one more seat in the lower house somewhere. I will do it.”
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
On Friday, at a press conference with Landry, Canavan shrugged off questions but did not rule it out. Landry denied she was pushed to resign from Capricornia to make way for another Nationals member, and declined to speculate on who could run as her replacement.
The Coalition leader, Angus Taylor, also declined to speculate about a Canavan lower house switch when asked at a separate press conference, only praising the Nationals leader as an “extraordinary colleague”.
Kos Samaras, director at polling group Redbridge, said Canavan faced losing his Senate spot in 2028, pointing to current polling showing a One Nation surge which he claimed could see Hanson’s party win upper house seats currently held by the Coalition.
Senators up for re-election in Queensland at the next poll include two LNP members in James McGrath and Canavan, two Labor, one Greens, and Hanson herself. But One Nation’s surge means the party could win one or more additional Senate seats, most likely at the expense of the second person on the LNP ticket – Canavan.
“He goes from a 0% chance of being elected as a senator, to potentially winning [in Capricornia],” Samaras said.
“That will also be difficult, because of One Nation, but he [Canavan] is in a better position going downstairs.”
Last month’s Guardian Essential poll showed One Nation with a 25% primary vote nationwide, with Labor at 29% and the Coalition at an all-time low 22%.
Landry took a parting shot at One Nation, and the prospects if Hanson were to attempt a run in Capricornia, in her press conference.
“I’ve had a lot of dealings with One Nation over the years, and I can tell you, most of it hasn’t been very pleasant.
“When I look at people that move into an area to run for a political position, it doesn’t usually end well,” Landry said.
Samaras pointed to Redbridge polling showing what he called “a complete wipeout” of the Coalition at the hands of One Nation, specifically a large analysis from May showing Hanson’s party winning up to 59 seats nationally – largely from the Liberals and Nationals.
“On current polling, they’ll win nearly every seat the LNP holds in Queensland,” Samaras said, including Senate spots.
“If there’s a state in this country that’s good for One Nation, it’s Queensland.”
However, Samaras noted large “volatility” in polling nationwide, noting that the Queensland’s state LNP government was polling well.

title: Mother sought advice from Alan Jones after broadcaster’s alleged indecent assault of her son, court hears
description: Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching Listen to the podcast Alan Jones on Trial The mother of the youngest alleged victim of Alan Jones continued to seek advice from the broadcaster after the teenager was allegedly indecently assaulted at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm, a Sydney court has heard. content:
Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching
Listen to the podcast Alan Jones on Trial
The mother of the youngest alleged victim of Alan Jones continued to seek advice from the broadcaster after the teenager was allegedly indecently assaulted at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm, a Sydney court has heard.
The divorced mother told the Downing Centre court she had developed a pattern of not trusting herself and she continued her correspondence with Jones because: “I knew he knew about everything; he had an opinion about everything.
“I was in a web of dependency with Mr Jones,” the witness said on her last day in the witness box on Friday.
She previously said she corresponded with Jones after he allegedly kissed the 17-year-old and put his tongue inside his mouth out of fear Jones would withdraw his financial support.
During cross examination, defence barrister Claire O’Neill suggested the mother continued to correspond with Jones not because she was scared but because she wanted more money out of him.
O’Neill asked: “You did not continue to communicate with Mr Jones because you were scared of his influence over your finances, did you?”
The witness replied: “I absolutely was.”
Her son, complainant A, is one of five men who allege Jones, 85, sexually touched or indecently assaulted them between 2003 and 2020. All five have now completed their evidence.
Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.
Under cross-examination by the defence, the witness agreed she wrote to Jones about her son’s late university application, a superannuation payment, outstanding legal fees and attaining a Sydney Cricket Ground membership for her son.
She was shown an email in which she provided Jones with an update on her son’s university application. The defence asked: “You wanted to lay the groundwork for having Mr Jones pay the [legal] bill?”
The mother said the suggestion was “absolute rubbish” and she was “proud of him” for finishing year 12 under difficult circumstances and wanted to convey that in the email.
She agreed she sent Jones information about the cost of repairs to her Land Rover but denied she was asking him to pay the bill.
“You have told lies in this court about why you continued to have contact with Jones?” O’Neill asked.
The witness replied: “Absolutely disagree, that’s rubbish.”
O’Neill: “You were taking advantage of Mr Jones’s generosity for as long as you could?”
When she was asked why she shared personal information with Jones about the deterioration of her relationship with her son she became emotional.
“My son, who was a child, suffered trauma and didn’t share it with anyone and it had an effect on his relationship with me and a lot of other people.”
Asked by prosecutor Georgina Wright what that trauma was, she replied: “I was referring to what happened to him at Fitzroy Falls”.
Listen to the podcast Alan Jones on Trial .

title: ‘I’ve killed people’: Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly confessed to friend and asked for help cleaning ‘mess’, court told
description: Friend tells jury Lamarre-Condon told him in early 2024 ‘I shot the first one through the head and the second one through the door’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly confessed to killing two men, telling his friend it was an “out-of-body experience”, before attempting to play it off as a joke, a court has been told. Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024. Continue reading...
content:
Friend tells jury Lamarre-Condon told him in early 2024 ‘I shot the first one through the head and the second one through the door’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly confessed to killing two men, telling his friend it was an “out-of-body experience”, before attempting to play it off as a joke, a court has been told.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon’s friend, whose identity is suppressed, told the New South Wales supreme court on Friday that the officer arrived at his workplace the day Baird and Davies were killed.
Lamarre-Condon told him “I’ve done something”, and when the friend asked for an explanation, the policeman said “I’ve killed people”, the jury was told.
“I said ‘are you fucking kidding me?’, he said ‘I wish I was’,” the friend told the court. “He said it just felt like an out-of-body experience and it just wasn’t him.”
The friend said when he asked how Lamarre-Condon did it, the officer said with a gun.
He then made a gesture with his fingers indicating a firearm and said “pew pew”, the friend told the court.
When asked for more details, Lamarre-Condon allegedly said: “I shot the first one through the head and the second one through the door.”
Lamarre-Condon then said the second person wasn’t meant to be shot but he “couldn’t leave any witnesses”, the friend told the jury.
The officer asked his friend to leave work to help “clean up his mess”, noting the bodies were heavy and he needed to buy a new door.
The friend then returned to his workplace and explained the situation to his team lead, who told him to tell Lamarre-Condon he had a meeting he couldn’t miss.
Lamarre-Condon later messaged the friend and asked “I should get an Oscar, hey?” before going on video call and saying “got you”.
The friend then got upset, saying, “it’s not a fucking joke, you’re mentally fucking with me”, the court was told.
The policeman responded: “OK it is real but I just didn’t want you to tell anyone.”
The friend told the jury that on 20 February 2024, the day after the alleged murders, the pair went to dinner and Lamarre-Condon said he needed to “throw out bloody clothes and things”.
He then made a gesture to indicate his legs were sore and said: “I didn’t realise bodies would be heavy.”
Shortly before Lamarre-Condon handed himself in to police, the friend contacted a lawyer who attempted to connect him with NSW police.
But police said: “Is it worth our time coming out? It’s really busy,” the court heard.
The lawyer responded: “You’ll want this information.”
Earlier on Friday, the friend revealed he had travelled overseas in late 2023 for a trip with Lamarre-Condon.
He said that while overseas, Lamarre-Condon told the friend: “I need to find a spot … to purchase a silencer.”
The officer explained he was going hunting on a mate’s farm, the jury was told.
The two found what they believed to be a gun store, but it had either closed down or there had been a fake ad, the friend said.
Back in Sydney, Lamarre-Condon drove his friend to a national park and took a police service weapon out of a paper bag, the jury was told.
Lamarre-Condon gave his friend a police-issued radio and asked him to listen for any reports of police movement towards them after the officer shot the firearm.
“I said ‘you can’t really shoot your police-issued firearm’. He then told me that they were training bullets he had taken previously from a police shoot they do once a year,” the friend told the court.
He said Lamarre-Condon then fired the weapon and asked his friend how loud it was.
Then, he tried again, shooting a bullet into the bushland before asking “does this make any difference on the sound?”, the jury heard.
“He’s asked me whether it would be louder or would you hear this in a house?” the friend said on Friday. “I proceeded to say ‘you could hear that anywhere, it was super loud’.”
On their way home, Lamarre-Condon then allegedly said “you can’t tell anyone about this”, the court heard.
The defence team claims Baird and Davies were accidentally shot when the accused acted in “self-defence”.
Lamarre-Condon then “panicked considerably”, cleaning up the scene and disposing of the bodies, the defence lawyer John Stratton SC said.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

author_name: Megan Davies, Claire Jones and Magdalena Shopova for MetDesk
content:
Storm Adam brings heavy rain to Valencia, Alicante and Balearic Islands, as Storm Austen gusts strike England and Wales
Storm Adam brought torrential rain to eastern Spain earlier this week. In Pego, Alicante, 632mm fell in 36 hours with 430mm of this falling in just six hours, while the Valencian town of Olivia received 600mm in 24 hours. As a result, 145 municipalities, approximately 850,000 people, across Valencia and Alicante were placed in a temporary lockdown on Monday due to the severe flooding.
At least five people have died and 500 have been rescued and 2,100 evacuated. The storm also affected the Balearic Islands, with more than 130 incidents recorded in Ibiza including standing water at the airport, which caused some flights to be diverted or suspended. Although the worst of the storm has passed and conditions improving across Valencia and Alicante, local disruption is expected to continue.
The first named storm of the winter for the UK is currently tracking through the Channel. Storm Austen is bringing damaging winds not only to south-west England and Wales, but also south-west Ireland and northern France. Gusts are expected to be around 50-60mph, but some exposed north-western coasts of France could experience winds of up to 80-90mph.
Following quickly on from Storm Austen is another deep low pressure system, Storm Boelo, which is expected to track across northern Scotland on Saturday into Sunday. Much of the UK and Ireland will see very unsettled conditions with further damaging winds and heavy and prolonged rain. Western Scotland will face the strongest gusts, but the rest of the UK and Ireland will see 40-55mph winds. Western parts of Ireland will experience 50-60mph winds with up to 70-80mph in exposed parts of north-west Ireland, similar to western Scotland. Again, heavy rain associated with Storm Boelo will reach 10-20mm with as much as 30-60mm in western parts of Ireland, Wales and south-west England. This, on top of the rainfall from Storm Austen, will increase the risk of flooding.
Super Typhoon Champi is headed towards China and Japan over the weekend after passing north-eastern Taiwan on Friday. While it has weakened since Wednesday, it is still a significant typhoon with the equivalent strength of a category 5 hurricane, producing 185mph gusts and sustained winds of 121 mph.Following torrential rain associated with the typhoon this week, up to 900mm of rain is forecast to fall in the mountainous regions of northern and eastern Taiwan from Tuesday to Saturday. As a result, there are school closures, cancelled flights and six-metre waves, with more impacts to come over the next few days.

title: EU leaders to press Burnham to pay more towards Ukraine’s defence
description: Officials will call on UK to ‘step up’ financial support at Brussels summit – with post-Brexit issues also on agenda EU leaders will press Andy Burnham at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort in 2027. EU officials argue that the UK, Canada and Japan should do more to support Ukraine, but entreaties to these G7 countries for extra financial aid at recent international meetings have not been answered, Brussels says. Continue reading...
content:
Officials will call on UK to ‘step up’ financial support at Brussels summit – with post-Brexit issues also on agenda
EU leaders will press Andy Burnham at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort in 2027.
EU officials argue that the UK, Canada and Japan should do more to support Ukraine , but entreaties to these G7 countries for extra financial aid at recent international meetings have not been answered, Brussels says.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen , will call on the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, to contribute to Ukraine’s looming financial shortfall at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next week.
A similar request to the British prime minister will be made when he meets von der Leyen and the European Council president, António Costa, for a long-awaited EU-UK summit on 20 November in Brussels. It comes as the UK chancellor, John Healey, prepares for his first budget next week, weighing numerous calls for more spending against the rising cost of government borrowing and a darkening economic outlook.
Healey said earlier this month he was “working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine – military, diplomatic and economic”.
Ukraine says it faces a €70bn (£58bn) funding shortfall in 2027 to pay for its defence and civilian needs.
The EU and its member states are paying for 80% of Ukraine’s financial needs, according to the commission, which considers a “fair” EU share to be two-thirds, with the remaining third covered by other allies. “We will continue to lead, but we urgently need other partners to step up,” von der Leyen told reporters last week, without naming countries.
The EU last year agreed a €90bn loan for Ukraine, intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s funding in 2026 and 2027. But as Russia escalates its attacks, dragging the war into its fifth winter, Ukraine’s costs continue to spiral.
EU officials have prioritised non-EU G7 countries, above all the UK, Canada and Japan. But they are now casting the net wider and may look to Switzerland, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand to promise additional aid to Ukraine.
The British government says it has committed £25bn to Ukraine, including £16bn in military aid.
The UK is Ukraine’s fourth largest donor, behind the US, Germany and France, according to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine Support Tracker . But the picture changes when the UK’s share is weighted to GDP. The UK was assessed by the Kiel researchers as spending 0.86% of national income to support Ukraine, compared with 1.1% from France and 1.5% from Germany. These three large European economies spent significantly less than the Nordics and Baltics, such as Denmark (4.2%) and Estonia (3.8%). The UK is more in line with France and Germany when their contribution to EU programmes is stripped out.
The UK government has been contacted for comment.
The European Commission declined to comment on specific countries, but referred to a recent statement: “We always said that we cannot walk this alone … therefore our partners in general must step up.”
Ukraine will be one of several issues on the agenda at the EU-UK summit, where leaders are expected to conclude three agreements: a food and animal health (SPS) deal to reduce Brexit paperwork; the linkage of the EU and UK emissions trading schemes (ETS) to protect British industry from European carbon taxes; and a youth mobility scheme to enable 18- to 30-year-olds to live, work, travel and study across both sides of the Channel.
In a positive sign for British negotiators, the European Commission proposed deferring the question of university tuition fees, one of the last big sticking points. The UK would like to charge EU students at British universities the international rate, about four times higher than the domestic fee. The EU, where many officials are alumni of British universities, wants to return to the pre-Brexit status quo, when EU students paid home rates.
Commission officials have proposed resolving this thorny question in technical talks within six months of the 20 November summit, rather than risk derailing the high-profile leaders’ meeting. But senior EU sources are confident they still have leverage on the issue, as the SPS and ETS deals will not come into force until there is a youth mobility agreement acceptable to the European side, including on tuition fees.
“The three elements are a sort of gift to the UK, but not a massive gift,” an EU diplomat said, adding that the EU would still have clout in the negotiations over the fees. “The leverage is that the UK needs this [the other agreements].” UK hopes to strike economic security agreements with the EU , to avoid British industry becoming collateral damage of Europe’s defensive measures against China, are seen as another source of leverage.
But a second diplomat said there was no consensus among the EU’s 27 member states on postponing the tuition fees question until after the summit: “There is no clear majority saying ‘let’s drop it now for six months’,” they said.

content:
In today’s newsletter: ​Born from the fury surrounding the deadly Novi Sad station collapse, Serbia’s Student List has taken its protests all the way to the elections in an unprecedented grassroots campaign
Good morning. As waves of youth-led protests swell across Europe , prompted by the cost of living, unaffordable housing and education standards, in Serbia the younger generation is taking on the apparatus of the state itself.
In tight-run parliamentary elections this Sunday, the country’s most consequential political movement in decades, Student List, is challenging former Slobodan Milošević henchman Aleksandar Vučić and his 12-year domination of Serbian politics.
Two years on from a singular national tragedy that galvanised public anger at state cover-ups and corruption, gen Z have channelled their energy and fury into a bold experiment in direct democracy, creating a genuinely leaderless, grassroots movement that is firing up disaffected voters across the country.
I spoke to Julian Borger , our senior international correspondent, who has just returned from Belgrade, about their hopes of emulating the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary and the potential for a democratic domino through central Europe. But first, the headlines.
UK news | Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.
Ukraine | Russia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations.
UK politics | Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader.
Europe news | Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years.
Energy | Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen.
It was, one Serbian student told me, “the drop that overflowed the glass”. On 1 November 2024, the collapse of a concrete canopy at the railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second largest city, killed 16 people. The youngest was a six-year-old girl, Sara Firic, who was sitting on a bench with her grandfather and older sister. The Serbian Times reported they were still holding hands when their bodies were dug out of the rubble.
In the aftermath of the disaster, student-led protests developed organically, with demonstrators blocking a nearby crossroads for the same number of minutes as lives lost. As details emerged of botched refurbishment work carried out in what critics described as a corrupt deal with a Chinese consortium, the anger mounted. Ongoing protests were brutally suppressed and Vučić himself branded demonstrators western-backed “terrorists”.
Two years later, that single tragedy has sparked a mass movement for accountability and inclusive democracy to counter the creeping authoritarianism of Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS).
“There was a deep well of public discontent, and the students were inspirational in keeping the protest movement going,” says Julian.
Vučić expected the protesters to dissipate – instead, the mounting pressure forced the president to resign and call a snap parliamentary election, as he endeavours to consolidate his 12 years in power in a Putin-inspired switch to become prime minister.
In response, the student movement is fielding a list of 250 candidates of its own, mainly locally respected academics but also actors, musicians and farmers, with each candidate approved by citizens’ assembly.
Some polling suggests that Student List is edging ahead; others that the SNS is consolidating support. Julian tells me he left Belgrade with the sense that anything could happen on Sunday.
How did a student network put together an election campaign?
The Serbian student I spoke to is buzzing ahead of Sunday’s vote: “We’re really excited,” he tells me over the phone from the Serbian capital. “We hope we win.” He is studying for a masters in dramatic arts at the University of Belgrade, and asks not to be named in accordance with the leader-less structure of his movement.
He talks me through the “big collective effort”, including collecting canvas data door to door, and the “A student in every village” programme targeting Vučić’s base of rural voters, all coordinated by democratic citizens’ assembly. The thinking is that a higher turnout of disaffected voters will favour Student List.
Julian encapsulates the Student List movement as “a bold democratic experiment”, and that is how my student describes it: “The essence of our movement is direct democracy. This collective effort is about making people feel part of the decision-making, not just spectators.”
When Julian joined Student List volunteers canvassing in the housing estates of Krnjača, a Belgrade suburb, they were met with overwhelmingly positive reactions – “the response was ‘bring it on’” – though he caveats that opinion in outlying suburbs varies from those of the urban intelligentsia and others in more rural settings.
“People were saying to the volunteers, ‘Take my contact and tell me anything I can do on election day.’ There’s a feeling of now or never.”
The demands of the student movement are focused on governance, Julian tells me, and their slogan, “Serbia or mafia?”, highlights repeated allegations of links between the SNS and organised crime, something the government denies. “Student List wants a rules-based order that conforms with the constitution on paper, not the system of classic crony capitalism that Vučić has established, where everything depends on your link to the SNS.”
Julian says Vučić is plainly taking the Student List threat seriously. He made 129 live television appearances in August, more than four times the previous month’s total.
But the elections are happening in a context of growing repression: Serbia has regressed in international rankings for press freedom and corruption in recent years. And only last week, the Guardian revealed that Vučić intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected landmark in Belgrade for a Trump tower, another spur for recent protests.
A September survey for Serbian pro-democracy group the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) found no negative coverage of the ruling majority on the country’s television channels, compared with 37% of the time for the opposition.
Student List has accused the foreign ministry of rigging the diaspora vote by keeping overseas polling stations open where support for Vučić is strong, while closing them in parts of North America where the opposition could expect to perform well. The ministry did not respond to Julian’s request to comment.
Meanwhile the digital rights group SHARE Foundation found that members of the student movement had been targeted by advanced spyware, while Reuters this week reported on intimidation and beating of protesters by police.
What is the likely aftermath of Sunday’s elections?
With preliminary results expected in the early hours of Monday morning, a fundamental problem for the country is that neither side sees the other as legitimate, says Julian. “So in the aftermath of the election, barring a really clear decision, it will be disputed one way or another.”
Indeed, the European Council on Foreign Relations has warned of further street protests and possible violent repression, depending on the outcome and the margin of victory.
Big questions remain around how Student List would configure themselves as a government. Reforming the state and economy after more than a decade of highly centralised SNS control will be immensely challenging. So far their policy platform has been decided by full general assembly, and divisive issues such as future relations with Kosovo or Russia, and stance on EU membership, have been played down.
Although Serbia is an EU-candidate country, public opinion on accession is split, and the SNS has counter-balanced relationships with the US, Russia and China, particularly after the Trump administration opened dialogue on energy and technology with them earlier this year.
A Student List win would throw this geopolitical balancing act, which protesters argue brings little benefit to the people of Serbia, up in the air and potentially bring the country closer to Europe. And a contested Vučić victory would challenge the EU on whether to freeze diplomacy and funding to the country.
The student organiser I spoke with is clear that regime change is just the beginning: “Once we remove the regime, the big debate starts in Serbia about what we should do next. Should we join the EU? What about foreign policy? How are we going to democratise the country? There’s a lot that’s not working because of corruption. But right now we’re focused on these elections.”

title: Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter
description: Official forecasts show country will meet energy demand by paying high prices to secure imports Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen. Energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand over the coldest months – in part because of paying higher market prices than neighbouring markets to secure imports. content:
Official forecasts show country will meet energy demand by paying high prices to secure imports
Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen.
Energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand over the coldest months – in part because of paying higher market prices than neighbouring markets to secure imports.
The official winter energy forecasts were published days after Europe’s gas market benchmark climbed to its highest level since December 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent prices rocketing.
National Gas, which runs Great Britain’s gas networks, set out its forecasts after striking an 11th-hour deal with the owner of a major Belgian pipeline to keep gas flowing into the country this winter by reversing a planned capacity cut.
The energy regulator, Ofgem, approved the deal – which will add around 10p a month to the average gas bill. Without the intervention there was a danger of gas running out in the event of a worst-case scenario where an important part of the country’s gas networks failed as temperatures plummeted.
In addition to gas imports by pipelines, Great Britain is expected to increase imports of seaborne liquified natural gas (LNG) cargoes by about 5% from last winter, according to National Gas forecasts, at a time when market prices are three times higher than they were before the Middle East crisis severely disrupted Gulf supplies.
Its winter outlook report suggested that prices could remain elevated if UK gas buyers need to compete more fiercely with countries in Europe for LNG cargoes amid low gas storage levels across the continent.
Europe ended August on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years owing to the slowdown in gas exports from Qatar, one of Europe’s biggest suppliers, and the increase in gas consumption over the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the record heatwaves caused by the global climate crisis.
The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea. UK production was forecast to fall by 6% this year compared with last winter, but the government’s controversial decision to approve the new Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea earlier this week, which was not fully accounted for in the winter forecasts, is expected to offer a modest boost to supplies when it starts up next month.
Great Britain is also forecast to be a net importer of electricity over the colder months, according to the National Energy System Operator (Neso) separate outlook report. That is also likely to come at a higher cost owing to tighter European power supplies compared with last winter.
The summer heatwaves reduced river levels across Europe, in a blow to French nuclear output and Norway’s hydroelectric reserves, which have remained below the 10-year minimum since late July.
The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics this week, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France. It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off due to bottlenecks in the grid.
Even though Great Britain will use gas power plants less overall this winter compared with previous winters thanks to rising renewable energy levels, the need for gas to play a role during power supply crunches could be 7% higher than previously assumed.
National Gas lifted its gas power demand forecasts for the most extreme electricity supply scenarios – when demand is unusually high and renewable output slumps – after noting over successive winters that gas plants have remained in high use when dark, still winter days lead to high electricity demand and lower renewable energy levels.
Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, a director at National Gas, said: “While supply diversity and flexibility remain sources of resilience, taken together these trends in demand and supply have resulted in tighter supply margins during periods of high demand and system stress.”

title: Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime
description: Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic. Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum. Continue reading...
content:
Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage
Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic.
Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum.
He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party.
The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America.
Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016.
It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links to another Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson , an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year.
Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being a bigger danger to the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.
The French judgment reveals that Ghandehari was the major investor behind a deal to supply and build a fibre-optic cable to carry telecoms traffic across Iran in a joint venture with a state-linked Iranian partner.
The businessman’s HP Trust was the ultimate owner of Ori Group, which took a 49% stake in the venture, called Omran Razavi International Co, in 2015.
The other 51% of the venture was owned by Astan Quds Razavi (AQR), a multibillion pound religious foundation in Iran’s second city of Mashhad.
AQR’s leader at the time was ayatollah Abbas Vaez Tabasi, who was appointed custodian of the foundation by the first supreme leader, Ruhollah Khomeini, and served from the 1979 revolution until his death in 2016. Vaez Tabasi had been an ally of some reformers but remained close to the next supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, and, according to the BBC , was reported by state media in 2009 to have said of opposition protest movements that those behind “sedition” in the country were “enemies of god” who deserved to be executed under sharia law.
The joint venture ended in about 2016, with the Ghandehari-backed entities being pushed out of the deal as a hardliner was appointed to replace Vaez Tabasi.
The US imposed sanctions on AQR in 2021, saying it controlled “large swaths of the Iranian economy, including assets expropriated from political dissidents and religious minorities, to the benefit of supreme leader Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian government officials”. It describes it as a bonyad, one of the “opaque, quasi-official organisations generally controlled by current and former government officials and clerics that report directly to the supreme leader”.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said it would be misleading to characterise him as “working with Iran” without the context that, after 2016, he was targeted by Iran’s supreme national security council with the false allegation that he was working with hostile western powers. They also said his involvement was intended to promote political change through greater access to information, which he believed was why the US and French authorities authorised the project.
Tom Keatinge, the director of the Centre for Finance and Security at Rusi, the foreign affairs thinktank, said dealing with Iran “has always been a risky business as a financial institution because of this blurring between kind of state and the private sector. The private sector is not free to operate. It’s just very hard to operate in that country without touching a live rail.”
He said there was clearly a range of positions among ayatollahs but it would be “pretty difficult to operate in an industry like telecoms” without the acceptance of the core leadership.
The judgment also revealed that, until 2016, Ghandehari’s HP Trust was the owner of Orico General Trading LLC, which was contracted to supply telecoms equipment from France’s Alcatel-Lucent and transport it from Dubai to Iran. After 2016, this company was transferred to Simpson, the administration professional, who was responsible for winding down Orico’s operations and taking hundreds of staff out of the region.
Simpson told the Guardian he acquired the company after Iranian extremists took over AQR, when the project’s assets were seized and those involved faced political persecution on national security grounds, including accusations of working for hostile western governments. He said his plan was to wind down the business, adding that he carried out detailed checks before acquiring Orico.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said AQR was independent and respected, and therefore the only viable choice for a joint venture in Iran. They said Ghandehari had never met Vaez Tabasi and that he did not regard him as an advocate for freedom or human rights but had believed him to be the only force in the Iranian hierarchy capable of holding back the hardliners in order for the project to go ahead.
The original contract for the deal was awarded to the Omran consortium in 2012 by the Iranian state-owned Telecommunication Infrastructure Company of Iran.
According to Iranian corporate filings, Omran Razavi International Co also owned stakes in two majority state-owned banks, Bank Mellat and Bank Tejerat, in 2013. Both were subject to sanctions over involvement in Iran’s nuclear programme at that point.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said Omran Razavi disposed of the small stakes in the banks before HP Trust’s Ori Group signed its agreement for a 49% stake in the venture in December 2014. They added that the deal was fully approved by authorities in France and the US.
In 2016, AQR took over the whole of the joint venture. Around the same time, the project’s chair, Mohammed Reza Noory, ended up in Iran’s infamous Evin prison, serving an 18-year sentence.
Ghandehari and Noory are both named on leaked judicial papers published by the hacktivist group Edaalat Ali as having being under investigation in Iran after the deal collapsed. Ghandehari’s lawyers say he first became aware of the “bogus allegations” during French court proceedings and that the intelligence services had not given him any further details. Ghandehari’s representatives said fabricating financial and social cases against its targets to discredit them was part of the Iranian regime’s playbook and had been widely documented and recognised by western governments, human rights organisations and independent journalists.
Ghandehari’s lawyers said he had not been to Iran for 30 years and his wealth had no connection to the country, since his ancestral property and assets were confiscated in 2016.
Farage has been highly critical of Iran’s government this year, supporting Donald Trump’s war against it, and attending a protest outside the Iranian embassy with pro-democracy activists in the spring. Last week he warned about Iranian agents entering the UK via small boats across the Channel.
In a joint interview with Farage and Ghandehari in July, the Telegraph described Ghandehari’s business deal in Iran without mentioning its connections to Iranian regime-linked companies. It described it as a project to bring access to high-speed internet to Iran that would help drive reform, but that it later went wrong and resulted in Ghandehari’s assets being confiscated.
It is still not clear how Ghandehari and his family have built up their extraordinary wealth. His fortune is said to have gone from an estimated $2bn, when his late mother bought a property on London’s “billionaire’s row” in 2008, to a reported $10bn now.
In a recent court case over a Picasso painting , Ghandehari was asked to provide proof that he could afford £1.5m in legal costs. His lawyers pointed only to a brochure from his Davos trip with Farage, with a description that he controls a trust with a “collective investment value in excess of $10bn”.
At one point, he offered a letter from a “partner in a leading accountancy firm” confirming he was the principal beneficiary of HP Trust, and drawing an annual income from it. However, this was later withdrawn, as Ghandehari decided he did not want its contents to enter the public domain.

title: Some US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
description: Similar withdrawals from UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain reported as concerns grow about restart of war on Iran after US midterm elections The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield. Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supported Houthis in Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. The state department spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.” Continue reading...
content:
Similar withdrawals from UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain reported as concerns grow about restart of war on Iran after US midterm elections
The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield.
Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supported Houthis in Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. The state department spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.”
The state department said the order covered its embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the US war on Iran and had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although in recent weeks some diplomats had returned.
Media outlets – including NBC and AFP – reported that families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, while the New York Times said the Trump administration was developing plans to restart the war on Iran.
However, in his statement on Wednesday, Pigott described the reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate” and said the state department order was for the departure of staff and their families from Saudi Arabia only.
Saudi Arabia has faced a succession of deadly attacks from the Houthis over recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport which was the kingdom’s deadliest in years as the war with the group escalates.
On Thursday the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced that two people had been killed in overnight attacks on King Fahd international airport in Dammam on the Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
Eight people were injured and there was material damage to the airport, according to officials. The global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said flights had been diverted away from the airport.
Separately, falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility in the country’s south-east killed two people and injured a further two, the Saudi energy ministry said.
The Houthis said on Thursday ⁠they ⁠had ​launched attacks on ⁠Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry in ⁠Riyadh, Saudi ​Aramco ‌facilities ‌in Yanbu ‌and King Fahd international airport in Dammam.
Essential workers at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in the east of the country were told to evacuate on Thursday, two sources told Agence France-Presse, after their non-essential colleagues were told to work from home since last week.
The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf in late February before the start of its war against Iran. NBC reported that the US military had been quietly scaling back its presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, but a spokesperson from US central command told the US news outlet that service members were regularly moved to “optimize mission readiness”.
The withdrawal of staff from the region coincides with reports that Trump has been presented with plans for restarting strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
The New York Times reported that the US and Israel had developed plans for a “short but intensive operation” after the defense secretary, Peter Hegseth, travelled to Israel earlier this week for meetings with the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Last week ⁠Trump said the US was hoping to knock out Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain , a site linked to the country’s ⁠nuclear program, however the US president has publicly said he does not intend to restart the war before the 3 November elections.

title: Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply
description: Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz Shipping workers: how is the Middle East conflict affecting you? Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May. Continue reading...
content:
Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz
Shipping workers: how is the Middle East conflict affecting you?
Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May.
Yemeni Houthis , who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield.
Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday.
It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases.
The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, which also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely.
Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran , oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt.
Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf .
However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman.
Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%.
In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%.
Shares in American Airlines dropped almost 4% in pre-market trading after the company warned that high fuel costs would push it into a loss this year.
American Airlines abandoned its previous forecast that it might achieve a profit this year as it faced “historic fuel cost pressure”.

title: Heidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attack
description: US photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incident The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians. Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah. Continue reading...
author_name: Julian Borger and Quique Kierszenbaum in Petah Tikva
content:
US photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incident
The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.
Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.
It is unclear whether the puncture wounds were caused by knives or other weapons. Levine said a witness to her attack had seen nails sticking out of some of the wooden clubs wielded by her attackers.
Levine, 64, has covered multiple wars and had just returned from an assignment in Ukraine before Friday’s attack. She said she would most likely have been killed had she not been wearing protective body armour and a helmet.
“I probably would have been dead, because for sure it doesn’t take much to kill a person with blows to the head,” she said shortly before being discharged from hospital on Wednesday in the Israeli city of Petah Tikva.
Levine pointed out that Palestinians did not have such protection and more than 20 had been killed in settler attacks so far this year, in the course of an escalating campaign of aggression – described as terrorism by Israeli security leaders – across the West Bank, aimed at driving Palestinians from their land.
“Every single journalist who looked at [the attack on me] are thinking they and I have gone to so many funerals of Palestinians killed by settlers,” Levine said.
She said the olive harvesting at Abu Falah had begun peacefully but at some point a group of young masked settlers appeared on a nearby hilltop watching the group of Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying them. Levine said the attack began only after the Israeli army arrived on the scene.
“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said. “Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw teargas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.
“I managed to keep my face to the ground, and I don’t know if I took that position to protect myself with my face down or it was their initial blow. Otherwise my whole face would have been broken and I could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye.
“They started kicking me and beating me with sticks. I can’t even count how many times, probably more than a hundred times. I actually tried playing dead so that they would stop. But it didn’t work.”
Witnesses said the beating only ceased when young Palestinian men used slingshots to aim stones at settlers forcing them back, allowing another American journalist, Jasper Nathaniel, to reach Levine and, with other reporters, help her to safety.
“The shabab [Palestinian youth] put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing. It was like a biblical battle,” Levine said.
After the attack, Nathaniel wrote : “Had the shabab not stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead. It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s.”
He said the army pursued the young Palestinians after the incident, rather than the settlers. Palestinians risk being shot by settlers or soldiers if they try to resist attacks, and can face long periods in detention without charge.
Levine, who has lived in Israel for four decades, said she would go back to reporting on the West Bank as soon as she recovered. “My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
Since the attack, she has received letters from Israelis expressing regret, and an apologetic phone call from the president, Isaac Herzog.
“He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she said. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they’re a dark stain, and he called them thugs.”
The office of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, however, put out a statement on X seeking to cast doubt on witness and video accounts of what he called an “alleged attack”.
Levine was particularly angered by Netanyahu’s claim that some video footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.
“That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why,” Levine said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.”
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, called the attack a “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions. Israeli police arrested 10 suspects after the Abu Falah incident and another attack on Saturday aimed at European diplomats near the West Bank village of Taybeh.
On Wednesday an Israeli court released four suspects in the attack on Levine and put them under house arrest, on the grounds there was insufficient evidence to keep them in custody.
Asked if she expected her attackers to be brought to justice, Levine said her level of confidence was “two out of 10”.
“I am not very hopeful,” she said. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it. But it’s not just arresting these teenage thugs. It’s going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they’re organised.”

title: Besieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warn
description: Water and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routes The humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area. Continue reading...
content:
Water and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routes
The humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned.
Iran-allied Houthi forces have largely encircled the city of more than 900,000 people, cutting it off from most supply routes. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area.
The conflict has intensified since forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on the Houthi-held airport in Sana’a in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that had largely stopped the fighting.
The UN has called for aid workers to be given access to Taiz. Oxfam in London called for the UK to send extra humanitarian aid to the country. The UK has allocated just £104m in aid to Yemen for each of the next three years, down from the £196m allocated in 2020. US aid to the stricken country has been virtually wiped out, and Germany, another leading funder, has halved its aid programme.
Donor countries have subscribed to only 23% of the cost of the UN humanitarian relief programme for Yemen this year, and pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia – itself cash-strapped by the cost of war – to make up the shortfall. The World Food Programme said wheat flour reserves in the city were nearly exhausted as of mid-October.
On Tuesday the UK government allocated an unspecified sum in extra military help to Saudi Arabia to help protect its airports and infrastructure, but London has yet to decide on whether to back a much more robust military response, including supporting the possible deployment of foreign ground troops to Yemen.
Fatma Jaffar, a Yemen-based advocacy manager for Oxfam, said local staff described an almost total siege of Taiz.
“All the main entrances [to the city] have been blocked. The clashes are continuing and the casualties are very high,” she said. “Even people that have money are not able to buy food. Supplies are becoming very limited in the markets. No fuel has entered Taiz for two or three weeks. Drinking water is a massive issue. Even our staff are struggling to buy water.
“Hospitals are struggling without medicines and a lot of people as a result are dying. Those that have been wounded by missiles – there have been attempts to get them out of the city, but because of the blockade they are not able to transfer anyone. Prices have rocketed.
“Our staff told me that people are even searching for apples right now and they cannot find any fresh fruit, and basic commodities are not found inside the city. Garbage is piling up since they are not able to transfer the waste outside the city. They are trying to burn it, but we can only anticipate there will be diseases such as cholera in the near future. If this goes on much longer and access remains blocked, there will be casualties from missiles, hunger and disease from lack of water right across the city.
“The situation was bad before the escalation – Yemen is one of the poorest countries on Earth – and now it is becoming unmanageable.”
Prices have rocketed: a 20-litre container of petrol that cost about $20 (£15) before the crisis is now worth $80 on the hidden market. Potato prices have doubled.
The Houthi focus on Taiz reflects the city’s strategic importance, but the level of resistance inside the city may swallow the group’s resources, weakening its response elsewhere.
Oxfam has been forced to transfer its limited resources from development to emergency humanitarian work, including offering cash transfers.
The Halo Trust, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine-clearance organisation, said 30 of its staff were among hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city.
In the Trump administration’s fiscal year 2027 budget request to Congress, the US state department has requested no economic support or development assistance specifically for Yemen. By comparison, the US committed roughly $760m in total aid to Yemen during the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.
UN diplomats are still mediating between the two sides, but there is no sign that either the Houthis or the internationally recognised government are ready for a ceasefire, let alone a long-term settlement.

title: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’
description: Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court. From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists. content:
Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed
The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.
From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees .
The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170% , with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.
A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.
“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.
Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.
As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line .
Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.
Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.
“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.
As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.
“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.
Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.
The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

title: Aung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five years
description: Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years. “Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday. Continue reading...
content:
Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions
The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup .
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.
On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

title: Indian court orders release of two leaders of Cockroach movement
description: Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdown An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests. The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week. Continue reading...
content:
Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in jail after defying restrictions on protests in Delhi amid government crackdown
An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.
The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.
On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.
Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, which led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.
Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.
The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.
After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.
The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.
The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.
The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.
He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.
“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

title: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
description: Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
