author_name: Miranda Bryant in Muhos and Otanmäki
content:
Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push
Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland . Now they are all gone.
After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.
“It doesn’t end. It goes on and on,” says Mari Annala, an ecologist from the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL), looking at drone footage of the former forest from the perimeter.
With 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, Finland has found itself at the forefront of the tech companies’ latest push. As well as its relative geopolitical and geological stability and abundance of land, the cool climate makes it especially attractive for saving on energy costs.
Earlier this month, Google was ordered by the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) to temporarily stop work on Muhos and another site about 100km south-east in the village of Otanmäki after it failed to complete the necessary environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land. The news has prompted widespread outcry and a national reckoning over what role, if any, the country should play in the global rush to build datacentres to keep up with rapid AI development.
Last week, Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”.
Muhos and Otanmäki are part of a €13bn AI infrastructure project by Google that has attracted criticism from Donald Trump, who would rather the centres were built in the US and has publicly called for the company to reconsider. It is the biggest ever project of its kind in the Nordic country.
The Finnish government, which has presided over deep spending cuts, has encouraged the investment. Last month, when the Google plans were announced, the country’s prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and “the value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment”. He said the Google deal would “deliver lasting benefits for both parties”.
But the revelations over Google’s misconduct have prompted public concern over what these deals mean for nearby communities, energy prices for Finnish households and Finland’s natural environment, a national source of pride. The datacentre push is likely to become a key election issue when Finns go to the polls in April.
In addition to the 250,000 trees felled at Muhos, Annala estimates that an additional 150,000 trees were felled at Otanmäki. Because the trees have been felled illegally, she says wood from the two sites cannot be sold to wood-processing plants.
The move has also prompted questions over why Finland’s renewable energy sources are being used to power international corporations.
More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and a fee to compensate local communities for environmental damage. Since the scandal broke, Orpo has described what happened in Muhos as a “cold shower”.
Hanna Halmeenpää, chair of SLL’s board, said she had been incredulous when she discovered Google’s law breaking. “At first I couldn’t believe it,” she said. “I have never heard that any company has done anything like this in Finland.” She said the system depended a lot on trust, which she believes Google took advantage of. “They bought the vast land area and they just started to cut it, just like that,” she said. “It’s pure arrogance and it’s amazing.”
The speed of developments had shocked the country, she said. “Many people are just watching the news and asking each other: ‘What’s happening now? What can we do about it? And do we have to take all these datacentre projects in Finland?’”
Jussi Kangasharju, head of computer science at the University of Helsinki, said that while datacentres brought a limited number of jobs, potentially boosting the local economy, the benefits on a national level were minimal. “Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” he said. “They are international companies serving international customers. Very little corporate taxes go to Finland. Datacentres ultimately have very little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.”
With legislation still playing catchup, there is a rush to get projects under way as fast as possible.
Some are calling for a centralised body to coordinate datacentre projects, rather than leaving so much of the decision-making down to municipalities that are likely to prioritise the immediate needs of the local area.
In Muhos and Otanmäki, there are people who support the projects, along with the jobs and land taxes they will bring into the local area. But many believe they have been sold short by municipalities.
Antti Jakonen, who lives in Muhos, said that, although the trees felled represented a small fraction of Finland’s overall forests, he objected to the manner in which it had been carried out. “It has been done in the wrong way. American style. No sense. No sense at all,” he said. The former entrepreneur and fisher wants Google to compensate by helping to restore the local salmon population destroyed decades ago by hydropower.
In Otanmäki, the disruption to nature and to residents’ daily lives is being vividly felt. When the trees were felled, the wolves who had lived there came to the village, said Anni Ranta, 53, whose family has lived there for generations.
A former mining village, the area is known for its rare earth elements. Ranta’s family live at the centre of the village next to a triangular church spire and a former bar that has been empty for years. The peaceful forest used to extend for miles from the village. Now the sound of building work next to the clearcut Google site reverberates.
“We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest,” said Ranta. “They fled. What worries me about the datacentres is also the noise because this is hardrock soil. Even when we are standing here talking,” she added, stamping her feet, “it’s like a drum.”
Such is her strength of feeling against the arrival of Google that she is thinking of moving out. She also fears the datacentre could make the village a target for Russia, with whom Finland shares a long border. “I don’t want them here,” she said of Google. “I don’t want them in Finland at all. I don’t like the whole idea of AI and the world changing and the way it’s changing. It’s going too fast, too soon.”
Her father, Pentti Korhonen, a retired wilderness guide, said that since the forest was destroyed, the water in the stream has turned brown. “There is no need at all for datacentres in Finland. No need for datacentres at all,” he said.
Vesa Hyyryläinen, chair of the local SLL district, said three-toed woodpeckers nesting in the forest had been pushed out. “All of us nature conservationists are very worried about our Finnish political situation and politics,” said the biologist and osprey expert. “I wonder why we have to sacrifice so much of our nature. They give everything away too easily.”
He said, however, that he understood why authorities were trying to bring in new sources of investment and jobs, given the region’s ageing population. “Young people go to Helsinki and Berlin and Paris,” he said. “There are so few people. We have to sacrifice.”
Veli-Matti Uski, director general of the ministry of environment, said the government was “monitoring the general development of the [datacentre] sector, [and the] application of its legislation, and is prepared to propose legislative amendments as necessary”.
Google said it was working to protect water quality at the Muhos site, and that it planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Conservationists say that figure is too low to have any real impact in comparison to the damage done by the tree felling.
A spokesperson said: “We have operated in Finland for 15 years and have always worked to meet or exceed zoning, environmental, health and safety requirements.
“After receiving the LVV letters on 6 October, we stopped preparatory works at Muhos and Kajaani [where the Otanmäki site is located] and have submitted a formal response to LVV confirming this.
“We will fully comply with LVV’s requests in this matter. We look forward to maintaining an active, open dialogue with all authorities to strengthen our partnership with Finland and local organisations.”

content:
In a few days the busiest shopping street in Europe will be closed to traffic. The hope is that an unloved and polluted thoroughfare will turn into somewhere that people actually want to spend time
I n February, the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan , announced that Britain’s best-known thoroughfare, Oxford Street, would be pedestrianised. To the surprise of every Londoner that I have spoken to in the past few months, it is actually happening. On Monday 26 October, the busiest shopping street in Europe – or, precisely, half of its 1.2-mile stretch – will be closed to traffic, putting an end to several decades of bitter arguments, obstructions and delays. Cars, lorries, vans, taxis, buses, bicycles, ebikes, scooters will be banned. Nothing but pedestrians (and emergency vehicles) will be allowed in.
This change will mark the most remarkable transformation to the streetscape of central London since at least 2003, when Trafalgar Square was turned from a glorified roundabout into one of London’s most recognisable public spaces. It will also form the most visible part of the mayor’s legacy, whether or not Khan runs for a fourth term in 2028. Three years ago, Khan published a memoir and manifesto, Breathe , attributing his asthma to growing up inhaling London’s polluted air. For the mayor, pedestrianising Oxford Street is the culmination of a mission to create a greener city that is oriented around public health, walking and cycling.
Pedestrianisation is one thing; making Oxford Street somewhere anyone actually wants to spend time is another. For weary Londoners and anxious visitors alike, it is a headache in the form of a high street. Its primary associations are crowds, stress, dirt, noise, the tackiest incarnations of consumer capitalism, and crime. At one point during my research I approached a harried police officer in the throng outside Tottenham Court Road tube station and asked if she thought pedestrianisation would be good for Oxford Street, or make her job harder. Both, she said.
This is not to say Oxford Street is an empty, dying high street. At the last count, it receives more than 500,000 visitors every day – equivalent to the population of Edinburgh. It seems reasonable to assume that most of London’s 22 million annual foreign visitors set foot on it at some point. The street generates 5% of the capital’s economic output , and lives in the national imagination the way few others do. “When I was 17, London meant Oxford Street,” sang Everything But the Girl, in their 1988 song of the same name: “It was a little world.” And yet, nobody loves Oxford Street. During the course of writing this article, I haven’t met anyone who will even admit to liking it.
On a Sunday evening in September, I did something I had always carefully avoided doing before and cycled its full length. Even at the end of the weekend, it was overwhelming – with teenagers careening on rented ebikes and gaudy pedicabs parked in the middle of the pavement, blaring music. The pavements were thick with people, in part because the road was still thick with traffic. On another occasion, I watched a late-middle-aged woman perch awkwardly outside Ikea on a narrow black electricity box, in the absence of anywhere else to rest. For most Londoners, Oxford Street is a necessary evil, to be visited with surgical precision before fleeing the scene: a site of crime, grime and perhaps some Christmas shopping. “Who,” wondered the FT’s architecture critic in 2020, “lingers any longer than they have to in London’s worst thoroughfare?”
The grime itself is no joke. In the 1990s, when Oxford Street was known for its huge record shops such as HMV and Virgin Megastore, I remember returning to my south London home on the tube, blowing my nose and seeing a tissue full of jet-black snot. Its narrow streetway and tall buildings on either side create an “urban canyon”, trapping the heavy diesel fumes emanating from its buses and taxis (private car access has been restricted since 1972). In 2014, it was found to have the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. In the same year, the crime had become so bad that the United Arab Emirates warned its citizens to avoid the area for their own safety.
Since then it has become better known for its lawbreaking small businesses, where substantial raids have hauled in counterfeit goods and illegal vapes. This decade has seen the rise of mysterious US candy stores and empty souvenir shops that allegedly thrive thanks to tax evasion . Covid and internet shopping hit Oxford Street hard: vacancy levels soared from 4.5% in 2019 to 16.9% by early 2023, and it was often these businesses that filled the gaps. The current Google Street View images of its shopfronts, taken just two years ago, already look like a postcard from the past.
That Oxford Street has been struggling hurts the reputation of London as a whole. This is in tabloid parlance, “the nation’s high street”, home to the flagship branches of iconic department stores alongside global retail brands. Khan’s gamble is that the pedestrianisation can reverse what he conceded in 2024 was a case of “managed decline” , and will flood the street with life again.
I n the offices of East, near London Fields, Julian Lewis and Archie Bashford were seated around a 4ft-long cardboard model of Oxford Street and talking animatedly about bollards. Lewis and his team are public realm architects, devoted not to buildings, but the world beyond them: signage, benches, perches, kerbs, paving, lighting, planters, trees and public art. East have carried out nearly 30 high street redesign projects in as many years, but this is the big one.
The first thing Lewis’s team did after being awarded the contract last year was to dive into the archives. The starting point was a little-known 1932 article in Good Housekeeping by Virginia Woolf. For Woolf, Oxford Street appeared as a “great rolling ribbon … the pebbly bed of a river … washed by a bright stream”. She saw it as gaudy, but also sparkling, thrilling and overwhelming, defined by the restless movement of its messy public. (Her essay also shows us how weird the street has long been – in 1932, it was apparently full of hawkers selling live tortoises.) It was these riverine characteristics that became the starting point for the thousands of material, small-scale design decisions that East are making. The “play of light on surfaces, the subtle reflectivity of a bench or a column” can all help bring out those tendencies, Bashford told me.
The pedestrianisation happening next week will cover 0.6 miles, stretching westwards from close to the Oxford Circus crossing to Selfridges. (Sadiq Khan has expressed his commitment to eventually pedestrianise all 1.2 miles of the street.) The most noticeable transformation will be how much greener it is becoming. The architects’ plan is to experiment with introducing young trees in pots, alongside new places to sit. They will use the test phase – which will last from next week until spring 2027 – to learn about how people respond to the trees. Will they become meeting points? Rest stops? Landmarks for wayfinding? Ideally they will provide respite, Lewis said, “a refuge from the flow of people, which is the river analogy again – maybe that’s optimistic, but instilling some relative calm”.
The pedestrianised zone’s edges will be marked by bollards. Lewis has strong opinions on this subject, and speaks about bollards as if they were people. “Bollards are generally horrible things,” he told me. Too often they seem “apologetic”, he said. “A misaligned, plasticky reflective strip [on a bollard] sends the message: ‘Sorry, I didn’t really mean to be here, but I need to let you know there are some vehicles nearby.’ Instead, they should be saying: ‘I’m happy to be here, because I’m doing a job.’”
An abundance of considerations go into designing the right kind of bollard, including security, maintenance, aesthetics, accessibility, climate, foot traffic, crowd flow and civic pride. Oxford Street’s bollards have to be exactly 1.2 metres apart, for reasons of HVM – hostile vehicle mitigation – but they also need to be helpful and use “the existing language of the street”. They will be made of ductile iron, because it is more resilient than cast iron: it’s springy, and doesn’t crack when you hit it. They are also matt, because shiny bollards are too flashy, and detract from the ambience. “They’re very sophisticated,” Lewis said, and he meant it.
One of the project’s primary ambitions is to better integrate Oxford Street with its neighbours. It is surrounded by four areas with strikingly different identities: Soho, Fitzrovia, Mayfair and Marylebone. “There’s this slightly numb connection to Oxford Street itself, like: where the hell is Oxford Street? It might as well not be there, with regard to the relationship with these incredible centres,” Lewis said. “People want to go to Soho. They want to go to Marylebone. People live in Fitzrovia. Oxford Street does not have a place yet, it’s a non-spatial space, which is unbelievable given how famous it is.”
This is where landscape architecture and design comes in. The noun the architects use over and over is “invitation” – how do you encourage people to do the unthinkable, and linger in the newly pedestrianised space, and move freely in and out of it? The built environment has to invite them to do so. One innovation Lewis’s team wants to explore is outdoor public dining – not outdoor tables for restaurants, because there are barely any on Oxford Street, but continental-style tables to sit and eat whatever you want; takeaway food bought in Soho, or a packed lunch you made at home. “The idea of sitting there having sandwiches at a picnic bench, next to a shop in which you can buy a Prada handbag, is a fantastic kind of paradox,” Lewis said with a smile. “And it’s also very London.”
T o understand where the idea of pedestrianising Oxford Street came from, you need to acquaint yourself with the work of a Danish urban planner called Jan Gehl. In 2003, when Ken Livingstone was mayor of London, Gehl was asked to spend 18 months researching the flaws in London’s streetscape, and in June 2004 he produced a 120-page report entitled Towards a Fine City for People. Gehl thought there was a huge amount of work to be done. “London comes only after Moscow in the contempt the city planners show for pedestrians,” he said that year. “You never see any children on London streets – what have you done with them all?” The answer is that they have been increasingly shut indoors: driven everywhere in cars or not trusted to play outside – compared both with earlier generations of Londoners, and with most other children across Europe .
Gehl wanted to transform the capital into one of the world’s most walking-friendly cities by 2015. But with the 2004 mayoral election taking place the same month, the radical edges of the final report that was published by Livingstone’s City Hall were sanded down. Gehl’s full recommendations were confined to a “secret document”, distributed to the capital’s decision-makers but never published. Among other things, it recommended the full pedestrianisation of Oxford Street. It has taken 22 years for that dream to be realised. “I see some signs of improvement in London,” Gehl told me recently on a video call from his home in Copenhagen, “but for God’s sake, the tempo and the amount of change have not been impressive.”
Gehl, who is 90, has long sought to turn cities into places that put the people that live there first. His motto is “the city at eye level, and at 5km/hour” – walking pace. Life Between Buildings, his first book, from 1971, was a challenge to the orthodoxy that had shaped postwar urban planning. Rather than judging the city principally by its buildings, its roads or the efficiency of its layout, Gehl asked planners to pay attention to what people actually did in public: where they walked, where they stopped, whether they met, talked or sat down to watch the world go by. These values are now finally at the centre of so much city planning – and it is no coincidence that his organisation Gehl Studio was appointed by City Hall to advise East on Oxford Street’s transformation.
For Gehl, city halls across the world should be looking to Australia. Sydney, Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide have moved dramatically towards pedestrianisation and light rail – they are “more ambitious, daring and faster in making decisions” than their peers in the UK. In Sydney, Gehl said, the rapid transformation of the equivalent of Oxford Street, George Street, is improving the atmosphere in the city around it. With ageing populations, “the end of the shopping era” for cities, and the need to reduce fossil fuel consumption, his once-radical ideas are becoming common sense. “If I am looking back at my professional career, it’s been one big struggle to reclaim public spaces from cars, which in the 1960s filled all of the streets and all the squares – they filled every possible place. We have spent many decades reconquering cities for their citizens.”
What we know as Oxford Street, which has been a street for the best part of two millennia, has always been a stage for the evolving society around it. It was previously called Tyburn Road, and for six centuries formed the processional path to the infamous Tyburn Tree, the gallows at what is now Marble Arch. Thronging crowds would line the route on hanging days, making for a rather different participatory public spectacle than that provided by its window-shopping era.
The evolution of West End neighbourhoods brought stables, barns, abattoirs and breweries, fortifications, countless pubs and coaching inns, and eventually department stores, theatres and music halls. Oxford Street has long been a centre not just of commerce, but culture and social life. Howard Carter gave his first public lecture about the discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb at the New Oxford Theatre in 1923, and the most famous punk gigs in history – featuring the Sex Pistols, the Clash, Buzzcocks and more – took place at the (still running, still pleasingly dingy) 100 Club in 1976. Oxford Street’s long list of fallen pubs – the Hog in the Pound, the Jolly Trooper, the Man Loaded with Mischief – today leaves just one survivor, the Flying Horse. At 6pm on a Tuesday in late September, the atmosphere inside the last was surprisingly gentle and convivial; the dark wood panelling and Victorian fittings offering a calming refuge from the rush-hour chaos outside.
There have been many experiments in recent decades to bring social life back to Oxford Street: tweaks to crossings, traffic restrictions and pavements, and, largely to accommodate more shopping, from 2005 to 2012, one single traffic-free day in the run-up to Christmas called Very Important Pedestrians Day.
One thing everyone agrees on is that a dramatic transformation is long overdue. By the time Khan replaced Boris Johnson as mayor in 2016, London had fallen behind cities such as Paris, Barcelona and Berlin when it came to infrastructure for cyclists and pedestrians, and measures to curb car numbers. Then, the systemic shocks of the pandemic, and an electorate voting ever more to the left (and more Green), offered Khan the opportunity and the mandate to catch up.
There are two big structural changes sweeping through the great cities of western Europe that have also shaped Khan’s ability to finally get this done. The first is that the motorcar is no longer king in the modern city. The second is that shopping has been displaced. Even though Oxford Street remains a river bobbing with more than 20 flagship stores, maximal spending is no longer the only consideration. In the age of same-day delivery, out-of-town fulfilment centres, and peer-to-peer secondhand marketplaces such as Vinted, what should replace shopping at the heart of the modern city?
T his week, I walked down Oxford Street with Nabeel Khan, CEO of the Oxford Street Development Corporation (OSDC). His earliest experience of Oxford Street was going to HMV to buy his first CD: 2Pac’s Me Against the World. Today, he is the man in charge of making pedestrianisation happen.
On our walk, the first signs of change were visible: the concrete bases of the new bollards were in place and the old wooden planters – “really poorly designed”, in Khan’s view – had had their dying shrubs removed. Outside the flagship UK store of the US shoe brand Vans, which styles itself as not merely a skateboarding attire shop, but “a space to express yourself” and a “cultural hub”, Khan spoke with gusto about the so-called experience economy.
In city centres post-Covid, there is “this desire, particularly among young people, for human connection,” he said, gesturing through the open concertina doors of the Vans shop, where a full drum kit, guitar and amps had been set up, facing out on to the street. “When you can buy almost anything you want, what’s the one thing that you can’t buy? That proximity to someone else and having that human experience.”
Given that everyone agrees Oxford Street needs overhauling, why has this taken so long? “The West End doesn’t have a single owner,” Khan said. “There are two local authorities, a transport authority, a strategic authority, five business improvement districts, hundreds of businesses and some major landowners.” The maestro trying to conduct this unruly orchestra is now the OSDC, which was created by the mayor. While reporting this story, I noticed the OSDC sought to keep an iron grip on press coverage. Perhaps this is because the local politics around Oxford Street have been fiercely contested for so long.
In fact, angst over vehicle traffic on Oxford Street is about as old as London’s mayor. In 1971, when Sadiq Khan was a baby, so many pedestrians were spilling from overcrowded pavements into the road and being hit by cars that an Oxford Street Action Committee was formed. During one protest calling for cars to be banned, 22 people were arrested. The Greater London Council introduced the first ban of private cars (between 7am and 7pm) the following year, marking the beginning of 50 years of gradual traffic restrictions.
Full pedestrianisation has faced decades of opposition and obstruction, primarily from the Conservative-run Westminster council – continuing when Labour took it over from 2022 to 2026 – but also from taxi drivers, disabled access groups, local residents, smaller traders and local neighbourhood groups such as the Soho Society and Mayfair Forum. The latter worry that plans to reroute buses, delivery lorries and taxis into quiet conservation areas surrounding the street will “destroy” those areas, as Tim Lord of the Soho Society put it. Accessibility advocates and the Licensed Taxi Drivers’ Association argue that pedestrianisation will create a transport desert for older people and disabled visitors. (In a statement, the OSDC admitted that journeys to Oxford Street will change for some, but said that accessibility has been at the “heart” of the planning process. Bus stops, it said, will be no more than about 200 metres from the pedestrianised area; it added that the street furniture was designed with input from specialist disabled groups.)
Khan’s predecessors tried, and failed, to transform Oxford Street. As mayor, Boris Johnson called pedestrianisation the “Schleswig-Holstein question of London traffic”, referring to the infamously complicated 19th-century German constitutional debate, because “everybody in abstract would love to do [it]” until they look at the “actual economic impact”. But by 2016, the tipping point had been reached – all the major mayoral candidates that year proposed pedestrianising it in principle, and when Khan won, he pledged that it would be completed by 2020. For a brief period, City Hall, Transport for London (TfL) and Westminster council appeared to be pulling in the same direction. Polling in 2018 and 2024 has shown about two-thirds of Londoners support the idea.
But the political fight over Oxford Street has often been less about how it is transformed than who gets to decide. In 2018, local opposition to Khan’s pedestrianisation plan crystallised into the creation of Capo, the Campaign Against Pedestrianisation of Oxford Street, which stood three candidates in 2018’s local elections, winning more than 1,000 votes between them. Spooked by this, Nickie Aiken, the council’s Conservative leader, used the backlash to nix the plan. Khan was furious, calling Westminster’s withdrawal “a betrayal” and claiming that £8m of public money had been wasted by the scheme’s collapse.
A decade and a pandemic later, it is finally happening because the planning authority is now held by the OSDC, which was established by the mayor’s office. The Better Oxford Street campaign, a coalition of local opponents to pedestrianisation, called this transfer of power a display of “jaw-dropping audacity” by the mayor, with the OSDC superseding the council “and its democratically elected representatives”.
As Jan Gehl observed to me, compared with some city halls around the world, London mayors have limited power. They can’t raise taxes (or introduce rent caps, legislate or control health services), which makes urban change that much harder to achieve. One thing that is under the mayor’s remit though is TfL: after he got the latter to agree to reroute their buses around the street, and with the OSDC up and running, Khan was finally in the driving seat.
W hat happens next week is just the beginning. The first half of Oxford Street will close to traffic on Monday – but the pedestrianisation process that follows will stretch on for well over a year. The people behind the project are anxious that the initial testing phase is not misunderstood as a permanent project that has been built cheaply, or half heartedly. The testing process will involve a lot of people standing around with clipboards and measuring things, observing the different ways and places that pedestrians dwell. Even the picnic benches they are installing will be engaging in data collection, thanks to a “beacon”, a sensor recessed into the seat, that will measure how many people sit down, for how long, and the ambient temperature at the time.
There are other problems to navigate. On my first “site visit” to Oxford Street with East’s Archie Bashford, he showed me an example of how not to do public-realm architecture. We were on a little side street behind Oxford Circus station. There stood three vast steel plant pots, each hosting a leafless, skeletal young tree. The soil base was crisscrossed with a lattice of slats, the gaps completely stuffed with cigarette butts. The planters had become giant ash trays, which presumably hadn’t done much for the dying trees. At the root of this miserable scene were security concerns, Bashford explained – the designers had wanted to keep the soil out of reach. I was confused. “Some planters,” Lewis later explained, “are quite conducive to hiding things.” Such as knives.
This might sound like Metropolitan police hyperbole. But the knife threat is not just a scare story: weapons hidden by organised crime groups are often found in “soft landscape”, usually soil, for easy extraction and future use, removing the danger of being caught in possession.
There is a delicate balance to be struck between public safety and a more sociable public realm. The social optimist’s view is that you minimise crime in the public realm not by making it so miserable that nobody wants to visit in the first place, but by overwhelming the minority of people behaving badly with people who are behaving well. The architects at East hope that some forms of crime, such as drug dealing, will become harder, for the simple reason that it will be more visible. “Sometimes you do have to mitigate [criminal activity],” Lewis said, “but I think it’s more successful in the long term to provide an infrastructure that supports social activity, and invites it.”
Another concern is that the new Oxford Street becomes something rather more mundane: a successfully pedestrianised but ultimately disappointing place. An open-air shopping mall, a tourist trap, a hyperbranded open-air events venue, or an empty corridor after closing time. Some observers worry it could acquire some of the same problems that Barcelona’s La Rambla is still tackling. In recent decades the Catalan boulevard has been a tawdry sacrifice to tourists, largely abandoned by local residents. In an effort to avoid that outcome, there has been a great deal of communication between Barcelona and London. Barcelona’s city hall is keenly watching Oxford Street, Nabeel Khan told me, and East’s architects have visited Barcelona to procure their data-gathering seating.
What would success look like in two years’ time, I asked Khan, as we lingered outside Selfridges, occasionally apologising as we sidestepped passersby. “Of course there’s an economic side,” he said. “We want to see retail doing well, we want to see the return of flagship stores. We want to see more people spending time and coming back to Oxford Street: not just first-time visitors, but return visitors.” It should also form the first stage of a wider transformation of London’s entire West End, he added. “We want to see Marylebone benefit from this, we want to see Soho benefit from this. We want to show people that this is how the heart of a global city should feel, should look, should be experienced. That will be success.”
Archie Bashford believes the change in atmosphere will be profound: “Even if we were doing nothing else, and they just shut the street, it would feel amazing and transgressive.” In just a few weeks’ time, visitors will be able to look up at Oxford Street’s glittering Christmas lights without worrying about being run over. People don’t tend to look up on Oxford Street, I’ve noticed, because they can’t – they’d be mown down.
But it turns out, if you gaze above shop-window height, that Oxford Street has a rich architectural history, stretching across styles and centuries, from the modernist Barbara Hepworth statue on the side of John Lewis to the imposing 18th-century Pantheon that hosts Marks & Spencer. It is worth your time to linger, even beyond the fundamental human right to sit down, have a sandwich and breathe some clean air.

title: ‘Jackdaw means we pay our mortgages’: relief in Aberdeen over gasfield approval
description: Few believe decision will bring back city’s boom years, but workers hope it will secure North Sea jobs for now UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea What does the UK’s approval of Jackdaw mean? content:
Few believe decision will bring back city’s boom years, but workers hope it will secure North Sea jobs for now
UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
What does the UK’s approval of Jackdaw mean?
As recently as 2012, Aberdeen boasted the highest concentration of millionaires in the UK. An ATM reportedly had the highest withdrawal rate in Europe in the 90s, as oil and gas wealth flowed through the city. House prices soared in the scramble for space as fossil fuel firms transformed the city’s grand granite houses into company offices. But that was then.
Today, “for sale” and “to let” signs punctuate the city’s main thoroughfares. Disposable income in Aberdeen has fallen by nearly 20% between 2013 and 2023 – more than any other large UK city – after a 2014 oil price shock sparked a brutal reversal in Aberdeen’s fortunes.
At the beginning of this year, demolition began on the former offices of Marathon Oil, once a base for hundreds of workers. Between 2010 and 2021, the number of people aged 20-29 fell by 16%. BP appears set to leave the city after announcing plans to divest from its North Sea business. On darker days, the spectre of former coalmining towns looms large in the minds of some residents.
“Years ago, a fund should have been set up that saved some of the oil money for Aberdeen . But that’s long gone,” said Scott, an assistant at a men’s clothing shop. “It’s a city centre like any other now. People blame the local council and the local government. I don’t know. It’s very different to how it was.”
“Twenty years ago this street was full. Now it is so quiet,” said one woman at a bus stop on Union Street.
For many Aberdonians, the government’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield , located 150 miles offshore, came as a relief.
Critics point to the climate impact and the modest number of jobs that the new gasfield would likely support. Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”
The UN Environment Programme has said global carbon emission targets need to be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin.
But for oil and gas workers in the city, this is about keeping as many North Sea jobs for as long as possible, which have so far not been replaced by the renewables sector and tend to pay less.
At the heliport, offshore workers returning to dry land after a flight across stormy North Sea waters were in good spirits about the prospect of a new field.
“Jackdaw means we pay our mortgages. Without oil and gas, what am I supposed to do?” said one woman, who works offshore as a cleaner on a rig.
Another offshore worker said: “Short-term, the green industry isn’t going to replace this. It’s a slow process. You can’t expect it to happen overnight.”
Few think that the new gasfield will restore the city’s boomtown years. Unlike other oil cities such as Houston, Abu Dhabi and Stavanger, Aberdeen has not been able to recover from the 2014 price shock and there is growing acceptance that the decline is permanent. Many offshore oil and gas workers acknowledge that they are likely to be the last generation of their kind – and increasingly work away for weeks at a time on rigs in Africa and Asia.
More than 90% of the UK part of the North Sea basin has been exploited, compared with just over 50% in Norway, which has not outlawed new exploration licences. Jackdaw is projected to supply only 6% of the UK’s gas output at its peak. In the approval, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, pointed to national security reasons behind her decision to back the project.
“This decision will support the country’s energy security with homegrown gas this winter and help minimise the UK’s use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear.
“The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050,” she said.
The rapidly growing renewables industry in the city has proved to be a boon for some firms: the shipping operator North Star once made all of its money from the oil and gas sector, but now nearly 80% of its operating profit comes from offshore wind. Great British Energy is headquartered in the city. Yet, the growth in the offshore wind industry has so far failed to offset the decline in oil and gas jobs in Aberdeen, and it is unclear it ever will. About 90% of offshore jobs in the northeast of Scotland remain in the oil and gas sector, supporting around 38,000 jobs compare to 4,200 in the renewables sector.
From the doldrums of the 2014 crash, Aberdeen has seen recent signs of recovery. Major regeneration works are taking place in the city centre. On a drive through the leafy west of the city, grand houses are not longer left on the market for months, said Joni Esson, a property lawyer with Simpson & Marwick.
“We’re seeing property sell for reasonable prices and a little bit of confidence coming back,” she said. “Loads of people who bought pre-2014 got in negative equity and then just couldn’t shift their homes.”
Our Union Street, a community group formed to reinvigorate the city’s main thoroughfare, has been filling empty shops after the vacancy rate reached 20%. For Bob Keiller, a former oil and gas CEO who oversees the effort, Jackdaw’s approval was a sign that the government was taking a more pragmatic approach to the fossil fuel sector – which would be a boost to the city.
“It’s symbolic. For a long time, it’s been ‘no, nothing, never, never again’. Whereas now there’s recognition that maybe it makes sense to produce your own fuel sources. It has to make economic and environmental sense, of course,” he said. “Before, it was, ‘No, not listening! Just stop oil.’ What does that mean? Everything we’ve got here just now relies on oil and gas at the moment.”

title: Too little, too late: Trump takes on gas prices as fuel costs hamper his midterm hopes
description: Polls show US voters are deeply upset by high gas prices and are likely to punish Republicans in the midterms as a result How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions With fewer than two weeks until the midterm s, US voters are unlikely to see relief on one of this election cycle’s main issues: gas prices. Airing up her car’s tires at a Speedway in Perrysburg, Ohio , Toledo resident Sharie Smith, 41, says soaring costs are having a direct impact on her life. Continue reading...
author_name: Debbie Carlson in Chicago, Chris Stein in Ohio and Sam Levine in Missouri
content:
Polls show US voters are deeply upset by high gas prices and are likely to punish Republicans in the midterms as a result
How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions
With fewer than two weeks until the midterm s, US voters are unlikely to see relief on one of this election cycle’s main issues: gas prices.
Airing up her car’s tires at a Speedway in Perrysburg, Ohio , Toledo resident Sharie Smith, 41, says soaring costs are having a direct impact on her life.
“It’s affecting my budget,” she says. “You got to take away certain things, you got to take away from your kids, like extracurricular activities.” She says high gas prices are making it harder to pay for the fees for her children’s football games.
Every 10 days, she used to fill up her gray Chevy Malibu for $30 to $40, but now it costs $50 to $60. It stings, she says. “Especially that with the price of groceries,” she adds.
“And I don’t even have a big car. I feel bad for those people with big cars, like trucks.”
Donald Trump has made many promises about bringing down gas prices and specifically touted several diesel cost-savings deals this month, but voters won’t see lower costs by 3 November, say energy analysts.
National average prices for gasoline and diesel are down marginally from a month ago, according to AAA , but remain substantially higher than last year. Compared with 2025, gasoline costs are up more than $1.25 a gallon, at $4.29, while diesel prices are up nearly 75%, to $6.30 a gallon.
Polls show that US voters are deeply upset by high gas prices and are likely to punish Republicans as a result. A 10 October poll by Politico showed that even if Trump were to bring the price of gasoline down by $1 a gallon, most voters polled would not likely be swayed to vote Republican.
Earlier this month, Trump announced several deals attempting to lower diesel prices, including promoting greater use of “red dye” diesel fuel normally reserved for off-highway use, temporarily lifting sanctions on Russian diesel imports, and now a one-time, $8bn diesel-fuel subsidy for farmers to help with harvest.
“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted on his social media site.
Ed Hirs, energy fellow at the University of Houston, says these moves will have no impact. “Zero. No elaboration needed,” he says.
Under the Russia deal, the US can import 2.24m barrels of Russian diesel, with more to follow. That initial figure amounts to just 14 hours of US diesel demand, says Andrew Critchlow, head of energy news for Dow Jones Energy. For context, the global diesel market uses nearly 30m barrels a day.
Hirs adds that the deal with Putin is not for new supply. “It was going someplace. It was going someplace at a discount. And now what Trump has done is, rather than have Russia sell it at a discount, they’re selling it for full value. He’s given them a huge windfall,” Hirs says.
Diesel fuel is an important transportation fuel globally, critical in the last-mile delivery of most consumer goods, so everyone feels the pinch, says Rob Thummel, senior portfolio manager at Tortoise Capital. Energy prices across the board are higher because of the US war on Iran, which closed the strait of Hormuz, through which much of the world’s crude oil flows.
Producing more diesel is difficult because Middle East refineries were damaged early in the war, and Chinese refiners are unable to get enough oil to produce any extra fuel for world markets. Recent attacks on Russian refiners by Ukrainian drones have further cut global supplies. US refineries have access to domestic oil but are running at maximum capacity, Thummel says.
The White House has characterized its recent executive order to temporarily allow greater use of red-dye diesel as a cost-saving measure for farmers and truckers. This fuel is exempt from federal excise taxes because it is intended for farmers and off-road machinery and is stained red to differentiate it from regular diesel. The White House says the 24.4 cents per gallon discount will save those drivers about $60 on a 250-gallon fill up.
Yet Hirs says it gives farmers more competition for fuel, which will raise their prices. Farmers already are being buffeted by higher operating costs across the board and losing China as a key export market because of the US’s trade war with the Asian nation.
Prices could rise as energy demand increases in the winter heating months, especially in places that use heating oil, experts add. Energy prices are seasonal, and prices are usually lower at this time of year since it’s neither cooling nor heating season, says Jay Hatfield, chief investment officer of real-asset investment firm InfraCap. Despite typically lower seasonal demand, prices are already high.
There are risks of higher prices if the fighting in the Middle East escalates, Hatfield says, pointing to a pickup of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as an example.
Critchlow says with many countries having depleted strategic stocks and few countries have released reserves, it might not take too much to push prices up. “I think that we are in a very fragile position now, marketwise,” he says.
The only moves that will lower energy costs are to open the strait of Hormuz to get more oil flowing, and to negotiate a peace accord between Russia and Ukraine, as these two conflicts are interlinked with energy markets, the energy experts say.
If those conflicts were resolved, Critchlow says the energy situation could be drastically different two years from now, with the world being oversupplied with fossil-fuel energy.
That change can’t come soon enough for some drivers. Lotanpa Jones, a home healthcare aide, was filling up at a Mobil in St Charles, Missouri, earlier this month. Regular fuel was $4.09 a gallon – last 1 October the national average price was $3.15 to $3.19, according to data from AAA . Diesel was $6.59 a gallon, up from $3.71 a year ago, according to data tracked by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA)
“I can tell you this is making me want to park my car,” said Jones.
She said she had last filled up her car two days earlier and now was adding another $55.
“It’s affecting a lot because you gotta decide what you’re gonna buy,” she said. “It’s major.”
Jones said she thought it would affect who people vote for. “Most definitely. Yes, this is extreme.”
Ironically, given Trump’s antipathy towards electric vehicles, Critchlow foresees the current crisis eventually pushing electrification for consumers, heavy industry and agriculture in the US. The shift in consumption and energy mix mirrors the 1970s energy shock, he says. “We are going to see something similar,” he says.
In the meantime, gas prices are likely to take their toll on Republicans come 3 November. Back in Ohio , Smith, a home health nurse, says she has already lost patients because of Medicaid eligibility changes made by the state, which she criticized Republicans for. “They’re thinking about the wrong things, and now the price of gas is going up,” Smith says.
As for who she is voting for, she says: “I’m going Democrat.” As for the Republican candidates, she adds: “They don’t have any idea what people are going through.”

title: Blockades, checkpoints and court action: fending off Brazil’s biofuel giants in the Amazon
description: After decades of violent displacement and land theft, the country’s quilombola communities are fighting back For most of his 39 years, Josias Dias dos Santos, known as Jota, has endured degrading cycles of displacement as a quilombola , a descendant of Black people once enslaved on Brazil ’s sugar cane and coffee plantations. He says his and other quilombola families subsisting in the rainforests in Pará, northern Brazil, were first forced out of their settlements by violent loggers, then by ranchers and miners. Yet, they say the worst came with the arrival of the palm oil industry in what is now the country’s most deforested state . Palm oil companies producing biofuels and supplying global customers, subsidised by the federal government, have laid claim to ever larger tracts of traditional quilombola territory over the past two decades. Continue reading...
author_name: Gisela Pérez de Acha, Sasha Schell, Cícero Pedrosa in Acará, Pará, with Luiz Monticelli and Kathleen Quinn
content:
After decades of violent displacement and land theft, the country’s quilombola communities are fighting back
F or most of his 39 years, Josias Dias dos Santos, known as Jota, has endured degrading cycles of displacement as a quilombola , a descendant of Black people once enslaved on Brazil ’s sugar cane and coffee plantations. He says his and other quilombola families subsisting in the rainforests in Pará, northern Brazil, were first forced out of their settlements by violent loggers, then by ranchers and miners.
Yet, they say the worst came with the arrival of the palm oil industry in what is now the country’s most deforested state . Palm oil companies producing biofuels and supplying global customers, subsidised by the federal government, have laid claim to ever larger tracts of traditional quilombola territory over the past two decades.
Since then, Dias dos Santos says, the companies have put up mazes of fencing , guard towers and security checkpoints , sometimes cutting communities off from their family cemeteries. Leaders who attempted to speak out for their land rights and against toxic industrial waste were often either jailed or gunned down in ambushes that went unprosecuted.
Now quilombolas fear the second round of Brazil’s presidential elections will heighten the threat to the forest and its people. Many say a victory for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro , would make securing the formal recognition of their land rights “impossible”.
Dias dos Santos was barely seven years old when loggers forced his and other quilombola families to flee their homes near an abandoned sugar mill, where their enslaved ancestors once worked.
After the loggers came the palm oil industry. With government encouragement , the industry set out to acquire large tracts of land in northern Pará. Today, about 202,000 hectares (500,000 acres), much of it near the Acará River, are used to produce palm oil for biofuels and a wide range of foods.
For years, quilombola communities complained that the companies were squeezing them off their traditional lands. They also claimed their families were being affected by a toxic chemical byproduct of palm oil production, which also plagued the Acará River with bloated, dead fish.
Quilombola activists who led protests and failed attempts to reclaim land met violent ends. One leader, Artemio Gusmão, was decapitated and dismembered ; another was shot 16 times in the back. “We were frightened,” Dias dos Santos says.
Tensions between the quilombolas and the palm oil companies increased in 2020 after Brasil BioFuels (BBF) took over a large operation in the region. It built a complex of fences, gates and watchtowers guarded by private security guards and began systematically filing more than 1,000 police reports accusing quilombolas of making threats, damaging property and stealing its equipment.
While many displacement cases in the Amazon end with companies forcing traditional communities off their land, the Acará quilombolas were different. The community acted to reclaim what they said was their land with a human blockade, then established borders that made it impossible for a palm oil company operating there to enter.
Behind their own security gates, the quilombolas began reforesting and restoring biodiversity to lands once degraded by palm oil monoculture. They built schools, community centres and hundreds of homes, despite a campaign to evict them.
In one incident in late 2021, BBF’s security chief, Walter Romero Ferrari, led scores of armed men to break up a demonstration against the company. Court records say that the armed men tied protesters’ hands behind their backs and used pepper spray on them. Ferrari and another BBF executive were eventually charged with torture (the case is still pending).
That event convinced the quilombola community members to pursue more radical forms of resistance: they planned to block BBF’s main entrance, a controversial move that many feared would lead to arrests.
On 24 February 2022, Dias dos Santos and others arrived at BBF, padlocked the gate, and refused to move, despite their lack of weapons against armed guards. BBF representatives later accused them of threats, which they deny. The quilombolas declared they would no longer allow the company to harvest palm fruits and insisted they owned the land behind the gate.
Over months, accusations of violence and theft arose, but the blockade endured, with the community expanding checkpoints and building infrastructure using income from selling palm fruit.
Finally, the courts have not only refused to enforce most of BBF’s land claims, but one key government body has already ruled that the quilombolas have a valid right to much of the land they have reclaimed.
They have also rejected eight of nine requests by BBF to lay criminal charges against Dias dos Santos. The exception – a charge of theft for allegedly disarming a BBF security guard and then turning the guard’s gun over to local police for safekeeping – is being contested.
In a 2024 interview, Milton Steagall, BBF’s chief executive, portrayed himself as a job creator and an environmentalist, combating deforestation by planting palm trees.
He rejected the idea that BBF had stolen land, saying that it acquired another palm oil company that had operated in the area for more than a decade. Steagall also presented the company as the victim of fraudsters who were falsely claiming Indigenous identity as a ruse to justify land theft.
“Imagine that I’m being accused of something that was planted 10, 12 years earlier and I’m responsible for having planted it in an Indigenous or quilombola area? Does that make sense?” he asks.
By 2024, BBF was struggling to pay its employees, and a court in Pará declared it bankrupt and put it into a corporate rescue procedure last year. New palm oil companies are leasing BBF’s former plantations next to the Acará community’s land.
In a statement, BBF’s lawyers said Steagall maintained his 2024 position that “the company entered into a palm cultivation activity that had already existed in the region for years”, and that this did “not mean that there are no territorial claims or controversies over areas in the region.
“The location, boundaries and legal status of each property require individual examination of the documents and the procedures conducted by the competent authorities,” the statement said, adding: “BBF respects the rights of communities and maintains that no accusation regarding a specific area should be treated as an established fact without such verification.”
The campaign marked the quilombolas’ first victory against biofuel companies in the region. About 2,300 community members have gained control over nearly 32,400 hectares formerly cultivated by BBF.
Yet, in the region, conflict between local communities and the palm oil industry is not limited to the quilombola communities or the Acará municipality. The Tembé and Turiwara Indigenous communities in Tomé-Açu, Moju and Tailândia also face another large producer operating on 22,972 hectares – 18,203 of which the quilombolas claim.
In a provisional ruling , the local court has already ruled partly in favour of the communities, finding that 72% of the disputed land overlaps with areas belonging to quilombola and riverside communities. The ruling has also led to the cancellation of 24 land registrations.
Independent reports by the Pastoral Land Commission (CPT), a Catholic advocacy organisation, indicate that at least four deaths, attempted murders, and 14 death threats have been recorded in the region.
For all these reasons, the Acará community says victory is far from assured. Dias dos Santos fears for his life and says they continue to repel violent attempts to evict them and are still awaiting formal property titles.
“I know that the risk of being killed is very high,” says Dias dos Santos, who travels in three-vehicle convoys for protection and relays his movements to other community members, who track him using a GPS app for security reasons.
The future may be uncertain, but for now, Dias dos Santos and his people are confident. “Our grandparents decided not to fight because they would die. Now, if we fight back, we run the risk of dying, too. But we have a mobile phone, where we can learn about our rights and report things,” he says. “So we have a chance of staying alive.”

title: A plan to ensure energy is affordable for all | Letters
description: Dr Alex Chapman calls for a government-funded price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas, in response to an article by Nils Pratley Nils Pratley thinks that the secretary of state, Miatta Fahnbulleh, should “keep things simple” and develop a targeted social tariff to protect vulnerable households from surging energy bills ( The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff, 14 October ). Unfortunately, there is nothing simple about such a scheme. Pratley’s proposal would mean creating a new benefits system inside our privatised energy industry. If the interminable debates about our current benefits system were not enough to put him off, we can look to the failing social care system to see where it might lead. Andy Burnham has made it his life’s mission to dismantle this lottery that can strip pensioners of their savings and the family home. content:
Dr Alex Chapman calls for a government-funded price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas, in response to an article by Nils Pratley
Nils Pratley thinks that the secretary of state, Miatta Fahnbulleh, should “keep things simple” and develop a targeted social tariff to protect vulnerable households from surging energy bills ( The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff, 14 October ). Unfortunately, there is nothing simple about such a scheme.
Pratley’s proposal would mean creating a new benefits system inside our privatised energy industry. If the interminable debates about our current benefits system were not enough to put him off, we can look to the failing social care system to see where it might lead. Andy Burnham has made it his life’s mission to dismantle this lottery that can strip pensioners of their savings and the family home. Just as he now plans a universal public provision of adult social care, we at the New Economics Foundation have such a plan for energy.
Every household should be able to afford the energy essentials: enough warmth to survive a winter; enough electricity to switch on the lights and run a fridge. We should recognise this as a universal right rather than waste time tinkering with a targeting system that arbitrarily separates the “worthy” from the “unworthy” (the “rough justice” of the Resolution Foundation’s proposal , which penalises households based on the income of the highest earner, is a case in point).
The long-term design of a universal offer can be debated. But as another energy crisis bears down on us, we should keep it simple: have the Treasury fund a true price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas. This would be a policy from which everyone wins (especially if electrically heated homes are allowed to transfer across their gas allowance).
In the longer term, one way to help pay for this could be to charge households with very high energy consumption more. But there are other ways. The Australian “ solar sharer ” scheme gives every household three hours of free electricity in the middle of the day, bringing hope that renewables could soon give true energy security. Dr Alex Chapman Head of economic and environmental policy, New Economics Foundation

We would like to hear from parents and teachers about their thoughts and experiences of two-week half terms
While it used to be standard for state schools in England to have one-week half terms, some pupils and staff are being given a fortnight off.
Councils set the holiday dates for state schools in England, while academies, free schools, foundation schools and voluntary-aided schools can set their own. Most schools still opt for one week, but more around the country are moving to, or considering the move to, a two-week break.
In the past, parents with young children have the said the longer holiday places an extra burden on them to find childcare . In Wales, plans to extend the half-term and reduce the summer term were shelved in 2024 after opposition from the teaching unions.
We would like to hear from parents and teachers about their thoughts and experiences of two-week half terms. Do you think they are a good idea or not? Do you have a fortnight off? Do you have any concerns?

title: ‘I can charge my car for £6’: could new rules cut costs for EV drivers?
description: Owners in England with no driveway can now slash their costs by installing a cross-pavement gully – but it’s a postcode lottery When Alison Williams bought her electric Volkswagen ID.3 two years ago, she thought she was making the right choice for the environment, having already upgraded her end-of-terrace London home with insulation and solar panels. However, charging the car has proved more costly than she hoped, as she is not able to install the cross-pavement gully – a narrow electric vehicle cable channel embedded in the pavement – that she would need to charge at home. That will remain the case despite a change in the law. Continue reading...
content:
Owners in England with no driveway can now slash their costs by installing a cross-pavement gully – but it’s a postcode lottery
W hen Alison Williams bought her electric Volkswagen ID.3 two years ago, she thought she was making the right choice for the environment, having already upgraded her end-of-terrace London home with insulation and solar panels.
However, charging the car has proved more costly than she hoped, as she is not able to install the cross-pavement gully – a narrow electric vehicle cable channel embedded in the pavement – that she would need to charge at home. That will remain the case despite a change in the law.
From Wednesday, drivers in England who do not have off-street parking will no longer need to get planning permission to put in a pavement gully outside their home.
The gullies sit flush within the pavement and allow an EV charging cable to reach a parked vehicle without creating a trip hazard.
By charging in front of their house via an energy supply in their home, rather than using a public charger, drivers can slash the cost by up to 90% .
But some of the 9.3 million households without off-street parking will be left frustrated as more than 20 local authorities will still not allow the installation of gullies after the law changes.
Williams’s council is Ealing, which does not allow them for cost and safety reasons. She charges her car at a public charger, at much greater cost than if she could do it at home.
“It’s really frustrating,” Williams says. “When we decided to buy an electric car … the reason we wanted to buy one was for the environmental impact.
“You either have to have enough money to have a house with a driveway, or you have to be able to afford the additional cost of charging at a public charger.”
Motorists are not allowed to string EV charging cables across the pavement from their home to the road, but many councils allow cross-pavement charging if you use a gully. To use one, a charging cable is run from the home through the gully and then plugged into the car.
This previously meant getting planning permission from the local authority.
Removing that step will save drivers between £300 and £500. However, anyone who lives in a conservation area will still have to apply.
Caroline Pidgeon, a Liberal Democrat peer, campaigned for the change in the law. She says one in three households in England do not have a driveway. Approval for the gullies has taken up to 15 months in some areas, she says. “Simpler rules will make it easier for people to switch to an electric car,” she adds.
The government has given £25m in funding to councils in England for pavement gullies for people with on-street parking, but the money is being distributed in different ways, depending on the local authority.
How much you pay for installation varies widely around the country.
If you want to apply for a gully to be installed, you should check with your council to see whether it allows them and, if it does, it should direct you on how to apply.
Kerbo Charge, a company that installs gullies, operates a postcode checker you can use to see whether you can get one in your area and sign up for an alert if that changes.
Ben Whitaker of Kerbo Charge says the average fee for the work is about £1,200 (including VAT) without a grant.
“Some [councils] are using it [the funding] to provide half-price channels to early adopters, others are making it totally free while funds last – but, after that, residents will have to pay full price,” he says.
“For example, Surrey is £499 for the channel and installation, South Gloucestershire is £250,” he adds. “Sadly, there is quite a variety of approaches and prices.”
To illustrate the difference in prices between local authorities, Redbridge council in London says the grant will cover up to £1,200 of installation costs. But applicants must pay £815 in fees and for a bond, as well as any additional installation costs.
On top of the cost of installing the gullies, some councils charge an additional annual fee for maintenance. For example, Redbridge charges an “ongoing annual licence fee” of £185. Enfield, also in London, charges £107 a year .
Shayne Rees of Gul-e, a company that has installed 400 gullies, says it takes between one and two hours to put the unit in place. “It’s a really heavy-duty steel channel that can take a truck driving over it, and once we put it in the ground, that will be there for decades and decades without any maintenance,” he adds.
It emerged in May that more than 20 local authorities appear to be holding out against having the gullies installed, among them Kent, Leicester and Worcestershire. Most of the holdouts are in London, including Waltham Forest and Hackney.
The reasons given often concern safety and maintenance, and because of issues over who will be liable if there is an injury. For example, Waltham Forest says gullies “raise significant concerns including safety and accessibility of footways, parking pressures, maintenance responsibilities and liability, electrical safety and earthing standards”.
Leicestershire county council says: “This is a new and very challenging area for local highway authorities to address.”
Ealing council says it decided not to proceed with a trial of the gullies.
“We took into account the needs of the people using the borough’s pavements, including elderly people and less able-bodied individuals, especially those on wheels and people with visual impairments,” a spokesperson says. “Gullies can have a significant impact on the feel and safety of pavements for residents walking or wheeling.”
Carl Cashman of the Local Government Association, which represents councils, says local authorities would like to support on-street charging as much as possible “but have limited resources and significant demands to meet”.
The different views of councils, sometimes neighbouring ones, have frustrated some drivers. Nick Theobald lives in Fulham in London, where he is not allowed to put one in yet. A pilot scheme with a small number of houses has been launched by Hammersmith and Fulham council.
“You’ve only got to go over the river to Richmond and it’s completely permitted there,” he says.
For people without off-street parking, charging an EV at home is much cheaper than doing so at public charge points.
Since the beginning of this month, the VAT charged on domestic electricity has been cut from 5% to 0%, while the tax on public charging remains at 20%.
Gregg Francis, who lives in Carmarthenshire in Wales, had a gully fitted outside his house two and a half years ago for free, as part of a scheme run by the local council. This allows him to fully charge his Vauxhall Vivaro Life for £6. He usually recharges it fully twice a week.
“If we went to the public charger, we could be looking at £30 to £63 for the same amount of electricity,” he says.
“We had a diesel Ford Focus that would cost about £70 a week to use on normal routine. That would now be considerably more as I’m comparing with two years ago.”
Figures from ChargeUK, the industry’s trade group, put the average cost per kWh for off-peak at-home charging at 8p, while the standard public charging cost averages 54p.
Vicky Edmonds, the chief executive of EVA England, which represents drivers, says people with a driveway can save an average of £1,400 a year compared with driving a petrol or a diesel car. Some of her members who do not have off-street parking estimate that they are now paying more than when they had a car using fossil fuels, she says.

title: AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened
description: Exclusive: Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco taskforce urges ministers to offer areas greater benefits from tech infrastructure amid fears of US-style opposition AI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.
