content:
An estimated one-third of adults in England have high blood pressure, with research showing that many are unaware of their condition. But thanks to the new Huawei Watch D3, monitoring blood pressure is easier, accurate and more stylish than ever
Wearable technology has come a long way in the past decade. Take a look around at your colleagues, friends and family, and you’ll be hard pushed to find anyone not wearing some kind of health monitoring ring, watch or band – there are even tracking insoles and patches, too.
These gadgets have myriad benefits – not least, allowing us more control and insight over our health and wellbeing than ever before. We’re able to monitor everything from sleep and stress to heart health and more, and the technology is becoming more refined and intuitive seemingly by the day.
It’s no surprise, then, that companies are laser focused on developing ever more advanced gadgets. But in a saturated wearables market, Huawei is leading the charge when it comes to stylish, performance-led devices.
Its newest bit of tech enables medical-grade* blood pressure tracking. Also known as hypertension, high blood pressure is a global health concern, and one of the leading causes of cardiovascular disease and premature death worldwide.
But the good news is that adequate monitoring and treatment renders these risks largely preventable. So, instead of (or perhaps as well as) tracking our sleep scores and steps, experts are advocating that we all take note of our blood pressure numbers, regardless of our age.
“Although hypertension becomes more common as we get older, one of the biggest mistakes we can make is thinking that we only need to start worrying about blood pressure and cardiovascular disease from middle age,” says Dr Lucy Hooper, GP and co-founder of Coyne Medical . “We increasingly know that cardiovascular disease is something that develops over someone’s whole life course.”
While there are now plenty of devices offering some kind of blood pressure monitoring, the new Huawei Watch D3 goes beyond the capabilities of a single, one-off reading, more closely resembling medical-grade instruments, for a detailed and reliable look at the whole picture, rather than a single snapshot.
Featuring an innovative first-of-its-kind wrist-worn mechanical airbag, the watch delivers effective yet comfortable compression and precise sensing across a minimal skin-contact area for all-day comfort and wearability.
This combination enables both real-time data and longer-term measurements, allowing you to track your personal blood pressure trends throughout the day and night (even while sleeping) via 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM).
Perfect for those wanting a deeper, more comprehensive understanding of their blood pressure, the ABPM data syncs to tailored reports available in the Huawei Health app , which is recognised and endorsed by healthcare professionals, too. In fact, the findings can be shared directly with your healthcare provider.
“Blood pressure is actually a great example of a measurement that can be potentially really useful and have a profound impact on someone’s health and longevity,” says Hooper. “That said, lots of things affect a blood pressure reading, from stress, caffeine, sleep, pain and alcohol, and we also know it is highly affected by the way the measurement is taken.
“Since it is so variable, just checking it as a one-off at the doctor’s surgery or pharmacy isn’t actually ideal. Having access to a 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitor gives us a much better overall picture of blood pressure.”
One thing we know helps keep blood pressure at a healthy level is exercise. However, this is also a physiological stressor in and of itself – if you’ve ever taken an intense Hiit class after a night out, you’ll likely have noticed that it felt tougher than usual.
The good news is that the Huawei Watch D3 can help you tailor those all-important workouts depending on how your body is faring, with its dedicated feature for pre- and post-exercise blood pressure measurements.
“The Huawei Watch D3 represents an evolution in blood pressure monitoring and management,” says Dr Jamie Edwards, senior lecturer in cardiovascular science, University of East London. “Exercise blood pressure responses and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring have long been recognised as providing valuable additional insight into cardiovascular health.”
“However, their application has traditionally been limited by the accuracy, practicality and convenience of conventional measurement approaches,” he says. “The D3 provides a gamechanging approach to accurately and conveniently assess these measures without the need for often cumbersome devices.”
But it’s not just about blood pressure: the watch has a range of other intelligent key health indicators in its Health Glance feature, from sleep tracking and physical readiness to heart rate and rhythm. All of which can be shared with your loved ones via the community function in the Huawei Health app.
If you’re concerned about how technological medical capability marries luxury aesthetics, don’t be. The Huawei Watch D3 delivers stylish and sleek curves, so you’re not compromising on style or substance. The slim, lightweight design offers all-day comfort, and doubles as a stylish accessory. Drawing inspiration from the colours found in nature, the watch is available in a choice of chic neutral colourways (black, white or mocha gold) meaning it’ll always blend seamlessly with your outfit of choice.
Other standout features include those nice-to-haves that make life that little bit easier in daily terms: contactless payments, a carefully selected suite of fitness and wellness apps, more than 100 sport modes, an impressive six-day battery life and compatibility with both Android and iOS.
Put simply, the Huawei Watch D3 is the most comprehensive, medically-certified wearable for people looking to proactively prioritise their health safely, effortlessly and in style, making those health goals simpler to achieve than ever, because wellness doesn’t have to be complicated.
The HUAWEI WATCH D3 is available from the HUAWEI Store from £399.99 and includes a complimentary 10-month Bupa Well+ Silver digital health subscription (worth £200). Plus, until 3 November, readers of the Guardian can claim £20 off the HUAWEI WATCH D3 with the code AGUARDIAN20 .
*The HUAWEI WATCH D3 is CE-certified as a medical device under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR)

title: Intuitive living is the latest wellness trend – meet the new tech making it work
description: Wellness culture can be overwhelming, but a more fluid approach is emerging. Smart devices such as the Huawei Watch Fit 5 perfectly embody this shift in direction – whether you’re regularly sleep tracking or just occasionally using data to support your lifestyle When it comes to the world of health and wellness, it’s easy to suffer from information overwhelm. content:
Wellness culture can be overwhelming, but a more fluid approach is emerging. Smart devices such as the Huawei Watch Fit 5 perfectly embody this shift in direction – whether you’re regularly sleep tracking or just occasionally using data to support your lifestyle
When it comes to the world of health and wellness, it’s easy to suffer from information overwhelm. We’ve never had more access to data, research and expertise which, while valuable, isn’t always applicable to our own lives. What’s more, few of us have time to spend hours sifting through content to devise a personalised health routine, let alone work out if a “routine” is necessary at all.
All this information and expectation can come at a cost: emotional strain, guilt and confusion about where to turn. Health and fitness then start to feel like abstract milestones that we’re blindly chasing rather than important components of our lives.
So in a world where our plans, priorities and interests are constantly evolving, developing the ability to live fluidly and to better tune in to our bodies and minds feels more valuable than ever.
In some areas, the gap between “health” and our contemporary lifestyles is starting to narrow. Smart devices have evolved from clunky accessories reserved for the disciplined athletic elite, to everyday companions for modern living. The new Huawei Watch Fit 5 series embodies a more fluid, perceptive approach to fitness that seems to be emerging as the antithesis to “lock-in” culture and extreme regimens that have flooded social media over recent years.
Aesthetically, there’s a colourway to suit every vibe. The Fit 5 Pro comes in orange, white and black while the Fit 5 is available in silver, purple, white, black and green. Style-wise, there are options to stand out or blend in. But these watches aren’t here to steal your valuable attention. Nor will they be loud and pushy about what you should be doing. The Watch Fit 5 series works alongside you to support and enable.
A standout feature is undoubtedly the contactless payment support via Curve Pay. On-the-fly purchases become both practical and seamless – because why scramble through pockets for your phone when your wallet can live on your wrist.
While your focus is elsewhere, the Watch Fit 5 remains proactive. The 10-day battery life means you can strap it to your wrist and move on with your day (or week), leaving it to monitor your wellbeing in the background. Cardio tracking keeps tabs on your heart health, detecting irregularities and flagging if there’s anything you need to know. Huawei’s latest generation of smartwatches also come with enhanced sleep tracking, offering an overview of your recovery levels and insight into when you’re best placed to tackle a long-distance run or advanced pilates class without putting yourself at risk of injury or illness.
Intuitive wellness is not about ignoring the breadth of information at our fingertips, but about editing our exposure to the noise. “Taking an intuitive approach to health and wellness is ultimately about allowing yourself to connect to what you really need as an individual, rather than changing parts of yourself to follow a regime that may not be suitable for you,” says Amber Fieldgate , a psychotherapist registered with the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy. “An intuitive approach asks you to take responsibility for yourself in a meaningful way. It also challenges you to check in and connect with yourself by asking: ‘What do I really need right now? What is best for me right now?’”
In the past, living life intuitively was typically interpreted as “trusting your gut”. Now, it’s more about identifying trusted tools and information sources and using that data to work out what you need, rather than letting alerts dictate your every move. That’s where something like Huawei’s TruSense System can become your best friend. This next-gen tech will monitor crucial health components such as blood oxygen, stress, heart rate and sleep with 15% better accuracy than previous models. Sure, the intricacy of some of this data isn’t going to be an everyday necessity for many of us, but knowing it’s there ready to explore only makes fluid living easier: the insights are there for you to examine on your own terms.
“Things like your sleep, heart rate and recovery can highlight how ready your body actually is to train,” says personal trainer Aimee Victoria Long . “Instead of relying purely on guesswork, you have something to guide your decisions. The key is using that information to support how you feel, not override it, so it becomes a tool that helps you tune in.”
Chartered physiotherapist and sleep expert Sammy Margo emphasises that sleep is an invaluable part of recovery, and making sure you feel your best throughout the day. “Deep sleep (also known as slow-wave sleep) is vital for physical recovery, immune function, and memory consolidation. Aim for 13-23% of your total sleep time in deep sleep,” she says. If you’re getting eight hours a night, that works out at roughly one to two hours. “REM sleep is where emotional processing, creativity, and long-term memory occur. You should aim for 20-25% of total sleep time in REM, approximately one and a half to two hours per night.”
“Tracking your sleep with a wearable gives you a clear picture of how much of each stage you are actually getting,” Margo adds. And for those days when you need to take some extra time out in the day, the watch’s nap tracking feature is super handy. It can identify short periods of sleep and incorporate them into your broader sleep score and recovery data. These moments can get lost in the big picture of what your body needs and where you are mentally, but being able to review your naps allows you to decide what type of daytime rest helps you feel your best: if napping for too long leaves you feeling groggy, for example, you can make a change.
And when the motivation to get moving does strike? Whatever kind of exercise you feel like doing, the Huawei Watch Fit 5 series has you covered with more than 100 different workouts available. The new cycling mode has enhanced metrics, automatically detecting when you’re in the saddle. Trail running enthusiasts can get segment-based navigation and elevation trends on the go. The Pro model, meanwhile, has in-depth support for other activities, such as golf, so you can get the information you need to perform at your best right on your wrist. Ultimately, there’s no need to stick to a certain type of workout or subscribe to one way of moving: with this smartwatch, you can do whatever feels right.
The emphasis on flexibility releases us from the “all or nothing” mindset. It also makes wellness more engaging. The Mini-Workout assistant built into the Huawei Watch Fit 5 series makes embracing this flexibility simple. The fact that this assistant takes the form of a virtual panda (undoubtedly the cutest PT known to remind anyone to do a few stretches) only adds a cute, nonchalant appeal to personal fitness. Whether you’re feeling sluggish after an afternoon sitting at a desk, are holding tension in your back after a stressful day, or want to shake off nervous energy before an important meeting, you’ll find short, guided exercises lasting from 30 seconds to a few minutes available on your wrist. The panda assistant can even offer exercise prompts based on your surroundings, so all you need to focus on is what your body needs in the moment.
Technology gets a bad rap for stealing our attention, but the Huawei Watch Fit 5 series demonstrates that so much of it comes down to design. Living intuitively doesn’t need to be a complicated lifestyle shift, and the right smart devices can make that step even easier.

content:
For millennia, humans have been captivated by ear decorations. Now, earbuds not only connect us to the digital world, they also showcase our personal sense of style – and the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 is at the forefront of that development
When we are born, a cry can let the world know that we are healthy and OK. When we first begin to talk, we learn to express our needs and understand the needs of others. As we grow older, we learn that the sound of a siren denotes danger, that certain notes swelling together create the sound of a favourite song which lifts our spirits, or that a warm familiar voice on the other end of the phone means our best friend has our back.
Our ears give us grounding and clues: they are our maps of the world, guiding us towards truth, keeping us from harm, giving us a constant stream of sensory information.
So it makes sense that humans have been highlighting this particular part of their anatomies for millennia. The power of the ear, as a portal through which good and bad could traverse was something that was clocked by ancient cultures who believed that evil spirits could enter through the ear canals. Metal earrings were thought to repel the malevolent forces.
In other cultures, ceremonial ear piercing would mark a rite of passage – such as coming of age or the ascension of a person to a particular status in the community. In some belief systems, certain parts of the outer ear were believed to be connected to other organs. And by piercing those parts of the ear it would lead to healing in the body. Meanwhile sailors wore gold loops in their ears as a sort of maritime life insurance, making sure they would get a respectful burial if they washed up ashore after being lost at sea. When the church banned the practice of ear piercing in the 13th century, it became subversive.
Of course, in different times, the wearing of ear jewellery also indicated wealth in societies, with gold and gemstones being worn to indicate status.
Currently, there are trends for multiple piercings throughout the ear – an aesthetic flex that’s as much an act of quiet-fashion rebellion as it is a visual insight into your unique style.
But there’s a revolution happening in ear adornments too. The act of listening has become increasingly crucial in today’s age of digital audio experiences, podcasts, personal assistants – as well as the need to maintain human connection and situational awareness as we move through our hybrid digital-IRL worlds.
We spend a great deal of time ingesting information through our ears, whether that’s having conversations with colleagues, listening to content or checking out a new band recommended by a trusted friend.
We spend so much of our waking day “plugged in” that it is increasingly important that our wearables work for us, mirroring our lifestyles. In this attention economy, we’re multi-tasking audio information the whole time so it’s important to have earbuds that meet us where our real lived experience is. Our listening habits – how we listen and what we listen to – are reflected through what we are listening on.
In 2023, Huawei changed the wearable tech game with its HUAWEI FreeClip: an open-ear earbud that clipped around the middle of the ear, resting outside a person’s ear canal in contrast with in-ear earbuds – marking a new stage in the history of ear adornments.
So lightweight and comfortable you forget you are wearing them, they offer crisp and clear audio that allows you to converse with ease. Now Huawei is launching a new iteration: the HUAWEI FreeClip 2, which elevates fashion, functionality, design nous and audio excellence even further.
Audio wise, the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 has had a multifaceted upgrade. The bass has improved thanks to a dual-diaphragm driver, offering a deeper low-end sound and more elasticity and richness in the lower frequencies, giving you more sonic details in the music you love. There are also “smart” features, where the buds automatically adjust the volume to match your surroundings, from a busy commuter train to your office. Not only that, the vocal content of what you’re listening to is then enhanced so the delivery is as audio perfect as can be.
And if you are taking an important call while you are listening to a new audiobook, you don’t have to worry about levels. The earbuds contain an advanced noise cancellation system that will kick in. It also identifies ambient noise in public spaces, so you will be able to be heard clearly and plainly even if you are in the middle of a busy coffee shop or restaurant.
With their hybrid ear-cuff design, the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 will be loved by the fashion set. The buds come in a range of colour schemes (black, white and blue, with rose-gold coming soon) and the blue and white editions feature a charging case with a denim texture produced through high-precision infrared scanning of real denim fabric. They’re also dust and water resistant, so they’re ready for any change in season (weather and fashion wise!).
The fashion set will also love that Huawei has announced its partnership with French jewellery designer, Les Néréides, which has created a series of three stylish, FreeClip 2 clip-on accessories which mirror the brands iconic pieces, so you can accessorise your tech with a perfect blend of tech and fashion.
Ergonomically, the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 is made with skin-friendly silicon and a shape-memory alloy, which enables it to hold its “C” shape while remaining flexible. The effortless fit makes the buds ideal for active users who want to incorporate them into their exercise activities such as running, yoga or dancing. Weighing just 5.1 grams, the earbuds themselves are also lighter than the first generation.
And don’t worry about running out of juice, the design team is on top of that too. Fast wireless charging offers three hours of playback after only a 10-minute charge, and you get nine hours of continuous playback after a full charge (38 hours with a fully charged charging case).
The HUAWEI FreeClip 2 is the next stage of human “earvolution” and we’re here for it.
Earbuds that are as individual as you are – find out how the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 could elevate your listening

title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher
description: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. content:
Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
A ustralia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way.
Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further.
It was an unusual step for our parliament to form a joint select committee on AI. It signalled that the decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations.
As a fresh round of hearings starts this week, the committee members must confront the gulf between the politics of AI and the stark reality on the ground. Some parts of the business sector are urging us to prioritise innovation and AI adoption, which is often another way of saying: “Do a better job of selling the upside of AI.”
Whether you’re an AI optimist or a sceptic, this is a terrible idea. Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and the other titans of Silicon Valley have a golden megaphone to spruik the benefits of their technology. Australians don’t want our elected representatives to do the same thing – especially when the technology is already bringing both opportunity and harm.
This doesn’t mean being blind to the benefits of AI. On the contrary, Australia is among the highest users per capita of Anthropic’s Claude and other generative AI applications. But we must also be clear-eyed about potential risks. And, crucially, we don’t see a compelling response to our concerns from government or the AI companies themselves.
Take the impact of AI on work. Our community is asking practical questions. How will AI impact our jobs and the jobs of our children? What is the government doing to ensure the AI systems used in Australian workplaces are safe?
Our new report, Drawing the Line , lays out how AI is propelling the rise of harmful tech-enabled worker surveillance. Often workers are unaware of the extent to which they are being monitored – including through their work devices and phones, and via software such as Microsoft Teams.
Unlike some of the hypothetical (and frankly terrifying) risks that the joint select committee on AI has already covered, such as AI-enabled biological weapons and engineered pandemics , this is happening today.
Australian supermarket workers are already being pushed to meet AI-generated productivity metrics that force them to work harder and faster under the threat of punitive repercussions – putting them at risk of injury and workplace accidents.
Remote workers are already being subjected to intrusive surveillance software capable of watching everything they do on their screen – including audio recording conversations they have with their families.
Rideshare drivers are already being penalised for road conditions and customer complaints that are unrelated to their performance, which can result in their account being deactivated and days of work lost.
Workers are being quietly crushed by commonplace AI-powered surveillance tools that have crept into our workplaces and home offices. And the impact is real. Think, for example, of the young woman who reported being sexually harassed by a boss that required her to be on video at all times. Or warehouse workers driven to suicidal ideation due to relentless micromanagement by machine.
Our workplace laws don’t protect workers from unreasonable surveillance. Nor do they give employers clarity about what types of monitoring are lawful.
Unlike existential risks from AI, which are outside the Australian government’s direct control, this problem could be addressed through straightforward law reform.
We urge the government to update the Fair Work Act to require any worker monitoring be “fair and reasonable”. This builds on the government’s commitment to require all personal information covered by the Privacy Act to be handled fairly and reasonably.
Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand. This is not a hypothetical future risk – let’s address it now.

title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka

content:
AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment
A utonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal .
That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.
People expect AI to lead to fewer jobs in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed by the Pew Research Center . In wealthy countries like the US, Australia and South Korea, about seven in 10 expect job losses over the next 20 years. And across countries, concern among young people is rising. While fears focus on job numbers, the bigger change will be what jobs become.
The nature of human work will move towards judgment. Experts refer to AI as “jagged”, superhuman at certain tasks but weak at others, with no clear boundary between the two. AI rapidly improves where work can be automatically checked and examples are endless. But it’s shaky where no automated test can determine whether the answer is right. Even if AI is correct a majority of the time on a task, it often doesn’t tell you when it’s inaccurate. If you’ve used AI, you’ve probably experienced how it can be confidently wrong.
Some of these errors will solve themselves as models get better. But jaggedness is a symptom of how these models learn. I see this often as a technology leader building with these systems.
A smarter model still needs a right answer to learn from. When one gap is closed, it shows up somewhere else no one thought to check. But many business decisions don’t immediately have a clear right answer. Whether a choice is good depends on a future no one can see and data no one has. That’s where judgment comes in. So AI will keep mastering tasks that have checkable results but struggle where a person has to decide what a good outcome looks like.
As a result, a new type of work is starting to appear. Someone tests whether the output of AI is correct based on real work, not just on benchmarks. Someone sets limits on what AI is allowed to do before it runs, so the worst mistakes are avoided. Someone runs and manages several agents the way a shift manager runs a crew. Picture an airport control tower. Radar and software track flight paths, with humans judging the few that matter to avoid collisions. No one is manually watching every screen. That would never scale.
Setting AI’s limits is harder than it sounds. In a 2026 study , after an agent was told to protect a secret, it destroyed its own email server, deleting every single email. It was given a goal, without any limits on what it could do. The researchers described it as the right values paired with terrible judgment. Deciding what is off limits and what a mistake would cost takes someone who knows the work and will answer for the result.
Here is the good news for people worried about their own jobs. The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done. Catching what a confident AI left out or got wrong takes someone who knows the complete answer. That knowledge is uncheckable, unwritten and takes the form of judgment honed over years of doing the task and watching it break.
Ford recently learned the value of human expertise. In recent years, it leaned hard on automating its quality control, cutting thousands of jobs. But earlier this year, it had to rehire 350 veteran engineers to oversee the process and hunt for failure points before a part reached the factory floor. They brought the judgment of watching parts fail over years. With humans at the helm, Ford’s quality ranking then hit first among mainstream brands for the first time since 2010.
But we are making a serious mistake with the jobs we’re eliminating due to AI: the entry-level, routine ones. That routine work is how judgment gets built over time. Junior employees work under the supervision of senior experts until their experience turns into instinct. AI eliminates the friction related to learning how to do the job. But the demand for judgment did not go away. We are just destroying the path to developing it.
The real question is not whether machines will take over our work. It is whether we will have the people who can tell when the machines are wrong. Right now, we are automating the training ground where judgment is learned. If you have hard-earned expertise about anything, the next few years will only make you more valuable. And if you are just starting out, the old apprenticeship model will not hand it to you. You have to go and earn it, deliberately, on tasks the machines cannot yet judge.
Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company
