content:
Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago
A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”.
Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago.
You could say that I fell down a Wiki rabbit hole, especially when it came to the website’s early years. Almost everything important about the project came together quite quickly. Its amateurish, homegrown ethos was off-putting to a lot of writers and journalists, and that meant many questions about why it had worked had no answers. Most of the people seriously interested in Wikipedia were a handful of academics – so I decided to write a book about it.
I’m not a tech journalist. Instead, I have a background in the humanities. Wikipedia actually does, too: philosophy, and even off-piste disciplines like town planning and poetry, played a much bigger role in its inception than pure technology. Ward Cunningham, who invented the wiki in the 1990s – that’s a webpage anyone can edit, and the foundational tool of Wikipedia – thought very carefully about how the power of computers might be democratised. He drew on all sorts of oblique concepts for it, such as constructivism and the Zen concept of wabi-sabi – beauty in imperfection – and it’s remarkable how well the culture he created has persisted. Especially wabi-sabi – Wikipedia is, after all, always in a state of incompleteness.
Philosophy drew Wikipedia’s co-founders together as well. Though Wales worked in tech and finance, he corresponded with philosophers for years. And though Sanger was an academic philosopher, he spent lots of time arguing online – only “amateurs” seemed to share his sense that philosophy had life-and-death stakes. Lots of people in the dotcom boom started online encyclopedias, but Wales was the only one to hire a philosopher. In fact, the only person he hired was a philosopher. It was such an unpredictable choice, and an important clue to what made Wikipedia work: it sprang out of this digital “republic of letters”, where all sorts of people were thinking about facts and why they were important.
Because Wikipedia is so massive, writing an “exhaustive” book on it is impossible, like trying to represent a mountain with a grain of sand. Instead, I concentrated on the human history – the small, sometimes very small, number of people who really influenced what Wikipedia became. Wikipedians can be difficult, and the most ornery get a bad wrap – even the Wikimedia Foundation’s leadership has made comments about their “Dorito-stained fingers”, or tendency to stay home on a Saturday night. But by the end of the process, I was in awe of them, and I still am.
Wales and Sanger are prominent, but many other important early Wikipedians are unknown. The first woman to edit Wikipedia, Gaytha Langlois, hasn’t had much attention. She wrote about two things dear to her: Rhode Island and standard poodles – small states and big dogs. Wikipedia has always had a gender imbalance, which has proved stubborn – Sandi Toksvig is only the latest in a long line of critics trying to address it . She is part of an effort to create a more balanced alternative to Wikipedia called Mappa Mundi, which has the potential to feed back into Wikipedia as well.
I became fascinated too with a little-known contributor who had the first biographical page for a woman on Wikipedia (today, it would be called a user page). Her name was Ruth Ifcher, and she was a very intelligent grammar pedant, with a PhD, who had been forced out of the workforce with severe agoraphobia. Wikipedia came along later in her life and opened a whole new avenue for creative and meaningful work.
Proust said that neurotics alone “composed our masterpieces”, and that’s true here.
Neurodiversity is so central to Wikipedia that one former head of the Wikimedia Foundation told me the encyclopedia is a “city built by Asperger’s”. You can sense that energy in familiar topics – planes, trains and automobiles, comic books, weather, and all the rest. Often, Wikipedians are so prolific that they write too much, a phenomenon called “fancruft”. “Road geeks” (like trainspotters for roads) kept having their work about minor roads deleted, so a whole lot of them left in a huff, and started a separate online wiki encyclopedia for roads . That’s almost a microcosm of the inclusionists v deletionists debate, which is the biggest philosophical rift on Wikipedia – a rolling argument about what should be included, and what shouldn’t.
The co-founders had once believed that 100,000 articles would be “a reasonable size” for an encyclopedia, because that’s how big Britannica was. Today, Wikipedia has 68m, and Pew Research estimates that it served 1.9tn page views between 2015 and 2025. Because it is so monumental, I never expected Wikipedia to feel fragile or vulnerable – but as I was finishing the book, AI had begun to encroach on Wikipedia in an existential way by diminishing the web traffic it relies on, for instance, or by editors contributing huge volumes of poorly written AI-generated text. People ask me “is Wikipedia under threat?”, and it is, but so is everything from Hollywood to pure mathematics. I do think it will survive, but the quaking foundations made it feel urgent to say “we saw this made, and we won’t see anything like it again”.
The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia by Richard Cooke is out now through Black Inc in Australia, and WW Norton in the US. It will be released in the UK on 5 November, via Granta

title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
description: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported . And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers , in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show. Continue reading...
content:
Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work
Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools.
Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported . And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers , in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show.
At Microsoft, which rolled out AI widely internally, executive vice-president Ryan Roslansky recently publicly lamented the prevalence of AI slop in his day-to-day work. After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”.
Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance, Business Insider reported .
Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses that started off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts.
C-suite leaders say when it comes to AI, there’s a sense that “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,” said Johnny C Taylor Jr, president and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management. “If we could all rewind … we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way.”
Despite billions of dollars that firms around the globe have invested in AI over the past few years, major returns remain to be seen: 90% of executives say AI efforts have yet to translate to productivity gains at their companies, according to an Atlanta Federal Reserve working paper . And an Ernst & Young survey published last month found that 36% of senior AI executives at companies with at least $1bn in annual revenue reported an AI incident that led to issues including data loss, financial damage, brand damage or operational disruptions.
Firms from Microsoft to McKinsey are limiting usage for employees, as the flood of new tools and rapacious consumption weighs on bottom lines. Others, such as Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and Nvidia, are restricting employee use over growing concerns about the security of their organizations’ data with AI companies, Reuters reported.
Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment. Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment.
“We initially treated AI like a traditional technology rollout: deploy the tools, provide training, drive adoption,” Kathleen Hogan, Microsoft’s chief strategy and transformation officer, said in a recent blogpost about the company’s AI adoption journey. “We learned that access and usage do not equal transformation.”
AI remains a mixed bag for managers and employees alike: more than half of employees said they “aren’t getting the AI training they need”, while most managers said they were outskilled in AI by their staff, according to an Indeed survey published in July. Just 45% of managers said they felt “equipped to effectively lead AI natives”.
Many workers feel “like they’re being asked to make use of these tools without any guidance about how they best could be deployed”, said Zack Mabel, director of research at the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce. Meanwhile, managers are balancing orders to “roll this out, find productivity gains and don’t compromise on quality”, he added.
Companies are trying to address these perceived gaps by moving away from one-off webinars for broad swaths of staff and toward “sustained, role-specific training”, Taylor said.
Microsoft found that “adding agents to a broken process still leaves a broken process” and “speeding up one step just creates a longer queue at the next”, Hogan’s blogpost reads. The company found that focusing on employee training, particularly pairing up early-career engineers with more seasoned employees, boosted productivity.
One barrier to bigger AI-induced gains is the technology’s tendency to produce “plausible-looking output” with weaknesses or mistakes that are not immediately apparent, explained Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.
“This makes it more likely that an error propagates through a workflow instead of being immediately corrected,” which can cause problems to snowball, said Reif.
Meanwhile, AI’s limited ability to assess human workers is still limited, which is creating tension at some companies. At Walmart , frustration is mounting among some rank-and-file store employees over inconsistent and inaccurate AI tools, Business Insider reported.
Employees described bots that set unreasonable standards for human workers while introducing a host of their own inefficiencies and errors. AI tools plotted nonsensical routes for fulfilment workers that made it harder to fill orders quickly, pumped out useless safety alerts and set unrealistic schedules that left store employees cutting corners to keep up.
These bots assume that workers are “going to be perfect every single time”, one manager told Business Insider. “We’re not going to hold people to these impossible standards.”
Neil Elan, attorney at Stubbs Alderton & Markiles LLP, said he had observed “a growing gap” between how his corporate clients think AI is being used and how it is actually being used, which is creating issues with confidentiality, intellectual property, efficiency and employee conduct.
It’s also creating headaches for companies when workers’ use of ChatGPT spills into public view.
The night before Will Moye was set to face 3M in court over a 2020 gas explosion at a Houston manufacturing plant that killed three and damaged hundreds of homes and businesses, the attorney received a report from the company’s independent expert witness.
Skimming on his iPad, Moye noticed telltale signs of AI: strange formatting and fonts and time stamps showing that 14,500 pages were assembled in a matter of hours. Moye suspected that the author, Josh Autenrieth of Knighthawk Engineering, lacked expertise and had relied on ChatGPT, despite billing 3M $90,000 for a report arguing the company was not liable.
Autenrieth’s chat logs, which Moye requested and shared in court, show he prompted ChatGPT, “What am I looking at?” after uploading a picture of the gas detector at the heart of the case.
The jury found that 3M had failed to properly inspect the gas detection system and ordered the company to pay $61.5m to 24 homeowners. Moye said after the verdict, the jury “expressed a profound disbelief” that the company would hire an expert who would make claims “without any foundation”.
“[3M] were trying to reset the narrative,” Moye said. “And they hired an expert who’d never touched the machine.”
A 3M spokesperson said that “after independently reviewing the facts and reaching his own conclusions”, Autenrieth “used AI as a tool in preparing his report”.
Autenrieth’s legal counsel Janina Wojtkowski said ChatGPT didn’t produce his opinions or replace his “professional judgment” but assisted in formatting, structuring and drafting amid “severe deadline constraints”.
As companies and workers muddle through the unknowns of early AI adoption, costs are still coming into focus, while broad productivity gains remain elusive.
In a study published in May , University of Pittsburgh researchers concluded that productivity didn’t rise after companies invested in AI and cut staff . Although executives have been overwhelmingly optimistic about AI’s potential impacts for years, “management optimism does not effectively translate into … better performance,” the paper states.
More than 112,000 job cut announcements in the US so far in 2026 have mentioned AI, making it a top reason for layoffs, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
Earlier this year, Meta paused its practice of tracking employees’ computer activity to train its AI, according to Reuters . Meta also recently told employees that their adoption and usage of AI tools would no longer be part of performance reviews, the Information reported.
Meta did not respond to a request for comment.
Mark Ma, University of Pittsburgh professor and researcher on the AI layoff study, said leaders are focused on short-term performance, “which is why they tried to rush ahead by investing in AI and laying off workers”.
But companies’ share prices tend to dip after they announce AI-related layoffs, he noted, suggesting that “the stock market also does not think these will work out.”
“A lot of these mistakes could have been avoided,” Ma said. “Now I feel some managers have learned their lesson.”

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max review: Apple’s biggest, heaviest and longest-lasting superphone
description: A giant screen, big battery, rapid chip and top cameras push the great iPhone 18 Pro to the max with a price tag to match Apple’s largest Pro iPhone gets its biggest battery upgrade yet to make it a true two-day phone with new Siri AI and a variable aperture camera. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the supersized sibling of the regular 18 Pro and, though it is no longer Apple’s most expensive phone thanks to the £2,000 iPhone Duo , it has a similarly large price tag to match costing from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299). Screen: 6.9in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi) Processor: Apple A20 Pro RAM: 12GB Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: iOS 27 Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins) Dimensions: 163.4 x 78 x 8.75mm Weight: 249g Continue reading...
content:
A giant screen, big battery, rapid chip and top cameras push the great iPhone 18 Pro to the max with a price tag to match
Apple’s largest Pro iPhone gets its biggest battery upgrade yet to make it a true two-day phone with new Siri AI and a variable aperture camera.
The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the supersized sibling of the regular 18 Pro and, though it is no longer Apple’s most expensive phone thanks to the £2,000 iPhone Duo , it has a similarly large price tag to match costing from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).
The 18 Pro Max follows the familiar formula of its Pro Max predecessors : take everything that’s great about the 18 Pro and supersize the screen and the battery. That means it has a first-class camera, the fastest performance and very long software support.
But it also means the 18 Pro Max is hard to use with one hand and pretty big to fit in a pocket. It weighs 249g, which is really heavy for even a very large smartphone, 23g more than its nearest rival , 38g more than its smaller sibling and heavier still than folding phones . It made my hand hurt after 10 days of use and is a two-handed phone needing some sort of handle or strap.
The 6.9in screen is a joy to behold. Super bright, crisp, smooth and with a very effective anti-glare coating it’s great for films, TV or games, and offers a similar level of real estate for video to most folding phones. It also has the new, smaller camera cut out and bigger dynamic island of the regular 18 Pro.
Screen: 6.9in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)
Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing
Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS
Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)
The 18 Pro Max has the same new A20 Pro chip as the 18 Pro , which is one of the fastest chips you can get in a phone, plus a resigned cooling system that helps maintain peak performance during long gaming sessions.
It has the longest battery of any iPhone, lasting almost three days of light usage between charges, actively using the screen for seven hours for apps, browsing, messaging and photos. That is about four hours longer than its predecessor and almost a day longer than the 18 Pro. Even with heavy use, the 18 Pro Max still managed to end the day with about 50% left in the tank, meaning most people will have to charge it only every second or third day.
The 18 Pro Max runs the same iOS 27 as smartphones from the iPhone 11 onwards. The new software speeds up app launches and other parts of the system, refines the Liquid Glass redesign from last year and revamps Apple’s AI tools.
The new Siri AI chatbot is a significant step in the right direction, able to better understand you and perform tasks. It has its own app to review previous conversations and can see what is on your screen or through the camera. It can also suggest data from your various Apple apps, similar to Google’s proactive tools on the Pixels . But it relies on you using messages and mail, rather than third-party apps such as the WhatsApp or Gmail apps.
The battery will last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity, and it can be replaced for £119 . Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £389 . The specialists iFixit awarded the phone seven out of 10 for repairability.
It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The 18 Pro Max has the same camera system as its smaller sibling , which includes an 18 megapixel centre stage selfie camera in the screen and three 48MP cameras on the back.
The three rear cameras are some of the best on a phone, including a 4x/8x optical zoom and 0.5x ultra wide.
The big addition for the 18 Pro Max is a variable aperture on the main camera, allowing it to open wider than other iPhones for better low light performance or to narrow to preserve depth of field. But it also allows additional creative photography possibilities, including shooting starbursts.
The 18 Pro Max also has new AI-powered focus tracking, improved Photographic Styles for greater customisation, Apple’s new digital negative feature and automatic cinematic mode for video.
The iPhone 18 Pro Max costs from £1,299 (€1,599/ $1,299 / A$2,299 ).
For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899 , the iPhone Air £1,099 and the iPhone 18 Pro £1,199 ; the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,279 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra £1,359 .
The iPhone 18 Pro Max is Apple’s biggest, longest-lasting and most expensive slab phone for 2026.
It takes what is great about the regular 18 Pro and supersizes the screen and battery, giving it a run time of up to three days, which is a good half day more than its smaller sibling. That places it shoulder to shoulder with some of the longest-lasting phones available on any platform.
But similar to superphones from Google and Samsung , the 18 Pro Max is too big to use one-handed and tricky to pocket. It is also too heavy and made my hand hurt without using a Popsocket or a similar handle attached to it.
Otherwise, it is a fairly iterative upgrade on the 17 Pro Max, with the same design and feel. The screen is still one of the very best on a phone, and the improved dynamic island is a useful upgrade. The A20 Pro chip is seriously quick, the cameras are some of the best you can get on a phone and the variable aperture on the main camera opens up some new creative opportunities, even if its impact on image quality is fairly minor.
Pros: fabulous 6.9in screen, better dynamic island, very long battery life, great cameras with variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.
Cons: very expensive, very heavy, hard to use one-handed, small upgrade on last year, AI tools still lag top competitors.

title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differences
description: Longer battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s model Apple’s smaller Pro iPhone gets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera. The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongside Apple’s first folding phone , the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced. Screen: 6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi) Processor: Apple A20 Pro RAM: 12GB Storage: 256GB, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: iOS 27 Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins) Dimensions: 150 x 71.9 x 8.75mm Weight: 211g Continue reading...
content:
Longer battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s model
Apple’s smaller Pro iPhone gets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera.
The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongside Apple’s first folding phone , the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced.
It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous models courtesy of RAMageddon .
Having fully revamped the design of the body for the iPhone 17 Pro , the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades.
Apple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models.
Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too.
Screen: 6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)
Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing
Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS
Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)
The 18 Pro has Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which is about 27% faster than the A19 Pro in last year’s model, with about 45% faster graphics performance. Since the A19 Pro was no slouch, that’s quite the leap and puts it miles ahead of the competition, ready to handle anything.
The phone has a redesigned cooling system for longer peak performance, too, which is especially useful for running games on top settings.
The battery lasts a solid six hours longer than the iPhone 17 Pro, managing to stretch to about two days between charges with more than six hours of active screen use across apps, browsing, messaging and photos. Even with the heaviest of use while out and about, the 18 Pro managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. Most people will only need to charge it every other day.
The 18 Pro ships running iOS 27 , which was released for the rest of the iPhone line on 14 September. It refines the relatively controversial Liquid Glass redesign from last year and speeds up the system, including app launches. But the big new addition is Apple’s revamped Siri, backed by Google’s AI technologies.
Siri AI, as the new system is called , is significantly more capable of understanding and answering questions than previous iterations. It is a chatbot like most other AI assistants, but it is less chatty and sycophantic than others, being more likely to just get the job done. As well as a choice of voices, there are sliders to control how fast it talks and how expressive its responses are. It has its own app where you can review previous interactions, but it is accessible anywhere on the phone via the side button, is built into Spotlight search and can see what’s on your screen, including when using the camera.
It can also offer suggestions, such as adding an event to your calendar from the messages or mail apps, and attempts to display relevant information from your emails in the phone app when you call a business. But Siri can only do so if you use Apple’s apps, so if you use WhatsApp for texting and Gmail for your email, none of it works.
The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £119 . Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £349 . The specialists iFixit awarded the phone a seven out of 10 for repairability.
It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The 18 Pro has a similar camera system to last year’s 17 Pro with one big addition, a variable aperture for the main camera.
That means it has a very good 18MP centre stage selfie camera on the front and three 48MP cameras on the rear: main, 0.5x ultrawide and 4x telephoto.
The ultrawide is one of the best on a phone, handy for landscapes and group shots. The 4x telephoto is very good too, full of detail and manages lower light settings well. It shoots excellent photos with a crop zoom to reach 8x before digital zoom is required, which is a little behind rivals with 5x/10x telephoto zooms.
The variable aperture on the main camera can be left on automatic or controlled manually. It allows the camera to open wider than previous models for better low light performance, speeding up night mode shots and reducing unwanted motion blur.
But it also enables a number of creative uses, such as making starbursts by narrowing the aperture when shooting lights, which is very fun, or controlling the depth of field in your photo. However, because the iPhone’s camera is tiny compared with an APS-C or full-frame camera, the difference in depth of field – where the foreground and background of the image are either in focus or blown out for a nice bokeh effect – is pretty minor. When shooting something up close, manually closing the aperture to f / 4.0 can bring things in the foreground or background into focus, but otherwise the difference for most shots is small.
The 18 Pro’s camera has a number of other useful upgrades. My favourite is AI-powered focus tracking that keeps a subject in focus as it moves about or into and out of the frame, which has been one of the best features of a Pixel camera for years and is extremely handy for fast-moving children or pets.
Apple has also added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles feature to customise how the camera shoots photos beyond what was introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro , including film simulation. Finally, the new Apple Reference Image feature can sign an image for authenticity, on a per pixel level directly on the sensor, to help later prove a shot is not AI-generated, similar to a digital negative.
The camera shoots some of the very best video on a phone, too. New for this year is the ability to convert a regular video to a cinematic one after the fact , a bit like the excellent automatic portrait mode for photos.
The iPhone 18 Pro costs from £1,199 (€1,449/ $1,199 / A$2,099 ).
For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899 , the iPhone Air costs £1,099 , the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs £1,299 , the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,359 .
The iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade on an already great device from last year. Inside, it has some quite big changes, but their impact is fairly minor on the whole experience.
The new A20 Pro chip is super fast, but you can’t really notice the difference day to day, as previous iPhone chips have already been very quick. The extended battery life is great, but most people will still have to charge it every other day. The smaller camera cutout in the dynamic island now shows three continuing activities instead of two. Even the variable aperture in the main camera makes only a small difference to image quality unless you’re really trying to get creative.
The screen is fantastic and big enough. The aluminium body feels great to hold. The cameras are some of the best on a phone and even Siri is better now.
All of these things add up. The 18 Pro is without doubt the best iPhone ever made and at this size is one of the very best smaller phones available. It’s just not a transformative change unless you’re upgrading from a much older model and it now costs even more thanks to RAMageddon.
Pros: relatively compact, great screen, better dynamic island, longer battery life, great cameras, variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.
Cons: small upgrade on last year, expensive, heavier than previous model, AI tools still lag behind top competitors.

title: Pixel 11 Pro Fold review: the foldable with the best triple camera
description: Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed Google’s latest folding phone sticks with its tried and tested design of a traditional phone shape when closed and almost square when open, in the face of new competition from Apple’s squat iPhone fold . The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as the pressure of RAMageddon continues to push up prices. Continue reading...
content:
Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed
G oogle’s latest folding phone sticks with its tried and tested design of a traditional phone shape when closed and almost square when open, in the face of new competition from Apple’s squat iPhone fold .
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as the pressure of RAMageddon continues to push up prices.
The 11 Pro Fold looks identical to previous models, but it is 19g lighter and fractionally slimmer in all directions with a slightly larger outside screen. Unlike Samsung’s slender Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra or squat models such as Apple’s iPhone Duo or the Galaxy Z Fold 8 , the Pixel has the same ratio screen as Google’s slab phones and so handles precisely like them when shut with a bright and smooth 6.5in display.
Opened up, the internal screen is essentially square, which allows you to run two full-size apps side by side but is less ideal for video. The display is very bright, crisp and smooth, but the crease where it folds is more visible and detectable with your fingers than the best rivals. Like all foldable phones the screen is also delicate compared with standard hardened glass phones.
The back of the phone hides the excellent Qi2 magnetic charging and accessory support from last year , while Google’s gimmicky HiLight notification LED, as seen on the other Pro Pixels , replaces the camera’s flash.
Outside screen: 6.5in FHD+ 120Hz OLED (399ppi)
Camera: 48MP wide, 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP 5x telephoto; two 10MP selfie cameras
Connectivity: 5G, eSim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, Thread, GNSS
Water resistance: IP68 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)
Dimensions unfolded: 155.2 x 150.4 x 5mm
The 11 Pro Fold has the same Tensor G6 chip from the other Pixel 11 models with 16GB of memory, which works very well for all kinds of multitasking, remaining snappy and responsive with multiple apps on screen. It handles light gaming, but can’t match rivals for raw performance.
The battery life is a little shorter than last year’s model and rivals, lasting about 36 hours between charges when used on a mix of 5G and wifi with the screens in active use for about 2.5 hours each for browsing, messaging, apps and photos. Most will have to charge it nightly, but even on the heaviest of use days the Pixel managed to end the day without requiring a top-up.
The Fold runs the latest version of Android 17 with all of Google’s AI tools, including Gemini’s proactive system, the new supercharged voice dictation feature and six months of Google AI Pro subscription .
Many of Google’s more creative AI tools, including the Omni video creation tool, Circle to Search and Gemini’s information cards benefit from the larger internal screen. Google has made a number of modifications to Android to better fit the folding form, including a floating taskbar and a split-screen mode that can resize apps beyond the bounds of the physical display introduced last year .
The bubbles system , which was primarily used for messaging apps, has been revamped to allow as many as five apps of any kind to be opened as floating windows on top of a single or split-screen apps and minimised to a little taskbar. But it isn’t as flexible as Samsung’s true desktop-like floating window system that can be resized and placed anywhere on the screen.
The 11 Pro Fold will be supported until August 2033 with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest supported devices available.
The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google and third-party shops, and self-repair with manuals and parts is due to be available .
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold contains 24% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free.
The Pixel Fold has some of the best cameras on a foldable phone, including three on the back and two very good selfie cameras, one in each screen.
The rear cameras include a new 48MP main camera with a larger sensor, matching that in the regular Pixel 11 , which captures better detail and has significantly better lowlight performance than its predecessor. The 10.5MP ultrawide camera is the same as last year and is still as solid this year. The 10.8MP 5x telephoto is also the same and shoots good photos that meaningfully reduce the distance to objects. It has a solid digital zoom that stretches up to 30x magnification, but not the generative AI zoom of the Pixel 11 Pro .
The Fold also has the new software features from the other Pixel 11 phones, including Camera Looks, which allows you to customise the processing of your photos for different styles. Magic Capture shoots video and photos automatically with one button, while the Creator suite helps you storyboard, trim and produce video content for social media.
The camera also has tricks to make use of the folding form, including modes to shoot when propped up and the excellent Made You Look feature that displays an animated character that reacts to your kid’s smiling to help take better photos.
Overall, the 11 Pro Fold has an excellent set of cameras that don’t feel a significant downgrade on top regular smartphones.
The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799 (€1,999/ $1,899 / A$2,799 ).
For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879 , Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079 , the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279 , the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899 , the iPhone Duo costs £1,999 and the Honor Magic V6 costs £1,499.99 .
The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a fairly minor hardware update for Google’s folding phone line, which makes it slightly lighter, smaller, brighter and faster, while keeping its overall look and feel the same.
It has great AI tools, slick software and some of the very best cameras. The inside screen is super bright and crisp, but the crease down the middle is more noticeable than rivals, the battery life is a bit short and it is thick and heavy compared to the best from rival Samsung .
As with all foldables the inside screen can be permanently marked by a fingernail if you press hard enough, so you must still be careful with it compared with a standard Pixel.
But if you want a folding phone to be exactly the same as a regular one when closed, the Pixel Fold is the one to get.
Pros: just like a regular Pixel when closed, good tablet screen, dust and water resistant, Qi2 magnetic accessory and charging, good performance, great cameras with 5x zoom, great software packed with cutting-edge AI, six months of Google AI Pro included, seven years of software updates.
Cons: very expensive, more fragile and costlier to repair than a regular Pixel, thick and heavy, cameras can’t match regular Pixel 11 Pro, battery life could be better.

title: Pixel 11 Pro review: Google’s best pocket camera goes customisable
description: Solid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer camera Google’s latest Pro phone is out to prove it has the best camera on a smartphone while embracing customisation, allowing you to change the look and feel of your photos far beyond simple filters even if that means making them technically worse. The Pixel 11 Pro packs the best of Google’s hardware and software into a still-pocketable and easy to handle frame, instantly making it a contender for best smaller phone of the year. Screen: 6.3in 120Hz QHD+ OLED (495ppi) Processor: Google Tensor G6 RAM: 12 or 16GB Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: Android 17 Camera: 50MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 5x tele; 42MP selfie Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 7, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes) Dimensions: 152.7 x 71.9 x 8.4mm Weight: 204g Continue reading...
content:
Solid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer camera
G oogle’s latest Pro phone is out to prove it has the best camera on a smartphone while embracing customisation, allowing you to change the look and feel of your photos far beyond simple filters even if that means making them technically worse.
The Pixel 11 Pro packs the best of Google’s hardware and software into a still-pocketable and easy to handle frame, instantly making it a contender for best smaller phone of the year.
Being smaller doesn’t make it cheap. The 11 Pro sits above the regular £879 Pixel 11 and costs from £1,079 (€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) – £80 (€100/$100/A$150) more than last year, with double the storage but less memory owing to the cost of RAMageddon .
Little has changed on the outside for the Pro Pixels in several years . The new model is 0.1mm smaller in all directions and 3g lighter but has the same size 6.3in OLED screen, same polished aluminium and glass body and a large camera bar sticking out the back. It is an attractive design that has aged well.
The temperature sensor from previous Pixel Pro generations , which always felt like a gimmick, has been replaced by a coloured HiLight LED that works as a camera flash and notification light. The LED glows when you talk to Gemini or pulses with one of five colours when your favourite contact calls. But it doesn’t work for notifications of any other kind, so is a wasted opportunity.
The 11 Pro has the same Tensor G6 chip as the regular Pixel 11 and has 12 or 16GB of RAM depending on the storage version. It can’t match the raw performance of the top Qualcomm or Apple chips for games but is snappy in day-to-day tasks.
Battery life is just shy of two days with the screen actively used for about seven hours across a mix of wifi and 5G for browsing, messaging apps and photos. This is a bit behind the regular Pixel 11 but should see out even the heaviest of use days with some left in the tank. Most people will need to charge the 11 Pro every other day for general use.
Camera: 50MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 5x tele; 42MP selfie
Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 7, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread and GNSS
Water resistance: IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes)
The 11 Pro runs the same Google version of Android 17 as the regular Pixel 11 and will be supported until August 2033 with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest-lasting devices available.
It’s a polished experience with smooth animations, nice touches of haptic feedback across the system and enough customisation to make it yours. But as with other Pixel devices, the phone is a showcase for Google’s most advanced AI tools that are littered throughout the software.
The 11 Pro comes with six months of Google AI Pro subscription , which gives you access to Gemini Omni to generate surprisingly good eight-second videos, higher AI usage limits, 5TB of cloud storage and Google Health Premium.
But the most interesting tools are the local AI ones, including the new Rambler voice dictation feature in Gboard, which produces fully formed succinct sentences and paragraphs from your ramblings, removing unnecessary pauses, ums, ers and deviations. Gemini’s proactive assistance has also improved with more time-saving suggestions, although it only works in certain apps and not WhatsApp, Signal or other third-party apps.
The reason you buy a Pixel Pro is for the camera. The 11 Pro has a very good 42-megapixel selfie camera on the front and a similar winning triple camera system on the rear from last year: a 50MP wide, 48MP ultra wide and a 48MP 5x telephoto camera.
All three cameras capture really fantastic photos across a range of lighting conditions with very little effort. The wide and telephoto cameras now capture more light and slightly better detail, but the biggest boost is the new Instant Night Sight. It dramatically speeds up low-light photos by up to 4.5 times, which makes taking great shots in very dark scenes a lot easier.
The 5x telephoto camera manages a very good 10x crop zoom before stretching up to 120x magnification, first with a very good traditional digital zoom to 30x then using local generative AI to go beyond. The camera keeps the regular digital zoom image and the one processed by AI to add back lost detail, which can be remarkable or filled with artefacts.
Magic Capture takes video and photos automatically with just one button for point-and-shoot recording, which works well for events such as a birthday party.
But Camera Looks is the most interesting feature for getting creative with photography. It allows you to modify how the camera processes your photos, starting with subtle changes such as darker shadows and ranging to more distinctive looks such as “minimal”, which reduces the computational photography processing for a more raw photo. Other options include “digi”, which replicates the look of old digital cameras that have become popular , and “velvet”, which mimics the look of some film cameras. Each look can be further customised, allowing great creative licence.
The Pixel shoots great video with lots of stabilisation and processing tools including the new “ Creator Suite ”, which captures clips straight into a folder for storyboarding and trimming, with a teleprompter, framing for social media and speed enhancement.
The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repair with manuals and parts available .
The Pixel 11 Pro contains 31% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free.
The Google Pixel 11 Pro costs from £1,079 (€1,199/ $1,099 / A$1,849 ) in a choice of four colours.
For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879 , Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279 , Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799 , the Pixel 10a costs £499 , the Samsung Galaxy S26 costs £879 , the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,279 and the Apple iPhone 17 Pro costs £1,099 .
The Pixel 11 Pro is a refinement of multiple generations of Google’s Pro phones rather than an outright revolution, but that’s no bad thing.
It is one of the very best smaller phones, packing all the top-end hardware, cameras and AI features of Google’s most biggest and expensive model into a slightly cheaper and more pocketable form. You buy a Pro Pixel for the camera, which doesn’t disappoint with arguably the best photography on a phone at the moment.
The ability to customise the processing of your photos goes far beyond rivals for interesting creative potential. The dramatically faster Night Sight is also a significant improvement.
Gemini’s proactive tools show great potential but depend on using the right apps. The supercharged Rambler voice dictation system is fantastic, and there are many other little AI tools that are useful from time to time.
With just shy of two days battery life, a decent chip and quality software, the Pixel 11 Pro is a great pocketable phone. It just isn’t a massive upgrade on the already excellent Pixel 11 or recent Pixel Pro models.
Pros: great camera with extended zoom and extensive customisation, seven years of software updates, excellent screen, impressive dictation and local AI features, Qi2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, good battery life, great size, fast fingerprint and face recognition, six months of Google AI Pro included.
Cons: quite expensive, less memory on cheapest model than before, face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance and battery life short of best-in-class, no physical sim card slot in the US, not a massive upgrade.

title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
description: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out. For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/ $899 / A$2,299 ) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks. Continue reading...
content:
Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android
G oogle’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out.
For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/ $899 / A$2,299 ) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks.
While Google does not make these machines directly, it has set strict hardware quality standards that the laptops must reach. That includes backlit keyboards, haptic trackpads, fingerprint readers, crisp touchscreens, decent speakers and modern fast chips with at least 16GB of RAM.
It is a list of specs you should expect with a premium Windows PC, but those start at a much higher price, primarily thanks to RAMageddon .
As such, the Acer Googlebook 14 and the Asus Googlebook 14 I’ve been testing have excellent hardware with satisfying keyboards, great trackpads and quality screens.
The Acer is a convertible that allows the screen to fold over the back of the device turning into a tablet of sorts. It is 1.14kg and 13.9mm thick, with a glossy 14in 3K OLED screen and a smooth aluminium-magnesium body, costing £999.99 .
The Asus is a traditional laptop with a matt 14in 3K OLED screen and a magnesium-alloy body that weighs just 0.99kg and is 11mm thick, costing £1,199.99 .
Top quality hardware aside, anyone familiar with a Chromebook would be forgiven for thinking it was ChromeOS running on these machines. It has the familiar taskbar at the bottom, Chrome-based web apps and access to Android apps.
But the software is essentially Android underneath, which means getting it up and running is just like setting up an Android phone: scan the QR code with your phone, enter a passcode and transfer your apps and accounts. It is all done and dusted in about four minutes, which is faster than setting up a modern Windows 11 machine even if you know all the shortcuts.
Access to the full gamut of Android apps is the Googlebook’s biggest strength and its greatest weakness. Practically any app you have on your phone can be installed and run on the laptop. But almost all those phone apps are just that, mobile versions, with most not even aware that they are not installed on a phone.
Those that have at least some tailoring to the laptop form come in a few different types, categorised by Google broadly under “compatible with desktop”, which means they should support mouse and keyboard controls; “optimised for desktop”, which means they should scale properly to the laptop’s display; and “made for desktop”, which are a handful of Android apps redesigned with the laptop in mind.
Only the last category really seems to make any difference to the quality of the app, and even then most of them are still not of the same calibre as their equivalents found on Windows or macOS.
Even Google’s apps are a mixed bag. Google Calendar can only show one account at any one time, so you can’t see your personal, work and shared calendars on one screen like you can on Android.
Google Docs starts as its own app, but when you actually open a document it just becomes another Chrome window hidden behind the Chrome logo on the task bar, not the Docs logo.
The Files app shows your Google Drive files, but you can’t pin locations to the side bar to quickly access your commonly used folders, making it a time-consuming dig through endless folders to find things each time.
Even the Chrome browser is not quite up to par with its Windows or macOS counterpart, lacking features such as split-screen tabs, the auto-hiding vertical tab bar or the ability to have multiple profiles, such as a personal and work account.
Google has an app-gap problem and one that will only be solved if developers are convinced Googlebook OS is going to take off and be worth spending time and money making better apps for.
The other big selling point is deep integration with your Android phone. Google calls this “better together”, which is a collection of features that mirror capabilities of iPhones with Macs or Microsoft’s Link to Windows.
Some of the features are like magic. You can search the files on your phone straight from the Files app on the laptop without plugging it in, see your notifications from your phone, continue tasks on your laptop from your phone and even use apps cast from your phone.
As useful as these features sound, many are not up to scratch. Streaming apps from your phone is so slow that I feel as though I can type entire sentences before they appear on screen in chat apps, and it is restricted to one app at a time. If you click on a synced notification from your phone, it will open in a cast app, even if you have the full app installed on your Googlebook. Even viewing files on your phone from the laptop is irritatingly slow.
The only apps I’ve reliably managed to get to appear with the ability to continue from where I was are Google Docs and Chrome on the phone.
It also took me two hours of troubleshooting to get an up-to-date Google Pixel 11 Pro to actually connect with the Googlebooks, despite using the phone to set them up in the first place.
The other big selling point for Google is its Gemini integration into Googlebook OS. The Gemini app is just like it is on macOS and Windows . But it is the Magic Pointer feature, which appears when you wiggle the mouse to click or highlight something on your screen to send it to Gemini, that is the most novel.
You can use it to get Gemini to summarise text, explain something, search for things or generally chat. But I often hit a road block, such as Gemini refusing to generate images or saying it cannot add a date into my calendar in the mode Magic Cursor opens, which oddly isn’t within the desktop Gemini app. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, and it is simply not joined up.
Magic Cue has been imported from Google’s Pixel phones , which is meant to pop up with helpful information such as calendar availability or a location in maps when you highlight a date or a place in a chat or email. But unlike on a Pixel phone, I have yet to get it to successfully activate in two weeks of testing.
Google’s super-charged voice dictation system called Rambler , also from the recent Pixels, does at least work as described. Press the dictation key and just speak naturally. Rambler will condense your speech into concise sentences removing filler words and errors.
Googlebooks are full of excellent ideas about how a modern laptop should work. The hardware of the Acer and Asus machines I’ve tested is top notch, but the software just isn’t ready for prime time.
When it works it’s great, but it is filled with limitations that might be acceptable on a super-cheap laptop but never on a £1,000 premium machine.
Chrome is not as good as it is on a Mac or Windows PC. Google’s various apps are generally better on an Android phone and the third-party app ecosystem is a mess of poorly optimised mobile apps. Even the best desktop-optimised Android apps pale by comparison to their counterparts on Windows or macOS.
The Android phone-linking system should be the killer feature, but it is partly broken or simply not up to scratch. Even the Gemini integration is flakey.
Most of the Google-specific issues and software bugs are eminently fixable. But the app gap will take serious time, effort and money to convince third-party developers to fix.
Unless you want to spend at least £1,000 to be a beta tester, your money is better spent elsewhere for now.

title: Apple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yet
description: Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips Apple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price. The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors . Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, H2 chip Battery life: four or five hours with ANC (22 hours with case) Water resistance: IP57 (up to 1 metre for 30 minutes ) Earbud dimensions: 30.2 x 18.3 x 18.1mm Earbud weight: 4.3g each Charging case dimensions: 46.2 x 50.1 x 21.2mm Charging case weight: 32.3g/34.7g Case charging: USB-C or wireless (Qi or Watch) Continue reading...
content:
Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips
Apple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price.
The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors .
The earbuds and case are almost indistinguishable from the AirPods 4, which makes the case very small and easy to pocket, fitting in the watch pocket of a pair of jeans.
The buds are some of the most comfortable open-fit designs available and stayed put when commuting, running for the train and generally going about the day. But for those that didn’t get on with the previous design of the AirPods, these are unlikely to change that, and they have no stability wings or similar to keep them in place for vigorous exercise.
The stalk has a pressure-sensitive panel you squeeze once, twice or thrice for playback controls. A squeeze and hold changes the noise cancelling mode or activates Siri. On the more expensive versions with a wireless charging case, the panel is also touch-sensitive for swipe volume controls – the same system used in the AirPods Pro to great effect.
Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, H2 chip
Battery life: four or five hours with ANC (22 hours with case)
Water resistance: IP57 (up to 1 metre for 30 minutes )
Charging case dimensions: 46.2 x 50.1 x 21.2mm
Case charging: USB-C or wireless (Qi or Watch)
The cheapest AirPods 5 have up to four hours playback with noise cancelling and a case that can charge them four times for a total of 20 hours playback.
The AirPods 5 with wireless charging case have longer battery life lasting slightly more than five hours of playback with noise cancelling with a total of 22 hours playback using charges in the case. That’s long enough for a week of commuting, but far behind the best in the business. A compromise for the design and super-compact case.
The new AirPods have noticeably improved noise cancelling and sound. They produce fairly detailed sound with good separation of tones and can handle complex and overlapping tracks very well. But it is the additional bass that helps them produce a fuller, more rounded sound that wipes the floor with most other open-fit rivals and compares well to many decent earbuds with silicone tips. They may not satisfy audiophiles but they are a great listen.
The noise cancelling is equally effective, managing to quiet busy roads, the drone of engines or fans, and dampen background chatter. It struggles with higher tones, such as loud keyboard clicks or the screeches from train wheels, but does as good a job as many similarly-priced noise cancelling earbuds with silicone tips and is miles ahead of the open-fit competition.
They suffer a little from wind noise and can’t rival the sound dampening of the best earbuds with tips from Sony, Bose or the AirPods Pro 3 , but still do a solid job.
The transparency mode is first class, sounding almost exactly like not wearing them at all, which is great for awareness on the street. Call quality is equally good coming through loud and clear with only a hint of sudden background noise when passing something particularly loud.
The AirPods 5 support Apple’s various smart features with an iPhone, such as direct access to the new Siri, live translation, automatic volume adjustment, spatial audio, audio sharing, the ability to pause music when falling asleep and optimised battery charging to increase its longevity.
Batteries in earbuds typically maintain at least 80% of their original capacity for 500 charge cycles. Apple offers a battery service for £49 per earbud or case and replacements cost from £69 . The specialists iFixit awarded the earbuds two out of 10 for repairability. The AirPods 5 are made with 40% recycled material, which the company breaks down in its environmental impact report . The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The AirPods 5 cost £119 (€149/ $129 / A$219 ) or £139 (€169/$149/A$249) with a wireless charging case and touch controls.
For comparison, the AirPods Pro 3 cost £219 , the AirPods Max 2 cost £499 , the Google Pixel Buds 2a cost £129 and the Shokz OpenFit Air 2 cost £129 .
The AirPods 5 take the comfortable open-fit design of their predecessors and upgrade the sound and noise cancelling to rival many plugged-in earbuds with silicone tips, which is quite a feat.
They provide a good amount of bass for a full, detailed sound that’s a great general listen and a step above most open-fit rivals. The noise cancelling is capable of dampening unwanted sound to tolerable levels, comparing well with better than average silicone-equipped earbuds. It can’t match the best plugged-in earbuds, but it is certainly good enough. Apple’s transparency mode and call quality are top-notch, and it’s hard to fault the earbuds for daily use with a compact design that’s easy to pocket.
The battery life is a little short, and while they work with any Bluetooth device, I wouldn’t recommend them to people who don’t have at least one iPhone, iPad or Mac.
There are few great open-fit earbuds, but if you didn’t get on with other AirPods, these won’t tip the balance. The extra money for swipe volume controls and longer battery life is worth it, if you’re considering them.
The fifth-generation earbuds are marginally more repairable than their predecessors, which opens up the possibility of replacing the batteries down the line, but otherwise they are just as disposable as most other earbuds .
Pros: comfortable open fit, good sound and noise cancelling, great case, great playback and volume controls, great connectivity, special features with Apple devices including spatial audio, great call quality.
Cons: battery life could be better, little passive noise isolation, lack of features when connected to non-Apple devices, no Bluetooth multipoint or higher quality audio format support, difficult to repair.

title: Mac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more pricey
description: Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse Apple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere. The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has been hit by RAMageddon , driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor. Continue reading...
content:
Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse
Apple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere.
The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has been hit by RAMageddon , driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor.
Apple introduced the Mac mini’s dainty form with 2024’s M4 model, which remains the same for the new M6 version. A lot has changed since the M2 Mac mini , which was pretty compact. The current mini measures just 12.7cm square and 5cm thick, with rounded corners and a solid aluminium body. It’s happy to sit on a desk, but is small and light enough to mount behind a monitor to turn any screen into a DIY iMac .
The machine is fairly minimalist. A small LED on the front shows you when it’s on. The back has three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports, a 2.5Gb ethernet socket, an HDMI 2.1 port, and a figure-eight power cable. It lacks any USB-A ports, but adapters are readily available for legacy devices not yet converted to USB-C, such as flash drives or printers.
It has basic speakers built in, which are good enough for macOS’s notification sounds.
The mini runs the latest macOS 27 Golden Gate , which brings welcome refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design that was introduced last year. But the big update is a relaunch of Apple’s Siri assistant and AI tools. Siri AI, as it is now known, is vastly superior at understanding and performing tasks, such as finding information on your Mac or the web, and has a dedicated app to see previous interactions. It can read what’s on your screen, so you can ask it to track parcels from just a code in your email or find an object from an image with the CMD+Shift+Space keyboard shortcut.
Siri is integrated into Spotlight search, which is handy but sometimes results in it trying to search the web instead of launching an app or a file on your Mac if you mistype, which can be frustrating.
Apple Intelligence is smarter too. Writing, proofing and summarising tools are built in and accessible from most apps, along with a collection of other features. The most surprisingly useful tool I found was file and folder naming suggestions, which made matching long file-naming schemes a doddle. Boring but very useful.
Ports back: 3x Thunderbolt/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, 2.5Gb Ethernet
Ports front: 2x USB-C (USB3), headphones
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread
The Mac mini is offered with the newest Apple Silicon chip, the M6 (as tested) or with an M5 Pro, which has greater performance in multicore or graphics applications.
For most people the M6 is more than enough, with the fastest single core performance of any of Apple’s chips by about 8.5% in testing. That means it absolutely flies along with apps launching near instantly and tasks just flying by. Compared with the previous generation M4 Mac mini, the new machine is about 25% faster in single core tasks, 50% faster in multicore tasks with graphics performance about 75% faster. That makes it a giant leap over older machines coming to the end of their useful lives.
The machine is also power efficient and runs silently unless pushed to the limit, and even then is very quiet.
The Mac mini is made with 50% recycled materials. Apple breaks down the computer’s environmental impact in its report . Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The Mac mini M6 costs from £899 (€1,049/ $899 / A$1,449 ) with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage.
For comparison, the A18 Pro MacBook Neo costs from £699 , the M5 MacBook Air starts at £1,299 , the M4 iMac starts at £1,499 and the Mac Studio costs from £2,499 .
The Mac mini is a fantastic general computer squeezed into a tiny box that fits just about anywhere. The new M6 chip has buckets of power and performance for practically anything. If you know you need more graphics performance the M5 Pro chip is also available, but at a significant cost.
The port selection is very good for a machine of this size, only lacking traditional USB-A ports of those commonly needed. With three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports it’s easy to add a dock or hub if you really need more connectivity.
The only downside is the RAMageddon-linked price hike that makes the Mac mini M6 slightly less of an instant recommendation than its predecessor. At £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449), it is still a lot of Mac for the money, just not the total bargain the M4 version used to be.
Pros: very fast M6 chip, quiet and cool running, plenty of ports, headphones socket, 2.5GbE, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: price hike, no expandable/replaceable storage or memory, no USB-A ports, no SD card slot, only 256GB of storage in base model, power button on base is difficult to reach.

title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game
description: Activision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game And so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was a sales disappointment for Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. Fortunately, this developer – like series heroes Price, Gaz and Ghost – seems to thrive on pressure. As you may have read , this year’s campaign is based around a fictitious North Korean ruling family that has seized an opportunity to invade its southern neighbour. Amid the chaos, a small group of Korean and American marines must help lead the fightback, while in the shadows, SAS hard man John Price makes an unlikely new comrade in his own morally ambiguous quest to put the world to rights. Mads Mikkelsen pops up as evil mastermind The Archer, but like Kiernan Shipka in Black Ops 7 he’s rather wasted, with very little screen time. Continue reading...
content:
Activision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game
A nd so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was a sales disappointment for Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. Fortunately, this developer – like series heroes Price, Gaz and Ghost – seems to thrive on pressure.
As you may have read , this year’s campaign is based around a fictitious North Korean ruling family that has seized an opportunity to invade its southern neighbour. Amid the chaos, a small group of Korean and American marines must help lead the fightback, while in the shadows, SAS hard man John Price makes an unlikely new comrade in his own morally ambiguous quest to put the world to rights. Mads Mikkelsen pops up as evil mastermind The Archer, but like Kiernan Shipka in Black Ops 7 he’s rather wasted, with very little screen time.
Nevertheless, it’s a bombastic, thrilling airport novel of a game, crammed with classic CoD set pieces, including but not limited to parkour over Manhattan rooftops, a car chase in Paris and a shootout in a train yard that somehow feels like a cross between Frogger and Time Crisis. A climactic battle at a North Korean airbase throws absolutely everything at you from sniper firefights to helicopter gunship attacks.
There are also moments where you’re forced into stark unethical actions, faintly recalling the notorious “No Russian” mission from 2009’s Modern Warfare 2. Elsewhere, a whole open-world section lets you explore a snowy landscape, carrying out story missions and side quests to improve your armoury. It’s a nice break from corridor shooting, and somehow it doesn’t stall the game’s momentum. Throughout the six-hour campaign, bullets fly and buildings collapse, friends become enemies, enemies become friends, and a breathless story of geopolitical skullduggery emerges. It’s a shame, though, that the Capt Price arc gets a little overlooked toward the end and his denouement lacks the intended emotional clout, but it’s fun and at least a little bit emotional while it lasts.
The multiplayer mode is a refinement of the turbo-paced, ultra-lethal experience of Black Ops 7. Players are still extremely agile, able to vault over obstacles and skid around corners, blasting their guns like John Wick on a recently polished vinyl floor. But movement is a touch more naturalistic here, and weapons have a heft to them that makes you feel deadly, even if you’re getting shot in the face every five seconds.
Alongside all the classic modes there are decent newcomers, such as the epic, up-to-64-player, Combat Outpost, and Collateral, a round-based shootout where you buy new weapons and items at the start of each bout (the better you do, the more cash you get to spend on goodies). The highlight though is Kill Block, which takes place in a modular training centre where three landscape types are randomly selected from dozens of possibilities, then slotted in to a play space at the start of the round so you’re never sure how everything will fit together. You might have to move from a train yard to a storage depot to a trench network, and weapons are randomised too, so you could all be fighting with pistols or sniper rifles, adding to the unpredictable challenge.
The last part of the package is a reconstructed take on Call of Duty’s extraction shooter mode, DMZ. Taking place in and around Hajin City, abandoned during the events of the campaign, you parachute in with up to two teammates, then carry out various PvE missions to earn cash and gear, before calling in for air rescue – all while avoiding or attacking other players on the same map. New to this version is the Forward Operating Base, a safe house you return to after each expedition where you can upgrade your weapons, 3D print new gear and get info on the current roster of boss characters. There’s also a three-branch skill tree for your character, which you populate by earning in-game XP. This gives you a range of new abilities and improvements including taking more loot from downed enemies, faster revives and reducing damage from explosives.
DMZ, then, is a huge mode with lots to do, set in a dynamic world with a real-time weather system. So far, we’ve only been able to play an early access version, but exploring the world and gambling on just one final side quest before extraction promises to offer the sort of tension and excitement this genre thrives on. However, its success will depend on how many players Activision can attract and retain, and to survive it’ll surely have to tempt people over from established rivals such as Arc Raiders and Escape from Tarkov. That could be the toughest mission of all.
Infinity Ward and its co-developers have thrown everything they have at this game, and it shows. The campaign is short but polished, the multiplayer still grabs you by the neck and DMZ is richly detailed and exhaustive. It’s all rendered in incredible audiovisual detail, delivering the spectacle we expect from the series. I’m not sure it’ll bring in a vast new audience, especially with GTA 6 on the way – Call of Duty remains a gung-ho Hollywood fantasy of armed conflict that glorifies the military-industrial complex. But if it’s a glossy, bombastic thrill ride you’re after, there is plenty here to keep you locked and loaded for months to come.
