content:
Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo/Nintendo Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game
W hen the first Nintendo Switch Sports brought the effortless fun of Wii Sports back into my living room in 2022, I was frankly delighted . My small children discovered the pleasure of waving a controller around in enthusiastic imitation of a tennis player, and the surprising subtlety of virtual bowling, working out how to twist the wrist just right to guarantee a strike. I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto.
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. Thumb wrestling in particular is cheerfully absurd, giving your characters gigantic thumbs on hands the size of their heads.
Every sport here is fun. In skateboarding you use the controller like a mouse, pulling it towards you to propel yourself forwards on the board and tilting it to steer through surprisingly challenging courses, lifting it into the air to jump and spin for tricks. Archery is perfectly intuitive, boxing enjoyably frenetic (especially when played with a seven-year-old), table tennis energisingly competitive, letting you spin and smash the ball with nuanced wrist movement. Almost all of these sports work exactly as you’d expect, with the exception of basketball, whose real-world speed and flashiness are replaced here with methodical turn-taking.
Touring the resort on a jetski or in a plane is more peaceful, reminiscent of Wave Race and Pilotwings, two long-dormant Nintendo series whose DNA is clearly evident in the Wii Sports lineage. On the jetskis, you can follow pink dolphins leaping through the waves. As you pass over the island’s stadiums, cafes and beaches in the plane you will see that they are busy with tiny people, watching a match or lazing on the sand. When you’re skating or soaring around you realise just how big and lively it actually is.
This gloriously unnecessary attention to detail gives this collection of sports games a sense of place and a holiday atmosphere that’s irresistibly appealing. The music is a sunny as the setting, full of guaranteed earworms. I spent a bunch of time dressing up my little character in outfits that you win by ranking up in the island leagues for each sport, a welcome addition that gives some structure to playing by yourself when you aren’t handing controllers around to friends and family. Variants on every sport also up the longevity: obstacle courses in bowling, for instance, or a three-pointer shooting contest in basketball.
After a week of daily play, it has become clear that Switch Sports Resort will not be going back on the digital shelf for some time yet. It is perfect for a Saturday afternoon with friends, but it also has enough going on beneath the surface to sustain the long-term attentions of an enthusiastic child. In other words, it is exactly what you want from a family video game – and as a bonus, it gets everyone off the sofa.

content:
As video games chase spectacle, Modern Warfare 4 makes a case for putting character and consequence at the heart of its biggest battles
Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
I n these strange, subdued weeks before the much-anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI, there have still been some welcome surprises. Onimusha: Way of the Sword revived a half-forgotten samurai action series with much aplomb, while Silent Hill: Townfall transported all of the franchise’s bloody, dread-filled psychological horror to … the picturesque Scottish coast. Even more shocking to games writers , though, is the fact that the forthcoming Modern Warfare 4 has one of the best Call of Duty campaign modes for at least six years – and might even be up there with the original Modern Warfare trilogy.
The setting is an invasion of South Korea by its northern neighbour – a setup that could have fuelled a hundred instantly forgettable Netflix films, but has proved controversial in a video game. The authoritarian regime has a new (fictitious) ruler and a powerful experimental weapon, which it’s not afraid to use as the opening gambit in an explosive attack. You take on the role of Park Hyun Jun, a conscripted South Korean soldier who, along with his small unit of similarly inexperienced grunts, gets caught in the firestorm as cities burn and enemy paratroopers fill the skies.
On the other side of the globe, meanwhile, series hero Capt John Price has gone rogue, teaming up with cartel boss Valeria Garza to track down his nemesis, Makarov. How these narrative strands intertwine is the propulsive engine of the story, and along the way this game throws an arsenal of gigantic set-piece battles at you, edging you closer to a layered finale.
Most positive reviews of the campaign mode have mentioned how the story combines its own ideas with themes and plots from the previous titles. So how did the game’s lead developer, Infinity Ward, set about creating a story that could support a giant first-person juggernaut such as CoD? “The DNA of a Modern Warfare story is that it is something you believe could happen in the real world,” says narrative director Jeff Negus. “‘Does it feel grounded?’ is the first question. Additionally, we ask, ‘What is going to resonate with a modern audience?’ It was important to us not to tell the same story again, not to show the same characters being the same people, because what they’ve been through has deeply affected who they are.”
Infinity Ward brought in a range of military and cultural consultants to ensure the story’s accuracy. “Some of our actors were conscripted in Korea, so they’re able to identify with some of what’s happening,” says Negus. “We use a wide array of military consultants across many different branches and types of service. Our dialect coach, June Yoon, was invaluable because he understands the dialectical differences between North and South Korea, and he could help us reword lines in a more colloquially appropriate way.”
One key element of the game is the combination of quieter, character-led narrative moments and apocalyptic action set-pieces. “There is a very healthy symbiosis between both parts,” says Negus. “We start with strong narrative and gameplay, and the very first thing that we ask is, ‘How can we interweave these things in a way that feels intentional?’ One must be complementary of the other, in such a way that we’re able to say, ‘I can’t imagine telling the story without this mechanic.’” Negus compares it to an explosion in an action movie, saying: “It can be spectacular, but if you don’t know the people who are a part of it, it won’t be meaningful. Back when I was working at Naughty Dog, and now with the team here, we talk about player-protagonist parity, and how, when you feel what the character feels, you’re all a part of the same story – the audience gets to be in on it.”
Surprisingly, iteration is an important part of the process – even though this is a game filled with cinematic sequences that may have to be filmed and animated early in the development process. “We certainly map out the story visually,” says Negus. “Justin [Harris], our lead writer, will put in these story beats, much like a season of television or a movie would do, but we do it with levels. And sometimes we’ll need to move things around, particularly in a story where we can shift the timeline in certain ways. When someone comes up with something, it gets moved around, it gets debated and analysed, and it’s road-tested pretty hard before it becomes inked.”
To me, the Modern Warfare 4 campaign is a story of dysfunctional families – the actual North Korean ruling family, Park Hyun Jun’s ragtag squad and Price’s Task Force 141. The tensions between these groups gives the story its human underpinning. Disaster movies usually centre on one or two main characters so that we, the audience, get to experience the drama vicariously through them.
Infinity Ward has successfully brought that structural and emotional toolkit to the finale of the Modern Warfare series, and that’s at least partly why it works. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 might not be a Pulitzer prize-winning story, but in these odd days before the arrival of GTA VI it certainly gives you something to think about – and people to root for – as you blast away with your rifle, grenade launcher or helicopter gunship.
If you like the look of extreme off-road driving sims such as MudRunner, but are put off by their unyielding difficulty level, Over the Hill is definitely for you. It’s a cosy exploration game where you drive a 4x4 through a bright low-poly landscape of babbling brooks and lush woodlands, occasionally using a winch to get out of muddy puddles or up steep hills.
Along the way, you unlock cabins to allow fast travel and visit a mechanic to customise your vehicle. Spot an interesting bird or critter and you can photograph it, adding it to your scrapbook. The pace is slow and gentle, but there is a fulfilling challenge in mastering the winch and getting yourself out of tight spots.
I wish more games simply gave you a world to explore and the tools to do it and then left you alone – although, if the solitude gets to you, there’s a co-op multiplayer mode too, so you can disappear into the wilderness with pals. Bliss.
Available on: PC (coming to Switch, PS5 and Xbox in 2027) Estimated playtime: 10-plus hours
“Let me be honest from the start: nobody was waiting for this.” Thus begins a lovely Eurogamer feature on the Game Boy Museum , or more accurately, the museum’s creator, Marcel Pflug, and his attempt to fit the whole of his website on to a cart that actually plays on a Game Boy. I love projects like this, which use games and games hardware as repositories of information. See also: The Uncensored Library , which collects banned books inside a Minecraft server.
A question that haunts me, as a 55-year-old, is: “Why do I still play video games?” People are often ecstatic to tell me there are more constructive things I could be doing. I enjoyed this essay by Lene Clement about the non-utilitarian nature of games and the annoying lifestyle influencers who instruct us that “uselessness” is a bad thing because everything has to be productive now.
I am reading There Is No Antimemetics Division by Sam Hughes, better known as qntm . Now out in paperback , it’s a novel about a government agency tasked with finding and battling “antimemetic” entities that feed on humans but can’t be seen, remembered or recorded. It’s a very video game-like premise and the staccato, almost episodic nature of the chapters reminds me of game missions. This is very much a recommendation.
From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era
Penguin Colony – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors | ★★★★☆
This week’s question from Kate via email is something I think all gamers have wondered:
“If I had an idea for a game but no idea of how to create it, who would you suggest I contact? It’s more a game to learn things rather than [one with] combat or sci-fi, etc .”
Remember that old saying, often attributed to Thomas Edison: “Genius is 10% inspiration, and 90% perspiration”? The same goes for video-game design, or indeed film-making, painting and writing novels. Nobody will pay you for an idea, because everyone is having them practically all the time. The most realistic way to realise your idea is to sign up for a game development course , where you may find like-minded people who enjoy your concept and want to work with you. You could invest in an application such as GameMaker and start building your own prototype, or you could study game design via books or YouTube videos.
I also highly recommend A Theory of Fun by Raphy Koster, The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses by Jesse Schell and Challenges for Game Designers by Brenda Romero and Ian Schreiber. All of these provide a really good way to structure your ideas and think about how they may work as a functioning game. This way you can work on a design document that lays out all the rules and systems of your game, and this will help you discover if a) there’s something practical in it, and b) you have the drive and time to work on a game project. A great idea is a great start, but it is really only ever that: a start.

content:
PC; Origame Digital This odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appears
A Nazi kneels down on frozen snow, staring at an endless Antarctic horizon. Another holds a gun to his head, ready to end his own life. I direct a small waddling penguin up to them, trying to imagine what it could be thinking. Dismay, perhaps. Likely bewilderment. But then a faint smile seems to break out across its beaky face, as if amused by these silly humans and their misguided belief that they could ever best this howling, harsh landscape.
For most games, the idea of playing as a penguin observing Nazis losing the plot near the south pole would be weird enough. But Penguin Colony, developed by Origame Digital, pushes further. This is an audacious, frequently brilliant retelling of HP Lovecraft’s 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness, in which eldritch horrors are just as common as Nazis. Further weirdness abounds: the many collectibles scattered about this place are not shiny gold objects à la Super Mario or Sonic. Rather, they are words. So tottering about as a semiaquatic bird, you have a unique mission: collect human language.
But let’s zoom out for a moment because playing Penguin Colony is more straightforward than this description suggests. First and foremost, it is a semiopen world exploration game in which you direct a penguin to the same unearthly entity that the Nazis are chasing. You hop, swim and glide about tummy-first, chewing up miles of frozen wasteland like an indefatigable snowboarder. Tapping a button next to another penguin lets you swap into its body. Some of these, like the rockhopper penguin, are nimble movers, capable of jumping especially high. Fluffy penguin chicks, meanwhile, can squeeze through tiny gaps.
At first, the game’s polar levels are straightforward: snow drifts and ice floes peppered with the remnants of human habitation such as fishing huts. But your surroundings quickly grow stranger: supersized stone labyrinths whose architectural splendour evokes Dark Souls , alien-looking obelisks and abyssal crevasses. Everything in the world is rendered in jagged, low-poly graphics, looming from the screen like a hallucinated PlayStation 2 game.
As you navigate these spaces, a deep-voiced narrator relays the expedition of a scientist from decades before. It’s clear he is driven by the same hubris and racism as his Nazi successors.
The layering of space, time and narrative is terrifically unsettling. At one point, having just hopped my way through a challenging platform section, I came across a Nazi cannibal feasting on his fellow soldier as a researcher delivered yet another verbose pontification on his God-given right to plunder Earth’s southernmost tip. At times, jarring cuts to archive footage and what seem to be Indigenous art interrupt the low-poly action. My head was often spinning, trying to reconcile all these conflicting, contrapuntal elements. Better, I found, to let go and soak up the unnerving, discordant whole.
Penguin Colony is a little uneven technically: I experienced a small number of audio glitches and, at times, bugs with the controls. Yet this does not overly detract from an experience that builds to an incendiary conclusion: a takedown of Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism while also, intriguingly, inviting the player to see the world in newly reenchanted terms.
This latter point is made with aplomb at the game’s end: a spectacular cosmological map that details everything you discovered on that playthrough. More tantalisingly, it shows you all the things you missed. This reveal is liable to induce a feeling of vertigo and wonder: Penguin Colony, one of 2026’s boldest, most original games, is far bigger than it first lets on. To access all of its secrets and excavate all of its meaning, one must think and act less like a human mainlining towards their objective. On the contrary, you must embrace the spirit of a renegade penguin, waddling carefree towards whatever piques your interest: atrocity, beauty and all.

title: ‘Bespoke’ mRNA vaccine significantly reduces risk of melanoma recurrence or death, clinical trial shows
description: Trial results represent ‘foundational shift’ in approach to cancer, allowing scientists to harness immune system in more personalised way Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast A personalised mRNA-based melanoma vaccine significantly reduces the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years, new clinical trial results show. author_name: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science
content:
Trial results represent ‘foundational shift’ in approach to cancer, allowing scientists to harness immune system in more personalised way
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
A personalised mRNA-based melanoma vaccine significantly reduces the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years, new clinical trial results show.
The vaccine, intismeran, is custom-made to target genetic mutations unique to an individual’s melanoma. It is the first individualised cancer vaccine to show positive results in a phase III clinical trial .
The Australian-led trial included 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but were at high risk of it returning.
All were treated with an immunotherapy drug called pembrolizumab for twelve months, and some were also given the personalised intismeran vaccine.
The trial found that at two years post treatment, the combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% compared with treatment with pembrolizumab alone.
Prof Georgina Long, medical director at the Melanoma Institute Australia and 2024 Australian of the Year, described the findings as “a foundational shift in our approach to cancer”, allowing scientists to “harness … the immune system in a more personalised way to reduce the risk of melanoma recurrence or death. This has not been achieved before in the history of cancer drug development.”
Long will present the results at the European Society for Medical Oncology’s annual congress in Madrid on the weekend.
The results have been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine and will need to go through a process of peer review.
Patients in the trial – conducted across 157 sites worldwide – had not previously received any cancer drug treatment. Of those receiving the combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab, 82% were alive and recurrence-free after two years, compared with 70% of participants treated with pembrolizumab alone.
In a phase III trial, a treatment is tested in a large group of people and compared with standard treatments; it is necessary before drug regulators can approve a medicine for use in the general population.
In recent years, developments in immunotherapy drugs have significantly increased survival rates for people with advanced melanoma.
Dr Jessamy Tiffen, acting deputy director of the Centre for Cancer Innovations at the Centenary Institute, who was not involved in the research, said what was “truly remarkable” about the vaccine was the “deeply personalised nature of the treatment, something cancer researchers have been striving to achieve for decades”.
“Where previously oncologists could pick a targeted therapy based on a single gene mutation present in the melanoma, this bespoke mRNA vaccine targets up to 34 gene mutations, unique to each patient. This vaccine, in combination with another type of immunotherapy, then trains the immune system to recognise and eliminate the melanoma, and most importantly, stop it from coming back.”
She noted that the treatment, if progressed, would not benefit all people with melanoma. “ A significant portion do not respond to the vaccine in the first instance ,” she said.
“ Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them. Only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years, but the results are clear that the combination works better than immunotherapy alone, and that’s a very exciting development.”
The drug manufacturers said it was too early to tell from the data whether the combination treatment improved long-term survival.
Prof Christopher Sweeney, director of the South Australian immunoGENomics Cancer Institute at Adelaide University, described the vaccine as “a step-change approach for how to improve the body’s immune system to see cancer cells as foreign and then augment the ability to prevent the cancer cells growing and recurring”.
He said more research was needed to see if the approach was effective in patients “who have cancer we can see”, or who were not responsive to the immune enhancer pembrolizumab.
The personalised vaccine will not be available as a standard melanoma treatment until it has gone through further study and regulatory review, a process that may take several years.

content:
With the climate crisis and diseases threatening one of the world’s most popular fruits, researchers are hoping a breakthrough in breeding techniques could give the Cavendish banana a certain future
Love them or loathe them, bananas are one of the world’s most popular fruit . But a combination of the climate crisis and new killer diseases have had growers concerned over the banana’s threatened extinction , something that would impose a huge toll on farmers in countries from Guatemala to Malawi, alongside eradicating a staple food.
Now researchers say they have made fresh advances in the race to save them from disaster. This month, Yelloway – a research collaboration between Chiquita, the world’s largest banana company , and the crop-improvement company KeyGene – announced it had developed a fully fertile Cavendish banana, meaning it may be possible, through cross-breeding, to create new banana varieties that are commercially viable and resistant to disease.
Second only to the tomato in terms of fruit consumption globally , the world grows about 139m tonnes of bananas a year . While there are more than 1,000 varieties, it is the Cavendish that is now found in most fruit bowls, taking over from the Gros Michel cultivar, which fell victim to Panama disease from the 1950s.
But the Cavendish itself is under threat from diseases including a strain of Panama known as Tropical Race 4 (TR4). Dr Jose De Vega, an expert on crop genomics at the Earlham Institute in Norwich, said TR4 had spread from south-east Asia to Australia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America.
“The most worrying recent report came in December 2025 from Ecuador, the world’s largest banana exporter,” he said, noting that the disease threatened both global supply chains “and the food security of millions of people in the tropics for whom bananas and plantains are a staple food and a source of income”.
Cavendish bananas have three sets of chromosomes, meaning they are typically sterile. “Combined with the ability to set fruit without pollination, this gives us the seedless banana,” said De Vega.
There are several different types of Cavendish, including dwarf versions, which have arisen as a result of random mutations in the Cavendish genome.
But in each case new plants are grown from offshoots, so they are virtually genetically identical to the plant from which they came. While this results in uniform fruit, it also means they are vulnerable to the same diseases.
Peter Stedman, Chiquita’s sustainability director, said: “We are not trying to preserve Cavendish. We’re trying to replace Cavendish because we believe at the core of any sustainable farming system is biodiversity and genetic diversity.”
Other researchers have taken different approaches. In Australia, a team at Queensland University of Technology led by Prof James Dale has created a genetically modified Cavendish by using a bacterium to introduce a gene from a wild banana that produces resistance to TR4.
The upshot, a type of Cavendish called QCAV-4, has been approved for human consumption in Australia and New Zealand, with researchers confirming that it tastes like the traditional banana.
De Vega, by contrast, is collaborating with other researchers to explore gene-editing techniques. These involve using “molecular scissors” to cut parts of the Cavendish’s DNA and replace them with genes from other banana cultivars.
His team have been sequencing the genomes of banana varieties that have different responses to TR4. “We are looking for the [immune genes] that resistant varieties have and that the Cavendish lacks, carries a broken version of, has too few copies of, or doesn’t switch on strongly enough,” said De Vega.
“Once we identify a candidate gene, the idea is to edit the Cavendish’s own copy so it matches the copy in the resistant cousin. That keeps everything that makes a Cavendish a Cavendish.”
In England and elsewhere in Europe, De Vega added, gene-editing was seen as precision breeding rather than genetic modification.
“That is because the change is one that could happen naturally or through conventional breeding,” he said. “The catch is that with a sterile Cavendish, conventional breeding has never really been an option, which is exactly why editing is so attractive for bananas.”
But Stedman said there were drawbacks to such approaches. “Every time you are editing or improving Cavendish, you’re not creating a new variety, you’re not creating biodiversity – you’re just maintaining a monocrop,” he said, noting that brought susceptibility to disease.
Yelloway’s production of a fully fertile Cavendish line – known as “Yellowdish” – using non-GM technologies potentially opens up a new route.
Dale and De Vega noted that details on exactly how Yellowdish was produced, and with how many chromosomes, had not been revealed – meaning questions remained.
Dale said the approach with Yelloway of crossing a fertile Cavendish with other types of fertile banana resistant to TR4 – and potentially other diseases – could have benefits, including in the regulatory environment and in public perceptions.
But while it may result in disease-resistant progeny, he noted it could also yield a very different type of fruit.
“Whatever they generate is going to be different to Cavendish,” Dale said, pointing out that crosses could produce a huge range of types but any new variety needed not only to be resistant to disease but also produce high yields and taste good.
For Stedman, the challenge boils down to a numbers game. “If you have enough progeny, if you have enough children, the chances of one of them having … the traits that you want is much, much higher,” he said.

content:
An app and a camera phone are all that’s needed at more than 200 spots to help researchers monitor coastal areas
The shoreline changes with the weather. Tracking these changes over time is a labour-intensive task, and an army of citizen scientists with camera phones is a great asset.
The CoastSnap project started in Australia in 2017 and has spread to beaches worldwide. You may have spotted the setup while out walking along the coast: a cradle to rest your phone on while taking a picture and a sign explaining where to send the snap.
Large waves and high tides remove sand from a beach, while gentler conditions deposit sand and build the beach up again. Sandbars migrate in and out, and change shape with the waves and tides. Some shifts are temporary, some permanent. CoastSnap enables researchers to follow these changes day by day.
The cradle ensures each picture is taken from roughly the same position and angle. Software aligns each photograph, then performs a geometric flip to transform it into a bird’s-eye view of the beach. An algorithm maps the shoreline, correcting for the tide based on the timestamp.
CoastSnap helps researchers track coastal erosion over time, see the changes caused by a particular storm, or monitor the effectiveness of beach replenishment schemes adding sand or shingle.
There are now more than 200 CoastSnap stations in 21 countries, including the UK, constituting the largest coordinated, land-based coastal monitoring programme in the world.

title: Mystery of Roman sarcophagus unearthed at Westminster Abbey solved at last, expert says
description: Archaeologist says skeleton inside coffin inscribed to Valerius Amandinus is likely to be remains of 11th-century abbot It has all the ingredients of a chilling mystery: the skeleton of an unknown man discovered within a Roman sarcophagus unearthed in the grounds of Westminster Abbey. Now an expert has said he has solved the longstanding “who-is-it”, suggesting the remains belonged to a medieval abbot. Continue reading...
content:
Archaeologist says skeleton inside coffin inscribed to Valerius Amandinus is likely to be remains of 11th-century abbot
It has all the ingredients of a chilling mystery: the skeleton of an unknown man discovered within a Roman sarcophagus unearthed in the grounds of Westminster Abbey.
Now an expert has said he has solved the longstanding “who-is-it”, suggesting the remains belonged to a medieval abbot.
First discovered in 1820, the limestone sarcophagus was officially excavated in 1869 from what is now an area of grass along the north side of the nave, but was once the yard of a sacristy built by Henry III. But the discovery spawned a mystery: whose remains were inside?
While the sarcophagus itself was from the late Roman period, with a Latin inscription to one Valerius Amandinus and Roman decoration on one side, no Roman artefacts were found in subsequent excavations of the area.
“That was not its original place of burial,” said Prof Warwick Rodwell, a consultant archaeologist at Westminster Abbey, noting it was likely the sarcophagus was originally housed in the wall recess of a mausoleum, and that Valerius Amandinus was a wealthy individual.
What’s more, the lid of the fourth-century sarcophagus was decorated with a large, carved cross that was later shown to be a modification of the original lid. “It runs the full length and the width of the lid, and it’s a very specific late Anglo-Saxon cross type,” Rodwell said.
Writing in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association , Rodwell not only describes what was previously known about the sarcophagus but sets out the findings of a more recent investigation in 2018 as part of plans to display the sarcophagus in the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries.
As part of that work the sarcophagus was taken to a laboratory and its lid removed. “And there, inside it, was the skeleton,” Rodwell said.
The discovery was something of a surprise given written records had suggested the skeleton had been lost. However, Rodwell said the bones tallied with those depicted in 19th-century drawings. A subsequent analysis suggested the remains belonged to a man who was 5ft 9in tall and aged between 35 and 49.
In another twist, when the inside of the sarcophagus was cleaned, experts found a rectangular outline in a white substance in the bottom of the sarcophagus. Rodwell said this suggests the body had been covered in powdered lime before being placed into a wooden coffin that sat inside the sarcophagus.
Crucially, radiocarbon dating of the bones suggested they were from the late 10th or early 11th century. Now Rodwell said he had the answer to the identity of the dead man, suggesting it was most likely a medieval abbott.
“Nobody of lower rank would have been buried in anything like that,” he said, adding that the lid was another clue. “The Latin cross again points to a major ecclesiastic.”
According to Rodwell, there are two possible abbots who fit the bill: Ælfwig, who died in about 1020, and Wulfnoth who died in about 1049. Rodwell believes Ælfwig is the more likely candidate, noting he was already a monk at Westminster when the previous abbot died, and spent about 27 years in the role.
Rodwell suggested the re-used sarcophagus was most likely interred in the eastern arm of the abbey church, with the lid as a floor slab, before being dug up and reburied during the construction work of Henry III.
“It’s like so much in archaeology,” said Rodwell. “There’s a lot more complication than one initially sees.”

title: Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others
description: Research shows how seeing bigger violations by others can lead people to increase their own rule-breaking From politicians taking bribes to bullying and harassment in City firms , leaders have been quick to label those who break the rules as the odd “bad apple”. But new research backs up the idiom that one bad apple can spoil the barrel. Researchers have found that when people go beyond the rule-breaking they see in others, general compliance can swiftly turn into widespread rule-breaking. Continue reading...
content:
Research shows how seeing bigger violations by others can lead people to increase their own rule-breaking
From politicians taking bribes to bullying and harassment in City firms , leaders have been quick to label those who break the rules as the odd “bad apple”. But new research backs up the idiom that one bad apple can spoil the barrel.
Researchers have found that when people go beyond the rule-breaking they see in others, general compliance can swiftly turn into widespread rule-breaking.
Dr Lucas Molleman, from the University of Amsterdam and the first author of the research, said the goal was to explore how individuals make decisions about rule-breaking in a social context.
“Many people think of themselves as making sort of autonomous decisions, especially in these individualist cultures that we are from, like Netherlands, the UK,” he said. “But in actual fact, in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.”
Writing in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B , Molleman and colleagues report how they recruited 750 people in the US to take part in an online experiment, with the participants approximately evenly split between Republicans and Democrats.
The researchers asked each participant to complete an online task in which they saw an animated “shooting star” moving across a row of 100 squares as its intensity varied. Participants were instructed to pick the square that lit up most intensely to receive a monetary reward.
However, participants received greater rewards for selecting squares further to the right of the correct square, and smaller rewards for selecting squares further to the left.
Participants were then shown whether another participant had followed the rules or broken them, the extent of any rule-breaking, and their political affiliation, and asked if they wished to update their choice. The process was repeated six times.
The results revealed participants showed large degrees of rule-breaking even in their initial choices, with 23% of choices involving squares with the highest reward.
However, the choices of others mattered: seeing others following the rules slightly reduced an individual’s rule-breaking, while seeing others making small beneficial violations – choosing a square a third of the way to the right, beyond the correct square – slightly increased rule-breaking.
Crucially, seeing others flagrantly flout the rules by selecting a square even further to the right led participants to greatly increase their own level of rule-breaking. In some cases they went beyond the violations they had observed.
The team say the findings were stronger when a participant had the same political leanings as others – something Molleman said chimed with other research, suggesting people who are politically aligned are more influenced by each other.
The researchers used computer simulations to explore how the behaviour they had observed in the experiments would play out in a large group. The results showed that a situation could quickly get out of hand.
“A minority of escalating individuals, exceeding the rule violations they observe, they might cause a whole collective to spin out of control,” Molleman said.
However, he noted that about a third of participants consistently followed the rules even though it did not lead to the largest reward.
Prof Stephen Reicher, of the University of St Andrews, in Scotland, who was not involved in the work, said the study had limitations, including that the experiment was abstract and there was no penalty for rule-breaking, meaning the relevance of the work to real-world examples remained unproven.
Reicher also stressed that the results went against the concept of contagion, instead showing that whether we are influenced by others depends on who those others are.
“This is important because it implies that, say, we don’t riot simply because we see others rioting,” he said. “In fact, many people who see rioting respond by helping clear up after riots.”

title: Big pharma accused of ‘free-riding on nature’ as global fund attracts just $7,000
description: The Cali Fund, set up to raise $1bn a year for biodiversity from drug companies, remains near empty Big pharmaceutical companies have been accused of “free-riding on nature”, after a landmark biodiversity fund that invites businesses to put some of their profits back into conservation was left virtually empty. The Cali Fund set out to raise $1bn (£750m) annually, by asking companies that profit from nature’s genetics to contribute towards conservation in low-income countries. But more than 18 months after the fund was launched, it remains far below this target. Continue reading...
content:
The Cali Fund, set up to raise $1bn a year for biodiversity from drug companies, remains near empty
Big pharmaceutical companies have been accused of “free-riding on nature”, after a landmark biodiversity fund that invites businesses to put some of their profits back into conservation was left virtually empty.
The Cali Fund set out to raise $1bn (£750m) annually, by asking companies that profit from nature’s genetics to contribute towards conservation in low-income countries. But more than 18 months after the fund was launched, it remains far below this target.
As of Monday, at the start of the Cop17 biodiversity summit in Armenia, the fund had received just $10,656 in commitments , of which $7,085 had been deposited.
No money has so far been given by major pharmaceutical companies, despite the industry’s reliance on genetic information from organisms around the globe for the development of lucrative new medicines.
The industry’s participation could prove pivotal to the fund’s success. A study by Zero Carbon Analytics (ZCA) found the top 15 pharmaceutical companies could have contributed $756m based on their performance last year, if they had followed guidelines set out by the fund, which suggests companies make a voluntary contribution of 1% of their profits or 0.1% of revenue.
In 2025, the top 15 pharmaceutical companies generated about $161bn in profits, according to ZCA’s research.
“Look at how much profit these pharmaceutical companies are getting – and we’re only asking for a tiny percentage,” said June Rubis of Macquarie University, who is an Indigenous peoples and local communities representative from Asia and sits on the Cali Fund’s steering committee.
“Definitely, they’re free-riding” on nature, said Rubis, who added that businesses did not appear to recognise the importance of protecting nature or of supporting “communities who have been in the frontlines of defending biodiversity conservation and therefore their future profits”.
The Cali Fund is a key issue to be discussed at the UN biodiversity conference – Cop17 – in Yerevan, this week, and is part of wider efforts to plug a $700bn gap in funding for nature conservation.
At least half of the money from the Cali Fund will be directed towards areas identified as priorities by Indigenous peoples and local communities.
“The future of health is written in nature’s DNA,” said Victoria Kalyvas, who authored the Zero Carbon Analytics analysis. “The pharmaceutical industry stands to lose a great deal from its destruction , as do patients.”
According to Zero Carbon Analytics, the total sum given to shareholders by the top 15 companies in 2025 was 175 times more than the suggested contribution to the Cali Fund.
Ensuring that companies pay for their use of nature has become increasingly complex, due to advances in biotechnology that mean large volumes of genetic information, known as digital sequence information (DSI) , can now be stored in public databases.
The Cali Fund was designed to plug loopholes that have emerged as research has shifted from a reliance on physical samples to use of DSI.
However, pharmaceutical companies have criticised the fund, saying the blanket amount they are asked to contribute is not appropriate, arguing that not all medicines are built using DSI, and that the fund overlaps with existing laws.
Since its official launch in February 2025, the fund has received just three contributions by small private-sector companies: $5,000 from the UK-based biotech firm Prozomix; $1,000 from TierraViva AI, also based in Britain; and $1,085 from the Belgian firm E-Biom.
“More money has been spent on meetings talking about the Cali Fund than there is in the Cali Fund’s coffers,” said Brian O’Donnell, director of Campaign for Nature, who said it was too optimistic to expect companies to contribute voluntarily and that they should be compelled to do so.
Guilherme Cintra, director of innovation policy at the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations, said the industry was committed to biodiversity but had “ongoing questions about the design and implementation of the mechanism”.
“The current mechanism overlaps with existing law, relies on inaccurate assumptions about how data is used in the discovery of medicines, and asks companies to hand over a share of their total revenue, whether DSI was used to develop a medicine or not,” Cintra said.
A spokesperson for the Cali Fund said the amount raised so far was “disappointing but not entirely surprising”, adding that “comparable financial instruments have generally taken two to three years before contributions began to scale [up]”.
The spokesperson said: “Contributions will likely remain modest while the operational infrastructure is being completed and until the Cali Fund becomes better known.” They added that discussions at Cop17 would give greater information to companies, enabling them to come forward with commitments.
A spokesperson for the French pharmaceutical multinational Sanofi said the company recognised “the critical importance of biodiversity and healthy ecosystems to human health and the long-term resilience of healthcare systems” and that protecting nature was a core component of its environmental sustainability strategy.
A spokesperson for the British biopharmaceutical company GSK said open access to DSI was “critical to enable continued medical innovation and rapid response to public health emergencies, including pandemics”.
They added: “We support the intent behind the Cali Fund and will make a decision regarding voluntary contributions when there is more information about how the Cali Fund will work alongside other national and multilateral access and benefit-sharing mechanisms.”

title: Tesla beats earnings projections after Musk floats SpaceX merger plan
description: Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but declined to elaborate Investors were paying close attention to Tesla ’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executive Elon Musk floated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX . But they didn’t glean further information after the company announced there would be no questions on the matter. “With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX, I think I said everything that should be said yesterday,” Musk, the CEO of both companies, said on Tesla’s earnings call. He repeated a phrase he said on Tuesday: “I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.” Continue reading...
content:
Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but declined to elaborate
Investors were paying close attention to Tesla ’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executive Elon Musk floated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX . But they didn’t glean further information after the company announced there would be no questions on the matter.
“With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX , I think I said everything that should be said yesterday,” Musk, the CEO of both companies, said on Tesla’s earnings call. He repeated a phrase he said on Tuesday: “I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.”
On a call with SpaceX investors on Tuesday, Musk said it would be a “good idea” to combine the two companies and that “there’s a lot of merit” that would come with it.
Musk said on Tuesday that the board of directors for both of his businesses had put together special committees to explore the potential merger, but had not yet reached an agreement on the terms of the transaction. The move would require the approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders.
On Wednesday, Tesla reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings, with a reported revenue of $28.05bn and $0.48 on earnings per share. That beat Wall Street’s projections of $27.9bn in revenue, with $0.43 on earnings per share. Still, the company came in at a slightly lower revenue than last quarter , which was $28.23bn. And its automotive revenue dropped 3% from the year prior.
“We maintained strong momentum on many projects spanning Super Intelligence (SI), robotics and renewable energy that will be critical to building a future of Amazing Abundance,” the company wrote in its report .
Despite the stronger-than-anticipated quarter, Tesla has experienced a rough year with falling stock and increased competition from cheaper Chinese automakers. The company’s share price has fallen by more than 11% this year, although it appears to have rebounded some since last week with the news of the possible SpaceX merger.
Last week, Musk unveiled the company’s electric sports car , the Roadster 2, which he said uses technology from SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”. At a demonstration at a SpaceX facility in Texas, a remote-controlled version of the car drove up a steeply curved ramp and then used jet-like thrusters to flip over, hover and land. The vehicle is priced at upwards of $200,000.
“Flying cars are real … It can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics,” Musk said at the event, adding: “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.”
During Tesla’s earnings call on Wednesday, he added that the event was “the coolest demo of any product ever”.
Tesla’s vehicle sales are not as crucial to its market performance as they once were, as the company has pivoted towards robotics, autonomous driving and AI. Tesla’s Optimus robot has faced production hurdles, however; and its driverless taxi service, Robotaxi , has hit roadblocks in scaling its fleet and expanding to new cities.
“Tesla’s leaders continue to make big claims about autonomous mobility and physical AI. The company has achieved remarkable things but continues to miss some of its leaders’ bolder bets,” said Paul Miller, a principal analyst for market research firm Forrester. “Tesla robotaxis are undeniably carrying passengers, but not yet at anywhere near the levels the company promised.”
Musk has long declared the Robotaxi will have near-infinite demand and that “probably half the population of the US” would be using the autonomous ride-hailing service by the end of 2025. Similarly, the CEO has forecast the manufacture of as many as 1m Optimus robots each year. As Miller pointed out with Musk’s promises, he has failed to reach those lofty targets and rollout has been slow.
Musk once again touted the robots on Wednesday, saying: “I remain convinced that Optimus will be the biggest product on earth and humanoid robots in general will be the biggest product on earth.” He added that no other company compares to Tesla in developing humanoid robots – this is despite Chinese competitors making vast strides in the technology.

title: Orangutans prefer food associated with sounds of laughter, study suggests
description: Apes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learning Orangutans base their food choices on whether others appear to be having a good time, research suggests. Scientists studying captive orangutans have found that when the great apes heard the sound of their peers laughing before they searched a bowl for a tasty treat, they valued the reward more highly. Continue reading...
content:
Apes in study more likely to choose treats linked to sound of peers having fun, suggesting emotions influence learning
Orangutans base their food choices on whether others appear to be having a good time, research suggests.
Scientists studying captive orangutans have found that when the great apes heard the sound of their peers laughing before they searched a bowl for a tasty treat, they valued the reward more highly.
Erica Cartmill, a professor of anthropology and cognitive science at Indiana University and senior author of the work, said the study is part of a larger project exploring whether animals feel joy and what the implications of those emotions are in areas such as cognition and learning.
“One of our big motivations … is building on human research that shows that emotion has important effects on rational thought – and that they aren’t two separate things; they really influence one another,” she said. “We wanted to extend that to animals – in this case to orangutans.”
Writing in the journal Biology Letters, Cartmill and her colleagues report how they worked with six orangutans based at two zoological institutions.
The researchers first trained the orangutans to search through bowls to find food treats. They then presented each orangutan with two bowls. One contained a tasty morsel buried under a harmless substance such as moss or sawdust, while the other contained a different type of material but no treat.
Crucially, just before the researchers presented the bowls to the orangutans, they played a recording. This was either the sound of orangutans playing and laughing or environmental sounds such as wind, with the choice of soundtrack depending on which of two substances was used to cover the food that day.
On the fifth day the team presented the orangutans with two bowls, but this time each contained a treat buried beneath one of the two food-covering substances. They then asked the orangutans to pick a bowl.
The results from multiple trials revealed that, overall, the apes preferred to pick the bowl containing the substance associated with the sound of laughter, with four of the six orangutans showing a clear preference.
Cartmill said the preference could be rooted in the sound of laughter putting the orangutans in a more positive emotional state when they learned to associate the substance with food.
Dr Adriano Lameira, a primatologist and evolutionary psychologist at the University of Warwick, who was not involved in the work, described the results as fascinating.
“Effectively, hearing others clearly having a good time, orangutans placed their food order: ‘I will have what they are having, please!’” he said.
Cartmill added the results suggest it is not only the quantity or frequency of a reward that can be important when learning associations.
“What our work is showing is that it’s also about the state of the animal when they are learning that association,” she said.
“Who you are in that moment – the context, the emotional states, what you’re feeling, what you’re thinking about – can also influence and can carry over in how you remember these things that you’ve learned.”
The findings, she added, could have applications to humans, including in educational environments.
“Students might learn at similar rates if they are in a good mood or not, but our research suggests that they would value information more if they learn it when they are in a good mood,” Cartmill said.
She added that could be useful in helping to understand why some information is more trusted or why students choose to continue studying certain subjects.
“If a student is anxious when they are learning maths for example, it might impact whether they prefer maths versus other subjects when choosing what to pursue in the future,” she said.

title: Do people become less creative as they get older? Research makes surprising discovery
description: Study pitting preschoolers against adults mostly in their 20s finds fear of failure and anxiety hamper the grownups Ask a five-year-old to paint a picture and they will almost instinctively reach for the brush, but ask an adult to do the same and they will often hesitate and shy away. Now researchers say they know why. While it is widely assumed children are more creative than adults, a new study challenges this notion, finding adults outperform preschoolers on creative tasks but generally feel less confident and more anxious doing them. Continue reading...
content:
Study pitting preschoolers against adults mostly in their 20s finds fear of failure and anxiety hamper the grownups
Ask a five-year-old to paint a picture and they will almost instinctively reach for the brush, but ask an adult to do the same and they will often hesitate and shy away. Now researchers say they know why.
While it is widely assumed children are more creative than adults, a new study challenges this notion, finding adults outperform preschoolers on creative tasks but generally feel less confident and more anxious doing them.
Dr Mathias Benedek, the senior author of the study at the University of Graz in Austria, said: “Children are so intrinsically motivated and absorbed in play that we often mistake their engagement with greater creative ability.”
Writing in the journal Plos One, the researchers asked 92 preschool children aged four to seven and 70 adults largely in their 20s to complete three tasks.
The first involved coming up with as many creative uses for a tin as possible in three minutes; the second involved drawing anything they liked with no stated time limit; and the third involved drawing an imaginary animal within eight minutes.
The results were then rated by judges on originality, usefulness and overall creativity.
Participants were also asked to rate how much they enjoyed each task, how motivated and confident they felt, and how anxious they were doing it.
The judges deemed the work by adults to be more original, useful and creative than that of children, particularly when clear goals and time limits were set. Conversely, children reported feeling more confident, motivated and less anxious completing tasks.
“Adults outperformed children, demonstrating higher creative potential, but they had far less confidence. We need to look at what makes adults so anxious about their original ideas being rejected,” Benedek said.
He said children approached tasks with greater intrinsic motivation and enjoyed the process of play, “whereas adults place more focus on the goal or objective”, limiting their enjoyment.
As a result, children experimented more freely and treated mistakes as part of the process whereas adults, wary of judgment, often dismissed unusual ideas before trying them.
The study, conducted at the University of Graz in Austria in collaboration with UCLouvain in Belgium and Yale University, has limitations. Among them, the research is based on a snapshot comparison of just two age groups, making it hard to draw conclusions about the impact of ageing on creativity. Children are also more likely to pick extreme answers on rating scales and have obvious differences in cognition.
Nonetheless, Benedek and his colleagues suggest that the idea of creativity fading as we grow into adulthood is a misconception. “Adults don’t lose their creativity, instead they lose the confidence to use it,” Benedek said.

title: Can AI really predict cancer survival better than a doctor? I have my doubts | Devi Sridhar
description: Take a selfie to see how healthy you are: the idea is enticing and this new research is promising. But so many factors have been ignored The idea that a single selfie could predict how long someone with cancer may live sounds like an incredible breakthrough. AI is getting better at spotting patterns in medical data, but can it be used to reliably predict what will happen to an individual patient? I asked a clinical colleague what she thought about the recent headlines . She found it an interesting development given that doctors have long used facial appearance to assess patient health. For example, she noted that they may write “appears stated age” or “appears older than stated age” as a proxy for general health. Now, researchers from Mass General Brigham, a healthcare institution in Massachusetts, have taken this idea a step further. They have developed an AI model trained on more than 40 million facial images – called FAHR-Face – to assess biological age and predict survival in cancer patients. For biological age, they developed FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates age from certain facial features such as the forehead, the wrinkles between the nose and mouth and the temples. For cancer survival, they developed FAHR-FaceSurvival, trained using almost 35,000 photos of cancer patients. This model focused more closely on the area below the eyes and the bridge of the nose – regions of the face “ linked with dying ”. Dr Raymond Mak , one of the study’s authors, noted that these parts of the face are the same as those referenced by Hippocrates in 400BC as signs of muscle wasting and mortality risk: “the nose sharp, the eyes sunken, the temples fallen in”. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh Continue reading...
content:
Take a selfie to see how healthy you are: the idea is enticing and this new research is promising. But so many factors have been ignored
T he idea that a single selfie could predict how long someone with cancer may live sounds like an incredible breakthrough. AI is getting better at spotting patterns in medical data, but can it be used to reliably predict what will happen to an individual patient? I asked a clinical colleague what she thought about the recent headlines . She found it an interesting development given that doctors have long used facial appearance to assess patient health. For example, she noted that they may write “appears stated age” or “appears older than stated age” as a proxy for general health.
Now, researchers from Mass General Brigham, a healthcare institution in Massachusetts, have taken this idea a step further. They have developed an AI model trained on more than 40 million facial images – called FAHR-Face – to assess biological age and predict survival in cancer patients. For biological age, they developed FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates age from certain facial features such as the forehead, the wrinkles between the nose and mouth and the temples. For cancer survival, they developed FAHR-FaceSurvival, trained using almost 35,000 photos of cancer patients. This model focused more closely on the area below the eyes and the bridge of the nose – regions of the face “ linked with dying ”. Dr Raymond Mak , one of the study’s authors, noted that these parts of the face are the same as those referenced by Hippocrates in 400BC as signs of muscle wasting and mortality risk: “the nose sharp, the eyes sunken, the temples fallen in”.
The results, published in The Lancet Digital Health this month, are intriguing – but far from conclusive. Researchers found that AI-estimated facial age was significantly associated with survival in 18 of 28 cancer categories. So, basically, it works for some cancers, but not for others. In addition, Prof Miroslaw Bober noted, “The tool still needs testing against doctors’ own judgments and across different hospitals and patient groups. For example, the facial-age measure was not significantly associated with survival for Black patients after adjustment for other factors.” That finding adds to the growing concern that AI models can exhibit racial bias based on the data used to train them and underlying assumptions. For example, racial bias has been shown when AI models analyse cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) scans – used to diagnose and monitor heart disease.
Let’s go back to what the published study does and doesn’t tell us. These models are built on retrospective data looking at statistical associations across thousands of patients, and it’s a jump to then accurately predict future survival from this. A selfie may contain clues about a patient’s health, but that is a long way from being able to predict their future – and a longer way still from proving that the prediction is useful in clinical practice.
I also worry about how unreliable selfies are. Just think of the times you’ve met people in real life and compared them with their profile photos. Anyone who has tried one of the online AI “guess your age” tools will know how much the result varies with lighting, camera angle, facial expression or even time of day. And then there’s botox, fillers, facelifts and even GLP-1 drugs, which alter facial fat and shape. How much can a single photograph really tell us about someone’s underlying health?
As anti-ageing treatments become the norm , visible age and underlying health will become an increasingly complex relationship. A face in a selfie that looks younger may not be necessarily healthier. The researchers do note that they tested their age model against lighting, expression and cosmetic surgery – but if predictions are based on specific signs of ageing in parts of the face that those all affect, I can’t see how it would be possible to avoid a certain degree of error in AI estimates.
None of this means the research isn’t promising. This new tool and the research team behind it are impressive. Alongside other tests that a doctor may perform to assess a patient’s health and future prognosis, it could take some of the guesswork out of “looks stated age”. But the question is whether it’s actually useful in daily practice beyond what clinicians are already doing when using experience and years of training.
If you’re tempted to go to the project’s public website to find out your biological age, even just to brag to friends about how young it says you look, be aware that by uploading your selfie, you will become part of the study too, as their consent forms indicate. Your face is not only being assessed, it’s contributing to the data used to develop the technology. Currently, the tool will only tell you your biological age, but I would be sceptical of what that may tell you about your overall health.
Finally, a pop quiz (I’m in the middle of the teaching semester): what top three things did the researchers find made people’s face age? Alcohol, drugs and smoking. No surprise there, but possibly an explanation as to why doctors can broadly read someone’s health status from their face. Something that perhaps we didn’t need AI scanning 40m faces to tell us.
Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

title: The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information | Editorial
description: In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics Is there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases. It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future. Continue reading...
content:
In the three weeks since a health worker’s death in Siberia, officials have stonewalled the WHO – setting a worrying precedent for future pandemics
I s there a plague outbreak in Russia? If the answer were a clear yes, there shouldn’t be much reason to worry. With swift medical intervention, plague is treatable. But in the nearly three weeks since a worker at a Siberian plague research unit died of a mysterious respiratory illness, state officials have been consistently tight-lipped about what happened and whether there were any further cases.
It is this uncertainty that has the World Health Organization (WHO) and international community worried: partly because there is a – very small – risk of an outbreak, and partly because it is yet another warning that the international coordination we rely on to prevent pandemics is fraying along with the rest of international politics, and could easily fail to protect us in the future.
The key to containing an outbreak is quick disclosure and open sharing of information. Russia reportedly held high-level meetings about the case, quarantined the hospital where the worker was treated and traced about 200 contacts. That response suggests officials believed the infection was plague, and yet they did not report any of this to the WHO, as international law requires. Russia later revealed that the worker died of a pneumonia of unknown origin – hardly useful information. It undoubtedly gathered lab results and genetic sequences that could shed more light on the case, but has not shared them.
Earlier this year, the hantavirus outbreak originating on the MV Hondius cruise ship was successfully contained , showing that the global health system can still work well when countries cooperate. This latest incident suggests that one recalcitrant nation can jeopardise everyone’s safety. It is not the WHO’s fault that Russia is essentially a rogue state, but the body must be ready for such eventualities. International politics is fragmented, and only becoming more so.
Earlier this year the US left the WHO (though it is still party to some of its treaties). States follow international laws when they believe in them, or when they believe that there will be penalties – reputational or otherwise – for not playing along. The WHO has not attempted to play hardball with Russia, or set off a round of international condemnation from leading member states. Some might be heartened that on 7 October the US state department officially requested that the Russian government share information with the WHO. However, it is likely that this reflects Washington’s increasingly ad hoc approach to international politics – using every lever available as situations arise – rather than a renewed commitment to international law. President Trump said on the same day that he would speak to Vladimir Putin about the issue. If that happened, no one has heard about it or what information may have been revealed.
The keen US interest may give credence to speculation that what in fact happened was some kind of bioweapons research leak. This is thought to be unlikely, but not impossible. The fact that such a scenario can even be plausibly entertained three weeks after the initial event speaks to a serious breakdown in the system. Western states probably do not hold much sway with Russia . But the other Brics nations may have more. The WHO used to rely on US backing for its requests. It may now have to find support among wider, more multipolar coalitions. This potential outbreak may come to nothing, but there will be another soon.

content:
Russia’s silence over the death of a lab worker underlines that pandemic preparedness amounts to nothing if information on threats is withheld
I n pandemic preparedness work , scientists like to focus on the technical challenges: identifying pathogens, diagnosing infections, understanding their effects and developing vaccines and treatments. Each step promises progress through human innovation, investment and planning. The World Health Organization (WHO), for example, brings experts together to identify and prioritise emerging disease threats and collect the evidence needed to prepare for them. But preparedness depends on more than scientific innovation.
As the past week has shown, politics is the elephant in the room in all of this. No one could have predicted we would be talking about pneumonic plague, and that the death of a single lab worker in Russia would cause global headlines. It might feel like an overreaction: the WHO deals with thousands of potential disease signals worldwide every month . But the circumstances of this case are unusual given the lack of transparency from Russian authorities on what happened – and ongoing concern about biological weapons research.
The 28-year-old lab worker died after developing severe pneumonia. She worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, established in 1934, which studies plague and other dangerous pathogens including anthrax and cholera, and is rumoured to be involved in biological weapons research. Prof Ashish Jha, who was the US White House Covid-19 response coordinator, and who co-chaired an Ebola commission with me, wrote on social media : “US intelligence assess that Russia’s scientists continue developing biological weapons capabilities. Those programmes operate in secret. Nobody outside inspects them and nobody inside has much incentive to admit when something goes wrong.”
On top of that, initial local media coverage suggested that she had died from pneumonic plague after a lab accident, possibly a broken test tube. Pneumonic plague is caused by a bacterium ( Yersinia pestis ), and can spread through respiratory contact and is always fatal if untreated . If antibiotics are given in the first 24 hours after symptoms, or even before onset of symptoms post-exposure, it is largely treatable. If she knew she had been exposed, why was treatment not given in time? (Pneumonic plague is a different disease to the more common bubonic plague, which transmits through flea bites.)
Despite Russian health authorities denying that it was a case of plague and insisting it was pneumonia of unknown origin, they quickly placed about 200 contacts of the lab worker under quarantine. The authorities reported that no high-threat pathogens were detected and monitoring had ended. The WHO released a statement noting a potential second linked case, but Russia denied this. The cause of death remains unconfirmed.
The WHO has pushed the Russian government for more information – including confirmation of the diagnosis and details of the investigations, the reason why it put so many people in quarantine and more information on the second case – but it has not yet received this information.
On the one hand, if this infection was spreading further, additional cases would have emerged by now. The lab worker died on 2 October, and the testing of contacts and release of those in quarantine indicates that any spread has been contained so far. However, given that the incubation period can be one to three days, continued monitoring is important.
There are three hypothetical scenarios if we assume the illness was pneumonic plague. The first is that the lab worker was accidentally exposed to the bacterium while doing research, and either didn’t know, or didn’t tell anyone out of fear – and therefore didn’t ask for treatment immediately. So when she became sick, her window of treatment had been missed.
Second, the lab worker was exposed to an antibiotic-resistant strain. This may sound like a conspiracy theory, but senior academics have raised concerns given the history of the Soviet biological weapons programme and the potential for pathogens to be engineered for hostile purposes.
Third, Dan Singer (the former White House director for countering biological threats) has suggested that this lab worker might have been given an outdated vaccine, which is only available in Russia as it is not approved by the WHO or most other countries. This is a live-attenuated vaccine, meaning a weakened version of the bacteria is given, but it doesn’t always provide protection and sometimes can cause disease.
In short, we don’t know what happened because there is insufficient information from the Russian authorities. To understand what happened, investigators would need access to laboratory and clinical evidence, including genomic sequencing, pathogen identification and details of the worker’s research. Without this, we are left with speculation when only scientific certainty will do.
As a member of the WHO, Russia has an international legal obligation to share information with the agency. The WHO’s health regulations specifically cover “unusual and unexpected” events, as well as those with serious public health impact and with significant risk of international spread, or that risk affecting trade or travel. But unfortunately, as with most international law, there’s no real enforcement mechanism. There is a reliance on broad cooperation across countries, with the understanding that sharing information on disease spread is in all nations’ best interests.
The US government has also put pressure on Russia for answers, with Donald Trump saying he would speak to Putin about the situation. The US state department also formally requested further information under the international health regulations – the irony being that the US withdrew from the WHO in January 2026, but is now invoking the international framework it left behind.
As a scientist watching this unfold, I’m reminded that while we can have research and expert conferences into better diagnostics, faster genomic sequencing, more effective vaccines and accessible treatments, none of these advances can compensate for a failure to share the information needed to identify a pathogen in the first place. Preparedness is a political challenge as well as a scientific one. And without transparency, it will be a case of one step forward, two steps back.
Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
