content:
Some change in our lifestyles and environments over a generation has caused this increased risk. What, exactly, is a mystery
Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
I n the field of global health, we often talk about each generation living longer and healthier lives than their parents. We’ve seen this in the gains in life expectancy, the sharp decrease in child mortality and in the near elimination of many vaccine-preventable diseases. But since the turn of the century this progress has stalled, and in some cases several health metrics have gone backwards.
Take cancer, which was long thought to be a disease linked to old age. While most cancers do indeed still occur in elderly people, a new report highlights that a number of cancers are increasing in people who are under 50 , often referred to as “early onset cancer”. The report, undertaken by the World Cancer Research Fund, looked at data from 12 different cancer types in England, the US and the Netherlands over the past 20 years. What they found isn’t pretty.
While there were slight variations among the three countries, larger patterns are clear. Among women who are under 50 in England, breast, bowel, uterine, kidney, liver, pancreatic and stomach cancers have increased . For men under 50 in England, there were increases in bowel, kidney, liver, pancreatic and prostate cancers. This is the opposite of what we would hope to achieve in public health – and no, it isn’t only because we have better diagnostic tools, or are doing more testing. While this explains some of the increase, it doesn’t account for it all. The data indicates that younger generations are experiencing a higher incidence of some cancers than previous generations at the same age. Put more simply: you have a higher chance of cancer at a younger age than your parents.
Scientists are now working to unpick what has changed between generations that might be driving this uptick, especially trying to find things people may have been exposed to during childhood or adolescence in the 1990s that they wouldn’t have been in the 1950s.
Here are some potential explanations: what we eat has changed significantly over the past 50 years, with the rise in ultra-processed and fast foods as well as sugary drinks. We also are more sedentary as a population. These changes are linked to rising levels of excess weight and obesity. Body fat, especially around the vital organs and waist, is a risk factor for chronic inflammation, insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction, all of which are linked to higher cancer incidence. Globally, obesity rates have more than doubled among adults and quadrupled among adolescents since 1990. Data collected in 2024 found that about 66% of adults in England were either overweight or living with obesity .
But diet, physical activity and excess body weight doesn’t fully explain the rise of certain cancers – such as breast cancer – in young people. Studies have shown that for women before menopause, a higher BMI is, in fact, linked to a slightly lower risk of cancer (which is in contrast to older women, where a higher BMI significantly increases risk of developing breast cancer.) Going further, scientists are looking at the health impact of sustained exposure to environmental toxins like air and water pollution, chemicals and plastics that have become widespread and almost impossible to avoid over the past 50 years.
It has been scientifically challenging to identify one toxin that explains the global increase in cancers. Cancer can develop long after exposure to a toxic chemical, and over our lives we encounter a range of chemicals and pollutants. Saying which one, or whether it was during childhood, in utero, or adulthood, is difficult to pin down.
On the positive side, one area that we have made progress with in young people is lung cancer, largely driven by anti-smoking campaigns and widespread awareness of the links between smoking and lung cancer. So not everything is getting worse.
None of the continuing research into risk factors for early onset cancer should mean attaching blame to patients. One of the first human impulses when getting a diagnosis is to think “what caused this?”, and even further, “what have I done?” – and this isn’t helpful. In addition, scientists estimate that only 40% of cancers at a population level are because of an “individually modifiable” behaviour like smoking, alcohol consumption, diet, physical activity, or weight. The other 60% is a mix of ageing, genetic susceptibility, infection, possible environmental factors, and sometimes just bad luck.
With the research and investment continuing into scientific research, we will eventually learn what’s driving the rise in cancer in younger people. But for now, that mystery is still to be uncovered.
Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

content:
My brother Norman McCubbin, who has died aged 77, was a scientist who worked at the forefront of experimental particle physics.
A leading light in experiments that took place on the Large Hadron Collider , the world’s biggest and most powerful particle accelerator at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (Cern) in Switzerland, he spent the last five years of his working life as director of the particle physics department at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) in Oxfordshire, until his retirement in 2012. Afterwards he became a tutor to undergraduates at St Anne’s College, Oxford, and was still in that role at his death.
Norman was born in Pinner, Middlesex, the first child of Hugh, an accountant, and his wife, Pat (nee Rosenberg). The family moved to Leicester, where his brothers, Richard and I, were born, and then in 1958 to Kenya for Hugh to take up a post as finance director of the Kenya Farmers’ Association .
When Hugh joined the UN’s World Food Programme, the family moved to Lesotho and later, Taiwan, while Norman went to Repton school in Derbyshire as a boarder. After moving on to New College, Oxford, he gained a first-class physics degree and took a PhD.
Between 1973 and 1979 he was a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Lancaster and then at RAL, working with the laboratory on the first hadron collider at Cern to study the dynamics of proton-proton collisions. He then worked at Cern as a senior (then principal) scientific officer, where he concentrated on the collisions of heavy ions.
From 1990 to 1999 Norman led RAL’s Zeus experiment in Hamburg, studying the structure of the proton, and from 1999 to 2003 he was computing coordinator for the Atlas experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Later he became divisional head of RAL’s particle physics department while continuing with some of his work at Cern until, in 2007, he became the department’s director.
In retirement as a stipendiary lecturer in physics at Oxford, he was a popular tutor, relishing the core subjects of thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, relativity and symmetries. More prosaically, he relished answering questions, via video from New Zealand, from his ever-curious seven-year-old great-nephew Hugh, about issues such as gravity, centrifugal force and quantum entanglement.
Despite his dedication to his work, family and friendship always came first for Norman. We all basked in his warmth, love, humour and kindness, as well as that illuminating intelligence he wore so lightly.
He is survived by me and Richard, two nieces, two nephews, three great-nephews and a great-niece.

description: Australian of the Year would become the first astronaut in space to qualify under the Australian flag if she embarks on the 2028 mission Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The federal government has sent an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send the Australian of the Year, astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, to the International Space Station. author_name: Donna Lu Assistant editor, climate, environment and science
content:
Australian of the Year would become the first astronaut in space to qualify under the Australian flag if she embarks on the 2028 mission
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
The federal government has sent an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send the Australian of the Year, astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, to the International Space Station .
The mission, slated for 2028, will mark the first time a qualified astronaut has flown to space under the Australian flag.
The ESA offer for Bennell-Pegg to join a future ISS mission garnered support from philanthropists and the Australian space industry, but has previously described by the office of the science minister, Tim Ayres, as “a very expensive undertaking” which no government alone could fund.
Announcing the decision on Friday, Ayres said:“The government has been engaging extensively with the private sector, philanthropists, and other levels of government to raise funding to support a space flight – which is a significant cost.
“We are grateful to the philanthropists who have committed over $6m in cash, plus in-kind support, and some indicative support from some state governments.”
Bennell-Pegg is director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency (ASA) and completed astronaut training with the ESA in 2024.
She is not the first Australian astronaut, but she is the first to qualify under the Australian flag. Dr Andy Thomas and Paul Scully-Power, both Australian-born, went to space as US citizens on Nasa missions. Elaine Hyde, a dual Australian and US citizen, last year took a suborbital flight aboard Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin NS-30.
In May, the ASA announced it had entered into “treaty-level discussions” with the ESA, which “would establish a formal framework for enhanced cooperation between Australia and Europe”.
In August, Ayres and the assistant science minister, Andrew Charlton, wrote to state and territory leaders asking them to “partner” with the federal government to fund the mission. The letter, according to The Australian , described it as a “complete Australian mission that includes locally developed experiments and ­technology”.
South Australia, where the ASA is headquartered, has publicly committed to supporting Bennell-Pegg’s space bid.
“South Australia stands ready to partner with the commonwealth in what should be a national endeavour,” the premier, Peter Malinauskus, said. “Katherine Bennell-Pegg has the potential to inspire a new generation to dream big and address the single biggest challenge to our economy which is productivity.
“Australia has a massive shortage of young people taking up the fields of science, technology, engineering and maths, and we need more of it if we’re going to grow the nation’s productivity … Nothing would motivate young people more to take up these fields of endeavour than seeing Australia’s first ever flagged astronaut in space.”
A campaign to secure Bennell-Pegg’s spaceflight mission was supported by entrepreneurs Dick Smith and Jim Whalley – who had each pledged $1m funding for the mission – and former prime minister Kevin Rudd, who said on social media that the “project makes long-term economic sense for Australia beyond the usual sensibilities of the Treasury bean counters”.
Richard de Grijs, a professor of physics and astronomy at Macquarie University, said of Bennell-Pegg: “She is qualified, she has undergone significant training, so she is set to go up if a suitable mission can be found.
“The government has actually contributed quite a lot of money to that education already,” he said. The ASA paid $466,000 for Bennell-Pegg to complete her astronaut training at the European Astronaut Centre in Cologne, Germany.
“There is an inspirational value in sending a citizen from your country to space who is also the Australian of the Year … but the question is, is that worth $100m?” De Grijs said.
“It’s a lot of money, but on the other hand, it might actually lead to returns that are way more than the estimated number.”
De Grijs pointed out that Australia was also involved in “inspirational spaceflight” by another means: an Australian-built lunar rover, named Roo-ver , will be sent to moon on a Nasa mission in 2030.
Darin Lovett, chair of the Space Industry Association of Australia, said the industry had “a strong track record of return on investment”.
“For around $100m, less than the price of a single coffee for every Australian adult, this is not a ticket to space. It is a down payment on Australia’s future in one of the defining industries of this century.”
In a speech Bennell-Pegg delivered earlier this month, she described space as “a gateway – a lure – into the full breadth of STEM fields. Especially for those that dream of going up there.”

title: Did you solve it? The treacherous puzzle of the round table

content:
Earlier today I set you these six puzzles. Here they are again with solutions.
Three people sit at a round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.
Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left.”
1. What is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?
2. What is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?
1. The oldest person must be lying, so the maximum is 2. Here is an example with 2 people telling the truth:
30-40-20 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table)
2. The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the minimum is 1. Here is an example with 1 person telling the truth
Seven people sit at a different round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.
Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left, and I am younger than the person two places to my right”.
3. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?
4. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?
3. The two oldest people must be lying, so the answer cannot be six or seven.
It turns out that the answer cannot be five either. If five were telling the truth, the third oldest would be one of them, and so the three oldest people would have to be arranged in one of the two cases below (suppose the ages are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70).
* * * 60 * 50 70 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table)
But now there is nowhere for the next oldest (the 40-year-old) to sit and be telling the truth.
It is, however, possible for four people to be telling the truth:
4. The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the answer cannot be zero. If you order everyone in descending order of ages, no one is telling the truth apart from the youngest:
999 people sit at a third round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age.
Each of them says “I am younger than the person three places to my left, and older than the person three places to my right”.
5. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth?
6. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth?
5. We might think about this by colouring the seats gold, silver and bronze in a repeating pattern, like so (in the illustration there are only 21 people, but the idea works for 999 people as well).
It can now be seen that each person makes a statement about people sitting on seats with the same colour as them; in particular, the closest people on either side with the same colour seat.
Consider those 333 people sitting in gold. The youngest and oldest of these must be lying, so there cannot be 333 or 332 gold truthtellers. But, as the example below helps to illustrate, it is possible for every other gold person to be telling the truth, by seating them with age increasing as we move clockwise around the table. Applying the same reasoning to those seated on silver or bronze, we can have all but six people telling the truth.
The same idea with 999 people has 999-6=993 telling the truth.
6. If the people are sat with age decreasing as we move clockwise around the table, then everybody is lying.

title: Did you solve it? Isaac Newton’s tower drop puzzle
description: The solution to the seventeenth century stumper Earlier today I set you a puzzle that Isaac Newton posed in 1679 in a latter to Robert Hooke. I mentioned that the answer is counter-intuitive, and also gave you the hint that it might have something to do with figure skating. Here’s the problem again, with its solution. The tower drop slightly to the west slightly to the east exactly at the bottom Continue reading...
content:
The solution to the seventeenth century stumper
Earlier today I set you a puzzle that Isaac Newton posed in 1679 in a latter to Robert Hooke. I mentioned that the answer is counter-intuitive, and also gave you the hint that it might have something to do with figure skating. Here’s the problem again, with its solution.
An object is dropped from a high tower. Bearing in mind the rotation of the Earth itself, where will the object land?
Our first thought might be that the object falls slightly to the west, on the grounds that as the object is falling the Earth will rotate slightly to the east.
But such an argument ignores the fact that the object is originally – like the tower itself – rotating with the Earth . Our second thought might be that it lands exactly at the bottom of the tower.
Again wrong! The object lands slightly to the east because as it falls it spins about its axis slightly faster, by essentially the same mechanism that makes a spinning ice-skater spin faster when they pull in their arms. It is in this way, then, that the object lands slightly to the east.
The effect is small, but not absurdly so. If the Eiffel tower were on the equator the deflection to the east would be about 11cm.
In more technical detail, the result follows from conservation of angular momentum, which is a measure of the momentum of an object rotating about an axis.
When an object is falling from a tower, gravity is pushing it towards the centre of mass of the Earth. Yet the object is also spinning in a circle around the centre of the Earth.
As the object falls its angular momentum stays the same. Which means that the expression wr 2 – where w is the object’s angular velocity and r is its distance to the rotational axis (in this case, the centre of the Earth) – stays the same.
Since the value of r decreases during the fall, the value of w must increase, which means that the object spins faster. If it spins faster than the Earth is spinning it will land slightly to the east of the position directly underneath the tower.
Thanks to David Acheson for today’s puzzle. He is the author of a new book, Wonders in Motion, The Story of Dynamics, which among other things explains the background to Newton’s puzzle in more detail.
I hope you had fun. I’ll be back in two weeks.
Wonders of Motion by David Acheson is on sale at the Guardian Bookshop.

title: Can you solve it? Isaac Newton’s tower drop puzzle
description: The problem that changed the world UPDATE: Solution is now up Today’s puzzle played a pivotal role in the birth of classical physics. The tower drop slightly to the west slightly to the east exactly at the bottom Continue reading...
content:
Today’s puzzle played a pivotal role in the birth of classical physics.
An object is dropped from a high tower. Bearing in mind the rotation of the Earth itself, where will the object land?
The answer is counter-intuitive. Or, in the words of Isaac Newton, who posed the problem in a letter he wrote to Robert Hooke in 1679, the answer is “quite contrary to ye opinion of ye vulgar.”
Some hints. Think about how the spin of the Earth might affect the downwards trajectory. Also think about what happens when a spinning figure skater pulls in their arms.
I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solution.
PLEASE NO SPOILERS. Instead discuss your favourite seventeenth century scientists.
Today’s puzzle was suggested by David Acheson, emeritus professor of maths at Oxford and the author of several excellent popular maths books. His latest is Wonders in Motion, The Story of Dynamics, a beautifully accessible introduction to the science of motion.
Acheson’s book includes more background about the tower drop puzzle. Hooke’s correspondence with Newton rekindled Newton’s interest in gravity and motion, which ultimately led to his formulation of the mathematical foundations of classical physics in the Principia.

title: How to face the end of the world – according to Plato and the Stoics
description: Fearing future catastrophe is nothing new – ancient Greek and Roman philosophers all visualized the apocalypse
content:
Fearing future catastrophe is nothing new – ancient Greek and Roman philosophers all visualized the apocalypse
Do your feelings of existential dread extend beyond your own personal mortality? Do they include fears about the survival of our culture and institutions, our species, nonhuman life and the Earth itself? Do you feel like there’s nothing that can help to wrap your head around the biggest problem we face: the end of the world as we know it?
Apocalyptic expectations are on the rise. According to a 2022 Pew Research Center survey , 39% of Americans believe that we are living in the end times.
Yet the feeling that the world is coming to an end is nothing new. Anticipating and preparing for the end of the world is an ancient practice. In fact, many of the ways in which we envision future catastrophes can be traced back to the ancient Mediterranean world.
Greek and Roman authors set up their accounts of the end of the world as the product of reason rather than divine revelation – the product of the rational study of the laws of nature that govern the universe. They saw the end of the world as an inevitability and typically saw the aftermath, if there was one, as a repeat of the cycle of human development. The main piece of wisdom they seek to provide is how to face catastrophe without fear.
This is particularly true of the Epicureans and Stoics. Their goal is to meet all events up to and including the end of the world with equanimity. The Roman poet Horace offers a summation of this ideal in his Odes: the “righteous and resolute man” will remain “undaunted even if the sky should fall and the ruins strike his head”.
These ancient texts do not explicitly offer solutions or means of avoidance, and as Horace makes clear, they can envision the end of the world as the ultimate test of masculine endurance. Yet they also provide an understanding of the long perspective of human history, and how humanity relates to cosmological and geological history. Unlike our doomsday prepperism, their form of preparation did not require any building projects or financial expenditures; rather, they encouraged preparation that was psychological, epistemological and ecological. This required one to study nature in order to understand its workings and the place of humanity within it.
My new book, How to Face the End of the World , offers several passages from ancient Greek and Roman authors about the end of the world in the original Greek and Latin, along with my translation and introduction. The collection begins with a passage from the archaic Greek poet Hesiod’s Works and Days. The other texts are by ancient philosophers: Plato, Lucretius and Seneca. Each developed different scenarios for how the world could end, but all posited that the end would come from the forces of nature, rather than the wrath of the gods.
Ancient Greek and Roman accounts of world destruction, as well as Jewish and Christian apocalypses, tap into what is likely an underlying psychological truth about these types of stories. They are a means to understand the future, and to realize the hidden natural and divine forces at work in the cosmos. Their power to reveal ultimate truths and to prepare us to face the future may explain why stories about the end of the world are found across cultures and why they have persisted from the ancient world to today.
Hesiod (ca 700BC) is the classical world’s intellectual forefather for envisioning the end of humanity. One of Hesiod’s most famous stories is the myth of the metallic races. It traces the succession of humanity from the ideal time of the primordial “golden race” to the present “iron race”.
Hesiod predicts that at some point in the future, Zeus will destroy the current iron race. He enigmatically makes no mention of what will happen after this destruction. His silence served as an impetus for later authors to imagine different scenarios, ranging from a continuation of the cycle and a return to the Golden Age, to the end of humanity and the world itself.
Also contained in Hesiod’s account is the suggestion that humans can avoid Zeus’s wrath by honoring the gods and living a just and simple life. The prophecy of doom is not a fixed certainty, but rather a warning of what could happen.
Plato (420sBC–347BC) is perhaps most famous today for the portrayal of his hero, Socrates, and for the political philosophy of the Republic. Less well known is that he invented the story of Atlantis , which serves as part of his theory of cyclical global catastrophes.
In his dialogues Timaeus and the Laws, Plato posits that the world will exist for eternity, but that human development will be continually hindered due to periodic terrestrial catastrophes. In short, the world does not end, but advanced societies do.
With his stories, Plato appears to be testing the imagination of his audience. In the Laws, it seems clear that he is engaging in a thought experiment about how human society might rebuild after a global catastrophe. Unlike the violent post-apocalyptic narratives of today, Plato imagines that the survivors would live in peace and work together.
Epicurus (341BC–270BC) believed that the goal of life is pleasure and freedom from disturbance. For Epicurus and his followers, there was a strong connection between ethics and physics. In other words, understanding the nature of the universe was linked to living a good life.
Epicurus theorized that the cosmos consisted of atoms and void, as opposed to the other elements of earth, air, fire and water; that the gods existed, but did not care for humans. As a result, death was nothing to us – simply the dissolution of atoms back into the void. There was no punishment or reward to expect in the afterlife.
Very little of Epicurus’s work survives from the reported 300 volumes he composed, but a brief account of how worlds end is preserved in one of his letters: “A world is an encasement of a heaven, which contains stars and an earth and all phenomena and is separated from the infinite; it ends with a boundary that is either thin or thick and when this boundary breaks apart everything within it will be ruined.”
Epicurus’s most famous disciple was the Roman poet Titus Lucretius Carus (ca 98BC–ca 55BC). One key way in which Lucretius departs from and develops Epicurus’s teachings can be seen in his accounts of the end of the world. Lucretius offers two scenarios: slow, gradual decay, or one sudden day of destruction.
When we come to Stoic cosmology, we seem to leave the realm of plausibility and have to abandon our deep-seated notions of time’s arrow moving in one direction. But if you prefer to think of time as moving in great cycles of creation and destruction, or ever had the feeling of deja vu, the Stoics are for you.
Founded by Zeno of Citium (ca 334BC–ca 262BC) in Athens during the late fourth century BC, the Stoics argued that “creative fire” was the primal building block of the cosmos. Eventually this fire would consume everything and then the cosmos would be reborn, events known as the ekpyrosis (conflagration) and apokatastasis (restoration).
Only brief fragments and reports, some of them hostile, remain of the early Stoics on this theory. Some Stoics even rejected the idea of cyclical conflagrations. There are no detailed accounts of how the conflagration would unfold or how humans should prepare for it in the fragments that survive of the early Stoics. Most likely, it was believed to lie in the distant future.
The Stoic perspective on the end of the world changed during the Roman period. For example, as part of his daily practice of ethical philosophy, the emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote a brief reminder to himself in his Meditations that the end will come very quickly.
The most detailed Stoic accounts of the end of the world survive in the works of Seneca the Younger (ca 4BC–AD65). Among Greek and Roman authors, Seneca had the greatest interest in the end of the world. He wrote about it throughout his career, exploring different apocalyptic scenarios in several of his philosophical works, as well as one of his plays, the Thyestes.
Although Seneca’s descriptions of destruction go into great detail, he is not solely focused on the catastrophe itself. Rather, exploring the end of the world serves a deeper philosophical and therapeutic purpose. Like the Epicureans, the Stoics closely connected the study of ethics and physics. Understanding nature’s cycles could help one to live a better life by understanding that death is a part of nature, both for the individual and for our world.
In his Natural Questions , Seneca also considers how people would react when experiencing a global catastrophe. Seneca states that the destruction is close at hand, so perhaps his interest in human reactions to catastrophe was part of his own psychological preparation for the event.
What is the wisdom provided by these Greek and Roman authors? How might their visions of the end of the world help us today, if at all? On one level, we can see the origins of several narratives and ideas that are still very much alive today: the myth of decline from the Golden Age, Plato’s story of Atlantis, the Epicurean theory of total planetary destruction, as well as the Stoic theory of eternal return. Overall, however, it may simply seem depressing to read account after account of the end of the world.
Nevertheless, there may be value in envisioning the various forms that future global catastrophes could take. In 2020, a group of scholars published a piece arguing that morbid curiosity and exposure to apocalyptic and similarly frightening narratives can provide psychological tools and resilience when real catastrophes hit.
One of the members of the team, the literary scholar Mathias Clasen, wrote that mental time travel, the ability to imagine possible futures, has been important for human development. Apocalyptic narratives serve a key purpose in that they allow humans to imagine and plan for the “worst-case scenario”.
Other scholars, such as philosopher Hans Jonas, have urged us to accept that the odds are high that catastrophe awaits us in the future. We should not only envision the future as catastrophe but wager that the future will be bad rather than good. Yet this is not simply a prediction of doom and despair. As the contemporary philosopher and cultural critic Slavoj Žižek noted in Too Late to Awaken: What Lies Ahead When There Is No Future?, perhaps envisioning the future catastrophe as inevitable is paradoxically the way to avoid it.
Ancient philosophers might be best known for writing lengthy tomes. They did not compose works summarizing their theories of the end of the world but rather included them within larger philosophical arguments on nature, ethics and politics. But there also was the tradition of distilling ideas into a short work, or enchiridion, that one could keep close to hand – the literal meaning of the word. We can perhaps let the ancient Greek and Roman apocalypses discussed here and collected in my book serve as a low-stakes method of doomsday prepping.
Excerpted from How to Face the End of the World: An Ancient Guide for Apocalyptic Times (2026), published by Princeton University Press and reprinted here by permission
Christopher Star is professor of classics and director of the Axinn Center for the Humanities at Middlebury College. His books include Apocalypse and Golden Age: The End of the World in Greek and Roman Thought

title: Macron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest
description: French president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrations
content:
French president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrations
Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases
Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend.
Speaking after a ​meeting with intelligence officials and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed.
Protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but they might have to use alternative routes.
The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.”
Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the republic”.
“The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.
An initial police ban on a student protest planned in Paris for Thursday was overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for the day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted.
Authorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze.
Authorities in Marseille, Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at the Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre.
However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said.
France’s main student union, UNEF, has also called ‌for rallies on Saturday. Businesses in central Paris and other cities had already begun boarding up their windows and hiring private security in preparation for violence, French media reported.
The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 174 of the 2,500 people arrested since last weekend’s rioting had been remanded in custody and more than 900 were being prosecuted. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big-city mayors later in the day.
The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Élysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations.
The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high-school pupils around the country.
Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections, which will choose Macron’s successor.

title: South Africa beat Boland and weather to force series decider against Australia
description: Scott Boland batted for more than three hours but South Africa beat Australia by an innings and 31 runs in the second Test in Gqeberha
content:
Rabada and Mulder lead hosts to victory in second Test
Boland bats for more than three hours as nightwatchman
It took time, it gently frayed nerves, but South Africa sealed the second Test in Gqeberha deep into the final day, clear by an innings and 31 runs, levelling the series with one to play. Although Australia made 295 and got within 28 overs of safety, they did not deserve to save this game, even if Scott Boland and Travis Head did.
Letting South Africa escape from 40 for four to pass 400 was the first offence, then came Australia’s capitulation for 99 to be forced to follow on. The salvage operation was in waters too deep.
Australia got an early boost from a washed-out morning session that cut the day’s ration from 98 overs to 82. The next boost came from Boland: having done it all with the ball while nobody else could match him, he then led with the bat. He had the nightwatch job in the first innings, batting briefly on the fourth morning, then had to do it a second time that evening, taking Australia to stumps at 156 for four.
On day five, though, his stay was anything but brief. With his team four wickets down and 170 runs behind, Boland settled in for the most substantial innings of his Test career, a personal best of 166 balls, while his 40 runs nearly doubled his previous best. He outlasted century-maker Head, outlasted Steve Smith and passed the tea break after an extended session.
There was the odd dabble at the wrong ball, the odd bit of luck with an edge, but the rest was an exercise in careful defence on the front foot, evasion on the back, batting out maidens with relative ease and taking rare chances for a stylish cut.
At the other end, Head did not tarry in the 90s with a few carved boundaries through the off side, then settled right down after raising his first official hundred in an away Test – his World Test Championship final ton against India at the Oval in 2023 being defined as neutral in venue. By his standards it was a sedate 121 from 190 balls and while it continued the spectre of the draw became a little more material, even though change hovered one wicket away.
It was fitting that the day was defined by Wiaan Mulder, the shortest, least rapid and least celebrated member of South Africa’s fast-bowling stocks. Humility is at Mulder’s core, the man who declined a shot at breaking the world record score , the man who does whatever job his team asks of him: new ball in Durban with two spinners, old ball when Kagiso Rabada returns, stepping up for more overs when Anrich Nortje is injured, bowling into a serious wind, batting three when nobody else wants it, batting seven when they do, attempting to bat time when Australia were bowling for victory, stopping them from batting time when the tables had turned.
Here, his approach was simple and skilful: hit the seam, wait for jag. Head got plenty, shorter and faster than expected, making him jump, forced to glove down on to his stumps. Boland got a better one, fuller and decking into the gap for the right-hander, even his set defence no chance of keeping it out.
An over later, Mulder repeated the dose to Pat Cummins, the ball moving a little less this time to make him play inside the line. Mulder’s three for 64 will not be written on any walls, but it won the match.
That left the score 262 for eight, with Smith already gone, and while reputation would suggest that he was the most important wicket, that belies his long record of having no effect on fifth days. Showing no sign of the stiff neck that had hampered him the previous day, Smith nonetheless torpedoed his brief innings with an atrocious shot, trying to pound a pull shot off Rabada from outside off stump, hitting a catch up in the air.
With nothing needed but to bat time, it was a decision as poor as Marnus Labuschagne’s attempted six off Simon Harmer’s spin the previous day. The comparison of either to Boland’s determination is catastrophically unflattering. While the lower order is not primarily to blame, you could equally ask why Mitchell Starc tried swinging Rabada over the leg side, instead finding fresh air and losing leg stump. Or why Josh Hazlewood tried a booming drive through cover to nick to slip, stranding Alex Carey on 37 not out. Marco Jansen got that last wicket, Rabada finished with four.
With so few overs to go, and with heavy cloud starting to roll in, this was a match that could have been saved with more application from one or two players. It concluded an Australia performance riven with fundamental failures of decision-making, from players whose celebrated wealth of experience gives them no excuse for that shortfall.
For South Africa, it is a dramatic comeback from their own heavy loss at Durban and a reminder that all revelry and disappointment is temporary. There will be another portion of each, however, to be doled out next week in Cape Town. The decider beckons.

title: Russia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine
description: Experts say Russia is trying to destroy energy infrastructure before winter and US ‘appeasement and flattery’ will not achieve peace
content:
Experts say Russia is trying to destroy energy infrastructure before winter and US ‘appeasement and flattery’ will not achieve peace
Russia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations after talks with the US envoy Steve Witkoff.
Overnight, Moscow pounded the Ukrainian capital, killing at least two people and wounding 22, including four children. Targets included the southern bridge over the Dnipro River, civilian houses, energy infrastructure, an ambulance station, office buildings and a clinic.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , said three of the missiles carried cluster warheads. One struck the Pecherskyi district, damaging several historic structures, including a monastery.
“This is another extraordinarily revealing strike – revealing, because it was no accident,” Zelenskyy said. “The choice of weapon was deliberate; the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible.”
He said the strikes showed Russia was not serious about peace, adding: “Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening.”
During negotiations on Wednesday in St Petersburg, Witkoff lavished praise on Putin, who was sitting across the table. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said.
In a social media post after the strikes in the early hours of Thursday, Zelenskyy issued a sardonic reply: “Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles.”
Zelenskyy said he was grateful to those among Ukraine’s western partners who saw “the situation for what it is” and “acknowledged the reality” that the Kremlin had little intention of stopping its war. He called for stronger air defences, Patriot interceptors that could bring down enemy missiles, and more sanctions against Moscow.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, ⁠Andrii Sybiha, ⁠added that “appeasement, ⁠servility ​and flattery” ‌would ‌not ‌stop Russian aggression.
Downing Street said it did not recognise Witkoff’s description of Putin, pointing out that the Russian president had killed “thousands” of Ukrainians and his own frontline soldiers.
On Wednesday, the Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said Putin had agreed “in principle” to resume three-way negotiations involving Russia, the US and Ukraine after 10 November, a week after the US midterm elections. In reality, Russia’s intention is to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in the coming weeks, leaving millions in the dark and cold , officials in Kyiv believe.
According to Zelenskyy, the US has resumed intelligence warnings of Russian missile attacks. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump called Elon Musk to ask him to reverse the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Musk’s Starlink internet satellite system, which had left Ukraine unable to intercept enemy drones or carry out mid-range battlefield strikes. Some Ukrainian officials reportedly told the Journal that the system had been working marginally better since the call, but others said it was still heavily restricted.
The New York Times reported that when the slowdown was imposed last week, dozens of armed drones heading to Russian military targets fell from the sky. The video feeds streaming their flight paths suddenly went fuzzy as the connection with Starshield was lost, the paper said.
Vladimir, the commander of an air-defence unit protecting Kyiv, said the US restrictions had hampered his unit’s ability to intercept Russian drones. “Of course it’s hindering us. Our drones can no longer reach the speeds needed to intercept enemy targets,” he said, adding that he felt betrayed by Washington.
The decision to cripple Ukraine’s successful drone programme came amid the most serious row between Washington and Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. It began after Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel , to lower US fuel prices, a move that Zelenskyy criticised as “weak”.
The Trump administration denies it is deliberately helping the Russians. But European diplomats concede that the US appears to have switched sides. Ukrainian civilians are dying as a result, they say.
Russia, meanwhile, said it had shot down hundreds of Ukrainian drones launched in overnight attacks. One man ⁠was ⁠killed ​and another was ⁠wounded as a ⁠result ​of ‌a Ukrainian aerial strike in Russia’s Belgorod region, local ‌authorities said.
Details also emerged of a Ukrainian counterattack through a tunnel in the north-eastern city of Kupiansk, which Russia partly occupies. As part of Operation Veles, the Khartia corps carried out the world’s first underground counteroffensive, advancing 15km into enemy rear lines.
“We observed how the enemy operates underground and studied their methods. The Russians intended to use gas pipelines to infiltrate the rear of our forces. So, we went underground ourselves,” Khartia’s commander, Brig Gen Ihor Obolienskyi, told Ukrainian media.
The Ukrainian soldiers crawled 15km through tunnels – without communication, GPS or light – having developed their own navigation and life-support technologies in advance. About 100 Russians were killed in the operation, and 30 taken prisoner, the Khartia corps said.
Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

title: Post-Ferguson worn-out horror show continues at Manchester United
description: In today’s Football Daily: A stake through the Michael Carrick era
content:
Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!
We’re in the midst of what the kids call “spooky season” – or, for our fellow fusty old-timers out there, “autumn”. If you’ve been cosying up with a few horror flicks this month, you’ll know nothing good can come from hanging around a lake at this time of year. And so it proved for Manchester United, who endured an early Halloween nightmare on the banks of Lake Como that may have driven a stake through the Michael Carrick era. Hailed as the interim anti-Amorim not so long ago, Carrick has overseen two wins this season, against Ipswich and Sabah Baku . Como were in Serie D when Carrick won Big Cup with United as a player in 2008 – now, 18 years on, he watched the Italian upstarts dance, twirl and shimmy through the set of training cones he had sent out to represent his storied club.
In the dugout, Carrick appeared frozen by fear. If there had been a sofa perched on the touchline, he may well have crouched behind it to avoid the series of jump-scares served up by his players. At the end, he walked over to the three United fans who had stuck around and held up his hands, looking like a cross between Ole Gunnar Solskjær and a doomed Squid Game contestant. But somehow, things were about to get worse. A week after Lisandro Martínez had taken aim at (or, in truth, just below) United’s hapless hierarchy, Bruno Fernandes decided to swing a little lower. Asked about his side’s tactics, Fernandes said it was “ on the manager and staff to see ”, before offering a surprisingly detailed dissection of Carrick’s pressing techniques. Now 32, perhaps Fernandes is eyeing the lucrative podcast market, where former United players are busy making hay by stating the obvious. Perhaps he’s just full of it. Carrick fired back with a maxim that works for horror-movie protagonists and lazy footballers alike: “If you don’t run, you ain’t going to win.”
In truth, Manchester United’s entire post-Ferguson era feels like a worn-out horror franchise, a repetitive cycle of diminishing returns that has churned through managerial victims, while still finding new ways of scraping the barrel. United fans might have dared to dream that City’s guilty verdict marked the end of the nightmare; instead, a new team of FFP-baiting waifs in shiny blue shirts have appeared, also led by a crafty Catalan. Carrick might not make it past United’s trip to Stamford Bridge on Halloween, but could Cesc Fàbregas replace him? Asked before the game, the Como head coach snapped back: “I don’t think that shows enough respect to a great footballer and manager like Michael Carrick, at the helm of a wonderful Manchester United side.” Tone it down a bit, Cesc, it’s giving sarcastic. Fabregas is on the bookies’ speculative longlist to replace Carrick, but it’s hard to fathom why he would take the job. At Como, he has total oversight of a talented team, a financial stake in the club and all the perks of Italian lakeside living. It’s a lot to give up just to be pushed around by Jason Wilcox.
Big Website reports that Frightfest tropes Julian Nagelsmann (hipster lost in woods) and Unai Emery (vampire) are the leading candidates . Our personal pick, purely for content reasons, would be Antonio Conte, who would surely combust with rage within a week. Ultimately, will it matter? We all know the big reveal by now: the real villains at Old Trafford are in the boardroom, hollowing out the mistreated mega-club like an overripe pumpkin. Much like reading a tea-timely email packed with too-early Halloween gags, bringing United back to relevance is a tortuous process that nobody has the strength to complete. For now, the nightmare continues.
Join Daniel Harris for an all-encompassing clockwatch taking in the early (5.45pm BST) and late (8pm BST) kick-offs in Bigger Vase, with updates from Lech Poznan 0-3 Sunderland, Bournemouth 1-2 Milan, Celtic 2-2 Celta and more.
“We’re not against anyone and we’re not in favour of anyone” – the president of the Asian Football Confederation, Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, gives no hint about the body’s support – or opposition – to the re-election of Gianni Infantino as Fifa overlord. How very helpful.

title: Pete Hegseth reportedly authorizes DHS to test ‘heat ray’ at US-Mexico border
description: The Pentagon’s Active Denial System shoots energy beam that causes ‘sensation of intense heat on surface of skin’
content:
The Pentagon’s Active Denial System shoots energy beam that causes ‘sensation of intense heat on surface of skin’
Pete Hegseth , the US secretary of defense, reportedly signed a memo last month permitting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to test a non-lethal “heat ray” for potential use at the US southern border.
The “heat ray”, known as the Active Denial System , is a military-grade weapon that shoots an energy beam causing “a sensation of intense heat on the surface of the skin”, according to a 2009 National Defense University case study on the weapon.
The sensation “creates an intolerable sensation and reflexive movement” such as ducking or running.
In a memo, first obtained by CNN , Hegseth authorized a “temporary loan” of the Active Denial System to the DHS for seven months beginning in September. The DHS can request further use of the Pentagon system if needed.
A spokesperson for Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said in a statement it was “continually evaluating new technology, especially technology that can save lives while simultaneously enhancing national security effectiveness”.
When asked for comment, the Pentagon referred the Guardian to the DHS, which shared the CBP statement.
It is unclear what the DHS plans to use the Active Denial System for exactly, but the memo permits the department to use it for potential operations at the US-Mexico border .
The US military initially brought the system to Afghanistan nearly 20 years ago, but it was quickly returned home without ever being used, the Washington Post reported .
Previously, CBP officials reportedly considered using the Active Denial System in areas with a large number of illegal crossings or for crowd dispersal, but it was never deployed.
When used, the Active Denial System can produce an invisible beam of 95 gigahertz that penetrates about 1/64th of an inch into the skin, causing a burning sensation. (The system is technically not a “heat ray” because it uses millimeter waves, not infrared, Forbes reported in 2020 .)
Pentagon officials have compared the feeling to a blast of heat when opening a hot oven, according to CNN. The feeling is temporary, lasting between 10 and 15 minutes.
In 2012, the Marine Corps announced that the system was compliant with international legal obligations of the US, and officials said they felt “comfortable” that it was safe.
The new memo, seen by CNN, states that the DHS will be solely responsible for the system’s “employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures”. It also states that no Department of Defense personnel shall operate it.
During the first Trump administration, officials sought to use the Active Denial System, first in 2018 to stop migrants from crossing the border, the New York Times reported. Later, in 2020, the administration also sought it to control protests in Washington DC after the killing of George Floyd, the Washington Post reported .

title: One in 10 adults in England and Wales experienced domestic abuse in last year, ONS finds
description: Charities say ‘tip of iceberg’ figures show government is not fulfilling pledge to halve violence against women and girls
content:
Charities say ‘tip of iceberg’ figures show government is not fulfilling pledge to halve violence against women and girls
Almost one in 10 adults in England and Wales have experienced domestic abuse in the last year, a survey from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) has found.
The Crime Survey for England and Wales (CSEW) found that 9.6% of people aged 16 and over had experienced domestic abuse in the last year – which equates to about 4.7 million people.
This marked an increase compared with the year to September 2025, when the same survey found that 7.8% of adults – about 3.8 million people – had experienced domestic abuse.
Domestic abuse charities said the figures were concerning, as they indicated the government was “not on track to fulfil its pledge” to halve violence against women and girls in a decade.
The increase was driven by a significant rise in intimate partner abuse, which had increased by almost 2% compared with the previous year; there was no significant difference in family abuse, which had only grown by 0.1%.
The survey also found that 2.1% of people, equating to about 1 million, had experienced sexual victimisation, and 3.9%, or about 1.9 million, had experienced stalking. These figures were based on new questions, so are not comparable with previous estimates.
The ONS estimates that in total, 10.9% of people aged 16 years and over, or about 5.3 million adults, have experienced at least one of the three crimes of domestic abuse, sexual victimisation, and stalking.
Prevalence was higher among female victims, at 12.8%, or about 3.2 million women. But 8.9% of men – about 2.1 million – were also affected.
Meghan Elkin, head of crime statistics at the ONS, said: “While minor survey changes and the usual uncertainty around gathering data on this sensitive topic are likely to have affected these estimates, our assessment is that the rise in domestic abuse includes real change. More data points are needed to further understand the uncertainty and what this tells us about trends in domestic abuse.”
The statistics will be used as the main measure for monitoring the government’s ambition to halve violence against women and girls.
The CSEW is a face-to-face household survey based on more than 30,000 adult interviews annually. The data is released by financial year, with this year’s statistics relating to the year ending March 2026.
Alice Russell-Harris, the public affairs lead at Refuge, said: “The government has pledged to halve violence against women and girls … by 2034, but latest domestic abuse data from the ONS tells a troubling story.” She added: “This figure reflects what we sadly know to be true at Refuge: domestic abuse is devastating an unacceptable number of lives.
“Domestic abuse often goes unseen and unreported, so these figures likely represent the tip of the iceberg. While ONS has highlighted that changes in data collection, such as the introduction and implementation of new survey questions, may have contributed to this increase, what remains steadfast is our concern that the government is not on track to fulfil its pledge.”
She called for “vital investment” before next week’s autumn budget, urging the government “to provide the vital investment required to meet rising demand”.
“Refuge has been clear that this ambitious goal is simply not achievable without sustainable, long-term funding for specialist domestic abuse services,” she said, “but we have yet to see a financial commitment that matches the scale needed for every survivor to access timely support.
“Specialist support services, and the survivors which depend on them, cannot afford to bear the brunt of underfunding any longer.”
Farah Nazeer, CEO of Women’s Aid said the statistics represented “a staggering number of people affected in the last year” and were “a reminder that if domestic abuse doesn’t affect us directly it will be affecting someone we know”.
She said the charity was particularly concerned about the rise of online harassment “and how new forms of abuse are being perpetrated in line with digital trends”.
As government considered how to respond to these statistics, ministers should ensure their approach included investment in specialist responses, including in support services by and for the women that used them, and in the public services on the frontline of responding to domestic abuse, from policing and probation to health and education. “We hope that as the chancellor prepares the budget for next week, these shocking prevalence figures are at the top of his mind,” she added.
Sam Smethers, the CEO of Surviving Economic Abuse, said the statistics were “shocking, but sadly not surprising”.
“This rise highlights the urgent need to challenge the harmful attitudes that normalise men’s control over women’s money and tackle the rising living costs that give abusive partners further opportunities to tighten their control,” she said.
She added that research by SEA found that “young women and girls are twice as likely to experience economic abuse as any other age group, with abuse often beginning in the very first month of a relationship”.
She called on the government to act on its commitment to halve violence against women and girls “by transforming systems to stop abusers from taking economic control and ensuring victim-survivors have the support they need to escape and rebuild their lives”.
In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid . In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org .

title: Trump’s Fifa peace prize was a sham. A reimagined award can still have meaning
description: The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer
content:
The first awarding marked the apex of Gianni Infantino’s hubris. A new version could highlight the good in the world of soccer
P oor Fifa peace prize. Unloved, unliked, mocked, tainted by association with its first winner. And now demoted, too, after Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino, dumped the thing on the global governing body’s “social responsibility committee” to look after. To redeem it, rather than to ditch it, to spare Infantino the embarrassment of acknowledging that his fake prize was really just a fake prize all along.
Here is where we should probably acknowledge that, as fake prizes go, and in the context of what it was intended to accomplish, the first awarding of the Fifa peace prize was an unqualified success. It achieved exactly what it was meant to, made by Infantino to flatter Donald Trump, the man he needed to keep on his side to safeguard the riches to be extracted from the North American market in order to consolidate his power base within Fifa. Trump, the gullible buffoon, was pleased as punch – handed a big, golden bauble and a medal he placed around his own neck – and briefly forgot about the Nobel peace prize he desperately covets .
The 22-person social responsibility committee is one of the dozens of standing committees Infantino has created to dole out generous per diems to his allies. It has been charged with recasting the prize into a recognition of social harmony and responsibility, as the Guardian has reported , and will probably seek to depoliticize it – or at least stop awarding it to politicians. There are no aspiring autocrats to placate for the foreseeable future, after all, since Saudi Arabia’s de-facto ruler and host of the 2034 World Cup, Mohammed bin Salman, doesn’t seem to go in for that kind of thing.
That first incarnation of the prize will stand as a monument to Infantino’s folly, as the apex of his hubris and his era of genuflecting to strongmen. That is, of course, assuming he survives the fallout of his attempt to privatize a chunk of the World Cup and re-emerges somewhat chastened and cautious, if either of those behaviors are still within his capacity. And if he makes it through another presidential election in March.
But a second version of the Fifa peace prize holds genuine potential to highlight some of the good the sport occasionally does, to platform and recognize those who leverage soccer’s vast cultural influence to improve the lives of others. The magic of soccer is that it transcends the field and reflects cultures and geopolitics; it becomes anthropological ritual, spoken as the world’s common language. Sometimes, it transforms into a vessel for virtue.
You could give the new prize to Afghan Women United for getting recognized as the official representatives of their country all while playing as refugees in exile. In June, they contested a pair of friendlies against the Cook Islands in New Zealand. They lost both matches, yes, but that’s beside the point. Their mere existence doubles as a towering protest against the Taliban, which has resumed its violent oppression of women since storming back into Kabul in 2021.
You could give it to the Ukrainian club Shakhtar Donetsk, for persevering and even thriving in spite of Russia’s invasion – either through proxies or outright – of their Donbas region a dozen years ago, forcing the club to play elsewhere ever since.
Give it to former Spain international Juan Mata, for his work with Common Goal in convincing other players and managers to donate 1% of their earnings to charity; to Marcus Rashford, for shaming the Tory government into feeding children during a pandemic; to Sadio Mané, for bankrolling the construction of a hospital and other infrastructure projects in his native Senegal; to N’Golo Kanté for doing much the same in Mali.
Give it to Scotland’s Tartan Army, for raising money for children’s charities wherever they play. Hell, give it to the England players for donating their match fees to charity causes since 2007, adding up to more than $6.7m (£5m).
How would any of this relate to peace? Fair question. The peace prize could stand to be rebranded, the better to disassociate it from the least peaceful leader of a western nation in generations. It should probably have clearer qualifications and regulations, too, which is to say that it should have qualifications and regulations. And it’s probably best to shy away from the notion of steering entirely clear of politics. You can either have an award that acknowledges social good or you can be apolitical. You cannot do both.
But that needn’t be a bad thing, if this prize is sincere in rewarding one of the sport’s best citizens – and so long as it serves more than the Fifa president’s selfish interests.
Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now . He teaches at Marist University.

title: What would make neonatal units safer for babies?
description: Letters: Dr Pamela S Melding highlights how New Zealand has created a healthcare culture where patient safety, interests and consent are the overriding principles. Plus letters from Mark Hanson, Paul Whiteing and a reader who lost her baby
content:
Dr Pamela S Melding highlights how New Zealand has created a healthcare culture where patient safety, interests and consent are the overriding principles. Plus letters from Mark Hanson , Paul Whiteing and a reader who lost her baby
I support Mark McDonald’s submission that the Thirlwall recommendations will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS ( 17 October ). We often hear of hospital scandals where trusts are intent on preserving their reputations, internal inquiries go nowhere, defensive clinical staff deflect blame on to others, non‑disclosure to patients of errors and “lessons learned” rhetoric that is quickly forgotten. There is also an industry of ambulance-chasing lawyers. None of this is conducive to a no-blame, honest, open culture in healthcare. The Thirlwall recommendations of more surveillance will make it worse.
There is an alternative. Most of my professional life as a hospital consultant, clinical director and deputy chief medical officer has been spent in New Zealand, whose publicly funded NHS is the same model as the UK’s – but with a major difference. In the 1970s, New Zealanders lost their right to sue for damages for medical accidents or injury through the public court system with the Accident Compensation Act . This got rid of the grievance culture and ambulance-chasers, and the system provided remedial care for any injury. In the 80s, after a huge scandal regarding medical investigations, the Cartwright inquiry ushered in the creation of the independent Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC) and overriding principles of patient safety, interests and consent.
All complaints – from patients, public and staff – about any health facility, organisation or practitioner go first to the office of the HDC for investigation. If the HDC deems it necessary, it goes to the various professional disciplinary bodies or to the Medical Council of New Zealand . HDC reports on complaints are publicly available.
In 2005, the government passed its “no fault, no blame” legislation. This brought in a duty to report “any risk of harm to the public from authorities responsible for patient safety”. This freed clinicians to engage with any compensation cases with openness. The system has its critics, but overall works well. Dr Pamela S Melding St Helens, Merseyside
Mark McDonald’s column is a breath of common sense. The Criminal Cases Review Commission is still considering Lucy Letby’s convictions, yet Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall has constructed a programme of reform on the assumption that the central conclusion of the case is beyond question. Meanwhile, barely enough time has passed for reflection on what would actually make neonatal units safer.
Thirlwall’s answer appears to be surveillance, suspicion and blame: cameras in cots, encouragement to report colleagues and an explicit retreat from the “no blame” culture developed precisely to make organisations safer.
But what makes a hospital safe? Is it a nurse wondering whether a colleague is about to report them, or a nurse confident enough to admit that they have made a mistake? Is it a doctor practising defensively, or one willing to report a near-miss before it becomes a tragedy?
Destroy candour and you destroy one of the most powerful tools of patient safety. A frightened workforce will hide mistakes, keep quiet about doubts and practise defensively. Patients will pay. Mark Hanson Hitchin, Hertfordshire
In March this year my daughter was born and died in the neonatal intensive care unit seven days later. I believe her death was preventable and one key mistake was made that resulted in her death. But I don’t blame the consultant who made (what I consider to be) the error. She was doing the best she could in a difficult situation.
What I find concerning is the follow-up from the trust’s management. They have bent over backwards to try to hide their tracks rather than discussing it openly and using it as an opportunity to learn and ensure other babies don’t suffer a similar fate. The response has been so heavy-handed that it’s an insight into the fear and blame culture doctors face, which I find so concerning. Mistakes are an opportunity to learn. Name and address supplied
Mark McDonald makes many good points. But sadly he overlooks the role that patients and families play in their healthcare and safety. The NHS needs staff who can speak up without fear. But it also needs patients who are listened to, informed, supported and involved. Some of the most important safety signals come not from systems, but from the people experiencing care. If there is one lesson from the Lucy Letby case, it is that patients and families must be recognised as partners in identifying risk, seeking answers and driving improvement. Paul Whiteing CEO, Action Against Medical Accidents

title: Carers can’t live on 51p an hour
description: Letter: Emma Sainsbury questions whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities shape their finances and ability to keep a home
content:
Emma Sainsbury questions whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities shape their finances and ability to keep a home
For 13 years, I have cared for my lovely 101-year-old adoptive mum who requires round-the-clock care. I feel blessed to care for her and have no regrets. But love does not pay the bills.
Carer’s allowance is £86.45 a week for 2026-27. Spread across 168 hours, that is roughly 51p an hour. As a sole carer, I have no downtime. I still work part-time as a self-employed therapist when Mum’s health allows, but when she is poorly, my work stops while the bills continue.
I do not claim carer’s allowance as the frequent paperwork required to report changes in my self-employed earnings is difficult to manage alongside my caring responsibilities.
Last winter, our electricity bill exceeded £400 a month because Mum needs heating round the clock. This is the reality of caring in a cost of living crisis. I worked hard to buy and pay off my own home. But it had no downstairs bedroom or bathroom, and was unsuitable for Mum. I had to rent it out, hoping one day to live there. Eventually, caring and the costs of maintaining the property forced me to sell, and I faced a capital gains tax bill.
I do not blame HMRC for applying the rules. I question whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities force them to make difficult decisions about their homes. Unpaid carers save society enormously, often at the expense of their own earnings, pensions and financial security. We need more than praise: we need practical support and a system that recognises the real cost of caring. Loving someone should not mean years of essential care leave you financially vulnerable. Emma Sainsbury Author, Love, Laughter and the Hidden World of Unpaid Carers

title: Do Stormont politics stifle the non-sectarian parties?
description: Letters: Responding to an editorial, Boyd Black deplores Labour’s policy of not fielding candidates in Northern Ireland. Plus a letter by Declan O’Neill
content:
Responding to an editorial, Boyd Black deplores Labour’s policy of not fielding candidates in Northern Ireland. Plus a letter by Declan O’Neill
Your editorial on the dysfunction in Northern Ireland politics ( 15 October ) does not mention the main cause: the denial of basic democratic rights to the people by the Labour party.
The party national executive committee refuses to run Labour candidates in any Northern Ireland election, whether to district councils, the Stormont assembly or the Westminster parliament.
This means people here, including affiliated trade unionists, are denied the basic democratic right to vote for our Labour government, which is setting our taxes and winding us up for war.
This undemocratic stance by Labour is not an act without consequences. By suppressing cross-community Labour party electoral politics, it forces the electorate into their ethnonational blocs and incentivises the sort of communal sectarian politics and stalemate that we are well used to. Boyd Black Secretary, the Labour party in Northern Ireland
It is undoubtedly true, as your editorial says that “Northern Ireland’s voters currently do not have the politics they deserve”. However, there are problems with your assertion that the current model of power-sharing “designed to reassure nationalist and unionist communities remains indispensable”. In fact, it plays a part in maintaining the current “cycle of dysfunction”.
I have family in Northern Ireland who would prefer to vote for parties that do not fit into this category, but doing so under the current rules would be pointless. They are part of a growing number of voters who do not primarily identify as being part of either “community”.
However, even if parties such as the Alliance, the Greens, People Before Profit were to win a majority at Stormont, they would under the current rules not be allowed to form an administration. In fact the current system reinforces sectarian division by stipulating that only those parties self-identifying as nationalist or unionist can “power-share”. Ireland needs real change. The current system cannot deliver it. Declan O’Neill Oldham, Greater Manchester

title: Storm names should tell a story or two
description: Brief letters: Storm Austen | Interpreting Hokusai | NI for pensioners | Creative car names | Queue for the Bayeux
content:
Storm Austen | Interpreting Hokusai | NI for pensioners | Creative car names | Queue for the Bayeux

But my excitement soon subsided when I read that Storm Austen has been named not for Jane, but Austen Nagle, the first director of the Met Office. Christine Shuttleworth London
Jonathan Jones rightly praises the new exhibition of Hokusai’s work in Dulwich ( Hokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji review, 19 October ). But in Japan the work is read from right to left. We go with the power of the wave, but if you reverse the print, the wave appears even more dangerous. David Cockayne Warrington, Cheshire
Re paying for sociall care (Letters, ( 19 October ), national insurance currently ceases at pensionable age. A simple way to raise funds for social care would be to reinstate NI for well-off pensioners. It could then be renamed social care insurance. Peter McCartney Bristol

The current crop of Chinese cars is a veritable seam of rich pickings: Jaecoo (cleaning cloths); Omoda (washing powder); Chery Tiggo (fruity gobstoppers). Struggling with Ora Funky Cat… Phil Thomas Frodsham, Cheshire
