title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular pleads not guilty to raping teen
description: The social media personality denies allegations he gave a girl alcohol until she was drunk and sexually assaulted her
content:
The social media personality denies allegations he gave a girl alcohol until she was drunk and sexually assaulted her
The “looksmaxxing” livestreamer Braden Peters, better known by his stage name Clavicular , pleaded not guilty on Thursday to charges that he raped a 17-year-old girl at his family’s Massachusetts home.
A social media personality known for promoting extreme devotion to male beauty, Peters, 20, is accused of giving the girl alcohol until she was drunk and then sexually assaulting her when she visited him in Chatham, on Cape Cod, in May 2025.
Peters has denied the allegations through his lawyers, saying the sexual encounter was consensual.
Peters arrived at the courthouse in Orleans, Massachusetts , wearing a dark suit, walking a barking dog on a leash. He spoke only to the dog as he entered the courthouse and ignored reporters’ questions. Peters maintained a neutral facial expression during the brief arraignment.
He has agreed to a $10,000 bail, surrendered his passport and will not contact or post about the woman who has accused him of assault.
He and his lawyers also did not comment as he left the courthouse.
The case is the latest legal challenge for Peters, who has a million followers on Instagram, and whose hours-long live streams feature him rating people’s looks and talking about methods of becoming better looking that include surgery and drug use.
Earlier this year, he was charged with misdemeanor battery in Florida after police said he provoked a fight between two women and then posted a video of it online. That charge was later dropped. In a separate Florida case this year, he was sentenced to probation after pleading no contest to a charge that he fired a gun in public.
The woman who accused Peters of rape told police he had been paying her to appear in his “looksmaxxing” videos. She alleged that during her visit to a Peters family home, he gave her two or three shots of vodka, then livestreamed himself kissing her while she was drunk. She told police that when she woke up the next morning, Peters was raping her.
The Associated Press generally does not name people who say they were victims of sexual assault unless they consent to being identified publicly.

title: Virginia Democrat indicted on federal drug and money-laundering charges
description: Federal authorities allege L Louise Lucas, a state senator and vocal Trump critic, led a ‘criminal marijuana enterprise’
content:
Federal authorities allege L Louise Lucas, a state senator and vocal Trump critic, led a ‘criminal marijuana enterprise’
Virginia state senator L Louise Lucas, one of the state’s most powerful Democrats, was charged on Thursday in connection with what federal authorities alleged was a role leading a criminal enterprise that acquired and distributed large quantities of marijuana and laundered the proceeds.
An indictment unsealed on Thursday charged Lucas and six other defendants, including several of her relatives, the Department of Justice said in a statement. Lucas surrendered on Thursday, a justice department spokesperson said.
The charges, including drug trafficking and money laundering, came after the FBI searched Lucas’s home town office and a cannabis shop in which she has a stake in May. At the time of the search, Lucas – who has been a vocal critic of Donald Trump’s administration – characterized it as an attempt to intimidate her.
“This is the circus we always expected it to be, and we will wait for further details to have a more specific response,” Brian Woolfolk, chief counsel for the L Louise Lucas Legal Defense Fund, told the Associated Press on Thursday.
The brash 82-year-old lawmaker has spent decades ascending the ranks of Virginia politics and has served since 1992 in the state senate, where she is the president pro tempore, overseeing the chamber in the lieutenant governor’s absence. More significantly, she leads the powerful senate finance committee, through which all legislation with any budget impact must flow. She’s used the position to stop and ultimately kill legislation she opposes.
Kash Patel, the FBI director, said in a statement that the charges alleged: “Lucas and a close-knit group of family members and associates orchestrated a multi-year scheme to enrich their own criminal marijuana enterprise, ‘the Lucas Enterprise’ – using Lucas’ position as Chairwoman of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to insulate the enterprise from criminal scrutiny and influencing legislation to financially benefit themselves.”
“No one is above the law”, the statement said, “and this FBI will continue to follow the facts with our Justice Department and ensure those responsible for criminal conduct are held accountable.”
Lucas has been a leading voice in Democrats’ ultimately failed attempt to redistrict the state’s congressional map this year, a bid to hedge against Republican efforts in other states to redraw maps for their advantage in the midterm elections.
A forceful advocate of legalizing marijuana, Lucas partnered in opening the the Cannabis Outlet shop in 2021, selling hemp and CBD products. While marijuana is legal to possess in Virginia, recreational retail sales of the drug are not yet under way, though shops across the state do sell other cannabis-derived products.
Lucas also runs a network of companies that provide residential, transportation and other services to adults with intellectual disabilities.

title: Zadie Smith among authors letting public bid to name new characters for charity auction
description: Other prizes at Freedom from Torture event include rare Mary Wollstonecraft book illustrated by William Blake
content:
Other prizes at Freedom from Torture event include rare Mary Wollstonecraft book illustrated by William Blake
Margaret Atwood, Zadie Smith and Ian McEwan are among a number of literary stars auctioning off the chance for readers to name characters in their next novels to raise money for survivors of torture.
The auction is part of Freedom from Torture’s 10th anniversary literary festival, which brings together leading authors and survivors for a celebration of storytelling, featuring a poetry competition and live readings at the London Library on 11 November.
More than 75 authors, poets, artists and illustrators are supporting the festival, with other prizes including original artwork by Quentin Blake, a rare book of Mary Wollstonecraft stories illustrated by William Blake, and a book club visit from the author Louise Doughty.
A bookmark raffle will feature more than 30 original designs by authors, each paired with a signed copy of the book that inspired it. Contributors include David Nicholls, Mark Haddon, Felicity Cloake, Nathan Filer, Nikesh Shukla, Sathnam Sanghera and Jeremy Vine.
The festival also features a poetry competition centred on the experiences of torture survivors, judged by the Booker prize-winning novelist Alan Hollinghurst and the poet Rachael Allen.
It comes amid growing concern over asylum policies in Britain and across Europe, with the charity warning that changes to legal protections could put torture survivors at risk of being returned to the countries they fled.
Samuel Morton, the special events and philanthropy manager at Freedom from Torture, said that the festival is inspired by their creative writing group, Write to Life, which is the UK’s longest-running refugee writers group, and believed to be the only one in the world for survivors of torture.
“They meet weekly and put pen to paper, and it’s a brilliant way to support each other and to process the things that they’ve been through in their trauma, as well as their hopes for the future.”
Four members from Write to Life will perform their own work at the London Library alongside acclaimed writers including Max Porter and the poet John Hegley.
Tracy Chevalier, the bestselling author of Girl with a Pearl Earring and The Last Runaway, is another of the authors joining the auction. She has supported the charity’s literary auctions since 2006, but admitted she was initially nervous about letting strangers name her characters.
“Names are important to me in my books,” Chevalier said. “What I choose to call a character, who I’m going to live with in my head for the next few years, they need to mean something to me.”
To her delight, her first winning bidder was Laura Devine, whose name she gave to a circus performer in her novel Burning Bright. The pair have remained friends ever since.
Chevalier has taken part in three more character-naming auctions, including one that saw her turn the name Dody Bienenstock into a “no-nonsense landlady” in San Francisco. She also praised the festival for giving survivors the opportunity to share their experiences in their own words.
“The story of your life is inside of you and for a lot of people it’s not great,” she said.
“They’ve had really terrible experiences and that pressure builds and to not only let it out, but control how you let it out. [To say] this is my story and I’m going to tell it. I’m not going to have a journalist tell it for me or a famous writer. I’m speaking.
“And the incredible power of that, of writing it down, so that it gets out of you and on to the page, and then you can shape it and do with it what you will, or throw it away if you want.”
Chevalier said many authors were drawn to the cause by concerns over the worsening treatment of asylum seekers in Britain. “I’m an immigrant myself, but nobody’s ever questioned my right to be here. And that’s because I’m white and American,” she said.
Morton criticised the government’s proposals to weaken the appeals system and raised concerns over the growing appetite across Europe to weaken legal safeguards, such as Article 3 of the European convention on human rights.
“Poor-quality asylum decisions risk sending survivors back into the hands of their torturers,” Morton said. “These protections are fundamental and must not be weakened for political convenience.”

title: Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’
description: Exclusive: Michael Aboud, whose actions in what he believed to be a documentary are likely to come under considerable scrutiny, has expressed anger at the film-maker• This article contains substantial spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I?
content:
Exclusive: Michael Aboud, whose actions in what he believed to be a documentary are likely to come under considerable scrutiny, has expressed anger at the film-maker
This article contains substantial spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I? Review: Ali G: Who Iz I?
The chair of the El Paso County Republican Party has said he intends to sue Sacha Baron Cohen over footage of the local politician used in new satirical comedy Ali G: Who Iz I?
In the film, Michael Aboud is shown taking part in a training programme with another Cohen character, ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, who instructs Aboud and fellow Maga sympathisers in self-defence techniques including the wearing, over clothes, of protective plastic buttocks. He also schools them in how to fire bullets from the middle of these buttocks by the repeated up and down manipulation of a rubber penis.
Aboud and a fellow student, former preacher and aspirant actor Joshua Loudermilk, are then recruited by Morad to help in a mission to prevent the birth in the US of the baby of a (fictional) South American drugs kingpin.
This involves Aboud and Loudermilk abducting his heavily-pregnant girlfriend and driving her in a phoney ambulance to a remote unstaffed medical facility, where she gives birth (to a lifelike prosthetic).
They then abandon her, Morad having placed her live baby in a zipped bag, and drive with it towards Mexico. Loudermilk is later seen attempting to discharge fire from his fake buttocks, while Aboud takes the decision to drop the baby – at that point being dangled from a drone at a substantial height – to the ground to prevent it touching US soil. The actions could not be anything other than extremely serious for a real infant.
Until the Guardian contacted Aboud on Tuesday, the businessman was unaware of his participation in anything other than what he believed to be a nonfiction film. In a statement, Aboud called Baron Cohen “and his entire film crew … a bunch of liars [who] deceive people to benefit themselves. They claimed that this would be a documentary about the illegals crossing the border. Then they said they were adding in this self-defence guy from Israel.”
He added: “It is my opinion that Sasha Cohen [sic] is a pervert. Plus he talked about how Muslims are all gay because they follow the sex practices of Mohamid [sic]. No one should spend one penny watching anything he produces or appears in. I plan to sue him.”
Pressed further on whether he stands by his actions in the film, Aboud declined to comment.
The film repeatedly stresses that neither Aboud nor Loudermilk are “in on it”. Loudermilk has not responded to requests for comment, but his social media feed suggests a level of understanding about the project not shared by most of his fellow participants.
Earlier this week, Loudermilk posted on Facebook that “I got to spend 12 hours one on one with Sasha [sic] and he taught me soooo much about the fun of making others laugh” as well as a link to a video promo for the film, saying, “I am in the trailer.” On 10 January, he also posted a headshot of himself, saying: “Howdy. Done with Sasha Cohen movie and ready for more.”
Representatives for the film have told the Guardian that Loudermilk was unaware of the true nature of the film.
Aboud’s shock at his involvement is particularly surprising given that he, along with Loudermilk, features in the second trailer for the film, which was released a fortnight ago.
That clip alone contains considerable clues to those involved that all is not what it seems. In his address to the recruits, Morad, who was a fixture of Baron Cohen’s 2018 show Who is America?, advises the group that they should not be fooled, for the immigrants they are set against “are not coming here to mow your lawn, trim your trees, rake your leaves, clean your house, care for your babies, bus your tables, wash your cars, paint your houses, build your fences, install your roofs, drywall, plumbing or electric. They are coming to kill you.”
Another section of the film involves Ali G hosting a “free speech” web show in which he is given a questionable script to read by South African producer Dirk Visser, who could not be contacted for comment.
The character also presides over a gameshow of Visser’s invention in which contestants, against the clock, must stuff mannequins depicting “undesirables” including rappers, gay people, Muslims and Mexican babies into pretend shower cubicles, before pressing a button to seemingly activate the release of the poisonous gas Zyklon B. The segment ends with a mass Nazi salute.
One of those who takes part is the disgraced former Republican congressman George Santos, who tells the camera his takeaway from playing the game is that next time he would try to grab more babies, as they’re easier to fit in the shower. In correspondence with the Guardian, Santos also suggested he was unaware of the true nature of the film, “as me and my team had no involvement”, and declined to justify his behaviour.

title: Criminals who refuse to attend sentencing face losing prison privileges under new rules
description: England and Wales judges to be able to keep inmates in cells for longer or stop visits if they refuse to face victims’ families in court
content:
England and Wales judges to be able to keep inmates in cells for longer or stop visits if they refuse to face victims’ families in court
Offenders who refuse to face their victims’ families in court for sentencing could be stripped of privileges or kept in cells for weeks under government changes granting wider powers to judges in England and Wales.
The imposition of new prison sanctions, coming into effect next year, builds on existing laws that order offenders to attend sentencing or face a fine or be jailed for a further two years for contempt of court.
“Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice. Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences,” said the prisons minister, Catherine McKinnell.
The new rules, to be laid before parliament on Thursday, will grant judges new powers to impose a loss of prison privileges for 84 days, cell confinement for 21 days, a loss of social visits for 27 days and a restriction on visits to once every four weeks, for 84 days. They could result in offenders already facing decades behind bars facing additional punishments.
The Ministry of Justice has said that while no measure could guarantee offenders would attend their sentencing hearing, the widened powers strengthened the consequences for offenders and ensured they could be “appropriately punished”.
Pia Sinha, chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, raised questions for ministers as to whether the new rules would achieve the aim of getting offenders to attend sentence hearings.
“These measures will inevitably affect not only prisoners but also family members, including children, who rely on prison visits to maintain contact, and who have committed no offence themselves,” Sinha said.
Younger offenders aged 18 to 20 could have privileges removed for up to 21 days or be confined to cells for up to 10 days, said the MoJ. Visits from prisoners’ children will be exempt, to help maintain family ties and when in the child’s best interests.
Claire Waxman, the victim’s commissioner for England and Wales, who has worked with relatives of the murder victims Sabina Nessa , Zara Aleena and Jan Mustafa, said the announcement reflected the “tireless efforts” of victims’ families.
“I know how offenders’ refusal to attend sentencing hearings compounds trauma and robs families of one of the very few moments of accountability in the justice process,” said Waxman. “It is now essential that these powers are used consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve.”
The move comes after nearly 2,000 prisoners across England and Wales were released from prison this month as part of a government plan to ease prison overcrowding.

title: Shamonda virus detected in human for first time in France
description: Investigations under way to determine whether virus normally found in livestock contributed to man’s death
content:
Investigations under way to determine whether virus normally found in livestock contributed to man’s death
A man in France has become the first human known to have contracted Shamonda virus, with investigations under way to explore whether it contributed to his death.
Shamonda virus is a type of bunyavirus and is spread by bites from infected midges. According to the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety , in animals such as cattle, sheep and goats it can cause diarrhoea, lack of appetite and a decline in milk yield, “as well as abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn calves, lambs and kids”.
“In Switzerland and Germany, the presence of Shav [Shamonda virus] genetic material has also been reported in the brains of horses that died from neurological symptoms,” the agency said.
The virus has previously been found in farm animals outside Europe, but was first detected in livestock on the continent in the summer. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said the patient in France was the first recognised human infection.
It also noted that he had already been seriously ill and had a compromised immune system, meaning it was unclear whether the virus played a role in his death this month.
“Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing,” the ECDC has said.
Prof Tom Solomon, the director of the pandemic institute at the University of Liverpool, said the risk to the general public appeared to be very low.
“Shamonda virus has been circulating in animals, particularly cattle, but also sheep, goats, horses and alpacas, for many years, yet this is the first recognised human infection,” he said.
“This suggests that transmission to humans is extremely unusual.”
But unknowns remain, he said: “We don’t know whether healthy people can become infected without developing symptoms, what symptoms the virus might normally cause, or how frequently it might cause serious disease.
“French authorities believe the neurological complications in this patient were very likely linked to the infection, although investigations are continuing.
“This is clearly concerning, but one exceptional case does not necessarily mean the virus poses a significant threat to the wider population.”
Dr Ben Brennan from the MRC-University of Glasgow’s centre for virus research, said there was currently no evidence of sustained transmission between humans.
“While this discovery warrants further scientific investigation and continued surveillance, it does not currently suggest a significant new public health threat to the UK,” he said.
“For most people, there is no reason to change their normal activities or take additional precautions.”

title: Emery and Nagelsmann are top targets if Manchester United sack Carrick
description: Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann have emerged as leading targets to replace Michael Carrick as Manchester United’s manager
content:
Carrick expected to be in charge for Bournemouth game
Compensation could be obstacle for Aston Villa’s Emery
Unai Emery and Julian Nagelsmann have emerged as leading targets to replace Michael Carrick as Manchester United’s head coach should the board decide on a change after the club’s poorest start to the season since 1986.
Carrick is expected to remain in place for Sunday’s visit of Bournemouth – he is due to hold his pre-game media conference on Friday – but the 45-year-old’s job is in the balance after two wins from 11 games this season.
Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation at Como in the Champions League has focused attention at United on a potential candidate to succeed Carrick should he be removed. Emery and Nagelsmann have admirers at board level.
Emery is contracted to Aston Villa until 2029, and Nagelsmann is unemployed after leaving his position as Germany’s manager in the wake of the team’s last-32 World Cup exit in the summer.
Emery has impressed since taking over Villa in 2022, last season winning the Europa League, the club’s first major trophy since 1996, and finishing fourth, one place behind United.
But Emery earns between £10m and £12m a year, so the compensation package United would have to pay Villa may be a stumbling block. He has also won trophies with Sevilla, Paris Saint-Germain and Villarreal and had a less successful spell with Arsenal.
Nagelsmann has managed Hoffenheim, RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich, with whom he won the Bundesliga in 2022 before being sacked in March 2023. He is highly regarded by United’s head of recruitment, Christopher Vivell.
The 39-year-old Nagelsmann guided Germany to the Euro 2024 quarter-finals, where they were knocked out by the eventual winners, Spain. It is understood Nagelsmann would be interested in an approach from United.
Other potential candidates who may be considered include Antonio Conte, Eddie Howe and Kieran McKenna. They are out of work after leaving jobs with Napoli, Newcastle and Ipswich respectively. It is understood Fabian Hürzeler is not open to leaving Brighton at this stage.
Bruno Fernandes’s house was the target of a break-in while United’s captain was away with the team at the Como defeat. His family were not at home, it is understood, and the intruders were inside for less than five minutes before the police arrived.
The club is supporting Fernandes and his family and have asked for privacy regarding what it said was a difficult time.
Meanwhile, the 32-year-old midfielder is not expected to face any disciplinary action for his criticism of Carrick on Wednesday. Fernandes questioned the head coach’s tactics following the Como defeat.

title: Pete Hegseth’s staff break priceless historic globe he requested for office
description: Hegseth’s aides, who attempted to move Eisenhower globe themselves, dropped it during relocation, army officials say
content:
Hegseth’s aides, who attempted to move Eisenhower globe themselves, dropped it during relocation, army officials say
A priceless pre-second world war globe coveted by the US defence secretary Pete Hegseth for his office in the Pentagon was damaged by his staff in a botched attempt to relocate it, army officials have admitted.
Photographs published by the Washington Post on Thursday show the shattered 30-inch Eisenhower globe, said to have been used by Dwight D Eisenhower, the 34th US president, as he plotted the D-day landings as allied supreme commander.
The fragile item was broken when Hegseth’s aides eschewed the services of specialist movers, then dropped it after deciding they would transport it themselves, the Post said, citing sources familiar with the February incident.
A US army spokesperson, in an email to the newspaper, conceded the damage occurred during “an attempted move”.
“The spherical portion of the globe was detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate,” the spokesperson said.
One photograph shows fragments of the globe below its wooden frame on a blue hallway carpet. A second shows an inches-wide gash in the bottom of the globe, with its base punched through.
According to the Post’s sources, Hegseth took a liking to the globe, one of two similar artifacts dating to the 1930s and housed in the Pentagon, and asked for it to be placed in his office.
The defence secretary has a well-documented fascination in the history of war, and has boasted of instilling a “ warrior ethos ” in the US military since his January 2025 confirmation.
The globe’s historical significance was attractive to him, the Post’s report noted, and aides moved quickly to enact the relocation.
Such was their haste, the sources said, that instead of waiting to engage specialist movers who would have packed the globe with precision and care, they dispatched their own team.
“They lost control of the artifact and dropped it, sending the globe crashing on to its base and impaling the fragile shell near Antarctica,” one of the sources said, blaming an “apparent lack of patience”.
Ultimately, the globe was not relocated, and is now undergoing repair.
An account of a successful 2022 relocation of an Eisenhower globe, between two army facilities in Alabama, appears on the website of specialist movers Craters & Freighters, which highlights the level of expertise and care necessary for such an undertaking.
“Since the globe is considered priceless, we knew its value was much greater than financial, and that our team was heavily relied upon for a safe delivery,” the article said, describing how the company designed and precision-built protective crating.
A spokesperson for the “war department”, as the US Department of Defense has rebranded itself during Donald Trump’s second term, dismissed the significance of the incident in a statement to the Guardian.
“An accident occurred while staff were transporting a replica of the Eisenhower globe as part of its relocation,” the official’s statement said.
“Accidents happen, we are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired. It is unsurprising that the Washington Post is once again dedicating time to another inconsequential non-story.”

title: Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacks
description: Iran’s security chiefs say there will be ‘zero red lines’ if Trump and Netanyahu attack again
content:
Iran’s security chiefs say there will be ‘zero red lines’ if Trump and Netanyahu attack again
Iran will strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities across as many as seven countries in the Gulf in the event of a fresh US-Israeli attack, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, has said.
Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Mohammad Ghalibaf, the hardliner who led Iran’s negotiations with the US to end the conflict between the two countries, said Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed in principle on an attack, but could not guarantee a successful outcome. He added: “We see the next conflict as an existential threat. The third war in two years means a threat to existence. Our strategy is ‘zero red lines’.”
Mohammadi said: “We break the temporal and spatial dimensions of the conflict. The war will continue longer and in a wider geographical area than the enemy anticipates.”
Iran’s ability to mount such operations, including any unofficial help it receives from China or Russia, will be a key factor in any American decision to restart the war.
Iranian media reported that Rezaei had declared: “In the event of a war, cables, datacentres and artificial intelligence facilities could also be targeted. If the conflict breaks out again, we will have a broader plan.
“There can be no arrangement in which Iran’s economic lifelines come under attack while the economic architecture enabling those attacks is considered untouched and immune.”
According to recent reports in US media, US military advisers have drawn up a detailed list of targets for a fresh joint US-Israel assault on Iran to be implemented after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Foreign ministers from three European countries, as well as Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, will meet in Istanbul on Friday to establish agreed policies on the linked Iranian, Yemini and Palestinian crises. There is alarm that a further war is now the working assumption in Tehran and Washington.
The naval services of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed to have simultaneously struck four commercial ships seeking to navigate through the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The ships were said to be transferring oil from ship to ship.
The IRGC claimed a further three ships had been struck when they hit mines in the strait. There was no independent verification that this number of ships were hit, but Brent crude oil was trading at $113.4 a barrel, a recent high, propelled by US reports of the imminent renewed joint Israeli-US assault on Iran.
Trump has backed away from striking Iran again seven times in the past four months. However, a deadlock in diplomatic negotiations has led US government officials to brief about a potential new military campaign that would target missile sites, oil installations and nuclear sites.
The sabre-rattling by both sides has coincided with extended joint-training manoeuvres by the US and Israel, including practice runs over Iraq. Dozens of Israeli planes also flew close to the Iranian border earlier this week, according to the news site Axios. A big fire at a large aluminium factory in Arak in central Iran suggests sabotage operations may be under way inside the country.
Netanyahu met the US secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth , in Israel on Monday to discuss the timing and purpose of a joint attack, including the possible political implications for Netanyahu’s chances of re-election.
Netanyahu would prefer it if Iran attacked first, he reportedly told Hegseth.
A US military buildup is due to be completed by early November, before a possible newly Democrat-inclined Congress or Senate take their seats in January. Trump intends to have stationed three aircraft carriers, thousands of marines, fighter jets and special operations forces in the Middle East by November.
Reza Nasri, an international lawyer close to the Iranian foreign ministry, said: “A third wave of war would not stay contained. Power grids, desalination plants, refineries and ports across the region would burn. Tens of millions would be left without water or electricity, and a massive wave of refugees would move from Arab countries towards Europe.
“Hormuz would close completely, oil would spike, and the global economy would tip into recession. Israel’s economy, already bled by mobilisation and missile fire, would not survive a prolonged war of attrition. And Trump would be trapped in a crisis that consumes the rest of his presidency and leaves a wreck for his successors,” Nasri said.
Fars news agency, which is close to the IRGC, said Iran had issued directives to its various military and operational units “stipulating that in the event of a new widespread war, involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, the Iranian response will not be limited to military targets, but will also include political targets”.
Mediators from Iran and Pakistan this week again explored familiar if reconfigured options for a ceasefire, including proposals that Iran receive billions in frozen assets in return for lifting its blockade of the strait, allowing UN weapons inspectors to view its bombed nuclear sites and to export its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country.
Iran has offered to end the Hormuz blockade within seven days and start talks on its nuclear file, but only if preconditions are first met, including lifting US sanctions.

title: Ali G: Who Iz I? review – Sacha Baron Cohen’s high-stakes satire punches up and down with spectacular bad taste
description: Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation
content:
Baron Cohen’s live-ammo prankster is back, 20 years on, but has to battle with his own irrelevance in search of big laughs and the approval of a new generation
Exclusive: Republican leader embarrassed by film says he plays to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’
I f you liked Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G the first time around, you’ll like this less; if you disliked it, you’ll dislike this more; if you suspected it was racist, you’ll be more emboldened to say so – especially as Baron Cohen has dreamed up a whole new character apparently to pre-empt and mock precisely that objection. Broad and crass as it often is – in fact always is – this Ali G sequel is sometimes funny: the athletic vigour of our hero’s pranking and punking is like the umpteenth Jackass film at which you might find yourself laughing, and Baron Cohen blunders with the semi-intentional force of an XL bully into the issue of whether jokes are still allowed.
Unlike the first film, Ali G in Da House from 2002, this is not a full written-through narrative. It is basically another live-ammo series of hoaxes with some spectacular bad taste perpetrated upon the deserving and less deserving; it satirises the shamelessness of anti-woke free speech martyrs, punching up and down with grossout cringe, and the targets include some big names who shouldn’t be revealed here. There are two other subordinate characters: Erran Morad, a sinister Mossad/IDF officer turned US security consultant (who appeared in Baron Cohen’s Who Is America? TV series ), and a new figure: Dr Nira Cain-N’Degrocello, a grotesquely supercilious white liberal who is the self-appointed scourge of cultural appropriation. The dupes are built into a big silly climax fabricated with body doubles and (presumably) covert reshooting.
The insurmountable problem is that the film keeps having to tell you who is and isn’t “in on it”: at the beginning, over the closing credits at the end and even briefly in the middle of the action. Well, Ali G was from so very long ago, and even the high-water mark of Baron Cohen’s Borat popularity was quite long ago, and the online media scene now so fragmented that … yes … people have forgotten, a whole new generation doesn’t know. People really don’t recognise him.
The high concept is that Ali is now washed up, short of money and unpopular, and old-school media figure that he is, he disapproves of a plan by his heavily pregnant partner Julie (Morgana Robinson) to launch an OnlyFans account. But on trying to sell his fax machine in a Staines high street pawn shop, an old fax chunters out of it with an offer from HBO for a new show. Overexcited, Ali and Julie head off to the US to sucker some people in the traditional style; the smallscreen setup blown up to high-def cinematic proportions. His fictional woke tormentor decides to take him down and, by employing the Israeli hardman, tries to convince credulous and aggressive Republicans that Ali is a Mexican terrorist whose baby must be prevented at all costs from being born on US soil. The movie does make a few people look silly, yes, although Baron Cohen doesn’t land a huge punch on a big name the way he did in the Borat sequel.
So who iz Ali G and what iz the point of trundling him out again? The first film implied he was once a Robert Smith-type goth, but that is now forgotten about. Interestingly, one person who this film doesn’t allude to is Tim Westwood, the BBC Radio 1 hip-hop DJ and son of the Bishop of Peterborough whose speech mannerisms were held to be one influence on Baron Cohen’s great creation, and proof positive that white people did indeed patronisingly ape a street way of speaking. Westwood’s subsequent all-too-unfunny history , perhaps, doesn’t mesh with trying to revive Ali G now as comedy IP. The movie outings of Ricky Gervais’s David Brent and Steve Coogan’s Alan Partridge worked better because they could more plausibly represent the melancholy of getting older and irrelevant. Ali G feels older in the wrong way, and the On-the-Buses humour with Julie is tired. The best bits will be available on TikTok and Instagram reels soon enough.

title: Astronomers challenge dating of Van Gogh’s Starry Night
description: Study suggests much-loved work was based on a real dawn sky in July 1889 rather than just the artist’s rich imagination
content:
Study suggests much-loved work was based on a real dawn sky in July 1889 rather than just the artist’s rich imagination
It was long assumed to be a product of Vincent van Gogh’s rich imagination – but scientific sleuthing now suggests The Starry Night may be based on a real dawn sky.
Researchers say the celestial bodies depicted in the famous painting match the sky the Dutch artist may have seen on about 22 July 1889, a month later than the usual date given for the work.
At that time, Van Gogh was living at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he had admitted himself after a series of mental health crises.
The June date rests on a letter Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo on about 18 June, describing “a new study of a starry sky” and on a mental breakdown in July, thought to have left him unable to paint for weeks. However, the authors of the new paper argue that the idea of the sky being imagined also rests on the assumption that the celestial arrangement of the painting did not match what would have been seen in southern France in June.
Moving the date to July, they say, means the moon, Venus and a star cluster called the Hyades that are shown in The Starry Night could have been seen by Van Gogh from his window at the asylum, making the painting an exaggerated reality rather than pure fantasy.
To make their discovery, researchers in South Korea identified a ridge south-west of the asylum and matched an earlier sketch by Van Gogh to the real landscape.
The sketch showed he drew a surprisingly narrow slice of the scene. “I was standing where Vincent had stood 130 years earlier,” said Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the study’s first author and an astronomer at Kyung Hee University in Yongin, South Korea.
The team used astronomy software to recreate the dawn sky for every day in June and July 1889. In the painting, the moon sits above Venus, so they looked for dawns where this occurred and both fitted inside the narrow frame. Only three dates qualified, and 22 July was the closest match, with a thin crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades arranged as in the painting.
“To bring the question into science, which needs quantitative data we had to measure the degree of resemblance between the star patterns in the painting and the real sky, using shape geometry and statistics,” Kim said.
The study is published in the journal Scientific Reports. However, the researchers acknowledged the results were not conclusive, with Kim noting that Van Gogh may have combined the skies of several days.
The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, which was not involved in the research, said its experts had established that Van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889. It said the painting was made on a roll of canvas he received in early June, and on 2 July Van Gogh sent his brother Theo a drawing based on it. The museum also said the artist had a severe breakdown on about 22 July that left him unable to paint for more than a month.
“Van Gogh was not concerned with exact likenesses,” a museum spokesperson said. “The positions of the celestial bodies depicted can therefore not form a reliable basis for dating the work.”
Donald Olson, professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at Texas State University, was also not convinced by the study because the positions of Venus and the Hyades cluster in the painting do not match their calculated position.
He added: “The authors’ assumed narrow field of view, essential for their theory that the stars of the Hyades fill most of the canvas, is inconsistent with the much wider field of view required to encompass Starry Night’s round hills and cliffs.”

title: The Audacity review – cracking TV packed with even more gloriously awful people than Succession
description: This Silicon Valley satire follows a CEO in trouble after the collapse of an acquisition deal. Created by Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, each character is more hideous than the next – and it is stuffed with twists and treacheries
content:
This Silicon Valley satire follows a CEO in trouble after the collapse of an acquisition deal. Created by Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, each character is more hideous than the next – and it is stuffed with twists and treacheries
W hat if Mike Judge’s cult hit sitcom Silicon Valley were remade as a dramedy and we had in the meantime come to appreciate tech and its titans as existential threats to humanity, I hear you ask. Well, wonder no more – the answer is here, and it is The Audacity. It comes at you in hour-long episodes, which rush past at breakneck speed and leave you panting and deeply unsettled in their wake. Rather like modern life itself, of course, except for the relief available while the credits roll, before the next chunk of horrors arrives.
The Audacity has a sprawling cast (especially in the opening episodes, which really are frenetic) but the figure around which most of the narratives move is Duncan Park (Billy Magnussen). He is the part-bullish, part-neurotic and wholly unbearable CEO of Hypergnosis, a data brokerage company he founded with a friend, who has since been struck by tragedy.
Duncan, who has not absorbed the key point of the Silicon Valley maxim and spends his time moving fast and breaking his own stuff, is in trouble. Hypergnosis was in acquisition talks with Cupertino (named after the location of Apple’s real-world headquarters and just possibly meant to evoke the behemoth) until Duncan leaked the news to boost his share price before the company valuation. That brought the deal to a screeching halt. He is now on the hunt for a play that will enable him to avoid the humiliation and (relative) poverty that will occur once word of the cancelled acquisition gets out.
Duncan’s wife, Lili ( Lucy Punch ), and daughters are weary of and maddened by him, and his therapist JoAnne (Sarah Goldberg) even more so. She is almost as gloriously hateful a character as Duncan, and that is before he gets the goods on her with an eye to blackmail. This feels like the right time to note that The Audacity’s creator, Jonathan Glatzer, was one of the writers on the first two seasons of Succession, the show that made “gloriously hateful characters” an art form.
JoAnne is married to Gary (Paul Adelstein), a slightly more ethical member of the same profession, though in the Valley this still means a lot of time spent administering ADHD tests to students in the hope that a diagnosis will buy them extra time on tests, and other such small corruptions. She shares custody of her son, Orson (Everett Blunck), with her equally unlovely ex-husband, and although she uses Orson’s birthday as her computer password, it’s not the right date.
Like most of the younger characters – including the Parks’ older daughter, Jamison (Ava Marie Telek), whose weight and academic results are ceaselessly monitored by her mother – Orson is a sweet child. Heartbreakingly resigned to his fate as an afterthought in his parents’ lives, he forms a growing friendship with Jamison’s little sister, embryonic kleptomaniac Tess (Thailey Roberge). The younger characters’ quiet endurance of, and resistance to, the chaos, greed and narcissism that surrounds them gives emotional heft to the show’s satirical thrust. Is gen z a reservoir of hope, or is youth just a brief period in everyone’s lives before the venality of the world – especially in its tech-aggravated modern iteration – gets to work? The bleakness of the latter gives us pause.
Add to the mix a potent turn from Zach Galifianakis as Carl Bardolph, another self-obsessed tech titan (worshipped for inventing “Bardolph’s Law”, a principle of infinite growth and profit “based on the logic of a cancer cell” that he once scribbled on a napkin while high); a genius coder called Harper (Jess McLeod), whose new algorithm may save Park or destroy the last vestiges of society; Rob Corddry as a rep for the Veterans’ Association, begging for a morsel of aid from billionaires; and about 700 supporting characters, twists, treacheries, good deals, bad deals and ayahuasca trips, with no clear way to distinguish what is satire and what is reportage – and you have The Audacity.
Once you’ve calmed down – and in later episodes, as the show gains confidence, it does too – it will fill both the Succession and Silicon Valley (sitcom)-shaped holes in your life. Unlike Hypergnosis, that’s an acquisition worth making.

title: Heartbreak, hope and human imperfection: Leonard Cohen’s greatest songs – ranked!
description: A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and grief
content:
A decade after his final album, and his death, we rate the best of the Canadian singer-songwriter who brought a deep, spiritual wisdom to love and grief
The synth-heavy production on 1988’s I’m Your Man has always been divisive – even Leonard Cohen’s longtime collaborator Anjani Thomas subsequently expressed misgivings – but on its opening track, it really works. The Pet Shop Boys-ish arrangement chafes against Cohen’s growling vocal, amplifying First We Take Manhattan’s shiver-inducing sense of brooding menace.
Seven years – and a personal financial crisis – after 2004’s half-hearted Dear Heather, Cohen returned to the studio with his powers freshly marshalled. As if to underline the point, Old Ideas opened with the sharply witty Going Home, on which Cohen’s muse addresses the listener directly, disparaging the artist himself as “a lazy bastard in a suit”.
Cohen famously called his 1977 LP Death of a Ladies’ Man “a catastrophe”, which perhaps reflected more on its drug- and booze-soaked recording with dangerously erratic producer Phil Spector than the finished album. It’s an outlier in Cohen’s catalogue, but one with much to commend it. Certainly, he maintained an understandable fondness for the rock’n’roll-influenced Memories, often performing it live.
Cohen’s renaissance continued apace on Popular Problems. Released the day before his 80th birthday, it sounded suspiciously like a masterpiece. Almost Like the Blues found him reflecting sorrowfully on man’s inhumanity to man – not merely torture, killing and war, but “all my bad reviews” – and staring down his own mortality, replete with a jab at Richard Dawkins.
Shruggingly titled, largely recorded in collaborator Sharon Robinson’s garage and packaged in a sleeve featuring a selfie, Ten New Songs was an understated return to recording after Cohen’s five years of Buddhist study. But beneath its unassuming veneer lurked beautiful songs: the chanson-like A Thousand Kisses Deep is an exquisite reflection on regret and time’s passing.
Nowhere else on this album does the cocktail of Cohen’s songwriting and Spector’s more-is-more approach to production gel so perfectly: the title track is a fantastic song. Moreover, the weight of Spector’s arrangement, the way it causes the tempo to drag, seems to complement rather than suffocate its mood.
Other artists have made albums that looked imminent death in the face – Warren Zevon’s The Wind, Queen’s Innuendo – but You Want It Darker, released less than three weeks before the end of Cohen’s life, may be the most poised and affecting. “I’m ready, my Lord,” he sang on its title track, a complex, thorny examination of faith.
In which a brief tryst with Janis Joplin – “We fell into each other’s arms through a process of elimination,” he later recalled – turns into a kind of eulogy, not just for the late singer, but for the era in which they met. It’s haunted by the sense of optimism extinguished.
Rock stars of a certain vintage were wont to write despairing state-of-the-world addresses in the late 80s – Lou Reed’s New York is full of them – but Everybody Knows is a cut above, its relentlessly bleak worldview leavened by black humour: “Everybody’s got this broken feeling, like their father or their dog just died.”
Against stiff competition, Songs of Love and Hate may be Cohen’s darkest album. Avalanche is its claustrophobic heart, a relentless, shimmering guitar figure, a confusing but compelling tumble of imagery, with his voice at its most poisonous. Nick Cave called it one of “the essential pillars that hold up the structure of my artistic world”.
Inspired by the story of the Lagerkapellen – concentration camp orchestras whose music accompanied forced labour and executions – there’s something eerie about Dance Me to the End of Love’s klezmer-inspired melody and lyrical pleas for lifelong fealty. The latter are filled with intimations of darkness; it’s never entirely clear that love will overcome them.
“I’ve seen the future, baby, and it’s murder”: Cohen’s apocalyptic response to the sociopolitical upheavals of the early 90s – most obviously the Los Angeles riots – depicted a world in which “attitudes are all extremist and they’re all defensive”. Thirty-four years on, it sounds grimly prophetic, its upbeat soft-rock backing only serving to amplify the unease.
Cohen found writing a trying experience – lurid stories abound of him beating his head against the floor while working on Hallelujah. He poured it all into the thrillingly vivid, mordantly funny Tower of Song, which has often struck a chord with other artists, covered by everyone from Phoebe Bridgers to Tom Jones to the Jesus and Mary Chain.
Anthem is home to perhaps Cohen’s most-quoted lyric: “There is a crack in everything, that’s how the light gets in.” But in truth, it’s just one among a plethora of memorable lines in the song’s gospel-infused paean to hope and human imperfection, a song he later suggested represented “everything my whole work and life had gathered around”.
Even by the standards of Cohen’s synth era, the backing of I’m Your Man is low-rent and cheesy, but it fits perfectly with a song about abasement. Its emotional tone shifts from lustful to desperate to hopeless: “A man never got a woman back, not by begging on his knees,” he notes in a moment of clarity, then carries on regardless.
Hallelujah’s progress from an album Cohen’s US record label refused to release to his most famous song – via, of all things, a cover by John Cale that appeared on the soundtrack of Shrek – is fascinating. Cohen later proposed a moratorium on its use in films, but, in truth, it has survived ubiquity with its power to move intact.
Cohen’s original intention was to try his luck as a Nashville songwriter. If you squint, you can just about make out the shape of a country song in So Long, Marianne’s beautiful admission of guilt, although it’s hard to imagine the Music Row treatment could improve on its wonderfully ramshackle string accompaniment.
Another Cohen classic with country music in its bones – Kris Kristofferson said he wanted the opening lines on his gravestone – Bird on the Wire was coaxed out of a depressed Cohen by his then girlfriend, Marianne Ihlen. It sounds utterly, authentically defeated, like one long sigh, destined to soundtrack moments of gloomy self-reflection for the rest of time.
There are infinitely worse ways to start your debut album than with a song so good, it immediately becomes a standard, covered by Nina Simone, Neil Diamond, Roberta Flack and Aretha Franklin. Some recompense, perhaps, for the titular lady’s refusal to let Cohen touch her perfect body with anything other than his mind.
Reducing Leonard Cohen’s oeuvre to 20 songs is a thankless task: the compiler is abundantly aware that umpteen deserving songs have been neglected. Similarly, there’s no head-and-shoulders “best” song, merely personal favouritism. Still, you listen to Famous Blue Raincoat’s disconsolate depiction of a love triangle – in the form of a letter to the other male party – and boggle at the idea Cohen was dissatisfied with such an impossibly beautiful song, which so perfectly conjures up an atmosphere of shadowy small-hours reflection, and which comes complete with one of his loveliest melodies (subsequently pinched on – crikey – Leo Sayer’s When I Need You).

title: Glee’s pro-LGBTQ+ vision captured 2010s hope. Can a reboot handle Trump’s America?
description: The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs
content:
The beloved high school TV show is returning in a different political climate. I’m skeptical that Ryan Murphy has the nuance this moment needs
F or months, Ryan Murphy has been discussing Glee . In July, he expressed his love for the musical comedy drama he created. In September, he said that he had finished writing a pilot for a potential reboot, adding that he had reached out to some of the cast about a reunion. And now it is official : Disney+ and Hulu have commissioned a Glee revival.
Glee, which ran for six seasons between 2009 and 2015, was a cultural juggernaut during its initial tenure . The show won six Emmys, four Golden Globes and made stars of actors including Lea Michele, Jonathan Groff, Chris Colfer , Darren Criss and the late Cory Monteith and Naya Rivera. Centred on the trials of New Directions, a scrappy show choir at the fictional McKinley high school in Ohio, the show became known for its peppy covers of show tunes, 80s power pop hits such as Journey’s Don’t Stop Believin’ (a Glee signature), 2010s chart-toppers and some truly baffling mashups (the amalgamation of Scissor Sisters’ Let’s Have a Kiki and Turkey Lurkey Time from Promises, Promises remains … a choice).
Nevertheless, these musical numbers worked: compilation albums regularly scaled the charts, and the cast even embarked on a US and UK tour, which was recorded and later released in cinemas as Glee: The 3D Concert Movie . Even today, the show’s soundtrack cast generates more than 4 million monthly listeners on Spotify.
It’s this longevity that is probably behind Glee’s return. On social media, videos featuring people recreating the show’s take on I Say a Little Prayer – complete with McKinley cheerleaders’ choreography – continue to rack up views, while over a million videos on TikTok are tagged with “#Glee”. Gen Z audiences, meanwhile, have revisited the show – albeit not always so favourably – thanks to streaming services, with recap podcasts and YouTube videos cropping up in response. “That show is interesting because it’s come back around,” Murphy said in July. “So many young people now watch it.”
Still, this extended shelf life is surprising given Glee’s politics: no show exemplified Obama-era optimism and liberal identity politics more. Murphy utilised Glee as a vehicle for representation, filling the show with characters from marginalised backgrounds. This was particularly apparent with the show’s numerous LGBTQ+ characters. Glee’s arrival on TV in the year after Proposition 8, which banned same-sex marriage in California, provided Murphy with an opportunity to shift public perception of LGBTQ+ people. While its pro-queer messaging was about as tactful as a neon green American Apparel “ Legalize Gay ” tank top, there’s little doubt that its emphasis on queer representation – even if said queer people were covering the novelty EDM monstrosity The Fox (What Does the Fox Say?) while wielding puppets – was significant.
Glee cleared the path for Lady Gaga ’s Born This Way and Dan Savage’s “It Gets Better” campaign, ushering in an age of hopefulness about the trajectory of LGBTQ+ rights. While it would take until the summer of 2015 for same-sex marriage to be legalised in the US – an issue covered in Glee’s final season with the nuptials between queer couples Brittany and Santana, and Kurt and Blaine – the increasingly queernormative world of Glee presented a utopian future for LGBTQ+ people, one where those in high school were no longer bullied for being queer, young trans people could transition without interference and gays could live in harmony alongside their heterosexual counterparts. A post-Glee world suggested that, no matter your differences, everyone would be equal.
The last 11 years, however, have highlighted what a fantasy Murphy’s egalitarian vision for the future was. The pandemic, a second Trump presidency and vast economic disparity have stoked divisions and cemented inequalities. Anti-LGBTQ+ legislation, both in the US and the UK, has created a hostile environment for the queer community, particularly for trans people, with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue reporting an increase in anti-LGBTQ+ hate crimes in the US, the UK and Europe. In this context, the identity politics propagated by Glee 1.0, which prized individual visibility, regularly weaponised victimhood, and made a (literal) song and dance about liberalism to promote a vision of societal equality, feel dated. Despite any good intentions, it is these very values that, some hypothesise, have contributed to the so-called “ war on wokeness ”.
Since its conclusion, Glee’s legacy has also tarnished. Along with allegations of on-set bullying, racism and favouritism, a number of the cast have died: Monteith, who played football star Finn Hudson, died from an accidental overdose in 2013; Mark Salling, whose character Noah Puckerman was the school’s bad boy, was arrested for possession of child sexual abuse material in 2015 and later died by suicide; and Rivera drowned in 2020. The writing, too, has been criticised, particularly for how it handled its characters of colour, disability, bisexuality, and the dynamics between students and teachers.
It’s this environment in which Glee returns. Some former stars, including Michele, Heather Morris and Chord Overstreet, are already on board . But whether Murphy will be able to produce something that speaks to our current climate is debatable. The prolific showrunner’s allergy to subtlety, as evidenced by recent output The Shards , All’s Fair and his exploitative Monster anthology series , suggests not.
Instead, this reboot feels like a shallow and desperate attempt by a streaming service to reclaim a dwindling gen Z audience. Meanwhile, Murphy’s ham-fisted identity politics feel incongruous at a time where nuance, tact and self-awareness feel more necessary than ever. Personally, when it comes to the Glee revival, I’ve stopped believin’.

title: Seth Meyers on JD Vance: ‘The integrity of a used-car salesman and the charisma of a wet ham’
description: Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s seeming cognitive decline and Vance’s rock-bottom approval ratings
content:
Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s seeming cognitive decline and Vance’s rock-bottom approval ratings
Late-night hosts recapped a tough couple of days for the Oval Office, as Donald Trump waved to an imaginary crowd and JD Vance bombed softball interviews.
On Wednesday’s Late Night, Seth Meyers addressed the “real issue” from the midterms campaign trail that could no longer be ignored: “Donald Trump might no longer be able to tell the difference between what is real and what is fake, be it polls or anything else,” he said, “as evidenced by this video taken Monday, where he seems to be waving at someone before boarding Marine One, only for the camera to zoom out and reveal that no one was there.”
Indeed, Meyers showed footage of Trump waving to no one, as if a crowd was there. “When the helicopter pilot saw that, he probably wanted to call in a new flight plan,” he joked. “‘Hey. Yeah, this is Marine One. We’re gonna scrap Kansas and head straight for the Whispering Pines Retirement Home.’
“Trump loves going to rallies,” Meyers later added. “One, because unlike on the helipad, he’s not the only one who can see the people. And two, he gets to talk uninterrupted. And he’s landed on an interesting way to describe his performances at those rallies.”
Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump described his own rallies as “two hours” of “ranting, raving”.
“You know, you don’t have to go for two hours,” Meyers responded. “They’re rallies. They’re not feats of endurance. You’re the only one who wants to treat these things like dance marathons from the 1920s.”
In other news, JD Vance, attempted during a town hall to blame high gas prices not on Trump’s war in Iran, but on Joe Biden, for allegedly taking US oil refining capacity offline during his administration.
“You guys have to stop talking about Joe Biden,” Meyers responded. “Most people don’t even remember that he was president. Biden probably doesn’t even remember that he was president.
“This is such a shameless lie,” Meyers added. “You want us to believe that a spike in gas prices that started in March of 2026 was because of a drop in refining capacity under Joe Biden, whose presidency ended in January 2025, and not because of the Iran war that Donald Trump started in February 2026. That’s like walking out of a bathroom and saying: ‘Hey everyone, I think someone clogged the toilet 14 months ago.”
It doesn’t appear that voters are buying it, as the vice-president’s approval ratings have hit rock-bottom; he’s now the least popular Republican vice-president at this point in his term since modern polling. “Oh my god, JD Vance is less popular than Mike Pence,” Meyers laughed. “And don’t forget, Republicans tried to kill that guy.
“It doesn’t surprise me that Vance is so unpopular,” Meyers added. “He’s got the integrity of a used-car salesman and the charisma of a wet ham.”
And on the Daily Show, Ronny Chieng also checked in with Trump’s PR-challenged vice-president. Vance “is probably going to run for president in 2028, assuming AI doesn’t kill us all next year”, the host explained. “Which is probably why he’s been doing softball interviews that are impossible to screw up – unless you’re JD Vance.”
During an interview onboard Air Force Two, Vance was asked by a reporter: “What are you good at in politics?” He still dodged the question, instead going into a tangent about loving life as a senator, forcing the journalist to cut him off with: “Sorry to interrupt, but tell me what you’re good at.”
“How is that a gotcha question?” Chieng said. “JD, tell us one thing you don’t suck at! ‘Uhh, can I phone a friend? Oh wait, I don’t have any.’
“He does have a sense of humor, though,” Chieng continued. “In fact, I saw him tell a really funny joke this morning.” Chieng then played a clip of Vance addressing press in Cincinnati, Ohio, where he claimed the “entire” Trump administration “rejects pay for play, we reject anybody getting rich off of their connections to the government”.
Chieng could only laugh. “Maybe JD’s right – when have you seen allegations of corruption in the Trump administration? I mean, yeah, there was his ambassador to Greece, and his crypto deals, his IRS slush fund, his son’s wedding party, his son-in-law’s real estate deals … But those were weeks ago!” Chieng joked. “When have you ever seen corruption allegations this morning ?”

title: Carrick joins Wilcox under the bus after Manchester United’s latest night in crisis
description: Bruno Fernandes followed Lisandro Martínez in revolt after his team’s 4-1 defeat to Como in the Champions League
content:
Bruno Fernandes followed Lisandro Martínez in revolt after his team’s 4-1 defeat to Como in the Champions League
Y ou have to credit Manchester United . Your local rivals have turned the Premier League into an almost meaningless farce. We are questioning the validity of anything we’ve seen over the past 20 years; wondering how many goals Erling Haaland will get in the Championship. We are looking at the league table from second position down and wishing we’d invested in inflatable bananas a month ago.
And yet here comes the Old Trafford machine: from players to the captain to the manager to the director of football, to the director of the director of football, to a minority owner who feels the UK is being “colonised by immigrants” , to debt-leveraging majority owners who take vast sums out of the club and are collectively saying hold my Ineos-sponsored high-performance wellness immune boost smoothie.
Yes, it’s time to dust down the Manchester United bin-fire article. Read this and compare and contrast. From 11 August 2022: “Reds rinse and repeat: will we ever break the Manchester United crisis cycle?” There are others.
It is some feat to be more newsworthy than Manchester City, even for an evening. The defeat in Como wasn’t surprising. We’re getting to the stage where the large pieces of furniture Barney Ronay keeps comparing Harry Maguire to are fighting back. @19thCenturyArmoire: “mate i’m a hundred and sixty years old, of course my legs have gone.” @CoffinFridge69: “#BeKind Ronay, appliances have feelings too.”
Everyone knows the problems at Old Trafford lie deeper than the defensive line held by Maguire and Matthijs de Ligt on Wednesday.
Perhaps it was only a matter of time before Bruno Fernandes’s constant on-field complaining spilled off the pitch . An exercise in throwing his manager under the bus, where presumably Michael Carrick found Jason Wilcox, still lying in hiding under the 250 to the Trafford Centre after Lisandro Martínez’s post-match intervention in Madrid .
Carrick did push back on the criticism: “Whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you aren’t going to win. ” But it’s hard to throw someone under the bus when you’re already under the bus you’re trying to throw people under.
Poor Carrick, who may well be gone by the time I finish this tram ride, never mind by the time you get around to reading this. It was one of those funereal press conferences: Carrick being as earnest as it is possible to be, while journalists take it in turn to sound even more earnest, as if they’re questioning a man who’s just failed to blow up the asteroid coming to destroy the Earth.
At this rate, that meteor will arrive long before United have recaptured past glories. Ineos presumably has a big blame pie chart constantly updating on a PowerPoint. Spin the wheel – who’s to blame today? Maybe the players?
Does anyone genuinely know any more whether any United player is good? I have analysis paralysis when trying to work out whether Fernandes is world class or why Youri Tielemans never lumbered at Aston Villa. How bamboozled will we be when Joshua Zirkzee has 25 goal involvements for Real Sociedad next season?
As for Carrick, while most of us (me included) felt he’d earned the right to manage the side this season, a more ruthless and efficient ownership would have made a different call. It wouldn’t have been popular.
He may turn out to be a world-class manager – he may not. Football decides pretty quickly about these things. But if he is sacked, there is a path to redemption. Daniel Farke has moved beyond “only good in the Championship”. Frank Lampard could reasonably expect an apology from anyone who comments on the game for his achievements at Coventry.
But at this stage it is fair to say Carrick doesn’t have the tactical ability or experience of almost all his competitors in the division.
Above him, is Jason Wilcox good? Perhaps the last time someone yelled at him like Martínez, it was Mike Newell after an overhit cross at Ewood Park in 1991. What will Omar Berrada’s CV look like after the independent panel delivers its punishments?
It is fair to say that barring the odd All or Nothing documentary, I have almost no knowledge of what happens behind the scenes. But £1bn spent by United to create this squad over the past five years, plus the randomness of Rangnick/Ten Hag/Van Nistelrooy/Amorim/Carrick, gives us limited evidence to suggest high performance.
And at the top, what does Jim Ratcliffe care about? Apart from enjoying the tax rates of Monaco while opining about the fallen British empire. The good old days where you could just colonise and get a pat on the back, eh Jim.
And then there’s the Glazers. Even for someone whose brain shuts down as soon as they hear the words “leveraged debt” the fact they have extracted about £1bn out of the club since the takeover in 2005 is an outrage. Perhaps if they had overseen a period of sustained success, but it is the opposite.
So when you add bad (maybe bad?) players, bad (or at least disrespectful) captain, bad (not great yet) manager, bad technical director, bad chief executive, bad minority owner, bad majority owners – apologies if I’ve missed anyone – it is, well, bad.
So what’s the best plan of action now? Did someone say Antonio Conte? For the wind and the rain make it happen. As Paul Watson said on the latest Guardian Football Weekly , he might resign during his unveiling.
Lots of us who lived through the Fergie success can’t help but enjoy a Manchester United crisis, but it’s possible to laugh and at the same time sympathise with powerless United fans under that dripping roof in the East Stand.
Football is so stupid that Conte, or Eddie Howe, or even Carrick could turn this into a good season. Perhaps everyone’s expectations still cling to a Manchester United that do not exist any more. Perhaps the odd trophy, the occasional foray deep into Europe, may be the new normal. But right now, how many Premier League teams are worse than they are? Did someone say a Manchester derby in the Championship next season? I can hear David Prutton’s excitement already.

title: Amy Winehouse: Back to Black 20 review – trying an all-star Amy tribute show is a losing game
description: With Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson and others reinterpreting Back to Black for its 20th anniversary, most of the singers are eclipsed by the memory of Winehouse
content:
(Roundhouse, London) With Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson and others reinterpreting Back to Black for its 20th anniversary, most of the singers are eclipsed by the memory of Winehouse
I t’s 20 years since Amy Winehouse released her masterpiece Back to Black and 15 since she died at a frighteningly young age. A good way to appreciate how special she was is to watch the Amy Winehouse Band trot through a few lesser songs and cover versions and spot what’s missing: her playfulness, bite, anarchic charisma and taste. Winehouse mixed soul, jazz, hip-hop, two-tone and 60s girl groups because she loved that music more than anything. Without her animating fandom, a cover of Monkey Man by Toots and the Maytals is just a cover of Monkey Man by Toots and the Maytals; for all her old band’s precision and gusto, it has no pressing reason to exist.
The main event, in which Back to Black producers including Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi hand-pick singers such as Jorja Smith, Lianne La Havas and Corinne Bailey Rae to recreate the album, is stronger except that it’s primarily staged for a BBC TV show, which means the flow is broken by onstage interviews and hagiographical patter from Jo Whiley. It’s a little grating to be constantly told that a concert is amazing even as it unfolds, but that’s TV for you.
Even performed out of sequence, Back to Black remains a miraculous set of modern love songs in vintage clothing – tragic, defiant and bitterly funny – but re-enactments can be limiting. One distinctive singer after another faithfully emulates Winehouse’s sly, gutsy phrasing and thus submerges herself. The show really crackles when something new materialises, such as Jessie Reyez tearing through Rehab with conviction or London trio Flo splitting the difference between TLC and the Supremes on He Can Only Hold Her. Yebba’s spectral, minimalist take on Love Is a Losing Game, with Ronson on guitar, would delight the Twin Peaks Roadhouse.
The ecstatic, mic-passing ensemble finale of Valerie is unexpectedly moving in that it presents a diverse tableau of Winehouse’s musical sisters and daughters and allows for a rare element of chaos. It ensures that this lovingly curated tribute leaves a pleasing glow. It’s just that Amy didn’t glow; she burned.

We reviewed Revolve’s 12- and 25-day beauty advent calendars to see if offerings from Summer Fridays to Sol de Janeiro provide value for your money
The best beauty advent calendars of 2026 in the US
Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things
October is too early for Bing Crosby and peppermint cocoa – but if you’re considering a beauty advent calendar, you’re right on time.
We have tested popular calendars from Anthropologie, Lush, Charlotte Tilbury and Amazon’s sold-out edition to see if any live up to the hype – and we math-ed out the true value of each.
Thus far, Revolve’s has had the best cost-to-value ratio of them all. The brand, perhaps best known for its huge catalogue of high-end, trendy clothing, doesn’t offer glitzy dresses or funnel-neck jackets in its calendar, just a ton of the best beauty products packed in a charming pink suitcase.
Its 25-day beauty advent calendar has a listed value of $953, but only costs $150. As we are always on the lookout for truly good deals, we tested it alongside its cheaper 12-day option . Below, we reviewed the de-bloating supplements, body lotions and sleep masks in each calendar. In the end, one came out on top.

If you or someone in your life is a beauty obsessive, chances are they have heard of most of the buzzy items in this calendar.
We were impressed with the fairly even ratio of hair, makeup and skincare items, too. The packaging is also the best we have seen – the magenta pink suitcase, complete with metal handle and clasps, is reusable and each product comes in its own pink box, which is perfect for gifting each item separately.
Summer Friday s Dream Lip Oil (full size): My mom introduced me to this lip oil, which feels hydrating and weightless on the lips, and thankfully, not sticky. Lauren Gould
Ilia The Base Face Milk (full size): This milky toner is one of my skincare staples, so I was excited to see it included in the calendar. It leaves my skin refreshed and smooth, without feeling too harsh. LG
Tower 28 SOS Daily Rescue Facial Spray (mini): I recommended this popular spray in my running guide , but I also love it for post-gym sessions or when I come inside from a walk but don’t have the energy for a whole skincare routine . LG
Ouai Detox Shampoo : Most shampoos don’t work for me, so I’ve stayed loyal to this one for years – it actually removes the grease from my scalp and leaves my hair feeling clean and soft. LG
Foreo Mini UFO Device + Call It A Night Mask Pack (full size): An early Christmas gift to my mother, who now uses this combo nightly as a 90-second spa routine. You place the mask pack (ginseng, hawthorn extract) on to the device, then glide it around your face. The heat is soothing, like warming your face with a hot towel, and the LED therapy is doing … something that she hasn’t noticed the effects of yet, but it doesn’t matter when the routine itself is so relaxing. Karen Yuan
Salt & Stone Black Rose & Oud Body Lotion (mini): Out of everything I’ve tried, this is the one item I will be buying again and again because the scent is so rich and fragrant. It smells like reclining on a throne in ancient Greece while being fanned and fed citrus fruit. KY
Abbode Sleep Mask : I gave this to a friend, who said it felt like a cushy pillow for her eyes. She only wished the strap were adjustable. KY
Dr Barbara Sturm Glow Drops (mini): Sort of like a serum and highlighter combined – a few drops brightened my face with a faint shimmer. A nice touch if you’re going for a no-makeup look. KY
Lavender dry shampoo: This did nothing. It was messy to apply and didn’t revive my unfortunately greasy scalp. LG
Lemme Mini Debloat Daily Digestive Gummies: These have an indiscernible fruit flavor and did not affect me at all, positively or negatively. Like the stale gummies you may stumble upon in the back of your pantry. KY
This $150 calendar is worth it. While I would love to say that the 12-day option is just as good, I simply can’t (more below). Though the 25-day option only costs $60 more, it gets you about $540 more in value in product and has six more full-sized items.
Revolve’s 25 days of beauty advent calendar punches far above its weight, just like Liberty London’s nearly $400 calendar (valued at $1,700) that we also liked. It’s a more affordable way to gift higher-end items to multiple people, a trendy larger gift that looks like you are really in the know when it comes to beauty or something to keep for yourself as you count down to the holidays.
Listed value: $409 Filter calculated value: $435 Full-size items: Six Bestsellers included: Five
The product selection is strong. Nearly half of the items included are bestsellers, such as Sol De Janeiro’s Bum Bum Cream and Ilia’s mascara , which I have used for years. Like the 25-day version, it practically comes gift-wrapped, with an adorable, large gift tag fastened to a light pink reusable suitcase. (And because each item is in its original packaging, you could also dole out each product as individual gifts.)
Ilia Limitless mascara (full size): I have lost count of the number of times I have repurchased this mascara. It doesn’t clump and adds much-needed length to my lashes. LG
Summer Fridays Cloud Dew moisturizer (mini): My slightly oily skin loves this lightweight moisturizer, which hydrates my skin without leaving it feeling like I rubbed grease all over it. LG
Mutha Exfoliating Detox Body Bar (mini): Satisfyingly scratchy on the skin, like those Japanese exfoliating bath towels. A little goes a long way – just a few passes covers your body in a creamy lather. I’ve always preferred body washes, but this may have converted me into a bar soap person. KY
Arrae bloat gummies: These felt a bit diet culture-esque to me (ie useless), and I didn’t notice that my stomach felt less bloated after trying. LG
Compared with the 25-day calendar, no. While nothing in this calendar is bad , only a quarter of the products are ones we would go out of our way to buy individually. Sometimes the costlier item is worth the splurge .
