title: The great moth revival: how bogongs have bounced back
description: This animated map shows the insect’s population exploding in Australia’s eastern states, with the endangered species coming back from the brink
content:
This animated map shows the insect’s population exploding in Australia’s eastern states, with the endangered species coming back from the brink
If you live anywhere on the eastern side of Australia, you’ve probably noticed that bogong moths are back in a big way .
While we don’t yet have figures from ecologist-led surveys to compare with previous years, there is a wealth of data on the great moth revival being generated by citizen scientists across the eastern states.
In this animated map you can see bogong moth observations posted to the citizen science platform iNaturalist via the Bogong Watch project . Every dot is a sighting, which may include one or more moths.
While there are some caveats to keep in mind with citizen science data (observation numbers over time can be skewed because of differences in effort and participation, for example), it does clearly show how the moth population has exploded this year.
Bogongs were once so common they numbered in the billions, according to researchers , with as many as 4 billion moths migrating to the Australian Alps in summer to aestivate in cool caves. The moths famously caused panic at the Sydney Olympics closing ceremony in 2000, and were known to invade Parliament House in Canberra each year .
But the bogong population declined slowly between 1980 and 2016, then crashed dramatically in the summer of 2017.
Moth numbers were so low the species was described as “undetectable” in the alpine regions.
Ken Green, an ecologist who has been monitoring bogong moths for more than 40 years, previously told the Guardian that Australia’s drought through 2017, 2018 and 2019 was probably the largest contributor to the population crash , with pesticides and urban light pollution contributing to the slower decline from the 80s.
After those years of catastrophic decline, the explosion of bogongs across the skies of eastern Australia this spring is great news for the plants the moths pollinate and the endangered species that rely on them for food, including the mountain pygmy possum .

title: Surfing faces a cultural reckoning as women’s voices grow louder over sexual abuse allegations
description: A culture of silence has buried the stories of women who allege sexual assault in surf industry settings
content:
A culture of silence has buried the stories of women who allege sexual assault in surf industry settings
W hen news broke last week that a surfer had been provisionally suspended from international competition, after what the International Surfing Association (ISA) described as “recent reports of serious allegations of abuse within the surfing community,” the response online was unprecedented in the world of surfing.
While investigations into those allegations are ongoing, the story prompted a deluge of comments detailing other alleged experiences of sexual misconduct and assault in surf industry settings, ranging from corporate brand houses in Hawaii to organised surf trips. While horrifying, for women who have existed in this subculture across the decades, those broader stories are sadly no surprise.
In 2019, as I stood in a bar in New York City at the afterparty of a World Surf League (WSL) Longboard Tour contest, I took stock of my surroundings. It was after midnight and the bar was packed with competitors who had just wrapped an event on a windy North Atlantic Ocean earlier that day. From the women’s side of the tour, teenagers gathered; nearby, other competitors and event staff, many well into their 40s, were dotted across the room. Alcohol flowed freely; the event was private, so there was no one checking IDs. In fact, surfers themselves could be found behind the bar pouring drinks. I reflected on the moment: who was tasked with keeping these young women safe while in a setting like this? And if something were to happen, how would we report it, and to whom?
Over the years, the stories between women working and competing in the industry have accumulated in private. Ranging from sexual harassment to assault, none of these stories ever ended in accountability. When I raised this issue with Surfing NSW a few years ago, I was told the process for something that happened at a Surfing NSW event would be to make the complaint to the event director, and it would then be passed on to the state body’s CEO. At the time, Surfing NSW said they had never received any such complaint. It’s not difficult to understand why.
In the WSL context, while I have competed in sanctioned events for more than a decade, I have never received any information about how to report an incident of sexual abuse to the WSL, or how that report would be treated. And in a male-dominated industry that is tight-knit and insular, where the same people move from institution to institution, where work is often contract to contract, and sponsorship decisions and other opportunities are relationship-based, trying to act against these ranks in search of accountability carries potentially career-ending risk.
Without any clear independent reporting mechanism or track record of taking these reports seriously, these institutions create a culture of silence that protects the accused and buries the stories of women who may have faced sexual violence while competing or working at surfing events.
What was most surprising about the recent allegations that prompted a statement from the ISA was not that they are being made, but that there has actually been a response. A surfer has been suspended, pending investigation, in a culture that had previously glorified a lifestyle where women’s bodies were sacrificed in favour of surfing talent.
Australian surfer Nat Young, who was the 1966 world champion and is credited with being one of the pioneers of the shortboard revolution of the 1970s, described a disturbing scene in the opening chapter of his memoir Nat’s Nat and That’s That. Young writes in the book published in 1998 that a friend “had strategically positioned the girl so that she was lying on her back with her head facing away from the youthful group of lechers and so was able to give the nod over her shoulder”. He adds that when the friend “slipped out”, another “slipped in”, then a third person and Young “had our turn in the same manner”.
“The Grunter”, as Young describes the girl in the book, “was really into group sex and we all greeted her with open flies every time we saw her getting off her school bus”. “The scene was starting to get a bit out of hand, the line getting longer and longer as friends and acquaintances from other beaches joined in,” he writes.
Young’s account is not the only one of its kind that exists in the pages of surfing’s magazines and memoirs that have been published over the years, serving as a tool to not just validate and normalise such experiences but laud them, weaving them into the central fabric of the industry.
Now it appears that wind has started to blow under the cladding that has kept this conversation confined to the private spaces of women, spoken in secret for fear of professional or social reprisal. For the first time since I joined the surfing community, I have seen the rumours written down, albeit so far in comment sections and Instagram posts. But will this be a reckoning beyond a passing moment of outrage? Will it lead to actual reform of the structures that have maintained this culture?
Lucy Small is a professional surfer, journalist and film-maker from Sydney, with a special interest in women’s sport

title: Sexualised, violent threats: female Victorian MPs fear for their safety as they fight more than just next month’s election
description: Hostility from constituents is not new for the state’s politicians, including its premiers. But the alleged attack on Helen Haines has sent a chill down the collective spine
content:
Hostility from constituents is not new for the state’s politicians, including its premiers. But the alleged attack on Helen Haines has sent a chill down the collective spine
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
On Monday night, Georgie Purcell shared a statement on social media in support of Helen Haines , who earlier that day had been allegedly attacked by a constituent in her regional Victorian electorate.
Purcell, a Victorian upper-house MP whose region partly overlaps with Haines’s federal electorate, wrote that the alleged attack had sent chills down her spine. Being a woman in politics, she said, had changed the way she moved through the world – where she parked her car, which route she took home, even whether she held public events at all.
It didn’t take long to receive validation of why her precautions were necessary: a constituent commented on her Haines statement, saying he wished it had happened to Purcell. Another, a little while later, said: “You should be scared.”
Purcell reported them both. Beyond that, she says, there is “nothing else” she can do as the threats lack the specificity police require to take further action.
It leaves her on “high alert” with just five weeks until the Victorian election.
“One thing that is on my mind is there is 10 days of pre-poll approaching where anyone who does want to undertake a targeted attack on a candidate or a member of parliament, it won’t be hard to work out where they are,” she says.
Purcell is not alone. Nationals MP Annabelle Cleeland, whose electorate of Euroa covers 11,452 square kilometres, says, due to threats, she shares her live location with her husband and staff when on the road.
“I don’t feel like I signed up for this job to put my children in harm’s way and, right now, I’m frightened about that,” she told ABC Radio Melbourne on Thursday.
“It’s sexualised, it’s violent and they target your weaknesses and your vulnerabilities – your children, your home.”
MPs across Victoria’s political spectrum – predominantly women – have said that threats to their safety intensified during Victoria’s prolonged Covid lockdowns and have remained a constant since.
Few Victorians can forget that, during the pandemic, an effigy of the then premier, Daniel Andrews, was subjected to a mock execution on the front steps of parliament amid debate over pandemic legislation.
The next day, Andrews said: “There are some people who are threatening me. They’re threatening my family. They are essentially attacking the safety of my family.”
It is understood the premier was receiving around-the-clock close personal protection at the time. During the 2022 election campaign, Andrews’ press conferences were largely kept out of public view. One exception, an event at a Caulfield dog park, drew a man intent on heckling him. In 2023, another man faced court on charges of stalking and harassing Andrews.
When he resigned in 2024, Andrews lost his security but remained as much a public figure. Just recently, images of where he has been living appeared on the front page of a national newspaper.
His successor, Jacinta Allan, also faced much hostility, particularly in regional Victoria, where communities opposed the government’s emergency services levy and laws that allow state body VicGrid and its contractors access to private land for transmission projects – without a landholder’s consent.
There was the 2025 Bush Summit – a day after the latter laws passed parliament – where, during her speech, Allan was relentlessly heckled, including by an audience member who stood on her chair with a noose around her neck. Allan’s staff left in tears.
On other occasions, cars believed to be carrying the premier have been blocked or followed, only for those inside found to be staff members or other ministers – including at a press conference during the January bushfires .
For six weeks a mobile billboard carrying the message “ditch the witch” and AI-generated images of Allan travelled around Melbourne’s CBD before being reported on.
Each incident generated footage that was widely shared by the media and on socials.
A former staff member of Allan’s said the former premier “legitimately feared for her safety”.
“She would say ‘Someone is going to be killed.’”
For the entire four years she has been in parliament, Purcell has received abuse and rape and death threats on social media over her positions on issues such as duck hunting and racing.
But since beginning a relationship with federal Labor MP Josh Burns, Purcell has had access to more security measures – not because she is a Victorian MP, but because her partner is a federal one.
In Canberra, the Australian federal police manage threats against federal MPs , building up intelligence about repeated behaviour and patterns over time. In Victoria, Purcell says, individual complaints are dealt with separately by police.
With a state election looming, this may be about to change.
On Wednesday, the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, met with the Victorian electoral commissioner and the chief commissioner of police, Mike Bush, as well as his cabinet, to discuss stronger safety measures for MPs.
“This work will happen progressively and as soon as possible. What has happened must be a turning point for political debate in Victoria and around Australia. We must go forward with more respect and understanding of one another,” Carroll told reporters.
Earlier that morning, Bush said police were working to establish a centralised process for monitoring threats against MPs.
“We want a single-stop shop to report these things and have the ability to be very proactive,” he said.
As of Thursday afternoon, changes were yet to be communicated to Victorian MPs, who have been asked to attend a briefing with police on Friday. For now, their only guidance remains a Tuesday morning email from the Department of Parliamentary Services that advises them to monitor and control access to their electorate offices, check external areas on CCTV before leaving, and to remember that a duress button is available in an emergency.
It leaves MPs weighing the risk of being out in public with their constituents against the possibility that one may try to harm them.
Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

title: ‘I can’t sleep at night’: international students forced to navigate the impact of Labor’s sudden visa changes
description: Masters student Fatima Bonna says her visa runs out before the end date of her course. She feels overwhelmed by the uncertainty
content:
Master’s student Fatima Bonna says her visa runs out before the end date of her course. She feels overwhelmed by the uncertainty
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Fatima Bonna has pored over her student visa conditions. When she began studying in Adelaide last year, she memorised the maximum number of hours she could work – and checked again, just to be sure.
She knew exactly when her visa would expire, what it expected of her studies and the rules surrounding partners and dependants.
But then came this month’s changes to student visas. Suddenly, she feels overwhelmed by uncertainty.
Having changed degrees and institutions after her first semester, the end date of her visa no longer aligns with the conclusion of her course.
How can she manage to finish a master’s in early childhood education after her current visa expires?
Bonna’s visa expires next September – four months before her course at the Ikon Institute is due to finish.
Under the new student visa rules – designed to slash the country’s net migration – she will be required to travel offshore to apply for a new student visa.
“If I had any idea of it, I wouldn’t have changed,” the 27-year-old student from Bangladesh says.
“I don’t want to be humiliated, I don’t want to be told that ‘you are the reason for our housing crisis’, because I am paying for it … and I am happy to go back to my country after getting the experience.”
International students around Australia are facing uncertainty amid a flurry of announcements targeting the cohort and the Albanese government’s changes to student visa rules – in an attempt to curb “permanently temporary” migrations – which came into effect this month.
The crackdown targets “visa hopping” and onshore student transfers and requires most temporary visa holders to leave Australia to apply for a new visa, with some exemptions.
Labor’s changes also restrict secondary applicants – partners and dependent children – on most student visas, although applicants from Pacific and Asean member countries and those studying a PhD are exempt.
But the assistant minister for international education, Julian Hill, said other exceptions could apply as the government was “not in the business of separating families already onshore in Australia”.
“Sympathetic consideration would be given to visitor visas where required to keep families together while a student completes their stay in Australia,” he said.
A Melbourne-based migration agent, Gurpreet Dhawan, says requiring students to travel offshore to apply for a new visa can leave them in limbo.
“It’s a huge risk,” she says. “We will send them offshore to lodge the visa but how long will they have to sit there?”
According to dethe Department of Home Affairs website , about 50% of applications for a student visa (subclass 500) in higher education are now estimated to be processed within 16 days, and 90% within four months.
While the federal government has made exemptions for PhD students bringing dependants, all student visa holders can no longer add a relative after their visa has been granted.
“They have done everything correctly as per the law until 1 October,” Dhawan says. “They woke up on 2 October and their life is upside down.”
Wina Satria, a PhD candidate from Indonesia, travelled to Australia with her then two-year-old son last year. Satria planned to add her husband to her student visa next year so he could help raise their son.
The family’s plans to reunite have been thrown into disarray by the new restriction on adding relatives to a previously granted visa.
“I was shocked,” Satria says. “It’s hard if we can’t have our family with us.”
Satira, who is studying at the University of Sydney, says she hopes the federal government will create a further exemption for further PhD students.
“The hardest part is seeing my son when he misses his dad a lot,” she says.
Labor’s changes are designed to help bring net overseas migration down from its annual level of almost 300,000 to 225,000 by mid-2028.
University leaders have warned their institutions are struggling to fill international student places due to visa uncertainty, high visa refusal rates and a heated political debate on immigration as contributing factors.
The Coalition and One Nation’s immigration policies have also targeted international students , compounding uncertainty ahead of the 2028 election.
Daniel Martin arrived from Colombia in 2024 to study a master’s in education, and completed his course in July. He now holds a temporary graduate visa – which the Coalition has proposed abolishing – allowing him to stay in Australia for at least another two years.
Martin is applying for teaching and educational adviser jobs, and hopes to undertake a PhD in the coming years. But he says he is reconsidering his plans, due to the uncertainty around the visa system.
“It’s quite tricky right now … the instability, the uncertainty, it’s extremely difficult to navigate,” he says.
A spokesperson for the Department of Home Affairs said the reforms strike the right balance and would “welcome genuine students” and strengthen “the integrity of the student visa program”.
There could also be some “sympathetic consideration” given to the families of PhD students now in Australia, the government says.
“Australia’s high-quality education system, post-study opportunities and quality of life continue to make it an attractive destination for international students,” the spokesperson said.
“Demand for student visas has remained strong following increases to student visa application charges and the introduction of a range of integrity measures since 2023.”
The spokesperson said the changes would not affect the ability of genuine students to study in Australia.
“Requiring affected student visa applicants to be outside Australia at the time of visa application and grant reinforces the intent of the program, which is to facilitate temporary stay in Australia for study purposes and encourages temporary visa holders to maintain strong ties to their home country.”

title: Delays, deodorant and ripped up carpet: how airlines handle mid-flight ‘biological hazards’
description: When stomach bugs meet turbulence, air travel can become a health hazard for all onboard – and it happens, unfortunately, ‘more regularly than you would think’
content:
When stomach bugs meet turbulence, air travel can become a health hazard for all onboard – and it happens, unfortunately, ‘more regularly than you would think’
A little over an hour into their transatlantic flight, Kate Carson’s daughters had just lain down to sleep when suddenly their Air New Zealand “cuddle class” skycouch became a “nightmare” scene.
A stomach bug that had been troubling their family during the holiday reared its head again: her youngest, three years old, started throwing up. “The first time, she was asleep, and no one saw it coming, and it went all into the seat … down the side and into the crack,” Carson says.
Her daughter did not stop vomiting until an hour before they landed in Los Angeles. “Everyone’s worried about their kid crying on a plane – no, no, no – this is so much worse,” Carson says.
Her husband spent “10 straight hours just trying to catch whatever else she threw up into the barf bag” while Carson cleaned the plane bathroom “top to bottom”. After she’d “nuked” it with what she thought was a cleaning product, supplied by the crew, she realised all she had been given was “deodorising spray”. (When contacted by Guardian Australia, Air New Zealand declined to comment.) Carson and her husband decided to abandon the plan to surprise their daughters with a visit to Disneyland during the layover. Instead, they booked into a hotel to do laundry.
As the other passengers disembarked, ground crew were waiting to take away the family’s chairs, clean around them, then replace them with an entirely new row. “I was so grateful … you come in and you sit on a seat of a plane and you just don’t know who was there, you don’t know what happened,” Carson said.
But some passengers have been left with clues. A Delta passenger sat in the faeces of an ill service animal from the previous flight; a man travelling with Air France found blood and faeces on the floor from a passenger’s haemorrhage two flights before; while Air Canada passengers were threatened with being placed on a no-fly list for refusing to sit in vomit-soaked seats . In a statement, Delta said their safety and security protocols are “top customer priorities”; Air Canada said “for any extraordinary situations” the airline “follows the standards as set out by the health authorities to deep clean and disinfect aircraft cabins using professional grade products”; while Air France did not respond to requests for comment.
While these incidents suggest airlines don’t always allow hygiene issues to hinder the schedule, they can also cause major delays. In 2023 a woman’s trail of diarrhoea forced a Delta flight from Atlanta to Barcelona to turn back, while a 2008 flight diverted after several passengers from the same New England tour group were struck with norovirus mid-air – and was the subject of a study by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention .
Travel is a major risk factor for gastrointestinal illnesses, with travellers’ diarrhoea thought to affect between 30% and 70% of travellers during a two-week period. Combined with turbulence increasing nausea and logistical barriers sometimes hindering passengers from making it to the lavatory on time, air travel can become not just messy but a biological hazard .
Flights are delayed due to biological hazards from passengers “unfortunately more regularly than you would think”, says Justin Brownjohn, a former operations manager for Singapore Airlines, Qatar Airways and Virgin Australia.
While there is no publicly available data on the subject, and multiple airlines refused the Guardian’s requests for internal data, Brownjohn says that, from his experiences, an airline would probably be delayed due to a biohazard issue roughly once a week.
The extent of the delay depends on what the substance is, “how bad it is”, where it is on the aircraft and where the flight has landed, says Brownjohn, now manager of the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology’s Aviation Academy.
When an incident happens midflight, cabin crew will attempt to contain the contamination, using biohazard kits they have on board for this purpose, which include an absorbent powder that can turn liquid into clumps so it can be scraped away. Then the area will be sanitised with a spray.
“But depending on the severity of the contamination, the aircraft may need a more thorough cleaning and disinfection by the ground team before it can operate again,” says Leila*, a flight attendant from a low-cost carrier airline in the Middle East.
She says that “the really extreme cases”, when body fluids get into carpets, seat cushions or other areas that are difficult to properly clean, can cause a delay. Sometimes whole sections of carpet have to be removed.
Flight attendants may also be able to swap out seat covers, block off a row of seats if the flight isn’t full, or close off a bathroom, says Seth Heiple, a flight attendant for a major US carrier and a safety representative for the Association of Flight Attendants. “Unfortunately, we’ve had faeces all over the walls of a lavatory.”
Flight attendants will notify the pilot, who will warn the ground crew, or other teams who may need to be involved, such as maintenance crews if seatbelts need to be replaced due to contamination, Heiple says.
Most airlines have third-party contractors who provide the ground crew cleaning services. Osman Yılmaz is the managing director of one such service, Çelebi Aviation, which contracts for airlines including Lufthansa, Emirates and Air China at their stations across five countries.
Yilmaz says crews are “well trained” in cleaning up vomit and spills. “But something beyond that, they don’t have to touch it.”
For more extreme cases, especially if there is blood, specialist cleaning companies with training in biological messes are called in. These experts can usually resolve issues fairly quickly in major ports, Brownjohn says.
However, when incidents occur in smaller airports without access to cleaning and engineering support, “the airline quickly runs out of options about what they can do”, Brownjohn says.
“It’s usually one of two: do the best they can – by cordoning off areas, changing seat covers, using air freshener – the other option is usually cancel the flight,” he says.
Heiple says in these situations “if the smell’s really bad, they might be legal to fly, but it’s not something that we want to accept if it’s going to maybe trigger more people to throw up on the next flight”.
The captain has the final authority on whether to accept an aircraft, Heiple says, but the crew will occasionally demand additional cleaning through a consultative process.
These kinds of delays are becoming more common with the advent of low cost carriers who turn planes around in short windows. “The system is not designed to accommodate last-minute problems like this,” says William McGee, who previously worked in airline operations management.
Last century, aircraft spent more time on the ground between flights, while airlines had a much lower rate of seat occupancy (about six in 10) and in-house cleaning staff. This meant “they had more ability to address this stuff”, says McGee, now a senior fellow for aviation at the American Economic Liberties Project.
While long-haul international flights are generally cleaned between flights – because these are the routes that make the most money – domestic short-haul routes are often only thoroughly cleaned at the end of the day, McGee says.
Aircraft are typically deep-cleaned every two weeks or so – which involves cleaning nooks and crannies and steaming carpets and seats, Brownjohn says.
McGee says: “My best advice is take the first flight of the day because chances are that’s the cleanest that plane is going to be all day.”
Heiple agrees. “Between flights during the day, [a passenger] might not realise that somebody used the tray table to change their baby and now it’s contaminated.
“Anything that can come out of the human body has and does on the aircraft unfortunately.”

title: Black Bag by Luke Kennard audiobook review – brilliant Booker-shortlisted campus comedy
description: The author reveals his mastery of comic timing in his narration of this novel about a cash-strapped actor paid to live inside a black leather bag
content:
The author reveals his mastery of comic timing in his narration of this novel about a cash-strapped actor paid to live inside a black leather bag
T he unnamed narrator of Luke Kennard’s novel is an out-of-work actor living in London. His last job was three months ago, he is behind with his rent and has “measured out my life in coffees I cannot technically afford”. So when he comes across an advert – “Male actor required for psychological enquiry. Non-speaking but discretion and devotion to restrictive performance requirements obligatory” – he offers his services.
The job, he discovers, is at a university working under a psychology professor named Dr Blend. There he must strip to his underpants and zip himself into a black leather bag, in which there are two eyeholes and further holes for his feet. The actor is expected to sit silently in the bag during seminars while students contemplate his presence.
The inspiration for Kennard’s Booker-shortlisted campus comedy is a 1967 social experiment, conducted at Oregon State University, where a student attended classes inside a black bag in a test to see whether other students would grow attached to his presence. It also nods to Yoko Ono’s 1964 conceptual artwork Bag Piece, in which gallery-goers were asked to climb inside a large black bag.
Kennard, who is the reader, mines this surreal conceit for laughs as the protagonist does battle with revolving doors and tries to pay for coffee using a card taped to the inside of the bag at chest height. As with his prose, the author’s delivery reveals him as a master of comic timing and a mordant bon mot . Yet beneath Black Bag’s winningly oddball exterior are more sober reflections on human relationships and what it is to be a man.
Battle Axe: A Memoir Margaret Hodge, William Collins, 14hr 43min The veteran Labour politician narrates her book detailing 50 years in frontline politics, from her early career as a leader of Islington council to her time as an MP during the Tony Blair and Gordon Brown premierships and her recent work as the UK’s anti-corruption champion.

title: Zach Braff: ‘You can be talented and good-looking, but acting success is still like winning the lottery’
description: The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman
content:
The Scrubs and Garden State star answers your questions about working with megastars, getting his hair to look good and being brutally killed on BoJack Horseman
How do you manage not to act starstruck when directing people like Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Harrison Ford? TopTramp That’s where my acting comes in – I pretend that I don’t know how famous they are. Every actor really wants a leader. They want someone who knows the script really well, has a plan for how the scene is going to be executed, and – in the case of comedy – knows how to make it funny. The last thing any of those guys wants is someone coming in starstruck and wide-eyed. So I use my acting skills to pretend I’m not starstruck and treat them like normal people.
Your Fake Doctors, Real Friends podcast was a real help through lockdown. You were very emotionally open and personal; it was like catching up with friends. I still think about your line that making it in acting, even if you’re talented and good-looking, is like winning the lottery. Do you think that early 00s Zach Braff would make it in the present day the way you did? KamesJ Back then, the broadcast networks were making so many pilots, at least it was work for people. Now, I think it’s a much harder landscape to break through. I firmly believe that you can be talented and good-looking, but success is still like winning the lottery. I know plenty of brilliant actors whose lottery ticket hasn’t come up yet. I started auditioning at 14 and barely got anything for years, so I’ve always felt very lucky.
And as far as the podcast, that’s so great to hear. We didn’t plan to start it during Covid, but it became a nice sort of warm hug for people who wanted a little bit of nostalgia. Donald [Faison, who plays Dr Turk] and I loved getting together, making each other laugh and reminiscing. So much so that we’re actually bringing it back.
Have you thought about Garden State 2? Haggisneepsnfatties We did an anniversary concert for the soundtrack last year – we got most of the bands together and did a charity show for the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles – and that was really cool. Natalie Portman was there. I had told her that people have come to me about doing a musical of the movie. I love musicals, but I’ve always thought: “I don’t know if that I want to do that.” Then she said: “Why don’t you do it with the songs from the soundtrack?” It’s funny, because I never thought of that. I haven’t taken any steps to make it a reality, but I do daydream of somehow using the music that people love so much from the soundtrack to make it into a musical.
When you agreed to join the cast of BoJack Horseman , how did you feel about your character having such a grisly end? topfoot I love the show, so it was so fun to play a cartoonish version of myself, and I just did whatever they said. I never said: “Don’t kill me that way. Don’t have Jessica Biel feast on my carcass,” or whatever the hell it was.
How much fun was it playing a small role in Arrested Development – to my mind the funniest, cleverest and silliest of all the US sitcoms? Manofthesouth It was amazing, especially because I didn’t know I was going to be a never-nude until I got the script. In the world of Arrested Development, a never-nude is someone – mainly Tobias – who can never be fully naked, even in the shower, so he wears denim short-shorts.
Scrubs and Arrested Development were both doing really well. Jason Bateman and I were at some big event with the heads of both networks – we were NBC, they were Fox. We were laughing, saying: “It’d be fun if we each guested on each other’s show, but the networks would never let us do that.” Then we realised: “They’re all here. Let’s just go ask them.” They said “Sure,” so I guested on Arrested and Jason did an episode of Scrubs as an ostrich farmer.
Who would you most like to cast in Dr Acula : The Movie – JD’s vampire-doctor screenplay in Scrubs? PickleMan Michael B Jordan and Leonardo DiCaprio, if we’re in the fantasy where we’re going to make an amazing, huge-budget version. Remember at the end of Pee-wee’s Big Adventure when they make the movie of his life and cast beautiful movie stars, and Pee-wee ends up as a bellhop? That’s the version of Dr Acula I want: megastars, while Donald and I are just in the background.
You’ve had huge success whether you’re acting, writing or directing. If you were to pick one standout pinch-me moment, what would it be? Turnipsnitzel Morgan Freeman saying yes to my film was one of those great moments. So was standing in the back of the Eccles theatre in Park City when Garden State premiered, thinking: “Holy shit, how did this happen?”
When I got Scrubs, I was waiting tables. I put my Motorola StarTAC phone on the passenger seat as I was driving home from the final callback, and was just eyeing it to see if it was going to ring. Then it rang, I pulled over, called my parents, then I called the manager of the restaurant. She said: “I’m so happy for you, babe, but you got to work tonight still.” I said: “Oh, don’t worry, I’m coming in.” So I worked the whole shift knowing I probably wouldn’t be waiting tables for a couple of years.
If you were on a plane and there was an announcement asking if there’s a doctor on board, would you put your hand up? MrSOBaldrick Absolutely not. I don’t know anything. I really don’t. We have the most amazing consultants on set, including this wonderful nurse who’s just a badass. She shows us what to do and tells us what the hell we’re saying. Anyone who thinks we know anything for real is crazy.
Scrubs taught me a lot about illness, life and death. Did it do the same for you? waydgroods I was so young when we did the original series that I don’t think I had any experience with loss and being in hospitals and grief. In the years since, I’ve lost so many people. I’ve sat in hospital and ICU waiting rooms, waiting with bated breath for the doctor to come in with good or bad news. I’ve seen how the nurses run the whole hospital. I’ve witnessed it first-hand in a way I hadn’t as a young man. So I think now I have even more respect. I feel more like I’m playing a superhero as the guy who’s the chief of medicine at an underfunded hospital who’s meant to be a particularly badass doctor.
Does your hair have its own agent? Dr_J_A_Zoidberg My hair’s agent is that I take a shower at night and then I go to sleep on it and you get magical bedhead.

title: Bruno Guimarães had sleepless nights before Newcastle exit but hopes for same ‘love’ at Arsenal
description: Midfielder says there were a lot of tears as he said goodbye at St James’ Park but he is enjoying the remorselessness at his new club
content:
Midfielder says there were a lot of tears as he said goodbye at St James’ Park but he is enjoying the remorselessness at his new club
F or Bruno Guimarães, it was a time to show his steeliness, to fix his eyes on the prize – even if he knew it would surely mean them welling up. And then some. It was a tumultuous summer for the Brazil midfielder. A fine World Cup on a personal level was marred by a crucial penalty miss in the last-16 loss against Norway . Now he had the dream move lined up to Arsenal but it could not happen without breaking some hearts at Newcastle.
Guimarães admits he lay awake at night as the emotions swirled. How could he leave Newcastle, the club where he made so many connections and enjoyed so many highs after joining from Lyon in January 2022 ? There were the Champions League qualifications and, above all, the Carabao Cup triumph in 2025 that ended a 70-year wait for a domestic trophy. On the other hand, how could he resist Arsenal and the prospect of competing regularly for the game’s top honours?
Sometimes, you simply have to take a deep breath and the plunge. Nobody wants to die wondering. Guimarães knew the Newcastle team was breaking up. Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali had gone to Barcelona and Tottenham. The manager, Eddie Howe, was at the end of the line and would also leave . Guimarães went through with the £75m transfer and nobody can say it has not worked out so far.
Arsenal felt he would provide a different element for them, different ways of unlocking defences, plus his trademark work rate and snarl. Guimarães has brought all of that. Already he has made a difference. He even gave a little back to Newcastle when he scored his first Arsenal goal at Sunderland in September , paving the way for a 2-0 victory. Two Premier League games later, he scored the winner at home against Leeds .
Guimarães almost got another vital goal on Wednesday in the Champions League tie at Bayern Munich only for Manuel Neuer to deny him with an outrageous save. That would have put Arsenal 2-1 up. The game finished 2-2 , Arsenal fighting until the end and equalising through Declan Rice in the 82nd minute. Still, it has not been easy for Guimarães and he surely has Arsenal’s visit to Newcastle on 21 November circled in his diary. His greatest hope is that he can build the same relationships at his new club.
“It was not just hard to tell Eddie but to tell the owners and my teammates [about deciding to leave Newcastle],” Guimarães says. “But I think the club went to a new rotation; a lot of players left, as well. The gaffer left. It was tough because my connection with the club was unbelievable. I never felt so loved like the way I was at Newcastle. I hope I can have the same love here at Arsenal .
“It was hard for me to say bye. I remember when I said bye to the lads, I was crying. They were crying as well because we were a family there. I lost many, many nights of sleep because it was difficult for me, for my family. But sometimes in your life you have to make decisions and in my mind, I needed a new challenge. I wish Newcastle all the best because they were so nice to me. It is just time to move on and I’ve been enjoying my time here at Arsenal, as well.”
Guimarães is enjoying his burgeoning midfield partnership with Rice, not to mention Martin Ødegaard, who tends to be the most advanced of the trio. That said, there is plenty of fluidity between the positions. There is the sense that the manager, Mikel Arteta, is searching for the perfect balance.
“Declan can play – like me – as a No 6, No 8 or No 10,” Guimarães says. “The manager is still trying to get the best version of ourselves. Against Bayern, I played more as a No 6, Declan played more as a No 8. I enjoy playing with him a lot; with Martin, as well. We have been on a good run so far.”
Guimarães’ battles when he was at Newcastle against Rice have been well documented. He said Rice had messaged him as he prepared to sign for Arsenal, saying: “No more fights, now we’re friends.” Guimarães is the player you loathe when he is against you but love when he is in your ranks.
What was the worst thing Guimarães said to Rice when they were in opposition? “It is difficult to say,” he replies with a smile. “I am like this when I play against teams. When we were playing against each other, I was not nice to him, he was not nice to me! Now we try to help each other on the pitch.”
Guimarães cannot believe how Neuer kept out his close-range header; the 40-year-old goalkeeper clawed the ball up against the crossbar and away. “He pulled off a miracle,” Guimarães says. “I asked him after the game: ‘How did you manage to save that?’ He said: ‘I don’t know. I just saved it!’ He’s unbelievable, one of the best keepers in the world. No matter how old he is, he is top.”
What Guimarães has seen with clarity is the remorselessness of the collective attitude at Arsenal; the insatiable will to win, which comes from Arteta. Next up for them is Everton at home on Saturday. Guimarães knows he is in the right place.
“The mentality of the club has changed a lot and Arteta shows this perfectly,” Guimarães says. “We don’t accept a draw at Bayern. We always want to win. That is the mentality that we go to the training ground with every day. Arteta is always a little bit addicted to videos and the way that he can make us feel better on the pitch. We have a top manager with a top mentality. We want to win everything possible.”

title: The best bread makers in the UK for easy homemade loaves – tested
description: Want fresh bread without the hard work? Our expert baked her way through nine machines to find the best for white, wholemeal and gluten-free loaves
content:
Want fresh bread without the hard work? Our expert baked her way through nine machines to find the best for white, wholemeal and gluten-free loaves
Everything you need to make great sourdough
A s a bread-loving lazy person, easy access to plump, airy loaves is always appreciated. And while buying it from a shop might be considered the laziest way to acquire it, I think making it at home can be just as convenient, especially with a decent bread maker to do all the hard bits for you.
Bread machines mix, knead, prove and bake your loaf at the touch of a button and most, including the ones I’ve tested here, produce loaves that are above and beyond your standard sandwich bread.
This is a real treat if, like me, you enjoy letting your imagination run wild with all the different loaves you can make. Sweet chocolate-chip breads, Italian pesto loaves, super-seeded high-fibre slices for your lunchtime toasties – the possibilities are almost endless. Making bread from scratch also means you can cater to dietary preferences – and most of the models here make an outstanding gluten-free loaf.
To find the best bread makers, I put nine machines through their paces – munching my way through an unimaginable amount of white, wholemeal, gluten-free and olive loaves in the process. These are the models that proved to be worth their salt, and more importantly, worth your money.
Having spent almost 10 years testing and writing about kitchen appliances and cooking gadgets, I’ve built a wealth of knowledge on just about every cooking tool out there. From emerging trends to tried-and-true chef favourites, I’ve seen it all.
All of this experience means I can spot a worthwhile product a mile away, but also know when something might not quite hit the mark. I’m also dough-obsessed, making pizza and bread from scratch most weeks, which makes the pursuit of finding the perfect bread machine all that bit easier.
When it comes to bread, consistency is key. A good bread maker should be as adept at making a basic white loaf as a crusty wholemeal or gluten-free variant. This is why I made and taste-tested multiple such loaves (36 in total) across nine bread makers, using the same recipes each time.
For machines with a mix-in function, I also made an additional olive loaf to assess the reliability of the mechanism that drops ingredients into the loaf. Testing the various flours gave me a good indication of how well each bread maker is suited to specific tasks, as well as how well they perform in general.
Most bread makers allow you to use any recipe, as long as the weight is correct for the bread pan you’re using. As they’re automated, they are, however, a little more slapdash with the mixing, so if you’re used to making your favourite loaf by hand, you might find a little trial and error is involved to get it right in a bread machine.
I also measured the energy consumption of each bread maker using a power meter, noting the result in the specs below. Functionality and how easy each machine was to use and clean were also factored into my testing and reviews.
All the bread makers sourced for this article will be sent back to their manufacturers after testing.
Most of the bread makers on this list offer a range of programmes for different types of bread, including white, wholemeal and gluten-free, as well as rapid settings for baking a white loaf in about an hour. You can also choose the crust colour – usually light, medium or dark – and the best bread makers have a delay timer if you want a fresh loaf ready by a specific time.
Ultimately though, the most important part of using a bread maker is finding a recipe you like. Most bread makers come with a couple of basic recipes included as part of the manual and occasionally a recipe app. If they don’t, there are lots of bread-maker-specific recipes online. Just ensure the recipe size matches the loaf sizes your bread machine can make. For example, to find a good gluten-free recipe for my testing benchmarks here, I searched for a “500g and 1kg gluten-free bread maker recipe” and found the Freee Gluten Free bread recipe to be most consistent. I used the quantities for the 3-litre pan and halved them for 500g loaves.
Once you have a recipe, the rest is relatively simple. For most bread makers, you add the wet ingredients first, but always check the manufacturer’s instructions, as the order can vary. Adding the wet ingredients first can help the bread paddle inside the maker mix more evenly and consistently, leaving no clumps around the edges of the pan.
After this, the machine pretty much takes care of the rest, automating the mixing, kneading, proving and baking with no need to work the dough by hand or monitor the proving. You can, if manufacturer instructions permit, remove the bread maker’s paddle before the baking starts to minimise the hole in the bottom of your loaf.
Once the full cycle finishes, remove the loaf from the pan and leave it to cool before slicing. If you try to cut into it while it’s still hot, the structure can tear and collapse, leaving you with broken slices and a sad-looking loaf.
You can make sourdough bread in some bread makers to speed up the process somewhat, but the crust and crumb structure won’t be the same as making it by hand. What’s more, as traditional sourdough relies on a live starter, which ferments dough more slowly than fast-action dried yeast, most basic bread maker presets don’t allow enough time for the dough to rise.
More advanced bread makers, such as the Graef model reviewed above, have dedicated sourdough settings that automate the process and allow more proving time (although the sourdough recipes provided by Graef also use yeast and require a separate fermentation stage). You can also consider a bread maker with a custom setting, such as Sage’s the Custom Loaf, as this will allow you to set your own longer proving and bake times.
Bread makers are surprisingly versatile machines once you get to know them. As well as kneading, proving and baking your bread, many models have programmes for other food prepping tasks. Most machines have presets for various mixing and cooking tasks, including anything from yoghurt and cheese to pasta dough and compote.
If you’d rather give an old bread maker a new lease of life and save yourself a bit of money, there are plenty of refurbished and secondhand bread makers available online if you know where to look.
Good places to look include eBay and Direct Vacuums . I found a refurbished Tefal bread maker , featured in our best of the rest list, for £64.99 on the latter. You can also search Amazon Resale or Amazon Renewed for secondhand and refurbished options. It’s also worth paying your local charity shops a visit, as larger ones, such as the British Heart Foundation’s, tend to sell used and tested electrical goods. Before buying secondhand, check that the appliance hasn’t been recalled, that the plug and cable are undamaged, and that all the parts are included.
For more, read everything you need to make great sourdough and the best stand mixers to make baking easier

title: A financially comfortable friend has set up a GoFundMe for vet bills. Is this socially acceptable?
description: Your friends may have had good intentions when making this request, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But that needn’t dictate how you feel about it
content:
Your friends may have had good intentions when making this request, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But that needn’t dictate how you feel about it
A friend, who I believe is financially comfortable, set up a GoFundMe page to pay for vet bills for their sick dog while on holiday overseas.
The family appears to be financially comfortable; both adults have good jobs, own two cars, have all the latest gadgets like expensive bikes and sporting equipment, take an annual holiday overseas and domestic holidays throughout the year, and live in a big house in a well-to-do area.
Is it socially acceptable to ask for money publicly in these circumstances?
Eleanor says: I’ll never forget someone posting their household expenses as proof it’s hard to get by on two six-figure incomes. By the time they’d paid for holidays, two cars, private school fees, insurance, extracurriculars, the mortgage and savings, there was nothing left!
They really did think this was proof they weren’t well-off. I suppose in some sense they’re right. Once you use your money to secure your financial future and have a high quality of life, you don’t have a Scrooge McDuck pile left over.
Point of story: moving up the wealth hierarchy moves your sense of what’s normal. Comparison looks up, not down, so people lose track of how many people they’re above. What they first experienced as an advantage slowly starts to seem like background. It’s possible your friends feel and are genuinely burdened – “we can’t cover this!” – in a situation other people would covet. And importantly, we don’t know their finances. They may not be liquid, precisely because of the holidays and the house and the equipment.
But in the ethics of asking for and giving money, it’s important that money isn’t just money. It has social meaning. Money talks, in the sense that it says things.
What it says isn’t always exhausted by how much people have. It may be important for the less well-off child to take their parents to dinner because that says “thank you”. Or for colleagues or dates to split the bill, because that means neither owes a debt of gratitude. Or to help pay for your child’s wedding even though they could afford it themselves, because that feels significant as a parent.
Where we go wrong is when our interpretations of what money says differ. Somebody thinks they’re being generous; others experience their largesse as domineering. Somebody – like a newlywed drafting the gift registry or, possibly, your friend – thinks they’re making it possible for people to give them money without any expectation of receiving it. Others experience that same action as tone-deaf and entitled.
If money talks, what does their GoFundMe actually say?
They might feel as if it says one thing: “Something unexpected happened, we’d be touched if anyone wanted to contribute.” You might feel as if it says another: “We expect you to cover our bills.” One is an appeal to friendship, the other is an appeal to need.
In fairness, a GoFundMe isn’t means-tested. They can ask, and other people can say no. In their social circle, they may be the least well-off, which would change the dynamics of making this ask.
They’re the authority on what they meant when they uploaded this, but they don’t get to be the authority on what everybody else hears. Meaning isn’t determined solely by our intentions. Their motivations might have been totally benign at the same time as their impact was gauche.
Asking for money introduces a question that nobody had beforehand; why should I help pay for this? They may think that’s a mean-spirited question, if they intended this as an appeal to friendship. But it’s a question they’ve invited people to ask, and you’re allowed to decide your own answer.
