title: Three things the Albanese government could do right now to make people feel better off
description: There are plenty of reasons why Australians feel ‘mad as hell’ at the moment. These three economic policies could restore faith in politics and bring some relief
content:
There are plenty of reasons why Australians feel ‘mad as hell’ at the moment. These three economic policies could restore faith in politics and bring some relief
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
I n the 1976 movie Network, news anchor Howard Beale tells TV viewers to stick their heads out their windows and yell: “I’m as mad as hell, and I’m not going to take this any more!” It’s a sentiment that resonates today in Australia and across the world.
In October, consumer sentiment at home fell to levels more often associated with recessions, despite the fact that the latest GDP numbers show the economy grew by a real 2% over the year to June (that is, 2% over and above the rate of inflation).
But there are plenty of reasons why Australians are unhappy and even angry. The combination of war-induced energy shocks, rising tariffs, ageing populations, increased military spending, more frequent climate shocks and even the datacentre frenzy are all pushing up inflation and public-sector debt, which in turn have led to rising interest rates . These are not short-term trends. Add to that falling house prices , rising unemployment, rising inequality and a general malaise around what AI might or might not do, and you might wonder why sentiment isn’t even lower.
Sadly, in Australia and across the world, pessimism is turning to rising frustration, anger and even violence. After the appalling alleged attack on the independent MP Helen Haines this week, there have been calls to “lower the temperature”. Which begs the question: what might the federal government reasonably do to make people feel like their concerns are really being heard and that action is being taken to rectify the situation (while noting that many challenges are global in nature)?
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
There are many ready policy options that could leave us collectively better off. Shifting the tax burden from income to spending , or increasing the supply of housing and childcare places, could all deliver productivity and wellbeing gains but they will take time. However, some more immediate measures, such as the $3.3bn in cuts to fuel excise levy and road user charges, if unfunded will just worsen the budget position and may end up forcing the RBA to increase rates again.
Measures must help households most in need, deliver a return to taxpayers over time and consider the long-term budget deficit (so that future generations aren’t paying for the policy mistakes of today). Ideally, such policies would also deal with some of the overarching challenges we face, too, such as climate change.
There are (at least) three things that the government could do right now that make economic sense to me, and that might restore some faith in the political system – assuming opposition parties (and the public at large) play ball and choose economically sensible options over costly ideologies . And while they might take some time to implement (and to recoup costs), they would represent a demonstration of intent that might restore some of that missing trust. The good news for the government is that others have already done the groundwork for them.
I’m a big fan of the Grattan Institute idea this week of raising the GST to 15% (still below the OECD average of 19.4% ) with appropriate income tax reductions targeted at low-income households, along with increases in jobseeker and youth allowance payments, rent assistance and pensions. Grattan suggests handing the remainder of the additional $76bn a year back to the states, which would help with woefully underfunded health and education systems; reduced reliance on gambling revenues could be an added bonus. There’s plenty in this to feel good about.
Another excellent, if more complex, idea is to implement a carbon pricing system. Yes, really! The Superpower Institute’s latest proposal to make polluters pay for the emissions that hurt us all and to tax the super profits of gas exporters would generate $35bn a year over 25 years. This can be redistributed back to those most affected and still leave room for wider supports and/or budget repair. This idea combines climate action and support for future industries with equitable support for households and businesses.
On a less grandiose scale, better targeting of existing supports might go some way to reducing household inequality. For example, encouraging electrification has never made more sense, given high energy prices. But government supports for EVs, solar and batteries generally benefit the wealthy , who have the money (and the rooftops) needed to take advantage. The New South Wales government’s Solar for Residential Apartments scheme, which is partly funded by the federal government, gives us a template for helping households electrify more equitably, while adding to the country’s energy security. The scheme specifically targets $5m of the total $30m package to apartment-dwellers in postcodes which score in the lowest 40% of the Australian Bureau of Statistics socioeconomic index of disadvantage. There’s room for improvement but more policies that improve equity – like pulling back on super tax lurks for the uber-rich – should be a high priority.
This is just a taste of what is possible. There’s no shortage of sound policy ideas from thinktanks, universities and even government departments themselves. It is vested interests, partisanship and a lack of spine that block progress. Political leaders of all stripes need to find more courage, more sense and a determination to bring people with them. Easier said than done but we need to start doing things differently if we want different (and better) outcomes.
This article was amended on 23 October 2026 to clarify that the federal government partly funds the NSW government’s Solar for Residential Apartments scheme

title: I longed for my big break. Then a Nobel winner and my girlfriend showed me why success isn’t everything
description: I was reducing a creative life down to public recognition. Anne Carson’s career deserves more respect than that, and so does mine
content:
I was reducing a creative life down to public recognition. Anne Carson’s career deserves more respect than that, and so does mine
I am one of those funny little people who is creative and has made the dubious decision to try to make a career out of it.
I didn’t fully commit until I was about 30, and I’ve spent the last 14 years in an up and down ride, trying to chip away until I reach the mysterious and elusive level of success where nothing bad happens ever.
I have had more heartening bits than many aspiring writers, but they have never coalesced into any kind of stability. Somewhere in the distance is the dream: I get to make my own TV show or movie, and everything finally falls into place and I never struggle or doubt myself again. The vague-but-strengthening-with-each-passing-day sense that I’ve made a terrible mistake that is too late to fix will vanish.
One of the things I have done to keep my head above water is collect stories about people who have achieved that kind of success later in life. Morgan Freeman was 52 before his breakthrough role in Driving Miss Daisy. Charles Bukowski was 49 when he quit his job to write full time. Yesterday a guy I follow on social media posted that a movie he co-wrote was about to start shooting, a first for him – and he is 43.
There are many artists who quietly beaver away (not all of them lesbians like me) for half their life or more until they finally get their “breakthrough”. When you’re younger than them, a late bloomer is a huge reassurance. It’s proof that even if it hasn’t worked out for you yet, it still conceivably can. These are stories I’ve gathered like precious stones over the years, clutching them to my breast when my own creative life feels impossible to sustain, as my bones weary, and the cohort of people also trying to make a splash in dying industries get ever younger and more beautiful.
Earlier this month, there was a shiny new precious stone up for grabs when the genre-defying 76-year-old writer Anne Carson won the Nobel prize in literature . Carson was 42 when her first book of poems was published by a small Canadian publisher, and since then she has lectured and published consistently. Usually, this is a story I would pounce on with my greedy little fingers, and use it to comfort myself. I’m only 44, look how much time there is to get beloved!
For a few reasons, I didn’t have that same feeling this time. The most obvious one is that Carson was already so successful, respected and well read. Another is that my ever-optimistic and very honest girlfriend has promised to break up with me if I give up on my dreams, which has shifted my perspective somewhat. And another was reading Carson’s own words about her artistic practice and attitude to success. She was once quoted as saying “ I’m going to be famous 15 minutes after I’m dead .” After winning the MacArthur Fellowship in 2000, when asked what difference notoriety had made, she said, “ Doesn’t make a lot of difference. It’s nice to be met at airports, I’ll say that .”
She went on to talk about how it meant she could make more work. That is the real success. Not that she won this or that award at her age, but that she has never stopped pushing herself; she has continued to make work of distinction, because that is what she’s here to do. I realised that my habit of hoarding these late-in-life success stories was doing a disservice to us all. I was placing recognition and milestones above the work, reducing someone else’s creative life down to their public victories. Carson’s career deserves more respect than that, and so does mine. I find it hard to say, but I am proud of the fact that I have come from almost nothing, with no connections, and have worked hard in a tough industry for over a decade to scrape together a living doing what I am here to do. I find it hard to accept, but that is worth recognition on its own. I’ve been treating this part of my life as a waiting room for victory, instead of the victory.
Don’t get me wrong, this is not an argument against wanting or striving for success. I would love to be given a huge creative opportunity that I can become very annoying about. I would LOVE for the creative industries to be supported to thrive so that many other annoying people can find their voice and get it heard. We shouldn’t have to choose between being who we are and being able to survive. It’s no good telling artists that the work itself should be its own reward when the rent still needs paying. Nor should we pretend that recognition, financial security and the chance to reach an audience don’t matter. They do. They really do.
But I’ve been reminded that outcomes are not everything. Your creative life will continue to change. It can take decades to hit the right thing on the right head at the right moment. It also may never happen. Carson (and my girlfriend) continue to remind me the point is to keep making things, to keep finding out what I think, to keep trying to inject my voice into the world. If I ever get a big break, it won’t be in the form of a Nobel prize, but I still hope for something. I can’t be dishonest about that. But whether or not it happens, I’ll still be here, chipping away at the dream until I fall into the big sleep.

title: ‘Jane Austen is for everyone’: novelist Diana Reid on adapting Sense and Sensibility – and surprising Brits with her accent
description: The Australian author of Love and Virtue says her nationality didn’t give her pause when she wrote the script, but Ang Lee’s ‘perfect’ 1995 film did
content:
The Australian author of Love and Virtue says her nationality didn’t give her pause when she wrote the script, but Ang Lee’s ‘perfect’ 1995 film did
T he summer Diana Reid spent writing her film adaptation of Sense and Sensibility , she found herself having some oddly formal conversations down at the pub. The Australian author used only about 25 lines from Jane Austen’s first published novel for her screenplay, inventing most of the dialogue herself. To be able to mimic that very distinctive voice, Reid had to dive headfirst into studying Austen’s rhythm and sentence structure.
“I got so immersed in the language it infected my own speech. I would be describing someone I just met, and I’d be like, ‘Oh, he was most amiable!’” Reid says, laughing. “It was a kind of insanity.”
Until now, Reid has been best known as the novelist behind bestsellers such as 2021’s Love and Virtue and 2025’s Signs of Damage , which are set among the university campuses and Euro holiday destinations of the modern world. Adapting a book published in 1811, then, was a very different job – but one that became oddly freeing.
“So much of writing contemporary dialogue is trying to make it sound believable, which often involves making people inarticulate,” Reid says. “Writing this, I got to sit at my computer and be like, ‘What is the most elegant way this sentiment could possibly be expressed?’ … It was actually a joy.”
Reid is speaking to me via Zoom from a chandelier-clad hotel room in Santa Fe, New Mexico, where she has been flown to promote the film (one of the perks of screenwriting is that the film industry has much “deeper pockets” than publishing, she says).
Her adaptation, directed by Georgia Oakley and released in Australia and the US this month, retells the story of Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, who are forced out of the landed gentry and into more precarious financial circumstances after the death of their father. Elinor falls for Edward Ferrars, a man who can’t seem to articulate his obvious reciprocal feelings for her, and Marianne is soon swept off her feet by the roguishly charming John Willoughby – but neither romance is what it first seems.
Reid and producer India Flint pitched the idea of a new adaptation because they wanted to tackle something by Austen, who Reid loves and considers a “genius”. Pride and Prejudice had been very successfully remade in 2005 and Emma more recently in 2020 – but the Dashwood sisters hadn’t been revisited on film in 30 years, when Ang Lee delivered his beloved 1995 take on the tale.
The Oscar-winning screenplay for that adaptation was penned by Emma Thompson, who also played Elinor. Unlike that thoroughly British star, Reid’s Australian accent has been tripping up some British fans and media.
“In recent weeks it’s almost felt like in Britain, perhaps [Austen] is viewed as a piece of cultural inheritance and that there are worthy and unworthy successors – and it seems striking or hubristic that an Australian would think themselves worthy,” Reid says. “But I never thought of Jane Austen as a possession. I just thought that she was something for anyone who was interested … if you don’t think of her as a possession, then it doesn’t occur to you to worry about whether it’s your right to receive it.”
What did give Reid pause, though, was how high a bar Ang Lee’s adaptation set.
“I love the 1995 film, and my initial instinct was that there was a reason it hadn’t been [adapted] for 30 years, and that was because the 1995 film was perfect,” Reid says. “But then I read the book and I rewatched the movie, and I felt that I did find something to say that I didn’t think had been said on screen before.”
Reid believes the main love story of Sense and Sensibility isn’t between Elinor and Edward or Marianne and Willoughby (or Colonel Brandon), but between the two sisters themselves – one logical and level-headed, the other utterly free-spirited.
“The spine of the story was about how these two women depend on each other, challenge each other and ultimately change each other,” Reid says. “And while there are romances in it, it’s almost as if the men are the rewards that the two women get for having gone on this journey of growth together.”
So in structuring the script, Reid tried to approach it almost as a romantic comedy but with the story arc plotted along tension between the sisters, not two love interests: the film’s climax comes when Elinor and Marianne are at odds, and their happy ending requires each to adapt qualities from the other. “Which is a very typical romcom structure,” Reid says.
Purists will be pleased to hear that Reid’s adaptation is a fairly faithful one – Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights this is not. But she did make some tweaks to the romantic fate of the younger Dashwood sister, feeling that Austen’s original ending wouldn’t sit well with modern audiences, who “respect what Marianne represents” – a bold, headstrong woman who goes for what she wants in life and accepts no substitutes.
Instead of “scene after scene of women sitting down in the parlour drinking tea, as Austen can sometimes feel”, she and Oakley opted to depict the Dashwood sisters cooking, chopping firewood and tending the veggie patch. Aesthetically, the film feels far drearier than the 1995 film, too, as the typical aestheticisation of Austen’s work – “very floral and bonnets; cosy, comfy escapism” – didn’t sit right with Reid, who considers her work very dark and imbued with an often cruel sense of humour.
What hasn’t changed is the heart of Sense and Sensibility. As Reid sees it, Austen’s work possesses “a generosity about the possibility of love” that is both romantic and timeless – and why it’s perennially reinvented.
“I don’t feel like Austen is, like, my cultural property now as a result of having written it,” Reid says. “I just feel like it is this thing that’s endlessly adaptable – there’s probably someone else doing their Sense and Sensibility adaptation right now. It is for everyone, and it’s still for everyone.”
Sense and Sensibility is in cinemas now in the UK, Australia and the US

title: This mighty cry for a goddess to help Earth proves Dickson Mbi is a bold force in dance
description: The Olivier-winner draws on his Cameroonian heritage in a visceral show, with music and movement that speak as one
content:
Sadler’s Wells East, London The Olivier-winner draws on his Cameroonian heritage in a visceral show, with music and movement that speak as one
D ickson Mbi won an Olivier award for his last major dance piece, Enowate , a result that surprised some of us who saw a talented artist still mastering the craft of choreographing a full-length work. But his new one, Tellus, is a much more sure and expressive work that creates a confident, textured world. Plus, Mbi is now not only a choreographer, but also a composer – a skill he honed during the pandemic – and the score is an essential part of the choreography (there are musicians on stage behind the eight performers), full of haunting melody and emotional pull. The music effectively shapes and enhances the action and speaks with the dance.
Tellus is a kind of folk tale about finding hope in a world that’s in environmental turmoil. The gist of the story (you may need to refer to the programme) is of a lost and stumbling central figure, a community struck by fire and drought, and an appeal to a goddess, Mami-Wata, for help. It draws on Mbi’s Cameroonian heritage, as does the music and the movement, which also takes in Mbi’s roots in hip-hop, with contemporary, South Asian and classical dance seemingly all in the mix. There are flashes of brilliance in the choreography, rousing ritual movement for the group and individuals with strong movement signatures: a spinning, leaping Nathan Goodman; an imperious, tottering Hannah Joseph.
Mbi has brought in some expert collaborators, including video designers YeastCulture, who provide a little magic in the visuals. He has been mentored by Complicité’s Simon McBurney , and worked with poet Nick Drake on the scenario; however, the result is a work of instinct and visceral impact rather than detailed narrative, although the message of reconnecting with our precious Earth is a simple and essential one.
At Sadler’s Wells East, London , until 24 October

title: Ilhan Omar says she plans to move out of Washington home after federal raid
description: Democratic lawmaker says family’s safety is at risk amid death threats and raid making apartment’s address public
content:
Democratic lawmaker says family’s safety is at risk amid death threats and raid making apartment’s address public
Our reporters answer your questions about ICE, immigration and the midterms
Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar said she plans to move out of her Washington DC apartment after federal agents raided her residence last week as part of a larger immigration investigation.
“I mean obviously, I can’t continue to live there,” Omar told MS Now in an interview that aired on Wednesday. “So we have to figure out where to move to, because our address has been public and with the death threats that I deal with, it’s no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids, like, visiting off and on, having people track them.”
The congresswoman, a Democrat who has been subject to Donald Trump ’s attacks, also denied allegations of immigration fraud.
Those in the president’s orbit – cabinet officials and rightwing influencers alike – have promoted baseless theories about the Democratic congresswoman, accusing Omar of being in a sham marriage with her brother and fudging details of her immigration paperwork.
The brother rumors circulated on a Somali blog, Omar told MS Now host Chris Hayes, before it gained traction with rightwing conspiracy theorists in Minneapolis.
She believes the raid was designed to appease Trump loyalists.
“They kept alluding to the fact that something was going to happen to me,” Omar told Hayes. “They had to do something, I believe, to say, ‘Hey, look we raided her house.’”
The 12 October raid marked an escalation of a years-long feud between Omar and Trump.
Trump has repeatedly denigrated Omar’s character, faith and Somali heritage, most recently on Tuesday, when he called her a “sick, very dishonest person who hates our country” while answering reporters’ questions at the White House.
Trump had been asked if Omar could face deportation over alleged misstatements in her immigration paperwork, to which he replied: “Well, she could be. She could also go to jail.”
In the MS Now interview, Omar also shared further details about how the raid was conducted.
About 15 to 25 Homeland Security Investigations agents surrounded Omar’s home and pounded on her door at 6am while she, her husband and her 20-year-old son were home.
“I thought something was on fire,” Omar said, recounting how she scrambled to put clothes on and answer the door before agents broke her front door.
The agents then executed a search warrant. According to Omar, after scouring her residence room by room for nearly five hours, the agents took 17 items, including several phones.
“You don’t show up to somebody’s house that early in the morning unless you’re trying to freak them out,” Omar said.
“Obviously, they’d like to see me locked up, deported and all of those things. But I think the bigger satisfaction for them would be for me to be like, ‘I’m tired of all of you and I’m going to leave,’” she said. “I have a legal right to be a member of Congress.”

title: Champions League review: PSG take a hit, Man City’s empty seats and teenage hope for Liverpool
description: The reigning champions must deal with the absence of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia for some time, while fans at Anfield were thrilled by Rio Ngumoha
content:
The reigning champions must deal with the absence of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia for some time, while fans at Anfield were thrilled by Rio Ngumoha
Paris Saint-Germain beat Barcelona 4-2 on Tuesday , but the reigning champions lost the best player in last season’s tournament, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. This autumn has seen much lobbying for the Ballon d’Or, with the Georgian a popular choice, despite his absence from the World Cup. He is expected to be out for six months, although Rodri’s comeback from serious injury – he was rested by Barcelona on Tuesday until coming off the bench in the 60th minute – shows it can take far longer than that for players to rediscover their highest level.
“Why me?” Kvaratskhelia asked his Instagram followers. The PSG policy of resting players in Ligue 1 to save them for the Champions League failed to protect him. By resting Rodri, Barcelona followed a wider practice among major clubs in European competition of saving stars’ legs for big domestic occasions. Barcelona face Real Madrid this weekend though Lamine Yamal is not being spared; his brilliant goal in Paris made it 10 goals, matched by 10 assists, from 10 matches.
Another heavyweight battle saw Arsenal lose Bukayo Saka to a first-half quad injury in an entertaining 2-2 draw at Bayern Munich . Declan Rice powered in a late equalizer after Harry Kane had put on a show that included a goal and an assist. Does the Ballon d’Or beckon for Kane? The prediction markets suggest so.
Matching Barcelona’s perfect record this season at home and abroad are Manchester City, who continue to thrive amid infamy. A resurgent Phil Foden scored a hat-trick and new signing Allan impressed. The official crowd for their 5-1 defeat of AEK Athens was 40,402, but it looked smaller, and mockery duly descended on the club. There is mitigation for those who stayed away, including high ticket prices for Champions League matches in tough economic times, and a run of five home matches in 17 days. Still, City remain in the crosshairs, and the empty seats raise eyebrows for a club reporting record revenues. Equally, it is fair to point out that Anfield was not full, either, for Liverpool’s 4-3 defeat of Villarreal.
A clean sweep of wins for Serie A, with three of their clubs scoring four goals. Inter let the side down with their 1-0 defeat of Shakhtar Donetsk. Roma defeated Slovan Bratislava 4-0, and Como beat Manchester United 4-1 , but the game of the week came in Naples. Scott McTominay scored twice, his first goals since a procedure on a benign heart arrhythmia as Napoli beat Bodø/Glimt 4-3 for their first win of the group stage. “I still need to find my best form, but I am not far away,” said McTominay.
Liverpool were a mess in the first 30 minutes against Villarreal and it was Rio Ngumoha who led the recovery. The 18-year-old played off the right, supplying two assists with his left foot: the long-term replacement for Mohamed Salah may already be at Anfield. Liverpool have nursed Ngumoha along, though this was his fifth start of the season. “Everyone is chipping in but for him to work with Mo [Salah] last year was obviously massive,” Virgil van Dijk said of the teenager.
With traditional Serie A giants Juventus and Milan in the Europa League, Como are enjoying their first season in the Champions League. If Manchester United were dreadful on Wednesday, Como’s rise hit its highest point yet. The club’s success carries echoes of Brighton and Bournemouth’s ascents, although Como’s is even more remarkable. They were a Serie D club in 2008, and the city is now known for something beyond its glorious scenery. Champions League winner Thierry Henry is among the investors in the club as is Como’s coach, Cesc Fàbregas, although the prime financiers are the Indonesian billionaire Hartono brothers.
Jamestown Analytics, the Brighton owner Tony Bloom’s company, has been consulting Como . Arsène Wenger, Pep Guardiola, José Mourinho and Antonio Conte are the elite coaches Fàbregas played under, and he has forged a high-pressing style against Italian orthodoxy. As United labored, they were swarmed by Como’s worker bees. Real Madrid have a buy-back option for Nico Paz, bought by Como in 2024, and the scorer of two fine goals against United. Argentina’s latest Messi replacement is rather beefier than his country’s idol.
As Como deepened Michael Carrick’s plight, thoughts moved to potential replacements. Fàbregas has been mentioned, though United fans will recall the summer of 2013’s unsuccessful chase for him. Had a deal been done, his midfield partner would have been … Carrick.
Another week, another Manchester United PR crisis. This one involved Carrick hitting back at his players, a rarity in his managerial career. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” Bruno Fernandes said.
Carrick’s riposte: “If you don’t run and you don’t run forward and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”
On CBS, Jamie Carragher weighed, saying of Fernandes: “They all think he’s working hard. He’s not. He’s killing the rest of the team doing it.”
The Amazon All or Nothing documentary series currently in production for United’s season will be appointment viewing.
After two consecutive weeks of action, we have a fortnight off. Will Carrick still be at United by the time they host Roma on 3 November? Aston Villa, who have three wins from three and are second place in the table, have a glamour trip to Barcelona . Real Madrid, another side on three wins, travel to AEK.
After defeat to Inter, Shakhtar’s adopted home, Stamford Bridge , hosts Sporting Lisbon, who this week were on the wrong end of Lask’s first ever group-stage win.

title: ‘If my brother hadn’t died, my life would be so different’: Olympic boxer Ramla Ali’s incredible journey
description: From fleeing the Somali civil war to fighting at the Tokyo Olympics, Ali’s life has been remarkable – and now she is being played by Top Boy’s Jasmine Jobson in a new biopic. We hear from both on this ‘positive migrant story’
content:
From fleeing the Somali civil war to fighting at the Tokyo Olympics, Ali’s life has been remarkable – and now she is being played by Top Boy’s Jasmine Jobson in a new biopic. We hear from both on this ‘positive migrant story’
B oxer Ramla Ali sweeps into the green room of a West End cinema, tiny in a frothy dress with a huge skirt of cascading black feathers. It’s an absolute showstopper. She’s just introduced the premiere of a new film about her life. There are messages on her phone from Bear Grylls and Malala Yousafzai, who are in the audience watching.
But the person who matters most is her mum, who is seeing it for the fourth time. What does she think? “She loves it,” says Ali quietly. The film is In the Shadows, directed by Anthony Wonke and stars Top Boy actor Jasmine Jobson. It tells the story of Ali’s journey to the 2021 Olympics in Tokyo.
And what a journey. Ali was born in Somalia . When she was a baby, her older brother Abdulkadir was killed in an explosion while playing. The family fled Somalia, making the perilous crossing by boat to Kenya, finally arriving in the UK as refugees.
Ali grew up in east London, joining a boxercise class at the local gym after being bullied at school about her weight. When she started boxing seriously, she kept it hidden from her family. As a Muslim girl, it would not be allowed. And she knew that her mother, having moved heaven and earth to get the family away from violence, would be devastated seeing her in harm’s way. These days, her mum is the first person Ali calls after a fight.
It was eight years ago that the idea of a film first came up. Ali’s husband Richard Moore has just walked into the room. He used to be her coach and is also an executive producer on the film. He explains that one of the biggest reasons for pitching it back in 2018 was practical: they were broke. “We were down to our last hundred quid. We were lucky at that time, we had friends who took us in and housed us.” For a while they were a living in a home owned by Idris Elba and his wife, Sabrina. “They were our saviours. Then we got Covid and had to stay for ages,” giggles Ali.
Did she have any doubts about making the film? She nods: “Yes. I wasn’t sure I wanted to be so vulnerable, to sit down with a writer and tell her everything about my life, things I haven’t shared before.” There was her family’s trauma to consider, too: “I remember thinking, how is it going to affect my mum? It’s my story, but it’s her story as well. When I talked to my family, none of them were really up for it.” In the end, unexpectedly, it was her mother who came round first. And she had strong opinions about the script too: “My mum was adamant that the scene when my brother got killed be included. It had to be in.” Moore thinks it was a way of keeping him alive: “Remembering him, and making his death mean something bigger.”
Ali has gone quiet. After a moment she says that Abdulkadir being killed set in motion a sequence of events that changed all their lives in her family: “His death is the ripple effect. If my brother hadn’t died, we wouldn’t have come to the UK. I wouldn’t have taken up boxing. I wouldn’t have met Richard. My life would be so different.”
She says the film is not a pro-immigration statement. But it does offer another point of view to the fearmongering about migrants arriving on boats and stealing British jobs. “It’s depicting a human migrant story. Immigration has been weaponised politically to drive division in this country. Positive migrant stories don’t sell newspapers in the same way, so they rarely get told. But they are far more representative of the people who come here and build lives, families and careers. If audiences walk out seeing a person rather than a headline, the film has done its job. ”
She is the living proof of a positive migration story. In 2015, Ali became the first Muslim woman to win an English amateur boxing title. Six years later, she competed at the Tokyo Olympics as the first boxer in history to represent Somalia. She has modelled, appearing on the cover of British Vogue guest edited by the Duchess of Sussex. In 2018, she set up Sisters Club, a charity providing free boxing classes to vulnerable women. She is a Unicef ambassador.
Ali tells me she worked hard behind the scenes of In the Shadows, reading every draft of the script, on set every day of the shoot. “Some exec producers just write their names on the film. But I worked for that title. I earned it.” She even body doubled in the boxing scenes.
Ali has been thinking lately about life after boxing. She and Moore have written and directed a comedy film together, Not Like Us, and she’s dipped her toe into acting too. “Boxing’s not for ever. There comes a day where you think: It’s time. Everyone laughs at me, but I keep saying it’s very similar to boxing. The dedication you’ve got to put into your boxing will show on the night in the ring. It’s the same with film-making. The level of dedication you’ve got to put in will show on screen.”
What kind of films does she want to make? “I feel like in America there are so many films made for black people. I would love to be able to be in a position to tell more stories focused on the Black British experience.”
It’s a sunny afternoon when I catch up with Jasmine Jobson, who plays Ali in the film. She took over from Letitia Wright, who was initially attached to the project. Jobson arrives at the BFI Southbank with a full entourage – publicist, makeup and hairdresser. “There’s not one part of my team that can be missing,” I hear her say as she strides across the room in Louboutin heels.
She looks in fabulous shape. Is that the boxing? “Thank you. No. I haven’t continued boxing. I do need to get back into it.” She is focused on physio for an old shoulder injury, picked up years ago at the gym. “At college, I was training to be a personal trainer. I just pulled a bit too much weight down on a lat-pull.”
Did she get into the swing of the boxing easily? “Yeah. Straight in. When I was young, I did karate, kickboxing, things like that. But I only had two weeks to prepare for this job. Literally two weeks to become a champion.” She spent eight hours a day training: “I absolutely loved boxing. I just don’t like getting my face touched. No one’s allowed to get my face. This is my money maker.”
Jobson says she fell in love with Ali the moment they met for coffee. “We had a nice little chat and got to know each other on a bit more of a deeper level. She’s overcome so much. To come out the other side, and to be an international success, to be able to change perceptions …” Jobson pauses. “Something might feel distant, or not necessarily accepted. But if you are passionate about it, and you are very good at it, if it’s your talent, go for it. You can be a success story no matter what your dream is. She’s a testament to that. Kudos to her, man.”
Did it feel intimidating taking on the part of a real-life person, I ask. “No. Not all. Any role I’ve played, I’ve incorporated myself into it.”
Like Ali, her experience of childhood adversity makes her achievements doubly impressive. As a young child, Jobson’s parents encouraged her talent for performing. But when she was in secondary school, social services became involved with the family. Jobson moved out of her mother’s house to live with her grandmother. Then, aged 14, she took the decision to place herself in foster care: “I had to do a very very deep dive within myself and take myself away from bad crowds, and figure out what my destiny was. My brain got a little bit clouded, and I had to find Jasmine again.”
A family friend suggested she try out for The Big House, a theatre company in north London that works with care leavers, and there she got an agent. Like Ali, she is a grafter, and learned lines in Somali for In the Shadows. She gives me a phrase in Somali: “It means: ‘I just want you to be proud of me.’ That’s all I’ve ever wanted – for my family and everybody to be proud of me.”
It sounds as if she put a lot of herself in the role. “Oh, 100%. But at the same time, I had to make sure it was authentically Ramla.” She can see the similarities, she admits: “It’s not that we’ve had the same life experiences, but we both had struggles and we both had a dream.”

title: Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra / Wigglesworth review – phrasing with hospital corners
description: BSO’s concert with their chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth mixed Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius. Best of all was the Tippett, and the Sibelius 5 had personality to burn
content:
Lighthouse, Poole BSO’s concert with their chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth mixed Tippett, Vaughan Williams, Adès and Sibelius. Best of all was the Tippett, and the Sibelius 5 had personality to burn
O n paper, it was a curious programme: Tippett’s Concerto for Double String Orchestra and Vaughan Williams’s The Lark Ascending, followed post-interval by Adès ’s Märchentänze and Sibelius’s Fifth Symphony. A calculated mix of more and less familiar works, certainly – but an otherwise unlikely foursome. The common preoccupations with folk music (threaded jauntily through the Tippett and the Adès) and the natural world (VW’s lark, Sibelius’s swans) only take us so far. In practice, the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra’s performance under its chief conductor Mark Wigglesworth revealed a shared creative tussle with existing musical forms and with finding new means of expression without breaking entirely with the old ways.
The Lark Ascending thus abandoned the Smooth Classics at Seven-mode for a covered, sometimes icy sound in the BSO’s world-class strings and a more risk-taking, more improvisatory approach from soloist Anthony Marwood . The tone of his Stradivarius was expensively sweet and his cool, no-vibrato opening compelling, though his performance was marred by intonation problems. Marwood fared better in Adès’s Märchentänze, which reworks folk tunes with unexpected timbral combinations and harmonies, and where the solo line tangles deliciously with the orchestra’s violins. But this work, written for the ultra-charismatic violinist Pekka Kuusisto , was rather less interesting without such a compelling soloist.
By contrast, Sibelius’s Symphony No 5 had personality to burn in a performance that front-loaded its modernist strangeness. There were shadowy wind solos, creepy string tremolos and double basses that lurched nastily instead of settling comfortably into the finale’s swan business. There were also tuning difficulties in the wind and the BSO’s trombones were almost comically direct from where I was sitting. But Wigglesworth’s detailed, sensitive conducting came into its own in the work’s transitional passages, as he eased the weight out of dense textures and managed the journey to the symphony’s climax as a slowly, inexorably cresting wave.
Best of all was the Tippett. Wigglesworth’s tempi were unhurried, even laid-back. Yet there was an angular neatness to Tippett’s neoclassical lines – this was phrasing with hospital corners – and the string sound was subtly malleable: from a striking, frosted tone in the first movement to the generous warmth that spread euphorically through the finale.

title: Judi Dench says sight loss means she can no longer perform but she is still ‘besotted by’ Shakespeare’s sonnets
description: Age-related macular degeneration has also left actor, 91, unable to read or recognise faces any more
content:
Age-related macular degeneration has also left actor, 91, unable to read or recognise faces any more
Judi Dench has said she can no longer perform on stage or in films because of her deteriorating eyesight, more than a decade after revealing she had been diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration.
“I can’t be on stage. I can’t do a play any more. I can’t do a film any more. I can’t read any more,” the 91-year-old actor told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Thursday.
Dench, one of Britain’s most celebrated actors, was diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in 2012. The condition causes progressive sight loss and has increasingly affected her ability to work, as well as her independence in everyday life.
She described how she can no longer read or recognise faces. “I go up to lots of the wrong people and give them an almost hug and say: ‘Oh sorry, didn’t realise’,” she said. She also told the presenter Emma Barnett: “I can’t see your face at all.”
Dench’s comments mark a stark development in a gradual deterioration that has affected her ability to work for years. In 2014, she said her failing eyesight made reading difficult, but insisted she would continue working for as long as she could.
By 2023, she said she could no longer see on film sets and relied on friends to teach her scripts, learning lines through repetition. Last year, she revealed that she could no longer go out alone because she feared walking into objects or falling over.
The actor also told Barnett of her sadness at no longer being able to see bluebells. “They said this summer was absolutely sensational with bluebells; I couldn’t see one,” she said. “But I know what my trees look like, and part of it is in my memory and part of it is about hopefully what I can make out.”
Asked about ageing, Dench replied: “There’s nothing to say for it at all. [I] don’t think about it too much.”
Despite the impact of her sight loss, she spoke warmly of her enduring love of Shakespeare’s poetry . “I am besotted by the sonnets, I just love them,” she said, describing their ability to capture human feelings simply. “It’s the rhythm of it. It’s the rhythm of your heart. It’s the way he’s summed up so simply the way that any of us feel about, well, anything.”
Dench was speaking before the publication of her memoir, Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?, written with the theatre director Brendan O’Hea.
Dench’s career spans more than seven decades. She won an Oscar for playing Queen Elizabeth I in Shakespeare in Love and became internationally renowned as M, James Bond’s boss, appearing in eight films in the franchise. Her stage work included celebrated Shakespearean roles such as Juliet, Lady Macbeth and Cleopatra.

title: Florida police officer finds man dead and steals his house and identity, authorities allege
description: Officer says he took possession of property and renovated it ‘to prevent criminal activity’ and ‘squatting’
content:
Officer says he took possession of property and renovated it ‘to prevent criminal activity’ and ‘squatting’
A Florida police officer who discovered a man dead during a welfare check stole his house and identity and spent years renovating the property for himself, authorities said.
Brian Louis Sguros, 35, an officer with the Lauderhill police department near Miami, appeared in court on Wednesday on charges including criminal use of a deceased person’s identification.
Sguros was part of a team sent to check on a Lauderhill resident, Dennis West, in July 2022, after the department received a call from a worried neighbor, a press release from the Broward sheriff’s office (BSO) said. West was found deceased in the home of natural causes.
Within weeks, the officer embarked on what BSO said was “a complex scheme to take control of the individual’s home” by involving himself in West’s post-death affairs.
“Sguros represented himself to the Broward county medical examiner’s office as West’s friend, although there is no indication he knew West, and stated that West had no living family, which was untrue,” the press release said.
“The investigation also revealed that Sguros paid the taxes and utilities at the home in West’s name and used West’s identification to make it appear that West was still alive to get the city of Lauderhill to issue a permit to facilitate repairs.”
A 21-page arrest affidavit alleges Sguros forged West’s signature on multiple documents, and between August 2022 and February 2025 spent more than $210,000 of his own money upgrading the property, including replacing doors and windows in 2024.
The affidavit said that Sguros, in sworn statements and civil pleadings, maintained he took possession of the property and worked on it “because it was hazardous and he wanted to prevent criminal activity and people from squatting”, NBC Miami reported.
During that time, Sguros allegedly used law enforcement databases to improperly access West’s driver’s license record, date of birth, social security number and other personal information.
Then in February 2025, he and his spouse filed a claim with the Broward property appraiser’s office seeking to establish a claim to ownership, the affidavit said.
A neighbor told WSVN TV that Sguros often talked with her, and told her he was renovating the property with a plan to rent it out on Airbnb. She said Sguros told her West was his friend, and had given him the property before he died.
The alleged scam came to light in August 2025 when a real estate company that bought the property legally from West’s heirs sent an employee to take possession and encountered Sguros, NBC reported.
Sguros surrendered the keys, but filed civil litigation against the real estate company demanding compensation for the money he had invested in renovations, the news outlet said.
The officer was placed on administrative leave with pay following his arrest on Tuesday after a months-long investigation by BSO detectives. He appeared in court in Fort Lauderdale on Wednesday on charges including official misconduct and criminal use of deceased person’s identification, and was released on $25,000 bond.
Sguros could not be reached for comment, and it is unclear if he is represented by an attorney.

Iranian attacks on container ships in the Strait of Hormuz have increased in recent weeks. Iran reported that seven tankers were struck on Wednesday night and over the last fortnight at least 15 container ships , passing through the waterway, were hit.
Most of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman , a route that Iran sees as unauthorised. title: Bartók: Miraculous Mandarin Suite, The Wooden Prince album review – vivid colours and astute pacing
description: Edward Gardner and the LPO are taut and dramatically alert in fine performances of these two theatrical works
content:
London Philharmonic Orchestra/Gardner (LPO) Edward Gardner and the LPO are taut and dramatically alert in fine performances of these two theatrical works
R ecordings of The Miraculous Mandarin used to outnumber The Wooden Prince 10 to one, so it’s good to see Bartók’s earlier ballet getting equal billing here. Unlike the Mandarin with its grimy, urban, modernist vibe, the Prince is rooted in pungent Hungarian folk music, viewed, of course, through the composer’s unique 20th-century lens.
It’s the story of a princess who falls in love with a decoy prince rather than the real thing and Edward Gardner revels in the vivid colours of its nature-inflected score. The London Philharmonic Orchestra is taut and dramatically alert throughout. There’s an unnerving sense of foreboding underpinning the Dance of the Trees; the Dance of the Waves churns with kinetic energy and the foot-stamping Dance of the Princess with the Wooden Doll cuts a rustic dash.
The live recording is less clinical than Boulez’s crystalline 1991 studio performance (still essential listening), but Gardner’s astute pacing is more theatrically involving than recent accounts by Cristian Măcelaru or Susanna Mälkki.
As for The Miraculous Mandarin Suite, this is as fine a performance as any, sleek and sinister in its evocation of the honeytrap antics of the sex worker and her thuggish pimps, swaggering or shy in her encounters with the old rake and the young man, and prickling with jagged pentatonic scales once the mandarin arrives on the scene. To open, Gardner paints a brutal portrait of the dystopian city with its honking car horns and concludes with a raw-nerved depiction of the desperate final chase.

title: McDermott blames Rugby League World Cup format as England face exit
description: Brian McDermott has conceded England’s hopes of reaching the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals may already be over, blaming the tournament’s format and their opening loss to Tonga
content:
Big wins and help from Tonga needed to reach semi-finals
‘You’ve got to hit the ground running, which we didn’t do’
Brian McDermott has conceded England’s hopes of reaching the Rugby League World Cup semi-finals may already be over, the head coach blaming the tournament’s format and their opening loss to Tonga .
The World Cup has been reduced to 10 teams, down from 16 four years ago. That is largely due to financial reasons when the hosts, Australia, stepped in after France’s withdrawal. That has led to a unique format, with different levels of jeopardy for different countries based on their group.
England are in the three-team Group B with the top two from a combined six-team table of Groups B and C progressing to the semi-finals. Defeat by Tonga last Saturday has made it difficult for England to qualify, with expected victories against France on Saturday and Papua New Guinea next week unlikely to be enough.
For England to progress, Tonga must beat Samoa on 1 November and England need to win their two group games by a bigger margin than Samoa. McDermott conceded the odds are stacked against his side and was critical of the format.
“The jeopardy of losing one game in a pool of three is so harsh, it’s almost like we don’t get another chance to straighten things out,” he said. “It’s just harsh that we have to take a standing eight count in that first round, but we’re ready to go again.
“Nothing has gone wrong, it’s just a harsh competition in which you’ve got to hit the ground running, which we didn’t do.
“I’m trying to be diplomatic here. If France held the World Cup, there would have been more teams in it and it would have been more like the usual format. I completely understand that if it has to be reduced to a 10-team competition.
“It’s not the easiest thing to do and we end up with situations like this. If you lose one game, you don’t really get a chance to fix it. It’s tough because we now need to rely on other results if we are to go through.”
In contrast, New Zealand are in the four-team Group A where two teams progress and despite losing to Australia last week wins over Fiji and Cook Islands will secure qualification.
“New Zealand have lost their first game as well, but they’re going to get another go at it,” said McDermott. “The likelihood is that they’ll quality, their destiny is not lying in other people’s hands.”
England have to inflict a second heavy defeat on Les Bleus after France’s 78-4 loss to Samoa last Friday.
England’s 30-12 defeat by Tonga drew criticism, but McDermott had promised his side would try to play a more enterprising brand of rugby. Also, England had been in Australia for less than a week, after a 48-hour journey from Manchester via London, Singapore and Sydney to reach their camp in Perth.
That is perhaps why McDermott has resisted the temptation for wholesale changes, with the Warrington winger Matty Ashton replacing Zach Eckersley in the sole change to the starting lineup.
England may be going home in a fortnight barring a minor miracle, but McDermott is upbeat about the national team’s long-term prospects. “I’m really pumped about what we’ve done over a short period of time; it’s been remarkable, really,” he said.
“We’ve come together and looked pretty good. We’ve laid some foundations and we’re pretty excited about where this could go. I don’t think there’s a great need for change, just give me another three or four games with this mob. Let’s build some layers of preparation with each other.”
However, for that to happen there is likely to be a post-tournament inquest into the national team’s place on English rugby league’s priority list.
With no mid-season camps, let alone games, and the schedule for a home three-Test series against New Zealand next autumn not yet confirmed, McDermott and his players need more support from above if England are to prove they are victims of the format and not drifting from the top tier of the international game.

title: ‘Former inmates want to come back to visit’: inside Florida’s prison zoo
description: Prisoners look after a kinkajou, zebu and ostrich at Monroe County detention center in the Florida Keys. It is the only correctional facility in the world with its own zoo
content:
Prisoners look after a kinkajou, zebu and ostrich at Monroe County detention center in the Florida Keys. It is the only correctional facility in the world with its own zoo
A t the Monroe County detention center on Stock Island in the Florida Keys, most of the prisoners do the type of work you’d typically imagine people doing in jail. Preparing meals in the kitchens, cleaning the common areas, working in the laundry, and so on.
But for about five prisoners at a time the work looks a little more exotic. They’re working in the jail’s on-site zoo, taking care of animals including a capybara, a kinkajou, a zebu and an ostrich.
The zoo was started in 1994, after a sheriff’s deputy noticed that ducks living near the jail were often getting hit by cars while crossing a highway. He gathered a group of prisoners and relocated the flock to a disused area beneath the jail, which sits on stilts as it is in a hurricane-prone area.
Word of the rescue spread, and people started showing up at the jail to drop off rescued or unwanted animals. “People started bringing in a goat, a pig, a cow, pets they’d gotten that they didn’t want or couldn’t keep,” said Jeanne Selander, the zoo’s supervisor. “We got a blind horse from the Miami area that had been abandoned, and then the sheriff thought, ‘Well, there’s a need for this.’”
The Monroe County detention center is the only correctional facility in the world with its own zoo. There was, briefly, another one. In Venezuela, a gang took over a prison and installed various resort-style amenities for the prisoners, including a pool, night club, and a zoo, with big cats, monkeys and flamingoes. But the Venezuelan government forcefully retook control of that prison a few years ago. Several of the zoo’s animals were reportedly killed in the battle for the prison and the ones that survived were relocated.
According to Selander, all of the animals in her zoo were either rescued, donated or confiscated. Rocky the fox was rescued from a fur farm in Minnesota. Jack the ostrich was donated as a tax write-off by a breeder that was unable to sell him because he’s blind in one eye. Harriet Houdini, a red-tailed boa constrictor, was donated by a school after the teacher that kept her as a class pet retired. “I had some alligators one time that came from a raid on a crack house,” said Selander.
But the zoo doesn’t accept all of the animals it is offered. Selander said she previously declined a camel and a bear as they presented too much of a risk to the residents.
You are unable to see the zoo from the inside as the building’s windows are frosted. Selander said that, when she is upstairs in the jail, the prisoners will ask her about the sounds they can hear coming from outside. She has been told that, from inside the jail, the peacock can sound like a woman screaming.
The prisoners that work on the zoo spend around six hours a day feeding and cleaning the animals, and performing maintenance tasks. Those selected are typically low-level offenders and are not allowed to have charges for violence or animal abuse. “It’s kind of hard to get down [to the zoo] because if you have a high bond or you’re in any way shape or form a risk to run away, they’re not going to let you come outside,” said Peter Faraco, a former inmate who worked on the zoo in 2021.
Inside the jail, prisoners sleep on concrete bunk beds with no pillows. “Stuck in them cells all day, or in the kitchen; it’s not that nice,” said Rodney Cox, who previously worked on the zoo. “There’s no air.”
Boredom is also an issue. “It’s a lot of time,” said Nicholas Sheldrake, a current inmate who is working in the zoo. “It’s just very boring. Watching the same TV shows and movies over and over, hoping a football or baseball game or something comes on.”
The zoo offers a respite for the prisoners that get to work there. “I love it down here,” said Sheldrake. “It makes my time go by fast. Nobody bothers me. I love working with the animals and talking to them.”
“And we can see stuff like birds and trees,” he added.
It is important to Selander that the zoo not look like it is part of a jail, as she hopes to make it appealing to visitors on the zoo’s regular open days. She has planted trees around the property, and had inmates paint murals of animals on the walls and support pillars. “People will come in, they’re like, ‘You don’t even realize you’re at a jail,’” she said.
In the 20 years she has worked there, she said, the number of visitors on open days has grown from about a dozen to more than 300.
Studies have shown that access to animals can have a positive effect on incarcerated people, leading to improvements in mental health , as well as a decrease in reoffending after release.
There are animal programmes of various kinds in prisons around the world. There are prisoners in Chile living alongside cats, and in New Zealand training service dogs, and in the UK receiving equine therapy, and in South Africa raising birds. Selander said that she believes working on the zoo has had a positive effect on the prisoners she has worked with, and has, over the years, received positive feedback from her workers.
She was recently out for brunch and her server was a man who’d worked at the zoo. “He was like, ‘I wanted to thank you, Miss Jeannie … Being able to be on the farm and have peace while I served my time just made it so much easier,’” she said.
Selander said that it’s not uncommon for former incarcerated zoo workers to come back and visit during open days to see the animals. Some will bring their family members. “One of the greatest compliments is that the inmates want to come back to visit,” she said. “What a compliment. Who wants to come back to jail?”

title: BBC News to axe education editor role in cost-cutting move
description: Fears over lack of scrutiny for key sectors as health editor position also to go in cuts aimed at saving £5.5m
content:
Fears over lack of scrutiny for key sectors as health editor position also to go in cuts aimed at saving £5.5m
The BBC will no longer have a dedicated education editor as part of a cost-cutting drive in which 100 jobs are to go across BBC News under a plan that school leaders described as “deeply regrettable”.
BBC staff have been told that the roles of education editor and social affairs editor are to be combined into a single position as part of a round of changes that will save £5.5m. However, prominent unions and campaigners are saying the reform will dilute scrutiny of two specialisms that are too important to go without a dedicated BBC role.
The education editor at BBC News is Branwen Jeffreys and the social affairs editor is Alison Holt.
In a message to staff seen by the Guardian, Richard Burgess, the director of news content, said he was proposing the change after a review of on-air editor roles. He said the review looked at “audience demand, editorial requirements and how we ensure these roles remain relevant in a changing news environment”.
There will also be no health editor title at the BBC when the current incumbent, Hugh Pym, leaves in the spring. That job will be incorporated into the role of medical editor, currently held by Fergus Walsh.
“These are difficult decisions, but I have given the changes careful consideration, taking into account levels of audience interest and editorial demand, as well as how we can work as efficiently as possible across the department,” Burgess said.
It appears BBC executives have opted to combine the education and social affairs jobs as they attempt to reduce duplication and cut wage costs. Sources said experienced education and social affairs specialists would remain at the BBC, but others inside the corporation have been left puzzled by a change that will leave the world’s oldest national public service broadcaster without a dedicated education editor.
School leaders and teaching unions questioned the move. “On the face of it, this announcement suggests that the BBC is proposing to dilute leadership of its education coverage,” said James Bowen, the assistant general secretary at the school leaders’ union NAHT. He urged the BBC to rethink the plan.
He said: “This would be a deeply regrettable move by our national broadcaster, which plays a vital role in shining a light on important issues affecting the education sector and holding the government and Department for Education to account.”
Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union, said the move would “diminish the public’s understanding of education matters in this country”. Matt Wrack, the general secretary of the NASUWT teachers’ union, said: “At a time when schools are grappling with rising child poverty, crumbling buildings, teacher shortages and major funding cuts, the public needs to hear from strong public interest reporting in the sector.”
Nadra Ahmed, the co-chair of the National Care Association, said she was concerned that the lack of a social affairs editor meant the sector could lose attention at a critical time with the prime minister drawing up social care reforms .
One BBC insider said combining the education and social affairs editor roles “further erodes our ability to give sufficient coverage to the breadth and depth of two materially distinct topics”.
However, others inside the BBC said the issues of education, social affairs and health all had dedicated teams of journalists that would ensure proper coverage. A BBC spokesperson said: “The BBC remains committed to covering education, and will continue to do so both at editor level, and with its team of expert reporters and producers.”
Burgess said that alongside the editor role changes the job requirements of on-air editors would be reviewed to place “greater emphasis” on making an impact on social media and digital platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.
The BBC is making renewed efforts to boost its presence on those platforms as it attempts to reach younger audiences who are increasingly using the sites for news.
The new head of BBC News, Rachel Jupp , used one of her first memos to staff to tell them that the department’s target of finding £51m in savings could be increased “given the BBC’s financial pressures”.

title: Six-year ban for top marathon runner who submitted fake prescription
description: One of the world’s leading marathon runners, Ruti Aga, has been banned for six years after anti-doping investigators found she submitted a fake prescription to explain a failed drug test
content:
Clinic named by Ruti Aga did not exist, testers found
Prescription signed by a family member, not a doctor
One of the world’s leading marathon runners, Ruti Aga, has been banned for six years after anti-doping investigators found she submitted a fake prescription to explain a failed drug test.
The Ethiopian athlete won the Tokyo marathon in 2019 and has reached the podium at the Berlin and New York marathons. She tested positive for the banned substance methylprednisolone after winning a half-marathon in China in March, the Athletics Integrity Unit said on Thursday.
Aga said she had been given the substance by a doctor in Ethiopia to treat knee pain, but the AIU said it found the clinic named on the document did not exist and the supposed prescription had been signed by a family member who was not a registered doctor.
After that, Aga failed to respond to charges for the use of methylprednisolone and “tampering” with the anti-doping process, the AIU added, meaning the six-year ban was issued without a hearing. The 32-year-old runner’s ban includes two years for the use of the substance and four more for tampering.

title: America gets new national park with designation of Chiricahua’s rock spires
description: Arizona’s Land of Standing-Up Rocks, formed from ancient volcanic eruption, gets new status with bipartisan support
content:
Arizona’s Land of Standing-Up Rocks, formed from ancient volcanic eruption, gets new status with bipartisan support
An area of towering rock spires in south-eastern Arizona known among Native Americans as the Land of Standing-Up Rocks has become the nation’s newest national park.
Legislation to create Chiricahua national park was sent to the White House and Donald Trump signed it on Tuesday. It passed Congress with bipartisan backing and is now the 64th US national park.
The 19-sq-mile (49-sq-km) site is within the historical territory of the Chiricahua Apache tribes. It was designated a national monument in the 1920s to preserve hundreds of pinnacle-shaped rocks formed from an ancient volcanic eruption.
For centuries the site of the proposed park was home to the Apache, nomadic tribes who often resisted European newcomers to North America. They clashed with settlers until surrendering to US troops in 1886 and being forcibly removed to the San Carlos Apache reservation.
“Chiricahua’s towering rock spires, rich Apache heritage and remarkable biodiversity make it one of America’s most extraordinary landscapes,” said Doug Burgum, the interior secretary. “This new designation will shine a national spotlight on one of Arizona’s hidden gems, creating opportunities to welcome more visitors, strengthen local economies and share this incredible landscape with more Americans.”
The bill creating Chiricahua national park preserves tribal access for traditional ceremonies. It allows temporary public closures within the park to protect those cultural uses, although Juan Ciscomani, a US representative from Arizona, said specifics had not been decided.
Early settlers called the site Wonderland of Rocks. The name Chiricahua comes from the surrounding mountains.
“This is a win for the communities in south-eastern Arizona and for everyone who worked to protect this extraordinary place so our kids and our grandkids can enjoy it,” said Mark Kelly, a senator from Arizona.
The area has evidence of thousands of years of human use, according to the park service. That spans from prehistoric people to Buffalo soldiers – US troops who were Black and stationed at the monument site after the civil war, during a government campaign against the Apache leaders Geronimo and Cochise.
Calvin Coolidge named the site a national monument in 1924 under the federal Antiquities Act. Franklin D Roosevelt expanded the site in 1938.
It gets roughly 60,000 visitors annually.
“While its name is changing, our commitment remains the same: protecting this remarkable landscape and its cultural heritage while providing opportunities for visitors to experience and enjoy it for generations to come.” said Jessica Bowron, comptroller and acting director of the National Park Service.
The park service has undergone deep cuts to its workforce under Trump. Maintenance projects at many sites – including Chiricahua – were ranked “low priority” by officials who have instead focused on projects wanted by the White House, including repairs to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool .
The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: ‘Nunchucks’ wielded by agitated man in Hannah Beazley’s office may have been drumsticks, court told
description: John Lawrence Smart charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear but Perth lawyer expresses concern for mental health
content:
John Lawrence Smart charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear but Perth lawyer expresses concern for mental health
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
A man accused of making threats while armed with “improvised nunchucks” at a Western Australian MP’s electorate office could have been holding a musical instrument, not a weapon, a court has been told.
John Lawrence Smart appeared on Thursday in the WA magistrates court, where his lawyer expressed concern for his mental health. He was not required to enter a plea.
Smart was accused of making verbal threats at the office of state Labor MP Hannah Beazley in the inner-Perth suburb of Victoria Park on Wednesday afternoon.
He was charged on Thursday with being armed in a way that may cause fear, making an unlawful threat and possessing cannabis. Police alleged Smart “made verbal threats while in possession of an improvised martial arts weapon (nunchucks)”.
During the court hearing, the highly agitated 56-year-old held his head in his hands and said he had been a musician for 20 years and he was holding claves.
“People, they don’t understand what I’m going through,” he said from the dock. Smart claimed people had “destroyed” his head.
Prosecutors said Smart entered Beazley’s office physically agitated and screaming, and holding two pieces of wood tied together.
He had a second similar implement attached to his belt, the police prosecutor said.
Smart allegedly demanded to see the politician while raising one of the implements above his head in a threatening manner before leaving the premises.
Smart’s lawyer said he was known to carry percussion sticks in the community and play drums.
The magistrate Heidi Watson suggested to the prosecutor that Smart might have been holding “drumsticks”.
The court heard Smart had previously been involuntarily admitted to hospital with schizophrenia and displayed delusional persecutory beliefs. He believed he had the “devil inside him”.
Watson ordered that Smart remained in custody for further medical assessment.
Beazley earlier said two of her staff were present in the electorate office when Smart allegedly entered.
“It was confronting,” she said in a social media post. “My staff did an amazing job and did everything right.”
No one was injured in the alleged incident, which comes after the federal member for Indi, Helen Haines , was struck by a 4WD vehicle outside her electorate office in northern Victoria on Monday.
That incident sparked a nationwide debate about whether public officials were sufficiently protected from threats against their safety.
The WA premier, Roger Cook, said state parliament had been shocked by both incidents.
“We have got to start to turn the temperature down,” he said.
Cook said discussions were under way about potential upgrades to security measures to protect parliamentarians and their staff.
“Everyone deserves to feel safe at work, at home and in their communities,” he said.
“It’s not OK for people to take out their aggressions, their disagreements on staff in a politician’s office.”
Cook said security measures could be improved at state parliament but they must be balanced with the need to maintain public access.
The Labor leader said he would support making an allowance available to MPs for security upgrades at their homes.
Beazley is the Labor state minister for local government and the daughter of former federal Labor leader Kim Beazley.
Smart was scheduled to return to the same court next Thursday.

title: Low-alcohol, high-calibre: the best super-session ales
description: Increasingly full-bodied and flavourful, low-strength British pale ales are growing in popularity, especially on the dinner table
content:
Increasingly full-bodied and flavourful, low-strength British pale ales are growing in popularity, especially on the dinner table
T here is nothing like discovering something for yourself to engender a fierce sense of loyalty, and that’s exactly what happened a decade ago when I fell upon the Kernel Brewery’s Table Beer , a pale ale of roughly 3% ABV. This is a brew that never fails to meet me where I am as a working parent with multiple identities but one brain, who often craves a delicious little buzz without loss of function.
Kernel brewer Evin O’Riordain tells me that sales have steadily increased over the past decade, and that 2026 has seen a tipping point. “For the first time ever, Table Beer became the thing we made the most,” he says. This is entirely consistent with the population’s collective interest in no-lo drinks, although, when it comes to beer, zero-alcohol examples are much better represented than low-alcohol ones (in the major retailers, at least). There are only a handful of the latter available in supermarkets, including Small Beer’s 2.3% IPA, Jiddler’s Tipple’s 3.8% Everyday Pale Ale (both Ocado), and Beavertown Satellite (2.8%) and Dark Star’s Hophead (3.4%), both at Waitrose.
So what makes a good super-session beer? Flavour and body tend to be sacrificed when alcohol is reduced or removed, so maintaining those is key. With Table Beer, O’Riordain says he was trying to emulate traditional British cask beers, albeit using “clean and neutral” American yeasts instead of “spicier” English ones, so the bright, New World hops can shine through. The result is a citrussy flavour profile (in a classic IPA, says O’Riordain, the alcohol catalyses the flavour of the hops distinctly, often becoming more tropical).
Texture, meanwhile, results from residual sugar. When he mashes the beer (the process of mixing crushed grain with hot water to activate the natural enzymes that convert starches into fermentable sugars), O’Riordain does so at very high temperatures, disabling the yeast from converting all of the sugar into alcohol. The result is a beer that has the satisfying body of something stronger. A second fermentation in bottle (rather than a forced carbonation, as many breweries do) “also adds a layer of depth”, he says, even though this does increase the alcohol, but only by about 0.2%.
Beavertown describes its Satellite beer as a “super session”, and most beers in that group pitch themselves as supreme session beers – although the Table Beer moniker implies something to drink with food. Always one to refer to past examples, O’Riordain says his research revealed “a whole family of low-alcohol British beers made in the 1700-1900s that were grouped together less by style than by ABV”. These included “boys bitter”, “dinner ale”, “mild beer” and, yes, “table beer”. “Strangely, the lower-alcohol things were more appropriate with food,” he says. All my picks this week are great with flavourful foods; I drank them variously with fish tacos, mattar paneer and donburi. They aren’t just good low-alcohol beers, though; they’re really excellent beers full stop.
Table Beer £3.25 (330ml) The Kernel Brewery , about 3%. My go-to beer, day or night, food or none; for ever and ever, amen.
Beavertown Satellite Super Session IPA £6.50 (4 x 330ml) Waitrose , 2.8%. Refreshing and soft, fruity and swiggable; eke out the sunshine with one in hand.
Dark Star Brewing Co Hophead Golden Ale £2.75 (500ml) Waitrose , 3.4%. The highest ABV here, which comes through in the body, plus there’s an amazing hoppy kick to finish.
Small Beer IPA £3 (330ml) Ocado, 2.3%. Golden, ultra-low ABV number from a brewery that specialises in “mid-strength” brews.
