title: Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet faces ecosystem collapse by 2075, UN advisors say
description: Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’
content:
Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’
Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here
Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet, including Australia’s Great Barrier Reef , faces a high risk of ecosystem collapse before 2075 because of global heating, according to an assessment by United Nations nature advisers.
About 24% of the planet’s reefs across more than 80 countries are already critically endangered, the assessment said, but when the expected impacts of global heating were added this rose to 96%.
Coral reefs are known as the rainforests of the sea. A quarter of all known marine species are found in and around them and they support hundreds of millions of people with food, as well as protecting shorelines and supporting tourism.
Overfishing, pollution, coastal development and global heating have already caused declines in the ecosystems over the past 50 years, measured by the loss of live coral as well as changes in fish populations, the assessment said.
But the scientists said while the prognosis was dire, the findings should serve as a “wake-up call” because reefs could survive with rapid cuts to fossil fuel use and strong conservation action at local levels.
Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter
“The risk is real and very concerning,” said Dr Mishal Gudka, research director at Cordio (Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean) East Africa and the scientific lead for the assessment.
“We stand to lose one of the most valuable ecosystems we have – the impacts of which will affect millions of people around the world.”
The assessment analysed the current status and future threat levels of 127 coral reef regions and was coordinated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), an international group that advises the United Nations.
The assessment assumed greenhouse gas emissions – mainly from burning fossil fuels – would follow a “middle-of-the-road” pathway, causing about 2.7C of global heating by the end of the century when compared with temperatures before the Industrial Revolution.
Current climate policies and targets adopted by countries around the world are likely to cause about 2.6C of global heating, one assessment finds .
The share of coral eco-regions considered critically endangered would likely be even higher, the IUCN said, but four regions did not have enough data to assess them and the coral reefs of the western Galápagos had already collapsed.
The critically endangered classification meant an “extremely high risk” of ecosystem collapse before 2075.
The group considers a coral reef ecosystem to have collapsed if the reef could not maintain itself because of a near or complete loss of living reef-building corals.
The assessment did not fully account for the impacts of the fourth global mass bleaching event from early 2023 to mid-2025 – the most widespread global mass bleaching event on record, the US government’s Coral Reef Watch has confirmed .
That global event was bookended by the worst mass bleaching event on record for reefs in Western Australia where a heatwave killed corals across 1,500lm (930 miles).
Marine heatwaves can cause corals to separate from the symbiotic algae that provides them with colour and nutrient. While not always deadly, bleaching can weaken corals and make them more susceptible to disease.
Gudka said the results were a “wake-up call” and were “alarming, but certainly not hopeless”.
He said: “They should be seen as a call to action – an early warning sign before the worst outcomes eventuate.”
Dr Grethel Aguilar, the director general of the IUCN, said: “It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming.
“We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them.”
Four of Australia’s 17 reef regions were considered critically endangered. Five were endangered and five more were classed as vulnerable.
But all 17 regions, including the Great Barrier Reef, were critically endangered once the expected impacts of climate change were accounted for.
Dr Ben Fitzpatrick of the University of Western Australia Oceans Institute led the Australian assessment. He said even after accounting for the ability of some corals to adapt to warmer water, the rising heat “overwhelmed everything”.
“Reefs are like Picasso paintings under water,” he said. “They have all these wonderful inhabitants in their millions. You can spend a lifetime trying to understand how all these weird critters go about their daily lives.
“To think we might lose that is devastating. There’s one message. We have to stop burning fossil fuels.”
This story was amended on 23 October 2026. An earlier version misstated Mishal Gudka’s organisation name.

title: Marine life in Gulf of Mexico has still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spill
description: New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after the Deepwater Horizon spill
content:
New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after the Deepwater Horizon spill
Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and has still not fully recovered, according to a new study .
The April 2010 explosion of an offshore drilling unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean. According to the study published Monday in PNAS, the disaster – which also killed 11 people and injured 17 others – led to the “sudden, severe and persistent declines in the abundance” of marine life for more than a decade.
Conducted using acoustic sonar, multi-depth trawling nets and genetic studies, the study revealed dramatic population drops across the gulf between 2011 and 2015: fish declined by 63.5%, macrocrustaceans including shrimp and krill fell by 62% – severely affecting a primary food source for whales – and cephalopods such as squid and octopus dropped by 59.7%.
Researchers found that the post-spill population crash outpaced any decline recorded in similar waters over the past 60 years. They also noted that natural factors like temperature, oxygen and food availability did not vary with the decline, confirming the spill as the primary cause.
The marine species most severely affected were also among the most vital to open-ocean ecosystems and global food webs. Krill, a primary food source for deep-sea fish and shrimp, plunged by 72.8%. Bristlemouths – likely the most abundant backboned animals on Earth – fell by 69%. Meanwhile, lanternfishes, which sustain seabirds, dolphins, sharks and commercial fisheries, dropped by 62.9%. A 2023 survey of the area found that many of these populations have not recovered sustainably.
Because large amounts of marine species were instantly killed or affected due to chemicals stored in their eggs, this led to sharp reductions in population sizes, in turn leading to reduced genetic variations, the study found.
Scientists examined genetic diversity in three lanternfish species that suffered severe population crashes, which subsequently led to inbreeding among the survivors.
“The rate of genomic diversity decline is remarkable given the short temporal scale,” the study noted.
The study also examined chemical dispersants applied during the oil spill cleanup. While these agents break oil into smaller droplets, they also spread polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) – among crude oil’s most toxic components – deep into the water column, increasing toxicity exposure for mid-water and deep-sea marine life.
Six years after the spill, researchers found elevated levels of PAHs in deep-sea fish eggs and cephalopod tissues, which severely impaired reproduction. The study further highlighted that residual oil – even at sublethal concentrations – may have hindered the ability of certain species, including damselfish and stingrays, to locate mates through olfactory cues.
“If you keep the oil from coming to the surface, then it won’t be affecting as many shallow water [animals] or humans that were there to work on the spill,” the study’s lead researcher, Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at Florida’s Nova Southeastern University, said.
“That was the idea [of the dispersants]. What that tends to do is break up the oil into smaller droplets, which allowed it to stay deep in the water column. So that probably was not a good thing for these deep pelagic things that we work on, because now you’ve got this kind of minefield of small oil-laden particles floating around and staying at depth instead of coming to the surface,” he added.
“We need to consider the deep ocean to be a very fragile system, not this thing that is so large we can’t disturb it. We need … to be as absolutely careful as can possibly be,” Sutton continued.
Similarly, Pedro A Peres, one of the study’s co-authors and a researcher at Florida International University’s Institute of Environment, said: “Our findings are particularly concerning because these are species that are abundant, widespread and historically might not have been considered vulnerable. What we are seeing suggests that even species that appear abundant can experience substantial changes that may go unnoticed without monitoring.”
Meanwhile, BP spokesperson Paul Takahashi in a statement said: “We will never forget the 11 people who lost their lives. Sixteen years later, we remain keenly aware that we must always put safety first … We have worked hard to build a safer and stronger BP. We have made many changes intended to help prevent an event like this from ever happening again. He added that the company has spent more than $69m for the Gulf region’s recovery.
In 2015, BP agreed to pay a record $18.7bn in penalties and damages after the US justice department and four states sued the company over the spill. The disaster also affected coastal communities in Mexico, which, as of 2020, had yet to receive any compensation. BP has denied that the oil from the spill reached Mexican waters.
Since the spill, thousands of people have also filed lawsuits over long-term health problems they attribute to their involvement in cleanup efforts. Research conducted after the disaster has linked exposure to the spill with a range of health issues including increased cancer risks , higher rates of chronic respiratory conditions, heart disease , headaches, memory loss and blurred vision .

title: Helen Fielding launches Bridget Jones prize for northern comedy writing
description: The Yorkshire-born author says that the 1,000 word competition is for people ‘just living their lives being quietly hilarious’
content:
The Yorkshire-born author says that the 1,000 word competition is for people ‘just living their lives being quietly hilarious’
Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding has launched a comedy writing prize in the name of her most famous creation, aimed at unearthing funny new voices from the north of England.
The Bridget Jones prize for northern comedy writing will go to the funniest self-contained, first-person prose of 1,000 words. The format echoes the anonymous diary columns in the Independent that first brought Bridget to readers in the mid-1990s.
Fielding, who grew up in Yorkshire, wrote the original columns and four Bridget Jones novels , as well as co-writing the blockbuster film adaptations starring Renée Zellweger .
She said Bridget’s humour was drawn from the people she grew up with: “laughing together at our mess-ups; bringing the fancy and pretentious down to earth”.
“There are lots of famous northern comics,” she said. “But this prize is for the comic voices of people who aren’t famous: just living their lives being quietly hilarious.”
Writers living in the north who have neither been published nor signed with an agent are eligible to enter. There is no entry fee and the winner will take home £2,000, plus a session with Aitken Alexander Associates, the agency that represents Fielding, and tailored support from the charity New Writing North. One runner-up will get £1,000.
Fielding was strict about the word limit. “I always tried to make the Bridget columns exactly 1,000 words long – like making the petrol pump stop at exactly 20 quid,” she said. “If it’s slightly under you won’t be punished. Just DON’T MAKE IT ANY LONGER!”
Fielding will judge alongside an Aitken Alexander agent and a representative from New Writing North, and the winner will be revealed at next summer’s Northern Writers’ awards in Newcastle, with the prize presented by Fielding. The prize will be given out each year until 2029.
Will Mackie from New Writing North said: “This is the first time the Northern Writers’ awards have featured an award exclusively for comedy writing.
“There is no one more fitting to identify an original comedy voice than Helen, who created one of the nation’s most beloved comic characters of the last 30 years.”
Fielding cited Victoria Wood, Alan Bennett, Les Dawson, Thora Hird and Morecambe and Wise as inspirations.
Submissions open on 23 November and close on 1 February 2027.

title: Australia bowler Megan Schutt apologises after ban for medication misuse
description: Australian women’s cricket stalwart Megan Schutt has been banned for two matches for a prescription medication breach
content:
Bowler handed two-match ban over ‘single incidence’
Final T20 of series with New Zealand succumbs to rain
Australian women’s cricket stalwart Megan Schutt has been banned for two matches for a prescription medication breach. Schutt has apologised in the wake of her ban, announced on Thursday, which is not related to performance-enhancements.
The 33-year-old strike bowler served the first match of her suspension on Thursday night when Australia’s T20 international with New Zealand was washed out in Sydney. Schutt failed to adhere to requirements under Sports Science and Sports Medicine guidelines with regard to prescription medication, Cricket Australia (CA) said.
“I fully accept the penalty handed down and apologise for failing to meet the standards expected of me,” Schutt, a mainstay of Australia’s women’s team since her debut in 2012, said in a statement. “I’m sorry for the attention this has caused and appreciate the support I’ve received.
“While this occurred out of competition and was not performance related, I understand that I am responsible for following the Sports Science and Sports Medicine Guidelines, which players receive regular education on and I should have adhered to these guidelines.”
Cricket Australia said Schutt’s breach related to “a single incidence which occurred while out of competition and was not for performance enhancing purposes”. It added in a statement: “The two-match ban includes all international and domestic cricket. We will continue to provide appropriate support to Megan and reinforce the standards and responsibilities expected of everyone representing our game.”
Schutt is among the top-10 all-time wicket-takers in women’s cricket. The South Australian has taking 319 wickets in her 244 internationals – four Tests, 114 ODIs and 126 T20s. The bowler most recently played for Australia in the three-match ODI series against Bangladesh, when she starred with 10 wickets in the series.
Schutt is expected to serve the second game of her ban when her Adelaide Strikers open their WBBL campaign against the Melbourne Stars on 31 October.

title: Shovel Dance Collective: Everything in Readiness review – ecstatic, dissonant folk music fighting for sonic and spiritual freedom
description: The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its present
content:
(tak:til) The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its present
T hose thus far unaware of Shovel Dance Collective’s bracing approach to folk should probably note that their third album is not much interested in breaking newcomers in gently. Everything in Readiness kicks off with a three-song suite that lasts more than 10 minutes and takes you, via a series of dramatic sonic jump-cuts, from a grinding one-note drone to a reel that seems to split the difference between trad folk fiddle-playing and the punishing squall of the Velvet Underground’s Black Angel’s Death Song. It then leaps to Tally Ho! Hark Away!, which sets a hunting song first collected in the late 1940s over a blast of what might best be described as ecstatic noise. It’s genuinely hard to work out what instruments are involved in the clattering arrhythmic chaos behind the vocal – there’s definitely a heavily distorted guitar in the mix – but the effect is weirdly euphoric rather than claustrophobic: a kind of purgative release after the mounting weirdness of the preceding reel.
If you’re looking for evidence that the nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to folk music, then there it is. The glib shorthand is that they’re doing for traditional English music what Lankum have done for its Irish equivalent – joining the dots with the kind of out-there experimentation that fills the pages of the Wire magazine – although it should be pointed out they sound almost nothing like Lankum. Anyone who already has an interest in leftfield explorations of British musical history might suggest their chaotic collage approach feels more akin to the fascinating collections of field recordings, folk song and avant garde composition released by Todmorden-based label Folklore Tapes. The music on Everything in Readiness careens unpredictably from gentle lo-fi recordings caked in distortion and tape hiss to the tumultuous, surging racket they serve up on their version of the traditional coalminer’s song Jowl, Jowl and Listen; from singing unaccompanied by anything but the sound of birdsong to the disquieting ambient shimmer of Who Killed Cock Robin? A Summoning (Kind Morning in our Fists), which sounds like it was recorded in a vast, echoing crypt.
It’s an experience that leaves you feeling faintly punch-drunk and disoriented. Everything in Readiness ultimately doesn’t sound like anything else around, but perhaps it’s not so surprising that a bunch of experimental musicians – various members also serve in post-rock band Caroline, improv trio Sullow and the deeply unpredictable Gentle Stranger – have embraced traditional music. English folk in particular has a tendency to slip its standard moorings at times of crisis and find musicians and an audience outside the usual clubs and festivals. The electric folk wave of Fairport Convention, Pentangle and Steeleye Span took root between 1968 and 1972 as the optimism of 60s counterculture curdled into the dark reality of the early 70s. The indie-folk movement that begat folktronica and the founding of Green Man festival, repurposed traditional music’s more sinister overtones, its eerie bleakness, for the twitchy, post-9/11 years.
It’s an impulse you could view as a retreat into “the certainties of a historical music that spoke of a more stable past”, as Rob Young’s peerless history of “Britain’s visionary music” Electric Albion called it. Equally, given folk’s visceral bloodiness and bursts of political radicalism, it could be a search for connection, a reaffirmation that this country has always been turbulent, violent and deeply strange. Shovel Dance Collective, with their loudly trumpted leftwing politics and willingness to dig out contemporary resonances in material hundreds of years old, clearly fit the latter category. You could view the closing I Wish There Was No Prisons as the 19th-century equivalent of those anarchist stickers that have proliferated during the cost-of-living crisis (“if you saw someone shoplifting, you didn’t”), although their approach is clearest on Bold Captain Avery, a 1694 broadside that hymned the “King of Pirates” as a bold freedom fighter, “disowned” by his native country but having at the foreigners and “heathens” in the name of St George. The reality is that Avery was a monster driven by the accumulation of wealth, whose most famous raid – on the Ganj-i-Sawai, a ship en route to Mecca – descended into an orgy of violence that seemed to shock even his own men. It doesn’t take a genius to grasp why Shovel Dance Collective might have repurposed it for 2026.
It’s intended as no shade on the band’s political leanings to suggest all this feels less important than the way their third album sounds: it’s there if you want to find it and that’s undoubtedly a good thing, but the most immediate pleasure of Everything in Readiness lies in the head-spinning sonic surprises it delivers. As it lurches wildly around, you find yourself struggling to keep up, a sure sign that you’re in the presence of music that feels entirely fresh and different. It makes songs that are centuries old feel messily, hectically alive.
Darren Hayman – Close Your Eyes and Face the Sun The latest of singer/songwriter Hayman’s idiosyncratic DIY projects involves making an album using only the once-ubiquitous, now outdated DX7 synth. Here, it (and he) sound fragile and lovely in equal measure.

title: Enzo Maresca says honest talks have revitalised Foden’s Manchester City form
description: Enzo Maresca has revealed he held heart-to-heart conversations with Phil Foden to help the midfielder back to his best
content:
Player has scored four goals in last two games for City
Aston Villa the next test for Premier League leaders
Enzo Maresca has revealed he held heart-to-heart conversations with Phil Foden to help the midfielder back to his best. Foden has struggled over the past two years but has scored four goals in his past two games to give hope he can recapture the form that won him the Professional Footballers’ Association player of the year award in 2023-24.
City travel to Aston Villa on Saturday lunchtime aiming to continue their perfect Premier League start under Maresca, with Erling Haaland fit after sitting on the bench for Wednesday’s Champions League win over AEK Athens .
“Since we started I sat down with Phil two or three times, especially at the beginning,” said Maresca, who knew Foden from a spell as Pep Guardiola’s assistant. “Maybe love is not the right word to use but just to show him how important he is.
“I said many times that I know Phil from years ago so I know how good he is. For different reasons the last few years he was not good enough, but again I think when you have more players like Phil available you are a better team because at the end it’s a matter of improving players. If you improve the players you improve the team, so for me it’s my duty to try to help Phil to be again one of the best players in England. But it’s not just about one game – the season is very long.”
Foden, 26, needs to remain consistent to keep his place in the team, with plenty of competition for the attacking roles, including from Rayan Cherki, who Maresca has described as “one of the best players in Europe”.
City’s only competitive defeat under Maresca came against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League, and they have seven straight wins in the Premier League to sit three points clear at the top. Maresca is waiting to find out whether Matheus Nunes, Mateo Kovacic and Nico O’Reilly are available after missing the AEK game. “The mood is good, we are happy with our start but we are still hungry for more wins,” Maresca said.

title: ​Make the most out of the last spoonful
description: ​Before you throw away that jar with only a bit left inside, turn it into a dressing, sauce, glaze or even a drink instead
content:
​Before you throw away that jar with only a bit left inside, turn it into a dressing, sauce, glaze or even a drink instead
Sign up here for our weekly food newsletter, Feast
I t has been almost three months now, and we still haven’t replaced the cupboards that fell off the kitchen wall. It is also disturbing how well we have adapted to the chaos and having half the room covered with plastic crates that once contained vegetables and that now contain the hundreds of items that used to fit in the three cupboards, the collective weight of said items explaining the incident. The lack of cupboards has put pressure on the fridge, too, which has become a depository. That’s why, when I finally looked inside it properly, I found three jars of honey, each with between 2mm and 2cm at the bottom, as well as two jars of peanut butter, and a pretty much scraped-out jar of chocolate spread. At least all of those jars provided inspiration for today’s newsletter.
Making a dressing with the last inch of honey is perhaps the most efficient and satisfying way to deal with a near-empty jar. Pour in a bit of boiling water and some lemon juice, orange juice or red-wine vinegar, screw on the lid, then shake aggressively so the honey dislodges and dissolves into a syrup. Now add everything else – olive oil, a bit of mustard and whatever else you fancy – and shake again to emulsify. This dressing is great with one of the most useful, speedy and cheap salads in existence, namely shredded red and white cabbage, grated carrot, possibly with grated apple. Alternatively, use the same dressing on a seasonal salad of radicchio, hazelnuts and gorgonzola . And if the remnants in a jar happen to be mustard, do exactly the same as above, just inverting the order and adding honey later.
Felicity Cloake also suggests a dressing in her four healing honey recipes , which also function as suggestions for using the stuff up. Her suggestion of a hot toddy is great – add hot water into a jar with a centimetre of honey left, shake, then pour the now syrupy liquid into a glass or mug and add a curl of lemon peel, a knob of ginger, a cinnamon stick, a few cloves and a large dose of whisky, too, for a really effective cure. Her honey peanut butter is another way: put two tablespoons of hot water in the peanut butter jar, shake, then add honey to make a dip for celery and carrot, or add the mixture to cake batter.
It isn’t just honey, either. The most efficient way to use up the end of any jar, and especially peanut or any other nut butter, is to add a little hot water, then shake the jar violently to turn its contents into a paste. And a good way to use peanut paste is in the base of a soup (especially one with pumpkin and white beans) or with pasta or noodles .
I used to think I was controversial (and therefore interesting), until an Italian friend rolled her eyes and said that she also often makes pesto with peanut butter – pesto being a generic word for “a pounded paste”. Let me explain. In a food processor, blend a large handful of herbs (basil or parsley are ideal), a clove of garlic, salt and enough olive oil to make a paste. Then, while the pasta boils in well-salted water, add a little of the cloudy pasta water to the end of a peanut butter jar and shake to make a thick paste. Add this paste to the herb paste, stir in some grated cheese (grana padano or parmesan), and mix the lot with the cooked, drained pasta, maybe including a handful of baby spinach, which will wilt in the heat.
Fuchsia Dunlop does more or less the same thing for her spicy peanut butter noodles . While dried udon cook in water, she lifts a little of the hot water into the jar, shakes to make a thick paste, then adds two to six tablespoons of chilli oil, two teaspoons of sesame oil and a minced clove of garlic, and shakes again for a sauce the consistency of single cream (if necessary, add more water). Once the noodles are done, she lifts them into a bowl, pours on the dressing, tosses well, divides the now slippery noodles between plates and tops each serving with minced spring onion and toasted sesame seeds.
Next up, jars with an inch of jam in them, which can also be used in a dressing, or to thicken gravy or to add to stews. More fun and slightly more work is to make a jam tart. Dan Lepard has good advice and an excellent shortcrust pastry recipe, which he suggests turning into individual jam tarts . I have also used his pastry to make a large tart filled with a mixture of leftover jams and marmalades, which I tried to keep in sections, but was not very worried when they blurred into a multicoloured mess. The last bit of jam can also be loosened with a little water and used as a glaze for roast vegetables or pork chops. It is also a reason to make semolina pudding.
The jar of chocolate spread that looks empty, meanwhile, should be turned into a drink: add hot milk to the jar, shake, then pour into a mug, add a bit of sugar, if required, and a generous pour of rum. Now, does anyone have the number of a good handyperson in Rome?
Where the art is | The most exquisite cookbook of the year is Paola Gavin’s Still Life Cookbook , a collection of vegetarian recipes inspired by great paintings. An art expert and the editor-in-chief of Epoch Review, Gavin has written many cookbooks, including the excellent Italian Vegetarian Cooking . In this, her ninth book, her two worlds meet and still-life paintings from throughout the centuries are paired with recipes. So, Giovanna Garzoni’s 17th-century Still Life With Pumpkin Flowers and Vine Leaves sits next to a recipe for flowers stuffed with ricotta and spinach. The publisher must be praised for producing such a beautiful but practical edition: the images are breathtaking, the fonts fantastic and the recipes gorgeous.
The Kei to my heart | Running down Wardour Street in London’s Chinatown the other day, on our way to see My Neighbour Totoro , the musical (go before it finishes in January), and desperate for something good and quick to eat, I saw a “CASH ONLY” sign in the window of a restaurant. “That has to be Wong Kei ,” I thought, remembering an article by Angela Hui . As promised, the setting is stark but comfortable, the service fast and functional, and the vegetarian mapo tofu with mushrooms and peas, in a soft gravy warmed with chilli on a mound of sticky rice, was exactly what we needed.
Go with the grain | Last week, I had the pleasure of cooking with chef Fatmata Binta at the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN in Rome. Originally from Sierra Leone and now working in Ghana, Binta is an award-winning culinary innovator and advocate for African agri-food systems. A particular focus of her work and advocacy is a tiny, millet-like grain called fonio that is not only densely nutritious and gluten-free but also incredibly versatile: it can be used like couscous, rice or semolina, as well as in breads, cakes and biscuits. As part of the demonstration, she made a porridge from fonio, which was new as a taste while at the same time reminding me of creamy oat porridge and semolina – made even better with the last of the jam scraped from the jar.

title: The joy of strap-ons, Sherman’s plump pearls and a hypnotic apocalypse: five free exhibitions to see
description: An inflatable Lady Godiva is just one of the thrills in a Pia Camil’s ode to lust. But why is Mark Leckey feeling so doomy and Cindy Sherman so bougie?
content:
An inflatable Lady Godiva is just one of the thrills in a Pia Camil’s ode to lust. But why is Mark Leckey feeling so doomy and Cindy Sherman so bougie?
All sorts of secret, shocking things happen behind closed doors, but they probably pale in comparison to what’s happening behind the saloon-style screens in Mexican artist Pia Camil’s debut UK exhibition. Swing them open and you’re greeted with eye-popping paintings of lust and sexual freedom. A demonic, fanged creature humps away at a blindfolded woman in one, a blue-skinned being with a curly little pig’s tail performs cunnilingus on another. Everywhere you look there are bodies writhing in ecstasy, hair being pulled, stilettos being pressed into bare skin. Most of the time when you see sexual art these days it carries a big political message about exploitation and abuse, but this is the opposite: this is about the joy of sex, about liberation through desire, about a feminist reclamation of eroticism. In the middle of the room, a huge inflatable sculpture of Lady Godiva inflates and deflates, rises and falls, over and over.
The whole show is like all your favourite erotic surrealists put through a Mexican art filter. It’s shocking art, not because of the strap-ons and genitalia, but because it’s so rare to see a painter this fun, an artist so obviously and totally devoted to pleasure, hedonism and joy.
The end is nigh in Mark Leckey’s latest video work. The influential English conceptualist has gone all apocalyptic, with a wild found-footage video that draws parallels between medieval cultists, 60s hippy freak-out gigs and millennial raves. It all starts with a renaissance painting by Uccello, which sends Leckey’s brain tripping across doom-mongering conspiracy theories, biblical prophecies and stock market crashes. It’s freeform and weird, almost unfollowable, but also pretty mesmerising. The film is unfinished, and it’s housed in a barren gallery in an abandoned former hospital, but this is exactly what you want from this kind of project space: challenging, strange, totally uncompromising and blatantly uncommercial art. These kinds of places give room for art and ideas to bloom and evolve, and are becoming rarer and rarer. The shows here are by appointment only – you message them through their Instagram – but you have to take advantage of experimental art spaces while they’re still around. Doom and gloom never felt so hypnotic.
Marcin Dudek has become an archaeologist of the self, digging through his past, his memories, trying to figure out how it all came to this.
His work has always been largely based on the Polish housing estate he grew up in: the basement gyms and football violence that marked his childhood and youth. But this show takes us into something a little more mundane: the local supermarket. He has recreated its metal walls here, rusted and filthy, a dead mouse petrified against the corrugated steel. Inside, he has laid out bottle caps, stones and torn cigarette packets excavated from outside the shop itself. Proper archaeological stuff, but useless, worthless, and meaningless except to him.
The metal collages on the wall are covered in burn marks and images of crowds and police vans. In the communist 1980s, the supermarket was a hub, a sanctuary. But by 1989, capitalism had arrived, bringing with it abundance – and crime.
Dudek’s whole look is dystopian abstraction, taking all the wreckage of his past and reassembling it into fractured grey images and threatening installations. All the rusted and twisted metal here is full of anger and incomprehension, but you get the sense that if he keeps digging, keeps uncovering and excavating the past, it might eventually start making sense.
Cindy Sherman has always been way ahead of the curve. Her photographic playacting has seen her dealing with ideas of identity, fiction and reality for decades, way before every young artist with an internet connection started doing the same thing. She’s brilliant, influential and important.
And this new exhibition is more of what you’ve come to expect from her. This time, her characters are lounging, they are draped over sofas, reclining in bed. These are wealthy, elderly, powerful women in moments of repose. They all wear extravagant undulating fabrics, their wrists and necks weighed down with the thickest gold chains, the plumpest pearls.
How do the rich construct their identities? How do once-young, once-beautiful women continue to project their importance and vivacity into old age?
It feels like a bit of an in-joke, as if she’s taking aim at the kind of people who can afford to buy her work. I don’t mind that: it’s neatly ironic watching ladies with expensive facelifts staring right into these works as they walk around the gallery, unaware that Sherman is holding up a mirror.
They are neurotic, vulnerable ruminations on ageing. But they’re not Sherman’s best work, not by a long shot. What makes it uncomfortable though is that it was all made at Chanel’s invitation, and a lot of the jewels and clothing the characters are wearing come from the fashion house’s archive. It makes the whole thing feel like an ad instead of an artwork. Selling out comes at a price, and this time it might be too high.
For people like me who are cursed to forever ask the universe where our hair has gone, the answer might be Nicola Turner’s exhibition. There are massive, curling, dreaded coils of the stuff tumbling out the front of the building, and things just get hairier inside. Big mounds of twisted wool and horse hair have grown out of the floor, reaching up the walls. Hair has coalesced into strange beings with tripods and shears for legs, stomping through the gallery.
The whole thing is half repulsive, half attractive, part kink weirdness, part psychological horror. Turner is talking about medical procedures and grief, about fashion and the body, about how we cover ourselves and expose ourselves at the same time. It’s good: unsettling, theatrical, but you get a bit too lost in gawping at the giant hair installations to feel much warmth from any of it.

title: Economy set to worsen, with higher unemployment and weaker growth on the way, Jim Chalmers reveals
description: Treasury is revising all the numbers for the midyear budget update as economists warn of a difficult six months ahead
content:
Treasury is revising all the numbers for the midyear budget update as economists warn of a difficult six months ahead
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
Jim Chalmers has revealed December’s midyear budget update will project weaker growth and higher unemployment, as economists warn of a difficult six months ahead for the Australian economy .
Two days after a senior Reserve Bank official foreshadowed the potential for another interest rate rise in under two weeks’ time, the treasurer in a speech on Friday morning will say “higher inflation is putting people under pressure, tighter monetary policy is weighing on domestic activity, and we can see that in the softening of the labour market”.
“Treasury is in the process of revising all the numbers for the midyear update,” Chalmers will say, according to speech extracts seen by Guardian Australia.
“Higher interest rates and higher inflation are likely to mean softer growth and slightly higher unemployment.”
With the Albanese government already suffering the fallout from its ambitious tax reforms , the deteriorating economic situation will be a further blow to Labor and Chalmers’s popularity into the new year.
Australian households are deeply pessimistic about the outlook and Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said “things have to get worse before they get better”.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
Jobs data last week showed unemployment reached 4.7% in September , the highest in nearly five years. Despite this, financial markets on Thursday lifted the probability of a Melbourne Cup day rate hike to nearly 60%, according to ANZ.
Kearns said the full impact of this year’s four interest rate hikes were yet to fully flow through to the economy – and that was before the prospect of a fifth.
“The unemployment rate will increase further from here and we are yet to see the full decline in housing prices, so they are two pretty high-profile things that will impact how people feel about the economy,” he said.
“We could be seeing unemployment at 5% and that will be a difficult threshold for the government.”
ANZ economists on Thursday said they now expected capital city home prices to eventually fall by 13.5% – a record peak-to-trough fall – before regaining some ground in 2028.
With little end in sight for the Middle East conflict, high fuel costs could also be a pain for motorists through the festive season and summer holidays.
Sally Auld, NAB’s chief economist, agreed that “the next six to nine months will be pretty challenging”.
“Growth needs to slow. The RBA is facing an inflation challenge that’s worse than they thought it would be as recently as August,” Auld said.
By this time next year, however, the economy should be sailing in smoother waters.
“Hopefully by that point we should have lower inflation than we have today,” Auld said. “That would be a step in the right direction.”
The government will hope for an economic tailwind before the next federal election in 2028.
But Kearns said Chalmers’ policy options were limited for now, as any additional cost-of-living relief threatened to exacerbate the inflation challenge.
“The challenge is that the government has been criticised, and probably fairly, for contributing to inflation through high government spending.
“But if they pull back on government spending to reduce inflation, they will be gonged for contributing to the rise in unemployment.”

title: Blackpool, Sheffield, Milton Keynes and Wrexham shortlisted for UK city of culture 2029
description: The winner will receive £10m and each shortlisted city will be given £125,000
content:
The winner will receive £10m and each shortlisted city will be given £125,000
Blackpool, Sheffield, Milton Keynes and Wrexham have been shortlisted to be the UK city of culture 2029, an award viewed as a way to boost local economies, foster civic pride and, above all, have some fun.
The four places were chosen from a longlist of nine. The title will be announced in the new year and the three runners-up will each be given £125,000.
That winner will be given a further £10m to help fund what has, in previous years, been a blizzard of events and ideas that create jobs, increase arts engagement and bring in tourists.
All four previous UK cities of culture – Derry (2013), Hull (2017), Coventry (2021) and Bradford (2025) – said afterwards that the designation had been transformative and brought lasting legacies.
Before the shortlist was announced, Wrexham was the bookmaker’s favourite to win. The city is already surfing a Hollywood wave after its football team was bought by the actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney .
“We’re on the map and on the up,” said Wrexham’s council leader, Mark Pritchard, adding that making the shortlist was “fantastic” news. “Our reputation is growing.”
He said Wrexham still had huge challenges around socioeconomic opportunities and inequalities but “winning this competition would be another step towards overcoming those challenges, building confidence in our communities and showing the world what Wrexham is truly about”.
Blackpool is bidding to become the first seaside resort to win the prize. The council leader, Lynn Williams, said it was a place that never stood still. She said: “Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of.
“It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen. We have always been a town that entertains the country and there is nowhere quite like Blackpool.”
Perhaps more than most places, Milton Keynes is a city burdened with misconceptions that it is just concrete and roundabouts. “We do still have concrete cows and, yes, we do have a lot of roundabouts – but I think that there is more to us than that,” Jane Carr, the leader of Milton Keynes council, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.
“We’ve got an amazing amount of homegrown talent. We’ve got our own orchestras. We’ve got lots of performing artists. We have an international festival every two years … we want to develop and move forward.”
Of all four shortlisted places, Sheffield’s artistic heritage probably shouts the loudest, whether that’s electronic music, Pulp, Arctic Monkeys or England’s largest theatre complex outside London.
Fran Belbin, the leader of Sheffield city council, said being shortlisted was a proud moment for everyone who had shaped the bid. “Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit,” she said. “From our world-renowned music heritage and vibrant independent arts scene to our festivals, libraries, theatres, museums, galleries and grassroots creativity, culture is part of who we are.”
The unsuccessful candidates on the longlist were Ipswich, Inverness, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon. Phil Redmond, the Brookside and Grange Hill creator who headed Liverpool’s European capital of culture year in 2008, chairs the advisory panel that will choose the winner.
He said: “Once again there is a hard choice ahead. The four places on the shortlist continue to demonstrate both the variety and strength of creative ambition across the UK.
“Each place represents a different view, or aspect, epitomising what culture is, the sum of all we do together, and while each approaches it differently, they all share the common aim of reminding the rest of the UK of who they are, where they are and why they are worth visiting.”

title: Nottingham Forest’s false start places early focus on Glasner and Delap
description: Austrian’s tactics need adapting to but Forest are in the bottom three and their owner is not the patient type
content:
Austrian’s tactics need adapting to but Forest are in the bottom three and their owner is not the patient type
S itting 19th in the Premier League was not the plan for Nottingham Forest after the arrival of a highly acclaimed manager and a £45m striker to fuel their ambitions. The fates of Oliver Glasner and Liam Delap are intertwined and with the stark stats of zero home goals and a solitary point at the City Ground it is not the dream start they were aiming for.
As Delap prepares to return to Ipswich, where his career ignited, on Friday night, Forest are remaining calm. There is a desperation to get away from the short-termism that caused so many problems; 12 months ago, they were on their third head coach of a disappointing season. This summer they were ruthless with the removal of Vítor Pereira, who had done a fine job to escape the drop, because they saw an opportunity to upgrade with Glasner, hoping he could transform Forest like he did Crystal Palace.
It cost plenty to acquire Glasner and Delap, which many fans believe should lead to instant results, but that is rarely the case in an industry as complicated as football. For the coach, it is a case of learning the club inside out while influencing performance through his carefully choreographed methods. For the striker, he needs to rebuild confidence and that comes via goals.
In Glasner’s first full season at Palace, they won one of their first 13 league matches but ended comfortably in mid-table and FA Cup winners . It was similar at Eintracht Frankfurt, getting one victory in 10, but going on to win the Europa League .
Learning the Glasner way is not straightforward. Playing three at the back is rarely the norm and nor is having two No 10s, all with the background of Forest losing their best player in Elliot Anderson .
The recruitment was measured, targeting positions that required strengthening and avoiding needless purchases that dogged the club after promotion. Replacing Anderson became a priority, but Glasner felt James McAtee could adapt to a deeper role in midfield alongside the shrewd free signing Xaver Schlager. Ousmane Diomande was a coup in defence and Glasner convinced Daniel Muñoz to follow him from Selhurst Park.
Behind the obvious figures, there is plenty of underlying encouragement for Forest. Based on chances created and conceded, Glasner has had the best start of any Forest manager in the Premier League era. His team rank seventh, according to Opta, for expected goals (xG), but have scored the fewest – five – and are the biggest xG underperformers at -6.2. It is a huge discrepancy, missing out on almost a goal a game. It includes 62 shots at home that have come to nothing and if Glasner wants buy-in from the fans, that needs to change quickly. If every team had scored and conceded the goals measured by xG, Forest would be fourth.
It is understandable that Delap is yet to find his feet after a disappointing year at Chelsea and the lack of pre-season set him back. Forest tried to sign him before he went to Stamford Bridge and have great faith in him, but he needs to improve his record of one goal every five league appearances. He is the ideal No 9, possessing pace, power and sharp finishing, but unless he is on peak form, turning that into guaranteed output is not straightforward.
Delap has scored once for Forest, but is putting in the effort through being the front line of defence, relentlessly pressing opposition centre-backs. He has shown plenty of quick thinking, demonstrated by his quick throw-in to set up a goal at Anfield, something almost replicated against Arsenal only for Chris Wood to miss the chance.
Forest allowed Arsenal a single shot on target last Sunday – it just happened to be deflected in for a winner . Glasner can also point in that match to the absence of his captain, Morgan Gibbs-White, the team’s attacking fulcrum. “It feels very unfair,” Glasner said of the result. “We have to accept we are missing some bits. But the performance in many parts was very good.”
In two full seasons at Selhurst Park, Glasner won two major trophies for a club that had gone almost 120 years without one. He has two European titles and his own distinctive formation and execution, something he has harnessed over 12 years in coaching, so he knows how long it takes to develop the complexities.
The picture looks clearer after almost four months together. The hope at Forest is that the endeavour is rewarded with greater luck, the missing ingredient among well thought-out recruitment led by the chief football officer, George Syrianos, and his team and clever coaching. Syrianos is Glasner’s biggest advocate and told fans the manager would be given time.
Friday will be Glasner’s eighth Premier League match at Forest, three more than Ange Postecoglou was permitted before being sacked this time last year by the owner, Evangelos Marinakis. Glasner, unlike the Australian, can show progress and will be justifiably confident points will come.

title: Introducing the new host of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating, Siobhán McSweeney
description: The award-winning podcast returns with ten new episodes, famous faces, a fresh format, and new host Siobhán McSweeney to lift the lid on the joys of comfort food.
content:
The award-winning podcast returns with ten new episodes, famous faces, a fresh format, and new host Siobhán McSweeney to lift the lid on the joys of comfort food.
Today (Thursday 22 October), the Guardian announces Siobhán McSweeney as the new host of the award-winning podcast Comfort Eating when it returns in November.
A previous special guest on Comfort Eating herself, Siobhán is renowned for her roles in Derry Girls and Amandaland, as well as hosting popular shows the Traitors Ireland and the Great Pottery Throw Down. She takes the hosting reins from food critic Grace Dent, who stepped down after ten series .
A foodie at heart, Siobhán stays true to her Irish roots. When alone she enjoys nothing more than tucking into a unique mix of cheese and onion Tayto crisps and Dairy Milk chocolate, finished off with a swig of Guinness.
The new season of Comfort Eating will serve 10 weekly episodes. Each week, Siobhán will welcome a new guest to lift the lid on what they eat when no one else is watching. As they introduce Siobhán to their favourite comfort foods, she’ll explore the memories and relationships behind them, and the role food has played throughout their lives. The first episode features comedian and actor Asim Chaudhry, with upcoming guests including actress Nicola Coughlan, journalist Caitlin Moran, and Good Morning Britain host Ed Balls.
For the first time, full episodes of Comfort Eating will be available to watch on YouTube , alongside the podcast on all audio platforms. Audiences can also follow the show on social media for highlights and exclusive content.
Siobhán McSweeney, Comfort Eating host, says:
“Even though it is impossible to fit into the elegant shiny stiletto heels of the incomparable Grace Dent, I am so excited to be gifted with the very special hosting crown of Comfort Eating. Food is such a big part of our lives, and I just love that with each weird and wonderful meal comes a beautiful story, endless memories and nostalgia. I can’t wait to hear and taste it all. Tune in and join me!”
Phil Maynard, global head of podcasts, Guardian News & Media says:
“We’re delighted to have Siobhán on board as the new host of Comfort Eating. Siobhán brings her quick-witted humour, sense of fun, honesty and warmth to a brilliant new series of celebrity interviews based around food and nostalgia.”
Read an exclusive interview with Siobhán in this weekend’s Saturday magazine.
For more information or to request interviews please contact media.enquiries@theguardian.com.
Guardian Media Group is one of the world’s largest and most-trusted quality newsbrands, publisher of the Guardian, theguardian.com and the Guardian app.
Founded over 200 years ago, the Guardian now serves audiences through five editions: Australia, Europe, International, UK and US. With no billionaire owner, the Guardian is renowned for its fearless investigative journalism, holding power to account and amplifying the stories that need to be told. Its independent ownership structure means it is free from political or commercial influence.
Today, millions of people worldwide choose the Guardian’s journalism every day and more than two million readers across 180 countries have supported the Guardian’s work.
Audiences can listen to the Guardian’s top-rated podcasts, watch its award-winning documentaries and interact with its growing digital portfolio, from a premium live news app to the recipe app Feast.

title: Tour de France 2027 routes revealed with British stages, time trials and a volcano
description: Edinburgh will host the most northerly Tour de France start in 2027 while the Pyrenees will provide the competitive finale of next year’s route
content:
‘Britain offers us a symbol that ties the races together’
Tour de France Femmes will conclude on Puy de Dôme
The most ambitious Grand Départ in the long history of the Tour de France was unveiled in Paris on Thursday as the race organisers fleshed out the details of next summer’s men’s and women’s race starts in Edinburgh and Yorkshire.
Over six days of racing, Scotland, England’s Lake District and Peak District, Lancashire and Yorkshire, Wales and central London will be taken over by the snaking race caravan on a route that is expected to lure millions to the roadside.
Christian Prudhomme, the men’s Tour director, said he expected “a warm and massive welcome for the champions”. “From the start at the foot of Edinburgh Castle – the northernmost in the history of the Tour – to a team time trial in London, Great Britain offers us a symbol that further ties the two races together,” he said.
The sports minister, Stephanie Peacock, confirmed that £65m has been allocated to fund the six stages and said the Tour’s visit would “shine a spotlight on women’s cycling like never before”.
The men’s race starts in Edinburgh on 2 July and finishes in Paris on 25 July, with a final stage that maintains the tradition of racing up and over the cobbled streets of Montmartre.
Paul Bush, the managing director of Grand Depart GB, has big ambitions of his own for the race. “One of my aspirations will be to turn the UK yellow next year, for two weeks, so everybody is in yellow,” he said. “Now that would be pretty special.
“Now that would beat 2014. Not that I’m looking to beat 2014, because it’s not a competition. But if we could encourage everybody, workplaces, communities, old age pensioners’ homes, schools, everything to become yellow, I think that would really embrace the thing.”
In fact, the men’s Tour will begin and end on cobblestones. From the Royal Mile to the Champs-Élysées, the peloton will cover 3,479km of racing and take in two individual time trials, three summit finishes and a potential decider in the climbs of the Pyrenees.
The first British stage, from Edinburgh to Carlisle, will head through Midlothian and the Borders, while stage two, from Keswick to Liverpool, will cover 223km and take in Lancashire’s Trough of Bowland before finishing on Liverpool’s waterfront.
The final British stage will include eight climbs on the winding road from Welshpool to Cardiff, and is likely to be one of the hardest stages of the race.
After the transfer across the Channel, the peloton races across central France, from Cherbourg to the Jura, for the first summit finish on the Grand Colombier, followed by mountain stages to Sallanches and Les Saisies.
From the Rhone Valley, where the furnace conditions that characterised this year’s race are likely to return, the convoy heads into the Cévennes and the Tarn for finishes in Mende and Albi.
The second time trial is centred on Toulouse and comes before two brutal Pyrenean stages, the first crossing the fearsome Col du Tourmalet before a finish on the Col du Portet, and the second, to Laruns, taking in four major ascents and 4,300m of climbing.
The Tour de France Femmes begins in Leeds on 30 July, 13 years after the men’s race staged its Grand Départ there, with an opening stage from the Headrow to a likely sprint finish on Deansgate in Manchester.
The next day’s challenge, from Manchester to Sheffield, includes both Winnats and Snake Pass on a route which features almost 3,000m of climbing and which the race director, Marion Rousse, called the cornerstone of “the hardest opening in the history of the women’s race”.
But the showpiece stage will be in central London, with an 18km team time trial, routed from Westminster to The Mall, taking in Tower Bridge, St Paul’s Cathedral, Trafalgar Square and Buckingham Palace.
London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, said the Tour’s visit would “not only cement London’s status as the undisputed capital of women’s sport, but also inspire more people to take up cycling, as we build a better, greener London for everyone.”
After the transfer to northern France, the women’s peloton heads south, via Calais, Magnanville and Bourges, to a first mountain finish at La Loge des Gardes before a penultimate mountain stage through the Auvergne to Clermont-Ferrand. The nine-day race climaxes on the steep volcanic Puy de Dôme, after a stage that climbs almost 4,000m.
Both routes were unveiled at Porte Maillot even as curfews remained in place in some parts of central Paris, including Place de la République and Les Halles. The French media described the nation as sinking “deeper into crisis”, but in the aftermath of the Covid pandemic and the controversies of climate change, the Tour has become well-versed in puffing out its chest in the face of adversity and threats.
However, disruption, due to both civil unrest and extreme temperatures, remains possible. Race organisers ASO faced a similar situation in July 2023, when climate activists and rioting threatened the race. That year, Prudhomme said the Tour was “in constant liaison with the state” and would “adapt if needed”.

title: Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases
description: Politicians have called for ruthless sentencing, but lawyers blame the politicians for the poverty, and anger, behind their clients’ looting
content:
Politicians have called for ruthless sentencing, but lawyers blame the politicians for the poverty, and anger, behind their clients’ looting
Awa, 18, stood in the dock in the tribunal de Paris , a small, mute and bewildered figure seeming unable to understand, let alone answer, the simplest of questions.
The court was told she had joined young people who looted an Yves Saint Laurent store on Boulevard Saint Germain in Paris’s Left Bank late on Sunday and stripped it bare within minutes.
Awa was arrested at a nearby Métro station with a black balaclava and black gloves in her backpack along with four YSL handbags worth a total of €5,000 (£4,200).
In the dock, dressed entirely in black – the clothes she was wearing when arrested two days earlier – she appeared panicked, clutched at her hair, picked her lip. Unable to speak, she covered her face and began to weep; first silently, then uncontrollably, her sobs punctuating an almost palpably painful silence.
Awa was just one of 2,500 people arrested during last weekend’s rioting and looting across the country , more than 900 of whom are being fast-tracked through the courts using a procedure called comparution immédiate (immediate appearance). It sends them to trial straight or shortly after being taken into custody, or within three days if they are held in pretrial detention.
The process of handling this sudden influx of cases has overwhelmed the courts and angered defendants’ lawyers, who say they have no time to meet clients.
The violence erupted after high-school student and union demonstrations. In Paris, the authorised march passed through the capital without major incident. But on the fringes and afterwards, black-clad, masked people rampaged through cities and towns, setting fire to public buildings, bikes and rubbish bins, smashing up restaurants and shops, and looting local and luxury goods stores.
Initial reports blamed the destruction on those protesting against a raft of unaddressed grievances against the president, Emmanuel Macron, and successive governments, including “ultra-left” disrupters spurred on by the France Unbowed leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. The reality was, in many cases, more prosaic.
Most of those charged with vandalism, violence, theft, or damaging public or private property appeared to have been what officials have described as “opportunistic delinquents” with mundane rather than political motivations.
The majority were young men. In Paris, 68% of those taken into custody were adults, according to the public prosecutor’s office, not high-school teenagers.
As police escorted the defendants into court from the cells where they had been held since their arrest, it was clear that, apart from black clothing, they could not be categorised. Some were confused, others more confident. Many, like Awa, seemed completely nonplussed at finding themselves before a judge whose first question was: “Do you want to be tried now or later?”
Laure Beccuau, the Paris public prosecutor, told French radio: “The vast majority of those we’ve sent to the courts have never been convicted [before].”
Most were young and unemployed, others in work with families. There was Aboubacar, 23, employed by the charity Emmaüs; Boumedine, 25, a TikTok influencer; Oussama, 37, a delivery driver; Victor, 21, a student who appeared in court with a black eye, accused of attacking a police officer.
In Lyon, there was, Yanis, 20, a restaurant worker, caught with a friend with 30 pairs of trousers and two jackets from Zara; Nathan, from Perpignan, arrested carrying fireworks (often used to fire at police); Julien, 27, a freelance artist accused of “serious and worrying behaviour” for throwing a traffic cone at a police car.
Lamine, 38, a builder, was discovered inside the Louis Vuitton concession at the Printemps department store in Paris, with Sofiane, 34, an Amazon worker, after the building’s grills closed in an emergency lockdown on Saturday. Lamine said he had gone to buy clothing for his five children, but the court heard his criminal record included convictions for violence, theft, resisting arrest and contempt of court. The pair, found with €37,000 of luxury goods, were convicted: Lamine sentenced to “semi-release”, allowing him to work during the day but return to prison at night, and Sofiane ordered to wear an electronic bracelet for six months.
A 19-year-old student with no previous criminal record who had taken part in the official march was caught on his way home with several stolen black pullovers from a looted clothing store. He was fined and given a 14-month suspended prison term, a sentence his mother said was too severe.
“It was just a question of opportunity,” he said. “I thought: everyone else is doing it why not me? I regret it.”
The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, had extended the time those arrested could be held in police custody from 48 to 72 hours and called for courts to “to be extremely firm, to be ruthless towards the c asseurs [rioters and vandals]”. In response, 125 lawyers wrote an open letter to the president of the Paris bar association denouncing “the ultra-repressive turn taken by the Paris public prosecutor’s office”.
“The nationwide protest on 17 October revealed to us, as lawyers, a historic, politically motivated, orchestrated, and deliberate crackdown. We refuse to allow summary trials to become the tool of a political response to social anger,” they wrote.
Back in court number 6.04, Awa managed to explain in mumbles and monosyllables that she had stolen the bags to sell, and regretted it.
Her lawyer, Hamma Bouchareb, told the court her client, who passed her baccalaureate and was studying for an advanced technical diploma in international business, has been living in sheltered care since fleeing her violent father who beat her, forced her to take cold showers, fractured her skull and broke her arm.
“She’s only just 18 and barely out of childhood. She can hardly express herself. Awa stole and I am not excusing that, but she stole because she needs money,” she said.
“This immediate court appearance is complicated and we need to reflect on what we are doing,” Bouchareb said. “These people have lost their bearings, they are afraid. The response to the outbreak of anger should be political not legal. Politicians are responsible for an economic situation in which some don’t have money to buy food or clothing, like my client.”
In a courtroom of lawyers, judges, prosecutors and press hardened to melodrama and often tall tales of woe, Awa’s story touched a nerve.
The lawyer representing Yves Saint Laurent said he would not seek to “aggravate the situation” but pointed out two of the company’s stores had been looted and hundreds of bags taken. The prosecutor agreed it was “a sad situation” and he would not seek a custodial sentence.
Awa was given a 12-month suspended sentence, ordered to pay a fine and damages, and perform 140 hours of community service.

title: What Chris Rock’s film Misty Green misses about Black characters
description: Director Rock establishes the film’s setting of Los Angeles better than the lead character, played by Rosalind Eleazar
content:
Director Rock establishes the film’s setting of Los Angeles better than the lead character, played by Rosalind Eleazar
I n the opening scenes of Misty Green, a new film from Chris Rock , a Black actor starts to perform her lines in an audition for the role of Andy Sachs in The Devil Wears Prada . The whimsical, pastel color palette of the scene collides with her deadpan recitation of lines meant to convey nervous excitement. If this unevenness weren’t uncomfortable enough, Misty’s nose suddenly starts to bleed down to her white button-up shirt. It goes without saying that she doesn’t get the role. She hasn’t gotten much of anything as of late, and she is in a very bad place.
Misty Green is an out-of-work, Emmy award-winning Black actor with substance abuse issues and a penchant for affairs with married men. The propulsion for the film is that the widow of one of her now dead lovers is kicking her out of the luxury waterfront property that Misty claims was gifted to her by him. Misty, who’s played by Rosalind Eleazar, has seven days to find a new job so that she won’t become homeless. In a different director’s hands, this plot could have been a comeback story in which false starts lead to eventual triumph, making for a traditional feel-good movie. But with Rock’s treatment, the premise isn’t compelling enough to sustain a feature-length film.
At the start of the movie, Rock establishes the film’s setting better than he establishes the lead character. In a voiceover, Misty describes “the bag”, or the money that she’s chasing, followed by a photographic montage of Los Angeles icons interspersed with harsh realities: the luxe Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel followed by a homeless encampment, Venice Beach and In-N-Out Burger, wildfires before a rapid transition to a billboard promoting thinness. Hollywood is full of beautifully packaged contradictions. Rock issues the same amount of contradiction to Misty; however, he falls short in facilitating an emotional connection between her character and the audience.
In one scene, for instance, Misty laments to her best friend, Naomi, played by Anna Kendrick, that she deserves a well-paying gig because she’s talented, yet repeatedly turns down Naomi’s suggestions for whom to contact and where to audition. When Misty finally finds an open role that piques her interest, she indulges in an all-night coke bender before her audition the next morning. Without any meaningful insight as to why she self-sabotages, it is difficult to empathize with her character. Chasing “the bag” is not a sufficient reason for a viewer to continue watching a marginally entertaining movie without much else to say. It’s difficult to have faith in a leading lady who is emotionally adrift and erratic for the majority of the film. Who exactly is Misty Green?
Rock has been focusing on Black women in his work as a means to convey institutional inequality for decades. He showed the ups and downs of marriage in the 2007 film I Think I Love My Wife and the race discrimination towards Black women’s hair in the 2009 documentary Good Hair . While those two efforts were measured and thoughtful, Misty Green is scattered and superficial. In the aforementioned works, we hear and see Black women who are psychologically complicated because of and in opposition to the barriers that prevent them from feeling seen and affirmed. In Misty Green, that depth is glaringly absent. Rock, who plays the director Jordan Green, does too much of the legwork to belabor to the audience the problems within Hollywood: the futility of audition tapes, the shoddy pay and the narrow opportunities for Black artists. At the same time, there is an overemphasis on the system without much examination of the woman navigating it.
In one of the most tender scenes of the film, Jordan and Misty are dining out, and the line between business meeting and a romantic date is blurred. The warm-colored lighting evokes a sense of intimacy as they poke fun at their mistreatment as Black creatives. Misty tells Jordan about her struggles growing up as a biracial girl, with the film leaning on the recognizable and overdone trope of the “tragic mulatto”. The admission aims to evoke pity, but lands as simply another detail in how much she has suffered. Misty has no real community, no money and no passion towards acting whatsoever besides an angry, relentless need to prove something to others.
By saddling her character with hardship after hardship, Rock leaves no breathing room where Misty’s humanity can emerge and the story can subsequently expand. Instead, Misty is the stereotypical “mule” – the Black woman who shoulders all burdens – without demonstrating her selfhood through resistance or, at the very least, self-reflection. Eleazer delivers a fine performance, given the material, but her efforts gradually become monotonous. The film moves along, but Misty remains static.
In an interview about the film, Rock says that he stole from movies like Legally Blonde and Dumb and Dumber, where audiences believe they are watching dumb characters who are actually smart. “So I knew Misty had to be great,” Rock says. “You can’t just be a fuck-up.” The difference in those aforementioned movies is that they have heart: the lead characters had arcs where they, alongside the audiences, discover something bigger than their initial objectives. Misty Green doesn’t accomplish this. Female characters don’t have to be likable, but audiences need to understand their fears and desires in order to have an investment in the story.
Rock tries to add layers to Misty’s personality through a severely underutilized Daniel Kaluuya, who plays her mentally ill brother, Jay. But even their bond and history of shared trauma is gratuitous and tacked-on. Audiences don’t understand until the last 20 or so minutes of the film why his presence is crucial to her character and how he influences a morally dubious decision she eventually makes. These expository details are presented as flashes across the screen rather than interwoven revelations within the overall narrative. Their tragedy could’ve been an entry point that would’ve made for a better, more textured film. But in the end, Rock is too reliant on pain as the vehicle for a Black character’s narrative momentum.

title: ‘America, this is a warning’: pro- Trump Maga media in a froth over Europe protests
description: Fox News and others have toed president’s line – seemingly hoping unrest abroad will make people vote Republican
content:
Fox News and others have toed president’s line – seemingly hoping unrest abroad will make people vote Republican
Donald Trump sought to capitalize on the scenes of unrest in France, telling a crowd in Kansas on Monday that “migrants” and “communists” were responsible, and that the scenes were “what the radical ‘Dumocrats’ want to do to America”.
As Republicans struggle to convince voters across the country ahead of November’s midterm elections, Trump’s allies in the conservative media have followed suit, seemingly hoping that the scenes in France can scare people to the polls.
Sean Hannity, perhaps Fox News’ most prominent host, delivered his version of the message on Tuesday. Speaking over clips of fires in France, with the chyron “A warning from Europe” emblazoned on the screen, Hannity said : “This is, sadly I argue, by design – an attempt by the left to destroy the free world, western civilisation, if you will.”
He added: “This is a preview of coming attractions here in America.”
Hannity wasn’t alone. On Monday, Fox News host Laura Ingraham had on Jamie Metzl, who describes himself as a “technology and healthcare futurist [and] geopolitical expert”, to draw the same comparison.
“If you like what you’re seeing in France then you should support these DSA candidates who are essentially calling for the same thing here,” Metzl said .
He was only echoing something Ingraham herself had said a few days earlier , in front of a cartoon version of a police flashing light with the words “A warning to America”. The chyron, as she spoke, could not have had a clearer message. It said in all capitals: “Don’t let America become France.”
“America, this is a warning. From the immigration disaster there, to the fiscal mismanagement, the same promises: free college, government-funded healthcare, tax the rich, climate change, open borders – they’re all being sold here, and they were implemented, some of them, here by AOC, Bernie, El-Sayed,” she said.
Most of the rest of Fox News agreed. Jesse Watters played clips of protests of violence in France on Monday, announcing that the goal is “to replace communism with capitalism”.
“It’s already started to happen here,” Watters added .
Lawrence Jones was of the same mind on Tuesday, reading out a tweet from JD Vance in which the vice-president said of the situation in France: “I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country.”
Jones responded : “The vice-president is exactly right.” He then interviewed Ben Domenech, an editor at the Daily Wire, who also agreed with Vance. The scenes in France, Domenech warned, are “the consequences of becoming apologetic about their values, viewing nationalism as something which is a dirty word”.
Fox News wasn’t alone. On Newsmax on Monday, Bianca de la Garza was busy asking Rick Santorum , the former Republican senator, if the situation in France is a “wake-up call for America”.
Santorum said it was. “The people who are running as democratic socialists or really just any sort of mainstream Democrats if you will, leftists, they want to bring the economy and style of government of Europe to this country,” he said. That, Santorum said, would lead to violent protests in the US.
“The standard of living of the average European is far below the standard of living of Americans,” Santorum said, which would come as a surprise to the people who are paid to research such things .
The same day Greta Van Susteren had interviewed Tom Emmer , the Republican congressman from Minnesota, who trotted out the same line.
“Look, we’ve got the same example in this country that we better be watching what’s going on in France. We want everyone to come to this country and chase their American dream. We want them to come here legally. And we also, Greta, want them to come to be Americans. We celebrate culture in this country like no one else,” he said.
“If you don’t come to this country to be an American, what you’re seeing in Paris is what is going to happen. You cannot have a different country within your country,” Emmer continued.
One America News (OAN), arguably the most rightwing of the three channels, was not about to be left out.
On Monday, OAN invited Andrew Fox , whom it described as a “cultural expert”, on to the channel to discuss the protests. Fox, who has 433 followers on X, said: “If we pay attention to what’s happening in Paris we can see our near future, if we don’t really toughen up immigration policy and the integration of how those immigrants become one with the nation they’re joining.”
Rounding out the message was David Pollack, one of OAN’s hosts, who at least adjusted his message slightly by looping in Italy. He tweeted a video of protesters in Italy, adding: “Now it’s happening in Italy: import the third world, and this is what you get. The sad thing was, this was all by design. And the Marxists are coming for the United States next.”

title: Snowy Hydro 2.0 has blown out to 12 times its original cost – but the CEO says it ‘could have been worse’
description: New projections by the Snowy Hydro company show tunnelling work is now 65% complete but the completion date has been pushed back to 2029
content:
New projections by the Snowy Hydro company show tunnelling work is now 65% finished but the completion date has been pushed back to 2029
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
The cost of Snowy Hydro 2.0 has blown out to as much as $25bn, with a major reassessment finding the long-delayed renewable energy project will not be completed until the end of the decade.
First touted by the Turnbull government in 2017 with a price tag of $2bn , the cost of the project in the Kosciuszko national park has increased dramatically over time. In 2023 it was revised to almost $13bn, with construction due to completed by the end of 2028.
But new projections by the Snowy Hydro company, released on Thursday night, show it will now cost at least $22.2bn, with contingency for a further increase to $25bn.
