Machine tunnelling is now 65% complete and major excavations are in their final stages. Work to build the new underground power station is under way, with about 5,000 people at work on the project.
But the project reset shows Snowy 2.0 won’t be completed and fully commissioned until 2029.
The Albanese government plans to announce additional project oversight and financing structures for Snowy 2.0 in coming weeks. Another injection of taxpayer funds is expected, along with possible private financing components.
Beset by challenges – including major delays when a specialist boring machine became bogged and wedged in hard rock – the project’s timeline and extraordinary cost overruns have been blamed on its unique nature, significant risk and technical complexity.
The boring machine, known as Florence, is still not yet at the halfway point of its 15km tunnel work.
Principal contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV) also faced “cost estimation challenges”, according to the company.
Since the project was signed off on in late 2018, more detailed technical analysis has been required, while FGJV has missed productivity targets and failed on cost and planning performance. Global price rises for construction equipment, services and staff have all exceeded early estimates.
The project aims to link two existing Snowy reservoirs with tunnels up to 27km long. Once completed, it will be able to generate 2,200 megawatts of power and provide 350,000 megawatt-hours of storage.
Despite the soaring cost and repeatedly delays, the Snowy Hydro chief executive, Dennis Barnes, said the situation could have been worse.
“This project is incredibly complex, it is off the charts even for mega projects,” he said.
“The original contract had so many flaws and the project was stalled. The thing I’m pleased about is that, if it wasn’t for the reset, if it wasn’t for the collaborative relationship we now have with the contractor, I think this would have been worse.
“The silver lining is the project is beginning to hit its straps.”
Asked if he was concerned community confidence in Snowy 2.0 was shot, Barnes said the project would provide half the storage capacity needed for renewables in Australia and would help lower electricity prices.
Snowy 2.0 is expected to be the largest source of stored dispatchable energy in the national electricity market, with its functions to include firming intermittent wind and solar generation and absorbing surplus renewable generation during periods of low demand.
It will provide peak-load generation during periods of high demand and boost supply during prolonged periods of low wind and solar output.
Critically, it is designed to reduce extreme wholesale price spikes by adding substantial supply when the market is stressed.
“I’m confident that we can get the message out that the lowest cost system of the future is renewables backed by Snowy pumped hydro, batteries and gas,” Barnes said.
The energy minister, Chris Bowen, and the finance minister, Katy Gallagher, blamed the former Coalition government for the poor design and cost projections but insist Snowy 2.0 is necessary to strengthen Australia’s national energy grid.
Labor looks set to attempt to place blame for the delays and overruns at the feet of the former energy minister and current opposition leader, Angus Taylor.
“The government remains transparent about the pressures facing this project and securing the best possible outcome for taxpayers, energy consumers and the grid,” they said in a statement.
“Once complete, the pumped hydro expansion of the Snowy Scheme will provide more than half of the total energy storage the grid needs by 2050, strengthening energy security and putting downwards pressure on energy prices.”

title: ‘Bodies, pornography and disgust’: did 2 Girls 1 Cup change the way a generation thinks about sex?
description: A New York theater show about the infamous viral video explores the effects of growing up with internet porn
content:
A New York theater show about the infamous viral video explores the effects of growing up with internet porn
Among the first questions posed in Two Girls , a verbatim play reconstructing the events of the shock-porn video 2 Girls 1 Cup, is a seemingly simple one: “Can you describe the cup?”
The cup was plastic, insists one interview subject, transparent but also red, “like you get at a pizzeria”. Another man describes the cup, with certainty, as “a tapering, slightly green glass”. A third subject, sounding less certain, suggests it was a clear Ikea glass, six inches tall, adding: “You see into it, which is important.”
And a fourth interviewee simply declares: “No, I cannot describe the cup.”
The playwright Eliya Smith’s strange, unexpectedly tender theatrical investigation draws on interviews with eight men to unpack the legacy of the infamous viral phenomenon 2 Girls 1 Cup, a 60-second trailer for the Brazilian scat fetish pornographic film Hungry Bitches that took the internet by storm in 2007.
Created with buzzy experimental theater company The Goat Exchange and subtitled, “A Homeric Retelling in the Oral Tradition”, Two Girls is currently playing at the Cherry Lane Theatre, a historic venue in New York’s West Village now owned and operated by the indie film studio A24, until 29 November.
Back in an age of MySpace when something close to an online monoculture still existed, 2 Girls 1 Cup sparked waves of screaming, revulsion-filled reaction videos. Teens dared each other to watch, framing it as an endurance test: how long can you last?
“We didn’t know what we were being exposed to, we had no business,” declared actor Keke Palmer in a recent Hollywood Reporter roundtable , after her mention of the video sparked hysterics across the table. “They should have protected us!”
We all saw it. We all remember it. Or do we?
Smith conducted hours of interviews with a group of male friends and acquaintances for Two Girls, none of whom are identified. Interviewer and subjects are all played by Chloe Claudel and Juliana Sass, who trade off with each scene, swapping places opposite a plain white table on a nondescript set. (Claudel also directs, alongside Mitchell Polonsky, her Goat Exchange co-artistic director.)
And since the subjects interviewed for Two Girls struggled to even recall the cup in question, no surprise that the video’s exact content also proves a challenge. One says the two women are topless, “obviously”; another says they start out in bikinis; a third says he “pictures” them wearing pantsuits.
Some of the men then grow uncomfortable, hesitant to describe the memories bubbling up. Others are less shy, launching into evocative descriptions of defecation into a glass, the mutual consumption of said feces and finally projectile vomiting. “It definitely has an arc,” insists one interviewee.
So too does Two Girls, which begins as an attempt to reconstruct the video in question but grows into a deeper examination of coming of age in the early era of internet porn and coming to associate sexuality, however unconsciously, with a certain kind of shame or disgust. Did 2 Girls 1 Cup play a part in that?
The playwright, who made her off-Broadway debut last spring with the melancholic Grief Camp , began interviewing acquaintances about 2 Girls 1 Cup about two years ago, uncertain if the conversations would make for anything interesting.
“I was thinking a lot about bodies, pornography and disgust,” said Smith. “But I don’t know that I totally understood why I was interested in these themes, at least at the beginning.”
Smith is also a longtime collaborator with Claudel and Polonsky, dating back to the trio’s time at Harvard. Goat Exchange had a breakout hit this summer with Smith’s teen-girl focused Dad Don’t Read This, a meta-theatrical tale of sleepovers and living vicariously through The Sims. (Goat Exchange also made their Ireland debut with Radio Bette at the Dublin Theatre Festival in September.)
The company’s subjects are varied, but each production sees Goat Exchange artists building a new and peculiar kind of narrative structure that ultimately breaks down to reveal the story’s emotional center.
“Chloe and I are really interested in structures and systems, building the scaffolding around the heart and finding the things that move us,” said Polonsky.
Their theatrical work Time Passes (For Ellen Brody) toggles between Virginia Woolf’s To the Lighthouse and Chief Brody’s wife from Jaws flirting with a giant inflatable shark, finding an existential ennui in the strange mash-up. And Deadclass, Ohio , also a verbatim piece by Smith, literally “breaks” at the halfway point and begins to loop, poking at the instability of memory by adjusting small details with each repetition. Both shows will play return engagements at the Under the Radar festival in January.
In Two Girls, the subversion comes in the awkward moments of strange social tension between Smith and her subjects who, in discussing the video, reveal themselves in disquieting ways. One subject confesses, seemingly to his own surprise, that he first understood sex as its own kind of game of chicken.
“For years, until it all gets demystified a little bit, what’s hot is not the blowjob, but that you got her to do it,” he admits. “And that you both knew she wasn’t supposed to if she was going to be, like, a good person.”
Far from censorious of their male subjects, the show’s writer and performers feel almost protective of them. “There’s something very vulnerable and honest about telling someone over the phone how something affected you as a 12-year-old,” said Claudel. For her and Sass, the task is to channel those vulnerable admissions (piped directly into their ears with in-ear technology) as honestly as possible.
“I was interviewing people who encountered internet pornography when they were very young, and didn’t understand their own bodies or the bodies of people around them,” said Smith. “Once I provided the space for them to answer questions, a lot of them really wanted to process the way that had shaped them.”
2 Girls 1 Cup becomes a container, of a sort, for all the ways in deconstructing the conceptions of empowerment, attractiveness and health we hold around our own bodies, built into us by teen confusion never fully disentangled. “This video, and the way we relate to it, synthesizes all of that,” said Smith.
In its final moments, Two Girls makes an unexpected pivot that reframes the play’s tension around the question of voyeurism. And until this moment comes along, it may not have occurred to you that the women who actually performed 2 Girls 1 Cup have scarcely, in all of this deep dissection, been mentioned at all.
Yet still, the conclusion is not one of finger-pointing or shaming. “We’re just trying to figure this out together,” said Smith. “What it means to live in this world that we participate in shaping, and started shaping when we were really young, and didn’t understand much.”
Two Girls is at Cherry Lane Theatre, New York, until 29 November

title: Donald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes appeaser Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle
description: Europe’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish Trump, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
content:
Europe’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish Trump
H istorical comparisons are always inexact. No one conflict precisely mirrors another. Yet Donald Trump’s shameless appeasement of Vladimir Putin carries more than a noxious whiff of Neville Chamberlain’s failed attempt in Munich in 1938 to head off war with Nazi Germany. To be fair to the former UK prime minister – and history largely hasn’t been – his peacemaking efforts had the enthusiastic backing of most people in Britain and France who, like him, were desperate to avoid a repeat of the horrors of the first world war. Trump enjoys no equivalent public support for his treachery . Nor does he face the prospect of a US war with Russia. His betrayal of Ukraine is cynically self-interested, globally dangerous and utterly contemptible.
US-Russian talks on agreeing the shoddy terms of a precedent-setting American sell-out of Ukraine are at an advanced stage, after meetings in St Petersburg this week. Trump has zigzagged over the war ever since returning to office. Now, panicked by record-low poll ratings , he seems determined to scapegoat Ukraine and force its de facto capitulation. Recent steps – his shocking decision to fund Putin’s war machine by buying Russian diesel, his waiving of tougher sanctions, his mysterious, lethal interruptions in US satellite and intelligence sharing with Kyiv, and his renewed attempt to oust Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – mark Trump out as the skulking Judas, the craven Brutus of the modern age. He makes Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle. All that’s lacking is an umbrella.
Why does Trump act this way? Partly, it’s personal. He doesn’t like Zelenskyy and it’s obvious why. Ukraine’s leader is everything he is not: courageous, principled, morally unimpeachable, hard-working and politically savvy. Partly, it’s money and power. Trump has set his shrivelled, grasping heart on normalising relations with Putin’s repressive rogue regime, opening the way for lucrative deals on energy, raw materials, and control of the Arctic and outer space. He likes the idea of a world dominated by three all-powerful blocs and authoritarian leaders: himself, Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. And partly it’s the unexplained, sinister hold Putin appears to exercise over this former society playboy, New York real-estate developer and serial bankrupt .
Whatever Trump’s motivations, the short-term consequences of his betrayal are potentially fatal for Ukraine’s bid to repel the Russian invaders and survive as a sovereign democratic state. For much of this year , Ukraine has been winning, or at least holding its own, in the contested lands of the Donbas and along the Black Sea littoral. More than that, by using homemade missiles and drones, it has taken the fight to Russia’s industrial heartlands and oil refineries, significantly undermining Putin’s ability to fund his war. Zelenskyy has also been winning the battle for international opinion, particularly in Europe, which itself is under escalating Russian hybrid attack . Amid Trump’s egregious backsliding, European nations have taken the lead in supporting Kyiv militarily, financially and diplomatically.
It’s hard not to wonder whether there’s a connection between Trump’s sudden, divisive, decisive lurch towards unabashed support for Putin and the fact that Russia , suffering unsustainable battlefield casualties, severe economic damage and deepening international isolation, is at increased risk of regime-toppling humiliation. Whatever the truth, Trump’s Putin bailout – his duplicitous Russia rescue act – could turn the tide.
Trump’s perfidy is the shame of the world, and it is the world – and not only Ukraine – that will pay the price over the longer term. This calculated attempt to force Kyiv’s submission imperils everyone. Ukraine, if it is allowed to fall, will haunt Europe and the wider geopolitical biosphere for decades, as was the case with Czechoslovakia after 1938. Trump’s Molotov-Ribbentrop-style pact with a warmongering dictator, an indicted war criminal , a smirking, bigoted mass murderer, may fatally compromise the western alliance and spell the end of Nato as an effective defence against eastern totalitarianism. Who among the democratic governments of western Europe, in the Elysée, in the German and Polish chancelleries, in Brussels or in Downing Street, can now trust a word that comes out of Washington? Its bond is broken, its honour in shreds.
Trump’s betrayal follows a pattern of lesser treacheries: arbitrary tariff wars waged against trading partners, the traducing of loyal allies, threats against Canada and Greenland, abandonment of a two-state solution in Palestine and most recently, his disastrous war against Iran – the real reason why US midterm voters, facing inflated fuel prices, are turning against him and his Republicans. But his Russian folly may be the most egregious and consequential. As MI5 has warned , Britain and Europe are under daily attack from Russia, its spy networks, saboteurs, cyber warriors and paid agents. Reports this week suggest it is menacing western space satellites, too . Don’t look to turncoat Trump for help. He’s on the other side.
Trump’s Munich moment is a disaster in the making for Europe’s security and defence. A Putin victory, accepted and facilitated by the US, would fatefully damage respect for international law and sovereign borders. Untold numbers of war crimes and crimes against humanity would go uninvestigated and unpunished in a partitioned, fractured Ukraine. China and others might soon follow the precedent established by successful Russian aggression. For all these reasons, Britain and its European allies can no longer afford to hold back. Indignant speeches at the UN, off-the-record murmurings and carefully calibrated verbal slaps on the wrist will not suffice, if they ever did. Andy Burnham, France’s Emmanuel Macron, Germany’s Friedrich Merz and Canada’s Mark Carney must lead the way in confronting Trump head-on, even at the cost of a definitive break with Washington.
Tell Trump publicly to knock it off. Take concrete steps to punish him for rewarding Putin and prove that the democracies of the world will not be bullied and sold out. Tell him if he really wants to be remembered as the US president who shattered the western alliance and ensured the triumph of authoritarianism, then keep on licking Putin’s boots – but he will be on his own. The UK, EU and Nato member states, Japan, South Korea and other like-minded countries, are far from powerless, economically, militarily and in numerous other ways. And despite what polls may suggest, healthy majorities of their citizens reject the hateful far-right lies and sick populist myths on which Trump and his pitiful emulators feed.
The US ultimately leads the west by consent, not by right. Consent can be withdrawn. Burnham could start by ordering the closure of US military bases in Britain, offensive symbols of a hostile occupying power. At all costs, Trump’s treachery must not stand.
Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

title: First Thing: Israel using US-made electroshock weapons on Palestinian detainees
description: An American company is still supplying Taser weapons linked to prisoner abuse by Israeli forces
content:
An American company is still supplying Taser weapons linked to prisoner abuse by Israeli forces. Plus, 12 valuable lessons about life and death by hospice workers
Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here
Good morning. An investigation has revealed that Israel is using US-made electroshock weapons on Palestinian detainees . The American company Axon is still supplying the Taser weapons despite evidence they have been used to torture prisoners. The news comes as US volunteers including a lawmaker helping Palestinians harvest olives were detained, and Heidi Levine revealed more details of her violent assault by Israeli settlers.
Human rights groups have condemned allegations of the repeated torture and ill-treatment of detainees held in Israeli detention centres and prisons using electric shock devices, with Amnesty calling for restrictions on exports of such devices. A spokesperson for the Israel Defense Forces said the abuse of detainees was strictly prohibited.
Who was detained by Israel near Nahalin in the occupied West Bank? The Israeli military detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander, several rabbis and Israel’s former deputy attorney general. Soldiers said the area had been declared a closed military zone.
What more has Levine said about the Israeli settler attack on her? The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians . Witnesses said thee attack on her ceased only when young men used slingshots to aim stones at the settlers, forcing them back.
What is the latest development with US diplomats in the Middle E ast? The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia , as it faces a barrage of near-daily attacks from Yemen’s Houthis. Reports have emerged of similar US withdrawals in UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain amid concerns of a return to conflict with Iran after the midterm elections.
Democratic state attorneys general, other top state officials and civic groups have accelerated planning to thwart any federal meddling in the November midterms by Donald Trump as he continues his false charges of widespread voting fraud and veiled threats of interfering in the process. The enhanced cooperation is significant because many secretaries of state are responsible for supervising elections, and state attorneys general are charged with defending the laws governing them.
Where has Elon Musk been spending his election campaign money? Elon Musk’s Super Pac has spent more than $500,000 in New York’s highly competitive 17th congressional district race to help Mike Lawler, the Republican incumbent, hold his seat. Lawler, a moderate Republican, is fending off a challenge from the Democrat Cait Conley in one of the most-watched races that could determine who controls Congress.
What has happened with letters containing white powder being sent to Congress? Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members. The offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum have received envelopes containing white powder in recent days.
What is Trump’s polling as the election looms? Donald Trump’s approval rating has sunk to 36% , the lowest recorded, with most respondents expressing frustration over his handling of the US economy, cost of living and Iran war. The president was heckled at least nine times during a campaign event yesterday, and reacted to a supporter punching a demonstrator by saying: “Man, I loved that.”
The US supreme court went against Donald Trump’s administration on Wednesday , refusing to allow the immediate enforcement of sweeping restrictions on gender-affirming care for transgender individuals held in prisons and federal facilities.
The decision marks an unusual victory for transgender rights before the nation’s highest court, which has largely sided with the administration and other opponents of transgender rights in several major cases.
Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. Several European governments took down sites temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70% of websites.
The US National Security Agency told all organisations using PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately. Our technology reporter Josh Taylor has this explainer on what PHP is, and how bad the flaw is.
Emmanuel Macron has accused Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of making “stupid comments” about France’s street unrest for political gain. The US president blamed France’s violence on “migrants, jihadists and communists”.
A 24-year-old Kansas man has been arrested for allegedly threatening to shoot Donald Trump . Jaden J Read allegedly wrote “I’m killing this pedo” on Facebook.
Pope Leo will not need any further ⁠treatment after undergoing lung cancer surgery last week , his doctors said, indicating ⁠that his tumour had ⁠not ​spread.
Jeffrey Epstein’s attorney and accountant have been accused of ‘facilitating and concealing’ his crimes in a civil lawsuit filed by New Mexico’s attorney general.
The Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar has denied allegations of immigration fraud in an interview , and said that after scouring her residence room by room for nearly five hours, agents took 17 items, including several phones.
Forget the familiar favorites and try these sweets from around the world – from caffeine-boosted chocolate drops to dragonfruit gummies – all available before Halloween.
Xan Brooks speaks to director Taika Waititi , who has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film.
Hospice and end-of-life workers discuss with Madeleine Aggeler what they have learned from their work and patients in their last moments.
Oliver Milman reports from Kerrville, Texas, where survivors are united on the need for urgent action after floods killed 136 people last year.
Bless her, but Bukang-i, the nearly 10ft-long female dusky shark that became a viral sensation after getting stuck in a South Korean canal for a month, has returned to it just hours after finally being coaxed out to sea.

title: Cathinka Tandberg: ‘Spurs fans hate Arsenal. That’s how it is’
description: Norwegian forward might look to Harry Kane for inspiration on the pitch, but when north London derby comes around, she needs no lessons on what the rivalry means
content:
Norwegian forward might look to Harry Kane for inspiration on the pitch, but when north London derby comes around, she needs no lessons on what the rivalry means
“I t means more than just three points. It’s for the whole club. It’s for the whole place. It’s for the whole of Tottenham.” One only needs to be in the presence of Tottenham Hotspur’s Cathinka Tandberg for a few minutes to feel the passion that emanates from her when it comes to this weekend’s north London derby. As a lifelong Spurs fan, the forward understands more than most the intensity of the rivalry that exists between her side and Arsenal, one that she cannot wait to experience once again on Saturday.
“It will just be an incredible feeling,” she tells Moving the Goalposts. “I think you will feel a few nerves that you maybe don’t feel in a normal game but that’s good.”
“All the Spurs fans hate Arsenal and Arsenal hate Spurs. That’s how it is. You want to show that you’re the best team. Simple as that. You just want to fight for the club, the badge and for the people around you.”
It has been a significant 13 months for the 22-year-old who made her dream move to London in September 2025. After catching the eye as a goalscorer in the Damallsvenskan at first Linköping and then Hammarby, the Norwegian was signed by Martin Ho on deadline day to bolster the team’s attacking options. She made her mark on her first start, scoring a spectacular 40-yard goal against Everton.
“I settled really well,” she reflects. “I’m really enjoying it and want to push myself forward. It’s been a tough start [to this season] and I haven’t really got what I wanted. But there’s loads of games left. I’m still young. I’m still improving and learning. I just have to trust the process and trust what I’m surrounded by.”
“It’s a big difference from Sweden,” she continues. “You meet World Cup players week in, week out so you have to perform every week if you want results. I feel like my physicality has changed a lot. I’ve got stronger and fitter. Playing under Martin has made me think more away from the goals. I think more about how I play with the ball, how I press and all of those things that I maybe didn’t focus on before … it’s a bit like Harry Kane. The older he gets, he has developed his game as well. He needed to be deeper in the pitch because that’s how they wanted to play and then he has to be better with the ball. That’s a bit how I also need to be. I can’t only just stand in the box. I need to be good everywhere else.”
Spurs have been transformed under Ho and finished fifth last season. However, with success, comes expectation, ambitions that Tandberg clearly shares but with a sense of perspective.
“Tottenham has always been a Champions League club for me,” she says. “But I’m a fan so I can’t really talk for the other players. When I came to the club, I said that I want to get top three. But you also need to be realistic and to see where the team has been before. The transformation that Martin has done in a season is unbelievable. I don’t think anyone else could do that. That tells you everything about him. He’s one of the greatest coaches I’ve worked with and I think everyone that comes here, one of the reasons is because of him. We all trust him and the process.”
That faith is currently being tested. After an unbeaten start, Tottenham have suffered back-to-back defeats, shipping six goals to both London City Lionesses and Chelsea.
“You can call it a dip in form but I still feel like we also showed our qualities in those games,” Tandberg says. “It’s just about ourselves. We maybe need to change our mentality a bit, find that fire and dig a bit deeper when we play those top teams. I feel like maybe it’s good that it’s come because it had to at some point. It’s about how we respond.
‘We also have to realise where this team has been. Two years ago, it was a relegation club. We need to realise how quickly it has [changed]. But, of course, we have expectations and levels that we want to come to and we know that we can. I feel like we’re working so well … we just have to believe in everyone.”
For Tandberg, putting that right against a struggling Arsenal in front a home crowd would be the perfect tonic. “I’ve always been a passionate player and I’ve been a supporter,” she says. “I play for the supporters because I just enjoy it and I know how it is to be in the stands. I think [that connection] is very important because we have their back and they have ours. To give them something back is important and to show that we see and hear them every time.”

title: Watching the watchers: Meet the volunteers observing Trump’s poll monitors on election day
description: Thousands of people are training to be observers to look out for any interference or ICE presence during the midterms
content:
Thousands of people are training to be observers to look out for any interference or ICE presence during the midterms
Our reporters answer your questions about ICE, immigration and the midterms
S tevie Lyn is angry at what she’s seen in her Phoenix, Arizona, neighborhood over the past year. Since US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) began conducting raids all across the city, her Latino neighbors on the west side have had to hide in their homes, too scared to grocery shop, work and vote. That’s why she volunteered to become a poll observer.
“I had to take the anger, because it was eating me alive, and direct it towards a constructive activity,” she said.
Lyn was trained by the grassroots non-profit organizations Living United for Change in Arizona (Lucha) and the Arizona Center for Empowerment (Ace), both focused on immigrant rights, to work the primaries in July. Sitting on the back hatch of her SUV 75ft from her local polling place – the legal distance allowed for poll observers in the state – she watched the area for any disorder or disturbances. She only encountered one problem in 10 hours: a campaigner for a local legislative candidate repeatedly walked with voters beyond the legal line. When she reported it, poll workers asked the campaigner to stay back.
Lyn, who has been through observer training three times, called the primary a dress rehearsal. She has taken election day off work to observe again. She hopes she won’t have much to report. “I just want to be bored to death on 3 November,” she said. “That’s my goal.”
Lyn is one of the thousands of volunteers trained by organizations like Lucha and Ace to safeguard the polls against election interference. The US justice department plans to send about 1,000 federal monitors to polling sites, in what it has called the “biggest DOJ election observer effort in history”, claiming the effort will ensure elections are carried out fairly. But critics suing the government over the plan said it could intimidate voters. And the administration hasn’t ruled out sending ICE and other law enforcement officials to the polls. Poll observers want to be prepared to counter any intimidation, even if many expect election day to be business as usual.
“I am not naive about this administration and have my eyes wide open,” said Justin Levitt, a Loyola Law School professor and former Barack Obama justice department official. “But this administration wants to project power that it doesn’t have and finds it in their interest to get the electorate freaked out.”
On a Monday night in late September, about 20 people logged on to learn how to protect voters in Arizona.
First, though, Karime Rodriguez, an organizer with Ace, told volunteers why the job “constitutional observer” exists. As immigration raids began surging in neighborhoods across Arizona earlier this year, Republican state lawmakers introduced a bill to station ICE agents at polling places. That’s when Ace decided to recruit and train volunteers for double duty: to monitor ICE activity in the Phoenix area’s most vulnerable neighborhoods and to keep watch at the polls during the midterms season.
“These aren’t abstract polling places,” Rodriguez told the trainees during the call. “These are our schools, our churches, our community centers where immigration enforcement has already been taking place.”
When Ace started mapping ICE activity in Maricopa and Pima counties, the map showed a pattern that the neighborhoods hit hardest by raids were often the same ones already facing barriers to voting, including polling place closures . In the two weeks before the July primary, the group recorded a spike in reported raids. There was also ICE activity around a few polling places in West Phoenix, a primarily Hispanic neighborhood. That alone discouraged some people from voting, Rodriguez said. Turning Point USA had a presence at a voting center in south Phoenix, and some voters told the groups they felt intimidated.
“ICE is in our neighborhoods and even people who are citizens are afraid that they’ll be taken if they go to vote,” said César Fierros, a spokesperson for Lucha. “We see the trucks driving by, the unmarked vehicles driving by. And we’re scared because we never know who is going to be in that vehicle.”
Organizers said the heat map had become the backbone of their election protection effort, using it to decide where to station observers and deploy its rapid response volunteers on election day. The groups’ plan is to have three or four observers at every polling place who must simply observe; if they see something suspicious, all they have to do is report it back to the leadership team. If ICE agents show up, they should also alert Lucha and Ace leaders, who will then send an alert within the group’s chat, post on social media or call for community members to show up. Volunteers who can’t be at the polls will answer phone calls and texts.
Groups like Lucha and Ace are preparing volunteers for election day all across the country. In Pennsylvania, more than 250 people participated in poll watcher training hosted by the state’s Democratic party on the same Monday night in September. They flooded the chat with questions: could an ICE officer challenge a voter’s eligibility? Almost certainly not, a party lawyer said. Law enforcement officers can’t come within 100ft of a Pennsylvania polling place unless they are voting or the site is in a police building.
Larry Hailsham, the executive director of the Pennsylvania Democratic party, said Democrats were building “an unprecedented voter protection program” that will deploy thousands of volunteer observers to priority locations, backed by volunteer attorneys in every county and a hotline staffed in English, Spanish, Mandarin, Vietnamese and Korean.
The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has seen a similar surge. Since June, 68,000 new volunteers have signed up to be “democracy defenders”, said Molly McGrath, the ACLU’s director of national democracy campaigns, people who are ready to be called upon to watch polling places or protest in the event of election interference. The organization is focusing on battleground states, close House races and polling sites that serve historically disenfranchised communities and students, particularly in the south. The organization has recruited 1,700 poll monitors in Texas, 650 monitors in Georgia and 120 monitors in Arizona’s Maricopa county.
Asked in May whether he would send ICE or national guard troops to polling places, Donald Trump said he would do anything necessary to ensure honest elections. After months of vague and contradictory statements, “administration officials confirmed a policy purporting to allow armed federal officers to conduct certain immigration and law-enforcement operations at polling locations despite acknowledging federal law that prohibits it”, according to a recent Democracy Forward report .
Still, voting rights experts are skeptical about Trump’s election monitoring plan, which Levitt said was not the largest in history. Before the supreme court’s 2013 Shelby County v Holder ruling weakened the Voting Rights Act, the justice department’s election observer operation was far bigger – and 1,000 monitors was the right size for spot-checking compliance with federal law, not for disruption, Levitt said.
Justice department monitors also carry no special authority. “They are subject to the exact same laws that any other observer in the state might be subject to,” said Lauren Miller Karalunas, senior counsel at the Brennan Center for Justice. In most states, she said, local election officials and law enforcement officers can remove observers who break the rules, federal ones included. Levitt pointed to Wyoming, where two justice department monitors sought access they weren’t entitled to during the primaries. Officials told them no, and they left.
What is unusual, Levitt said, is the publicity. The justice department typically doesn’t reveal details about its monitoring plan until days before an election. “To the extent there’s a strategy – it is very clearly messaging,” he said, referring to the administration’s election monitoring announcement. “Voters should continue to trust their local officials to deliver elections that are free, fair and well run.”
Organizers have raised some concerns that Trump could declare a national emergency to take control of elections. But no statute gives the president that power, Levitt said, and states and localities run elections. “The president is free to declare a national emergency all he wants,” Levitt said. “State and local election officials who do run the election process will likely ignore him.”
Sending armed federal personnel to active polling places, unless an agent is voting, has been a federal crime since the civil war era, he said. And the logistics would be daunting since most Americans can vote early or by mail, spreading any such operation across weeks.
Other ways Trump could undermine the election go beyond routine election day activities, including claiming election fraud (including claiming that noncitizens voted illegally), election machines were compromised, late-counted votes should be questioned or local election officials interfered with the results. The administration could also pressure local officials to delay or reject certification results or use a warrant or subpoena to take election materials, including ballots or voting machines. “These potential outcomes are all reasons why our work will continue past election day,” Rodriguez said.
Experts say the larger danger is that fear keeps people home. Karalunas worries that in addition to the messaging from the Trump administration, headlines about dueling armies of observers could lead some voters to skip the polls. Organizers, including the No Kings coalition , have encouraged voters to vote early and together to avoid any election day setbacks.
“For most folks, elections will go exactly as planned,” she said. Past predictions of mass observer deployments haven’t materialized and skeptics who watch the process up close often come away reassured, she said.
Levitt expects most poll observers will be “massively overprepared” and will spend election day pointing voters to the right polling place.
Organizers in Arizona say preparation is the point. Fierros said the groups want voters to feel confident, even joyful, when they arrive at the polls. “We’re not the ones fearmongering,” he said. “We’re the ones responding to the moment.”

title: How Democrat Mary Peltola is on the verge of flipping right-leaning Alaska
description: Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the state
content:
Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the state
How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions
M ary Peltola’s campaign to represent Alaska in the US Senate has taken her to parts of the huge state’s interior that are inaccessible by road and on the frontlines of the cost-of-living crisis she hopes will make her the first Democrat to win the seat in nearly two decades.
She has been to towns where paper towels retail for $40, a half gallon of oat milk goes for $21 and the cost of a new freezer can be quadruple what it is in the state’s largest city, Anchorage, simply because it’s so complicated to get there. Along the Arctic Ocean, she’s heard of communities where power bills have climbed to $1,500 a month because they rely on generators for power and the Iran war has pushed the cost of diesel to new heights .
“Nobody can afford that,” Peltola said in an interview.
Alaska, a right-leaning state that’s about twice the size of Texas but the third least-populous in the country, has always been among the more expensive places to live, and the price increases in the state’s rural areas haven’t necessarily been felt to the same degree in the more populous cities and towns.
Yet the state’s Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the 3 November midterms. The Senate seat currently held by two-term Republican Dan Sullivan is a top prize.
“In 23 short days, we’re going to be voting both [Republican congressman] Nick Begich and Dan Sullivan out of office, and they richly deserve it,” the chair of the state Democratic party, Eric Croft, said at a press conference last week.
“They are self-serving, self-dealing DC politicians who repeatedly voted to make life harder and more expensive for Alaskans.”
All signs indicate that Republicans are taking seriously the threat posed by Peltola, an Alaska native and former US House lawmaker who supports oil and gas and gun rights. Outside groups have poured in tens of millions of dollars into supporting both candidates, and last week Donald Trump made the long journey from Washington DC to the conservative Matanuska-Susitna valley to rally voters behind Sullivan, who has trailed in some recent polls .
“Here in Alaska, the Democrats are running radical left Mary Peltola for the Senate. If she gets in, you’re screwed,” the president told a packed sports center in Wasilla, which is best known outside the state as being the home town of Sarah Palin , the Republican former vice-presidential nominee.
On the campaign trail, Peltola and Sullivan have dueled over who would do a better job lowering costs for Alaskans, and also representing its vital fishing and oil and gas industries in the US Capitol. There have been mutual accusations of allegiances not to a state known as “the last frontier” but to special interests in the Lower 48, while Sullivan has accused Peltola of denigrating Alaskans after a report that she mistreated her staffers.
The incumbent has his own unique vulnerability in the form of a similarly named Republican challenger who made it through the state’s top-four primary, and could split his support. And while polls open on 3 November, the outcome may not be known for days – Alaska has always taken a long time to count its votes, since absentee ballots are allowed to arrive up to 15 days after the election.
Since becoming the 49th state in 1959, Alaska has only once supported a Democratic candidate in a presidential election – Lyndon B Johnson in 1964. But its politics are nuanced – bipartisan majorities currently control the legislature and the frontrunner in the governor’s race is a Democrat . In the race for the state’s lone US House seat, the party has coalesced behind the independent candidate Bill Hill to take on Begich.
“Sixty per cent of Alaskans do not identify with the Republican or the Democratic party. We are a great example in this state of how government should work,” Hill, who is receiving support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in an interview.
A former state lawmaker, Peltola rose to prominence in 2022 when she won a special election to replace Don Young, the long-serving Republican congressman who died aged 88 , and became the first Alaska native in Congress. She was elected to a full term later that year, then lost re-election to Begich in 2024. This year, Peltola is viewed as the best candidate Democrats could field to take on Sullivan.
Centering her campaign on the slogan “fish, family, freedom”, she has added an Alaskan twist to the cost-focused platform many Democrats have adopted nationwide. Visitors to her campaign website can play a video game intended to highlight her views on bycatch, or the accidental netting of other species by trawlers, which has become a major controversy in Alaska as salmon runs have dwindled.
Peltola opposes Trump’s tariff regime, noting it has driven up costs for imports from Canada, which separates Alaska from the rest of the country. She has also condemned his decision to attack Iran and spark a conflict that has driven costs for gasoline and diesel – which typically arrive by barge or ship in the state’s interior and island communities – even higher than usual.
“These really frivolous decisions are just putting Alaskans in a bind, and we’re really paying the price for these weird partisan wars,” Peltola said as she visited a picket line of flight attendants at Anchorage’s main airport. With a laugh, she added: “I don’t know what’s funny about that, but it’s funny.”
Sullivan, her opponent, was first elected in 2014 after ousting a Democratic incumbent. He serves alongside Republican Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s senior senator who is one of the most outspoken Trump critics in the Senate, but has nonetheless remained a firm ally of the president, even as his popularity has waned , unlike many vulnerable Republicans who have sought distance. Sullivan has emphasized his advocacy for Alaska’s military installations, as well as the state’s long list of proposed oil developments and major infrastructure projects that he argues will only come to fruition if Republicans are kept in charge.
“Joe Biden, Schumer, their Democratic allies came after Alaska with a barrage of executive orders to shut down our state, kill jobs, drive up the cost of energy, and my opponent, Mary Peltola, not only did nothing to stop it, she enabled it,” Sullivan said as he rallied with Trump.
“They try to kill our jobs and turn us into a national park. Ladies and gentlemen, the conflict in the Middle East is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs.”
He gained new ammunition against Peltola in September, when the New York Times reported allegations that she had verbally and physically abused her staff and used slurs. “My opponent really doesn’t like her fellow Alaskans. She just doesn’t,” Sullivan told supporters in Wasilla.
Peltola’s campaign has said parts of the report are not true, and noted some of the behavior occurred when she was grieving the death of her husband in a plane crash, and the death of her mother around the same time. When Peltola was asked about the report during a debate with Sullivan last week, she replied: “I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day, and I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications.”
Alaska is one of the nation’s top oil-producing states, and every year its permanent fund pays each resident a dividend that’s usually upwards of $1,000 . But production, which is concentrated on the state’s North Slope, has steadily declined since peaking in the late 1980s, and how to manage the resource is a constant topic in the state’s politics.
Sullivan is all-in on oil production, supporting moves by Trump to open up more protected federal land and waters to drilling, which could offer new revenue opportunities. He cheered the president’s announcement that South Korea would invest $54bn to build a long-discussed natural gas pipeline across the state, although reports have since emerged that Seoul has agreed to no such deal.
Though she was in the House of Representatives for just over two years, Peltola has taken credit for pushing Joe Biden to approve the vast Willow oil project , over the objections of environmentalists. But she also emphasizes the opportunities renewable energy could present to Alaska’s communities, and is cognizant that she is a member of a party that prioritizes fighting the climate crisis, which many believe requires curbing oil and gas production.
“We do need more oil production in our state for our state revenues to pay for our schools, our roads, our public safety,” Peltola said.
But the sky-high prices for gas in parts of Alaska are proof to the candidate that oil is not the solution alone.
“When you’re paying $26 a gallon for gas or diesel, we’re priced out of petroleum,” she said.

title: Experts alarmed by ‘less transparent’ CDC as US measles deaths rise
description: Agency declines to reveal in which state latest measles death occurred as it delays reporting other measles deaths
content:
Agency declines to reveal in which state latest measles death occurred as it delays reporting other measles deaths
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) added a third measles death to its dashboard on Wednesday, but the agency would not reveal whether the death occurred in Pennsylvania or another state – which is “notable” as the agency delays reporting other measles deaths, experts say.
The CDC cited privacy laws in not sharing the name of the state, but experts say there are no privacy concerns in doing so – and this information is important for the public to have as the outbreak continues accelerating, growing by 8% in one week to 4,410 confirmed cases so far this year, nearly double last year’s count.
“Due to privacy laws and legal restrictions, NCHS [the National Center for Health Statistics] cannot identify a state or provide additional details about the third individual,” a spokesperson with the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) told the Guardian in response to questions about where the death took place.
The spokesperson did not respond to follow-up questions about which laws and restrictions prevented that information from being shared.
“I don’t buy it,” said Dorit Reiss, a professor of law at UC Law San Francisco. “Naming a state won’t be giving personal details, and they give the number of cases in each state,” she said, adding there was “nothing to prevent giving numbers of deaths in each”.
The CDC is not governed by Hipaa as health providers are. The agency is instead guided by the Federal Privacy Act, which usually prohibits disclosing government records about specific individuals, said Lindsay Wiley, professor of law and faculty director of the Health Law and Policy program at UCLA Law.
“But this general prohibition only applies to information that reveals an individual’s identity,” Wiley said. “It’s hard to see how identifying the state where a death occurred would allow the public to identify the patient.”
At the same time, it’s “not unheard of” for agencies to use an “overly broad, unwarranted interpretation of privacy protections to decline to share information that they prefer not to share anyway, because it may be seen as damaging to their reputation or agenda”, Wiley said.
The CDC switched in September to using NCHS rather than the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS), a system that usually reports deaths quickly and provides the state where a death occurs. The agency has not given a clear reason for the change.
When only a few deaths have occurred, NCHS usually does not say where those deaths are happening, which is one of the weaknesses in using it to report information like this.
“But it’s also in the news, so it already is likely identifiable,” said Debra Houry, former chief medical officer at the CDC. And the agency still has access to other reporting systems, like NNDSS, to know which state has deaths, Houry said.
Pennsylvania has strict privacy laws about not reporting demographic information or medical details, but “that still wouldn’t limit state and deaths”, she said.
Pennsylvania has now reported a total of six deaths, with the most recent case still under investigation by state officials. By carefully tracing the cause of death before reporting it on the state dashboard, officials in Pennsylvania are “doing the right thing”, Houry said.
The CDC dashboard only lists three deaths from measles this year, despite five confirmed deaths in Pennsylvania. The agency has not given a reason for the delay; usually, the NCHS system is updated within days of states sending information.
Reiss said it was “a change from past practice, and not a good one. [The] CDC is being less transparent than in the past.”
Not having a clear picture of what’s happening in each state, including a possible death from measles, makes it hard to understand risk levels, said Paul Offit, an infectious diseases physician at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “You’d like to know what the activity is in your state.”
Offit said he wondered if the secrecy was “coming from the top”, since officials such as Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary, or Erica Schwartz, CDC director, have reportedly given orders to decrease the measles death count.
It’s also not clear if the public is receiving accurate numbers of cases, Offit said. A 39-year-old woman in Franklin county, Pennsylvania, died of an acute cardiac event, a known but very rare complication of measles infection, Offit pointed out.
“When you see something like that, you’re looking at the tip of a much bigger iceberg,” he said. “Are you really monitoring how many adults are getting infected? I doubt it.”
It’s also harder to reach adults who may be at risk because they’re not vaccinated, because most vaccination requirements happen at the school level, Offit said. “What do you do for adults?”
The decision not to include all deaths from measles is “notable” and will likely have wide-ranging consequences, Offit said. The CDC has offered to send a support team to help Pennsylvania with the outbreak, but state and local officials may be wary of working alongside staff at an agency that is refusing to record accurate data, Offit said. “You wonder, ‘Can you trust them?’ It’s really that bad.”

title: Who needs sleep when you can scroll through home makeover videos instead
description: I’m not talking about frenetic whole-house renovations and stripping wallpaper but the slow, thoughtful design tweaks that are perfect for bedtime viewing, writes Bim Adewunmi
content:
I’m not talking about frenetic whole-house renovations and stripping wallpaper but the slow, thoughtful design tweaks that are perfect for bedtime viewing
I have been doing more than my fair share of revenge bedtime procrastination. Night-time is when I get to have complete silence, but nature abhors a vacuum, and my phone agrees. Right now, all I’m watching are home makeover videos. People – usually women – try to do something new with something old, throw together all their influences, and get their hands dirty to make it all come out splendidly. I’m struck by how quick makeovers are nowadays. The time pressure of the television show, Changing Rooms, was clearly manufactured by the producers; why else would you attempt to redecorate that much square footage in less than a week? But I get it: the tension is exciting, and it leaves room for regret, which is TV gold.
I am drawn more and more to the slower projects. People who take years to redo their entire house, and then walk me through each and every design decision. This is what our parents and grandparents did, no? The homes so many of us grew up in were not subject to annual refreshing – who had the time or will to strip all that wallpaper? Not my mum! And we were no poorer for it.
One of my faves is Medina Grillo . She and her family were long-term renters until they recently bought their own home, and I adore how she makes room for trial and error. Her design choices always charm me (I’ve copied her idea of turning dish racks into book and vinyl shelving), and she is so calm and chill.
I also follow Anna Stephens on TikTok. She has a series called “three tweaks per week”, in which she undertakes three little projects and slowly shifts the vibe of her home. It has been almost a year of the videos, and I’m not sick of them yet. It’s such a simple, no-pressure idea. An ideal bedtime scroll destination.

title: In reliably blue Minnesota, could Democrats do the unthinkable and lose a Senate seat?
description: Frustration with a sprawling fraud scandal has cut Peggy Flanagan’s poll lead – could ex-NFL reporter Michele Tafoya win a first statewide election for Republicans in 20 years?
content:
Frustration with a sprawling fraud scandal has cut Peggy Flanagan’s poll lead – could ex-NFL reporter Michele Tafoya win a first statewide election for Republicans in 20 years?
Our reporters answer your questions about ICE, immigration and the midterms
A s Democrats fight to regain control of the US Senate, hopes are rising in states – from Kansas to Texas – where they have not prevailed in decades. But in Minnesota, where Republicans have not won statewide election since 2006, the contest for an open Senate seat is closer than expected.
Should Peggy Flanagan – the state’s Democratic lieutenant governor – win the election, she will be the first Native American woman to serve in the US Senate. But history has not yet been made. The closely watched Cook Political Report shifted its rating on the race this week from “likely Democrat” to “lean Democrat”.
Flanagan has made hundreds of stops throughout Minnesota this year, first in a contested primary where she beat out a more moderate congresswoman, and now as she faces Republican challenger Michele Tafoya.
Tafoya, a more pragmatic choice for Minnesota Republicans than in previous US Senate elections, has sought to cast herself as a pro-choice Republican, though she has not spelled out what her stance is on access to abortion. She has also broken rank with the Trump administration on the Iran war after previously supporting it.
Unlike some Republicans who have sought Trump’s support, Tafoya didn’t rush to embrace the president’s recent endorsement. “I heard about that,” she said.
Most polls have shown Flanagan ahead – but not with a large lead, and lagging behind those built by Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic US senator now running for governor, in polls against her challenger, Minnesota house speaker Lisa Demuth. The most recent poll by the Minnesota Star Tribune earlier this month showed Flanagan up four points.
Flanagan’s central liability comes from her current job. As the lieutenant governor in Tim Walz’s administration, she is tied into a sprawling fraud problem in the state’s social services. Without an incumbent on the ballot for governor or US Senate , some voters may take out their frustration on Flanagan.
Walz decided not to seek a third term as governor, after initially saying he would, because of the fraud issue and the political response to it.
Republicans have not won a statewide race in Minnesota in 20 years. “There is a path. It’s not a wide path, but there is a path for Republicans,” said Blois Olson, an independent political analyst in Minnesota.
While Minnesota Democrats have dominated statewide races the past two decades, the state is not deeply blue: the state legislature is now split, with the house tied and Democrats controlling the senate. Some see Flanagan, a progressive who supports the proposed Medicare for All model of universal healthcare, as farther left than the statewide electorate.
“It sets up a race where Republicans are as optimistic as anything,” Olson said. “But until Republicans win statewide, you can’t think they’re going to win. It’s kind of like Democrats in Texas.”
Trump’s approval rating among Minnesotans is at a personal low . His surge of immigration agents into the state sits heavy on the minds of many, and features in campaign ads against Republicans. Two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – were killed by federal agents in Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge earlier this year.
Trump has continued to attack the state and its leaders, often rails against the state’s Somali population. In the only debate for Minnesota’s US Senate seat ahead of the general election, Tafoya wouldn’t say whether she would attend if Trump staged a rally in the state.
National Republicans have so far not swooped in to boost Tafoya – a signal that the race is not a top priority, or that their money is more needed to defend their seats in unexpected places, including Kansas .
Flanagan, at a union press conference earlier this month, said she always runs for office as though she’s 10 points behind, including when she ran unopposed for the state legislature, when she still knocked doors most nights. In the primary, she noted, polls showed a close race between her and Craig, but Flanagan won by nearly 20 percentage points.
“I’ve always been underestimated, and that’s OK. That just means I work a little bit harder,” she said. “And frankly, there are more people in the state of Minnesota who understand that they are being squeezed, and when the response to that pain from my opponent is to say that people should take one less trip to Starbucks and keep a stiff upper lip , that is a slap in the face to working people all across Minnesota.”
Tafoya did not respond to multiple requests for an interview.
S igns for Tafoya dot the yards of the Twin Cities suburbs. Olson, the analyst, said he heard from people who knock on doors to talk to voters that the conversations at people’s doors in swing districts after the primary changed.
“I have somebody to vote for, and it’s not Mike Lindell,” he said, explaining how some Republicans felt about the pillow salesman and election denier who lost the party’s gubernatorial primary. Lindell had been endorsed by Trump.
Voters are getting hit with ads on social media from Flanagan, too, who talks about the competitiveness of the race and offers up her wild rice hotdish recipe to anyone who donates to her campaign.
Tafoya, 61, made her career as a sports broadcaster, and worked for NBC as a sideline reporter covering the NFL. After she left that job, she became a political commentator. She has never run for, or held, elected office.
Flanagan, 47, has, by contrast, spent her career in politics – first as an organizer and then working her way up in elected offices, from school board to state legislature and then to lieutenant governorship.
Tina Smith, the Democrat who now holds the US Senate seat, decided not to seek re-election this year, saying she wanted to retire and spend time with her grandchildren. Smith endorsed Flanagan in the primary and has campaigned with her.
Tafoya, needing independent and centrist votes to win in a left-leaning state, calls herself a pro-choice conservative. In her prior public comments on abortion, she has said she supports bans on abortion after 12 or 15 weeks.
During the debate, hosted by Minnesota Public Radio last week, she could not explain what her position entailed. “Reasonable access is reasonable access,” she said.
Republicans in Minnesota need the anti-abortion community’s votes, as well as those of gun rights advocates and diehard Trump supporters, said Michael Brodkorb, a commentator and former deputy chair of the Republican party of Minnesota. Some, including a prominent pastor , have said they will not vote for Tafoya because of her approval of abortion to any degree. A write-in candidate is running for the seat in large part because she wanted voters to have an anti-abortion option on the ballot.
In her most recent ad, Tafoya says she’ll stand up to Trump if she needs to. “If she had delivered that message from the beginning, then it would be more credible,” Brodkorb said.
On fraud, Flanagan has said she believes fraud of any kind is unacceptable and supports harsher penalties and an independent inspector general. But, she has said throughout her campaign, Walz has said the buck stops with him on fraud.
One of the central questions for voters lies in someone who isn’t on the ballot: Trump, and whether the state’s next senator would provide a check on presidential power. Flanagan has said Tafoya would be a rubber stamp for the president, citing her opponent’s previous reluctance to publicly differ from Trump’s positions. Tafoya has said she would be an “equal-opportunity pain in the ass to any corrupt career politician”.
“You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who is a very respected person,” Trump said when he recently endorsed Tafoya. “It’s hard to win because they cheat on their elections too, you know, I thought I won Minnesota three times.”
Trump lost Minnesota three times. Minnesota has not voted for a Republican president since 1972.
As soon as Trump endorsed Tafoya, Flanagan put up a campaign ad highlighting the endorsement, his stamp of approval a likely negative for a swath of Minnesota voters.

title: Christiane Amanpour’s parting advice to journalists is right on the mark
description: The CNN star’s wise advice to ‘be truthful, not neutral’ should be tattooed on our souls
content:
The CNN star’s wise advice to ‘be truthful, not neutral’ should be tattooed on our souls
After decades as a renowned international journalist, the CNN star Christiane Amanpour is calling it a career, saying she’ll soon leave the cable network which she joined in 1983.
She will be missed for the courage in war zones and forthright presentation that have made her one of the most famous names in media.
Amanpour leaves behind not only the legacy of her extraordinary work, but also four words of advice that everyone in the news business should heed.
“Be truthful, not neutral,” she has urged many times, including again this week.
For what Amanpour is saying in those few words would vastly improve much of the media coverage we see today, as mainstream news organizations desperately try to gain the largest audience by not offending anyone, and by tiptoeing around the reality of today’s corrosive politics.
In so doing, they too often soft-pedal the truth.
They refer to politicians’ falsehoods not as lies but as “baseless claims”. They describe would-be authoritarian officials as “sidestepping norms” rather than attacking democracy. They “sane-wash” lunatic behavior and they present both sides of every controversy as roughly equal.
Amanpour certainly isn’t urging journalists to be activists. She isn’t urging them to drop the ideal of objectivity in which reporting and evidence, not ideology, prevails. She’s not suggesting they become partisans and echo the talking points of any political party or candidate.
She’s urging them to drop the false pretense of neutrality and to focus instead on getting to the heart of the matter – yes, the truth.
I don’t mean to make Amanpour out to be a saint. Like anyone who has been in the media world for decades, she has her detractors, those who think she has favored one side or another, and been unfair in her reporting.
But at a time when journalism – under great pressure from corporate ownership and the realities of a transformed business model – hasn’t consistently hewed to its core mission of informing the public honestly, her words are a lodestar.
The historian Garrett Graff wrote recently about the failures of the American press in the dangerous Trump era, especially as the important midterm congressional elections approach and as threats to democracy grow more dire.
“The media – which is under immense un-ordinary pressures of its own – continues to fail to convey just how un-ordinary these developments and shifts in our daily life” are, Graff wrote. “Too often, these stories are covered individually, but not as a pattern.”
In essence, then, the media is failing Amanpour’s directive to “be truthful”, because it is missing the big picture.
Was Amanpour’s decision to retire affected by the “un-ordinary pressures” in the media sphere?
She didn’t say so directly as she announced her decision, but her earlier comments about the coming changes at CNN suggest that there was some worry on her part that truth-telling might be threatened by corporate pressures.
It’s easy to see why that might be on her mind.
CNN’s parent company has just been acquired by a media behemoth, Skydance, headed by David Ellison, the son of one of the world’s richest people, Larry Ellison. The younger Ellison’s moves at CBS News – particularly the installation of the controversial opinion journalist Bari Weiss – have thrown the venerable broadcast network into turmoil. Prominent journalists including Scott Pelley and Anderson Cooper have left or been fired, and insiders have charged that network leadership has intruded on editorial independence.
This past spring, Amanpour noted, during a public appearance in London, that she was concerned about the “ideological realignment of CBS and the destruction, potentially, of 60 Minutes”, the network’s flagship news magazine program.
She leaves, however, on good terms with the CNN chief executive, Mark Thompson, who will remain at CNN for the time being, which is reassuring to the cable network’s staff.
Announcing her departure, Amanpour made a point of saying she’d be cheering on her longtime home and “its history of independent journalism”.
It’s hard to believe the uncertain future of CNN wasn’t at least some part of her calculation, although she’s certainly earned the ability to ease away from the tumult and demands of foreign reporting and commentary.
Will the younger and less-seasoned journalists who remain in the daily fray be able to heed her “be truthful, not neutral” words? Or will corporate and business pressures push them further toward the performative neutrality that undermines truth-telling?
With her stellar career and her pithy advice, Amanpour has set a high bar.
Let’s hope reporters and their bosses – not just at CNN but far beyond – can clear that bar, better than in the past. So much depends on it.
Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

title: John Anderson, five-time US country chart-topper, dies aged 71
description: Florida-born singer-songwriter had major hits with Swingin’, Seminole Wind and Straight Tequila Night
content:
Florida-born singer-songwriter had major hits with Swingin’, Seminole Wind and Straight Tequila Night
John Anderson, the traditionalist US country singer whose extensive body of work included five No 1 hits on the country charts, has died aged 71.
The news was announced on social media by his family, who said: “To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely and made every ordinary moment feel special.”
So woven into the culture of country music that he once worked as a roofer on the genre’s focal point, Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry, Anderson’s career spanned nearly 50 years and resulted in him being inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024.
Among those paying tribute to Anderson was country singer and friend Blake Shelton: “I am a very lucky man. I got the opportunity to find out that my hero wasn’t just the guy I hoped he’d be.” Shelton’s wife Gwen Stefani wrote: “We loved him!! His music is part of our family’s hearts for ever!!”
Born and raised in Florida in a music-loving family whose tastes spanned big band jazz to the Rolling Stones, Anderson headed to Nashville after graduating high school to try to make it in the city’s country music scene by playing live sets at night while doing manual labour during the day. “I’d fill up the truck with gravel and take the truck to wherever the order was and drop it off. A lot of odd jobs, but never lost sight of the fact that I really wanted to play,” he said in 2024.
Writing his own material as well as performing that of others, he released his debut single in 1975, but broke through two years later with I’ve Got a Feelin’ (Somebody’s Been Stealin’), and inched his way up the country charts with each subsequent release. He had his first country Top 5 single in 1981, I’m Just an Old Chunk of Coal (But I’m Gonna Be a Diamond Someday), which earned him his only Grammy nomination, for best male vocal country performance – and was a typical showcase of his wry, earnest and pure vocal tone.
It ushered in a number of years of commercial success, with the songs Wild and Blue, Black Sheep and Swingin’ all becoming country chart-toppers – the slick, hard-driving sound of the latter gave it crossover appeal and it became Anderson’s only hit on the US pop chart.
The latter half of the decade was a frustrating time for Anderson as he was dropped by his label Warner Bros and shuttled between others, before finding his groove again with 1992 album Seminole Wind, containing three Top 3 hits; the title track, an ode to his birth state of Florida, and Straight Tequila Night have endured as country radio staples and streaming successes. Follow-up Solid Ground was also a hit, containing the chart-topping Money in the Bank.
Anderson ended up recording 22 studio albums, most recently 2020’s Years, recorded with Dan Auerbach of blues-rockers the Black Keys. That was a proud and hard-fought return for Anderson, who faced illness with a non-cancerous tumour in 2017 that left him hospitalised. “I had been very, very ill,” he told Billboard in 2020. “I had almost 100% hearing loss … that really almost put an end to me. I just started praying and praying harder than I’ve ever prayed in my life and you know what? My hearing started coming back.”
Anderson continued to perform live thereafter, saying in 2024 that since his recovery, “I’ve really been enjoying every day. I live out in the woods and take a lot of lessons from my little wildlife friends. They pretty much live day to day, minute to minute. Enjoying that minute, enjoying this time. I’m very thankful to be able to go out and play any music at all.”

title: Harry Kane says wait to learn if he has won Ballon d’Or is stressful for family
description: Harry Kane would love to know now whether he has won the Ballon d’Or because the uncertainty and questions are driving his family to distraction
content:
Bayern Munich and England striker is odds-on favourite
‘I try not to think about it. Obviously it is hard not to’
Harry Kane would love to know now whether he has won the Ballon d’Or because the uncertainty and constant questions are driving his family to distraction. But the Bayern Munich and England striker accepts the ­suspense before the big reveal at the London Palladium on Monday night is part of the show.
Kane is the odds-on favourite to win the prestigious individual ­honour after a prolific run of form. The 33-year-old scored 61 goals for Bayern last season and 12 for England. This time out, he has 10 for Bayern and six for England.
He scored from the penalty spot in Wednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw against Arsenal at the Allianz Arena, although his standout moment was the inch-perfect through ball that set up Alphonso Davies to make it 1-1.
Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal is the second-favourite for the Ballon d’Or and Kylian Mbappé of Real Madrid is next in the betting.
“I think my wife would prefer to know and my family … it’s very stressful for everyone,” Kane said. “I can see why they don’t tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names, and there will be more people watching it if they don’t know so I can understand why.
“From my point of view, I’d love to know to just kind of see and not have to wait throughout the whole night. But it is their decision, I can’t control that. We’ll have to just enjoy it and try not to stress out too much.
“I try not to think about it. ­Obviously it is hard not to. There are always rumours and stuff flying around so you try to stay away from it.”
Kane’s fellow Bayern forward Luis Díaz will be out ⁠of action for the “foreseeable future” after suffering a minor muscle ⁠tear in his ⁠left ​hamstring during Wednesday’s game.
The 29-year-old Colombia international came on in the ⁠68th minute at the Allianz Arena but ​was forced off ‌in stoppage ‌time after suffering the injury.
Examinations carried out ‌by Bayern’s medical staff confirmed the hamstring tear, the club said in a statement. “The 29-year-old forward will therefore be sidelined for the time being,” Bayern said.

title: Welcome to the trap: swaggering Atlanta Dream turn WNBA finals into a hometown spectacle
description: Atlanta’s hip-hop royalty brought the star power as the Dream turned their long-awaited WNBA finals homecoming into a celebration of everything the city does best
content:
Atlanta’s wounded sports fans know better than to get carried away. But the Dream’s first WNBA finals game in 13 years showed this might finally be a team worth falling for
T he Atlanta Dream were exactly where they wanted to be on Wednesday night, comfortably ensconced inside their downtown arena for Game 3 of the WNBA finals against the Golden State Valkyries . Kerry Washington, Ludacris and Cam Newton led the courtside celebrity delegation. Quavo and TI headlined the half-time show, while two more hugely popular Atlanta rappers performed during other extended play stoppages – a mini-spectacle that speaks to the city’s deep bench of hip-hop talent.
But it was the crowd that really made State Farm Arena a house of horrors for Golden State. They didn’t just fill the 17,608-seat venue. They donned matching sky-blue T-shirts and waved rally towels. They sang along with their favorite emcees and lived and died with every point. They were so loud in the first quarter that I couldn’t hear the referee’s whistle from my 100-level press seat. They stayed to the end – well, two minutes from the buzzer anyway (gotta beat traffic) – and, with the 97-71 win sealed and DJ Khaled’s All I Do Is Win blasting through the arena speakers, serenaded the departing Valkyries with the unofficial Atlanta battle cry: “ATL hoe!”
Angel Reese never knew basketball could be like this. “When you can have at the end of the quarter a performance,” she gushed after a 21-point, 12-rebound effort. “And at the timeout, another performance. You smell the chicken, you smell the fish. It’s a blue-out in here. I didn’t even get to see Kerry. You don’t know who you gonna see in the A.”
