We’ve been leaving bowls on the counter for ages: this is only a problem now because we’ve moved to a new place, and I said I’d change my ways. But I think the issue is more about how James organises our home than hygiene. He doesn’t like to see a cup or bowl out of place; he’s much tidier than me. But this is only a bowl filled with water on the counter. It’s not a big deal, but he doesn’t like to see a bowl left out.
James is Juçara’s favourite, but she ignores me. I think that’s what love is: doing something for someone again and again even though it’s not reciprocated. James and I work in the same company, but I come home first and put the water out for the cat so he doesn’t see. I do the same in the morning at 7am, before James wakes up. I will always do this for Juçara and I will always defend her. If she needs me, I’m there. Names have been changed
While I support Tony’s pet care, cat hair in food areas is unpleasant. The home belongs to James too. Tony could try leaving the water on the floor longer, or commit to cleaning the kitchen counters more regularly. Serrena, 31
Tony saying “There’s few things as relaxing as the sound of a hydrating cat” makes me want to be on his side. But I can’t agree to kitties on counters. I’m a cat lover, but the idea of them pawing around food preparation or dining areas is a cardinal sin. Tony has to concede. Maddie, 28
Tony shouldn’t view himself as defending Juçara against James. They need to work as a team, and not have Tony sneaking about while James is asleep. Try properly with the water on the floor. Or if a raised location is important (it makes some cats feel safer), perhaps try a windowsill. Imogen, 19
Cats on worktops aren’t ideal, but Tony tries hard to strike a balance – keeping Juçara content and James happy. When clever Juçara asks for a drink (and Tony’s love, clearly), a countertop bowl is fine. But once she’s done, the bowl belongs on the floor. Sharing the dining table is downright unnecessary. Frank, 40
Tony, Juçara respects James because cats are fur-natical about hygiene. Give Juçara a chance to form some new habits, which takes at least a month. So put the water somewhere hygienic where she will not contaminate her loving owners with parasites! Maria, 49
In our online poll, tell us: should the cat be brought down to earth?
The poll closes on Wednesday 28 October at 9am GMT
We asked whether Abdeen should stop looking up menus before eating out with his wife.

title: Shola Ameobi: ‘I thought: how can I be most useful to Newcastle? Then the cog started turning’
description: From experiencing racism growing up in Newcastle to becoming a derby hero and now a member of the executive team, the former striker tells Sam Dalling about his remarkable journey
content:
From experiencing racism growing up in Newcastle to becoming a derby hero and now a member of the executive team, the former striker has been on a remarkable journey
“T here were times where I feared for my life as a kid, being harassed and chased by different groups of people,” Shola Ameobi says. “There were situations where I had to sprint to get away from groups of lads who didn’t like me because of what I looked like.”
Ameobi is recalling growing up in Newcastle during the late 1980s and 1990s, having moved from Nigeria aged six. There were lots of moments like that.
“It was almost as if I had to hide myself to be able to do what I love to do,” he says. “It wasn’t a very nice feeling, having to worry about getting from A to B. It was just part of my world. I had to be more aware of my surroundings and what I was doing.”
Ameobi’s “A” was often the family home, situated within a few pitch lengths of Newcastle’s St James’ Park, and “B” was frequently the club’s base at the time in Benwell, where he would head for academy training.
“It built incredible resilience in me,” he says. “That really helped me in a sporting context in my career, but also as a person, understanding that, irrespective of what people thought of me, what really mattered was the value I put on myself.”
That young boy running in fear became the scorer of 79 goals in 397 appearances for Newcastle including seven against their local rivals, Sunderland. The likelihood is that some of those he fled from while wearing a club tracksuit subsequently cheered him.
Since July, Ameobi has been Newcastle’s head of corporate affairs, after seven years as the loans coordinator. His role is to ensure “we’re doing things that are valuable not only to us as a football club but to the region”.
He adds: “We want to make this club the heartbeat of this city. But by being the heartbeat of the city, it’s making sure we integrate well into everything the city is about, whether that’s civically, whether that’s through our sport or through our community engagement.”
Ameobi’s job switch followed the 100-day review conducted by the CEO, David Hopkinson. At the end of a preliminary discussion, Hopkinson told Ameobi to take the weekend to consider things. But Ameobi, while grateful for the “level of trust and commitment”, pushed back, wanting to consider what the role would look like in practice. Six months and plentiful discussions later, he accepted.
For Ameobi, the leap to an executive position was not as huge as it might appear. He started his previous role in the Mike Ashley days and built that department “from nothing”, he says. “That’s really helped me understand how to business-plan and build a team.”
Ameobi has been part of the Premier League’s Black participants advisory group since it formed in 2019. Its successes include implementing the No Room for Racism action plan in 2021 – this weekend marks the second of two match rounds this month dedicated to the initiative – and the pilot launch of the player to executive pathways scheme in 2022. That is designed to help those from underrepresented groups into executive roles and Ameobi was part of the initial seven-strong cohort.
“It gave me a really good framework,” he says. “It took us through, at a very high level, what the different streams of executive work look like, whether that’s finance, brand, the future of working, how organisations work. That gave me a little bit of confidence, if I’m honest, more than anything, to go: ‘Actually, a lot of the things I’m already doing translate into that world.’
“One of the biggest things was working in a pressurised environment, which is what I’ve done for 20 years, and learning how that can really help you in those moments when things get a little squirrelly, when they aren’t going as planned.”
Completing the programme fuelled a fire in Ameobi that had flickered for two decades. In November 2006, having struggled with a hip injury for several years, he had career-saving surgery. The resulting time out was “the start of my thought process beyond the football pitch”. Whether he would return to playing at his previous level, or at all, was uncertain. So, Ameobi’s thoughts turned to: “How can I best be useful to my teammates and this football club? That’s when the cog started turning.
“Football wasn’t always going to be there so who am I outside of the footballer? There were some really hard questions I had to answer during a very, very difficult time. There were some dark moments.”
Ameobi navigated those moments with the help of a psychologist and by leaning on his family. “I’ve always been fascinated with leadership, right from an early age,” he says. “My father was a leader of a church and he’s been the biggest influence of my life when it comes to leadership and how to lead well.”
He cites the late Sir Bobby Robson, who gave him his professional debut aged 18, and Alan Pardew, who managed him at Newcastle and Crystal Palace, as footballing influences. The former “still to this day has such an impact on the way I think about the game, the way I think about the person more than what you’re doing”, while the latter “used me to channel my leadership within the dressing room and wider squad to help him deal with some of the issues we were going through”.
Ameobi holds a master’s in strategic leadership and it is obvious at an event to celebrate the supporters’ group The Black Geordie Club that he is a natural with people. There is a presence to him, a warmth, that puts others at ease.
He is unrelenting in wanting to use his position to improve society. He grew up watching Andy Cole at Newcastle and memories of Tino Asprilla’s 1997 Champions League hat-trick against Barcelona bring the broadest of smiles. “That was the moment where time stood still. It was almost like I said to myself: ‘What’s wrong with you, Shola? You should be giving everything to be there.’
“You need to feel like you belong, you need to see yourself there, and that is so important when it comes to inspiration and people who aspire to be great in whatever sphere.
“It’s so important those who are in those positions give back and share their experience and share what helped them get to where they’re at. Being a young Black kid who has walked the walk throughout the club, from youth team to first team and now into this executive role, I want to show anything’s possible for anybody.
“Part of the reason I want to continue to push myself is because, yes, I want to be successful, but I want to show that anything’s possible if you’ve got the hunger, irrespective of what you look like and where you come from. I want to be an inspiration to the next generation.”

title: Is this Prince Harry or David Brent in The Office? Either way, we’re watching a masterclass in awkwardness
description: The wayward prince and his wife seem to be aiming for a reboot – searching for purpose, but not self-awareness, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
content:
The wayward prince and his wife seem to be aiming for a reboot – searching for purpose, but not self-awareness
Y ears ago, I was in Washington DC when Prince Harry blew through on an official engagement. He was 28, with a full head of hair, a slightly louche gait and a public image that, on a tour of the Senate led by a baffled-looking John McCain , caused people to lose their minds.
Senate staffers stood five deep to get a glimpse; women materialised from every corner, more glamorously dressed for the office than usual. The excitement was so great that there were actual screams from behind the security line. I remember noting the prince’s prominent ears, the high colour in his cheeks and his habit, when addressed, of bowing his head, as if humbled by what he was hearing. Aw, I thought. Bless him.
But that was a long time ago. This week, Harry, now 42, appeared on camera in an interview in New York with GQ, playing to a very different audience. He looked older and schlubbier – don’t we all – the diffidence of youth replaced by something more pompous and belligerent, undergirded by what, in recent years, has appeared to be his bottomless well of hurt feelings. Harry was promoting something – a masterclass on “grief science”, which he has undertaken with Dr Mary-Frances O’Connor. But the question of why on earth he would double down on previous US media appearances, none of them successful, sat alongside the bigger royal question of the season: namely, what are he and his wife, Meghan, going to do ?
Since the pair arrived back in the UK this summer after a six-year absence, watching them try to settle on a role has been a veritable festival of awkwardness, not least because it’s not entirely obvious where they have left to go . In March, Netflix ended its partnership with Meghan’s lifestyle brand, As Ever, less than a year after it replaced the pair’s $100m mega-contract with a first-look deal. These well-publicised failures were compounded by the previous death of Meghan’s podcast , the couple’s parting with Spotify and what might politely be called their low productivity metric when it comes to anything not immediately related to the royal family.
In this, the Sussexes are no different to any other creators endlessly raking over their own lives for content. The difference, of course, is that Harry, with a lofty mindset inculcated from birth and which is presumably incredibly hard to shake, presents his every gesture as automatically belonging to that higher calling, public service. “I don’t do it for myself,” he says in the interview in New York when explaining the venture with MasterClass. (Side note: the real masterclass here is in watching the GQ hack trying to use Harry’s grief project as a Trojan horse for questions about the royal family, among them: “Do you grieve that?” in relation to Harry’s fallout with King Charles, and a sleight of hand reference to “anticipatory grief” in a reach to get his father’s health on the table. Honestly, I tip my hat).
“Trying to make an impact in the world, that is genuinely what energises me,” says Harry, sinuously pivoting away from the awkward questions. And if he stuck to harmless banalities about grief and, oh God, what he calls his mission as a storyteller, one might be inclined to say good luck to him. Harder to stomach is what appears to be his and his wife’s need for the public to participate in their grandiose delusions.
Witness the Sussexes in Nottingham last week , going on a walkabout under the auspices of a charity event that, to me, looked more like an exercise in self-gratification. As the king had already sternly warned the pair : they’re private citizens, now, with no officially sanctioned public engagements, and yet here they were, working a crowd like any active-duty royals. While Meghan smiled excessively with her “hello, little people!” act, her husband alternated between mild engagement with the well-wishers and sending category-five death stares to the hacks, poor sods, who’d turned up to cover this non-event. It was embarrassing, and awkward, and as someone pointed out on the internet, like watching David Brent return to the office after being fired.
And so, while the top line from the interview in New York focused on Harry’s indirect call for reconciliation with his family , it was another takeaway that struck me more forcefully. More than once, the prince talked about the importance of knowing yourself, adding that he had “put in the work” and clearly positioning himself as more evolved than his father and brother. I would suggest Harry’s journey of self-awareness has a way to go yet.

title: Proms, parties and gender politics: amazing photos from American dancefloors – and what they tell us about a changing nation
description: From George Balanchine to the Rockettes, the US magazine regularly ran lavish photo spreads dedicated to dance, with the myriad ways people moved their bodies holding up a mirror to the changing times
content:
From George Balanchine to the Rockettes, the US magazine regularly ran lavish photo spreads dedicated to dance, with the myriad ways people moved their bodies holding up a mirror to the shifting times
L ife magazine launched in 1936. Its aim: to show the US the world, in pictures. At a time when television was still an experimental medium, a golden age of photojournalism brought the outside world into people’s homes. Life ran weekly until 1972, spanning a transformative time in US culture. Photographers were dispatched across the globe, covering wars, political manoeuvres, social trends, hemlines and Hollywood. And in December 1936, the magazine dedicated its cover feature to dance, with dancers from the new School of American Ballet gracing the front page. As such a vividly visual medium, dance would become a regular feature in Life’s pages across the years. When I was asked to write the text for a new book featuring a collection of dance-themed images from the Life archive, it was a kid-in-a-candy-shop situation. For a dance fan there were some absolute gems to be found: the great George Balanchine crafting his ballet The Seven Deadly Sins – and cooking dinner in his Manhattan apartment; Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev taking New York in a piece headlined The Hottest Little Team in Show Biz; or an ageing Agnes de Mille going full-throttle in rehearsal.
But the archive told a much bigger story than that. It was fascinating to see the reflection of society through the way people danced: in ballrooms, nightclubs, proms and parties. In the array of social dancers: from the waltz and tango to the lindy hop, mambo, twist and the frug, themes of the 20th century play out. You can see a story of growing individualism in the shift from structured couple dancing to going freeform on the dancefloor – gender politics, too, as it was out with “May I have this dance?” and in with the democracy of the disco. Life columnist Albert Goldman asked: “Has there ever been a decade for dance like the 60s?” as he wrote of a power shift from the stage to the dancefloor, from the professional performer to the “inventive amateur”. There’s the birth of the teenager, too, bringing an explosion of pop culture and spreading dance trends on TV shows such as American Bandstand.
The archive also tells a story of the US’s shifting relationship with race, showing dancers in segregated bars and newly desegregated schools. But more than that, we see the way music and dance styles from Black communities and from Latin America were adopted, appropriated and absorbed into the US mainstream, whether tap, jazz, Charleston or cha-cha-cha.
Dance even had something to say about cold war politics and paranoia. For a series comparing American and Soviet education systems, which found the US lagging worryingly behind, Life took photos of Moscow students in a dance class to demonstrate their iron-clad discipline, compared with easygoing American schools. The magazine captured visiting folk dancers from the USSR, as well as reporting on Khrushchev denouncing the dancing in a Hollywood film, and by extension, casting judgment on western culture.
So much of life can be observed through dance, in the ways people choose to move their bodies and how they display themselves, how they relate to each other, celebrate and communicate. There’s a real treasure trove of images to explore.
LIFE. Let’s Dance is published by Taschen.
On the set of Can-Can, 1959 (main image) The sheer raucous joy in this picture of Shirley MacLaine and Juliet Prowse leaps off the page, captured on the set of movie musical Can-Can, the story of a Belle Époque Paris cabaret whose dancers are arrested for public indecency. It was a stance approved of by Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev, who was visiting the 20th Century Fox studios during filming and pronounced the dance routines depraved.
Willa Mae Ricker and Leon James, 1943 Ricker and James were members of Whitey’s Lindy Hoppers, one of the finest, and most awesomely acrobatic, dance troupes of the 1940s. The lindy hop originated among Black dancers in the clubs of Harlem (it was named after pilot Charles Lindbergh’s “hop” over the Atlantic in 1927) but by 1943, Life was calling the lindy hop “America’s national dance”.
The Rockettes, 1958 Modelled on high-kicking British group the Tiller Girls, all-American precision dance troupe the Rockettes took things up a notch with their machine-tooled synchrony. Launched in 1925, they’re still going strong today, proving the enduring allure of the showgirl (Taylor Swift can’t be wrong), and have even trademarked their signature dance technique.
Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev in La Bayedère 1965 It is hard to imagine now that two ballet dancers could be as famous as Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev were in the 1960s. Rudimania peaked on the Royal Ballet’s 1965 tour to the US, when mounted police were stationed outside New York’s Metropolitan Opera House to save Nureyev from being mobbed.
School prom, 1967 Teens dancing at the annual prom at Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. Ten years earlier, after the supreme court had ruled against segregation in public education, Arkansas’ governor called up the National Guard to stop nine Black students enrolling at the same school. Life’s journalist at the prom reported that “the school sees itself as desegregated rather than integrated”.
Michael Caine on the dancefloor, 1966 Such a keen dancer he was once known as Disco Mike, here’s Michael Caine at an LA club. Decades later he gave a tutorial on doing the twist on Jonathan Ross’s chatshow, a dance craze that had swept the world, meriting a seven-page feature in Life in 1961. From hipsters to socialites to suburban grandmas, everyone was caught up in “pulsating, gyrating, hip-swinging mania”, it reported.

title: Female Life on Planet Earth by Laleh Khadivi review – a mother’s secret past in the Iranian revolution
description: A woman living in California discovers her mother may have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic revolution, in an intriguing novel of inheritance and identity
content:
A woman living in California discovers her mother may have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic revolution, in an intriguing novel of inheritance and identity
“I t’s a little scary, isn’t it, inheritance?” That’s what Heti, the protagonist of Laleh Khadivi’s latest novel, remarks to a “soccer mom” as they watch their daughters play. “We don’t get to choose what we inherit. Or what we pass on.” Heti, who lives in Los Angeles, is Iranian-American and works for an accountancy firm. She has two daughters, Ava and Zora, and her mother has recently died. When Ava scores a goal, the soccer mom asks, “Did she get that from you?”, but Heti is less interested in the skills that parents pass to their children than the secrets they keep from them.
Khadivi’s novel is about mothers and the mysteries they contain. In Female Life on Planet Earth she asks what happens when the people closest to us turn out to be strangers. How do we manage our grief and memorialise our loss when those we love have hidden awful parts of their lives? At the beginning of the book, Heti receives strict instructions from an Iranian aunt about the correct way to mark her mother’s passing. “One year after the death you throw a party,” she is told, “so that [people] can think about your mother, really remember and mourn her.” But then Heti receives a startling set of photographs from an unknown sender. In one image, a younger version of her mother stands veiled in black, a machine gun slung over her shoulder. In a second image, the weapon is extended towards a group of handcuffed women, “their miniskirts uneven on their hips, rips in their tight sweaters”, some crying before the camera, another lying prone, “face pressed into the concrete floor”.
Could her mother have been a merciless enforcer of the Islamic Revolution in Iran? Khadivi doesn’t pose the question so bluntly. Instead, she allows the impact of the images to reverberate for Heti. The pictures with the gun are disturbing, but it is the “shock of affinity” that startles her most of all. “Even though I’m terrified by these pictures, I understand her urge to have control … For the tiniest second I was weirdly reassured that my mother wasn’t all manners and sweetness and that maybe we had more in common than I thought.”
Later, she visits her local library and reads about all-female militias, women who in “their newfound zeal … found the punishment of their sisters, the task assigned them by the revolutionaries, to be a satisfying outlet of power”. It’s a grimly fascinating history, but Khadivi is less interested in raking over the political complexities than in attending to the dissonance it stirs in Heti. She allows Heti to puzzle through her uncertain feelings in a novel that fluctuates in tone, serious and sardonic, analytical and droll by turns.
The drollery is partly an effect of the book’s structure – a series of vignettes dotted over the course of a year in which Heti wrestles with big issues in incongruous places. On the soccer pitch, she is bemused by the mom who complains, “You can’t believe all that Barbie feminist crap.” At the wholesale supermarket, with its “maze of open freezers filled with thirty pound turkeys”, she wonders if she is remembering her mother “as she really was or as I want her to be”. Doing the accounts on the set of a soft porn film, she decides that what “happens in these shoots is a kind of freedom … Where I came from, where my mother and I were born, a woman’s pleasure can destroy her.”
Standing in contrast to the comic parts of Heti’s suburban life is Khadivi’s more cosmic sensibility – suggested by the book’s title. Chapters are named for planets or taken from terms in physics, but the shift between the domestic and the metaphysical can make reading an uneven experience. Khadivi can be grandiose: “At night, Heti’s soul ranged and she followed. Without direction or orientation her thoughts spread into undefined time and limitless space.” At other times, the cosmos is an effective analogy: the “emotional gravity” of Heti’s experience pulls her “into a freefall” that feels like grasping at Jupiter’s vaporous atmosphere. In such circumstances, as Heti tells her daughters, “either you fall and fall or you figure out how to fly …”
When Zora later expresses her determination to act on the climate crisis, she tells her mother that “it’s going to be our job to do the extreme things, like take hostages, or destroy oil tankers, or stop eating meat just to get people to care. I’m ready to do any of those.” Khadivi positions Zora’s radicalism as an intriguing mirror to that of her grandmother, quietly challenging any easy assumptions a reader might have about the rights of one and the wrongs of another. If mothers can conceal their lives from their daughters, Khadivi is right to point to how daughters can carry forward, resist or remake the legacies they inherit. As Heti comes to understand in this intriguing and unusual novel, perhaps the more important question may be not what we inherit, but what we choose to become.

title: ‘I wanted to create the female version of a man’s suit’: how Roland Mouret’s Galaxy dress took over the world
description: One the most famous dresses of this century, it was worn by royalty and A-list celebrities in the noughties. Its latest fans are Maga women. Here, the designer, and former mentor to Victoria Beckham, reveals the story behind it
content:
One the most famous dresses of this century, it was worn by royalty and A-list celebrities in the noughties. Its latest fans are Maga women. Here, the designer, and former mentor to Victoria Beckham, reveals the story behind it
T he story of one of the most photographed and ripped-off dresses of the last 50 years came together with a simple zip. It was 1998; the designer Roland Mouret had shown his first collection at London fashion week and was looking for a way to produce good clothes at speed. He connected with a small British atelier and it was there that some old-school industry wisdom would alter his course: he learned that a longer seam doesn’t actually cost any more than a shorter one.
Despite his brilliantly instinctive approach to design, it was like cracking a code – and steered him towards the dress that would make his name. “My brain was buzzing!” he says. “I hadn’t thought about it before – if you extend a top by 50cm, it becomes a whole outfit. You just need accessories. Focusing on dresses gives you a signature piece at the right price.”
The hyper-bodycon Galaxy dress, with its industrial zip on the back, was born, embedding itself in the public consciousness via the backs of Beyoncé, Halle Berry and Victoria Beckham . Creating a singular silhouette, it helped Mouret define the look of the late 90s and early 2000s in London as much as John Galliano or Alexander McQueen did a few years before him.
“I really earned my two lines in the fashion bible,” says Mouret, whose new autobiography, I Am Roland Mouret – The Butcher’s Boy Who Dressed the World, documents the era. “It had what we call in French ‘the lunch neckline’, with the sharpness of a table, and a waistline cinched in like that of an iconic 1950s actress, but comfortable and not too girlie. It had masculinity.”
While Elizabeth Hurley culturally owned that Versace safety pin dress after wearing it on the red carpet in 1994, leaving its second life solely to museums, the Galaxy reappeared in Mouret’s collections “in the colour and fabric of the season” for years – and continued to be seen on a who’s who of Hollywood, from Scarlett Johansson to Naomi Watts.
“I always saw the people I was dressing from the back,” he says now over a video call from his home in London. “I wanted to position myself behind them so I could see their point of view. The zip was part of that – it was at the back of the dress. As soon as you see a face, your imagination stops and the real person is there.” It was a way of designing clothes that he would later impart as a mentor to Victoria Beckham; the Galaxy’s silhouette could be seen in her early collections.
In the book, which is a candid and moving account of his life in rural France, Paris and London, Mouret writes about sexual exploration as a teenager. It would become part of the R&D for the Galaxy: “I had sex with women but knew I wasn’t straight,” he says. “It was a collaboration. I wasn’t trying to prove my masculinity, it was just an amazing experience, discovering a body in a carnal way. The dress was about equality. I wanted to create the female version of a man’s suit.” One of the celebrities who wore it, Dita Von Teese, who Mouret describes as “an athlete”, epitomised the woman who suited it best after a period of size zero ubiquity.
The way the Galaxy fastened was practical, but also part of the pleasure of wearing it. It was literally sensational. “It was lined in power mesh fabric,” says Mouret, “and when you unzip it at the back, whether yourself or with your partner, the flesh jumps out – it’s a rollercoaster of carnal experience, an explosion of emotion.”
But while Mouret describes the zip as about “strength and choice”, some notable women chose to wear it minus the hardware. Catherine, Princess of Wales, had one made without it because, when faced with paparazzi, it was a weak spot. Ditto the female president on House of Cards, Claire Underwood. The actor Robin Wright, who played her, explained to Mouret that his usual gold zip needed to go. In the book she explains: “I love it as a woman but as a woman in charge, a female president … that part of me has to be invisible.”
Perversely, some of Mouret’s Galaxy energy is now evident on podiums in Trump’s America. While the Galaxy is no longer being made new, similar sheath dresses by the Mouret label are still finding their way on to women including Ivanka, Melania and Lara Trump. And that bodycon silhouette, favoured by so many in the Trump administration , which has always been severe, now connotes a Trumpian aesthetic and style of politics, accented with extreme eyelashes, ironed hair and injectables.
Does Mouret know why the look has been co-opted? “Fashion is just a reflection of the sociopolitics of its time,” he says. What “[Maga women] wear is extreme now. The clothes are so tight, and heels so high, that you couldn’t run from anything to protect yourself. The future is fear, and the look is decadent.”
The past was a better-looking place, according to the memoir, which documents the optimism and subsequent collapse of possibilities in fashion for independent designers. But the book is a full stop on fashion as Mouret knew and lived it – it doesn’t define him today. He is no longer at the helm of his brand: after Covid depth-charged his niche of eveningwear and event dressing, the label went into administration in 2021 and then changed hands. Mouret now describes himself as a queer artist, and a lot of his imagery still harks back to being the rural butcher’s son who wanted to explore bodies regardless of gender.
Clothes are still made with Mouret’s name sewn into them, but they are not his. It’s unlikely lightning will be caught in a bottle again. As he says in the book: “The Galaxy proved to me that my signature was not my name, but my technique.”
In 2015, 10 years after the dress first appeared, customers could buy one for £1,750 new. Now you can get one on resale sites for not much more than £200. Its time has passed, but it has also passed into fashion history, along with Mouret’s journey. It was autobiographical. As he writes in the book: “It was a dress born out of my collective consciousness; it was my mum getting dressed in the morning, it was my dad’s precision with meat, fat and bone.” It was the product of his biggest inspirations, Azzedine Alaïa and Yohji Yamamoto, filtered through his psyche. “Making it,” he writes, “was like the moment you find yourself speaking another language without thinking.”

title: Some enchanted evenings: 10 of the best after-dark adventures for families in the UK
description: The clocks go back this weekend, so embrace the longer nights with these family-friendly activities and events, from a stargazing festival to moonlit crazy golf
content:
The clocks go back this weekend, so embrace the longer nights with these family-friendly activities and events, from a stargazing festival to moonlit crazy golf
Legend has it that Faskally Forest – the Pitlochry location of Scotland’s most famous sound and light show – steals an hour from time itself every 25 years. This year marks a quarter of a century since the first Enchanted Forest, and the theme taps into the legend: Stop the Clock: The 25th Hour. The trail is a mystical, atmospheric wander through jewel-hued woodland, with misbehaving clocks, time-themed installations and immersive soundscapes creating the sense of a dreamlike world. There are autism-friendly sessions and free carers’ tickets and an accessibility bus for those with mobility issues. Until 8 Nov , adults from £28.50 , kids from £15.50 , family from £78.50 , including shuttle bus to and from the event
Even a beginner stargazer will find it easy to navigate an autumn night sky, when the stars are at their clearest and constellations such as Orion’s Belt and the Plough flicker and gleam with an iridescent glow. The North Pennines has some of the darkest skies in the country, along with the highest number of official Dark Skies discovery sites in the UK – 16 – making the region’s stargazing festival one of the best. Choose from a family astronomy event at Grassholme Observatory (pictured), a dark skies stroll or stargazing on Alston Moor . All events need to be booked in advance. Until 1 Nov , prices vary
The banks of the Mersey and some of Liverpool’s most iconic spots blaze with colour during this annual free outdoor light art festival, which brings together 13 original works on the theme of “together”. Installations include 6-metre high peonies at the Cunard Building, which remain white by day but glow with ever-changing colours after dark, and Dream Herd, a floating cloud of sheep with interactive “legs” that trigger lighting and sound changes when touched. Over on Williamson Square, Pop! consists of five tall, colourful boxes that spring open like jack-in-the-boxes when people clap, sing or talk to them, revealing inflatable puppets. The installations will light up from 5pm–9pm each night, with quiet hours 4pm-5pm on 28 Oct and 1 Nov. 23 Oct – 1 Nov , free
From badger banquets to batwatching safaris, many wildlife trusts and nature reserves run special late openings and events at this time of year to allow visitors to enjoy the nocturnal activities of their resident species. At RSPB Frampton Marsh in Lincolnshire you can look out for hunting owls, marsh harriers and starling murmurations on a sunset walk (fortnightly on Saturdays, adults £19, adult members £15.50, children £10), while RSPB Mersehead in Dumfries and Galloway will be running its popular badger banquets , where visitors can observe the shy mammals feeding through the glass windows of the reserve’s Sulwath Centre (24 & 30 Oct, 6, 14 & 20 Nov, adults £28, adult RSPB members £22.60, children £14.50). The Kent Wildlife Trust is hosting a family bat detecting event at Sevenoaks Wildlife Reserve (29 Oct, £10pp) which includes hot drinks in the visitor centre and a guided night hike with bat detectors. Search for more events on the RSPB’s Dusk Discoveries page
Nature gets super-sized at this refreshingly un-Halloween-themed lantern trail at Slimbridge wetland centre, where giant frogs loom out of illuminated ponds, bats and kingfishers hover and swoop in the tree canopy and luminous giant bugs glitter between flaming scarlet fungi. Each creature is handmade and inspired by real wetland wildlife, with wings, fur and scales transformed into light sculptures. Arrive early to fuel up on street food at the Kingfisher Kitchen, or save yourself for toasted marshmallows around the firepit. Kids can make their own lanterns and the buggy-friendly trail takes about 45 minutes to explore. Until 1 Nov , £14.95pp
The original (and some would say best) location for autumn illuminations, Blackpool is celebrating 10 years of the Lightpool festival, with interactive installations, illuminated artworks and live performances across the city. The Light Art Trail includes walk-through tunnels of light, glowing stone circles and glittering “sky orchards”. A specially designed VR arena at the Winter Gardens conjures spectacular visuals, while the Firefly Field uses LEDs to creates the illusion of hundreds of beetles hovering and darting above the ground. Until 31 Oct , 6pm-9pm , free
As if scrambling across rope bridges and whizzing down from treetops isn’t challenging enough in daylight, every autumn more than 20 of the Go Ape high ropes courses open up for an evening adventure. This year, for the first time, there are adults-only sessions at selected locations , but the continuous belay harness system means the course is reassuringly safe for families and suitable for all children over six. The course is illuminated and takes about an hour to complete. Until 8 Nov, but dates vary according to location, from £31.95pp . Min height 1.2m; max weight 130kg
Polish up your putting with a spot of moonlit golf at Heatherton World of Activities near Tenby, where the 18-hole Pirates of the Caribbean-themed course will take on a distinctly different feel, with atmospheric lighting and music. It’s just one of the After Dark offerings, along with climbing the Tree Tops tower before stepping off into the pitch black and whizzing down the 165-metre zipline, with the park illuminated below. For older kids, the Heatherton maze has been transformed into the full-on Institute of Terror – a not-so-abandoned asylum with live scare actors. Until 31 Oct , prices vary according to activity
This immersive rail adventure at the Bluebell Railway whisks passengers into the past to unravel a 100-year-old mystery of an engine explosion, a derailed train and a possible injustice as to who got the blame. The station platforms are peopled with characters from that fateful day in 1926, while clues about the real perpetrator wait to be discovered, and the air is thick with rumours of ghostly figures on empty platforms and the sound of a steam train that never appears. Spooky rather than properly scary, this is ideal for older children, with plenty of chances to interact with characters and explore independently. Until 1 Nov , adults from £42, children from £21
Get ready for a Jurassic Park-style adventure with an after-hours visit to the World of Dinosaurs, where 40 life-size, animatronic dinos roam and roar; all the more terrifying when they loom out of the darkness. The woodland trail winds past a pair of towering T rexes, stegosaurus and the startling, dome-headed pachycephalosaurus, with velociraptors springing out and flying reptiles swinging through the trees. Alongside the trail, UV-lit Halloween drummers provide a thrilling soundtrack, with face painting, a silent disco and glitter tattoos also on offer. 23 Oct–1 Nov , £18 .99pp

title: Man charged after allegedly making threats at Hannah Beazley’s electorate office while armed with nunchucks
description: Perth man charged with ‘being armed in a way that may cause fear’ – days after Helen Haines was allegedly attacked with 4WD outside her Victorian office
content:
Perth man charged with ‘being armed in a way that may cause fear’ – days after Helen Haines was allegedly attacked with 4WD outside her Victorian office
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
A man has been charged after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the Western Australian local government minister, Hannah Beazley.
The Perth incident came days after the federal independent MP Helen Haines was hospitalised with severe injuries following an alleged attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta in Victoria on Monday.
Electoral staff at Beazley’s Victoria Park office called police after a man caused a disturbance on Wednesday afternoon.
Police said they received reports the man was making verbal threats while in possession of an “improvised martial arts weapon” described as “nunchucks”.
They arrested the 56-year-old man nearby and took him into custody. On Thursday he was charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear, making unlawful threats and cannabis possession. Nobody was injured in the incident.
The man was refused bail to appear at Perth magistrates court on Thursday.
Beazley was not in the office at the time but told reporters on Wednesday evening her staff were “rattled” by the “confronting situation”.
“He was [allegedly] being very threatening. He did want access to me, I believe, but we don’t know his motivations at all,” the minister said.
Beazley said there had been two staff members in the office at the time. The man allegedly attempted to lean through the security screen but her staff were a safe distance away, she said.
“It’s not the first time I’ve had threats made against me.
“My primary concern is the welfare of my staff, obviously. That was very rattling for them. They called the police.”
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Hannah Beazley was a friend “because I’m a good friend of her dad”, the former Labor defence minister Kim Beazley.
“This is far too prevalent,” Albanese told Perth radio on Thursday. “It’s not who we are as Australians. We can have our discussions and debates and settle those issues at the ballot box.”
The governor general, Sam Mostyn, speaking generally on Thursday, discussed the gendered dynamics of threats and abuse directed at women in high-profile positions.
“Like any woman who has stepped up into any position across any part of our society, there is a unique and pernicious form of attack that comes our way,” Mostyn told ABC TV.
“I still receive that online. In fact, I was just saddened this morning to see some of the comments on my own Instagram page, in capitals with expletives, once again questioning the very nature of what it is that I do.
“Women across the country know that there are certain things that are reserved for women … that go to our gender and they are often vicious and just despicable.”
A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.
Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.
McGowan had spent time with Haines’s staff and she told Guardian Australia they were “all crying together because of the emotion that’s been building up”.
“The people here tonight don’t want violence … but that’s not to say when violence happens in their communities they know what to do about it,” McGowan said.
“There’s a lot of violence in our communities, there’s a lot of violence online … there’s nothing new about this.
“What the attack on Helen has brought to our mind is, this is us. We can’t just pretend that everything’s OK in the regions and we’re doing fine.”
Haines’s chief of staff, Kaz Rourke, said on Thursday that the team was “devastated” by Monday’s alleged attack.
“Helen is adored by her team. She is a remarkable leader, a truly wonderful boss and someone we all care about deeply,” Rourke said in a statement.
“Most of us were in the office when the incident occurred and some of us were involved in Helen’s immediate care, so this has been deeply traumatic for the team.
“We are receiving a great deal of support and my priority right now is making sure Helen’s staff are as OK as they can be. I’m so very proud of them and know Helen would be too.”
Rourke said Haines’s staff were planning to reopen the electorate office “later next week”.

title: Thursday briefing: The crisis putting maternity units in England at risk of closure
description: In today’s newsletter: rising rates of C-sections, staff shortages and years of unresolved concerns are preventing some hospitals from delivering babies safely
content:
In today’s newsletter: rising rates of C-sections, staff shortages and years of unresolved concerns are preventing some hospitals from delivering babies safely
Good morning. Over the summer, doctors in the emergency department at the North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple, one of the most remote in the UK, received a crash course on delivering a baby. Their training covered subjects nobody wants to hear about when they’re imminently expecting: shoulder dystocia, postpartum haemorrhage, and neonatal collapse. “I’m hoping that we won’t see such emergencies,” one doctor said. “It’s been an intense time.”
That crash course was necessary because maternity services at the hospital have been indefinitely suspended due to staff shortages. Other remote hospitals across the country are expected to do the same, as NHS trusts struggle to recruit enough staff to safely deliver babies. Earlier this week, the Guardian reported that up to 20 maternity units in England could shut. The story sheds light on a maternity care crisis that has been rumbling on for years, and shows how childbirth has changed dramatically over the last decade.
The Guardian’s health policy editor, Denis Campbell, has been reporting on this story, and has covered nearly every major maternity scandal in the health service’s recent history. In today’s newsletter, he reveals the alarming stakes involved in this one. First, here are the headlines.
Oil | Miatta Fahnbulleh is leaning towards rejecting the giant Rosebank oilfield, the Guardian understands , in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners.
Reform UK | Farage’s party has been fined more than £2,000 for failing to declare it was the publisher of campaign material seen by voters – including an additional penalty for failing to pay on time.
Defence | Britain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability of Royal Navy submarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said.
Technology | Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web.
Israel | The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.
Matthew Hopkins, NHS Alliance’s lead director of acute care, recently suggested to Denis that up to 20 of the UK’s 155 NHS maternity units could be at risk of closure. Two units, the one in Barnstaple and another in Yeovil, Somerset, have already suspended maternity services because of staffing shortages, while a hospital in Newry, Northern Ireland, plans to permanently shut down its maternity services.
One reason for these potential closures is that people are having fewer children. The Royal Free hospital in North London recently announced that it was permanently closing its maternity unit because the number of women having babies locally has fallen by almost 30% in the last seven years (four of the area’s primary schools have shuttered during the same period). But the main concern for many units at smaller hospitals in rural and coastal areas is staffing. These are often areas without alternative provision nearby.
At the same time, childbirth has changed. More women than ever are now getting C-sections or having births that require medical intervention from doctors, and smaller maternity units are also grappling with a widespread lack of obstetricians. “If you don’t have enough doctors, you can’t run a service safely, so more and more smaller hospitals are considering losing their maternity units altogether,” Denis says.
The rapid growth of caesareans, both planned and emergency, appears to be one of the primary reasons that some smaller hospitals are considering suspending maternity services. The proportion of births performed by caesarean increased from 31% in 2019 to 45% in 2024 , and last year was the first time in England that more babies were born via c-section than “natural” births (a term that many women find pretty grating because it implies there’s a hierarchy between births with medical intervention and those without).
“England’s rate of caesareans is unusually high compared to similar European countries, and all of the experts I speak with think this is just going to keep going up and up,” Denis says. This dramatic rise in caesareans has several causes , including changes in clinical practice designed to reduce the risk to babies and (quite rightly) give women more choice over how they give birth, as well as an increase in pregnancies among women who are over the age of 35 (the average age of parents in England and Wales has been increasing steadily for the last 50 years).
But this isn’t the whole story. Some women are also worried about the type of care they might receive during vaginal births. Successive reviews portray a state of crisis, with burnt-out and exhausted midwives, a growing risk of serious injuries, and women of colour experiencing persistent racism and discrimination. A national review of maternity services in England from 2022 to 2024 by the Care Quality Commission warned that serious harm in maternity care risked becoming the norm.
“There’s real concern among maternity doctors that women are reading endlessly negative headlines about the poor quality of NHS maternity care, which is leading them to ask for C-sections,” Denis says.
As the rate of caesareans increases, trainee midwives are struggling to gain the experience of dealing with more complex births, potentially creating a cycle in which more women end up having caesareans. “Rather than building huge obstetric units and planning for a far higher caesarean rate, which is where we’re currently heading, the NHS should be investing in community-based and continuous midwifery care, alongside excellent obstetric care for women who need it,” Debbie Garrod, a midwife and antenatal educator, tells me.
How is the fear of medical negligence claims affecting childbirth?
Another reason for this rising rate of caesareans is something known as “defensive practice”. This is when doctors, nurses and midwives make decisions to avoid blame or complaints, rather than because those decisions are necessarily in a patient’s best interests.
The cost of settling all outstanding maternity-related claims in England was estimated at £37.5bn last year, nearly two-thirds of the NHS’s total £60bn clinical negligence liabilities bill. It’s a figure that senior MPs have described as “jaw-dropping”. In fact, the bill for maternity negligence claims in England since 2019 could be more than the health service’s budget for newborns during the same period.
“If a baby ends up suffering a catastrophic injury because it was deprived of oxygen for a few minutes during birth, that can cost the NHS £20-30m,” Denis says. “Doctors are so aware of these risks, and of being pilloried with scandals and inquiries, that they often try to take a no-risk approach to childbirth.”
There have been four inquiries into maternity scandals in England since 2015, one national maternity review led by Valerie Amos, and a further two inquiries led by Donna Ockenden, which are now ongoing. Denis estimates these have made no fewer than 700 recommendations for improving maternity services. “Experience shows that many of these have gathered dust on a shelf, and by almost every metric, maternity care has got worse, not better,” he says.
By all accounts, this shouldn’t be happening. The number of births has decreased significantly since the first of these inquiries was published in 2015, while the number of staff in maternity units has increased. So why is maternity care getting worse? “That’s the big question,” Denis says. “You could give about 65 different answers.” So I pressed him on the most important ones.
Childbirth, he says, has become more complicated, as the NHS has attempted to reduce its risks through measures such as early inductions and increased monitoring. As the population has become less healthy, more women also now have underlying health issues such as diabetes and obesity. Meanwhile, women from poorer backgrounds, and Black and Asian women, continue to experience the worst maternal outcomes, as the Amos review demonstrated .
The government’s maternity and neonatal taskforce is expected to publish an action plan before Christmas, building on the recommendations from the Amos review. “There is great scepticism among maternity doctors about this plan, given how little has changed after previous reviews,” Denis says. “I think it’s going to need the best luck in the world to address this sense of fear and failure.”

‘Disgraceful’: Jackdaw gasfield approval condemned
Climate campaigners have condemned the UK government’s decision to allow the drilling of the Jackdaw gasfield. Critics argue the move will put climate targets at risk, while failing to reduce energy bills and the cost of living crisis. But there could be a significant victory for green activists when it comes to the much larger Rosebank oilfield, with the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, leaning towards rejecting approval. A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Finally, Lake Windermere might be clean again. After years of being pumped with sewage, a creative solution to remove sewage from England’s largest lake has been agreed by campaigners, the Environment Agency and a local water company. title: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
description: Accommodation platform acts after long-standing guest complaints over doing dishes, taking out rubbish and stripping beds
content:
Accommodation platform acts after long-standing guest complaints over doing dishes, taking out rubbish and stripping beds
Airbnb hosts will no longer be able to ask guests to strip beds or wash dishes under the accommodation platform’s new rules.
The changes, which apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform’s global policy, will come into effect on 20 November and limit chores imposed on guests.
Airbnb had long fielded complaints from guests about having to pay cleaning fees, which can be hundreds of dollars, and still complete a list of chores for their host.
Since April 2025, cleaning fees have not been shown to guests. Instead, hosts have been allowed to choose to factor cleaning costs into the total price of the stay.
In a community policy update posted on its website this week, Airbnb said hosts would “generally” no longer be allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
Examples of such tasks include stripping beds of linen, taking rubbish offsite, and washing and putting away dishes, the company said.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules which must be displayed in full at the time of booking – and can also add other “reasonable” requests.
Examples of house rules include check in and check out times, limits on how many guests can stay at the property, smoking restrictions, quiet hours, and whether or not pets are allowed.
Reasonable requests depend on “relevant local considerations”. For example, it may be reasonable to ask guests to limit shower time due to local water restrictions, or to dispose of rubbish in an animal-proof container.
While guests shouldn’t be asked to wash and put away dishes under the new guidelines, hosts can ask them to put used dishes in the sink.
“House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage,” an Airbnb spokesperson said.
“So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”
