title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for chicken with citrus and oregano
description: This dish has been handed down through generations of Roman restaurateurs
content:
This dish of chicken in a lipsmacking citrus and oregano sauce has been handed down through many generations of Roman restaurateurs
I f you look through the window of Piatto Romano between 10am and midday, there will almost certainly be two, maybe three people at the round table trimming vegetables: chicory, artichokes, poppy greens, amaranth. After midday, the crates and trimmings will have been cleared away and the table will now be home to trays of bright-green boiled vegetables and, maybe, baked salt cod. By 12.30pm, everything will have been moved into the small kitchen in time for service, which starts at 12.45pm.
When I first moved to Rome in 2005, Via Bodoni 62 was home to a restaurant called Da Rafaelle, which had white plastic chairs (inside as well) and served traditional Roman food with plenty of offal. We went to Da Rafaelle a few times before it closed in 2009. But, mostly, we went to La Torricella, which is on the other side of Testaccio and serves mainly fish. The owner is Augusto D’Alfonsi and, during lunch one day, he mentioned that he was taking over via Bodoni 62, and that his daughter Francesca would run it. They’d serve traditional Roman food with plenty of offal and it would be called Piatto Romano. This was 2011. My son was born later that year and my memories are not unpleasantly foggy; of the vegetable trolley in the corner, of chicken with red peppers and of Francesca and her father negotiating strongly. I also remember Francesca’s brother, Andrea, starting to be around more, before he eventually took over in late 2013.
Andrea grew up riding his bike along the pavement in front of La Torricella, which his parents had opened in 1973, a few years before he was born. If his lunch didn’t come out of the kitchen at La Torricella, it probably came out of the kitchen at Da Antonio on Via dei Pastini, where Andrea’s maternal grandma cooked, or from the kitchen of his maternal grandfather’s restaurant, Da Giovanni on Via dei Barbieri. As a teenager, Andrea also ate at his paternal grandfather’s osteria, Gran Sasso in Trastevere, and in the various branches of Insalata Ricca , a chain of salad restaurants opened by his entrepreneurial uncle Gino in the 1980s. All the various parts of the family have Abruzzese roots, but Andrea mentions Gino, eccentric and single-minded about history, vegetables and nutrition, as being a particular influence.
The way Andrea continues to evolve Piatto Romano (which for many is the embodiment of an ideal Roman trattoria) would require several columns. For now, though, I will note his singlemindedness about the vegetables he picks up every day from his various sources. The other night, we had courgette greens – a little hairy and very succulent – with Leprino rabbit (typical of the Tuscia area of Viterbo) braised in wine and citrus, which produces a lipsmacking sauce/gravy. And head chef Umberto Mussato, who has worked with Andrea since 2021, has adapted his recipe for this column, but using chicken instead of rabbit. The dish is made even more tasty by the addition of three to five anchovy fillets mashed with a tablespoon of red-wine vinegar, plus a sprig of fresh thyme or oregano, which is then left to sit for at least half an hour before it’s served with greens and potatoes, if you wish.
1.2kg skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (or a mix of legs and thighs) Salt 4 tbsp olive oil 100-150ml dry white wine 1 tsp dried thyme or oregano 400ml fresh citrus juice – a mix of orange, lemon, grapefruit, mandarin 3-5 anchovies mashed with 1 tbsp good-quality red-wine vinegar A few stalks fresh oregano
Season the chicken with salt, rubbing it into the skin. Working in a heavy-based pan, warm the olive oil, then brown the chicken pieces in batches so as not to overcrowd the pan. Once all the pieces are brown, look at the amount of fat in the pan – I suggest leaving it all in there, but remove some, if you prefer.
Return all the browned chicken to the pan, raise the heat and add the wine, which should sizzle and evaporate. Add the dried oregano or thyme, stir, then pour over the citrus juice. Lower the heat so the pan simmers, then cover.
Leave the chicken to cook for 45 minutes to an hour, lifting the lid to turn the pieces every now and then, then lift off the lid and cook for another 20 minutes, so the sauce can reduce. By the end of the cooking, the chicken should be tender and the sauce thick. (If the sauce needs significant reduction, remove the chicken, simmer hard so the sauce reduces to your liking, then return the chicken pieces to the pan.)
To finish, stir in the anchovies mashed in vinegar and a sprig of fresh thyme or oregano, then leave to sit for 30 minutes before serving.

title: How autumnal high pressure brings on the dark doldrums
description: With no wind to disperse the low cloud, mist and fog and less sunlight to burn it off, anticyclonic gloom can set in
content:
With no wind to disperse the low cloud, mist and fog and less sunlight to burn it off, anticyclonic gloom can set in
In summer, a high-pressure system over the UK usually means fine weather. But in the colder months it can result in anticyclonic gloom, characterised by grey skies, mist, fog and drizzle.
A settled high-pressure system brings stable conditions and impedes the usual vertical movement of air. This is a recipe for sunshine when humidity is low, but can act like a lid, trapping atmospheric moisture near the surface.
The moisture condenses as low stratus or stratocumulus clouds, and sometimes as fog or mist. Wind normally disperses these and in summer the sun is strong enough to burn them off. But there is little wind when high pressure dominates, and in winter the shorter duration and low angle of the sunlight make it less effective.
The weather may be mild and even warm during anticyclonic gloom, but dull conditions persist day after day, with frequent drizzle and occasional mist or fog.
In northern Europe in the renewable energy sector, this situation is called Dunkelflaute , German for “dark doldrums” because it brings a reduction in both solar and wind power. Spells of such weather pose challenges for the smooth transition to renewable energy, highlighting the need for pumped storage or other backup energy sources until the high pressure moves on and the weather changes.

title: Strongmen like Trump would destroy the planet out of pure spite – and Brazil shows we’re all in peril
description: If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poor, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
content:
If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, Brazil’s ecosystems will face collapse. The ruling class would rather burn the world than share it with the poor
H owever grim the trajectory might seem, I’ve always believed that sense will ultimately prevail. As the great perils of dismantling the living world become increasingly obvious, even the most rapacious exploiters must come round. Nobody wants to live on a dead planet, do they?
There are – or were – signs that this wasn’t just wishful thinking. Since 2015, mostly thanks to China, the area of the planet being reforested has increased , while thanks in large part to Brazil, the global rate of forest destruction has declined. The area of the Brazilian Amazon forest cleared each year is one-sixth of what it was when records began in 1988. In the past four years, as a result of Brazilian government policy, the deforestation rate has fallen by 71% . If Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is re-elected president on Sunday, the country could reach zero deforestation by 2030. The arc of the moral universe seems to have bent towards justice.
But what my faith in human nature failed to account for was a perverse delight in destruction among a small cohort of the economic elite. There are people who appear to hate life and love death. Donald Trump’s removal of protections on public lands , the small bite – doubtless the first of many – he wants to take out of Yosemite , his assaults on the US National Park Service and the US Forest Service , his trashing of the Endangered Species Act : all are partly a response to lobbying by ranchers, loggers, frackers and miners. But this, I think, is not the primary driver.
More important to him, I’ve come to believe, is a vengeful desire to hurt. I doubt Trump hates the monarch butterfly. I’d be surprised if he knows what it is. But he does appear to hate people who love the monarch butterfly. Destroying the habitats on which this and many other endangered species in the US depend seems to be part of the “retribution” he promised. The New York Times was unable to find evidence that Trump has ever visited a national park. He probably doesn’t hate them either. But seemingly anything valued by the enemy – greens, liberals, socialists, feminists, anti-racists, “bureaucrats” and “blockers” – should be attacked on principle.
Wiping ecosystems off the map is an obvious demonstration of power. Extinction leaves a permanent mark, which is every dictator’s dream. It’s also a highly effective means of hurting those who resist him: the Indigenous people and other people of colour so often on the receiving end of environmental destruction; the regulators; the scientists and the rest of the intelligentsia; above all, people who care .
Caring could be seen as the far right’s meta-target. The “suicidal empathy” theme now crops up repeatedly in videos, newspaper columns and speeches: a professed belief that those who care about other people or species should be destroyed by those who don’t. This belief, by definition, is psychopathic. What exhausts my optimism is that, conned by shallow promises such as the use of brutal methods to address crime, people keep electing those who subscribe to it.
Physically and politically, Flávio Bolsonaro is the spitting image of his father, the jailed coup-plotter , Jair. When Jair Bolsonaro was president of Brazil, he appeared to see ecological destruction as a kind of a holy duty. The deforestation rate rose by 59% in his four years, and attacks on Indigenous people and other forest defenders, as well as invasions by illegal ranchers, loggers and goldminers rocketed. The crudest forms of extractivism – regardless of their costs, or how they might hold back all kinds of progress – were a matter of policy.
The ideology of the far right in Brazil has been described as “ beef, Bible and bullets ”: violence against those who resist the seizure of their resources, an ultra-conservative evangelism and the expansion of cattle ranching, which is both a potent symbol of far-right machismo and the primary driver of deforestation in the Amazon.
Jair Bolsonaro looked back with nostalgia to the military dictatorship of 1964 to 1985 – which was actively supported by the US government – during which local oligarchs could do as they pleased, and those who opposed them were tortured and disappeared . The warnings couldn’t be clearer, but Brazil seems determined to revisit its nightmares. Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October, and is likely to become president.
If he wins the second round this week, the gleeful rampage of his supporters, catalysed by government policy , threatens not only the Amazon but the Atlantic forest in the south, the Pantanal wetlands, the Pampa grasslands and the savannah habitats of the Cerrado. This is politics as an orgy of destruction. Let’s eradicate our life support systems – that’ll teach the liberals!
Trump has been using all possible means to help Bolsonaro win . He gives the impression of seeing Latin America as the conquistadores did – one big heap of treasure, ready for looting. The region’s far-right demagogues are only too happy to help. Mass deforestation and the sudden ecosystem collapse that is likely to result offers a finality to their politics: there’s no coming back from this. You Indigenous people, you greens, you carers: you’ll have nowhere left to hide. The world will be ours, even if it is a world of ashes.
What might Bolsonarismo teach us? First, it appears there is no limit to the perversity of the ruling class, which would rather there was nothing left to share than cede any fraction of the planet to the poor.
Second, that it possesses all the tools – social and traditional media, the pulpit and the gun – required to make its perversity look like common sense, or at least irresistible, as force is deployed. Third, that the only defence we have against suicidal gullibility is what the Brazilians call conscientizaçao : raising awareness about the relations between exploiters and exploited, and the violence that underpins them. Otherwise all that is good, trusting and hopeful in humanity can be harnessed for a war against everyone and everything.
As for the idea that nobody wants to live on a dead planet, Elon Musk, with his preposterous plans for living on Mars – “Fuck Earth! Who cares about Earth?” – has killed that too. Extending the frontier of destruction, even to the point of human extinction, comes across as a matter of pride. The four horsemen ride again, not in cloaks but in stetsons and denim shirts, driving their cattle before them.

title: Wanted: new No 10 adviser to help citizens deal with rise of AI
description: Andy Burnham advertises for policy experts in technology, economic growth and cost-of-living challenges
content:
Andy Burnham advertises for policy experts in technology, economic growth and cost-of-living challenges
Andy Burnham is to recruit a number of advisers to plug gaps in No 10, including an expert on how AI will affect society.
The roles advertised by Downing Street give a glimpse into the biggest challenges facing the prime minister – and what he has decided to prioritise.
The new hires will flesh out the threadbare No 10 policy unit – where many of the roles are still vacant after Keir Starmer’s departure. Senior sources have said the prime minister wanted to take time to recruit advisers.
The adviser on AI, who will be expected to have “deep expertise” in the sector, will be expected to lead preparations for the impact of the AI boom on the workforce, amid significant concerns for lower-level professional services jobs, in particular for new graduates.
They will also be expected to be the main adviser to Burnham on frontier AI, the effects and benefits of AI in public service transformation and other major societal impacts.
Several cabinet ministers have openly expressed concerns about the UK’s readiness for the impact of AI on the workforce and economy, as well as the dangers of unregulated systems.
In his Labour conference speech on 28 September, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , said there were “daunting” dangers of AI, saying they could not allow technological advances “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.
Burnham will also hire an adviser to develop policy on greater public control over everyday essentials – with a roving brief across transport, energy, housing, water and the environment.
The adviser will be asked to focus on the cost of living. The job advert specifically demands an individual who can “bring challenge and external perspectives into policy development”.
Burnham is known to be frustrated with the cautious and limited options presented to him by Whitehall on areas where he is seeking greater public control.
The Guardian reported on Tuesday that Burnham had told officials to rip up their plans on how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical choices for what to do with the stricken company, including options that could cost more taxpayer money or carry higher legal risk.
Burnham will also recruit an economic adviser to replace Starmer’s aide, Minouche Shafik. The job, which will examine growth and macroeconomic policy, requires “a strong understanding of the economic, fiscal and political context shaping government decision-making”.
Before he became prime minister, Burnham took advice from Andy Haldane, a former Bank of England chief economist, as well as from Richard Hughes, a former chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, and Jim O’Neill, a cross-bench peer and former Treasury minister.
However, none have agreed to take roles in No 10. Haldane and O’Neill have been critical of Burnham’s economic approach since he entered government, particularly on increased public spending and a lack of growth-oriented policies.
Other roles will include a new adviser on Scotland, an adviser on work and welfare who will report to the new growth director, as well as another post working across immigration, security and justice, looking at cross-border crime, exploitation and illegal migration.

title: ‘This isn’t greenwashing’: thousands of butterflies surprise experts on restored West Sussex farmland
description: Rare small blues and dingy skippers among species found on former wheatfields two years after start of transformation under commercial nature project
content:
Rare small blues and dingy skippers among species found on former wheatfields two years after start of transformation under commercial nature project
An “amazing” abundance of 5,290 butterflies, including rare small blues and dingy skippers, has appeared on land that was barren wheatfields just two years ago.
The speed with which nature has bounced back at Halnaker Hill farm in West Sussex has surprised experts after 133 hectares (330 acres) of intensively farmed land were turned into a commercial nature restoration project.
The farm’s relatively unproductive soils on the South Downs were cropped for wheat for 40 years, but after a final harvest in 2024 the arable land was sown with a special wildflower mix. Seven kilometres of hedgerows have been planted, seven hectares (17 acres) of new woodland created, three ponds dug and 54 hectares (133 acres) of herbal leys seeded, with carefully controlled mob-grazing on existing chalk grassland to improve its wildlife and biodiversity.
Halnaker Hill Natural Capital is a commercial nature restoration project that derives its income from selling biodiversity net gain (BNG) credits, which enable houses to be built in the wider region. Under BNG rules, developers are legally obliged to deliver an increase in nature on new housing estates or by buying credits for nature restoration elsewhere.
The independent ecologist Neil Hulme, who has advised Halnaker Hill on nature restoration and surveyed for butterflies, said he found “clouds of butterflies” on the former wheatfields last summer.
“The speed has amazed me, from a sterile landscape to one brimming with butterflies,” he said. “Despite being tiny, the small blue is very good at sniffing out its foodplant, kidney vetch. I knew it would come, but what I didn’t expect was it to come so soon and multiply so soon.
“Some people are a little bit unsure about BNG and the idea of monetising nature, but projects like this are showing so clearly how BNG can deliver nature by the bucketload. This isn’t greenwashing; this is the real deal.”
As well as seeing a profusion of skylarks, corn buntings, hobbies and dragonflies on the site, Hulme recorded 85 small blue butterflies and seven dingy skippers, which have never previously been recorded on the fields.
Surveys also found 547 small heath butterflies, and scores of common blues and green hairstreaks, alongside eight sulphur pearl moths, a highly localised species restricted to coastal areas of southern Britain and usually observed in ones and twos.
Halnaker Hill farm, which is delivering more than 850 units of BNG, forms part of the South Downs national park authority’s “ ReNature ” programme, which is tackling biodiversity loss and adaptation to global heating in the region. More than 7,700 hectares (19,027 acres) of land is being transformed into natural havens.
Nick Heasman, the head of natural capital for the South Downs national park, said: “It’s been wonderful to work with the team at Halnaker Hill to bring about real, positive change, demonstrating that BNG can make a big difference for nature, and this survey proves that. Just two years ago this was largely an arable landscape – showing how quickly nature can bounce back, given space, time and love.”
According to Hulme, it is relatively simple for any land manager to boost nature on chalk, simply by scraping off nutrient-rich top-soil and sowing specialist chalk grassland wildflower mixes if the site is not near any existing chalk grassland.
Next year he is planning to reintroduce the rare Duke of Burgundy butterfly to the site, with wild pansies also being sown to attract the Queen of Spain fritillary, a once-rare migrant that is increasingly common visitor to southern Britain.
“Projects like this fill me with optimism,” said Hulme. “If we can achieve this in just two years, the sky is the limit.”

title: Country diary: From Mexico’s Day of the Dead to a Shropshire allotment
description: The Marches, Shropshire: Symbolically a flower of the ancestor-honouring Mexican festival, the dahlia appeals to the British gardener’s appetite for the spectacular
content:
The Marches, Shropshire : Symbolically a flower of the ancestor-honouring Mexican festival, the dahlia appeals to the British gardener’s appetite for the spectacular
G ardeners are a deviant lot. Despite our passion for wildlife gardening and the drive to be sustained by, and share, our own fruit and veg, our appetite for novelty, aberrancy and even the spectacularly monstrous is insatiable.
Take a look at this. The flower is the size of a plate and the brightest orange, like Mark Rothko’s painting No. 210/No. 211 (Orange) , with a kind of vibrating stillness, maybe the colour of a sugar maple in autumn sunlight. The ray florets are a mass of long, pointed, half‑curled petals, wildly dancing, writhing away from the central boss of golden disc florets.
This exotic vision is a dahlia . We bought a bag of dahlia tubers from the supermarket and planted them in the allotment back in May. We lost the label and, anyway, they grew into three different varieties together, so we’d be none the wiser. One was a small white-tinged pink pompom that flowered in the heatwave, another was a larger white-orange-yellow ball and now this, a semi-cactus in audacious orange.
These flower shapes are part of a dahlia culture that has flourished since their introduction from Mexico in the 18th century. The semi-cactus type originated from a single tuber of Dahlia juarezii sent to Holland in 1872. Since then, hybridisation from all forms of dahlia seeds has resulted in 50,000 varieties.
Although the dahlia’s position in gardening fashions waxes and wanes, dahlias are respectable again, but they have long been an allotment favourite as a cut-flower crop or grown competitively for shows. Our allotment neighbour has rows of gorgeous blooms and immaculate veg in the vernacular tradition.
The stories dahlias have travelled with add to their exoticism. Their symbolic role as the flower of Día de los Muertos ( Day of the Dead ) has made them the national flower of Mexico, and the festival’s link to Halloween is a potent folklore connection. Even so, the marigold is more historically correct as the primary flower of los Muertos.
Much of what we read about dahlia history from the Aztec and Inca periods is myth, curated by European imperialists. Nevertheless, just like tomatoes, also from Mexico , funky and transgressive dahlias now have a special place in the traditions of British allotments and in our deviant little hearts.
Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: 18 again: I returned to my life in 1983 – to reckless adventures, in a world soaked in alcohol
description: Sundays were deadly, the generation gap between parents and their kids was enormous, and a pint cost 50p. The frisson of casual violence was everywhere. When I left school and set off to travel, I had no sense at all of where I was going or what I would find
content:
Sundays were deadly, the generation gap between parents and their kids was enormous, and a pint cost 50p. The frisson of casual violence was everywhere. When I left school and set off to travel, I had no sense at all of where I was going or what I would find
I am wandering down a steep and unfamiliar street in Saint Peter Port, Guernsey, a force seven gale blowing in my face, when I look up to cross the road and see a back garden running up the hillside opposite. It ends in a granite rock face about 30ft high, and in that moment, I have a vivid flashback to being sat on top of it, watching a group of people in the garden below. I can’t conjure their faces, but the memory is all too real: the sun on my face, a woman calling up: “Don’t break your neck!” I can tell she’s not worried and neither am I. Nobody is. It’s a party and we’re young and we’re drunk and we’re carefree, without a worry in the world. Or at least, that’s how I remember it.
I continue down the street, spooked by the power of the recollection, how it has ambushed me. I stand outside the house. I could swear I’ve never seen it before. Did I come to the party over the cliff? Should I knock on the door? Hi, this is going to sound weird but I was in your back garden about 42 years ago and I haven’t a clue why but I’ve just remembered it like it was yesterday …
There are no lights on, no car outside. I carry on down to the coast, where huge waves crash against the sea wall.
“A single person’s memory, uncorroborated and unsubstantiated by other evidence, is a feeble guide to the past,” the novelist, Julian Barnes, wrote in the Guardian last year. I am in Guernsey because it’s where I lived when I turned 18, even though I spent most of that year working and travelling abroad. I’m trying to recapture what my life was like then and it’s a good place to start. In Back to the Future, Michael J Fox’s Marty McFly gets in a DeLorean time machine. I have flown in an ATR 72-600 turboprop, and it is only my second time on the island in 35 years.
O n 26 May 1983, a 7.8 magnitude earthquake in the Sea of Japan triggered a tsunami that devastated Honshu. Across the Pacific, the US conducted a nuclear test in Nevada, while Candy Girl by New Edition topped the UK charts. Manchester United beat Brighton & Hove Albion 4-0 in the replay of the FA Cup final (a painful fact to write as a Liverpool fan and now Brighton resident) and Star Wars: Episode VI – Return of the Jedi was bossing it at the box office. It was also my 18th birthday. Two weeks later, on 9 June, the Tories had a landslide general election victory that cemented Thatcherism for the next decade, a far more unpleasant detail to recall than the football result.
I don’t remember any of that – a quick internet search has filled me in. But it can’t tell me what I did that day. A Thursday in the middle of my A-levels, I would have probably been revising in my bedroom (although I remember spending more time doing keepy-uppies in the garden, struggling to focus), eager for the exams to be over, to leave school and home and go travelling. Top of the Pops was on that evening but it was no longer the weekly ritual of my earlier teens. Apparently the Police performed Every Breath You Take, today the most-streamed track of the 80s. I didn’t like it back then. The month before, Bowie’s Let’s Dance had been No 1 for three weeks. I loved Bowie and bought the album, but was disappointed: it was too polished, too commercial, a new direction for him I disapproved of, all tan and white teeth, a sign of much of the 80s to come.
When I was 11, my family moved from Wirral (or the metropolitan county of Merseyside, which it became part of in 1974) to Guernsey. My dad worked for the Midland Bank on Dale Street in Liverpool and was being transferred. Five days before I was due to start secondary school in Birkenhead, we drove south and caught a ferry. I’d never been on one before, never been abroad (neither had my parents). I told my mates I was going to live on the equivalent of a Caribbean island. It was the heatwave of 1976; the sun had clearly gone to my head. That first winter in Guernsey it seemed to rain incessantly and as a family we struggled to adapt to a very different way of life in a rented bungalow. My sister, Sue, who was two years older than me, never adjusted. When she was 16, three years after our move, she went back to Birkenhead to finish her education, living with the family of a friend of hers, only returning to the island for holidays. Which meant that from the age of 14, I was essentially an only child.
I had a troubled relationship with my parents, as did my sister; it was a big reason she left. The generation gap was huge. My parents had no experience of being a teenager. Born in the 1930s, they grew up in north Wales before youth culture. My father had a motorbike, but he wasn’t a biker. He couldn’t understand why I had to question and challenge everything. Because I did. I struggled with authority and I saw him as compliant. We were chalk and cheese. Even my being left-handed, which he jokingly called “cack-handed” when I laid the table with the fork on the right, was further evidence of our difference. A friend said once: “Everything we did was a way of saying to them: ‘I don’t want to be like you.’” Their politics, their clothes, their music, the TV they watched and the jobs they did (my mother was a housewife) were anathema. Such rejection must have been difficult, but perhaps not that unusual. Late 70s punk shocked not only my parents’ generation but its own. Rebellion was in the air. Another friend, who had a similarly difficult relationship with his conservative father around the same time, puts it: “He didn’t have the tools to deal with me.”
There was also the growing disparity in our educations. My parents left school at 16 but their ambition was for me to go to university (about 7% of 18-year-olds in the UK went to university in 1983, compared with 40.6% in 2025, despite there being grants and not crippling loans). English was my favourite subject (I was a big reader) and two books I studied for A-level helped broaden my horizons: As I Lay Dying by William Faulkner introduced me to stream of consciousness and more experimental writing, while Strait is the Gate by Andre Gide for my French A-level got me reading Sartre, Cocteau, Camus and Kafka – and opened the door to a morally ambiguous and transgressive world that I embraced for its essential absurdity. This was perhaps not the education my parents had in mind.
B efore going to Guernsey, I arrange to meet my old friends Paul, Jay and Steve, who still live there. In the pub, as we chat about the past, I am initially struck – and a little alarmed – by how much more they remember than I do: people, pubs and clubs, parties and incidents. I tell myself it’s because they still live there, the constant reminders, but I also wonder if it is more about what we choose to remember.
Over dinner, we talk about how we understood the world in 1983 and what shaped us, with no internet and only four TV channels. Apart from our peers, we agree that NME and other magazines such as the Face were hugely influential, along with the John Peel show and Radio Caroline. I first started reading NME when I was 14 from cover to cover (the classified ads were as fascinating as the editorial). A review or interview might mention an older band or influence, and at the record shop (No.19 in Saint Peter Port, today a White Stuff), you’d search through the racks for them. Did the Teardrop Explodes and Echo and the Bunnymen trigger an interest in the Doors and 60s psychedelia, acid and Carlos Castaneda, the beats and counter culture?
You often had to take a punt on a record, parting with your hard-earned cash (I had a job as a milkman on a Sunday and in the holidays throughout my school years). Did I buy Thermonuclear Sweat by Defunkt in 1983, a band I’d never heard of, because I picked it up in No.19, drawn to the title, and saw a Joseph Bowie in the lineup and I was a Bowie fan? Its punk-jazz threw me, but I grew to love it, learned that Joseph was the brother of Lester Bowie, co-founder of The Art Ensemble of Chicago, my hardcore introduction to jazz. In that random way, one thing could lead to another, so slow compared with today, when we have a world of knowledge at our fingertips.
The early 80s were tribal: punk, mod, skin, rude boy, new romantic, indie: you dressed like the bands you listened to (on Saturday afternoons, we would go to jumble sales and find clothes to customise). The music you bought spoke volumes. Talking to my own three children, Connor, 27, Ella, 23 and Jake, 21, I get the impression that they didn’t listen to music with the same prejudices when they were 18. Fleetwood Mac, Genesis, Led Zeppelin and all those 70s “rock dinosaurs” would never have darkened my turntable (or increasingly, my cassette player; although I still have a lot of my records, not a single cassette has survived, all those cherished mixtapes, often painstakingly recorded off the radio, gone).
I remember being interested in the news, what was happening in the world (it was easy to feel cut off on an island). I read the Guernsey Evening Press (I liked the crime pages) and the Times, which my parents got, every day. They listened to BBC Radio 2 at breakfast, Terry Wogan to start the day, and watched The Nine O’Clock News in the evening. The news events that I remember were acid rain destroying the forests of northern Europe, high unemployment of 11.5% in the UK (though in Guernsey the rate was negligible), the Soviet Union invasion of Afghanistan and the tensions of the cold war growing with Reagan in the White House. There had been the Falklands war in 1982, a 74-day conflict that saved Thatcher’s premiership but seemed a world away. (The landlady of Taylor’s Long Bar in Saint Peter Port didn’t like serving groups of young men, but made an exception for servicemen. My friends and I happily told her we were back from the Falklands and she served us underage.)
The biggest threat was nuclear Armageddon. In September 1983, only the quick thinking of a Soviet officer averted catastrophe, when he interpreted a reported US nuclear strike as a false alarm and didn’t push the button – the closest the world has come to nuclear war since the Cuban missile crisis.
We all knew the name of Greenham Common, but I didn’t fully understand what was happening there. We would laugh about the advice of hiding under a table, in the case of a nuclear attack. Yeah, right.
Alcohol played a massive part in my life when I was 18, as it had done throughout my teens. It was easy to get served underage, so turning 18 wasn’t a landmark moment in terms of legally buying a drink (no one carried ID). Alcohol and tobacco were cheap on Guernsey: we all drank and smoked. You could go out with a fiver and have a night of it at about 50p a pint, the same for a packet of cigarettes. (It’s no longer cheap there, more or less the same as the UK.) During my visit, I pop into a pub at lunchtime that we used to frequent. It has seen better days. There is one customer, a woman at the bar having a large glass of wine. While I am chatting to the barperson about why I am on the island, the woman turns and says: “Love, all you’ve got to write about Guernsey is: 70,000 alcoholics clinging to a rock in the middle of the sea.”
There is certainly a wild and reckless alcoholic haze to a lot of my memories. A time and a pub would be agreed and the night would go on from there. Afterwards, we might go to a club or a house party, invited or not. We were all sexually active, quite promiscuous. Aids was still a few years off from being widely reported and we took few if any precautions. We drank and drove, motorbikes when we were younger (my friend Paul was a mod and we went round on his Lambretta), cars once we were 17. Guernsey didn’t have breathalysers at the time. If you were pulled over, you had to walk toe to heel for about 10ft, bend down and pick up a coin, and toe to heel back. If you didn’t lose your balance, you were fit to drive. I got away with it several times.
Apart from the record shop, the bookshop was another important place of discovery. It was there that I bought Jean Genet’s Miracle of the Rose when I was 17 and got chatting to the owner about literature. He invited me to his house for a cup of tea and showed me around the place. The last room was the cellar, which turned out to be a sex dungeon: handcuffs on the wall, whips and masks. He casually explained that he threw parties down there and if I ever fancied coming to one … I declined as casually as I could. Maybe we’d talked about De Sade earlier in the bookshop. The next time I saw him we chatted as if it had never happened. He must have trusted me not to tell anyone, which I didn’t (it would have been scandalous in such a conservative place). But it seemed like confirmation of the edgy and exciting world that books could lead to.
It’s hard to say if our lives were better or worse than they are for 18-year-olds today. We experienced boredom more – Sundays were deadly, everything closed. Sexism and racism and homophobia were commonplace, as was casual violence; parents physically disciplined their kids and corporal punishment wasn’t banned in state schools until 1986, so it’s perhaps no surprise that, with a few drinks, punches got thrown. Football hooliganism was rampant, making headlines. On a night out, there was a mild expectation of trouble.
We would occasionally go to London to see bands (in my early teens, bands came to Guernsey – Elvis Costello, the Jam, Depeche Mode, Adam and the Ants – but then stopped. I’m not sure why, but logistics, costs and the island not having a big enough venue were all probably part of it). There was a world out there – and I was desperate to explore it.
T hree months after my 18th birthday, my friend Joel and I set off travelling. I had saved £400 from working all summer in a greenhouse that was pioneering the cultivation of kiwifruit on Guernsey, to replace the dying tomato industry (it never took off). Our vague plan was to work our way across Europe, maybe end up on a kibbutz (which still had a reputation as socialist paradises), then travel further. A gap year before university. In the bookshop I had chanced upon Work Your Way Around the World, which was in its first edition; we’d never heard of Lonely Planet and were perhaps as informed by the spirit of On the Road and Genet. Our only map was of all of Europe, taking in the top of north Africa and some of the Middle East. It was somewhat lacking in detail. No one else we knew was going travelling or had been. Looking back, Joel and I agree that naivety was as much our guide.
After grape picking in the Champagne region, we hitchhiked to the south of France. Often, no one would pick us up (including Björn Borg, who drove past us twice in his black Porsche near Monaco) and we would walk for miles, sleeping rough. On the French riviera, we bought a cheap summer tent and crossed northern Italy, sleeping in railway stations. In Venice, a guy tried to rob us in the middle of the night. When I woke, he threatened me and carried on going through my bag so I pulled out my knife to scare him off. I’d had it since I was 14, when I saw it glinting at the bottom of the marina in Saint Peter Port and dived down to retrieve it, a British second world war Fairbairn Sykes stiletto fighting knife; no plaything. He looked at it and laughed, whipped out a switchblade and waved it in my face, to show I didn’t stand a chance, before strolling off. I vowed to never pull a knife on anyone again. But what amazes me now is that I carried that knife through dozens of border checks and on numerous flights, and it was never an issue.
We continued through Yugoslavia and into Greece, where Work Your Way Around the World said there was orange picking on the Peloponnese. We met a few other northern Europeans, older than us, also looking for work. They told us the harvest was late. We wandered around Greece for weeks, ending up in the small town of Gargalianoi, where we stayed for three months, helping with the olive harvest, working in construction and an olive oil factory. Most of the time we slept in woods on the edge of town, our own little squatter camp that the locals turned a blind eye to, once a week going to the fleapit hotel in town, for a cold shower and the comfort of a bed. We were the only foreigners, apart from a couple of French guys, Gilles and Eric. They were recovering heroin addicts (Gilles had done nine months in Paris’s notorious La Santé prison for possession) and were planning to stay out of France for seven years to avoid military service, that length of absence granting exemption. We became friends and also increasingly aware that being British, we were the envy of European youth for not having national service: a Greek friend we were working with, Tomas, was about to start his two-year military conscription, a bleak posting on the troubled Turkish border.
That eight-month journey sometimes feels like a fever dream. It defines being 18 for me: freedom and adventure, living on your wits, never knowing what the next day might bring. From Greece we went to Egypt and across north Africa, back up through Spain and France and home. There were tough times, but no question of turning back. People on the whole were kind – we were kids and they wanted to help us. Our map was so basic, we had little idea where we were going, following the setting sun. For a time, we used a copy of David Copperfield we picked up in a hotel in Cairo as toilet paper, each reading the same 20 or so pages a day and then tearing them out.
There were two threatening periods: in Tunis, we became the target of unwanted sexual attention, followed night and day, men waiting outside our hotel room, every invitation for coffee turning into aggressive attempts at seduction; and in Tétouan in Morocco, we were hounded by dealers for days, sold hash and then told we would be shopped to the police unless we bought more. They were still threatening us as we left on the bus.
“The stories we tell most often about our lives are likely to be the least reliable, because we will have subtly amended them in every retelling down the years,” Barnes wrote in the same article. “It’s salutary to discover, from time to time, how other people’s memories are often quite different from our own – not just of events, but of what we ourselves were like back then.” Joel had forgotten the use of Dickens as toilet paper; I’d forgotten the level of hassle in Tétouan. Maybe I was too stoned. The truth is there, somewhere, among the stories.
In 2019, when my mother went into a home, I was clearing my parents’ house with my sister when I came across a folder of old documents and papers of mine that they’d kept. Looking through them for this article, I found five letters I wrote during my time away – I’d forgotten they existed, this was the first time I’d read them since I wrote them 42 years ago. Would they corroborate what I was really like as an 18-year-old? The fact that I sent only five letters and made no phone calls in eight months shocks me now as a parent (my sister says she asked my mum if she worried about me when I was away and she said she did, but that she felt there would have been disapproval, possibly from my father and no doubt from me, if she had expressed it).
To be honest, I’m surprised I wrote any letters at all, from how I remember our relationship. Instead, I find myself joking to them about being hungry, about roughing it, my hair getting longer, losing weight. There are things I had forgotten – our plan to go to a kibbutz in Israel thwarted by “war and conflict”; another plan to take a two-week boat trip from Athens to Alexandria (why would it take so long?!); our intention to cross the middle of the Sahara, only to find out in Egypt it would take three months to get a visa to enter Sudan and continue into Chad. I can see I am trying to shock them at times, but not too much. I tell them about Gilles and Eric and getting drunk on New Year’s Eve with them, Gilles throwing up in our hotel room, but I don’t mention their heroin addiction or the pills we took that had me hallucinating large insects crawling over my body, something that I thankfully found hilarious rather than terrifying. I say how beautiful Venice is, being kicked awake by Italian cops at dawn, but I don’t mention the incident with the knife. I complain about being sexually harassed in Tunis, but brush it off.
What surprises me most though is a warmth I hadn’t allowed for. Maybe distance did. Letters tell their own stories.
Most of us look back at our 18-year-old selves and do a little editing. As F Scott Fitzgerald wrote: “At 18, our convictions are hills from which we look; at forty-five they are caves in which we hide.” What were my convictions? Is the unheralded memory of being sat on that rock face – acting fearless, reckless, carefree, about to leap into the unknown – as accurate a picture as any? I spent most of my 20s after university travelling, living abroad. I still love to travel, even if kids and a career and the realities of adult life have restricted the opportunities. I still love the feeling of the bag on my back containing all I need. My kids love to travel too; I like to think my wife and I have given them that sense of adventure. We plan to go travelling for a year when we stop working. I like to think that 18-year-old is still with me.

title: A violent and coordinated youth uprising? That’s exactly the picture Europe’s enemies want to paint
description: Each country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernable, says law professor Alberto Alemanno
content:
Each country’s protesters have distinct grievances. Listen to them, not the voices telling us Europe is ungovernable
L ast Saturday night, the town hall of Limoges in west-central France was set ablaze . By Sunday, images of the fire destroying a symbol of the French republic, and other scenes of unrest across France , were everywhere, but being used to tell very different stories about what is happening in Europe.
For some, the flames announced a pan-European youth revolt , proof that a single movement was sweeping the continent. Donald Trump, who had already insisted that the French schools protests were not about schools but about migration and Islam , urged Europeans to “close the borders”. The mayor of Limoges saw the fingerprints of an alleged ultra-left insurrection.
I lost count of how many mainly rightwing media outlets were contacting me suddenly. Most were based in India, China, Singapore and the US. They sought voices to validate the idea of a “teen revolt” spreading across Europe , driven by the same grievances and violence.
None of these narratives, each serving a different political agenda, adequately explains what is happening. Europe’s protests have different causes, constituencies and demands. Portraying them as a Europe-wide rebellion erases those differences and makes Europe look ungovernable. That picture is a gift to anyone who wants to exploit the unrest.
What set off the protests varies from country to country. In France, the mobilisation began in schools in mid-September in frustration over longstanding failures to address overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings and facilities. By the time of the huge demonstration on Saturday, public-sector workers had joined, and the grievances had widened to encompass the cost of living .
In Belgium, meanwhile , students have challenged tuition-fee increases in the country’s French-speaking region and demanded additional teaching hours. Greek students have mobilised over housing costs and access to accommodation, while German pupils have protested against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.
Look beyond western Europe, and the differences become even more distinct. In Albania, student unrest builds on a pre-existing anti-government mobilisation, rather than a standalone youth revolt. In Serbia , students have led nearly two years of largely peaceful protests following the Novi Sad railway station disaster . Their movement centres on demands for an end to corruption, a lack of institutional accountability and political inaction. Now the students are running in this weekend’s election on their own list. This is a battle over power and accountability, and goes well beyond education or generational frustration.
Italian students may occupy schools and shout slogans in French, but the cross-border spread of images, slogans and tactics does not prove a shared organisation. Rather, 24-hour news coverage can turn separate protests into a single story of youth rebellion, creating, deliberately or not, the illusion of a common movement and programme where neither exists.
Rejecting the idea of a single European youth revolt does not mean denying the existence of a shared generational anxiety. Housing has become increasingly unaffordable, public services are under pressure, and the transition into secure employment is uncertain. Eurostat reports that EU house prices rose by 55.4% and rents by 26.7% between 2010 and the fourth quarter of 2024. The 2026 TUI Foundation Youth Study found that 52% of young people aged 16–26 across seven European countries expected to be worse off than their parents, compared with just 25% who expected to do better.
Youth unemployment in the euro area remains substantially higher than overall unemployment. One study of French firms found a sharper decline in permanent hiring among workers aged 21–29 in occupations exposed to artificial intelligence. The European Central Bank cautions that the evidence does not yet establish generative AI as the cause. But the uncertainty itself can create a shared sense of insecurity across national borders.
Such anxieties help explain why protests in one country resonate with young people in another, and why images of school sit-ins or street demonstrations can inspire imitation. But they don’t translate into common demands, let alone a coordinated political movement.
France’s demonstrations last Saturday exposed another danger: how quickly violence can overshadow a protest’s message. Most demonstrators marched peacefully, but a minority resorted to violence. Their actions should not define hundreds of thousands of demonstrators, just as peaceful protest should not provide cover for criminal acts.
What happened in Milan showed how the two can blur . A peaceful cost of living march alongside protests over education cuts and race-based reform, was followed by looting carried out by hooded, mostly teenage groups organised partly via TikTok. More than 200 were detained, most of them minors, and the march’s organisers disowned them. Defending public order must go hand in hand with accountability for violence and scrutiny of police conduct .
But when images of burning buildings and looting dominate coverage, peaceful protest and criminal violence become harder to distinguish in the public mind. A single incident can come to define an entire mobilisation.
The misleading narrative of a pan-European revolt has consequences, because it allows images of unrest to be taken out of their national contexts and presented as proof that a chaotic Europe is ungovernable.
This is particularly useful to those seeking to deepen divisions and undermine European democracy: it turns distinct national problems into a sweeping story of European failure.
For the radical right, the idea of a continent in flames proves that open societies cannot protect their citizens, hence the call to “close your borders”. For those on the radical left who celebrate every burning building as the dawn of a continental uprising, the flames prove that liberal democratic institutions are beyond repair. Both need Europe to look ungovernable but neither offers an answer to the disorder it complains about. And both serve the interests of those beyond Europe’s borders who gain from a divided union, from the Trump administration to Vladimir Putin.
President Macron had a point when he lashed out at the “stupid” comments of foreign leaders about events in France. AI-generated images of scenes that never took place in France had been circulating, he said. Macron is hardly neutral, but certain forces clearly have an interest in amplifying images of chaos.
Governments should neither romanticise protest nor use violence as a pretext to dismiss legitimate grievances. They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold perpetrators accountable and address the pressures that leave many young people uncertain about their future.
Europe’s democracies will be judged not by how they withstand these protests, but how they address the distinct grievances behind them and restore confidence in the future. That is how generational anxiety can become a force for democratic renewal rather than fuel for those seeking to portray democracy as broken.
Alberto Alemanno is the Jean Monnet professor of EU law at HEC Paris and the founder of The Good Lobby
