Send your questions by email now to conversations@theguardian.com or post questions in the comments from 0900 BST here .

title: Waitrose opens first new supermarket in eight years in north London
description: Grocer launches Cricklewood store as part of £1bn investment plan, with Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, to follow next month
content:
Grocer launches Cricklewood store as part of £1bn investment plan, with Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, to follow next month
As part of a £1bn investment plan , Waitrose has chosen Cricklewood in north London as the location for its first supermarket in eight years.
The upmarket grocer will open the store on Thursday and another supermarket in Hale Barns, Greater Manchester , next month. It also plans four smaller stores next year, including a supermarket in Oakham, Rutland, and three convenience stores in Bedminster (Bristol), Chalk Farm (London) and Springstead Village (Cambridge).
In 2024, Waitrose, which has more than 300 supermarkets, said it planned to open up to four large supermarkets and 100 convenience stores over five years and would also refurbish a number of outlets introducing meat, fish and sushi counters, on-site bakeries and fine wine sections. The company has since ditched these specific targets and said it wants to focus on finding the right locations for new outlets.
Tina Mitchell, the retail director at Waitrose , said: “Our supermarkets provide the ultimate showcase for everything that sets Waitrose apart – from our unmatched quality and industry-leading welfare standards to the expert service of our partners.”
This year the company – led since January by the former Tesco executive Tom Denyard - also plans to refurbish 29 stores.
After a difficult period, when sales were hit by IT problems which led to gaps on shelves, Waitrose is holding market share, according to the latest figures from market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. However, the chain is coming under pressure from Marks & Spencer, which now has a higher share of the grocery market, under some measures, after opening a number of new food-led outlets.
Sales at Waitrose rose 4% in the six months to 1 August. However, its underlying operating profit slid by £7m to £103m as it invested in keeping prices down and improving its loyalty scheme. It was also hit by higher energy costs during the summer heat wave.
Waitrose’s parent company, the John Lewis Partnership – which is owned by its staff – reported a £98m pre-tax loss in the half-year to 1 August, as sales fell at the department stores despite heavy investment in updating the outlets.
The company has been reducing the number of staff it employs directly as it tries to trim costs.
On Wednesday, the partnership announced it had signed its first company-wide union recognition deal. The collective agreement with Usdaw, the shopworkers’ union, comes ahead of new rights of union access in workplaces that come into force at the end of this month.
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said: “Usdaw already has members working within the business and this agreement will strengthen that presence and help us in supporting and representing members across the partnership. We now look forward to growing our membership and influence within the partnership and to working with the partnership’s management on finalising the details of how the agreement will work in practice.”

title: ‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the Sun
description: The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?
content:
The director has turned Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel about an ailing adolescent and her glitchy robot friend into a thought-provoking film. What do the pair think this story says about tech, love and grief?
I n the wings of the London film festival, a group of young influencers are discussing their personal highlights. Klara and the Sun, says one, and her colleagues agree. It’s not just that the film is still so fresh in their memory, or that they have gathered today to meet its creators and stars. Klara is funny and moving; it’s their festival favourite so far. I relay this exchange to Taika Waititi , the film’s director, who is sipping bottled water in a room down the hall. His gaze widens. He almost chokes. “Thank God!” he exclaims with just a bit too much heat.
Everybody has a perfect film, just as everybody has a perfect friend, and they vary because everybody is different. In the film, sick 14-year-old Josie loves her discontinued robot doll Klara, whereas most kids her age opt for brighter, shinier models. And the young influencers love Klara and the Sun – Waititi’s adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s acclaimed novel – while most older critics vehemently, violently disagree . All of which shows that there’s no accounting for taste, that people are confounding, and that our hearts and our brains are not always in sync. That keeps life interesting. It’s partly what the film is about. “The emotions that we give very simple labels to are really complex,” says Ishiguro, who is seated alongside the director. “The thing we call love, for example, is incredibly noisy and multifaceted. Nobody knows what the hell love is.”
For what it’s worth, I loved Ishiguro’s distinctively spare and poignant source novel and am less convinced by Waititi’s screen version, which is certainly noisy. Jenna Ortega stars as Klara, the perky solar-powered AI who plays soulmate to adolescent Josie (Mia Tharia), at a remote country house. She’s a warm splash of sunshine in an otherwise frosty environment, a fish out of water in a tragicomic sci-fi caper. But there is a glitch in the matrix; the component parts don’t align. Waititi adds sugar and caffeine, pratfalls and one-liners. Klara misreads social cues and steers the family car off the road. She fears she’ll be shipped back to the factory and melted down for scrap.
Perhaps the perfect friend is independent, self-directed. Ishiguro has seen several of his Nobel prize-winning books – The Remains of the Day, Never Let Me Go, A Pale View of Hills – adapted for the screen. He feels that the best films break away and that the worst are too faithful. “Sometimes it’s not just loyalty but laziness,” he says. “You can’t just have the text there in front of you. You need to use your imagination to move it on. A film needs to step forward, out of my book on a journey to being something bigger.”
Waititi agrees. “Why would you do a cover of a song with exactly the same instrumentation? You make the film because you love the book. But you at least want to bring some original ideas to the table.”
The book and the film are so different, it follows that their creators would be too. Ishiguro is sober, soft-spoken and writes delicate dramas about the deep mystery of life. Waititi is voluble, peacockish and makes uproarious films such as Jojo Rabbit, What We Do in the Shadows and Hunt for the Wilderpeople . He tends to view the world through a comic lens. “Yeah, that’s my instinct. I can’t make a Schindler’s List, that’s not in my wheelhouse. I want to push everything towards comedy and then reel it back.”
It’s a defence mechanism, he admits, part of his cultural DNA. “I’m from New Zealand,” he says. “In New Zealand, my friends and I always had a very sensitive cheese-o-meter. We thought the Americans loved cheese and saw sentimentality as a good thing. But of course that’s also me being scared of it. Now I think there’s a way of being more emotional and dramatic. Hopefully that’s a sign of me maturing.”
Waititi’s work, though, has always carried a pleasing eddy of sadness. His 2010 feature Boy was a comedy about child abuse, while What We Do in the Shadows reframed the vampire as a lost, lonesome immigrant. Klara and the Sun is a love story but it’s also about isolation: the gap between people; the limits of understanding. “Oh, I’m definitely interested in loneliness,” he says.
Ishiguro chips in. “Yeah, I think you’re right, there’s a crossover between our preoccupations,” he says. “But this isn’t just everyday loneliness, it’s something more fundamental. It’s about the human experience. There is part of each of us that remains alone. There is stuff that we all have to face alone. Not least death.”
That’s the other big looming topic of Waititi’s film: death. Klara works as an “artificial friend” while other robots serve as “bereavement dolls”, filling in for lost spouses, siblings and children. That’s a sound business model, the director insists. “As a father with two kids, I always fear I’ll lose one. The younger me would have thought, ‘Oh, you can’t replace someone special.’ But the older I get, and the more in love with my kids I get, I think, ‘Oh, eventually I’d believe it was them.’ The human brain is easily adaptable. A therapist will tell you that you can programme anyone to fall in love. Tell someone you love them 50 times a day and in a few months your brain will give up and believe it. So I’d definitely consider replacing one of my children.” He laughs. “They don’t even have to be dead. I’d just like a version that’s nice to me and doesn’t ask for money.”
Ishiguro once joked that he essentially writes the same story in a variety of guises. He is drawn to flawed eyewitnesses and a partial view of events; groping narrators who try to make sense of their places in the world. The Remains of the Day’s rigid butler doesn’t know he’s in love, nor that the stately home where he works contains Nazis. Never Let Me Go’s hothoused schoolgirl finds out she is held captive and being used in terrible ways. Ishiguro’s books are unique but each connects to the world, and sometimes in ways he could not have foreseen. Klara and the Sun, for instance, was recently cited as a potential handbook for the development of generative AI. Tom Lue, VP of global affairs at Google Deepmind, suggested it be used as an “ethical touchstone”, the centrepiece of a “human-centred” approach to the future of frontier AI.
So the book has been co-opted. It has taken on another fresh life of its own. Waititi turns to the author. “It’s all your fault,” he says. “That’s incredible,” says Ishiguro. It’s the first he’s heard of it. “I know a lot of people within the AI industry are worried about its impact on society. It’s got to the point where they feel the need for a handbrake. So they are surprisingly keen to talk to creative people and road-test various ideas and scenarios.” He frowns. “But here I do become protective of both the book and the film. Because our story really isn’t about all that. If someone is trying to figure out the ethics of AI and where we should all be going, I’m not sure they’d be well-guided by this story. There are other, better places to go.”
Waititi pipes up. “The Terminator’s a good one.”
Klara has been built with a sweet, simple purpose: to provide friendship and support. But the human world is hazardous, unstable, which means she has to update her files and adapt her approach. Waititi’s film veers and darkens, riffing off its downbeat source novel, finally closing in towards death. “There’s another version of this story where Klara would turn into a murder-bot,” he points out.
Robot dolls fill a need, plug a gap and ideally make life better. But artificial friends, by their nature, are replaceable too. In the press room next door, the influencers are still comparing notes, killing time between interviews. Klara and the Sun is receding; the conversation has already moved on. One says: “You have to see La Bola Negra. It’s my film of the year.”

title: ‘Wow, logging that as a microaggression!’ Sophie Duker on trolling masculinity, lesbian cruises and her stripper fantasy
description: The standup on the bizarre gifts she’s received from fans, the intoxicating power of being an author and her aim of becoming a ‘fiercely intellectual slutty grandma’
content:
The standup on the bizarre gifts she’s received from fans, the intoxicating power of being an author and manifesting her ‘fiercely intellectual slutty grandma’
How did you get into comedy? If you want anything badly enough, the best way to get it is to feign absolute indifference while pouring in 110% effort. I was telling outrageous jokes about colonialism in tiny pub rooms five nights a week alongside a rotating lineup of lunatics and sexual deviants, all the while gaslighting myself into believing it was a casual hobby and I could stop any time.
What’s been one of your all-time favourite gigs? I loved performing on a lesbian cruise, despite the debilitating impostor syndrome (I’m an omnivore). I got a record number of fist-bumps from appreciative butches and met so many incredible older sapphics. One was a black witch from California who communed with my ancestors directly after the show – you don’t get that kind of service on Live at the Apollo.
Can you recall a gig so bad, it’s now funny? I was headlining at a festival and my right breast fell out of my top about 10 seconds in. I didn’t address it because I thought it would weaken my authority; the audience didn’t address it because they were kind and possibly scared. My tit was swinging in the breeze like Tarzan from the vine! I think through sheer bloody-mindedness we all managed to trigger a Mandela effect where after the half hour ended no one present was sure it had ever actually happened. Until now.
How would you describe your new show, Hot Beef Injection ? A stunning, silly, angry show where we (me, Sophie, and you, the audience) troll masculinity for an hour. I love the men who come to my shows (hot dads, fun nerds, miscellaneous) but the men outside, who roam the streets, have me tired and distressed on the daily. In a world where we’re processing rape academies , frat-house group chats and private islands it feels not only punk but necessary to rugby tackle the toxic elephants in the room.
Was there a particular incident that triggered the show? Hoo boy. When I was but a tiny baby girl comedian I had a non-consensual experience with an older man in the industry. At the time I sort of walked it off. But our paths crossed again in late 2025, and I thought, in the light of all the hideous bleakness of Everything Happening Right Now, why not sneak the anecdote into a standup set and make it my best-reviewed show to date?
Your debut novel, Dong , is out in the new year. What interested you in fiction writing? I’ve been writing fiction my entire life – alibis, flirtatious texts, hastily drafted email excuses and backstories for social media catfish. But sandwiching a feature-length story inside a hardback and putting my name to it has always felt like seducing Pedro Pascal – technically possible but unattainable for me, at least at the moment. The carte blanche you get given as an author to fantasise is intoxicating. I was tapping it out at the hair salon while the aunties ravaged my edges, sneaking my laptop into bed at sunrise so I could get a fix before my partner woke up.
Best advice you’ve ever been given? “If you’re doing well, get off; if you’re doing badly, get off.” This was said to me by a male comedian, but I think it’s still valid. I really hate when any work becomes more about the performer’s vanity than audience enjoyment. It reminds me not to let success make me too self-indulgent, or to scrabble for extra scraps of approval if I feel short changed by the room’s reaction. Do the thing you came to do, to the best of your ability, then dip.
What’s one of the strangest fan encounters you’ve had? My fans’ love language is bizarre gift giving. A man in York offered me freshly baked bread (I accepted). One man from France offered me his credit card details (I declined). On tour in Australia, a woman gave me a card which contained a lock of her dog’s hair. (I kept it – the card, not the dog.)
What’s a joke you’re convinced is brilliant, but just doesn’t land with audiences? Wow, logging that as a microaggression. All of my brilliant jokes land with all my audiences – but I do notice that sometimes they are slightly more tepid when I try to sneak in niche references to Lord of the Rings.
What’s next for you? I want to nail my Ayesha. Not referring to the Baroness Hazarika. Nailing my Ayesha is part of my nonagenarian stripper fantasy. The Ayesha is a pose where you hang upside down, legs splayed, labia facing heaven, just two contact points on the pole. I’m manifesting a level of physical and mental dexterity in my 90s where I can be this fiercely intellectual slutty grandma and every other month I throw big debauched parties where I’m fed psychedelic-laced frozen grapes by my absolutely smitten, smoking hot entourage.

title: Tied up and tortured: Israel using US-made electroshock weapons on Palestinian detainees
description: Investigation suggests American company Axon still supplies Israel with Taser weapons despite evidence they have been used to torture prisoners
content:
Investigation suggests American company Axon still supplies Israel with Taser weapons despite evidence they have been used to torture prisoners
T he soldiers drag the man into a section of the prison known as Hell’s Wing, a metaphor for its notoriety for acts of brutality. Shoving him violently into a corner, they take a step back before one of them draws his weapon and fires two rubber bullets at his body. The man, a double amputee, collapses to the floor.
After tying him up tightly, the soldiers continue their assault until one of them pulls a stun gun from its holster. The soldier approaches the man, brandishing the gun, before applying it to his body, engulfing him in an electric shock.
This is what Essa* says happened to him during a period in Israeli detention. Today, more than a year and a half later, the scars from the electric shocks remain visible on his body. The close proximity of double scars suggests he was subjected to repeated shocks while in a “tightly restrained” position, says the International Rehabilitation Council for Torture Victims.
Essa, now 43, was arrested in the Jabalia refugee camp in January 2024, where he had been staying since having both feet amputated after an Israeli missile attack on his home. He was held at Israel’s Ofer Prison before being released in October 2025.
According to an investigation by the Guardian and Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism, Essa was likely to have been tortured with a Taser electroshock weapon manufactured by the American company Axon Enterprise, formerly known as Taser International.
The alleged torture is one of a number of incidents that have been linked to the use of Axon weapons, which the company appears to continue to supply to Israel. Three other detainees since released allege they were tortured using Axon weapons between 2024 and 2025.
Human rights groups have condemned allegations of the repeated torture and ill-treatment of detainees held in Israeli detention centres and prisons using electric shock devices, with Amnesty calling for restrictions on exports of such devices.
A spokesperson for the Israel Defense Forces said the abuse of detainees was strictly prohibited and that the use of restraints on detainees was carried out “only in exceptional circumstances that justify their use, and in subject to Israeli law, international law and IDF orders”.
An investigation conducted by the Israeli military advocate general, Itai Ofir, against five Israeli soldiers accused of committing a sexual assault against a Palestinian detainee inside the Sde Teiman detention camp in July 2024 found they had used a Taser weapon while torturing the detainee, leaving him needing hospital treatment.
In November 2025, the UN’s Committee Against Torture reported on allegations of torture, including the use of electric shocks, within Israeli detention facilities and noted that “torture and ill-treatment had escalated sharply since 7 October 2023”. The committee also expressed its “serious concern over widespread allegations of sexual abuse of Palestinian detainees … including allegations of rape … sexualised forms of torture … electrocution of the genitals and anus”.
Despite such concerns, Axon appears to have continued to sign contracts with Israeli entities to supply either the Taser gun or its accessories. As recently as June 2025, the company was showcasing the latest models of its electroshock weapons to Israeli security agencies at a conference in Israel .
Two video clips produced by the Israeli prison service over the past year show a gun that appears to be a Taser electroshock weapon produced by Axon. Both Essa and the three other detainees interviewed say it was the weapon used to torture them inside Israeli detention centres and prisons.
One of the detainees interviewed says he had water poured over his body – which can intensify the torture – before he was given an electric shock with a Taser weapon, during a spell in detention in 2024. He says he still suffers from severe visual impairment, spasms and recurrent fainting spells.
In August 2025, the Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs highlighted the torture of detainees at Gilboa prison with electric shocks, before they were dragged to the shower stalls in the prison’s courtyard, doused with water and then shocked again. It did not state the model of weapon used. Amani Al-Sarhanah, from the Palestinian Prisoners’ Club, a human rights group, says: “The use of electric shocks may be just one of dozens of types of weapons that have been used against them [Palestinian prisoners]. We do not actually know what types they are or which companies supply them. Nevertheless, we certainly know that most weapons imported by Israel originate from the United States in one way or another.”
Since October 2023, 92 Palestinians are reported to have died while in detention, but only one Israeli soldier has been tried for mistreating Palestinian prisoners from Gaza, according to a report by a group of Israeli NGOs.
Amnesty says it has published extensively on the human rights risks involved in the use of electric shock weapons and has previously called for such law enforcement equipment to be included in the UN’s Arms Trade Treaty that regulates the trade in conventional weapons. Axon Enterprises and the Israel prison service were approached for comment.

title: History comes home as St Louis City top Columbus Crew to win US Open Cup
description: Substitute goalkeeper Ben Lundt made a key shootout save to help secure St Louis City’s first-ever title.
content:
Title is club’s first-ever since 2023 founding
St Louis clubs have won 11 Open Cups all-time
Daniel Edelman nets winner in 5-4 win on penalties
For much of the 20th century, winning the US Open Cup required a team to beat someone from St Louis. The Gateway City was home to many of the nation’s best teams during some ramshackle eras of soccer in the United States, with six different clubs combining for 10 trophy lifts. The most recent came in 1988, when St Louis Busch Seniors beat San Francisco-based Greek-American AC in the last throes of a tournament history dominated by amateur and semi-pro teams. MLS has won every Open Cup but one since starting play in 1996, and St Louis didn’t have an MLS club until 2023.
From the beginning, club figures spoke of their aim to restore the city to soccer prominence. Well, mission accomplished. St Louis City are US Open Cup champions, outlasting the Columbus Crew 5-4 on penalties to end the city’s 38-year wait for a major US soccer title and earn a place in the field for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.
Daniel Edelman scored the decisive penalty, with backup goalkeeper Ben Lundt making a save on Columbus’ first attempt, himself having entered the match in the second half.
Fittingly given their home’s rich soccer history, City’s first trophy is also the nation’s oldest. Wednesday marked the 109th Open Cup final.. The first was held in 1913–14 and the competition has run continuously save for a two-year hiatus during the Covid-19 pandemic.
St Louis won this season’s tournament with MLS’s youngest manager – Yoann Damet, the 36-year-old Frenchman who was previously Wilfried Nancy’s top assistant in Columbus but was passed over for the top job after Nancy left. St Louis will be thankful that he was.
Often two of the nation’s most aesthetically pleasing teams, Columbus and St Louis opened the final by minimizing risk. For the opening half-hour, St Louis carried a 60% share of possession but failed to muster a single shot. The hosts were a bit more incisive whenever they found the ball, working to advance upfield and trying to fashion chances for Brais Méndez, but failed to threaten Roman Bürki’s net.
Referee Guido Gonzales Jr promptly blew his half-time whistle after the 45th minute. No need for stoppage time after that half, and few could argue.
Both teams returned with intentions to sustain the caginess after the break. Columbus continued to dramatically tilt the field, taking 11 touches in St Louis’ box after half-time before the visitors managed a single one. Still, Bürki kept their sole on-target effort from rippling the net. The visitors responded by upping their fouling volume to further impede the Crew’s efforts.
The 69th minute provided an inflection point as Columbus again entered the St Louis box, where Santi Rodríguez took a clattering from behind by Carlo Holse but saw the referee play the advantage. Méndez picked up the loose ball, strafed across the top of the box to his left, and played a through-ball to former Morocco international Anass Zaroury, whose shot was blocked by a fearless Bürki who took contact to his head from the wing-back’s knee, staying down as the play fizzled.
As the former Switzerland international received medical treatment, the VAR had ample time to review and, ultimately, clear the potential penalty on Holse’s initial tackle. Ultimately, a six-minute examination led to Bürki exiting the match on a stretcher, leaving to a stadium-wide applause. Later, the CBS Sports broadcast relayed that Bürki was “OK” shortly after his departure, though he was taken to the hospital for an evaluation. In stepped Lundt, a backup since coming to MLS in 2019 – but one who had played shootout hero before for St Louis, winning their quarter-final shootout against Houston.
Another injury, seemingly a leg muscle issue to promising Columbus midfielder Taha Habroune, brought Eric Bailly off the bench with captain Sean Zawadzki pushing into midfield to accommodate. The fourth official showed 11 minutes of stoppage time, perhaps cashing some rollover minutes from the first half on top of the lengthy delay as Bürki was examined. The Nordecke increased the volume of their support, but the game’s established physicality hardly waned for their efforts. St Louis seemed to fashion a clear look inside the box in the 10th minute of stoppage time, but US international Damion Downs took too heavy a touch to fashion a shot.
A minute later, the whistle blew. Despite Columbus outshooting St Louis 16-3, both teams finished the 90 minutes without a goal to their name or a trophy to their claim. Another 30 minutes of brawling followed.
Neither team ceded an inch in the opening minutes of extra time, exchanging hard challenges and failing to maximize their ensuing set pieces.
After Timo Baumgartl started the sequence with a make, Columbus’ Santi Rodriguez sent his attempt to Lundt’s left only to be stifled by a strong left hand. The teams each converted their next three attempts, although Lundt nearly ended the sequence with a finger to Andrés Herrera’s effort in the fourth round. Edelman stepped up and made no mistake with his trophy-winner.
The MLS schedule-makers did the finalists no favors as both teams played on the road this weekend, although St Louis enjoyed an extra day of rest. St Louis also entered the final at a known disadvantage, playing without striker Rafael Navarro. A front-runner for the year-end MLS Best XI, Navarro played for the Colorado Rapids through the quarter-final stage, cap-tying him for the remainder of the tournament.
While Columbus was recently a contender on all fronts under Nancy, his departure at the end of 2025 forced the Crew into a stylistic reset. Rather than hire his top assistant, Damet, Columbus looked beyond the league and hired Henrik Rydström, a self-proclaimed acolyte of “relationism”. The Swede never adapted to MLS, quickly leading Columbus toward the bottom of the East before being shown the door in May after just 17 matches.
His replacement, Laurent Courtois, was another Nancy disciple. Meanwhile, Damet is a frontrunner for coach of the year, is in line for a top-three finish in the Western Conference – and, now, is the Open Cup champion.
In an era where fiction fixates on multiverses, Columbus will no doubt wonder what could have been had they opted for continuity and retained Damet. Their loss is St Louis’ gain, as the Western Conference club will hope this is the first of multiple trophies to be won under MLS’s youngest manager.

title: Anthony Edwards scores 45 as Timberwolves spoil Giannis Antetokounmpo’s Heat debut
description: Edwards joins Wilt Chamberlain and Michael Jordan in an exclusive NBA club as Minnesota overwhelm Miami despite 35 points from Antetokounmpo
content:
Edwards hits nine threes in 45-point explosion
Antetokounmpo scores 35 in first game with Heat
Minnesota rout Miami 131-106 in season opener
Anthony Edwards scored 45 points as he and the Minnesota Timberwolves spoiled Giannis Antetokounmpo’s debut with the Miami Heat in an emphatic 131-106 season-opening win on Wednesday night.
Edwards became just the third player in NBA history to record multiple 40-point games in season openers, joining Wilt Chamberlain and Michael Jordan.
Antetokounmpo scored 35 points and grabbed six rebounds after joining Miami in an offseason trade with the Milwaukee Bucks.
Edwards checked out with 3:51 remaining and Minnesota leading by 28. He shot 16-for-29 from the floor, including 9-for-17 from three-point range, and added 10 rebounds.
His 45 points were the most by a Minnesota player in a season opener and marked his 125th career game with at least 30 points.
LaMelo Ball, making his Timberwolves debut, hit five three-pointers and finished with 21 points and six assists. Jaden McDaniels scored 17 points, and Rudy Gobert grabbed 15 rebounds for Minnesota.
Antetokounmpo checked out with seven minutes remaining after hearing MVP chants from the home crowd early in the game. He shot 13-for-19 from the floor but also airballed a free throw and was assessed a flagrant foul after elbowing Terrence Shannon Jr in the head on a drive.
Antetokounmpo was Miami’s most productive scorer. Bam Adebayo had 15 points, Andrew Wiggins and Davion Mitchell added 11 apiece, and Mitchell also dished out 10 assists. Klay Thompson scored 10 points in his Miami debut.
Minnesota made 21 three-pointers, compared with eight for Miami.
Edwards and Antetokounmpo each scored 21 points in the first half, but Minnesota carried a 10-point lead into the break.
The Timberwolves opened 11-for-14 from the floor and led 27-19 after eight minutes. Miami pushed back in the second quarter and briefly took a 50-49 lead on a three-pointer by Bobby Portis Jr.
Minnesota controlled the final five minutes of the half. Shannon hit a pair of corner three-pointers, Edwards recorded a steal and an easy dunk, and Ball scored on a drive and added two free throws to make it 69-59.
The momentum carried over into the third quarter. Edwards and Ball each hit a three-pointer in the opening two and a half minutes. Edwards added another as Minnesota extended their lead to 78-61, and the Timberwolves remained in control the rest of the way.

title: ‘Almost looks fake’: two Sydney beaches closed after whale carcass washes up
description: Swimming banned at Maroubra and Coogee while council prioritises ‘culturally respectful’ approach to remains
content:
Swimming banned at Maroubra and Coogee while council prioritises ‘culturally respectful’ approach to remains
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
A whale carcass has forced the closure of two busy swimming and surfing spots after washing up between Coogee and Maroubra beaches in Sydney – but there are no plans to remove it.
The whale’s heavily decomposed body was found on Thursday morning at Lurline Bay, a rocky cove surrounded by cliffs in Sydney’s eastern suburbs.
It’s believed to be a juvenile humpback.
Local council said nearby Coogee and Maroubra beaches would be closed until further notice to protect oceangoers as whale carcasses have been known to attract sharks.
“We have cordoned off the area to leave this creature in peace and safe from the attention of people,” Randwick Council mayor, Dr Clare Willington, told reporters.
The council has also contacted Surf Life Saving about introducing extra drone patrols, but Willington said it was a precaution as there had not yet been reports of an increase in shark activity.
Willington said there were no plans to remove the whale and that staff were working with Gamay Rangers about a culturally and environmentally sensitive approach to take.
“This is a natural occurrence and in time nature will deal with the carcass,” Willington said.
The Gamay Rangers are an Indigenous ranger team who undertake natural and cultural resource management activities like protection work, conservation, and threatened species management in the La Perouse Local Aboriginal Land Council area.
The whale is an important totem animal to the local Bidjigal people, and Gamay Rangers manager Robert Cooley said previous instances where beached animal carcasses were taken to landfill had distressed his community.
However, Cooley said he was not “super confident” the rising tide would return the carcass to the sea.
“We’re got a reasonably strong north-east wind here and a bit of a swell pushing it back up – so that’s going to be a challenge,” he said.
“We’ll just have to wait and see what happens but the animal is in a pretty advanced stage of decomposition, so if it did go out into the ocean, I don’t think it would take long for nature to break it down.”
If intervention is necessary, the rangers would be discussing plans with cultural advisers, he said.
The whale is believed to be a young humpback, but it is difficult to confirm due to its state of decomposition, Cooley said.
The carcass was first spotted on Wednesday in Sydney’s northern beaches near Manly, where attempts were made to tow it out to sea, which is why there are pieces of rope found with the whale.
The council is encouraging residents and visitors to avoid the area and follow directions from lifeguards and authorities.
It comes as authorities are working to free a large whale found stuck in shallow waters off Turners Beach on Tasmania’s north-west coast.
“Members of the public are asked to avoid the area and not enter the water on the incoming tide due to the anticipated danger,” Tasmanian police said.
Curious locals have stopped by Lurline Bay throughout the morning to try catch a glimpse of the whale.
Meeri Pajala, an au pair from Finland who is living in Sydney, said she had never seen anything like this before.
“It almost looks fake to me,” she said. “That skin looks so weird.”
Glenda, a local who did not want her full name published, says she usually watches whales swimming by the coast and was curious when she heard the news.
“My interest is in if it’s newborn, or if it’s juvenile,” she said. “I thought it would be more complete.”
It was nudging up against the rocks as the waves ebbed and flowed but had become stuck in a crevice due to low tide.
To the surprise of many onlookers, it doesn’t seem to have a smell.

title: Bukang-i is back: shark returns to canal in South Korea hours after being coaxed out to sea
description: Animal attracted 1.6m visitors after getting trapped in September, now a new attempt to free it is under way
content:
Animal attracted 1.6m visitors after getting trapped in September, now a new attempt to free it is under way
A shark that became a viral sensation after getting stuck in a South Korean canal for a month has returned just hours after being coaxed out to sea.
Nicknamed Bukang-i by fans, the 3-metre-long (9.8-foot) female dusky shark was first spotted in the waterway on 18 September.
On Wednesday, workers used nets fixed to floating pontoons to guide the shark free, but it dived beneath a net and returned to the canal in Busan overnight, authorities said.
“The shark is now between the outer net and an inner net installed 30 to 40 metres ... further inside the canal,” an oceans ministry official told AFP.
After it got trapped in September, officials initially opted to wait for the shark to leave on its own – but amid growing concerns for its wellbeing they took a more proactive approach. A fresh attempt to free Bukang-i was under way on Thursday morning, officials said.
Officials spent Thursday morning removing a screen that was potentially blocking the shark’s exit, replacing the net it had swum under and raising an outer barrier, before attempting to guide Bukang-i out again.
Before Wednesday’s effort, authorities had twice tried and failed to steer Bukang-i back to sea, using water jets and then nets.
As each attempt failed, the shark amassed a huge following, drawing more than 1.6m people to the canal for a glimpse.
The affection for Bukang-i has become an industry, with a commemorative soju , a baseball mascot in a shark cape and an honorary city ambassadorship, and nearby shops reporting a surge in sales. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, visited the canal in mid-October.
But concerns for the shark’s health are growing.
The canal temperature, now 21C, is near the lower range of what the dusky species prefers, and Bukang-i has not been seen feeding since September.
Choi Yoon, a shark expert at Kunsan National University, told the Hankyoreh newspaper the shark could die within two weeks, due to hunger, colder water and abrasions to its snout and fin.
An oceans ministry official said this week the shark appeared to have difficulty maintaining balance.
Environmental groups have linked the shark’s appearance in the canal to warming seas, saying rising temperatures are pushing warm-water fish northwards, with subtropical sharks following in pursuit.
The fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that sharks feed on.

title: Enes Kanter Freedom claims he was denied entry to WNBA finals game in Atlanta
description: Former NBA player says he was removed from State Farm Arena after officials arranged a private suite and additional security for his attendance
content:
Former NBA player says he was denied entry to arena
Arena had arranged private suite over safety concerns
Freedom was previously ejected from Chicago game
Reese stars again as Dream thrash Valkyries in Game 3
Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom said he was denied entry to Game 3 of the WNBA finals between the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream on Wednesday after a disagreement over seating arrangements at State Farm Arena.
Freedom posted a video at halftime claiming he had been removed from the arena. The reason for his alleged ejection was not immediately clear, though the footage appeared to show him telling security personnel that he wanted to sit in the seats he had bought rather than a private suite arranged for him.
The video posted by Freedom showed him being informed at the entry gate: “If you come in you have to agree to go to the suite.”
Freedom responded: “I purchased tickets, right? Just because I purchased tickets, I would like to sit in my seat. That’s all I want.”
An Atlanta police officer was also heard telling Freedom: “You’re free to go to the city of Atlanta streets. That’s another private establishment over there. He’s free to go there. He just can’t be here.”
A public relations official for State Farm Arena said Freedom “was offered the suite for his safety and he rejected it”.
Before the game, an arena spokesperson said in a statement that “Enes Kanter Freedom has contacted federal, state and local authorities, the WNBA, the Atlanta Dream and State Farm Arena officials to express concerns about his personal safety during his planned attendance at Game 3 of the WNBA finals tonight … Following consultations with the WNBA, Dream ownership, State Farm Arena leadership and security officials, we have directed Mr Freedom to watch tonight’s game from a private luxury suite. This arrangement is intended to address his security concerns and help provide a safe and positive experience for him and other guests. The suite will have additional security and will be his designated viewing location for the game. State police have also assigned an officer to Mr Freedom at his request.”
Freedom, who last played in the NBA in 2022, has made opposition to transgender participation in women’s sports a focus of his public commentary. This has led to his recent interest in the WNBA, which became a center of that discussion following Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham’s comments on the topic over the summer that drew a rebuke from many WNBA players and fans. His appearance in Atlanta followed an August confrontation with Chicago Sky guard Natasha Cloud that resulted in his ejection and a ban from the Sky’s home arena .
At that game, against the Indiana Fever, Freedom wore a shirt bearing the words “WOMAN noun adult human female”.
Ahead of Wednesday’s game, Freedom criticized comments by Golden State’s Gabby Williams supporting transgender athletes. In a social media post, he sarcastically claimed that Williams had inspired him to identify as a woman and enter the WNBA draft.
Freedom and fellow former NBA player Royce White have both publicly claimed to identify as women and announced plans to enter the draft. The league has said neither is eligible.
On Wednesday, Freedom also shared a letter from WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert responding to questions from Republican congressman Marlin Stutzman about the league’s eligibility rules.
“Only women are eligible to play in the WNBA and the individuals you cite in your letter are both men,” Engelbert wrote, referring to Freedom and White.
Asked about Freedom’s planned attendance before the game, Williams questioned the attention being devoted to him.
“Obviously the media has a responsibility in what they choose to cover,” she said.
Atlanta went on to beat Golden State 97-71 behind 21 points and 12 rebounds from Angel Reese, taking a 2-1 lead in the best-of-seven WNBA finals.

title: Angel Reese stars again as Atlanta Dream thrash Valkyries to seize WNBA finals lead
description: Reese records second straight double-double as Atlanta overwhelm Golden State 97-71 before a sold-out crowd to take a 2-1 lead in the WNBA finals
content:
Reese posts 21 points and 12 rebounds in Game 3
Dream cruise to 97-71 prevail before 17,099 fans
Finals opener draws record 2.1 million TV viewers
Angel Reese had 21 points and 12 rebounds to help the Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 97-71 on Wednesday night and take a 2-1 lead in the WNBA finals.
Rhyne Howard added 16 points and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who host Game 4 on Saturday.
It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for their first victory in the finals. She now has a double-double in each game of the finals.
“It feels good when you’re in the finals. It’s a long season and you play against everybody and go through and push through, but when you can do it at the highest level, this is what you live for, this is what the offseason is for,” Reese said. “I put the work in for this moment and I’m just happy I could lead the team to a win. We’re feeling good going into Saturday.”
With the game tied at 49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes’ layup, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter by scoring 12 of the final 14 points.
Atlanta have dominated the third quarter so far in the series, outscoring Golden State 63-35 across the three games.
With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who was fouled.
Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.
This game was originally scheduled to be played on Thursday at the Gateway Center Arena, where the Dream play most of their home games. The league was able to work with the Atlanta Hawks and State Farm Arena to play the next two games of the championship series there so that they could have a much bigger crowd. Gateway seats only 3,500. State Farm Arena can seat more than 17,000 fans.
“Protect home court,” Howard said of the team’s focus. “Giving our fans a show. We fought for this arena so we had to protect it. It’s big. We went and stole one but we can’t let them come in and do the same thing.”
Wednesday night’s game was sold out, as is Game 4 on Saturday, which will also be played at State Farm Arena. The crowd included several music stars, including Ludacris and 2 Chainz, as well as actor Kerry Washington.
Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom said he was going to be at the game. The Atlanta Dream and State Farm Arena offered him a private suite for his protection. He refused to sit in it and was removed from the game .
The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed their first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket for the Valkyries with 4:39 left. They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive three-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.
The hot three-point shooting continued in the second quarter as Atlanta built their lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State were able to hang around and trailed only 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48%) from behind the arc. That was more made three-pointers in the first 20 minutes than in either Game 1 or Game 2.
Reese had 15 points and WNBA sixth woman of the year Janelle Salaun had 11 for the Valkyries.
Games 1 and 2 had huge ratings, with the opener on NBC averaging 2.1 million viewers, the most ever to watch the first game of the finals. Game 2, which was broadcast on USA Network, averaged 1.33 million viewers.

title: Man fined after 700 frozen and taxidermied animals found on Victorian property
description: Antiques store owner, 74, pleads guilty to 13 charges after regulator uncovers hundreds of animals at his home and shop
content:
Antiques store owner, 74, pleads guilty to 13 charges after regulator uncovers hundreds of animals at his home and shop
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
The white-walled room packed with magpies, galahs and sulphur-crested cockatoos, foxes and possums is eerily quiet. As a video pans across shelves filled with these and many other species, there is no flapping or squawking or hissing; the animals are frozen and silent.
They are among the more than 700 native animals that were found illegally taxidermied and frozen that were seized from the property of a Victorian antiques store owner last year.
On Tuesday, 74-year-old Glenn Richard Rollo was fined $10,000 by a court after he pleaded guilty to 13 charges, including selling and possessing protected and threatened wildlife and failing to provide treatment to a sick animal.
The regulator searched his property as part of a broader crackdown on the illegal wildlife trade, executing search warrants for the man’s store and home in April last year. Restrictions on selling and possessing threatened and protected species apply to both living and dead animals.
During their search they found 14 freezers containing animals. Across the property they found hundreds of dead reptiles, native birds and mammals, including 78 emus, 42 brushtail possums and 26 echidnas. They also found the remains of threatened species, including the barking owl, diamond python and Murray River short-necked turtle.
In addition to the dead animals, 15 live reptiles were found in enclosures, including North American red-eared slider turtles and corn snakes. Six of the reptiles, the regulator said, were not being kept under the required animal welfare standards.
The regulator said the man did not have the licence of authorisation under Victoria’s wildlife laws to obtain or possess the animals.
Wildlife in Victoria is protected under the Wildlife Act 1975, which outlaws taking native animals without approval. A commercial wildlife licence or private wildlife licence is required to trade dead animals.
Victorians who wish to taxidermy animals are also required obtain a licence under the conservation regulator. The man did not hold a licence.
During an appearance before Kynton local court on Tuesday, magistrate Patrick Southey reportedly told the man: “It is bewildering that a man of your intelligence and knowledge and love of wildlife would arrogantly flout the law so comprehensively.”
The conservation regulator director of regulatory operations, Cal Heppell, said: “The scale of offending in this case highlights why Victoria has strong protections in place for wildlife and animal welfare.
“Our laws and permit systems help protect wildlife from unlawful exploitation, ensure animals are appropriately cared for and safeguard Victoria’s environment and biodiversity from potential threats.
“These requirements are not optional. Anyone who keeps, trades or possesses wildlife must comply with the law.”
Victoria Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell said the wildlife laws in Victoria are not strong enough and called on the government to modernise the 50-year-old welfare act. “This is a horrific case that has rattled our community of Kyneton but it should serve as a wake-up call as to just how broken our so-called wildlife protection laws are here in Victoria,” she said. Purcell said that the $10,000 fine for possessing 700 dead native animals and keeping reptiles in poor conditions was “barely a deterrent and doesn’t send a message to the community that wildlife are respected and protected in Victoria”. “The government talks a big game about protecting wildlife but cases like this show just how badly our native animals are being let down. If hundreds of native animals can end up dead in someone’s collection, questions need to be asked why the government has continued to stall when it comes to ensuring these laws meet community expectations.”

title: 860 review – Billy Crystal’s charisma powers rambling one-man play
description: The veteran actor charms with stories about his colorful life and losing his home in the LA fires while taking jabs at Trump
content:
Imperial Theatre, New York City The veteran actor charms with stories about his colorful life and losing his home in the LA fires while taking jabs at Trump
I n his review of the 1986 buddy comedy Running Scared, Roger Ebert wrote that Billy Crystal and Gregory Hines, the film’s leads, “don’t need a plot because they have so much good dialogue and such a great screen relationship”. With a bit of paraphrasing, Ebert’s description of that chemistry works just the same when discussing Crystal’s relationship to the New York stage, where the legendary funnyman has made a cozy home for himself this century.
His 2004 one-man show 700 Sundays won a special Tony and was brought back nearly a decade later to be filmed for HBO. Then came Mr Saturday Night in 2022, which Crystal adapted from an earlier movie and which was tepidly, politely received. Still, most agreed there is little that Crystal’s born charisma can’t overcome, and he scored a Tony nomination for best actor.
His latest solo show, 860 , proves again that there’s likely no such thing as a bad time in Crystal’s company, even if its structure stretches any notion of “plot”. Named after the address of the Los Angeles house he inhabited for most of his life, it finds Crystal in an existential but ultimately grateful mode, having lost that longtime home to the region’s fires last year and taking stock of his improbably rich 78 years on earth.
Under Scott Ellis’s direction, it’s a perfectly enjoyable 100-minute trip down memory lane – or, more accurately, into Crystal’s former home office, which he’d furnished with all sorts of career mementos. “It wasn’t a man cave, it was a ME cave,” he explains. “Every picture had a story.”
Much of the show takes the feel of arriving at Crystal’s favorite stop on his house tour. There’s a light sense of chronology, stretching from the home’s 1979 purchase toward the present day, but it’s mostly guided by Crystal’s delight in sharing his life’s stories as each loosely connects to the next.
He lends these tales a believable awe, evincing an everyman persona just as wowed by his achievements and highlights through a blend of his standup self-deprecation and the sheer length of his time in the public eye as a well-liked performer. He’s just as surprised as anyone to have built an ongoing rapport with, say, Muhammad Ali or with Mickey Mantle, one of his heroes and with whom he bonded over losing fathers at an early age.
The elder Crystal’s death formed the backbone of 700 Sundays, which focused on the 15 years they spent together and so had stronger thematic cohesion. Crystal was about a decade into his career by the time he and his beloved wife, Janice, moved into the Pacific Palisades home, and the wider pool of stories from which to pick occasionally feels too unfocused.
It does carry over some of that previous show’s sentimentality, sometimes through original music composed by Marc Shaiman, a longtime Crystal collaborator, or when recounting the aftermath of the fires, once he was able to return to the now-destroyed site.
There’s no mention of the catastrophic climate changes that have led to California’s recent fires, despite a handful of (eye-rolling inducing) anti-Trump potshots, which the audience heartily eats up. Crystal does get a good equal-opportunity jab at Biden, though, who apparently confused the comedian with Billy Joel at his own Kennedy Center Honors.
There’s also no deeper reckoning with the idea of loss, which could seem like asking too much from what is essentially a standup act, though it does include tributes to friends Rob Reiner and Robin Williams.
Scott Pask’s set is mostly suggestive, leaving Hana S Kim and Kylee Loera’s video designs to do the heavy lifting. Some of the choices, such as vertical iPhone videos taken by Crystal during and after the fires, are touching, like those shared by an older relative. Others are less graceful – firmly in the visual aids category – as when a film still accompanies a reference to the spooky twins from The Shining.
As a frequent Oscars host, Crystal is expert at maintaining an agreeable atmosphere without sacrificing character or zingers, and it’s tough to muster much to complain about this production, however slight it might end up feeling. The man has an iron-clad grip on an audience’s attention that feels unforced, only inching us closer. These days, an appreciation for the live art of the raconteur is as welcome as ever.
860 is at the Imperial Theatre , New York City, until 3 January 2027
