title: Ukraine war briefing: New peace proposals lack ‘substance’, says Kremlin after Witkoff-Putin meeting in Russia
description: US envoy Witkoff presented Putin with proposals drafted by Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo earlier this week. What we know on day 1,702
content:
US envoy Witkoff presented Putin with proposals drafted by Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo earlier this week. What we know on day 1,702
The Kremlin has criticised new peace proposals to end the war after US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian leader Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday. Commenting on the meeting, which followed talks with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in Norway, the Kremlin warned there was little “substance” in the Ukrainian and European proposals. Despite the lukewarm response from Russia, US president Donald Trump claimed it was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war. A day before travelling to Russia, Witkoff met Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo in a meeting aimed at smoothing over a bitter rift between the Ukrainian president and Trump.
Commenting on the Witkoff-Putin meeting, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Russia was “in principle, ready to resume” the trilateral talks in mid-November – after crucial US midterm elections – and that the Kremlin wanted them to focus on postwar security. Ushakov said Witkoff briefed Putin on “some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv” from the Oslo meeting, but added that “there wasn’t really much substance in them”. Zelenskyy said Kyiv backed resuming trilateral talks as soon as possible.
Witkoff said his talks with Putin were “constructive” but that “there is still important work left to do” . Discussions would continue between the US, Ukraine and Russia at the technical level, he added.
However, the US envoy has face sharp criticism at home for describing Putin as a “humanitarian” , after the Russian leader agreed to free US citizen Stephen Hubbard from a Russian prison. US Republican senator Thom Tillis posted on X: “WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian’.” Trump brushed off Witkoff’s comments, saying “I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other”, while US vice-president JD Vance said: “I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.”
Later, after a Russian ​strike on ⁠Kyiv that ​followed the talks, Ukrainian foreign minister ⁠Andrii Sybiha said that “appeasement, ⁠servility ​and flattery” ‌would ‌not ‌stop Russia’s war.
Putin’s order to release Hubbard as he met Witkoff appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections, writes Pjotr Sauer . Trump had previously asked Putin to free Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Trump said on social media: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Missiles struck Kyiv in the early hours of ⁠Thursday and Ukraine sent hundreds of drones towards Moscow overnight , authorities said, as the two sides kept up a barrage of attacks ⁠despite the latest ⁠US mediation attempts. The Russian strikes wounded 15 people and damaged subway infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River in the Ukrainian ⁠capital while also restricting traffic there, Kyiv authorities said. The strikes came after another attack on the city on Wednesday evening that wounded six people. In Ukraine’s north-east, a Russian strike ⁠killed a woman and injured another four people in the Kharkiv region, governor ​Oleh Syniehubov said. And a drone hit energy infrastructure in ‌the Kremenchuk area in the Poltava region, a local official said. In Russia, two people were wounded near Moscow after 630 drones were sent towards the capital during the night, mayor Sergei Sobyanin ‌said. Most of the drones were downed at long range, he added.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said decisions regarding Ukraine’s access to Starlink were ⁠up to its parent company ⁠SpaceX and Elon Musk, ​not the White House , comments that suggested Musk may have restricted Kyiv’s access to the service. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered the slowdown of a military-grade ⁠version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on to defend itself against missile attacks from Russia. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said the US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes after the Norway meeting with Witkoff.

title: ‘Man, I loved that’: Trump cheers South Carolina rally attender who hit protester
description: President was reportedly heckled at least nine times during campaign event for Darline Graham
content:
President was reportedly heckled at least nine times during campaign event for Darline Graham
How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions
Multiple protesters were removed from Donald Trump’s rally at South Carolina’s Clemson University on Wednesday, including one who was apparently punched by a rally attender – to the US president’s delight.
“That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that. I watched that,” Trump said. “That was incredible. Wow. That was unbelievable. Is everybody OK?
“Who’s the guy that threw that punch?” he continued. “You know, you reminded me of Evander, the real deal, Holyfield,” referring to the former heavyweight champion, who was also in attendance at the rally.
“You gotta give them credit. It takes courage to do that at a Trump rally,” he said. “He got whacked.”
According to a pool report, the president was interrupted at least nine times by hecklers. The crowd chanted “USA” as security guards escorted the ​protesters out of the arena.
One protester who was removed by security was followed by a rally attendee, who appeared to slap the demonstrator on the head.
Trump was in South Carolina to support Darline Graham, the sister of late senator Lindsey Graham who died suddenly in July from a heart condition. Graham, appointed to her brother’s seat, is facing Democratic challenger Annie Andrews in her bid for a full six-year term.
Protests have frequently erupted at Trump rallies in recent weeks, as the president has ramped up his campaign stops in the final weeks before the 3 November midterm elections. The president often brushes off the demonstrations as being carried out by “paid protesters”.
Trump’s 32-day campaign blitz has largely taken him to Republican-leaning areas that he won comfortably in previous elections, underscoring the challenges facing Republicans as they try to retain control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives.
The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, published on Monday, found that 31% of Americans approve of Trump’s performance in office, a record low for the president.

title: Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks
description: Russia frees Stephen Hubbard after US request while Steve Witkoff praises Putin, wanted by ICC as war criminal, as a ‘humanitarian’
content:
Russia frees Stephen Hubbard after US request while Steve Witkoff praises Putin, wanted by ICC as war criminal, as a ‘humanitarian’
Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American man from a Russian jail as he met Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine, amid increasingly close relations between Moscow and Washington.
Trump had previously asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine .
His release appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine , while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections.
Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia , rather than as part of a prisoner exchange as has often been the case with previous releases of Americans held in the country.
Writing on social media after the release was announced, Trump said it followed a request he had made “directly” to Putin last week.
He wrote on Truth Social: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Hubbard’s younger sister told the Associated Press she had spoken to her brother, who said he had thought he was “going to die in prison”.
“He’s out of Russia territory. He is free, praise God,” Patricia Hubbard Fox said, adding that her brother suffered beatings and starvation while he was held captive.
Witkoff, meanwhile, lavished praise on Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.
The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war.
More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher.
The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting: “We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.”
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.
Witkoff described his meeting with Putin as “constructive” but said “important work” remained and trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine “at the technical level” would follow.
The Kremlin said it had agreed “in principle” to the talks, which would focus on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended.
The latest rupture in relations between Washington and Kyiv was triggered by Trump’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal with Putin, followed by his call for Zelenskyy to be replaced after Ukraine refused to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv has since complained of disruptions to US intelligence-sharing and restrictions on its access to Starshield , the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Washington had resumed providing advance warnings of Russian missile attacks after his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo.
But Ukraine continues to face restrictions on Starshield, although it remains unclear who ordered them. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, while Reuters, citing sources, said the directive had come from inside the White House.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Wednesday that the decision to restrict Ukraine’s access came from Musk.
“I’m not aware that we knew ​about this decision beforehand. But that’s irrelevant,” Rubio told reporters ‌during a trip to India.
“The bottom ‌line is that, that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds ‌they’ll allow it to be used at.”
During Wednesday’s meeting with Witkoff, Putin thanked Trump and his wife, Melania, for “their attention to efforts to end the war”.
Yet there are few signs of an imminent breakthrough. Despite repeated Ukrainian calls for a ceasefire, including a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow has given little indication that it intends to end its bombardment of Ukraine as winter approaches, apparently confident that continued pressure will help it extract greater concessions from Kyiv.
The Russian leader remains intent on sticking to his maximalist war aims, including his demand for full Russian control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.
Putin also sought to emphasise the prospects for closer economic ties between Russia and the US once the war ends, suggesting that Moscow could significantly increase its exports of fertilisers to the American market.
Russian officials said the first tanker carrying diesel to the US would depart on Thursday as part of an initial shipment of about 300,000 tonnes.
Energy analysts and traders have questioned whether Trump’s agreement to temporarily resume Russian diesel imports will deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections, arguing that the volumes involved are too small to significantly ease the global supply squeeze.
The talks on Wednesday also touched on a possible meeting in China next month between Putin, Trump and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. The Kremlin said Beijing was already making preparations for what it described as an unprecedented summit between the three leaders.

title: Sam Wood makes bid for bail to supreme court over domestic violence charges
description: Former reality star and wellness influencer stands accused of choking and assaulting wife at Noosa in Queensland
content:
Former reality star and wellness influencer stands accused of choking and assaulting wife at Noosa in Queensland
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Former reality television star Sam Wood will go to the Queensland supreme court seeking release from custody, more than two weeks after he was denied bail over allegations he choked and assaulted his wife.
Wood, a 46-year-old wellness influencer from Melbourne, was arrested at Noosa on 4 October on domestic violence allegations.
He was refused bail by a Queensland court after police detailed evidence about a similar incident from Victoria about three years ago and argued that his behaviour was “escalating”.
Wood is now seeking for the bail decision to be reviewed by the supreme court.
Under Queensland’s domestic violence laws, serious charges including “strangulation in a domestic setting” carry a presumption against bail.
Wood appeared in a Sunshine Coast court earlier this month charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting.
The court heard that his wife, Snezana, was supportive of the charges and that “there was a cessation of breath” as she was allegedly choked.
“She articulates the banging of her head on the floor. She couldn’t breathe,” police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris said. “She thought she was going to die.”
In Wood’s first application for bail, lawyer Matthew Cuskelly said his client denied the allegations. He cited a psychologist’s report that said Sam Wood was suffering from “severe depression”.
“He ought to be given the opportunity to engage with mental health professionals,” Cuskelly said.
“And also try to salvage something of his professional reputation and career, which is taking a hell of a beating at the moment.
“Ultimately, as all families have, there was problems. And my client had been enduring the hardship of attempting to quarantine those problems from his family for some period of time. It was agonising.”
Cuskelly cited a psychologist’s report that describes “the difficulty that my client has been enduring in respect of the deterioration of his psychological state”.
“His depression is regarded as extremely severe.”
Wood spent four days in the Maroochydore police watch house after his arrest. He was subsequently held in the high-security Wolston correctional centre near Brisbane.
It is understood the supreme court bail hearing won’t take place until next month, meaning Wood will spend at least a month in custody.

title: Flaw in PHP computer language leads to shutdown of websites around world
description: Precautionary takedowns come as experts say vulnerability in PHP, which is used by 70% of sites, could be exploited
content:
Precautionary takedowns come as experts say bad actors could exploit vulnerability in language used by 70% of sites
Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web.
Belgian, Dutch, Finnish, French and German sites were among those that governments took down temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70% of websites .
The vulnerability in the programming language, which became public on Tuesday, sparked warnings from national security agencies in Washington and London. It means millions of websites will need to be fixed. One internet infrastructure expert said Russian state actors or organised criminals could exploit the flaw to carry out cyber-attacks.
WordPress, one of the most common website systems, uses PHP, as does Wikipedia, the messaging software Slack and – at least historically – much of Facebook. The Wikimedia Foundation said it had taken down several systems on Wednesday as a precautionary measure until they could be patched.
The organisation behind the language issued a patch on Wednesday after researchers testing cyberdefences discovered the flaw. The US National Security Agency told all organisations using PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately. It said the vulnerability could “provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database”.
The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for “backdoors installed by an attacker”.
Because a fix is now public and AI tools are able to reverse engineer the bug with little effort, experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers ⁠jumped to get ahead of the updates.
AI was powering a “race to exploit”, said Costin Raiu, co-founder of cybersecurity research and incident response firm TLP:Black. He said the next step was the “mass compromise of every vulnerable web server on the internet”.
Prof Alan Woodward, a cybersecurity expert at Surrey University, said: “It was very surprising and troubling because of the extent to which PHP was used around the world. PHP issued a patch very quickly. The big thing is for everyone using it to get that in to make sure their systems are safe.
“The troubling part is there is going to be a long tail of websites who may not be maintained as well and they are going to remain vulnerable, which means we may see weeks and months of ongoing attacks. For the big juicy targets, I hope to goodness they are being patched quickly.”
Woodward said there was a window of opportunity for bad actors. “There is this race and some people unfortunately don’t even know they are in the race.”
OpenAI said it led a coalition of researchers that discovered the flaw and claimed “frontier AI” had been key. The researcher who found the weakness, however, said they used models available to the public.
Cybersecurity company Calif said in a blog post it found the flaws with the help of a large language model on 1 August and had been working on a fix ever since. Alphabet-owned cybersecurity company Wiz said in a blog post that it too had discovered it with the help of Wiz Atlas, its autonomous AI vulnerability research tool, as well as Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol.
The vulnerabilities remained hidden ‌in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz’s post said.
In a blog post late on Wednesday, Amazon security chief CJ Moses said its security team detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities against one of its decoy “honeypot” systems on 17 October, four days before public disclosure.
The attempt on the system came from an anonymous internet address, suggesting the activity was conducted by a threat actor, Moses said, adding that it was unclear how the actor learned of the flaws while they were under embargo.
In a statement, the ​White House said it was made aware of the flaw on Friday.
In the UK, websites belonging to Edinburgh, Bristol and Oxford councils were taken offline. In France, local government websites including that of the Paris police prefecture went offline on Wednesday, as did in the Netherlands the national digital identity service, the website of the house of representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity centre.
The Australian Signals Directorate was temporarily affected by the outage overnight local time, with the national cyber defence agency noting other government websites may have been similarly affected.
Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said: “There’s going to be a lot of automatic exploitation of this.” The bug might allow cryptocurrency miners to exploit vulnerable servers at other people’s expense, he said.
He also said large crime organisations and Russian state actors could use the vulnerable sites as a launching pad from which to conduct distributed denial of service (DDoS) and other cyber-attacks.
The issue highlighted the poor state of internet infrastructure, Woźniak said, something that was being brought to light by advancing AI models but that had been a long-developing problem. The underlying vulnerabilities the researcher found were decades old.
“This is an environmental problem in an industry where there’s an incentive to move fast and make changes,” he said. “There’s an incentive to deploy a thing and then never update it and not think about maintenance.”

title: I spent a week watching Helen Haines in action in Canberra. It was the most inspiring week of my life
description: Somehow, among all the meetings, media commitments and delivering rousing speeches – she managed to bake seven sponge cakes for the people around her
content:
Somehow, among all the meetings, media commitments and delivering rousing speeches – she managed to bake seven sponge cakes for the people around her
Life has been feeling heavy for a while but since Monday it has felt overwhelming.
Our communities have been through so much: bushfires, floods, fugitives, lockdowns and bushfires – and that’s only since 2019. Throughout all this there has been one familiar face lightening the load during uncertain times: the smiling face of Helen Haines .
During past disasters it always felt as though there were things we could do to help each other. Right now it’s really hard to know what to do. It’s pretty simple to understand how a fire starts or why a flood stops but in this moment things seem so much more complex.
I had just returned from a run when I found out what had happened to Helen. The feeling is almost indescribable, a mixture of disbelief, anger and sadness.
My immediate thought was how could this have happened to her? Of all people? Surely this is not real. What do I say? What can you say to something so senseless?
I felt sick. I still feel sick. I keep asking myself: what do I do? How do we respond to this? What do we do when the person we use for strength is the person needing ours?
This grief and confusion is palpable throughout the hills and valleys of Indi, and it feels as though it has spread across the country. Everyone shares the same sense of bewilderment. We are all asking the question none of us can answer: how did we get here?
Two years ago, at the age of 30, I decided to move home to my small country town. Mansfield sits at the base of the Victorian Alps and is in the Indi electorate.
I’ve told people a multitude of reasons for moving home but, in truth, I moved back because I wanted to be more involved with what Helen and her team have been building up here. A genuine sense of community that is founded on the idea that democracy is for us and by us. Lasting outcomes are found in our commonalities, not our differences.
Helen’s courage and humility as a leader inspired me to stand to be a councillor in the local elections. Like Helen, I ran as an independent. I wanted to emulate the kind of compassion and honesty she demonstrates.
Representing your community is tough. Our communities are diverse, with an array of interests across a spectrum of issues. Some people agree with each other, some don’t. But that is the price we pay to live in a democracy. It’s between our differences that we find the best solutions.
Helen is the embodiment of this. Her mission to bring more integrity and transparency into politics is founded in the belief that compassion will prevail.
In May I spent a week in Canberra as part of Helen’s parliamentary volunteer program, attending meetings and observing how our representative serves our communities in the big house.
That week was the most inspiring of my life.
Somehow, during budget week – among all the meetings, media commitments and delivering rousing speeches – Helen managed to bake seven sponge cakes for the people around her. Seeing the way she interacted with people from across the political spectrum was inspirational. She gives everyone the same kindness, compassion and fair consideration.
The access and respect that we volunteers would get because we were associated with Helen was astounding. Not just from politicians but from staff, from at the library to those in the canteen – Helen’s reputation afforded us all the same veneration.
How many people can say that their reputation not only precedes them but rubs off on everyone around them too?
I’m still not sure how she made all those cakes in a tiny kitchen but, at the end of the week, when we sat on the couch in her office, she told me why she did it. In typical Helen style, she simply said it was because people appreciate a bit of kindness, and everyone loves cake.
The complex problems we face can feel insurmountable. But if we were all a bit more like Helen, we’d work our way through them together. Maybe it’s time for us to collectively do away with left-right polarisation and instead look forward together with a shared perspective.
Because it’s only together that we will find the best solutions. As a collective we all pretty much want the same thing: clean air, fresh water and to spend time with the people we love. I for one hope that Helen gets a lot more time to do just that.
Throughout all of this I come back to that same thought. What would Helen do?
I think she’d be getting out into her community, wrapping her arms around everyone, and saying, “C’mon, have another slice of cake.”

title: Officials confirm flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite found in US wildlife
description: USDA says screwworm found in elk in Texas, and warns hunters and ranchers to be vigilant to help stop spread
content:
USDA says screwworm found in elk in Texas, and warns hunters and ranchers to be vigilant to help stop spread
The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) said on Wednesday it had ⁠confirmed the ⁠first detection ​of the flesh-eating parasite the New World screwworm in US wildlife in an ⁠elk in Pecos county, Texas .
The elk was located on a game ⁠ranch and was reported after being killed by ​a hunter, the ‌USDA said ‌in a statement.
The Texas animal health ‌commission will modify a previously established infested zone, and the USDA and the Texas parks and wildlife department is conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area, the USDA said.
“We encourage all hunters and landowners to be vigilant for signs of New World screwworm while they are out in the field this season,” the Texas wildlife division director, Alan Cain, said in a statement.
Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central ​America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports.
The US halted livestock imports ⁠from Mexico last year to keep out screwworm, ​but ​resumed trade in August ​at an Arizona port as part ​of a ‌phased reopening ​plan.
The halt has tightened US cattle supplies and pushed beef prices to record highs for American consumers.
Despite those efforts, the screwworm was detected in June on a calf in Texas’s Zavala county, located near the US-Mexico border. There have since been dozens of cases detected in the US this year, including on a horse and on a dog.

title: Macron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest
description: Leaders criticised for spreading misleading information as France prepares for further protests this weekend
content:
Leaders criticised for spreading misleading information as France prepares for further protests this weekend
Emmanuel Macron has accused Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of making “stupid comments” about France’s street unrest for political gain, as the country prepared for more protests this weekend.
Speaking during a visit to Qatar, the French president did not name names but said “manipulation of information” after Saturday’s riots had led to “comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders”.
Asked if he was referring to Donald Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.” The US president has blamed France’s violence on “migrants, jihadists and communists” as he campaigns for his Republican party before midterm elections.
Macron told reporters in Doha that some leaders “in the middle of election campaigns, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic” were “naively spreading narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote”.
They were “using our country for their own political campaigns”, the French president said. “And we don’t need that. We already have difficulties to deal with.”
He said AI-generated images were circulating “depicting scenes that never actually happened in France . We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.”
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections next weekend, has also said that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Analysts have dismissed claims that migrants were the main factor in France’s protests.
Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has erupted six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday.
Largely peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living rapidly descended into rampant violence and extensive looting , especially in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges, where the town hall was set on fire and partly destroyed.
Police said that protests would be banned in parts of Paris on Thursday as the city braced for more demonstrations.
The ban, from 8am to 8pm, will apply to key landmarks, including the Elysee presidential palace, both houses of parliament, and tourist havens such as the Louvre museum and the Champs-Elysees.
Other areas where rallies will be prohibited include the Bastille and République squares, and the Châtelet-Les Halles shopping area which was heavily targeted by looters over the weekend.
The unrest has prompted several countries to issue travel warnings for France and rattled already nervous financial markets, with the yield on the French government’s benchmark 10-year bonds passing 5% on Wednesday , its highest since 2002.
Macron pledged to prevent any repeat of last weekend’s convulsions, as the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) grassroots protest movement formally filed plans for a march through the centre of Paris ⁠on Saturday that is likely to be the ⁠government’s next big test.
Student groups have also called for protests on the same day to push demands for greater investment in education. The gilets jaunes activists aim to revive their nationwide 2018 campaign against rising living costs and declining public services.
“Those who want to cause disorder in city centres next Saturday will be prevented from doing so,” Macron told reporters in the Gulf, where he was seeking energy deals to help offset rising fuel costs. “There must be no wavering at the top of the state.”
Government ministers have promised a “massive” and vastly reinforced security operation after acknowledging shortcomings in their initial response last weekend, with some troops expected to be deployed alongside police reinforcements.
Partial night-time curfews imposed on Monday and Tuesday in areas prone to violent protests and looting in cities around France, including Paris, Marseille and Lille, have helped ensure relative calm and were expected to be renewed on Wednesday.
France’s main trade unions have separately called a nationwide mobilisation for 5 November. Sophie Binet, the head of the CGT union, said: “There is huge and legitimate anger, and the answer to that situation is not repression. It is a political response.”
Macron insisted France “doesn’t need a state of emergency”, saying it “has the means” to control any further unrest. Union representatives met the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on Wednesday but no concrete announcements followed.
Justice minister Gérald Darmanin said on Wednesday that, of the 2,500 people taken into custody during and after the protests, 174 had been jailed. Another 917 had been formally prosecuted, he added.
Sometimes violent protests in European countries including Italy and Belgium have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading across the continent where with many nations, including France, face budget problems.
Italy’s government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there.

title: Labor, Coalition and crossbench MPs afraid at home and work after alleged attack on Helen Haines
description: Home and office safety a common concern in Australian federal police and Asio safety briefings with politicians following alleged attack on MP Helen Haines
content:
Home and office safety a common concern in Australian federal police and Asio safety briefings with politicians following alleged attack on MP Helen Haines
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
Security agencies will review safety precautions for MPs’ homes and offices after numerous federal politicians told police and Asio in safety briefings that they were worried about widening threats after the alleged attack on Helen Haines .
The Labor government and politicians across the parliament are still considering how they will respond when they return to Canberra next week, with ideas being floated including a new committee on MPs’ safety, greater resources for police, and motions of condolence for Haines, who lost both her legs after Monday’s incident . Renewed calls from the crossbench for reforms to question time and the tone of debate in parliament are unlikely to be taken up by the major parties.
In safety briefings with the Australian federal police and Asio granted to Labor, Coalition and crossbench MPs on Wednesday, security of homes and electorate offices was a common concern, according to Guardian Australia interviews with 10 MPs. While a broad review of safety and security is unlikely at this stage, multiple MPs across the political spectrum told Guardian Australia they had spent thousands of dollars of their own money to install safety features based on the advice of the federal police.
Federal ministers receive stronger security assistance but numerous backbenchers said they felt under-resourced, saying many angry constituents may see all politicians as a homogenous group, and may not differentiate between cabinet members and ordinary local MPs.
“People are getting activated now because they see us as part of the government. We represent the system to them, as much as anyone else,” independent Monique Ryan said.
Two years ago, the AFP recorded 951 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against office holders. Last year, that increased to 1,067.
On Thursday, a Western Australian man was charged after he allegedly made verbal threats while in possession of nunchucks outside an electoral office in Perth.
No one was injured as a result, Western Australia police said, and his bail was refused.
A number of politicians asked to speak anonymously to discuss reflections from the briefings. While many praised the AFP’s response when their staff contacted them – for instance, to seek advice on holding public events – some said they had received less timely assistance from local police when they requested help, such as to respond to aggressive visitors.
Numerous MPs said they did not want security guards or armed escorts for themselves in public but that they felt alarmed for the safety of their homes and families.
Some said they would feel more comfortable with cameras and floodlights at home, and had decided to pay for their own upgrades after not being offered such features in risk assessments conducted by security agencies. One independent MP said crossbenchers questioned whether extra home security features should be paid for by the public.
Several MPs said they wanted more security and safety support but questioned how much impact that would have on their overall safety and how much more the AFP could do.
Guardian Australia was told security officials had committed to assessing safety settings of MPs who raised specific concerns. While a broad-ranging government review is at this stage not expected, other responses could include giving MPs more information on the background work that policing agencies conduct year-round, such as threat assessments and periodic checks.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, told News24 his government had overseen “an increase in funding for security for members of parliament in the last couple of years”.
“We want to make sure that people can feel as much comfort as possible, that everything’s being done to maximise security,” he said. “But also, I think parliamentarians across the board are determined to make sure we can continue to engage as we need to in this great democracy of ours.”
A spokesperson for the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said: “Reviews of the threats faced by high office holders are constantly conducted by our agencies.”
Ryan, who is close with Haines, said she had rarely discussed safety arrangements with fellow MPs until recent times but claimed many colleagues were “now realising they’re having common experiences”. She was supportive of a broader review into safety and more resources to secure offices.
“If it makes my team feel better and safer to have bollards out the front, I’m happy,” she said.
Two Labor MPs said some government backbenchers had expressed frustrations towards the finance department for not adequately funding safety measures for their electorate offices or doing so in a timely way. One said money was “always an issue” with the department, and expected more MPs to be directly lobbying the prime minister to improve office security.
Nationals MP Sam Birrell, whose electorate neighbours Haines’s in Indi, said regional politicians had particular concerns, with many being highly visible in their communities and locals often knowing where they lived.
“Some of the MPs were frustrated there’s not clear advice on things like whether to advertise mobile offices or have signs on cars,” he said.
“There were some complaints about whether people are able to get fairly modest security measures … that needs to be reviewed.”
Multiple people across meetings raised concerns about how to protect electorate office staff.
Liberal senator James Paterson told Radio National electorate offices were “very exposed” and were “not well protected”.
Asio and AFP have been contacted for comment.

title: Aneurin Bevan’s personal security file was ‘remarkably tame’ – National Archives
description: Some in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interest
content:
Some in UK’s security services questioned why Welsh Labour firebrand was of interest
Aneurin “Nye” Bevan, the Welsh Labour firebrand who spearheaded the creation of the NHS, was monitored by security services for more than two decades, though his personal file was “remarkably tame”, according to official files released to the public.
Bevan came to MI5’s attention in the 1930s over concerns about his links with known communists, papers released to the National Archives show. Monitoring continued even after he became a minister in the postwar Labour government that created the NHS.
At one point, his links to a known Russian spy led to the then director general of MI5 approaching prime minister Clement Attlee to warn him.
However, the papers show, some in the security services questioned why Bevan was of interest. Although there is nothing in the files to indicate that MI5 ever tapped his phone or intercepted his mail, one officer wrote in 1943: “I do not think that Bevan’s activities are a matter in which we, the Security Service, should be involved.
“In fact he makes exactly the same remarks in the Houses of Parliament pretty frequently, as any copy of Hansard will show, and it would not therefore be possible to do anything positive.”
Reviewing the file after his death in 1960, another MI5 officer noted: “Considering what a controversial character Nye Bevan was, the file is remarkably tame.”
MI5 first opened a personal file on the backbench Labour MP for Ebbw Vale in South Wales in 1933. He was described in one entry to have “inherited the evangelical fervour of his Welsh forebears and knows how to use it in the communist cause.”
He was also noted to have been “in close touch” with Harry Pollitt, general secretary of the Communist party of Great Britain, and others in the party who backed his plan to organise “workers’ freedom groups” to defend against “capitalists”.
Bevan fell out with his communist allies who had complained he was not interested in workers’ unity and was intent on building “a movement of his own”. But by 1936 they had reconciled, with Bevan supporting an application by the Communist party to affiliate with the Labour party.
In 1949, MI5 became concerned about Bevan’s friendship with Wilfred Macartney, who had been convicted of spying for Russia in 1928.
Recordings of Macartney’s conversations suggested he was passing on information obtained by Bevan to Pollitt. It led the director general Sir Percy Sillitoe to approach Attlee, who dismissed Macartney’s claims as a “tissue of lies” but agreed to “warn” Bevan about Macartney.
The file was finally closed in 1975, 15 years after Bevan died.
Other newly released papers show MI5 feared communists could attempt to disrupt the coronation of King George VI, with Communist party activists closely watched before the Westminster Abbey ceremony in 1937.
While the party prepared a propaganda drive and printed a million anti-monarchist leaflets to be distributed during coronation week, members were warned to avoid antagonising a largely pro-royalist public.
One MI5 report from April 1937 noted that a “comrade” in Manchester had been “severely censured” for proposing a series of demonstrations as it would be “playing into the hands of the fascists and police”. “It has been pointed out that members will be ‘going against the stream’ in doing this and they must be careful to speak in such a way that they do not make themselves unpopular with their neighbours.”
Sir Michael Tippett, a leading British composer of the 20th century and a famed pacifist, was also monitored by MI5 as a suspected Trotskyist revolutionary, according to the files.
MI5 believed he joined first the Communist party and then the Trotskyists in the 1930s, and remained an active supporter until the end of the second world war.
The files suggest, however, he was unconvincing as a revolutionary. In one intercepted letter to a Communist party organiser in London, he complained of the difficulties of trying to combine his work as a communist with his life as a music teacher living in rural Surrey. His evening commitments meant that it was “quite impossible” for him to attend “cell” meetings in London, he complained.
A report from 1955 noted that Tippett “has not come to notice in connection with communist or Trotskyist affairs”.
However, his radical past meant that as late as 1959 he was blocked from taking up a Foreign Office-sponsored lectureship in Germany, and it was only in the 1960s that MI5 were prepared to give him a clean bill of health. In 1966, he was knighted for services to music. He died in 1998 aged 93.

title: Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn
description: Committee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decade
content:
Committee cites shortfalls of submarines and warships and says ‘dramatic progress’ needed by end of decade
Britain risks failing to deter future Russian aggression in the high north beyond the UK because of shortfalls in the number and availability of Royal Navy submarines and warships, MPs on the defence select committee have said.
The committee focused on the slow deployment of HMS Dragon to Cyprus this spring, declining numbers of frigates, and reports that all five Astute-class attack submarines were in dock this summer as evidence of a navy under-resourced for the threat.
“The UK needs to be willing to address a hard truth: it does not currently have all the capabilities to operate successfully in the high north,” said Tan Dhesi, the committee chair. “Publicly available evidence of low availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines calls into question whether the UK can meet its commitments.”
The high north, the seas beyond Scotland, have become increasingly strategically significant amid growing Russian interest in energy pipelines and undersea cables at a time when Arctic seaways are opening up because of global heating.
The navy shadowed a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, operating inside the UK’s economic waters in November and January last year, accusing sailors onboard of trying to map strategic cables and shining lasers at RAF pilots monitoring them.
Russia also wants to assert control over the emerging northern sea route, a 3,500-mile (5,600km) shipping lane running along the country’s Arctic coast. It is the quickest maritime route from China to Europe, navigable last year for four and half months.
The MPs argued the UK needed to make “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade, and they called on the Ministry of Defence to draw up a plan to ensure more warships and submarines are at sea by 2030.
The problem would be particularly acute, the committee added, if the US did not support the UK in a crisis, a rare cross-party acknowledgment that under Donald Trump, US military help cannot be relied on, particularly if a small Nato member in the region was threatened or attacked.
“There would be critical military gaps if the United States were not involved in countering such [Russian] aggression,” the MPs said, and they argued that the UK, as the next largest Nato military in the region, had to be prepared to increase its navy.
It took more than three weeks for HMS Dragon, a destroyer, to arrive in the eastern Mediterranean in March after an RAF base in Cyprus was struck by a drone. No warships were available and Dragon had to be hauled out of dry dock to deploy.
The navy has five frigates with sonar dedicated to detecting Russian submarines at distance, the committee noted, lower than a target of eight, as ageing warships have been scrapped without replacements coming into service. It could take until 2037 before it reaches its stated requirement, the committee added.
None of Britain’s five Astute submarines, also used to track Russian maritime activity, were at sea from June and into the summer. They were in dock for a mixture of short-term and long-term refits, the committee noted, and they also lack the capability to operate under ice, unlike their Russian equivalents, although certification exercises are in progress.
However, no significant extra money is expected to be available for defence until the next decade, with Andy Burnham’s government committed to medium-term spending plans agreed under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer.
Though Starmer agreed to lift defence spending by about £30bn a year to 3.5% of GDP in 2035, he would only sign off spending to the lower level of 2.7% by 2030. That prompted the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary, only for him to return as chancellor under Burnham, with the old spending plans intact.
In response to the report, an MoD spokesperson highlighted a recent £330m investment to protect undersea infrastructure, and noted that Wes Streeting, now the defence secretary, had visited Iceland this month and watched how HMS St Albans, a frigate, tracked Russian submarines in the north Atlantic. “We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses,” they added.

title: Former Australia sprint champion Jake Doran charged with alleged child abuse
description: Police charge 26-year-old with indecent treatment of a child under 16 while Australian Athletics ban sprinter from any involvement in the sport
content:
Police charge 26-year-old with indecent treatment of child under 16
Australian Athletics ban sprinter from any involvement in the sport
Australia’s 2022 men’s 100m sprint champion has been arrested in Townsville for alleged indecent treatment of children.
Queensland police arrested Jake Doran on 13 October and he has been charged with one count of “indecent treatment of child under 16 (indecent film etc)”. Police investigations covered the period between January 2025 and September 2026.
The 26-year-old was bailed to appear at Townsville magistrates court on 5 November.
Doran, who works in business development at Tafe Queensland, has been training athletes in Townsville.
Australian Athletics confirmed he has no paid or unpaid role with the national governing body, but has banned him from any involvement in the sport while the matter is ongoing.
“Based on information provided to Australian Athletics, the organisation has imposed a provisional action on the athlete, prohibiting him from attending club, member association or Australian Athletics events, as well as banning him from participating in athletics training,” a spokesperson said.
“The safety and wellbeing of all participants in our sport is paramount, and we take all allegations of this nature very seriously.”
Doran has deleted his Instagram account, and his profile no longer appears on the Australian Athletics website.
Queensland Athletics declined to comment.
A Tafe Queensland spokesperson said: “Based on the information available at this time, the allegations are understood to be unrelated to the individual’s employment with Tafe Queensland, and there is no indication they relate to Tafe Queensland students, staff, training delivery, campus activities or operations.
“The employee has been suspended from duty while the matter is before the courts.”
The sprinter was the winner of the 100m at the Australian national championships in 2022, when he crossed the line ahead of current Australian representative Eddie Nketia in a wind-assisted time of 10.05sec.
Doran went on to compete for Australia at the world championships and Commonwealth Games, and also won the national 200m title in 2023.
He has been unable to replicate his early promise, however, and has not run the 100m faster than 10.39sec since 2023.
Queensland police said investigations continue.

title: ‘Cut the umbilical cord’: Bougainville’s bid to break away from Papua New Guinea faces reckoning
description: MPs in PNG to decide on ratifying a 2019 referendum in which Bougainvilleans voted overwhelmingly in favour of independence
content:
MPs in PNG to decide on ratifying a 2019 referendum in which Bougainvilleans voted overwhelmingly in favour of independence
For decades, the distant island of Bougainville has fought for secession from Papua New Guinea , for a future as an independent nation of its own.
This week, that long-running aspiration faces further challenge, with PNG’s parliament slated to debate the ratification of Bougainville’s 2019 UN-sanctioned referendum, in which nearly 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence.
That referendum was a key element of the 2001 Bougainville Peace Agreement, which ended a 10-year long civil war estimated to have killed as many as 15,000 people.
Even as violence has reemerged around the controversial Panguna mine – a catalyst for the conflict, but now seen as critical to the island’s independent financial future – Bougainville’s government has insisted it will not be deterred from secession. It has committed to “self-government” from next year, and to breaking away from PNG, as a fully fledged independent nation, by 2030.
Sources in Port Moresby and Bougainville say they expect the independence referendum result to be rejected on the floor of the PNG parliament, given the threshold for ratification has been raised to three-quarters of all MPs, not the two-thirds usually required for constitutional amendments.
The autonomous island of Bougainville, PNG’s easternmost province and about 1,000km from the capital, is home to about 300,000 people, culturally and ethnically distinct from the rest of the PNG archipelago. It has for decades, sought to break free of rule by Port Moresby.
Port Moresby has long resisted acting on Bougainville’s post-conflict independence, anxious not to establish a precedent for the break-up of PNG’s vast and culturally diverse archipelago, or to lose a resource-rich and potentially lucrative province.
Bougainville’s attorney-general and vice-president, Ezekiel Masatt, said that the MP vote threshold was “crafted” by the PNG government to defeat the vote.“There is a national government strategy to poison the waters and make it impossible to come close to reach the voting threshold,” he said in a June statement.
Opinions in PNG’s parliament were divided ahead of the referendum vote.
Dr Allan Marat, chair of a bipartisan committee on Bougainville matters, told parliament last month that the island had met all the conditions outlined in the 2001 peace agreement and deserved its independence.
“It seems there is only one humane option for us members of this honourable house to do … to cut the umbilical cord connecting baby ‘Bougainville Independence’ to PNG,” he said.
Others are fiercely opposed. Former deputy prime minister Belden Namah, who served in the PNG army during the Bougainville conflict, said the question went beyond a political debate.
“It is an issue of national sovereignty, it is an issue of constitutional integrity, it is an issue of peace, unity, sacrifice and the future survival of Papua New Guinea as one nation,” he told the same parliamentary sitting.
In June this year, Bougainville’s president Ishmael Toroama presented his government’s “ final position ” on the island’s political future.
He said Bougainville would enter a stage of “self-government” from 1 September 2027, before declaring itself independent “separate from the state of PNG” in 2030.
Toroama said he did not want a return to violence or conflict with Port Moresby. “Our objective has never been confrontation,” he said. “Our objective has always been reconciliation, partnership and a peaceful transition founded on law and mutual respect.”
The Bougainville government hopes the controversial Panguna gold and copper mine will fund independence. Carved from a mountain in the centre of the island, it was once one of the largest gold and copper mines in the world, and still has an estimated $60bn in unrealised reserves.
“We closed the mine because of oppression,” Toroama told the Guardian in an interview last year . “Today the mine is the key to our economic growth and settling all unresolved issues from the war.”
Multinational Rio Tinto and other international investors earned nearly $2bn from Panguna over 17 years of operation from 1972. But less than 1% of the mine’s profits went to Bougainvilleans, whose homes and lands were destroyed by it. The mine and surrounding river deltas remain dangerously polluted. Rio Tinto has signed an MOU with the Bougainville government to address the ongoing environmental and human rights impacts of the dormant mine.
Disaffected landowners ran a sabotage campaign that forced Panguna’s closure in 1989. The PNG government responded by sending in police, then soldiers, to restore law and order. Bougainville was blockaded and the island descended into a brutal civil war – known as ‘the crisis’ – that ran for a decade.
Violence returned to the mine last month, when up to 30 men carrying high-powered rifles drove into the sprawling Panguna pit site and set fire to nearly 40 heavy haulage trucks, excavators and water tanks owned by the newly appointed contractor, India’s Lloyds Metals and Energy.
Toroama said violence would not intimidate his government from redeveloping the mine.
“We will not cower to terroristic acts of violence designed to cause disunity and distract us from our agenda of creating a socio-politically and economically viable Bougainville,” he said after the incident.
Oliver Nobetau, Pacific islands program director at the Lowy Institute, an Australian thinktank, said it was well known across the island that “not everyone is on-side to reopen the mine”.
He said the incident, while relatively minor, had damaged the independence cause by affirming Port Moresby’s often-overstated concerns that Bougainville was not ready for independence, including that the island had not fully disarmed.
Nobetau said a “no” vote was looking increasingly likely in PNG’s parliament.
“My assessment is that it’s not going to spill over into actual conflict and fighting the way that people fear,” he said. “I think there’s going to be a lot of social tensions, a lot of political tensions, but I think eventually they’ll come back to the table to discuss how to move forward.”
Nobetau said the independence movement on Bougainville would not be deterred by resistance from Port Moresby.
“I think most likely they will try to go at it alone through the self-government model and then rolling out a three-year plan towards independence by 2030.”
