title: ‘It doesn’t look good’: Arteta concerned as Saka limps off against Bayern Munich
description: ‘A player off with really sharp pain is never good news,’ the Arsenal manager said after his winger was forced off 10 minutes into the 2-2 draw in Munich
content:
‘A player off with really sharp pain is never good news’
Winger forced off 10 minutes into Arsenal’s 2-2 draw
Mikel Arteta made no attempt to conceal his concern over the quad injury that forced Bukayo Saka out of Arsenal’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich , saying it did not “look good at all”.
The manager was delighted with the fight that his players showed, Declan Rice earning a deserved point with an 82nd-minute equaliser. Arsenal had led through Eberechi Eze, who came on in the 10th minute for the stricken Saka, before Harry Kane took centre stage. The Bayern striker set up Alphonso Davies for 1-1 before giving his team the lead from the penalty spot.
It was Saka’s setback that provided the sour note for Arsenal. He collapsed to the turf after a routine battle with Davies and walked off slowly after treatment. Saka was still moving in a very limited way as he left the stadium.
“It doesn’t look good at all but we have to wait and see,” Arteta said. “They [the medics] are a bit concerned. A player who has to come off with a really sharp pain is never good news. Bukayo did not start the game against Lille last Tuesday, then he started at Nottingham Forest on Sunday and it happened very early in this game. The level of intensity that this game requires, as well, is something incredible.
“You could see it on Tuesday night, the PSG-Barcelona game , what happened [with players getting injured ]. This is man-to-man for 96 minutes in every action. There’s no breathing. The stress, the quality, the intensity, the level that you need … it’s unbelievable. It’s the highest level. And those things happen, unfortunately.”
Arteta insisted that he wanted more than the draw. “We take it, although that doesn’t mean we are really happy about it as we prepared to win,” he said. “You could see that right from the beginning – the mindset, the purpose and the intention that the team has, to be very dominant, to come here and cause problems to Bayern. To press them and attack them. That’s certainly what we’ve done. We were the better team in the first 25 minutes, we got the goal … unfortunately we also got the injury of Bukayo, which was a big setback.
“The team showed incredible composure, the spirit to keep going, to attack them. The finishers came in and made an impact, as well. After scoring the goal [for 2-2], you see the reaction of the team. We wanted to take the ball and go and attack them again to come and win the game.”

title: Nancy Pelosi’s office latest recipient of letter containing white powder
description: Former speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm elections
content:
Former speaker is latest target of mailings sent to various Congress members in the lead-up to the midterm elections
California representative Nancy Pelosi’s office received “a suspicious letter” on Wednesday in what appears to be the latest incident of ill-intentioned mailings targeted at US Congress members before the midterm elections.
The offices of more than three dozen members of Congress across the political spectrum have received envelopes containing white powder in recent days. One lawmaker’s office said preliminary tests indicated the powder was not hazardous.
A spokesperson for Pelosi said the letter was “consistent with mailings reported by other congressional offices” and that everyone in the office was safe.
“Speaker Pelosi remains focused on serving the people of San Francisco and is concerned for the members and staff whose offices have experienced similar incidents,” Nicholas Martin, a spokesperson for the speaker emerita, said in a statement.
“She is grateful for the efforts of the US Capitol police, the San Francisco police department and other law enforcement agencies to thoroughly investigate this series of intimidation across America.”
More than 100 letters thought to contain white powder were reportedly thought to be circulating in the US mail system. Election offices across the US have also reported receiving suspicious mail.
The mailings are under investigation by the FBI, the Capitol police and the US Postal Inspection Service. The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement earlier this week: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.”

title: The Experiment review – easily the most disturbing thing on TV
description: As members of the public tour a fake ‘residential home’ for disabled people riddled with Nazi ideology, you desperately hope someone will speak up. Prepare for the most excruciating viewing of your life
content:
As members of the public tour a fake ‘residential home’ for disabled people riddled with Nazi ideology, you desperately hope someone will speak up. Prepare for the most excruciating viewing of your life
I have never had to pause a programme halfway through before to catch my breath. That is until The Experiment – Channel 4’s highly controversial social exercise designed to find out “how susceptible the British public are” to Nazi ideology about disabled people. This is a show so disturbing, timely and surreal that within 90 seconds of viewing it alone, I am looking around for confirmation from an empty room that any of this is happening.
We start with a clip of Hitler. Against a backdrop of growing anti-benefits and ableist rhetoric, presenters Mat Fraser and Sophie Morgan fear the disabled community globally are once again being framed as a financial burden. Their question is: can the British public be persuaded that disabled people should live in “money saving” segregated institutions and be given low-skilled jobs to be productive?
Cue “Segrilife”, a residential home for disabled people that members of the public are invited to tour. In fact, every resident is a disabled actor, and the creepily jovial corporate films and posters are made using AI. Fraser and Morgan are watching events unfold on monitors in another room.
Each part of the tour is based on a different piece of Nazi ideology, much of which has a menacingly clear link to some modern-day ideas. First off, the group are shown “the workshop”, where disabled people are placing beads on to string to earn an allowance. “I used to be in marketing. I don’t know why I’m in this room now,” a character called Sonia says, threading monotonously in her wheelchair.
Soon, we are touring a dormitory (or “the nest”) – a room with threadbare beds lined up in a row for disabled people to use as a communal bedroom, with cameras placed on the walls to monitor them. “It’s safe,” one woman in the tour group says, approvingly. “That’s what the people we’ve just met need.”
On the walls are posters repackaging 1930s fascist concepts with a glossy contemporary face – the price tag of a disabled person’s care package in bold font next to their smiling photo, with mantras such as: “Normal life isn’t for everyone.”
It is excruciating and sinister and there is little letup, the producers building the tension methodically as viewers witness dehumanisation being normalised in real time.
Few TV moments this year have been more disturbing than when three members of the public and a manager (an actor) discuss the “cost” of a young disabled woman as she sits silently in the same room, with the “savings” the state has made by putting her in an institution glowing on an iPad.
You are, of course, waiting desperately for someone – anyone – to speak up. It’s a long wait. There are a couple of women who show some concern but it’s all rather tame given what they’re seeing. By the time one man on the tour finally declares, “This is hell on earth,” I don’t know whether to cheer or cry.
Threaded between these scenes is a harrowing history of “Aktion T4” – the Nazi’s programme to systematically segregate and murder disabled people. Fraser – visibly distressed – and Morgan visit Hartheim Castle in Austria, one of six facilities in which tens of thousands of so-called “mercy killings” of disabled people occurred in gas chambers from 1939.
You could argue that the programme-makers controversially pairing Nazi killings with 2026 rhetoric is counterproductive to winning over hard-to-reach critics. That the horrors of the past are of such unique depravity that discussing them in a modern context will let the Daily Mail et al dismiss the whole thing as woke hysteria. And yet you could also claim that’s the point: it is comforting to tell ourselves fascism and democratic ideas are always neatly defined, that the beliefs strangers held 80 years ago bear no relation to what our relatives post on Facebook today.
There is the standard reassuring reveal at the end of the programme, in which the participants discover the truth and make all the right noises to suggest they have learned something. But it is hard to shake off what we’ve seen: most of the public who take part are convinced it is quite rational to treat disabled people as less than human, and with remarkable ease.
Some excuse it for the strain on the taxpayer. Others say institutionalisation is for disabled people’s own sake. As one woman concludes, it’s “incredible” they are being looked after and “kept occupied”.
That’s the thing about prejudice towards disabled people. It is not always violent or cruel. Much of the time, it is an almost well-meaning belief that disabled people are not quite like other people. Not as complex. More infantile. Of less value.
There is a moment when Morgan covers her eyes with her open fingers, barely able to watch through the monitors what has been unleashed. Viewers would be forgiven for doing the same. But acknowledging that these attitudes still exist is the only way we might begin to rid society of them. None of us should look away.

title: Pope will not need further cancer treatment, doctors say
description: Medics indicate pontiff’s tumour had not spread, but doubts remain about planned trip to South America next month
content:
Medics indicate pontiff’s tumour had not spread, but doubts remain about planned trip to South America next month
Pope Leo will not need any further ⁠treatment after undergoing lung cancer surgery last week, his doctors said, indicating ⁠that his tumour had ⁠not ​spread.
The ⁠71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his ​right lung removed on 13 October and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most ‌common form of lung cancer.
Final histological examinations and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed confirmed the diagnosis, with the disease remaining localised, the doctors said in a statement released by the Vatican.
“A subsequent ‌oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the pope’s lead surgeon, ​Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said.
However, it was still unclear whether the pope would ⁠proceed with a planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, scheduled for 6-17 November.
Leo was discharged from hospital on Saturday and is gradually resuming his normal duties . On Wednesday, he returned to ⁠St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience with ​pilgrims.
The pope had been working from hospital, including making a phone call last Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
Last Sunday, the pontiff told a crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square that he would “gradually resume” his activities.
He also thanked those who had prayed for him, saying that he appreciated the support while adding that the experience had made him feel especially close “to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity”.
Margaritora said ​last week there ​were “no clinical reasons” preventing the pope from travelling ​to South ‌America, but ​the Vatican’s ​secretary of state indicated that the pontiff may need to adjust the pace of his schedule to aid his recovery.
Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys playing sports including tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.
In May last year, Leo became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church.

title: Champions League: Silva sparks Real Madrid’s demolition of Leipzig as Lask stun Sporting
description: Bernardo Silva opened the scoring as Real Madrid beat RB Leipzig 4-1, while Galatasaray swept past Lille and 10-man Inter edged out Shakhtar Donetsk
content:
Bernardo Silva opens scoring as Madrid win 4-1
Galatasaray sweep past Lille; 10-man Inter edge Shakhtar
Real Madrid claimed a third Champions League victory in as many games by thrashing RB Leipzig 4-1 on Wednesday, with Kylian Mbappé and Yan Diomande among the goals for José Mourinho’s side.
Bernardo Silva opened the scoring for Madrid from close range towards the end of a tight first half, with Arda Guler doubling the record 15-time European champions’ advantage soon after the interval.
Mbappé bent home a third before Tidiam Gomis pulled one back for the German side and Diomande rammed a volley into the top corner to cap Madrid’s triumph late on.
“We know every point is important to get into the top eight, we know we have to win as many games as possible – we’ve won three and there are five to go,” Mbappé said. The France forward, who hopes to win the Ballon d’Or next week , has netted in each of Madrid’s Champions League matches this season and has 12 goals in 12 games.
“I’m doing well [but] I think I can do more,” he said. “I’m one of the few players who always has to demand more from himself ... right now it’s a good moment, but we have to keep going and I have to do more.”
Lask launched an impressive comeback at Sporting to earn their first Champions League win of the season. The Austrian champions went behind when Luis Suárez scored from the spot after five minutes, but equalised 10 minutes later through Christoph Lang.
The visitors then stunned the Estádio José Alvalade as Sasa Kalajdzic and Krystof Danek put them 3-1 up, the former rounding off a smart team move and the latter firing in at the near post. Suárez scored again for the hosts late on, but it was not enough.
Galatasaray swept past Lille at the Stade Pierre-Mauroy, setting the tone with a goal after two minutes from Yunus Akgun.
Lille levelled the score via Soriba Diaoune, who then put them 2-1 up in the 39th minute. Aleksey Batrakov made it 2-2 just before half-time, however, before an own goal from Nabil Bentaleb and Victor Osimhen, in action against his former club, sealed a 4-2 victory.
Inter had Alessandro Bastoni sent off midway through the second half before Carlos Augusto’s late goal secured a 1-0 win at home to Shakhtar Donetsk , as the Italian champions got their first points of the league phase.
Bastoni was sent off for two yellow cards in as many minutes, putting Inter on the back foot. Carlos Augusto saved the day in the 77th minute, capping a lightning-fast counterattack with a low finish.
Real Betis , who beat Feyenoord 1-0 via a penalty kick from Isco, made it three from three in the Champions League to extend their strong start to the season.
Betis had the lion’s share of the chances, but only broke the deadlock when Jeremiah St Juste was adjudged to have handled in the box. Isco stepped up and fired low into the right-hand corner for what proved to be the winner.
Club Brugge defeated Lens 3-0 at the Jan Breydel Stadium in a ruthless home performance. The Belgians went 1-0 up through Hans Vanaken in first-half stoppage time before Joaquin Seys and Carlos Forbs secured the win in the second half.

title: My husband Hiep Tran is in a Vietnamese prison. He has done nothing wrong
description: No Australian citizen, or anyone else, should have to endure the terrible nightmare our family is going through
content:
No Australian citizen, or anyone else, should have to endure the terrible nightmare our family is going through
A bit more than a month ago my husband, Hiep Tran, went missing. It was the beginning of a terrible ordeal for Hiep, me and our entire family.
We now understand that he is being wrongfully detained in a Vietnamese prison.
My husband and I live a simple life, much like many other couples. We go to work each day, and every evening we come home and share a meal. I cook and he does the dishes. Afterwards, we watch movies and play with our cats. Some nights, he plays piano and I sing, although I’m never quite sure my singing is as pleasant as he makes it seem.
We both love nature and outdoor activities. On weekends we often go hiking, camping or fishing, sometimes with family and friends. We love to travel, enjoying good food and exploring new things together. These ordinary moments are what make our life together so special.
Hiep works in data analytics, but there are other things he has always been passionate about. He loves fixing things around the house and making wooden objects for our home. He also has a deep love of music. He used to play music at church. At family gatherings and get-togethers with friends, he often entertains everyone by playing the piano or guitar.
It breaks my heart to realise that it has been a month since we were able to share these simple moments together.
Just some days ago, I received a few fragmented details about his condition. I was told that he is in a fragile mental state, gripped by fear, and experiencing erratic blood pressure – symptoms which he had never experienced before. Knowing that my husband is suffering like this, unable to feel safe or at peace, is unbearable.
The only brief message I have received from him reads:
“Hi, how are you all going? I want you to know that I never entered Vietnam on my own. I never crossed the border. I am struggling mentally – traumatised and terrified by the situation.”
I read those words at 4am, in a report from a consular officer, and broke down in tears. It was truly heartbreaking. My husband had done nothing wrong to deserve being put through such a horrific experience.
Next week, we will celebrate our 8th anniversary together. Hiep had booked tickets for a trip to South Korea for us to celebrate this special occasion. But instead, he is now living in fear and panic, trapped in a prison where he should never have ended up.
His birthday was on 7 October. I thought being alone in prison would be the hardest part for him, but I was wrong. The “happy birthday” message and photos I tried to send him were not even allowed to reach him. Why are they so afraid of a simple message from his loved ones?
He must be feeling incredibly desperate, not knowing that out here, my lawyer, his friends and so many others still care deeply about him and are doing everything in their power to bring him home as soon as possible.
Living in a free country like Australia, we never imagined that helping others, speaking up for vulnerable people or simply travelling to another country could lead to a nightmare like the one my husband is now enduring.
Over the past month, the Australian government has provided tremendous support to me and my family, and I am deeply grateful. I sincerely hope the government will continue to do everything within its power to secure Hiep’s safe return. I also hope that people around the world with continue to speak up, raise awareness, and call for his release.
No one, whether an Australian citizen or anyone else, should ever have to endure the nightmare my husband and our family are going through. All I want is for my husband to be safe, to be free and to come home to the life and family waiting for him.
Please help bring my husband home safely to us.

title: House prices falling in every Australian capital city for first time in 15 years
description: House prices in Sydney are at a two-year low after falling 4.7% in the September quarter to $1.66m, according to Domain report
content:
House prices in Sydney are at a two-year low after falling 4.7% in the September quarter to $1.66m, according to Domain report
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
House prices are falling across every capital city for the first time in 15 years and the second time on record, according to figures from Domain’s September Quarter 2026 House Price report.
House prices in Sydney are at a two-year low after falling 4.7% in the September quarter, to $1.66m.
House prices in Melbourne have fallen for the third consecutive quarter, slumping 3.3% in the September quarter, but the city remains in the million-dollar club, marginally, with a median price of $1.014m after experiencing its largest quarterly house price fall in four years.
Perth recorded the sharpest drop, with house prices falling a record 4.7%, while Brisbane and Adelaide also logged their steepest quarterly house price falls on record.
“Geographically, the downturn has broadened, but also across property types with houses and units also falling,” Domain’s chief residential economist, Nicola Powell, said.
“Homes are taking longer to sell, there is greater scope to negotiate and sellers are having to be more realistic about price expectations.”
Higher interest rates, persistent cost-of-living pressures and changes to housing investment tax policy were driving the reductions, Powell said.
“What this has really layered is weak sentiment across buyers in particular,” she said. “Ultimately we could see Melbourne close the year with the median house price below $1m.”
Reduced borrowing capacity is also stifling sales, the data suggests.
While the statistics show weakened confidence from buyers and vendors, the diminishing market has created the best start to spring for prospective purchasers, according to Powell.
“We are in a buyer’s market and many of our capital cities have got the highest levels of supply that they’ve seen in a number of years,” Powell said.
“For buyers with secure finances and the capacity to transact, that creates opportunities that have been difficult to find in recent years.”
Prices could continue to fall for many months to come, Powell said.
“Something needs to shift to alter the confidence to transact and I cannot envisage the confidence changing until we see an interest rate cut or even the discussion that interest rate reductions are on the horizon,” she said. “And ultimately that prospect is in the latter part of next year.”
Morgan Stanley economists agreed, predicting the market will bottom out in the second half of 2027. They expect the downturn to run as deep as 15% from peak to trough.

title: Ellie & Natasia review – please give us more of this irresistibly weird comedy
description: The hilarious duo are back with deeply silly sketches about an evil trad-wife, Lime bike addicts and Dubai chocolate. There are only three episodes, but each one is gloriously unsettling – and packed with ridiculously good guest stars
content:
The hilarious duo are back with deeply silly sketches about an evil trad-wife, Lime bike addicts and Dubai chocolate. There are only three episodes, but each one is gloriously unsettling – and packed with ridiculously good guest stars
I n 2022, comics and actors Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou starred in six bite-size episodes of their self-titled sketch show. Among the highlights: a woman who makes wild swimming her whole personality before realising she hates freezing water; a pair of overbearing, overopinionated mums who vlog from a sterilely clean kitchen (“you’re not a real mum unless you’re redecorating or knocking through at least six times a year”) and, of course, Internet Nails, about two decidedly useless eastern European beauty entrepreneurs who were branching out into a variety of business ideas (“please let us scratch you with our ink today, and if you change your mind we can burn the tattoo off with professional match”). It was often hilarious, and was definitely weird, with many parallels to the offbeat Channel 4 series Stath Lets Flats (which White and Demetriou starred in alongside the latter’s brother, its creator Jamie).
Four long years later – reportedly due to scheduling clashes – the duo are back. Ellie & Natasia series two comprises just three episodes, although – gladly – these episodes are now half an hour long rather than a mere 15 minutes. Internet Nails, in particular, remains a crucible for unsettling comedy, with the salon having become a “premiere relax styling and elegance lounge for all makeup, hair straightening and spray tanning mother-baby needs”). The fact that both women were pregnant at the time of filming only makes it funnier, and the low-rent experience (“100% birthing penthouse with perfect lukewarm Jacuzzi”) is deeply silly and – for anyone who has gone to a slightly shonky beauty shop before – astutely observed. The judgy mums are back, too, complete with advice on how to make your wardrobe stretch from “conception to birth, birth to night, night to bed, bed to menopause, menopause to coffin, and coffin to hell …”
Influencers have become even more inescapable since White and Demetriou’s first series, and the parodies are plentiful. These include two women who speak gobbledegook into their podcast microphones, while their hats get bigger and bigger with every scene (“don’t just dress for the job you want,” White implores. “If you want the dress, job for it”). There’s also a bit about a sack-wearing, trad wife-style content creator (White) who enjoys eating croissants, making collages and, er, keeping the woman her boyfriend cheated with locked up in her basement. So silly, so irresistible.
Of course, this is a sketch show, so not everything lands. The two women who spend hours in posh shops fondling candles and cooing are relatable but the concept wears thin, even when Sian Clifford pops up as a wonderfully exasperated shopkeeper. An OnlyFans parody that involves the pair eating grapes and mashed potatoes out of their cleavages feels more like an in-joke. See also: Mary Poppins at the gynaecologist, complete with what can only be described as dangerously cavernous nether regions. Unfortunately, that four-year gap also means that Mitchell and Webb pipped them to the post with a Repair Shop send-up in Mitchell and Webb Are Not Helping, even if White and Demetriou’s version is funnier, with a better payoff.
Luckily, there’s much that does work – eccentric and sometimes touching vignettes of life that don’t punch down but do cock a snook at almost every area of society, from a “wee little shop selling tiny mini wee things” in Scotland to Lime bike addicts to aspirants like Donna and her cousin Nikki, who composes a rap about Dubai chocolate’s pistachio filling. A Crystal Maze-style gameshow about a man who needs to get rid of all the snakes that are ruining the foundations of his house (“I sleep with a knife on a stick!”) probably doesn’t say much about anything, actually, but it is totally hysterical. Ditto a Fonejacker-esque recurring bit where Demetriou pops up to declare “I made it, it was me!” about everything from a pot plant to a high-rise building to a pen. A special mention, too, for “Women’s-Only Only Fools and Horses”, a new musical stage adaptation of the TV series (a sheepskin-clad Demetriou explains: “Strip it back and at its heart it’s a very serious story about three generations of working-class men …”).
The series also manages to pack in a ridiculous surfeit of British comedy talents, from Jamie Demetriou to Steve Coogan, Katy Wix to Asim Chaudhry, Kiell Smith-Bynoe to Vicki Pepperdine. But, of course, its brightest lights are White and Demetriou. “Pregnant and doing a sketch show? Does that make it funnier?” asks Demetriou in one of the transition scenes where the two women natter to each other. Not necessarily, but I could easily watch another 10 episodes.

title: ‘Angry’ Carrick on the brink as Fernandes hits out at Manchester United tactics
description: The manager apologised to Manchester United fans after the 4-1 defeat in Como, while his captain criticised the team’s tactical approach
content:
Manager apologises to fans after 4-1 defeat in Como
Captain criticises ‘decision from the staff’ not to press
Michael Carrick’s future as Manchester United manager is in the balance after a humiliating 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como on Wednesday night.
Before Bournemouth’s visit to Old Trafford on Sunday his future may be discussed by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, Omar Berrada, the chief executive, and Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the co-owner who controls sporting policy.
On a torrid night an “angry” ­Carrick insisted afterwards that he had not given his position any thought and was forced to defend himself against Bruno Fernandes after his captain questioned the manager’s tactics of not pressing against Cesc Fàbregas’s team. Carrick also criticised his side for not running. The defeat by Como in the third Champions League group game leaves United with only two wins all season from 11 games. ­Carrick’s side are in 13th place in the Premier League and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup last month.
The 45-year-old was asked if he fears for his job. “Listen, I’ve not given my own position any thought,” he said. “[My thoughts are] for the supporters – I was one of them watching that and I wasn’t happy at all.”
Carrick was then asked if he could walk away following the latest defeat in Europe. “No. It’s not about me right now and my feelings in that regard,” the manager said. “It’s more of as a team and as a football club, what we want to look like, what we should look like. And as I said, the results can come and go at times, but you got to do it in a certain way. And that wasn’t it.”
700 United sup­porters travelled. At the end around 200 remained and Carrick went to ­apologise to them, noticeably ­ignoring his players. After United conceded Nico Paz’s second-minute goal, Carrick’s men were unable to mount any resistance. By 57 minutes Como led 3-0, due to Tasos Douvikas’s strike and Paz’s second, before Jacobo Ramón completed the scoring for the Italian side on 76 minutes. Joshua Zirkzee netted in added time for the visitors.
Fernandes openly challenged ­Carrick’s strategy during the match. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” he said.
The captain was asked if Carrick’s tactics were wrong. “That’s on the manager and staff to see, not me,” he said. “Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable. As you saw with them, the centre-back was coming to mark me in my own half. We need to do that as a team but we were unable to.”
Fernandes’s criticism was put to his manager after the match. “We actually half-pressed man-to-man the second half and then conceded a goal from that,” Carrick said.
“Whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”
Carrick was asked how he can raise the mood before Bournemouth’s visit. “I’m bitterly disappointed, I’m frustrated; more than frustrated, I’m really angry. But you’ve got to move on. You got to deal with what’s next and see what that looks like.
“At this moment in time, there’s a lot to do before that next game to get the team ready because that was a difficult night for everyone. I have to apologise to the supporters.”

title: Arsenal’s Declan Rice strikes late to deny Bayern Munich after Harry Kane penalty
description: Declan Rice’s late equaliser rescued a 2-2 draw for Arsenal in a blockbuster contest at Bayern Munich after Harry Kane had scored from the spot
content:
It is as if Harry Kane cannot get enough of tormenting Arsenal. The Bayern Munich striker has plenty of form from his Tottenham days. He remains the top scorer in north London derby history with 14 goals. He made an impact yet again here and yet it was not a night when he had the final word. That honour fell to Declan Rice, the Arsenal midfielder storming into the Bayern area in the 82nd minute to guide home a low finish that Kane would have been proud to call his own.
Arsenal were hunting their latest statement result. Only once had they ever won away against Bayern – the 2-0 in the Champions League last 16 second leg in 2013, although it did not prevent an away goals exit. Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player that night. When Eberechi Eze, who came on for the injured Bukayo Saka in the 10th minute, gave them the lead midway through the first half, their hopes surged.
Enter Kane. He wore his playmaker’s hat; some of his passing was sumptuous and it was his assist for Alphonso Davies that helped Bayern to draw level. He wore his finisher’s one, too, scoring from the penalty spot to put his team in charge. It meant he had scored in 10 consecutive Champions League games; one short of Cristiano Ronaldo’s record. There is a reason why Kane is the favourite to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday. He now has 16 goals against Arsenal; he has only scored more against one club – Leicester, against whom he has 20.
Rice loosened Bayern’s grip. It was a lovely goal from him and Arsenal even hinted at a late winner, Jurriën Timber drawing a tip over from Manuel Neuer in stoppage time. That would have been too much because Bayern shaded an absorbing tie in terms of clear chances created. But Arsenal made their point. They were value for it.
Arsenal knew they were inside a fortress. Bayern had not previously lost a Champions League group or league phase match at their own stadium since the 3-2 reverse against Manchester City in December 2013, 40 games ago. The following 39 featured 37 wins and two draws. Arteta’s players were not intimidated. They bristled with assurance at the outset and Rice rewarded their never-say-die spirit. Bayern had wanted revenge for their 3-1 defeat at the Emirates Stadium in the league stage last season. They did not get it.
Arteta’s idea was to go pretty much as strong as possible with his lineup. He made just two changes, Timber for Ben White and Noni Madueke for Eze, albeit the latter was not on the bench for long. Saka had tussled with Davies and it looked innocuous. The alarm bells rang when Saka grabbed his thigh and went to ground, waving his hand in the air.
Was it possible for the Arsenal support to think that Bayern had been stripped of their fear factor in the line behind Kane? Michael Olise was suspended, Jamal Musiala was injured and Luis Díaz was a substitute. He came on in the 68th minute only to be forced off before the end. Bayern were without the midfielder Joshua Kimmich for personal reasons.
Arteta moved Madueke over to his more natural position on the right wing when he introduced Eze on the left and Bayern will still be wondering how the latter was afforded so much space up the inside channel on that flank to put Arsenal in front.
It was a fabulous ball from Martin Ødegaard, who was in the mood, full of sharp turns and urgency, and Eze had the time to let it bounce before shooting first time into the far corner. An offside flag killed the Arsenal celebrations and there was one of those weird waits before the video assistant referee ruled that Eze was in fact onside.
Kane was booed by the Arsenal fans. Of course he was. He dropped deep to link the play and there was a moment in the 17th minute when he started a move with a pass from inside his own penalty area. There was a glorious ping over Gabriel Magalhães, who was the last Arsenal defender, for Ismael Saibari on 23 minutes, although his teammate could not control, and Kane’s fingerprints were all over the equaliser. He was on halfway when he sculpted the low through ball for Davies which took Timber out of the equation. The Bayern winger’s finish was clinical.
Bayern had other chances in the first half, none better than the one for Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, in the 21st minute. It was Kane who began the attack, taking a quick goal kick – yes, really – and Gnabry was the man over on the right when the Bayern forwards worked it that way. Gnabry’s shot was too close to David Raya. Kane also saw Ezri Konsa produce a fine block to keep him out.
It is never anything other than a pleasure to be at the Allianz for a showpiece match. All the staples were present and correct. The en masse scarf waving. The slightly slapstick oompah band notes. The fans at either end of the ground calling to each other. The non-stop drumbeat and songs from the Südkurve, who also bounced as one at times.
The pre-game surprise had been the sight of Vincent Kompany in the Bayern dugout; the manager made a Lazarus-like rise from his sickbed and the action after the restart kept the blood pumping. Arsenal thought they had gone back ahead when Bruno Guimarães rose to meet Rice’s corner only for Neuer to produce an extraordinary save.
The goalkeeper touched the ball up and on to the crossbar and away. Shades of Gordon Banks against Pelé. It was Raya’s turn next; his save to keep out Dayot Upamecano’s close-range header from Gnabry’s cross was of the highest order.
It was interesting to watch Kane after the penalty was awarded for handball against Timber. Bayern had worked the ball back to their No 9 and, when he shot, Timber’s arm was outstretched. Kane went through his mental processes. He could see that Raya did not retreat to his line for what felt like an age. Kane delayed even longer. He was in total control. He stuttered before banging the ball hard into Raya’s right-hand corner.
Bayern were close to putting the game to bed. Konrad Laimer dragged narrowly past the far post when well-placed but it was Arsenal who produced the sucker punch. Eze was dangerous throughout. And when the opportunity knocked for Rice after a pass from the substitute Viktor Gyökeres, he made no mistake.

title: Barkley and Buendía on target as Aston Villa sink Viking to maintain perfect start
description: An own goal from Henrik Heggheim completed Aston Villa’s 3-1 Champions League victory against Viking, their third consecutive win of the league phase
content:
For a little over 20 minutes, Aston Villa could look down on the rest of Europe. They had scaled the Champions League summit on goal difference when Henrik Heggheim put through his own net and the fact was not lost on the Holte End, who reflected their position in song and perhaps allowed themselves another glimpse back to the days when their supremacy was undisputed. “We’ve conquered before, we’re prepared for more,” the pre-match tifo display had read.
Perhaps Villa really will rekindle the spirit of 1982 but the frustration here, albeit minor in the wider scheme, was that they could not maintain their bird’s-eye view over the continent. A superbly taken volley by Peter Christiansen, awarded by the video assistant referee after initially being disallowed for offside, gave Viking a consolation their second-half display deserved and meant Unai Emery’s side must make do with slumming it just behind Paris Saint-Germain.
“Collectively and individually we did a good job and some players also made a step forward in their confidence,” said Emery, who was pleased with Villa’s seriousness against opponents still finding their way in a first campaign at this level. “Each match has an objective to get better, to be consistent and be very demanding.”
The hard work had been done in an opening period whose scoreline hardly did justice to Villa’s total dominance. Viking had drawn at home with Bayern Munich in their previous game, a fact that would look more explicable when they emerged from their shell later, but were barely afforded a kick and looked vulnerable every time the ball was delivered from wide.
Nicolas Jackson, electric in the 6-0 thrashing of Fenerbahce , fluffed two free headers in the opening seven minutes and a similarly resounding win came to appear possible. Emery had made four changes but Villa, working the play smoothly from side to side, were a consistent threat and unfazed by opponents whose attacking ambition was initially minimal.
The breakthrough arrived after a spell of pressure sparked when a cross from João Gomes, the makeshift right-back, deflected on to the bar. Two corners later, an inswinger from the livewire 18-year-old Ibrahim Mbaye was met by Ross Barkley, who leapt highest to plant a firm header across Arild Østbø at the near post.
Barkley had scored twice in the previous week’s big win but the rest of the first half resembled a quest for Emiliano Buendía to put his mark on the scoresheet. Straight after the opener Buendía looped a header wide of the vacant goal after Østbø had parried from Alysson, who was a rangy threat throughout, and then he charged on to a clever John McGinn corner only to aim straight at the keeper.
It was third time lucky when the VAR reviewed a needless challenge by the Viking captain Zlatko Tripic on Alysson, who had run into traffic in the box, and led the referee Sebastian Gishamer to award a penalty. Buendía rolled it in, his fourth goal in consecutive European games; 37 minutes had passed and Viking had still not produced a meaningful attack.
After the restart they showed some of the intensity and verve that had ruffled Bayern, the richly promising midfielder Tobias Moi warming Zion Suzuki’s midriff and seeing a goalbound effort blocked. Suzuki also beat away a Tripic drive. But Villa could now exploit space in behind and, after flashing an angled effort just wide, Alysson got away once again to create the third. This time his attempted centre snicked off Heggheim, who was desperately trying to recover, and gave Østbø no chance.
Now Villa were, as the home choirs gleefully announced, top of the league and they received further opportunities to hammer home the point. Alejandro Garnacho saw one of them saved by Østbø after a strong run but Viking remained a threat and Christiansen’s finish, emphatically converting Kristoffer Askildsen’s deep cross, was by some distance the best of the night.
“The second half was much more like the Viking we want to be,” said Morten Jensen, who co-manages the Norwegian champions alongside Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim. “Maybe we had too much respect for them in the first half, they were all over us.”
Nine points from nine, not to mention 12 consecutive home wins in Europe, mean Villa are flying. Sweeping Fenerbahce and Viking aside can “give us confidence and comfort for the next challenges,” Emery said. They will need plenty of it given a trip to Barcelona follows the relatively soft run presented so far. Maybe the peak is yet to come.

title: Paris Saint-Germain sparkle on the pitch while the city of light burns around them
description: PSG, the pet project of the state of Qatar, expresses the dualism of the city, a place of deprivation where the centre is perfect
content:
PSG, pet project of the state of Qatar, expresses the dualism of the city, a place of deprivation where the centre is perfect
The security deployment will be massive.
Those who sought to bring down the Republic will have to answer for it.
Tell you who would have loved this? Who would have been utterly engrossed scrolling the hashtag #Paris on Tuesday night as two things happened simultaneously, the harrowing of the Barcelona defence at the Parc des Princes, and the harrowing of Paris itself via tales of city-centre thuggery and end-of-days political doom‑mongering.
The big man, Guy Debord himself. The Society of the Spectacle, you say? Actually, I think we’re past that now. Hold the society bit. We’ll just take the spectacle.
The great Parisian Situationist philosopher wasn’t really one for managed fun. But it was impossible not to be bowled over by the extraordinary pre-match show for Paris Saint‑Germain versus Barcelona, Champions League Matchday Three.
The wild pyrotechnics, the plumes of smoke, the full-wrap light show, the lime-green robo‑text spelling out every player’s name on the pitch. Although not the Barcelona names, sadly, for anyone with an unrealised desire to see the words “ANTHONY GORDON” projected in vast letters for the delight of a shrieking crowd.
Admittedly, the Halloween‑themed tifo banner showing a masked Paris Saint-Germain serial killer-type literally butchering the Barcelona badge to death with his bloodied chainsaw was perhaps a bit much. As were the Barça Puta signs, which are now reportedly the subject of a complaint to Uefa.
But it was a wild and all‑consuming spectacle, annihilating every other impulse in your head to a green thought in a green shade. And in the process capturing the profound sense of cognitive dissonance in the city.
Just walking around the streets of central Paris earlier in the day generated its own mild whiplash. On the face of it this was still the same city of flâneurs and tourists and everyday bistro business, and not, repeat not, a civil war drama or some kind of emergent military caliphate.
But the sense of dread was also tangible. You still got the occasional crunch of glass underfoot. Here and there charred bikes and scooters had been politely piled to one side. Even close to the Parc, away from the main hotspots, shopkeepers could be seen emerging warily into their doorways at the sound of a police siren.
By Tuesday night, a total of 2,513 people had been taken into police custody after the events of the weekend . At least 420 rental bikes had been destroyed or maimed. Liberated high-value retail goods were already being sold on Vinted, a commendable show of entrepreneurial energy from the maligned younger generation.
Not that you’d suspect these two worlds had any kind of overlap, lost in the booming triumphalism around PSG’s 4–2 win, one of the most beautifully luminous football matches you’re ever likely to see. Or indeed reading the coverage of an event that seems to have been treated in France like its own clear, clean space, floating above the flames, all the chat about the brilliance of Monsieur Dynamite, Désiré Doué, the wonderful television audiences on Canal+ TV, the whole of European football “kneeling before the machine” (are we sure this isn’t to do with anarchic rejection of social control?). “ Paris est insubmersible !” was the headline in Le Parisien. But is it?
Remember when football used to reflect the world? Or just provide clues, a commentary, some kind of metaphor? This is no longer the case. At a time when even the most thunderous of commentators is struggling to summarise all this in suitably trite and damning terms, it was hard to avoid the feeling Paris Saint-Germain, the pet power football project of the state of Qatar, expresses this dualism perfectly.
Sometimes you just have to let football tell you things. “People who want to cause trouble in the city centres next Saturday will be prevented,” Emmanuel Macron announced on Tuesday evening, speaking, as it happens, from Doha, where he met Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, ultimate owner of PSG.
Macron is said to be considering deploying the French military to keep the peace on the streets before the next planned protests, although even here he may have to ask Qatar’s permission if he wants to deploy any of the French troops currently deployed working its missile systems, or embedded in the Doha security services.
The key event Macron is tooling up for is this Saturday night, 24 October, the date the gilets jaunes social media feed has set for an even greater swell of disorder. And again this will be football adjacent, with PSG playing Lyon at home on Sunday, a top‑of‑the-table capital‑city clash played out against whatever wreckage is left, however many thousands of Dot bikes are savaged, whatever guerrilla skirmishes are still playing out in the Marais.
What does this really have to do with football and the Ici C’est Paris brand appropriated by a state outreach project? Well, what are these demonstrations anyway? There have been many theories put forward as to what exactly is happening here, what is the spark, the kindling, the fire behind this disorder. School protests were the original line. Others have now roped in some kind of nebulous omni-cause, Instagram-activism, perhaps even a barbarian takeover, the decline of the west, savagery at the gates, of the type Donald Trump pretends to see.
Do you need a single reason? Take a look around. Modern life is pretty alarming on a minute‑to‑minute basis. Disaffection, alienation, a sense of being transformed in real time into a passive economic consumer unit, a set of eyeballs, an avatar of consumption. French youth unemployment is close to 20%. Robots nobody wants are being lined up to take jobs that don’t exist. Why don’t these young people want to join a youth club? Why don’t they sign up for the Liberal Democrats? Why are they enjoying empowered disorder? Maybe because nothing is yours around here, not even the things thrust into your brain as digital distractions. So why not grab something when you can? Debord would have called this “a vicious circle of isolation”, lonely crowd, technologies based on isolation.
On the other hand, what is PSG in Paris, other than the perfect expression of this? It often seems to surprise people that celebrations of PSG victories end up with riots and burnt-out cars. But Paris is both a beautiful and deeply dysfunctional city, a place of make‑believe and deprivation, where the centre is a perfect, performative relic, the suburbs shunted out to the ring roads, a life lived inside a box, noses pressed up against the glass, peering through your binoculars at the city of someone else’s love.
Paris is the divide between overclass and churn expressed in a single city. It’s everything you might have had but never will. And PSG represent this like no other entity, a football club owned as an act of outreach by a staggeringly rich inherited monarchy, weaponised passion, borrowed culture, engineered spectacle, deeply cynical but also deeply seductive.
Why are the Qataris splurging hundreds of millions into this project? Because they just really like high-pressing positional football? Qatar is the indentured labour state that employs Colin Kaepernick to promote its outreach projects. It will hymn its connections to the footballers of the banlieue , which is true and real and valuable, but not because of anything this political project wants or needs other than public relations.
It is in its own way a perfect human lab experiment, synthesised beauty, collectivism, with a cold, cold hand at its heart. And this is why there weren’t two versions of Paris in evidence on Tuesday night, just the same one, the dark side and the shiny side, an engine of the same divisions, the same kind of violence, right down to the sight of kids in PSG training gear dodging the police or taunting the barricades at the Place de la République.
And now we have Sunday night to come, more Ici C’est Paris , more PASSION. What kind of background will it be played out against? Does it matter under the lights? Will anyone notice?
Le Monde has described these events as a very basic test of the republic, its ability to bend, to remain essentially itself, the state’s willingness to pit itself against its own people. Football, as ever, holds these answers already. PSG’s Qatari owners have spent the past 15 years flaunting this city like a global luxury brand, extending its reach, creating its own ideal of conspicuous consumption, spectacle, triumph, son et lumière , bread and roses. As ever, if you want to know how and why, football has the answers.

title: ‘He was a great kid’: Chiefs mourn death of former player Allen Bailey at age of 37
description: Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid have spoken of their sadness after former Kansas City Chief Allen Bailey died at the age of 37
content:
Defensive end played for Chiefs for eight seasons
Andy Reid says player’s death ‘makes you sick’
Patrick Mahomes and Andy Reid have spoken of their sadness after former Kansas City Chief Allen Bailey died at the age of 37.
The defensive end was found dead at his home in Florida on Tuesday by his wife. He is believed to have died from natural causes.
“It’s terrible, especially with all the good he [did],” Chiefs head coach Reid said. “He’s got a family and that’s a sad deal. I know his father passed away young, too. It makes you sick when it happens to somebody that young … He was one of my favorite players, a great kid. I’m just sorry to see that happened to him.”
Mahomes spent two seasons with Bailey after the quarterback was drafted by the Chiefs in 2017.
“I tell this story every year: He was the first person I saw when I stepped into the locker room after the draft,” Mahomes said. “I see Allen Bailey and I’m like, ‘This isn’t [college] anymore.’ It was surreal to see him.
“Obviously, it’s terrible to hear the news. A great teammate – he’s one of those glue guys on the team. He makes plays. He’s not necessarily a superstar, but the guy that kind of makes everything go. We’re praying for his family. [As] teammates, we’ve talked and we know that we’re going to do whatever we can to support those guys.”
Bailey grew up on Sapelo Island, a barrier island off Georgia only accessible by boat and with a population of fewer than 70 people. “I’m from a place a little out of the normal,” Bailey told Distraction magazine in 2018 . “It’s relatively quiet; no stop signs, no traffic lights. It’s mostly dirt roads.”
From there he played college football for Miami before becoming a third-round draft pick for the Chiefs in 2011. He played for the team for eight seasons before spending the final two years of his career with the Atlanta Falcons .

title: ‘Huge moment’: long-awaited extension to Sydney’s metro line to open next week
description: The south-west metro extension will open on Friday 30 October, more than two years after the former T3 heavy rail line closed
content:
The south-west metro extension will open on Friday 30 October, more than two years after the former T3 heavy rail line closed
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
A long-awaited extension to Sydney’s metro line will open next week, bringing an end to more than two years of replacement buses for residents in the city’s south-west.
In a video shared on Instagram on Thursday morning, the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, announced that the south-west metro extension would open on Friday 30 October. In a statement, the government said the first service would commence at 4.31am.
Minns thanked “the thousands of commuters, families and local businesses for their patience while we’ve undertaken this major transformation.”
“This is a huge moment for south-west Sydney,” he said.
It comes more than two years after the former T3 heavy rail line, which serviced 10 stations in Sydney’s inner west and south west – Marrickville, Dulwich Hill, Hurlstone Park, Canterbury, Campsie, Belmore, Lakemba, Wiley Park, Punchbowl and Bankstown – closed in September 2024 to be converted to the driverless rapid transit system.
A continuous 66km metro line will span from Tallawong in the city’s north-west through the CBD to Bankstown in the south-west from next Friday.
After regulator approval delayed the opening date of the city metro section in 2024, the Minns government had been at pains not to commit to a date for the south-west extension, despite media reports that it was aiming for launch on 18 October.
Last week, the transport minister, John Graham, said that the opening was “very close” and “a matter of weeks, not months” after the operator, Sydney Metro, provided the final piece of safety data to the Office of the National Rail Safety Regulator (ONRSR).
The project to connect the stations to the city metro, which opened in August 2024, was estimated to take 12 months at that time. In the interim, commuters have had to use pink replacement buses to connect to metro services at Sydenham, where the line currently terminates.
The government says the pink rail replacement buses will continue to operate on 30 October and the first weekend of operation.
When the line opens, a journey from Bankstown to Central is expected to take 28 minutes – a six-minute saving compared with the former heavy rail line. Longer journeys are expected to yield greater savings, such as Lakemba to Victoria Cross, which will take 37 minutes – a 24-minute saving on previous travel times.
The government says the extension will deliver capacity for an additional 17,000 people during peak hours. Metro services run every four minutes during peak hours, five minutes during the day, and 10 minutes in the evenings and on weekends.
The project has been delayed amid challenges in converting the 130-year-old heavy rail line and historic stations, including the need to add mechanical “gap-fillers” to fill spaces between curved platforms and trains.
When the south-west metro opens, six of the 360 doors on the line where gaps are widest – three doors at Dulwich Hill, and one each at Marrickville, Canterbury and Campsie – will not be in use while data is collected on the reliability of the gap-fillers.
The project was first announced by the former Coalition government in 2014. Labor campaigned against it at the 2019 election but committed to completing it after Minns became premier in 2023. Amid blowouts, the city and south-west metro sections are expected to cost more than $20bn combined.

title: Morning Mail: MPs’ protections under scrutiny; Putin releases jailed US citizen; and National Geographic’s NZ pick
description: MPs paying to boost their own security; systemic nature of alleged abuse in youth detention; Vladimir Putin labelled a ‘humanitarian’ by US diplomat
content:
Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Morning Mail here , and finish your day with our Politics, really newsletter .
Good morning. After the alleged attack on Helen Haines, MPs have revealed they have been shelling out thousands of dollars to improve their security amid rising concerns over threats facing elected officials.
As we continue our Duty of care investigation, former child detainees have come forward to describe the systemic nature of physical and sexual abuse they allege they suffered within the youth detention system.
Overseas, a US diplomat has dubbed Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian” after he ordered the release of an American held in a Russian prison. And a new literary prize has been launched – for fiction written with AI.
Exclusive | Former detainees have alleged a system of state detention in which children – disproportionately of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander backgrounds – were left vulnerable to abuse .
MPs’ safety | Security agencies will review safety precautions for MPs’ homes and offices after numerous federal politicians reported they are worried about widening threats after the alleged attack on Helen Haines. The independent MP has lost both her legs but remains in a stable condition in hospital, her husband has said.
Allergy, or not? | The latest evidence shows up to 90% of those reporting a penicillin allergy in Australia do not have one , prompting a change in guidelines in a bid to tackle antimicrobial resistance.
Animals in research | More than 1 million mice and nearly 47,000 rats are used in scientific research in Australia annually, according to the first ever nationwide count described as “an overdue first step”.
Grogonomics | Yes, oil prices are going up, but let’s not pretend companies importing the oil are struggling. No, they are passing on the costs and then some, Greg Jericho writes.
Russia-Ukraine war | Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American from a Russian jail as he met with Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine; the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die, Andrew Roth writes.
French unrest | As further protests loom, Emmanuel Macron has accused Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of making “stupid comments” about France’s street unrest for their own political gain.
West Bank tension | A US photojournalist has recounted how Palestinian youths helped save her from attack by Israeli settlers; the Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democrat Brad Lander.
Russell Brand trial | A woman told Russell Brand he had treated her “like an animal” after an alleged assault at his London townhouse that left her bleeding for days and in pain, a court has heard.
‘Serious incident’ | Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and compared Xi Jinping to Winnie-the-Pooh.
Booksmart? | After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by the winners of prestigious literary awards, tech entrepreneurs have now launched a prize to reward fiction co-written with AI .
Can Japan’s firebrand PM survive a second year in power?
One year ago, Sanae Takaichi became Japan’s first female prime minister, taking over a party in crisis. Since then, she’s defied the doubters – not just surviving as leader in a country that struggles with its gender politics but winning convincingly at an election in February. But could she be at her most politically dangerous moment yet? Justin McCurry speaks with Reged Ahmad about whether Takaichi can ride out what comes next .
This weekend, the first commercial flight will embark from Sydney’s much-anticipated new airport. Passengers will depart from Western Sydney international airport’s architecturally lauded terminals amid much fanfare on Sunday. And so, the title of Australia’s leading secondary airport is now up for grabs. So how different will it be to Melbourne’s own second commercial airport, Avalon?
Almost 70 finalists were chosen from 6,000 entries for this year’s New Zealand Geographic photographer of the year competition, with works reflecting the country’s natural environment, wildlife, culture, history and traditions. Photojournalist Mike Scott took first place for his aerial shot of an island of green trees within the bushfire-scorched Tongariro national park, with judges praising his patience and craft.
Cricket | Australia collapsed in chaotic fashion to leave South Africa in sight of victory after day four of their second Test.
Football | In today’s Champions League action, Manchester United have been humbled by Como and German giants Bayern Munich are taking on Arsenal . Follow the rest of the matches here .
Netball | Australia’s hoodoo continues as New Zealand pile on pain – again – in the Constellation Cup.
Motorsport | The Austin Grand Prix is about much more than potential for Kimi Antonelli’s first F1 world title, Giles Richards writes.
There are calls for Australia to train “smoke jumpers” to parachute into remote fire grounds as part of a strategic shift to deal with longer and more ferocious bushfires, the Sydney Morning Herald reports. Australian government websites are among those exposed to a “critical” software flaw being exploited by hackers, ABC News reports. title: NSW passes ‘human compost’ laws with several MPs saying they will utilise practice after they die
description: Australian-first laws provide a third legal option other than burial and cremation for the treatment of bodies
content:
Australian-first laws provide a third legal option other than burial and cremation for the treatment of bodies
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Several New South Wales MPs say they want their own bodies turned into “human compost” after Australian-first laws were passed allowing the unusual practice.
The laws, passed on Wednesday, provide a third legal option other than burial and cremation for the treatment of bodies.
The private member’s bill was introduced by independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich, who travelled to Germany and the US to research the practice, which is allowed in some parts of both countries.
The practice, known as natural organic reduction, terramation or human composting, involves placing the body in a temperature-controlled vessel with organic matter such as alfalfa, straw or mulch.
Once inside, the vessel is turned or rocked to circulate air. The introduced matter reacts with the air and feeds the body’s naturally occurring microbes to rapidly decompose the body.
The process creates heat that, after about 30 days, transforms the body into soil. When rested for about 30 days more, the vessel contains about 110kg of “dry, rich soil that is fertile and free of pathogens”, Greenwich told the legislative assembly earlier this year.
In the legislative council on Wednesday, John Ruddick, a Libertarian MP, said he backed what Greens MP Dr Amanda Cohn said in supporting the bill: he thought it was likely he would choose terramation over a burial plot or cremation.
“Terramation will be voluntary. It is a choice. A lot of people may not choose it … I am pretty sure that I will put in my will that I wish to be terramated,” Ruddick said.
“I like the idea of being buried somewhere and having a nice big gum tree grow there for 100 years.
“The idea of being cremated or buried has always freaked me out. This is a much better option.”
The Labor MP Cameron Murphy also said: “I look forward to being able to utilise this service in the long-distant future after it becomes law”.
Liberal MP Susan Carter urged the government to consider when it implemented the bill how to ensure the dead were respected.
“Terramation should not simply become a human compost bin,” she said.
“Like all the many ways in which we approach death, it should help those who remain to mourn, and the respect shown to that person in life should continue into death.
“It is important for that person, for their family, and for the whole way in which we go forward as a society.”
Emma Hurst MP, the Animal Justice MP who introduced the bill into the legislative council, told parliament on Wednesday that terramation had significant environmental benefits.
She said it could avoid the need for large burial plots and can be wholly carbon neutral, compared with cremation, which she said was energy intensive and released substantial greenhouse gas emissions.
“Terramation provides possibilities to grow living things, like trees and plants, in honour of a life,” Hurst said.
“Because terramation is a slow process, there are multiple opportunities for ceremonies, including for the laying of the body in the vessel and for opening the vessel after a body has been terramated.
“Facilities overseas have allowed families to visit during the terramation process. It is a natural and gentle process that, for some, can help with grieving.”
The bill passed on Wednesday gives the NSW government 18 months to create regulations to control the practice, which would be limited to specialised facilities.

title: Titans coach says Jordan Elliott pulling gun in team parking lot was not ‘criminal act’
description: The defensive lineman, released on Tuesday by the Tennessee Titans, ⁠went to his car to retrieve a gun after an altercation during practice
content:
Player fetched firearm after altercation with JC Latham
Tennessee released defensive tackle on Tuesday
Robert Saleh calls situation ‘lapse in judgement’
Tennessee Titans coach Robert Saleh confirmed on Wednesday that defensive tackle Jordan Elliott was released after pulling a gun in the parking lot of the team facility but said it was a “terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a criminal act”.
The Titans had announced Tuesday that Elliott was released, but said only that it came after his involvement in an unspecified incident at the team’s facility five days earlier.
A person briefed on the incident told the Associated Press on Wednesday that Elliott had a gun in his car and went to the parking lot to retrieve it after a dispute with another player, believed to be right tackle JC Latham. Titans defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers is said to have helped deescalate the situation.
Speaking to reporters, Saleh defended Elliott’s character. “Unfortunately, rules are rules with regard to guns on property, and sometimes it’s far greater than the kneejerk reaction of kicking somebody when they’re down,” the coach said.
“He’s a good man. Made a terrible, had a terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a criminal act,” Saleh added. “He’s never committed a crime in his entire life and he pulled a gun, in the parking lot.”
Latham called the episode an unfortunate situation.
“I don’t really have too much to say about it,” Latham said Wednesday. “There ain’t never been no bad blood between us two. We were here on the summer getting treatment. Before that, we hung out whenever we were in the same city together. We actually had never had an argument leading up to it.”
Elliott appeared in five games this season with one start and had 11 tackles. He followed Saleh to Nashville after a two-year stint with the San Francisco 49ers, where he played in 31 games with 29 starts.
The 6ft 4in defensive tackle was selected by the Cleveland Browns in the third round of the 2020 draft. He spent his first four seasons in Cleveland before signing a two-year deal with San Francisco.
Tennessee added him as a free agent in the offseason on a two-year, $8m deal.

title: Clayface review – flesh-stretching DC body horror is very gory but not very good
description: Liverpool makes for an unconvincing Gotham City in this effectively gross but otherwise middling attempt to milk money from a lesser-known Batman villain
content:
Liverpool makes for an unconvincing Gotham City in this effectively gross but otherwise middling attempt to milk money from a lesser-known Batman villain
A sense of desperation is understandably in the air over at DC, the company, like Marvel, slowly realising that the mass superhero fever has finally broken. There’s still interest there, of course (this summer’s Spider-Man is now the biggest film of all time in the US after all), but it’s no longer good enough to leave a high-speed conveyor belt unmanned, purpose and quality control be damned. 2019 saw a staggering 10 superhero films released in cinemas, and the inevitable exhaustion that followed, also fueled by Covid, led to a gradual winding down, monster hits turning into minor ones and sure bets often becoming expensive flops.
As Peter Parker winged his way to box office records this summer, DC’s Supergirl bombed so hard that experts believe it might have cost Warners upwards of $200m in losses. It was just the latest disappointment for the brand after Black Adam, Joker: Folie à Deux, Blue Beetle and The Flash all underperformed while even last year’s much-heralded Superman reboot only grossed a solid $618m, a far cry from the $1bn heyday of the genre (things got so bad that even a fully filmed Batgirl adventure was deleted for the tax break ). Notably, the last DC film to swoop past that magic figure was Joker in 2019, a darker, lower-budget attempt to spotlight a villain rather than a hero, a big swing with relatively low stakes. Todd Phillips’s film might be best known by some for being brave enough to ask the question, “What if Taxi Driver sucked?” but for all of its many issues, it brought buzz and prestige and, shockingly, Oscars, to an easily ridiculed universe. It was also, crucially, something rare in that world: a close-to-good idea.
The evolution of Clayface, another R-rated villain origin story with a markedly lower budget than the DC norm, was not in direct response to Joker (it is allegedly the first in a new “Gods and Monsters” strand) but its path is one that head James Gunn would clearly like to emulate, albeit financially rather than awards-wise. One of many thoughts I had during Clayface, other than what I should have for dinner and how long I might be able to make a small popcorn last, was just how striking Phillips’s film stands in comparison. It remains shallow and smug and cursed with a grating lead performance, but it was visually punchy and, like the very best comic book adaptations, genuinely transporting, rich on dank atmosphere and thoughtfully curated production design. It was an undeniable moment.
Clayface is overwhelmingly not a moment. Admittedly its targets are way lower (Mike Flanagan’s original script, allegedly more texturally complex, was entirely rewritten ) but even as a similarly new way in, as a relatively standalone horror movie for those who wouldn’t now rush toward a superhero caper, it’s a clumsily missed opportunity and another reminder that those at DC don’t seem to know what they’re doing and why they’re doing it.
Rather than feeling like a lower-budget DC movie (it was made for around $40m), it looks closer to a network TV series, more Fox than HBO Max, more Gotham than Lanterns. With the standard there now so high (The Penguin looked every bit a blockbuster movie), the distractingly tinny aesthetic and lack of confident directorial style is disappointing both as a horror (especially at a time of micro-budgeted films such as Obsession and Backrooms looking so very distinctive) and as a tale that takes place in the DC universe. Liverpool was used as a stand-in here and if, like me, you found Manchester to be an unconvincing New York in Brand New Day, you won’t realise how good we had it …
Gotham is where working-class boy done good Matt (Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries, fine enough) is from and a place that he was desperate to leave. He’s a rising movie star, riding high after his first Oscar nomination (“Nominees don’t wait in line!”) and on a trip back to his home town, he makes the mistake of sleeping with the girlfriend of a violent gangster, introduced by Goldfrapp’s Ooh La La, one of the film’s many dated attempts at cool. As a result, he has his money-making face sliced up by goons and his career soon crumbles, back to a bedsit with all his money wasted on useless surgeries orchestrated by his viperous lawyer.
Matt is desperate for revenge and resurrection, and after stumbling upon a doctor working on experimental skin surgery (Naomi Ackie, trying her hardest), he thinks he’s found his chance. But before you can say Substance (the elixir is at least red here over Brat green), things go horribly wrong …
What the film does do is successfully gross us out, as Matt’s skin starts to morph in tune with his emotional state, which might be enough for some, and in the screening I attended, mostly filled with rowdy non-journalists, there was a vocal response to the goriest and gloopiest moments. The trailer scene, of Matt trying to cut through flesh growing over his eyes while on a bumpy flight, is brilliantly awful to watch, and it’s in these more intimate, uneasy moments where director James Watkins shows off his dusty genre mettle. His best films have been his earlier, smaller attempts – 2002’s genuinely creepy and forward-thinking reality TV horror My Little Eye and 2008’s brutal hoodie thriller Eden Lake – but he’s less assured when the canvas is expanded.
Clayface is as poorly lit and junkily made as the very blandest of streaming movies and never once do we feel transported to Gotham with a cast of exclusively non-American actors trying to out-accent each other (Eddie Marsan, as ever, loses that game). It doesn’t help that what could have been interesting at one point (perhaps when Flanagan was the sole author) with briefly pointed at issues of AI, unreality and method acting, has been sanded down to a kill-by-numbers revenge thriller led by a character who feels like an off-brand swirl of Venom, Hulk, Joker and Mystique. His abilities, and the rules of how they work, are so poorly defined, that he just becomes a screenwriting device, able to do whatever is needed in the moment.
Any tragedy that could and should have come from the character and his journey – boy from the wrong side of the tracks to privileged Oscar nominee to flesh-stretching, face-changing supervillain (!) – is excised for an easier video game trajectory, from one familiar level to the next (despite those involved comparing this to The Fly, this is very much not that). Clayface might be the start of a “bold” new era for DC’s superhero output but for anyone outside of a boardroom, it’s a face we have seen many times before.
Clayface is out in Australian cinemas on 22 October and in US and UK cinemas on 23 October

title: Ilford Boy review – Barbra Streisand teaches teen to smile about the way we are
description: In Danny Lee Wynter’s drama, a quiet boy struggles amid the swirl of his family until a mercurial friend offers him another future
content:
Donmar Warehouse, London In Danny Lee Wynter’s drama, a quiet boy struggles amid the swirl of his family until a mercurial friend offers him another future
B road Essex accents fill the stage in Danny Lee Wynter’s sprawling family drama. The busy script from the Black Superhero playwright is crammed with a fractious extended family treading heavily over old arguments, but the production sings when an old friend swans back into town. Set across the 80s and 90s in the shadow of the Aids crisis, this story’s beating heart travels around on tap shoes.
Quiet teenager Ted (Leo Whitfield Harris in his stage debut) is surrounded by the loud swirl of his feuding family, with everyone’s rusty views on queerness, race and masculinity grating against each other as they clear out his showtune-loving nanna’s house in Ilford. His father (a bolshie Gershwyn Eustache Jr) is pushing him towards boxing and girls, so Ted grits his teeth and resists anything seen as weakness, but in doing so he resists kindness too.
There is sharpness and humour within the core family’s spiky arguments, with an abundance of anguished love offered by Ted’s mum (Ria Zmitrowicz), though some of the wider family could have more substance. Flashbacks build up backstory, enabling the creative team to have fun with costumes and hair. In both timelines, Tim Sheader’s direction scatters the family across Peter McKintosh’s surprisingly sparse double-decked neon home that doesn’t quite reflect the chaos – or the occasional warmth – within.
But then there’s Pat, Ted’s mum’s old friend, played by the mercurial Craig Stein. While everyone else is telling Ted how to be, here is a Black gay man showing him another way. As Ted is drawn in by Pat’s knowledge of Barbra Streisand, the play begins to move away from the more predictable father-son dynamics and towards something more effervescent.
There’s a whole life in the way Pat looks with disgust at Ted’s father, in how he talks about his lost love, in the hand he stretches out to Ted when the teenager asks him to dance. Illuminated in a brilliant moment of boldness from the script, with glorious movement by Ebony Molina, this is the image we’re left with long after Pat’s left the stage and the rest of the family have turned away: a beautiful man, up above the audience, leg kicked high in the air, radiant with life.

title: Como demolish dismal Manchester United to pile more pressure on Carrick
description: Manchester United conceded in the second minute and never recovered as Como scored three more in the second half, coasting to a 4-1 victory
content:
In the shadow of the Alps, a boat ride from George Clooney’s villa, Manchester United’s torrid season plunged into chaos and infighting just 11 games in.
