Michael Carrick’s status as United manager is now precarious because witnessed here by Lake Como was a humiliation of the three-time European champions by Cesc Fàbregas’s competition debutants.
At the end about 200 of United’s 700 travelling fans remained. Carrick walked over to say sorry, raising his hands three or four times in supplication. But, markedly, he ignored his players, the manager later admitting to “anger” at what was witnessed.
He was then embroiled in a wrangle with his captain after Bruno Fernandes stated “the staff” decided on a tactic not to press. Carrick’s riposte, deep in the stadium at the post-game media conference, was pithy.
“We actually half-pressed man-to-man the second half and then conceded a goal from that,” he said.
And so, after Lisandro Martínez called out Jason Wilcox last week following the 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid (for the director of football’s recruitment; the defender later apologised), we now have the spectacle of the manager and his captain at loggerheads.
Whether the 45-year-old will be in place for the visit of Bournemouth on Sunday is the searing question because Carrick was unable to rouse his players when 1-0 down at half‑time after a dire start, and if he has a tactical plan this is a mystery. Carrick brushed away questions about quitting and fearing for his job, but the executive will surely discuss this.
The manner of the defeat will be top of the agenda because by 57 minutes this was over: Como were 3-0 ahead, and Nico Paz had destroyed Carrick’s men with a scintillating display featuring two goals and the assist for Tasos Douvikas’s strike.
When the Italian side attacked and defended it was as a unit drilled supremely by Fàbregas. Carrick, on this and the evidence of only two wins all term, is a coach struggling to match this. Como’s supremacy in the most famous victory of their 119 years came with only 62 total Champions League appearances by their players to United’s 242.
Or, more simply, this was the Italians’ men against United’s boys at a sold-out Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia, where the visitors went down to a club whose tagline is “the most beautiful football in the most beautiful location”. For United, though, this was an ugly night in Lombardy.
Disaster struck two minutes in. Carrick’s men snoozed, allowing a Paz curler from the right to beat Senne Lammens. This was a whole 60 seconds longer than Atlético were kept out, as United became the first English team to concede inside two minutes in consecutive major European matches.
The opener came moments after Diogo Dalot spurned a simple opening to dizzy the hosts, so here was United, in microcosm, at each end of the pitch: a basic lack of quality.
Mason Mount lined up alongside Andrey Santos in a midfield that had Matheus Cunha, Youri Tielemans and Bryan Mbeumo ahead, with Fernandes a false-ish 9. As Como hogged possession throughout, any United foray needed to threaten Jean Butez’s goal: Mbeumo’s corner from the right patently did not when failing to clear a first defender.
After a near 24-hour deluge the rain finally stopped but Como’s blue wave continued relentlessly. United’s press was piecemeal, as Fernandes identified, maybe involving one or two, but never a group act.
At the interval, Carrick had to earn his corn. In missing nine players because of injury, suspension or illness, there was mitigation. Matthijs de Ligt, partnering Harry Maguire in central defence, being thrown straight in for a first appearance in 325 days after a serious back injury illustrated Carrick’s straitened resources.
Carrick’s move was to take off Cunha and Santos for Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo in a reshuffle that took Tielemans into central midfield, Fernandes to No 10, and Mbeumo leading the line. The net result: Como’s second. Paz enjoyed a universe of time to thread in Douvikas, and he powered past Lammens. This was a mere four minutes into the second half and thoughts turned to the clock ticking on Carrick’s tenure, before Como scored twice more.
First came Paz’s second, the Argentinian skating along the right and beating Lammens for 3-0. Then, on 76 minutes, Como waltzed through for a fourth time. Up rose Jacobo Ramón to head in Kaiki Bruno’s cross from the left and United’s disintegration was complete – Joshua Zirkzee’s stoppage-time goal not even a consolation.
By the end Carrick seemed as broken as his team. Even if Carrick survives until Sunday, who knows how much longer he will remain after Bournemouth’s visit. He was let down in the summer market but at this club the manager usually pays, not the hierarchy.

title: Elon Musk’s Super Pac spends $500,000 to back New York Republican in midterms
description: Incumbent Mike Lawler is fending off a challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in state’s 17th congressional district
content:
Incumbent Mike Lawler is fending off a challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in state’s 17th congressional district
How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions
Elon Musk’s Super Pac has spent more than $500,000 in New York’s highly competitive 17th congressional district race to help Mike Lawler, the Republican incumbent, hold on to his seat.
Lawler, a moderate Republican, is fending off a challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in the Hudson valley. It is among the most-watched races that could determine whether Republicans hold on to their majority in Congress.
America Pac, the Super Pac founded by Musk , has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars over the last year to boost Lawler’s campaign, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
Most of that spending has funded voter outreach efforts such as texting, printing, and postage and digital media-related services. Gothamist was the first to report on Musk’s spending.
Musk, the Republicans’ largest donor so far this midterm cycle, has spent millions of dollars on conservative candidates. Since the beginning of July, Musk has funneled $276m into Republican groups and America Pac, the New York Times reported earlier this month.
The funding is helping push Republican candidates to the finish line as they try to convince disgruntled voters to back the conservative party again. Polling shows Republican candidates are at a slight disadvantage this cycle because many have grown frustrated with the cost of living under Donald Trump.
America Pac’s spending on Lawler’s race is notable because Musk’s Pac spent more than $2m to help re-elect Lawler in 2024.
Conley, Lawler’s Democratic opponent , and the former head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has accused Lawler of protecting Musk rather than regulating artificial intelligence.
“AI poses a very real threat to the safety and security of the American people, and it’s long past time that Congress took action to regulate it,” Conley wrote on X. “But Mike Lawler is standing in the way, because he’s looking out for his trillionaire backer Elon Musk.”
Ciro Riccardi, Lawler’s campaign manager, told Gothamist that they had “no say over what America PAC or any other outside group spends in this race” – referencing a law that prohibits campaigns from coordinating directly with Super Pacs.

title: Epstein’s attorney and accountant accused of ‘facilitating and concealing’ his crimes in lawsuit
description: New Mexico lawsuit claims ‘in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project, his associates received generous salaries’
content:
New Mexico lawsuit claims ‘in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project, his associates received generous salaries’
The attorney general of New Mexico on Wednesday filed a civil lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s longtime attorney, Darren Indyke, and Epstein’s longtime accountant, Richard Kahn, accusing them of having “facilitated and concealed” Epstein’s crimes, and is seeking to stop them from being paid by Epstein’s estate while the litigation plays out.
The lawsuit , filed in the US district court for the district of New Mexico, names Kahn and Indyke as defendants both in their individual capacity, and in their capacity as co-executors of Epstein’s estate. The complaint also names Epstein’s estate, and the 1953 Trust, which holds the estate’s assets.
“Epstein, with the help of his associates, trafficked, isolated, and abused survivors at alluring locations” including at Epstein’s ranch in Stanley, New Mexico , known as Zorro Ranch, the complaint claims. It goes on to allege that “in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project and remaining silent about it, his associates received generous salaries, access to elite social circles, and lavish gifts, including being named beneficiaries of his multimillion-dollar estate”.
In a statement on Wednesday, an attorney for Indyke shared a statement on behalf of both Indyke and Kahn saying that they “emphatically reject the New Mexico Attorney General’s allegations that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr Indyke nor Mr Kahn was present.
“Not a single woman has ever accused Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, nor claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to them any allegation of Mr Epstein’s abuse,” the statement added. “The New Mexico Attorney General’s complaint does not allege anything to the contrary.”
The statement goes on to say that “neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General’s investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit”.
Earlier this year, Kahn and Indyke told the US House committee investigating Epstein that they had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes during their employment.
Among the demands the lawsuit seeks is a court order preventing Indyke and Kahn from receiving estate payments while the case proceeds.
The complaint alleges that both men profited personally from their relationships with Epstein. It alleges that from 2011 to 2019, Indyke received more than $16m from Epstein and related entities and that Kahn received more than $10m.
In a statement on Wednesday, Raúl Torrez, New Mexico’s attorney general, said that Epstein “did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible”.
“The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico,” he said. “Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences.”
In the complaint, Torrez wrote that “through this action, the State seeks to hold these individuals accountable to the fullest extent possible and to ensure that Epstein’s assets are distributed to the survivors of his horrific crimes”.
Several survivors of Epstein’s abuse signed a letter on Wednesday in support of Torrez’s lawsuit “because it can expose what roles Indyke and Kahn played in Epstein’s operation, examine how they handled survivors’ claims, and prevent Epstein’s trusted loyalists from being rewarded for their roles in Epstein’s organization”.
“Survivors deserve accountability and answers under oath. Epstein’s chosen confidants should not get the last word – or the money,” they added.
At a news conference on Wednesday about the new filing, Epstein survivor Anouska De Georgiou thanked Torrez for “standing with survivors”.
“We have carried this burden for long enough,” she said. “It is time for those responsible to answer for their part in it.”
The announcement on Wednesday comes amid a separate ongoing dispute between New Mexico officials and the Department of Justice over files Torrez is seeking as part of the state’s investigation into Epstein ’s possible crimes in the state, including at his ranch outside Santa Fe, where multiple survivors have said they were abused.
Torrez sued the Department of Justice in August, accusing the department and Todd Blanche, the attorney general, of “stonewalling” the state’s investigation , which was reopened in February. Torrez asked the court for access to unredacted Epstein-related files held by the justice department, and said in its filing his prosecutors had requested access to the records but had “faced sustained resistance” from the department.
The case is ongoing and the justice department recently filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that “decisions about law-enforcement information sharing are committed to the agency’s discretion” and that turning over unredacted files would violate victims’ privacy.
Epstein’s Zorro Ranch came under renewed scrutiny after the justice department’s release of roughly 3m files related to Epstein late last year and early this year. The Guardian reported in early February that the newly disclosed Epstein files contained thousands of references to Zorro Ranch, and numerous photos of men and young girls at the property, and that several survivors of Epstein’s abuse had also previously given testimony about abuse they say they were subjected to there.
The Guardian investigation also revealed that, unlike Epstein’s other properties in Palm Beach, in New York and on his private Caribbean island, federal authorities had apparently never searched the New Mexico ranch.
Epstein, who died in a Manhattan jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges , bought the property in New Mexico 1993. It was later sold by his estate in 2023.
In late February, Torrez announced that New Mexico would reopen its investigation into Epstein’s activities at the ranch, after the state’s initial investigation was put on hold in 2019 at the request of federal prosecutors in New York, who were pursuing the investigation into Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation that led to his arrest. In March, New Mexico authorities launched a search of the ranch.
Torrez has said that he wants to establish what took place at Zorro Ranch. New Mexico lawmakers also established a “truth commission” to examine activities at the ranch.

title: Thousands of California public employees begin strike over contract
description: SEIU Local 1000, representing nurses and teachers, pushing for higher wages, telework and affordable healthcare
content:
SEIU Local 1000, representing nurses and teachers, pushing for higher wages, telework and affordable healthcare
Thousands of California state workers walked off the job Wednesday in a sweeping one-day strike as tensions boiled over lapsed contract negotiations with Governor Gavin Newsom’s administration.
SEIU Local 1000, a union that represents roughly 100,000 public employees, has been at an impasse with the state since its contract expired on 30 June.
Negotiators say state officials rejected their key proposals: a 20% salary increase over three years, higher state healthcare contributions and flexible telework – Newsom has required state workers to be in office four days a week.
Union representatives also argued in a complaint filed with California’s public employment relations board that the state engaged in bad faith bargaining, by allegedly waiting until 30 June to respond to some of the proposals and saying there was “no money” for additional compensation.
In downtown Los Angeles, picketers dressed in purple-and-yellow union shirts circled the exterior of the Ronald Reagan state building under light drizzle.
Some motorists slowed down, beeping their car horns in apparent solidarity.
Joseph Santillan, a motor vehicle records specialist, began working at the Department of Motor Vehicles about nine years ago, when he was earning roughly $17 per hour. “As I got higher up in my seniority, we got our annual raises, but now I’m maxed out,” he said.
Santillan, who lives near West Covina, said he had to move out of an apartment he shared with two roommates because it was too costly.
“I’ve been living at home with Mom again for the past six years,” Santillan said. “It’s kind of sad. I’m 43. I should be on my own. I should be able to support myself.”
William Hernandez, a financial institutions examiner, said he was striking for fair pay and changes to the state’s in-office mandate. For his role, the 26-year-old often commutes from Hollywood to various banks around Los Angeles and southern California without a car.
“I personally don’t have a car because it’s too expensive to afford both a car and housing,” Hernandez said. About half of his monthly wages go to rent.
In the afternoon, David Huerta, president of SEIU-West, drummed up energy, sparking a labor chant: “Sí, se puede!” (Yes, we can!)
“Their fight is representative of the fight right now that’s happening across the state, across this country, as working people continue to get more and more squeezed. And the ability to be able to live becomes more and more difficult,” Huerta said.
Wednesday’s picketing marked a first for the union.
California’s department of human resources (CalHR) had reportedly attempted to block the strike, arguing the union did not have plans to exempt essential workers and thus was compromising public health and safety. The labor board determined a list of about 5,000 workers deemed essential, according to the union, who will report to work during the strike.
“The department remains focused on achieving a fair and responsible agreement and continues to be available at the bargaining table,” a CalHR spokesperson said in a Wednesday statement.

title: ‘It feels quite frightening’: readers rush to snap up Sally Rooney books as stocks dwindle amid Palestine Action ban
description: Booksellers have reported selling out of the Irish novelist’s works after it was announced that her books would be withdrawn from sale in the UK
content:
Booksellers have reported selling out of the Irish novelist’s works after it was announced that her books would be withdrawn from sale in the UK
Booksellers have reported selling out of copies of Sally Rooney’s novels, following the news that her books would be withdrawn from sale in the UK, given her support for the banned group Palestine Action. Sales shot up nearly 300% in a week, as a host of high profile writers signed letters in support of the Irish author, including Zadie Smith, Annie Ernaux, Arundhati Roy, Ali Smith and Kamila Shamsie.
Bookmarked, an independent bookshop in Bristol, had three Sally Rooney novels in stock when Faber announced last week that it would stop supplying the author’s books. Within hours, customers had bought all of them. Now the shop has none, and it cannot get any more. “In retrospect, I feel like we should have put them behind a glass casing, forever on display until the law is overturned,” says the shop’s general manager Evelyn.
Faber’s books “have just been immediately taken down from the suppliers’ website, which feels really eerie”, she adds. “What worries me most is the precedent that it sets … We’re becoming increasingly used to seeing this type of stuff happen in other countries, but this is happening on our doorstep.”
Rooney is arguably the best-known literary novelist of her generation. Normal People alone has sold more than a million copies in the UK, and each new book is treated as a publishing event, with launch-day queues and early openings. Now, her work is disappearing from British shelves.
Last year, Rooney said that she would use proceeds from her books and their BBC adaptations to support Palestine Action. The direct action group was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025 , and supporting it is now a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison (the high court ruled the proscription unlawful in February, but the court of appeal overturned that decision in June and the ban remains in force). Last week, Faber said UK legislation meant it could not pass on UK earnings to Rooney, and that it had decided, with her full agreement, to stop supplying her work. Copies already in shops can still be sold, they just cannot be replenished.
Readers have rushed to buy what was left. Nielsen BookScan told the Guardian that Rooney sold 4,531 copies last week, up 291% from the week before the announcement.
Restocking is now the problem. When a customer came into The Best of Times, a new bookshop and cafe in Kent, asking for Rooney, owner Gavin Boyter went to reorder. On the website of Gardners, the UK’s main book wholesaler, every one of her titles was marked as unavailable to order.
“Farcically, I can order Bucknell University Press’s Sally Rooney: Perspectives and Approaches for a mere £96,” he said. “I guess we’ll be out of stock for the foreseeable future, which is a great shame.”
“I can still order four different versions of Mein Kampf, though,” he added, which illustrates the “absurdity” of the situation.
In August 2025, weeks after Palestine Action was banned, Rooney wrote in the Irish Times that if supporting the group made her “a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it”. She has since said she could no longer safely travel to the UK without facing arrest, sending her editor to collect an award in London on her behalf.
At Juno Books in Sheffield, Alim Kheraj said the situation felt unprecedented. “We’ve had people coming in asking if they can buy the books specifically to support Rooney,” he said. “But we’re completely sold out. I can’t think of another time where a publisher has had to pull a book because of comments [an author has] made about a specific organisation,” he added. “It feels quite frightening.”
Across the Irish Sea, a kind of book smuggling – entirely above board, as far as the booksellers involved understand it – has sprung up almost overnight.
Kennys Bookshop in Galway, which ships worldwide, says its Rooney sales have risen tenfold since the announcement. Almost none of the new buyers are Irish: 95% of the increase, owner Tómas Kenny said, has come from Britain. “It’s almost exclusively the UK”.
British booksellers are also trying to get stock in by the back door. Kenny, who works closely with UK shops, said he had been contacted by “lots of people” looking to get hold of books.
For him, the reversal is striking. He grew up in an Ireland where books were banned for blasphemy. “Britain was where people escaped to, to read and watch what they wanted,” he said. “We’re in a scenario where it’s the opposite”.
Northern Ireland, which has access to both the UK and Irish markets after Brexit, has become a conduit. Some booksellers there are openly continuing to stock Rooney by sourcing her books from the Republic, and then posting them across the water. Lesley Price, who runs Bridge Books in Co Down, says she has been “inundated” with website orders, most of them heading to Britain, and that sales were up “tenfold, if not more”.
“I don’t believe in book banning,” she said. “I know it’s not a ban, but I guess it is a censorship of sorts, and that does not sit well with me.” When she posted online that Bridge Books would continue to stock Rooney’s books, she says the response has mostly been positive, with some exceptions. “There have also been quite a lot of people calling me a terrorist sympathiser and wishing harm on my business.”
Writers have also rallied behind Rooney. An open letter signed by hundreds including Patrick Ness, Damian Barr and Juno Dawson called on the government to act. A second letter, published by the New Statesman and signed by writers including Zadie Smith, Annie Ernaux, Naomi Klein and new Nobel literature laureate Anne Carson, declared: “Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist.” Normal People stars Daisy Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal are also signatories, along with Gary Lineker.
“I am troubled at this Orwellian suppression of ideas, all writers should be,” says Dawson. “Both throughout history and today, clampdowns on artistic freedom are a hallmark of rising fascism.” Nikesh Shukla said he signed to draw attention to what he sees as the wrongness of the ban on Palestine Action itself, which he said was “now damaging the arts sector, literature and freedom of speech”.
Proscribing Palestine Action “highlighted that the Terrorism Act is too broad in structure and application,” says Jemimah Steinfeld, chief executive of Index on Censorship. “The arrests of thousands of peaceful protesters that followed made this point even stronger.
“This is really a test case,” she continued, adding that Faber’s caution was “fully understandable” because “we’re on new ground”. Ireland’s foreign affairs minister, Helen McEntee, has said she will raise the matter directly with the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband.
The real test will come with her next release. Rooney’s latest novel, Intermezzo, was published two years ago. “What happens when she has a new book coming out, which I would say is not that far away?” Kenny said. “Will it be available in the UK? That, to me, will be a far bigger story.”
For independent shops, the stakes are high. “It’s really some titles, like Sally Rooney, that will make or break your year.”

title: Former Tory election candidate suspended over contract killing claims
description: Jack Ross was filmed allegedly discussing with an undercover reporter violent options to deal with enemies
content:
Jack Ross was filmed allegedly discussing with an undercover reporter violent options to deal with enemies
A former Conservative election candidate has been suspended from the party after he was seemingly filmed discussing the cost of hiring contract killers and offering to “broker” the services of a far-right activist with alleged paramilitary links.
Jack Ross was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter “What do you want done?” before listing the type of violent options that could be bought.
Ross appeared to tell the Al Jazeera journalist: “They can just kick the fuck out of someone. That’s a certain amount. They can start cutting people’s faces up, that’s another amount. And they can stab someone. They can shoot someone. They can kill someone.”
Police in Scotland say they will be reviewing and assessing the Al Jazeera documentary – Contract Killers and the Far Right – for any criminality.
Ross is the chief executive of Turning Point UK, a spin-off from the campaign group founded by the murdered US Republican commentator Charlie Kirk.
Footage released by TPUK last year showed Ross and others from the group meeting Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, after Kirk’s death.
A profile page for Ross on the website of the Bow Group, a Conservative thinktank that lists him as a research fellow, states he has advised MPs and candidates on political and digital strategy. He has been pictured alongside Boris Johnson and other high-profile figures including James Cleverly, Jacob Rees-Mogg and Liam Fox.
Ross was reported by Al Jazeera to have introduced an undercover reporter to a violent criminal from Glasgow with links to the paramilitary Ulster Volunteer Force, who offers to have people killed for money.
Al Jazeera approached Ross with a fictitious family problem where a deceased uncle’s business was at risk of being taken over by a gang, whose members were supposedly warned they would “get fucked” if anything happened.
Ross replied to this: “Yeah, you have to deliver on that as well. You’ve got to explain to me what’s needed … I can then go and broker from there. But I’ve got to say, even to myself … if there’s lashback I’ve got to keep my name out of it.”
The Scottish paramilitary contact was then filmed at a London hotel offering to arrange different types of killings, ranging from a hit-and-run that could be made to look like drink-driving to a stabbing.
The meeting took place after Ross, apparently acting on behalf of the Zimbabwean government, had reportedly paid thousands of pounds to the Glasgow activist to organise a fake political rally in support of lifting UK sanctions imposed on the African country.
Ross said: “I have had a few things and some of the Zims [Zimbabweans] have said to me they want stuff done. They wanted a fucking shooter.”
He said he had asked them to talk to the paramilitary, adding: “I said I was not putting fucking prints on anything.”
While TPUK was launched as a student movement, it has become increasingly involved in anti-migrant street protests. Its chief operating officer is Nick Tenconi, the leader of the far-right UK Independence party, who visited the Conservative conference in 2022 with Ross.
Ross was filmed in 2022 telling an undercover reporter they should chat to him about what they wanted, adding “keep it simple” and then listing the various violent options that could be bought for cash, including murder.
A Conservative party spokesperson said: “Mr Ross’s membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation. We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing.”
At another point, Ross expressed concerns that journalists could be recording the sort of things he was saying and could pass them to police.
“The journalist will put it out there and then the police will pick it up and fuck you,” he said. “You’ve got to think that what we were talking about and had someone film it we’d be fucking done for conspiracy.”
Tenconi was filmed alongside Ross as they outlined a plan to use football hooligans to stir up trouble.
Tenconi said: “So let Labour get in. So we build the new right and we have these armies … so, three-pronged. We keep winning MPs over. Then we build the second prong, we build an army, and that’s street demos, protest, just fuck things up, basically.”
A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the documentary. It will be reviewed and assessed for any criminality.”
Al Jazeera reported that Ross had “completely” denied its investigation’s findings, claiming that everything he said to the undercover reporter was not meant seriously.
Ross, who was a local elections candidate for the Conservatives , was approached by the Guardian for comment through TPUK. Tenconi was also approached for comment via his party.

title: ‘It should never be forgotten’: families recount care home victims’ experiences in wake of Covid findings
description: Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy
content:
Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy
“A t the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.
“I spoke to Grandad on the phone when it was possible – it often wasn’t possible due to staff not being able to take him a phone – and he was desperately lonely, isolated in his room, unable to talk to anyone because they were worried about [the spread of Covid],” says Amy, 39, who lives in Milton Keynes and works for a large software company. “I consoled myself that they were keeping him safe. That all the isolation was necessary.”
Instead, she says, he was depressed and very afraid until he finally caught the virus in 2022. Amy saw him for the first time on a Covid ward, “when I had to beg and beg and beg the hospital staff to let me visit him”. Eric died shortly afterwards.
Six years after Covid struck, the latest report from the public inquiry into the pandemic, published this week, has convinced Amy that the policy of isolating residents was “cruel and pointless”, she says. “I want to smash something. I can never get that time with them back.
“The impression I had at the time was that [the government] were doing their best in the face of an unstoppable tidal wave, but it sounds like they put out a hand and expected it to stop the ocean.”
The inquiry concluded that the entire care sector had been an “afterthought” to government planners, and that a claim by the then health secretary, Matt Hancock, to have put a “protective ring” around residents was entirely unfounded. Instead, the decision to discharge untested patients from hospitals into care homes led to the virus spreading “like wildfire”, while blanket restrictions on outside contact led to “immense emotional harm” and “profound isolation” for vulnerable residents.
The findings are no surprise to the family members of care home residents, many of whom have told the Guardian of the immense distress their loved ones went through. Roger Dennison’s father, Lucius, was a sprightly 90-year-old care home resident when the first reports of the coronavirus emerged; they watched the news together in Lucius’s room and wondered how quickly it would peter out.
Weeks later, Lucius’s care home had firmly locked down, and the only way Dennison could talk to his dad was through a window that had been opened a few inches at the top. “You’re standing on tiptoe, trying to shout in and then be heard on the other side,” he says. “It was very confusing. It wasn’t very happy as an experience.” They tried it just once but stopped because it was too distressing for Lucius.
After that, Dennison, who had previously visited every other day, was reliant on passing messages through staff, while Lucius was “in his room, largely on his own”. The disease “became a growing apprehension for me once it became clear people were coming into the home and bringing it with them”, says his son. “I think there was a sense of inevitability.” Lucius caught Covid in the first wave and died in hospital in April 2020.
To care workers, too, the situation was terrifying and immensely distressing, says Nick (not his real name), who was a senior worker at a home in West Yorkshire. “The situation from the very start was frightening because we all thought that if you got Covid, you died or were going to be seriously unwell. I remember having to strip naked at the back door of my house because we had a resident return from hospital who had shared a ward with Covid patients. As a care home, we tried to refuse their return based on the risk of infection but were told [by the hospital] that we couldn’t.”
From that point, he says, “all hell broke loose”. “Our first case of Covid was about a week later.” They had already run out of personal protective equipment, he says.
“The mental health impact on all staff was huge. Watching people die at such a high rate in such a small space of time; having to say goodbye to so many people we came to know and love; putting our own health on the line every day and then quite possibly carrying that home to your family. Mentally, we were all spent.”
Like many, Catherine Bennett, a retired teacher from Lewes in East Sussex, says she was not shocked by the inquiry’s findings: “We knew what was happening. I am, however, very angry.” Her father, who had been in a care home since 2018, “felt a terrible sense of abandonment” that no one was able to visit and became paralysingly afraid of catching the virus.
“For a long time he didn’t go down for meals; he stopped doing all his activities so he wouldn’t meet anybody.” After some months, she says, the care home built a room where residents could talk to relatives through a glass panel and speakers. It was, she says, “very distressing for a man of his age to be separated from his loved ones in that way, to be able to see us through the glass but not be able to touch us or have any meaningful contact”. Her father died in the home in 2022.
Diana, a retired social worker from Derby, feels a similar lasting anger about the experience of her sister, Helen, whose mental health needs meant she was living in a care home in Carlisle when the pandemic struck, and who experienced a similar bewilderment at her sudden isolation. The first time Diana was able to sit with her was after a year of lockdown when Helen was very unwell; she died the same day.
“I just think they threw care homes under a bus while they partied in Downing Street, and I do feel rather cross about that,” says Diana. “I think it is a major trauma for this country and I think it should never be forgotten.”

title: US charges six people in alleged Massachusetts marriage fraud ring
description: Accused allegedly arranged hundreds of sham marriages for immigrants to obtain green cards
content:
Accused allegedly arranged hundreds of sham marriages for immigrants to obtain green cards
Federal prosecutors on Wednesday charged six people with participating in a long-running scheme to reportedly arrange hundreds ⁠of sham marriages in Massachusetts in order to help immigrants unlawfully obtain green cards and potential US citizenship.
US attorney Leah Foley during a press ⁠conference in Boston said ⁠the scheme’s alleged ​mastermind, Jennifer Gonzalez, helped organize sham marriages for over a decade in Massachusetts , a Democratic-led state the defendant described as a “sanctuary” jurisdiction where “you get ⁠a lot of help as an immigrant”.
It marked the latest such case by the US Department of Justice as part of Donald Trump ’s immigration ⁠crackdown. In August, it brought one of the largest such cases when in New York it ​ charged 11 people over a scheme prosecutors said ‌facilitated about 1,000 sham ‌marriages.
Gonzalez, 43, told a cooperating witness posing as a client that her group helped obtain hundreds ‌of permanent resident cards, or green cards, for undocumented noncitizens living in Massachusetts, charging between $38,000 and $40,000 for marriages to US citizens, according to a criminal complaint.
Authorities said the operation ran for about 12 years and averaged about 18 to 20 fraudulent marriages annually, generating more than $6m in profits.
Gonzalez, a US-born citizen, told the witness her goal was “for you to get the American dream”, but ‌that her business had become more difficult after Trump returned to office in 2025, the complaint said.
Foley, whom the Trump administration appointed as the state’s top federal prosecutor, ​called it a sophisticated scheme that Gonzalez was “operating with impunity under the last administration”.
“My hope is that today the charged defendants and others like them realize that the American dream is not for sale,” Foley said. “It is earned. And when you try to pilfer it for profit, we will hold you ⁠accountable.”
Gonzalez is charged with harboring immigrants living illegally in the US and ​marriage fraud. Her lawyer did not ​immediately respond to a request ​for comment.
Other defendants include people accused of aiding Gonzalez’s scheme or entering into ​sham marriages with immigrants.
Foley ‌said Gonzalez entered ​such a marriage ​herself and obtained Snap food benefits from Massachusetts without listing any income from her scheme, which she used to buy property in the Dominican Republic.
Foley said the investigation was ongoing and could result in future charges against anyone found to have obtained legal status through the scheme.

title: ‘You are a humanitarian also, sir’: the US feeds Putin with lies as Ukraine’s children take cover and die
description: Steve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’
content:
Steve Witkoff’s flattery of the Russian leader could be just the start of a mendacious stratagem from a US president who says Moscow ‘has been fine on Ukraine’
They say the first casualty of war is truth. For the Trump administration , the road to peace with Russia now encompasses some extraordinary lies.
Steve Witkoff delivered one as he sat down with Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday, aiming to close the deal on Russia’s land grab in Ukraine with the White House’s strategy of maximum pressure on Kyiv and saccharine flattery of the Kremlin.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” said Witkoff, a real-estate mogul who, thanks to being Trump’s friend, is now the US’s senior envoy and diplomat to end the largest European conflict since the second world war. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you.”
In Putin’s 26 years in power, it is a rare moment when he has been granted that specific honour. Skim through Russia’s past wartime exploits – from the bombing campaigns in Chechnya and Georgia and Syria, to the thousands of Russian citizens jailed for dissent, to the violent deaths of prominent opposition journalists and politicians in barely disguised assassinations and poisonings – and it will be difficult to identify Putin’s credentials as a humanitarian.
And that is before looking to Ukraine, where Russia chose to launch a full-scale invasion that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives. The Guardian recently obtained a Russian strategy document showing the Kremlin’s potential to black out Ukrainian cities this winter, cutting off up to 90% of electricity to cities such as Kyiv and Odesa and Kharkiv – where millions of people live – to intentionally create a humanitarian catastrophe. And judging by the nightly barrages levelled at power plants for cities across Ukraine, the Kremlin has decided to move forward with that strategy until Kyiv surrenders.
As Witkoff met Putin on Wednesday , schoolchildren in Kharkiv hastened down a reinforced stairway, sirens announcing the arrival of Shahed drones overhead. This is no ordinary bomb shelter; it is one of 10 underground schools Kharkiv has constructed because of Russia’s regular bombing of the city less than 20 miles from the border.
Parents had welcomed the schools because they were safe, said teachers, and this was the one way that young people could have an uninterrupted school day during a war that could last years more – and reignite even if a shaky peace deal is reached.
“We all believed in Trump. We all really had hopes for America and for Trump to stop this monster Putin,” said Olena Svytlychna, the head of the education department of the Novobavarskyi region in Kharkiv, sitting in the school’s cafe on Wednesday.
“And now we have doubts, we don’t believe them. And we are very scared.”
As Witkoff spoke, the families of six people killed in a drone strike in a park near Kharkiv this week were holding funerals. The youngest victim of the strike was a one-year-old girl, Anhelina, who was killed as she was sitting strapped into her stroller in a playground. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, a local schoolteacher, was also killed in the strike. The final death toll was four adults and two children, Anhelina and an 11-year-old girl.
Those lives have barely earned a mention from the White House as it pushes for Ukraine to capitulate as quickly as it can this week – and crucially before the 3 November midterm elections when voters will deliver a referendum on Trump’s leadership for the last two years.
Shortly after the bombing, Trump told reporters on the White House lawn that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine”. After taking criticism for that remark, he mentioned the attacks in passing just to downplay the shelling of civilians: there were “some people in a town that got hit or whatever, but mostly young soldiers” died, he said from the Oval Office on Tuesday.
For the White House, those words cost little. Witkoff’s goal was to bring home a US citizen, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan, who had been detained in Russia. But if Witkoff wants to buy a peace deal by 3 November through flattering Putin, then this will only be the White House’s opening salvo in its war on truth.

title: Drill, baby, drill? Climate campaigners condemn Jackdaw gasfield approval - The Latest
description: Climate campaigners have condemned the UK government’s decision to allow the drilling of the Jackdaw gasfield. But green activists may have secured a significant victory on the larger Rosebank oilfield with signs it won’t be approved. Michael Safi speaks to environment correspondent Matthew Taylor
author_name: Michael Safi, Matthew Taylor, Angus Neale, Leonore Schick, Zoe Hitch
content: Climate campaigners have condemned the UK government’s decision to allow the drilling of the Jackdaw gasfield. Critics argue the move will put climate targets at risk, while failing to reduce energy bills and the cost of living crisis. But there could be a significant victory for green activists when it comes to the much larger Rosebank oilfield, with the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, leaning towards rejecting approval. Michael Safi speaks to environment correspondent Matthew Taylor – watch on YouTube

title: The Guardian view on drilling in Jackdaw: a truly pragmatic approach would focus on Britain’s green transition
description: Editorial: Opening the North Sea gasfield will deliver minimal benefits for households, while sending a dismal signal before next month’s Cop summit
content:
Opening the North Sea gasfield will deliver minimal benefits for households, while sending a dismal signal before next month’s Cop summit
T his week a report from the UN Environment Programme concluded that holding global temperatures to a 1.5C warming limit – the centrepiece commitment of the Paris climate agreement – is no longer achievable. If the disastrous consequences of a significant overshoot are to be mitigated, it argued, governments must start delivering the short-term actions to meet long-term targets on reducing fossil fuel consumption.
Disappointingly, Andy Burnham and his energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, took a different view of short-term priorities on Wednesday. Before the November Cop summit, where regaining lost momentum on climate action will be crucial, their decision to approve new drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield sent a dismal signal. The prime minister justified it as a pragmatic move “at a time when people are really struggling”. But the pragmatic arguments don’t stack up.
Going ahead with Jackdaw will have no impact on bills this winter and little in the longer run. It will deliver only a small number of jobs for a very limited period. Tax revenues from new drilling will be substantially negated by the various concessions and breaks enjoyed by the oil and gas industry. Claims that Jackdaw will enhance the UK’s national energy security are hugely overblown, given that it will satisfy a mere 2% of national demand. The country’s heavy reliance on natural gas imports will remain unaltered.
So why? Mr Burnham would doubtless have preferred not to be landed with the judgment call on either Jackdaw or the much larger Rosebank oil and gas field (on which an announcement has yet to be made). Both were already in the licensing system, having been approved by Rishi Sunak as he sought a dividing line with Labour. A successful legal challenge meant the final decision fell in the present prime minister’s lap.
On Jackdaw at least, Mr Burnham appears to have judged that political expediency, particularly in Scotland, was best served by waving it through. A failure by governments to invest gamechanging sums in the green transition has made the politics of net zero more fraught. The recent Tory byelection victory in Aberdeen South followed a campaign focused on reviving oil and gas production in the North Sea. One of the first acts of Scottish Labour’s new leader, Michael Marra, has been to back both the Rosebank and Jackdaw developments.
Mr Burnham inherited this complicated set of circumstances. But rather than rubber-stamping a regressive rearguard action by the fossil fuel industry, he should be using his rhetorical gifts to make the pragmatic case for Britain’s green energy future. As research by the E3G thinktank has laid out , the dubious benefits of drilling for disappearing oil and gas reserves are dwarfed by the potential economic impact of insulating Britain’s homes and investing in heat pumps. The government’s warm homes plan , it estimated, would significantly reduce household energy bills and generate 50,000 new jobs. Yet Ms Fahnbulleh is reportedly under pressure to find cuts so spending can be diverted to defence.
The best way to achieve energy security, back British workers and bring down bills – the three imperatives identified by Mr Burnham in his statement on Wednesday – is to invest ambitiously in the country’s climate goals. Proceeding with Jackdaw does not, in itself, signify a prime ministerial reluctance to do that. But this decision suggests there are grounds for concern about which way the wind is blowing in Downing Street.

title: The Guardian view on the Republicans’ midterms struggle: Trump has circuses, but voters also want bread
description: Editorial: As prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promised
content:
As prices keep rising, more of the president’s supporters are asking what happened to the economic good times he promised
I t is no great revelation that Donald Trump is enriching himself as president. He raked in $2.2bn in 2025, with his position and his personal interests frequently overlapping. Yet this week’s poll finding that 34% of Republicans (and 66% of all American voters) think that he is using his position to make himself rich merits attention . Separately, voters in a Fox News poll last week put government corruption at the top of their list of concerns – just ahead of inflation and high prices.
Mr Trump pledged that people would be better off if they voted for him. Billionaires are; not the rest. He promised to lower grocery costs (they have risen) and to cut the price of gasoline to below $2 a gallon. It’s more than double that, thanks to his illegal war on Iran. Tariffs haven’t helped. Incumbents struggle when life feels unaffordable, and polling for the Guardian has shown the disenchantment of key voting groups. The gulf between his own prosperity and the lives of his base now looks less like an inspiration and more like an insult. Cash offers seem unlikely to help much.
The president’s popularity rating sank to a record low of 36% in a poll on Wednesday. Mr Trump, of course, is not on the ballot. But he is touring red states as he seeks to shore up the vote in places where the idea of a Democratic victory looked laughable two years ago. Democrats are rightly cautious about their midterms prospects, having been burned too many times. But less than a fortnight from 3 November, with many votes already cast, polls suggest that they will take the House and could well claim the Senate too.
The party is still unpopular, though impressive candidates are performing far better than anyone expected in surprising places – notably Texas and Kansas. But they are now more trusted on economic issues . Independents are turning away from Mr Trump and his party, and many Republicans seem unenthused, for multiple reasons. The “Maga-sympathetic” pollster Rich Baris argues that “Donald Trump did this to himself”. His base believed Mr Trump was their champion. Now they suspect that he is “just another politician”.
There is merited concern about how the president has already used his power to tilt the midterms , and more about what he may do if his party fares as badly as forecast. Republicans still hope to reclaim ground through traditional if unsavoury means, massively outspending Democrats.
Yet while some polls are tightening , culture war attacks and salacious lies about opponents such as James Talarico in Texas do not seem, at least so far, to be as powerful as Republicans hoped. That’s not just because Democratic candidates are repositioning themselves. The toxic messaging of the presidential race – that Kamala Harris “is for they/them, President Trump is for you” – doesn’t land if voters believe that he’s actually for himself and his friends.
Republicans now point to France’s unrest and claim that a Democrat-dominated Congress would bring chaos and destruction to America. Their fearmongering has often motivated core voters. But while Democrats stick to the economic attack, Republicans are trying to change the subject instead of offering answers. Mr Trump’s bread-and-circuses politics is floundering, cage fights on the South Lawn of the White House notwithstanding, as voters ask what happened to the bread.

title: Chemical tank explosion in Toledo, Ohio, prompts mass evacuation
description: Officials say the explosion released an airborne irritant that can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin
content:
Officials say the explosion released an airborne irritant that can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin
Officials are investigating a tank explosion in Toledo, Ohio , that released a chemical into the air, causing a mass evacuation in the area.
One person, a first responder, was injured and taken to the hospital, but officials believe the injuries are non-life-threatening. They are also unsure about the cause of the explosion.
An employee at the company, MC Tank Terminal – which specializes in transporting bulk liquid chemicals and provides tank container transportation, storage and maintenance – called on first responders late Tuesday night to address the explosion.
Wade Kapszukiewicz, Toledo’s mayor, announced in a news conference on Wednesday that residents within a 1-mile radius of the explosion needed to evacuate and those within 3 miles were being asked to shelter in place with their windows sealed. He said executives from MC Tank Terminal were en route to Toledo to assess the situation.
“We understand the seriousness of what has happened here,” Kapszukiewicz said. “That’s why we took the actions that we did. That’s why we’re going to continue to monitor and communicate with the public throughout the day.”
The chemical released was glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial coating product used in plastics, rubbers and resins. Local officials say the airborne irritant can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin; they have suggested Toledo residents who experience serious symptoms like difficulty breathing, nausea and vomiting, dizziness or confusion, go to the emergency room or call 911.
When the chemical was released in the explosion, it became a gas, but when it settles back into the tank, it will turn again into a liquid, Kapszukiewicz said at Wednesday’s conference.
“The hope is that at that point, the risk of explosion will have expired, and that efforts can be made to contain and eliminate the hazard,” he said.
Local news outlets in Toledo have reported a visible, dense fog over the town and a lurking plastic-like odor .
The city, which has a population of roughly 265,000 people, per the US Census Bureau, had already issued an evacuation order on Tuesday night for about 300 people who live within a half mile of the explosion. That was later expanded to a full mile, evacuating about 1,000 people.
City officials said Wednesday that as far as they knew, all residents had been evacuated. Kapszukiewicz said officials were unsure how long the evacuation and shelter orders would last.
Residents were being asked to communicate with local businesses and schools within the evacuation zone to see what their plans were during the evacuation. Some schools were closed Wednesday and others delayed their opening, according to NBC News.

title: John Staley obituary
description: Other lives: Field director for Oxfam in India who went on to be a lecturer in development studies in Birmingham
content:
My father, John Staley, who has died aged 88, was field director for Oxfam in south India and Sri Lanka during the late 1960s and early 70s, when he was responsible for Oxfam’s funding of several hundred local, national and international voluntary agencies.
His role included aid administration, policy formulation, project appraisal, recommendations for funding, disaster relief and liaison with government and non-government organisations. He led Oxfam’s response in India to a drought in Maharashtra in 1973, which fed more than 20,000 people as part of a work-for-food programme, and was made MBE in 1974 for services to the Indian people. John was born in Epsom, Surrey, the only child of Robert, a doctor, and Sylvia, a housewife. He went to Marlborough college in Wiltshire, and then, after national service, to Cambridge University, where he studied natural sciences and economics (1957-61).
At Cambridge he met Elizabeth Pott, and they discovered a shared love of travelling on an overland expedition to Pakistan with friends. They married in 1962 and did PhDs together at the University of the Punjab in Lahore, studying the economics and geography of mountain communities in northern Pakistan.
In 1966 they returned to the UK, where they finished their PhDs and where John did some freelance lecturing at the Commonwealth Institute, the Pakistan Society and the Royal Central Asian Society before taking up his field director post at Oxfam in 1967.
John eventually became research director for Oxfam in India (1975-76), and during that time discovered the concept of experience-based training, by which small groups of people learn about the behaviour of groups and organisations from their own analysis of their experience of the group.
In 1976 he and some Indian colleagues founded Search, an organisation that developed and used these experience-based training methods to train people in development work in India. He was seconded by Oxfam to Search from 1976 to 1980, and then, in 1982, returned to the UK to become a lecturer and later senior lecturer in development studies at Selly Oak Colleges in Birmingham – remaining there until his retirement in 1999. Thereafter he wrote, travelled, took part in his local U3A in Great Malvern, Worcestershire, and cared for his garden and a small local wood that he and Elizabeth bought as a retirement project. Over the years John wrote three books, Words for My Brother (1982), People in Development (also 1982), and Enticing the Learning (2008). Elizabeth died in 2019. John is survived by their children, Eleanor, Joanna and me, and grandchildren Isabelle and Freddie.

title: Shabana Mahmood urged to ‘read the room’ on Labour opposition to immigration policy
description: No 10 declines to rule out watering down plans to extend waiting period for indefinite leave to remain as cabinet split widens
content:
No 10 declines to rule out watering down plans to extend waiting period for indefinite leave to remain as cabinet split widens
Shabana Mahmood has been urged to “read the room” on Labour opposition to her immigration policy, as No 10 declined to rule out watering down her plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.
She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.
However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”
There is already a cabinet split over the policy, which deepened on Wednesday when Miatta Fahnbulleh , the energy secretary, repeatedly refused to back the specific plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency in the UK.
This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”
This year the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, publicly criticised the plans , and dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.
One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.
“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.
MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the reforms.
Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.
“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”
In her interview with Sky News on Wednesday, Fahbulleh repeatedly avoided the question on whether she would back an increase in the waiting period for permanent residency to 15 years. She said: “We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution. And so there is a package of reforms. The home secretary has been consulting on this. She’s looking at the range of responses, and she will come out with the measures that we take forward.
“No one can look at our immigration system – and I say this as someone that came to this country as a refugee – and not believe that it’s broken and not believe that we need to fundamentally reform it.
“But our principles has to be a system where we’ve got control, but ultimately a system that when people do come to this country, they are able to integrate, they are able to contribute, and that we both respect but also value that contribution.”
She said she supported “reforms that say that people have to contribute and make a contribution to this country in order to get citizenship”, adding: “I 100% back Shabana Mahmood and everything she is trying to do.”
But she avoided multiple questions on the prospect of a 15-year wait. When it was put to her that she did not back that specific proposal, Fahnbulleh said: “Don’t … put words in my mouth.”
A government source said that “the minister clearly supported the policy and process” in her interviews, “but while subject to review of the consultation, the final policy is not set – so ministers cannot offer opinions on specific parts of it”.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

title: Olivier Mourgue obituary
description: Designer whose flexible furniture for informal 60s living gave a futuristic look to Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey
content:
Designer whose flexible furniture for informal 60s living gave a futuristic look to Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey
Olivier Mourgue always wanted to design the future. Growing up in Paris in the 1950s, he took against the ornate antique furniture of his parents’ apartment, the formality of a dining room with a table surrounded by elaborately uncomfortable chairs and a living room dominated by a sofa used only on special occasions. “Furniture like that has nothing to do with life,” he would suggest later. “One is never at ease in such rooms.”
Mourgue, who has died aged 87, set out to design furniture that belonged to the modern world, and blurred the boundaries between furniture and architecture. In his view, that meant that it should be flexible, informal, affordable and as close to the floor as possible. He succeeded in a way that he could not have expected.
The film director Stanley Kubrick made Mourgue’s designs an essential part of popular culture’s expectations of how the future would look, even though Mourgue’s work was produced by the thousand rather than in millions. Kubrick used a cluster of Mourgue’s Djinn armchairs to equip the lobby of the Hilton hotel orbiting the moon on Space Station V for one of the key scenes of 2001: A Space Odyssey. The Djinn seemed to float almost weightless, like a colourful bubble of air. There were no conventional arms or legs to be seen. Instead there was a lightweight steel structure and some sturdy rubber webbing to support the foam upholstery, all hidden inside a seamless surface.
Kubrick had a preternatural gift for finding what might be called “real” objects, such as Djinn, from his own time, that seemed to belong to the future. He used them to give a sense of authenticity to his sets. Kubrick filmed A Space Odyssey in 1968, when Djinn looked entirely at home in a plausible version of 2001 that did not yet exist. Almost 60 years later, Djinn still looks like a version of the future, fluid and colourful, covered with a specially made stretch fabric that was available in 15 different bright colours and light enough to carry under your arm.
Mourgue wanted to do more than change the way that things looked. He believed in designing furniture that reflected the way that people want to live. He created a low-cost range of mass-produced designs for the department store chain Prisunic, in the days when it was a French version of Ikea, selling through its catalogue as well as its network of stores. The 1969 Prisunic edition launched a collection that Mourgue described as “bringing beauty at the price of the ugly”. It included bookcases, beds, tables, and seating made from lightweight chipboard that could be easily dismantled if required. One piece was a floor-cushion seat with raised edges that formed a place to sit.
Olivier was born in Paris, to Denise (nee Lesieur), a physiotherapist, and Jean, who owned an art supply store. His uncle, Pierre Mourgue, was a successful illustrator, working for Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar in the US. Olivier’s younger brother, Pascal, also became a successful furniture designer.
Influenced by the radical spirit of 1968, Olivier was impatient with tradition. But he was also the product of one France’s historic institutions. At the age of 15 he went to the École Boulle, a school named after Louis XIV’s cabinet maker, André-Charles Boulle, and set up to train apprentices in the art of marquetry.
After graduating, he studied at the École Nationale Superieure des Art Decoratifs. He also went to lectures at the Conservatoire National des Arts et Metiers by the architect and designer Jean Prouvé, whose ideas about prefabrication would have a lasting impact on Mourgue. He spent six months interning as a furniture designer for the Stockholm department store Nordiska Komaniet. His travels in Sweden and Finland, in those days Europe’s leading centres for innovative design, gave him an important new perspective.
Mourgue was still a student in 1959 when he designed Joker, his first chair to go into production. One of his teachers at the Boulle school introduced him to the Bernard family, founders of the Airborne furniture company. He caused something of a stir at Airborne’s factory in Montreuil, on the outskirts of Paris, when he arrived on his Solex moped carrying a full-scale prototype. It was the beginning of a long collaboration. Airborne launched Joker in 1964 and made the Djinn range, which included a two-seater sofa and a chaise longue. The company also manufactured a version of Montreal, the lounge chair that Mourgue designed for the French national pavilion of the 1967 Expo.
In 1966 Mourgue had set up his own studio in Paris. His projects included a consultancy for the motor manufacturer Renault for a low-cost version of the Renault 4 and lighting for the French company Disderot.
Despite Mourgue’s radical approach, he was part of the teams that designed the French national pavilions for both the Montreal Expo in 1967, and the one in Osaka in 1970. He designed the Bouloum chaise longue for Osaka and gave it a playfully anthropomorphic human form. But then the French state has always been determined to present itself as modern and forward looking. It was the Mobilier National , the state-run foundation originally set up in 1663 as the Royal Furniture Depository, that made the Montreal chair from fibreglass.
The Mobilier National was also responsible for Mourgue’s most radical project, an experimental scheme to equip 500 flats in the prefabricated Grand’Mare social housing development in Rouen with a furniture system. The architect was Marcel Lods, one of Prouvé’s collaborators. Lods used factory-made steel and glass compontents for the project, and designed the 80m² floor-plan that Mourgue worked with. He came up with a series of prefabricated units that could in theory be used to take the place of internal walls to equip it. There was a sleeping pod on wheels, a kitchen that could be shifted as required and an integrated bathroom unit that could be plumbed in where needed.
Mourgue had a personal fondness for mobility. In the 1970s he built himself a series of travelling studios, one based on a Land Rover, another on a VW van. By now married with children, he took his family on an extended tour of central Europe on a specially adapted Saviem truck made by Renault for military use. In the 1970s he began to teach, first in Paris at the École Nationale Supérieure des Art Décoratifs, then, after moving to Brittany, at the École des Beaux Arts in Brest, where he was a charismatic and inspiring presence for 30 years, retiring in 2004.
Alongside his design work, Mourgue pursued painting and sculpture. He created a series of what he called “Imaginary Gardens and Little Theatres”, exhibited in 1992 at the Sainsbury Centre at the University of East Anglia, among other places. They can be seen as a more personal exploration of possible futures.
Mourgue is survived by his wife, Anne, a former kindergarten teacher, and their five children, Thomas, Mikael, Armel, Gaetan and Maria.

title: Jimmy Anderson set to retire from cricket as Lancashire opt against renewing contract
description: Jimmy Anderson is expected to call time on his remarkable career at the age of 44 after being told his contract at Lancashire will not be renewed
content:
England bowler may have played last game at age 44
Lancashire tell Anderson he does not fit their plans
Jimmy Anderson is expected to call time on his remarkable career at the age of 44 after being told his contract at Lancashire will not be renewed for next season.
A change of direction is under way at Old Trafford after the club finished second-bottom of Division Two in the County Championship this year and failed to get out of the group stages in both men’s white-ball competitions.
Richard Kenyon has since arrived from Nottinghamshire as Lancashire’s new chief executive and hired Paul Farbrace from Sussex as director of cricket. While Farbrace does not start officially until next month, the pair informed Anderson on Monday that he does not feature in their plans, as first reported by the Times.
Anderson had been on season-by-season contracts with his boyhood club following his retirement from England duty in 2024, and he captained the first team in their most recent campaign. He combined this with 50 wickets at a princely average of 17, even if it could not prevent the club’s lowest finish in the two-division era.
Unless an overseas deal follows this winter, or a hopeful county comes calling, it appears Anderson has played his final game of professional cricket. If so, then he will finish with 1,193 first-class wickets, and more than 400 in limited-over matches, to go with the knighthood he was awarded 12 months ago for services to the sport.
Reports at the end of the season suggested Anderson was unlikely to remain as Lancashire captain but there were also indications that he wished to play on. This was only ever going to hinge on the new leadership’s view, however, after Daniel Gidney stood down as chief executive and Mark Chilton lost his job as director of cricket.
The call has now been made by Chilton’s successor, Farbrace, who was head-hunted to revive the ailing county. Farbrace, a former England assistant coach, had been poised to remain at Sussex on a part-time basis – a new arrangement triggered by their financial difficulties – only to be swayed by the lure of a Test county.
For all that Anderson has raged against his advancing years, the decision is a bold one that has put sentiment to one side. A product of Burnley cricket club, and having made his first-team debut for Red Rose in 2001, there will doubtless be a large section of the membership who would have wanted one more season.
The same went for a significant number of England supporters two years ago when Anderson was ushered into retirement by Rob Key, Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes. With 704 Test dismissals he finished as England’s record wicket-taker and the third highest in history overall – even if he personally remained unsated.

title: Supreme court blocks Trump’s bid to restrict gender care for trans prisoners
description: Decision stands in contrast to recent trans rights actions from court that often sides with Trump administration
content:
Decision stands in contrast to recent trans rights actions from court that often sides with Trump administration
The US supreme court went against Donald Trump ’s administration on Wednesday, refusing to allow the immediate enforcement of sweeping restrictions on gender-affirming care for transgender individuals held in prisons and federal facilities.
The decision marks an unusual victory for transgender rights before the nation’s highest court, which has largely sided with the administration and other opponents of transgender rights in several major cases.
In its latest action, the supreme court turned away an emergency appeal from the justice department seeking to overturn a federal judge’s order that prevents the Federal Bureau of Prisons from putting the controversial restrictions into effect while a lawsuit challenging them moves forward.
Two conservative members of the court, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito , publicly opposed the decision.
At the center of the legal battle is a policy introduced earlier this year that would sharply limit medical care and other accommodations available to transgender people in federal custody.
Under the measure, medical and surgical treatments related to gender transition would be prohibited. The restrictions would also extend to “social accommodations”, including access to clothing and hair-removal devices intended to help prisoners present themselves in a way that matches their gender identity. Psychiatric care would remain available under the policy.
The restrictions prompted three transgender people incarcerated at federal correctional facilities in New Jersey, Florida and Minnesota to bring a class-action lawsuit challenging the government’s actions.
The proposed changes represent a big departure from longstanding federal prison practices. According to the plaintiffs, the federal prison system has provided hormone treatment to prisoners experiencing gender dysphoria since at least 1992.
The dispute comes amid Trump’s broader campaign to roll back transgender rights since beginning his second presidential term.
On his first day back in the White House, Trump signed an executive order declaring that the federal government would recognize only two genders, male and female, while portraying transgender identity as false.
The order directed multiple federal agencies to revise their practices, including requirements ensuring that “males are not detained in women’s prisons” and ending government funding for medical procedures provided “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex”.
In defending the prison restrictions in court, government lawyers have characterized gender-transition medical treatment as “unproven sex-rejecting interventions”.
But the plaintiffs challenging the policy have warned that allowing the restrictions to take effect could have devastating consequences. In their legal filing, the plaintiffs argued that a decision favoring the administration would result in “immediate and catastrophic” harm.
They pointed to serious mental health concerns, warning: “Patients who are denied hormone therapy can suffer from increased depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation and self-harm.”
Wednesday’s decision stands in contrast to several recent supreme court actions involving transgender rights. The court, which holds a 6-3 conservative majority, has issued multiple decisions since last year that have favored restrictions affecting transgender Americans.
Among those decisions, the justices supported state laws preventing transgender athletes from competing on female sports teams at public schools, including colleges and universities.
The court also permitted the Trump administration to enforce its ban on transgender people in the military. In another decision, the justices allowed the administration to prevent passport applicants from selecting gender designations reflecting their gender identities.
The legal fight carries potential consequences for thousands of people within the federal correctional system. More than 2,000 transgender prisoners were housed in federal prisons and halfway houses in 2025, according to reporting from NPR .

title: Energy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield
description: Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaigners
author_name: Kiran Stacey, Jessica Elgot, Fiona Harvey
content:
Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaigners
Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners.
After approving the smaller Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, officials say the energy secretary is leaning towards refusing approval for what would be one of the biggest oilfields in the North Sea.
But she could still be overruled by Andy Burnham, who may hear different representations from the chancellor, John Healey. A final decision is expected before the end of this year.
In comments that will be read as a signal of her intent, Fahnbulleh told the Guardian that the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it.
