“One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.”
In contrast, Healey told ITV he expected “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, a suggestion he is anticipating new oil revenues. Burnham would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.
Labour MPs warned on Wednesday there would be a major pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessity as part of the transition to net zero.
MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent.
Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet taken a final decision on Rosebank. The field would emit about seven times the carbon of Jackdaw and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe that it would do less for UK energy security, given most of the oil would be exported.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This is speculation. As the energy secretary has said, each project will be assessed on its own merits.”
On a visit to Aberdeen, Fahnbulleh said she had been satisfied that Jackdaw, which is due to begin producing gas within weeks and will add an estimated 36m tonnes of carbon emissions, would not violate the UK’s climate commitments.
“As we make the transition, we are going to need gas,” she said. “At a point when we have got conflict in the Middle East that is triggering an energy crisis, energy security is vital, and homegrown energy is key.”
She admitted, however, it would not help achieve the government’s main energy target of bringing down bills, saying: “This is not about bills.”
The UN Environment Programme has recommended that global carbon emissions be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin.
The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland , where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.
But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.
One Labour MP close to the energy secretary said she knew her credibility was “on the line” and that she was able to show she was pragmatic by approving Jackdaw but drawing the line at Rosebank. “She’s putting up a fight and I want to be supportive of Miatta – I understand what she is fighting,” they said.
But they said the decision would ultimately come down to Burnham. “Andy is not a climate guy – he is under pressure. If he wants to do it, he’ll do it.”
Several serving ministers have said they would find Rosebank a more difficult decision to back and it would cause greater problems in their constituencies.
The former minister Catherine West said climate change “is not a future threat but a present reality” and that the answer to job losses in the North Sea was not to “double down on new fossil fuel developments”.
Afzal Khan, the Labour MP for Manchester Rusholme and chair of the all-party parliamentary group on climate change, said: “Approving projects on the scale of Rosebank, on top of today’s decision to approve Jackdaw, cannot be justified.”
Burnham is seeking more ways to lower energy bills, telling MPs on Wednesday that ministers would consider whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills to ease cost pressures on households.
While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfield project have sought approval for existing licences.
The Greens said on Wednesday they intended to fight seats directly on the issue of Jackdaw and Rosebank. The Green MP Carla Denyer said: “We have identified dozens of seats where we are Labour’s main challenger and the climate is one of the top issues and voters have been mobilised by the heatwave and wildfires.
“Our strong advice to Labour MPs is to stand up to Andy Burnham and his act of climate violence, both to save your seats and, far more importantly, to protect the planet for future generations.”
Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through a new energy wealth fund. She said the fund would be given £2bn in the budget.
“When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes.
However, she could not say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the new fund, or how much that might generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.

title: Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen
description: This foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demands, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
content:
This foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demands
W hen the news broke that the UK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield , I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom?
There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring. The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them. The Jackdaw announcement will face immediate protest and legal challenge, but it sends a very clear signal from the government: we don’t mean what we say about ending emissions.
It turns out you can take all imaginable personal responsibility to arrest the climate crisis, make lifestyle adjustments that even five years ago you wouldn’t have dreamed of, miraculously summon the energy to take collective action from what is often private despair, but it will be insufficient as long as corporations – assisted by the government – are working against you, in effect with impunity. At some point, you need to get the people you elected to do what we all know – and they acknowledge – is necessary.
The Jackdaw decision had been quietly parked during the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when the threat of the Greens seemed greater to Labour than it turned out to be . But while Labour successfully buried the issue during the campaign, the underlying issues surrounding Jackdaw – and Rosebank, which is yet to be decided upon – persist.
Since the 2015 Paris agreement, we have been committed to try to limit temperature rises to 1.5C, and we’ve known for at least five years that means the vast majority of fossil fuels have to stay in the ground. As of 2024, there’s been scientific consensus that the target of 1.5C is “deader than a doornail” , while this week’s emissions-gap report could not be clearer: the threshold will be breached and it will cause unimaginable damage, yet with urgent emissions reduction, there is a way back from the abyss. There is no workable argument that runs: “Everyone has to leave their fossil fuels in the ground, as a matter of the utmost urgency, except for us; everyone has to prioritise the long-term survival of a livable planet over energy bills, except for us; we all need to reach carbon neutrality and worry about high-skilled jobs later, except for us.” The Jackdaw field isn’t huge, will peak in a short time and won’t on its own reduce energy bills , which are determined by global markets. So it’s tempting to shuffle it off as a side-order issue, but it matters: it destroys our moral authority as a nation and it extinguishes hope.
The climate debate operates on two tracks that don’t meet. On the one hand, we talk about non-linear irreversible tipping points whose effects would be so seismic that the question of mitigation is too vast and, frankly, too painful to consider. The only bearable discussion of the collapse of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) – a system of currents within the Atlantic Ocean – is how to avoid it, and the contested matter of whether that is even possible. We talk about heat deaths across 854 European cities over the past summer, and we talk about areas in the UK of environmental deprivation, flood risks and poorly insulated housing. We also talk about food security both in the short term, with potato crops destroyed by the weather, and in the long term, with supply chains subject to the incomprehensible devastation of every country going through its own particular climate crisis simultaneously. We look at the social unrest across Europe – which is the fastest-warming continent – and ask to what extent the deprivation created by an unstable climate is being weaponised by a far right hell-bent on choking off climate action.
Then we gate off all that knowledge, all that anxiety, all that will to action, and turn our attention to the UK’s immediate energy compromises. The arguments here run that since we’re going to import gas from somewhere anyway, because any transition will take time, we may as well get it at home. Even though it’s well known that household energy prices won’t be reduced , the government can use the tax take to reduce VAT. Some categories of emission are lower from UK gas than they would be from energy imported from the Gulf.
We need to bring these conversations together, because what they describe is one shared reality. Alongside the carbon that Jackdaw and Rosebank would release, they’ve “sucked all the oxygen out of the debate around what to do about climate change”, Chris Stark, the former CEO of the Climate Change Committee, has said. A warm homes initiative would create vastly more jobs, research recently found , and by reducing bills would also bring far more prosperity, with the additional advantage of not undermining the climate goals we claim to hold.
Thinking of agriculture alone, the headroom, investment and planning we’re ploughing into carbon extraction could make an immeasurable difference to building resilience for an already uncertain future. The most meaningful way to reduce household bills is to reduce reliance on increasingly turbulent world markets, by separating the renewable price from the fossil fuel price, which would immediately boost the already flourishing wind and solar sectors.
Gas and oil proponents beg us to be pragmatic, while their own arguments are floridly impractical: conducted as though the outside world doesn’t exist; as though carbon emissions are tomorrow’s problem; as though there aren’t better solutions for high prices and insecurity everywhere you look; as though we have time to quickly exhaust all our bad answers before we move on to good ones.
One depressing aspect of the Jackdaw announcement – although by no means the most depressing – is that it’s all about the optics. Even its most trenchant supporters would admit that it’s not a long-term solution to energy security. Rather, it’s a flag to the fossil-fuel industry that the government isn’t an enemy. It’s a toxic smoke signal to the US that the UK might not be with it, but definitely isn’t against it. It’s a feeble attempt at domestic politicking by Labour , trying to deflate the Conservatives’ anti-net zero bubble. It’s a statement of intent to make no trouble, when the trouble is already upon us.

title: Pollster admits to fabricating data for ‘social experiment’ to expose flaws of industry
description: Wedgewood Polls said project was designed to highlight lack of scrutiny over polling sector by mainstream media
content:
Wedgewood Polls said project was designed to highlight lack of scrutiny over polling sector by mainstream media
A polling firm has admitted to using fabricated data in surveys that were picked up by national media outlets in the US, claiming the project was a “social experiment” designed to expose the lack of scrutiny over the sector.
Wedgewood Polls released a statement on Tuesday on social media, after the polling and election analysis site FiftyPlusOne reached out for comment on an investigation it had conducted into their surveys and data.
In its statement, Wedgewood Polls admitted to fabricating its numbers, and said the project was designed as a “wake-up call”, intended “to demonstrate the vulnerabilities, lack of oversight, and overall low barrier to entry in the modern political polling industry”.
“Our fabricated numbers were given instant credibility across national media platforms,” the statement said. “The ease with which unverified figures were absorbed into mainstream political narratives highlights a systemic breakdown in media vetting and data aggregation.”
Publications that reproduced Wedgewood Polls’s fraudulent surveys included Newsweek, the Hill, Breitbart, the Daily Beast and the Washington Examiner, and those that included its results in their polling databases included the New York Times, Nate Silver, VoteHub and FiftyPlusOne.
After Wedgewood’s admission, the election results and analysis site Decision Desk HQ said it had removed 17 polls from its race-level polling lists and averages, and the New York Times said in an editor’s note that all of its polls had been removed from its poll tracking project.
Wedgewood Polls first came on the polling scene in June, billing itself as an election survey firm that conducted independent political research. Within weeks, on 10 July, a Washington Monthly columnist noted that its first poll of the Louisiana Republican primary runoff had been “wildly wrong”.
In August, Straight Arrow News then looked into Wedgewood’s background, finding that its website, hosted on Google Sites, listed no employee names, phone number or location. Its website had been registered on 26 June, and its X account created that same month.
On 16 August, an Urban Milwaukee journalist referred to Wedgewood as “a shady outfit” after one of its polls regarding the Wisconsin Democratic primary for governor showed Francesca Hong at 30% “at a time when legitimate polls had her with far less of the vote”.
Adam Carlson, a Democratic pollster at a different firm, told Straight Arrow News that he had communicated with someone at Wedgewood after he raised a question about them on X. Carlson said the person told him the two-person firm includes one progressive and one conservative. They declined to reveal their identities or participate in a video call, claiming that one of the two people at Wedgewood had previously experienced doxing and online harassment.
Then FiftyPlusOne researchers received a tip – after having previously received other tips about Wedgewood that lacked evidence – earlier in October suggesting that Wedgewood had been faking its data. They obtained Wedgewood’s raw data for its Mississippi Senate survey, their most recent survey, which the company said had been conducted using online survey platform Pollfish.
FiftyPlusOne said it identified discrepancies in the data and confronted Wedgewood with its findings. The firm then published its statement on X.
Michigan state senator Mallory McMorrow, a Democrat, who dropped out of a contentious US Senate primary campaign on 5 July, said that Wedgewood’s numbers indicated that her support had plunged in the weeks prior. As a result, her donations dried up, volunteers were left “devastated”, and reporters “hounded” her with calls to drop out of the race, she said.
McMorrow wrote on X: “Sure, a point was proven. Polling is broken. But tens of thousands of people poured their hearts, time, energy, hard-earned money into something they believed in – for a year-and-a-half, and it was treated like a game. Our volunteers gave their all. And then some. I felt like I had let so many of them down.”
She went on: “Trust is already at an all-time low. We don’t get out of this mess without rebuilding trust. And media – who loves to ride the drama of a pollercoaster – needs to take a hard look at what’s legitimate and what’s not.”
The affair followed a similar story in August in which the Guardian tracked down a 21-year-old recent college graduate who was found to be behind an anonymous website that put out widely shared fake election polling in Wisconsin, Nevada and California.
That site, Median Strategies, had abruptly shut down and withdrawn its polling the week prior after questions from a Los Angeles Times reporter. In an unsigned statement , it similarly described a “short-term social experiment” to examine how fake polling “could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification”.
“I wanted to see if fake polls could really penetrate the ecosystem that easily,” Rahil Prakash told the Guardian when reached by phone. “And as it turned out, it could.”

title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy
description: Government decision is about how much oil and gas is sensible for UK to produce on the way to net zero
content:
Government decision is about how much oil and gas is sensible for UK to produce on the way to net zero
A ndy Burnham hit the nail on the (well)head in his first fortnight as prime minister when he said : “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is, where does it come from?”
It was a nod towards several awkward energy facts. First, oil and gas provided 75% of the UK’s energy in 2025, government data shows. Second, even with the rollout of domestic renewables for generating electricity, about 43% of overall energy was imported last year.
Third, all credible paths to net zero emissions by 2050 involve using a lot of oil and gas on the way because we’re still in the foothills of electrification. Fewer than 2% of UK households have heat pumps, according to the lobby group Electrify Britain.
While sales of EVs are accelerating, nearly 95% of vehicles on the road run on petrol and diesel. Meanwhile, hydrogen and biomethane have barely taken off as alternatives to gas for those industrial processes that require higher temperatures than electricity can achieve – tricky for a government pursuing “reindustrialisation ”.
Fourth – and this one must alarm Downing Street – the global energy market has simply become less reliable. The strait of Hormuz can close overnight. The US president can threaten to ban diesel exports . Russian ships prowl the North Sea . Even the nice Norwegians, with an eye on their own energy consumers, scrapped a planned electricity cable to Scotland in 2023.
It is no longer a world of always-available “just in time” supply. Thinking has shifted to “just in case” scenario-planning. And a truly scary scenario would be disruption to the 725-mile Langeled pipeline that is the primary route for gas supplies from Norway, 40% of the UK’s consumption last year. The pipeline is a security vulnerability if ever there was one (if you doubt it, watch Sky News’ recent report ).
Now we have the start of an answer to Burnham’s “where should it come from?” question. The Jackdaw gasfield, 150 miles east of Aberdeen, has finally been approved to produce in time for winter. About time, too.
All the arguments from pragmatism were in the field’s favour. As this column has said in the past , less North Sea gas would inevitably mean more imported liquefied natural gas, with the extra carbon emissions created by chilling the fuel to -160C for shipment and then “regasifying” it at the other end.
Such cargos were 20% of UK gas imports last year, mostly from the US. It already feels absurd that the 24m UK households with a gas boiler burn any gas at all from the shale fields of Texas and Pennsylvania. Why increase the exposure if lower-polluting supplies are available off Aberdeen?
More UK North Sea gas production won’t lower the price for consumers much, if at all. But that was never the argument. It was always about tax receipts, jobs, the national balance of payments, relative emissions and the security that comes with having domestic volumes piped straight into the national gas network.
Jackdaw is not a gamechanger – it will be 6% of UK North Sea gas production at peak – but it’s definitely worth having while the UK is still using gas, which will be at least as long as the field’s 11-year life. The next question is whether other “tie-back” gasfields in already-explored areas, such as Tornado, west of Shetland, will follow. The line in the government’s announcement about “asking the regulator to consider urgent cases that could benefit from similar measures now” suggests so.
Rosebank, also near Shetland, is a trickier political proposition because it’s mostly oil, which is more polluting, and will be producing for longer. But the arguments aren’t wholly different. The common elements are still jobs, investment, taxes and the government’s ability to impose higher environmental standards during the production stage.
Meanwhile, the “it’s all exported” objection to Rosebank misses the fact that the UK oil industry operates within a European network. If the UK had more than four refineries (compared with nine at the turn of the century), a chunk of Rosebank’s output might be processed at home. As it is, some – perhaps the majority – will come back to the UK as petrol, diesel and jet fuel once it’s been refined in Rotterdam or elsewhere in north-west Europe.
Take a step back and the North Sea debate is really about how much oil and gas it is sensible for the UK to produce itself on the way to net zero. On the current trajectory, only about a third of consumption will come from domestic sources on a net basis. Even offshore lobbyists reckon a boost to North Sea production would only get the ratio up to about a half, albeit the figure would obviously increase if consumption of fossil fuels can be made to fall faster. Nobody is talking about the UK becoming a net exporter again.
Commitment to net zero by 2050 was intact, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted. We wait to see what the new “energy wealth fund”, which will reinvest oil and gas revenues into renewable and low-carbon projects, means in practice. But the financial logic is sound: recycle the receipts from the old system to quicken the transition. Electrification, enabling consumers to make use of lower-carbon energy, is still the main story.
The bizarreness in the government’s previous approach was that, even as it proclaimed the virtues of “clean homegrown energy” such as wind, solar and nuclear, it pursued an approach that maximised imports when it came to oil and gas. Many, including the general secretary of the GMB union, Gary Smith, pointed out the flaw: it was hard for the UK to claim real climate leadership if it was simply off-shoring emissions.
In a small way, Jackdaw addresses the UK’s extreme reliance on imports. It is a step towards a joined-up commonsense approach to energy security. The real transition test remains the pace at which the UK stops using fossil fuels.

title: Gas go-ahead ignites oily response from Trump, while speaker seems ready to blow
description: The energy secretary’s trip north provokes Hoyle’s futile rage, while ITV’s Reform exposé leaves Zia Yusuf immensely sad
content:
The energy secretary’s trip north provokes Hoyle’s futile rage, while ITV’s Reform exposé leaves Zia Yusuf immensely sad
W hen is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party conference and a byelection to negotiate first – the government finally gave the go-ahead to drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too.
There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill. So the inconvenience of a Labour manifesto that promised no new North Sea licences could be rethought. It was now merely re-allowing a licence that had already been granted and then deemed unlawful by the courts. AKA dancing on the head of the pin.
Donald Trump greeted the decision with wild enthusiasm. Though he appeared to be under the impression Jackdaw would be drilling for oil and would turn the UK into a land of plenty overnight. No one in the UK could quite bring themselves to enlighten him. Fair to say, that not everyone in the UK was quite so thrilled. Not least Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, and Miatta Fahnbulleh , the current one.
Miatta had sought permission to be as far away as possible from Westminster for prime minister’s questions and the subsequent ministerial statement on Jackdaw. So she had taken the trouble to go all the way to Aberdeen to make a television statement that she could have made in her own department. And she is the one worried about her carbon footprint.
Only it turns out that any amount of emissions is a price worth paying for a minister anxious not to have the hypocrisy of her former opposition to Jackdaw replayed to her by many of her own backbench MPs. Life comes at you fast when you’re a politician climbing the greasy ministerial pole. You find yourself in some awkward places, the most awkward being the House of Commons . Hence the – ahem – unfortunate diary clash.
The speaker was less than impressed . Lindsay Hoyle sounded as if he had swallowed a fistful of amphetamines and steroids and was mid-roid rage. He only just stopped short of calling the Labour frontbench a bunch of fucking fucks. Maybe he was just having a bad day.
For decades now, governments of all colours have been going out of their way to make sure that junior ministers take the flak to save their bosses the embarrassment of an hour’s humiliation at the dispatch box. The parliamentary equivalent of droit de seigneur. Lindsay demanded assurances this would never happen again, and the junior energy minister Michael Shanks duly nodded sheepishly. Not that he cared. He mainlines oil for breakfast. Inside, he was just counting down the seconds till the speaker had calmed down a bit. And then carried on as normal. Of course it will happen again. Maybe even next week.
PMQs itself also took on a familiar look, with Kemi Badenoch unable to make any inroads into Andy Burnham. You could even sense her frustration. There were times when she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, but now both she and the Labour party have seen him off, she is faced with Mr Congeniality.
Against him, Kemi’s attack lines feel half-arsed. Not properly thought through. Everything she tries just bounces off him. He seems almost untouchable. Mostly because he’s a better politician, but also because he has the air of a reasonable grownup. Someone you feel is doing his best and comes across as someone you can trust. Well. As close to honest as you get in Westminster.
By contrast, Kemi feels like a second-rate opportunist. She tried making something of Labour taking years to approve the Jackdaw licence, a charge that rather melted away when Burnham pointed out we could have been drilling ages ago if the Tories had bothered to get the necessary legalities right in the first place. This was about putting pragmatism before ideology, Andy insisted . Fair enough. Though expect him to say precisely the opposite when it comes to the Rosebank oilfield. Then ideology will take precedence over pragmatism. Fahnbulleh had already as good as confirmed that Rosebank was dead in the water.
For the rest of PMQs , it was Kemi who was dead in the water. Seemingly having no other real questions she wanted to ask. It felt like she was sulking. Or underprepared. Her pre-budget attack lines went nowhere. First Andy pointed out that he was the only one with a plan to ditch the triple lock and sort out social care – still more vibes than policy – and ended by making fun of Liz Truss’s forthcoming new book on the mini-budget.
It wasn’t her who had screwed the country, apparently. Liz had been captured by the Blob. But it could have been any number of the current members of the shadow cabinet. Including the shadow chancellor who was part of the Trusster’s team. Incidentally, Liz was due to be interviewed by a robot on Wednesday afternoon at a Lincolnshire fair. But how would we know which was which?
That just left time for Burnham to take one question from a Labour backbencher about the ITV exposé of Reform. Though Nigel Farage had already left the chamber by then, so he couldn’t get all heated and declare that it was all a London plot and that it was perfectly normal for people to be as racist as possible in the comfort of their own homes. It was political correctness gone mad.
As if by telepathy, Zia Yusuf had chosen just that moment to post a video on social media in which he expressed his immense sadness that the media had stooped so low. He would be reporting ITV to the police, he insisted, because they had betrayed the racist code of honour.
How could everyday racists feel comfortable expressing their racism in the workplace if they couldn’t be sure that their colleagues weren’t undercover journalists looking to expose them? The world had gone mad. Who would have guessed that deep down, Zia – the man even the Reform elite have come to hate – was a snowflake at heart.

title: US Park Police spend $343,000 on mobile surveillance cameras in Washington DC
description: Cameras reportedly set up near site for Trump’s proposed arch, Arlington Memorial Bridge and reflecting pool
content:
Cameras reportedly set up near site for Trump’s proposed arch, Arlington Memorial Bridge and reflecting pool
The US Park Police are spending $343,000 to lease mobile surveillance cameras from a company that also supplies Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) , federal contract records show. The deal comes as Donald Trump has insisted that vandals damaged the reflecting pool, one of Washington’s best-known landmarks – charges that have since been dismissed.
The Department of the Interior, which oversees the Park Police, awarded the lease to the Utah-based company LiveView Technologies (LVT) on 14 September, on a fully obligated government contract that runs through the end of February. The records do not say how many camera trailers are covered.
On Monday, the president posted on Truth Social that “we are watching very closely, and security cameras have been installed” at the reflecting pool. He also warned that anyone who vandalized the newly refilled pool would “GO TO JAIL”.
The Washington Post, which was first to cover the contracts , reported that LVT’s cameras had been installed at Memorial Circle, where Trump wants to build an “ Arc de Trump ”, and near statues by the Arlington Memorial Bridge, and that Park Police put up other cameras at the reflecting pool as early as June.
The Guardian has not independently confirmed where the leased cameras are, and the contract records do not say.
Trump also did not say who supplied the cameras or where they would be placed, and the records do not say whether the leased equipment is what he was describing.
LVT’s main product is its camera trailers that can be towed to a parking lot, construction site or street corner and set up without permanent wiring. On Tuesday, LVT announced it would add a “thermal-plus-visual” camera from Axis Communications, meant to detect people in low light and “total darkness, glare, rain, fog and smoke”, with shipments expected in December.
The trailers also run software with AI capabilities that LVT says would flag people loitering and read license plates, a feature the company began offering this year to private customers. LVT says its systems “do not actively apply facial recognition”, and that its “customers own their data”.
The latest order adds to LVT’s frequent business with the federal government, particularly with ICE. In March, ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations division ordered a one-year lease of 26 camera trailers at 10 locations, worth $760,400. In June, another ICE office awarded the company about $2.2m in a separate contract for mobile security units, with a potential completion date of June of next year.
The company has been an approved federal vendor since 2023 , when the General Services Administration under Joe Biden added it to its schedule of contractors.
The company’s cameras have drawn controversy from the public and from local governments that have used them. In New York, a Monroe county lawyer complained in 2024 that an LVT trailer placed outside a government building during protests tied to county legislature meetings could see into his office windows, though county officials said the cameras were aimed at the building to protect speakers and attenders and that footage was saved only when needed for an investigation. The company has also faced questions about reliability: last year, Colorado ended a contract for 136 highway cameras after the state said many were offline for long stretches, and said it had withheld about $494,000 in payments.
The interior department did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. LVT declined to comment.

title: Israel’s fault lines: inside the 23 October Guardian Weekly
