title: Maro Itoje seals England future by agreeing new deal with Saracens
description: Maro Itoje has reaffirmed his long-term commitment to England, rejecting interest from France by agreeing to a new deal with Saracens
content:
Captain will resist lure of big-money move to France
‘Maro is everything we want at the club – a brilliant leader’
Maro Itoje has reaffirmed his long‑term commitment to England, rejecting interest from France by agreeing a new deal with Saracens.
Itoje’s existing deal, signed in 2024, was due to expire after the World Cup next year but he has agreed terms with his club despite interest from Top 14 sides. A move to either Perpignan or Bordeaux had been mooted but the 31-year-old is to commit his future to the club he first represented in 2013 with a new deal, believed to be until 2029.
The extension is a significant boost for Saracens , who are in a period of transition with Brendan Venter at the helm for a second time and will enable Itoje, who has 102 caps, to continue his international career. It remains to be seen whether Steve Borthwick will still be in charge of the England side but either the national head coach or his successor is to benefit.
“He is staying,” Venter said of Itoje. “He has agreed with the owner. It’s brilliant of Maro, Maro is everything we want at the club. He’s an unbelievable human being, he’s a brilliant leader, he’s such a good rugby player, I’m so glad the owner and him could agree terms.”
Itoje was rested for England’s summer Tests against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina after showing signs of fatigue throughout the season on the back of several gruelling campaigns. He has made more Test appearances than any other player in the world game since his international debut in 2016 and revealed last month that this summer he had enjoyed his first full pre‑season with Saracens since 2014.
“He’s always got energy so Maro’s been so good in the pre-season for us,” Venter said. “We’re lucky because Maro is always developing.”
Itoje has been linked with a move to France before and was said to have explored the option of going to the Top 14 on loan when Saracens were relegated in 2020. Such a severe workload in recent seasons added to the speculation that he may seek a lucrative move across the Channel.
He was also linked with the mooted R360 breakaway league but said at the time that “playing for England is the mecca”. Itoje was among the first tranche of players to receive an enhanced England contract worth £150,000 in 2024 and has since stayed in the selected group. It is understood, however, that none of the existing deals go beyond the World Cup in Australia next year.
The Lions lock Hyron Andrews’s death was caused by an aortic dissection, a tear in the body’s main artery, the South African rugby team have said. The former Sale player died at the team hotel last Friday, a day before the Lions played the French side La Rochelle in the European Champions Cup, a game that went ahead in honour of the 31-year-old. French media reported that Andrews was found unconscious in a shower cubicle at a hotel on the Île de Ré in France, where the team had been staying.

title: Letter: Paco Robles obituary
description: Stephen Pound: I used to sit with him outside his flat in Northolt while he sipped his favourite brandy, drew on a good cigar and recalled his displacement from the Basque country during the Spanish civil war
content:
Paco Robles was a constituent of mine as Labour MP for Ealing North for more than 20 years. I used to sit with him outside his flat in Northolt while he sipped his favourite brandy, drew on a good cigar and recalled his displacement from the Basque country during the Spanish civil war and arrival in Britain in 1937.
Always a man of the left, Paco had a great admiration for Jeremy Corbyn , and asked if I could arrange for them to meet. I did so happily, and when I drove him home afterwards I asked how the conversation – all in Spanish – had gone. He looked rueful and said that Jeremy had problems with his Galician accent, and Paco thought Jeremy spoke Latin American Spanish. Nonetheless, they managed to communicate.

title: Australia collapse in chaotic fashion to leave South Africa in sight of victory
description: Australia were bowled out for 99 and forced to follow on, with the tourists’ batters left to conduct a desperate rearguard on the last day of the second Test
content:
Tourists all out for 99 and forced to follow on
Batters left to conduct desperate rearguard on last day
There it was, another entry in Australia’s hall of infamy against South Africa. There was 47 all out, in the innocent days when the 2011 Test was the worst humiliation in Cape Town. There was 85 all out in Hobart, 2016, that led to half the side being sacked. Now there is 99 all out in Gqeberha, one day after the home team blew past 400 , only for the visitors to follow on halfway through day four.
At 156 for four, still 170 behind, Australia could yet save the second Test on its final day, but another batting failure has left the door wide open to defeat, and the table laden with defeat’s favourite snacks.
When Nic Maddinson’s first innings lasted four balls on the third evening, nobody would have predicted that his second innings would be done an hour after lunch the next day. Between times, nine other Australian wickets fell in 38.3 overs. Marco Jansen and Kagiso Rabada bowled spells of ferocity, cranking up the speed gun while beating edges with the ball pitched up, and peppering batters when it wasn’t.
As well as they bowled, though, their best was not always required, with some dismal Australian decisions giving wickets away. Not Scott Boland, the nightwatch, who nicked one early, or Travis Head lbw to a ball angling in from the left-armer, nor later could you place much blame on Matthew Renshaw, who got a ball that reared to take the shoulder of a defensive bat.
But Alex Carey and Beau Webster both played senseless punches off the back foot to rising balls, nicking them to round out Jansen’s five for 33. Mitchell Starc did the same for Rabada’s second. Marnus Labuschagne got in a footwork tangle and tipped towards the off side, edging Anrich Nortje to set up Simon Harmer’s sizzling slip catch. Pat Cummins slogged to the deep, having given up.
Steve Smith hung in for 28, becoming the dozenth player to pass 11,000 Test runs, though he looked awful in the process. It transpired that this was related to a neck problem, making it difficult to turn his head, and when he was eventually bowled by Wiaan Mulder’s nip-backer he was as far away from hitting a ball as he’s ever been in his life.
With South Africa’s lead at 326, and a session and a half to go, they had the option to bat for a couple of hours to buffer the lead before bowling late, or to go straight into a new bowling innings. Even with Nortje out with a groin strain, having bowled just 3.3 overs, Temba Bavuma asked his bowlers to go again. Maddinson lasted 10 balls this time, with two fours, before rewarding Bavuma’s call, the batter’s back foot creeping away from Rabada’s line while his hands dangled the bat out for a nick.
The Maddinson selection continues to be the nightmare that it promised to be. No doubt we will be told he was unlucky: to face one over from Rabada in the gloom, to face Rabada again with his tail up. This is not luck: this is simply the job that a Test opener is picked to do, facing the best bowlers in their freshest state with the newest ball in the most difficult conditions. This is why you don’t give that job to players whose last good streak in first-class cricket was closer to three years ago than to two.
For a time, Head and Labuschagne looked like they had the blessing of some roadside saint to take Australia to safety, Head flashing edges past cordon catchers, Labuschagne hitting short leg twice before overturning an upheld lbw that was missing leg stump by a Rizla. They passed the team’s first-innings score for the loss of one, not 10. But while Labuschagne beat his recent bogey of 37, he fell at 39, discomfort against Harmer’s spin leading to an attempted launch over leg. With so little to gain, he gave up a catch in the deep.
From 100 for two, more South African rewards came: with Smith absent injured the key man, Renshaw, was bowled for 11, leaving Rabada’s ball that decked in sharply from around the wicket. Harmer also went around the wicket to the promoted Webster, straightening an off-break to trap him for eight. Incongruously, Boland was next, asked to perform nightwatch duties for the second time in the same day.
Still 170 behind, any last-day rescue must be undertaken by the sore Smith, the keeper Carey, and by Head resuming on 87. His 50 average as an opener is split markedly between 33 in his first innings and currently over 70 in his second. Where Cummins has spoken recently about batting orders changing by innings, Head provides the strongest argument for trying it. If he’s not able to save the day with a little help from his friends, something about this batting order will have to change for good.

title: 24-year-old Kansas man arrested for allegedly threatening to shoot Donald Trump
description: Jaden J Read was arrested after federal authorities say he posted threats online before president’s Wichita rally
content:
Jaden J Read was arrested after federal authorities say he posted threats online before president’s Wichita rally
A 24-year-old Kansas man has been arrested for allegedly threatening to shoot Donald Trump .
Authorities arrested Jaden J Read, of Clearwater, Kansas , last Saturday after he allegedly posted threats to kill the US president at his rally in the Wichita area on Monday, according to the justice department.
According to federal authorities, a Crime Stoppers tip on 15 October led investigators to a Facebook post responding to a KAKE News article about Trump’s upcoming Wichita visit. Read allegedly commented: “Let’s shoot Trump honestly, where’s our shooter? I’m tired of living this money life.”
Immediately afterward, he allegedly posted a second comment on the same article: “I just got a 308 and 305 round and I’m killing this pedo.”
Authorities also found two additional comments allegedly posted by Read in response to a KWCH 12 News article about Trump’s planned visit.
“Can we shoot him in Kansas please I will myself,” Read allegedly wrote. A minute later, he allegedly posted another comment, saying: “IK where your speech will be. Already mapped out roofs around. Finna get kirked since yall couldn’t help him.”
Read was arrested in Clearwater last Saturday and taken into federal custody, where he will remain pending a detention hearing. The district of Kansas filed a criminal complaint against Read for making threats against the president.
“Political violence and threats of political violence will not be tolerated,” US attorney Ryan A Kriegshauser said, adding: “The first amendment allows for robust disagreement but there are constraints. I caution people to stay within the bounds of constitutionally protected speech.”
The Secret Service, the US Marshals Service, the Kansas bureau of investigation, the Kansas highway patrol and the Wichita police department investigated the case.
Trump held his 6,000-person rally in Park City on Monday, a city about 10 minutes from downtown Wichita. According to local reports and the Sedgwick county sheriff’s office, one person was arrested near the designated free-speech area for failing to comply with a lawful order to regulate traffic, while 11 other “uninvited individuals” were escorted out of the Heartland Credit Union Arena for causing disruptions.

title: In the age of AI, learning maths is even more vital
description: Letters: Readers react to Simon Jenkins’ article that said it’s more important for children to learn how to speak fluently than study mathematics
content:
Readers react to Simon Jenkins’ article that said it’s more important for children to learn how to speak fluently than study mathematics
Simon Jenkins must have had a deeply unpleasant experience of learning maths at school because he seems to have a pathological antipathy towards it ( We are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently?, 16 October ). I have no qualms with his insistence on the importance of oracy. But his argument breaks down with the claim that it is either oracy or maths, but not both. This is nonsense. Oracy and maths skills should exist side by side. Both contribute to a person’s ability to realise their full potential, and to employment opportunities.
Maths drives the understanding of the natural world and contributes vastly to the solutions of problems that humanity needs to solve to exist. It is fundamental to science and technology, health and medicine, communications, the study of the Earth, finance and economics, distribution of resources and supply chains, architecture, warfare, and much else besides.
The negative economic, social and health and wellbeing impacts of poor maths skills in adult life are well known, yet the maths skills gap – the difference between the numbers of mathematically literate people we need and the number we have – remains too large in the UK.
Many young people suffer from maths anxiety, but that is not an argument for not teaching maths and its importance. It is a social problem that needs addressing by improving the quality of schooling and attacking the root causes of social issues that affect how young people engage with society. Dr Jack Abramsky London
The idea that calculators and AI reduce the need to learn maths is mistaken. Maths is about far more than calculation. It teaches us to reason, analyse evidence, solve unfamiliar problems and question whether an answer makes sense. These abilities are more important, not less, when technology can produce apparently authoritative answers in seconds. The public need to know when they can trust those answers, and maths underpins that.
The government’s 2025 curriculum and assessment review recognised this, stating that “Being secure in core subjects such as Maths and Science will remain pivotal for young people, now and in the future”. The review also highlighted the growing importance of critical thinking and digital skills in a world increasingly shaped by AI.
Maths is also fundamental to the economy. Analysis by the Academy for the Mathematical Sciences found that more than 5 million people worked in mathematical-science occupations in 2024, contributing £489bn, or 19% of the UK’s total gross value added. Ensuring young people develop strong maths skills is therefore important not only for individuals, but for the UK’s future productivity and prosperity.
We should strengthen young people’s ability to communicate, but not at the expense of their ability to reason mathematically. In the age of AI, both are more important than ever. Mark Chaplain President, London Mathematical Society Heather Tewkesbury President, Institute of Mathematics and its Applications
Much as I understand the advantages that oracy confers, it is no gift when it is combined with entitlement and dishonesty. It was Boris Johnson’s silver tongue that got him into Downing Street and kept him there, despite outlandish transgressions and fabrications. I would prefer that schools embedded behaviour, integrity and sincerity into the curriculum. These are the building blocks for sound character. Mona Sood Southend-on-Sea, Essex
I think Simon Jenkins may be slightly behind the times. My five-year-old child goes to a state foundation primary with two sites in south London. Oracy is a core part of the curriculum. Her professional state-educated parents attended the workshop the school provided on the subject; it was certainly not something familiar to our own education.
Our daughter has flourished in confidence and speech. Previously a naturally shy child, she now regales kind strangers on public transport with stories. Her teacher encourages simple but critical interaction daily – each child says hello and goodbye to their teachers and each other in a way that is comfortable to them and respectful to others. This is in a classroom that has lots of children with education, health and care plans, who qualify for free school meals, and who have English as a second language and parents who do not speak English. The benefits are obvious, but Winchester it is not. Dr Elaine Seymour London
All public schools know the answer to Simon Jenkins’ question, hence their debating societies. All state primary schools also know how to develop confidence and ensure that all have the opportunity to take part in community events.
Never overlook the importance of early-years festive productions, class assemblies, concerts, school councils and school plays. These vital aspects of our state curriculum need to be celebrated. Never forget the insignificance and misery of log tables and slide rules. Sally Bates Retired primary headteacher, Cotgrave, Nottinghamshire

title: The Green party hasn’t lost its way, it’s just broadening its appeal
description: Letters: Marianne Gemmeke and John Ashby respond to criticism of the party and its leader, Zack Polanski
content:
Marianne Gemmeke and John Ashby respond to criticism of the party and its leader, Zack Polanski
The two eloquent letters on the super-rich ( The problem with living in a rich man’s world, 14 October ) explain perfectly why I, as a longstanding Green party member, could not agree less with the letter writers who claim that the party has lost its way ( Has Zack Polanski forgotten what the Green party is for?, 14 October ).
Social justice has always been at the heart of the Greens’ policy, which also means that unless we have a change in our dysfunctional economic system, we cannot achieve the green agenda. The Green movement has always been about having a moral framework, standing up for oppressed people and bringing about a more just society both at home and abroad.
People tend to know about the green agenda; it is the other messages that need clearer communication, which is where recent campaigns have focused, leading to a surge in membership. Marianne Gemmeke Eastleigh, Hampshire
The complaint about the Green party used to be that it was a single-issue pressure group. In response, it diversified into general politics, and now the complaint is that it talks about things other than climate change. You just can’t win. John Ashby Oxford

title: Does a Trump press aide have a half-life?
description: Brief letters: Katie Zacharia | From Aberfan to Jackdaw | EU re-referendum | Other lives and Wikipedia
content:
Katie Zacharia | From Aberfan to Jackdaw | EU re-referendum | Other lives and Wikipedia
As a trained physicist, I am delighted that we have a new unit of time. A “ Scaramucci ” was the unit of time derived from the 11-day career of the White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci. But we now have an even shorter career unit of five days, the “Zacharia”, for Donald Trump’s press secretary Katie Zacharia ( Report, 16 October ). In the final stages of Trump’s presidency, we may find that members of his media team come and go at ever shorter intervals, possibly asymptotically approaching the sub-zeptosecond lifetime of a Higgs boson. Dr Martin Treacy Cardigan, Ceredigion
On the 60th anniversary of one man-made fossil-fuel catastrophe ( ‘I survived for a reason’: Aberfan fights to preserve memory of disaster 60 years on, 20 October ), we are subjected to another – the approval of the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea ( Report, 21 October ). Do our leaders never learn? Douglas Currie Edinburgh
My late mother, Barbara Hulme, is a perfect example of the idea that Wikipedia only covers people who have already been written about elsewhere ( Letters, 16 October ). She has a Wikipedia page as a result of the obituary published by the Guardian ( Other lives, 9 February 2021 ). Janet Hulme Wadebridge, Cornwall
Re another EU referendum, Polly Toynbee says “not yet” ( Shall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet, 19 October ). When we can’t even sort musicians’ access to the EU, let alone start the young people’s exchange scheme, wouldn’t “sometime never” be more realistic? John Bishop Codsall, Staffordshire

title: Reform UK fined for failing to declare it was publisher of campaigns material
description: Party given additional penalty by Electoral Commission for not paying original fine on time
content:
Party given additional penalty by Electoral Commission for not paying original fine on time
Reform UK has been fined more than £2,000 for failing to declare it was the publisher of campaign material seen by voters – including an additional penalty for failing to pay on time.
Nigel Farage’s party was sanctioned by the Electoral Commission after four items of election material were missing an “imprint” – a declaration of the publisher so voters know who has paid for the promotional message.
It was due to pay £1,750 on 23 September, but the fine was increased by a quarter to £2,187 because Reform missed the payment deadline. The penalty was eventually paid on Tuesday.
Jackie Killeen, the commission’s director of electoral administration and regulation, said: “The UK’s political finance and imprints laws are there to ensure transparency in both the finances of political parties and the materials produced to influence voters.
“As a regulator, we take proportionate action based on the facts and circumstances of each case, as set out in our enforcement policy. We seek to support compliance and deliver transparency, and we will take enforcement action where necessary.”
The fine related to three social media accounts run by Reform, on X, Instagram and LinkedIn, that did not have digital imprints between at least November 2025 and January 2026.
The party also published an advertisement in the Telegraph in February 2026 without an imprint, promoting its shadow chancellor, Robert Jenrick. The watchdog’s investigation found that the purpose of the advertisement was to promote Reform and its electoral success in the May 2026 elections, so the ad required an imprint.
There has also been a separate complaint about the Reform candidate’s election material in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February this year.
On that occasion, the party sent out a letter designed to look as if it had been handwritten by the local resident Patricia Clegg, who said she no longer wanted to vote Labour, but who was in fact working for Reform – without including an imprint.
The party said it was caused by a printing error, and that the company had accidentally left the imprint off the material.
Reform’s censure from the Electoral Commission came as the party said it had reported ITV to the police after the broadcaster’s exposé which revealed racist remarks by members of the party.
Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, announced it would also launch a legal challenge against the ITV journalists involved and the broadcaster’s board of directors.
The channel’s undercover investigation included footage of Reform councillors and candidates using racist language.
In one excerpt, black children were referred to as animals, while in another a Reform member said his area had become infested with Asian families.
In a social media video, Yusuf said: “We have reported multiple ITV journalists and their board of directors to the police, and will be taking legal action against all of them. Journalists are supposed to report the news. These ones set out to create it.”
He claimed that the undercover ITV reporter who became employed as a Reform press officer had “doctored” her passport to gain the job.
He also said two undercover reporters who joined Reform members campaigning in Portsmouth had been reported to the police, as it is illegal to pay someone to canvass for a candidate.
An ITV spokesperson said: “ITV stands by its journalism. The programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom broadcasting code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest.
“All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme’s producers. Should the police get in touch, we would fully cooperate.”

title: Getting into the swing of playing golf
description: Letters: Readers respond to Adrian Chiles’s article on his antipathy to the game
content:
Readers respond to Adrian Chiles’s article on his antipathy to the game
I have some sympathies with Adrian Chiles’s war of attrition with golf ( I hate golf, 14 October ). I too have suffered with shots to the right followed by shots to the left, and have had rounds with many bad shots, only to then have a perfect drive down the middle, or by sinking a 20-yard putt on the last green that inevitably brought me back the next week thinking that I had finally cracked it.
Over the 60 years that I have been playing, I have learned that it is possible to master some of this game some of the time, but not all of the time. There are many other pluses to this wonderful game. I have played golf on many courses in this country and in Europe, enjoying great views and friendships along the way.
At 81 years of age, I still play twice a week, walking just over five miles each time, and still play to a respectable nine handicap. Come on Adrian, look on the bright side and continue your search for the perfect swing, even if it’s only one per round. Bob Dawson Greenmount, Greater Manchester
Adrian Chiles has it all wrong. If he removed the competitive element from his approach, he would see that golf doesn’t sit in isolation from the world around it. I was coerced into playing golf for the first time at the age of 60. I didn’t have that elusive isolated “Wow!” moment. The whole round, from a golf point of view, was lousy. But I loved the camaraderie, the walk through nature, the science attached to equipment and performance, the exercise on most fronts and the knowledge that, even with time against me, I could get better. I did … and plateaued. I fully expect to get worse as age takes over – I don’t care. As has been said, golf is not a game of being perfect, it is a holistic experience that is hard to match. Joe Waddle Bedlington, Northumberland
I can readily identify with the myriad frustrations that Adrian Chiles identifies in his experiences of playing golf. However, after more than 50 years of playing without any discernible improvement, I still soldier on o’er hill and dale, wielding my mashie niblick.
I do so because of all the positive benefits to be gained from a four-hour walk unspoiled: the exercise, the beautiful scenery, the fresh air and, as much as anything, the banter and bonhomie with my old schoolmates as we mercilessly mock our collective inability to master the game.
Get back out there, Adrian Chiles, it’s fun and good for your mental health! Kev Ward Quorn, Leicestershire
I stopped playing baseball at the age of 65 (exploded achilles tendon); ice hockey at 70 (Covid). I took up golf. Now five years in, I’m a reliable bogey golfer. I’m not a great athlete, absolutely average in size (5ft 9in) and took one formal lesson. But God bless YouTube. All the answers are there. Play with people who are better than you (not difficult in my case) and be willing to improve gradually.
There are tons of people who can tell you what you are doing wrong. Find one person who simplifies the game and follow them exclusively. For me, it’s a YouTube star called Jimmy Tropicana. And his best skill is making you believe you can play the sport well.
And stop keeping score until you develop some consistency. Just think about the next shot – not the good or bad ones already taken. The score will settle itself. Chris Gargan Verona, Wisconsin, US

title: Ex-tennis pro Megan Rose appointed to lead 2031 men’s Rugby World Cup in US
description: World Rugby has appointed Megan Rose, a USTA executive, as managing director of the the men’s Rugby World Cup in 2031
content:
Tournament coming to the US for the first time
Rose says tournament is a huge opportunity
World Rugby has appointed Megan Rose, an American tennis pro turned United States Tennis Association (USTA) executive, as managing director of the 2031 men’s Rugby World Cup , a key appointment as the governing body prepares to host what is by some measures the third-biggest global sporting event on American soil for the first time.
Rose said: “Rugby World Cup is one of the iconic events in global sport, defined by unforgettable moments on the pitch and the passion of fans around the world. To be entrusted with bringing Men’s Rugby World Cup to the United States for the first time is an extraordinary honour, and I’m thrilled to join this team.”
As a tennis player, Rose was a five-time collegiate All American out of the University of Miami, and a national indoor champion. After competing on the WTA Tour, she coached Princeton to an Ivy League women’s tennis championship then worked for the WTA and the USTA , becoming managing director of major events and team leader for USA Olympic Tennis.
Measures vary but on a world scale, the Rugby World Cup is generally placed third in size and prestige behind the Fifa World Cup and the Olympic Games. Australia will host the next two Rugby World Cups, men in 2027 and women in 2029. The US will host the 2031 men’s tournament and the women’s World Cup in 2033.
Rose’s appointment comes a little more than a month since more than 68,000 fans traveled to Baltimore, Maryland, to see South Africa’s men beat New Zealand in the fourth Test of the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series, an attendance record for rugby union on US soil. Smaller-scale internationals will be played this weekend in Nashville, Tennessee, where the US Eagles women will face Italy before the Eagles men take on an Australia XV. The following weekend in New Jersey, the Eagles women will play England, the world champions, while the men face the Australians again.
Rose said the 2031 World Cup was “a once-in-a-generation opportunity to bring millions more Americans into the game and create a lasting impact for rugby in this country. I look forward to working closely with USA Rugby, and the clubs, players, supporters, and stakeholders who have built rugby across the United States, alongside the global rugby community, to deliver an incredible Rugby World Cup and build something that lasts well beyond 2031.”
The World Rugby chief executive, Alan Gilpin, said: “Megan is an outstanding leader with a proven track record of delivering world-class sporting events and driving innovation. She joins us at a pivotal moment as our US project enters its next phase – an appointment that reflects the scale of our ambition. Her experience, vision and deep understanding of the US sports landscape make her ideally placed to deliver a defining chapter for rugby in the United States and around the world.”
The US currently supports a men’s pro competition, Major League Rugby, and a women’s semi-pro league, Women’s Elite Rugby. MLR has survived since 2018 but is now down to just five teams after a series of failures, with a possible sixth entrant for 2027 mooted but not confirmed. WER has just five teams too . The US college game has deeper roots and greater strength than is generally known around the rugby world but is politically split and subject to steep challenges in funding and facilities. The US Eagles men failed to qualify for the 2023 World Cup in France but will compete in Australia next year. In England last year, the Eagles women fielded breakout social media star Ilona Maher but failed to get out of their pool.
Such hard realities have fueled skepticism around the global game about whether a US World Cup can be successful, at least in terms of engaging the American public and boosting the American game. In Baltimore, around the Springboks-All Blacks fixture, executives from World Rugby and the competing unions expressed confidence that it can.
Announcing the appointment of Rose, World Rugby said: “With more premium match content being played in the US than ever before, 25 highly engaged cities involved in the applicant process and stakeholder engagement building and fan and media interest continuing to grow, the US is poised to provide an unprecedented stage for Rugby World Cups that will redefine the sport’s future and support the ambitions of its global growth strategy.”

title: Jeffrey Donaldson investigated over alleged rape in UK parliament
description: Met police investigating after referral from PSNI about allegation former DUP leader raped woman in 2016
content:
Met police investigating after referral from PSNI about allegation former DUP leader raped woman in 2016
The Metropolitan police are investigating an allegation that the former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson raped a woman inside parliament in 2016.
Scotland Yard confirmed it received a report from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) on 13 October about an alleged rape in the Palace of Westminster involving a man now aged 63.
The Belfast Telegraph first reported the allegation concerning a woman from Northern Ireland. The newspaper reported that Donaldson invited the woman on a tour of the Commons where he introduced her to high-profile figures. He was said to have taken her for dinner before bringing her into the DUP’s offices in parliament.
The newspaper also reported that the woman received a photo of Donaldson during the Covid lockdown showing a filter on Snapchat across his face with a message saying: “Ready to face the world as soon as this isolation lark is over.”
The woman has been interviewed by PSNI officers, who referred the case to the Met because the alleged offence was said to have taken place in London.
The Met confirmed that the alleged rape was reported to have taken place inside parliament in 2016.
A Met spokesperson said: “On Tuesday 13 October, the Met received a report, referred to us by Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), relating to an allegation of rape in 2016, by a man now aged 63.
“The allegation relates to one victim who is being supported by specialist officers. The investigation is in its early stages. No arrests have been made and inquiries remain ongoing.”
Donaldson was the leader of the DUP from 2021 to 2024.

title: Husband and wife charged in shooting death of teen driving to St Louis Halloween party
description: Alyssa Wilson, 17, was driving to a party at city zoo when prosecutors say Willie Herndon fired a gun at her car
content:
Alyssa Wilson, 17, was driving to a party at city zoo when prosecutors say Willie Herndon fired a gun at her car
A Texas husband and wife are facing criminal charges following the fatal shooting of a 17-year-old girl who was driving to a Halloween celebration at the St Louis zoo when gunfire struck her vehicle on a Missouri highway.
St Louis county prosecutor Melissa Price Smith announced on Monday that Willie Herndon, 43, has been charged with first-degree murder and armed criminal action in connection with the death of Alyssa Wilson. His wife, 45-year-old Taiya Herndon, is also facing a charge of hindering prosecution.
The charges follow an investigation into the deadly 14 October shooting along Interstate 170 in Overland, Missouri , a community north-west of St Louis.
Wilson was traveling southbound at about 7pm, heading to meet a friend for the zoo’s Halloween festivities, known as Boo at the Zoo, when the shooting occurred.
Court documents reveal that at least one bullet was fired into the back of the teenager’s vehicle.
The gunfire left Wilson “incapacitated,” according to court records, and her vehicle subsequently slammed into a concrete median barrier. Emergency responders transported the teenager to the Barnes-Jewish hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
Investigators say security footage captured crucial details that helped authorities identify the suspects.
Jack Abell, chief deputy commander of the region’s major case squad, said during a news conference that Wilson had just driven past a white Buick Enclave parked along the highway shoulder when a single gunshot could be heard.
“A person exited the vehicle and stood outside for a short period of time,” he said. “There was a gunshot, got back in the vehicle. The vehicle turned its hazards off and continued on.”
Authorities used surveillance footage and automated license plate readers to trace the Buick, which carried an out-of-state registration, which ultimately led authorities to the Texas couple.
During Monday’s press conference, Wilson’s father, Robert Hickman, spoke about the devastating loss of his daughter and the future she will never get to experience.
“Alyssa was 17, excited about her life, excited about her future,” he said. “She had 60 days until she turned 18, and we were getting ready to take our first family vacation together to go to Disney for her to see her favorite person in the world, Princess Tiana, and unfortunately, she’s not going to get to do that any more. This was a senseless act.”
Investigators did not disclose what may have prompted the deadly encounter. Abell confirmed that Wilson had no relationship with either of the accused individuals.
Willie Herndon now faces first-degree murder and armed criminal action charges, while Taiya Herndon has been charged with hindering prosecution in connection with the teenager’s death.

title: ‘A vehicle to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity’: Sacha Baron Cohen defends Ali G as satire
description: The actor defended his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, saying his aim is to bring people ‘face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories’
content:
The actor defended his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I?, saying his aim is to bring people ‘face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories’
Sacha Baron Cohen has launched an impassioned defence of satire, the right to offend, and his Ali G character on in a lengthy article for Time magazine .
On the eve of the release of his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I ?, Baron Cohen described satire as “more important than ever”, adding that “along the way, some people, instead of laughing, wince or worse, take offence.”
Comparing modern satirists to the traditional figure of the “bouffon”, Baron Cohen described satire as “the humour of the dispossessed … using biting and at times cruel humour to undermine systemic injustice”.
Having previously released films containing controversial characters including Kazakh journalist Borat Sagdiyev, Austrian fashion show presenter Brüno Gehard, and a thinly disguised Colonel Gaddafi parody called Admiral General Aladeen, Baron Cohen directly took on critics of the Ali G character, who has been criticised in the past for laughing at black street culture and described as a “black caricature” .
Baron Cohen writes: “I made this latest film for the same reason I’ve always done this work. Not only to make people laugh, but also to bring them face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories.”
He added: “I’ve always designed my characters and comedy as vehicles to expose prejudice, bias and stupidity, though I realise not everyone sees them that way. Ali G is a white imbecile – a delusional cultural appropriator – who steals the fashion and lyrics from his favourite gangsta rap and dancehall idols, from Compton to Kingston. The joke is on him, and on the predominantly white male establishment who take him seriously.”
“The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him. The world he’s returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven’t just lingered – they’ve metastasised ... 20 years ago, Ali G would sit next to world experts spouting absurdities. Today – fed a steady diet of disinformation and conspiracy theories by social media influencers and TikTok news – we have created an entire world where ignorance reigns and truth is inverted.”
Saying that “each of my characters has a specific mechanism to encourage people to drop their guards and show what they really believe, prejudices and all”, Baron Cohen suggests that “yes, satire can offend people other than the intended targets.” Aware that the release of his new film is likely to attract protests, he said that his university dissertation was a study of Jewish and black cooperation during the 1960s struggle for civil rights in the US, and added: “As someone who has opposed bigotry and injustice throughout my life and partnered with civil rights groups, I don’t recognise myself in the warped portrayals of me that I sometimes see on social media, lumped in with the bigots I lampoon.”
Pointing to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s path from TV comic to president of Ukraine, Baron Cohen suggested that “satire doesn’t just needle politicians or regimes – it occasionally helps bring them down”, and that the Trump administration’s actions against Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel showed that “ridicule is [far from] irrelevant”.
Quoting George Orwell’s observation in his 1945 essay Funny But Not Vulgar that “every joke is a tiny revolution”, Baron Cohen concluded: “Maybe [satire] can even help shame more of our governments into finally making our Silicon Valley overlords – unelected billionaires who decide what billions of people see and believe – liable for the lies, conspiracies, and hate on their platforms that have already gotten people killed and will likely kill many more.”
“We are once again entering an age of ‘virtuous’ violence, where any atrocity – by racists, Jew-haters, or Islamophobes, the right or the left – can be somehow justified. It is not a place any of us should want to live.”

title: No sour grapes: Venter on vintage form as he lays out Saracens vision
description: The head of rugby culture and wine consultant wants people to see ‘the bigger picture’ as he builds the club to win the Prem again
content:
Head of rugby culture and wine consultant wants people to see ‘the bigger picture’ as he rebuilds club to win the Prem
A rm wrestling with Chas & Dave. Youth hostelling with Chris Eubank. Wine tasting with Brendan Venter. Two of those are among the suggestions made by a flailing Alan Partridge in the famous “smell my cheese” sketch, the other took place on a chilly Tuesday night in north London this week. No prizes for guessing which, given recent events, but 12 months ago it would not have been so easy. Things move fast in the Saracens world, however.
When the invitation arrived, you could not help but smile. Saracens would dispute that Venter’s temporary job title change from director of rugby to head of rugby culture and wine consultant was, to put it bluntly, taking the mickey. But, still, there was something delicious about it. Curiosity took hold, invitation was accepted. A poisoned chalice or a peace offering?
It soon became clear this was a charm offensive. Saracens have been through the mill of late and felt the need to issue a fierce statement this week defending themselves. To recap, they were fined because Prem Rugby executives felt Venter was dodging media obligations. They have endured mixed results to date but the performance against Sale , witnessed by a worryingly sparse crowd, was cause for concern. And they sacked the 21-year-old Totoa Auvaa after his latest brush with the law. Accordingly, Saracens threw open the doors and wheeled out the big guns. Chief executive, chairman, owner, Owen Farrell, Ben Earl and George Martin and, of course, Venter, in his element with dozens of bottles of red to get stuck into.
Venter’s reasons for not wanting to fulfil media duties are roughly threefold. One, because he does not like the banality of it all. “What are your thoughts on that match?” is a question for which life is too short. Two, he wants to promote his coaches such as Joe Shaw. Three, he does not trust himself to bite his lip and avoid disciplinary proceedings.
The first two points are more persuasive than the third but Venter has acknowledged things played out regrettably and here we are, in Saracens’ home dressing room about to discuss notes and tones. Venter is deeply passionate about wine and that he loves to talk about it. “You get to explore wine,” he says.
“It’s like rugby, you’re never going to beat rugby, there are always better ideas and different permutations. I know I’ll never master either of them. Just when you think you’ve got it, you don’t have it and it slips away. Just when you think you’ve figured it out then you are humbled.”
We are blind tasting to avoid preconceptions, just as he did with the Saracens squad during pre-season, before running out on to the training field. “We are so subjective as human beings,” adds Venter. “We can’t help it. We see things, we hear things, and we are influenced. When I tell you this wine costs £100, or it’s this fancy label, or it’s this old, or it comes from this country, you will think it is a good wine.
“The lesson was brilliant for [the players] that day. I am not going to know how much you earn. I don’t want to know how old you are. I’m going to measure you by how you taste, and it was for the players then to get an opportunity to get a seat at the table. If you’ve got a seat at the table, you are going to be up for selection.”
Venter is in full flow. Cabernet is the base of most Bordeaux, he says, and as a result, represents the defence. Merlot, by virtue of being softer, is the attack. Cabernet franc represents kicking, petit verdot and malbec the unseen work that knits everything together. South Africa wines, in Venter’s eyes, are big, meaty and they’re the props.
“The Italians would without doubt be the wings, the flamboyant style,” he says. “The French would be the centres, the same thing, the Aussies would be the meticulous people, the scrum-halves, the fly-halves, the New Zealanders would be the sevens, really tough. And then the Georgians would be the hookers.”
Venter’s stock at Saracens is sky-high despite indifferent results this season. The wonders he worked in his first spell, laying the foundation for players such as Farrell, Maro Itoje, Jamie George and the Vunipolas – Mako and Billy – to form England’s most dominant team for more than a decade make sure of that. Put simply, he has returned to do so again.
“In rugby we see today so much, we don’t see the bigger picture,” he says. “The bigger picture is developing people over a longer period to try and win a Premiership. We need to build again. If you think about it, we were so good for so long with these superstars. And they’re at the end of their time and we need a new group. They’re not going to fall from the air, we need to develop them.”
Farrell is one of the few remaining. He has taken his first steps into coaching – the smart money is that he is still at the club long after hanging up his boots – but he too sees reasons for optimism in Venter’s second stint. “We’re doing it in a bit of a different way from what we’ve been used to but we feel like that will benefit us in the long run. We did the same thing with the wine tasting and then we went out to train after. I can’t remember if it was one of our best sessions. Not because I had too much! He’s very clear and makes it about what we’re doing now – not about what’s been before.”
Time will tell if Venter’s second stint is a success but in wine, there tends to be truth.

title: ‘Don’t sweat the small stuff’: hospice workers share 12 lessons about life and death
description: Hospice and end-of-life workers discuss what they’ve learned from their work and patients in their last moments
content:
Hospice and end-of-life workers discuss what they’ve learned from their work and patients in their last moments
“Hospice” can be a loaded term. Some see it as synonymous with death and “giving up”, as Courtney, a full-time hospice nurse practitioner in Missouri, puts it. But Courtney, who asked that her last name be withheld for privacy reasons, doesn’t see it that way.
“Hospice is giving someone a gift,” she says of her patients, who have typically received a terminal diagnosis with a timeline of six months or less. “It is giving them the gift of being able to stay at home and eat or not eat whatever they want. It is the gift of comfort.”
Courtney first started working with dying patients when she was an oncology nurse. Patients would come to her from the intensive care unit (ICU) or other areas of the hospital when they had a limited time to live and were on comfort measures only – a medical term for care that focuses on relieving pain and distress rather than prolonging life.
“I fell in love with it,” says Courtney. She loved getting the rooms ready, dimming the lights, and creating a gentle, pleasant atmosphere for the patient and their families to say their goodbyes.
After a brief stint working in the ICU, Courtney began working in hospice care full-time. She says her job has reshaped how she approaches her life both personally and professionally. We spoke to her and other hospice and end-of-life workers about what they’ve learned from their work and their patients.
“The best way to have a good death experience for all involved is to be able to have conversations about it with your loved ones,” says Penny Smith, a recently retired hospice nurse of 20 years who lives in Washington state.
People are often reluctant to discuss death, experts say, either because they are worried about upsetting their loved ones or because of superstition.
“People think that talking about [death] is going to make it happen faster,” says Dr Luyi Kathy Zhang, director of the palliative care serenity unit at Bellevue hospital in New York City. “It seems silly when you say it out loud, but it is a real fear people have because the topic is so uncomfortable.”
But open dialogue “ensures that your end of life wishes are met”, says Smith, whether it’s what music you’d like to listen to when you’re dying, or whom you would like to be in the room.
Death often brings up painful feelings like fear, loss and discomfort. But Courtney says it can be a beautiful experience as well.
“That’s something we get to see with hospice. Someone dying at home, surrounded by loved ones, listening to music and sharing stories,” she says.
“Death can be sad,” agrees Zhang. “But there’s so much beauty in being able to witness the amount of love and devotion between people which gets magnified at the end of life.”
Too often, we put off our goals and dreams indefinitely, figuring we’ll get to them when we have more time, more money, more energy. But our time is not infinite, hospice workers emphasize.
“So many of my patients waited to take the vacation of their lifetime and were never able to,” says Smith.
Zhang hears lots of patients talk about how they regret not following their dreams or pursuing what they wanted because of fear of judgment, risk and the unknown.
“We all think that we’re going to live to 80, 90 or 100, but that’s not the case for everyone,” she says. “Just go for things.”
Working with death highlights how little of life is in our control, says Courtney.
“I cannot control what is happening in somebody’s body,” she says. “I can’t control cancer, I can’t control COPD [chronic obstructive pulmonary disease], I can’t control any of those things.”
But knowing what is outside our control can make more clear what is in our control.
“By the time someone gets to be my patient, I can’t control those other things they have going on, but what I can control is making sure that they have their wishes honored, that their loved ones are cared for,” Courtney says. “I can ensure they have dignity, and that their death is a phenomenal, beautiful thing.”
“A lot of people are alone at the end of life for one reason or another,” says Zhang.
Many of Zhang’s patients tell her about people they miss or friends they regret losing touch with.
Seeing this, she says, has made her more intentional about cultivating the relationships in her life. She tells herself: “‘I am going to be the one to reach out and try to have a meetup. And if people aren’t reaching out to me, I’ll be the one to do it, because it’s important to me.”
Put differently: “Don’t sweat the small stuff,” says Courtney.
Working with death day in and day out has made this easier for her, she says, because it “puts into perspective what is worth reacting to and what’s not”.
When she’s stuck in traffic or dealing with minor inconveniences, Courtney says she tells herself: “If I’m fortunate enough to live to be 80 years old or I’m on my deathbed, I’m not going to be thinking about this.”
Zhang says the greatest lesson she has taken from her work in end-of-life care is “being present, and taking advantage of and being grateful for the life I have”.
Before joining this field, Zhang says she was always wondering about the next thing she had to do or achieve. This isn’t necessarily a bad idea, she says, but it led her to neglect where she was at that moment.
“I’m so much more grateful for the little things – even waking up and being able to enjoy coffee,” she says.
This reminder from a colleague years ago changed the way Courtney worked.
“We are so used to compartmentalizing death,” she says. “But when we step into that room, that isn’t just Mr Johnson – it’s also Sara’s dad.”
This can help you remember that other people are human, and make you feel more patient and generous, even if someone is cutting you off in traffic.
Courtney considers hospice work her passion. But even so, her patients remind her all the time that a job is just a job, and that there is more to life.
“Even though it’s meaningful, we have to be able to leave that at the door sometimes,” Courtney says.
When trying to comfort someone in their last moments, loved ones will often tell them that it is “OK to go”. But in Smith’s experience, what people really want to hear at the end of their days is that “their life had meaning and purpose”.
A patient said this to Courtney once, and it has stayed with her. “It was just so funny,” she says: a reminder that life is delightful and messy, often at the same time.
This doesn’t just apply to those we love the most, but also so many others, Courtney says. “There are little interactions with patients that I remember from years and years ago,” she says.
“I think that’s beautiful, because at the end of the day we don’t get to leave much on this earth except the impact we had and what we’re remembered for,” she adds.

title: Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine review – turgid tribute to pioneering star
description: Barbican Hall, LondonJulia Bullock is magnetic in this discourse on Josephine Baker, but the 100-minute piece is slow-moving and lacking in intimacy
content:
Barbican Hall, London Julia Bullock is magnetic in this discourse on Josephine Baker, but the 100-minute piece is slow-moving and lacking in intimacy
Josephine Baker was many things: a civil rights activist; a spy for the French resistance; a woman who, born into poverty, became the best-paid stage star in Europe. But before she was any of these, she was an entertainer. So one wonders what on earth she would make of Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine, a turgid 100-minute piece developed by the soprano Julia Bullock, composer Tyshawn Sorey, poet Claudia Rankine and director Peter Sellars.
This was its UK premiere, although Bullock and Sorey have been performing versions of it in the US and elsewhere over the past decade. It isn’t a tribute in the usual sense, but a discourse on racial discrimination, in Baker’s day and our own. Bullock, magnetic as ever, sings and speaks alongside six musicians, who include Sorey himself on piano, drum kit and percussion, plus electric guitar, violin, alto flute, saxophone and bassoon. On a platform, in front of a saturated square of brightly coloured light, Bullock declaims Rankine’s words and sings Sorey’s music, in which Baker’s songs are deconstructed, reformed, and mostly slowed right down. A riff on Bye Bye Blackbird has guitar and saxophone sounding suspiciously like the playout on a 1980s power ballad. Later, more rewardingly, the guitar gives a highlife flavour to a version of Je t’aime. But mostly the score is bloated and the instrumental episodes don’t unify the piece so much as draw it out. Ear-splitting bass drum and tam tam indicate emotional climaxes. Everyone is mic’d up, which works against any sense of intimacy.
Surtitles translate the French, laying bare the sentiments that she slipped into unsuspecting ears. “Should I be white to please you more?” Bullock sings, holding a half bow and gazing out as if simultaneously accusing us and seeking our approval. One episode alludes to Baker’s famous “danse sauvage”, for which she wore a skirt made of rubber bananas, and almost nothing else. Braless under the sheer fabric at the top of her jumpsuit – and yes, the sight of a woman’s breasts is more transgressive on the Barbican stage today than it was in the Folies Bergères a century ago – Bullock dances, making some of Baker’s grotesquely caricatured “savage” moves, and the effect is properly disturbing. Here, Perle Noire is hard-hitting. Otherwise, it’s hard going.

title: Woman told Russell Brand he treated her ‘like an animal’, court hears
description: Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women
content:
Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women
A woman said Russell Brand degraded her and treated her like “a piece of meat” when he raped her at his London townhouse, a court has heard.
She alleged she repeatedly begged the 51-year-old comedian to stop the assault which left her bleeding for days and in pain.
Months later she bumped into Brand who texted her saying: “You’re dirty and I wanna push you further.”
Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.
The TV personality listened intently in the dock as the woman gave evidence from behind a screen at Southwark crown court on Wednesday.
Brand is accused of anally raping the woman at his three-storey Victorian townhouse after picking her out from a crowd at one of his stand-up performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009.
The woman told police she was a “massive fan” of Brand and had performed oral sex on him after the gig despite having a boyfriend at the time. Days later, she went to Brand’s home in Hampstead, north-west London, knowing she would have vaginal sex with him. But she alleged Brand anally raped her after consensual vaginal sex.
In tense exchanges with Brand’s barrister Ian Winter KC during cross-examination, the woman denied she had consented to anal sex but later regretted it because she was in pain and feared she had contracted HIV.
The woman told the court that Brand “didn’t act like he’d done something criminal” after the alleged attack, to which Winter replied: “That’s because you consented.”
She insisted she had not, telling the barrister: “We’re not here to discuss my morality.”
“I didn’t consent to what happened to me,” she continued. “I have said that repeatedly in questioning. I made it very clear that I thought I was going to have penetrative vaginal sex with a condom.
“I agree that I haven’t painted myself in a very good light. I did just meet Mr Brand at the Hammersmith Apollo and I did have a partner who I really loved and I made a huge mistake.”
The woman was also questioned about her pre-recorded police interviews which were played to court on Tuesday and Wednesday. She told officers she ran into Brand at the Edinburgh Festival months after the alleged rape, and then received a “random” text from the comedian.
The woman, who was in her early 20s, said she challenged Brand: “Why are you even messaging me?” She claimed he responded: “Because you are dirty and I want to push you further.”
She said she replied saying: “I think you’ve pushed me far enough, you treated me like an animal,” to which Brand responded: “I’m sorry.”
She told police: “I feel how I’d felt at his house, that I felt completely degraded and fucking treated like an animal, like a piece of meat.”
Winter questioned why she had not replied to Brand saying he had raped her. He told the woman: “That’s because he had pushed you and probably had treated you like an animal, but he didn’t rape you.”
Earlier, Winter said the woman was aware of Brand’s reputation, to which she replied: “I had not heard about Mr Brand raping somebody.”
Winter replied: “Of course not. You knew that he was extremely sexually active with multiple women. You knew that he won the Sun newspaper’s Shagger of the Year three years running.”
He went on to describe how Brand’s show at the Hammersmith Apollo was “extremely sexually explicit” and that women were throwing their bras at the comedian and flashing their naked breasts. “I didn’t do that,” the woman replied.
The barrister said that after the show the woman had performed oral sex on Brand “who was effectively a total stranger, because you were obsessed with him at the time”. She replied: “If what you are asking is, would I have met someone … and then perform oral sex on him had he not been the person that he was, the answer is no.”
The barrister said the woman was aware that Brand was interested in “transactional” sex when he persuaded her to go to his house after the gig. “I didn’t think I was going to be his girlfriend,” she replied.
But the woman denied Winter’s suggestion that Brand had told her he wanted to have anal sex with her.
Winter said: “In a way, you went along with what he wanted because you were young and impressionable and obsessed with him. I’m putting to you, you agreed to do that.”
She replied: “I didn’t agree to do that.”
“The reason I made the comment about going there willingly and regretting it afterwards was because I did not consent to that,” she said.
The woman said she had not been able to immediately tell Brand to stop the alleged rape because she was in shock and pain. “In the very first instant I couldn’t speak, I couldn’t breathe,” she said.
She said she carried a lot of guilt and shame about what had happened, saying: “Because I went to his house willingly, because I engaged in a consensual type of sex, I didn’t feel I had as much right to feel as bad about it as I did.”
When Winter pressed her, she replied: “I felt a lot of burden. I carried that feeling of guilt and shame and I felt lots of things but particularly for exactly the reason that you are doing right here, making me feel like I brought it on myself. That just because you go somewhere willingly and the outcome in the end is not consensual – it’s a different scenario.”

title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: don’t want to get your Big Winter Coat out just yet? Try ‘onion dressing’
description: It’s time to learn the art of layering – and we’re talking a crew neck with a ballet wrap and blazer, not full-on outdoor explorer
content:
It’s time to learn the art of layering – and we’re talking a crew neck with a ballet wrap and blazer, not full-on outdoor explorer
I s layering an art? Probably not in the traditional sense. We are not talking the Bayeux tapestry here. No one is going to queue round the block to admire the subtle interplay between your Uniqlo Heattech and your cashmere crewneck. Still, I think it’s nice to romanticise this stuff. The deeply unpoetic truth is that it is going to get cold and wearing one item of clothing at a time simply isn’t going to cut it. So let’s pretend that the sliver of white T-shirt beneath a jumper, the shirt collar poking out above a cardigan, or the ballet wrap over a snug top are not acts of basic thermal self-preservation, but composition. A creative statement about proportion, texture, colour and self-expression. If you have to wear half your wardrobe at once, you may as well make a masterpiece out of it.
The avant-garde layering term to drop in order to sound like a connoisseur this season is onion dressing. Not the most romantic name, but a clear visual for the most refined form of layering, which is fine layers rather than hefty ones. And instead of the top layer covering all beneath it, each piece should be visible. As if we were slicing through the onion and looking at a cross-section if you will excuse me labouring the allium thing. This is layering with finesse rather than brute force. Hems and collars and cuffs give an outfit depth and texture without adding too much bulk. You want to look intriguing and multi-dimensional, not like Joey in Friends wearing all of Chandler’s clothes .
Onion dressing is your sartorial safety blanket in an increasingly uncertain climate. Autumn was unpredictable enough to start with, and our new weather reality is constant chaos. The merry-go-round keeps spinning even when you are indoors: will the train carriage be arctic and draughty or stuffy and overheated today? Who knows, comrades. You are invited for Sunday lunch, but will your pals have their heating on full blast or not at all? One can neither ask in advance, nor comment. Best to be stylishly prepared for all eventualities.
The greatest joy of onion dressing is that you can put off the moment when you start wearing your Big Coat. As a psychological upside, this is not to be sniffed at. In January and February you will be stuck in that thing, so you don’t want to be sick of the sight of it by then. Imaginative combinations of less bulky pieces can keep you warm, offer temperature flexibility, make getting dressed less dull, and get some extra use out of jackets that would otherwise be sidelined for six months.
Start with the science. The allure of layering is looking relaxed, effortless and ready for anything. Red-faced, sweaty and unable to move your arms because your sweater is too bulky for the sleeves of your jacket is not elegant. Follow the principles of hardy folk dressing for the outdoors and start with a fine base layer, something breathable to keep you warm without cooking you. A polo neck is extra cosy, but a crewneck looks chic. Check that the neckline is clean and tidy, because this part will be on show and that needs to look deliberate. Then a middle layer: this could be a plaid or plain cotton button down shirt, or an interesting cardi, or a sweater. Outdoors, all you need now is a “shield” layer: an easy on-and-off piece, which could be a blazer, a chore jacket or a puffer vest. Oh, one last practical point: consider either the middle or top layer being sleeveless to avoid feeling like you’ve been stuffed like a Christmas turkey.
You need some flair, too. This is style, not pass-the-parcel. If all the layers are utilitarian the effect can veer a bit “Duke of Edinburgh award”. A pop of colour works. Contrasting textures will add sophistication. A collar or layered necklines are good for elevating the vibe. Layering is not going to get you a retrospective at the Tate, but it does take an eye for colour, composition and texture. Keeping warm is much more interesting when you use your imagination.
