title: Bush’s brother crosses party lines to vote for James Talarico for Senate
description: Republican Neil Bush says he was ‘deeply troubled’ by Ken Paxton’s conduct and ‘enormously impressed’ with Talarico
content:
Republican Neil Bush says he was ‘deeply troubled’ by Ken Paxton’s conduct and ‘enormously impressed’ with Talarico
Neil Bush, a son of former president George HW Bush and a lifelong Republican, announced on Tuesday that he crossed party lines to vote for James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas.
In a Facebook post, Neil Bush said he chose to vote early for Talarico over Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate and current Texas attorney general, because he was “deeply troubled” by Paxton’s conduct and was “enormously impressed” by Talarico’s principles.
As a moderate Republican, Neil Bush’s statement on the competitive Senate race in Texas reflects views from a faction of the party that often disagrees with Donald Trump while holding traditional conservative views. It comes just two weeks before the midterms, when Democrats and Republicans are battling for the seat in Texas.
“I have been deeply troubled by Paxton’s conduct as Texas Attorney General, particularly his decision to challenge the results of the 2020 presidential election in other states in an effort to help Donald Trump remain in power,” Neil Bush, 71, wrote.
The former president’s son and brother of George W Bush expressed concern about Paxton’s past controversies , including Paxton’s 2023 Texas state legislature impeachment and acquittal, as well as Paxton’s loyalty to Trump.
“I have been a Republican for most of my life, and I still believe deeply in many traditional Republican principles. But character matters more than party affiliation. Our democracy depends on leaders who respect our institutions, tell the truth, accept accountability, and seek to unite rather than divide,” Neil Bush wrote.
His departure from the party’s nominee comes amid the Bush family’s distancing from Trump’s influence on the party. The former president George HW Bush was vocal about his dislike of the president, and voted for Hillary Clinton in 2016. Another former president George W Bush, meanwhile, has not voted for or endorsed Trump in any of his elections. The family exception appears to be George P Bush, a Trump supporter who who lost to Paxton in a bid for Texas attorney general in 2022.
Neil Bush said he saw Talarico as “a principled, pragmatic leader” who has a “willingness to listen to those with whom he disagrees”.
“He speaks with respect, seeks common ground, and seems genuinely interested in bringing people together rather than driving them apart. His faith appears to be a deeply rooted source of humility, compassion, and conviction rather than a political weapon,” Neil Bush wrote.
Talarico, a progressive liberal candidate who uses faith-based messaging, is the Democratic party’s latest hopeful to flip the seat in the deep red state. No Democrat has secured the Senate seat in Texas since the 1980s.
“Today, I voted against a style of politics that I believe has damaged our country. More importantly, I voted for the kind of character and leadership I hope will help heal it.”
The Guardian has asked the Talarico campaign for comment.

title: Seth Meyers on Elon Musk: ‘Nobody likes him’
description: Late-night hosts discussed Donald Trump’s praise for Elon Musk as well as the physical appearance of several male US Senate candidates
content:
Late-night hosts discussed Donald Trump’s praise for Elon Musk as well as the physical appearance of several male US Senate candidates
Late-night hosts recapped Donald Trump ’s recent comments on Elon Musk and the physical attractiveness of numerous male candidates in the upcoming US midterms.
Seth Meyers opened Tuesday’s Late Night with a nod to the world champion New York Knicks, who kicked off their season that evening with a ceremony to raise their NBA championship banner at Madison Square Garden. “Meanwhile, over at the Brooklyn Nets stadium, they raised a ‘help wanted’ sign,” Meyers quipped.
The president, meanwhile, said in a post on Truth Social that the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool was repaired, 70% filled with water and “looking good”.
“Oh man, well, you keep us posted,” Meyers laughed. “I think Trump missed his calling as a condo board president. ‘The koi pond is almost filled and the new mailbox keys are in, come find me when you can.’”
Similarly, at an executive order signing ceremony at the White House, Trump praised the Rose Garden and said “that stone is so beautiful”.
“Said reporters: that’s RFK Jr,” Meyers quipped.
In other White House news, according to numerous reports, Trump is considering several replacements for former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, including the New York Yankees president, Randy Levine. “Because any time someone goes 17 years without winning a championship, you gotta capture that magic,” Meyers joked.
And at a recent White House science summit, Trump praised Elon Musk and said “quite honestly, there’s nobody like him”.
Meyers made an edit: “I read that wrong – nobody likes him.”
And on the Daily Show, Michael Kosta checked in with Trump’s efforts on the midterm campaign trail. “As we all know, he has a very important day job looking for things on the map to rename,” he joked. “But with the midterms in the home stretch, he’s also been holding daily rallies in support of embattled Republican candidates. And lately, he’s hit upon a very interesting observation about many of these men.”
Kosta then played several recent clips of Trump referring to the physical appearance of male candidates, calling them “good looking”, “beautiful looking”, or in the case of Ohio Senate candidate John Husted, “I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete … I looked at his ass.”
“Yes, you live your truth, Donald!” Kosta joked. “It doesn’t matter what anyone says! You find a man with a nice tight ass and take him dancing in your big gay ballroom.
“And Maga, if you’re upset by this, you are the ones who love Trump because he ‘says whatever he’s thinking’,” he added. “But that’s a double-edged sword. Because sometimes you get ‘I hate immigrants’, and sometimes you get ‘reincarnate me as a desk chair so this guy can sit on my face all day’.
“But if Donald Trump is not secretly gay, what he definitely is, is an 80-year-old man,” Kosta continued. “That’s the age where the filter starts to slip and grandpa just says out loud anything that pops into his head.”
Kosta made sure to caveat, there’s “nothing wrong with being an ass guy, OK? But Trump has now spent more time thinking about this guy’s butt than how to end the Iran war,” so he had some advice: “Mr President, rub one out and get back to work!”

title: ‘He had this electrical charge’: the short life and long legacy of Jason Molina, master of Americana
description: As a documentary celebrates the late US musician, friends and collaborators describe an incomparable storyteller who brought ‘myth and magic to everyday life’
content:
As a documentary celebrates the late US musician, friends and collaborators describe an incomparable storyteller who brought ‘myth and magic to everyday life’
J ason Molina grew up in a trailer in the working-class city of Lorain, Ohio. The city’s skyline once flickered with blue flames and a warm orange glow emanated from clattering steel mills, but by Molina’s teenage years, Lorain was in a tailspin. “Things were really on the economic decline,” says Tommy Nickoloff, Molina’s childhood friend and director of a new documentary: You Fuckers Figure It Out: A Jason Molina Story. “Nobody had any money and we were encouraged to get out. It’s a place where the American dream was born and died. And we watched it die.”
Molina did indeed get out: the singer-songwriter released almost 20 studio albums and numerous EPs, primarily under the monikers Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co, spanning lo-fi to slowcore via polished Americana and alt-country. By 2009, he estimated he had written thousands of songs. But he died in 2013, aged 39, after years of alcoholism.
The documentary is a warm and intimate look back on Molina’s early life and how his rust belt upbringing, along with notions of home, place and landscape, became recurring themes in his bountiful songs. The audience for them has kept growing after his death: there’s been a biography, cover albums, a touring tribute band titled Magnolia & Johnson Electric Co made up of ex-bandmates, and he’s got a new generation of fans in Phoebe Bridgers, MJ Lenderman, Clairo, Kevin Morby, Waxahatchee and hyped young singer-songwriters such as Greg Freeman. “You have a moment with a handful of artists in your life where you hear their music and it clicks and you immediately fall in love,” says Freeman. “That happened with Jason’s music.”
But this wasn’t always the case. “It still shocks me how few people are aware of Jason and his legacy, especially around home,” says Nickoloff, recalling a 2006 show in nearby Cleveland that drew just 70 people.
When Songs: Ohia started in the mid-1990s, it was via lo-fi skeletal songs recorded to tape that were tender yet raw and delivered with a quivering high tenor reminiscent of Neil Young and soon-to-be collaborator Will Oldham. As grunge and alt-rock boomed, Molina went against the grain. “There was nothing less cool than a ukulele in 1994,” laughs his former bandmate Max Winter in the film. “Holy shit, he may as well have been playing bagpipes.”
But Molina was unique from a young age. A voracious reader as a child, he consumed everything from instruction manuals to foreign language poetry. His teenage years were spent as a metalhead and by the time he was at college, his fervent, enthusiastic – sometimes annoying – energy earned him the nickname “sparky”. Now writing a song a day, he would sometimes play impromptu 5am shows on a roof or porch to show them off. “I’ve never met anyone like him,” says Nickoloff. “He’s like a 20-sided die in Dungeons and Dragons. Most people are lucky if they have six sides.”
Chris Swanson, co-founder of record label Secretly Canadian, heard Molina’s first single, Nor Cease Thou Never Now, and was besotted. “We obsessively played it and drove 19 hours to New York to go see him,” he says. Songs: Ohia was the label’s second ever signing and a lifelong relationship began. “Without him there would be no us – plain and simple,” the label said after his death. A pattern of releasing at least an album a year followed, including 2000’s The Lioness, in which he decamped to Scotland to work with Alasdair Roberts and members of Arab Strap on a ghostly yet beautiful record of post-rock-folk-blues.
Emma Niblett, who performs as Scout Niblett, was a friend, collaborator and touring partner of Molina’s. “He had this electrical charge around him, which matched his nickname,” she recalls. “And he had this ability to bring myth and magic to everyday life as a master of storytelling. You never quite knew if his stories were true or fantasy or a bit of both.”
The late producer Steve Albini, who worked with Molina, also recalled this blurring of truths. “He was a big bullshitter,” Albini said in 2014. “A lot of the things that he said were fantastic and it seemed like he wanted things to be magical and awesome, and that he needed to create fables for himself to inhabit in order to do that.” Swanson describes this unusual quirk as “the elephant in every room with Jason”, adding: “He was just a consummate storyteller and if that meant him saying he was bitten by a tarantula which ended up quasi-paralysing him, then that’s the story.”
This seeped into his songwriting too: Molina’s obsession with ghosts and hauntings added an otherworldly element to his work. “The songs belong in his own secret world,” says Freeman. “There’s an internal logic and language to his songwriting, the way motifs reappear and build this imaginary psychic place. Like he’s painting a dream.” Niblett describes him as “a magician”, “incomparable” and “a one-off, playing in a major league by himself”.
In 2003, Molina released his magnum opus, Songs: Ohia’s The Magnolia Electric Co (confusingly, the name of the album then became the name of the band afterwards). Mike Brenner’s stunning, shimmering lap steel is all over the record. “When I was sent the demos, I was stunned by how much of a quantum leap it was,” he says of the progress from the previous record. “It sounded like a whole different game.” Swanson felt similarly. “You can hear it in the demos but when they made the album, it just became effervescent,” he says. “The songs had stepped up by a full magnitude of order and they just sounded timeless. It was like, holy shit! These are all-time country songs.”
Produced by Albini, with a full band, it was a lightning in a bottle moment for all involved. “The most otherworldly experience I’ve ever had in a studio,” says Niblett. “It felt like some supernatural powers were present. His writing felt like pure channelling. It was so clear, vulnerable, yet insightful, and undeniable. We all knew that something special was occurring.”
However, changing your name halfway through your career is not an ideal scenario to help boost your profile. “It was very tricky,” says Swanson. “And this was also during the era when he’d go on tour and not play any songs from the album he’d just released, and only play ones that no one’s heard before.” Molina was driven, prolific, and at times stubborn and impatient: “He wasn’t super interested in doing things twice,” says Brenner.
He was also capricious, says Brenner, which Swanson also recalls. “Very generous, sometimes to his own detriment,” he says. “He’d be like, ‘I just gave away our guarantee [fee] for the show to someone on the street who looked hungry.’ He would do very irrational things out of a generous impulse.”
Molina continued to release albums and EPs at a remarkable pace but by the end of the 2000s things slowed down. “The later it got in the story, the more stressful and darker the touring became,” says Brenner. “It became less enjoyable and I don’t think the quality of the shows were at the forefront of his mind.” Niblett recalls seeing a change when watching him perform. “He seemed to slowly disappear,” she says. “Although he was present on stage, his presence diminished. He started leaning on the band to take the weight, so his powerful, unique, and nuanced way of carrying a song was fading. I could hear and see he had lost himself. He was literally hiding behind his band in the later years.”
Unbeknown to many, Molina had begun to drink heavily. “He was a very light drinker in his 20s,” says Swanson. “But in his 30s, he went whole hog.” This eventually led to debilitating alcoholism that meant he retreated and stopped releasing music in 2009. The last four years of his life are described by his family as “pure chaos” in the documentary. For those who knew the young Molina, “it was unbelievable,” says Nickoloff. “It made zero sense. To the degree it was like: I don’t know anybody else named Jason Molina but they have to be talking about that person.”
Swanson recalls visiting him a few months before his death in Indianapolis. “He had given away all his belongings, which was something he would do routinely,” he says. “So he was living in a shell. We made the decision to move him to Bloomington, where he had more of a community, as his community was with street people in Indianapolis around the projects he was living in.”
But a week after that decision was made, Molina died of organ failure related to his alcoholism. “I honestly wouldn’t have believed it if you’d have told me years earlier that’s how his life would end,” says Niblett. “I don’t think the shock ever leaves.”
Despite being a heartache of enormous magnitude, for Nickoloff it ended up changing his life in numerous ways. “Jason’s death saved my life,” he says. “I was in a terrible spot emotionally and psychologically. He’d always been this beacon for me, and then he’s gone. But as a kid he was the only voice that was encouraging and believed in me to do something. So, in that spirit, we made this film and what a tremendous pleasure it is to be a small vehicle in helping make people more familiar with him, his work and his life. He was my homeboy.”

title: I’ve booked my first proper holiday – and it’s pulled me out of winter grimness like a magic spell
description: Anticipating a potential spring in which I am bathed in sun on a Greek island is giving me the kind of glee that makes anything feel possible
content:
Anticipating a potential spring in which I am bathed in sun on a Greek island is giving me the kind of glee that makes anything feel possible
R eader, it’s important to tell you that I’ve never been to Greece in my life. Not once. But I might be going, for the very first time, in the spring. And so, for the last week or so, all my dreams have featured fresh fish cooked to flaky perfection, a swimming pool into which I shall venture no deeper than my waist (I can’t swim), and the heat of the sun that not even the climate crisis can make happen in the UK in April.
I don’t come with a history of exotic foreign holidays. Travelling abroad fell under the umbrella of familial duty: “Going Home”, AKA a brief return to the place where my parents were born (and coincidentally more and more foreign to them the longer they lived in the UK) in order to keep the ties of kinship going and remind us of our roots. I should say we didn’t do idyllic UK-based holidays either. I read about caravans in Enid Blyton books and watched Vaseline-lensed ads for CenterParcs and knew neither was in my immediate future. I made peace with it. We just weren’t a “going on holiday” type of family. It didn’t bother me. I harbour no resentment, and honestly, feel largely equanimous when I consider this “gap” in my life experience.
But this potential Greece trip? It’s been on the back burner of my mind for years. A low-level, always-running app on my personal CPU, taking up very little energy but alive and constant. Almost as soon as I found out I was pregnant, I had a full-fledged fantasy. Picture it: somewhere in Europe 2027. A villa, a group of friends, two weeks of deep chats, delicious local cuisine, reading books and afternoon swims (remember, I can’t even swim). Our children? I dunno, somewhere safe and/or soundly asleep. My mind? Unencumbered, dreaming up the outline of my next play. My body? Relaxed but strengthened by the daily yoga session that also magically happens shortly after every sunrise. Before you ask, yes, I can hear myself. I know I sound insane. And I’m fine with it!
My friend, newly a mother of two also, is the planner of this Greece trip. She sees the vision, works at the same foolish bank of romantic illusion where I have my account. But she’s not just a dreamer. She’s done solid, boots-on-the-ground research. She’s checking dates, curating the invite list: who likes cooking? Whose vibe matches our knackered-but-trying-to-be-a-good-friend situation? How many childfree adults can we ethically invite until we have the optimal number of eyes to cover all the children who’ll be around? She’s checking availability, organising the group chat, working to make my dreams a reality. I could kiss her. And perhaps in Crete, with the permission of all affected parties, I shall.
More than the treat of a fortnight somewhere far away and yet in the company of old, dear friends, what I’m feeling most acutely is the pleasure of a promise. Having something to look forward to? A balm in the best of times. But especially so right now. I am re-emerging from beneath the cloud of the fourth (and fifth!) trimester. I read – and finished – a book the other week. I worked out with a kettlebell at some point in the past month. I went to a gig! Things are feeling viable again.
Outside of my little sphere, having something pleasurable on the horizon feels like a magic spell. There is a grimness to reading headlines in the morning that can’t be shaken off. Going on holiday clearly won’t solve these problems but my Cretan dreams give my soul small moments of uncomplicated anticipatory glee that make life worth living despite the horrors of near and far. Spring will come again, as it always does. The human race trudges on.
Perhaps I feel my most human when I am anticipating. Inside of that anticipation is the incredible knowledge that while everything is possible, sometimes I get to imagine only delightful things. It’s an excellent exercise. Like I said, a magic spell.
So here goes: I might be going to Crete with my children. What if we have an amazing time? What if this is the beginning of a new family tradition? What if the baby takes his first steps there? Could I master a couple of new recipes with new ingredients before we return home? Will 2027 be the year I start and finish Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan quartet? In Crete, anything could happen.

title: Popcorn with your Puccini: can opera on screen ever work?
description: Composers have harnessed TV and cinema since Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors pulled in five million viewers 75 years ago but for my money Kombat Opera’s satire showed us how to do it best
content:
Composers have harnessed TV and cinema since Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors pulled in five million viewers 75 years ago but for my money Kombat Opera’s satire showed us how to do it best
I t’s not even Halloween, but here’s an operatic Christmas story for you. This is the 75th anniversary of the first opera made for television: Gian Carlo Menotti’s Amahl and the Night Visitors, broadcast at Yuletide in 1951 and watched by five million people across the US in a production sponsored by Hallmark. You can watch the original broadcast on YouTube : it was introduced with wit, self-deprecation and early 50s elegance by Menotti himself (vastly less charmingly, the role of King Balthazar was played by a singer in blackface). Chet Allen’s performance as the boy, Amahl, is staggering, and even more moving is Rosemary Kuhlmann’s Mother, especially in her aria, All That gold!.
Amahl is “an opera for children because it tries to recapture my own childhood”, Menotti said. It was played on US TV every Christmastime throughout the 50s, and was recorded and remade in new productions the next decade, while the BBC picked it up in 1953, and there was even an Australian TV version. Less than an hour long, Menotti’s festive fable works because of the intimacy of its story, and its refusal to patronise its intended audience.
But Amahl was a high-water mark. Another opera-made for-telly anniversary this year is Benjamin Britten’s Owen Wingrave , composed for the BBC and first broadcast 55 years ago. Britten’s piece definitely wasn’t made for children. Based on a gothic novella by Henry James, it’s the story of the pacifist Owen Wingrave’s struggles against his military forebears and his fiancee who is ashamed of him. Britten’s opera is uncompromisingly claustrophobic and intense, one of his most underrated scores – but it’s a piece that wasn’t designed to capture Amahl’s popularity on screen.
The later story of operas made for TV in Britain is more about exploration of the possibilities of the medium rather than following in Menotti’s audience-first footsteps: in the 90s and 00s there are pieces composed for TV including Judith Weir’s Armida or Jonathan Dove’s When She Died … , written on the fifth anniversary of the death of Princess Diana, and there were filmed productions of existing operas especially remade for television, such as the director Margaret Williams’s scintillating versions of Thomas Adès’s Powder Her Face or her version of Britten’s Owen Wingrave , produced for Channel 4 in 2001 to mark the opera’s 30th anniversary.
These days, opera is more often found on the big screen: cinemas all over the world can take you to a night at the opera, and here’s another anniversary for you – this autumn marks 20 years since the Metropolitan Opera started streaming its productions to cinemas , an innovation that the Royal Opera House in London quickly followed, finding new audiences, as well as a parallel stream of income and impact.
The Met: Live in HD has been controversial: Peter Gelb, the Met’s general manager suggested in 2013 that the cinema audiences were “ cannibalising” the audience for live shows ; but surely, from Japan to Brazil, and here in the UK, these broadcasts reach opera-lovers who are unable to go to the Met in person.
On cinema screens there are huge gains in seeing close up what the singers are doing as actors, subtleties of facial expression and the relationships between the characters on stage that you can’t pick up when you are sitting at the back of the gallery. But the essential problem with broadcasting live opera on any screen remains the same as it was in 1951. We are watching performers who are projecting through the acoustic miracles of their voices into an auditorium that seats thousands.
The intimacy of film, and especially TV, requires precisely the opposite mode of delivery. In drama on TV or film, the wonder and the illusion lies in sharing an intimacy of space and feeling with the actors, whereas the mechanics of opera work through the other end of the telescope, zooming out from their voices towards us in the audience, rather than zooming us in to be with them in each scene. Opera and film are essentially made for entirely different purposes.
But if you do want to see what happens when opera is made for television from the ground up, there’s another anniversary to tell you about: it has been 19 years since Richard Thomas’s Kombat Opera Presents, half-hour shows broadcast in 2007 that sent up TV staples from The Apprentice to the South Bank – Bragg! – Show . Thomas was hot on the heels of the success of his theatre show with Stewart Lee - Jerry Springer: The Opera , but the origins of Kombat Opera also go back to sketches in Simon Munnery’s Attention Scum series that aired on the BBC in 2001, with the soprano and contemporary music catalyst Loré Lixenberg, who made a new art-form dressed as a gothic uber-diva , filmed on the white cliffs of Kent.
Lixenberg, and trained singers including Leigh Melrose, Janis Kelly and Sophia Ragavelas made every half-hour long episode of Kombat Opera their own, but it’s the way Thomas included parts for actors including Kevin Eldon, Hugh Dennis and Jon Culshaw, and mixed all the media together, that makes these shows so compelling.
The format never feels as if it is selling either medium short: the heightened emotionalising and ridiculousness of opera serves the satire perfectly, joyously and concisely. Seems opera on screen works best when its turns its attention to the screen itself.
Talking of taking the artform into new places, Raymond Gubbay celebrates his 80th birthday with the Choir of King’s College, Cambridge at Wigmore Hall, London tonight. Gubbay’s Classical Spectaculars, his Christmas shows, his operas at the Royal Albert Hall – which included flooding the arena with 65,000 litres water every night for Puccini’s Madame Butterfly, a Turandot at Wembley Arena in collaboration with the Royal Opera House, and even his Savoy Opera venture , a brave but doomed attempt to make repertory opera work in the West End without subsidy, are some of the most brilliant, energetic, and imaginative ways of popularising classical music over the last 60 years.
To make large-scale classical music profitable is a vanishingly rare phenomenon. (Even if, while it’s true to say that as a business, Gubbay never took a penny from any Arts Council, most of the musicians and orchestras he worked with wouldn’t exist without it.) Gubbay’s 80th birthday concert will give its profits to another now Arts Council-free organisation, Wigmore Hall itself. Gubbay’s subsidy-free business model remains an impossible dream for most, but Wigmore Hall is an unlikely contemporary torchbearer for the same spirit of entrepreneurship.
This week Tom has been listening to: Anna Meredith’s Dusky , the single from her new album.
You know that feeling when you’re on the summit of the rollercoaster Stealth at Thorpe Park, and there’s that microsecond where your heart’s in your mouth before the drop? Dusky is like six and a half minutes spent in that place of delirious freefall, as rhythms grind against each other, melodic arcs rising and falling, to make time warp and your stomach pitch and yaw.

title: Home Office lifts deportation order for man, 62, who has lived in UK for 50 years
description: Department drops efforts to return Tony Hall to Barbados, a country he left at 12 and where he has no living relatives
content:
Department drops efforts to return Tony Hall to Barbados, a country he left at 12 and where he has no living relatives
The Home Office has lifted a deportation order handed to a 62-year-old man who has lived in Britain for 50 years after criticism of the department’s attempts to remove him to Barbados, a country he left as a child.
The Home Office wrote to Tony Hall on Tuesday to inform him that his deportation order had been revoked. His case had been highlighted in the Guardian a day earlier.
Hall had repeatedly tried to get the deportation order lifted, arguing that as the child of parents who emigrated to the Britain as part of the Windrush generation, he had the right to remain in the UK. He has no surviving relatives in Barbados and has not visited the country since arriving in London aged 12 to join his parents and five older sisters in 1976.
The Home Office had previously stated that he was liable for deportation because of a 2001 conviction for conspiracy to rob and having a firearm with intent. Police stopped Hall and his co-defendants before the robbery was committed. Hall spent eight years in prison.
Officials have been attempting to deport him since the end of his sentence in 2009. As a result of his precarious immigration status, he has been prohibited from working, renting somewhere to live, receiving benefits or receiving full access to NHS treatment.
Hall had argued that he should not continue to be punished as a result of a crime committed 25 years ago, and for which he had served prison time. The Home Office put him on a flight to Barbados in January 2010 in an attempt to deport him to the country of his birth, but he was returned to London on the same plane, arriving the next day. Officials in Barbados appear to have been unwilling to issue him with papers to enter because of the length of time he had been in the UK.
His lawyer, Naga Kandiah at MTC Solicitors, welcomed the decision but said: “The historical injustice at the heart of this case remains unresolved. For over 17 years, our client has endured fear, detention, relentless uncertainty, exclusion from work and housing, and ultimately destitution.
“The Home Office may revoke a deportation order, but it cannot give our client back 17 years of his life.”
Hall said the protracted period of limbo had been very difficult, and that he was relieved that he now had “the chance to live in the country I call home without fear”.
The Home Office indicated that the timing of the decision to lift the deportation was coincidental.
Clive Foster, the Windrush commissioner, the independent advocate for victims and families affected by the scandal, also intervened with the Home Office, arguing that a compassionate approach should be taken in Hall’s case.
Fiona Bawdon, the author of Will I Always Be British? , a recent study of people with precarious immigration status, said: “Either the government wants to do right by all of those it harmed or it doesn’t. What ministers fail to realise is that each time they treat someone in the way they treated Tony Hall, other Windrush victims – even those who’ve now had their citizenship confirmed – feel as if they could still be at risk, as if they are not really seen as British and this could be taken away from them again.”

title: Why is Liz Truss trying to be Danny Dyer with her new book?
description: Bank Job, the former prime minister’s forthcoming publication, is about a shady cabal that brought down the bond market. Seemingly she has forgotten that this was her doing
content:
Bank Job, the former prime minister’s forthcoming title, is about a shady cabal that brought down the bond market. Seemingly she has forgotten that this was her doing
Appearance: Etiquette dictates that you should never judge a book by its cover.
Yes, but do it anyway. It looks like a poster for one of those bad gangster films Danny Dyer used to make, featuring a shadowy set of tough guys – except, instead of Dyer front and centre, there’s Liz Truss.
So you’re saying this is a book – by Truss? Yes. The former prime minister’s new book is out next week. Its subtitle is A Short Book on How the Bank of England Broke the Bond Market and Brought Down the Government.
I have so many questions. Who wouldn’t? The response to her first book , Ten Years to Save the West, didn’t seem to guarantee that she’d get to publish a second.
OK, first : how short is short? Amazon states that the book comes in at just 99 pages. For reference, that’s about 13 times shorter than War and Peace, or three times shorter than the 2012 memoir by Tulisa from N-Dubz .
Next : who on earth is publishing this? That would be Free Speech Press, which says it is “dedicated to publishing books that challenge conventional thinking”. Its authors include Jennifer Arcuri , who you might remember as that woman who claimed she had an affair with Boris Johnson, and the guy who went viral for saying you can grow concrete .
Mike Graham ? That’s him. Actually, this is an interesting link: Graham also owns UKLive, the YouTube channel that now hosts Truss’s show.
Is that still going? Sadly yes. And by the look of recent videos – which include “Why Britain’s political system is completely broken”, “Britain is becoming a LOW-TRUST society” and “Defund the BBC” – she’s still scratching around the US right’s favourite talking points in the hopes that someone will love her again.
What has been the response to the announcement? Are people excited ? Well, when Truss announced Bank Job on X, just six days before its publication date, replies variously retitled it as “Bankrupt” and – inevitably – “Lettuce Job”.
I suppose we should ask what the book is actually about. It’s the same drum that Truss has been banging since her embarrassment as PM: the country is secretly run by the Bank of England, the Treasury and the Office for Budget Responsibility, with this unelected cartel ensuring that Britain will never change.
Still, at least it’s nice and short. Exactly – it’s a toilet book, in the sense that it will probably do in a pinch if you run out of Andrex.
The book is about breaking the bond market, and bringing down the government , but … But wasn’t it Truss who did that? Yes, it was her.
Do say: “Liz Truss knows who broke the bond market.”
Don’t say: “Presumably because Liz Truss owns a mirror.”

title: Poland’s parliament votes to ease abortion ban but faces likely veto from president
description: Measures would remove some penalties for those helping women access abortion but are ‘small-scale step’, say campaigners
content:
Measures would remove some penalties for those helping women access abortion but are ‘small-scale step’, say campaigners
Poland’s lower house of parliament has approved two bills aimed at loosening a near-total ban on abortions, in what campaigners have described as a “small-scale step” ahead of protests calling on the government to fulfil its promises to overhaul the country’s laws.
The new measures, which are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s nationalist president, would remove some of the criminal penalties for those who help women to access abortion care and allow terminations in cases of foetal abnormalities.
Leah Hoctor, of the Center for Reproductive Rights, said: “These bills represent a very small-scale change. Even if these pieces of legislation are ratified and signed into law by the Polish president – which remains to be seen – they would change very little for most women in Poland who need abortion care.”
This view was echoed by the NGO Legalna Aborcja (Legal Abortion), a reproductive rights and advocacy initiative. “What does this mean for women who need an abortion right now? Nothing, because none of these bills would help them,” said a spokesperson.
The Fundacja Widzialne (Visible Foundation) asked people to keep up the pressure on the government by taking to the streets on Thursday. “Poland still has an inhumane abortion law,” it wrote on social media as it announced rallies in 27 cities. “We demand the full decriminalisation of abortion and access to abortion covered by the National Health Fund!”
The rallies, backed by a range of groups across Poland, mark the sixth anniversary of a 2020 ruling that tightened the country’s already-restrictive abortion rules. The ruling prompted the largest protests in Poland since the fall of communism as people poured into the streets wielding placards that read “The revolution has a uterus” and “My body, my choice”.
The protests were later credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk into power in 2023, with promises to overhaul abortion laws within 100 days. Last year Tusk backtracked on the pledge to legalise abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy, saying there was “simply no majority” to reform the laws.
Even if the two bills passed this week are signed into law, Poland would remain “completely out of step with the rest of its EU peers”, said Hoctor. Currently, abortion is only legal in Poland when a pregnancy results from a criminal act, such as rape or incest, or when it threatens the life or health of the mother.
The Center for Reproductive Rights instead called on Tusk to skirt around Poland’s polarised politics by putting in place an interim moratorium on the application of all criminal law provisions concerning abortion. “This would ensure that those caring for women no longer do so under the threat of criminal investigation and prosecution,” Hoctor said.
The idea was first floated by the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, which in 2024 concluded that women in Poland faced severe human rights violations due to restrictive abortion laws.
Hoctor said: “The reality is that thousands of women in Poland every year access abortion care. So they are doing that illegally, or they’re travelling for it. That’s not what a modern European country needs to be. They’re not living up to the promise of what it is to be a modern healthcare system and a modern democracy.”

title: Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams
description: European Commission calls accommodation website’s approach to fraudulent listings and phishing scams as ‘absolutely substandard’
content:
European Commission calls accommodation website’s approach to fraudulent listings and phishing scams as ‘absolutely substandard’
EU regulators have opened an investigation into Booking.com, alleging that the accommodation website has not done enough to protect consumers from fake listings and scams.
The European Commission , which regulates the world’s biggest tech companies operating in the EU, said Booking.com may have breached the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) with its “absolutely substandard” approach to tackling fraudulent listings and phishing scams, where criminals impersonate a third party to trick people to hand over money.
A commission official said Booking.com should be carrying out risk assessments and acting to prevent fraud as required under the DSA. “We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” said the official. “Although they take measures, they could go much further and they could have much more solid systems to prevent fraud.”
EU officials will also investigate whether Booking.com has breached advertising transparency rules, by potentially not making clear to users that some accommodation providers had paid to make their business more visible on the website.
Under the EU’s DSA, which aims to protect people from harmful and illegal internet content, a company could be fined 6% of its worldwide annual turnover.
The commission said that opening the investigation did not prejudge the outcome.
Booking.com, which is headquartered in Amsterdam and claims to have 28m accommodation listings, said it was engaging constructively with the commission. “Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com,” a company spokesperson said. “We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to ‌combat cybercrime and online fraud, and protect travellers and partners.”
The investigation comes after researchers at the UK consumer group Which? exposed security lapses at Booking.com when they used the site to set up – and accept payment for – a fake offer to stay at 10 Downing Street.
EU officials are investigating similar scams, with less high-profile addresses, where consumers thought they had booked a stay, only to find on arrival at a property that it had been fraudulently listed on Booking.com.
Officials are also assessing a second category of scams, dubbed “reservation hijacks” where scammers use hacked data to impersonate an accommodation provider. Criminals send WhatsApp messages and have even used Booking.com’s own platform to request payments from Booking.com’s customers, supposedly to secure a stay. Cases seen by Guardian Money in 2025 involved the theft of several hundred pounds.
EU officials will examine whether the company has sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused.
The Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said it had received 200 reports of scams costing people €65,000 that involved Booking.com in 2025, up from 89 reports worth €25,000 the previous year. These cases were “just the tip of the iceberg”, it said, as many victims would not report to its fraud helpdesk.
Booking.com told the BBC in 2024 it had seen a 500 to 900% increase in scams in the previous 18 months, driven by generative AI tools that enable fraudsters to create very realistic-looking fake emails and internet booking links.
Agustín Reyna, director general of the pan-European consumer group BEUC, said: “It is positive to see the European Commission investigating Booking.com for failing to meet EU digital rules. This is a systemic problem.”
Henna Virkkunen, the commission’s lead official on tech policy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.”

title: New prize launches for books co-written with AI
description: After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs
content:
After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs
A prize for AI-written books has launched this week.
The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA invites submissions of manuscripts co-written with AI tools, with the winner promised publication.
Entrants are asked to submit an unpublished manuscript of between 10,000 and 50,000 words, along with information about which AI model and prompt were used to generate the text. All major language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Entrants can be based anywhere, but entries must be submitted in French.
The Prix Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal, a French polymath who helped invent one of the first mechanical calculators and also wrote theological texts, including Pensées, which Pope Francis praised for its “philosophical depth and literary charm”.
While the terms and conditions ask for a work of fiction, the prize also states that submitted texts should help solve an ethical, social or ecological problem threatening humanity. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré, all of whom are technology entrepreneurs.
Rodriguez is a founding partner at the mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Avolta, and is described as a “leading figure in the European crypto and blockchain industry” on the company’s website. Serviant is a digital media entrepreneur and former chair of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu. Meanwhile, Mentré is a former civil servant with a PhD in philosophy who teaches at Harvard and the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Mentré also co-founded Electis, an online voting platform.
The Prix Pascal is launching after months of controversy over the possible use of AI by finalists and winners for a number of literary prizes this year, including the Commonwealth short story prize , the Caine prize and the Prix Goncourt , France’s most prestigious literary prize.
Applications for the Prix Pascal opened on Tuesday, with entrants invited to submit via the prize’s website , and are set to close at the end of November. A shortlist of 10 will be drawn up before the winner is announced in early December. The jury will be made up of a panel of five or six writers, critics, journalists, philosophers and publishers, to be announced early November.

title: Can UK pop cut immigration and stop the boats? I suppose we’ll find out with GB News Music Radio
description: An ‘all British, all day’ station is a nativist dream come true – but good luck with the playlist. And anyway: how many artists will want to be on Farage FM? asks Guardian columnist John Harris
content:
An ‘all British, all day’ station is a nativist dream come true – but good luck with the playlist. And anyway: how many artists will want to be on Farage FM?
I f you want a quintessential “It wouldn’t happen now” story, try this. Two months before Margaret Thatcher became prime minister in May 1979, a national Militant Entertainment Tour was organised by Rock Against Racism .
On 20 March 1979, it came to the West Runton Pavilion near Cromer, the (very) small town on the coastal edge of East Anglia. The bill mixed the black and white musicians in three bands then at their artistic peak – the post-punk maestros Gang of Four, the punk-reggae hybridists The Ruts, and Misty in Roots, the renowned reggae collective from Southall in west London – and thereby made a stark symbolic point: that the multiracial nature of large swathes of the UK was not to be decried or attacked, but actively celebrated.
The UK was then – and some of this may sound familiar – in a bitter, polarised state, seemingly locked into deep economic problems, amid rising fear about the neo-fascist National Front. The previous year, Thatcher had said – and this may feel familiar, too – that British people “were really rather afraid that this country might be rather swamped by people with a different culture.” Amid such a grim political atmosphere, RAR and the musicians who supported it felt duty-bound to try pulling their audiences away from such toxicity, and point out that what we now call diversity was something to be celebrated.
Nearly half a century on, the lack of any comparable cultural response to this country’s equally unsettling current state seems quite remarkable. There is, then, a vacant cultural-political space – and look what has now come along to fill it. GB News, that bracingly rightwing TV channel whose regular faces include Nigel Farage, the Reform MP Lee Anderson and the party’s failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin, is about to launch a music radio station .
According to its promotional blurb, it will be “dedicated exclusively to artists from Great Britain and Northern Ireland”, with tagline “all British, all day”. By way of further explanation, one of its presenters, the black GB News host Nana Akua, says that “It’s easy to forget how this country has shaped the global music landscape” – a strange point instantly disproved by a mention of any number of artists (such as those four fairly successful fellas from Liverpool). But here, perhaps, is the strangest thing of all: according to GB Media, every track on the station’s playlist will be an “artist from Great Britain or Northern Ireland, or where the main proportion of the band is British.”
This sparks no end of questions. Does anyone in the ordinary world actually perceive music like this? Will someone frantically be employed to sift through Wikipedia, finding out whether this or that band fits the “main proportion” criterion? What will happen in the case of, say, the Gallagher brothers, who self-identify as Irish – and should, therefore, be excluded for the same reasons as U2, CMAT and Fontaines DC? Should the Jimi Hendrix Experience be ruled in or out, given that the two supporting members of the trio were respectively from Ealing and Folkestone? And to get into the real nitty-gritty, how exactly are the programmers defining “British”?
We all know the jaw-dropping conversations taking place in GB News-adjacent circles about national identity. The Tory-to-Reform defectors Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman see Englishness as an ethnic identity . If this definition wins out, which is quite conceivable, what will happen then? A playlist cull that will leave little apart from the musical equivalent of sliced white bread?
There are more fascinating questions to ask. There has been an on-off debate about whether Britpop was partly responsible for Brexit. As the writer of a book about that cultural wave , I have always clung on to the idea that because its nationalistic(ish) animus was focused on the US, and the demographics of Leave voters do not map on to the Britpop generation, no one had any case to answer. But this latest development brings on a slight pang of unease. In retrospect, the large-scale whiteness of Britpop was, as we say these days, rather problematic. On a musical level, it accounts for its chronically limited range of influences and inputs, which led to it burning out pretty quickly. But it also left it open to what might turn out to be a belated act of appropriation: whatever music the new station plays, I would imagine that Oasis, Blur, Pulp et al will be an integral part of its output. Put another way, the Farage-ist tanks are now surely heading for Britpop’s metaphorical lawn.
Inquiries to a couple of music lawyers established that musicians cannot stop radio stations that possess the relevant licences and pay the required royalties from playing their material. Self-evidently, however, they could quite easily express their displeasure at the prospect of being part of a constant Farage-ist soundtrack. In the excellent new Oasis documentary, Don’t Look Back in Anger, Noel Gallagher rightly says that his band was never “a rightwing thing … All are welcome. It’s we and us.” In the context of GB Music Radio, he should translate that into something slightly more specific. So should the already embattled Ed Sheeran, Adele, what remains of the Rolling Stones, the former members of Dire Straits and everyone else who is – and isn’t – mentioned in the station’s launch statement. The music all of them make, after all, is founded on precisely the kind of cultural mixing that so many voices associated with GB News take against.
Oh, and one last thing. This message needs to be out there in the fabric of people’s lives, not only pouring out of their phones, but arriving in their towns. The West Runton Pavilion was demolished in 1986. But imagine some modern equivalent of Militant Entertainment pitching up on the Essex coast, the old Nottinghamshire coalfield, the seaside towns of Kent, or any number of Reform’s supposed heartlands. Is that really now as inconceivable as it seems?

title: The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped
description: These graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of Representatives
author_name: Chris Stein, Alex Clark, Andrew Witherspoon, Ashley Kirk
content:
These graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of Representatives
A turning point in Donald Trump’s second term will soon arrive. On 3 November, voters across the US will decide whether to keep the president’s Republican allies in control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority.
Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of the House of Representatives , and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration.
These charts and maps reveal where the battle for Congress will be fought.
Polling shows there has been a nationwide shift towards the Democrats in the run-up to the midterms, even in states Republicans have dominated for decades.
Many recent surveys of the generic ballot, a key indicator of voters’ intent in congressional elections, give the Democrats an edge ranging from the high single digits to the low double digits.
The events of this year – notably the Iran war and its impact on inflation – have undoubtedly changed the race, and much of the advantage seems to have swung towards the Democrats.
Across all key races, Democratic candidates have been campaigning on affordability, at a time when the Trump administration’s actions in the Middle East have pushed up prices, particularly for gasoline and diesel.
It is a reflection of just how concerned US voters are about the economy, rating it as the most important issue in surveys, far ahead of immigration, healthcare or civil rights.
Meanwhile, Trump’s personal ratings have also fallen, with Reuters/Ipsos finding only 32% of US adults now approve of his job performance.
That is worse than his previous low of 34%, recorded by Gallup at the end of his first term in 2021 after the January 6 attack on the US Capitol.
The 2026 midterms may be another brutal reckoning for the US president – the question is whether punishment from voters will lead him to change course.

title: Burnham backs mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after parent-carer Matilda Davis’s death
description: Former art teacher, who cared for her disabled son, ‘received almost no support’, said her local MP Manuela Perteghella
content:
Former art teacher, who cared for her disabled son, ‘received almost no support’, said her local MP Manuela Perteghella
Andy Burnham has backed mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after the “devastating” death of Matilda Davis, a parent-carer who killed herself minutes after meeting professionals.
The Guardian revealed in August how the “absolutely inspirational” 36-year-old had taken her life after feeling “completely exhausted” and failed by England’s social care system.
Davis, a former art teacher, had told multiple professionals she was struggling to cope with the significant care for her seven-year-old son and “paralysed with anxiety” about her looming divorce from her estranged husband.
She died on 3 October last year, minutes after an emotional meeting with social workers who had not received suicide prevention training.
Burnham was asked about Davis’s case at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday and said he supported the extension of this training to all local authorities in England.
Manuela Perteghella, the Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-upon-Avon, where Davis lived, said: “My constituent Matilda Davis was a wonderful and devoted mum and a full-time carer for her disabled seven-year-old child. Despite providing round the clock care, she received almost no support leaving her physically and emotionally exhausted.
“Last October, social workers visited Matilda and she took her own life 15 minutes after they left. She was 36.”
Perteghella highlighted University of Birmingham research showing that 41% of parent-carers have contemplated suicide, and asked Burnham to meet her and Matilda’s family to discuss “mandatory suicide prevention training for local authorities and other measures so that no more normal families suffer such a devastating loss”.
Burnham replied: “I will ensure that a minister meets the honourable lady to discuss that proposal because I find myself in agreement with it.”
The prime minister praised the Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, for his work campaigning on behalf of unpaid carers, whose failure by the state has been brought into light by an award-winning Guardian investigation into the carer’s allowance scandal .
Burnham said these carers, who often gave up work and other commitments while saving the government billions of pounds to look after severely disabled loved ones, could often “sink under their responsibilities and find it very, very difficult”.
He added: “Sadly in the case of Matilda, [Perteghella’s] constituent, obviously a devastating situation. I will arrange that meeting and I thank [Perteghella] for raising it in the House [of Commons] today.”
At Davis’s inquest in March, social workers admitted they did not ask her whether she had thoughts of suicide despite knowing she was in significant distress, nor was she directed to crisis organisations.
As a result, the coroner, Deborah Sewell, issued a rare prevention of future deaths notice ordering Warwickshire council to make suicide prevention training mandatory for 600 members of staff, primarily social workers.
Davis’s brother, Joel Harley-Davis, said the family was “really reassured” by Burnham’s response and that his sister would have been “proud” to make a positive difference.
“We all believe that this training would have been enough to save Matilda’s life,” he said. “If those social workers had asked her [whether she was considering ending her life] Matilda was so honest she would have said yes.
“This needs to be made mandatory – you can’t leave it up to councils to decide whether to put it in place because it creates a postcode lottery. It doesn’t need to be this really expensive thing. All the literature and advice says that if in doubt about whether someone is suicidal, ask that direct difficult question.”
Guidance issued by the mental health charity Mind states that it is best practice not to “skirt around the topic of suicide” and instead ask direct questions such as: “Are you having suicidal thoughts?” when speaking to someone who might want to kill themselves.
Harley-Davis, 30, said his sister felt “failed and let down” by England’s social care system and was passionate about advocating on behalf of other parent-carers. He added: “Matilda was an incredibly stoic individual but that’s not to say she didn’t need someone to offer that respite.
“Matilda needed that professional support and a degree of empathy and I don’t think she got that, especially on the day she died.”
In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org , or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counsellor. title: Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda
description: Nationalist leaders are framing unrest as consequence of failed liberal governance and open borders
author_name: Jon Henley, Deborah Cole, Sam Jones, Angela Giuffrida
content:
Nationalist leaders are framing unrest as consequence of failed liberal governance and open borders
Europe’s far-right leaders have jumped on the violence that rocked numerous cities last weekend, framing it as the inevitable consequence of failed liberal governance and open-border policies and insisting only they can restore law and order.
Months away from key elections in Spain, France and Italy, authoritarian nationalists are eager to weaponise the wave of street unrest, originating in peaceful protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services but hijacked by violent rioters.
Those in opposition have not held back. In France, where cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon faced widespread rioting and looting, the far-right National Rally (RN) has denounced centrist incompetence and promised a crackdown.
The party’s president, Jordan Bardella, said the government was “impotent”. The RN leader, Marine Le Pen , said on Wednesday the state was “collapsing” and had “lost control of everything” amid “migratory, budgetary and security chaos”.
Ahead in presidential polls and seeking voters beyond her base, Le Pen has resisted explicitly racialising the unrest, but has framed it more broadly as a result of state and policy failures leading to “anarchic immigration” and “a total loss of authority”.
In Germany – where there were no major protests – the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has stoked fears rioting could spill over the border. Its co-leader Alice Weidel said France’s “violent excesses” were a “warning for Germany”.
Weidel also linked the unrest to immigration, posting: “The dangerous mix of mass migration and leftwing extremism threatens to lead to civil war-like conditions here too … There will only be a turnaround on migration with the AfD!”
In Portugal, populists have used peaceful protests to blame immigration for the country’s housing crisis, which André Ventura of the far-right Chega party said was chiefly a consequence of an “uncontrolled influx of people from abroad”.
In Spain, where the housing crisis has led to huge protests and a Madrid encampment, and prompted the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap election next month, the far-right Vox party has sought to demonise the protesters. “They’re not defending the right to housing, or asking for work, they’re serving Pedro Sánchez,” the party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said. “They’re Sánchez’s militias.”
Vox has also attempted to link the housing issue to migration. In a message posted on social media last month, the party falsely suggested that the 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked the mammoth protests would have had a home had she been an immigrant from north Africa.
In Belgium , where cost of living protests also escalated into street clashes in Brussels and Liège, the far-right Flemish nationalists of Vlaams Belang framed the rioting as a failure of integration and open borders, characterising it as “imported violence”.
Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni , has adopted another strategy – as head of a far-right government she has headed for four years, she cannot simply blame failures of the state. Instead, she has expanded her law-and-order agenda, and framed rioters as extremists.
“Demonstrating is a right, but setting our cities ablaze is not,” Meloni said after rioting in Milan and Bologna. “Hooligans have exploited the protests to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security, and hold entire cities hostage.”
Meloni has previously enacted sweeping security measures aimed at hindering public dissent, including jail terms for blocking roads, tough sentences for resisting police officers, and pre-detention for demonstrators thought likely to cause trouble.
This week she passed emergency decrees creating an offence of violent participation in ⁠a demonstration, imposing tougher penalties on ⁠rioters and organisers of violent groups, and penalising parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
But she too has highlighted immigration as a factor, noting that “nearly half of those stopped or arrested” after the Milan riots were “of immigrant background, including individuals born abroad and second-generation children of immigrant families”.
Beyond Europe’s orthodox far-right parties, anti-immigration polemicists have gone further, interpreting the violence not as state and policy failures but as evidence of a looming civilisational war fuelled by multiculturalism and non-EU immigration.
Éric Zemmour, the founder of France’s Reconquête! (Reconquest) party, demanded an immigration halt and the deportation of “foreign delinquents”, declaring: “These are not riots, but the warning shots in an ethnic war. Either we establish absolute order or we yield.”
The far-right narrative has been reinforced by similar comments from the US, where both the president and vice-president have sought to turn the unrest in France in particular into a cautionary tale for voters before midterm elections.
Donald Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”, adding on social media that immigration “has shattered that once great country”.
JD Vance echoed the same view, saying: “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion.” In doing so, they “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”, he said.
Deborah Cole in Berlin, Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Sam Jones in Madrid contributed reporting

title: ​Europe stands by Ukraine – but how long can that last?
description: As US support ebbs away, looming European elections and growing financial strains across the continent could fracture the precious coalition that has kept Ukraine afloat
content:
As US support ebbs away, looming European elections and growing financial strains across the continent could fracture the precious coalition that has kept Ukraine afloat
E urope woke up last Friday to another belligerent outburst from Donald Trump – this time berating Ukraine’s wartime leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy again. Just a few days after his diesel deal with the Kremlin, the US president said Zelenskyy was more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin and blamed Ukraine’s leader for rocketing oil prices – without any reference to the impact of his own war on Iran.
The contrast in Europe was obvious. When Zelenskyy walked into the multi-coloured summit room of the European Council headquarters in Brussels that Friday morning, the EU’s 27 leaders burst into applause, getting to their feet to offer big hugs and brisk handshakes. European Council president António Costa told Zelenskyy and the media: “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine ,” calling instead for increased pressure on Russia. Zelenskyy was thankful, pointedly saying he was happy to have “huge support” from “real leaders”.
The symbolism was powerful. As US support crumbles, Europe seems to be stepping up. According to the Kiel Institut’s Ukraine Support Tracker , Europe – including non-EU countries such as the UK and Norway – has spent €236bn supporting Ukraine from 2022 to April 2026, compared with a US outlay of €115bn.
While Trump is weakening sanctions, Europe is promising more. The EU has passed 21 rounds of sanctions against Russia and last year agreed to raise a €90bn loan for Ukraine – an unprecedented sum for a non-member state. Meanwhile the EU has opened accession negotiations with Kyiv and given shelter to 4.4million Ukrainian refugees.
Behind the declarations of Europe’s enduring support, the outlook is more complex and less encouraging for Ukraine, as it approaches its fifth winter since the launch of Russia’s all-out invasion.
First, Europe is not able to replace US military dominance in areas such as intelligence. This was brutally exposed by the disruption to the US SpaceX technologies that Ukraine uses in frontline drone operations and air-defences protecting civilians from Russian air attacks. Zelenskyy said the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access, a charge that senior figures in the Trump administration have denied.
Ukraine also depends on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles. Deepening the spat, Zelenskyy this week accused the Trump administration of preventing European countries from passing on their Patriot stocks to Ukraine.
Secondly, Europe’s monetary support for Ukraine is not evenly spread. Germany is the second-largest donor, having spent €54bn since the start of the war, a particularly crucial contribution since Trump ceased virtually all new US funding. But a report from the Kiel Institut describes this funding as “sizeable but not exceptional” given the scale of the German economy. Four Nordic countries together have given more than Germany, even though they total only a third of Germany’s population, the researchers note. The EU’s other big economies, France and Italy, give less than Germany.
The Nordic, Baltic and other north European states are Ukraine’s most generous donors when contributions are measured against national income, according to the Kiel Institut. Denmark, for instance, spends an equivalent to 4.17% of its gross domestic product supporting Ukraine, and Estonia 3.77%, compared with 1.49% spent by Germany, 1.1% by France, 1% by Italy and 0.86% by the UK. With Ukraine’s huge bill to defend itself growing, and Russia’s relentless attacks continuing to wreak a heavy toll, these more generous donors might arguably feel Europe’s biggest economies – and other western allies – could do more to shoulder these ever-rising costs.
Top donors to Ukraine by percentage of GDP
Thirdly, and most critically, Europe’s support for Ukraine could be reaching its limits, as Europe enters a supercycle of elections in which the far-right are expected to make gains. National votes are due in Spain, France, Poland and Italy, four of the five biggest EU member states by population. Mujtaba Rahman , managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group, argued that the biggest risk for Ukraine is not Trump’s opinions, but the potential for European support to fragment. There is a risk 2027 will be the year “when political reality, electoral reality, policy reality, economic reality catches up with Europe and prevents it being able to go further in its support for Ukraine”, he said.
France’s elections could be the most consequential. The far-right leader and frontrunner Marine Le Pen is seeking to present herself as the candidate to restore order and security, after days of rioting and looting across French cities. She has also vowed to cease aid to Ukraine within six months of taking office “because we simply cannot do it any more”. Speaking to the Financial Times (£) , Le Pen vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget, which raises questions about a proposed €100bn fund for Ukraine in the upcoming 2028-34 budget cycle. Beyond Ukraine, her election could plunge the EU into a deep internal crisis that will consume political energies and attention.
“European support for Ukraine is already fragmenting,” argued Rahman, who points out the €90bn loan for Ukraine was agreed by only 24 EU countries (Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out). But a Le Pen victory could tilt the balance, especially if anti-Ukraine parties make gains in Spain, Poland and Italy. “Le Pen is the biggest gamechanger because she will provide cover for many other countries to say: ‘enough is enough, we can’t keep funding,’” Rahman said.
That scenario paints “a really dark picture for Ukraine, a really sad picture for Ukraine” he said. “Because it’s not about Ukraine’s performance on the battlefield – Ukraine has done a remarkable job of holding the line. This is the risk Europe has been talking about for a very long time, and has promised Ukraine many times it would not allow to happen: that through strategic patience, Russia gains in the negotiating room what it has not been able to gain on the battlefield. And that is precisely the risk Ukraine is now confronting.” To head off this risk, EU leaders will seek to shore up support for Ukraine by agreeing another funding plan. The head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, confirmed that Kyiv has a €70bn funding gap in 2027, although she expects Ukraine’s other international partners to help raise the sum.
Jana Kobzová, co-director of the European Security Programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said an EU leaders summit in December will be the moment when “we should have a clear idea and mechanism” on providing the €70bn for Ukraine ahead of key elections. “I think the urgency and the consciousness on the side of the European leaders is already there.”
To some extent, EU Russia policy is protected, after a recent decision to keep sanctions in place for three years, avoiding the need for divisive rollover decisions every six months.
But a Le Pen victory in six months’ time could lead to a bigger problem than financing Ukraine, suggests Kobzová. “If there is a huge shift in Europe as a result of these elections that are going to affect the way the EU itself works, then Ukraine might become collateral damage.”

title: Champions League goals and drama galore – so why do we feel hollow?
description: In today’s Football Daily: 40 goals in nine games but where’s the jeopardy?
content:
Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!
Now then, which one of you hipsters decided to put Porto 0-1 PSV on? Oh dear. This was another night of Bigger Cup at its Bigliest self, comebacks everywhere, 40 goals in nine games, six of those in a best-v-best clash as Paris Saint-Germain rallied late against Barcelona. Even in defeat, Lamine Yamal found space to decorate the room with a ludicrous toe-poke equaliser, and there was a wholesome tale in Italy as Scott McTominay scored twice for Napoli in their 4-3 win against Bodø/Glimt. These were his first strikes since returning from heart surgery, taking his tally at the club to 29 goals in 86 appearances. No wonder Erik ten Hag was peeved with his bosses at Manchester United for shipping the midfielder off to Naples.
But even after all that, Football Daily feels hollow, as it does for most of Bigger Cup’s group stage. The absence of jeopardy in the 36-team table remains a sore point, as PSG magnificently demonstrated during their back-to-back title-winning campaigns. In 2024-25 they finished 15th, taking seven points from their first six games; in the old days this meant a third-place finish in your group and a humiliating retreat to Big Vase. In 2025-26 Luis Enrique’s side settled for 11th and, once again, embraced their punishment of an extra knockout round. To be fair, this season they look as if they want to put their feet up in February, sitting pretty at the top with three wins from three.
Liverpool, too, would have been OK without a special night at home, having won their first two games, but try telling that to the Kop. They got the thrills of coming back from two goals down to beat Villarreal, under-the-pump Florian Wirtz hit the decisive goal, and Rio Ngumoha received plenty of love . The visitors got the full Anfield experience, with Villarreal’s manager, Iñigo Pérez, confessing: “We weren’t able to handle the emotion.”
Having said all that, try telling Michael Carrick that the match in Como doesn’t really matter, that it’s perfectly fine if his United side make it two wins in 11 games this season. Cesc Fàbregas’s side are the opposition, which should make you feel really, really old. The boy who infamously flung some pizza in an Old Trafford melee, splattering Sir Alex Ferguson, is enjoying himself on the touchline. All grown up, he could make life seriously messy for another Manchester United manager.
Join Simon Burnton from 5.45pm BST for Como 6-4 Manchester United in Bigger Cup, while Scott Murray will be all over Bayern Munich 5-3 Arsenal and Sarah Rendell will be on hand for a clockwatch covering the night’s other goalfests.
