title: Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years review – old pals back on the toon as TV series gets squished
description: They have appeared in epic BBC dramas since their RSC debut but Peter Flannery’s immortal foursome now return in an 80s-focused play
content:
Theatre Royal, Newcastle They have appeared in epic BBC dramas since their RSC debut but Peter Flannery’s immortal foursome now return in an 80s-focused play
T he four thwarted, postwar north-eastern dreamers created by dramatist Peter Flannery have now played more than a whole day of drama across different formats. The 1982 RSC world premiere of Our Friends in the North featured almost four hours in the lives of lawyer-councillor Mary, drifting philanderer Tosker, photo-journalist Nicky and petty criminal Geordie. The award-winning 1996 BBC Two version ran 10 hours, as did the 2022 Radio 4 adaptation. Now Flannery brings the quartet home to the stage and to Newcastle (where the first version toured) in another play.
Starting in 1964, with Labour PM Harold Wilson promising a new Britain, the first stage version ended in 1979, as Margaret Thatcher’s victory heralded a rightwing transformation. Exploiting the way that saga dramas test characters against landmark events, the TV version took them to 1995 (brink of Blair) and the radio one to 2020 (Boris Johnson and Covid). It would be intriguing to know if the idealism of these now triple-locked pensioner characters burns again under Burnham, but Flannery has tracked back to 1979-85, adapting the sixth (Thatcher in) and seventh (miners out) TV episodes.
A piece begun when he was an RSC writer in residence always had Shakespearean ambitions and these continue with the tremendous Trevor Fox, like the Chorus in Henry V, galvanising our imaginations and dropping historical footnotes. Fox, who starred in the TV and radio series, doubles as Nicky’s dementia-affected dad, Felix, a subplot especially poignant in what will be a memory play for much of the audience.
All forms of the story have used soap opera domestic tension to offset socialist history and here the epic courtship of Sam Neale’s Mary and Ryan Nolan’s Nicky affectingly shows campaigners for social change yearning for romantic conformity. The largely wasted lives – the piece’s bleak sub-theme – of Tosker and Geordie are caught by Jack Robertson, pointlessly optimistic, and Scott Turnbull , accepting defeat. Jude Nelson makes a small part large as a Tory MP who achieves a prophetic early breach in Labour’s “red wall”. The politics are Kinnockian, accusing Labour’s Militant tendency and miners’ union leader Arthur Scargill of swelling a rightwing electorate that led to 18 years of Tory rule.
The different Our Friends in the North directors have tended to panic at its politically expository dialogue and in this case it sometimes feels as if director Jack McNamara is searching for action such as slow-motion strobing for clashes between colliery pickets and riot squads.
For completists, this is a must-see but, paradoxically, it feels incomplete. In all media, the story has had length and breadth and, though these two episodes were a logical choice, Flannery perhaps acknowledges losses from selection and compression when Fox’s Chorus laments: “There’s always so much more to say.” The events depicted partly explain why a regional theatre would struggle to put on an all-day epic, but this dramatically immortal foursome needs it.

title: Trump’s approval rating drops to 36% two weeks before midterms, poll finds
description: Voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of economy and cost of living, says poll in new low recorded by NY Times/Siena
content:
Voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of economy and cost of living, says poll in new low recorded by NY Times/Siena
Donald Trump ’s approval rating sank to 36% just two weeks before the midterm elections , the lowest recorded in a poll by the New York Times/Siena College , with most respondents expressing frustration over his handling of the US economy, cost of living and Iran war.
In an October survey of approximately 3,494 likely voters, 59% said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of his job, and 52% said they planned to vote for the Democratic candidate in the upcoming election.
Much of the disapproval toward the US president was associated with frustrations over Trump’s handling of economic and cost-of-living-related issues. On gas prices, 73% of registered voters said they disapproved; on the cost of living, 69% said they disapproved, and on the economy , 64% said they disapproved.
Approximately 65% said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war , which has dragged on for nearly eight months and pushed gas and oil prices up.
The new polling numbers paint a gloomy picture for Trump and Republicans , who have embarked on an uphill battle to defeat Democrats in the upcoming midterms to maintain their majority control in Congress.
Trump, whose name recognition has largely helped Republican candidates in past elections, has been on the road campaigning for Maga-aligned candidates. However, some candidates have sought to distance themselves from the president, who has become increasingly unpopular over his economic policies.
In 2024, Trump promised to lower everyday costs for Americans, keep inflation low and to keep the US from starting more wars abroad .
But as of 21 October, gas prices were more than $4.25 a gallon , inflation increased to 3.7% last month and the president’s war with Iran remained steady.
Between September and October, the US president’s approval rating decreased by two percentage points in the New York Times/Siena College polls.
Democratic candidates , meanwhile, have seized on the cost-of-living issues to appeal to independents and undecided voters, promising to rein in the president’s policies that have pushed costs up, such as tariffs.
While polling from the New York Times/Siena College indicates Democrats have the upper hand headed into next month’s election, the party is still fighting against a massive financial war chest in competitive races in Texas , Ohio , New York , Alaska and Iowa .
The Guardian has asked the White House for comment.

title: The six best slip-on shoes in the US – tested for comfort and style
description: After a back injury, bending to put on shoes was unimaginable. I’ve since been testing pairs easy to glide my feet into – and on the eyes
content:
After a back injury, bending to put on shoes was unimaginable. I’ve since been testing pairs easy to glide my feet into – and on the eyes
What do you want to know about kitchen and food safety?
Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things
I popped a disc in my spine a few months back, and one of the things that saved me a lot of pain during my recovery was slip-on shoes . With these, I could wear shoes that looked normal without the pain of bending over to put them on and do up the laces. I have been testing new pairs since then, looking at the various ways that manufacturers such as Kizik, Skechers and others create a shoe that you can slip on as easily as a pair of slippers, but which still look like normal shoes you could wear to work, socializing or anywhere.
I tested seven different pairs of shoes, rating them for ease of use, style, comfort and the intangibles that make you feel comfortable and more confident, no matter how much your back might be aching.
I have tested consumer products ranging from automatic coffee makers to Xbox peripherals for publications including PC World, Reviewed.com, CNET and many others. For all of those publications, I bring an objective scientific eye to testing products and helping consumers make better buying decisions. For the Filter US, I’ve tested the best gadgets if you live with back pain , the Kiziks hands-free shoes and an eco-friendly mattress .
A good pair of slip-on shoes should be comfortable, cool looking and ridiculously easy to put on. So, I wore each pair for dog walks and ambles around town, logging how comfortable they felt on the move and around the house. I asked friends, family and strangers on the street to tell me what they thought of the look of the shoes, talking to sneakerheads, comfort fans and all those in between. To test the slip-on feature, I looked at how easy it was to step into the shoes and put them on, when paying attention and without looking down: imagine leaving a shoe-free friend’s house encumbered with leftovers and stepping into them by the door. A good pair of slip-ons should guide your feet into place, with a clean action to the heel mechanism that makes them work. A bad pair will need you to move your feet in a certain way, or, God forbid, reach down and move the shoes to get them on.
After this review was completed, I donated all of the slip-on shoes to Goodwill.
For more, check out our guide to tech neck fixes , the best seat cushions and products that offer help with back pain .
Magic. Well, sort of: these shoes rely on a combination of clever design and flexible materials, all covered with a tasty sauce of patent law. The specifics vary, but the gist is that a precisely formed piece of plastic in the heel provides a specific mixture of flexibility and rigidity. This makes the heel part flexible enough to bend under your foot when you put your heel into the shoe, but rigid enough to snap back into its initial shape when you move your foot forward, pushing the heel part back without you having to pull on it
The real fun starts when the lawyers get involved. Kizik, for instance, has several hundred patents on what it describes as “rapid entry footwear” , while rival Skechers has their own portfolio of patents covering what they describe as their “hands-free slip-in” shoes . Kizik is now suing Skechers in the US and Europe , claiming that Skechers has used their patent designs without a license. Skechers have denied this . This case is continuing, but it hasn’t yet reached a point where either company has stopped making shoes. The winners? The lawyers, as the case is likely to drag on for some time.
Yes. Although older slip-on shoes and slippers have a reputation for loose fits and slipping off when you move your foot, none of these modern shoes have this problem. No matter how vigorously I shook a leg, danced or gyrated, they all stayed on. (Oh, the things I do for the sake of journalism.)

title: A grieving female elephant carrying a stillborn baby: Federico Veronesi’s best photograph
description: ‘She carried the dead calf for hours even though it wasn’t hers. She had had a miscarriage two years before – and now picked up the stillborn babies of other mothers’
content:
‘She carried the dead calf for hours even though it wasn’t hers. She had had a miscarriage two years before – and now picked up the stillborn babies of other mothers’
M y love of African animals, in particular elephants, dates back to when I was three or four years old, growing up in Milan in a house full of old nature books. When I was six, my parents took me on my first safari in Kenya – I cried on the plane home, feeling I was being torn away from the savanna I’d dreamed of, somewhere I really loved. But for the past 20 years, that’s where I’ve lived, guiding photographers on the Maasai Mara National Reserve and elsewhere in Africa.
I’ve spent time photographing other animals, especially big cats, but elephants are still my favourite subject. They have this extraordinary presence, dominating the landscape and making it come alive. I love to follow them in different habitats. They are extremely adaptable – in Kenya they’re associated with the savanna and acacia woodland, and they can also live in extremely arid areas, such as the deserts of Namibia, where this photograph was taken.
I was there last September, guiding a group of photographers. We had been following a group of elephants walking along a dry riverbed as night fell. Even though there is no water in these rivers, they retain some vegetation and act as a lifeline for the elephants, who follow them from the hills in the west towards the Atlantic Ocean.
Because it’s a sandy river, it was quite easy to follow their tracks until we found them again the next day. But among the tracks was something quite unusual, like a dragging mark. Sometimes bull elephants, when they’re full of testosterone, will do crazy things to demonstrate their power and intimidate their opponents – I’d seen one lift a log before, and thought perhaps that’s what was being dragged.
We drove on until we found them, and that’s when I realised one of the females was carrying a baby. When people see this picture, they sometimes think it’s of a young elephant hugging its mother, but in fact the calf is dead and the leg you can’t see is wedged between the adult’s tusk and trunk. As I took this photograph, another elephant was approaching and the female swung her head so the baby was lifted up and out of its way. I have other photographs that make the reading of the scene more straightforward, but this one leaves the interpretation open and adds a layer of mystery.
We followed the herd for several hours, and the female carried the calf for the entire time, only putting it down so she could feed before picking it up and continuing on her way. She was still carrying it when we last saw her – eventually the elephants started climbing into some rocky hills where we couldn’t follow.
I’ve since read that 17 out of the 19 calves born in that area during the past four years have not made it. There’s clearly a problem, but researchers aren’t yet clear why this is happening. What has come to light, however, is that the elephant carrying the calf was not its mother, as I had assumed. Her mammary glands were not swollen as they would have been if she’d recently given birth, and the researchers were able to identify her as a female who had a miscarriage a couple of years before, and had since been seen picking up the stillborn calves of other mothers. In a sense, that makes the image even more deep and profound, as it implies that she perhaps hasn’t moved past that trauma.
Most of my elephant photographs are in black and white. Sometimes I use colour – in Tsavo, Kenya, elephants are often covered in red earth, which makes for a striking contrast against green vegetation, and in Etosha, Namibia, there’s a place where they visit a waterhole full of white clay and end up looking like ghosts. But black and white highlights the texture of elephants’ skin, and also, as here, removes distracting elements and exposes emotion in a more straightforward way.
This is a painful image to look at, but at the same time it reveals so much of the psychology of elephants, their interior complexity, personality and feelings. Here we see a creature that feels just as much as we do, that experiences the same grief at losing a baby, the same sense of not wanting to let it go. My hope is that photographs like this help people realise how important it is to coexist peacefully and respectfully with animals that look different to us on the outside, but inside are very similar.
This image is the adult grand title winner of Wildlife Photographer of the Year. The exhibition is at the Natural History Museum, London, until 11 July 2027.
Born: Milan, Italy, 1975. Moved to Kenya in 2002 High point: Probably this award, and the three books I published Top tip: Explore ways to convey emotions to the viewer through your photographs, carefully choosing light, atmosphere, shooting angle, framing, backgrounds, and so on

title: Israeli military detain US and UK volunteers in West Bank including Democratic NY politician Brad Lander
description: About 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers held near Nahalin in West Bank and taken to police station
content:
About 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers held near Nahalin in West Bank and taken to police station
The Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander, several rabbis and Israel’s former deputy attorney general.
“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis and volunteers,” Lander posted from a bus taking him to a police station. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nahalin in the West Bank. The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”
Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government, describes himself as a liberal Zionist. He believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot be a true democracy while it denies Palestinians their human rights and freedom.
An ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, Lander’s critical approach to Israel was a key factor in his resounding primary victory against Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel.
He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide.
Settler militants have unleashed extreme violence on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives from their trees across the occupied West Bank, and anyone accompanying them.
A vicious assault on a US photojournalist and attacks on European diplomats and a French mayor over the weekend drew international condemnation and calls for the Israeli government to crack down on militants.
Wednesday’s olive-picking from trees outside the village of Nahalin was uneventful until a large contingent of Israeli security forces arrived, the organisers Protect the Harvest said in a statement.
“All volunteers were peacefully harvesting on the private land of a Palestinian family who had invited them. For reasons that remain unclear, the Israeli army showed up and detained approximately 80 people who were present.”
Soldiers said the area had been declared a closed military zone, separated the group by nationality and drove them to a nearby police station in minibuses for the Israelis and a larger bus for Americans.
Joshua Schoffman, who served as Israel’s deputy attorney general for more than a decade, described the mass detention as a “complete hallucination” in a post on social media .
“Just now, they told me that I’m being detained for the crime of olive harvesting,” he wrote. “We were asked to stop, and everyone complied. There was no friction whatsoever with settlers or with the security forces.”
Lander was released with a warning but all the others were still being held, Protect the Harvest said. Detainees include Jill Jacobs, the chief executive of T’ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, and 11 other American rabbis affiliated with the group.
The detainees have been given water but no food. The Israeli military and police did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
On Monday, Lander made a first post about his journey to Palestine. “Our goals for the trip are to help protect the olive harvest – and to shed a light on the reality of the occupation,” he wrote. “Thankfully, our corner of today’s harvest was peaceful and successful. But violence unfortunately is never far away.”

title: Sir Donald Insall obituary
description: Conservation architect whose projects included restoring and renewing Windsor Castle after the devastating fire of 1992
content:
Conservation architect whose projects included restoring and renewing Windsor Castle after the devastating fire of 1992
Donald Insall, doyen of conservation architects, who has died aged 100, was very clear about the distinction between preserving buildings and conserving them. “Preservation,” he pronounced, “is what you do for marmalade.” Though Insall could see the value of preservation, he was an adroit conservationist rather than a stodgy marmalade maker, always seeing how historic buildings could be revived and put to new uses.
Marshalling teams of architects, craftsmen and builders, he brought Windsor Castle back from the brink following the devastating “ annus horribilis ” fire of 1992. The exacting rescue scheme encompassed a range of strategies, from complete restoration to renewal in spirit. “As well as keeping things as they were, or putting them back as one thinks they were – which is chancy and not the main aim – we had to find new solutions to parts that had been irreparably destroyed,” Insall told Country Life in 2018.
Other high-profile projects included the renovation of Kelmscott Manor, the Oxfordshire country home of the writer, designer and socialist William Morris, following its acquisition by the Society of Antiquaries in 1961, and the restoration of Kedleston Hall in Derbyshire, Robert Adam’s Palladian masterpiece, now in the care of the National Trust. “Kedleston was our first big job,” Insall recalled. “I used to take a scooter on the train, hop off at Derby and go to the hall, where I was met by the butler and the dogs. Once or twice, Lord Scarsdale, the owner, came on the back of the scooter for a ride around the estate.”
Insall was also involved in the lengthy rebuilding of Wotton House in Buckinghamshire, which had previously been remodelled by John Soane following a fire in 1820. Derelict and teetering on the brink of destruction, it was bought in 1957 by the enterprising Elaine Brunner, daughter of King George V’s valet, who had first arrived there, chauffeured by an antique dealer friend, to scavenge columns to adorn her swimming pool and then embarked on a decades-long programme of restoration.
Commissioned by custodians of the country’s most significant historic buildings, from town halls to royal palaces, Insall changed the scope and ambition of conservation practice, shaping pioneering approaches to heritage management at a time when historic buildings were widely seen as impediments to progress rather than assets to be cherished. In deftly addressing issues of heritage, sustainability and contemporary use, his approach has a renewed resonance and relevance. When Insall once worked for the College of Arms, he was granted a personal coat of arms. Aptly, he chose the motto “Bring Forth the Best”.
The son of Phyllis (nee Hill) and William Insall, he was born in Bristol into a family of long established manufacturers of traditional luggage, such as trunks, cricket bags and portmanteaux. He attended Bristol grammar school, and his interest in architecture was piqued when his father commissioned and built a new family home at Henleaze, in the north of the city. During the blitz, Insall witnessed the wartime destruction of Bristol’s ancient churches and historic buildings, and in 1942 started architectural studies at the Royal West of England Academy School of Architecture . He saw wartime service from 1944 in the Coldstream Guards, completing his education after being demobbed in 1948.
Insall studied civic design in London at the Royal Academy Schools and later at the RA’s School of Planning. In 1951 he was a Lethaby scholar with the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings, the organisation founded by William Morris in 1877 in response to the activities of Victorian architects, whose misconceived enthusiasm for restoration often caused calamitous damage. As a Lethaby scholar, Insall worked with and learned from an array of traditional craftsmen, including thatchers and lime plasterers, going on to spend 18 months measuring and surveying Winchester college for the medieval historian John Harvey .
It proved a formative education in which he got to know and understand historic buildings from different periods. He claimed to have no favourites. “I love them all,” he said, relishing how social change was reflected in architecture. “It’s all part of a lively continuity.” What also mattered to him was not just the quality of individual buildings, but their wider contextual relationships with streets, towns and cities. The role of conservation architects was, Insall believed, to help make “every place to be truly more itself”.
Insall initially joined Phillimore and Jenkins, a London-based practice specialising in the restoration of country houses in the greatly altered postwar milieu. In 1958, together with a fellow Lethaby scholar, Peter Locke, he founded Donald Insall Associates, working from the kitchen table in his flat in Belgravia. His father and then his wife, Libby (nee Moss), a lawyer, whom he married in 1964, did the accounts. From these tentative beginnings, the practice is now over 100 strong, operating out of eight offices across England and Wales.
With modernism then in the ascendancy, it was a bleak time for historic buildings. Country houses that did not find a saviour were all too often demolished, as were urban swathes of Victorian and Georgian terraces. While conservation fired Insall’s imagination, taking an interest in old houses was regarded as perplexingly antiquarian, as he recounted to Country Life. “Nice to meet you, but when will your father be coming?” asked the builder on one early job.
Insall’s 1968 study of Chester was a landmark for urban conservation and town planning. Undertaken as a part of a government pilot project surveying four historic towns (the others were Bath, Chichester and York), it recognised for the first time the importance of groups of structures with historic or architectural value. Insall and his team “crawled in overalls” over some 400 buildings, evaluating their merits and advocating that the best ones should be retained.
This led to his appointment as conservation consultant for Chester, and, ultimately, to the establishment of municipal conservation officers in local councils across the country. It also helped formulate many of the principles that underpin today’s conservation management plans and historic building appraisals.
Over time, Insall became a driving force in the workings of the Ancient Monuments Board and the Historic Buildings Council for England. There he befriended the architectural historian John Summerson, and the historians and conservation activists Nikolaus Pevsner and John Betjeman. These liaisons seeded the formation of English Heritage in 1984, of which Insall was a founding commissioner.
Conservation techniques are continually evolving and Insall kept abreast of developments. In the decade-long restoration of Westminster Hall completed in 2020, for instance, nanolime (nano-sized particles of calcium hydroxide dissolved in alcohol) was used to consolidate weathered limestone, and latex poultices employed to remove staining. Insall was also a thoughtful writer, summarising his philosophy, principles and practice in Living Buildings (2008), reprinted a decade later with a foreword by the then Prince of Wales.
For the last three years, Insall projects have won the Europa Nostra award, Europe’s highest accolade for heritage conservation: for the restoration of Westminster Hall (2024), the saving from dereliction of the 18th-century Camellia House at Wentworth Woodhouse, in South Yorkshire (2025) and the revitalisation of Rochdale’s imposing neo-Gothic Town Hall (2026).
Whether resplendent in elegant tweed suits on Instagram, commuting to the office on a BMW 750 motorbike, or vertiginously face to face with Nelson at the top of his column, Insall cultivated a suavely swashbuckling persona, laced with charm and humour. Though he retired as practice chairman in 1998, he continued to work as a consultant until his death.
“Buildings are so very much like people,” he observed. “They all have their own characters, their own strengths and weaknesses, their own message, their own background in terms of the influences that have made them. People change throughout their lives – so does a building.”
Insall was knighted in 2010. He is survived by Libby and their three children, Robert, Christopher and Hilary.

title: More than 1 million mice used in Australian research annually, ‘overdue’ study finds
description: Advocates say having national data about numbers of rats and mice used in research can help boost public trust in science
content:
Advocates say having national data about numbers of rats and mice used in research can help boost public trust in science
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
More than 1 million mice and nearly 47,000 rats are used in scientific research in Australia annually, according to the first ever nationwide count.
Dr Malcolm France, a veterinarian who compiled the data, described the count, released today, as “an overdue first step” towards publishing national statistics for all animals used in research, including fish, rabbits, birds and monkeys.
National statistics on the use of animals in research are important for establishing public trust and informing policy, he said, but unlike comparable countries Australia has historically lacked overall data .
“Publishing national statistics has long been the norm in the United States, Canada, the European Union, the United Kingdom and New Zealand, where year-on-year comparisons help inform animal welfare priorities and resource allocation and also contribute to greater transparency, which is important for public trust in science,” he said.
The research, undertaken for the Australian and New Zealand Council for the Care of Animals in Research and Teaching, found 1,193,619 mice and 46,961 rats were used in scientific research, teaching and testing in 2024 (the most recent comparable year), although the total did not include animals that were bred for research purposes but not used .
The pilot study focused on mice and rats in the first instance as they are widely used laboratory animals with clearly defined roles in biomedical research.
Establishing a national figure required a range of approaches, including in one case a freedom of information request, France said. Only three states – New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania – consistently publish their animal use data, while other jurisdictions collect statistics without sharing them and some did neither.
“What the whole process has shown is that there is a pathway to get national statistics,” he said.
Bella Lear, the chief executive of Understanding Animal Research Oceania, said nationwide data is “absolutely vital” for Australia to be able to demonstrate the scope and capability of its research, alongside its animal welfare practices.
“It’s very hard to show that you are a great place to do research, and that your research is very welfare-focused and top of the line, if nobody can say for sure how much research takes place or how many animals are used,” she said.
Lear said mice are commonly used, particularly in biomedicine, because the mouse genome was one of the first to be sequenced. The animals also breed quickly, enabling scientists to study subsequent generations. Rats are also routinely studied, in part because they were easy to train and keep.
Dr Suzie Fowler, the chief science officer at RSPCA Australia, said transparency and accountability were critical for establishing trust and understanding with the public and that included public reporting on animal use and welfare outcomes.
Mice and rats are social and intelligent animals, she said, and enjoy a variety and activities such as exploring and building nests. While some behavioural preferences could be provided for in a research environment – such as nesting material for mice, or more social interaction for rats – some practices and procedures could significantly affect their ability to have a good life and could negatively impact their welfare, she said.
Paula Wallace, director of the Liberty Foundation – which earlier this year opened Australia’s first adoption centre specialising in small research animals – said statistics would assist organisations like hers in identifying how many animals might be suitable for rehoming.
“Animals used in research are no different from the dogs and cats and rabbits we call pets,” she said, adding that the animals deserved the chance to find loving homes and experience a different kind of life beyond facilities.

title: Can Japan’s firebrand PM survive a second year in power? – Full Story podcast

title: Sydney’s second airport will soon be up and running. How different will it be to Melbourne’s Avalon?
description: With Western Sydney international airport due to start commercial flights, the title of Australia’s leading secondary airport is up for grabs
content:
With Western Sydney international airport due to start commercial flights, the title of Australia’s leading secondary airport is up for grabs
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
T his weekend, the first commercial flight will take off from Sydney’s much-anticipated new airport. Passengers will depart from Western Sydney international airport’s architecturally lauded terminals amid much fanfare on Sunday.
It is not the first secondary airport to open in an Australian capital city with grand plans to transform transport for residents of the metropolis and its surrounds. More than two decades ago, passenger flights began at Melbourne’s own second commercial airport: Avalon.
Both airports share comparable footprints, similar distances to their respective city centres (roughly 60km away), and a first flight operated by Jetstar.
But the airports are at pains to distinguish themselves from each other.
Avalon’s chief executive, Ari Suss, says examining the similarities and differences between Avalon and Western Sydney is “not really comparing apples with apples”. A WSI spokesperson says “conceptually, the two are chalk and cheese”.
In 2015, the entity that runs Avalon airport said it “maintains the passion to make Avalon airport the nation’s leading secondary airport”. Asked if this is still the ambition, or if he expects WSI to overtake Avalon in this respect, Suss says: “I’m concentrated on Avalon.”
Avalon, which was built in 1952 primarily as a military airfield, has never really taken off, so to speak, as a major passenger alternative to the city’s main airport at Tullamarine. How will WSI be different from Melbourne’s longstanding second airport?
Seven airlines are already signed up to operate flights out of Western Sydney, which opens amid promises to relieve congestion at Kingsford Smith and offer Sydneysiders more competition for flights. It is in sharp contrast with Avalon, which launched its passenger operations with just Jetstar on board.
Suss says Avalon has the capacity to handle 1.2 million passengers a year. “It’s up and down,” he says.
The airport resumed international flights earlier this year, after a six-year break precipitated by the pandemic. The only international route offered is to Bali. Altogether, there are about 55-60 commercial flights a week including 35 return flights to Sydney, and services to Brisbane, Adelaide and the Gold Coast, Suss says.
By contrast, the federal transport minister, Catherine King, has said WSI will serve up to 10 million passengers annually, with “scalable expansion” to meet future demand. The airport plans to serve up to 80 million passengers a year by 2060, which a spokesperson says is “a larger capacity than Dubai, Hong Kong and New York’s JFK today”.
At first, however, WSI will service a handful of domestic and international destinations with its multiple airlines, including legacy carriers Singapore Airlines, Air New Zealand and Qatar Airways.
The airport’s spokesperson acknowledges WSI will “launch with a modest volume of services, relative to its future capacity” but says it has been “built for long-term growth and will serve Sydney’s growing population for the next century”.
Western Sydney has an advantage as a secondary airport in that its alternative, Kingsford Smith, is subject to strict movement limits of 80 takeoffs and landings – known as slots – in any one hour alongside an 11pm-6am curfew, to curb noise pollution. WSI, in contrast, is approved to run 24 hours a day.
Melbourne’s Tullamarine is not as restricted as Kingsford Smith. It has greater capacity for flights and, crucially, room to expand, which, Suss says, makes competing with the bigger airport for passengers more difficult for Avalon than likely for WSI.
For now, Sydney’s Kingsford Smith has the advantage of a quick rail link into the city’s CBD with promised rail links for the western airport not due to come online until 2027 or 2028. Neither of Melbourne’s airports has such supporting rail infrastructure.
Associate Prof Chrystal Zhang, an aviation expert at RMIT University, says WSI will have to show there is the passenger demand and connecting flights to keep the airlines using its runways.
“That would be an ongoing challenge,” she says.
Suss says Avalon “of course” wants to grow its passenger services, but it has other things on the agenda. Linfox, which effectively bought the airport from the commonwealth in 1997 with a 99-year lease, runs the site more as a logistics operation than a passenger hub.
“We have different advantages,” Suss says. “We’ve got opportunities that are uniquely ours and that’s what we’re pursuing.”
Avalon handles a large amount of freight and recently opened an industrial precinct whose tenants include the Cotton On Group, Australia Post and defence giant Lockheed Martin. It is a portal for Australian food and pharmaceutical exports and e-commerce deliveries from cut-price online retailers Shein and Temu.
WSI also has freight ambitions: its 24-hour cargo precinct opened in July, with Qantas Freight and Dnata among its clients, and plans to “ultimately cater for up to 1.8m tonnes of air cargo annually”.
Prof Rico Merkert, an aviation expert from the University of Sydney, says WSI may need 10 years before it becomes commercially viable and may require financial support from the government to sustain it until then. WSI would not say whether it expected to take a decade to become commercially viable.
On the other hand, Merkert says, the fact that Avalon is privately owned by Linfox means it may not matter whether or not the airport is profitable on its own. The airport has strategic value because it is a linchpin of the company’s broader logistics operations.
“If [Avalon] airport doesn’t break even it doesn’t really matter so much as long as the rest of the organisation benefits financially from that activity,” Merkert says.
Suss says the company does not comment on profits publicly but is “certainly very happy with its growth”.

title: Cost-of-living crisis? You wouldn’t know it by looking at these companies’ profits
description: We are so locked into believing the market must not be questioned that we just assume everything is happening as it should
content:
We are so locked into believing the market must not be questioned that we just assume everything is happening as it should
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
It is always quite striking just how greatly the overseers of the economy defend the status quo in order to ensure company profits keep rising.
Right now, Australians are suffering from a cost-of-living crisis.
It’s pretty obvious why this is happening.
Click here if this graph does not display
But we too often default to the view that oil prices are rising, so petrol prices must also rise and nothing can be done about it. We are so locked into believing that the market must not be questioned that we just assume everything is happening as it should.
Well this week Ampol released its third-quarter report to the ASX. It noted that the growth in its operating profits “reflects the strength of the integrated supply chain to capture the benefits from prevailing market conditions”.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
It also reported that the “escalation of geopolitical tensions in the Middle East in recent weeks and ongoing constraints in supply of fuel products … continue to be net favourable for Ampol’s integrated supply chain”.
This isn’t about them selling more fuel. It’s about them increasing margins at Ampol’s Lytton refinery. Ampol noted that the margin in the third quarter of US$23.92 was more than double what it was a year earlier (US$10.62).
This accords with earlier reports from Ampol showing just how good the US and Israel war on Iran has been for them:
Click here if this graph does not display
It’s why Ampol’s net profit in the first half of this year was up a rather stunning 376% from $180.2m to $857.2m.
Then there is Viva Energy , which owns the Geelong oil refinery and supplies, among others, Shell-branded fuel. It has announced “strong first half earnings”, with its operating profit up 154% from $304.9m to $774.4m.
Again, this did not come from more sales – the volume of fuel it sold only rose 1.3%.
It’s pretty astonishing when you are outperforming even the gas companies:
Click here if this graph does not display
So yes, oil prices are going up, but let’s not pretend the companies that are importing the oil are struggling. No, they are passing on the costs and then some, as we can tell from the increase in the prices charged by the petroleum and coal product manufacturing companies compared with the cost of their inputs:
Click here if this graph does not display
This is important because on Wednesday at his fireside chat the deputy governor of the Reserve Bank, Andrew Hauser, was asked about strong “corporate profitability” and whether companies needed to adjust “to a lower level of profitability over time in order to get the balance right … in order to have the social licence to operate”.
It was a good question, and in reply Hauser suggested “companies are extremely conscious … about what is called in the trade their social licence” before talking about small business and then future problems with AI companies.
But we don’t need to ponder what will happen in the future, because the problem of excessive profits leading to hardship for workers is happening right now and the RBA is saying nothing.
And as for caring about their social licence, companies care about ensuring their marketing budgets are spent making them look like good corporate citizens rather than actually being so .
They also spend an inordinate amount lobbying governments to ensure any concerns about social licence are overlooked.
Consider that Japanese gas companies , including Inpex, are currently complaining loudly about the proposed gas reservation policy and agitated against a 25% tax on gas exports because (as it wrote in a Senate committee submission ) “Inpex’s contribution to Australia extends beyond taxation”.
In August Inpex reported that the times were very good, despite its Abu Dhabi operations being disrupted.
It noted that “despite continued uncertainty surrounding the Middle East situation, full-year profit is expected to be a record high ¥510.0 billion, supported mainly by higher sales prices and stable operations at Ichthys LNG”.
That Ichthys LNG operation is rather beloved by our current minister for resources, Madeleine King. Back in 2018, when she was the shadow minister, she attended the celebration of its first LNG shipment and said “it plays a vital role in the economy of Northern Australia and will continue to contribute to the Australian economy for decades to come”.
More recently she crowed about how “this project provides resilience and security for Japan”.
That’s nice. Especially given so much LNG is exported to Japan that it sells more of that gas to other countries than is used each year in all of eastern Australia .
And it sure is good to know that Inpex’s profits are going to reach a record high due to the Ichthys LNG project, given how much it pays in tax and royalties that helps Australians:
Click here if this chart does not display
But don’t worry, I’m sure when AI firms make massive profits that increase inflation and pay little tax our governments and central banks will speak up and households won’t again be hit with higher interest rates or cuts to services.
Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia Institute

title: First a strip-search goes too far, then a boy is isolated in a cell … the former detainees who tell all-too-similar stories
description: Exclusive: Guardian Australia has spent five months talking to men and women who are speaking out at last, alleging systemic assaults in custody across the country
content:
Exclusive: Guardian Australia has spent five months talking to men and women who are speaking out at last, alleging systemic assaults in custody across the country
Warning: This article contains allegations of child sexual abuse some readers might find distressing
Find more from the Duty of Care investigation here
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Sexual abuse disclosed by former youth detainees often follows a “typical pattern”, Dr Sivasankaran Balaratnasingam says.
First they mention invasive strip-searches which go one step too far, then two. They speak of being isolated in their cells, or assaulted while being escorted to use the toilet.
“There is also an atmosphere where institutional abuses are unchecked,” the psychiatrist says. “The detainees can be abused by other detainees, older boys … It can be very traumatic in these sorts of communal environments with older detainees who themselves have been sexually abused.
“There’s a smaller number of teachers and ancillary support staff, rehabilitation providers who come in, and there’s some abuse there as well. But the majority in my experience, [are] guards and custodial officers, and it often happens at night-time.”
In the past five years, Balaratnasingam has spoken to up to 200 survivors of institutional child sexual assault who were abused within the youth detention system.
The former chair of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mental health committee for the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists tells Guardian Australia that the number of reports is growing as more survivors begin to break decades of silence.
But while the royal commission into institutional responses to child sexual abuse led many survivors to speak up, those abused in youth detention are still burdened with the knowledge that they are less likely to be believed.
Guardian Australia has spent five months speaking to former detainees and their lawyers and advocates, who are lifting the veil on the alleged rapes, sexual assaults and bashings of young people spanning decades. They claim youth detention centres that were supposed to rehabilitate children have left them traumatised, struggling with addiction to drugs and alcohol, and trapped in a revolving door of juvenile and adult incarceration.
Former detainees describe a system in which children – disproportionately of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander backgrounds – were left vulnerable to physical and sexual abuse, isolated and ignored, or disbelieved when they tried to speak up. Years later, they are fighting a sluggish and adversarial legal system which they say causes further trauma and has led some to abandon their push for justice.
It is a national phenomenon, appearing in courtrooms and legal offices across the country. Men and women, some barely out of their teens and others shaking off decades of silence and shame, are coming forward with claims of systemic sexual abuse inside state custody.
In Tasmania in 2023, an inquiry into the state’s only youth detention centre found evidence of widespread sexual abuse and rapes of incarcerated boys. A 2008 inquiry in South Australia heard from 792 people who said they had been sexually abused in state care – a figure the commissioner, Ted Mullighan, said was the “tip of the iceberg”. The royal commission into the protection and detention of children in the Northern Territory heard evidence of “sexualised attention” to female detainees by male guards, and excessive use of strip-searches.
In South Australia last month, a 73-year-old man with access to Magill youth training centre was charged with sexually abusing, raping and intimidating dozens of detainees , the majority of whom were Aboriginal children.
Former detainees speak of being left emotionally scarred, physically brutalised and systematically broken, all while held under the explicit care, and at the behest, of the state. Class actions filed in Western Australia and Victoria have alleged sexual abuse and rapes as well as physical assaults, lockdowns and a lack of psychological and educational support.
A solicitor at Angela Sdrinis Legal, David Longano, is working with dozens of clients who launched a class action in early 2025, alleging that they were physically and sexually abused or raped while incarcerated at Melbourne’s Parkville youth justice centre. The allegations date back 50 years, with the latest from 2023.
“The allegations span across officer- or staff member-to-inmate and or inmate-to-inmate [assaults],” Longano says. “We’re also currently looking at intentional torts arising from forced isolation and unlawful strip-searches.”
Two lead plaintiffs identify the same alleged perpetrator, who they say repeatedly sexually assaulted them and threatened or coerced them to conceal physical and sexual assaults. The individual, who has since died, is the subject of complaints dating from 1998 to 2015, the law firm says. Dozens of other staff have been identified by various plaintiffs as having allegedly sexually or physically abused detainees, the firm adds.
Court documents describe one plaintiff’s allegations of three separate sexual assaults while incarcerated for various periods between 2011 and 2013. According to a statement of claim filed this year with the Victorian supreme court, he was groped underneath his pants in a game room while he was playing on Xbox, and verbally threatened when he tried to resist. He also alleges that the staff member digitally penetrated him during a strip-search.
The same person assaulted him a third time while he was watching a film with four other detainees in a small cinema room, he claims. In the back of the darkened room, he alleges that the officer touched his genitals and forced him to masturbate him, then threatened to withhold access to family visits if the detainee reported the alleged abuse.
In the words of one lawyer who spoke to Guardian Australia: “It’s like Spotlight , they never seem to slow down.”
Balaratnasingam says many of the survivors he has spoken to are First Nations people, reflecting the over-incarceration of Indigenous Australians . The incarceration rate for Indigenous adults as of June 2026 is almost 12 times the rate for non-Indigenous adults, while Indigenous children aged 10 to 17 were 21 times more likely to be in youth detention than non-Indigenous children of the same age, according to 2025 figures.
He says First Nations children are “more vulnerable with less family support when they’re taken into care, and more susceptible to abuse because abusers think they can get away with it”.
The royal commission into institutional responses to child sexual abuse found that Indigenous people were twice as likely to report that they had been abused while in the care of the state than non-Indigenous children.
Jackie Mead, the chief executive of Knowmore, a free national service supporting survivors of child sexual abuse and the Stolen Generations, says a large percentage of clients say they were sexually abused in youth detention.
“It’s alarming, the number of people in adult prisons who refer back to their abuse in youth justice settings, and we’re seeing that pattern of continuation into adult jails,” Mead says.
“We also have cases where people in adult prison settings are telling us that the abuser from their youth justice setting is now working in an adult prison as well, so they are re-facing the traumatisation of their abuser in a power position.”
The gruelling and adversarial court process, fighting against the well-resourced legal teams of state governments, is further traumatising, Mead says. Every phone call, text message, email and document request from their lawyers compounds the hurt.
“When we’re speaking to them and saying that this is the road that lies ahead, it deters them from coming forward,” she says.
Indigenous Australians can call 13YARN on 13 92 76 for information and crisis support; or Lifeline on 13 11 14, Mensline on 1300 789 978 or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636. Support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse is available at Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. Children , young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800.
