title: The best Kindles in the UK for every bookworm and budget – tested
description: Whether you want a colour screen, somewhere to scribble notes or a child-friendly model, here’s what we recommend from Amazon’s e-reader range
content:
Whether you want a colour screen, somewhere to scribble notes or a child-friendly model, here’s what we recommend from Amazon’s e-reader range
F rom that fresh paperback smell to the wrinkles in the spine, nothing beats a real book. But if you’re sick of the space they take up in your home, or the weight they steal from your holiday luggage allowance, it might be worth considering an Amazon Kindle . It can fit thousands of weighty reads into as little as 158g, and as tech goes, it’s almost immune to the sort of pathological time-wasting features that come with modern phones and tablets.
Amazon Kindles have been available in the UK for more than 15 years, so they’re an old-school gadget at this point. But in 2024, the biggest update yet arrived: colour, which added an important extra option to the existing Kindle lineup, alongside readers for children, for note-taking and for tighter budgets.
With so many modern versions available now, I spent months testing them to analyse their pros and cons to help you find the best Kindle for your needs.
Amazon clearly has a sense of humour, because no less than one day after I’d finished writing this guide the brand announced a whole new range of Kindles. I will keep this page updated with how the new line compares once I have fully tested them.
Available to preorder ahead of their release on 11 November, the Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft will be a little lighter and thinner than their predecessors, with a fetching new array of colours.
More significant changes have been made to the Signature Edition models, trading plastic backing for an aluminium one. But it’s the basic Kindle that’ll get the biggest upgrade, with the raised screen border replaced for a flat end-to-end design like the Paperwhite. There are Kids editions of these e-readers coming, too.
The good news about fresh launches is that the models tested here are far more likely to be slashed in price, so you could save some money.
I’m a long-term e-reader user; I first tried one in place of paperbacks in 2009, the Sony PRS-505, a year before the first Kindle arrived in the UK. Since then I have tested almost every member of the Kindle family going. From the Kindle Fire HD (which some say never deserved the Kindle name at all because it’s more tablet than e-reader) to fondly remembered classics such as the Kindle Voyage and Oasis, I’ve lived with them all, for better and worse. I keep coming back to Kindles over other e-readers for their simplicity and reliability – and for Amazon’s ever-changing Kindle book sales.
Most of my book reading is done on e-readers these days. Light, portable and ideal for bedtime reading, e-readers are among my favourite pieces of tech – even if nothing can quite replace the nostalgic charm of a real paperback.
To test a Kindle, you need to live with one for a while. Many keep ebook readers for a decade or more – they can be remarkably long-lasting – so a cursory test wasn’t going to cut it.
While I’ve tried each of these devices as my personal e-reader for several weeks (at the very least), I’ve used the key Colorsoft and Paperwhite readers for about six months, on and off. And for the Kindles designed to offer more than just reading, such as the Kindle Scribe, I wrapped them into my day-to-day routine, using the Scribe (for example) in place of a paper to-do list.
Unlike a tablet, raw power is not important in e-readers. Page-turn speed does matter, but is now good across the whole Kindle lineup. What matters more is how comfortable the screen is to read from, how comfortable the e-reader is to hold, and of course how well it slots into your day-to-day life.
Any remaining devices from this Kindle group test will be donated to Cancer Research UK.
Kindles cannot borrow ebooks from digital lending libraries in the UK.
The two common digital book-borrowing services used across the UK are BorrowBox and OverDrive’s Libby. Unfortunately, Kindles don’t support either of these platforms in the UK. Kindle users in the US do, however, get to borrow books through OverDrive.
To get library book loans, consider a Kobo or PocketBook e-reader . Both support Libby. Head to your local library to see whether it supports such loans with a membership.
A case is highly recommended, particularly if you use a Kindle Colorsoft or Paperwhite. I learned the hard way. These e-readers have a border layer of rubbery material that sits between the rear casing and the screen. It acts as handy impact protection, but can become tatty through general wear in a few months if there’s no case to help out.
Amazon’s own Kindle cases are good quality, if a little expensive, but alternatives are available. If you mostly read in bed, you may want to try one with a hand strap, which I’ve enjoyed using in the past.
An Amazon Prime membership doesn’t include Kindle Unlimited, but Prime Reading does provide access to a rotating but limited library of titles – the number of included novels tots up to a figure in the low thousands.
That’s plenty to be getting on with for the casual fiction fan, but it’s going to be down to luck if a book you already want to read happens to be in there. It has never happened to me.
Prime Reading is a borrowing service. You don’t have permanent access to these books once you pick them, but you can borrow up to 10 at a time for as long as you have an active Prime membership.
Kindle Unlimited costs £9.49 a month and includes “unlimited access” to a large number of books, audiobooks and magazines.
There are a couple of limitations, though. You can borrow up to 20 titles at once, but unlike a library loan, there are no return dates. For most, this won’t be a major limitation, especially since you can just “return” one of the books if you hit the limit and want something new.
The Kindle Unlimited collection doesn’t encompass the entire Kindle library either, giving access to about 4m titles. (Amazon doesn’t publish stats on how many books are in the full Kindle library, but some estimates have the figure at above 10m.) As such, if you are the kind of person who gets your heart set on reading something specific, you may find Unlimited frustrating.
Happy to have a browse and pick something from a glance at its cover, summary or reader reviews? It could end up a real bargain for the voracious readers out there. You can try a month for free, and occasionally longer trials are available too. You can check over at the Kindle Unlimited landing page.
Kindles can fetch a good price secondhand on platforms such as eBay or Vinted. The main turn-off for buyers is usually scratches or damage to the screen. Alternatively, CeX accepts Kindles, although phone trade-in fave musicMagpie does not.
If this sounds like too much effort, Amazon has a trade-in scheme for many sorts of Kindles – although you won’t get much for older-generation models – and you’ll get a 20% discount off a new Kindle. Digging a little deeper into the terms and conditions, your old Kindle needs to work, hold charge, be free of cracks and defects, and have no stickers or decals on the screen. Otherwise, your trade-in value will tank.
Amazon sells refurbished Kindles at a slight discount. And while you don’t quite get the level of promised quality that Apple’s Certified Refurbished iPads have – including a guaranteed new casing and battery, for example – Amazon does claim a refurb should “ look and work like new ”.
If you’d rather buy a brand-new device, it’s probably a good idea to wait for one of Amazon’s sales. Such sales periods are the best time to buy a Kindle.
These are typically Black Friday in November and Prime Day in the summer, with additional sales in October and around Christmas. I’ve seen sub-£100 refurbished Kindle Paperwhites during these sales, representing £44 off the current refurbished price, £85 off the “new” cost.
When you buy most Kindles, you have the option to buy it “with ads” or without, and there’s a £10 to £15 saving if you pick the ads version. That means adverts will be displayed on the lockscreen when the e-reader is not in use.
They are pretty inoffensive, as ads go, typically advertising a book – and are not shown while you are actively reading.
However, you can also upgrade a Kindle with ads to ad-free software for a one-off fee whenever you like.
The Paperwhite and Colorsoft are available as Signature Edition models at a price bump. Upgrades include wireless charging, double the storage and an auto-adjusting front light. By tech standards, it’s not a pricey upgrade. However, none are all that noticeable unless you’re a real wireless-charging household.
Kindle batteries last for several weeks, and getting close to running out of storage isn’t something most need to worry about. And the auto-screen-brightness feature is far less reactive than that of a phone, at times making you wonder if it’s doing anything at all.
Like several of the key tech manufacturers, Amazon likes to talk up the recycled materials used in its key products. All Kindle packaging uses 99% materials from “responsibly managed forests or recycled sources”. Here’s how the devices themselves stack up:
Kindle Paperwhite (2024) – 29% recycled materials in total, internal frame is 90% recycled magnesium
Kindle Colorsoft (2024) – 28% recycled materials in total, battery uses 100% recycled cobalt
Kindle (basic) – 75% recycled plastics, 90% recycled magnesium
Scribe (2024) – 18% recycled materials in total, 100% recycled aluminium
Scribe Colorsoft (2025) – 11% recycled materials in total, battery uses 100% recycled cobalt
Amazon provides a sustainability data sheet for all key models on its sustainability website .
For more, read the best e-readers and the 100 best novels of all time
Andrew Williams is a consumer journalist who has written about technology since before the first iPhone came out. As his flat is filled with the cardboard boxes of gadgets, he tries to get out for a run whenever possible to avoid them – often while testing a fitness tracker and a phone camera at the same time

title: Majority of Australians who report penicillin allergy not truly allergic
description: Peak body for immunologists changes guidelines as evidence shows up to 90% of those reporting allergy don’t have one
content:
Peak body for immunologists changes guidelines as evidence shows up to 90% of those reporting allergy don’t have one
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
The majority of Australians who report a penicillin allergy are not truly allergic, prompting the peak body for immunologists to change its guidelines in a bid to reduce hospital stays and tackle antimicrobial resistance.
Penicillin, one of the most commonly prescribed antibiotics in Australia, was thought to cause allergies in 10% of Australians, or about 2.8 million people.
But the latest evidence shows up to 90% of those reporting a penicillin allergy do not have one.
The changes to the Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy guidelines, which have been published in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology , give the first peer-reviewed and updated advice to GPs and other health professionals about how to diagnose and manage the allergy, and when to refer to a specialist.
Prof Michaela Lucas, a clinical immunologist, said misdiagnosis occurs for a number of reasons, with people sometimes experiencing a rash or nausea after taking penicillin and assuming it is an allergy, or doctors wanting to be cautious and recording side-effects as allergies.
Other people were told by a parent that they suffered a reaction when they were a child and carry that diagnosis through to adulthood without questioning it, she said, while some side-effects may also be due to the illness itself and not the medicine.
Penicillin is an important antibiotic option, as it treats common infections, said Lucas, a professor at the University of Western Australia’s medical school.
“It is also what is known as a narrow spectrum antibiotic, which means it is targeted at the bug specifically causing the infection,” she said.
“Once you have to avoid narrow classes of drugs, you have to use broader spectrum antibiotics which have a bigger impact of your gut microbiome as they are associated with also killing good bacteria and allowing superbugs to come in and take residency.”
Superbugs are strains of bacteria that are highly resistant to multiple standard treatments.
“Antimicrobial resistance matters beyond the individual patient, because resistant bacteria can spread between people and through communities,” Lucas said.
“If someone develops a serious infection that is resistant to several antibiotics, doctors can be left with very limited treatment options.”
Dr Nick Cooling, the chair of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners’ allergy special interest group, said the guidelines were based on the latest evidence, and a consensus report from a range of medical specialities.
He hopes the guidance will cut health costs in the community and ease the burden on immunologists.
“We know that people who have a penicillin allergy label go to hospital more,” he said.
“They spend longer in hospital, and they also cost the system more.”
This is because of more treatments needing to be trialled, side-effects from those treatments, and delays in finding alternative treatments.
“The ability to clarify that with these patients will reduce hospital costs but also the whole health system cost,” he said.
“We need all health professionals to be involved in this because if we’re going to de-label some 2.8 million people in Australia, you can’t just rely on the 300 immunologists to do that.”
Cooling urged affected patients to raise the question of a penicillin allergy with their GP, and with cases where the potential risk of harm is low, doctors could give their patient penicillin and monitor for symptoms. The National Allergy Council is launching a campaign on Thursday encouraging all Australians with a recorded penicillin allergy to discuss it with their doctor.
But Cooling warned: “No one should try taking penicillin themselves to find out whether they are allergic. Antibiotics should only be taken when prescribed for the individual taking them.”
For Tammy Prescino, the issue of penicillin allergy is a very real concern. She welcomes the changes, with her 70-year-old mother and 12-year-old daughter both diagnosed.
Prescino worries that if her mother were to get an infection she could miss out on the benefits of penicillin. She plans to see a doctor and to get her family reassessed.
“Because if she doesn’t have the penicillin allergy, then we wouldn’t have to withhold medicine … that could help her,” Prescino said.

title: ‘A complete threat’: Rio Ngumoha’s electric display excites Van Dijk and Liverpool
description: Teenager produced man-of-the-match performance against Villarreal and has learned from Salah, says Virgil Van Dijk
content:
Teenager produced man-of-the-match performance against Villarreal and has learned from Salah, says Reds captain
T he shot sailed wide of Peter Gulacsi’s top corner and into the Kop, affording Villarreal much-needed respite at 4-2, but for Andoni Iraola it was a standout moment in a scintillating Champions League display from Rio Ngumoha. To a coach who called for versatility from all of his wingers this summer, here was a significant step forward among many from the 18-year-old at Anfield.
There were questions over how Ngumoha would adapt to playing on the right even before Liverpool increased the likelihood by signing Bradley Barcola for £123m from Paris Saint-Germain. On his fifth start under Iraola on Tuesday, which his side won 4-3 , Liverpool witnessed an answer: quickly, incisively and confidently. The teenager’s willingness to cut inside from the right and shoot from distance with his left foot captured Iraola’s imagination as much as the devastating run that created Alexis Mac Allister’s second goal of the game.
“I’m happy with his attitude because he’s eager to improve the things that we think he needs to improve,” the Liverpool head coach said after the comeback win against their Spanish opponents. “He has played a lot on the right lately. He’s feeling so comfortable now that he’s even adding some shots with the left. He hasn’t scored but he’s getting there, and if he can add these small things to his game it will put him in an even better position.”
Ngumoha’s 71st-minute attempt was reminiscent of Mohamed Salah in its intent, if not in execution. The Liverpool great’s final season at Anfield may have been the exception to the exceptional in terms of his own contribution but, as an education to a gifted and hungry young winger, it was not wasted.
Virgil van Dijk noted that “a few senior players” have taken Ngumoha under their wing. “I would say Cody [Gakpo] is definitely part of that. Everyone is chipping in but for him to work with Mo last year was obviously massive. Mo was one of the best wingers at the club and experienced everything so why not soak in all the information and show it on the pitch and show your own qualities? I think he has shown it this season but there is still much more to come. He’s pretty electric at times and he showed it again. He was a complete threat constantly and their defender had a tough time.”
The Salah comparison was not the only throwback for Liverpool against Villarreal. It was a flawed performance with Van Dijk’s early mistake, Iraola’s initial formation and Liverpool’s lethargy on the ball all punished by Iñigo Pérez’s slick side. “It was a terrible start,” the Liverpool captain said. “I think the saying is you fight an uphill battle and as a defender it is pretty difficult to come back from it. I tried but it was a bad day at the office personally but we do it together with 11 players. We turned it around and that’s the main thing.”
The rousing recovery, the relentless high press, Iraola’s bold changes and the character required to overturn a 2-0 deficit all carried echoes of the Jürgen Klopp era. Given that was where Liverpool wished to return when replacing Arne Slot with the Basque coach this summer, Iraola’s 11th game in charge showed development is not confined only to Ngumoha.
Van Dijk said: “If you look at it from that perspective, it is like that. We train a lot, tactically as well, but because there are so many games you learn playing games and this was a test in that sense because Villarreal were good on the ball. They also rotated a lot so you have to find moments when you can press them and when you can win the ball high.
“Is this squad used to that [pressing style] because I don’t think many players have been part of that? What the manager wants us to do is something which resonates with Liverpool and it is down to us to show it in each and every game. It’s not easy, it’s demanding, but if you want to win games and win games in the Liverpool way then we have to do it.
“The first half was obviously not good at all and the second half was solid and we turned it around and that’s a good sign. Now we have to get ready for Brighton, a super team, which is coming.”

title: Kagan says supreme court conservatives have made US political system ‘a nightmare’
description: Liberal justice says recent decisions on redistricting and campaign finance have undermined democracy and polarized US even more
content:
Liberal justice says recent decisions on redistricting and campaign finance have undermined democracy and polarized US even more
Elena Kagan criticized rulings made by the US supreme court’s conservative majority this week, arguing that its recent decisions on redistricting and campaign finance had undermined America’s democracy.
“The court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works,” said Kagan, one of the court’s three liberal justices, during a discussion at Catholic University’s law school in Washington DC on Tuesday, according to multiple reports.
She emphasized that the court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, “has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should”.
Kagan’s remarks come just two weeks before the midterm elections and amid battles over congressional redistricting . Earlier this year, the supreme court struck down Louisiana’s congressional map, effectively gutting a major section of the Voting Rights Act. In June, the court also struck down campaign finance restrictions limiting how much political parties may spend on candidates. Both decisions were split 6-3 along ideological lines.
During Tuesday’s discussion, Kagan, who was appointed by Barack Obama, described voting rights as “foundational” and said: “If you basically get democracy down, if you get a well-functioning, healthy political system then you can count on that political system for a wide range of outcomes.”
Kagan also took aim at the court’s 2019 decision that held that federal courts should not police a practice known as partisan gerrymandering.
As a result, she said, “both political parties have been engaged in a race ​to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting ​equality”.
Kagan said that decision was pushing political candidates “away from the center, toward the wings, toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about ⁠any more is being primaried”.
“It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” she continued. “In ​this election, and the next election, we are seeing large states with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who ​vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is very destructive to our democracy.”
Kagan also criticized the court’s decisions on campaign finance rules, and the increasing amounts of money in politics.
“The people of America look around this political system and think that all this money chasing all these political candidates is a nightmare,” she said. “And they’re right.”

title: Mark Allen reveals he made snooker return after 10-week stay in mental health clinic
description: Mark Allen has revealed he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic before discharging himself to play in this week’s Northern Ireland Open
content:
Former world No 1 vows to show ‘fighting qualities’
‘I see the light now that I couldn’t see before’
Mark Allen has revealed he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic before discharging himself to play in this week’s Northern Ireland Open . In a long statement posted on X, the 40-year-old said he was “not OK” but vowed to show his renowned “fighting qualities” as he continues his recovery.
Allen’s 4-2 defeat by his friend and compatriot Jordan Brown on Tuesday was his first match since his world championship semi-final loss to Wu Yize in April, when he missed a black off its spot that would have given him the win.
After losing to Brown, Allen conducted an emotional interview with TNT Sports in which he said he was “really overwhelmed”, and suggested his career could be over. He wrote on Wednesday: “Everything I said in that interview was true. However, rest assured I’m doing my best to turn things round.
“I have been in a mental health clinic for the last 10 weeks, finally discharging so I could attempt to play in Belfast. I owed that to my family, in particular my daughter to see me play for what could be the last time … I also owed it to the fans who have supported me throughout my 21 years on tour.
“I also owed that to World Snooker who have been amazing from day one in all this, in particular [chief executive] Simon Brownell and [WPBSA Players chief operating officer] Neil Tomkins who have remained in touch regularly, even Simon paying me a visit in the clinic itself.
“I’m not OK, but I’m OK in that itself. I’ve been much worse in the last few months than you saw yesterday. I literally didn’t see a future in anything. My daughter kept me going, the therapists, staff and all the other patients were amazing and helped me through some really dark days.
“I see the light now that I couldn’t see before but I do now. I also know it won’t happen overnight. I’m a work in progress. My fight and determination on the table has always been there for ones to see. I need to show those same fighting qualities off it now for a while.
“Please don’t detract anything from Jordan yesterday, he’s been aware of my struggles and that can’t have been easy to play in but he handled it with grace and skill as I knew he would. I’m proud to call him a friend.
“I hope the rest of the event is a success and I will continue my treatments going forward and then see what’s ahead.”
Since his defeat by Wu, Allen has stayed away from the tour for unspecified personal reasons that are understood not to relate to any repercussions from the manner of his defeat at the Crucible.
Allen has won both UK and Masters titles in a total of 12 ranking tournament wins, and has reached the world championship semi-finals three times. He was ranked world No 1 for four months in 2024.

title: As fans reject AI-generated music, even boosters are drawing the line
description: Enthusiasts like Grimes and A$AP Rocky may embrace AI-generated content, but they won’t produce it themselves
content:
Enthusiasts like Grimes and A$AP Rocky may embrace AI-generated content, but they won’t produce it themselves
Streaming services, notable musicians and fans are confronting the growing presence of AI-generated music and drawing lines in the sand.
On Tuesday, Spotify announced it had removed about 50m songs considered AI slop from its recommendations to users over the past year.
“Our editors hold the same standard and don’t program content identified as slop or spam,” a statement from the company read. Spotify requires “AI persona” badges on artist profiles that don’t represent a real human being, but it does not require individual songs generated by AI to be labeled. Other streaming services have taken more stringent stances.
Though it is cracking down on slop tracks, Spotify is far from AI-shy. The company allows users to create playlists with generative AI and has promised a tool for making AI-generated remixes and cover songs.
Unable to ignore the tide, even early AI boosters like the singer and producer Grimes , former paramour of Elon Musk and mother to three of his 14 children, have declared their limits on allowable amounts of AI. She and other musicians say they are open to AI-generated music but wary.
Fans, by contrast, have little tolerance for it. They are voting with millions of streams against artifice in music. Songs and albums harkening back to analogue instrumentation are dominating the Billboard charts, no futurism wanted.
Both A$AP Rocky, rapper and partner to Rihanna, and Grimes have taken the same position: accepting AI-generated music but not making it.
“I prefer to do things myself, practically,” A$AP Rocky told Billboard : “If somebody does a totally AI-generated song where all they did was prompt something, then I think that’s their thing. But who am I to say what’s standard and what’s not? I’m just doing me out here, and I’m doing my music practically – the right way.”
Kelly Clarkson similarly outlined her own boundary while expressing enthusiasm for AI.
“I love AI. Controversial, I don’t care,” she told the Las Culturistas podcast. “Here’s the thing, I love AI. There are very amazing things with AI that I’m obsessed with. But also, and I’m very into it artistically too, I have fun with it just like everybody else does. But when you see AI artists competing on a chart with humans, I have an issue. I think there should be a separate chart.”
Grimes, one of my own favorite musicians, has begun promoting her first new album in six years, Psy Opera, which she described to the Paris Review as capturing the “emotion of being thrust into the future”. Stereogum described the album as “AI-inspired but not AI-generated”, citing Grimes’s own insistence that her team of 70 be credited rather than reduced to machines.
Grimes offered a free license of her own voice to AI enthusiasts to make what they would three years ago. That she declined to generate her own music indicates that, even to a futurist like her, AI-generated music is lacking, similar to Rocky’s stance.
I have also found myself listening to an AI-generated song, Bomboclat Wallahi, brought to my attention via frenetic , overstimulating videos on Instagram. Despite the song’s comical sonic maximalism, it lacks any staying power. Listening to it the day after I first heard it left no impression, similar to the way low-quality food leaves me hungry again just a few hours after eating. “Slop” is still the best word to describe AI-made content.
In contrast with artists’ nuanced stances, fans are making their position on tech-made music clear: they don’t want it. Billboard’s charts of the most popular albums and charts of the past week showcase a preference for music without obvious modification. Songs and albums that feature a simple voice-and-guitar arrangement are dominating. On the Top 200 album charts, most of the Top 10 albums foreground a singer over analogue instrumentation – Olivia Rodrigo’s You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, Ella Langley’s Dandelion, Olivia Dean’s The Art of Loving, Taylor Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl, Noah Kahan’s The Great Divide and Stick Season, and Morgan Wallen’s I’m the Problem. In the Hot 100 singles chart, the top four songs bear the same sonic signatures: Swift’s Patient Zero, Langley’s Choosin’ Texas, Stella Lefty’s Boston, Wallen’s Been by Now.
Incredibly, the Beatles’ Rubber Soul, released in 1965, also made an appearance at No 4 on last week’s Billboard rankings. Some listeners want to return to a time when producing music with artificial intelligence wasn’t even an option.

title: What is Black journalism for?
description: In honour of Claudia Jones’ memory, I reflect on how diasporic reporting provides community and avoids being defined by the western white experience
content:
In honour of Claudia Jones’ memory, I reflect on how diasporic reporting provides community and avoids being defined by the western white experience
Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
T his week, I had the great honour of delivering the Claudia Jones memorial lecture, hosted by the UK National Union of Journalists. It is partly inspired by the Long Wave and the extraordinary response it continues to receive from readers. As the newsletter turns two, I reflect, in the abridged version of the lecture below, on the importance of making space in an embattled political climate.
It feels like a particularly difficult time to say anything with much certainty. We stand today in the shadow of the Black Lives Matter Movement – as well as the wreckage brought about by neoliberalism, the rise of the far right, and ongoing culture wars. In the last decade, several moments have swelled with possibility and then melted away – not quite into nothing, but certainly, less than we would like. Where do we go from here?
It feels to me, as someone who began writing as a columnist and journalist proper less than a decade ago, that I broadly could always tell what my marching orders were – who the antagonist was. In Britain, a Conservative government enacted large-scale cuts to public services, and the police and Security Service institutionalised Islamophobic and anti-Black policies such as the Prevent duty and stop and search. It was a hostile environment that meted out treatment so cruel that I am still haunted by some of the stories I heard from victims I met while reporting on it. And it was a broader political culture that refused to acknowledge that institutional racism existed. Things were said to us, and about us, while we lived an entirely different reality. The sense was of a particular sort of psychological agony, one which powered much of my writing.
I remember when the lies began, after what appeared to be giant breakthroughs in 2020. There were always lies but these had a different quality – a coordinated feel. The Daily Mail would print something, and then Tory ministers would run with it, conveying outrage and dismay at the special treatment Black people were supposedly demanding and receiving. Then, the airwaves and social media would hum with discourse and debate for days in the aftermath. One particular episode comes to mind: when the BBC shortened its Last Night of the Proms broadcast due to Covid-related precautions, and the rightwing media claimed Land of Hope and Glory was cancelled because of the BLM movement. Even then-prime minister Boris Johnson joined the condemnation.
After the death of George Floyd, similar stories followed. Trying to correct and counter media coverage, rightwing myths, and mainstream discourse about race became like playing whack-a-mole. The right and those influenced by them worked together to produce a blanketting account of Blackness. If you challenged or complained, you were labelled as entitled, and addicted to a victimhood that the government had disproved once and for all in the form of an official report . Even if you said or did nothing, stories would be made up about you for sport.
The progressives were the most infuriating of all. Posting black squares and taking the knee when the cost was low and reward was high, but then retreating to the pompous and disingenuous argument of “going high” in the face of Black vilification because culture wars aren’t “salient” to voters. They were pretty salient to Black people. I experienced this time as one of almost physical savaging.
In hindsight, I see we were rapidly boxed in, with no room for manoeuvre. I felt a sinking realisation in my work: every objection I wrote or spoke was happily gobbled up by the very ecosystem it fought. Journalism regarding Black concerns and public figures became a matter not of reporting and opinion, but instant recruitment into a war. Our opponents were a disparate bunch, but were the product of a majority white establishment that just did not want to listen to the experiences of Black people, to the facts about disproportionate policing and racial profiling, and vastly unequal maternal health, unemployment, education and income. It felt like a trap. In responding to this climate, our orientation was not towards each other, even though it felt like we were defending each other. We needed to turn away from white-facing discourse and into Black-facing and intra-communal discourse. A step back became necessary. What was journalism for?
How can multi-faceted Blackness take up space?
In 2024, we began publishing the Long Wave. I have learned a lot in the past two years, but the main lesson is just how much more distinctive the Black experience is, even more than I thought or intuited, because no other people were enslaved, traded and removed from their lands in such numbers and over such a long time. The Black diaspora is among the largest and most sprawling of them all, connected by similar histories that often shock myself and the team with the specificity of practices, ways of living and challenges on entirely different continents. Whether it was in common linguistic heritage, musical influences, resistance politics, and in one particularly bewildering report , shared mystical pre-Abrahamic practices.
Diaspora is not a people scattered from a homeland, but a homeland that has travelled with the people and remains, in different forms, still within them. It makes space for a multifaceted form of Blackness, which can incorporate co-existing identities. For me, these identities have included being Sudanese, from a certain tribe, and Muslim. Following that, I have found other ways of self-defining – African, pan-African, and Black. I have found that Black can mean belonging to part of something bigger. Acknowledging this follows the legacy of Claudia Jones herself, who inspired this speech. Jones’s journalistic endeavours at the West Indian Gazette supported anti-racism in the UK, but also fostered dialogue between West Indians and international freedom movements. And in establishing the precursor to Notting Hill Carnival, she also galvanised a form of Black culture that insists on its endurance on its own terms.
In these forms of thinking, writing, organising and community-building, we might find that space for manoeuvre. That breathing space as a Black British journalist, and a Black Briton who gives a damn. That space to be Black and care and write about racism – because it is simply a fact of one’s life. That space to do so without being limited by it and defined by it. And that space to be confident and ambitious and global with our own stories, without having to worry about how this looks to “them”. This feels all the more pressing to me as a Black journalist who is also Muslim and Arab. None of this will change the media or the environment we live in, but it will help us navigate it without being subsumed by it.
This is the process of identifying with a diaspora, and actively seeking ways in which we can re-connect with it. It is also a process of divesting from the particular, and embracing something more whole. To think in different strategies and approaches to surfacing Black life beyond its treatment by white majorities and hegemonic histories. To understand that wherever we feel kettled in, suffocated and disempowered, so much exists beyond the reach of the online troll or rightwing columnist. There is history, literature, political activism, carnivals, music, travel and, wherever we stand – community and gathering in the spirit of what Claudia Jones created. There are also vast opportunities for journalism that reports the diaspora not simply as an addendum to a western white experience. What is journalism for? For me, it is to exist on your own terms.
