Next week, the Long Wave marks its second anniversary. What, to you, is the most memorable edition of the Long Wave? Perhaps there was a piece you deeply related to, or one that drew your attention to a shared diaspora experience?
Send us your name, location, your chosen edition, and 3-5 sentences explaining why. Our favourite responses will receive a copy of former Long Wave editor Jason Okundaye’s book Revolutionary Acts: Love and Brotherhood in Black Gay Britain – part of the Guardian bookshop’s Black History Month collection . They may also be published in next week’s anniversary edition of the Long Wave.
Entries should be submitted to thelongwave@theguardian.com by 9am on Monday 26 October.
Last week, Long Wave editor Micha Frazer-Carroll shared her experience of attending a Jamaican Patois class, and the barriers to Caribbean diasporans learning Creole languages. Here’s what readers thought:
double quotation mark Living in Scotland, I rarely speak patios, but I enjoy hearing it and sharing a few words. Its etymology is what fascinates me. I cried when I learned that nyam , our word for eat, comes from the Fulani word, nyami , meaning to eat. Also unu is plural for “you” in Yoruba. I cried because it brought home all those lost voices, words from home, and people displaced against their will.
Pauline Brown, based in Glasgow, Scotland
double quotation mark I grew up also surrounded by Indo-Guyanese English Patois. My grandmother’s Patois included many Bihari, Sanskrit, West African and Indigenous Arawak terms. I remember speaking on my first day of kindergarten and my teacher being quite confused. My grandmother died a few years ago and when she was admitted to hospital the staff did not know what language she spoke. Her doctor very rudely joked: “we thought she was from another planet and that she was speaking some Martian language.” I feel that she could’ve lived many more years had there not been a perceived language barrier during her care.
Rajendra Kapila Basdeo, based in Montréal, Québec, Canada
double quotation mark I’m a Jamaican living in Canada, but I go to Jamaica every year. The Jamaican language is much more recognised, taught at university, translated into the New Testament and celebrated thanks to the work of many people. I write poetry in Jamaican (the term that marks it as a language as opposed to a dialect). I think we have come some way away from the stigma. You should hear my Canadian born 10-year-old grandson speak it as his mother practices with him and teaches him the grammar!
Jennifer Walcott, based in Toronto, Canada
double quotation mark I am pleased to know someone is teaching Jamaican Patwa, but I did not agree with parts of this newsletter’s description. I doubt that anyone would overstand kin for “skin” or kalp for “skyalp” (the usual pronunciation). For me, when I returned from England speaking “the Queen’s English” I learned Patois by being in and around Patois speakers. It blended into my language and musical rhythm until it is completely a part of how I now speak. However, may the students press on. Learning more languages is always good for everyone.
Barbara Blake-Hannah, based in Kingston, Jamaica
double quotation mark As someone born and raised in Jamaica, I’ve never even thought about how Jamaicans born and raised abroad may feel about speaking Patois. This newsletter was enlightening and opened my eyes to how they suffer a pain that I cannot understand, and instead of teasing them about how they sound when they try to speak like a native Jamaican, I need to give them grace and help them with their Patois. I’ll make sure to tell my friends as well.
David P.A. Mullings, based in the US and Jamaica

title: Double blow to Healey as inflation rises to 3.5% and monthly deficit hits £24bn
description: Consumer prices rise by more than expected while government’s debt interest payments surge to record high for September
content:
Consumer prices rise by more than expected while government’s debt interest payments surge to record high for September
Inflation surged to 3.5% last month while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn, in a double dose of bad news for John Healey before next week’s budget.
The Office for National Statistics said annual inflation rose from 3.1% in August , overshooting City forecasts of a rise in the consumer prices index (CPI) to 3.4%, as a result of the surging cost of fuel.
Oil and gas prices have soared since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran , throttling the flow of fuel through the strait of Hormuz.
Rising inflation has also contributed to higher government borrowing costs – the key factor behind the deterioration in the public finances since the spring statement in March.
Official figures showed the government paid £10.9bn in debt interest last month: the highest September figure since records began, and only the eighth time the monthly number has been above £10bn.
Payments on some government bonds rise in line with inflation. The ONS said higher inflation had added £4bn to debt interest costs in September alone.
Total government debt is estimated to have hit £3tn for the first time – although as a share of the size of the economy it has fallen to 94%, from 95% a year ago.
In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £97.8bn, the ONS said – £4.4bn lower than last year, but still £6bn higher than the independent Office for Budget Responsibility had expected.
The twin pieces of bad news underline the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure.
The ONS said a rise in the cost of motor fuels was the single largest factor pushing up inflation in September. The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p a litre from August compared with a fall of 0.2p in the same period last year.
Diesel, which is often refined in the Middle East, rose by 10.7p a litre last month compared with a fall of 0.4p a litre in September 2025. Air fares, which are heavily affected by the price of fuel, dropped in September by much less than usual after the traditional summer peak.
In better news for the chancellor, the cost of clothing fell slightly and food prices growth remained steady at 1.3% as competition among supermarkets offset increases in transport costs.
Rising prices make it even more likely that the Bank of England will raise interest rates from their current 3.7% level when its monetary policy committee (MPC) meets next month. Rate setters are concerned that inflation will jump above 4% next year as the price of a wider range of goods increases in response to higher oil and gas prices.
September’s reading commits the chancellor to raising most working-age welfare benefit payments from next April by more than expected. For instance, the 3.5% rise will uprate weekly child benefit by 95p, to £28 for the first child.
It also means a bigger than forecast inflation-linked rise in business rates in England. The tax firm Ryan said this could raise more than £1bn in extra receipts for the Treasury and would be paid mostly by organisations in the hospitality, leisure, education, health, transport and utility sectors.
September’s CPI reading came in lower than the 3.9% wage growth figure for the three months to July , meaning that the state pension will almost certainly rise by the latter figure under the formula that dictates the triple lock.
Healey blamed the inflation rise on the war in the Gulf. “We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide,” he said, adding that his budget would “drive for growth in every postcode” to improve living standards.
Charlotte O’Leary, an economist at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said the run of three months of rising annual inflation was likely to continue through the winter, even if there was some resolution to the conflict in the Middle East.
“Higher fuel and transport costs will likely push up food prices, and January’s large price cap increase will land as household energy demand peaks. Given this, inflation could reach 4%, double the Bank of England’s target, by early 2027,” she said.
Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultancy WPI, said the higher than expected inflation rate meant it was almost inevitable that the MPC would raise interest rates when it met on 5 November, but he cautioned against persistent rises in the cost of borrowing.
“Raising interest rates cannot produce more oil or gas, and further tightening risks weakening an already fragile economy,” he said.

title: French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets
description: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests
content:
Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests
France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.
With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor ( Oat ) , issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%.
The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks.
Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living.
Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics , sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges.
No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024 . The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending.
France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action.
International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans.
Matthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies.
“The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”

title: UK cinemas report ‘bonkers’ demand for documentary You Can See Everything
description: Tickets for film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes said to be selling out after $15m opening weekend in the US
content:
Tickets for film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes said to be selling out after $15m opening weekend in the US
It is the film everyone seems to be talking about, spawning memes and fuelling feverish online debate about its subject, the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.
Now, a month before Nathan Fielder’s documentary You Can See Everything reaches UK cinemas, tickets for screenings are already selling out after its remarkable $15m (£11.3m) opening weekend in the US.
Clare Binns, the creative director of Picturehouse Cinemas, said the excitement was reminiscent of the response to Greta Gerwig’s Barbie, which became a global box-office phenomenon in 2023.
“People are hungry in a way that we haven’t really seen since then,” she said. “And for it to be a three-hour documentary, it’s bonkers.”
Tickets for the film, which opens in the UK on 20 November, went on sale at Picturehouse Central in London before its US opening, Binns said, and demand has prompted the chain to add extra screenings. At the Ritzy in Brixton, the first screen had almost sold out, leading the cinema to sell tickets for a showing at a second.
“It’s fantastic, it proves again that there’s a different kind of audience coming to the cinema,” Binns said. “They came to see Backrooms, they came to see Obsession, they came to see NAZA .
“There’s a real appetite for smart films that talk to an audience differently than the studios have talked to them before. With this documentary, you’ve got a story that has been mined to some extent with the Dropout and podcasts. But I think the fact that Nathan Fielder spent a month with Elizabeth Holmes is a huge draw. He’s a smart guy, and audiences want something they can relate to.”
Cineworld has also reported strong demand. Stuart Crane, its international vice-president of content, said “the speed and scale of demand has been remarkable”.
Initial screenings at Cineworld Leicester Square sold out after tickets went on sale at about 40 cinemas on Sunday. The chain has since added more screenings at Leicester Square and expanded bookings to a further 35 cinemas nationwide.
Vue has reported similar excitement. Dean Cross, its senior screen content manager, said it was “seeing incredible buzz both within the industry and amongst cinemagoers”, and it was “particularly encouraging to see a documentary capturing the attention of younger audiences”.
The momentum for You Can See Everything has been building since it was unveiled at a secret screening at the Telluride film festival in Colorado in September, where audiences were required to surrender their phones. A teaser trailer released the same day quickly went viral, with Holmes herself joining the online conversation, responding to tweets about the film and its trailer.
Co-directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the film has won widespread critical acclaim. The Guardian described it as “a modern masterpiece of deceit”, praising its unsettling exploration of Holmes and the blurred boundaries between documentary and performance.
Its US opening was the biggest for a documentary in more than 20 years, with more than 2,000 screenings selling out at 855 cinemas. More than 70% of its opening-weekend audience was under 35.
“People want to enjoy films in a cinema with other people,” Binns said. “The younger demographic want shared experiences. They want to talk about it with their friends, and you can’t do that when you’re sitting on your own watching a TV.
“Cinema has been ruled out so many times. Covid, the rise of streamers. Everybody is aware cinema has to change, it has to offer customers something different. But never rule us out.”

title: NYC built a monument to Khalil Gibran and Little Syria. Why was there global uproar?
description: Lebanese officials were furious, claiming the city erased Gibran’s identity. Yet there was a time when Arab immigrants in the US thought ‘we were all Syrians’
content:
Lebanese officials were furious, claiming the city erased Gibran’s identity. Yet there was a time when Arab immigrants in the US thought ‘we were all Syrians’
This is Muslim New York: artists, thinkers and politicos on defining a new era for the city
On the morning of 30 April, in the shadow of the financial district’s skyscrapers, a gold cloth slid off a bright yellow sculpture of painted stainless steel, 7ft (2 metres) tall, that spells an Arabic word: “ al Qalam ”, the pen.
The monument, Al Qalam: Poets in the Park, stands in Elizabeth H Berger Plaza and honors the writers of the vanished neighborhood that New Yorkers once called Little Syria: an Arabic-speaking immigrant community that ran along Washington Street, blocks from where the World Trade Center would later rise. The monument was the first commemorative artwork unveiled under Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Little Syria produced one of the most famous poets ever to live in New York: Kahlil Gibran, author of The Prophet, a book of poetic prose that has never gone out of print. The monument honors the Pen League, the circle of writers Gibran led in Little Syria in the early 20th century.
Its designer, the French Moroccan artist Sara Ouhaddou, wept as she addressed the crowd . Discovering the story of this community, she said, had made her “truly aware of my position in the world as the child of immigration”.
“Thousands of people are going to see Arabic every day of their lives, and it’s in perpetuity. It’s for ever,” the historian Dr Linda Jacobs, who led the Washington Street Historical Society through the project’s final years, told me.
In the weeks that followed, the piece settled into the anonymity that is the fate of most public art, with tourists pausing to gawk on their way to the Statue of Liberty. That would have been the end of the story, until the government of Lebanon found out about the small parks department sign beside the artwork.
Lebanese diplomats, politicians and cultural leaders were incensed at what they read on the sign. Henri Zoghaib, director of the Philip A Salem academy for Lebanese heritage at the Lebanese American University, called the monument “wrong in time”. The Gibran National Committee, which runs the poet’s museum in Bsharri, Lebanon, his birthplace, issued a formal objection. Two Lebanese ministries complained through diplomatic channels, and in May, Lebanon’s foreign minister, Youssef Rajji, announced that he had directed his ambassador in Washington and his consul general in New York to contact “the relevant authorities, with the aim of correcting the text”.
What was the problem? As Beirut saw it, Gibran and most of his fellow honorees should not have been labeled Syrian. They were born in Mount Lebanon. To call them Syrian – as the sign did in six places – was to erase their Lebanese identity.
This might seem like a petty fight over a sign, but the circumstances are not abstract. Lebanon has been battered in recent years – economically collapsed, politically paralyzed, under Israeli bombardment and its south occupied. Two weeks before the unveiling, an Israeli airstrike razed the shrine of Shamoun al-Safa at Shamaa in Tyre, a holy site. A nation in that condition holds hardest to the things that prove it exists, and no one is more indispensable to Lebanon’s cultural identity than Gibran. Why else, under bombardment and occupation, would a foreign ministry spend its diplomatic capital on a park sign an ocean away?
The problem for the dignitaries demanding the change is that Gibran never thought of himself as Lebanese. Though he was born in Mount Lebanon, he has always called himself Syrian.
This could not be more explicit. In January 1929, for example, 200 guests in evening dress filled a ballroom at the Hotel McAlpin in New York to honor Gibran’s 25 years of work. The community’s English-language magazine, The Syrian World, ran the story under the headline : “Syrians Show Pride in Writer Who Has Brought Honor to Race”.
The paperwork tells the same story . When he first landed at Ellis Island in 1895, traveling under his mother’s name, he was recorded as “Jubran Rhamé”, nationality: Syrian. In 1902 he returned as “Gibran K Gibran”, Syrian again in 1910 as “Kahlel Gebian”, nationality: “Turkey, Syrian”. Never once Lebanese, because Lebanon, as a state, did not yet exist.
From 1861, Mount Lebanon was an autonomous Ottoman district with its own Christian governor. It was a province of an empire, not a nation, and it lost even that autonomy in 1915. Beirut, Tripoli, Sidon and Tyre were never a part of it: they belonged to the Ottoman province of Syria, and from 1888 to a Beirut province carved from it.
Lebanon was assembled only on 1 September 1920, decades after Gibran’s generation had relocated in Manhattan.
Historian Hani Bawardi – who has spent decades interviewing the children of the first wave of Arab immigrants to America and served on the committee for the Pen League monument – said that he heard “over and over and over” from the sons and daughters of the very first immigrants whose histories he archived: we were all Syrians. Though today they would be considered Lebanese, Syrian, Jordanian, Israeli or Palestinian, then they were all children of Bilad al-Sham , greater Syria .
Many of the writers in this monument spent their lives dedicated to unifying this community. They did so through creating a newspaper and literature publishing universe, on a few streets of downtown Manhattan.
Roughly 95,000 Arabic-speaking immigrants came to the United States between 1880 and 1924 , and New York was their “Mother Colony”. The neighborhood that would become Little Syria grew at Manhattan’s south-western corner, along Washington Street. Its arrivals were escaping conscription, sectarian pressure and economic ruin after the collapse of Mount Lebanon’s silk industry. They were overwhelmingly Christian: Maronites, Melkites and Orthodox.
They took what work they could. Men and women alike peddled goods through the city and beyond, and Washington Street workshops later turned out most of the cotton kimonos American women wore in the early 20th century. Jacobs’ own grandmother rolled cigarettes, taking one of the only jobs available to women.
And as the community stayed, grew and became more affluent, one of its first acts was to write home. In April 1892 the brothers Najib and Ibrahim Arbeely founded Kawkab America, the first Arabic newspaper in the United States. Over the following decades the working-class colony became a temple of the written word, its presses sending dozens of newspapers across the diaspora to Egypt, Brazil, and back to the Levant.
“I still have the stamps that my grandfather used to send his newspapers out,” said Bob Madey, one of the monument’s earliest advocates. His grandfather was Elia Abu Madi, featured in the monument, who founded the journal As-Samir and is one of the most beloved poets in the modern Arabic canon.
This literature of emigration was called the Mahjar, and New York was its western epicenter; it was one of the earliest literary movements from any willing immigrants to the United States from non-European countries.
Karen Zraick, a New York Times reporter and great-granddaughter of Little Syria writer and publisher Antoine Zraick, wrote to me that writers like her ancestor discussed “western colonialism, nationalism and the re-emergence of a shared Arab identity after centuries of Ottoman subjugation”. Antoine Zraick edited a vehemently anti-Ottoman satirical magazine, Jurāb al-Kurdī, from New York. On a visit home to Mount Lebanon in 1915, he and his brother were arrested by Ottoman officials and executed for what they had published.
Many of these diasporic New York newspapers and journals of literature dreamed of what the future held for greater Syria. The historian Stacy Fahrenthold has described the Mahjar press as “a place of semiotic contest”, where activists became “Syrian” or “Lebanese” by fighting in print for the right to speak for the community. During the first world war, Gibran and Rihani helped lead New York’s Committee for the Liberation of Syria and Lebanon. On the other side stood Lebanese nationalists such as Naoum Mokarzel, publisher of the longest-running Arabic-language daily, Al-Hoda, who championed a French-protected Lebanon. “He was an agent for the French,” said Bawardi.
Yet even those born in what is now Lebanon would describe themselves as Syrian. In 1926, six years after Greater Lebanon was proclaimed, Naoum’s brother, Salloum, founded an English-language magazine for the American-born generation called the Syrian World . In its first issue, Gibran published Message to Young Americans of Syrian Origin . To be a good American of Syrian origin, Gibran wrote, is to say: “I am the descendant of a people that builded Damascus, and Biblus, and Tyre and Sidon, and Antioch, and now I am here to build with you, and with a will.”
Little Syria, meanwhile, was disappearing. The 1924 Immigration Act capped each nationality’s annual arrivals at 2% of its foreign-born population in the 1890 census, and Syria’s quota was set at 100 people per year. A migration that had carried 95,000 people to America all but stopped, and the gates would not reopen until 1965.
The colony was thinning. As soon as families could afford to, they moved to Brooklyn, first along Atlantic Avenue and later to Bay Ridge. “There’s this idea that Robert Moses came in and put in the tunnel and just expelled everybody,” said Jacobs about the city’s master builder and his Brooklyn-Battery tunnel. “That’s not totally the case.” The historical society holds the tunnel’s eviction notices; she counted perhaps 10 Syrian names on them. They had gone already.
As the place emptied, the name changed. Paula Hajar, now the historical society’s interim president, watched it happen in her own Boston childhood. In 1958, Syria merged with Nasser’s Egypt to form the United Arab Republic, and in American eyes turned radical, Soviet-adjacent and suspect. “In the early 60s Lebanon was seen as a beautiful little country, a vacation destination, capitalist and pro-west,” Hajar said. “There was a pall over Syria and a bright light over Lebanon.” It was safer to switch. “When I was quite small, I was Syrian,” she said, “but by middle school, in the early 60s, I was identifying as Lebanese.”
Only three buildings of the old Little Syria survive on lower Washington Street, among them St George’s Syrian Catholic church, landmarked in 2009 as what the city’s preservation commission calls the most vivid reminder “of the time when Washington Street was the Main Street of Syrian America”.
With the homes paved over and the name fading, the history faded too. “No one – any of the Lebanese people I’ve ever met, or Syrians – has known about the Manhattan colony,” Even her grandmother, who lived at 2 Washington Street from 1897, “never, ever mentioned Manhattan”. And she understood why. “It was embarrassing, or not good memories. They were poor. They lived in these tenements, seven, eight people to a room. I think none of them wanted to remember that.”
A century after Arabs first made their home on Washington Street, catastrophe arrived. On 11 September 2001, the twin towers fell blocks from where the colony’s tenements had stood, and in the “war on terror” that followed, the US began treating their descendants as suspects. The NYPD spent years surveilling the city’s Muslim communities, including the mosque of Asad Dandia, now the Brooklyn borough historian. In 2013, Dandia and others sued the department , alleging unconstitutional religious profiling – the city settled.
And still, the community came back. More than 300,000 New York state residents now claim Arab ancestry . The city has a mayor who told supporters on election night, “ As we say on Steinway, ana minkum, wa ilaykum ” (“I am from you, and with you”), and who is married to Syrian American artist Rama Duwaji.
In August a New York magazine cover story declared the city “Habibi City”, heralding a Swana (south-west Asian and north Africa) renaissance. A century after Little Syria’s editors argued Ottoman politics in Arabic publications, reading series filled Brooklyn back yards; the Yemeni cafes of Atlantic Avenue and Steinway Street play the role Little Syria’s coffeehouses once did. Last winter the New York Public Library gave this history its first exhibition: Niyū Yūrk: Middle Eastern and North African Lives in the City , curated by Hiba Abid, the library’s curator of Middle Eastern and Islamic studies.
“There’s a sense of community that comes with a lot of the cultures involved in this renaissance,” said Madey. “I think it’s transformative, breaking down barriers between ethnic and nationalist sentiments … It’s a long time coming.”
The renaissance has arrived as the federal government ends the protected status Syrians have held in the US since 2012 and detains green-card holders for their politics. “The Syrian community was in New York City 60 years before Donald Trump’s mother became a naturalized American citizen,” said Dandia. “And the Trump administration is now revoking the status of a community that has been here for two generations before he was born.”
No one embodies this whiplash of identity like Mahmoud Khalil , the Columbia protest leader whose detention made him, for a season, the US’s most famous green-card holder. Khalil was born to Palestinian parents in a refugee camp in Syria, and holds Algerian citizenship through his mother’s ancestry. He calls himself Palestinian, and almost everyone, friend and enemy alike, identifies him as so. His son, born in New York while his father sat in a Louisiana detention center, is by the plain arithmetic of birthplace a young American of Syrian origin: the literal addressee of Gibran’s letter.
If Khalil’s chosen identity is honored even by the government persecuting him, why should Gibran’s identity be overruled by the two modern states that claim him? This monument, which cost $1.6m – $1.4m of it from the arts non-profit the Mellon Foundation – was supposed to honor him and to make Little Syria something to be proud of. So how did they settle the dispute over whether it was Syrian at all?
When the monument went up in late April, its sign, drafted by Jacobs and edited by Parks, described “immigrants from Greater Syria, which encompassed modern-day Lebanon, Syria, and historic Palestine”, in a neighborhood “known as ‘the Syrian quarter’ or ‘Little Syria’”, home to “about 1,200 Syrians”. Within weeks, Lebanon’s foreign minister announced on X that his ministry’s efforts had gotten the sign taken down, and that its replacement would reaffirm the writers’ Lebanese identity. By July, a new sign took its place .
Set the two side by side and the edit is surgical: “1,200 Syrians” became “1,200 immigrants”. “A Syrian school” became “a school”. The excerpts in the mosaics, once “the works of Syrian writers”, are now the works of “those writers”. The poets, once “respected members of the community”, now merely “performed”. The word “Syrian” has been removed six times ; apart from the neighborhood’s own name, it no longer appears.
Jonathan Kuhn, the parks department’s director of arts and antiquities, saw the change as routine. “They’re not permanent signs, they’re temporary signs, and they can be modified over time,” he said. Others among the monument’s original stewards were outraged. In July, Madey and the historian Todd Fine, a co-founder of the historical society, took their case to the community board. “This is not the way we normally do public history,” Fine said . Yet he sympathized with the Lebanese outcry. “The fact that a government, in the middle of a war in their country, took the time to intervene on this … shows that it’s worthy of serious thought.” But he believed the revisions went too far.
For Madey, whose grandfather’s verse is on the benches, the new sign “is an erasure of the writers and what they wrote about”, of “how they stood on the colonialist project, and how they saw themselves”. Yet Gibran’s call is still being heard. It was heard by Bob Madey, turning up at the community board to fight for his grandfather’s legacy. It was heard by Paula Hajar, who was Syrian as a small girl and Lebanese by middle school without moving an inch. It was heard by Linda Jacobs, who saw this monument through its completion, wrote its first sign and accepted its second.
Jacobs, for her part, would rather the fight not eclipse the achievement. “The history of the first Arabic-speaking community in the United States is finally being recognized and memorialized, in large part because of the beautiful monument in Elizabeth Berger Park,” she wrote in an email in October. “We as Arabs should be so proud of that accomplishment.”

title: Woman told she had cancer by NHS worker who inappropriately accessed her records
description: Pippa Boardman said she lost her dignity through data breach at Royal Cornwall hospital by man she barely knew
content:
Pippa Boardman said she lost her dignity through data breach at Royal Cornwall hospital by man she barely knew
A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee she barely knew who had accessed her medical records days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant.
Pippa Boardman said she lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall hospital in Truro.
Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said her personal information was accessed by a man she knew only vaguely who worked at the hospital.
She said: “I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play. This man said to me: ‘Pippa, I don’t want you to worry, but you’ve got cancer.’ I just couldn’t really believe it.”
Two days later, Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer.
Boardman, who is recovering well from the cancer, said Royal Cornwall’s handling of the case had reinforced her trauma, and she said the trust only apologised once it had been contacted by reporters at the BBC.
She told the BBC : “It really distresses me people can’t see just how invasive and intrusive it is if somebody looks at your information and then shares it inappropriately.”
A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall hospitals trust said: “We are truly sorry that Ms Boardman was contacted in this way. Whilst the member of staff had legitimate access to her records as part of their work, it was outside of their role to contact her and discuss her diagnosis. This should not have happened, and we recognise the distress and concern it will have caused.
“Appropriate action was taken following our investigation, which was carried out immediately after Ms Boardman raised her concern. While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously.
“We have reminded all our staff of their responsibility to protect patient confidentiality and that records must only ever be accessed for a legitimate work-related reason. We are also reviewing our policies and processes in light of the strengthened NHS England guidance on inappropriate access to patient information.
“We sincerely apologise to Ms Boardman for what happened and for the time she has had to wait for answers.”

title: Bristol student who stabbed housemate to death jailed for life
description: Zack Coughlan, 23, killed Jamie Collins, 21, in garden of home they shared and initially denied murder
content:
Zack Coughlan, 23, killed Jamie Collins, 21, in garden of home they shared and initially denied murder
A university student who lay in wait for his housemate to return home before stabbing him 30 times has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 28 years.
Zack Coughlan, 23, dressed in black and wore a mask and gloves to ambush Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home in Filton, South Gloucestershire .
Bristol crown court heard Collins was stabbed repeatedly and Coughlan left him dying in an alleyway as he cycled away on his housemate’s bike.
Coughlan had denied murder and a trial was under way at Bristol crown court but he changed his plea to guilty on Tuesday.
Sentencing Coughlan on Wednesday, Mr Justice Linden said: “He [Collins] was caught totally unaware by you and was utterly defenceless.”
He dismissed Coughlan’s evidence in court that Collins had previously threatened him, describing Collins as a “gentle soul”.
The judge said no one would know why Coughlan killed Collins.
Collins was attacked shortly before 6pm on 8 April this year after cycling home from University of the West of England (UWE) Bristol where he was studying robotics alongside his killer.
Adam Vaitilingam KC, prosecuting, told the jury: “This was a carefully planned and cold-blooded execution.”
Coughlan dumped the bike at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing in a pond, in carrier bags weighed down with bricks.
He returned to the house they shared at about 9pm, put a pizza in the oven and did some online gaming with friends.
At around 2am, Coughlan dialled 999 claiming he had just found Collins’s body in the garden.
The attack was caught on CCTV installed at the house they shared, which Coughlan showed the attending police officers who initially treated him as a witness.
The defendant’s blood had been found on Collins’s bike, and analysis of his mobile phone matched the killer’s movements afterwards captured on CCTV.
Coughlan also had injuries to his hands, and he told people who saw him bleeding that he had been climbing trees and had fallen and hurt himself.
After the murder, Coughlan told a university friend he wanted to hold a memorial for his housemate.
Coughlan and Collins, originally from Swansea, were both final year students and lived together in a £300,000 three-bedroom house owned by the defendant.
The defendant is half Danish and grew up with his family in Cork, Ireland, before moving to Bristol to study robotics at the age of 19.
In a statement issued following Coughlan’s change of plea, Collins’s family said his death had “affected our family in a deep, profound, and lasting way”.
“As a family we have had to explain repeatedly to people what has happened,” they said. “Every time we do so it reinforces the pain of him having been killed so suddenly, and in such a senseless and brutal way.
“Our family has been sickened that Zack Coughlan pretended to help Jamie when in fact he is responsible for killing him.”

title: Why has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped
description: Ibrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hope
content:
Fondation Cartier, Paris Ibrahim Mahama put an entire factory in this exhibition exploring Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism. And it’s just one dazzling installation in a show full of hope
Ibrahim Mahama has dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.
Sit on one of the Asante stools in his circular Parliament of Ghosts and you can almost feel a new future being worked out right in front of you. It’s the first installation in this huge exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris , and it sums Mahama up pretty neatly. He’s looking at the collapse of the Ghanaian government in 1966, the way the hope of the post-colonial project was crushed in a military coup, and he’s looking at ancient Ghanaian history, at the empires that fell centuries ago and the way colonialism tore them to shreds. But he’s not lamenting any of them. He’s not mourning. Instead, he’s reclaiming them, asking how things can be rebuilt, how we can move forwards by learning from the past.
And he does it over and over. In 2024 he bought an old bottle factory – a symbol of industry and its collapse. He’s rebuilt it here, in the centre of Paris. Its steel roof beams, rusted and crumbling, reach up to the ceiling, its walls are lined with thousands of green bottles in Coca-Cola, Schweppes, Kool and Club Minerals crates. It’s a whole history of manufacturing, of commerce in West Africa post-independence. Not left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new.
Nearby, he’s taken some of those bottles and piled them around a collection of local pottery. The industrial meets the artisanal, two lost arts creating a new one.
But this huge show isn’t really about Mahama, it’s about the people around him. Most of the work here is by nine other artists and collectives. Mahama runs three art centres near Tamale in Ghana , giving time, space and opportunities to local artists. Their work is given priority here, alongside art by his mentors and collaborators. He’s taken this massive exhibition opportunity and used it as a chance to celebrate his community. It’s almost as if he’s trying to make the rest of us feel bad.
Way up on the top floor, a long scroll of jute and bark by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke undulates across the floor. If it looks like Mahama’s work, it should: she was his art teacher back in 2013. Knowledge, and the past, gets reconfigured and reshaped once again.
Nearby, the wall of a farmhouse has been built by artist and architect Courage Dzidula Kpodo out of red earth clay, a material lost as modernism brought in concrete. Now, historic methods become a kind of resistance, a symbol of tradition’s ability to endure.
Those core ideas get repeated through pretty much every presentation here. Influential 97-year-old photographer James Barnor captures the communities around Mahama in large format, grainy Polaroids. Gideon Appah ’s hazy, dream-like paintings imagine fictional Ghanaian youths staring out to sea, congregating on beaches in utopian, idealised visions of the country’s past. Some of the works are absolutely stunning, like Peter Doig and Noah Davis transported to Accra.
The best work, appropriately enough, isn’t by one artist but a collective. On the top floor, a bunch of lumpy, surreal sculptures of birds, bodies and men wrestling bulls is by the Congolese Plantation Workers Art League (CATPC) . Each one is made of chocolate, sculpted in the DRC but poured into moulds in Amsterdam. Everything they make from selling the art goes towards buying back land confiscated in the early 20th century by the Lever Brothers, who we now know as Unilever. The work is a whole conversation about global trade taking place in sculptural form, an act of resistance and reclamation through chocolate.
This exhibition is essentially an ambitious, ultra-idealistic group show of West African art. It is art exhibition as political utopianism. Which is great, even if not everything in it is good. And the real draw is Mahama, with his archival approach to monumental installation art, and it’s a shame to not get a load more of it.
Mahama has sacrificed himself for the greater good, basically. But this collaborative approach is the point: he’s saying collective action, community, togetherness, that’s how we’ll build a future. It might sound a bit cloying and earnest, but then you see the results, you see the art and the ideas, you see the community and the hope and the idealism and you eventually say: “Get me a one-way ticket to Accra. I’m in.”

title: Red Roses drop Kildunne to bench for Canada rematch as Mitchell seeks England reset
description: Ellie Kildunne is on the bench for England’s third and final Test against Canada as the Red Roses look to bounce back from their first loss in four years
content:
Star back loses starting place following 24-21 upset
Head coach: ‘She adds huge value – she will get back’
Ellie Kildunne has been dropped to the bench for England’s third and final Test against Canada on Friday as the Red Roses look to bounce back from their first loss in four years.
The Maple Leafs defeated England 24-21 last Friday to end the Red Roses’ 41-game unbeaten streak. Kildunne starting from the bench, with Emma Sing at full-back, is one of four changes the head coach, John Mitchell, has made to his starting XV for the Test in Ottawa.
“She [Kildunne] adds huge value, she is just going through a difficult period at the moment,” Mitchell said. “It’s important for us to help her through that. She has to become consistent as well. She will get back. It is also important to create competition and to recognise that you have to become more consistent, especially when you are competing in the Red Roses.
“It’s really important to reinforce the behaviours we think are necessary to our game. That goes for everyone.”
The last time Kildunne did not start for England was in the 2025 Rugby World Cup quarter-final against Scotland after she suffered a concussion in the previous match. Kildunne has started the nine games England have played so far in 2026 but last Friday she committed four knock-ons and Canada managed to stifle England’s standout player.
Sing will win her 18th cap for England, with her last start for her country coming against Italy in the Six Nations. In that match, which the Red Roses won 61-33 in Parma, the 25-year-old played at full-back with Kildunne starting on the wing.
The other changes see Sadia Kabeya starting ahead of Alex Matthews, who is on the bench, with Claudia Moloney-MacDonald and Tatyana Heard dropped from the matchday 23 as Mia Venner and Helena Rowland start.
Of Moloney-MacDonald and Heard’s reactions to being dropped, Mitchell added: “Their response has been outstanding. Both individuals have different cases, that is between myself and them.”
The captain, Meg Jones, added the team have had “honest conversations” as well as allowing players to “feel sad, happy or indifferent” about the loss.
“Now we have the opportunity to not be defined by the outcome [the loss last Friday] and really solidify where your two feet are and where you are is the most important. That is where you find courage and bravery to stick where you are in the present moment. That is going to be huge for us this weekend.”
Canada lead the series against England after last Friday’s defeat and the 26-26 draw at Exeter in September.
The Red Roses have travelled to Ottawa to take on Canada again and while it will be the final time they play their rivals in this WXV Global Series, England’s matches do not end there. They face the USA on 30 October for their final match until the Women’s Six Nations in April.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo asked for punishment ‘without mitigation’, then fought to cut it
description: Cristiano Ronaldo put forward several arguments to an inquiry with a view to reducing his punishment for walking out of a Portugal training camp
content:
He presented several arguments after Portugal walkout
Inquiry chose to halve, then halve again his punishment
Cristiano Ronaldo successfully fought to reduce his punishment for walking out on a Portugal training camp, after saying publicly that his sanction should be imposed “without mitigating circumstances”.
After leaving the training camp in Denmark last month, Ronaldo said in a lengthy statement on social media that he should be punished as the Portuguese Football Federation saw fit and that his role as captain constituted “an aggravating factor”.
However, during the disciplinary council’s inquiry the 41-year-old put forward several arguments for cutting his punishment, including his clean disciplinary record in recent seasons and his services to football.
Ronaldo received a 30-day suspension and a €255 (£215) fine , and the document accompanying the ruling reveals he presented three arguments in mitigation: his disciplinary record this season and in the previous three seasons; his services to football including recognition for sporting merit; and his contribution to establishing the facts of the case.
To support these arguments, Ronaldo listed the club titles he has won and his achievements with the national team: the 2016 European Championship and two Nations League titles. His individual awards were also highlighted, including the fact that the Al-Nassr forward has won the Ballon d’Or five times. Beyond his achievements on the pitch, he mentioned the honours he had received from senior state officials.
The decision-makers accepted Ronaldo’s arguments concerning his achievements and services to the country, using them to halve his suspension and fine. The punishment was then halved again because Ronaldo had accepted responsibility for his actions.
Ronaldo’s suspension will be served in a period during which there are no international matches. It is unclear whether he intends to return to the national team – or whether the head coach, Jorge Jesus, will select him again.
The account of events provides a clearer picture of the circumstances surrounding Ronaldo’s departure from the training camp. After head coach Jesus held a press conference in which he reiterated that he was in charge of the team and that no player would influence his selection decisions, Ronaldo requested a vehicle from the FPF and set off for Copenhagen airport.
During the journey, he called the Portuguese federation’s president, Pedro Proença, and told him he was “not in the right frame of mind” to remain with the team.
“The defendant [Ronaldo] did not inform or provide prior justification to the federation or the men’s national team officials regarding his intention to leave the stadium and the training camp,” the ruling states. It says that between 30 September and 4 October, Ronaldo missed more than 30 team activities, including travel, training sessions and meals.
The federation says that Ronaldo’s promise on social media, after leaving the training camp, to tell his fans “the whole truth” brought further negative attention to the incident: “Given his prominence as a public figure on a global scale, the defendant could not have been unaware that his conduct, in the circumstances in which it occurred, would be subject to intense media scrutiny, as indeed it was.”
Ronaldo was therefore “expected to exercise particular caution in choosing the timing and manner in which he expressed his dissatisfaction with the manager’s decisions and conduct”. Instead, the player “further fuelled speculation and public curiosity by posting on Instagram on the very day he left Copenhagen, announcing that, ‘in due course’, he would tell ‘all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to his departure from the men’s senior national team’,” the inquiry concluded.
Portugal are scheduled to play Denmark again in their next game on 14 November in Braga.

title: ‘Invasive and extreme’: doctors fight anti-trans measure requiring genital exams for student athletes
description: A Washington referendum has drawn broad opposition from adults who work with queer and trans teens
content:
A Washington referendum has drawn broad opposition from adults who work with queer and trans teens
F or Kelsey Gellner, a Seattle-based pediatric nurse, a statewide proposal to bar trans girls from sports participation feels like a violation of her duty as a medical professional. The ballot initiative includes a requirement she calls “invasive and extreme”: all students who wish to compete on girls’ teams would have to undergo genital exams.
“I tell my kids and patients that my No 1 job is to keep them safe,” said Gellner, who is also a board member of the Washington State Nurses Association. “I can say with confidence that girls do not want to have an unnecessary exam that creates an unsafe barrier.”
As attacks on transgender rights have accelerated under the Trump administration, four states have placed measures on the November ballot to further erode those protections, with a focus on banning trans teens from participating in school sports. (Similar restrictions have already been implemented in 27 states.) Though LGBTQ+ groups have long fought against anti-trans policies, the proposal in Washington has drawn broad opposition from adults who work with queer and trans teens, including many healthcare providers, teachers and counselors.
Over the past few weeks, as midterm election organizing has ramped up, Gellner and nurses across the state have campaigned against the initiative by speaking at press conferences, canvassing and door-knocking. They are among more than 140 healthcare providers who have issued a statement opposing Initiative 638, while unions like the Washington Education Association and the American Federation of Teachers are actively mobilizing members across the state, organizers said.
Washington’s ballot measure was introduced last year by Let’s Go Washington, a political action committee founded by the hedge fund manager Brian Heywood, a multimillionaire who has bankrolled many conservative initiatives. It’s widely considered to be the most restrictive of the four statewide measures, mandating that girls show proof of female anatomy through expensive genetic or hormone tests, or a genital exam. Boys are not required to undergo the same sex-verification process.
“The way the measure is written says that I, as a physician, cannot rely on a birth certificate,” said Libby Loft, a family doctor in Spokane. “I have to examine someone’s reproductive anatomy – that seems inappropriate to me for a sports physical.”
The wave of measures targeting transgender youths’ participation in sports followed a supreme court decision in June that ruled such bans are constitutional . At the same time, dozens of hospitals have discontinued care for trans youth after Trump threatened to withhold federal funding. Yet the groups that such policies are supposedly targeting are often exceptionally small: the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association has said that it is aware of only about 10 student athletes who identify as transgender out of more than 200,000 in the state.
A sex-verification requirement adds another barrier for girls to participate in team sports, Loft said, when they are already twice as likely as boys to drop out by age 14.
“I don’t see this as a way to level the playing field for girls, and we’re making a villain out of trans girls who are children,” Loft said.
Let’s Go Washington and I638’s proponents have argued in the voter guide that the sex verification requirement is a standard procedure endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics – a claim the medical group has publicly rejected .
Gellner said a genital exam was wholly different from a sports physical, which is used to determine metrics like vision and heart health and, crucially, doesn’t require a student to remove her clothing. She added that any policy that puts girls through intrusive medical procedures “opens up a can of worms” given the horrific crimes of Larry Nassar, an ex-USA Gymnastics doctor who was convicted in 2023 of sexually abusing girls for decades.
“While I believe that a vast majority of people who enter the medical profession do it for the right reason, writing legislation that opens the door to predators is just not responsible,” Gellner said.
Libby Watson, campaign manager for No Hate in Washington State, said organizers have spent the past year and a half building a broad coalition against two ballot measures they consider detrimental to LGBTQ+ rights: the one that targets trans sports athletes, and another that would expand parents’ rights to access public school records.
The No Hate campaign has amassed nearly 600 endorsers, including prominent Democratic politicians like the US senator Patty Murray and groups such as Planned Parenthood and the Washington State Nurses Association. The group is now ramping up its door-knocking, phone-banking and canvassing efforts, powered by more than 6,300 volunteers, Watson said.
Public awareness about the anti-trans sports measure had increased dramatically over the past couple of months, Watson said, as the No Hate campaign held up to four phone-banking sessions a week. Organizers also found that messaging around the unjustness of the policy – the fact that only girls would be affected – and the invasiveness of the genital exams resonated most with voters, she said.
“We have people power,” Watson said. “We have many people who haven’t been involved before but care enough about beating these initiatives so that Washington remains a safe state for queer young people.”
John Gallagher, a Seattle-based high school teacher and former cross-country coach, said the measure put coaches in an especially tough position because their priority is to support all athletes, no matter their gender identity.
“To me, this particular policy is incredibly exclusionary,” Gallagher said. “It’s a lot of effort to exclude a very small population of kids who are just trying to be themselves.”
Despite being heavily out-funded by Let’s Go Washington, Watson said she was optimistic that the No Hate coalition is building up more than enough momentum to mobilize voters and defeat the two measures at the polls.
“These are culture-war wedge issues to divide and conquer us,” she said. “The cost of housing, gas prices – these are the real issues people are facing and want to see addressed.”
Advocates say the state’s school-records proposal also could disproportionately hurt LGBTQ+ youth. The measure would prevent school counselors from providing a safe space for students to disclose bullying, substance use or struggles with their physical or mental health. As LGBTQ+ youth are more likely to experience homelessness, domestic violence and suicidal ideation, Jaime Fineman-McKinney, a school counselor in Tacoma, said many may not feel safe at home and need protection from their parents.
“If they’re coming to me as a trusted person and I have to then out them, I just put them in a very unsafe situation,” she said.
Loft, the Spokane-based family doctor, said it did not surprise her that medical professionals have come out in droves to fight the two ballot proposals.
“We all have the goal of helping our kids live healthy lives,” she said.
