title: Trump suggests he could be ‘arbitrator’ in DoJ anti-fraud whistleblower scheme
description: President makes suggestion while announcing new program to reward tipsters who submit fraud allegations
content:
President makes suggestion while announcing new program to reward tipsters who submit fraud allegations
Donald Trump suggested on Tuesday that he would serve as “the arbitrator” of decisions in the justice department’s new anti-fraud program that awards compensation to those who submit tips resulting in conviction or significant federal enforcement.
While announcing the new program alongside JD Vance, the vice-president, who leads the White House’s taskforce to eliminate fraud , the president told reporters he had a solution for situations where multiple people submit a tip for the same alleged fraud.
“I was just thinking, when you do these things, sometimes there’s a dispute as to who turned ’em in and who didn’t turn ’em in, who’s supposed to get what and when, you know,” Trump told reporters.
“So I am going to do something, which I think people will like, I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions. In other words, I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous, believe me,” the US president said, resulting in laughter from the group.
It is unclear whether Trump was being genuine about his new role. The Department of Justice website says the department has “sole discretion” in issuing rewards and exercising its authority in the program.
When asked whether the president’s statement was true, the White House referred the Guardian to Trump’s Oval Office comments.
The Guardian has asked the justice departmentfor comment.
The new fraud whistleblower incentive program gives anyone who submits a tip the opportunity to receive a financial reward of up to $30,000 for tips in the “charging stage of a criminal case”.
The government already gives financial rewards to whistleblowers who file lawsuits against individuals and companies committing financial fraud through the False Claims Act. If the government intervenes in a suit and prosecutes it, whistleblowers can obtain 15% to 25% of the financial penalties.
Vance said the new program differs from the False Claims Act because it expands the opportunity for financial reward in cases of fraud related to the government.
“Over 99% of the fraud that we’re finding in the federal government isn’t covered by the False Claims Act,” Vance said.
The new program also provides whistleblower rewards at an earlier stage of investigation, rather than requiring it to result in large fines or forfeiture.
Vance said he and Trump decided to create the program to incentivize more people to report fraud like Nick Shirley, a conservative influencer who went viral earlier this year for accusing Somali-run childcare centers in Minnesota of rampant fraud .
During his Oval Office announcement, Trump indicated the program would result in whistleblowers obtaining 1% of however much fraud was uncovered, insisting people could make “millions and millions” of dollars from submitting tips.
However, the justice department website says the program is limited to a $30,000 reward.
“You’ll get your money immediately, but I’ll make the determination,” Trump added. “So if two people are fighting over it, maybe they’ll split it or maybe whatever, but I’ll make that determination. It’ll be done expeditiously and fairly.”
Trump encouraged members of the media to participate in the program by investigating and reporting instances of fraud. He said the government would be willing to give reporters the financial reward, so long as their respective outlet allowed it.
“We’re going to let the reporters partake because you know a lot of things that are happening,” Trump said.

title: State attorneys general step up plans to counter Trump’s meddling in midterms
description: Coordination by Democratic officials overseeing elections includes Zoom calls and in-person tabletop exercises
content:
Coordination by Democratic officials overseeing elections includes Zoom calls and in-person tabletop exercises
Democratic state attorneys general, other top state officials and civic groups have accelerated planning to thwart any federal meddling in the November midterm elections by Donald Trump as he continues his false charges of widespread voting fraud and veiled threats of interfering in the process.
Since early this year, 24 Democratic attorneys general have expanded coordination with about a dozen Democratic secretaries of state and several civic groups using weekly Zoom calls and in-person tabletop exercises to strategize about countering any federal intervention in the elections.
The enhanced cooperation is significant because many secretaries of state are responsible for supervising elections, and state attorneys general are charged with defending the laws governing them. The coordination efforts by the state officials are being spearheaded by the Progressive State Leaders Committee (PSLC), the public policy arm of the Democratic Attorneys General Association.
The Democratic attorneys general say they are especially worried about interference in the elections by the Department of Justice and other parts of the Trump administration given the president’s repeated false charges of rampant voting fraud in US elections.
On Trump’s first day in office last January, he falsely called the 2020 election “rigged” and has made similar claims hundreds of times since he lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden.
Nick Brown, the Washington state attorney general, said that the justice department and the Trump administration were “the biggest adversary to a smooth election”. Brown added that “Trump lies about the election on a regular basis. Truth is not a goal of his. That creates a whole host of concerns for us.”
The Department of Justice, for instance, announced dubious plans this summer to deploy 1,000 poll monitors, which prompted the NAACP to file a lawsuit on 4 October seeking details of how the monitors would be deployed; by comparison, in 2022 the justice department deployed 289 monitors, according to CBS News.
In another worrisome move, the justice department has sued 30 states to obtain their unredacted voter lists that contain sensitive personal information. Democratic attorneys general have been involved in challenging the justice department lawsuits, and the justice department has lost 26 of the lawsuits that courts have ruled on.
Furthermore, Harmeet Dhillon, who heads the justice department’s civil rights division, this summer wrote to state election officials threatening prosecutions if they didn’t cooperate adequately in hunting for voting fraud.
To counter threats of federal intervention in the November elections, Brown has led the weekly Zoom calls with PSLC partners including offices of secretaries of state and key civil society groups such as the Democracy Defenders Fund, the States United Democracy Center and the Brennan Center for Justice.
A former US attorney and federal prosecutor, Brown said the Zoom calls focus on election security issues in general and potential event scenarios – including the possibility of ICE agents showing up near some polling places and ballots being seized in some races.
Brown, who chairs the PSLC election-protection working group, also led two “tabletop” in-person exercises in Milwaukee in May and Detroit in September that included attenders from secretary of state offices and other PSLC partners.
Besides these efforts, Brown’s office co-led the legal moves that blocked Trump’s radical plans in his March executive order to overhaul and curb voting by mail, which the supreme court ruled against last month.
The fears of federal meddling in the elections have been fueled by Trump’s drumbeat of baseless allegations about large-scale noncitizen voting and voting-by-mail fraud, both of which the president falsely alleged in a nationalized televised address on 16 July.
In his TV speech, Trump made the factually inaccurate claim that noncitizen voting, which has long been illegal and historically rare, poses a “crisis of election security”.
Trump’s fixation with portraying noncitizen voting as a crisis has been significantly undercut by data from the conservative Heritage Foundation, which cited just 100 cases over a 25-year period.
Other concerns about federal meddling in the next elections were spurred by Trump’s comments to the New York Times that he regrets not calling out the national guard to seize ballots in the 2020 election, and his urging Republicans last month at a mini convention in Texas to “cheat like hell like they do”.
Oregon’s attorney general, Dan Rayfield, shares Brown’s concerns about the threat to the elections posed by Trump.
“From day one, Trump has been taking dead aim at our elections,” Rayfield said. “We’re trying to dispute some of the misinformation that the Trump administration keeps putting out,” including about the dangers of voting by mail.
Oregon, he noted, was the first state to adopt all voting by mail and has had two GOP secretaries of state in the last decade who have been happy with the voting system.
Elsewhere, Arizona’s Democratic secretary of state, Adrian Fontes, whose office has participated in a number of the Zoom calls and the two tabletop exercises, said the increasing cooperation this year with the attorneys general represents “an all-hands approach” to cope with the threats of federal interference. “We have an adversary we didn’t expect in the form of this administration,” Fontes said.
Fontes added that a central concern of his office was that the administration’s “constant drumbeat of lies is going to suppress the vote”.
The Democratic attorney general efforts have benefited from the input of several non-partisan groups.
Norm Eisen, the executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund who participated in the Milwaukee and Detroit tabletop exercises and has been on some of the Zoom calls, praised the work of the attorneys general preparing to combat federal election meddling.
“The pro-democracy AGs [attorneys general] are preparing for anything that this anti-voter administration may throw at them,” said Eisen, a former special counsel for ethics and government reform to Barack Obama. “The level of preparation by the AGs and the secretaries of state is off the charts.”
More broadly, Larry Norden, an elections expert with the Brennan Center who has participated in a handful of the Zoom calls and the two tabletop strategy exercises organized by the PSLC, warned: “Leaders in the administration, including at the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security, have repeatedly threatened or attempted to exert control over the midterm elections.”
Norden noted that “for the last 18 months, they have been met by pushback and consistently lost. I don’t expect that to change in the coming weeks, but everyone involved in this fight knows we must continue to be prepared.”
To better protect election results and bolster coordination between the Democratic attorneys general and Democratic secretaries of state, two new groups were created in 2026. One of them is called the AGSOS Election Protection Pac, and is working to raise funds to elect more Democrats to both state offices, and the other is dubbed AGSOS Election Protection Action, which serves as a policy arm.
Addressing the PSLC work to counter Trump administration election interference threats, Sean Rankin, the president of the Democratic Attorneys General Association, noted that “it is a concern that the administration will try to seize ballots, and the AGs and secretaries of state are working on responses to that to find solutions if that happens”.
Mai Ratakonda, a top election-protection attorney with the States United Democracy Center, stressed that since the justice department early this year in a highly unusual move seized 2020 ballots from Fulton county, Georgia, election officials are “ready and prepared to respond” to the threat of ballots being seized in the midterms.
More broadly, Rayfield cautioned that Trump “continues to take steps to interfere in our elections … This president has stretched our democracy more than any president in my lifetime.”

title: How to turn brown bananas into the best vegan bread of the bunch – recipe
description: Use over-ripe fruit to flesh out this loaf with chocolate, spelt and miso – truly top banana
content:
Use over-ripe fruit to flesh out this loaf with chocolate, spelt and miso – truly top banana
A fter nine years, I can’t believe I’ve never written a recipe for banana bread for this column, so it had better be a good one, especially after I picked up a huge bunch of brown bananas at the corner shop for next to nothing the other day. This is a vegan bread made with olive oil instead of butter and with the mashed bananas acting as a binder in place of eggs; I’ve also added some miso to boost the umami and overall satiety – the salt enhances the sugar, boosting the sweetness while rounding it off nicely. In the interest of biodiversity and flavour, I’ve used wholemeal spelt flour, but any will do.
This has become our go-to banana bread at home because it has crazy levels of deliciousness. The recipe is inspired by a plant-based banana bread recipe I found on Laura Wright’s wonderful The First Mess website , and my tweaked version of her loaf uses extra-virgin olive oil and wholegrain flour for nutrition, flavour and biodiversity; I’ve also used miso instead of salt, to bump up the umami factor.
280g wholemeal spelt flour 1 tsp ground cinnamon 1 tsp baking powder 1 tsp bicarbonate of soda 150g dark chocolate chunks 150g walnut pieces 6 very ripe bananas 120ml maple syrup , or brown sugar 120ml extra-virgin olive oil 1 tsp vanilla extract 1 tbsp miso , or ½ tsp salt
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and grease and line a 1kg bread tin. Mix the flour, cinnamon, baking powder and bicarb in a large bowl. Set aside about seven pieces each of the chocolate and walnuts to decorate the loaf later, then stir the rest into the flour mix until well distributed. Peel five of the brown bananas and, in a second bowl, mash them with the maple syrup, olive oil, vanilla extract and miso. Add the banana mix to the bowl of dry ingredients, stirring until properly combined, then pour into the bread tin and level out the top. Peel the last brown banana, cut it in half lengthways and arrange on top of the dough with the reserved chocolate and walnut pieces. Bake for an hour, until just cooked through, then leave to cool before slicing.

title: Michigan residents fight potential $6.4bn datacenter bill: ‘That is insanity’
description: DTE Energy, among the US’s biggest utilities, is requesting approval to build two new gas plants to meet datacenter demand
content:
DTE Energy, among the US’s biggest utilities, is requesting approval to build two new gas plants to meet datacenter demand
Michigan utility customers may pay $6.4bn for two new gas plants to meet datacenter demand, drawing outrage from residents.
The potential burden on ratepayers, especially residential customers, is a microcosm of similar tensions nationwide, highlighting how the utility industry benefits from unchecked datacenter growth.
The proliferation of energy-hungry datacenters in the state of Michigan is driving a DTE Energy proposal to double its electric grid capacity over the next 20 years. DTE is Michigan’s largest energy provider, and among the nation’s biggest utilities. It has asked regulators to approve a long-term energy delivery plan that includes developing a combined 2.1 gigawatts of gas plants in 2031 and 2032, in counties just outside metro Detroit.
The company has already contracted with Google and Oracle to provide a combined 2.4 gigawatts of electricity to hyperscale datacenters – enough to power more than 1.8m homes. It is also poised to announce two more hyperscale contracts, and a potential total of roughly 6 gigawatts’ worth of datacenters could be contracted by the year’s end. If all came to fruition, DTE could need more than two gas plants.
About 2.3 million electric customers in south-east Michigan could be affected. Any plan to saddle residential customers with datacenter costs was “deeply unjust”, said Yousef Rabhi, a public power advocate and former state representative who in August won the Democratic nomination for mayor of Ann Arbor.
“People who are struggling to feed their kids, to put diapers on their babies, to keep the lights on – those people are going to be subsidizing the wealthiest people on the planet to help them make more money, and that is insanity,” Rabhi continued.
The Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC), which regulates the state’s private utilities, has drawn fire over its previous decisions about whether residential customers should effectively subsidize datacenters. The commission’s leadership is filled with appointees of Michigan’s governor, Gretchen Whitmer, a pro-business, big tech ally who has seen her popularity in the state fall in part over her support for datacenters, which are unpopular .
DTE Energy wrote in a press release that “the plan reflects what [customers] told us matters most to them”.
“We designed this plan to be achievable and affordable – grounded in real analysis and feedback from customers and built to deliver cleaner energy while meeting Michigan’s growing needs for the next 20 years and beyond,” said DTE Electric’s president, Matt Paul. The plan also calls for a significant increase in renewable energy and battery storage, which consumer advocates praised as a positive step.
The MPSC will take input from industry and environmental groups and consumer advocates, among other interests, and issue a preliminary decision within 300 days.
DTE has said the gas plants will replace a coal plant that is being retired, but the retirement agreement was developed in 2023. While DTE around that time said it would need about 940 megawatts of gas in the long term, it now claims it needs about 2.3 times more gas generation than previously anticipated, raising questions about whether the coal plant closure is truly a driver of the gas expansion.
“We are very comfortable with saying that the amount they are currently requesting – the vast majority of that could be attributed to datacenters,” said Helen Li, a senior attorney with Earthjustice, which is representing the Sierra Club in the regulatory case.
The DTE plan includes some analysis of the effects on ratepayers, including residential, but protections will not be determined until later regulatory cases.
“DTE’s approach to the question of ‘who pays’ is unclear, convoluted, and does not ensure that ordinary ratepayers won’t foot the bill for these new, energy-hogging neighbors,” Li said.
The datacenters also may derail Michigan’s nation-leading climate transition laws. Michigan, in late 2023, passed legislation requiring utilities to transition to renewable energy by 2040. But the law included an “off-ramp” that allows utilities to continue running or building fossil fuel plants if renewable sources cannot handle the energy grid’s load.
At its peak, DTE’s grid already demands more than 9.5 gigawatts of power, while the grid’s capacity is 11 gigawatts. DTE may already exceed that with the datacenters for which it has contracts, and it may soon announce several more. The company also develops gas infrastructure across the US, so its parent company benefits from datacenters and is incentivized to add more to the grid.
The mix of energy generation DTE proposed appears to potentially get it close to meeting the climate law’s requirements, but part of that relies on installing unproven carbon capture technology. Additionally, more gas plants could be built if more datacenter contracts are approved, which appears likely.
“This blows a hole in the state’s clean energy laws,” Rabhi said. “Of course they are going to build fossil fuel, and there is a massive environmental cost to this.”

title: The night watch: the YouTubers who are guardians of a shark stuck in a South Korean canal
description: A group of self-appointed guardians wearing hi-vis and carrying selfie sticks watch over the animal that has been trapped for a month, drawing more than 1.6 million visitors
content:
A group of self-appointed guardians wearing hi-vis and carrying selfie sticks watch over the animal that has been trapped for a month, drawing more than 1.6 million visitors
I n South Korea , they call them jagyeongdan , a word whose meaning sits somewhere between vigilante group and neighbourhood watch. Each night they put on hi-vis vests, picked up their selfie sticks and gathered around the harbour in Busan to keep watch over an unlikely charge: a stranded shark affectionately known as Bukang-i.
On Wednesday, after more than a month in the canal and at the third attempt, the shark was successfully guided out, South Korea’s oceans ministry said. Officials expect her to move into open water in time.
For the month that she was stranded, the group of self-appointed guardians took turns to protect her, patrolling the waterfront at night for visitors who might disturb the animal.
Most are YouTubers who livestreamed the waterway, where the shark became a national celebrity. They stayed up through the night, calling out anyone shining torches or lasers into the water. Some of their videos have been watched hundreds of thousands of times.
“They bring fishing lamps, or the kind of lights people use at a campsite,” said Choi Won-jin , one of the shark’s protectors. He would arrive as the lights went out along the canal and wait for the offenders Koreans online call “lantern villains”.
The shark had been marooned in the canal since 18 September. Named after Bukhang, the Korean name for the city’s North Port, and about 3 metres long, the female dusky shark was one of a species classed as endangered worldwide. More than 1.6 million visitors came to see her, the city said, at a park that used to draw about 2,000 people on a busy Saturday.
Authorities had twice tried to guide her back out to sea and failed. Until she left, the shark remained in the canal, drawing crowds by day and leaving a handful of men to keep watch after dark. They patrolled the canal’s park to check everything was in order, ate snacks as the night went by, and shared their grievances on air about the behaviour they witnessed.
“We’re ordinary members of the public,” said Choi, who has had a YouTube channel for 10 years and covers trending issues in South Korea. “So we have no choice but to put it nicely, and get them to understand as best we can.”
“Don’t, please don’t switch the torch on,” said one of them, a YouTuber who lived nearby and went by the name Na Tae-soo . Most people complied, he said. “The animal thrashes about at night because of the torches, and it’s dangerous.”
His footage captured the shark twisting sharply away from a beam of light at 2am and striking the side of the canal. The national institute of fisheries science later confirmed an abrasion on her snout and said a visitor’s torch was likely to have startled the shark into injury.
Korean media reported that 105 officials from seven agencies watched over her, with a team on standby to reach the water within three minutes. Choi disputed this, saying that after dark it was almost up to him and the others.
The waterfront was closed to the public from midnight until 5am, a restriction the YouTubers said was impossible to enforce across a park that size. One night, livestreaming from the walkway, Choi filmed a man tipping food waste into the water.
Nobody saw the shark feed, though experts said feeding could happen in an instant and sharks her size did not need to eat often.
Further attempts to free the shark had been paused on the grounds that more force would distress her.
Cooler water had been expected to prompt her to move on. Dusky sharks prefer water between 18C and 26C, the fisheries institute said. Experts put 15C as the point below which her physiological functions would start to decline, and about 11C as the point at which survival would become precarious. Busan city officials had expected the canal to reach that temperature after the middle of November.
The fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that sharks feed on.
The affection for Bukang-i has meanwhile become an industry, with a commemorative soju , a baseball mascot in a shark cape and an honorary city ambassadorship, and nearby shops reporting a surge in sales. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, visited the canal in mid-October.
None of the shark’s guardians thought she should be forced out. Choi said the city should protect her where she was until she left of her own accord.
Kim Jong-hwan , who runs a small business, kept watch by day as well and livestreamed her almost every day. “I went to pass on information [to my followers], and after that I started observing her”, he said. “Watching her over time, with the water pumps being fired and then the nets, I came to find those things being done to her objectionable. So we ended up cheering her on.”
“She’s just an animal, and she came in by her own choice,” Kim said. “If it gets cold, if there’s no food, if the water doesn’t suit her, she’ll leave by herself. I’d like her to just be left alone, to rest there comfortably until then, and go.”

title: ‘We can go all the way’: Jonas Eidevall on life at San Diego Wave and lessons learned from Arsenal
description: The Swede’s team are second in the NWSL and, he tells Tom Garry, he hopes to create some special memories at their 35,000-seater Snapdragon Stadium
content:
The Swede’s team are second in the NWSL and hope to create special memories at their Snapdragon Stadium
“I love the ocean,” Jonas Eidevall says, and he references walks along the beach at Del Mar. “People are very relaxed, life is lived at a slower pace here. I’m a very simple person. I like to read a book, go to the gym and spend time with my wife and kids, that’s sort of all I need.”
The former Arsenal head coach is revelling in a calmer world as the head coach of San Diego Wave but it is not merely the beaches that are lowering his stress levels; his team are on a five-game winning streak in the NWSL and sit second in the table, one point off top spot, with two matches to go before the playoffs. Winning feels good and the club are targeting silverware, as he tells the Guardian: “It would mean everything. There are no guarantees in the playoffs, but the exciting part is saying: ‘We can also go all the way’ – that’s a possibility for us and we need to believe.”
Success did not originally look destined, when the Swede took charge 21 months ago, at a time when San Diego Wave were enduring something of an exodus of senior players; the United States defender Abby Dahlkemper’s sale to Bay FC in August 2024 and Alex Morgan’s retirement a month later were followed by the USA forward Jaedyn Shaw’s departing for North Carolina Courage and her international teammate Naomi Girma joining Chelsea in January 2025. A reconstruction was needed.
That is why, on a video call that winter, when Eidevall spoke to his players for the first time after taking charge, he began by quoting a proverb: if you want to go fast, go alone, but if you want to go far, go together. “My ideas are not worth anything if we don’t believe and buy into them altogether,” he says. “We focused everything on just building connections as human beings.” Detailed tactical discussions were initially kept to a minimum. They spent – as he recalls – around four weeks of their six-week pre-season focusing entirely on passing out from the back, to develop their style. Fast forward to the present day and it has paid off, with the Wave defenders Kristen McNabb and Kennedy Wesley being the division’s top two players for passes completed this season. More notable, though, has been the development of young players, such as the 18-year-olds Melanie Barcenas and Kimmi Ascanio.
“From 2024, when the club was not performing well on the pitch and it led to a complete rebuild, we had to find an edge, finding players that could fit into the way we wanted to play,” Eidevall says. “Back then it was a bit different to many other teams in the league, because the NWSL was seen as being dominated by athleticism and transitional play, which obviously then requires really fast players and maybe didn’t put a premium on technical supremacy.”
He adds that the club therefore eyed players who are “really, really good technically. We had some young, talented players already – that has given us a really good advantage because we’ve been able to develop players in a salary cap league. That’s huge, because if you only buy readymade players, you will run out of salary cap space pretty quickly.”
It is not just the salary cap that differs in the NWSL, compared to Eidevall’s previous jobs at Arsenal and Rosengård. The broad competitiveness of the American league means that, despite being second in the table, San Diego have lost almost as many games this season as Eidevall’s Arsenal across three English campaigns, and he says: “This was new for me. In European leagues the top teams very rarely go two games in a row without winning. Here, even the team that wins the league might go through spells where they don’t pick up points, so the way you handle those moments becomes very important.
“Training [here] is also a challenge – sometimes it’s very hard to get 22 players because you have a limited roster size. The moment you start to have injuries … there’s no real second-team academy system like we have in Europe, where you can always have the numbers that you want. Here you might not, here you would like to do something XI v XI, but you have 18 players and you just have to be creative with how you coach.”
Trying to play entertaining football has been a target in a campaign during which they have already set new club records for regular-season wins and goals scored. They have done it with the second-highest average possession share in the division, more shots on target than any other team and while facing by far the fewest shots on target.
“That’s the most pleasing part, results through an identity rather than getting results the other way around,” Eidevall says. “The identity we have is to allow the players to be creative.”
We are speaking around two years after Eidevall resigned as Arsenal’s head coach on 15 October 2024, following a disappointing start to that season. In his three full campaigns at the helm in north London he had won two League Cups, reached a Champions League semi-final and secured a second-placed top-flight finish in 2022 – but was unable to win the WSL. Reflecting on what he learned from that spell, he says: “We had a lot of fluidity with how our wide players could play in Arsenal, which at times created too few central options. So, how do we get better central connections? How do we get more players central on the pitch? That was a long-term reflection on my time at Arsenal. And that’s also led to some tactical changes that we’ve done here with San Diego.”
There is an aspect of his Arsenal tenure that he is determined to take inspiration from at San Diego, with his team having secured a home playoff quarter-final at their 35,000-seater Snapdragon Stadium.
The 43-year-old fondly remembers the first sellout crowd for a women’s match at Arsenal’s 60,000-seater Emirates Stadium, for their Champions League semi-final against Wolfsburg in 2023 : “We want to sell out Snapdragon Stadium and in order to do so we need to do exactly what we were doing at Arsenal – we need to create special experiences at the stadium,” he says. “That is what’s going to draw people into there. Yes, play exciting football, but we also need to play games that mean a lot to be there. The ripple effect of that, that’s so big.”

title: Bereaved civil service families could face ‘unjust’ tax bills due to pension scheme delays
description: MPs say ‘chaos’ at Capita-run scheme could mean some claims miss tax-free time limit on lump sum payments
content:
MPs say ‘chaos’ at Capita-run scheme could mean some claims miss tax-free time limit on lump sum payments
Bereaved families could face “unconscionable” tax bills because of “chaos” in the civil service pension scheme, the government has been warned.
Some lump sum pension payments to families are only tax-free if made within two years of a scheme being told of the member’s death.
MPs are now voicing fears that severe delays in the administration of the civil service pension scheme, which is run by the outsourcing company Capita , could push some families over that threshold. They would then be hit with a tax bill calculated at the recipient’s personal rate.
The families of more than 1,600 deceased civil servants have been waiting for more than 100 days for their “death in benefit” claim to be processed, according to the latest figures . Some of those have reported struggling to pay bills because of the delay.
The Conservative MP Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs the Commons public accounts committee (PAC), said: “The chaos currently engulfing the civil service pensions scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim.”
He added: “It is unconscionable that the families of loyal and dedicated civil servants, who are continuing to suffer through this serious government failing, could potentially face such an unjust financial penalty.”
The Cabinet Office, which is responsible for the pension scheme, said it was unable to prevent HM Revenue and Customs from taxing delayed claims, and that affected members would have to claw back the money by taking their case to the Pensions Ombudsman.
The ombudsman estimates an 18-month wait to resolve cases because of the volume of complaints from those affected.
The PAC has called for a change in legislation to prevent relatives paying the price for administrative delays.
The government has already been accused of letting down civil servants and their families by repeatedly outsourcing the 1.7-million-member pension scheme to private companies that failed to deliver.
The PAC last year urged ministers to take the scheme in-house after a previous contractor, MyCSP, was blamed for plummeting service levels. However, the £239m contract passed to Capita last December, despite concerns voiced by some that the company was inadequately prepared.
The Cabinet Office said it was confident that Capita would offer an improved service. It has since acknowledged that service levels were “unacceptable”. MyCSP and Capita were contacted for a comment.
In February, a dedicated email address was set up for unions to escalate cases of severe hardship caused by the delays. The cases referred included claimants at risk of suicide or of losing their homes.
Clare Norris has been waiting 11 months for the death benefit and pension payments she is due after her husband died last November.
“I was petrified – I am 52 and early death was not part of our financial plan,” she said. “Losing your partner is one of the most difficult experiences anyone can go through. The lack of clarity, communication and basic administrative handling from Civil Service Pensions has made it considerably worse.”
Capita said her case would be progressed under a new process. “It remains a high priority and the member can expect to hear on next steps as soon as possible.”
Under HMRC rules, in cases in which someone dies under the age of 75, tax-free lump sum payments must be made within two years, otherwise they will be taxed at the recipient’s marginal rate of tax.
The Cabinet Office said it was committed to ensuring scheme members were not left out of pocket. “We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure individuals do not experience delays,” said a spokesperson.
“If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses.”

title: Manchester City have been a joy to watch but they became detached from their roots
description: City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward
content:
City behaved much like other top clubs but their rule-breaking deserves to be punished. The Bundesliga, where members have a controlling stake, can show the way forward
D o we have to reassess Manchester City now? In my columns, I have repeatedly engaged with this club and its key figures. Looking back at what I have written over the years, I believe it remains beyond question that the team have achieved greatness. I always loved watching them: they were a true unit on the pitch, a finely tuned orchestra.
I would also write all over again that the conductor, Pep Guardiola, masters his craft like few others. I could recognise his teams even if they were wearing the wrong shirts and the game was broadcast in black and white – by the passes, the distances between the players and the intelligence of their interplay. It is no wonder Guardiola inspires others to become managers; look at Vincent Kompany, Mikel Arteta, Enzo Maresca, and perhaps some time Ilkay Gündogan and Rodri.
As a player and a columnist, I never had an issue with Manchester City – precisely because, for many years, the club avoided buying the most obvious superstars. Guardiola said it himself: the most valuable of the valuable do not go to a club such as City, who aren’t even the biggest football brand in their own home town.
Many became world stars in Manchester. Kevin De Bruyne had been discarded by Chelsea, Rodri’s true class was overlooked in Madrid for a long time, Gündogan’s career was on the brink after injuries, and most recently Gianluigi Donnarumma was no longer wanted in Paris. In Germany, City signed players from Hamburg, Frankfurt and Wolfsburg. Erling Haaland in 2022 was the first player they targeted who was also pursued by Bayern Munich. City did not operate like Paris Saint‑Germain did in the era before Luis Enrique.
From the outside, City fundamentally did not do much differently from the other 10 or so top European clubs. But what are achievements on the pitch worth if they are accompanied by rule-breaking? The club have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. It allegedly invested almost €1bn more than allowed and declared. The league leaders face potential forced relegation or titles being stripped. City continue to deny wrongdoing and are appealing against the decision.
It is right for the Premier League to crack down on unfair competition. I also appreciate that Germany is holding on to the 50+1 rule, which the federal cartel office recently upheld. It ensures that the majority of voting rights must remain with the parent club – the non‑profit section of a professional club. The exceptions that have applied to Leverkusen and Wolfsburg are under review.
The bedrock of our football culture is 50+1. This rule exists only in Germany, yet it speaks to a spirit that fits perfectly with the European sports model: 50+1 maintains a balance; on the one hand it allows for investment, on the other it guarantees participation. It strengthens the rights of members and fans. Perhaps it is because of this rule that the average attendance in Germany is higher than anywhere else in the world.
What is the ultimate purpose of football? It is a business, but its infrastructure is still developed by the general public. That is how I have always understood sport. Even as a professional, it was clear to me that my privileged life was made possible by many people working on a voluntary basis. Through my role as tournament director of the European Championship, these political connections have become even clearer to me.
The stadium and football clubs can remain the final places where people gather and society debates its issues only if the elite and the grassroots stay connected, and the public is involved in the process. Football must not be detached from its roots, as was the case with Manchester City. This becomes possible when rules are enforced by an institution. Ideally, not by a commercial entity but by a non-profit one such as Uefa.
In business, as in politics, I am observing a shift in mindset. Today, it is deemed necessary to invest in non‑profit institutions. More and more companies realise that football allows for a genuine exchange with the population – that it provides the perfect vehicle to set up corporate social responsibility projects.
This is what is needed in these politically turbulent times. In our fragmented world, political parties, churches and the media have lost credibility. In sport, however, people still come together. It is a tool to foster social cohesion. Therefore, I consider 50+1 to be a distinct competitive advantage for the Bundesliga.
I also welcome the fact that rules mean something in another case. Uefa is standing firm against Gianni Infantino , who recently wanted to privatise the World Cup and its profits. Along with his friend Donald Trump, he was seen by many as breaking the normal rules when Folarin Balogun’s suspension was lifted. The outcry from the global football community was loud, and it is possible that the Fifa president will fall.
When behaviour such as that in Manchester and at Fifa is punished, it is a good thing. Football must prevent questionable ideas from distancing it even further from its grassroots. Only then can it drive engagement in civil society, and only then can it strengthen Europe.
Philipp Lahm’s column was produced in partnership with Oliver Fritsch at the German online magazine Die Zeit .

title: ‘Sham tribunal’: one family’s battle with Louisiana’s ‘feudal’ eviction courts
description: In rural Louisiana, eviction hearings are held at kitchen tables and other unorthodox venues – and many justices have little legal training
author_name: Melissa Segura, Aliya Uteuova, Ana Lucía González Paz, Pablo Gutiérrez, Andrew Witherspoon, Angelica Alzona, Gail Fletcher, Michael Hudson, Cameron Armstrong, Mahesh Makani, Georges Lebreton, Izzy Kiff, Frederick O'Brien, Tom Richards, Oliver Laughland, Will Craft
content:
In rural Louisiana, eviction hearings are held at kitchen tables and other unorthodox venues – and many justices have little legal training
The eviction notice stuck to Lesley Wilson’s door, with two streaks of green tape and a hand-scrawled note, was left at a precise moment of crisis in her life.
It was April 2025 and Wilson, a 54-year-old mother of six, was living with her partner and her 11-year-old granddaughter named Kat in a stilted bungalow, surrounded by sugar cane fields and a small trailer park. She loved the peace and quiet of the place, about 10 miles from the rural city of New Iberia in southern Louisiana . A crawfish pond was a short walk away.
But the night before the notice was stuck to the door, her partner became abusive again, she told police. She called 911 multiple times, and she and her granddaughter cowered inside a locked room, according to interviews and her statement to police.
“It kept escalating and escalating,” she recalled. “And I don’t handle conflict well. My brain just shuts down.”
He eventually agreed to leave their home, a police report confirms. The following morning she obtained a temporary protective order to keep him away. As she returned from court, she was met with the eviction notice that Kat plucked from the door.
The handwritten note cited the reason as “disturbing the neighbors + fighting”.
Louisiana’s Violence Against Women Act , passed in 2015, limits landlords’ ability to evict victims of domestic violence, mirroring similar protections in federal law. But, Wilson said, despite her presenting the temporary order to her landlord, he made clear he wanted her gone.
“He told me he knew the justice of the peace,” she recalled. “And that: ‘All I’ve got to do is tell him what I want, and that’s the result I’ll get.’”
Three weeks later, Wilson arrived for her eviction hearing in Justice Patrick Broussard’s courtroom – the backroom of a small public library.
Across rural Louisiana, dozens of justices of the peace courts operate on the fringes of judicial formality. These elected justices, who are required only to hold a high school education and be of “ good moral character ”, are allowed by law to hold court in unconventional venues. They are required to complete 16 hours of training every two years. Many do not even comply with this basic requirement, a Guardian investigation has found.
Because operating expenses for these low-profile courts are paid with court fees, hearings can be held in almost any venue, except for those that sell alcohol . Living rooms. A spare bedroom. An old jailhouse. A small office next to a roadside daiquiri bar. A cellphone repair store. All have been used to hold eviction proceedings in Louisiana justice of the peace courts, according to interviews with 10 housing attorneys who have practiced within them.
The use of such venues “gives the signal to both parties that evictions are unimportant and uncomplicated legal proceedings”, argued Hannah Adams, a senior attorney at the National Housing Law Project. “But the stakes are so extreme for a tenant and these are often complicated cases.”
Adams is a former legal aid attorney in Louisiana and has fought evictions in venues including a pool house and a kitchen table. She described the process as “a real holdover from the feudal era”.
Documents released under a public records request reveal that dozens of justices mostly in these rural locations are failing to comply with their mandatory minimum training requirements.
For the past nine months the Guardian has been examining evictions in Louisiana’s justice of the peace system, which operates in every parish of the state except the city of New Orleans.
A handful of these justices earn hundreds of thousands of dollars a year via revenue from court filing fees. Critics argue the system is plagued with potential conflicts of interest and routinely denies tenants their rights to due process under the US constitution.
The majority of these courts sit in rural settings with lower populations, so most generate little income. A Guardian review found that 52% of Louisiana’s 390 justices declared less than $10,000 in fee revenue over the past decade.
Still, experts say, the conflicts of interest are baked into the system – they exist no matter how much money is made.
“Whether it’s a high-volume court or a low-volume court, the more landlords that file evictions, the more dollars go into the justice of the peace’s pocket,” Adams said. “It’s still extra money for the person who is supposed to be a neutral arbiter of these cases.”
Lesley Wilson’s hearing was scheduled for 4.45pm on 29 April last year.
She had found pro-bono legal assistance after the eviction notice was stuck to her door, a civil rights attorney named Donald Hodge.
She arrived at her local public library 20 minutes early and headed to the backroom that served as the courtroom. The corridor was daubed with canvases decorated with self-help quotes: “be humble & gentle”, “be patient & kind”. A librarian could be heard scanning books around the corner.
“It all felt illegal,” Wilson recalled. “I don’t know how else to describe it.”
As she waited inside, she spotted her landlord, named Steven Freyou, and Justice Broussard deep in conversation outside, she said.
“That’s not right,” she thought to herself. “That’s not how this should go.”
What followed, Wilson would later claim in legal filings, was a “sham tribunal”.
Justice Broussard sat behind a grey library table near a large US flag. “All rise,” his constable instructed the almost empty room. Wilson’s attorney, Hodge , listened in over the phone.
The justice first announced it was his intention to “wrap this up quick”, according to Wilson and Hodge’s recollection. It was his birthday and he had plans. It was also, the justice remarked, the first time he had ever presided over an eviction hearing where a tenant had secured a lawyer.
The grounds for Wilson’s eviction had now multiplied. Along with claiming she was “disturbing the neighbors”, her landlord was now also arguing that she had not paid her rent on time. This, Wilson said, was untrue. The cash-in-hand payments had always been delivered correctly, she claimed. Documents supported her: a petition of eviction signed by her landlord on 21 April recorded that “$00.00” rent was due.
The petition also stated her landlord was seeking eviction because her lease had expired.
To her horror, the court then called a witness. It was her ex-partner, who she now had a full restraining order against. He was invited to testify over the phone and supported the landlord’s claims that she and her ex-partner were behind on their rent, Wilson and Hodge recalled. His evidence was not sworn testimony, according to a lawsuit Wilson is currently pursuing in federal court.
“I was in shock,” she remembered. “Like, you’re really going to let him testify over the phone?”
At the hearing Wilson and her attorney also argued that her lease contained an unlawful clause that permitted eviction if law enforcement officers were called to the home.
But, as proceedings progressed, the lawsuit claims, Broussard “threatened” to charge Wilson three months’ rent as a bond if she appealed his decision and delayed the eviction. It was an amount she had no means to pay. She felt as though she was being bullied into submission.
After a few minutes weighing up her options she decided it would be impossible to stay in the house at this point, and asked Hodge to try to negotiate a deal. She was adamant she would not pay another penny in rent. After a 40-minute hearing, Wilson signed a “judgment of compromise” that compelled her to leave in a month’s time and forfeit her deposit.
It would not constitute a formal eviction, “but I was still being forced out,” she said.
The federal lawsuit that Wilson filed alleges she was harmed by violations of due process and seeks damages against Broussard and her landlord. It claims the agreement was “extracted by duress, by the threat of an unpayable appeal bond … by the admission of ex parte hearsay from her abuser, and by the deprivation of every procedural safeguard to which a litigant before a court of law is entitled.”
Hodge recalled in an interview: “There was no order. No rules. No procedure. No law.
“It speaks to why the justice of the peace system needs to be reformed,” he said. “Lesley is just one example of who this is happening to every day across the state. And most people don’t know their rights and can’t afford an attorney.”
Justice Broussard and the landlord, Freyou, did not respond to detailed questions from the Guardian.
In legal filings, Broussard laid out a lengthy list of defenses, including judicial immunity, and denied any unlawful conduct. He also claimed a lack of sufficient information to assess Wilson’s status as a survivor of domestic violence. His motions, which seek to have the lawsuit thrown out of court, were written by Louisiana’s attorney general’s office, which was representing him.
The landlord denied he violated any state or federal law in terminating Wilson’s lease, according to recent legal filings, which also seek to have the case thrown out. One document states Wilson’s lease was not ended “because she contacted law enforcement, obtained a protective order, experienced domestic violence or possessed any protected characteristic”.
Louisiana is among 17 states that allow judges, including magistrates, with no law license to preside over eviction hearings, according to research . The state mandates that all justices must attend a minimum of 16 hours of training every two years. Legal experts and housing advocates argue these basic training requirements are not enough to prepare many of the state’s justices to handle often complex areas of housing law.
A separate lawsuit being pursued as a class action in federal court in Louisiana argues the system routinely violates tenants’ due process rights. The case, which was filed by the Southern Poverty Law Center and the National Housing Law Project, notes that the state’s justice of the peace training manual contains just 10 pages on evictions “and does not include any relevant or even binding case law governing evictions”.
Justice Steven Sanders of East Baton Rouge, the named defendant in that litigation, acknowledged under sworn deposition that the training courses contain roughly “an hour and half of discussion” on evictions.
Despite these basic requirements, documents obtained by the Guardian under a public records request revealed that over a quarter of the state’s justices failed to comply with even these standards. An analysis by the Louisiana attorney general’s office, covering the years 2024 and 2025 showed that 98 justices and 142 constables had failed to complete mandatory training. The documents revealed that 37 of these justices and 52 constables had completed no training at all during that time period.
Broussard, a retired engineer who indicates online that he does not hold a law license, was among those listed as non-compliant, having attended only nine hours of training in two years.
“These courts are acting like their own fiefdoms, where they get to act with impunity and do not do the training they are required to,” said Micah West, a senior supervising attorney at the Southern Poverty Law Center.
The Louisiana attorney general’s office did not respond to detailed questions from the Guardian.
In the month after her case was heard in eviction court, Lesley Wilson scrambled to find a solution to impending homelessness.
She had been unhoused once before in her life, at the beginning of her last marriage when her partner lost his job and they lived together with their children in a tent for three months.
She always prided herself on being resourceful and working to solve problems in her life. Her only available option this time was to move with her granddaughter to the small, unincorporated town of Harwood in Texas and live with a friend, about 400 miles away from the rest of her close family. She borrowed money to rent a U-Haul, and put all of her belongings into storage: mattresses, bed frames, the balls of yarn for her crochet business, and her late daughter Kelsea’s ashes.
Wilson had become her granddaughter Kat’s legal guardian shortly after she was born. Kelsea, Kat’s biological mother, had died in 2018 after a fentanyl overdose at the age of 21. Kat had only been told about her birth mother two months before the eviction ordeal. She still calls Wilson “mom”.
They arrived in Harwood, a dusty railway town with a population of fewer than 200 people, and moved into a travel trailer that sat in the front yard. There was no running water. Electricity ran via a cable plugged into an outdoor shed, which frequently short circuited. It had only one bed.
She was able to get a job at a local Buc’ees, working a night shift at the bakery. The pay was decent, but the living situation became untenable within a month. They decided Kat would have to move in with relatives in New Mexico. Wilson would stay behind. It was the first time they had been apart in all of Kat’s life.
“I already felt alone,” Wilson recalled. “But now even more so. I just couldn’t see the way out. Every single thing that has happened in my life since is tied to that eviction proceeding.”
In 2009 a justice of the peace named Keith Bardwell from the rural parish of Tangipahoa caused outrage after he refused to conduct an interracial marriage , over four decades after the landmark US supreme court decision Loving v Virginia ended legal restrictions against people of different races being married. In a referral to the state’s judiciary commission, the ACLU of Louisiana argued that Bardwell’s “blatant bigotry poses a substantial threat of serious harm to the administration of justice” and highlighted he was “persistently failing to follow the law”.
The case was extreme, but Louisiana’s justice of the peace courts have faced recurring criticism for over a century. Ahead of a state constitutional convention in 1921 a local legal scholar named Edmond Bourgeois argued for complete abolition of the system, citing concerns over justices’ lack of legal training. In an article for the Loyola Law Journal , he wrote: “The procedure is a farce; the courts’ dignity a myth; justice is frequently absent; attorneys hold the courts in virtual contempt, and in some instances indignantly refuse to practice before them.”
Nonetheless, accounts from the time indicate that while the issue was considered, the lobbying in support of them “was too strong”.
The convention occurred at the height of Jim Crow segregation in the south, and was attended by only white delegates, who passed further laws to suppress black citizens from voting in the state .
The pro-justice of the peace lobby remains strong in Louisiana today. Along with voting earlier this year to expand the territorial jurisdiction of some high-earning justices, the Republican-dominated legislature passed a law in 2020 that exempted justices of the peace from mandatory retirement. While all other judges in the state must leave the bench when they turn 70, Louisiana’s justices of the peace can continue holding court at any age from 18 onward. A November “ Peace Talk ” newsletter published by the Justices of the Peace & Constables Association, announced the news under the headline “Mission Accomplished!”.
Last month, the state’s rightwing attorney general attended the annual justice of the peace convention and described their “vital role in serving our communities and upholding the rule of law”.
Part of Lesley Wilson’s salvation came in the form of a garden ornament. While scrolling online one evening earlier this year, she discovered a resurgence in the popularity of a beloved porch goose statuette and in particular the tiny custom stitched sweaters people were dressing their porch geese in. She put her crochet skills back into use, and started posting images of her unique goose sweater designs. They came in many colors and were selling for $50 a piece.
Wilson had spent eight months living in the travel trailer in her friend’s yard. But with the Texas winter setting in and no heating inside, the cold had begun to bite. She moved again to live with another friend in Colorado, hauling many of her belongings with her.
Two months later, Kat left New Mexico and rejoined Wilson in Colorado. They had been apart for more than seven months.
The funds from her increasingly popular porch goose knits had helped make it possible to think about moving back to Louisiana. She found a small place with two bedrooms and told Kat it was time to come home.
In May of this year they got the keys to their new rental unit, and spent two full days cleaning it out front to back. Wilson’s possessions were split between storage units in Texas and Colorado. Some items had been destroyed or damaged after a leak in one of the units; an antique mirror passed down between generations, a bedroom set now covered in mould.
“Unless you’ve lost everything, you just don’t know what it’s like,” she said.
After moving in, both were still sleeping on air mattresses as they waited for a final large delivery to arrive from Colorado amid persistent delays. The shifting timelines compounded her worry and triggered diverticulitis, a painful inflammation of the digestive system linked to stress.
One day in late August, the delivery arrived. There was one item she had thought about more than any other: Kelsea’s ashes, which she had left behind in Colorado.
She found them days later nestled in an unmarked box. She placed them on the kitchen counter and felt a moment of relief.

title: How the Guardian reported on Louisiana’s justice of the peace courts
description: Reporters scanned more than 11,000 pages and processed thousands of handwritten and often incomplete records
author_name: Will Craft, Tom Richards, Oliver Laughland, Melissa Segura, Aliya Uteuova, Ana Lucía González Paz, Pablo Gutiérrez, Andrew Witherspoon, Angelica Alzona, Gail Fletcher, Michael Hudson, Cameron Armstrong, Mahesh Makani, Georges Lebreton, Frederick O'Brien, Izzy Kiff, Sophie Sullivan
content:
Reporters scanned more than 11,000 pages and processed thousands of handwritten and often incomplete records
In Louisiana , justices of the peace are locally elected part-time judges who perform weddings and handle small claims, wage garnishments and, frequently, evictions.
They often hold court in ad hoc rooms around the state and, under state law, they are allowed to accept hearsay evidence. And importantly, for renters facing eviction across Louisiana , justices of the peace get to keep, as personal income, a portion of the money the court collects in fees.
Everyone who files a case in a justice of the peace court pays court fees. The judges then use the income from fees to run the court, pay constables and cover expenses. Whatever is left, the judge keeps as pay and reports on their annual financial statements.
At the start of this reporting project, the Guardian had questions about how these courts operate: How much have the judges collected in fees? How much are they paying themselves? How many evictions are the highest-paid judges handling?
Justices turn in sworn financial statements to the Louisiana legislative auditor, but the state does not put the data into any analyzable form. There are also no computerized records available to monitor what these courts are doing. Uncovering how this system operates took multiple different reporting projects, using a combination of software engineering, manual document processing, and a team of volunteers to process thousands of handwritten financial statements and more than 11,000 pages of court records.
After more than nine months of reporting, we uncovered a system that collects millions of dollars a year in court fees, much of it from poor tenants facing eviction, and a handful of judges who are earning hundreds of thousands of dollars from the fees they are collecting.
In the highest-volume, highest-earning court, we found a judge earning between $150,000 and $400,000 a year, overseeing a district with an eviction filing rate that is nearly three times the national average.
The only way that judges are required to report the fees they are collecting is by submitting annual financial statements to the Louisiana legislative auditor.
The statements are public records, and courts that earn more than $200,000 a year are required to report their earnings through a certified public accountant. The majority of the courts in the state, however, disclose their earnings through handwritten financial statements.
The Guardian digitized a decade’s worth of financial documents – covering roughly 3,400 sworn financial statements from 2016 to 2025 – to discover how much the justice of the peace system brings in and how much the judges are earning through fee income.
The reports were messy. The format changed year to year, the wording changed and most of the reports were handwritten. Justices also frequently failed to fill forms out correctly, and one version of the form did not require the justices to explicitly state the money they retained from the fees collected.
We tested several different AI toolkits to extract the data and digitize these documents, and settled on using Google Pinpoint, powered by Gemini. The data extracted with AI was a first step, but the results were a jumble and needed to be cleaned and verified.
Pinpoint by itself has limited functionality, so the Guardian made a custom Chrome browser extension to increase the usability of Pinpoint for data entry and verification. The modifications allowed us to more quickly automate the uploading and processing of the documents. The Chrome extension also modified the Pinpoint user interface to allow Guardian reporters and engineers to correct the data in Pinpoint, which then automatically populated a Google Sheet with the corrected data.
A team of seven volunteers manually verified and corrected every number extracted using AI. We also used a series of calculations to check for outlier figures that were the result of human error either by the Guardian or the justice filling out the paperwork. At least one volunteer eyed and verified every number, and we also double-checked the reports for each of the top 10 highest-earning courts. We tallied the total fees as well as the total the justices retained from these fees.
The Guardian calculated the likely salary for forms on which justices did not explicitly state the amount retained based on the fees and expenses listed. We used calculated salaries only for court and parish-wide totals. Any salaries listed in articles in connection with a single justice were verified and explicitly listed on financial disclosure forms.
Justices of the peace, in the highest-revenue courts, make the bulk of their money from eviction filings, but we do not know how many eviction cases they handle. They oversee a low-tech, ad hoc system, with little digitization and no way to publicly search for cases. No computerized records are kept, and there is no online docket to inspect. There are no lists of cases, which makes tracking evictions statewide impossible.
The Guardian team decided to focus on one court. We digitized a year’s worth of court records in the fifth justice of the peace court in Jefferson parish to count how many evictions occurred and track their outcomes. Reporters chose this court because it is the highest-earning justice of the peace court in the state.
Documents are stored in the courthouse, in dozens of bankers boxes. Reporters used a portable scanner to copy a year’s worth of eviction court records, covering 11,000 pages from June 2025 to May 2026.
After the documents were digitized, we wrote a series of computer scripts to use optical character recognition (OCR) and natural language processors to separate the pdfs and organize the pages into four groups: orders, judgments, writs and unrelated documents.
After the individual cases were organized, we scraped each case for information on the case and its outcome. Where possible, the computer scripts tried multiple passes over the same document for the information. In general the first pass was the most loose, using regular expressions and document cropping to capture the information. Where necessary, the scripts reran OCR. If the computer was not automatically able to capture case IDs, reporters entered the ID by hand.
Unlike the financial statements project, where we used AI to do first-pass data extraction, AI was only used to assist in writing the code to scrape the eviction court records. No AI was used in extracting or identifying data from the eviction documents.
After getting data out of the documents, we connected each order, judgment and writ by ID number in order to follow each case through the court system and determine the outcome.
We found that 41% of orders did not have a corresponding judgment and required hand classification. The presence of a judgment means that an eviction was heard in court. But eviction orders that did not have a judgment could only be classified by looking at the handwritten notes that the judge or clerk wrote on the order, as with this no-show case:
A team of three reporters and researchers classified 2,200 orders by hand and roughly 10% of the manual classifications were verified a second time. Every single denial was verified a second time.
We also identified landlords who repeatedly brought eviction cases to court, tenants who faced more than one eviction as well as rates of legal representation. We cleaned the list of landlords by manually creating a crosswalk between the dirty data and a cleaned list of landlords. It is possible that some may have been missed, so the cases per landlord are probably an undercount. We calculated the number of cases with legal representation by looking for eviction cases where the judge hand wrote “atty”, “esq”, “SLLS” or “SLLC” ( Southern Louisiana Legal Services and a misspelling of its acronym) on lists of defendants.
You can find some abbreviated datasets used in our investigation here .
