title: Austin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world title
description: The young Italian driver’s maiden championship is all but secured but Mercedes upgrades will inform next year’s run to the line
content:
Young driver’s maiden championship is all but secured but Mercedes upgrades will inform next year’s run to the line
There is nothing quite like a potential title decider to bring the fiercest of spotlights to bear as doubtless Kimi Antonelli will discover when he attempts to seal his first championship at the United States Grand Prix this weekend.
For the young Italian the goal is straightforward and the culmination of a childhood dream. However, for his Mercedes team there will be scrutiny over performance in Austin that has significant implications going into next season.
The 20-year-old Antonelli holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton is fifth or lower. It is not an entirely impossible scenario but even if he does not clinch the title in Texas, in all likelihood he will be crowned in Mexico a week later.
Antonelli has been exceptional in only his second season in F1, but also enjoyed what was for the opening half of the season an all but untouchable car. Mercedes can no longer boast that advantage. Max Verstappen has won the past two races as Red Bull’s upgrades finally unlocked the performance they felt was there to be exploited.
Ferrari, too, are now close to Mercedes, capable of beating them and have a raft of aerodynamic upgrades arriving in Austin. McLaren, having dropped back a tad in recent races, have repeatedly proved to have the measure of the championship leaders and have upgrades planned for the coming triple-header in the US, Mexico and Brazil.
Mercedes had not had it all quite their own way then when they brought their second and final improvements to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Yet an expected uplift of as much as three-10ths a lap was met with disappointment . The upgrades did not deliver as expected and the car became a handful to drive, gains in lap time unsurprisingly elusive.
The Mercedes is less forgiving, switching between understeer and oversteer in a narrow window, working the tyres harder.
Such was the discrepancy between what occurred on track and what was expected that after Malaysia they reverted to using the old spec on Russell’s car and the new one on Antonelli’s to better assess the issues at the following Singapore GP , after which the Italian felt there had been an improvement.
All of which is part of the development process, especially in a season of new regulations. But as the Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, noted these updates were not only intended to enhance and improve but were of paramount importance because they would inform next season’s car.
“Was it an easy car like the previous one? I don’t think it was. Does it have the performance that we were hoping the upgrade would bring? I don’t think so yet. But it was a step in the right direction,” Wolff said after Singapore. “In Austin, we should see whether we can continue to consolidate that and whether it has more performance, because it’s crucial for the development direction for the next year.”
While Malaysia and Singapore might be considered outliers, Austin is a typical circuit, with medium- and fast-speed corners on a flowing track where good balance and a quick, well-behaving car is rewarded – the type of track where Mercedes were in control for the much of the season.
That said, some at the team may be forgiven for experiencing a discomforting sense of deja vu. In each of the previous four years, with many upgrades not delivering as expected and in some cases setting the team back.
To be fair, Mercedes are far from such straits now and are still quick. Yet they have nowhere near the level of dominance they enjoyed in the 2014-2020 period when they remained all but untouchable and missteps along the way were almost unheard of.
At the time the opposition closed on them but in most cases that was because Mercedes were already switching resources to the following year, confident they were ahead of the game and in where they needed to go with next year’s model.
As this season draws to a close there is no such clearcut advantage. The frontrunners are all still feeling their way toward exploiting the maximum from the new regulations. The direction for 2027 is vital because the field is far more closely matched and developing at a fearsome rate, as Red Bull have demonstrated.
Mercedes’ lead this season is nonetheless formidable and while they cannot seal the constructors’ championship this weekend, Antonelli’s drivers’ title is surely all but done and dusted. Austin, however, might yet suggest whether they can repeat the feat in 2027.

title: ‘I never saw my son, until they handed him over in a bag’: inside El Salvador’s brutal crime crackdown
description: President Nayib Bukele’s campaign of mass arrest has been marked by allegations of torture and killing. Four years on, 120,000 people are still in prison
content:
President Nayib Bukele’s campaign of mass arrest has been marked by allegations of torture and killing. Four years on, 120,000 people are still in prison
At midnight on a Monday in December 2021, dozens of soldiers and police officers stormed into the home of Sandra Carolina Velasco Mena. They were looking for her 22-year-old son, Jefferson Alexánder Hernández Velasco.
“They wanted to arrest young people,” Sandra says. “Two of the policemen said it was because they were short of three people in their quota.”
The arrest came amid an intensifying crackdown on criminal groups in El Salvador, launched by Nayib Bukele, who won the presidency in 2019. For decades, the country of 6 million had been racked by extreme levels of gang violence, with its exceptionally high homicide rate at one point exceeding 100 per 100,000 inhabitants – the highest rate in the world outside a war zone.
Hernández was taken away. “They treated him like an animal,” says Sandra.
Homicide rates in El Savador had been falling, but in March 2022 an alleged truce between the government and gangs appeared to collapse when gangs reportedly killed 87 people in three days . Bukele responded by declaring a nationwide state of emergency.
What followed was an unprecedented campaign of mass incarceration. An estimated 90,000 people were arrested. About 120,000 people remain incarcerated – roughly 2% of the population, one of the highest rates in the world.
The crackdown has swept up tens of thousands of people with no proven links to criminal gangs, human rights groups say. The so-called state of exception allows the government to detain suspects for prolonged periods while curtailing constitutional rights. Thousands have been prosecuted for the vaguely defined offence of “unlawful association” in closed proceedings where evidence is kept under judicial seal and not made public.
Sandra insists her son is innocent and has no gang affiliation. “My son was a family man, very calm, very passive,” she says. “He worked on a farm where they cared for chickens. He loved soccer, and took care of his little brothers. He was a jovial boy.”
A judge ordered Hernández’s release at a hearing more than three years ago, she says, but instead of being freed, he was transferred to Cecot, El Salvador’s notorious maximum-security prison , the centrepiece of Bukele’s war on gangs. Sandra has not seen her son since.
“I don’t know what’s going on. We don’t have any communication with him, nothing. I don’t know anything,” she says.
Beatriz Magaloni, a politics professor at Stanford University and senior fellow at its Freeman Spogli Institute, says El Salvador has become a “carceral state of terror”.
“The atrocities are more than I ever expected,” she says. “The regime can perpetually condemn these people. There is no rule of law, no protection, it is really tragic.”
Bukele’s crackdown has also been marked by allegations of abuses, torture, sexual violence and beatings. At least 513 people have died under state custody during the state of emergency, according to Cristosal, a human rights organisation, while Amnesty International has said most deaths were of people who had not been not convicted of a crime .
Among them was Julio César Santamaría Flores, 32, who worked as a mechanic. His mother, Idalia Flores, 52, says he was arbitrarily detained on suspicion of gang affiliation on 1 December 2022. Idalia says she was initially told her son would be detained for 15 days, before being told his detention would last six months.
“My son was detained under the state of exception, arbitrarily detained, unjustly accused, of gang affiliation,” says Idalia. “I never saw my son again after he was arrested. Until they handed him over to me in a bag.” When she saw her son’s body, she says he had been “practically tortured”.
Behind the prison walls, former detainees describe a system of malnutrition, physical abuse, degrading conditions and torture.
Víctor Barahona, a journalist, was arrested in June 2022 during the wave of detentions, accused of illicit association. Before his arrest, he says, his life had been “joyful”. He spent 11 months and 12 days in custody, much of it in Izalco prison, which he describes as hell.
Barahona says he was also held in Mariona, or La Esperanza , prison where 230 men were crammed into a small cell, enduring degrading conditions. He describes most of his fellow prisoners as “innocent” and “hard-working people”.
“The guards tortured us psychologically and beat us constantly. They treat you like a rat, like garbage,” he says.
Detainees were denied medicine, deprived of sunlight, given just one glass of water a day and punished for worshipping, Barahona says. “When I was released, I had lost 80 pounds. I was malnourished. I had fungal infections. My health was very poor,” he says.
The scale of the crackdown has also raised questions about the incentives driving the arrests. Interviews with El Salvador’s police conducted by Human Rights Watch (HRW) found that officers faced pressure to meet arrest quotas, with those who fell short risking disciplinary action or losing their jobs. HRW says this pressure encouraged officers to accuse people of gang affiliation on the basis of flimsy or fabricated evidence, disproportionately affecting people in poor neighbourhoods who lacked the resources to defend themselves.
Barahona says an intelligence officer acknowledged the scale of the crackdown during his arrest. “Look, Don Víctor, right now they’re arresting everyone,” the officer told him, according to Barahona.
He also believes his work as a journalist made him a target. “I think my work made them uncomfortable. I think that is why they came to me. They did it to silence me, and they did.”
Almost four years into the crackdown, authorities have increasingly resorted to mass trials , trying hundreds of defendants at once by video link.
Defendants are unable to discuss their cases with their lawyers, says Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at HRW, while lawyers are prevented from calling witnesses and witnesses are threatened if they agreed to testify for the defence. “Defence lawyers also operate in a climate of fear, they too are sometimes threatened with being prosecuted or being surveilled,” she says.
“The whole process makes it impossible to separate the innocent from the guilty.”
Idalia Flores says she tried to build a case for her son’s innocence before his death, collecting documents to show that he had a life and livelihood unrelated to the gangs.
“I gathered information as best I could. Documents: proof of enrolment, receipts for [mechanic’s workshop] parts purchases, diplomas for the degrees he earned, the deed to the house where he lived, and letters of recommendation,” she says. “I presented all the evidence to prove my son’s innocence, but they disregarded the case entirely. He was treated like a criminal, despite having a clean record and all his documents in order.”
Yet Bukele’s crackdown has also brought him public support. Homicides have fallen sharply and the country has been transformed into one of the region’s safest. For many Salvadorans, the decline has brought a sense of security after years in which criminal gangs exerted control over neighbourhoods and daily life.
The fall in homicides has not prompted the government to lift emergency powers. The state of exception, initially presented as a temporary 30-day measure, has become a permanent fixture of Bukele’s government.
“This regime of exception is politically very profitable for him, because he can use this against anyone he wants. People are really afraid to express any dissent, any political opposition,” Magaloni says.
In 2024, Bukele acknowledged that 8,000 people who had been detained were innocent and had been released, but rejected estimates by human rights groups that 30,000 had been wrongfully arrested. He has responded to critics by dismissing them as “gang defenders”. The strongman has won the admiration of the Trump administration and conservative leaders around the world.
“I understand that those who commit crimes must pay the price. But not innocent people,” Barahona says. “Justice has been lost in our country.”

title: Stratford International on track to get cross-Channel trains in budget boost
description: Sadiq Khan says upgrade would unlock station’s potential and allow it to live up to its name and be truly international
content:
Sadiq Khan says upgrade would unlock station’s true potential and allow it to live up to its name
Stratford International train station in east London will receive funding in next week’s budget, according to reports, putting it on track to live up to its name and become a hub for cross-Channel services.
London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, has been making a case to ministers for funding to upgrade the station to allow it to start running international rail services.
Until now only domestic routes running to and from central London and Kent have stopped at the station, although Eurostar services pass through on the way to and from St Pancras.
Khan said: “We’ve been working closely with the government to make Stratford International truly ‘international’ for the first time – opening up new opportunities for jobs, investment and tourism, while connecting one of the UK’s fastest-growing economic centres directly to Europe.
“It’s time to unlock the full potential of this station and help write the next chapter in Stratford’s remarkable success story.”
Khan recently argued that growth in international rail travel and environmental concerns meant it would be better to improve Stratford International than expand Heathrow airport by building a third runway.
Stratford International would require a significant upgrade from its current two platforms to allow it to welcome international services, including adding a border post and security checks as well as a check-in zone, waiting area and facilities for passengers.
The work opening up the station and the mothballed international section of the station, including platforms and a waiting area, would cost an estimated £20m , according to the Standard. It reported Khan’s plan was for one in three trains to and from France to stop at the station, while it could also become a hub for rail services from the continent to the Midlands and the north of England.
The station, located close to the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, opened in late 2009 and was originally designed and built with the intention of handling Eurostar trains, but this was not fully developed.
The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly planning to greenlight the mayor’s proposal to create a business rate retention zone, according to the Financial Times, to help fund the station’s redevelopment. Such zones allow local authorities to keep all of the businesses rates growth collected in their area – rather than half of the rates collected, as is standard – to fund local regeneration directly.
In recent months, Virgin and other rail companies have been in talks with City Hall about operating future international rail services from Stratford.
Virgin is planning to launch rail services from London to the continent in 2030, bringing direct competition to Eurostar on the cross-Channel route for the first time since the opening of the tunnel. The operator has been granted access by the rail regulator to the track and to Eurostar’s nearby Temple Mills depot .
A spokesperson for the Virgin Group said the operator was “looking forward to exploring additional stops, including Stratford International”. They added that the company had been “actively engaging with stakeholders to explore future expansion” beyond its initial launch plans.
Gemini Trains, chaired by the Labour peer Tony Berkeley, is hoping to run trains to France, Belgium and Germany and has said it wanted to use Stratford as its London hub. However, it has not yet been granted depot and track access.

title: High School Musical review – Disney fave is sweet, slick and as squeaky clean as ever
description: Harry Judd is the coach while KayCee Stroh from the original movies is back to play a teacher in the hoop-shooting, pompom-waving romance
content:
Troubadour Wembley Park theatre, London Harry Judd is the coach while KayCee Stroh from the original movies is back to play a teacher in the hoop-shooting, pompom-waving romance
S ince soaring on screen 20 years ago, this Disney Channel favourite has cemented itself as a squeaky clean, painstakingly earnest but no less beloved descendant of Grease. Like Danny and Sandy, Troy Bolton and Gabriella Montez share a holiday romance and wind up at school together the following term, where the social pecking order initially keeps them apart. Driven by a shared love of singing, they defy conventions to end up together.
This new stage production, first seen at Salford’s Lowry, is directed by Hope Mill theatre founders Joseph Houston and William Whelton. No, it can’t escape the limitations of the story’s spectacularly two-dimensional characters, who are siloed into the camps of jock, brainiac or drama kid, and whose stock traits are indulged in the book by David Simpatico, but it’s bright and buzzy nonetheless.
The thrust stage of Andrew Exeter’s basketball-themed set positions us courtside, while Rory Beaton’s bright lights, Matt Peploe’s thunderous sound design and George Reeve’s videography – beamed on to screens surrounding the gym – help animate the spectacle playing out on court, where the school’s Wildcats team are shooting hoops and pompom-waving cheerleaders are drumming up hype.
It’s dizzying and dazzling – never more so than during the revival of Bop to the Top, led by Luke Bayer and Caitlin Tipping as siblings Ryan and Sharpay Evans, who are every bit as entertainingly grating as their screen counterparts. Aaron Renfree’s nimble choreography rotates montages from the all-important science competition, basketball game and musical callbacks, as Troy and Gabriella race against the clock to make it to auditions.
The headline names belong to the teachers: KayCee Stroh, who played hip-hop-loving Martha Cox in the films, is now over-the-top drama teacher Ms Darbus, while McFly’s Harry Judd plays austere Coach Bolton with brow-furrowed concentration.
As Troy and Gabriella, Tobias Turley and relative newcomer Leonor Correia bring a sweetness, but their chemistry is yet to fully bloom. Gabriella’s When There Was Me and You is, here, a duet sung by the pair of them in an arrangement that cops out of the high notes, but throbs with teenage longing. Breaking Free really does see them soar, albeit on a stiff-looking swing.
Still, if it skirts the ring more than it nets the ball, I suspect adoring fans won’t leave disappointed.

title: First Thing: Race for crucial midterms attracting vast sums of money on both sides
description: Billionaire Michael Bloomberg is spending $80m to help Democratic candidates, while Trump has promised Republicans $400m
content:
Billionaire Michael Bloomberg is spending $80m to help Democratic candidates, while Trump has promised Republicans $400m. Plus a vital investigation into justice in Louisiana
Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here
Good morning. Vast sums of money are being ploughed into November’s midterms , with the billionaire Michael Bloomberg spending $80m to help Democratic candidates, and Donald Trump announcing he intends to spend $400m to aid Republican candidates, with $300m already disbursed.
Bloomberg made the contributions in September and October, particularly focused on Democrats running to flip the US House of Representatives. Democrats believe they are favored to take back the House, though they’ve acknowledged trailing Republicans in fundraising. Republicans are also being aided by the president’s ally Elon Musk, who has spent $366m so far.
What are the main issues for voters in the midterms? In this explainer , Robert Tait looks at six key issues swaying how people might vote – the economy, Iran, immigration, Trump’s use of power, AI and datacenters and the state of democracy and voter rights in the US.
What is happening between the DoJ and California over voter rolls? The justice department’s list of suspected noncitizens in California includes a “high percentage” of people born in the US, Los Angeles election officials said . The statement, made in court papers, raises further questions about the reliability of the list of 20,000 people the DoJ is demanding be investigated.
What was strange about how the ADL reminded people about an antisemitic slur? The Anti-Defamation League ADL has denounced the use of the term “shylock” as antisemitic, without explaining that the slur had been used a day earlier by Trump in a speech in Kansas.
Some Republicans have spoken out against Donald Trump’s softening stance on Russia , threatening to pull financial support for his agenda over his handling of the Ukraine war. Don Bacon, an outgoing congressman in Nebraska, condemned Trump’s actions – which include an agreement to buy Russian diesel and pausing sanctions on Moscow – as “absolutely disgraceful” and accused the US president of cozying up to a “war criminal” in Vladimir Putin.
On Tuesday, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said his country was again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were seemingly suspended last week by the White House.
A sorority member at the University of Arizona has alleged she was sexually assaulted by two men at a fraternity house during a night of drinking in late August. The sexual assault allegations surfaced two weeks after the university had suspended activities for its 21 fraternities amid reports of misconduct, including assault, hazing and drug- and alcohol-related behavior.
What are the latest developments at Cornell University? The former Cornell University student who accused seven men of sexually assaulting her at a fraternity house in 2024 recently wrote a letter to campus faculty leaders saying that she felt “unsupported and disbelieved” by the Ivy League institution’s president.
Elon Musk has declared his support for combining the aerospace and AI company SpaceX with his electric vehicle company, Tesla. He said both companies had created special committees to explore a potential merger, but had not reached any agreement on terms of a transaction.
“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla merger is a certainty and I think that would be overstating it,” Musk said, adding it would require shareholder approvals and special committees at both firms.
Christina Applegate has revealed she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Having been an advocate for awareness of the condition, the actor said: “I’m back at square one – that I don’t know what’s going on with me.”
Australian MP Helen Haines has lost both legs after an alleged vehicle attack but “her heart and mind are in good shape”, her husband said. A man has been charged.
A judge has dismissed a sexual abuse lawsuit from Sam Altman’s sister. Ann Altman had accused the Open AI CEO of repeatedly abusing her decades ago.
The United Airlines CEO, Scott Kirby, is facing a rightwing backlash after calling for a nationwide US wealth tax.
A fifth foreign company has pulled out of a plan to build a cable car to East Jerusalem that threatens to involve the seizure of land and property rights from dozens of Palestinian families.
UK watchdogs have been urged to tackle suicide social media content after the death of girl, 14 . Adriana Retyte took her own life after viewing “high-risk” material on TikTok.
Although the “window has closed” on holding temperature rises to 1.5C, in line with scientific advice, limiting the “overshoot” of that target is still possible , according to the UN Environment Programme (Unep), which says the world needs to cut carbon emissions by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade to meet the goal.
It’s natural for reunions to trigger existential questions about how our lives have turned out, so Wendy Syfret has got experts and attenders to share how to go in prepared. We’ve also had articles over the last few days answering these two vital questions: is it true that you need to take 10,000 steps a day to be healthy, and should you store bread in the fridge ?
In Louisiana, justices of the peace pocket income directly from the filing fees charged to evict tenants. This Guardian investigation highlights an urgent, unconstitutional flaw in Louisiana’s legal system during a national housing crisis.
Julian Borger reports from Belgrade , where a mass student movement represents the most serious challenge Aleksandar Vučić has faced in his 12 increasingly authoritarian years in power. In the weekend’s parliamentary elections they hope to emulate the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary.
Failed rains and a dire El Niño are threatening the waterway that sustains Panama, with farmers left selling cattle to survive . They are also now lacking fresh water in Longyearbyen in Norway, thanks to contamination, where my colleague Karen McVeigh has visited one of the fastest-warming places on Earth .
Beatlemania may have been decades ago, but the Fab Four still have a magnetic hold on popular culture, especially in their home city of Liverpool. This new museum sounds like a “must see” for every fan , even if it requires a transatlantic crossing.
