title: Australia hoodoo continues as New Zealand pile on pain in Constellation Cup
description: Silver Ferns claim 12th consecutive win on home soil against Diamonds as Grace Nweke scores 49 goals from 52 attempts against world No 1 side
content:
Silver Ferns claim 12th consecutive win on home soil against Diamonds
Grace Nweke scores 49 goals from 52 attempts against world No 1 side
New Zealand have inflicted more pain on the under-fire Diamonds, pulling off a 62-50 triumph to maintain their perfect start to the Constellation Cup .
With Kate Moloney back from injury, Australia were determined to bounce back from an opening 56-50 loss in Auckland and end their five-year hoodoo across the Tasman.
The Diamonds cut an 11-goal deficit to three goals at the final break, but the Silver Ferns refused to relinquish their control over the netball world No 1 side in a highly physical battle at Christchurch’s Wolfbrook Arena on Wednesday night.
If coach Noeline Taurua’s New Zealand pull off a sweep of the four-game series it will mean Australia surrender top spot on the world rankings for the first time since 2013.
Grace Nweke (49 goals/52 attempts) was once again unconquerable in the circle, while the towering defensive duo of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger proved too difficult for Australia’s attackers.
Several players hit the deck during the tough tussle and the visitors gave away 84 penalties to New Zealand’s 53 in a desperate bid to force some turnovers.
The Diamonds started brightly, but made uncharacteristic mistakes to trail 17-14 at the first break.
Diamonds captain Liz Watson – playing as centre – was pinged for intentional obstruction after stepping into the circle as she tried to corral Maddy Gordon.
The experienced midcourter gave the ball away to Georgia Heffernan, and the Silver Ferns goal shooter converted easily to put the Kiwis ahead.
Watson was then warned for encroaching into New Zealand’s circle in the third quarter, prompting coach Stacey Marinkovich to bench her skipper.
With Amy Parmenter taking over as wing defence, Moloney’s influence as centre was felt immediately as the Diamonds claimed the third quarter 16-12 and reduced the deficit from seven to three goals.
So influential was Moloney that New Zealand’s Adelaide Lightning star Kate Heffernan was benched as centre in favour of Gordon.
Donnell Wallam also joined the fray in the final term to end her two-year hiatus from the national team and was tasked with helping Moloney complete the comeback.
The goal shooter could only manage seven goals from nine attempts as an under-pressure New Zealand adjusted aptly to contain the damage.

title: Gabby Thomas, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden and the doping tensions dividing sprinting
description: As women’s sprinting enters a golden era in the run-up to LA 2028, controversy surrounding a top coach threatens to overshadow the sport’s biggest stars
content:
As women’s sprinting enters a golden era in the run-up to LA 2028, controversy surrounding a top coach threatens to overshadow the sport’s biggest stars
W hen Olympic 200m champion Gabby Thomas came second at the recent track and field World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, she tried her best to be diplomatic: “I am an equal-opportunity doping hater,” she said. “If you are actively doping in sport, I do take issue with that. I’m not saying any names, no names are mentioned. But if you look at yourself and you think that’s what you’re doing, then so be it.”
Thomas then went out of her way to congratulate her compatriot Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, who finished ahead of her that day, aware of the territory into which she was straying.
Last year, Thomas posted on Instagram that “doping coaches should be banned for life from coaching in the sport.” Dennis Mitchell, who is one of the world’s leading sprint coaches, oversees Jefferson-Wooden’s training but had a long history of doping while he was competing. Most notably, he tested positive for testosterone in 1998, claiming the elevated levels were due to having sex four times with his wife the night before. He was cleared by USA Track & Field, but not by the IAAF and was banned for two years . He later testified under oath that his former coach Trevor Graham had injected him with banned human growth hormone. (Graham denied the allegations.)
Thomas and Jefferson-Wooden will probably represent Team USA at next year’s world championships, and then potentially compete to be the homegrown star of the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028. In that scenario, let’s just say that relay practice could be awkward.
Indeed, there is a brewing toxicity in the sprint world that may eventually rival the Ben Johnson-Carl Lewis clash at the 1988 Olympics, with the legally significant caveat that no one involved has failed any drugs tests nor is there any evidence they have taken drugs nor has anyone been officially accused of taking drugs. But the rumors, suspicions and bad blood are simmering just as they were in the two years running up to the Johnson-Lewis clash.
Throw into the mix that Jefferson-Wooden could soon smash the most controversial world record on the track – Florence Griffith Joyner’s 38-year-old 10.49sec 100m mark – and women’s sprinting is likely to be more talked about than at any time since that extraordinary Flo-Jo era.
Jefferson-Wooden is already the fourth-fastest women of all time – she ran the 100m in 10.61sec at the 2025 world championships in Tokyo. Last month in Budapest, she won the 100m at 10.62sec. But the two other athletes in front of her, other than Griffith Joyner, were aided by substantial (yet legitimate) tailwinds. Jefferson-Wooden, meanwhile, ran into a 0.2m/sec headwind in Budapest, meaning she could have come close to breaking Griffith Joyner’s iconic world record with a favorable tailwind. That would be a landmark achievement: there is widespread skepticism that the 1988 Olympic champion was clean. Griffith Joyner, who also still holds the 200m world record, died of epileptic fit at the age of 38. She never failed a drug test but her training partner Darrell Robinson said in a paid interview with German magazine Stern in 1989 that he had sold Griffith Joyner banned human growth hormone. Griffith Joyner vehemently denied the accusation and never failed a drugs test.
It wasn’t just Jefferson-Wooden who ran off with the prize money – she won $300,000 after claiming the 100m-200m double – in Budapest. Kenny Bednarek, another Mitchell-trained athlete, also took home $300,000 after winning the men’s 100m and 200m.
The issue for both of these athletes is not only that their coach, Mitchell, took drugs in his career. He has also been unfortunate in the company he has at times kept as a coach. His greatest success was guiding Justin Gatlin to world championship 100m gold in 2017 but that achievement was tainted by the fact that the Olympic gold medalist had served two previous doping suspensions, one for four years for testing positive for testosterone. Elite sprinting is a tight world of interconnectivity: Gatlin was banned while training under Graham, Mitchell’s own drug cheat coach in his competitive days. When Graham was banned for life as coach, Gatlin switched to train under Mitchell. (Gatlin has denied ever taking PEDs .)
In 2017 Mitchell and athletics agent Robert Wagner were filmed offering to supply testosterone and human growth hormone to a fake actor in an undercover operation conducted by the Daily Telegraph. Mitchell insisted afterwards that none of his athletes had ever taken drugs while Wagner said that they were playing along with the actors, who were pitching a film project. But Gatlin cut ties with Wagner and sacked Mitchell as coach.
More recently, the 2022 world 100m silver medalist Marvin Bracy-Williams tested positive for testosterone shortly after he joined Mitchell’s group and was eventually banned for 45 months. The United States Anti-Doping Agency confirmed at the time that it had been tipped off about Bracy-Williams’s drug taking and sources with knowledge of the case say the inside information came from within the Mitchell training group.
Mitchell’s lawyer, Ryan J Stevens, has told the Guardian that “Coach Mitchell is a different man than he was nearly 30 years ago. He’s committed to clean sport and strict compliance with anti-doping rules. He had absolutely no involvement in Mr Bracy-Williams’ personal choices that resulted in his sanction. Coach Mitchell insists on transparency, accountability, and integrity in every aspect of his coaching.”
The Guardian has contacted Jefferson-Wooden for comment.

title: ‘A powerful warning’: will Europe’s angry protests lead to real political change?
description: Hamstrung governments seem to have no answer to the public’s furious demands, making further discontent likely
content:
Hamstrung governments seem to have no answer to the public’s furious demands, making further discontent likely
I n France , it was the piles of wheelie bins stacked up against school entrances that first hinted at the scale of student anger over crumbling classrooms and teacher shortages. In Spain, it was a tent camp that steadily grew in the heart of the capital as residents railed against soaring housing costs.
Similar scenes have since sprung up in Belgium, Italy and Portugal , and clashes have convulsed Albania’s capital of Tirana, hinting at an autumn of protests across Europe.
Much of the news coverage in recent days has focused on the violence that played out on the fringes of the protests in France and Italy . The protests themselves, however, point to what seems to be a diverse response to a common crisis: the growing perception, particularly among younger generations, that governments are unable, or unwilling, to deliver when it comes to affordable housing, social equality and robust public services.
“This is the most powerful warning from Europe’s angry youth today, in France and across the continent,” the policy analyst Alberto Alemanno said.
The framing stands in sharp contrast to the many rightwing and far-right voices who have sought to exploit the violence in France and Italy, linking it without evidence to migration while brushing over protesters’ wider demands.
Officials in France have dismissed any link between the violence and immigration. The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, said on Sunday that the “unbridled violence” had been carried out by French people.
Alemanno, a professor of EU law at the HEC business school in Paris, said he had received an unprecedented number of calls from right-wing, xenophobic outlets in recent days, many of them seeking to fuel the idea of the protests as some sort of “pan-European revolt”.
It is a narrative that he describes as misleading. “The demonstrations have different causes and do not necessarily share political objectives,” he wrote this week . “Yet their rapid spread hints at a common weak point: too many young Europeans doubt that existing institutions can deliver the security, opportunity and voice they expect.”
The head of the Paris office of the European Council on Foreign Relations, Célia Belin, said some of those doubts were currently being reinforced in France.
“Faced with the high discontent of young people in high school, the government has no answer for them,” she said, citing an administration squeezed financially by a high deficit and debt-to-GDP ratio and limited politically by the country’s deadlocked parliament. “Basically the answer is: ‘There’s no money, there is nothing we can do.’ And that’s a huge problem.”
The view echoes that of the secretary general of France’s CGT union, Sophie Binet, after Saturday’s protests in which about half a million people turned up to rail against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services.
Binet condemned the violence, but she noted that the government had little choice when it came to quelling the protests. “Today’s mobilisation confirms the depth of the anger,” she said. “To get out of the crisis, there is only one way. Respond to the demands.”
Albania has also been shaken by mass student demonstrations for the past week after protests initially prompted by a proposal to build a resort backed by Donald Trump’s family.
In Milan, people took to the streets to protest against the rising cost of living, giving voice to the deep inequalities that now course through a city where an estimated one in 12 people is reportedly a millionaire .
In Lisbon’s Rossio Square, housing campaigners set up camp on Saturday surrounded by banners that read “homeless generation” and “I just want a home to live in” and vowing to stay on as long as possible. It was an echo of the protests that have sprung up in Porto in recent weeks as residents push back against housing prices that more than doubled between 2015 and 2024, rising roughly twice as fast as the EU average.
The managing director for Europe at the consulting firm Eurasia Group, Mujtaba Rahman, said what had burst into public view was not a single, coordinated European movement. Instead the events of recent days had laid bare a “convergence of distinct national protest movements”, each with substantially different triggers.
“What links them is a growing perception that European governments are unable to deliver affordable housing, functioning public services and economic security, particularly for younger generations,” he said, citing a growing gap between public expectations and governments’ fiscal capacity.
“This mismatch between political demands and economic reality is likely to remain and grow over time, which suggests further discontent and protests are likely over the medium term,” he said.
Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs and a former Spanish foreign minister, went a step further when asked this month about the similarities between the housing protests in Spain and the school protests in France.
“The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” she told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “Young French people are protesting for education, young Spanish people for housing, but in Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
In Portugal, the campers were dislodged on Tuesday, leading to a fresh call for more housing protests. Similar calls for protests in the coming days have been heard across France, Spain and Italy, hinting at the tremendous task that lies ahead for officials across Europe, said Alemanno.
“They must protect peaceful demonstrators, hold those responsible for criminal acts accountable, and address the underlying pressures, from housing costs and insecure work to strained public services and an uncertain technological future,” he said.
“Europe’s democratic institutions will be judged not by how forcefully they condemn disorder, but by whether they can turn generational anger into tangible political change.”

title: What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain
description: This summer alone, 26 local authorities in the UK had to stop accepting fridges and freezers for recycling. Now the appliances are piling up around the country – with no proper disposal date in sight
content:
This summer alone, 26 local authorities in the UK had to stop accepting fridges and freezers for recycling. Now the appliances are piling up around the country – with no proper disposal date in sight
N ot much is happening in the tiny Norfolk hamlet of Little Hautbois on the day I visit. The pub, once popular with airmen from RAF Coltishall, stopped being a pub a long time ago, even before RAF Coltishall stopped being RAF Coltishall. It’s not Saturday, so there are no weddings at Hautbois Hall. Nor is it 19 May, so the restless, headless ghost of Thomas Boleyn isn’t driving his carriage across the bridge over the River Bure, as he is said to do on the anniversary of the execution of his daughter, Anne. Today, a lovely autumn one, all is as it should be.
But half a mile down a narrow country lane is an incongruous and baffling sight: a strip of gentle hillside made up of large white rectangular blocks, piled up and sparkling in the sunshine. A glacier, you might think, if you were in Norway rather than Norfolk. (And ice is involved, as it happens.) As you get nearer, the picture becomes clearer; the blocks have coils on one face, doors and handles on the opposite one, plus the manufacturers’ names. It’s a glacier of fridges, more than 3,000 of them.
Kate Murrell, the assistant director of waste management at Norfolk county council, is here to let me in. The fridges are surrounded by a security fence with CCTV cameras. “It’s not what we want to see here, or what the local residents want to see either,” says Murrell. The nearest local resident, Stuart Brown, tells me over his garden fence that it is “a bit of an eyesore”.
These eyesores are not particular to Norfolk. All around the UK, old fridges are piling up, including in Nottinghamshire, Durham, Oxfordshire, Gloucestershire and Newport, the last of which found itself with a mountain of 80,000 appliances over the summer. So what is behind it?
In part, it is because fridges and freezers are difficult to dispose of. David Santillo, a senior scientist with Greenpeace Research Laboratories, based at the University of Exeter, explains that they contain gases and materials that are harmful to the environment if the appliances are not dismantled correctly. Thus, by law, fridges have to be dismantled at specialist processing plants. The problem is that the number of these plants is shrinking rapidly in the UK.
In Norfolk, a fire at an electrical waste and treatment facility in Thetford in April meant there was nowhere to recycle fridges and freezers for two or three months, which caused a pile-up. “If you got a new fridge and took the old one to the tip, they turned you away,” says Murrell. Then came this summer’s record-breaking temperatures, which caused more fridges and freezers to break down – and some processing plants to shut temporarily. As Murrell says: “During Covid, people upped their refrigeration capacity at home,” so there are even more appliances to deal with.
After the Thetford fire, Norfolk council ran out of treatment facilities to which it could send fridges. Thetford was one of just eight full-scale processing plants for fridges in the UK; another major plant in south Wales shut down when the recycling company Unimetals filed for liquidation and a plant in the West Midlands closed in February due to a fire. This summer alone, 26 local authorities had to stop accepting fridges and freezers. Compared with Newport’s 80,000 fridge mountain, this Norfolk site maybe doesn’t look so terrible, though the stark contrast with its bucolic surroundings certainly adds to the shock value.
“It’s nationwide,” says Jon Hubbard, the chair of the Local Government Association’s neighbourhoods committee. “I’m hearing more and more reports of councils struggling. In my own local authority in Wiltshire, I see large quantities of fridges and freezers piling up. It’s certainly not getting any better.”
Santillo says the main danger with these appliances is the refrigerants. “Lots of different chemicals are used as refrigerants. Very old fridges could contain CFCs, which are ozone-depleting substances. There are almost certainly going to be HFCs, which are potent greenhouse gases. Others will contain propane and isobutane. Commercial fridges can contain ammonia.”
Once removed and isolated, he says: “The refrigerants can be recycled and reused or, in the case of some of the old ones, they would need to be incinerated. Then you have the foams used for insulation, which can contain hazardous substances such as fluorinated compounds that also have to be recycled or incinerated.”
While some of the fridges at Little Hautbois are clearly quite old, others look pretty recent – in working order even. Murrell says they probably are. Often the fridges are disposed of because the owner wants an “upgrade, or it’s a new kitchen and they want one that fits in with this, not that”. Some just aren’t built to last or are impossible to repair.
Santillo says manufacturers could do a lot more to stop fridges and freezers needing to be disposed of. “They could find ways of making them last longer. They’re a significant investment and some of them aren’t very robust.” It doesn’t help that we no longer get things fixed. “The weakest link is always the compressor; once that goes, it becomes so expensive to fix that people tend to just get a new fridge.”
Hubbard points a finger in another direction – at the producer compliance schemes that coordinate the collection, recycling and disposal of fridges and freezers in the UK. The idea is that the polluter pays, but because treatment capacity has been hit so hard, producers haven’t been able to keep up, so councils are having to handle and fund the collection, storage and treatment of these goods. “We’re picking up the phone, and they’re not answering,” says Hubbard of the schemes. “They need to come up with a proper business plan to get back up to full-scale recycling again. In the short term, they need to come up with a solution to storage.” At the moment, this is also falling to local authorities. “It’s costing money that should be spent on libraries, sports centres, fixing potholes, delivering health and social care,” he says. Murrell says more help needs to come from central government: “What the country needs is a more resilient infrastructure to deal with fridges and freezers at the end of their lives.”
The other worry, says Hubbard, is the risk of fly-tipping when council disposal services are forced to halt. “Council-tax payers are being scammed by people who claim to be legitimate waste disposal organisations, collect your fridge and then dump it where they shouldn’t. And if that fridge can be tracked back to a resident, it’s the resident who gets prosecuted.” He advises people to take photographs of any disposal company’s licence.
And the piles of fridges building up? “Recycling fridges should be about containment,” says Santillo. “You have to take the refrigerant out, contain it, then that goes on for further treatment. That’s clearly broken down and they’re just being dumped. They certainly shouldn’t be left to fall apart and fragment in the environment.”
He has an additional concern. “If you have piles of fridges and freezers, they’re going to become home to wildlife; they’re great places to attract animals that like to live in small spaces.” Murrell says that here in Norfolk, pest control come in regularly and haven’t discovered any new residents, gnawing away at fluorinated insulation. But looking up at the kestrel hovering overhead, I wonder. I don’t think it’s after putrefied turkey twizzlers.
Norfolk is now accepting fridges, but only at seven of its 19 recycling sites, which is all that can be managed. “That’s a way of reducing the volumes we get in,” says Murrell. “Customers might have to travel a bit further and so think twice about disposal at the moment.”
A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs says these delays are “frustrating” and that the minister responsible for waste crime has written to producer compliance schemes asking them “to take all reasonable steps to fix this fast, as this cannot go on any longer”.
The spokesperson added: “We appreciate the challenges facing local authorities, and are working closely with them, the Environment Agency and industry to manage the impact of capacity shortages, including allowing temporary storage sites and looking at long-term solutions to ensure this does not happen again.”
In the meantime, the site here outside Little Hautbois is full, with no room for any more fridges. Nor are the ones already piled up here going anywhere at the moment, and Murrell is not hopeful that this will change any time soon. “Until we see national capacity really increase, councils like us are going to see disruption to the services. I think this one’s stuck for quite a while.”
Chances are then that next 19 May, when Thomas Boleyn comes riding through with his phantom horses and carriage, he’ll look to the side of the road and think: “What an eyesore!”

title: Florida gambling helpline director sentenced to nearly 10 years over $1.4m theft to fund addiction
description: Philip Sullivan, who sought to rebuild his life after gambling addiction, convicted of stealing from real-estate employer
content:
Philip Sullivan, who sought to rebuild his life after gambling addiction, convicted of stealing from real-estate employer
A Florida man who stole more than $1m from his employer to bankroll a gambling problem – before becoming the director of his state’s gambling addiction helpline in trying to make amends – was recently sentenced to nearly a decade in prison.
Bay county, Florida, authorities charged Philip Sullivan in March 2024 with stealing $1.4m from the Panama City Beach real-estate company for which he was the chief financial officer, Royal American, as local news outlets WMBB and WJHG had previously reported.
An internal audit revealing numerous company credit card transactions that were unauthorized thrust Sullivan under scrutiny. He ultimately pleaded no contest to a half-dozen felony charges of grand theft on 16 October, when the Florida state judge Timothy Register adjudicated him guilty and sentenced him to nine years, eight and a half months in prison, court records show.
Character witnesses on behalf of Sullivan asserted in court that he developed a gambling addiction after being prescribed the pharmaceutical stimulant Adderall around the time of the thefts. In March 2025, a year after his employment with Royal American ended, Sullivan became the director of 888-Admit-It, the Florida Council on Compulsive Gambling (FCCG)’s hotline, according to his page on the professional networking platform LinkedIn.
Sullivan, 43, appeared on the Addicted Recovery Show podcast a little more than a week before his sentencing and described his role at the FCCG helpline, which he undertook as he sought to rebuild his life in the wake of his criminal charges.
He said the helpline positioned him to speak with more than 460 people with struggles similar to his.
“It’s hard not to feel a certain way about gambling when it’s not only your account – but you talk to other people and you see … the pain that it’s causing them, too,” Sullivan – whom Register ordered to pay restitution – said on the podcast.
“I’m incredibly thankful for that opportunity. It has given me greater purpose than I feel like I’ve ever had in my life.”
On the podcast, Sullivan also recounted how he progressed from $25 sports bets to wagering $50,000 at a time – and losing more than $2m through gambling.
He said he was grateful his wife had stuck by him through his legal issues – and discussed how they would ready his sons, ages 12 and six, for the prospect of their father being imprisoned.
“We just have to prepare them for me being gone,” Sullivan said, becoming teary-eyed. “I can’t have them go to school that day [of the sentencing] wondering if … I’m going to be home.”
Sullivan was remanded to state custody after his sentencing hearing to begin serving his punishment. He received credit for 40 days he spent incarcerated between the time he was charged and when he made bail to await the resolution of the case from out of custody, court records show.
He has 30 days to appeal his sentence, WMBB reported.
The Guardian has requested comment from the attorney listed for Sullivan.
The National Council on Problem Gambling estimates that about 2.5 million adults annually meet the criteria for a severe gambling problem in the US, where commercial casinos as well as online betting and prediction markets are multibillion-dollar businesses. It estimates another 5 million to 8 million US adults would be considered to have mild or moderate gambling problems.

title: The best gifts for nine-year-olds, picked by nine-year-olds and parents
description: Popcorn makers, Lego Fortnite and the coolest water bottle around … surprise the mini tween in your life with our pick of the top gifts and toys
content:
Popcorn makers, Lego Fortnite and the coolest water bottle around … surprise the mini tween in your life with our pick of the top gifts and toys
The start of the tween years, nine years old, is a sweet spot between curiosity and growing independence, making it a fun, though sometimes tricky, age to buy for.
Kids at this age are up for a challenge, whether that means trying a trickier craft set, playing a more complex game or stepping up their sporting interests. Pitch a gift right and you’ll not only get the whoop of joy when they first receive it, but something that will hold their interest and help them develop their skills, interests and hobbies over time.
As an experienced toy tester, I have dedicated a lot of my career to observing children play. I’ve worked in schools as a teaching assistant and in children’s publishing, where knowing what makes children tick is essential. I also have three children of my own, so I understand what works on home turf once the gift-opening frenzy is over. When researching for this article, I aimed to strike a balance between children’s outlandish wishlists (one Christmas my son asked for a ghost for his present) and what a parent wants in their home (not a ghost).
I spoke to a lively gang of nine-year-olds with varied interests and hobbies who were only too happy to shout over each other about what they want for Christmas. I also checked in with their parents on the gifts that got their seal of approval – and offered long-term value – and spoke to childhood play experts about the best presents to suit this stage of development.
Testing primarily took place at home with one nine-year-old tester, with additional help from their friends. I also spoke to other nine-year-old children and had gifts sent to them for testing and feedback, so it wasn’t just one kid’s opinion. I noted the child’s initial reaction, how they used a toy and whether they returned to it. After testing, we had a lot of surplus toys in our house, so anything that could be donated went to the Salvation Army, which sells preloved items to raise money for its work.
“I want a game called Mexican Train dominoes. I played it with my older cousins on holiday, and it was fun,” says one of my nine-year-old testers. This game was pretty fast-paced and was easy to pick up, with some strategy when we played it. Players build their “train line” by matching tiles up to a central hub – but you can sneakily block each other’s play. “Peer-based play is really valuable for nine-year-olds,” says Laura Moore-Williams , an early years consultant. “Children value being part of a group at this age. More advanced games, team sports and long-term creative projects give them a sense of belonging and achievement.” This set comes in its own box, making it easy to take to their mates’ houses.
Materials: resin, plastic, wood, metal tin Suitable for: 6+
“I would like some really good colouring pencils. I’m really into comics – I started a comic club with my friends. And I’m trying to get my artwork better. I think colouring pencils might help my drawings look more grown up,” says one nine-year-old tester. Whether they’re into comics or other creative projects, a decent set of colouring pencils is a great open-ended gift for kids of this age. I spent a long time sitting with my tester, colouring side by side using these pencils. My nine-year-old loved how softly they glided across the page, and how they produced smooth, even shading. The non-slip surface is comfortable to hold for extended periods; there’s a great range of colours; and they’re made from a durable wood-based composite containing upcycled wood chips from PEFC-certified forests.
Materials: wood, oil, pigment, binder, wax Suitable for: 6+
“I really enjoyed doing this hanger project,” says one of my nine-year-old testers. “I did sewing in school on a project last year, and wanted to do more.” This little kit is an ideal party bag gift or rainy-day project to have in your back pocket for kids of this age. It’s not too prescriptive as there’s no set design, so it requires the child to work out what they want to create first. I found this called for gentle assistance when my tester tried it – although my ideas for letters or nature scenes got vetoed in favour of a Minecraft Creeper. Whether you get roped in or not, it’s a nice way to develop fine-motor skills for nine-year-olds working towards their pen licences at school.
Cotton Twist make your own stitched banner decoration
Materials: cotton, metal, wood Suitable for: 5+
I was stuck in a battle between my nine-year-old wanting to listen to music independently and my desire to keep them screen-free. Then I found the Mighty 3, and it has kept us both happy. It may remind some of the iPod Shuffle – it’s a tiny box you can upload music to and then whack your headphones into. My young tester has loved developing the art of playlist curation, poring over Spotify for hours with parental supervision. You then upload these playlists on to the Mighty using its app (Spotify Premium account required), and you’re ready to go. It has transformed long car journeys and even an 11-hour flight, and my tester has enjoyed the independence and grownup feeling it’s given them. It is worth noting that Mighty will stop supporting Spotify from April 2027 and only be compatible with Amazon Music.
Materials: plastic, electronic components Suitable for: 8+
“I love Lego and Fortnite,” says one enthusiastic nine-year-old. “This Lego is absolutely perfect!” Kids at this age are able to focus on longer-term projects – especially if they catch their interest. This is a good option even if they don’t yet play Fortnite but know it’s “cool”. My tester and I spent many happy hours sitting side by side building this set. The recommended age is 10+, but my nine-year-old relished the challenge. You end up with a toy (there are a generous nine minifigures in the set) that can be played with or put on display.
Water bottles are a big deal to kids – they’re a way for them to show off their personal style at school, where they’re otherwise in uniform. Many nine-year-olds are desperate to feel more grown up, and Owala’s FreeSip for adults won my best water bottle tests earlier this year. On a practical level,it’s durable, easy to use and (less important for the nine-year-old, but key for the adult) easy to clean. This is a smaller version of my winner, which makes it lighter for kids to carry around all day. The different colourways available allow for self-expression, and they’re popular, so they’re a big tick in the “trending” box.
Materials: BPA‑free Tritan plastic, silicone, stainless steel Suitable for: 3+
“My friends all play with Tech Decks at school during playtime,” a nine-year-old tester told me. “They’re so cool. You can learn tricks. And they fit in my pocket for school. I really want some new ones for my collection.” This enthusiasm for a finger skateboard might mystify adults – myself included – but nine-year-olds seem crazy for them. This set is a good place to start – there are various “ramps” you can invest in later if you want. This set comes with six boards, 20 wheels and four trucks, plus stickers. My tester enjoyed customising their boards with the trucks and wheels included (they’re interchangeable) and spent a long time trying to master tricks; I live in hope that this transfers to a love of actual skateboarding.
Materials: plastic, metal Suitable for: 6+
My nine-year-old tester loved this instant camera. They snapped photos, printed them off and coloured them in or stuck them up around their bedroom. The camera feels grown up but still has a foot in the “toy” arena. The Photo Creator is similar to the Fujifilm camera our 11-year-olds rated, but it’s less pricey to run for impulse-driven nine-year-olds as it prints on rolls of paper rather than Instax film. As it’s technically a thermal printer, it only prints in black and white, but there are kid-friendly filters they can put on the photos and an all-important selfie lens.
Materials: plastic, electronic components Suitable for: 8+
“I love this mini record player that really plays music,” one nine-year-old tester told me. “You can build up a mini record collection with the surprise balls.” (The balls in question are plastic spheres that have collectible items inside – in this case teeny records – and you don’t know which ones you’re going to get before you open them, which apparently adds to the fun.) Every child who came across this record player seemed totally transfixed. “It was the biggest hit for my daughter,” one friend told me. “I love that she’s listening to records – I hope it’ll get her into vinyl.”
Who knows if it’ll stick, but the delight of playing a record was palpable with my nine-year-old tester. It comes with one record – APT by Rosé and Bruno Mars – and you can add to your collection with the capsules , which are £15 for two capsules with four records each. Put a record on the turntable, and the record player will play an extract of the song using chips to trigger digital playback. I only wish I could play my vinyl on it – but alas it’s not compatible with standard records.
Materials: plastic, electronic components Suitable for: 3+
“We have family game nights at home, and I’d like a more grownup board game now I’m nine,” my tester told me. Kids at this age have a better understanding of cause and effect, helping them think critically and solve problems. “Valuable play for children aged nine includes social games for interaction,” says Sydney Piercey, former au pair and nanny, and author of Sustainable Play . Risk ticks all of those boxes, and should see them through game nights into adulthood. Wannabe despots can conquer territories and control the world by deploying armies, attacking opponents and forming temporary alliances. Fair warning though: nine-year-olds are probably going to need an adult or two to play with them to explain and supervise gameplay.
Materials: cardboard, plastic Suitable for: 10+
“My brother got a circuit set for his birthday, and now I want one too. I want to make the ultimate circuit that does loads of cool things,” says my nine-year-old tester. This set should cater to their every wish, with 175 different projects. You simply link the components together to make various circuits that do exciting things – the glow-in-the-dark fan was a favourite with my tester. Instructions guide you through simple circuits, but during testing I noticed how quickly kids of this age learn and experiment. It quickly felt like a miniature version of the Blackpool Illuminations had been created on my dining table, and when a circuit didn’t work, my tester did some problem-solving. I just sat back and became the battery supplier (unfortunately it rinses through them at an alarming rate – and they’re not included).
Materials: plastic, metal, electronic components Suitable for: 8+
“I love getting new pyjamas,” says my nine-year-old tester. No matter your age, a new pair of PJs rarely misses if you’re looking for a good gift. These by Polarn O Pyret are the best pyjamas I’ve found – and my research has been extensive. They’re made from organic cotton and are just the right weight for all but very warm weather. Plus, they wash so well – I’ve put pairs through so many cycles, and they haven’t faded, but the cotton softens beautifully. The foldable cuffs are designed to let the PJs grow with your child, the stripes are a crowd-pleaser, and they’re available in several colours to keep everyone happy.
Materials: organic cotton Suitable for: 1+
“Everyone in my class has been reading this book, and I want to get into it,” one nine-year-old told me. Diary of a Wimpy Kid is a great book for kids of this age as the format – drawings, onomatopoeia bubbles (eg “Boom!”) for making sound effects, and short chapters – makes it accessible. The story follows relatable but hapless Greg as various annoying (yet funny) things happen to him at school and in his family life. It made my nine-year-old roar with laughter. It’s quick to read, but this is the first in a lengthy Wimpy Kid series.
“My child enjoyed GraviTrax marble runs well below the recommended age … he continues to play with it aged 11,” says Daisy Upton, play specialist and author of the Five Minute Mum book series. These sets are brilliant for nine-year-olds who like to problem-solve and get creative in a hands-on way. The SkyTrax is a newer addition to the popular GraviTrax range, and allows builders to create complex marble runs that change levels, flip the marbles and spin them around. I found it almost dizzying how fast the marbles fly around the track. It’s definitely more complex than any other marble run I’ve tested, but a great “next step” for nine-year-olds who enjoy this kind of play.
Materials: plastic, metal Suitable for: 8+
“Movie night just got so much better,” whooped my nine-year-old tester when we fired up this popcorn maker. Many niche kitchen appliances feel like a bit of a novelty (we looked at chocolate fountains and slushie makers too), but this gadget felt exciting to use – my young tester loved watching the popped corn pouring out of the canister – and it gets plenty of use in our family, where popcorn is a movie-night must. This maker works without oil, which was a nice bonus for me.
Materials: metal electrical components, plastic Suitable for: 8+ with adult supervision
If you’re still stuck for an idea, an experience gift is great for a nine-year-old. They’re old enough to enjoy the anticipation and start to accept that “things” aren’t everything. It’s possible to buy vouchers for theme parks such as Legoland, and for other activity experiences. I took a nine-year-old to Legoland recently, and they completely embraced the day. They were able to tolerate queueing and were tall enough for all the rides. Otherwise, Virgin Experience Days offers a wider range of activities such as treetop adventures, theatre tickets and crafting days.
“The key developmental needs of nine-year-olds are building confidence, identity, teamwork and deeper problem-solving skills,” says Moore-Williams. “They’ll be interested in group games, coding and tech, creative expression (art, music, writing) and competitive sports. Toys I really rate for this age group include advanced Lego sets, Stem kits like Snap Circuits and coding robots, strategy games, arts and crafts kits and sports equipment.”
Kids of this age are able to dive into more complex play – and are desperate to do so and feel more grown up. They want to be challenged by trickier craft kits and board games, and many will enjoy more complex imaginative play too – character-based figures might scratch that itch well. All these types of play can give them a sense of achievement and boost their self-esteem and resilience. “So much holistic learning and development can be supported through opportunities to play games together in groups,” says Moore-Williams.
The experts I spoke to all acknowledged children’s need for sociable play with their peers. Getting them active with team sports or games is important at this age. More than one expert recommended buying a ball for a nine-year-old – they’re versatile for so many different types of play and easy to take around with you. “A small football is portable, sociable and can be played independently and together,” says Piercey.
Many of the nine-year-olds I spoke to mentioned an experience gift. There is a good variety to choose from, including theatre vouchers, an annual pass to an attraction and days out. Some parents I spoke to asked people to contribute towards sports-club membership as a gift too. While this may not have the immediate “play” factor, it should make the recipient feel seen and supported.
A Noble Gift lets you bid on experiences such as being a football mascot or tickets for kid-friendly concerts (though be warned, some are very pricey), with the winning bids going to charity (an additional platform fee applies). If you have something specific in mind, you can always contact the organisation to see if they will allow you to do something with them, even if it’s not readily available as a voucher.
For more, read our guides to the best toys and gifts for eight-year-olds , the best toys and gifts for seven-year-olds and the best sustainable toys for kids
Zoë Phillimore is a journalist with 20 years of experience. She’s tested many things, from mattresses to makeup, and she’s slightly obsessed with finding small new businesses to spotlight. Aside from this, Zoë loves travel, being outside – especially on the beach – and finding screen-free things to keep her three very active children busy. She shares her discoveries on Instagram

title: Troy Aikman and Joe Buck: what next for the NFL’s $165m TV power couple as they head for a split?
description: The duo have carved out lucrative and successful careers as TV audiences elsewhere are falling. It seems they won’t be together for much longer
content:
The duo have carved out lucrative and successful careers as TV audiences elsewhere are falling. It seems they won’t be together for much longer
T roy Aikman knew when it was time to go. His aching body made the decision for him when he ended his NFL career in 2001. A quarter of a century later, with one of the top quarterbacks of the 1990s established as half of the pre-eminent broadcasting duo in American sports, his potential exit from the booth is not so clearcut.
Aikman clearly feels his voice remains in fine working order, but his bosses at ESPN may not agree. The color commentator’s Monday Night Football play-by-play partner, Joe Buck, is reported to have agreed a new deal with the network worth $108m over six seasons (his previous deal was for five years at $15m a season), yet Aikman has claimed ESPN does not want to renew his contract.
The longest-running television broadcast partnership in NFL history looks set to end once ESPN broadcasts the Super Bowl in February. It would be Buck and Aikman’s seventh Super Bowl together. After that, Aikman’s existing five-year, $90m deal expires.
The prospective rupture is another tremor shaking the NFL’s media landscape only shortly after another ex-Cowboys quarterback turned high-profile TV personality, Tony Romo , was dropped by CBS. The network formally parted ways with the 46-year-old on 2 October, a month after he pleaded no contest to a civil charge of driving while intoxicated in Wisconsin in July.
Adding to the intrigue, Buck and Aikman argued at SoFi Stadium before the Los Angeles Rams hosted the Buffalo Bills on 12 October after Buck broached the matter of the contract-related tension between them, according to Front Office Sports .
The murky situation is an unwelcome distraction seemingly of its own making for ESPN, which will produce and show a live Super Bowl for the first time next year at SoFi. It wanted hype ; now it has hoopla. If Aikman’s version of events is accurate, it’s surprising the company would consider terminating the partnership having earlier this year hailed a “surge” in viewership that “coincides with the Buck-Aikman era”. ESPN representatives did not respond to a request for comment, but the network has previously said it “won’t be addressing talent contract specifics publicly before the Super Bowl”.
Aikman has been less reticent about giving his side of the story. He essentially confirmed the Front Office Sports report in an interview with a Dallas radio station, 96.7 The Ticket: “There’s probably a time and a place for all that to be discussed. I don’t know if now is the time. I don’t know that it’s hard to figure out kind of what’s happened. I’ll broadcast through this season and I’ll be a free agent at the end of the year and kind of see what happens. I’m looking forward to whatever the rest of this year does hold with the Super Bowl and all that and where my next landing spot might be.” He added to Underscore that he expects ESPN to “go in a different direction”. That is a logical assumption: why else enter negotiations with Buck during the season but not his partner?
It could also make sense for Aikman to advertise his imminent availability to alert potential suitors and perhaps galvanize ESPN into making a late offer to keep him away from the competition. But publicly airing his disquiet also seems characteristically on-brand for a man who has built a reputation for candid analysis since swapping the field for the booth.
A Hall of Famer, Aikman retired after guiding Dallas to three Super Bowl titles in 12 seasons. (True fact: the Cowboys used to win things.) He teamed up with Buck at Fox Sports in 2002 and cosplayed as Mr T when the network announced its new “A-Team”. Aikman and Buck loved it when a plan came together for them to jump ship to ESPN in quick succession in 2022, with Buck traded for the rights to a college football game. They have since broken the longevity record held by Pat Summerall and John Madden and brought stability to what was once a problem position for ESPN.
Buck, a 57-year-old NFL and MLB media veteran who is the son of the beloved late St Louis broadcaster Jack Buck, is steady, authoritative but unobtrusive. Aikman, who turns 60 next month, has remained perceptive long after his playing career ended. He has also had many plays in his business portfolio over the years: car dealerships, co-ownership of a Nascar team, a light beer brewery in Dallas and a minority stake in MLB’s San Diego Padres. He’s also been an informal consultant to the Miami Dolphins.
Star broadcasters command similar salaries to elite players and attract similarly feverish examinations of their performances, contract status and potential free-agent destinations. Fox Sports handed Tom Brady a 10-year, $375m contract in 2022 – inflating the market and presumably informing Aikman’s opinion of what his services are now worth – though the fast-evolving broadcasting landscape makes future negotiations hard to predict.
The rise of streaming services has led to more games on more platforms. Unlike when Aikman retired from playing at 34 after concussions and back injuries, he may not be short of suitors. Calling Thursday matchups for Amazon Prime would not carry the same prestige as Mondays on ESPN, though the viewing figures are similar. Amazon may be ready to freshen up its act, given that its lead commentator, Al Michaels, is nearly 82 and the analyst Kirk Herbstreit’s job security is reportedly tenuous . Netflix is streaming five games this season.
Among the legacy giants, CBS promoted former Houston Texans star JJ Watt from its No 2 crew to replace Romo. If it concludes that the solid but relatively inexperienced Watt isn’t ready for primetime, the network may be interested in Aikman as a permanent successor to Romo, who was its lead analyst since 2017.
There’s a lot at stake. Viewing figures for live televised football remain extraordinarily resilient in the era of on-demand streaming and social media. Advertising inventory for the Super Bowl sold out in August , while last season Monday Night Football averaged 15.8 million viewers over 21 games – ESPN’s second-best set of ratings for MNF in the 20-year history of the show at a time when TV audiences in general are plummeting. But anything that damages the product and turns off viewers – a new pairing who don’t have the chemistry and credibility of Buck and Aikman, for example – is a problem, considering the increasingly marginal economics of the media industry.
ESPN completed its acquisition of the NFL Network in January , with the league taking a 10% equity stake in the broadcaster. It pays the NFL $2.7bn a year in rights fees. But estimates suggest that ESPN’s reach via traditional bundled services has roughly halved over the past 15 years from a peak of 100 million households. Over that time, rights fees nearly doubled . And the league wants another huge increase for its next deals .
Half the customers and twice the cost (or thereabouts): it’s not the makings of a viable long-term business in any sector. And other strategies in the cord-cutting era – job cuts, launching on-demand streaming services , embracing betting , more intrusive and pervasive advertising – haven’t come close to replicating the lucrative success of the old-school cable and satellite subscriber model.
The old certainties no longer apply, whether in the boardroom or on the air. One source of intrigue over the next couple of months is whether the teamwork of Buck and Aikman, as professional as they are, is perceptibly affected as the season’s climax and the likely end of their partnership looms. But nothing seemed out of the ordinary on the broadcast Monday when the San Francisco 49ers beat the Washington Commanders.
Buck stressed his friendship with Aikman, and the importance of getting along, in an interview with the Associated Press in 2023. “I think you need to put as much work on the personal relationship as you do the professional. I don’t know that everybody does that,” he said. “I know a lot of stories of broadcast partners that have been together for a nice chunk of time that didn’t really enjoy being with each other. I just can’t imagine being in that situation in this kind of a job when you’re relying on each other in front of millions of people live.”

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: cream blush sticks for every skin type
description: With new shades and formulations, the latest cream blush sticks are eminently wearable
content:
With new shades and formulations, the latest cream blush sticks are eminently wearable
T here’s something so irresistible about cream blush sticks. The fact that one can scribble on and smoosh in the instant appearance of good health makes sticks a practical handbag essential that ticks off both lips and cheeks.
Whereas previous incarnations were broadly samey and could mostly be differentiated by colour alone, the new crop includes a formulation for any skin type – even oily.
Milk Makeup built an entire brand on easy, “back of a taxi” application sticks of cream colour. And so the new reformulation of their push-up bronzers, contours and blushers brings the excitement of a full relaunch. The opportunity wasn’t wasted. The new Lip & Cheek Blur (£24) is not for me, but it’s absolutely for someone blessed with some natural oil in their cheeks who might previously have struggled to make cream blush stay on. Shade, a very pretty brownish mauve that (it must be said) looks very similar to Merit’s popular Bespoke, is gorgeous and blends out softly with either fingers or brush.
Speaking of Merit (its Flush Blush creams are among the most popular out there, after all), Jones Road’s recently dropped Blushing Sticks (£30), feel and look pretty identical, so if you love those, you’ll love these. The shades are very different and, as is typical of Jones Road, very easy and wearable. Bare is a suits-everyone rose that gives a flush of good health on any skin tone.
Kosas’s recently launched Impressionist Multisticks (£32) are emphatically for skins, tastes and temperaments able to handle shiny, glassy colour that will probably need topping up in the afternoon. But one application of Nuance, a muted, pinky beige, and another of Intuition, a dusty shade of pink, had me fully on side. The shades here are exceptionally well chosen and hard to find elsewhere. The finish catches the light, but not in a year 9 school disco way – this looks healthy, carefree and chic.
My most worn of the lot has been Bobbi Brown’s Skin Enhancer Multi-Stick (£29), specifically Beach, an irresistible warm, toasty brown with a hint of pink that resembles – in the best possible way – slightly sunburnt skin. The formula is one of the brand’s best in a while – less shiny than the Kosas, but with more slip than the Milk Makeup and with a wear time that sits somewhere between the two. It can be daubed on carelessly, and the moisturising formula won’t rip up any foundation or powder you’ve laid underneath.

title: Cyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’
description: As she auctions off her treasures, the synth-pop savant opens up about her eccentric style and why she doesn’t believe in cancel culture
content:
As she auctions off her treasures, the synth-pop savant opens up about her eccentric style and why she doesn’t believe in cancel culture
B efore Cyndi Lauper rose to fame as one of the most singular pop breakouts of the 1980s, she was queen of the cash register at the edgy Manhattan boutique Screaming Mimi’s. The vintage emporium is still a downtown staple, but a little of its spirit comes uptown this month with Cyndi Lauper: A Suitcase of Memories , a two-part auction of her fashion and personal items at the New York auction house Bonhams.
On a recent Thursday morning in New York , the singer is sporting seafoam green hair and is in good spirits as she leads a private tour of the collection. It is an Aladdin’s cave of outfits from her five-decade career, with clashing prints, jutting tutus and statement headwear in every color you can imagine. As she strides around in her platform creepers, she gives a few final notes to the Bonhams team. Is that rainbow fan at the right angle? And can we confirm that more mirror balls are on their way?
“Over there is my grandmother’s pyjamas,” she says, walking over to a mannequin that displays the leopard print sleepwear Lauper wore in the Girls Just Want to Have Fun video . The ensemble was originally purchased from her family’s favorite mail order catalog. “Frederick’s of Hollywood gave people in Queens a glimpse of glamor and sexiness,” she says. “You know, they’re flannel pyjamas, but come on – they’re leopard!”
Born in Queens, Lauper was raised as part of a large family who worked in New York’s Garment District as cutters and seamstresses. After leaving home at the age of 17 armed with not much more than a toothbrush and a copy of Yoko Ono’s book Grapefruit, she honed her eclectic style while working at Screaming Mimi’s in between singing at downtown local clubs.
“I went to art school but I didn’t finish,” Lauper says. “So what happened is this, I guess.”
Lauper captivated a generation with performances which combined music with art and fashion, selling more than 50m records. Her fantastic debut She’s So Unusual became the first debut album from a woman to produce four top-five singles upon its release in 1983. Hits like True Colors and I Drove All Night followed, as well as new ventures: she co-founded the True Colors United foundation in 2008 to benefit homeless LGBTQ+ youth and, in 2013, won a Tony award for her Kinky Boots score.
After retiring from live performance last year, Lauper says she is enjoying the chance to take stock. Leading us past the metal bra and headdress from her True Colors video and a red plaid dress she wore to the inaugural VMAs in the early 80s, she seems nostalgic for the freedom of the decade. “It was a time where there was a little bit of a wildness,” she says. “We’ve been corporatized – we kind of have braces on our brains. You know, it would be nice if you could think for yourself sometime.”
As well as ephemera such as handwritten lyric sheets, the exhibition features a Raggedy Ann doll from the Girls Just Want to Have Fun video and a multi-colored spotted couch that could have come from the set of Pee-wee’s Playhouse. “I did this to inspire people,” Lauper says of the show. “To inspire us who are older to remember the individuality of creativity, and to inspire the young to discover that creativity is individual.”
Lauper is a great storyteller – I could listen to her anecdotes for hours – and as no-nonsense as you might expect from a born-and-bred New Yorker. As we admire the singer’s newspaper skirt from her True Colors album art, a guest asks Lauper if she worried that the fragile-seeming skirt would fall apart. “What do you mean? No,” she replies crisply. “It was a photoshoot . I was good.”
Last year, Chappell Roan wore a replica of the newspaper skirt while inducting Lauper into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Lauper says that Roan is the one of the few current stars whose creativity she relates to.
I can see that with Roan’s edginess and use of color. “It’s not just that,” Lauper tells me in a conference room later that morning, adding that she sees songs like Pink Pony Club as landmarks for LGBTQ+ representation. “It’s how she wrote about a lifestyle and made it normal. And then the clothes, sure.”
In 2022, Lauper released a new version of her abortion rights song Sally’s Pigeons to protest against the US supreme court overturning Roe v Wade. “If we don’t have control over our own bodies then we have no real freedom,” she said at the time. “We need to mobilize. We need to let our voices be heard.”
She sees the exhibition as coming at a “great time to have people inspired and come alive again” as the midterms approach. Despite gentrification squeezing out artists from the city, she says “the good news is that, because of Mamdani, the billionaires might be moving out, giving us our city back.”
In 2023, Lauper gave her blessing for Nicki Minaj to sample Girls Just Want to Have Fun in a song from Minaj’s Pink Friday 2 album; Lauper joined her on stage for a performance a few months later. Given Minaj’s recent alliance with Donald Trump, does she feel differently about the collaboration now?
“No,” Lauper says flatly. “First of all, I don’t believe in cancellation. And second of all, the fact that she did Girls Just Want to Have Fun musically – it’s a political thing anyway, babes.
“Girls just want to have fun. They’re entitled to a joyful experience in this world. Like it or not, we’re here. We’re not going out in the rice fields any more. Yes, rise up and put your foot down, and she did. I don’t know what she’s doing now. But I still don’t think you cancel people, because otherwise there’s no room for discussion.”
Lauper says that she learned the importance of breaking bread with those across the political spectrum through her advocacy work. “If you want people to listen to you, you need to listen to people,” she says. “If you don’t let people evolve, what are you doing?”
The exhibition shows how Lauper’s own tastes evolved too. In the 90s, she became increasingly drawn to sculptural pieces from Vivienne Westwood and Alexander McQueen , styling designer pieces with a DIY twist. For 1994’s Twelve Deadly Cyns album, she paired an electric blue Dolce & Gabbana shrug with a bowler hat that she spray-painted and decorated with feathers to match. “I wanted it to look like art,” she said, pausing by the ensemble as she wraps up the tour. “I remember that because it was another invention.
“That’s what makes it exciting,” she says. “That a young person would look and go, ‘I could do that.’”
Cyndi Lauper: Suitcase of Memories, Part I is a live auction at Bonhams New York on 22 October. Part II runs online until 23 October

title: After three disastrous years, Israel needs to rethink itself. A new government would be a start
description: Only a clear opposition victory would let us begin to heal, strengthen democracy and establish Palestinian rights, says Dahlia Scheindlin, a Tel Aviv-based political analyst
content:
Only a clear opposition victory would let us begin to heal, strengthen democracy and establish Palestinian rights
Dahlia Scheindlin is a Tel Aviv-based political analyst
I srael’s 27 October election is fast approaching, with little clarity about who will win. But Benjamin Netanyahu is more likely to lose . His polling is poor , and the fractious opposition parties may yet find a way to form the next government.
What would such a government do? Most of the Zionist opposition parties, the frontrunners to lead such a coalition, have offered bromides about good governance and unifying the country. Others have focused on more specific plans to establish a state commission of inquiry into the government’s failures around the attacks of 7 October 2023, and end the exemption from military service enjoyed by most ultra-Orthodox Jewish men.
But if a new government truly plans to build a better future, Israel needs more profound changes. Simply ousting Netanyahu will not be enough.
The two issues the opposition has highlighted are understandably important to Israelis. For so many citizens, the disaster of 7 October and subsequent two-year hostage crisis became a crisis of faith in the state itself. Without accountability through an independent inquiry, society cannot move on. And even staunch supporters of peace cannot tolerate the rank injustice of some citizens serving and dying in wars while others are systematically let off the hook.
But what then? Israel’s war in response to 7 October has continued to devastate Palestinian society. But the past few years have damaged Israel internally as well.
Social solidarity in Israel is abysmal . Hundreds of thousands of reservists have served for months, interrupting their studies, family life and income. Up to 30,000 people have been wounded, according to Israel’s ministry of defence .
Meanwhile, the current government has slashed social-service budgets in favour of defence spending. The psychological toll is immense, yet Israel had a shortage of psychiatrists even prior to the war . Dr Graciela Cors, a youth and child psychiatrist, told me: “The mental health situation is catastrophic, and so are the social systems that are supposed to support mental health, like outpatient clinics and Kupot Holim [Israel’s state-mandated health funds].”
These problems are urgent, but addressing them would amount to damage limitation. Without deeper change, better-funded services and greater conscription would do little more than help Israel cope with the next round of seemingly endless wars.
Israel desperately needs to confront the factors that brought the country to this point to begin with.
Before Hamas’s attack, 2023 was already the year these long-festering problems burst into full view. Society was torn apart by two unreconciled, deeply interconnected questions: what kind of democracy Israel should be, and what is the future for the Palestinians?
Historically, Israel has demonstrated a flawed, ambiguous commitment to democracy . It avoided writing a constitution, and has no law that explicitly guarantees equality to all citizens. But over roughly the past 15 years, that ambiguity has given way to a full-blown assault on democratic institutions. Attacks on the judiciary came from top governing officials , culminating in Netanyahu’s government’s plans in 2023 to drastically weaken judicial independence .
That top-down assault fell on fertile ground because of a deeper problem: the erosion of democratic values, shaped in part by education. Or Kashti, the former longtime education correspondent for Haaretz (where I also write), told me that the seeds of the judicial assault are found in the new civics textbook adopted in 2016 . He has traced a shift from vague treatment of democracy in earlier decades, to what he describes as “indoctrination”, with greater emphasis on Jewish identity and state power . This is a thin and misguided view of democracy, one that risks elevating the will of the majority above all other democratic values.
The curriculum can also be alarmingly parochial. Kashti says that history matriculation exams focus on the second world war and the Holocaust, the wars of modern Israeli history and the establishment of the Zionist movement. “All other topics in history of the world are marginal,” he says. Religion, he adds, infiltrates unrelated subjects. “In geography or weather lessons, children are told to learn the prayer for rain. What’s the connection between prayer for rain and a lesson on geography and climate change?”
This narrow conception of democracy helps explain how, in 2022, half the country elected parties that sought to hobble judicial institutions as part of the coalition government’s programme. And when education gives barely any attention to human rights, civil liberties and the equality of all citizens – it becomes easy to see why Palestinian self-determination has dropped off the Israeli agenda entirely.
For decades, Israeli society has increasingly acted on the assumption that Palestinians could be contained through military force or control. In the years before 7 October, most Israelis saw no contradiction between democracy at home and their active military occupation regime effectively ruling over all Palestinians, without giving them rights or representation.
Netanyahu’s current government has pursued the logical end of occupation – permanent annexation , ever-expanding settlements and ethnic cleansing. To do that, the government had to destroy the final guardrails on its power. The 2023 assault on the judiciary finally galvanised many Israelis, who feared that their own liberties were under threat. Massive protests followed, plunging the country into prolonged social turmoil.
No Israeli government can offer a different future without fundamental and comprehensive change on these deepest issues. What is needed is a fundamental reassessment of the country’s entire social ethos.
The good news is that such change is absolutely possible. Education curriculums can be rewritten to embrace the principles of a modern liberal democracy. Teachers, politicians and even religious leaders can embrace human and civil liberties, minority rights, checks and balances, good governance and the universal values that too many Israelis disdain today. Societies and people can change.
In such a society, it would be the occupation, rather than democracy, that would become an unsustainable affront to the values of Israel. This is a long way off; the current opposition leaders demonstrate no vision leading to such an outcome, and change is needed much more urgently. Israel’s right wing and many ordinary citizens, shaped by years of fear, would fight any change favouring Palestinian independence. But without embarking on the path, the country will never get there; needless to say, Palestinians will never be free.
None of this will transpire if Netanyahu wins or if Israel’s elections yield a stalemate. But an opposition victory should be the day when the hardest, yet most hopeful, work will begin.
Dahlia Scheindlin is a Tel Aviv-based political analyst and author of The Crooked Timber of Democracy in Israel
