title: A student protest movement has gripped Serbia for two years. This weekend it will try to take power
description: Unorthodox campaign is challenging the ruling party’s 12-year reign with a bold democratic experiment
content:
Unorthodox campaign is challenging the ruling party’s 14-year reign with a bold democratic experiment
O n a cool autumn evening, a team of Serbian student volunteers went canvassing in the housing estates of Krnjača, a Belgrade suburb. They were equipped with lanyards emblazoned with the word “victory”, a stock list of questions and a mobile app that mapped visited homes and the level of support in each.
The volunteers were part of a mass student movement, Student List, that has rocked Serbia with two years of constant protests. On Sunday, the group will represent the most serious challenge Aleksandar Vučić has faced in his 12 increasingly authoritarian years in power, by putting forward their own candidates in parliamentary elections.
They hope to emulate the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán , in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, in a domino effect that could bring a democratic resurgence to central Europe.
Opinion polls have varied wildly, but many expert observers say a close race is quite possible, with neither side prepared to accept a loss as a legitimate result, raising the risk of post-election unrest and clashes.
In order to win, the students’ list of 250 candidates would have to break the mould of Serbian politics, along with Vučić’s grip on the country. He stepped down as president last month, five months before the end of his second and last term in office under the constitution, but only with the aim of extending his hold on power as prime minister at the head of his Serbian Progressive party (SNS).
In the section of the suburb assigned to them, law student Zak Veličković and campaign photographer Danijela Radojković were welcomed with overwhelming support. Apart from a small handful of polite doorstep rejections, from those claiming they had no interest in politics, people seized the opportunity to air their grievances.
Most promised their vote and a large minority offered help: some taxi drivers with flats in the low-rise apartment blocks said they would help ferry voters to the polling stations.
“Turnout is the key,” one said, adding: “Orbán fell with 80%” – a reference to the Hungarian elections in April .
Veličković began each conversation by asking what was the biggest problem in Serbian society, a query that often raised a laugh and replies such as: “How much time do you have?”
Corruption was the most frequent single complaint. On the corruption index run by Transparency International , Serbia ranks far worse than any of its neighbours, as the most corrupt country in Europe bar the dictatorships in Belarus and Russia.
There are frequent allegations of links between the SNS and organised crime, and the Student List’s slogan confronts that widespread perception head on, posing the question: “Serbia or Mafia?” The government denies all accusations and officially claims to be tackling organised crime.
The key local issues in Krnjača were the poor repair of the road bridge linking the suburb and central Belgrade, and the sewage system, which repeatedly fails in heavy rain, despite a personal promise by Vučić, who residents said had visited a few years earlier, to fix the problem.
The economy has been growing in recent years, but there is a widespread opinion that the fruits are not being fairly distributed. Porsche and Land Rover car showrooms have been established in Krnjača but public spaces look neglected. Some of Belgrade’s trams are more than 50 years old.
It was a major infrastructure failure that sparked the student protests – the collapse of a concrete canopy in Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, killing 16 people. Evidence pointed to botched modifications made during refurbishment work, but so far there has been no official finding on the cause, and no official has been held accountable.
When Belgrade students blocked a road in a vigil for the victims three weeks after the disaster, they were attacked by a SNS mob and the protest movement went nationwide.
The students initially distanced themselves from opposition parties and avoided any kind of hierarchy or conventional leadership structure. That was partly an ideological choice and partly practical. The SNS and state-run media rule in part through smearing opponents and the student’s collective approach offered fewer targets.
Vučić rose to prominence in the 1990s as a radical nationalist, who supported the policies of Serbian expansion and ethnic cleansing led by Slobodan Milošević, who died of a heart attack in detention in The Hague during his trial on charges of genocide and crimes against humanity committed in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo. He served as Milošević’s information minister throughout the Kosovo conflict. As president, Vučić has not emulated his predecessor’s militarism, but he has maintained his nationalist playbook in domestic politics, dismissing the opposition as stooges of unspecified foreign powers.
So far those well-worn tactics have proved ineffective against the students. A survey published in July by a Serbian pro-democracy group, the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) and Stanford University showed significantly more support for the students (45%) than for the SNS (36%), but that was well before Vučić announced his resignation on 27 September and his election machine went into top gear. Other, more recent domestic polls show the SNS in the lead, though the pollsters in question are seen by the opposition as pro-government.
Vučić himself shows signs he is taking the political threat seriously enough to throw himself into the campaign, making 129 live television appearances in August, more than four times the previous month’s total.
“Serbia has been an electoral autocracy and in electoral autocracies only ruling political parties can win,” Raša Nedeljkov, CRTA’s programme director, said. But he added that the status quo was now in jeopardy.
“What we are seeing in the past days, weeks, months, is that strength; the homogeneous government that Vučić used to have is no longer there. He is faced with a completely unorthodox political actor and the toolbox that he has improved over the years since he came to power is no longer effective.”
Unable to crush the students by force, division or denigration, Vučić gambled, announcing his resignation as president and calling snap elections, in the apparent hope of catching the students off guard, but they responded by improvising a democratic experiment.
The 250 candidates were mostly nominated by university faculties (there are more than 160 doctorates among them) with a sprinkling of farmers and other professions, and each candidate was subject to approval by plenary sessions of the student protests.
The policy platform has also been decided by plenum, with the result that divisive issues, especially foreign policy, have been played down: the question of future EU membership has been left to a referendum and Kosovo is claimed as an integral part of Serbia.
One of the chosen candidates, Milica Jovanović, an assistant professor at the University of Belgrade, argued the List’s lack of political experience was not necessarily a drawback.
“We are political amateurs, but we are experts,” Jovanović said. “We are people who have led projects, led organisations, led our community, and actually I cannot see that we can do worse than these politicians … The only thing that matters is willingness to improve something, expertise to actually do it and support to do the actual change.”
The Student List is pitted against the political monolith of the SNS, in power for 14 years and with control of the state apparatus. It has accused the foreign ministry of rigging the diaspora vote by keeping polling stations open where support for Vučić is strong, such as the Serbian part of Bosnia, while closing them in parts of North America where the opposition could expect to perform well. The ministry did not respond to a request to comment.
The SNS grip on national media is meanwhile evident everywhere. A CRTA survey in September found that 69% of air time on Serbian television channels was dedicated to the ruling majority. Of the remaining coverage of the opposition, 42% was negative in tone and 53% neutral.
The student movement has sought to sidestep government domination of the media by, it says, going door to door, including sending a canvasser “to every village”, in the hope of making inroads into Vučić’s solid base in the Serbian countryside. The outcome could hinge on whether these student emissaries can change rural minds.
No SNS officials responded to a request for comment. Gordana Čomić, a former member of the opposition Democratic party who served as a minister in the SNS government, said the students were exaggerating the extent of their rural campaign and were deluded if they thought they could win.
“They are not in the field. It’s propaganda. They have no clue who their voters are,” Čomić said, predicting that the Student List would win about 80 of the 250 seats in the national assembly and then dissipate.
“They won’t have a clue what’s their role there. How will they work when they don’t want to talk with anyone from the ruling parties? They will just dissolve.”
Radivoje Grujić, a Serbian electoral consultant based in Warsaw, was also sceptical that the Student List could make gains in the countryside and argued the students’ only path to victory would be if the Novi Sad disaster mobilised Serbians who had previously stayed away from politics.
“These people were saying: I’m not involved in politics, and then politics got them killed,” he said. “This definitely triggered a lot of people to get involved and obviously those people will not vote for Vučić. I think that’s the only chance for a change – that reservoir of votes of people who never voted.”
In a close race, other factors are expected to come into play. Minority parties representing ethnic Hungarians, Bosniaks and Albanians could emerge as kingmakers.
Previous elections have seen multiple allegations of various forms of rigging, including vote-buying, voter intimidation and ballot box stuffing, so the Student List is planning to deploy an unprecedented number of opposition monitors on Sunday.
That could in turn raise the prospect of election day clashes. Attacks on opposition representatives by gangs of anonymous, black-clad burly men has been a frequent feature of SNS rule. In the days before the elections, one of those hired thugs has turned whistleblower.
“My role was to lead a group of guys to the riskiest and most critical places, to any gatherings where students or the opposition were on the other side,” Momcilo Marjanovic told the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network , saying that he was covertly paid through a fictitious job at a public utility.
“It was our job, as a last resort of course, to use force, although it often happened not as a last resort.”
Diplomats in Belgrade thought that Vučić’s plans to host a major international event, EXPO 2027, next year, could constrain any violence. If his hold on power is threatened, Vučić also has the option of forcing repeated recounts in the hope that the students’ momentum may eventually dissipate.
The movement is determined that will not happen and has focused its planning in recent weeks on post-election street tactics to defend any victory.
“I think there is a strong feeling of now or never,” Jelena Kleut, an associate professor of media studies, said at a recent demonstration outside the education ministry in Belgrade.
“I think that people have really felt in their skin what the regime is capable of and there is a sense you still need to stay strong because the job is not finished.”

title: UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
description: Decision was widely expected after lobbying by Shell but will dismay environmental campaigners
author_name: Peter Walker, Kiran Stacey, Aletha Adu
content:
Decision was widely expected after lobbying by Shell but will dismay environmental campaigners
What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?
The UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, a widely expected move that will nonetheless dismay environmental campaigners and a number of Labour MPs.
While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project, which is being decided on separately, have sought environmental approval for existing licences.
The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. The decision on Jackdaw had been expected last month but was delayed , seemingly to take it beyond the Holborn and St Pancras byelection on 8 October, where Labour was defending a seat against a Green challenge and ultimately won .
The Jackdaw field will start supplying gas to homes and businesses from the end of the month, the government said after approving the scheme.
Andy Burnham has said drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield will “protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter”.
“At a time when people are really struggling, it’s right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” the prime minister said. “We’re committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.”
Announcing the decision, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh , said: “Following careful consideration of all relevant factors, I have agreed that the regulator can grant consent for gas to be produced at Jackdaw, which will begin to supply the UK with gas from this winter thanks to the highly skilled and vital North Sea workers.
When asked to clarify how many jobs the gasfield would create, Fahnbulleh said: “It will create 27 jobs. It will secure 273 jobs. But, look, that was not the primary consideration.
“This decision will support the country’s energy security with homegrown gas this winter and help minimise the UK’s use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear.
“The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050.”
Fahnbulleh also said the government would launch a new energy wealth fund with a £2bn downpayment to reinvest oil and gas revenues into the climate transition. It hopes this fund will demonstrate that approving new gasfields is not at odds with Britain’s climate commitments.
Environmental campaigners have called for Jackdaw and Rosebank to be abandoned, while Donald Trump has urged Burnham to open them.
Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”
She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.”
The oil and gas industry says the fields will provide 10% of the UK’s output at their peak. But campaigners say they will cause so much environmental damage as to obliterate any economic benefit.
The UN’s Environment Programme has said global carbon emission targets need to be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin
Jackdaw is owned and operated by Adura, an independent joint venture half owned by Equinor and half by Shell . Both have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled that the companies needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be created by burning the oil and gas they produce.
The companies have been lobbying hard for the green light. Adura commissioned a report this week that said rejecting the two projects would cost the UK economy nearly £10.8bn over the next decade.
The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted. But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.
A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling. That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and about half of 18- to 24-year-olds.
Ellie Mae O’Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer. If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.”
The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, called the decision “climate vandalism”. He said: “Today’s decision by Labour is a betrayal of all of our futures, Labour has abandoned all credibility in the fight against climate change.
“The energy secretary has herself said it will make no difference to energy bills, the health secretary has admitted the summer heatwave added to pressure on the NHS and the industry’s own assessment is that will create only 27 jobs. This is a victory for Shell over the people.”
Ami McCarthy, the head of politics for Greenpeace UK, said: “Approving Jackdaw shows the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy. Andy Burnham promised pragmatism, but there is nothing pragmatic about rubber-stamping a project that won’t lower energy bills, won’t boost energy security and will create just 27 full-time jobs.
“What Jackdaw is guaranteed to do is generate record profits for Shell and Equinor while supercharging the climate chaos hitting families here and abroad. Going on to approve Rosebank would detonate an even bigger carbon bomb, releasing as much carbon as 56 coal plants operating for a year.
“True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates.”

title: Eddie Howe is Jason Wilcox’s choice if Manchester United replace Michael Carrick
description: Manchester United’s director of football believes Eddie Howe’s extensive Premier League experience places him above other potential targets
content:
Howe would seriously consider job if offered it
Head of recruitment Vivell prefers Julian Nagelsmann
Eddie Howe is the current preferred candidate of Jason Wilcox to replace Michael Carrick should Manchester United decide to change manager, with the director of football believing Howe’s extensive Premier League experience places him ahead of other potential targets.
Howe left Newcastle in late July to take a break from the game but would seriously consider a return for the United role, it is understood, should this be offered.
Howe would be less expensive to bring in than Unai Emery, another admired candidate, because Aston Villa would demand about £20m in compensation for their manager.
In five years managing Newcastle Howe impressed, leading the team to the 2025 Carabao Cup, ending a 70-year wait for a domestic trophy. After taking over from Steve Bruce in November 2021, Howe led Newcastle to 11th, winning 12 of the last 18 games. The team had gone 14 games without a victory at the start of the season.
Howe also took Newcastle back into the Champions League after 20 years in 2023 and qualified again two seasons later. He managed Bournemouth for five seasons in the Premier League from 2015.
Julian Nagelsmann, the former Germany and Bayern Munich coach, is highly regarded by Christopher Vivell, United’s head of recruitment, but Wilcox’s view may hold more sway with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls football policy.
Carrick is under serious pressure after the club’s poorest start since 1986. The 45-year-old is expected to remain in place for Sunday’s visit of Bournemouth – he is due to hold his pre-game media conference on Friday – but the 45-year-old’s job is in the balance after two wins from 11 games this season.

title: World Series 2026 predictions: will the Rays or Brewers claim their first title?
description: It’s Milwaukee and Tampa Bay in the 122nd Fall Classic. Our writers predict how it will be decided, who will shine brightest and who will break their World Series maiden
author_name: Alan Evans, Bryan Armen Graham, David Lengel
content:
It’s Milwaukee and Tampa Bay in the 122nd Fall Classic. Our writers predict how it will be decided, who will shine brightest and who will break their World Series maiden
Yes - and in fact, evidence that money actively undermines baseball happiness. For the big-market teams, anything less than a World Series is disappointing. Whereas for the Rays (who in April were given a 1.1% chance of winning the World Series by FanGraphs) or Brewers (2.1%), the season is already a success, and winning it all would give their fans more pleasure than a Yankees or Dodgers fan could ever experience. Alan Evans
No. It’s does offer proof that October remains gloriously resistant to being bought outright. But money buys depth and insurance, even if it can’t guarantee that your $300m hitters won’t spend an off week grounding into double plays. Better to enjoy this peach of a matchup – only the second Fall Classic since 1920 where a first-time winner is guaranteed – without letting baseball’s billionaire owner class weaponize it in the coming labor fight, with a salary cap on the table and the sport potentially heading for another protracted lockout. Bryan Armen Graham
Yes. High-end talent is nice, but to get to the World Series on a shoestring budget you also need a certain culture. There shall be no tolerating careless mistakes, no getting too comfortable in cushy MLB dugouts, and players must have a clear understanding of their roles and the brand of baseball they’re expected to play. That’s where Milwaukee and Tampa Bay have truly excelled this season. David Lengel
Jacob Misiorowski may be the best pitcher in the world, but the cliché that “bullpens win championships” is more true than ever in modern baseball. Luckily for Milwaukee, theirs is one of the best in the game – only the Yankees had a better collective regular season earned run average – and the sweep of the Dodgers means everyone will be starting on full rest. AE
Make Tampa Bay chase. Milwaukee have the pitching to win this series, but asking them to weather seven nights of high-leverage situations with traffic on the basepaths is inviting trouble. Get ahead in counts, limit free passes and force the Rays to string hits together. The fewer opportunities Tampa Bay have to improvise, the better the Brewers’ chances. BAG
The Brewers bullpen is lights out but don’t ask them to do too much. The Rays will try to pile up reliever innings in a bid to weaken the core. Also, Game 4 in Tampa will be a bullpen game for Milwaukee, so make sure the unit is kept fresh for that pivotal matchup. DL
Be inventive. Ace Shane McClanahan is injured, but their occasional gambit of using opening pitchers is arguably even more of a power move in a single series at the very end of the season. As for batting, if any two of the “big three” of Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero find their groove at the same time, they’ll be hard to keep quiet. AE
Turn every baserunner into a problem. Swipe a bag, take the extra base and make Milwaukee’s fielders execute under pressure. But don’t confuse small ball with giving away outs: Díaz, Aranda and Caminero still need to supply damage. The best version of the Rays makes opponents defend everything, including the outfield seats. BAG
Ensure the big three are up and running against the Brewers rotation. When Caminero, Díaz and Aranda struggled in the ALCS, the Guardians took two games and sent Rays fans searching for the nearest cliff. Kevin Cash also must excel in the dugout against healthy competition in Pat Murphy, who won’t make Dave Roberts-like mistakes. DL
Tampa Bay will clinch the title wearing their Devil Rays throwback jerseys, and within a year will revert to that as the franchise name. They went 12-3 in the regular season wearing them and are now 2-0 in the postseason. If it happens, fan demand will make it hard for the newish owners to resist. AE
Someone will lose a game after pulling a starter who looks untouchable , and the ensuing argument will briefly eclipse the actual World Series. The manager will point to the matchups, the broadcast will show the abandoned pitcher staring into space and everyone will pretend the alternative outcome was a matter of certainty. (And for Tampa Bay fans, it could be déjà vu .) BAG
Club Tropicana by Wham! becomes the theme song for the Rays and this World Series as the dumpy dome in St Pete becomes the epicenter of the October sports world. Tampa win in seven tight games and fall in love with the worst venue in all of Major League Baseball. They take a 180 turn on the Trop and demand that their new owners drop plans for a new stadium. Talk about bold! DL
Chandler Simpson, Tampa Bay. He’s become the talisman of a team increasingly focused on small ball, and is well on his way to becoming a folk hero for his homer-averse approach. Tight games are often decided by small margins such as a stolen base or a timely bunt. If it happens two or three times at key moments, the underdog could finally have his day. AE
Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay. There’s a temptation to choose someone whose candidacy explains the Rays’ entire organizational philosophy. I’ll take the less complicated option: the hitter who can put the ball into the seats with the purist-rankling, time-expanding home-run trot . In a series of infinitesimal margins, one emphatic swing can turn the whole thing. BAG
Drew Rasmussen, Tampa Bay. Like Freddy Peralta, Drew Rasmussen has spent some time in a Brewers jersey, and has benefited from whatever they’re sprinkling on pitchers in Tampa. The 31-year-old righty was a sixth-round pick who can miss bats and hit his spots with ease. In this World Series, he will reach the pinnacle. DL
Rays 4-3 Brewers. There’s not much between the teams, but the Rays have surpassed every expectation this season and easily won the toughest division in baseball. It’s close to a tossup, but the Rays’ versatility and Cash’s managerial nous might be enough to edge it. AE
Rays 4-3 Brewers. Milwaukee have the pitching to make every run feel precious, but I trust the Rays’ ability to manufacture offense to make the difference in a series where margins will be razor-thin. There’s something about this matchup that reminds me of the 1991 World Series between the Twins and Braves: Great Lakes v South, two evenly matched teams with no obvious weaknesses and barely a whisker between them. Expect seven games of mounting tension, managerial second-guessing and repeated reminders that neither of these teams arrived here by accident. BAG
Rays 4-3 Brewers. How could it not go seven? They’re so close in culture and approach that you’d be shocked if either of these teams went down without a fight. The Rays have just a little bit more, and a slight advantage at skipper with Kevin Cash. It’ll be super tight: Rays in seven. DL

title: Backrooms to The Monkey: the seven best films to watch on TV this week
description: Chiwetel Ejiofor stars in a heart-poundingly original horror, while Theo James plays twins cursed by a killer wind-up monkey. Happy Halloween week!
content:
Chiwetel Ejiofor stars in a heart-poundingly original horror, while Theo James plays twins cursed by a killer wind-up monkey. Happy Halloween week!
Director Kane Parsons was just 20 when he shot this genre-redefining horror, based on the “creepypasta” YouTube series he’d been developing since his mid-teens. Chiwetel Ejiofor stars as Clark, a failed architect who discovers an apparently endless liminal space behind the strip mall store where he works and, depressingly, also lives. Renate Reinsve is Clark’s therapist, Mary, a woman working through her own traumas around enclosed spaces, who nonetheless follows him into these backrooms to attempt a rescue. The wallpaper may be monotonously yellow, but there are scares of every shade here and, underlying it all, the heart-pounding thrill of pure originality. EEJ Monday 26 October, HBO Max
The scene where the knight (Max von Sydow) plays chess with Death (Bengt Ekerot) is among the most recognisable in the history of cinema, and endlessly parodied by the less cultured likes of Bill & Ted’s Bogus Journey and The Muppets. But that shouldn’t eclipse the rest of Ingmar Bergman’s 1957 classic, worth seeing in full for its allegorical depiction of plague-ravaged medieval Europe, the austere black and white cinematography of Gunnar Fischer, and a climatic rendering of the Danse Macabre, performed before slowly dissolving dark clouds. EEJ Saturday 24 October, 9.30pm, BBC Four
Is Cat Person a romantic comedy? Or is it a psychological horror? The erratic tone shifts of this 2023 film, adapted from Kristen Roupenian’s viral short story of the same name, are entirely in keeping with its subject matter: what it means to be a single, straight woman and, in the internet parlance, “date your only natural predator”. Emilia Jones stars as Margot, a 20-year-old college student who begins an ambivalent relationship with Robert (Nicholas Braun, AKA Greg from Succession), a harmless if slightly pompous nice-guy lunk. Or is he? EEJ Saturday 24 October, 11.40pm, BBC One
Tony Curtis turns up halfway through, playing against type as the now DNA-linked killer, Albert DeSalvo. The real stars, though, are the dogged detectives of Boston PD, featuring a host of reassuringly craggy-faced character actors such as George Kennedy and Murray Hamilton, and headed up by John S Bottomly (Henry Fonda). They run down seemingly every creep and kook in eastern Massachusetts before eventually landing on their man. Director Richard Fleischer’s use of split-screen adds to both the pacing and the period feel. EEJ Sunday 25 October, 10.10pm, Talking Pictures TV
Andrew Haigh’s film is an emotionally complex, fable-like story of regret and redemption. Andrew Scott, never better, plays Adam, an introverted, gay screenwriter who lives alone in a tower block. In search of inspiration, he revisits his childhood home, only to come upon the ghosts of his parents (Claire Foy and Jamie Bell), who died in a car crash when he was 12. He also meets Harry (Paul Mescal), seemingly the only other person in his building, and starts a tentative romance. These two encounters draw Adam out of himself, giving him the chance to reassess his childhood, his sexuality and his present. A heart-rending but hopeful tale. SW Wednesday 28 October, 9pm, Film4
Osgood Perkins made 2024’s scariest movie in Longlegs, but his 2025 follow-up, based on a Stephen King short story, is a raucous comedy horror with more laughs and more life wisdom. Theo James plays twins whose traumatic family inheritance continually resurfaces in the form of a cursed wind-up monkey. Whenever someone is foolish enough to turn its key, a spectacularly gruesome death ensues. This leaves the twins with a dilemma: how to go on living when death is all around? EEJ Wednesday 28 October, 10.40pm, BBC One
The Spanish-language zombie flick Apocalypse Z: The Beginning of the End was a huge international hit for Prime Video in 2024. In this sequel, also directed by Carles Torrens, much of the population has taken refuge in the Canary Islands, following the outbreak of the blood-borne TSJ virus. Roberto (Carlos Alcaide) joins a special return mission to the mainland, which soon becomes a scramble for survival as the infected hordes march on. Perhaps returning fan favourite Lúculo the cat (still played by Pedrito the cat) can come to the rescue? EEJ Friday 30 October, Prime Video

title: Loidis: From the Toolkit of Lovers review – epic 111-minute album is a teeming universe of detail
description: Brian Leeds, AKA Huerco S, keeps raising the temperature on his once-chilly ambient on an ambitious record full of delightful detail and ASMR-inducing sound design
content:
(Incienso) Brian Leeds, AKA Huerco S, keeps raising the temperature on his once-chilly ambient on an ambitious record full of delightful detail and ASMR-inducing sound design
T he sun barely seemed to rise in the earlier work of US electronic producer Brian Leeds. As Huerco S he put out the audio equivalent of 5pm November gloaming: lo-fi, low-lumen ambient and house music, flickering as if through a thicket of pine. But the light sharpened on his 2022 album Plonk, and for his project Loidis – on 2024 album One Day and this year’s stunning remix of James K’s Peel – the temperature seemed to rise along with the tempos. It wasn’t quite Balearic summer, but certainly Baltic spring or Adriatic autumn.
His new album is his grandest statement across either project: 111 minutes of music across six sides of vinyl, a scale he goes a long way towards justifying. In tracks reminiscent of the microhouse sound of early 00s acts such as Luomo, the synth chords have Leeds’ trademark degraded shimmer, paired with ticklish snares and delightful ASMR-inducing sound design, stereo effects panning from right to left with quicksilver physicality. It’s hugely pleasurable to let your mind zoom in and out of these arrangements, marvelling at the microscopic detail then appreciating the overarching sense of groove, further enhanced by big melodic motifs: the playful echoing notes in TT Stunt, or the Afrobeat bassline of Running Rich. A couple of tracks in the second half lack the adventure elsewhere, but at least 90 of the minutes here are riveting, psychedelic even on nothing stronger than a cup of tea.

title: Asian Football Confederation backs Gianni Infantino in U-turn on Fifa presidency
description: Sheikh Salman, the AFC president, has made an abrupt turnaround months after accusing Gianni Infantino of a ‘fundamental breach of trust’
content:
AFC president Sheikh Salman praises and hugs Infantino
It had stood with Uefa and Concacaf against him
The Asian Football Confederation has endorsed Gianni Infantino for another term as Fifa’s president in a turnaround in its stance from two months ago when it criticised the head of football’s world governing body for a breach of trust.
The AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, speaking at the body’s extraordinary congress in Tokyo on Friday, embraced Infantino with a large hug in front of the membership as he delivered his endorsement.
“We affirm our full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the Fifa president.” Sheikh Salman said. “You’ve visited a lot of countries in Asia. I’ve spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well.”
The AFC has 47 member associations. Even if all the members do not follow the direction of Sheikh Salman, those votes could be a key to guaranteeing another mandate for Infantino. The Fifa election is in March and nominations close on 18 November. So far no one is standing against him.
Addressing his remarks to Infantino, Sheikh Salman indicated not every AFC member would go along with the endorsement but that most will. “My feeling is, I’m sure, the feeling of most of my members,” he said. “And I’ve said that to you.”
This is an abrupt turnaround for Sheikh Salman. In August, the AFC joined Uefa and Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – in saying that Infantino had committed a “fundamental breach of trust”. They wrote an open letter calling for “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”.
Infantino apologised last week in Zurich to Fifa’s council – which he chairs – for “mistakes” he made in assembling a now-scrapped $4.2bn plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors. Sheikh Salman referenced the differences with Infantino in his speech but glossed over any details.
“Yes, we had some issues we spoke about in the past,” he said. “But let’s not relate the two things together. I think the last few [times] we met in Zurich you made it clear that there’s a true understanding between us.”
Even before the AFC endorsement the indications were that Infantino was edging toward a simple majority of the 211 Fifa member federations.
The largest applause came at the end of Sheikh Salman’s address when he repeated his support for Infantino. Fifa’s president took the podium after and acknowledged some errors. “When you do many things, you do – hopefully, as we did, many good things – you do some mistakes as well,” Infantino said.
The largest applause came as he mentioned how, under his leadership, more millions were flowing. “Before I started as Fifa president, each of you, some of you are still [here] and still remember that time … Each of you was receiving $1m every four years. As of the first of January of next year, it will be $25m.”

title: Basma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season
description: Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tension
content:
(Stroom) Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tension
T he new album from French-Moroccan vocalist Basma and Paris-based group Temir Alcy comes just in time for the changing of the clocks. It’s a dark and disorientating listen, exploring themes of loss and new beginnings over swampy, downtempo rhythms. The 11 tracks here linger somewhere between folk, shoegaze and ambient, with skulking percussion, droning passages and plucked strings soaked in reverb. Opening track Belati sets the tone with its spacious, shapeshifting composition, where ghostly drones and Basma’s layered calls give way to a sluggish beat. Most of the tracks follow a similar non-structure: amorphous but with an intermittent, sultry groove, like the winding bass on Khti Sarah, or the slow, swinging rhythm on Aji M3aya.
Basma’s performance is always captivating. Singing in a mixture of Darija (vernacular Arabic) and French, she delivers poetic snapshots in sensory terms that chime with the shifting seasons: “shy light”, blowing wind and bonfires. On Rised, breathy fragments are looped and reversed into a dreamy haze, while her lilting chants on La Tourne have a hypnotic effect. On standout Al Atlal, which lumbers along like a haunted lullaby, she drifts between soft wails and stoic spoken word.
Accentuating the murky atmosphere are the textural elements which lurk between Basma’s vocals and the sub-bass, often so subtle they are barely perceptible. On Belati, traces of oscillating electronics emerge; Khti Sarah features muted flecks of oud. Disembodied field recordings shimmer and glitch like static on Aji M3aya. Cha3ouka is immediately thrown off-kilter by the percussive krakeb, offering dissonant clatter over dubbed-out whorls. On Ana Jaya, where the experimentalism peaks, the line between instruments and vocals blurs as the sound dissipates. The effect is bodily: tension you can feel, but can’t quite pin down. It’s a brilliant, heady formula.
Dalga (Zel Zele) is an exciting compilation of wonky pop productions made in 1980s Turkey, most of which have never been reissued before. Across these nine tracks, traditional Anatolian psych and pop sensibilities combine with robotic samples, hi-NRG drum programming and delirious, glitching synths. Hysterical Love Project are part of an ever-expanding pool of artists making atmospheric, trip-hop-inflected pop. The Melbourne duo’s second LP, February’s Album (Motion Ward), is a gorgeous meditation on love and longing, channelled through mumbling vocals and warm, reverb-heavy instrumentals. The quietly pulsing Thinking Woman’s Lament is a highlight. The second album from experimental dubwise group Holy Tongue is an invigorating listen, propelled by Valentina Magaletti’s ritualistic drums and scattered with haunting samples and effects (AD 93). Ecstatic, echoing guest vocals from Dali de Saint Paul add to the whirlwind on two of the tracks, but it’s the rolling instrumentals that stand out most.

title: Chess: Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, can break another world age record on Friday
description: England’s talent from Harrow can become the youngest female international master in chess history
content:
England’s talent from Harrow can become the youngest female international master in chess history
Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, who needed just a few rating points to qualify for an open international master title and to break Judit Polgar’s world age record, went very close to a draw against the former world title challenger GM Aleksandra Goryachkina in round one of this week’s European Club Cup, then outplayed her IM opponent in round three to take her rating to 2399.4 against the 2400 needed. In her next game, she drew from a winning position against GM Nino Batsiashvili, rated 2426.
Sivanandan has thus already joined the 10 youngest 2400-rated players of all time, who include the new Russian star Roman Shogdzhiev, the world No 5, Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Argentina’s Faustino Oro, and Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus.
If Sivanandan wins her final round game against a 2034-rated opponent or draws against a 2116 on Friday afternoon, which will be shown live on lichess , starting at 1pm BST, she will also achieve her third and final international master norm and with it a historic title, breaking Judit Polgar’s female world age record from 38 years ago and joining the 10 youngest IMs of all time.
Shogdzhiev, like Sivanandan, was born in 2015, and is clearly being groomed as the heir apparent to Soviet legends Mikhail Botvinnik, Anatoly Karpov and Garry Kasparov.
For several years now his team of coaches led by the experienced GM Evgeny Tomashevsky have organised periodic blitz tournaments in Moscow where the youngster could hone his speed skills against strong rivals.
Shogdzhiev’s final record-breaking IM norm was organised at a so-called norm factory in Serbia, but he has since then registered two of the three required grandmaster norms in t he Asian Championship in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and more recently in the Serbian League. Now he requires just one more norm and a 2500 rating to capture Abhimanyu Mishra’s world age record as the youngest ever grandmaster. He could easily do it before his 12th birthday in February 2027.
Pride of place in this week’s column would otherwise go to IM Richard Pert, who scored a career-best result when he defeated GM Jorden van Foreest, rated 2716 and No 24 in the world, in the Cheddleton Savills Catering v SuperChess Romania round three match in the European Club Cup in Budva, Montenegro.
Pert, 45, an ECF national chess coach, is on a roll, with a 6/6 total before Friday’s final round. Richard’s twin brother, Nicholas, is a grandmaster of long standing, and his children Max and Nina both have Fide titles.
The Dutchman, who famously won Tata Steel Wijk aan Zee in 2021 and played No 2 in the SuperChess team behind Abdusattorov, opened with the experimental 2…h6 and 4…a6 but was still comfortably level at move 24 when his blunder 24…Rd6??, instead of 24…Rd5, instantly lost a piece to 25 a4. He resigned immediately , as 25…Nd4 allows 26 Bb4 skewering Black’s rooks. Pert scored another speedy win in round five of the European Club Cup.
Cheddleton Savills Catering have been a team revelation, after an opening round in Budva saw two of England’s other teams defeated 6-0. Seeded only 16th, Cheddleton have won five of their six matches by wide margins and now face the Israeli champions Rishon LeZion, whose top board is the former world title challenger Boris Gelfand, in Friday’s final round, with an outside chance for a medal.
The London Chess Classic returns next month, from 25 November to 4 December. Full details on how to enter, and details on who is already competing, are here .
The US Championship at Saint Louis went to a rapid and blitz playoff on Thursday night after Fabiano Caruana, the world No 3 and defending champion, caught up with the world No 6, Wesley So, in the final round. So won the playoff 1.5-0.5. He stood better in both games, but Caruana narrowly escaped defeat in the first.
So had led by a point before round 11 and faced the tailender Samuel Sevian, who had a favourable lifetime score against the former Filipino and said after winning the game : “He is really good in setting tricks in shorter time controls, but in classical I kind of figure out his little ideas.”
Final leading US Championships scores: Open So (playoff winner) and Caruana 7/11, Jeffery Xiong and Grigory Oparin 6.5, Andy Woodward 6, Mishra, Levon Aronian and Awonder Liang 5.5. Hans Niemann finished joint 10th out of 12 with 4/11.
Women Rachael Li 8.5/11, Alice Lee 8, Irina Krush 7.5. The holder, Carissa Yip, finished equal seventh with 4.5. Li, 16, is the youngest first-time champion although Krush, who debuted at 11, was 14 when she won the first of her nine US titles in 1998.
