title: Chaotic state of football in Brazil epitomises a nation where greed has conquered glory
description: The national game merely reflects the mood in a divided nation which is going to the polls with very little faith in the power of democracy
content:
The national game merely reflects the mood in a divided nation which is going to the polls with very little faith in the power of democracy
L ook, cards on the table: I don’t know for certain, and nor do you, whether Flávio Bolsonaro – the man widely tipped to become the next president of Brazil after Sunday night’s election – really did steal an island from Richarlison. There are lawyers involved, claims and counter-claims, and in any case, adjudicating land ownership disputes between right-wing strongmen and Tottenham reserve-team strikers lies very much beyond this column’s spectrum of expertise. It’s why, for example, this newspaper took no official position on the well-publicised battle between Rodrigo Duterte and Vincent Janssen over that Polynesian isthmus.
According to Richarlison, a few years ago he purchased an island off the southern coast of Rio de Janeiro, and has the documentation to prove it. Richarlison says Bolsonaro tried to buy it from him, and when he refused a lawyer named Willer Tomaz simply turned up and annexed it. “These guys took the island without spending a penny, as far as I know,” Richarlison claimed in an Instagram video that has been viewed more than 31 million times. Tomaz has accused Richarlison of lying, arguing that he has a public deed registered at the notary’s office. Bolsonaro, for his part, has denied any connection with the island in question and described Richarlison’s intervention as “politically motivated”.
All of which offers just the tiniest sliver of insight into an election that – in common with most modern Brazilian elections – has by turns been rancorous, divisive, wildly surreal and littered with contested facts, where the fake news sounds real and the real news often sounds fake. “Brazil is now a dystopian place,” said Renan Santos, one of the presidential candidates defeated in the first round of voting. “People do not talk about public policy. They just create entertainment content about politics.”
And this being Brazil, of course, it has been an election indelibly inflected by the ultimate entertainment content: football, its symbols and tropes, its ability both to explain and reflect a country torn along multiple planes. As president, Flávio’s father Jair – a deeply weird ex-military man who refers to his four sons by number – made a concerted effort to politicise the yellow national team shirt, appropriating it as an emblem of his campaign and wearing it at rallies. Numerous footballers – Neymar, Ronaldinho, Rivaldo, Dani Alves, Thiago Silva, Lucas Moura – allied themselves explicitly or tacitly to his cause.
In part this can be explained by the wider appeal of the Bolsonaros within Brazil’s evangelical Christian community, from which 20 of the 26 players in Brazil’s World Cup squad this summer came. Many are followers of neo-Pentecostalism, a highly commercialised brand of evangelism fuelled by 24-hour TV preachers, megachurches and vast ostentatious displays of material wealth, in which the individual is cast as the architect of their own fate.
The disaffected young urban men from which both Bolsonaros draw their base have little use for the minimum wage increases or welfare programmes established by current president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. They dream not of union membership but entrepreneurialism and influencer clout, conceive of society not as a collective struggle but as a game with winners and losers, where the aim is not to build order but to conquer the chaos.
In this world Neymar – currently whiling away the last of his fading light at Santos – is not a cautionary tale, a potential all-time great footballing career that essentially disintegrated into frivolity and waste. In this world Neymar is an aspirational hero, a man who accumulated wealth and celebrity status beyond his wildest dreams, and did it all with a defiant wink, by apologising to nobody. Neymar has, of course, publicly backed the younger Bolsonaro before this election.
But the real footballing battleground of this election has been not the players, but the clubs. Last month Lula incited fury within Brazilian football by imposing a ban on sports betting in a country where an estimated 7% of the population are problem gamblers. Online gambling is also one of the sport’s major sources of revenue: 14 of Brazil’s 20 top-division clubs advertise online betting sites on their shirts. Star players such as Neymar and Vinícius Júnior make a handsome living endorsing gambling companies. “How am I going to pay for [Lucas] Paquetá?” the Flamengo president, Luiz Eduardo Baptista, complained on a podcast. Bolsonaro has criticised the ban and suggested he may be open to reversing it if elected.
And in a sense the dividing lines in this election are also the very same questions with which football has been grappling for decades. Is this a team game or a vehicle for individual volition? Is it all about the scent of triumph, the cold hard certainties of winning and losing, the reaping of accolades and capital, the haptic thrill of crushing enemies underfoot? Or can it also be an expression of collective will, civic and regional pride, representation and inclusivity, the pursuit of a goal larger than the self?
Perhaps the modern Brazil is particularly sensitive to these questions: dysfunctional and chaotic, captured above all by a sense of endemic decline. By 2030 it will be 28 years since the men’s team won a World Cup. It still has no nationwide academy system or standardised youth development programme. The national federation has had eight leaders since 2012. This is a game that has essentially been broken down into its constituent parts, its players strewn across the globe, an entire country of entrepreneurs and sole traders.
We hear a lot about football’s power to unite a nation. Perhaps we underestimate the extent to which it can also divide; the way it can reflect the very worst of ourselves, our greed and vindictiveness, our lust for feuds and petty entertainment. There is a Women’s World Cup being hosted in Brazil next summer and while Lula has sought to fast-track the professionalisation of women’s football, Bolsonaro’s only public utterances in the field of women’s sport have been to assert his opposition to trans athletes playing it.
Occasionally voices of dissent whisper into the gale. Raphinha has shared posts on workers’ rights and social justice. Richarlison has pledged that if he ever recovers the money he spent on the island, he will donate a portion to the hospital in his home town of Nova Venécia. Former players such as Juninho Pernambucano and Rai have spoken out against the Bolsonaro family. Female footballers such as Carlinha and Tayla Carolina have used their platform to oppose the far-right. Perhaps they, unlike so many of their compatriots, realise that ultimately democracy is like an island retreat: one day it’s gone, and it’s not entirely clear whether you ever had it in the first place.

title: Murder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing?
description: Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland. With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should be
content:
Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland. With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should be
T owards the end of summer, a debate began raging in clubland, kick-started by an Instagram post from the esteemed DJ Jane Fitz. Ahead of the Houghton festival, where she is a regular fixture, she posted a request asking people to stop chatting so much during DJ sets.
“What I wrote was super respectful,” she tells me. “A bit of talking is obviously OK. But why would you stand completely still, where the sound is super loud, just to ask your mate about a new boyfriend or what they had for lunch? It’s called a dancefloor for a reason.”
Fitz’s plea exploded. It chimed with many, while others were up in arms, claiming that paying an entry fee allowed them to do whatever they wanted. “People were accusing me of being the fun police,” she says. “I’m not trying to stop your fun, mate. I’m trying to give you a better night out.”
“I think the dancefloor is dead,” Charli xcx sang on her tongue-in-cheek comeback single Rock Music this spring. Was she right? Many DJs and clubbers are worried it goes further than the yappers Fitz complained about, citing the rise of certain drugs – insular ketamine, chew-your-ear-off cocaine – and TikTok-boosted star DJs bringing in passive fans used to consuming dance music through a screen, who end up standing still filming the DJ and their visuals. Then there is the rising cost of clubbing, prohibiting younger, potentially bouncier dancers from attending raves.
As fewer purpose-made clubs have been built in recent years, clubbers have got used to squeezing into one-room raves often in converted arches, warehouses and garages. Josh Aitman, an organiser of the sober-friendly London queer party Good As You, complains that “some parties can be so packed in that I get looks just for dancing”. Separate bar areas are scarce and the 90s concept of a dedicated chill-out room is long gone, so the smoking area is often the only safe – if smelly – bet for a chat away from the music.
While the audiophilia boom has improved sound quality in many clubs, stricter council licensing demands often result in quieter dancefloors, making chat more liable to cut through and annoy other punters. One diehard group of clubbers detailed the science on cards they handed out this summer on dancefloors including at Houghton. One side read: “The Dance Floor Is For Dancing” with “Please take your conversation to the back” written underneath. The flipside featured a diagram of EQ curves. “Dance music is very bassy, meaning there’s loads of room on the top end of the EQ spectrum for vocals to punctuate,” says Paul M, one of the instigators of the cards.
“The sadistic side of me wishes I could just turn the music off for 10 minutes and give these people a lecture on all this so they understand,” says Paul. “The cards were a jokey way of doing that – but it’s no joke. I was watching a DJ I’d wanted to see for ages and two men next to me were having a 20-minute discussion about mortgage rates.” Astonishingly, this group of dancefloor activists wasn’t alone – someone else at Houghton gave out cards that just said: “Stop Talking.”
Not everyone in clubland wants the dancefloor to be treated as a sacred space. James Ronald, who plays as Hot Cross Fun and is a resident DJ for the nomadic party Disco Disco, posted a heartfelt rebuttal to Fitz’s post titled: “Please Talk on the Dancefloor.” It garnered a similarly huge reaction. “I get that you should be respectful,” says Ronald. “But she talked about treating it like a church, cinema or a theatre – places where you just observe and nobody communicates.”
Ronald tapped into an important reason why club culture is such a powerful force: the dancefloor is a place for people to connect. “Community is a really big part of clubbing,” he says. He defends the right for clubbers to get deep. “There’s been instances with a particular friend, for example, who only really opens up when he’s a bit wasted. We’ve had important chats about family and personal issues, chats we wouldn’t have had anywhere else.”
It’s a fairly new discussion and, apparently, an intractable one. Dan Beaumont, a DJ who is writing a history of London’s queer club culture, sees it like this: “Gossip is the glue that holds clubbing together. You need an equilibrium of yappers and dancers. Clubbing doesn’t work when it’s one and not the other.”
One possible way forward is for venues to set more direction for what they expect from punters. At Gaffe, an intimate DIY 150-capacity club in south London that opened in early 2025, a sign shows two arrows pointing in different directions. One says “Dancing”, the other “Yapping”.
“The sign is a bit tongue in cheek,” says founder Luca Marchal. “But the arrows point in different directions for a reason. We’re asking people to take the longer chats off the dancefloor. Having a proper catch up is a massive part of going out, so we want that to happen somewhere good.”
Until more venues spell it out quite so clearly with signs, interpersonal skills have become more important than ever in this delicate standoff, a challenge for conflict-averse Britons. Compare that with Berlin, where there is far less social stigma around asking someone to take their chat outside. “There’s a certain etiquette that leads to more satisfying and transformative experiences on the dancefloor,” says the British DJ Pandora, who is based in Berlin. “You’re more able to get into a flow state without the distraction of nearby conversations.”
British clubs have started to follow Berlin’s lead in banning phones on the dancefloor, a change that many have credited with restoring a bit of life. Michael Peacock, an almost ambassadorial figure for British clubbing, is one of those leading the charge. The 68-year-old likes to arrive at clubs barefoot, often wearing little, and proceeds to have the most fun in the room; he says his peak this summer was dancing for 30 straight hours.
In 2022, a video of Peacock going for it at Fabric in London was shared online by a punter with mocking intent. There was a huge outcry: not only are people not dancing because they are filming the DJ (or each other) but they may be worried about someone else filming them . “A lot of the debate on social media is about how phones destroy the vibe for the DJ,” says Peacock. “But there’s still scant regard for ravers who are filmed without their consent.”
Peacock now campaigns for less phone use in clubs. He praises Amber’s in Manchester which goes further than most “no-phones” clubs with a strictly enforced zero tolerance policy. “There are still times when I have to remonstrate with people,” he says with a sigh.
Sheffield DIY venue Plot 22 staff place a sticker over your phone camera on the way in, and will have a word if they catch you breaking the rules. “Our space is small and intimate,” says the venue’s manager, Mike Thompson. “Even just one person filming with a flash would really disrupt the vibe”. Co-owner Adam Seymour agrees: “People say they feel free to enjoy the dancefloor when you take away the ability to use their phone.”
If clubbing’s heyday was defined by ecstasy, today’s most popular drugs can pull the dancefloor in disparate and equally destructive directions. Many feel that the rise in ketamine use – a drug that creates a profound sense of dissociation – has made dancefloors markedly less buoyant in recent years.
Manchester DJ Luke Una stresses that he doesn’t want to be judgmental about drug use, but calls ketamine a “very solo” drug. “It breaks any sense of communal togetherness. For me, music has to be about connection. A nightclub should be about bringing people together and transcending and escaping together. The one time I had it, I’ll be honest with you, I thought I was listening to Underground Resistance for 12 hours until I came round and realised that I was listening to the air conditioning unit.”
Then there’s cocaine, the cost of which has plummeted in recent years and is now as omnipresent as ecstasy used to be. Clubbers have “gone from a drug that makes the music sound amazing, to a drug that makes you think you’re amazing and people need to listen to you instead,” says the DJ Wes Baggaley, a resident on NTS Radio, a London music station.
But Luke Una is keen to point out how a revival of a different drug is having the opposite effect. “In the last 12 months, there’s been a lot more unity, love, warmth and smiling – down to people taking mushrooms again. I played a party in Belfast and said to the person running it, ‘Why is everyone so fucking happy?” And he said, ‘Luke, they’re all on mushrooms.’ I’m not advocating using them – but you can see the difference.”
Now Jane Fitz feels optimistic: “We started a debate, which was a great first step. I have seen differences, I think people have realised there should be some kind of etiquette. During the breakdowns in songs, the dancefloor has been feeling quiet with people listening again.”
When a party pops off, Luke Una also sees optimism: “I believe something is going on which feels like a reaction to what has become a brutal, toxic world out there. It feels like people are coming back to life in 3D again, showing a need to be together and – without being cringe about it – to kind of transcend together too.”

title: Lupin review – the French super-thief is magnetic in his blockbuster return
description: The bizarrely salient French crime smash is higher stakes than ever – and its Houdini-style thrills are complemented with some interesting questions around race and infamy
content:
Houdini-style thrills, Marvel-style set pieces and relentless twists? The stakes are higher than ever in the hit crime series – but beneath the action, it asks some big questions
S omething strange has happened with Lupin. Two years after the French jewel heist thriller’s third season aired, its series one plotline played out in real life, in the form of a global news story turned viral sensation. The Louvre heist of 2025 happened by day – while Lupin’s main character Assane Diop (Omar Sy) stole jewels from the Louvre at night. The real-life robbers posed as construction workers – Diop posed as a caretaker. You couldn’t help but draw comparisons.
So it returns for the fourth series with a salience the makers could never have predicted – amid a renewed appreciation of the power of a cleverly crafted disguise to dupe even the world’s most revered cultural institutions.
Things are higher-budget, higher stakes and more cinematic from the title card onwards. The show’s central question seems to be: what happens when a mastermind finds themselves a victim of their own intelligence? We meet master criminal Diop, four years after he surrenders to the police at the close of the third season, in a maximum security prison. Diop is a week away from release, hoping to fulfil his fatherly promise to put the life of crime behind him and join his family in Senegal, when technology across Paris is hacked, and warnings of imminent heists signed with the name “Lupin” appear. Things are not looking good for Diop, who has modelled his life on fictional master criminal Arsène Lupin. He is swiftly straitjacketed and locked in a panopticon-style glass cell, allowing surveillance and mockery by prison guards and prisoners alike. We are only 12 minutes in to episode one. I repeat, things are not looking good.
Diop’s Blackness has often served as his strength – the racial stereotypes still rife in supposedly “colourblind” France allow him to camouflage as a janitor or delivery person for his crimes. But when he becomes a suspect, his racialisation is his downfall; blurry security footage shows that a robber was a Black man, which is taken as unequivocal evidence that Diop is guilty.
So Diop is hoisted by the petard of his own notoriety: despite being imprisoned in a high-security facility, the police still believe he was somehow involved in the jewel theft. He must have found a way to become invisible, to break out. He is implicated in a crime that doesn’t seem to bear his fingerprints, before it even happens.
Lupin eschews exposition and offers up Houdini-style thrills right from the start. I find myself wanting to believe that Diop is not responsible for the robberies, but it is hard to know what to trust in this show. The twists have been relentless: last season concluded with Diop’s nemesis, Hubert Pellegrini, revealing himself as the secret mastermind behind much of the series’ conflict.
Lupin asks complicated questions about what it means to attempt to leave things behind when you have achieved a certain level of infamy. Other thieves (in the show and in real life) become copycats. To those investigating, it becomes unthinkable that anyone else could have pulled this off. Yet Diop is no longer the puppet master – now, he is at the mercy of others. “I want to be done with Lupin once and for all,” he remembers telling his son. But there is an irony here: Diop embarked on his life of crime to avenge the death of his father, who was falsely accused of a jewel theft. Now, Diop finds himself falsely accused, while the potential impact on his son hangs in the balance.
This is all compelling enough to justify another series of the Netflix hit, which has been subject to delays that some fans have bemoaned as making it as drawn-out as the end of Stranger Things. Much like that show, Lupin has been scaled up from a five-episode series to eight. Sy, whose performance is magnetic as always, has graduated to co-showrunner and wants to lean harder into the show’s “superhero”-like qualities. These include tech and set pieces which undoubtedly add a sprinkling of Marvel.
Certain moments do feel over-dramatised – and it relies on that cliche of the old pro getting roped back in for one last hurrah. But will Lupin manage to shapeshift from a French drama punching above its weight on the global market to a big-budget thrill-ride? Watching on Netflix’s default US English setting (which is sacrilege, anyway) would certainly tip this Hollywood feel over the edge. Make sure you switch to French.

title: ‘The run ends in the centre of this beautiful village’: readers’ favourite small ski resorts in Europe
description: From cosy Alpine villages to queue-free skiing, you tell us where to head to avoid the crowds
content:
From cosy Alpine villages to queue-free skiing, you tell us where to head to avoid the crowds Tell us about a conservation tourism experience – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher
Bad Gastein is a relatively unknown gem. The Austrian state it sits in, Salzburg, offers free local transport (the guest mobility ticket ) if you are staying in the state, so you can travel to the resort via train for nothing. The slopes are directly next to the station, too. Rob Owen
Puy-Saint-Vincent in France is a wonderful, small, child-friendly resort. Our grandchildren learned to ski each morning with great instructors on the gentle slopes under amazing azure skies. Three generations then made memories of a lifetime, skiing the wide quiet slopes together each afternoon. We enjoyed dog sleds and cosy hot chocolate in the slopeside cafes. A wonderful trip. Barbara
Gausta , Norway, is such fun. Stay at Gaustablikk, the hotel built by Kirk Douglas’s stuntman , a wonderfully quirky piece of local history. Explore Vemork, the historic heavy-water plant where British and Norwegian resistance fighters carried out their daring sabotage during the second world war. For families, the on-piste skiing is friendly and accessible; while the cross-country trails are simply stunning. Then there’s the real adventure: an old US military train climbs Gaustatoppen , opening up spectacular off-piste skiing with views and terrain that rival much of mainland Europe. It’s a brilliant mix of history, skiing, scenery and adventure, and somehow remains a wonderfully under-the-radar destination. Fiona
As a family of four, we loved St Johann in Tirol . It’s a comfortable Austrian village with Christmas markets, picturesque churches and gorgeous frozen valley walks – with little marmosets and weasels to look out for along the river. Wherever you stay, you can walk to a gondola. It’s really near to Salzburg airport, too. In Austria, kids get all-day lessons, which is a big bonus. Parents can just kick back or wander around and have a gluhwein or two. Prices were very reasonable in the Christmas holidays. Nick
Tarvisio-Monte Lussari on the Italian-Slovenian border covers 24km (15 miles) of skiable terrain interconnected across two main sectors: the historic and stunning Monte Lussari pilgrimage peak and the Priesnig area. Used by local people and those in the know, it offers sufficient ski runs and good value ski passes and restaurants, and is much cheaper than neighbouring resorts in Austria. Neil
Stay in the attractive resort of La Rosière in France, in the foothills of the Mont Blanc region. Enjoy the short forest walk to the village, with wind chimes and magic in the air, for an après-ski drink and a cheese fondue in a local tavern with the kids. Oliver
About 50km (30 miles) from Ålesund, Strandafjellet has excellent pistes, but also some of the best off-piste skiing in Norway. Strap on a pair of randonnée skis and you can use the lifts to access spectacular backcountry skiing in the Sunnmøre Alps. The views down to the fjord make this truly special. Pistes are illuminated for evening skiing. Graham
Saint-Martin-de-Belleville , in the French Alps (Les Trois Vallées), is low at about 1,500 metres, so go mid-season. The single run ends smack in the centre of the village, which has retained its historical features along with small, friendly bars and places to eat. Plus, it gives access to the whole of the Trois Vallées ski area – absolutely amazing from one small but beautiful village. There are plenty of choices for accommodation, both expensive and cheap. Russell Walker
Brunico is tucked away in the Dolomites, just a 90-minute transfer from Innsbruck. I had a great week at the beginning of March. Unlike bigger resorts, queues were nonexistent here. There are runs for beginners through to experts. Great snow and plenty of opportunities to use it. Ian B
Oberstdorf in Germany continues to be my go-to for a quiet and restorative ski week away. There are 130km (80 miles) of pistes for all levels, stacks of Bavarian restaurants, a wide variety of mountain huts, plenty of hotels for all budgets and family sizes, and the novelty of skiing into and out of Austria daily. Neuschwanstein Castle is a short hop away for a day off. Unbeatable value. Daniel Stephens

title: ‘The biggest motivation is fear’: High turnout among Israel’s Palestinians could unseat Netanyahu
description: The Knesset is up for grabs next week and the Arab community is desperate to topple the far-right ruling coalition
content:
The Knesset is up for grabs next week and the Arab community is desperate to topple the far-right ruling coalition
As the sun set over the town of Kfar Qasim, Palestinian citizens of Israel gathered over hot knafeh pastries and shots of strong cardamom-laced coffee to hear an urgent pitch for their votes.
Palestinians make up about 20% of Israel’s population and their votes are likely to be critical to efforts to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition in elections next week.
“We are determined to do everything in order to bring this government down. And high turnout among the Arab community is one important tool in achieving this goal,” said Ahmad Tibi, a member of the Knesset for more than two decades as head of the Ta’al party.
Most polling shows Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority in the 120-seat Knesset but the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc will also fall short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.
Palestinian citizens of Israel are forecast to secure between 12 and 15 seats, divided between the Islamist Ra’am and the Joint List alliance of three smaller parties, one of which is Ta’al.
The mathematics of power are clear, even though most of the Jewish Israeli opposition has ruled out a coalition with Arab politicians, and Netanyahu and his allies have been doing everything they can to make such an alliance politically toxic.
Racist, fear-mongering campaigning includes posters reading “It’s [either] the right or Palestine”, while others on the right have coined the phrase “Bibi [Netanyahu’s nickname] or Tibi”, even though there is little chance Tibi will hold even a junior ministerial post.
In the history of the state of Israel, there have been just two Palestinian ministers: Raleb Majadele held the portfolio for sport for two years and Issawi Frej was in charge of regional coordination for just over one year.
There is recent precedent for breaking promises not to work with Palestinians, however. The Ra’am leader, Mansour Abbas, in 2021 took his party into a historic coalition government with Naftali Bennett, now part of the opposition bloc, and Netanyahu himself had previously started coalition negotiations with Abbas.
One prospective voter, Mohammed, works at a hi-tech company, managing both Jewish and Arab employees, which he sees as a template for a different future for Israel.
Although disappointed that most Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out a coalition with Palestinian parties, he understands the political logic, and he expects their position to shift once results are in.
“At the end of the day, everything is mathematics, right? One plus one is two. They cannot do anything without [those seats]. So they must do [some kind of deal] and they will do it.”
He is voting and urging all his friends, Jewish and Palestinian, to do the same. “You can say, ‘OK, they don’t like me and I want to relocate’. But if you want to stay here, you must vote. You must do that. Because if this government stays in power, it will be a disaster,” he said.
For Palestinian politicians, any alliance with a Jewish-Israeli opposition is also challenging. None of the parties are calling for a two-state solution, most vigorously oppose a Palestinian state and most support the settlement movement in the occupied West Bank.
“It’s between bad and worse. Any new government will not be my cup of tea, but I am choosing between Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, Itamar Ben-Gvir and the opposition,” Tibi said.
The scale of death and destruction in Gaza, militant violence and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and spiralling racism and discrimination inside Israel have created deep-rooted fears about what another four years of far-right ministers could bring.
“The biggest motivation is fear. It is more effective and important than our political parties or our campaigns or anything else,” said the Balad party leader, Sami Abu Shehadeh. “People are very politicised, and aware of the danger of what will happen if these criminals come back to rule again.”
Turnout has been suppressed in the past because some voters lost faith in a system that is stacked against Palestinians and their representatives.
Israel’s supreme court effectively forced Abu Shehadeh to drop out of the race last month over an article about the 7 October Hamas-led attacks, in a decision widely criticised for enshrining different standards of free speech for Jewish and Palestinian citizens of the state.
A motion to disqualify the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, for racist language, including calls for ethnic cleansing, was not upheld.
Other Palestinians do not take part in elections on principle. Nagham Zbeedat, a journalist with Haaretz newspaper, laid out her opposition in an article earlier this year.
“I do not vote because I refuse to legitimize a system that treats my rights as favors, my safety as optional and my humanity as negotiable,” she wrote. “I refuse to be grateful for crumbs while Palestinians are erased – slowly here, violently elsewhere.”
There is a new urgency to voting this year, however, because a far-right coalition returned to power would have a renewed mandate to accelerate its policies of ethnic cleansing and annexation, said Amjed Iraqi, a senior analyst for Israel/Palestine at International Crisis Group.
In Kafr Qassim, the date of the election is a reminder of Palestinian vulnerability. Two days after voting, the town will remember one of the most notorious massacres in Israel’s history, when in 1956 border police killed 49 men, women and children, shot because they broke a curfew they didn’t know had been imposed on them.
“From a Palestinian perspective this election is arguably primarily about mitigation. Everyone understands fully what the opposition represents and yet, for all that, Palestinians in Israel can see the difference between a rightwing government and a far-right government,” Iraqi said.
“There’s the sense you need to make your presence known and heard and shown, in the face of the far right, just by going to the ballot. There’s no clarity about what comes afterwards but that’s how powerless I think a lot of people feel.”

title: Under Fire by Humza Yousaf – a deeply affecting story of being stranded in Gaza
description: The former Scottish first minister writes of his in-laws’ plight and the tragedy of those who weren’t so lucky
content:
The former Scottish first minister writes of his in-laws’ plight and the tragedy of those who weren’t so lucky
A week into Israel’s bombing of Gaza in 2023, which followed Hamas’s deadly terrorist attack on Israel, Scotland’s then first minister Humza Yousaf received a text from his mother-in-law, Elizabeth. “Humza, I think we are about to die. I need you to promise me that you will take care of my girls.”
Elizabeth, a retired nurse from Dundee, and her Palestinian husband, Maged, had been visiting family in Gaza and become trapped there when the bombing began. Not only were people dying all around them, but their house was filling up with friends and neighbours whose homes had been destroyed, and they were running out of food. On the night Elizabeth texted, they had been told to leave their neighbourhood of Deir al-Balah ahead of a fresh wave of Israeli strikes. They later learned the evacuation order was a false alarm. Even so, Yousaf reflects, “in the four weeks from hell, this felt like the lowest point”.
Under Fire is a short yet deeply affecting book detailing Yousaf and his wife Nadia El-Nakla’s month-long nightmare as Elizabeth and Maged remained stranded in Gaza, during which they made repeated attempts to flee. The Israeli government had said it would let foreign nationals leave, though for Yousaf’s in-laws this appeared to be an empty pledge. More than once they made the perilous journey to Rafah, on the border with Egypt, only to be turned away when they got there. Meanwhile, Nadia’s brother was working in a Gaza hospital and sending desperate updates about civilian casualties, the lack of clean water and medical supplies and how he was performing surgeries without anaesthetic, often lit by the light from a mobile phone.
Yousaf and his family’s agonising plight unfolds as he goes about his duties as the newly elected first minister. The text from Elizabeth arrived during the SNP conference, on the eve of his first speech. As a result, much of the narrative concerns his efforts to meet his responsibilities in Scotland while trying to comfort and support his wife and children. All the while, he and his aides plead with the Foreign Office in London to help get Elizabeth and Maged out.
Yousaf is a natural communicator and, though his writing sometimes lacks flair, he effectively conveys the stress and torment that comes with attending meetings and delivering speeches while wrestling with what to make public and what to keep private regarding his family. In the end he decides to share what is happening to his in-laws to raise awareness about the horrors being visited on Gaza’s civilian population. The title Under Fire has a dual meaning, describing the terrifying ordeal of Palestinians in Gaza and the scrutiny and criticism that comes not just with being Scotland’s first minister but the first Muslim leader of a country that is 95% non-Muslim and overwhelmingly white.
There is another narrative here concerning Yousaf’s struggles to make his way politically and step out of the shadow of his mentor and predecessor Nicola Sturgeon, which sits awkwardly in a book that is primarily about a family in crisis. Similarly, his diatribe about Kate Forbes, his rival for the top job, and her “clumsy” leadership campaign would suit a straightforward political memoir, but here feels out of place.
More pertinent are Yousaf’s criticisms of the then British foreign secretary James Cleverly for initially failing to pick up the phone to him, even after he had spoken publicly about his parents-in-law being stranded. Neither does he mince his words about Rishi Sunak, whom he chastises for failing to provide updates for worried British citizens with family in Gaza.

title: Nocturne to The One About Matthew Perry: the seven best shows to stream this week
description: Stephen Graham nails another standout performance as a serial killer in a creepy thriller. Plus, laughter and tears in an intimate look at the life of the late Friends star
content:
Stephen Graham nails another standout performance as a serial killer in a creepy thriller. Plus, laughter and tears in an intimate look at the life of the late Friends star
Stephen Graham gives good serial killer. Even in isolation, in the bowels of a prison psychiatric ward, he’s the unnervingly calm yet relentlessly beating heart of this creepy, claustrophobic thriller. Somehow, Jurek Walter (Graham) is still making waves outside the facility: when a kidnapped child returns, seemingly from the dead (his sister is still missing), the cops are certain Walter must be involved. However, his alibi could hardly be more solid. Soon, Jonah Lynn (Liev Schreiber), the cop who put him away, is back on the case, sending his FBI agent surrogate daughter Saga (Zazie Beetz) into the prison, undercover, as an inmate. It seems risky and, sure enough, it is. Apple TV, from Friday 30 October
Filmed as a “vertical drama” (it’s short and the visual format is designed for smartphone viewing), this five-part series was made in partnership with a global beauty brand. But for all the presentational quirks, the premise is very traditional: four London women, in microcosm, over the course of an evening preparing for a night out. Along the way, they navigate everything from unreasonable bosses to a phone-snatching via laughter, gossip and friendship. It won’t win any Baftas but it passes muster as an innovative advertising campaign. Channel 4, out now
This fun mockumentary about a shambolic pizzeria run by incompetent teenagers made its name as a series of five-minute YouTube shorts. Netflix has expanded the format to 12 minutes an episode but Minimum Wage’s lo-fi charm remains intact. However, now the stakes are higher: the owner of the business, who was largely absent from the web series, has turned up and told the gang that unless they start turning a profit, the building will be sold to developers. Cue hapless promotions, health and safety crises and general slacker chaos. Netflix, from Monday 26 October
“God, you can do anything you want to me; just please make me famous.” Matthew Perry recalls thinking this as a struggling actor, but concedes that he hadn’t reckoned on what else might be in store. This three-parter is revealing and frequently very sweet – the excitement of Perry’s initial rise was clearly a caffeinated rush akin to a double espresso from Central Perk. But as the intimate interviews with friends and family members suggest, Perry was always troubled in ways that fuelled both comedy and tragedy. The series doesn’t shy away from the latter but much of it feels like a celebration of his talent, too. Netflix, from Tuesday 27 October
As we rejoin Dexter Morgan, he’s not living his best life. He’s in New York, gloomily driving a taxi. He has dispatched the Midnight Mangler and the Yonkers Slayer (the writers aren’t really trying with these names any more) but the New York Ripper remains elusive. On the bright side, his son Harrison has joined the NYPD so Dexter has a little inside help. Michael C Hall remains a compelling lead but this resurrection feels like a case of diminishing returns – both Dexter’s modus operandi and the show’s tangled moral code is now too familiar to feel essential. Paramount+, from Friday 30 October
The cream of the world’s darts players have struggled to beat Warrington wonderkid Luke Littler in recent times. So what chance do a bunch of amateurs have? The process won’t be quite as random and informal as the publicity suggests: after a series of open heats in Manchester and London, 20 contenders have been selected to play a single live leg of darts against the world champion – and the shorter the game, the more chance there is of unexpected outcomes. If anyone manages the seemingly impossible, there’s a share of £501k to be won. Game on! Netflix, from Friday 30 October
As the climax arrives, the Coven and Mr Nas (AKA Satan) are on a collision course after spending much of the season apart. It’s overdue: this run of the horror anthology has felt disjointed, and Ben’s triskaidekaphobia (fear of the number 13) plus the desire for conceptual neatness prompted by the season number have caused a certain sluggishness. Still, the endgame should be worth the wait: as the devil approaches the century on Earth that will grant him control of humanity, heaven and hell, only his son Ben or daughter Constance can stop him. Disney+, from Friday 30 October

title: ‘A form of anti-status status’ – how much would you pay for a plain tote bag?
description: The ubiquitous carrier has been given a four-figure makeover. But why has an everyday bag associated with running errands and US supermarkets become so aspirational?
content:
The ubiquitous carrier has been given a four-figure makeover. But why has an everyday bag associated with running errands and US supermarkets become so aspirational?
Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
I f you were in the blessed position of having £500 to spend on a bag, what would you look for? Would it be made of cotton? A nice light shade bound to sully quickly, like “paper white” or ecru? Would you want something that looks a lot like those ubiquitous totes sold by a certain US supermarket chain for a couple of dollars?
No, thought not. But there are plenty of options if you do. Phoebe Philo, former Celine designer and quiet luxury pioneer, offers a white canvas shopper , made entirely from cotton except for the silver brass hardware of its internal zipped pocket, for £450. Luxury Swedish brand Toteme’s “effortless tote bag” is made from organic cotton canvas and is available in dark brown, red or classic ecru. It goes for £510. Tom Ford’s version , at £1,600, differentiates itself a little, with a body made exclusively of cotton canvas but trims and handles from calfskin. Prada’s, which features leather details and metal hardware , could be yours for over £2,000.
These are the kinds of totes that have become a relatively inexpensive staple, thanks to Trader Joe’s, LL Bean, J Crew, museum gift shops and countless other brands stocking this pleasingly simple and in some ways hyper-practical bag. They have become a common sight on the shoulders of people doing their vegetable shopping or in need of a second bag for gym clobber on an office day.
So why have they been co-opted by luxury fashion? For Tiffany Hill, the founder of Trend Suite , “the appeal is partly that the canvas tote has become a form of anti-status status”. The “strange impracticality of their pale colour” is, she says, part and parcel of it. “A cream or ecru tote that costs hundreds, or even thousands, and is inevitably going to mark, almost makes practicality beside the point. You are buying into an aesthetic and a lifestyle rather than simply buying something to carry your belongings in.”
These ecru canvas totes are two a penny on the American east coast. Muffy Aldrich is the editor of the blog Salt Water New England: The Thing Before Preppy , where she offers tips on styling her LL Bean tote. (She has a couple of dozen of them in ecru.) If she includes those with different trim/handle colours, “it is embarrassingly in the triple digits”. She has bags in “medium, large, and extra-large. Occasionally the small. Long handles and short. Zip-top and open-top.”
Perfect for going from Nantucket beach to lobster roll shack, Aldrich thinks “they may be the single most iconic East Coast Preppy item today. And fittingly, it is almost impossible to walk through any coastal New England town without running into one.” In large part that’s down to design. For Aldrich, their handles are a case in point: “The straps wrap completely around the bag, instead of just being sewn on at the top, so the bags feel secure when you carry them.”
The fact they are so symbolic of Martha’s Vineyard is very much the point. “The canvas tote already carries this very specific visual language of boats, summer houses, farmers’ markets, weekends away and slightly old-fashioned American affluence,” says Hill. “Luxury brands don’t have to invent that mythology – they can borrow it.”
Where totes were once a symbol of sustainability in an era of disposable plastic bags, they have since become part of the overproduction problem – according to the UN Environment programme , the average cotton tote needs to be used between 50 and 150 times to offset its production. In reality, less than 10% of totes are used more than three times. So there has for some time been an appetite for tote bags that do more than clog up your cupboards, which explains the advent of the “forever tote” .
And these iterations are , apart from perhaps their colour, extremely practical. Boxy in shape, Anna Wintour famously carried “the book” (a dummy copy of the upcoming Vogue) in a monogrammed number. In the final episode of the TV show Furious, which depicts the sordid world of an Epstein-esque billionaire, his daughter reaches for hers when she needs a bag in a rush that’s sturdy enough to stash away all the drives harbouring her father’s collection of child sexual abuse images. It’s a smart piece of costume design from Claire Parkinson, who clearly understands that the character is exactly the type to have such a tote to hand.
What we could call “the Erewhon effect” may also be at play. Erewhon, a high-end LA supermarket frequented by the Kardashians and TikTokers – AKA a $19 powdered-beef-organ and unpasteurised milk smoothie kind of place – sells ecru totes. Emblazoned with “Erewhon”, they are about £74 and, in certain circles, aspirational.
“Consumers have become very fluent in these quieter lifestyle codes: the right grocery shop, coffee cup, baseball cap or canvas tote can communicate taste and belonging just as effectively as an obvious designer logo,” says Hill. “The status is increasingly in recognising the reference rather than displaying the price.” Even if the reference is a supermarket, albeit an extremely fancy one; fashion has always appropriated the everyday.
Marc Jacobs could be seen as playing an early role in this strange new world of expensive totes. In 2019, he launched The Tote Bag collection. The heavily branded canvas bags were hundreds rather than thousands of pounds, and marketed with the pithy slogan “No more Birkins, only tote bags”, they became a mainstream classic.
“The fashion houses are riffing,” says Aldrich. “They can add an inner pocket or outer pocket, or different handle lengths. A logo, of course. Zhoosh up the proportions.” But pleasingly for anyone who owns a similar bag that cost them a tenner: “fashion houses are not going to make an appreciably ‘better’ canvas tote than the original, because it is already perfect for what it is.”
In fact, Aldrich suggests, these new luxury iterations are antithetical to the tote’s allure. “When we get to a point where a tote bag is so precious – so expensive and made of softer materials – that we are afraid to toss it from boat to boat or let it get covered in sand … we get very close to losing what made it iconic to begin with.” Paradoxically, then, “it becomes temporary. Disposable. And that may be exactly what the fashion houses are counting on as the next season rolls around.”

title: At Cop17, the pressure is on to rescue a deal that could end the destruction of nature
description: ​As world leaders struggle to meet deadlines to halt nature loss set four years ago, a rare leopard in host country Armenia offers a symbol of what is at stake
content:
​As world leaders struggle to meet deadlines to halt nature loss set four years ago, a rare leopard in host country Armenia offers a symbol of what is at stake
Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
T he Armenian capital Yerevan is chock-a-block right now with officials, scientists and environmentalists from all over the world gathering for Cop17. Everyone is here to try to rescue a historic deal to end the destruction of nature.
The pressure is on. Targets set for 2030 are woefully off track , and the nearly 200 countries present need to agree on a plan to speed things up. All this is happening at a time when national budgets are tight and leaders are distracted by conflict, protests and the global energy crisis.
But first, this week’s most important reads.
This Norwegian village is one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. How can its people save it?
What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?
US extreme weather survivors are a growing group – now they want to be a political force
There have been snippets of positive news. Just a week before the conference began, a Persian leopard, one of Armenia’s rarest and most endangered animals, was spotted in the southern-central region of the country.
“It was late, we came home and then one of my caretakers [rangers] called me and said, ‘I have amazing news,’” Syuzi Karapetyan, a teacher who also leads the Gndasar Social-Environmental NGO, explained when I visited her village on Saturday. She had goosebumps when she heard the news, she said.
Persian leopards, also known as Caucasian leopards, were once widespread across western and central Asia, but their range has shrunk dramatically. There are thought to be no more than 10 leopards in Armenia, as poaching and habitat destruction have devastated its population .
The discovery of a new individual, never spotted before in the country, has delighted Karapetyan and local people, who in partnership with WWF have rebuilt the population of bezoar goats, one of the leopard’s key prey species, and found ways to protect its habitats.
The question of how to save our most endangered species is a critical issue being discussed at Cop17. Scientists have warned of the rapid annihilation of wildlife, far above natural background levels, with some saying we are in the midst of a mass extinction event , driven by human overpopulation and overconsumption.
A commitment to protect endangered species was one of 23 targets that governments set four years ago, and which they are not on track to meet .
Lots of governments still haven’t mobilised resources, partly because they don’t know where to focus, says Dr Kira Mileham, who co-chairs the Reverse the Red Action Partnership, which supports governments to tackle species loss.
There might be hundreds of species at risk within a country’s borders; which should they prioritise?
This week, Armenia and Colombia announced an initiative, the Coalition of Action to Recover Endangered Species (Cares), a government coalition that aims to help countries assess where to focus their efforts. Some species might not need much dedicated action, as long as parallel efforts – for example to protect their habitat – are under way. Others might need more focused, species-specific interventions such as protection from disease or, if their numbers are very low, help to enable them to breed.
The Cares alliance will help governments to assess which of the species in need of specific support are already receiving attention from NGOs or research institutions, and which are falling through the cracks, and connect them with experts, says Mileham. Reverse the Red will serve as the secretariat of Cares.
It’s then up to governments to develop a plan, and find resources to support it. So far, 17 countries, including the UK, have joined the Cares alliance to share best practice.
Separately, nine private funders and organisations, including Leonardo DiCaprio’s Re:wild, have said they will commit more than $500m over the next five years to recover the world’s most threatened species.
The money has been welcomed, but it also matters how it is spent. There is still a huge bias in how conservation funding is allocated , with larger, charismatic animals such as leopards, tigers and elephants sweeping up the majority of resources. “Decisions need to be taken based on the scientific information that is available, and not just because some are cute, which unfortunately is what happens,” says Benoit Guénard, associate professor at the University of Hong Kong, who has researched the distribution of conservation funds.
Many conservationists hope money will be better targeted, with resources spread more evenly – and that fungi, algae and amphibians might see some of the success enjoyed by the Persian leopard.
‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in decline World must cut emissions by 18% in four years ‘to find our way back’, UN says As a former minister who once climbed a tree to save it, I know there is passion to protect nature. We just have to show it | Steven Guilbeault

title: Son of Wallabies great named in spring tour squad as Les Kiss turns to new faces
description: Teddy Wilson and Tom Lambert part of 33-man group as Australia prepare to face England, Scotland and Wales in the Nations Championship
content:
Teddy Wilson and Tom Lambert part of 33-man group to tour Europe
Australia to face England, Scotland and Wales in Nations Championship
Son of a gun Teddy Wilson and prop Tom Lambert are the new faces in the Wallabies’ spring tour squad, which welcomes back some international reinforcements.
Coach Les Kiss on Friday unveiled his 33-man group to tour Europe for Tests next month against England, Scotland, Wales and another yet-to-be-determined side in the maiden Nations Championship finals weekend.
NSW scrumhalf and former Australian under-20s captain Wilson is the son of Wallabies great David Wilson, with the flanker part of the 1999 World Cup-winning side among his 79 caps.
“There’s a few [Wallabies] jerseys up at home, the 1999 World Cup winning jersey’s there as well,” Wilson said. “Dad, he’s been there and done that so he tells me a few things but lets me play my game.”
“[The main advice was to] just work hard. He was always that type of player and … if we were slacking off when I was younger he’d get us down to the oval, doing extras.”
Wilson was in superb form as Easts won Sydney’s Shute Shield competition and has vowed to back his running game if given a shot at Test level.
He has replaced Kalani Thomas as the third No 9 with the latter playing Australia A this weekend against the United States.
Ryan Lonergan has established himself as the standout No 9, with Wilson to push fellow tourist Tate McDermott in the battle to support him.
The Wallabies had gone six Tests undefeated, including Kiss’s first five in charge, before back-to-back Bledisloe Cup hidings opened old wounds.
Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper, who play club rugby in France and England respectively, performed crucial bench roles in the Wallabies’ defeat of back-to-back World Cup champions South Africa.
But Australia were without the pair’s services against New Zealand, given the All Blacks Tests fell outside of World Rugby’s global player release period.
It exposed the Wallabies’ bench depth and, after a one-sided second half in Auckland , forced Kiss to shift prop Angus Bell to the reserves for the Sydney rematch.
That contest was over inside 30 minutes, before Bell got on the field.
Kiss will have access to his international arsenal though for the four-Test tour that begins in London on 9 November.
Flyhalf Carter Gordon is recovering from a fractured leg and has been included alongside Ben Donaldson and Declan Meredith, with Harry McLaughlin-Phillips squeezed out following his debut off the bench in Sydney.
Kiss has also included Japan-based Hunter Paisami, who was suspended for the Bledisloe Cup for a high tackle and lock Miles Amatosero, who will also play for Australia A in the US.
NSW junior, loosehead Lambert – who will join the Queensland Reds this season – has replaced Aidan Ross, who started against New Zealand in Sydney, in the squad.
Unused fullback Jock Campbell has also missed a spot on the plane.
Kiss said ahead of the Sydney Test that he had been in conversation with veteran playmaker Kurtley Beale who, like fellow experienced halves James O’Connor and Bernard Foley, was a known quantity who remained in the frame ahead of the World Cup.
“There’s a real buzz among the squad as we prepare for what will be four incredibly demanding matches against high-quality opposition,” Kiss said.
“We’ve made some tough selection calls to keep building depth across the board and we know a tour like this will challenge the whole squad on many levels.”
Wallabies: Allan Alaalatoa, Miles Amatosero, Angus Bell, Josh Canham, Massimo De Lutiis, Tom Hooper, Isaac Kailea, Tom Lambert, Fraser McReight, Josh Nasser, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Billy Pollard, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Lachlan Shaw, Carlo Tizzano, Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Jeremy Williams, Harry Wilson. Filipo Daugunu, Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon, Isaac Henry, Len Ikitau, Max Jorgensen, Ryan Lonergan, Tate McDermott, Declan Meredith, Hunter Paisami, Harry Potter, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Teddy Wilson, Tom Wright.
