title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for chocolate and pumpkin spice choux buns
description: I like to get pumpkin into everything – including dessert – at this time of year
content:
Whip winter squash puree into a creamy filling and pipe direct into the heart of a cracking seasonal pudding
A t this time of year, I aim to get as much pumpkin as I can into my meals, including desserts. If I’ve been organised, I’ll roast and puree some from scratch, but I seem always to have at least one tin of pumpkin puree to hand, which I can use quickly in anything from pumpkin pies to cookies and muffins. Here, it’s whipped into cream with some spices, then piped into crackly puffs of choux for a chic, autumnal dessert.
Prep 10 min Cook 1 hr 15 min, plus cooling Makes 12
For the chocolate craquelin 60g unsalted butter 65g light brown sugar 10g cocoa powder 65g plain flour
For the choux 50ml milk 45g unsalted butter 60g plain flour 1 tsp sugar 1 pinch salt 1-2 large eggs For the filling 150g pumpkin puree 1 tsp ground cinnamon ¼ tsp ground cloves 1 tsp vanilla bean paste 90g cream cheese 75g icing sugar 150ml double cream 20g pecans , roughly chopped
Briefly mix the butter and sugar for the craquelin in a small bowl, until smooth and well combined, then work in the flour and cocoa powder to make a thick paste. Spread this evenly over a sheet of baking paper, top with a second sheet, then roll out to about 2-3mm thick and pop it in the freezer to firm up.
Meanwhile, make the choux. Put the milk, butter and 50ml water in a saucepan and heat until steaming and the butter has melted. Off the heat, add the flour, sugar and salt, and stir quickly to bring the dough together. Return to the heat, cook, stirring, for one or two minutes, then transfer to a clean bowl and leave to cool for a few minutes.
Meanwhile, whisk the eggs in a jug, then bit by bit work some into the dough, mixing until it’s all incorporated before adding more. The dough will look lumpy at first, but it will come together. Continue mixing in the eggs (you may not need all of them) until the mixture is glossy, falls easily, and leaves a V shape hanging when lifted with a spoon. Transfer to a piping bag, snip off 2½cm from the end and pipe 12 blobs of the choux dough on to a lined tray.
Heat the oven to 210C (190C fan)/410F/gas 6½. Take the chilled craquelin out of the freezer and, working quickly, use a round cutter roughly the same width as the piped choux to cut out 12 discs. Gently place a disc on each choux, then bake for 15 minutes. Turn down the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and bake for another 10-12 minutes, until the buns are puffy and firm to the touch. Remove and leave to cool completely.
Meanwhile, whisk the pumpkin puree, spices, vanilla and cream cheese in a bowl until smooth, then mix in the sugar. In a second bowl, whip the cream to very soft peaks, then fold into the pumpkin mix.
Use a sharp, serrated knife to trim the top off each choux bun just above halfway. Spoon the cream into a piping bag with an open-star nozzle, then pipe swirls into each bun. Sprinkle chopped pecans on top, then gently top with the choux “hats”. Serve at once.

title: Imagine if, for once, Labour decided to tell the truth about immigration
description: Our economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integration, says the Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
content:
Our economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integration
M y mum’s carer was uncharacteristically late one morning. She didn’t want to say why at first, but it turned out she’d found her previous client – an elderly lady living all alone, with no family to visit – collapsed on the floor, barely alive. It was a lot to cope with for someone only in their early 20s, a reminder of the heavy responsibility this job carries. Watching the carers who helped both my parents in their respective final weeks taught me that while the work itself might seem mundane, the emotional and social skills needed to do it well – to coax some sense out of the confused, to jolly along the lonely, and to soothe the dying, to walk in and out of unfamiliar houses all day long without quite knowing what you might find – are anything but.
Yet like so many jobs predominantly done by women, care has long been relentlessly undervalued. That means lousy pay, little public recognition, and now – at least for the disproportionately large chunk of this workforce who are migrant workers – the disorientating realisation that the government can snap its fingers and all your life plans are upended overnight.
Under the latest attempt by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, to ratchet immigration numbers ever further down, “low-skilled” foreign workers will now have to wait up to 15 years for the right to become permanent residents. The new rules would be backdated to 2021 to catch what the right dubbed the “Boriswave”, that unexpected surge of workers who came to Britain in the Boris Johnson years – many on health and care visas – and would under the old five-year rule have started qualifying for settlement in 2027. What has unsettled some of Mahmood’s own cabinet colleagues is the sense of the state reneging on what was understood to be the deal when those workers came here. Having to be continuously employed for 15 years instead of five without a break means in practice that some will have to leave, while others will live in mortal fear of losing a job. A growing cabinet revolt against Mahmood’s reforms is now becoming the first real challenge to Andy Burnham’s authority as prime minister, but also more broadly a test of where he really stands on immigration.
This month’s budget throws a problem that governments have been trying to ignore for a decade into sharp relief: kneejerk hostility to foreign workers is costing Britain dear, and not just because public services would fall apart without them. Last month, the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned that falling immigration would inevitably mean falling tax revenues, shrinking John Healey’s headroom at the budget by about £4bn. So much for the rightwing myth that migrants are a drain on their host country: if anything, they’ve been bailing Britain out.
It’s not just taxes, either. Immigrants pay a surcharge on top for the right to use the NHS if needed while they’re here, which is now raising £2.5bn a year , according to new research from the Nuffield Trust. It seems all those pesky liberals who argued that migrants are generally healthier than the average Briton – and therefore less likely to need a GP – were right after all: the trust estimates that migrants are on average paying in 60% more in surcharge per year than they take out in healthcare services, a handy little revenue stream that for some reason we never talk about. But immigration crackdowns threaten that income too. The trust notes that falling immigration can lead to “a sharp drop in income” for the NHS, much as slashing foreign student visas has hurt universities that were reliant on their fees.
As the Office for Budget Responsibility spelled out in 2024 – when it calculated that the surge of immigration under Johnson that so offended Tory voters at the time would help knock more than £7bn off projected government borrowing by 2028-29 – economically speaking, immigration is basically good news. If the country really wants it to fall, then something else – higher taxes, lower spending or more borrowing – is going to have to plug the resulting hole in the finances. Yet for years now, successive governments, fearful of confronting leave voters, have tried manfully to pretend that that choice does not exist.
Mahmood’s plan is essentially yet another attempt to square the same old circle, gearing the system around letting in as few people as possible – in keeping with what a furious public has for the last decade seemed to want – while trying to cherrypick those most likely to make an outsize economic contribution. Under her reforms, the highest paid workers (who are likely to pay lots of tax over their lifetimes) would be fast-tracked to settlement , while those judged more likely to be an economic burden on the state overall would be pushed away. What she doesn’t seem to have bargained for, aside from the fact that the rest of the world is in hot competition for high-skilled migrants, is the sense of deep disquiet that engenders. As the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has pointed out, endlessly prolonging settlement risks undermining social cohesion. A country that makes very clear its foreign workers are here at best on sufferance, even if they do hold lives in their hands at work every day, does nothing to encourage them to integrate and put down roots.
The logic of Burnham’s announcement that a future Labour government might consider rejoining the EU , meanwhile, leaves Mahmood’s reforms looking strangely like the relics of a bygone era. If rejoining the single market or customs union would inevitably mean accepting freedom of movement again, what’s the point?
The truth is that grimly ratcheting immigration down to next to nothing has come at extraordinary fiscal and social cost, and if the aim was to destroy Reform’s raison d’etre then it hasn’t worked. The mainstream right has switched seamlessly from the pre-Brexit days of complaining that Polish plumbers were taking Britons’ jobs, to a much darker post-Brexit stage of painting migrants as rapists and criminals. The far right, meanwhile, has simply moved on from cheerleading for deportations to insisting that even people who were born here aren’t English unless they’re white.
Legal migrant numbers are at a historic low and small boat crossings have halved , yet that didn’t stop anger at asylum seekers spilling on to the streets again this summer. There is no level of migration low enough to satisfy some people. There is, however, very much a level of migration low enough to make us all even poorer, and the angry somehow even angrier. And right now, we’re living with it.

title: Milan braces for more unrest as debate intensifies over Italy’s ‘lost generation’
description: Protests and fringe violence expose sharp divide between marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects
content:
Protests and fringe violence expose sharp divide between marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects
M artina Miccichè was filming riot police kicking and beating a teenager with batons as they dragged him along Piazza del Duomo, the central Milan square hosting its cathedral, when she was struck by a flying object, causing a deep gash and bruising near her right eye.
The journalist had joined hundreds of mostly young people marching through the northern Italian city on Saturday afternoon to protest over soaring living costs and unaffordable housing, echoing the wider wave of economic discontent fuelling protests across Europe .
It wasn’t the first time Italy’s youth have loudly aired their grievances during Giorgia Meloni’s four years as prime minister, despite the risk of falling foul of her ruling coalition’s ever-expanding crackdown on security and public dissent. On Saturday afternoon they plan to protest again in Milan and other major Italian cities.
Miccichè said the atmosphere last Saturday was peaceful until about 5pm, when police blocked access to Via Broletto, a street about a 10-minute walk away from Piazza del Duomo.
“People were angry because they were being repressed,” she said, claiming the police turned “suddenly violent” as they pushed the crowd back with their shields. “The violence escalated. They started to grab people at random, hitting and kicking them. It was shocking.”
As the clashes continued and police filled the square with teargas while astonished tourists looked on, a group of masked youths on the fringes headed to the surrounding fashion district, tearing down road signs, setting bins alight and smashing shop windows – among them Footlocker and Levi’s – then looting them.
The vandalism resumed on Sunday as the gangs – many baited by the promise of luxury goods through a network of social media chats – descended on the city centre again, mostly from marginalised areas on the outskirts.
During the two days of unrest, police detained more than 271 young people. Of those, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals.
As the Italian media published images of injured police officers, Meloni’s government rapidly enacted more measures targeting minors and further empowering the police – including holding parents financially accountable for their children’s vandalism and looting – while dispatching 500 troops to Milan.
The latest legislation also criminalises violent participation in ⁠a demonstration and toughens penalties for ⁠rioters.
Some of the government’s security measures are now being applied in the south of Italy , where lorry drivers have been protesting against high petrol prices for more than a week, blocking roads and disrupting supermarket supplies. In response, 71 people have been reported to judicial authorities and 242 fined over the blockades – a protest act made illegal in a previous security bill. A government official also warned the lorry drivers that obstructing public highways could carry jail terms.
“This government just tries to repress protesters instead of listening to them and addressing the issues,” said Miccichè, who needed stitches for her injury. “It is all connected. There is anger in the south over fuel prices and young people everywhere are angry – they don’t even have a chance to think about the future because they are so terrified of the present.”
Furthermore, “we are not feeling safe”, the 34-year-old added, “because we can see how much space the police have now and how shielded they are”. Racial profiling had become the norm in Milan, especially in the centre and close to its train stations, she claimed.
The weekend’s urban unrest, including protests in Turin and Bologna, has intensified debate over Italy’s “lost generation”.
Furthermore, the youth protests and subsequent fringe violence have exposed the sharp divide between Italy’s marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects.
Working-class Italians or third- and second-generation immigrants are regularly labelled by rightwing politicians and the press as maranza , a derogatory term used to describe groups of young people who usually congregate in city centres.
They come from areas like Barona, a sprawling council estate in the south-west of Milan. Young people there have been reflecting on the events of last weekend. “There is a lot of discontent – we are all children of this widespread malaise,” said Domenico Ricci, who along with Luca Orlando manages a bar that is part of Barrio’s , a cultural hub where the district’s youth come together.
Orlando believes the vandalism and looting were a symptom of anger and years of feeling unheard and invisible. “So when an opportunity arises, these kids take revenge. They don’t do it simply because they want to steal something. All this government does is introduce new crimes – they never listen or engage in dialogue.”
Orlando, whose parents came from Calabria, is feeling the nationwide discontent. “But the protests there [in the south-west] have hardly had any coverage,” he said. “And we are only talking about Milan because of the violence and not the real issues.”
Thomas, 18, who has grown up in Barona, is training to be a chef and wants to leave Italy “as soon as possible”. He said: “I see no future here.” His friend Mohamed, an Italian citizen of Moroccan origin, is still at high school and wants to become a lawyer. “If you make a mistake, then you must pay,” he said. “But this is also a characteristic of protests – the more a government doesn’t listen, the more people get angry.”
Mauro Magatti, a sociologist at Milan’s Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, said socioeconomic discomfort and a sense of abandonment affected “an entire generation” and responding to the anger with excessive repression risked enlarging the protest. “Violence always needs to be condemned but now we need to lower the tone to overcome this burst of anger and violence and focus on addressing the real problems,” he said.
Police and military presence in central Milan has been building in recent days before Saturday’s protest, organised by a new online movement which has pledged to gather each weekend “until this government of thieves falls”. Security guards stood outside shops that had been damaged or looted last weekend.
Italy’s politicians from across the spectrum must take heed, warned Miccichè, as the protests were only set to amplify ahead of general elections next year. “There is no perception at all of how young people feel,” she said. “Even if they took just a minute to listen, they will understand that it is a generation full of ideas – they just want to be heard.”

title: Country diary: Slugs? Dull? This one is pure showbiz
description: Falmouth, Cornwall: The rainbow sea slug is a bizarre and breathtaking animal, and with warming seas it’s gaining a toehold in the south-west
content:
Falmouth, Cornwall: The rainbow sea slug is a bizarre and breathtaking animal, and with warming seas it’s gaining a toehold in the south-west
I have never seen a species quite so flamboyant in appearance. A couple of centimetres in length, it was curled beneath the submerged rock like a piece of gaudy costume jewellery.
When the cry went up that one had been found, I had to prevent myself from breaking into a run as I navigated the slippery seaweed-covered boulders to catch my first glimpse of this rarity.
A sea slug. And yet a species that does everything possible to dispel any idea that slugs are drab and dull. The extravagant rainbow sea slug comes with a “ta-da!”. Typically found along the coasts of Spain and Portugal, this multicoloured member of the Aeolid nudibranchs family has spread north with warming seas , and was first recorded in the UK off the Isles of Scilly in 2022. It has since secured a toehold in southern bays of Cornwall and Devon.
I had joined a “bioblitz”, run by the Rock Pool Project , on a low spring tide in Falmouth. The community organisation’s monthly challenge engages members of the public in a citizen-science survey of seashore life. The rainbow sea slug was a star find, drawing an admiring huddle of enthusiastic rockpoolers. Breathtaking and bizarre, its outlandish confectionary of candy colours looks almost artificial. The vivid pink body is decorated with a mane of blue finger-like projections known as cerata, which are topped with yellow and orange. A pop-art palette of colours designed to warn predators that it is unpalatable.
This one was found on the underside of a rock beside white circles of recently laid eggs – the next generation of these sensational little sea creatures.
The project volunteer and marine biologist Ellie Maynard told me that she encountered her first rainbow sea slug last Christmas. “Since then I have seen upwards of 20 here,” she said. “It has been really rapid how they have grown in number.”
It was far from the morning’s only rarity. Others included the wonderfully named hair curler slug , which first reached the UK last September and has wavy brown cerata that give it a permed appearance.
The rainbow sea slug we were watching eventually trundled off, like an overdressed performer late for a carnival. Show time was over.

title: ‘Slow news day at the office’: LeBron James shrugs off Trump’s national anthem attack
description: The US president accused the NBA superstar of disrespecting the national anthem after footage showed him warming up before Philadelphia’s season opener
content:
Trump calls James a ‘TOTAL DISGRACE’ over anthem
US president demands apology for pregame warm-up
James helps Sixers erase 29-point deficit against Cavs
Donald Trump lashed out at NBA superstar LeBron James on Thursday for what he called disrespectful behavior during the playing of the national anthem.
Trump posted a video of the basketball legend making apparent warm-up movements while lined up with his Philadelphia 76ers teammates before their season opener against the New York Knicks on Tuesday.
“While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country! I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.
“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!” he wrote.
The video used by Trump had an on-screen caption that read: “LeBron working on his golf swing pregame.” It showed him making lateral swinging motions and basketball shooting movements.
Trump, speaking at a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday night, renewed the attack, calling James’s actions “a big scandal kind of a story”.
Trump and James have traded barbs before, and the NBA’s all-time leading scorer shrugged off the president’s latest criticism.
“It must be a slow news day at the office,” he said after the Sixers completed an epic comeback to beat the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106 in Philadelphia. “Slow news day at the office.”
James, 41, is entering a record-extending 24th NBA season with his fourth team.
Sixers coach Nick Nurse said Trump’s comments were the kind of distractions he was schooling his team to tune out.
“I think that goes right in with other outside noise we’ve already had,” Nurse said. “I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor.
“The focus that they’ve had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding.”
Philadelphia’s win on Thursday marked both the largest comeback by the Sixers in the play-by-play era (since 1996-97) and the largest comeback win of James’s career.
James finished with 17 points, 10 rebounds, five assists and three steals, while Tyrese Maxey powered the rally with 32 points and a crucial defensive effort on James Harden. Jaylen Brown, also making his home debut in a 76ers uniform, scored 17 of his 21 points in the second half and 10 in the fourth quarter.
Trump has been critical of athletes before – particularly Black athletes – for their behavior during the playing of the Star-Spangled Banner before games.
During his first term, Trump singled out NFL star Colin Kaepernick for his decision to kneel during the Star-Spangled Banner to protest against racial injustice and police brutality.

title: Decomposing whale near Sydney’s Coogee beach should be towed out to sea, Indigenous rangers say
description: The juvenile humpback carcass is wedged between rocks and attracting sharks, but is too decayed to be moved for burial
content:
The juvenile humpback carcass is wedged between rocks and attracting sharks, but is too decayed to be moved for burial
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
A First Nations ranger group says a whale carcass that closed two of Sydney’s most popular beaches after washing up this week should be towed out to allow it to decompose in the ocean.
Coogee beach reopened on Friday after closing on Thursday , when a whale carcass, believed to be a juvenile humpback, was found washed up in Lurline Bay, between Coogee and Maroubra beaches. Randwick city council confirmed the reopening on Friday but said Maroubra beach remained closed due to “dangerous surf conditions”.
But the council said the carcass remained wedged among rocks after high tide had failed to move it out to sea as hoped.
“People should avoid Lurline Bay and not swim or enter the water in the immediate area. The area remains barricaded off,” the council said.
They said a drone flyover on Thursday evening had not spotted any shark activity, so lifeguards decided Coogee was safe to reopen. Swimmers were urged to swim between the flags.
But they added that high tide on Friday evening could move the carcass closer to the water’s edge one again, potentially attracting sharks.
The whale is an important totem animal to the local Bidjigal people. Robert Cooley, a senior ranger at the Gamay Rangers, who have been working with the council on a culturally respectful way to deal with the remains, said the tide had pushed the carcass higher up towards a coastal walkway, requiring an intervention.
“The preferred option now is to tow it back out to sea.” he told Guardian Australia ahead of an afternoon briefing with the council.
“Now that it’s up there and decaying and several vertebrate and other bits of bone are showing, people have a habit of taking collections home, which is quite distressing to us.”
The Gamay Rangers undertake natural and cultural resource management activities like protection work, conservation, and threatened species management in the La Perouse Local Aboriginal Land Council area.
Cooley said that because the whale was in an advanced stage of decay, it was too challenging to lay it to rest on conservation land owned by the land council, as a young humpback that washed up on Cronulla beach earlier this year had been.
“It’s just a big pile of blubber now, but the priority is to let nature take its course [out at sea]. The second priority would be lay it to rest on our conservation land.”
He said the Gamay Rangers did not support taking the whale to landfill.
“It’s really distressing to know that a significant ancestor of ours is taken to landfill with the rest of the city’s rubbish.”
Concerns were raised earlier this year about the towing of a sperm whale carcass along a 20km stretch of coast south of Sydney to Wollongong before being taking it to landfill, resulting in increased shark activity and catching swimmers off guard.
Olaf Meynecke, manager of the whales and climate research program at Griffith University, has been involved two successful whale tows this year in New South Wales and one in Queensland.
He said taking whale carcasses to landfill was “unethical, and … not very environmentally friendly”, towing them far out to sea, typically to the start of the continental shelf – up to 50km offshore – allowed them to decompose naturally and support the marine environment, including sharks.
“We actually do want the sharks to bite into these carcasses because it helps to decompose it quickly,” he said.
“It’s actually a pretty good thing because then you get rid of the sharks from the nearshore areas where people are bathing.”
He said while explosives had been used in the past to break up whale carcasses onshore, now they were typically only used while towing to “open up one side of the whale so that the decomposition will happen a lot faster”.
“The only thing that keeps the whale buoyant is is the intestines and the methane that’s being created through gut bacteria.
“Once that compartment is opened and the guts release all the methane, the whale will start sinking.”
In Western Australia this week, the popular Cottesloe beach was closed amid fears of shark activity due to a three-metre decomposed partial whale carcass.
The Cottesloe mayor, Melissa Hawkins, t old the ABC the council had organised a bulldozer to take the remains to landfill.
With whale migration season in full swing, the ABC reported that watchers in Jervis Bay off the NSW south coast were greeted by the a rare sighting of an orca pod, believed to be hunting a humpback.

title: Heat killed ‘staggering’ 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, scientists warn
description: People succumbed to heat at highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, with health issues, loneliness and poverty exacerbating toll
content:
People succumbed to heat at highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, with health issues, loneliness and poverty exacerbating toll
Heat killed a record 50,000 people in European cities this summer, new research suggests, with scientists blaming climate breakdown for two in every three of the deaths.
Morgues and funeral homes filled with bodies from June to August as the heat added by planet-baking pollution cut short an extra 32,000 lives in urban areas, the researchers found. Hot days pushed vulnerable bodies into overdrive and warm nights prevented them from recovering.
The “staggering” death toll, modelled using historical relationships between heat and health in 854 cities, was the worst on record, the study found. Hot weather marked by relentless heatwaves killed nearly twice as many people as it did in each of the two next most dangerous years.
“In some sense, the absolute numbers of the heat-related deaths estimated across the 854 urban areas are indeed staggering,” said Malcolm Mistry, a climate and health scientist at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who co-authored the study. “But perhaps what is even more alarming is the proportion of these deaths that we attribute to anthropogenic climate change.”
The share of deaths due to climate breakdown has risen from about 40% at the start of the century to 65% this summer, the study found.
People succumbed to heat at the highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, while absolute death tolls were greatest in Italy, France, Spain, Germany and the UK. Because death certificates rarely record contributing factors – such as dangerous temperatures that push a stroke victim or lung cancer patient past their limits – families rarely know that heat and human activity hastened their relatives’ death.
“These shocking figures represent thousands of families who have lost a loved one this summer due to the climate crisis,” said Katie White, the climate transition minister for the UK, where scientists estimated 4,354 heat deaths this summer.”
In Naples, the hardest-hit city on the continent, 815 people per million died from the heat, according to the study’s age-standardised estimates. Mario Guarino, an emergency doctor at Ospedale CTO in the north of the city, said he witnessed a 15% increase in emergency room visits during the hottest weeks.
The “defining characteristic” of the period was the complexity of health problems exacerbated by heat, he added, with loneliness and poverty worsening the situation further.
“We took in a terminal cancer patient who lived in a hot attic simply because his family couldn’t find a company to install air conditioning during the summer,” said Guarino. “An elderly man with dementia was abruptly abandoned by his Ukrainian caregiver who returned home to say goodbye to her son, who had been called to war. Emergency services found [the man] lying on the floor one night with a fractured pelvis, desperately trying to call the tenant next door.”
The study found people over the age of 85 made up almost half of the death toll, though younger people were not immune, with 833 people between the age of 20 and 44 also thought to have died due to the heat. The scientists said the death toll from the cities studied, which account for about 40% of the European population, could not be easily extrapolated to estimate the full death toll including those in towns and villages.
The scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, the EU’s climate monitoring service announced this month , with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C. Slightly less punishing temperatures in eastern Europe brought the continental average to its third-hottest level on record.
Greenhouse gases have warmed Europe about twice as fast as the global average, exposing more people to intolerably hot summers and fewer people to dangerously cold winters. While cold is a bigger killer than heat, scientists expect rising temperatures to claim more lives than they save, as heat deaths are projected to rise faster than cold deaths fall.
The study combined established relationships between heat and mortality with temperature data for 2026 to rapidly estimate the fallout from this summer’s heat. The death tolls for individual countries differ from what national public health agencies have calculated using their own methods.
David García-García, a researcher at the mortality monitoring system at the Carlos III health institute in Madrid, who was not involved in the study, said it was a “valuable contribution” that allowed for comparisons across the continent. “However, it is important to bear in mind that these are estimates based on observed temperatures and epidemiological models, which do not incorporate actual data on deaths occurring in the summer of 2026,” he said.
Doctors have urged governments to burn fewer fossil fuels – the core driver of rising temperatures – while bolstering health systems, greening cities, rolling out air conditioning and encouraging people to drink water and seek shade. They have also stressed the benefits of people checking in on vulnerable neighbours and family members so they can get help before tragedy strikes.
“The real epidemic these days is loneliness,” said Guarino. “Many elderly people are left alone during the summer, abandoned by their families, and due to their low income, they can’t afford air conditioning or, if they do have it, avoid turning it on because of the cost of electricity.”

title: Experience: I’ve climbed Mount Everest 20 times
description: In 1996 doctors told me I wouldn’t walk again unaided, but in 2022 I took the record for the most Everest summits by a non-Sherpa
content:
In 1996 doctors told me I wouldn’t walk again unaided, but in 2022 I took the record for the most Everest summits by a non-Sherpa
I grew up in Slough, Berkshire, in a bungalow beside a farm. My father was a scout leader, and I was always outside, building dams and dens, sleeping out and hiding in trees. In my teens, family holidays were two weeks in Wales. At home, nature was my playground.
When I was 17, a school friend took me to a climbing wall where he was a regular. I loved the physicality of it and trying to work out where to put my hands and feet next. We would go there twice a week. In sixth form, we headed to the south coast in Dorset for my first real climbing outing. The waves were crashing and it felt scary and exhilarating. I thought it was magical.
We would go climbing there or in the Peak District whenever we could. After A-levels, we caught a bus to Chamonix, in the Alps, for five weeks of camping; we climbed Mont Blanc and made stupid mistakes like starting too late in the day. It was a huge learning curve, but it was fabulous.
I did a geology degree at the University of Leeds and joined the climbing club. I wanted to see the Himalayas, so organised a trip to Pakistan. That was a turning point. The climbing was wonderful, but it was the people I fell in love with.
Over the next decade, I spent half my year working in ski and climbing shops, and the other half climbing across Europe, New Zealand and Asia. It was treacherous at times. In 1996 I fell from a rock face, shattering both heel bones, and was told I wouldn’t walk again unaided. After several surgeries and three months in a wheelchair, I defied doctors to climb – and even ski – some of the world’s highest peaks. A group of us took on harder and higher routes and were nominated for a Piolet d’Or – the Oscars of the climbing world – after establishing a trail on Annapurna III, a 7,555-metre peak in Nepal, in 2003.
That caught the attention of a Sheffield adventure company, which asked if I would guide an expedition of two to Everest. I was an accomplished climber, but I had never been to 8,000 metres or led at high altitude; it was a huge leap of faith.
The ascent took eight weeks and I relied heavily on Sherpa expertise. We climbed through the night, with thunderstorms and stars lighting the sky, and I soaked in the feeling of being on the summit at the highest point on the planet, looking down at the Himalayas spread below.
I loved facilitating someone else’s journey. I did three more Everest ascents for the company before setting up my own in 2006. Now I take on one client a year, preparing together for up to three years.
I’ve climbed Everest most years since that first time. This May, I clocked up my 20th summit. There have been testing times – once, we encountered a catastrophic oxygen delivery failure and had to share tanks.
But there have been beautiful moments, too. The best was in 2017: we had summit day to ourselves – warm, no wind and just the right amount of snow. I could see Kangchenjunga and Makalu, the third and fifth highest peaks, respectively, and into Tibet. In 2013, I climbed Everest’s neighbouring peak, Nuptse, looking back from 7,900 metres and recalling years of memories.
That same year, I encountered my hardest night when I came across a dying climber who passed away in my arms. Another time, I pulled a dead Sherpa off the fixed line ropes, the barriers designed to stop people falling. The mountain doesn’t respect whether you have climbed it 20 times or once – anybody can die there.
In 2022, I took the record for the most Everest summits by a non‑Sherpa after my 16th ascent. Meanwhile Kami Rita Sherpa holds the general record. I still hold mine, although it has never been about numbers; it’s about experiences.
There will be a time when I stop climbing Everest, but it won’t be soon. It has given me everything and I feel humbled by that. But it’s the place and its people that mean the most to me – Sherpas I have climbed with; locals who fed me in their homes or nursed me when I was ill; people who have become my friends. The mountain is simply the vehicle that got me there.
Do you have an experience to share? Email experience@theguardian.com

title: Liechtenstein prince’s ‘surreal’ abortion veto dismays campaigners
description: Alois uses the first veto of his reign to quash parliament-approved bill backed by a national petition
content:
Alois uses the first veto of his reign to quash parliament-approved bill backed by a national petition
The hereditary prince of Liechtenstein has used his veto for the first time in his reign to quash a bill aimed at bringing abortion laws in line with much of Europe.
The legislation was approved by Liechtenstein’s parliament last month after the presentation of a citizens’ initiative signed by roughly a quarter of the nation’s voters.
The news left campaigners in the principality, home to some of the strictest abortion laws in Europe , reeling. “We’re not really surprised, but still disappointed,” said Tatjana As’Ad, who led the initiative to overhaul the law and who works for the small leftwing party, Free List. “It’s surreal what’s happening right now in 2026 in a state in the middle of Europe.”
The veto would do little to actually prevent abortions from taking place, she said. “Liechtenstein will continue to have a situation where abortions are banned, but we know they’re happening. The veto just means they will continue to take place abroad.”
Abortions in the principality are allowed only in limited circumstances such as when a woman’s life is at risk or a pregnancy is the result of rape. Since 2015, women have been legally permitted to travel abroad to terminate a pregnancy to skirt around the restrictions.
After campaigners launched the citizen’s initiative in February, more than 4,970 people – far more than the 1,000 signatures needed to send it to parliament – backed the call to decriminalise abortion up to 12 weeks. The initiative also called for the procedure to be covered by health insurance and for a repeal of a nationwide ban on sharing information about abortion access.
The hope was to do away with the many barriers that women face by being forced to travel abroad, often to neighbouring Austria or Switzerland, which include the cost, the need to arrange childcare and the lack of a vehicle.
As the initiative gained steam, Liechtenstein’s hereditary prince, Alois, said he would use his veto to counter any overhaul of the laws. The promise loomed over the initiative, even as parliamentarians voted narrowly to back it and an August poll suggested that 62% of voters were in favour of reforming the law.
This week the royal house confirmed Alois’s decision to “withhold his sanction from the bill” in a statement. It said: “Following careful consideration, he remains convinced that the proposed reform is not compatible with ensuring adequate protection of unborn life as a fundamental legal value.”
The royal house did not respond to a further request for comment from the Guardian.
Campaigners, who said they had met Alois hours before he announced his decision, described it as a blow to Liechtenstein’s identity as a monarchy underpinned by democratic principles.
“A single individual is overriding a decision initiated by almost a quarter of eligible voters and passed by the parliament,” the committee behind the citizens’ initiative said in a statement.
“Hereditary Prince Alois has only threatened to veto legislation twice in his reign, and both times it concerned the legalisation of abortion,” the statement added, referring to a 2011 pronouncement by the regent.
“This is the first time he has actually exercised this veto. The conclusion is clear: when it comes to abortion, there is only one decision-maker.”
It was a nod to the tremendous power the monarchy holds over the Alpine nation, with the ruling prince able to appoint judges and fire the government or individual ministers, said Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel, a journalist and one of the campaigners behind the citizens’ initiative. “He has a veto over everything, really,” she said.
In 2012, voters cast their ballots overwhelmingly to uphold his veto powers, in a referendum that was described at the time as a proxy debate over whether or not Liechtenstein should have a monarchy.
Alvarez-Hummel described this week’s decision as “very troubling”, given that Liechtenstein was the last in Europe to grant women the right to vote in national elections in 1984.
“Liechtenstein has a history of being the last when it comes to women’s rights,” she said. “I had hoped that we wouldn’t be the last in abortion rights as well, but it doesn’t look good at the moment.”
The campaign had managed to chalk up a few successes, she said, pointing to how it had chipped away at the decades-long taboo in talking about the topic in the nation.
In his statement this week, Alois also said he was open to lifting the nationwide ban on information about abortion, suggesting that women might one day be able to consult their healthcare provider on where to access the procedure abroad and receive support afterwards.
Even so, Alvarez-Hummel worried that the estimated 40 women a year who are forced to carry out the procedure abroad would now face greater stigma and more deeply entrenched taboos.
“You live in a country where it is forbidden, where the prince who lives in a castle made sure it stayed forbidden,” she said. “The one time he used his veto was against this – I can only imagine how difficult it must be for them to know this.”

title: Last One Laughing: Halloween review – still a total treat, despite the new twist
description: No screaming is allowed in the spooky spin-off, but the stars are only in danger of cracking up over these golden comedy moments. Even Jack Dee looks delighted to be there!
content:
No screaming is allowed in the spooky spin-off, but the stars are only in danger of cracking up over these golden comedy moments. Even Jack Dee looks delighted to be there!
B ritish comedy is a broad church united by a simple adage: less is more. The most acclaimed and beloved shows – Fawlty Towers, The Young Ones, Brass Eye, The Office – tend to be exceptionally short-running. Compared to the Americans, our series are brief anyway, but we also seem anxious to bow out well before a premise is squeezed dry. We don’t milk it, we don’t money-grub. In a weird way, comedy is viewed as a precious finite resource liable to become exhausted at any moment.
Which is why I feel slightly sceptical about this Halloween special of Prime Video’s Last One Laughing, the reality gameshow that involves a group of comedians competing to see who can remain straight-faced for the longest. The enormous success of the first two series – incredible ratings, healthy media coverage, a pair of Baftas – was well deserved: the show produced some of the most hysterical TV comedy in recent memory. You can understand why the streamer would be keen to capitalise on the interest of the circa 6 million-strong fanbase with this four-part miniseries, which whittles down the usual 10 contestants to seven. But might this snacky stopgap dilute the precious joy of the yearly series proper?
At first, the whole thing does come off a bit half arsed. Why Halloween, except that it falls six months after the last edition? While some contestants do seem specially chosen – series one returnee Daisy May Cooper has authored a book about the supernatural, while Reece Shearsmith (The League of Gentlemen, Inside No 9) is known for his love of horror – others are shoehorned into the theme: we’re told Lou Sanders (who also appeared in the first series) “genuinely believes in crystals” and that Phil Wang once presented a podcast about his hatred of horror movies. Tom Allen, Jack Dee and rising standup Harriet Dyer, meanwhile, are merely introduced with a spooky joke.
The twist this time is that the comedians are not only banned from laughing, but screaming too. I thought this might solve one of the format’s only flaws: that the challenge is too easy for a certain kind of personality. In the last series, both David Mitchell and Sam Campbell got to the end of the allocated time without cracking, forcing producers to bend the rules with a tie-breaker. Yet in the first three episodes of this series – the finale wasn’t made available to reviewers – this new caveat barely features.
Well, none of it matters … Last One Laughing: Halloween is just as hilarious as the show’s previous iterations. There’s little chance of this particular comic well running dry – even second-time contestants Sanders and the defensively screwfaced Cooper prove they have plenty more to give. Wang provides the quick wit, Allen brings the camp asides (and a ridiculously funny breakdancing interlude), Dyer a touch of surrealism and Shearsmith a seemingly never-ending box of gruesome tricks. Ironically, the typically gloomy Dee is a delight – the man has never looked so happy to be on TV. And there’s another irony: what was previously the show’s most groan-worthy quality – the lameness of host Jimmy Carr’s script – has been almost completely rectified (credit, perhaps, to the new blood in the writers room).
Aside from everything Shearsmith says and does, the Halloween of it all is most evident in the “jokers”, pre-planned performances the comedians are periodically called up to do in an effort to make their peers laugh. These seem more gratifyingly weird than ever before, while the special guest appearances are starrier still. Yet the best value comes from the random conversational turns and strange little bits of prepared material the contestants spring on each other. You might go in thinking certain standups are more to your taste than others (not everyone will find Sanders’ dance about frogs as funny as I do), but by the end you’ll be impressed by all of them. Obviously comedians are funny as a rule – here, however, they’re working especially hard to prove it. In a sense, Last One Laughing is the polar opposite of the podcast: the bloated medium in which two comics chat about banalities over a thousand hours while laughing liberally at almost anything the other says.
Despite the impulse to equate comedy with scarcity, Last One Laughing turns out to be pure treat, no cynical trick. Bring on series three – and any other spin-offs the producers come up with in the meantime.

title: The White House Farm massacre – exclusive: new forensic evidence suggests Sheila Caffell killed herself. Is Jeremy Bamber innocent?
description: In 1986, Bamber was sentenced to life imprisonment for killing five members of his family. Now analysis of crime scene photographs by a leading forensic biologist could exonerate him
content:
In 1986, Bamber was sentenced to life imprisonment for killing five members of his family. Now analysis of crime scene photographs by a leading forensic biologist could exonerate him
On 7 August 1985 , five people were found dead at White House Farm in Essex , England: 28-year-old Sheila Caffell (familiarly known as Bambi ); her six-year-old twin sons Daniel and Nicholas ; and her adoptive parents, June and Nevill Bamber . All five had been shot with a rifle. Caffell’s 24-year-old brother, Jeremy Bamber , who was also adopted, had alerted Essex police to a disturbance inside the farmhouse – he said his father had called to tell him – and was outside with the police for four hours before the bodies were discovered. Caffell, who had recently been hospitalised with schizoaffective disorder and is said to have feared her children were going to be taken into foster care, was found with the rifle lying on her chest, pointing towards her neck. There were two gunshot wounds to her neck and chin, and a bloodied Bible by her side.
The case was initially thought to be open and shut, a tragic murder-suicide committed by Caffell. But a month later, Jeremy Bamber was arrested, after relatives went to the police to voice their suspicions about him, and his former girlfriend, Julie Mugford , then told police he had confessed the murders to her. The relatives went on to inherit from Nevill and June Bamber’s considerable estate after Bamber’s conviction. It was later discovered that Mugford had agreed to sell the story of their relationship to the News of the World for £25,000 if Bamber was convicted . Essex police and Crown prosecutors had also agreed to drop charges against her for burglary, chequebook fraud and selling cannabis, because “prosecuting her could jeopardise her availability or credibility as a key witness ”.
Bamber has now been in prison for 41 years, and questions have always been asked about the safety of his convictions. These have grown recently. The proper body to examine these questions is the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) , but it has already taken the CCRC four years to consider less than half the evidence that Bamber has submitted to it, and it has concluded that the four points (out of 10) in the submission that it has so far considered do not meet the high evidentiary threshold to refer the case back to the Court of Appeal . In the second piece in our series considering discrete pieces of evidence, the Guardian commissioned forensic biologist Sue Carney-Gannon to analyse the bloodstain patterns at the crime scene for the first time.
Forty years ago, the jury at Jeremy Bamber’s trial was given a binary choice. Either the 24-year-old son of well-to-do farming stock had killed five members of his adoptive family, including his sister, Sheila Caffell. Or Caffell, 28 – also adopted, but from a different family – had killed their parents and her six-year-old twin boys before turning the gun on herself.
What became known as the White House Farm massacre was a horrific case: brutal, chaotic, shockingly policed and, to this day, hugely controversial. On 28 October 1986, Bamber was convicted of the five murders in a 10-2 majority verdict at Chelmsford crown court, Essex, England.
But now a leading forensic biologist has presented evidence that Caffell took her own life. After analysing the crime scene’s bloodstains for the Guardian, Sue Carney-Gannon has concluded that the patterns on the clothing and body of Caffell point to suicide. “In my opinion, if Sheila Caffell took her own life using the rifle, as the defence for Jeremy Bamber assert, then this explains the distribution of blood on her nightdress and right arm,” she writes in her report. “In my opinion, these findings are accounted for by her having taken her own life with the rifle; blood from the wound under her chin running down the upper right front of her clothing and splashing on to her right forearm, then veering to her right side as her body and arms fell.”
Carney-Gannon’s conclusion challenges the prosecution case, which maintained that Bamber meticulously staged Caffell’s suicide after he shot their parents, June and Nevill Bamber, and her twins Nicholas and Daniel.
The crimes occurred in the early hours of 7 August 1985. It was originally reported as a murder-suicide committed by Caffell, who had been diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder and had been hospitalised earlier that year after a psychotic episode. Caffell’s delusions included the belief that she was possessed by the devil and her twin sons were evil.
Three days after the murders in the picturesque village of Tolleshunt D’Arcy, Bamber’s uncle and cousins went to Essex Police to suggest he had been behaving strangely and that they suspected him. His uncle, Robert Boutflour, provided the police with an elaborate theory to explain how he thought Bamber had killed his family. These relatives went on to inherit from June and Nevill Bamber’s considerable fortune.
On 3 September 1985, Bamber split up with his girlfriend, Julie Mugford, after she discovered he had cheated on her with her best friend. Four days later, exactly a month after the murders, Mugford gave a statement to the police, implicating him.
It soon emerged at Bamber’s trial how seriously the crime scene had been contaminated. At least 43 officers had trampled through the farmhouse, clothing and bedding had been destroyed, clumsy reconstructions resulted in bodies and murder weapons being displaced. Alarmingly, the crime scene was not secured for 32 days. The most reliable record of the crime is the series of photos police photographer Detective Constable Bird started taking two-and-a-half hours after officers first entered the farmhouse, although the scene was already heavily compromised.
A bundle of crime-scene photos was disclosed to Bamber’s defence before the 1986 trial. Fifteen years later, in 2001, a second bundle was disclosed to his new team, to prepare for his appeal. Finally, in 2011, following decades of legal battles and multiple court orders regarding non-disclosed evidence, Essex Police handed over 406 crime scene negatives to the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), the body tasked with investigating potential miscarriages of justice. When the CCRC refused to pay to have the negatives developed into hi-res photographs, Bamber’s supporters paid £2,295 to have them developed.
Late last year Bamber agreed to hand the crime scene photographs to the Guardian so we could get them forensically analysed. We asked Carney-Gannon, who has given expert evidence in more than 2,000 cases, to examine the bloodstain patterns, focusing on the master bedroom. In the 41 years since the murders, these photos have never been analysed in this way before. Bloodstain analysts use biology, chemistry, physics and maths to examine the size, shape and location of blood left at a crime scene, to reconstruct violent events.
Once seen, the crime scene photographs cannot be forgotten. Nevill Bamber was found in the kitchen, his head slumped in a coal scuttle. The twins were dead in their beds.
The Guardian asked Carney-Gannon to focus on the master bedroom. We believed that the crime scene there suggested a struggle had taken place between Caffell and June Bamber.
Caffell was found on the far side of the master bedroom with a bloodstained Bible by her side and the rifle on top of her. June Bamber lay in her bloodied nightdress against the door. There were multiple blood drops on the carpet between Caffell and June Bamber.
While Carney-Gannon stated she could not tell from the bloodstain pattern whether there had been a struggle in the room, her other findings were more interesting and seem more significant.
At Bamber’s trial, the prosecution argued that he had led Caffell into the master bedroom, asked her to lie down, then shot her twice in the neck. The prosecution argued that she must have been murdered, because it was impossible for her to shoot herself in the neck twice. This has long been refuted by scientific evidence showing the first shot, into her lower neck, was not fatal.
At trial, the pathologist Peter Vanezis was called by the prosecution, but the evidence he presented challenges the prosecution case. Vanezis believed Caffell had been sitting up when she received both injuries, and fell backwards immediately after the second shot. He indicated that Caffell could have walked around briefly after receiving the first of her neck wounds. Vanezis told the court that, from the pathological evidence alone, he could not say whether Caffell had been murdered or taken her own life. Despite being a witness for the prosecution, he testified at the trial: “My examination did not reveal anything to contradict the suicide theory.”
Carney-Gannon’s analysis of the bloodstain patterns reaches the same conclusion – that Caffell was sitting when she was shot. “In my opinion, the blood stains to Sheila Caffell’s clothing and right arm suggest she was sitting upright as the shot entered under the chin, and blood began to run down her upper front and splashed on to her right forearm. As she began falling backwards, blood on the front of her clothing began to run to the side, and as her arms fell, blood on her forearm adjusted direction due to gravity.”
The forensic biologist says the blood pattern analysis cannot help determine whether Caffell shot the rest of the family or whether Jeremy Bamber did. However, throughout the trial Mr Justice Drake laid out the zero-sum nature of the case to the jury. In summing up, he said: “On the facts of this case, the killer was either Sheila or Jeremy Bamber and therefore it follows that if you are sure that Sheila did not carry out the killings, then it must be Jeremy Bamber who did.”
Carney-Gannon refutes the theory proposed at trial that Bamber shot Caffell while she was lying down. “If she had been lying on the floor when he shot her, then in my opinion, this would not readily explain the pattern of blood on Sheila Caffell’s clothing, particularly the veering of the blood to her right side, since she would not have fallen after the shot.” She says she assumes that if he had shot her while she was lying down, he would have had to first incapacitate her.
At trial, it was never suggested that Bamber had incapacitated Caffell. The prosecution argued that Caffell was passive and compliant due to the high dose of haloperidol, an antipsychotic drug, that she had been taking. In fact, her dosage had just been dramatically reduced because it was causing severe side-effects, including muscle stiffness and a “zombie-like” state. The defence argued that the sudden reduction had caused a psychotic episode that resulted in the massacre.
Carney-Gannon does not rule out the possibility that Bamber shot his sister, but suggests the only feasible way he could have done so is to have shot her under the chin while she was standing up. “The possibility that Ms Caffell was upright and Jeremy Bamber held the rifle barrel under her chin and fired, cannot be ignored.” Even here, though, Carney-Gannon says she struggles to explain the blood patterns she has analysed. “In my opinion, that scenario might result in similar blood patterns to her upper clothing, but might not readily explain the blood on her forearm, if her arms were by her side at the point she received the shot.”
At trial, Vanezis, the pathologist for the prosecution, explicitly ruled out the possibility that Caffell had been shot while standing. He pointed out that her nightdress would have been more heavily stained if she had been standing when shot the first time, or if she stood up after having been shot. In his expert testimony, Vanezis said: “The nature of the blood stains to the nightdress suggested that Sheila Caffell was sitting up when she received both injuries. After the second injury she would have immediately fallen back.”
Carney-Gannon’s analysis of the blood patterns around June Bamber suggests she suffered a horribly slow, messy death. June received wounds to her chest, arms, upper back and head. Carney-Gannon believes the bloodstains on the bed suggest June sat on it after being shot. “In my opinion, this distribution of blood on this location of the bedding is explained if June Bamber sat in this position while injured and bleeding from wounds in her arms, back, and possibly other areas, and with blood on her hands,” she writes.
Her report, which has been peer-reviewed, comments on the “numerous blood drips on the carpet around the body of June Bamber, across the floor at the foot of the bed, and on the floor at the far side of the bed where the body of Sheila Caffell was found ... The number of drips and the extent of the distribution suggest a person (or persons) who was actively bleeding has moved around these areas … In my opinion these findings are explained if June Bamber was the injured person moving around the bedroom whilst bleeding.” The blood staining on June’s feet “supports the suggestion she walked around the bedroom whilst bleeding and dripping blood on to the carpet”.
Carney-Gannon has also identified two bullet holes and a cartridge casing on the bed – indicated by green arrows in the photo above – where the shooter appears to have missed their target. She says she cannot discount the possibility that the bullet holes may be the result of bullets that hit and then exited June Bamber, but she believes they are likely to be “the result of shots that did not strike any of the deceased parties”.
At trial, ballistics expert Malcolm Fletcher stated that every shot had hit the target area, saying there were “25 hits out of 25”, indicating that 25 bullets and 25 empty cartridge cases had been found. The prosecution argued that Bamber – a skilled huntsman – had to be the killer, because Caffell was insufficiently experienced with a rifle to have a 100% hit rate. The defence argued that Caffell did have limited knowledge of handling .22 rifles because she had grown up on the farm and attended rural shoots.
The bullets identified by Carney-Gannon imply that the shooter was less skilled than has been suggested. After all, not only does Carney-Gannon suspect that some bullets missed June Bamber, she believes June probably moved around for some time after being shot.
Carney-Gannon’s findings support a forensic investigation the Guardian commissioned from the prestigious forensic physician Professor Jason Payne-James, earlier this year, into whether or not a silencer was used in the shooting of Caffell.
The silencer in question was found three days after the massacre, in a downstairs storage cupboard at White House Farm, by relatives who went on to inherit from the Bamber estate. This silencer was crucial in the case against Bamber. The prosecution argued that Caffell’s arms were not long enough to kill herself had the silencer been attached to the rifle, and, if she had shot herself, she would obviously have been unable to replace the silencer in the downstairs cupboard. At trial, it was stated that blood belonging to Caffell was found inside this silencer.
Mr Justice Drake told the jury that if they were convinced beyond reasonable doubt that a silencer was used, then Bamber was guilty of the murders. Minutes before they convicted Bamber, the jury returned to ask whether the blood in the silencer definitely belonged to Caffell. The judge told them it did. In fact, it was merely her blood grouping, which she shared with Robert Boutflour, who regularly used the guns. Later testing suggested the blood found in the silencer might not even be human.
Payne-James concluded that a silencer had not been used, and that the two shots to Caffell’s neck and chin were either contact or close-contact wounds. This dismantled much of the prosecution’s case against Bamber, and is consistent with Carney-Gannon’s view.
The new findings will be handed to the Criminal Cases Review Commission, the body responsible for investigating alleged miscarriages of justice and referring them to the Court of Appeal if it concludes there is a “real possibility” that a conviction may be unsafe. The commission spent four years examining four out of 10 points in the latest submission by Bamber, before rejecting them.
After being criticised for its low referral record in recent years (1.5% of total applications in 2023/24 were referred to the Court of Appeal), the CCRC’s chair and CEO were forced to resign last year. Under the leadership of interim chair Dame Vera Baird KC, there has been a sharp increase in referrals – 45 cases were referred in the 2025/26 financial year, compared with 31 in 2024/25. Baird accused the previous regime of “almost looking for reasons not to refer”.
It is hard to see how the commission will not be swayed by Carney-Gannon’s findings, especially under its new leadership. After all, the new evidence regarding stray bullets that were shot at the bed; June Bamber sitting down and walking around after being hit by an unskilled shooter; and, most importantly, the blood stains suggesting that Sheila Caffell shot herself, turns the case on its head.
A spokesperson for the Jeremy Bamber Innocence Campaign says: “This report supports what Jeremy has said all along, that he did not murder his family. The report is clear that the blood patterns present at the scene are consistent with the initial conclusion drawn by the police at the scene, that his seriously mentally ill sister Sheila killed her family and then herself. These two terrible tragedies have been compounded by how long it is taking the appeal system to recognise this in the light of the scientific evidence now available.”

title: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films
description: New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movie
content:
New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movie
S andra Hüller is crying, and it feels very strange. A wildly gifted actor, she can convey every human emotion there is. On screen, though, she is most often asked to embody deep self-possession. Even doing karaoke, Hüller is in control. And in real life, life is good. Her 2026 will end with four high-profile movies this year alone. Two (Fatherland and Rose) are black-and-white arthouse films that centre on her brilliance, and though one of the others (Digger) is already a Hollywood cautionary tale, a second (Project Hail Mary) was a giant $684m hit. (There may also be a fifth movie, bigger still. We will come back to that.)
And yet, dressed in film star black, she is in tears. “This is really hard for me,” she says.
We are talking about Fatherland. Directed by acclaimed Polish film-maker Paweł Pawlikowski, Hüller plays the German polymath Erika Mann, who in the film drives her novelist father Thomas Mann through newly divided postwar Germany. The Nazi past shadows everything – but the movie is also tied up with the birth of East Germany, where Hüller grew up. (She still lives in what was once the GDR.) I tell her I’ve never before seen a film that acknowledged the utopian dreams of that place and time, however damaged they became. Yes, she replies: German directors don’t know how to approach it.
“But Fatherland has a grief that you feel clearer coming from the East.”
And then her voice cracks, and she cries. We reflexively apologise to each other. “I’m just grateful Pawel gave space to this political idea that didn’t survive in Germany , but is one maybe people can still think about. The socialist idea.”
Hüller wipes her eyes. Finally, she laughs. “You’re going to say I cried, aren’t you? I can see the headline.”
And yet she has always been open about the nuance to the East Germany she remembers from childhood – a place defined by more than the Stasi men of cold war thrillers. “What fascinates me is that in East and West were two systems that for a certain time could have learned from each other.” She apologises again; I’m not sure why. “It is this situation we live in now. I feel like I’m on thin ice.”
Inevitably, we come to the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The subject is doubly unavoidable in light of Fatherland. The Manns originally fled the country in 1933 and they would end up in the US. “It’s no secret there are similarities now,” Hüller says. “Fascism doesn’t arrive overnight. It gets here slowly, in little doses.” Her tone turns businesslike. “The question is what we do about it.”
We all contain multitudes, but Hüller more than most. At home in Leipzig, she is a co-founder of the experimental Farn Kollektiv theatre group; a politically engaged woman of 48, she is the single mother to a teenage daughter. She is also deadpan funny. An account of her excellent safety record as a driver is a comic treasure. “ That should be your headline. ‘Sandra Hüller – a clean licence.’”
She is also a movie actor with snowballing momentum. In 2024, she astonished twice over as the wife of the commandant of Auschwitz in The Zone of Interest and a woman suspected of murdering her husband in Anatomy of a Fall. The latter saw her Oscar-nominated. Now, after Project Hail Mary, Digger and Fatherland, there will also be Rose, a stark 17th century fable in which she plays a war veteran – who is, in fact, a woman passing as a man. Oscar talk is simmering once more. America is freshly excited.
“OK, so what is happening is that I made very different movies at different times, but they’re all coming out together. It’s nothing I control.” What is good, she says, is that, with her as the common thread, Hollywood marketing budgets end up spotlighting the likes of Fatherland too. “On the other hand, I struggle with seeing myself as someone special. I still consider myself part of a group. That is actually the highest praise I can give myself.”
Curiously, a collective spirit might also apply to the fifth film Hüller is strongly rumoured to be in this year: Marvel relaunch Avengers: Doomsday. Whatever else Marvel movies represent, they have a reputation for an oddly egalitarian vibe on set. I wonder aloud if that’s true. “Me too!” She gives an impish tilt of the head. Ah. For the record, then, Hüller still may or may not be part of the new Avengers.
But in theory, a Marvel film might feel unexpectedly non-hierarchical? “I heard that as well! Which would show having a lot of money available doesn’t have to mean abusing your power. And that would be a great thing. In theory.”
If the thought of Hüller doing Marvel takes getting used to, it makes more sense after Project Hail Mary. In a deft piece of Hollywood feelgood, she proved the perfect foil for Ryan Gosling’s reluctant spaceman as stone-faced mission controller Eva Stratt. The air of ultra-competence was very Sandra Hüller for Beginners. The film even harked back to her 2016 breakthrough in skewed German comedy Toni Erdmann. Hüller has a glorious singing voice. Then, she karaoked Whitney Houston’s Greatest Love of All. Now, it was Harry Styles’ Sign of the Times.
“But I think Eva Stratt made some people uncomfortable. It can feel unusual to be governed by a woman.”
Still, making Project Hail Mary was another pleasant surprise – her first Hollywood set where the directors – Phil Lord and Christopher Miller – actually lightened the mood. “They made sure we could actually play. Have fun.” She did, though, find it strange being wrangled by runners on the kind of blockbuster where producers want to know where a star is at all times. (Unlike almost every actor on her level, Hüller doesn’t even have an assistant.) “But you can always hide in the bathroom.”
Would she spend more time in the US than necessary? “Not right now. No. It’s a workplace.” Anyway, she says, she likes where she lives. “It’s simple. America is just very far away.” And she smiles.
She believes audiences embraced Project Hail Mary because the film-makers sought to unite them, inside a cinema at least. “And entertain them without the usual things – death and weapons. So you have a story about a human with a task that lets them be bigger than themselves. That inspired people.”
But what about their response to Digger? Directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, with Tom Cruise as a cartoonish oil tycoon, the movie got poor reviews, then did cataclysmically at the box office. Can we talk about it? “Sure!” she says brightly. “I mean, we expected a strong reaction. It’s a polarising movie. And a political movie, which we weren’t able to say in interviews. For whatever reason.” A beat. “But personally – I was surprised by the harshness of the rejection. People really hated it!”
Hüller, though, says she loves it. “Years from now, it will be seen as a document of our times.” But time won’t be able to fix a problem like the thinness of her role as the sister of Cruise’s character. There should have been more of her, I say. “Well, there was.” Naturally, she smiles. Ah. (Again.) More rumours put forward that her role was heavily cut by Iñárritu. “You’d have to talk to Alejandro.” Are they still friendly? “Of course!”
At the movie’s royal gala premiere in London, the audience spent hours watching on screen the introductions of Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, to the cast and many others. I tell Hüller a cameraman briefly focused on her, waiting in a red carpet frock with a look that suggested a looming medical procedure. The memory clearly tickles her.
So what was she thinking? “Well, I thought of the people in the cinema, waiting for us to start the movie, and not being able to leave. Also, my feet really hurt.” But she has a surprise in store. “I mean, I’ve never met any royalty in my life, so I was also fangirling.” Really? Hüller seems an unlikely monarchist. “I don’t find the monarchy interesting. But they are fascinating, remarkable personalities.” So what did she finally talk about with the royal couple? “Oh, I can’t remember. I was in shock!” Would she like to meet them again? “Of course! I want to have tea with them! I want to talk about everything with them!”
If we do include the Avengers, her fifth film of this most productive year is Rose. Like Fatherland, it is a story of the German past, in black and white. And yet, after fun with royals and Ryan Gosling, Rose now brings her back to modern Germany. It was filmed in Saxony-Anhalt, “where a certain party recently won power”. (This is the German state where the AfD claimed 43.8% of the vote in September.)
In preparation to play a character passing as male, Hüller says she watched men more closely than she ever had before. The result was a study of all that goes into being read as male. “Honestly, it left me astonished. I realised that as a woman, I rarely enter a room and think of it as a battleground. But male behaviour is so related to that. Where is the enemy and how can I defeat him?”
So do men make bad socialists? “No! Some of the most famous socialists have been men.” Could that be why we don’t have socialism, though? She grins and wags a finger. “You forgot Mamdani?” She also has a related point. “One advantage of being born in the GDR and seeing it fall apart, or reunified, however you want to call it, is you learn no system is for ever. And that is interesting in a time when the things we’ve done so long don’t work any more. So maybe it is good to think of different ways they could work in future.”
Hüller is having to rethink the present too. Despite still seeing herself as a theatre actor who sometimes makes films, her German stage career is now on hold – at least in front of the curtain. Fame complicates. “If you are part of an ensemble but people come to see you as if the others matter less, I don’t enjoy that.” But she has a workaround. Farn are now creating two new plays she will instead direct. (“One is about revenge. The other goodbyes.”) So far, she says, the new role has been a pleasure. “I love the discussions. I love watching people invent. And we will see how long this wave continues.”
She tells me she is also curious how my piece will turn out. In Germany, she says, interview subjects give notes on a draft before anything goes to print. We don’t do that in the UK, I say. “I know. But as the interviewed person, it gives you a feeling of being respected. Not that I don’t feel respected here. Anyway, I never change much.” She smiles. “Sometimes just a comma.” So will she read this? “No, because I have no say.”
And yes, she agrees, laughing, that means I can write whatever I want.
