title: Giorgia Meloni is Italy’s great political survivor. Could one man be about to bring her down?
description: With elections looming in 2027, Roberto Vannacci’s new far-right movement could fatally outflank the prime minister, says Riccardo Alcaro, head of research at Istituto Affari Internazionali
content:
With elections looming in 2027, Roberto Vannacci’s new far-right movement could fatally outflank the prime minister
G iorgia Meloni’s government became the longest serving in Italy’s republican history last month. This unusual political longevity, a moderate foreign policy, a certain personal charisma and even a recent spat with Donald Trump have combined to sharpen Meloni’s profile as the go-to leader on the European right.
Meloni’s personal approval rating – at about 41% – is one of the highest among west European leaders. Her far-right Brothers of Italy party has retained most of its support – a striking feat in our anti-incumbent era and by Italian standards, an achievement.
Yet all this may not suffice for her ruling coalition to be returned to power at Italy’s next election, in 2027.
Even before this week’s riots in Milan, Meloni’s greatest challenge was emerging from her far right, in the form of a new movement led by the former army general, Roberto Vannacci. The firebrand demagogue will, like Marine Le Pen in France, certainly seek to exploit the unrest to promote his party’s law-and-order credentials. If he succeeds, it could come at the expense of Meloni’s ruling coalition.
Vannacci was a high-ranking officer of almost 40 years’ service when in 2023 he self-published Il mondo al contrario (The World Turned Upside Down). Filled with hyper-conservative misgivings about such supposed western ills as cosmopolitanism, multiculturalism and feminism, Vannacci’s book became a sensation and the general was suspended from the armed forces.
But Vannacci’s extreme positions and abrasive style quickly made him a regular media presence, and with public attention came political interest. Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right League and a junior partner in Meloni’s coalition, calculated that pulling the general into his ranks could boost his dwindling ratings. Salvini’s instincts were not wrong: in 2024 Vannacci was elected to the European parliament. However, he soon quit the League and this year founded a new far-right party, National Future, to which, polls suggest , the League has been losing support , imperilling Meloni’s coalition’s chances of re-election.
Electoral logic and a common ideological background would point to a Meloni-Vannacci alliance, but Vannacci’s ideological extremism makes that difficult.
Vannacci has made the “remigration” of foreign nationals – an idea promoted by such radical forces as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) – a central plank of his programme. While opposition to migration is one of the defining features of Meloni’s government, it has never gone that far.
Vannacci’s emphasis on the traditional family is so uncompromising that he proposes giving parents additional votes in elections and an advantage in public recruitment. His programme insists that abortion “is not a right” while it promotes the so-called “ Mediterranean patriarchy ”, and advocates abolishing the specific crime of femicide . These positions sit uneasily with Meloni’s politics, which combine conservative values with her own self-image of female empowerment.
The sharpest divide relates to foreign policy. Vannacci aims at easing the burden of eurozone fiscal discipline and opposes plans for greater defence integration. Tellingly, he has joined the AfD-led Europe of Sovereign Nations grouping in the European parliament, a group shunned even by Salvini’s League, the most nativist member of the Meloni government. On Russia and Ukraine, the gap is wider still. Echoing the AfD, Vannacci has argued that Russia is not an imminent threat to Europe and has called for the reopening of trade and diplomatic channels with Moscow, including by buying Russian gas. Vannacci also opposes support for Ukraine. For Meloni, by contrast, backing Ukraine is a pillar of her international positioning, most recently attested by her open criticism of Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russian diesel exports, ahead of a hard winter for Ukraine.
Meloni’s reluctance to enter an alliance with Vannacci is understandable. Forza Italia, her centre-right coalition partner, fears it would drive away the moderate conservative vote. The League is so shaken that some of its members want to disavow Salvini’s nativist ideology and go back to the party’s roots, representing the interests of business and local communities in Italy’s northern regions .
For the time being, Meloni has responded to the far-right challenge by doubling down on migration. Vannacci’s presence in the electoral wings explains some of the background to her suspension of the Schengen free-movement rules for air and sea passengers from Spain after the Ceuta tragedy. The same applies to the recent decision to put a 30% ceiling on students of foreign origin in schools. But it is far from certain this strategy can work, and pressure to strike a deal with Vannacci may build, not least to prevent the former military man from claiming to be the only politician promising a hardline law and order response to vandalism and looting in Milan. Meloni’s dispatch of 500 troops to the city ahead of further planned cost-of-living demonstrations was aimed partly at taking the wind out of Vannacci’s sails.
While an alliance could increase Meloni’s chances of re-election Vannacci would be a restive and unreliable coalition partner.
The alternative is to delegitimise Vannacci as a nationalist force, pointing to his extremism and proximity to Russia. Meloni would hardly regain the most extreme nativist voters lost to Vannacci but could convince a section of the moderate electorate to choose her coalition over centrist parties.
This strategy entails a real risk that Meloni will lose the next election. Still, the onus is on her now to articulate why Vannacci’s mix of anti-EU nativism, homophobia and misogyny is incompatible with both her own brand of national conservatism and Italy’s place in Europe . Doing so would send a powerful message that the commitment to the EU’s democratic principles – and European cohesion – is a moral red line. It is also one that can be imposed by conservative nationalists like Meloni on fringe forces to their right. As the now-seasoned leader figures out how to juggle her political ambition against the challenge posed by Vannacci, she should consider how high the stakes are, not just for Italy, but for all of Europe.
Riccardo Alcaro is head of research at IAI, Istituto Affari Internazionali, in Rome

title: ‘Hot Santa’, Raging Bull and a Toy Story vibe help to rebuild The Snowman for a new generation
description: More than 30 years after Raymond Briggs’ story became a stage show, director Will Tuckett and Paddington designer Tahra Zafar have given it a hi-tech refresh with a hunky Saint Nick
content:
More than 30 years after Raymond Briggs’ story became a stage show, director Will Tuckett and Paddington designer Tahra Zafar have given it a hi-tech refresh with a hunky Saint Nick
“T op of the show!” says Will Tuckett. On the grand piano, musical director Andy Massey strikes up an arpeggio that could melt the most frozen of hearts: “We’re walking in the air …” It is The Snowman, of course. Raymond Briggs’ 1978 picture book was animated for the screen in 1982 with a score by Howard Blake and became a hit stage show in 1993, an annual outing for Birmingham Rep ever since. Now it’s getting a reboot, directed by Tuckett, former Royal Ballet dancer turned choreographer and director of everything from the National Ballet of Japan’s Nutcracker to a stage adaptation of In the Night Garden.
We’re in a studio in Birmingham. As the overture plays, a large wooden box in the centre of the room opens like the cover of a book, to become a house. There’s a kitchen, a couple at the table with a pot of tea and an endearing puppet cat winding round their legs. Upstairs, a boy wakes up, looking forward to Christmas .
The Snowman is a perennially popular show but “it needed a bit of a refresh,” says Tuckett. “Theatre’s changed a lot in 30 years – expectations have changed.” Audiences are so used to the latest effects that the scenes where the Snowman takes the boy flying, for example, were starting to lack the wow factor. The old show used a one-point harness to lift the actors, and if you drifted in the wrong direction “you had to swim back,” says Tuckett, miming the breaststroke in mid-air. Now they have a fancy automated system that lets them dance through the air against a backdrop by video designer Nina Dunn. “I was blown away,” says Tuckett. “She made all the snow feel 3D, the landscape 3D.” The effect will be much more filmic and immersive.
Puppetry is also much more sophisticated and ubiquitous than it was in 1993, from the trailblazing War Horse to the Paddington musical whose designer Tahra Zafar has created a Snowman costume, which can blink and smile as well as dance. Daisy Beattie has designed a menagerie of puppets, which the dancers manipulate: the curious cat, two pheasants on wheels, a lone fox and some sweet rabbits. Other things you can’t change too much. “The score is the score,” says Tuckett, although there are always tweaks. The original used lots of synth-y samples on keyboards, but the quality of sound you can generate electronically now is completely different.
Most important, though, is the story. “And it’s a story told through dance, it’s not a ballet with a story,” Tuckett clarifies. We might think of The Snowman as a bit saccharine, but “it’s a book about loneliness, and ultimately, it’s a book about loss”. He’s rejigged scenes to show that there’s lots of love, too. The simplicity of this story is the antidote to the fast-cut craziness of modern kids’ entertainment where “there’s a glitter shower – and then all the pyros go off,” he says. “This is very simple, very honest. It’s really about human relationships and family, but none of it is too heavy.” His job is “to slow things down, but keep things moving”.
Tuckett and the team had multiple visits to pore over Briggs’ original artworks. “It’s really emotional seeing it, because I was given the book as a kid at Christmas,” says Tuckett. “Going back and seeing his original marks and little notes on it, and the original cover – he used Tippex for some of the snow – it was just amazing.”
Tuckett opens his laptop and brings up an illustration of the boy and the Snowman flying. “It’s really hard to look at it and not well up and remember when you were small and when your kids were small.” He zooms in on the details. “I don’t want [the show] to look like a panto – it should feel like the drawings.” He and Zafar had been discussing how the simplest things are often the hardest. “Have you seen Raging Bull?” he asks, a reference I was not expecting. He describes how in Martin Scorsese’s film, all the boxing rings were different sizes and shapes, to give different visual effects, even though it’s ostensibly the same setting. The video projections will do some similar changing of perspective, but there are painted sets too. In the workshop, I find a giant snowy tree taking up the whole room.
The book is only around 30 pages long, the film was 26 minutes, and the stage show will be around an hour, so Tuckett’s job is to expand on the material, yet stay true to it, while making it all a bit less gendered. “Like, could the dad not just sit in his chair smoking a pipe and falling asleep while his wife does the washing up and the ironing?” says Tuckett. The biggest change will be more proper dancing. There are some new characters “who are really zoomy” and a Father Christmas who is “a beautiful classical dancer,” says Tuckett. “His jacket is a bit like one of those huge North Face ones, and when he takes it off, he looks like Hot Santa,” Tuckett laughs. “And it means then he can properly dance.”
In the previous show, they cast actors in the role of the young boy, but Tuckett has brought in dancers. Four of them, aged 11-14, will rotate the role. “We tried the flying the other day and it was really fun,” says one dancer, Tristan, while Tate, another, adds: “We get all those features from the film and the book and make them come to life.” Jake says: “It’s really cool being part of a new production and seeing how it’s made.” He watches the Snowman film every Christmas with his mum. Tuckett felt that the show, as it was, had become increasingly something for little kids. “I felt there was a bit of a disconnect with the adults in the audience.” The book, he says, is “so well observed, and the humour in it works if you’re a kid, but as an adult, it’s really clever”. Briggs’ illustration of the melted snowman still brings a lump to the throat. Is it going to be a Toy Story vibe, I ask: the kids will be laughing, the parents crying? “It’s totally that,” smiles Tuckett.
The Snowman is at Birmingham Rep until 1 November, then Peacock theatre, London , 21 November-3 January 2027

title: Caleb Williams outduels friend and rival Drake Maye as Bears beat Patriots
description: Caleb Williams threw for 308 yards and two touchdowns, and the Chicago Bears cooled off Drake Maye and the New England Patriots with a 30-24 win
content:
New England Patriots 24–30 Chicago Bears
Bears QB throws for 308 yards and two TDs
Caleb Williams threw for 308 yards and two touchdowns, and the Chicago Bears cooled off Drake Maye and the New England Patriots with a 30-24 win on Thursday night.
Williams was 22 of 33 passing in his second game back after being sidelined by a hamstring injury . He became the first Bears quarterback to throw for more than 300 yards in consecutive games since Mitch Trubisky had a three-game run in 2018.
“It’s amazing [having Williams on the field]. His leadership, his competitiveness, everyone around here feels it. He gets us going,” said Bears running back D’Andre Swift after the game.
Williams outdueled Maye in their second meeting since the longtime friends were part of the 2024 NFL draft. Williams went No 1 to Chicago, and Maye was selected by New England at No 3.
Luther Burden had four catches for 130 yards for Chicago (5-2), and Colston Loveland had a 12-yard touchdown reception. Cairo Santos kicked a 58-yard field goal with 1:34 left, a career long and matching the franchise record, after he missed a 53-yard attempt earlier in the final quarter. That made it 30-21 but Maye then drove New England into range for Andy Borregales’s 47-yarder with 37 seconds to go. However, Chicago recovered the ensuing onside kick and ran down the clock.
Maye was 24 for 31 for 321 yards and two touchdowns. He also threw a costly interception in the end zone in the first half.
New England (4-3) had won three consecutive games behind Maye, who threw 10 TD passes and one interception during the win streak. Rhamondre Stevenson had five catches for 93 yards and a touchdown for the Patriots. Eli Raridon had a 30-yard TD catch in the third quarter.
It was Chicago’s first home game since Mike Ditka died on 9 October. The Bears saluted the Hall of Fame tight end and longtime coach with a pregame moment of silence, and they also handed out fake mustaches to the crowd of 60,520 at Soldier Field. Ditka’s No 89 jersey dotted the stands, and fans also donned Bears sweaters in a callback to the gear he wore on the sideline as a coach.
The Bears jumped out to a 10-0 lead in the first quarter thanks to a ‌Santos 43-yard field goal and Swift’s four-yard touchdown run.
New England responded when Maye scored on a seven-yard run early in the ​second quarter, but Santos made a 31-yard field goal to give Chicago a 13-7 lead.
The teams traded touchdowns in the final 14 seconds of the half. After Williams connected with Burden for a 24-yard TD pass, ⁠New England scored on a 48-yard pass from Maye to Stevenson ​with no time remaining ​on the clock. Stevenson caught the ​pass on the Chicago 47 and eluded several defenders ​on his way to ‌the end zone. ​Borregales made the ​extra point, which pulled the Patriots closer at 20-14. Chicago extended the margin to 27-14 when Loveland capped the second half’s opening drive with a 12-yard TD catch, but New England answered with a 30-yard scoring pass from Maye to Raridon on the ensuing drive.

title: 2GB touts ‘Ben Roberts-Smith day’ as Fordham interviews alleged war criminal
description: Nine newspapers factcheck Roberts-Smith interview. Plus: Daily Telegraph links French riots to reusable coffee cups
content:

“It’s Ben Roberts-Smith day!” 2GB host Ben Fordham declared on Thursday, followed by forward sizzles for stories about gender-neutral language being used about breastfeeding and Bogong moths.
And so it was. About 250,000 people had watched the two-and-a-half-hour long interview between the shock jock and the alleged war criminal by Friday morning.
That was plenty of time to hear all about Roberts-Smith the soldier, the father, the lover, the “proud warrior” (Fordham’s words). Time to hear about the man who’s here to do his duty, to talk about his missions, his heroics, his meeting with the Queen, his naivety when the war crime allegations began, and his denials of wrongdoing. There was even enough time to learn that he had to put Y-fronts over his eyes to block the light while he was in prison.
And to admire the Epic 1 Two logo across his chest, his old call-sign now part of his new activewear range “for the underdog who refuses to stay down” (slightly unfortunate wording for the war-inspired range).
Roberts-Smith has strongly denied all charges.
The Nine newspapers, which published a series of award-winning investigations into Roberts-Smith, did a handy factcheck on the chat .
And if too much BRS was barely enough, News Corp ran exclusive interviews with Roberts-Smith and his girlfriend, Sarah Matulin.
Fordham asked him why he was doing the interview now, with “a really serious trial coming up” (effectively answering his own question).
It’s about putting “facts on the table”, Roberts-Smith said.
The interview ended with Roberts-Smith saying he doesn’t know how they’ll find “a jury that hasn’t already to some degree formed an opinion”.
“Can there be a fair trial? I can’t answer that question,” he said.
The continuing riots across Europe began with young people protesting about the state of schools, and has escalated to encompass cost-of-living concerns. Others who “destroy, ransack and loot”, in French president Emmanuel Macron’s words, have joined in and fuelled the violence. There, the far right have linked it – without evidence – to migration.
Nevertheless, Pauline Hanson and a host of One Nation-adjacent folk insist mass migration is behind the European riots and Australia could be next.
Not to be outdone in the hunt for a one-dimensional explanation, the Daily Telegraph found a different culprit – the Minns government’s planned ban on single-use coffee cups.
“Now might not be the best time to adopt an idea that began in riot-torn France,” the Tele’s editorial said, adding that instead of reusable coffee cups the French would now “be better off carrying fire extinguishers and medical kits”.
France brought in a range of bans on single-use items more than a decade ago, although not all of the bans are yet in force. And it did cause some consternation among restaurant owners about who would foot the bill. But widespread, violent riots? You’re milking it, sugar.
Like the Rorschach test , people found their own meanings in the social media feed of Brendan Nugent, the man who allegedly attacked independent MP Helen Haines .
The Tarrawingee man’s posts on X (formerly known as Twitter) sparked a frenzy of political point-scoring as Haines lay in a critical condition in hospital.
Some saw an old, seemingly sarcastic post about “Dame Pauline Hanson” as proof he was a One Nation acolyte.
One News Australia, formerly the One Nation Supporters Network , called him a “radical, green activist”.
News24 (formerly Sky News) revealed a Greens “link” – that leader David Shoebridge had unfollowed him in the wake of the attack.
The Australian Jewish Association labelled him an “anti-Israel extremist”.
So far, no one has taken particular umbrage at his handle – @notLaoTzu – to furiously accuse him of hating the Daoist Chinese philosopher, but it’s probably just a matter of time.
Also missing in the maddened finger-pointing was the logical end point – if he allegedly carried out the attack due to his views on climate change and Gaza, why on earth did he go after Haines, a progressive independent?
Many so-called “mainstream” media outlets took care to look at the nuance of Nugent’s history and to mention that, at this point, we don’t actually know of any motive behind the alleged attack.
Southern Cross Media – which merged with Seven West earlier this year and includes Seven, TripleM, the West Australian and more – unveiled its lineup for next year at its Seven Upfront 2027 event on Thursday night under the Big Top in Luna Park.
Hopefully the razzle dazzle wasn’t undermined too much by the ABC’s report on Wednesday about sexism and bullying allegations.
Reporter Paddy Manning got hold of the secret 2024 review of Seven West Media’s “diabolical” company culture and the story came out just in time for the big party.
Anthony Albanese backflipped on the idea of a royal commission into antisemitism after heavy pressure from the victims of the Bondi attack, Jewish community groups, the Coalition and his own caucus .
This week’s 22nd annual News awards also credited “11 straight front pages” in The Australian for the move, which won it the title of state/national campaign of the year. The broadsheet also won brand of the year.
The Daily Telegraph took out the best coverage of a major event award for its Bondi terror attack reporting at the in-house awards.
Now here’s a journalist who deserves an award. ABC reporter Will Murray saved a man from drowning in flood waters on Thursday.
The man was trapped in his sinking car at Morayfield when Murray made the call to swim out to him, and he and another man were able to pull him out and to safety.
“All three of us gave each other a big hug and were just so relieved,” Murray said.
“It was very scary, but happy everyone is safe and relieved it is OK.”
You have to wonder if it will change the tone when the BBC World Service moves some of its operations from overnight in London to daytime in Sydney.
The broadcaster has been forced to make a number of cuts due to its dire financial situation .
The shift for the radio bulletins, the Newsroom program and the Global Newscast comes as part of the Beeb’s “Follow the Sun” strategy. The “big move” is about “building a multi-platform operation in Sydney to fulfil our output commitments when London is asleep”, according to an internal briefing.
“This means the current UK night shift for both teams would end [while] media operations roles would remain in London.”
Twenty-six jobs will be lost in London and 19 created in Sydney.
The BBC already has a bureau in Sydney to cover its websites in Australia’s daytime hours.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Uncertainty over Kyiv’s Starlink access after Trump claims Musk restored service
description: US president says Starshield military communications system is back, but declines to comment on whether he spoke to Musk on the matter. What we know on day 1,703
content:
US president says Starshield military communications system is back, but declines to comment on whether he spoke to Musk on the matter. What we know on day 1,703
Donald Trump has claimed that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk fully restored Ukraine’s Starlink access , restrictions on which have hampered Ukraine’s attack missions and air defence. However, a senior European official told the Associated Press on Thursday that nothing has changed in the operation of the military-grade Starshield service. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine’s use of ⁠the system. Trump on Thursday appeared to confirm that the service had been down, but claimed it was once again working at optimal speeds. “You know, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference,” he said. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back.”
Questions over who ordered interruptions to Starshield – which plunged relations between Kyiv and Washington to a new low – have ignited a blame game within the Trump administration and its allies . Trump has denied being involved in the decision concerning the slowdown, while US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said that decisions regarding Ukraine’s access to Starlink were up to its parent company SpaceX and Musk, not the White House. Musk last week posted to X: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ⁠on Thursday – before Trump’s latest comments – that Starlink had not ⁠been fully restored.
Russia pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight , after US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin to discuss the resumption of peace talks. Russia’s aerial attacks hit 12 regions of Ukraine, killing at least four people and wounding scores of others, including five children, Zelenskyy said on social media Thursday. Two women, aged 50 and 60, were killed and dozens of other people were wounded in a Russian strike on a market in Lozova, in Ukraine’s northeeastern Kharkiv region, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration. Another person was killed in other strikes on Kharkiv.
Downing Street has rejected the description of Putin as a “humanitarian” made by Witkoff after meeting the Russian president. When asked about the US envoy’s comments, a Downing Street spokesperson said: “We certainly do not recognise that characterisation, and President Putin has killed thousands of people, both innocent Ukrainians and his own Russian people, who he has sent to their deaths on the frontline.” Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha chided Witkoff for flattering Putin, saying on social media the latest “brutal” Russian attacks demonstrate “what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like.”
Nato member Denmark said on Thursday it has agreed to buy its first ⁠long-range precision missiles as ⁠it seeks to bolster its security to deter Russian aggression in Europe, drawing condemnation from Moscow. Defence minister Jeppe Bruus said the new missile systems would boost Denmark’s capabilities and enable strikes “behind enemy lines” ⁠if attacked. “We’re in a serious and deteriorating security situation and that ​is why we are ‌building up the defence ‌and strengthening our combat power,” he said. The Russian embassy in ‌Copenhagen said Denmark’s missile policy aimed at confrontation with Moscow and warned of “inevitable disastrous consequences”.
Romania will accelerate development of surveillance capabilities and equipment to counter mines ⁠and drones in the Black Sea after a series of drone attacks on commercial ships off ⁠its coast , its ⁠top defence council ​said on Thursday. At least seven cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Nato members ⁠Romania and Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with 30 sailors reported dead or missing.
No ⁠deals should ​be made to buy gas from ⁠Russia as long as Moscow’s war ⁠in Ukraine continues, Finland’s prime ⁠minister Petteri Orpo said in Kyiv on Thursday . The EU banned Russian pipeline gas under short-term contracts ​from 17 June, and will ​apply it to long-term contracts from 1 November next year. Senior Russian political and energy officials meanwhile have urged the EU to reconsider plans to ban imports of ⁠Russian LNG, arguing the bloc’s ⁠low storage levels ​had put Europe in a precarious position. “I ‌hope there is still time to reconsider these decisions,” Leonid Mikhelson, the head of Novatek, Russia’s largest liquefied natural ‌gas producer, told an economic forum in Istanbul on Thursday. “Europe should support its industry, in my view. There is still time.”

title: Embattled Queensland minister Amanda Camm quits Crisafulli frontbench citing health and safety reasons
description: Camm, who resigned following months of pressure over her handling of state’s child safety system, cited Helen Haines attack as reason for departure
content:
Camm, who resigned following months of pressure over her handling of state’s child safety system, cited Helen Haines attack as reason for departure
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
The Queensland minister Amanda Camm has resigned from cabinet following months of pressure over the state government’s handling of the child safety system and efforts to prevent domestic and family violence.
Camm told reporters on Friday the decision to step down was “mine alone”.
She suggested that some criticism of her had gone beyond “public scrutiny and accountability” and cited the recent alleged attack on federal MP Helen Haines .
Over the past year she had experienced harassment, threats, bullying and vilification, she said.
Camm had recently taken six weeks of medical leave, including undergoing a surgical procedure. She said she had realised her recovery would be “ongoing” and that she would not be able to continue perform her ministerial duties, given the workload and “the ongoing stresses”.
“It would be unfair to the government for me to take further leave,” Camm said.
A replacement is expected to be announced later on Friday.
Before taking leave, Camm had been the government’s most under-pressure minister. Her relationship with Tim Mander , the sport and Olympics minister, had placed both under scrutiny in parliament and the press.
But it was her dual responsibilities – child safety and the prevention of family violence – that had heaped pressure on Camm over her job performance.
The government came under fire over claims of children in state care sleeping on the floor of government offices , which child protection workers linked to government policies including the cancelling of contracts to some residential care providers.
Camm also came under pressure over budget cuts to domestic and family violence prevention, and a lack of progress on reforms demanded by the former government’s women’s safety and justice taskforce.
Guardian Australia reported that Camm had buried the findings of a panel of domestic and family violence victim-survivors, which was highly critical of police. Her office told one member she was no longer welcome to contact them by phone .
Camm said the attack on Haines had “reinforced the importance of taking concerns about personal health, safety and wellbeing of people in public life very seriously”.
“Public scrutiny and accountability are central to democracy and to our institutions. Harassment, threats, bullying and personal vilification are not. And for the past year this has been my experience. There is much more work to be done.”
The premier, David Crisafulli , said he wanted to “support Amanda” and that she had not been removed over her performance.
It is understood that the government will not instigate a broader reshuffle but will appoint a new face to the ministry to replace Camm.
Among those considered in the frame for a promotion is former senator and Morrison government figure Amanda Stoker, who was elected to the state parliament in 2024.

title: Indigenous girl, 16, shackled to hospital bed after being allegedly dragged through her home by police in Perth
description: WA government has defended the practice of shackling people in hospital as ‘part of standard custodial management practices’
content:
WA government has defended the practice of shackling people in hospital as ‘part of standard custodial management practices’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
The Western Australian justice department has defended its use of restraints after a 16-year-old Indigenous girl was shackled to a Perth hospital bed after she was taken into custody.
A photo shared by the family showed the teenager’s ankles bound in chains and locked to the underside of a hospital bed.
The girl’s grandmother, who cannot be named to protect the identity of her grandchild, alleged police used excessive force while arresting the teenager over allegations of child neglect, including dragging her while she was topless.
The teenager gave birth to a child several months ago.
The grandmother, who visited her granddaughter in hospital, where she was taken after the arrest in the custody of department of justice staff for an undisclosed health issue, said her grandchild had scratches on her breasts and stomach from her handling by police. She said the use of the shackles in the hospital was appalling and called for the practice to stop.
“I would like for her to have been treated like a human being because she is one,” the grandmother said.
A spokesperson for the WA justice department said it could not comment specifically on the girl’s case but that restraining people in custody was in accordance with its policies and procedures.
“Where a person in custody is being treated in an unsecured medical facility, appropriate restraint measures are used as part of standard custodial management practices,” the spokesperson said.
“Medical practitioners can request that restraints be modified or removed where deemed clinically necessary. These measures are in place to ensure the safety of the person in custody, hospital staff, custodial officers, and the wider community.”
Mervyn Eades, a Noongar man and community advocate, said the practice of using shackles was an “abomination”.
“We’re talking about a child, not a serious criminal” he said. “With past atrocities against our peoples I look at those chains on her legs and I automatically think of colonisation and how our people were placed in them.”
In response to allegations excessive force was used to arrest the teenager, a spokesperson for WA police said: “A review of officer body-worn camera vision has been conducted and the officers were found to have acted within policy during the arrest.”
They said police went to the girl’s house in response to concerns about the welfare of her child and found upon arrival the children was unharmed.
“After a short verbal exchange, it will be alleged the female, who was present at the time, resisted arrest by attempting to push past officers and enter the residential premises. She was subsequently brought to the ground and placed into custody,” the spokesperson said.
Police charged the girl with one count of breaching protective bail conditions, one count of endangering the life, health or safety of a person, and one count of failing to protect a child from harm.
Australian state and territory governments have been coming under pressure over their use of shackles on incarcerated people in hospital settings, including women while they give birth.
In October, Victorian senator Lidia Thorpe, a Gunnai, Gunditjmara and Djab Wurrung woman, introduced legislation to ban shackling of incarcerated women during childbirth and to stop children being strip-searched.
Its passage was blocked by Labor and the Coalition, with Labor saying “the responsibility of the criminal justice system predominantly sits with state and territory governments”.
Days later, an incarcerated Indigenous woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while she was in labour.
In 2016, a Noongar man was handcuffed and shackled to a hospital bed in Western Australia while he was comatose after collapsing during a court appearance for a driving offence.
Debbie Kilroy, a spokesperson for advocacy group the National Network, said the latest incident in Perth demonstrates why the federal government needed to step in to regulate state actions.
“When politicians tell us that shackling is a state issue, what they are really saying is that they are prepared to leave women and girls at the mercy of police and prison officers,” Kilroy said.
“We need to ask ourselves what it says about this country that we can look at a 16-year-old mother and see someone who needs to be chained down rather than someone who needs care.”
The WA attorney general and police minister were approached for comment.

title: In allowing coal expansion in the Hunter, Chris Minns is pouring fuel on the climate fire. His decision will come back to hurt us all
description: The high court found NSW is responsible for emissions from burning exported coal. What message does it send when the government can step in and bypass the law?
content:
The high court found NSW is responsible for emissions from burning exported coal. What message does it send when the government can step in and bypass the law?
Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here
As someone who lost their home in the black summer bushfires, I was buoyed by the high court finding in favour of a small community group in the Hunter Valley earlier this month.
Led by two retired science teachers, Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan, the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group took on a massive coal corporation and won . As a fellow schoolteacher, I felt a particular sense of pride seeing these ordinary Australians act on their care for their community and future generations.
In their four-year fight against MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant coalmine in Muswellbrook , they argued it is no longer OK for big mining corporations to dig up coal and bank piles of cash while pretending the climate pollution from burning that coal is someone else’s problem.
The high court agreed that conditions aimed at reducing the climate pollution from burning Australian coal overseas had not been properly considered when the rosily named “Mount Pleasant Optimisation Project” received New South Wales approval.
Mining interests quickly responded to the high court’s decision, saying it was a threat to investment. Well, of course it is. But only to the wrong kind of investment – the kind that brings us all more frequent, worse and very costly climate-driven disasters.
Now, less than two weeks later, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, has announced plans to introduce special legislation that will allow the very same coal company to increase production at Mount Pleasant by nearly a third, bypassing the state’s usual planning approval process and scrutiny by the courts.
Minns says this is necessary to protect 400 jobs. But the mine already has approval to operate until 2032. What message does it send when ordinary Australians fight for years to uphold the law, win in the highest court in the land and then watch our government step in to change the rules?
The premier tells us he has agonised over the environment versus jobs dilemma. Both, he says, are important. I strongly agree. A just transition for workers into new, good, climate-positive jobs is a core principle of thorough climate action.
Two brave, retired science teachers have shown what ordinary Australians can achieve when they act on the science and stand up. The Minns government must look beyond the next election and the demands of powerful fossil fuel lobbyists, search its own conscience and respect the rule of law. Even the big coal corporations need to play by the same rules as the rest of us.
On New Year’s Eve 2019, my partner Cath and I saw our home go up in flames before being separated. The fearful feeling of not knowing if each other had made it out alive is a memory that will never fully leave us. Nor will the widespread devastation we witnessed across our NSW coastal community. I knew then that an awful climate future had crashed right through into our present. It was a huge wake-up call. And yet Australian governments have continued to approve new coal and gas mines, pouring more fuel on to the climate fire.
The evidence is clear: Australia and the world already have enough coal, gas and oil in the pipeline to see us through the transition to renewable energy and reach global net zero emissions by 2050. No new or expanded coalmines, or oil and gasfields are needed on that pathway. This has been the view of the authoritative International Energy Agency since 2021. That agency, of which Australia is a member, is technology-neutral and was created back in the 1970s to ensure the reliable supply of fossil fuels. That reliability is still a big part of its remit. Somehow Australian governments have been missing the IEA’s emails.
For Wales and Lonergan, it was hugely stressful spending years taking on a massive coal corporation. But they stepped up, persevered, and they won.
Inspired by people like them, I have joined nine other ordinary Australians in taking our concerns to the United Nations human rights committee. The kernel of our Hard Truths case is that we are asking the United Nations human rights committee to assess whether Australia is breaching our human rights by continuing to approve and support coal and gas exports that fuel dangerous climate change. These are rights that belong to all of us – the right to life, family and home, and the rights of First Nations peoples to protect their Country and culture.
It gives us no joy to complain about our own government. But we have tried everything else and yet continue to see huge coalmine extensions approved and vast new gasfields opened. Their pollution will come back to hurt us all. We need the Australian government to come to their senses and act.
Jack Egan is a teacher, climate advocate, partner, father and grandfather living on the NSW south coast. On New Year’s Eve 2019, Jack and his partner Cath lost their home when the Currowan fire tore through their community during the black summer bushfires
