title: ‘The Bird Reich’: Atlanta Falcons roasted over throwback logo with Nazi resemblance
description: Atlanta’s retro design ahead of Sunday’s game against San Francisco prompted an avalanche of second world war jokes and Nazi comparisons online
content:
Retro design features red, white and black stripes
Social media users draw Nazi Germany comparisons
Falcons’ X post attracts roughly 26m views
Social media erupted in jokes and memes on Thursday after the Atlanta Falcons unveiled a logo that instantly drew comparisons with the imagery of Nazi Germany.
The logo – posted by the Falcons on the NFL team’s social media channels – shows the team’s old falcon symbol from the 1960s and 1970s, emblazoned on a background of red, white and black stripes.
The “throwback” design is being used in the run-up to Atlanta’s game against the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday.
But the design prompted an avalanche of comments from social media users who said it resembled iconography of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi Party.
The Falcons’ post revealing the design on X had attracted more than 26m views since being published early Thursday.
Comments beneath the post lampooned the logo mercilessly over its perceived Nazi resemblance.
“I must say, I was not expecting to wake up this morning to see that the Atlanta Falcons are preparing to invade Poland,” one user wrote.
Another referenced the Falcons’ notorious 2017 Super Bowl collapse against the New England Patriots.
“Falcons were up 28-3 at Dunkirk,” the user commented.
Others found ways to combine football terminology with second world war references. “Falcons leading the league in blitzkrieg,” one user joked.
One commenter dubbed the team the “28-3rd Reich”, combining the Nazi reference with Atlanta’s infamous Super Bowl meltdown.
“Now they just need to hire Frank Reich and it’ll be complete,” another wrote, referring to the former NFL head coach.
Another user commented that after this weekend’s home game against San Francisco, the Falcons had “road games in Dunkirk, Normandy, and Stalingrad”.
Others suggested the Falcons might need to change the NFL’s “End Racism” end-zone slogan to “Start Racism”, while one commenter offered a new billing for Sunday’s matchup: “49ers vs 39ers.”
Several users mocked the Falcons as the “Bird Reich”.
The Falcons did not immediately comment on the logo.

title: ‘We can’t just pretend that everything’s OK in the regions’: what went wrong in Wangaratta?
description: After Indi MP Helen Haines was allegedly attacked on Monday, people across the electorate are questioning how something like this could happen – and if anything could have been done to prevent it
content:
After Indi MP Helen Haines was allegedly attacked on Monday, people across the electorate are questioning how something like this could happen – and if anything could have been done to prevent it
S omething changed a few years ago. Brendan Nugent had been a reasonably prominent conservationist when Helen Haines – a longtime friend of his family – became his federal MP in 2019. He would sometimes visit his state MP’s electoral office, raising issues about forest preservation. Other locals in the north-east Victorian city of Wangaratta remember him back to his junior footy days, when he played alongside future stars of the AFL.
But a few years later, according to those who knew him, he changed. His physical and mental health issues became more apparent.
By the time he allegedly ran down Haines in Wangaratta on Monday, he was living in a ramshackle farmhouse outside town, surrounded by long uncut grass and empty beer cans.
Victoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon. He has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. The police investigation is ongoing.
At his first court appearance on Wednesday the magistrate noted Nugent had mental health and neurological concerns, and that it was his first time in custody. His lawyer, Chirag Patel, said Nugent suffered from idiopathic transverse myelitis – a rare neurological condition caused by inflammation of the spinal cord, which can result in muscle weakness, pain and bladder dysfunction. He was also concussed, Patel said, not on any prescribed medication and not withdrawing from any substances. The magistrate asked a mental health professional to see Nugent immediately.
He was estranged from his father, Rob. A well-liked member of the community, Rob is the vet you call first, people say. They describe him as a well-built man who is kind and well loved. He owns the Tarrawingee house his son lived in, but rented it out to him through a real estate agent.
Tarrawingee is a tiny town of just a few hundred people, a 10-minute drive from Wangaratta down a tree-lined road that passes farms, cattle and horses. In addition to the butcher, there’s a cafe van that closes at 11am and an upmarket bistro. Nugent’s property is off the beaten track and stands out against flower-lined lawns and houses with wraparound verandas.
Several of the locals say they have never met him. Others say they knew he lived there, but have not seen him in years.
At Nugent’s court hearing this week, the only local to attend was a neighbour who told Guardian Australia she wanted to “look him in the eye”.
Afterwards, a woman rode past the court house on her bicycle and provided some detail into his background. Jacquie, who once taught Nugent, had hoped to come and support him.
She has campaigned for Haines in previous elections, and says she feels “sick to the core” for her, Nugent and their families.
“I don’t condone what has happened to [Haines],” she says, while adding she hasn’t known Nugent to be an extreme or violent person.
“I wanted to reach out. He was a good kid. I could see there were possibly some issues with him. He was a bit withdrawn, sometimes, but he was a beautiful kid.
“He’s been reaching out for help for a long time.”
The last time she says she saw Nugent was two-and-a-half years ago, when he was hanging out with mates on the Ovens River. He seemed distressed and was suffering from mental health issues, she says. Since then, they have lost touch.
In the days after his arrest, Nugent’s X profile has been trawled over by the media and internet sleuths. It provides little insight into any motives for the alleged attack on Haines, but does indicate a possible withdrawal from public life.
In the past year, he has posted just 13 times, mostly sharing links about international issues including the war in the Middle East, paedophilia and global conspiracies. Before January, he hadn’t posted anything since December 2024.
Before that, his posts were longer and more coherent. He shared fundraising causes, pictures of local flora and fauna, his dog and nights at the MCG watching Geelong.
He was passionate about the environment, regularly attending protests before the pandemic. In 2018, he was at a conference in Melbourne, where he shared a paper he had written at the University of Melbourne’s School of Ecosystem and Forest Sciences.
Online, he was often critical of politicians from all sides, but he does not appear to have criticised Haines. In late 2019, he replied to her tweet about the ABC’s Q&A program, saying it “would’ve been nice to include a politician who takes climate change seriously, such as yourself”.
A hint of his struggles, though, came in mid-2022, when he professed that he had spent time living with a “significant disability” and was in “a lot of chronic pain”.
“I’ve had plenty of time … having to cook on a fire and wash my clothes in the river,” he wrote. “I have a proper house at the moment … I’m also on DSP unlike 1000s of other people with disabilities in Australia. But why keep ppl on disability support pensions when they want to work? I just want to work again.”
Nugent said he had a master’s degree, but still couldn’t get the “basic assistance” needed for ongoing employment.
“I’m constantly broke spending on health, NDIS is unavailable. We are left to sit in pain 24/7,” he wrote.
Before the alleged attack on Haines, some locals saw normality. Others saw things they didn’t like.
Speaking on background, they have described erratic behaviour. He often played loud music – heavy metal, rap and Bob Marley. Sometimes, they say, they would hear him screaming.
Nugent had started secondary school at Wangaratta high before transferring to Assumption College.
He played footy for his school and a club league, with success. In 1998, Wangaratta high’s intermediate team were state champions, defeating Belmont high school 73 to 56. A celebratory photo remains online with Nugent in the middle row, serious-faced. In the same picture are three future AFL players: Sean O’Keefe, Steve Johnson and Karl Norman.
Many locals remain close-lipped when asked about Nugent, but not all of them.
The local butcher, Russell, says he often came into the shop; his storefront is just a few hundred metres from Nugent’s property. Russell says he never noticed anything out of the ordinary, describing Nugent as relatively normal and quiet, but says he didn’t know him in any depth.
Across the electorate, people are questioning how something like this could happen. On Wednesday evening, a community vigil for Haines was held in Wodonga. It took place less than an hour after it was revealed she had lost both her legs – but would survive. Her recovery could take at least 12 months.
There were many tears and many hugs, but also moments of celebration – as when Cathy McGowan, the former federal member for Indi, repeated words of promise delivered to her by the governor general, Sam Mostyn: “We now know that Helen’s heart and head are good. She is going to get better, and she is going to come back fighting.”
The crowd, visibly moved and emotional, burst into cheers.
McGowan says the community is grappling with “mixed emotions”.
“The people here tonight don’t want violence … But that’s not to say when violence happens in their communities they know what to do about it,” she says.
“Because there’s a lot of violence in our communities, there’s a lot of violence online … There’s nothing new about this.
“It’s made it really visible. We can’t just pretend that everything’s OK in the regions and we’re doing fine … We own it.”
Many are pointing at a political climate, where discourse has increasingly become volatile. Others are talking about violence towards women. In between, some are questioning whether Nugent fell between the cracks of a stretched mental health system.
A police summary shows additional charges have been laid against Nugent, including possession and cultivation of cannabis.
At this week’s vigil, the chief executive of Regional Development Australia, Sarimah Hellyer, says it isn’t lost on her that one of the main issues Haines had fought for over the past seven years was better mental healthcare.
“There’s just so many holes in [mental health] service delivery,” she says. “There’s actually whole cohorts who aren’t catered for from a mental health perspective … We have one Headspace that basically supports the same catchment.”
Dr Lachlan McKeeman was endorsed by Haines as an independent candidate in the upcoming Victorian election at a campaign launch she had attended with her husband on Saturday, just days before the alleged attack.
She was sharing photos of her grandchildren, who were only born weeks ago. They had spent the morning together.
“The smile and energy she gets from her family makes it a really hard time at the moment,” he says. “To think what they’re all going through.”

title: Massive student-led rally marches in Belgrade ahead of Serbian election
description: Student List movement hopes to oust the party of veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic in a pivotal vote on Sunday
content:
Student List movement hopes to oust the party of veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic in a pivotal vote on Sunday
Explained: what’s at stake in Serbia’s election? The key players, main issues and potential fallout
About 150,000 supporters of Serbia’s opposition student movement rallied in central Belgrade on Thursday, seeking to oust the party of veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic in crunch parliamentary elections this weekend.
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, wants to end more than 14 years of rule by Vucic’s rightwing populist Serbian Progressive party (SNS) in Sunday’s vote.
Civil society groups have said the campaign has been marred by intimidation, arrests and misuse of public resources.
“I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country,” Marija Nedeljkovic Radic, 47, said as she arrived for the students’ rally.
“Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible.”
Sunday’s vote comes after nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The tragedy, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of Slobodan Milošević in 2000.
The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, snowballed from demands for a transparent investigation into the tragedy into calls for an early election.
Waving “Students are winning” flags, chanting and blowing whistles, students and their supporters marched through Belgrade before converging on Slavija Square, the site of some of their biggest protests.
The Archive of Public Gatherings, an independent crowd-size monitoring group, estimated about 150,000 people gathered at the rally.
“We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours,” university professor Jugoslav Gasic – one of 250 candidates on the Student List – told the crowd, which chanted “Victory, victory!”
“You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!”
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade, serving as either prime minister or president.
Amid mounting pressure, Vucic announced the snap vote last month, setting up his biggest electoral challenge since his party took power in 2012.
Vucic, who addressed supporters at a sports hall in the capital on Thursday, has regularly accused the student movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
“Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it,” said the 56-year-old, who resigned to run for prime minister.
“Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!” he said before white ticker tape and balloons showered the crowd.
Many of the 250 candidates of the Student List running for the 250-seat parliament are drawn from academia or are deliberate political outsiders.
The movement has a broad platform, but at its core is a pledge to fight corruption.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling, and surveys have produced widely differing results.
Days before the vote, Serbian civil society groups warned that conditions for “free and fair elections” were lacking.
On Wednesday, Belgrade prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting “violence, riots and attacks” on election day.
Reports of threats and intimidation targeting student demonstrators have grown in recent months, but their rallies have remained largely peaceful since they began.
“I’ve been following this fight since the very beginning,” 35-year-old student rally attender Igor said.
“Today is the last rally, and it’s important that we all come here to send a message of love and peace and that we see each other on the 25th at the polling stations.”

title: Rebel Wilson secures another Australian court win as co-producers of The Deb awarded just $10
description: NSW supreme court judge otherwise dismisses case brought by film’s co-producers and awards Wilson almost $400,000 after star countersued
content:
NSW supreme court judge otherwise dismisses case brought by film’s co-producers and awards Wilson almost $400,000 after star countersued
Rebel Wilson has been ordered to pay A$10 (US$7, £5) in damages after emerging victorious from a bitter legal spat with her latest film’s co-producers.
The Pitch Perfect star directed, co-produced and starred in The Deb, a musical comedy that became the battleground for multiple legal battles in Australia and the US.
Filmed on a $22m budget, The Deb made just $335,000 (US$235,000, £175,284) at the local box office and is yet to screen outside Oceania.
Wilson’s co-producers allege that shortfall could be traced to her false and derogatory statements about them online.
The Bridesmaids star claimed in July 2024 that producers Amanda Ghost, Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden tried to block The Deb’s release, embezzled money, and behaved inappropriately towards the film’s star, Charlotte MacInnes.
The producers alleged Wilson caused their company financial and reputational damage in an attempt to devalue her debut film so she could buy it from them.
On Friday, Justice Elisabeth Peden awarded the trio a mere $10 in damages and otherwise dismissed the summons in the New South Wales supreme court.
Wilson had denied her co-producers’ allegations and countersued, claiming their involvement in the film was marked by a troubling pattern of illicit, egregious behaviours, including theft, bullying and sexual misconduct.
Peden awarded her $359,000 (US$251,830, £187,868) plus interest in a brief decision, which will be followed by a written judgment.
Wilson took to Instagram to welcome the victory with a photo of herself in a graduation gown holding a degree from the University of NSW.
“This girl never knew how much she was going to need that law degree!!” she wrote.
“I spoke up because I believed there were serious concerns that needed to be raised on my film The Deb.
“Defending myself has come at an enormous personal, emotional, and financial cost. But I’m proud I stood my ground – for myself and for others I was trying to protect.”
Wilson said she struggled to remain positive throughout the proceedings and thanked her family and followers for their support.
It’s the second victory for Wilson after she was cleared of defaming MacInnes earlier this year following a fiery federal court hearing.
MacInnes claimed Wilson defamed her in four social media posts that implied she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.
The posts alleged the young actor confided in Wilson – and later recanted – that she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together.
MacInnes denied making or retracting a complaint, saying she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023.

title: With albums under threat, Raye’s Mercury win is a triumph for grand statements
description: Her winning album has its longueurs, but there’s something heartening about its risk-taking – and the Mercury prize needs big bold records like this to stay relevant
content:
Her winning album has its longueurs, but there’s something heartening about its risk-taking – and the Mercury prize needs big bold records like this to stay relevant
I t was generally agreed that last year’s Mercury prize ceremony was a vast improvement on its predecessor. In fairness, the bar was set pretty low: hosted without an audience – or indeed a corporate sponsor – in what looked like a broom cupboard at Abbey Road, the 2024 Mercury prize seemed to suggest the whole jig was up.
Instead, the event was relocated to Newcastle’s Utilita Arena, the general public rather than record label grandees provided the audience, and something approaching a sense of genuine excitement attended the event.
And yet somehow, said excitement didn’t sustain. The announcement of this year’s nominees seemed to be greeted with something approaching a shrug: a smattering of headlines noting that Paul McCartney had been nominated for the first time, aged 84, and that was about it.
You wonder what the problem is. Not the albums nominated, all of which had plenty to commend them, from the punk-y “Geordie noir” jazz of Knats’ A Great Day in Newcastle, to the appealingly off-message take on pop proffered by former Little Mix star Jade on her solo debut, That’s Showbiz Baby!
Perhaps the Mercury shot themselves in the foot by giving the 2025 award to local boy Sam Fender’s People Watching, an album that’s exceptionally good, but was already hugely successful, clearly not in need of any kind of profile or sales boost (Fender gave his prize money away to the Music Venue Trust).
That People Watching actually won the Mercury is easy to forget, a minor consideration lost amid its platinum sales figures and string of hit singles, one of which went on to spend nearly six months at No 1.
Perhaps people are just losing interest in albums in an age defined by streaming, a means of distribution that privileges single tracks and playlists? More than half of the 40 biggest-selling albums of 2026 thus far are either greatest hits collections or longstanding back catalogue classics; that chart contains only seven albums that actually came out this year, which hardly suggests a widespread hunger for new releases in the format.
One of those, though, was Raye’s This Music May Contain Hope, the winner of this year’s Mercury . It was an album that spawned a single huge hit single – the retro soul of Where Is My Husband! – but that nevertheless made spawning a huge hit single seem beside the point: 73 minutes and 17 tracks long, divided into four sections, it’s an album that flies in the face of the suggestion that no one really listens to albums from soup to nuts any more.
Its saga of romantic despair, which stylistically leaps from soul to swing to house music to 50s easy listening schmaltz, is clearly intended to be consumed in toto .
Not everything the singer-songwriter tries over its lengthy course works. Fabulous songs – The WhatsApp Shakespeare, Beware.. The South London Lover Boy, the Hans Zimmer-assisted Click Clack Symphony – coexist with moments where it slips into self-indulgence: Fields offers a lengthy dialogue between the singer and her grandad, and the closing track, Fin, lasts six minutes, four of which consist of Raye reading out the album’s production credits.
Still, the highlights are hugely impressive, and there’s something to be said for the degree of risk-taking involved, given the risk-averse tenor of the times.
Moreover, choosing it as the Mercury winner sends out a defensive signal. This is what an award that has occasionally seemed surplus to requirements now exists in order to celebrate: the grand statement, the right for artists to indulge themselves at length in a climate that favours short and sharp releases.
But after two years in a row of awarding No 1 hit albums, in future will the judging panel see fit to award grand statements from underground artists too, or only to A-listers?

title: King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit
description: Caricom commission chair Hilary Beckles wants king to ensure Commonwealth becomes a ‘moral institution committed to human justice’
content:
Caricom commission chair Hilary Beckles wants king to ensure Commonwealth becomes a ‘moral institution committed to human justice’
The head of the Caribbean’s reparations commission has appealed to King Charles III as a “human brother” whose family he said had benefited from slavery to support reparations talks at next month’s Commonwealth leaders meeting in the Caribbean.
Speaking at a press conference ahead of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting ( Chogm ) in Antigua and Barbuda next month, professor Hilary Beckles urged the king to use his influence to advance slavery reparations talks between Britain and the Caribbean.
Beckles, the chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, said: “My personal appeal to King Charles III, not so much in his role as head of the Commonwealth, not so much in his role as the constitutional monarch of the United Kingdom … I’m appealing to Charles Windsor, a parent, a grandparent, a man today who reflects upon the history of his family, and he can see the enrichment that slavery has presented to his family.”
He declared that he believed the king was aware that the wealth he is passing on to his children and his grandchildren came from chattel slavery.
Referring to the king as “a man, as a human brother”, he urged Charles to ensure the Commonwealth, historically “the site of this crime”, becomes a “moral institution committed to human justice”.
Beckles’s appeal comes amid growing calls from Caribbean leaders and groups for Charles to formally apologise for slavery when he visits Guyana and the Bahamas next week ahead of Chogm, which he will attend in Antigua.
On Thursday, Commonwealth secretary-general Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey told Sky News that a formal apology for slavery from King Charles “wouldn’t hurt” and that the “time has come” for a serious conversation regarding reparations.
Eric Phillips, head of Guyana’s reparations committee and vice-chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, joined the calls for an apology from the king.
“The king is a decent monarch based on his lifelong commitments to the world in which the environment for him is sacred. We Africans are also part of that sacred environment. As an enlightened monarch, I strongly believe King Charles will want to promote a conversation of decency that reflects his character and values,” he said.
“The citizens of the United Kingdom say, long live the king. We in Guyana say, long live the king, so he can apologize and call for reparations,” he added.
Last month, when Jamaican officials lodged a landmark petition to King Charles for legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations, which will be heard by the privy council in March, a palace spokesperson said Charles “has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today”.
But David Comissiong, the deputy chair of the Barbados National Task Force on Reparations, said he was concerned about a lack of unanimous agreement on commitments on reparations in a draft of the 2026 Chogm communique, which records agreements made by leaders.
Comissiong said a paragraph that referenced the commitment to dialogue made at the previous Commonwealth summit in Samoa and highlights subsequent developments at the UN, African Union and Caricom, was confirmed, but there was disagreement about a second paragraph mandating Commonwealth foreign ministers to advance discussions on historical harms from the transatlantic slave trade through “structured, inclusive, and good faith dialogue”.
“It is very peculiar, to say the least, that the second paragraph which speaks about the Commonwealth foreign affairs ministers coming together to engage in these discussions … has not been unanimously agreed upon,” he said.
Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations commission, said that campaigners are expected to raise the issue of reparations during the conferences’ major forums, and that discussions between governments are expected to take place at their meetings.
He said the reparations movement will launch a “Global Reparations Caravan”, described as an international movement combining reparations advocacy, demonstrations and culture, at a separate event on 3 November.
O’Marde added that, while there will be stringent security measures around the event, he expects physical demonstrations from groups who are “inflamed” by the blanket statements of no apology coming out of the UK.
“Blanket no apologies from both government and monarchy reek of gross insensitivity to the demands of the citizens of the Caribbean,” he said.
Beckles stressed that the absence of a dedicated official event at Chogm does not mean that reparations would remain peripheral to the summit. He described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations” and the “first round of reparations negotiations”.
“This is the meeting of the Commonwealth in the Caribbean, and the number one item in the Caribbean as far as this gathering is concerned is reparatory justice,” he said.
“I can assure you that [for] everyone in the Caribbean right now, everyone who’s going to be at that meeting from the Caribbean, with an interest in the Caribbean, from Africa, and an interest in the global African movement, this will be the number one item on the table.”

title: Child health in England at risk from sharp rise in NHS waiting times, report says
description: CQC research finds long delays are making conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in care
content:
CQC research finds long delays are making conditions harder to treat and highlights regional disparities in care
Thousands of children in England are experiencing some of the sharpest rises in waiting times for healthcare in the history of the NHS, a report has revealed.
While some adult waiting times have improved, children and young people are being “hit hardest” amid soaring demand and falling numbers of staff, according to the annual state of care report by the Care Quality Commission.
In community health services alone, 80,000 children and young people have been waiting more than a year for an appointment – almost 11 times the number of adults, the report said. Experts said that was “wholly unacceptable”. Children’s health conditions were getting worse and becoming harder to treat as a result, they added.
More broadly across health and social care services in England there were signs of improvement, including more GP appointments, increased use of digital solutions and shorter waits for elective care. The report also highlighted examples of local innovation, including neighbourhood models and integrated care teams.
But improvements were struggling to keep pace with rapidly rising demand for health and social care. In many areas, including mental health services, patients’ needs are also becoming more complex.
Persistent inequalities across the entire health and care system mean people’s experience of care is fractured and heavily dependent on where they live and who they are, according to the report.
Across all areas of the country and every part of the health and social care system, there was “unwarranted variation” in access to services, quality of care and outcomes, the CQC said.
Some adults with cancer were waiting far too long to begin treatment after being diagnosed, while there remained “sustained pressure” in urgent and emergency care.
But the report highlighted how children in particular were bearing the brunt of long waiting times. And, despite growing demand, health visitor and school nurse numbers were “continuing to decline”, the CQC said.
It also raised concerns about regional variations in rates of children being admitted to hospital for diabetes and asthma, and sounded the alarm over particularly high rates of rotten teeth among children in some areas.
Dr Ronny Cheung, of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health , said community health services existed to support some of the country’s most vulnerable children outside hospital, including those with complex conditions, developmental disorders and safeguarding needs.
“Yet these children face some of the longest waits in the NHS , while waiting times for adult community services have improved. It is wholly unacceptable that more than one in four children still wait over a year for treatment, and without urgent action, too many more will be left to suffer unnecessarily.
“As a paediatrician, I am sick of seeing children wait so long for support that they miss crucial opportunities to improve their health and development.”
Behind the figures were children struggling at school, families pushed to breaking point and conditions becoming more complex while they wait, Cheung added.
The CQC chair, Julia Neuberger, said that while some health and social care services were “working well”, improvements were not keeping pace with demand. “To repair a fracturing system, there must be a collective response,” she added.
The Department of Health and Social Care said the report showed “the scale of the challenge this government inherited” when it was elected in 2024. “While the CQC recognises signs of progress on waiting lists, cancer care and general practice, patients and families rightly expect faster improvements – which is why the secretary of state has committed to go further to end corridor care, transform support for mothers and children, and deliver a new national care service,” a spokesperson added.

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
description: Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends
content:
Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends
After seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea that marked the end for Ange Postecoglou , the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing the narrow defeat by Arsenal , while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season. Niall McVeigh
It was five months ago but it feels a lot longer. When these two sides met in May to finish the season, the contest doubled as Pep Guardiola’s leaving party after 10 years in the job and twice as many trophies, an era now laden with asterisks. It must be surreal for Aston Villa supporters, too. Their 2-1 victory at the Etihad Stadium, inspired by two goals from Ollie Watkins to complete a league double over City, came only four days after their Europa League triumph in Istanbul, where Youri Tielemans, Morgan Rogers and Emi Buendía were the scorers. Buendía is the only one left in claret and blue as Unai Emery builds a new side, one that has picked up in form after a single point from their first four league games. City, meanwhile, are thriving on the pitch: victory would make them just the third side to win their first eight games of a Premier League season. Taha Hashim
Max Dowman became the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history with his dazzling solo strike against Everton at the Emirates in March. But the supremely talented 16-year-old has found opportunities limited this season. Dowman has played only nine minutes in the Premier League despite scoring twice against Ipswich in the Carabao Cup last month as Arsenal have tried to protect their rising star. Yet the suspected quad muscle injury suffered by Bukayo Saka in Wednesday’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich means Mikel Arteta is short of attacking options. With David Moyes’s side back in north London, it could be the perfect chance for Dowman to step up in his favoured position on the right flank. Ed Aarons
Coventry and Fulham have only met twice in the English top flight – back in 1967-68, when the promoted Sky Blues took a single point from two meetings, but stayed up by a point while Fulham went down. It is too early to call Saturday’s game a six-pointer in the relegation battle, but the two teams sit either side of the dreaded dotted line after shaky starts. Coventry have shown glimpses of their Championship swagger, particularly in the 4-1 rout of Newcastle , but Frank Lampard wants his players to start thinking like a Premier League team. “I can’t keep applauding the players, believing they deserve to be here,” the Coventry manager said. “Now we have to get over that. We can’t be too soft.” Sunderland, Crystal Palace and Ipswich all visit the CBS Arena in the coming weeks, so there is an opportunity to consolidate. Fulham were linked with Lampard in the summer, and questions remain over whether Álvaro Arbeloa is pragmatic or flexible enough to succeed. Will these sides meet in the Premier League again next season? The jury is out. NM
Tottenham’s recent record against Chelsea is miserable. They are on a six-match losing streak against their London rivals and have collected a paltry two points at Stamford Bridge since last winning there in April 2018 . Tottenham finally have a league win – they beat Coventry 3-1 on Monday – but remain unconvincing. Roberto De Zerbi used a 3-4-2-1 system against Coventry. He had problems in midfield but now has to work out whether to change a winning team. Does he stick with James Maddison after the No 10’s excellent goal against his boyhood club? Spurs still looked short of energy at times. There is an argument to bring back Conor Gallagher’s dynamism, but would that hurt the side’s quality on the ball? Mateus Fernandes is another option but is yet to establish himself since joining from West Ham. Spurs’ approach remains hard to decipher. De Zerbi likes possession, but Chelsea want teams to open up as the Blues have searing pace on the break. Given their history in this fixture it seems Spurs should focus on tightening up. Equally they can’t be passive and need a threat on the break. De Zerbi will be searching for the right balance. Jacob Steinberg
Talk of Brighton achieving Champions League qualification for the first time will gain more credence, even at this early stage, should Fabian Hürzeler’s confident side extend their unbeaten run to nine matches in all competitions. There have been six clean sheets and 23 goals scored in sequence that featured six wins in a row and the Premier League’s highest scorers will take encouragement from Liverpool’s defensive problems in the comeback against Villarreal , which were not limited to Virgil van Dijk’s early lapses. Andoni Iraola is yet to savour a first home league win as Liverpool head coach – Anfield has seen only four home wins in 13 league games this year – and he will be wary of Brighton’s various threats. But with Rio Ngumoha electric in the Champions League win, Florian Wirtz improving and Alexander Isak increasingly decisive, the ingredients are in place for another enthralling spectacle. Andy Hunter
Who can or will lift Manchester United after the latest dismal/embarrassing week? Bruno Fernandes’s abdication of captaincy duties – accusing his manager of being tactically inept – showed what a rabble the team has become under Michael Carrick; and beyond the double footballer of the year, is there another star act who can win a game? Bournemouth will hope to take advantage, register only a second league win of the season, and deepen the misery for their hosts and fans. If his side goes down to the Cherries, Carrick will surely follow: the latest victim of the United circus. Jamie Jackson
It’s been six months since Crystal Palace recorded a clean sheet in the Premier League at Selhurst Park and the pressure will be on Pierre Sage against Newcastle on Sunday. Palace have conceded eight goals in four home league games this season, although they welcome back Axel Disasi from suspension after his reckless red card against Ipswich . The French defender was brought in on loan from Chelsea to add experience but cost Palace in the defeat by the newly-promoted side and had to watch from the sidelines as the Eagles were humiliated against Brighton last weekend. Disasi owes Sage a favour and he will be desperate to make up for his poor start to life in south London. EA
Something unusual will happen at the MKM Stadium on Sunday; either Hull City or Brentford will register more than 50% possession. In seven league games, Brentford only had more of the ball in their 1-1 draw at Leeds . The hosts, meanwhile, are comfortably the most possession-averse team in the top flight so far this season, at an average of just over 30%. Both teams have been effective on the break and successful at set-pieces, with three goals apiece from dead balls. This may prove to be a match for the purists, where one clinical moment makes the difference. The Bees head coach, Keith Andrews, will hope it comes from Igor Thiago, yet to recapture the prolific form of last season. “Thiago at the moment is a very marked man, but we’ve got goalscorers throughout the team,” Andrews said of the Brazilian forward, who has scored one goal in seven this season. “Thiago being Thiago wants to score more goals, and he’s certainly not far away.” NM
Nordi Mukiele ranks among Sunderland’s best players and most influential dressing-room figures. Tellingly the former Paris Saint-Germain defender has been scathing about his team’s dismal start to the Premier League campaign and expects a reaction when Leeds visit Wearside on Sunday. “Leeds will be the right moment to show everyone we are not dead,” says Mukiele, well aware that Régis Le Bris’s side start this weekend on the bottom of the table. “We have not been good enough. Right now it’s not us; we are not Sunderland. I believe we can go back to the top. I believe in this team and this staff. We have quality.” Sunderland must use their three league fixtures before the international break – Leeds, Coventry away and Chelsea at home – to remind everyone why they finished seventh last season. Louise Taylor
