title: New York city council votes to ban horse-drawn carriage rides
description: City’s council passed Romanch’s Law, named after teen who died when he was ejected from carriage earlier this year
content:
City’s council passed Romanch’s Law, named after teen who died when he was ejected from carriage earlier this year
The New York city council has voted to ban horse-drawn carriage rides in the city by 2028 in a decision that has widespread implications for hundreds of jobs.
The council voted on Thursday on Romanch’s Law, legislation named in memory of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died this summer after he was ejected from a runaway horse-drawn carriage in Central Park.
Under the measure, carriage operations will cease completely in June 2028. The legislation also called for a plan to help affected employees and business owners transition out of the industry in 2027.
Earlier on Thursday, the city council’s committee on health voted six-three in favor of the ban, clearing the way for the full council vote later in the day.
The final vote came just hours after workers and members of the Transport Workers Union (TWU) Local 100, which represents horse carriage drivers, gathered outside city hall in a last-minute push to stop the legislation.
Protesters called on lawmakers to either vote against the proposal or postpone the decision to allow further negotiations. They rallied and held signs decrying the vote, including one person who raised up an actual bag of horse poop in protest.
At the center of their objections is the uncertainty surrounding what happens to workers once the industry shuts down. Carriage operators maintain that their livelihoods are being taken away without a clearly established path forward.
John Samuelsen, president of TWU, told Spectrum NY it is “utterly false” that the bill includes real plans for retraining the workers. “There’s nothing concrete at all,” he said. “The language says consideration will be given. The language should not say that.”
The measure could also put dozens of carriage medallions in jeopardy, including those belonging to immigrant-run family enterprises that have been passed down through generations.
Industry advocates argue that the carriage trade has significant financial importance, saying operators conduct more than 100,000 rides each year and contribute to the city’s tourism sector.
Some carriage drivers expressed disappointment that Zohran Mamdani , the New York City mayor, who has championed himself as a voice for the working class and unions, would take a stand in favor of the ban.
One longtime driver, Conner McHugh, told Gothamist that the mayor “gets up on his podium and announces that he’s just shutting us all down, putting us out of business, doesn’t even talk to us”, adding, “I think this guy is as phoney as a $3 bill.”
McHugh, a second-generation driver, had previously told the Guardian that he feels there is an ongoing effort to drive people like him off land and buildings in Manhattan that coincides with the rezoning of the area where horse stables are located.
“Intimidation has taken various forms,” he said, including “reporting us to ICE and the IRS, keyboard warriors trashing us on social media, animals rights volunteers who have come to Central Park to harass our drivers and create an unsafe situation”.
But advocates pushing for the ban have repeatedly raised concerns over the years about the dangers associated with the rides and the risks to passengers and pedestrians, with those dangers gaining national attention after Mahajan’s death.
The treatment of the carriage horses has also been controversial. Animal welfare campaigners have questioned conditions in the industry, pointing to several horse deaths since 2020, including incidents in which animals collapsed while pulling carriages.
Before the decision, Donald Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform he is “so sad to see the beloved Central Park Horse-drawn Carriage Industry ending after over a Century, based largely on one tragic accident.
“When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don’t stop cars from entering the Park,” he wrote. “So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition. Another piece of History that’s gone. It will be missed!”
In a separate post, he added: “The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience. So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!”
The Transport Workers Union had already informed city officials that it plans to pursue legal action in federal court if the legislation passed. Union officials maintain that the measure would unlawfully deprive carriage owners of their operating licenses, valuable medallions and businesses built over many years.
Thursday’s vote follows an agreement reached earlier this month between mayor Mamdani and the head of the city council to eliminate horse-drawn carriage rides across New York City.
Mamdani previously made clear that the administration intended to move ahead with ending the practice while addressing the consequences for those involved. “The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected and the horses are safe,” Mamdani wrote on X .

title: Europa League: Celtic lose to Celta after leading, Mateta returns in Palace draw
description: Celtic fell to another defeat after taking the lead against Celta Vigo, while Jean-Philippe Mateta scored on his first start for Crystal Palace since the opening day in a 2-2 draw at Besiktas
content:
Sunderland drop points in 1-1 draw but stay unbeaten
VAR rules out Juventus winner in draw with Rennes
Celtic suffered more Europa League pain as Spanish side Celta Vigo came from behind to win 2-1 at Parkhead. After defeats by Ferencvaros and Benfica in their first two league phase fixtures, Martin O’Neill’s side struggled to impose themselves on the visitors who were neat and tidy without really testing Hoops keeper Sam Johnstone.
Germany midfielder Mika Baur fired the home side in front just over a minute into the second half to thrill the Celtic fans but Spain defender Javi Rodríguez scored twice in three minutes – a header then an unstoppable drive – to stun the home side who could not find a way back.
It was another damaging Euro night for the Scottish champions, knocked out of the Champions League qualifiers by LASK on a 5-4 aggregate after being 4-0 up at one stage earlier in the season.
Celtic’s ultras group, the Green Brigade, boycotted the game in protest at the running of the club, albeit there appeared to be only a couple of hundred empty seats, while 3,000 raucous Celta Vigo fans helped the noise.
Jean-Philippe Mateta scored on his first start since the opening day but Crystal Palace could not capitalise on a Besiktas red card to produce a winner in their 2-2 Europa League draw in Istanbul.
Palace were looking to bounce back from Sunday’s humiliating 5-0 defeat at Brighton, and were the superior side before Wilfred Ndidi opened the scoring for the hosts in first-half stoppage time.
Yéremy Pino drew the sides level six minutes after the restart and Mateta – who had a first-half goal chalked off by the video assistant referee – fired Palace to a first-time lead four minutes later.
Junior Olaitan netted a 73rd-minute equaliser, and Palace could not find a winner after Umit Akdag was sent off for a clumsy 77th-minute challenge on Jørgen Strand Larsen, who was subsequently forced off.
Sunderland ’s winning start in the Europa League was ended with a 1-1 draw away to Lech Poznan . The point keeps Sunderland unbeaten in Europe this season after back-to-back victories over AZ Alkmaar and Torreense.
In a thrilling opening Sunderland went in front early through Timur Tutierov, who was making only his third competitive start since arriving at Sunderland’s academy in 2023.
The visitors had opportunities to extend their lead when Malick Fofana hit the post and Nordi Mukiele forced a strong save from Mateusz Lis, but Lech responded in the 70th minute through the substitute Leo Bengtsson’s low strike.
Régis Le Bris made six changes from Sunday’s Premier League defeat to Bournemouth , including a first start of the season for Habib Diarra following his return from injury.
Sunderland took the lead in the second minute when Nilson Angulo pounced on a tame pass from Lis, and the winger crossed into Tutierov in the middle of the box to comfortably nod home for his first Sunderland goal.
Robin Roefs was called into action at the opposite end with a double save to deny Patrik Wålemark and palm away Antoni Kozubal’s header before Diarra charged up the pitch and fired into the side netting.
The hosts had two good chances to level when Pablo Rodríguez blasted just past the post and Daniel Håkans was played through in a one-on-one with Roefs but flicked his shot wide.
Sunderland enjoyed a good spell of possession during which the skipper, Granit Xhaka, had a strike parried away by Lis and the rebound fell to Fofana, who rattled the woodwork. Moments later Dayann Méthalie was denied at the near post by Lis as the visitors pushed for a second goal.
Early in the second half, Fofana cut into the box but could only send his effort over and Poznan looked to strike when Wålemark scuffed a shot wide following a good solo run.
Diarra fired wide for and Angulo’s low strike was scooped up by Lis, who moments later made a great save to tip Mukiele’s shot over the bar.
Bengtsson looked to make an instant impact from the bench when his effort from Wålemark’s cross was sent wide. However, the midfielder made no mistake when next presented with an opportunity as a corner rebounded towards him just inside the area and he fired into the bottom corner with 20 minutes to play.
Poznan almost took the lead moments later when Roefs made a brilliant point-blank stop from Michal Gurgul. Fofana skewed an effort wide as Sunderland looked to restore their advantage and the substitute Chris Rigg’s powerful shot landed on the roof of the net, but the spoils were shared.
Juventus dropped their first points of the Europa League campaign after coming ⁠from behind to draw 2-2 with visitors Rennes .
Zeki Celik gave Juventus a fifth-minute lead, but ⁠the French side ⁠kept their ​composure and were level 10 minutes later when the Jordan international Musa Al-Taamari finished from close range for ⁠his first goal in the competition.
Rennes then stunned the hosts with a Boulaye Dia penalty two minutes before the ⁠break as the Italians struggled to create chances until Nick Woltemade equalised ​from the spot in the 67th ‌minute.
The Germany forward ‌twice went close to scoring again as Luciano Spalletti’s team upped the ‌pressure, and Juve thought they had won it in the 88th minute when Jhon Lucumí found the net from close range, but his effort was ruled out for offside.
The draw at least spared Juventus a second successive defeat following Sunday’s 3-0 home loss to Lazio ‌in Serie A.
Jonas Hofmann made the most of his surprise start for Bayer Leverkusen , scoring twice in three minutes ​to give the Bundesliga side a 2-0 victory at OFI Crete to go top of the table with their third straight win.
Crete, who stunned Hoffenheim 2-0 in their opening league-phase match, were twice caught napping by Hofmann, ⁠who was added to the side following an injury to ​Martin Terrier. Leverkusen have ​nine points and lead Ferencvaros ​on goal difference after the Hungarian side beat Torreense ​4-1.

title: It Gets Worse review – Leo Reich is a rare star and the future of TV comedy
description: The hot comic has made Fresh Meat for generation Z with this London sitcom. Produced by A24 and guest starring Andrew Scott, it is profound and properly funny – even if you’re easily triggered by houseshare horrors
content:
The hot comic has made Fresh Meat for generation Z with this London sitcom. Produced by A24 and guest starring Andrew Scott, it is profound and properly funny – even if you’re easily triggered by houseshare horrors
I n his 2023 standup special Literally Who Cares?!, Leo Reich bemoaned the fact that his life wasn’t more like a TV comedy . “All the sitcoms I watched as a teenager really made me imagine that being in my early 20s would involve a lot more navigating the dating scene in the big city,” he groaned. “And a lot less Googling the words ‘death toll’.” Reich was playing a caricature of a self-absorbed zoomer, who had taken up smoking during the pandemic because “some part of me decided it might be worth cutting 20 years off my life”. Behind this performance there was, of course, a rather big dollop of truth: life for gen Z has – for the most part – been less sitcom, more doom-filled rolling news bulletin.
Reich – now 28 – is a rare comic to land an HBO special, and now an A24/Channel 4 series, putting him in the ideal position to redress the balance with his very own sitcom. Like HBO’s I Love LA (spiritually gen Z, if written by a millennial, Rachel Sennott), it juxtaposes grossness with aspiration. And like Girls before it, it is helmed by a perfectly un-self-aware protagonist, Ethan (Reich), whom – we are told at the outset – has had “one of the easiest lives in recorded human history”. There are hints of Fresh Meat, too, and traces of Reich’s comedy hero Simon Amstell in its dry neuroticism and Jewish-themed LOLs. Sometimes, it verges on the satirical – as when Andrew Scott cameos as a hookup who offers Ethan free therapy as foreplay. (Ethan tempers his complaints by saying that at least he hasn’t “lived through Aids” – Scott’s character, Brian, snaps back: “How old do you think I am?!”)
As well as Ethan, we follow his uni pals Sam (Olive Gray) and Abi (Emily Fairn), who have been living with him in a London houseshare. They’re all moving out and need their deposits back, except Ethan has somehow made a ginormous hole in the wall with a drill, and doesn’t seem fussed about fixing it. As someone who has lived in more houseshares than I can remember, this feels particularly triggering. Reich might have been trying to shock the audience with lines like “my last therapist rimmed me”, but seeing someone play fast and loose with their household’s finances is more likely to solicit an emotional response from Generation Rent. Despite being chronically unemployed, Ethan will be fine, his friends say, because he has his parents’ house to go back to. Except that he doesn’t want to go home, so decides to inflict himself on an ex (as moving home, he reckons, would mean “[paying] rent in bad vibes and homophobia”).
Meanwhile, Sam – artsy and queer like Ethan – ends up in an anarchist warehouse with a shared Mubi account, while Abi – northern, conformist, seemingly hiding all kinds of stress behind her rictus grin – moves in with her normie boyfriend Tom (Sean Delaney), and the cracks between the friends begin to deepen. “You want to pretend like you’re an adult!” Sam snaps at Abi. “Better than pretending I’m a child,” says Abi. Sick burn.
It Gets Worse is, in many ways, a classic sitcom about surviving your 20s, complete with intensely awkward sex scenes (“Pull out!” “I’m not even in!”) And yet there’s a lot more going on here. Zadie Smith – at first inexplicably; later somewhat explicably – is our narrator. As well as Scott, Lena Dunham makes an appearance as the horrifying girlboss CEO of the data-mining startup where Abi works, and “fellow badass white woman with zero fucks left to give”. Amelia Dimoldenberg pops up as a university frequaintance who sparks Abi’s jealousy. Every episode is named after the characters it features, except when they aren’t (see: a chapter set at a funeral with the Auden-parodying title “Stop all the Cocks”). There’s an episode about a rather sexless sex party, which ends up feeling like a plot device for more beef between the characters, while references to “incel” culture, Andrew Tate and ChatGPT seem more like period-appropriate window-dressing than anything deeper.
But, gladly, It Gets Worse is truly funny, propelled along by Reich’s zinger-filled, often profound script. The cast are solid, too, not least Vicki Pepperdine as Ethan’s highly-strung mum, plotting a move from the London suburbs to the Kent countryside because “almost everyone we know has been stabbed”. At the end of the second episode, Tom inadvertently calls Ethan a flop, to which he says: “We’re too young to be failures – in 10 years, then we’ll have failed.” In 10 years, Reich will probably be running British television – and, you imagine, breathing a sigh of relief to have his 20s far behind him.

title: Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval
description: PM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’
content:
PM pledges commitment to address climate crisis, saying in Guardian article that his ‘determination is unwavering’
Andy Burnham: We will make the net-zero transition work for Britain
Andy Burnham has said he will not “abandon the responsibility” of fighting the climate crisis after the government approved the Jackdaw gasfield, pledging to block new North Sea licences and keep Britain on track for net zero by 2050.
The comments are the prime minister’s most forthright yet on net zero, after many MPs have privately cast doubt on the authenticity of his commitment to tackling the climate crisis.
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh , insisted that she alone would make a decision on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield – a decision sources say she is minded to block.
Burnham has been under pressure from industry and political opponents, as well as some Labour MPs, to water down Labour’s manifesto promises on new oil and gas licences and the net zero targets.
“There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering,” the prime minister said in an article for the Guardian .
He said he was conscious of the “acute global instability” affecting energy security and wanted to treat oil and gas workers with more dignity.
Burnham said that would not stop the government from abiding by its climate targets, saying he was “personally committed to confronting” the challenges of the climate crisis.
“Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires,” he wrote.
“More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.”
Meanwhile, Fahnbulleh doubled down on her insistence that she would not be influenced by other departments on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield, setting up a potential standoff with the Treasury.
The chancellor, John Healey, has said he expects “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, but Fanhbulleh said “only I can make that decision”, insisting that she bore the legal responsibility to ensure the UK did not violate its climate commitments.
Dismissing speculation that Burnham, or his chancellor, would make the final call, she said: “[It] sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because, in the end, only I can make it. And if it is overturned by other colleagues, all that means is we’re going to be overturned in the courts. So we will do the process and we will do it properly.”
Fahnbulleh said she was “really concerned” and “quite sad” about the breakdown in consensus about the climate crisis. She said: “I think it’s a sad place where Reform has gone and got to. But I’m even sadder about the Tories because they know better, and they’ve had a long tradition, including Boris Johnson, of working cross-party on climate action.
“It has been really painful and tragic to watch that consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change this summer.”
The climate crisis was having a real impact on communities, she added. “It’s people’s livelihoods, it’s their jobs, their communities. Even if you don’t care about climate – care about that, you’ve got to take action.”
Reflecting on the decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield, Burnham said he wanted to make the transition to a greener future “on our terms”, saying that meant giving oil and gas workers a path to new jobs and using homegrown rather than imported gas.
“At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter.”
He said he had been moved by the plight of oil and gas workers in Aberdeen, adding that it was an industry that had suffered from deindustrialisation “with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives.”
Fahnbulleh echoed the prime minister’s words, saying the private sector had invested £100bn in clean energy in the last two years. “It’s a huge opportunity for parts of our countries that have been left behind,” she said. But that investment had to have a real-world impact, she added. “When you say jobs are going to be created, don’t say it. People need to see it.”
Burnham said the energy wealth fund that was being created to convert North Sea oil and gas tax revenues to clean energy programmes was long overdue – “something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago”.
It comes as Burnham announced that military planes and helicopters would fight wildfires for the first time, ahead of a major wildfire summit with fire chiefs, local leaders and experts.
The RAF’s chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft will fight fires and help crews across the UK tackle blazes on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.
“Heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs,” said the prime minister.

title: Woman charged over shooting of police officer in Nottingham
description: Aisha Zaman, 27, charged with two firearms offences after incident in city centre on Sunday
content:
Aisha Zaman, 27, charged with two firearms offences after incident in city centre on Sunday
A 27-year-old woman has been charged after a police officer was shot while attending an incident in Nottingham.
Aisha Zaman, from the Hyson Green area of the city, has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence.
She has been remanded into custody and will appear before Nottingham magistrates court on Friday.
The officer, who is in a stable condition in hospital, had approached two people at a bus stop at 4.50am last Sunday when he was shot in the foot, Nottinghamshire police said.
A weapon was recovered and a large crime scene cordon put in place around Angel Row in the city centre.
Several other people have been arrested in connection with the incident including two men, aged 24 and 30, and two women, aged 25 and 21, on suspicion of assisting an offender.
A 35-year-old man and a 33-year-old woman have also been arrested on suspicion of possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life and assisting an offender. Both suspects remain in police custody, the force added.
DCS Rich Bull said: “We would just like to take this moment to thank the public. The outpouring of support for the injured officer has been greatly appreciated.
“We continue to support him as he undergoes further treatment in hospital and are keeping him and his family fully informed of the developments in this investigation. He has asked for privacy during this incredibly difficult time.”
The Police Federation sent its best wishes to the officer and said it was a “stark reminder of the dangers police officers face every day”.
Following the incident, Neghat Khan, the leader of Nottingham city council, said she was “deeply shocked and saddened”.
She said Nottingham was a “safe city” and praised the bravery of police and community protection officers, adding: “My thoughts and full support are with the injured police officer, their family and their colleagues across Nottinghamshire police.”

title: Raye wins 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain Hope
description: Singer who has had record-breaking Brit awards success adds to haul thanks to massively ambitious big-band album
content:
Singer who has had record-breaking Brit awards success adds to haul thanks to massively ambitious big-band album
Raye is the winner of the 2026 Mercury prize , for her second studio album, This Music May Contain Hope.
Her win – for a hugely ambitious 73-minute record that spanned big band jazz, power balladry, funk and more – caps an ongoing renaissance for a British singer who at one point was in the doldrums, lashing out publicly at her record label for not letting her release a studio album.
Since that low in 2021, she split from that former label and found huge success with two albums: My 21st Century Blues, which won her six Brit awards – still the record for a single Brits ceremony – and This Music May Contain Hope, which topped the UK charts and contains the global hit Where Is My Husband!
The judging panel said: “Raye displays real imagination and scope in showing what an album can be, going beyond any one style or genre to realise her vision. The judges agreed that Raye’s superb album will serve as a huge inspiration for years to come.”
The award, handed out yearly to the best British or Irish album as voted for by a panel of music industry figures, comes with a £25,000 prize.
While This Music May Contain Hope didn’t have universally positive reviews – “there are flaws, but in fairness it pays off more often than it fails”, was the opinion of the Guardian’s pop critic Alexis Petridis – the judges hailed its “scale, structure, ambition and sheer charm”.
Where Is My Husband! proved to be a powerhouse lead single, reaching No 1 in the UK, No 6 in the US and delighting audiences globally with Raye’s witty rat-a-tat-tat delivery as she expressed her frustration at her romantic failures including “lonely acrobatics, unzipping my dress at 2am”.
It adds to a strange and heartening career for the 28-year-old singer, born Rachel Keen in west London, who started out by shuttling between genres and netting hits as a guest vocalist on pop-dance singles before finally being able to let her stylistic diversity shine on her album projects.
As lighthearted as songs like Where Is My Husband! are, she has also written about more serious subjects, such as a sexual assault she faced from a music producer.
Accepting the award at the ceremony in Newcastle, Raye said: “I cannot tell you how grateful I am to be holding this. I’m shaking, I’m jet-lagged, I’m tired, I’m grateful!”
She alluded to her difficult years with her former label, saying: “Albums are so important, and not to be bitter – because I feel like I’m mostly at peace with my past – but to come from a place where it’s all about singles and chasing the next thing, I just feel so grateful to be recognised.”
She also talked about the central topic on the album: “Hope is a very cheesy word, especially for us British people, we don’t do that deep stuff like that, but hope is something we all need … so I hope that message comes across to anyone who needs it.”
Elsewhere on the shortlist, Paul McCartney missed out in the first year he was nominated for the prize, for his reflective album The Boys of Dungeon Lane . In a video message, he said he was “chuffed” and “surprised” to be nominated on a shortlist alongside “such a group of really amazing artists”.
Suede, who opened the ceremony by performing their stridently pro-European anthem Dancing With the Europeans, weren’t able to add a second Mercury win to their trophy cabinet, after winning for their self-titled debut in 1993, the second year the award ran.
Nor could Dave, who won for his own debut album, Psychodrama, in 2019; he and McCartney were the only artists not to perform at the ceremony.
Pulp – the winners in 1996 – performed for the second year in a row: last year for their nominated album More, and this year representing the all-star compilation album Help, created to raise funds for the charity War Child.
Florence + the Machine now have the ignominious honour of being the Mercury’s joint highest nominee without winning, tying with Radiohead on five unconverted nominations.
Raye also beat stiff competition from Olivia Dean, whose album The Art of Loving has been one of the most successful albums by anyone in the singer’s generation, spending every one of its 55 weeks since release in the UK Top 10.
After losing its sponsor in 2024 and taking place in a rather low-key ceremony, the Mercury prize has repositioned itself, moving away from London to Newcastle in 2025 and scaling up in size to the city’s Utilita Arena.
In its inaugural year in its new home, the Mercury was awarded to local boy Sam Fender – though Newcastle jazz band Knats, who wowed the arena crowd with virtuosic bass soloing and spoken word poetry, weren’t able to secure back-to-back Tyneside wins this year.
There has been some consternation, though, that its focus is becoming more commercial than in the past – and not distinct enough from the Brit awards.
In 2025, seven of the 12 nominated albums reached the UK Top 3, while this year six of the nominations reached No 1, and another two were Top 3 hits. All but two of the albums (Suede’s Antidepressants and the Help charity compilation) were released by or in partnership with the three major labels: Universal, Warner and Sony.
Previously the UK’s independent music scene has been better represented, including in winners such as Arctic Monkeys, Dizzee Rascal, Sampha and Ezra Collective.
This year’s judging panel featured musicians, broadcasters, journalists and consultants: Afrodeutsche, Danielle Perry, Jamie Cullum, Lea Stonhill, MistaJam, Phil Alexander, Sian Eleri, Sophie Williams and Will Hodgkinson, with Jeff Smith as chair.

title: James Bond finalists to screen-test for role this week – reports
description: Actors in the mix to play 007 in Denis Villeneuve’s installment include Callum Turner and Jack Lowden
content:
Actors in the mix to play 007 in Denis Villeneuve’s installment include Callum Turner and Jack Lowden
The search for the next James Bond may finally be nearing its end: according to reports, a very select group of actors will screen-test to become the next British agent 007 this weekend.
According to the Hollywood Reporter and Variety , citing several sources, a group of actors reportedly including Callum Turner and Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, will appear in front of cameras as the secret agent this weekend in London.
The tests supposedly include three elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Reports vary that between three and five actors are finalists for the role, which was vacated by Daniel Craig after 2021’s No Time to Die. Despite speculation to the contrary, Sinners’ Jack O’Connell and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi are not testing, according to the Hollywood Reporter.
Dune film-maker Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next installment of the Bond franchise for Amazon MGM studios, which bought the series rights as part of an $8.45bn (£6.9bn) deal in 2022. The Peaky Blinders writer Steven Knight will pen the script.
The company, which paid more than $1bn last year to wrest “creative control” from the Broccoli family, has neither confirmed nor denied the reports, and referred the Hollywood Reporter to its earlier statement: “The search for the next James Bond is under way. While we don’t plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we’re excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right.”
In April of this year, Amazon film executives urged fans to exercise patience in waiting for the casting announcement, citing an abundance of caution in making the closely watched decision. “I know you’re all wondering when we’re going to announce who’s playing James Bond,” said Courtenay Valenti, the company’s head of film. “Don’t get too excited. Please know that we’re taking the time to do this with care and deep respect. It is the dream of a lifetime for all of us to bring audiences this next chapter, and it’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly.”
Villeneuve, a “diehard Bond fan”, has said the opportunity to add to the beloved franchise is what drew him away from the Dune franchise that has consumed the better part of a decade of his life.
“I said, ‘Maybe it’s a good idea to go back to this project, not out of nostalgia, not because I miss it, but the opposite – I’m tired of it,’” he told Empire of Dune: Messiah, which will premiere this December. “I want to make sure that I will be severe with the material. That I will not be complacent,” he said. “I thought, ‘When it’s done, I need a very powerful rocket to pull me away from Arrakis.’ When I was asked to do the next Bond, I said: ‘OK, this is what I need.’”
It’s been more than 20 years since the last full screen test for Bond; future Superman Henry Cavill was reported to be a finalist, but the role eventually went to Craig, who first appeared in 2006’s Casino Royale.
Speculation over the new Bond has intensified in the months since Villeneuve was revealed as director in 2025. The film is still reportedly positioned for a 2028 release.

title: Inter Alia by Suzie Miller review – an urgent play about rape and justice is undermined by its novelisation
description: Bogged down by extra padding and a poorly crafted narrator, Miller’s book dilutes the potency of the original and diminishes its scope
content:
Bogged down by extra padding and a poorly crafted narrator, Miller’s book dilutes the potency of the original and diminishes its scope
S uzie Miller’s acclaimed 2019 play, Prima Facie, was a visceral exposé of the cruelty of due process in rape trials that has, on any analysis, been tremendously successful. It has been staged in more than 50 countries, won countless awards and been adapted into a film starring Cynthia Erivo ; it has been used to educate judges and even resulted in changes to jury directions in rape trials, energising debate about better outcomes for survivors.
Miller is a prolific playwright (her latest of more than 40 plays, Strong is the New Pretty , is currently touring Australia), and Inter Alia , which premiered at London’s National Theatre in 2025, picks up themes that animated Prima Facie. The 2025 production starred Rosamund Pike as Jessica Parks: a feminist judge whose ethics are shaken when her 18-year-old son is accused of sexual assault. Pike gives a captivating performance of a desperate and disoriented woman working within a broken justice system. From the bench, Jessica has watched in dismay as defence lawyers exploit loopholes to keep their clients out of jail in rape trials. But when her son is accused, inconsistencies in the testimony of a traumatised victim give Jessica reason to hope he will be let off.
Inter Alia was an effective piece of theatre – but Miller has transformed it into a novel and the results are infuriating. The book is presented as a legal drama about the collision of the ethical and the emotional but, unlike the play, it’s a story about a privileged woman coming to a belated understanding of her life and circumstances. If Prima Facie gained moral momentum by centring the experience of a survivor, the teenage rape victim in the novelisation is a prop in a personal growth narrative. And without the nuances and vulnerabilities conveyed by Pike, Jessica is a much-reduced character.
We learn a lot more about Jessica in the novel but she always seems surprised by the moment, as if her backstory crept up on her out of nowhere. Her marriage to the smug KC Michael is expanded too but, despite all the padding, the reader is given no grounds for the longevity of this relationship. Jessica tells us that Michael resents her for being named a judge before him; that he insinuated she only got the call because she was a woman. Michael is a sexist git but you wonder whether he might be on to something: in the play, Jessica exudes a competence carried by brazen confidence; but, in the novel, thanks to clunky writing, Jessica strikes the reader as imperceptive and foolish.
Often she’s making brisk, empty statements about how things work: “I can read my courtroom. I can read the barristers, the court staff, the public, the defendants. And I can read the witnesses, the complainants. It’s here that I can effect real change.” We know she’s kidding herself about her ability to effect change; the plot is so heavily signposted that the novel’s laboured ironies work to diminish the narrator without inspiring much sympathy for her.
And while on stage we’re with Jessica as she tries to make sense of it all, leaping from past to present at a dizzy pace, that’s not the case in the novel, where urgency is deflated by asides and cliches. Jessica looks in the mirror in her chambers after putting on red lipstick and observes her reflection: “I want to be a judge who is also a woman, who is also herself completely. And this is me. Jessica.” Inane bromides like these add up to a caricature of an ambitious but insecure woman. She may be a complex character onstage but she’s one-dimensional and unconvincing on the page, unable to communicate the moral tangle of her circumstances.
In an early scene, she contemplates reprimanding a barrister from the bench: “The power I have is exciting. If I was telling it as a story in chambers, I would laugh with the delight of it. But only to those other judges who understand the dynamic.” So much of the writing is of this order: lifeless and dull. This is less a matter of Jessica being an ironically unreliable narrator, tragically unable to see what is in front of her until it is too late, I think, than the novelist’s poor command of her craft.
The novel also drags thanks to Jessica’s habit of posing strings of questions that she should be able to answer. For instance: “Somehow since I’ve become a judge, I seem to be pushing myself to be something of a domestic goddess … Why do I need to prove myself at home? Am I catering to Michael’s insecurities around me being more successful in the law?”
These are small questions compared with the moral compromise Jessica must wrestle with later. Harry is the son of two legal professionals, who has been educated about consent – and who is now accused of raping a teenage girl at a party. Jessica cannot believe it . Where the play rushes on, as if to demonstrate Jessica’s powerlessness, the novel plods, as if to emphasise her foolishness. Jessica cannot believe it – until she must. She talks the reader through every doubt, every I couldn’t believe it moment. And, in doing so, Miller’s systemic critique of a culture in which privileged boys raised by progressive parents still feel entitled to the bodies of girls is lost, sucked into the vortex of Jessica’s bewilderment.
Certainly Inter Alia shows how difficult it is for women to parent and to work, and the different standards mothers must meet in the legal profession. But for all that, when it comes to understanding who’s to blame for rape culture, this novel still lays a heavy burden of responsibility on mothers for being – as Jessica sees herself – both overprotective and neglectful. Jessica comes to a limp realisation late in the piece: “In my failing Harry, in our failing a generation of boys by neglecting to mentor them, guide them or show them the way, we are failing a whole generation of girls.” There’s a nod to collective failures – but the novel’s scope is constrained by the lack of complexity and limited perspective of its narrator; and by Miller’s limitations as a novelist too.
I read Inter Alia as the shocking alleged sexual assault at Cornell University made headlines; if I’d read it a month earlier or later, there would have been another assault in the news. We need feminist artists to keep holding rape culture to account, to keep asking why perpetrators are treated with impunity. But in turning Jessica into such a weak character, Inter Alia’s powerful rebuke to a patriarchal legal system that benefits rapists is diluted. It’s not that the problems with the novel are entirely absent from the play – but an actor can convey the pathos of Jessica’s desperate efforts to fix everything in a way that Miller’s narrator simply cannot.
When Miller novelised Prima Facie, the book received a lukewarm reception. Why has this accomplished theatre-maker delivered another underwhelming version of another celebrated play? Moving from the stage to the page is less common as adaptations go, but this one seems to show an indifference to the narrative craft of the novel – and undercuts the original as a result.

title: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm
description: When it rains, it pours for Ruben Amorim as his Milan side were beaten 3-0 by Bournemouth after Mike Maignan’s mad red card
content:
This was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. Whatever this rotten impersonation of a Milan side was, it bore no relation to those that forged such a celebrated history. The visitors resembled holograms even before their goalkeeper Mike Maignan, with an extraordinary rush of blood resulting in a penalty and red card, rendered their task impossible. They never showed the slightest hint of putting up a fight.
Bournemouth simply swamped the seven-time European champions and, amid a swirling south coast storm that rarely let up, could depart singing in the rain. Amine Adli’s sumptuous late free-kick, curled left-footed from 22 yards, meant they could finish the evening with the flourish they deserved. Their joy was clear at full time and met disapproval from some of Milan’s staff, who appeared to take umbrage in a short-lived fracas near the tunnel afterwards.
It was certainly an abject return to English soil for Ruben Amorim, who could have been excused in seeing this particular week as the opportunity to prove a point. Amorim may view Bournemouth as kryptonite given they beat his Manchester United side by an identical scoreline at Old Trafford in December 2024. As it happens that is where the Cherries head on Sunday. On this damning evidence the modern version of Milan share more than a few similarities with his former employers.
“A difficult night in every aspect,” Amorim said. It began with a downpour and waves of Bournemouth pressure, an incisive move ending with Justin Kluivert missing his kick and Ben Gannon-Doak’s drive deflecting wide. Milan failed to clear their lines from the resulting corner and were punished when VAR found Koni De Winter had deflected Evanilson’s header wide with his arm. Kluivert converted the spot kick coolly and the die was firmly cast.
Amorim’s attempt to divide the match into two parts, before and after Maignan’s 27th-minute dismissal, cut no ice. Bournemouth’s tempo had been far too much for Milan before that, Maignan saving untidily from Ryan Christie after Yunus Musah’s pocket had been picked. “We just suffocated them, we didn’t give anything to them,” said a satisfied Marco Rose. “The way they did it today was just brilliant from the first minute until the last.”
When Maignan clawed James Hill’s deflected shot wide, everybody on view set up for a left-sided corner. Nobody was prepared for Maignan, who perhaps expected to be manhandling a taller opponent, to shove Tyler Adams in the face as the ball was sent in. It was a moment of supreme idiocy from the captain; the penalty award was inevitable and so, even before confirmation via VAR, was his departure. This time Marcus Tavernier did the honours, beating the replacement keeper Lorenzo Torriani.
Barely half an hour in, the outcome had been settled. Bournemouth could hardly have imagined, in making their “great escape” from the fourth-tier trapdoor in 2009, that they might land in such a position against Italian royalty. Past luminaries looked on from the stands, Harry Redknapp among them, while their polished successors turned the screw down below.
The relentless Gannon-Doak, called “a special player” afterwards by Rose, thrilled and frustrated in equal measure; the substitute Rayan almost set up a goal for Christie with a delightful piece of skill. It was Adli, another replacement, who applied a delicate garnish.
What a night, then, for a club that knows what it is to gaze into the abyss. “How did we end up here?” asked the public address announcer before kick-off, a question repeated on a banner hoisted by the Steve Fletcher Stand, but it was worth posing in a different sense too. The sizable elephant in the room was how the Premier League’s 15th-placed team could face down one of Serie A’s most decorated institutions, unbeaten domestically this season, and simply sweep them off the park.
In truth nobody could feign too much surprise; certainly not the bookmakers, who deemed Bournemouth the pre-match favourites. Scoffing at Milan’s inadequacy is, up to a point, simply plucking low-hanging fruit. Football’s ecosystem has arrived in a glum place where outwardly fairytale occasions like this are packaged with caveats: even the English top flight’s relative minnows are, through financial and physical power, playing on a different pitch to representatives of leagues once deemed its equals.
For those understandably immersed in the here and now, Rayan came close to a superb fourth. “I’m happy for our fans especially,” Rose said. It is unlikely to be Bournemouth’s last European gala show.

title: Tom Skerritt, Alien and Top Gun actor, dies aged 93
description: Actor also had roles in M*A*S*H, A River Runs Through It and Picket Fences in career spanning 60 years
content:
Actor also had roles in M*A*S*H, A River Runs Through It and Picket Fences in career spanning 60 years
Tom Skerritt, the actor known for roles in Alien and Top Gun , has died at the age of 93.
His publicist confirmed to Variety that he died from natural causes.
“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” a family statement shared with People read.
Stars who paid tribute to him on Thursday included his Steel Magnolias co-star Julia Roberts, who remembered him as “a shining light of a gentle man”, as well as his Picket Fences co-star Cathy Baker.
“My heart is broken to hear of the passing of dear, lovely, loving, Tom, my TV husband, my partner, my darling friend,” Baker told People . “He taught me so much … I couldn’t have asked for a more gracious and kind actor to work with, and it was very special to share with him the incredible run of the show.”
In a career spanning more than 60 years, the actor had more than 170 big and small screen credits, winning an Emmy and receiving Golden Globe and Screen Actors Guild award nominations.
After serving a four-year tour of duty in the US air force, Skerritt made his big-screen debut in the 1962 war film War Hunt alongside Robert Redford and Sydney Pollack, but his breakout came in 1970 with a role in Robert Altman’s hit satire M*A*S*H. The film was a major box office hit and was nominated for the best picture Oscar.
The 1970s saw Skerritt follow the film with roles in the cult black comedy Harold and Maude, Altman’s crime drama Thieves Like Us, Roger Corman’s sexploitation comedy Big Bad Mama and the Oscar-nominated ballet drama The Turning Point.
The decade closed out with a role in Ridley Scott’s smash hit Alien, a film he had earlier turned down due to the low budget. “At two million bucks and with other actors that I don’t know about, this is a film that could have been directed by Ed Wood,” he said in a 2019 interview . “I was uncertain about it because my training with Altman and Ashby had proceeded me, so I had that approach that I had absorbed from watching those two guys going about their work.”
The following decade saw him feature in David Cronenberg’s The Dead Zone, the sci-fi adventure SpaceCamp, horror sequel Poltergeist III and female-led comedy drama Steel Magnolias.
Skerritt also worked with Tony Scott in the 1986 blockbuster Top Gun, a role he almost didn’t get. “There was some question about me playing that role because I was … I think they used the word, laconic,” he said in a 2021 interview with Vulture . “It pissed me off. I went into it with [producer] Don Simpson, who was still alive at that point … don’t tell me, as a producer, what you think I’m going to be doing. You’re going to get what you need.”
In the 1990s, he reunited with Robert Redford for A River Runs Through It and also starred with Jodie Foster in Contact, Drew Barrymore in Poison Ivy and Diane Keaton in The Other Sister.
Skerritt also received an Emmy for his role in David E Kelley’s family drama Picket Fences, a show that ran for four seasons.
The 2000s saw him star with Bruce Willis in Tears of the Sun, Kate Beckinsale in Whiteout and on the small screen he had roles in Will & Grace, The West Wing and Brothers & Sisters.
His last film role was in the western drama Broke in 2025 with Dennis Quaid.
In 2012, he also co-founded an initiative called the Red Badge Project, which aimed to help veterans process their PTSD through storytelling. “It starts with that wanting to help someone else rather than talking about it,” Skerritt said to CBS News . “I just got tired of talking about this if I could do something about it.”
“I’m just a lucky guy, man,” he said in 2021. “Strength is measured in how you confront your weaknesses. I have had a lot of weaknesses. I still have them.”

title: Teacher wounded in Oregon school shooting played dead after she was shot
description: Becky Drury says she was hit by gunfire before she could intervene in attack that killed four, including three children
content:
Becky Drury says she was hit by gunfire before she could intervene in attack that killed four, including three children
A teacher wounded in last week’s shooting at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school shared her account of the incident, and how she was shot before she could intervene and “[pretended] to be dead”.
Becky Drury was seriously wounded at Silver Rail elementary when Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school armed with a shotgun, broke in and headed toward a special education classroom. He shot six people, killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.
Drury and Saylor Graham, a seven-year-old student, were also shot. Another teacher threw her phone at John and tackled him before a parent fatally shot the teen gunman.
Drury, who is still hospitalized, released a statement on Wednesday.
“Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on. I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there. Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground,” Drury said.
Her left hand was almost completely severed, and her other arm was also badly injured, Drury said.
“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again,” she said. “I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act.”
Drury’s account contradicted some reporting that she had thrown herself on top of a student in an effort to protect her, and the 54-year-old said she wanted to ensure “the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately”.
She described the violence as “unimaginable” and said: “My heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy.”
Public schools in the central Oregon city began reopening this week. Dozens of officers have welcomed students as they return to their classes.
The shooting remains under investigation. The Bend police department said this week that the shotgun used in the incident was purchased legally.

title: Trump attacks Ohio governor over call for Ramaswamy to drop ‘deeply troubling’ ad
description: Republican Mike DeWine said ad featuring estranged mother of Democrat Amy Acton was ‘wrong’
content:
Republican Mike DeWine said ad featuring estranged mother of Democrat Amy Acton was ‘wrong’
Donald Trump issued a swift rebuke against Mike DeWine, Ohio’s Republican governor, who on Thursday said gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy was “wrong” to release an ad critical of his Democratic rival Amy Acton that featured her estranged mother.
DeWine had implored Ramaswamy to take the ad down, but hours later, Trump urged Ramaswamy to keep airing it and accused the Republican governor of disloyalty.
Acton, who has led the Republican nominee Ramaswamy in recent polls of the governor’s race, has said she has not seen her mother Donna Arthur for decades, after her mother married a man who sexually abused Acton when she was 12 years old and stayed with him even after police stepped in.
Calling the ad “deeply, deeply troubling”, DeWine told reporters at the Ohio state capital. “It’s wrong to run this ad,” the Associated Press reported .
“I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down,” the governor added.
The video, which began circulating on social media earlier this week and which Ramaswamy’s campaign later told Ohio media outlets is their work, shows Arthur calling her daughter “a liar” and saying she should not be put in charge of the state. Ramaswamy’s campaign said later in the week it would spend $4m to air the ad across the state.
DeWine noted that “family members have always historically been off limits” and Acton had earlier this year mentioned Ramaswamy’s mother’s involvement in an alleged “pump and dump” scheme, though with less prominence than the Ramaswamy ad.
On Truth Social Thursday afternoon, Trump excoriated DeWine for his comments, saying DeWine was “disloyal to the Republican party”.
“He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing,” Trump wrote. “I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!”
Connie Luck, a spokesperson for the Republican’s campaign, said: “We refuse to accept the media’s double standards when Democrats have regularly used family members of President Trump, RFK Jr, and other Republicans in ads. Voters shouldn’t buy it.”
Speaking to reporters in Cincinnati on Wednesday, Vice-President JD Vance dismissed criticism of Ramaswamy’s campaign. “Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern,” Vance said.
“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America. Politics is a tough business.”
In a statement released by Acton’s campaign, her brother, Philip Stearns, called the ad “a despicable low” for Ramaswamy, and noted that he and his sister were removed from Arthur’s custody after her stepfather was arrested.
The Republican US senator Jon Husted, who is facing a election bid that could decide which party controls the chamber in the 3 November midterm elections, joined in the condemnation. “I would not have run that ad,” he told the Associated Press.
His Democratic opponent, former senator Sherrod Brown, has called the video “disgusting”, and said all candidates should denounce it.
Ohio’s Republican secretary of state, Frank LaRose, also criticized Ramaswamy, telling the Columbus-area broadcaster ABC 6 : “I probably wouldn’t run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision.”
DeWine nonetheless declined to drop his endorsement of Ramaswamy in the governor’s race, saying he wanted to support the “full ticket” of Republican candidates in the midterms.

title: Aipac halts candidate endorsements amid US backlash against Israel
description: Political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability
content:
Political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability
When the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most prominent pro-Israel lobby group in the US, announced on Wednesday that it would stop endorsing candidates or make direct contributions to them, its many critics were quick to hail the development as Aipac’s admission of how toxic its brand had become.
The announcement marked a significant reversal that underscored just how profoundly US public opinion of Israel has shifted over the latest war in Gaza , and how political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability .
But Aipac, which only launched its political action committee and started endorsing candidates three cycles ago, is hardly getting out of US elections. It pledged to maintain the work of its deep-pocketed Super Pac, United Democracy Project, and to continue to funnel millions of dollars to prop up pro-Israel candidates through individual donors and Aipac members. The shift in strategy was a sign it was adapting to a changing political landscape, not that it was giving up its efforts to shape it.
“Historically, AIPAC sustained an aura of invincibility that ensured it won most battles by walkover – if you are perceived as invincible, the other side doesn’t even bother to fight you,” the political analyst Trita Parsi wrote . “Rather than invincibility, AIPAC’s name now carries such toxicity that the group doesn’t want its own name on its political donations.”
Aipac did not respond to a request for comment. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Aipac, which normally backs Democrats, was planning to give as much as $9m to a Pac supporting Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. The group had already spent $32m seeking to defeat El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel, in the primaries.
But the announcement that it would stop directly backing candidates going forward was seen as tacit recognition that Aipac’s open support risked hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them.
“Through this shift, AIPAC openly admitted that their brand has become toxic in the political world,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, one of Aipac’s most vocal critics, said. “Fewer and fewer candidates are willing to be publicly affiliated with this extremist, warmongering group. This is a clear signal: being pro-genocide is bad politics and bad policy.”
In a letter from Aipac to members first reported on by Jewish Insider , the group’s leadership seemed to acknowledge that its once formidable power in US elections had suffered as more candidates openly distanced themselves from Israel and from the group itself. In the letter, they noted that the 2026 election was “one of the most challenging environments in recent memory” for the group and predicted that the “challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead.”
“To win the fight for the future of the country and the U.S.-Israel alliance, we must build a more strategic, consequential, and nimble political operation,” they wrote. “The only tactic we’re married to is the most effective one.”
While Aipac boasted that it helped 290 candidates this election cycle, leading to the defeat of 29 candidates it described as “anti-Israel”, the group has also suffered major blows – including in Michigan and New Jersey. More than a dozen candidates who took Aipac contributions in the past have since publicly distanced themselves from the group, and New York congressman Pat Ryan announced last week that he would return nearly $250,000 from the group, the latest of several elected officials to return Aipac funds or say they would turn it down .
Dion Nissenbaum, a journalist whose documentary on Aipac was published this week , featuring interviews with former Aipac insiders, told the Guardian that the announcement appeared to be the “first real admission from Aipac that their campaign strategy has backfired”.
Still, he warned, “if Aipac’s super PAC – the main source of its campaign donations – is going to keep operating, it may be an attempt to reinvent itself without ceding the battlefield.”
Tuesday’s announcement would change little in practice, those who have monitored Aipac’s political funding say. An Aipac spokesperson told Jewish Insider that Aipac members had contributed over $90m to candidates this election cycle – far more than the $3m in donations the group contributed directly through its Pac.
“This is not new,” Hady Amr, a former secretary for Israeli and Palestinian affairs with the US state department, noted . “This is Aipac going back to their tried and true approach.”
Groups like TrackAipac and initiatives like the Reject Aipac campaign, that have in recent years played a growing role in calling out candidates over their ties to the group, are already attuned to the varied avenues through which the pro-Israel lobby funnelled contributions to candidates, some more visible than others.
“[Aipac] has already been experimenting with ways to make their support more untraceable,” said Hamid Bendaas of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, one of the groups behind the Reject Aipac campaign. By dropping endorsements and direct contributions, Aipac was giving up one tool available to lobby organizations to signal to politically-aligned donors who may not be active members which candidates to back. Aipac had calculated that approach was more risky than worth it, he added, but it had plenty of other tools available.
“It’s akin to an animal that chews its leg off to get out of a bear trap. It’s a last resort choice to survive and stay relevant, which they will on both counts,” Bendaas added. “Aipac is going to continue influencing elections. If you’re someone who wants Aipac out of politics entirely, this is not that.
“We know they’re going to continue driving tens of millions of dollars into our elections to support Israel’s atrocities,” echoed Miller of JVP. “And we will continue to fight to fully get them, and their dirty money, out of our politics and out of Congress.”

title: Terry Lee obituary
description: Other lives: Artist and art teacher who was originally associated with the Kitchen Sink painters of the 1950s
content:
My father, Terry Lee, who has died aged 93, was an art lecturer at Sheffield College of Art in South Yorkshire for almost three decades, and a well-regarded painter for more than half a century.
In his early years he was associated with the “Kitchen Sink” painters , who portrayed ordinary people in scenes of everyday life. But as his work evolved it became more figurative, lyrical and contemplative, and was influenced by landscape, music and literature.
Terry’s early success came with inclusion in John Berger’s Looking Forward exhibition in 1956 and prize-winning entries in successive John Moores exhibitions, but the creative energy to paint continued across five decades as he produced successive collections of work and exhibited at a series of London galleries, including the New Art Centre, Agnew’s and the Piccadilly Gallery during the 1960s and 70s.
In the 80s he was included in the British Art Show, curated by the critic William Packer, and a series of exhibitions in Maastricht in the Netherlands. A retrospective exhibition of his work was held at the Wildenstein Gallery in London in 1992.
Terry was born in Sheffield to George, a draughtsman for Firth Brown Steels, and Phylis (nee Senior), a housewife. He went to King Edward VII school and began his creative life at Sheffield College of Art in 1953, progressing to the Slade School of Art in 1955, after which he taught at his old college from 1958 until he took early retirement in 1986.
At the Slade School of Art, Terry had met fellow Sheffield artist Rosie Peters. They married in London in 1956 before returning to Sheffield, eventually settling in a dilapidated farmhouse at Calton Houses near Chatsworth in Derbyshire. There they raised four sons and worked on their art.
Beyond painting Terry loved the hills. He was a rock climber, and an early series of abstract paintings reflected this, taking inspiration from Heinrich Harrer’s book The White Spider, detailing early attempts to climb the Eiger’s infamous north face. Terry passed this passion on to his sons, whom he took on climbing trips to local Derbyshire crags and farther afield to north Wales and the Dolomites.
His marriage to Rosie ended in separation in the mid-70s; afterwards he met the artist Pamela Firth, and they married in 1998. The last chapter of his life was lived out in the mountainous beauty and solitude of Spain’s Costa Blanca, where both he and Pam continued to paint, taking inspiration from a landscape full of light.
Terry is survived by Pam and three sons, Daniel, Dominic and me, from his first marriage. His fourth and eldest son, Adam, predeceased him.

title: Morning Mail: Victoria’s female MPs ‘on high alert’; Snowy Hydro’s $25bn bill; and Tour de France routes revealed
description: Safety concerns before Victoria’s state election; visa changes could leave students in the lurch; dire warnings for coral reefs
content:
Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Morning Mail here , and finish your day with our Politics, really newsletter .
Good morning. With just five weeks until the Victorian election, female MPs say they are “on high alert” over potential threats after the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines.
International students across Australia say they fear disruption to their lives as they are forced to navigate the impacts of Labor’s sudden visa changes.
There are dire warnings for the future of the world’s coral reef ecosystems, including the Great Barrier Reef. And we look at the resurgence in bogong moth numbers across eastern Australia.
‘I can’t sleep’ | International students in Australia are facing uncertainty amid the Albanese government’s sudden changes to student visa rules, which have left some fearing the disruption ahead .
‘On high alert’ | The alleged attack on Helen Haines has sent a chill down the collective spine of female MPs before the Victorian election. “Nunchucks” allegedly wielded by an agitated man at WA MP Hannah Beazley’s office may have been drumsticks , a court has heard.
‘Could have been worse’ | The cost of Snowy Hydro 2.0 has blown out to as much as $25bn , with a reassessment finding the renewable energy project will not be completed until the end of the decade.
The road ahead | Jim Chalmers has revealed December’s midyear budget update will project higher unemployment and weaker growth, as economists warn of a difficult six months .
Analysis | If you live on the eastern side of Australia, you’ve probably noticed that bogong moths are back in a big way. Data from citizen scientists reveal how they are coming back from the brink .
Opinion | There are plenty of reasons why Australians feel “mad as hell” at the moment, Nicki Hutley writes. Here are three things the government could do right now to make people feel better off .
Russia-Ukraine war | Russia has carried out a massive attack on Ukraine , bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume negotiations; Downing Street has rejected US envoy Steve Witkoff’s description of Putin as a “humanitarian” .
Middle East crisis | Iran will strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities across as many as seven countries in the Gulf in the event of a fresh US-Israeli attack , Tehran has said.
‘Wake-up call’ | Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet, including Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, faces ecosystem collapse before 2075 because of global heating, UN advisers warn.
French unrest | “Illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned in the coming days, Emmanuel Macron says, as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years.
Active Denial System | Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, has reportedly signed a memo permitting officials to test a non-lethal “heat ray” for potential use at the US southern border.
‘Pure arrogance’ | There’s anger in Finland as it was revealed that Google illegally felled 250,000 trees and stripped an entire area – even taking the topsoil – to build a new datacentre project.
Alan Jones on trial: Alleged victim’s mother ‘trusted’ Jones
The mother of the youngest complainant wept on the stand after being presented with a note written by her son alleging “something happened” at Alan Jones’s property at Fitzroy Falls. As the prosecution questioned the mother, she told the court she had “trusted” Jones with her then teenage son. Amanda Meade joins Nour Haydar to unpack an emotional week in the courtroom .
Air travel can become not just messy but a “biological hazard”, with stomach bugs combined with turbulence increasing nausea and leaving passengers caught short while making it to the lavatory. Airlines don’t always allow hygiene issues to hinder their schedules but they can cause major disruptions. Changing seat covers, using air freshener and cancelling flights: here’s how airlines tackle mid-flight contamination .
Diana Reid only used about 25 lines from Jane Austen’s first published novel for her film adaptation of Sense and Sensibility, inventing most of the dialogue herself. But as she toiled over her screenplay, the Australian author found herself having some oddly formal conversations down at the pub. She talks about how Austen infected her speech, the impact of Ang Lee’s 1995 film, and surprising Brits with her accent .

title: Barbara Jay obituary
description: Singer who worked with Ronnie Scott and Benny Goodman, and in a musical partnership with her husband Tommy Whittle
content:
Singer who worked with Ronnie Scott and Benny Goodman, and in a musical partnership with her husband Tommy Whittle
Being a dance-band vocalist in the early 1950s meant sitting at the side of the stage in a pretty frock awaiting the call to perform, and the stylish singer Barbara Jay, who has died with dementia aged 94, described this as serving her “apprenticeship” in the business. Greater success and satisfaction followed when she sang with Ronnie Scott and Benny Goodman , and later with her husband, the jazz tenor-saxophonist Tommy Whittle .
It was 1953 when the saxophonist Pete King , then managing Ronnie Scott’s feisty nine-piece group, called Jay to offer her the job of singer with the band. Vying to make it the UK’s top jazz outfit, Scott and King had assembled the best upstart jazz musicians in the country. This was not an easy billet musically for a young vocalist, since Scott himself was never “very happy with girl singers anyway”. The band member Benny Green recalled: “She stayed longer than all the other girl singers put together and she certainly came to play an integral role in the band’s performance.” For all its many indignities on the road, with the ladies’ dressing room often doubling as a toilet or vice versa, Jay relished her time with Scott and company, remaining friends with King and Scott and appearing often at their famous London club in Frith Street.
After working with the pianist and entertainer Cab Kaye in Amsterdam for 18 months and then with a German big band, Jay returned home, and joined Billy Ternent’s orchestra, broadcasting frequently, until another game-changing moment. A vocalist rang to ask Jay to deputise for her with Whittle’s group at the Savoy dance hall in Catford, south-east London. This went so well that Jay joined the group, and in 1967 she and Whittle were married, their musical and marital partnership lasting until Tommy’s death in 2013.
She also took on his two young sons (their mother had died some time before) and ran the family unit. It was then at Tommy’s suggestion that she sent a tape to Goodman’s entourage in 1970 and was hired to tour Europe with the last of the King of Swing’s all-star British big bands as featured vocalist for six weeks, “earning more than I had ever done in my life”.
Thereafter she helped Tommy run their very successful jazz club at the Hop Bine pub in Wembley for 10 years, while appearing with his bands or with the Pizza Express All-Stars, which he led. There were albums, too, on the Spotlite label, but her greatest breakthrough came when a promoter challenged her in 1993 to devise a concert show. This became the wildly successful Ella Fitzgerald Songbook show, which starred the singers Maxine Daniels and Rosemary Squires alongside Barbara, with their neatly packaged tribute programme backed by Tommy’s jazz quartet. This eventually ran for some 400 performances in Britain and abroad, with Lee Gibson and Tina May joining Barbara in a further variant entitled Ladies in Jazz.
Born in Cardiff and raised in London, Barbara was the daughter of Barbara (nee Weyman) and Billy Jones. Her father was a professional trumpeter who toured (and recorded) with the Joe Daniels Hot Shots before playing with many top palais bands. “He was a lovely trumpet player,” Barbara said. “Well, all daughters would say that, wouldn’t they?” Evacuated during the second world war to Alnwick in Northumberland, she moved around while spending time with her father, then an RAF musician in a band led by the saxophonist Claude Cavalotti. Having attended 11 different schools during this period of upheaval, she always bemoaned her educational shortcomings.
Brought up to appreciate the great jazz singers and star trumpeters such as Louis Armstrong and Harry James, she tried out for her school choir in 1946 and liked it, so her parents paid for her to have proper vocal training. The war over, her father continued to play summer seasons with Cavalotti’s dance band and “of course we used to go along and spend a couple of days with him. My dad said, ‘why don’t you learn a song and come up and sing with us?’ I was so nervous! But that’s what got me started.”
Newly enthused, the 16-year-old Barbara Jay (taking the initial J of Jones to become Jay) began to sing with local musicians around south London until the bandleader Bill Collins hired her for occasional Saturday nights at the nearby Streatham Locarno Dance Hall. This, incidentally, was where her parents had first met, when her mother was a dance hostess and father Billy “the young tearaway” band trumpeter. Always pro-active, Barbara answered a Melody Maker small ad placed by the trombonist Geoff Love and headed “Wanted – Girl Singer”, auditioned successfully, and was booked with his jazzman-stuffed Octet to appear in summer 1951 at the Astoria, Charing Cross Road, for six afternoons and six evenings a week, this her first entry into the “name” band world.
After a season in Brighton with Love, Jay began a sequence of increasingly rewarding engagements, always honing her skills, first with the Joe Saye Trio, then with the Ken Mackintosh band at the Wimbledon Palais. She joined Tito Burns ’ popular sextet in 1952 as maternity cover for his wife, the vocalist Terry Devon, on their German tour, the band including the brilliant bassist Coleridge Goode , whom Jay credited with “helping me relax”. Then came the call from Ronnie Scott’s band.
In the years after Tommy’s death, Barbara gave talks about the music business to social clubs and put together impromptu groups until her health began to fail. Always positive and adept at making connections, and glamorous too, Barbara was a trouper to the end. She is survived by her stepsons Martin and Sean; her sister Carol predeceased her.

title: Neon joins the Guardian and MK2 on Academy Award-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s NAZA
description: Documentary, produced by James Wilson and executive-produced by Jonathan Glazer, premiered in Venice and won the special jury prize
content:
Documentary, produced by James Wilson and executive-produced by Jonathan Glazer, premiered in Venice and won the special jury prize
Neon, the award-winning studio behind some of the most daring and celebrated films of the last decade, has joined the Guardian, MK2, James Wilson and Jonathan Glazer on NAZA from Academy Award-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the co-directors of No Other Land, which won an Oscar for best documentary feature in 2025. The urgent documentary received its world premiere in competition at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize and received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation. The film later screened at the San Sebastián international film festival (winning the audience award) and the New York film festival. This week, it won the critics prize at the Hot Springs documentary film festival. The film is nominated for three Critics Choice documentary awards including best documentary, best director and best political documentary. It is also included on Doc NYC’s Short List.
Neon stated: “Yuval and Rachel have created one of the best films of the year; it’s an extraordinary work of art and eyewitness testimony that stands alongside landmark documentaries like Laura Poitras’ Citizenfour and Joshua Oppenheimer’s The Act of Killing. At the heart of Neon’s mission is a commitment to championing the best cinema from around the world. We’re proud to join the incredible team already working on the film and help bring it to the widest audience possible.“
The Guardian’s head of investigations, Paul Lewis , and global head of multimedia, Nicole Jackson , said:
“We’re delighted that Neon is joining the NAZA team – a global network of distributors, producers, journalists and film-makers intent on bringing this remarkable documentary to as many audiences as possible. The film is currently in cinemas in more than 50 countries around the world and, with Neon’s backing, we are confident we can further expand our audience in the US.
“Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are exceptionally talented directors. Their partnership with the Guardian has resulted in an urgent film that is informing and moving audiences all over the world. We believe with Neon’s support that impact will only grow.”
NAZA was released independently in the US on 30 September in 85 theaters across 30 cities. Overseas, the film has secured theatrical distribution in more than 50 countries. Neon will work with the film-makers to expand its footprint and to reach larger audiences and communities. In NAZA , which was the only documentary in the Venice competition, secret conversations on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night reveal the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza by the people who designed and operated them.
The documentary is produced by the Guardian with producer James Wilson’s JW Films in association with Placeholder Films and Unseen Hand. Jonathan Glazer (The Zone of Interest, Under the Skin) executive-produced. The deal was negotiated by MK2 Films, which led sales for the film before the Venice film festival, and Neon.
