Abraham is an Israeli film-maker and investigative journalist and Szor is an Israeli film-maker and cinematographer. They are two of the four co-directors of the Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land.

title: ‘It’s all God’s creation’: farmers continue a ‘Jewishly inspired’ agrarian tradition
description: In the US, a growing number of Jewish people are seeking purpose and community through farming
content:
In the US, a growing number of Jewish people are seeking purpose and community through farming
Wendy Rhein is trying to round up the sheep hanging out among the hazelnut and walnut trees of her Chutzpah Hollow farm in Tryon, North Carolina .
“Hi, Brea. Come on down. I hear you,” Rhein calls to the bleating queen of the flock. If the Barbados black belly ewe moves, the rest will follow.
Brea, a bottle-fed lamb named Hadassah and their flock mates bound down the hill when Rhein rustles a box of kosher tea biscuits. The small treat reveals something different about this farm. Rhein is remarkable for several reasons: she’s a female farmer in a male-dominated industry and a single mother who had no farming experience when she launched her farm at age 52. She’s also Jewish.
Rhein, who also works as vice-president of a faith-based advocacy organization, is part of a renewed interest among Jews in farming as an expression of their religion, culture or values. Shani Mink, co-founder of the Jewish Farmer Network, often hears “Jewish farmer – isn’t that an oxymoron?” Mink’s organization serves about 1,800 farmers, most of them first-generation agriculturalists, and offers conferences, classes and farm-to-table Shabbat dinners.
There is no solid estimate of the number of Jewish farmers in the country; the US Department of Agriculture’s census of the farming workforce doesn’t collect data on religion. But as Mink points out: “Jews have been farmers from time immemorial. The Jewish tradition is an agrarian tradition” – evidenced by how many holidays, such as the autumn harvest celebration Sukkoth, are tied to the agricultural calendar.
The Jewish Agricultural Society, chartered in 1900, helped people facing persecution in eastern Europe relocate to US farmland, where they could gain skills and independence. By 1933, more than 100,000 Jews earned some or all of their living from farming, according to Gary Moore, professor emeritus at North Carolina State University. But as the US population shifted away from agricultural work, many Jewish people moved into cities and suburbs. Some are returning to rural environments and family roots to farm, inspired by principles of their faith and building better food systems.
Rhein grew up in Detroit, the daughter of a man who was raised on a dairy farm he couldn’t wait to leave. In contrast, she loved the idea of raising livestock and being closer to her food sources; she challenged herself to prepare every ingredient she and her two sons consumed, down to the ketchup, while living in a high-rise with a kitchen “the size of a postage stamp” in Washington DC. When the pandemic hit, she started to search for land and research a new venture selling starter flocks of sheep.
Her brother, who lives about 45 minutes away in Asheville, showed her properties for sale over FaceTime. “I did not step foot on to this land or into this house until the day of our closing,” she said. Now she owns a 10-acre property.
Despite rising Jewish interest in land stewardship, Mink noted that most Jewish growers are “the only Jewish person in their farming community or the only farming person in their Jewish community”. In Rhein’s case, the nearest synagogue is almost an hour away. For her, that means “how I practice being a Jew on a day-to-day basis is how I farm and how I am attached to and care for this land”.
Rhein donates 10% of everything she raises to a local food bank, a reflection of pe’ah , a Talmudic concept that describes giving part of the harvest to the needy. She prays over every duck, chicken and sheep she slaughters so her family may eat.
“It’s all God’s creation,” she said. “It is a gift that we get to be part of it. We are stewards. We are not owners.”
But she also differs in her interpretation of some principles. The concept of bal tashchit focuses on limiting waste, so she keeps a pig to eat food scraps – a controversial decision for some Jews who don’t eat pork due to kosher dietary practices, many of whom disagree with her choice online.
“I am very clear this is not a quote-unquote ‘Jewish farm’,” Rhein said, “but I do consider us to be a Jewishly inspired place.”
A number of Jewish farming organizations focus on both community building and skills building. The Sacred Slaughter Institute trains students to become a shochets , ritual slaughterers of kosher meat; the butchering process calls for prayer, a highly sharpened knife and a single clean cut to lessen tza’ar ba’alei chayim , or animal suffering . Elsewhere, at the 20-acre non-profit Adamah Farm in Falls Village, Connecticut, Jewish people in their 20s and 30s come for three-month farming fellowships. Located at the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center, Adamah sells vegetables and herbs through membership in its community-supported agriculture (CSA) model.
Adamah Farm co-founder Shamu Sadeh said the work “is a process of reinvigorating Judaism and the Jewish community with an ecological perspective, and of reinvigorating the ecological environmental community with people who feel spiritually connected”. Graduates work in food rescue programs, food policy, environmental groups and Jewish social services, among other fields; a small percentage are farmers.
Rabbis Shoshana and Philip Ohriner run the 16-acre Ma’alot Farms in Los Gatos, California, with grants from community organizations and foundations. The farm nurtures hundreds of varieties of produce, from olives and broccolini to marionberries, a type of blackberry. Almost everything is given away to people facing food insecurity, including kids in afterschool programs and seniors with nutritional needs.
Ma’alot’s marketing doesn’t refer to Judaism. Still, “you cannot step on to Ma’alot Farms without feeling our Judaism permeate everything”, Philip Ohriner said, “from the way in which we care for our staff and provide a living wage for them and benefits, to the ways in which we seek to share our abundance to feed the hungry, to seek to bring equity and justice more fully into our world.”
At Ekar Farm , located at an eldercare community in Aurora, Colorado, executive director Jason Plotkin offers intergenerational gardening programs and donates about 20,000lb of organic produce annually to groups including Hope Communities, which serves refugees, and Spirit of the Sun, an Indigenous-led organization. The farm grows epazote, Thai hot chilies and bitter melon among its crops based on requests from recipients. Plotkin grew up Jewish but wasn’t religious. “I actually have learned more about my Jewish identity working for Ekar,” he said, “than what I brought into it.”
Non-profit farms exemplify the idea of tzedakah , or charity, a requirement in Jewish tradition. Small-scale for-profit farms strive to be community partners in their own ways.
Zalman (Robbie) Friedman operates a subscription and delivery service for local kosher meat from Robariah Farms in South Deerfield, Massachusetts. A certified shochet , he tends to about 1,000 birds, including meat chickens, egg layers and turkeys. About a quarter of his customers aren’t Jewish but appreciate Robariah’s regenerative farming practices. His birds have plenty of room to move and dine on fresh pasture every day thanks to mobile coops. “We raise a slower-growing variety that’s very active on the grass,” he said.
The laws of kashrut , or keeping kosher, outline how to slaughter an animal but are less specific about its care, Friedman said. “Why can’t it be done in a way that also honors the life of the animal, which is also a very important Jewish value and Jewish practice?”
Jewish guidance can show up even in crop selection. Ian Yosef Hertzmark grows ancient grains such as emmer, einkorn, spelt and Persian wheats, among other crops, on the 32-acre Migrash Farm in Baltimore county, Maryland. He plants ancient grains in the fall to be yoshon, or “old”, taking root before Passover (the Torah forbids eating chadash , or “new” grain). Hertzmark finds fulfillment in having “a relationship with land in an observant and seasonal context”.
Rhein agrees. She feels “more self-aware, more confident, more alive and whole as a human being here, doing this, than I ever felt living in Manhattan … This way of life – attaching yourself to land and animals and seasonality – is a constant sense of joy.”

title: Flo & Joan: With Feeling review – sisters turn an old rock setlist into hilariously neurotic songs
description: Richly wrought lyrical wit and sumptuous harmonies enhance the duo’s clever new show – along with plenty of backchat
content:
Shepherd’s Bush Empire, London Richly wrought lyrical wit and sumptuous harmonies enhance the duo’s clever new show – along with plenty of backchat
T he last time Flo & Joan played Shepherd’s Bush Empire, they found a setlist on stage left by beloved indie-rock band the Feeling on the previous night. It made the sisters contemplate their own relationship to the music industry. Are Flo & Joan a proper band or doomed for ever to remain “musical comedy”? The problem with which, they deadpan here, is that “no one takes it seriously”. Cue this new show, its structure inspired by that chance discovery. Tonight, the duo play a suite of new songs that, title by title, matches the setlist of the band who preceded them four years ago.
And so goes the first half of With Feeling, which by turns delivers on and subverts that challenge – and proves handsomely entertaining either way. In the sisters’ hands, Fill My Little World becomes a neurotic number about the surfeit of stuff (cheap food, fast fashion, AI slop). Never Be Lonely returns to a favoured topic, Flo & Joan’s toxic co-dependency – with an added sight gag involving Joan (AKA Rosie Dempsey)’s questionable trumpet skills. Further numbers address the risks of poor punctuation and the need, in a society giddy on unfiltered self-expression, to “bring back shame”.
Elsewhere, those secondhand titles inspire bits of business or bad puns rather than whole new songs. That’s just as much fun: Flo & Joan are more expansive on stage than they used to be, amusing one another very infectiously as they navigate – via a wide array of musical styles, sibling backchat and surprise interventions – to the end of their setlist stunt.
Then comes act two, in which they unleash their rock band fantasies (leathers, bandanas, drumkit) on some well-loved numbers from their back catalogue: the one about social gaffes and the eternal cringe they engender (The Rest of My Life); the nonsense spoof folk song Lady In the Woods. As ever with Flo & Joan, you get richly wrought lyrical wit, sumptuous harmonies and musical surprises – this time with a droll top layer of bathetic rock posturing. A proper band, they may never be – for which, when improper is this much fun, we should all be grateful.

title: Super Graphic Spectacular review – Chappell Roan dazzles at her gloriously gay mini-festival
description: With performances by Christina Aguilera, Lola Young and Tinashe, the pop star brings a colorful vision to life in support of LGBTQ+ charities
content:
Shrine Auditorium, Los Angeles With performances by Christina Aguilera, Lola Young and Tinashe, the pop star brings a colorful vision to life in support of LGBTQ+ charities
A t Chappell Roan ’s Super Graphic Spectacular, the sincerely camp pop star imagines a world where the most vulnerable among us aren’t wielded as scapegoats, and where life can be good, so long as we are good to one another.
That better world takes the form of a two-night extravaganza at Los Angeles’s Shrine Auditorium, part kiki ball, part fabulous revue, celebrating the first anniversary of the Midwest Princess Project , the non-profit Roan founded in 2025 to support transgender youth and LGBTQ+ communities.
Named after her breakout album, The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess, the non-profit has raised more than $800,000 and supported more than 60 organizations in its first year. Its work extends the promise at the heart of Roan’s music: that queer people, particularly those who grew up feeling estranged from their surroundings, can find somewhere to belong. For an artist whose rise has been inseparable from the extravagant performance of identity, the event offers a way to translate that feeling of collective recognition into practical support.
The Shrine Auditorium, with a capacity of about 6,300, is at least 10 times smaller than the crowds Roan usually plays to. The bill, however, is hardly modest. Pop stars Lola Young and Tinashe share the stage with drag acts and burlesque performers whose influence on Roan’s gleefully excessive presentation is unmistakable. Hosting the festivities is Caleb Hearon , everyone’s favorite algorithm-touted gay guy. “Why’s a man here? It feels like Chappell doing Make-A-Wish,” he jokes at the beginning of the night.
On the first of the two nights, straight men are in the minority. They dangle from the arms of their fabulous girlfriends, who wear sequins and cowboy hats, like accessories themselves, dressed in black bandanas and Spider-Man tees. Both groups queue for the same bathroom. “Restrooms are non-binary tonight,” a security attendant announces. Roan has not skimped on a single detail.
She has transformed the Shrine into a rococo burlesque ballroom, its gilded scrollwork set against great, swooping red velvet curtains. Blaine Petrovia , the night’s opening act, slides down a tall pole at the center of the stage, executing extravagant, sensual flourishes in a slutty circus routine.
There is hardly a pause between the night’s five acts as Hearon ushers performers on and offstage, vamping about straight men (why are they all fake photographers?) and straight women (ditto, but witches?).
Lola Young, the first of the night’s two guest singers, takes the stage in what might be called normal-people drag, looking a little out of place. She performs just three songs, closing with her hit Messy. An extraordinary vocalist still early in her career, Young has yet to master stage presence or crowd management, though her awkwardness remains charming, much as it did when PinkPantheress used to sheepishly carry a bag on stage.
The house band remains the same throughout, presumably to lend the night some cohesion, but Roan’s two guest singers struggle to distinguish themselves from it. The coherence of Roan’s universe is also its limitation: the show is so thoroughly organized around her sensibility that its glammed-up, exaggerated arrangements don’t quite work for everyone. Tinashe, the night’s second guest singer, is a case in point.
Tinashe’s latest album, for my money one of the best of the year, is supremely chic. Here, the band distorts its sleekness into chintz. It’s a testament to Tinashe’s deftness as a performer that she rises to the occasion, delivering Roan-filtered versions of her songs with ease, but the crowd doesn’t quite respond in kind. When she sings Nobody Wanna Dance Anymore , the audience largely proves her right. Devastatingly, that is one of the only two (two!) songs Tinashe is allotted.
The space made for Roan proves worthwhile when the headliner launches into an extraordinary hour-and-a-half set. It confirms her status as one of the greatest performers in pop, and possibly in any genre, working today. She emerges relatively understated, by her standards, in a gray gown, with a long red fishtail woven into her hair.
Roan’s world is one of ballroom, drag, glam rock, girlhood splendor and sex. She hiccups her way through Midwest Princess hits – Femininomenon, Casual and Super Graphic Ultra Modern Girl – without a hair out of place.
By now, Roan’s production is so perfected that the cracks that peek through tonight feel graciously illuminating. Several songs into her set, she begins to look noticeably nervous, taking swigs from her lilac Stanley cup, forgetting lyrics and smiling diffidently. “I have a surprise,” she announces, telling the crowd that she is about to bring out a guest who has “paved the way”. Cyndi Lauper? I think. Madonna, if we’re being incredibly ambitious.
Then Christina Aguilera appears in black lingerie, and Roan, who has spent the evening functioning with the precision of the well-oiled Femininomenon she is, suddenly becomes a giggling fan. Aguilera sings Beautiful, accompanied by piano, while Roan watches from the bench in disbelief.
There is something especially moving about hearing a song you have taken for granted, through sheer ubiquity, suddenly acquire a new resonance. As Aguilera sings Beautiful to a predominantly queer audience, the familiar becomes elemental again. “Words won’t bring you down.”
Roan appears charmingly nervous as the two duet her indie-folk ballad Coffee , forgetting her words again and regaining her composure only after Aguilera leaves the stage. Then she becomes the slick, precise performer again, leading the crowd into the YMCA’s sexier, uncloseted cousin, Hot to Go!
She closes with the song that traces her escape from her conservative Missouri upbringing into a world of her own making. In Los Angeles , surrounded by fabulous gays, Pink Pony Club needs little explanation. Pink confetti bursts overhead, and the fantasy she once sang about is no longer somewhere else. It is here.

title: Christa Pike’s IV team warned vein might be ‘blowing’ before failed execution
description: New account from Pike’s lawyer suggests team was racked by doubts even before pentobarbital began to flow
content:
New account from Pike’s lawyer suggests team was racked by doubts even before pentobarbital began to flow
The Tennessee execution team tasked with setting an intravenous line in the arms of the death row prisoner Christa Pike through which she could be injected with a lethal dose of pentobarbital repeatedly warned that her vein might be “blowing”, before they went ahead with the procedure, her lawyer has revealed.
Members of the intravenous (IV) team used up to 10 needles as they sought to establish a line through which Pike could be killed with a massive dose of the sedative. About 20 minutes into the attempt, they began discussing among themselves whether the prisoner’s vein “might be blowing”.
Two unidentified members of the team began poking the site through which they were trying to set up the line, and both agreed that they couldn’t tell whether they had succeeded in finding the vein. “One of them said something like: ‘It’s either blood or blown, I need to know,’” the lawyer’s new account says.
The potentially critical new details of how Tennessee’s execution team failed to kill Pike, 50, on 30 September are contained in the most detailed account yet given by Pike’s lawyer Randy Spivey.
In a declaration that was released as part of separate legal proceedings, Spivey gave a minute-by-minute chronology of Pike’s ordeal, which he personally witnessed in the death chamber.
The account suggests that the IV team was racked by doubts even before the pentobarbital began to flow, as they struggled to find a vein for almost an hour. The search began at 6.35pm that evening, and was completed at 7.24pm, at which point the team left the chamber assuming everything was going according to plan.
But Pike remained alive, making snoring and choking sounds.
The execution was eventually called off, and after 10 days in hospital Pike was returned to prison in Nashville. She is the only prisoner in modern times to survive a full dose of a lethal injection drug.
Though she can now talk and walk, her long-term prognosis is still unknown. The gruesome events of her failed execution have prompted nationwide soul-searching about the death penalty in the US, and forced the Republican governor of Tennessee, Bill Lee, to call off all executions in the state pending a review.
Spivey’s blow-by-blow chronology gives agonizing new details about the lengths to which the IV team went to find a vein, as well as their profound anxieties about whether they were doing the right thing. A person on the IV team named by Spivey as “member two” first expressed the fear that Pike’s vein might be blown at 6.53pm.
The team then discarded the 20-gauge needle that they had been using, saying: ‘“It’s not long enough. What is the longest you’ve got?”
Three minutes later, at 6.57pm, member two repeated it “might be blowing”. Spivey reported: “Member two and IV team member 3 inspected the insertion site and poked it. Both said that they ‘can’t tell’.”
Despite the uncertainty, the IV team agreed among themselves that they had established a line just two minutes later, only to discover that it was not, in fact, properly working. “I need to work again,” member two said, pulling the needle out of Pike’s left arm. “It appeared to be severely bent,” Spivey records.
At 7.08pm member two called on the team to think again. “Let’s regroup,” he said. They began checking Pike’s right arm again, and poking around the insertion site. At 7.13pm, member two told Pike directly that they “have it”, and the injection of pentobarbital that they thought would kill her was set to begin.
The revelations of so many doubts and foiled efforts to find a line, including the critical fears that her vein might have blown, lend added weight to one of the most prominent theories that have emerged for how the execution failed and Pike survived. Had the drug entered her bloodstream at such a extreme dose she would almost certainly have died, but if her vein burst, the pentobarbital would have been diverted into her arm tissue, causing her severe injuries but falling short of killing her.
As Spivey noted in his chronology, at 7.34pm Pike cried out: “I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns.”
Spivey’s detailed minute-by-minute account is attached as an exhibit in a new legal motion filed on behalf of Tony Carruthers and other death row prisoners. Tennessee attempted to execute Carruthers on 21 May, but he too survived after the execution team failed to find a vein in more than 30 minutes.
Carruthers’s lawyers have asked permission from the Davidson county chancery court to file a supplemental complaint challenging Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol. They made an initial complaint in March 2025 in which they warned that the prisoner could face a torturous death by pentobarbital poisoning because the team administering the lethal drug were “incompetent, insufficiently trained, insufficiently dedicated to doing their jobs, and/or insufficiently attentive”.
As such, they warned, the execution ran an unacceptable risk of violating constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
The failed executions in May, and Pike’s subsequent failed execution in September, bear out the lawyer’s advance warnings, the new motion asserts. “The specific failures that Mr Carruthers and Ms Pike endured were predicted, in detail and at length,” the new motion states.
Kit Thomas, an attorney for the death row plaintiffs, said: “Instead of addressing the problems in the 2025 Protocol when we identified them last year, the Tennessee Department of Correction and the Attorney General’s Office doubled down on secrecy and refused to make changes. The result was just as we predicted: extreme pain and suffering for our clients, in botched execution attempts that also inflicted lasting harm on victims’ families, corrections staff, and media witnesses, among others.”
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of her friend Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 at the time of the murder, and spent the next almost three decades in solitary confinement.

title: Next in line? Main contenders for the Manchester United hot seat
description: With Michael Carrick’s future at Old Trafford a matter of some debate, we examine the credentials of those who could succeed him
content:
With Michael Carrick’s future at Old Trafford a matter of some debate, we examine the credentials of those who could succeed him
The German was of interest to Manchester City while Omar Berrada was part of the hierarchy on the other side of town. He is highly thought of and would come with an impressive CV for a 39-year-old, having taken charge of Bayern Munich and Germany. Nagelsmann is regarded as an innovator who is very demanding of his players and builds teams to press relentlessly, a concept not currently used at United, as Bruno Fernandes will testify . His spell with Germany was underwhelming, concluding with a 2026 World Cup last-32 defeat by Paraguay , and at Bayern – with an exceptional squad – he won the Bundesliga in his only full season and was sacked the following March with the team second and still in the Champions League.
The King of the Europa League is tactically astute and knows about working on a budget. If he is intrigued by the prospect of managing United, it would come down to whether he believes they have more potential than Villa, who are one point and place above them in the Premier League and faring much better in the Champions League, and whether United are willing to pay significant compensation. Emery likes a 4-2-3-1 but has always had a central striker at his disposal, and United lack someone strong in this department. Very calm but with a ruthless edge when required, he has plenty of silverware to back up his credentials. He is regarded as one of the game’s great pragmatists and is happy to play on the counterattack, which would suit the United squad.
The Italian, who left Napoli in the summer, knows the Premier League from spells with Chelsea and Tottenham, winning the title with the former in 2017. A fierce competitor and disciplinarian, he would shake up the dressing room with his high standards. His fiery temper can also result in fascinating interactions with the media, including telling a post-match press conference after losing to Burnley that maybe he was not the right man to manage Spurs. His willingness to speak out when it may not necessarily be wise could put United off. His preference for playing three at the back could be problematic considering the personnel at United, as Ruben Amorim found out .
The Northern Irishman worked within the United academy before stepping up to be part of José Mourinho’s backroom staff alongside Carrick. He stayed when Ole Gunnar Solskjær replaced the Portuguese and was credited with having a strong tactical influence as United secured second place. It is often a strength to have a link to a club but considering the struggles Solskjær and Carrick have endured, an external candidate seems more appropriate. He departed to become a head coach at Ipswich and his work there meant he was linked with a return to United to replace Erik ten Hag. McKenna resigned in June after securing promotion to the Premier League for a second time to take time away from the day-to-day grind of management. Would he want to end his sabbatical by jumping into a precarious situation after five or so months?
The English option and a manager with plenty of Premier League experience who took Newcastle to the Champions League . Arguably this makes him the safest pair of hands. A hard worker, Howe was often first in and last out at the Newcastle training ground as he pored over every detail. A lover of wingers and 4-3-3, he would be reliant on a central striker such as Benjamin Sesko to step up. He likes to work closely with his nephew Andy, who held senior roles at Bournemouth and Newcastle, which would create an interesting dynamic if he wanted similar at United. Howe, like others in contention, would not cost anything in compensation – and every penny counts at Old Trafford.
The 33-year-old has a growing reputation, with his Brighton team third after scoring 23 goals in seven games. This could explain why he is not particularly keen on leaving at the moment. His team are outperforming United with a squad that looks stronger. The size of United is alluring for many coaches but moving mid-season to a struggling club is not always advantageous because it means stepping into a firefight.

title: CDC denies approval for high-volume measles test, citing ‘other priorities’
description: California, Oregon, Washington and Hawaii health officials ask CDC ‘prioritizing emerging technologies’ to reconsider
content:
California, Oregon, Washington and Hawaii health officials ask CDC ‘prioritizing emerging technologies’ to reconsider
California and Washington asked the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in May to validate a new way to test for measles – but after waiting two months, the CDC denied the request, citing “other competing priorities”, according to a letter from the West Coast Health Alliance to the CDC director, Erica Schwartz.
The letter, signed by health officials in California , Hawaii, Oregon and Washington, asks Schwartz to reconsider and validate a rapid, high-volume measles test in preparation for major outbreaks. The alliance also asked the CDC to create protocols to test for other high-priority pathogens to prepare for future outbreaks.
The CDC is “ensuring state and local health departments have the support needed to strengthen measles detection and outbreak response”, said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The agency was “prioritizing emerging technologies” to respond to the measles outbreak, Hilliard said.
The spokesperson did not answer questions about whether the CDC had plans to validate a high-throughput measles test or assay.
Such a test would “dramatically strengthen” the ability of laboratories to respond quickly to outbreaks, the health officials said – which would help preparedness for known pathogens like Ebola or hantavirus as well as emerging threats.
Right now, laboratories have to rely on lower-volume tests for measles, like individual polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests.
In the Covid pandemic, most public health labs bought high volume equipment, like the Hologic Panther Fusion, a PCR platform for diagnosing illness that can process up to 500 tests in eight hours. That way, labs could process large batches of Covid tests very quickly.
But there is no high-throughput test to diagnose measles that has been validated by the CDC.
Texas state laboratories developed such a test during the measles outbreak in west Texas last year, but they have not distributed or published the protocol. ARUP Laboratories, a national, academic, non-profit reference laboratory, published their assay for measles in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in December. The CDC could validate this or another protocol so other public health labs could run diagnostic tests.
High-throughput tests can process a lot of samples at once, but the automated instruments can also be faster and easier than manually conducting tests. “One of the big advantages that they offer is essentially more flexibility,” said Benjamin Bradley, an assistant professor of pathology at the University of Utah and medical director of virology at ARUP.
That’s especially important in a fast-moving outbreak. “With a measles outbreak, time is really of the essence,” Bradley said. One measles patient can infect 12 to 18 other unvaccinated people, and the virus can linger in the air for two hours. “You can quickly see how that goes exponential, from a handful of cases to an entire community of cases,” he said.
Quicker tests can help curb an outbreak like that, helping to identify and isolate positive patients as quickly as possible and leading to faster contact tracing. It also means officials can promptly offer vaccines to anyone who was exposed and isn’t already vaccinated. If vaccines are taken within 72 hours of exposure, they can prevent infection.
There are no commercially available tests for measles; the current tests are developed by laboratories. Validating and publishing the process for creating these tests is crucial for labs to be able to create and conduct them.
“You essentially have to do science for it,” said Bradley. That means planning, undergoing and documenting experiments, and then checking to make sure the test is reliable. “A lot of that work is very burdensome for laboratories to put together. So by having groups that can share their protocols, that helps labs.”
The CDC has reportedly completed studies on the assays from Texas and ARUP Laboratories, “but they were not full validations or a comprehensive comparison”, the west coast officials said in the letter.
The alliance asked Schwartz to develop an assay, or test, for measles diagnostic testing on the Panther Fusion and to publish that protocol so any lab can run the tests. Having tests ready to go is an essential part of preparing, the letter said: “If a large outbreak were to occur in our region, without high-throughput capacity, it would be more difficult to scale up diagnostic testing appropriately, impairing patient care and public health investigation.”

title: Video footage of Kohen Wiley shooting released after toddler’s death deemed ‘justified’
description: ‘The word ‘justified’ has haunted me since Monday,’’ the child’s maternal grandmother says
content:
‘The word ‘justified’ has haunted me since Monday,’’ the child’s maternal grandmother says
Since the Mississippi attorney general, Lynn Fitch, announced on Monday that the police shooting of Kohen Wiley, a one-year-old baby, “was justified”, footage of the shooting has been made public. It was first reported by Darkhorse Press, a Mississippi outlet.
On Thursday, attorneys Ben Crump and Van Turner, who are representing the Wiley family, held a press conference at the Senatobia Church of Christ, in Senatobia, Mississippi . The press conference came shortly after members of the family were able to view footage of the shooting.
“The word ‘justified’ has haunted me since Monday,’” Veronica Roberson, Kohen’s maternal grandmother, said during the press conference. She fought back tears as she spoke. “I went to work and I had to find out through news sources … no one reached out to the family. A single call, a heads up, anything to prepare us for what we was about to face.”
Roberson said that the leaked videos of the shooting from multiple outlets were “slaps in the face”. In the footage, she said, five officers with guns drawn descended on a car with two women, Vellesiya Wiley, the baby’s mother, and Latoya Ferrell, a friend, and Kohen Wiley.
Crump called the footage “excessive from the very start”, and said that the officers approached the women and baby with guns drawn. According to initial reports, officers were responding to a shoplifting call. Allegedly, Wiley and Ferrell stole a pack of diapers.
“We’re the most prosperous nation in the world and we’re going to draw guns to shoot people over misdemeanor allegations of baby diapers?” Crump said.
Crump noted that neither woman was ever arrested for shoplifting. Even if they had been, shoplifting is a misdemeanor, which does not qualify for the death sentence, he said.
“After what I’ve seen today, I’m having a difficult time understanding the word ‘justified,’” Lasandra Williams, Kohen’s paternal grandmother, said. “I don’t understand how it’s OK for someone to take a sweet, innocent soul – Lord knows I miss him so much.”
Crump and Turner were joined by both of Kohen’s grandmothers, his father and representatives of Senatobia Committee for Accountability and Building Bridges Coalition, local civil rights organizations. Crump said that the footage would officially be released later this afternoon by investigators.
Turner and Crump are calling for a federal investigation into the shooting.
Next Sunday, 1 November, would be Wiley’s second birthday.

title: Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises
description: Be Ready campaign aims to prepare UK for impact of climate crisis, technological dependency and threats by hostile state
content:
Be Ready campaign aims to prepare UK for impact of climate crisis, technological dependency and threats by hostile state
Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.
The Be Ready campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.
Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”. It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, added that Britain also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
“Terms like ‘hybrid warfare’ and ‘grey zone threats’ do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as ‘state-sponsored terrorism’,” he said.
“So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.
“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready? Do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves?”
People are advised to keep a ready supply of blankets and cash at home plus a first aid kit, a torch with batteries and a wind-up FM radio. Three litres of water per person per day should be stored for drinking – and more is needed for cooking and washing, the guidance adds.
The government had indicated in August that UK citizens would be told to stock up on tinned food but the Be Ready campaign from the Cabinet Office is more specific. It will be followed up with an advertising campaign on social media and radio.
Stocking up for three days is considered to be a realistic and practical proposal for households and would bring the UK in line with France, the Republic of Ireland and the Netherlands in advising people how to prepare for serious disruption.
Ministers timed the launch of the campaign to come before the winter storm season after a series of intense storms that have battered the UK in recent years. Tens of thousands of homes were left without power in the Midlands, the south-west and Wales after Storm Goretti hit in January , with winds reaching nearly 100mph.
There is also concern about the potential impact of the “super El-Nino”, a global phenomenon that could lead to 2027 being the hottest year ever recorded and uncertain weather patterns, affecting global food supplies and energy systems.
The guidance emerged as 32 UK government websites were taken offline in a precautionary measure in response to the discovery of a security vulnerability in the PHP programming language used by millions of websites around the world.
Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, in a reminder of the high degree of dependency that modern societies have on the internet and other critical technologies.
Spain and Portugal were suddenly left without power for several hours in April 2025, in a cascading failure triggered by voltage instability in the network. About 55 million people were affected in the incident, the worst blackout in Europe in recent memory.
People also need to consider how to respond to hybrid warfare attacks by Russia or other hostile states, including cyber-attacks that could knock out payment systems used by businesses or cause supply chains to collapse, Streeting said.
The minister was speaking at a new tank gun barrel factory in Telford in the West Midlands . The factory, owned by the German manufacturer Rheinmetall, is part of efforts to accelerate rearmament in the face of Russian military threats, but Streeting also emphasised that the public should be prepared for hybrid warfare, or sabotage actions that stop short of outright war.
Russian spy ships have been tracked by the Royal Navy monitoring undersea pipelines and cables that connect the UK to the continent of Europe and elsewhere, raising concerns they could one day be attacked, though this would represent a major escalation by Moscow.
European states have become increasingly vocal about the threat of sabotage efforts by enemies , particularly Russia, which can cause disruption or even directly threaten safety. These efforts have included an explosives-laden drone found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport in August, and a series of explosions and fires at defence facilities.
Britain has only rarely embarked on public information campaigns, with governments of both parties reluctant to be accused of scaremongering. A 1980 campaign advising people on how to survive a nuclear war, Protect and Survive , advised people how to build a bomb shelter at home and retain enough food for 14 days.

title: Minister insists she backs migration policy after joking she couldn’t lie about supporting it
description: Miatta Fahnbulleh says reference to ‘awkward’ interview was meant to be lighthearted and self-deprecating
content:
Miatta Fahnbulleh says reference to ‘awkward’ interview was meant to be lighthearted and self-deprecating
The energy secretary has been forced to clarify that she backs Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy, after earlier joking that she had not been able to “lie” about supporting a key element of the changes.
Miatta Fahnbulleh made the original remarks to a journalists’ event in Westminster, referring to an “awkward” Sky News interview in which she repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
She told the event: “I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments, including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge yesterday.”
The implication that she could not bring herself to lie about supporting the changes appears to have gone down badly among colleagues in government, although No 10 refused to be drawn on whether they requested her to issue a clarification.
Fahnbulleh posted a statement on social media on Thursday evening saying: “Today I made what was meant to be a lighthearted, self-deprecating remark. I didn’t get it right and it hasn’t come off as I intended.
“I fully support our home secretary and the government’s position on migration reform. As I said earlier this week, it’s absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship.”
The clarification represents a twist in the cabinet split over the issue of the migration changes, with Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner among those not keen on elements of the original plan.
Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.
She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.
However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”
This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”
And earlier this year, Rayner, the housing secretary, publicly criticised the plans , while dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.
One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.
“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.
MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the planned changes.
Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.
“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”
Earlier this week, a Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

title: Amy Winehouse musical in development for West End
description: Stage show based on late singer reportedly set to feature her best-loved songs with involvement from her father Mitch
content:
Stage show based on late singer reportedly set to feature her best-loved songs with involvement from her father Mitch
A musical based on Amy Winehouse is in development for London’s West End.
The project is still in early stages with Catherine Schreiber, a Tony award-winning producer (Cabaret, Rent), attached to the project, according to Variety . Casting is reported to currently be under way.
Mitch Winehouse, the late musician’s father, is also said to be involved with the show, indicating that it will probably feature her most loved songs.
The Guardian has approached Amy Winehouse’s record label for comment.
This week, the 20th anniversary of her landmark album Back to Black was celebrated with a tribute concert at London’s Roundhouse featuring performances by Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson, Lianne La Havas and Corinne Bailey Rae.
“Back to Black remains a miraculous set of modern love songs in vintage clothing,” wrote the Guardian’s Dorian Lynskey, adding that “re-enactments can be limiting”.
On 23 October, an expanded reissue of Back to Black will be released, including four unreleased demos, B-sides and a live album recording at Amsterdam’s Paradiso in 2007.
Mitch Winehouse has hinted at the possibility of a musical based on the singer over the years.
“A musical celebrating her life and music is being talked about for the near future,” he said in a 2017 interview . “It is something I’d really like to happen, and I’ve said I’m happy for it to go ahead.
“It would be for the West End . We want to do something that remembers Amy for what she was; there’s so much more to her than just the drugs and the alcohol.”
That is now set to come to fruition, joining the multiple posthumous music releases, films and TV specials that have been released since Winehouse’s death in 2011, aged 27.
In 2011, the rarities collection Lioness was received as a “flawed memorial for a flawed star”, while Sam Taylor-Johnson’s 2024 biopic of the musician was slammed as a “grotesque insult” by the Guardian’s Laura Snapes.
Meanwhile, Asif Kapadia’s 2015 documentary about the singer won the best documentary Oscar, and was praised by the Guardian as “an intimate and passionate tribute, tracing the awful trajectory of her celebrity destiny”.
A current London exhibition by the artist Alex Margo Arden assembles ephemera from Winehouse’s life in a Chelsea apartment, with items including ballet flats laid in tribute to the singer and a birthday card from Ronson and Adele that she never had the chance to open.

title: US judge orders Trump administration to halt noncitizen voting investigation
description: Federal judge says government’s investigation into alleged noncitizen voting in nine states is relying on flawed data
content:
Federal judge says government’s investigation into alleged noncitizen voting in nine states is relying on flawed data
A federal judge in California has ordered the Trump administration to halt investigations in nine states into whether noncitizens are registered to vote.
US district court judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland found the government’s effort was relying on data that is full of errors and that it was leading to intimidation of groups performing voter assistance efforts. She said it should be halted until polls close on election day on 3 November.
She put her ruling, which was made on Wednesday, on hold until Friday to give the administration a chance to appeal.
The ruling applies to investigations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.
It comes as the Trump administration has been hunting for noncitizen voters throughout the country in the months leading up to the midterm elections. The administration has signaled that it is a widespread problem, when in fact it is quite rare, as even its own investigations have shown.
The lawsuit was filed by the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United, along with the Voto Latino Foundation, San Francisco and Santa Clara county.
In response to the ruling, the Department of Homeland Security issued an email statement on Thursday saying it was focused on “removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens”, while adding: “We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens.”
According to legal filings in the case, investigators were told to target naturalized citizens to see whether they had voted before they became US citizens. The lists of voters to check came from sources that included state and local governments and publicly available information. Martínez-Olguín called them “voluminous and unreliable”.
“Even under the best conditions, there is a high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents,” Martínez-Olguín wrote in her ruling. “The time limitations implemented during the Surge further exacerbate the risk of error.”
The Department of Justice has been demanding detailed and unredacted voter roll data from the states and has sued the 30 states that have refused to turn the information over, losing each of those cases so far. The judge noted that for states that refused to share their records, the administration was trying to obtain them through “unreliable commercial versions of voter roll data”.
Martínez-Olguín said during a “surge” phase of the investigation starting in late August, agents were ordered to complete reviews of flagged individuals taking no more than 12 minutes per person to assess whether they were legally qualified to vote.
In their challenge, the plaintiffs said some US citizens felt they were wrongly identified and investigated as part of the inquiry. Martínez-Olguín said those fears “are well understood as intimidation” that has chilled people from attending campaign events and working as poll monitors during the election.
Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer representing the unions and voter group, said in a statement that the ruling affirms the groups’ position.
“It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people’s homes weeks before an election,” Tremitiere said.
Details of the investigation, known as the “Unlawful Voter Initiative”, came to light last month after Chuck Schumer, the Democratic Senate minority leader, of New York and Alex Padilla, the Democratic California senator, released a whistleblower report about it.

title: Nana Patekar obituary
description: Indian actor known for his roles in Salaam Bombay! and the Bollywood hits Parinda and Krantiveer, who had a controversial personal life
content:
Indian actor known for his roles in Salaam Bombay! and the Bollywood hits Parinda and Krantiveer, who had a controversial personal life
The Indian actor Nana Patekar, who has died of a heart attack aged 75, first broke through in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! (1988), and the Bollywood hits Parinda (1989) and Krantiveer (1994). These early credits established Patekar as a performer of rare versatility: he and Irrfan Khan remain the only performers to have won Filmfare’s best actor, best supporting actor and best villain awards (considered India’s “oscars”). Yet the question of whether Patekar was better suited to heroism or villainy lingered unresolved: allegations of sexual harassment and intimidation first made by his former co-star Tanushree Dutta in 2008 kickstarted India’s #MeToo movement when she raised them again in 2018.
Until that point, Patekar’s rougher edges had mostly been celebrated. As an actor, he demonstrated a baggy-eyed naturalism that spoke more to Bombay streetlife than Bollywood fantasy. He was given to writing out his dialogue until he had internalised it, and his growling line readings were both idiosyncratic and much imitated. Satyajit Ray counted among the actor’s most illustrious admirers, but apparently could not find a suitable project for him ; Patekar instead had Nair to thank for launching him to international prominence in Salaam Bombay! as Baba Golub, the brutal pimp and drug dealer lording over an army of street children.
Yet the Bollywood studios also made good use of his grouchy grit. He was commanding as the kingpin Anna in Parinda, Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s inventive relocation of On the Waterfront, for which Patekar won two best supporting actor awards; he was appointed an honorary captain in the Indian territorial army after undergoing three years of army training for Prahaar: The Final Attack (1991), a film he also ended up directing. He crossed paths with the emergent megastar Shah Rukh Khan in Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (1992) and was momentarily in the running for Subhash Ghai’s blockbuster Khalnayak (1993), losing out to Sanjay Dutt.
Relations between Patekar and Dutt deteriorated further after the latter was linked to the 1993 Bombay bus bombings in which Patekar’s brother was killed. (Patekar’s wife, the Marathi actor Neelakanti, was also due to board one of the targeted vehicles.) Even after Dutt’s comeback, Patekar remained defiant: “I have not worked with [Dutt] in 22 years of my career. I will not work with him in the future.”
A comparable rage powered Krantiveer, in which Patekar played a dissolute gambler reviving his fortunes via social activism. Heart problems meant he shot his final scenes with a doctor on standby; while distributors thought Patekar a commercial risk, the film struck a chord, becoming one of that year’s biggest Hindi hits.
Born Vishwanath Patekar in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra, Nana was one of the three sons of Dinkar Patekar, a textile painter and businessman, and his wife, Nirmala. He was educated at the Samarth Vidyalaya and the Bandra School of Arts in Bombay (now Mumbai), supporting his family after his father’s business collapsed by painting zebra crossings and cinema posters. He went on to the Sir JJ Institute of Applied Art, where he also joined the drama society.
After graduation, he briefly worked as a police sketch artist before joining the Marathi theatre group Rangayan. Switched on to films by his friend the celebrated Indian actor Smita Patil (“I was happy doing theatre, but she insisted”), he made his screen debut in the 1978 social drama Gaman, starring Patil.
A string of supporting roles followed: two years before Salaam Bombay!, he played Gandhi’s assassin Nathuram Godse in the Emmy-winning TV miniseries Lord Mountbatten: The Last Viceroy.
Despite his success in Krantiveer, for which he won several best actor awards, Patekar was not always the easiest fit with the studio system. He was replaced on Raja (1995) after spending two days hectoring his co-stars Madhuri Dixit and Mukesh Khanna with acting notes. And he paused his career during the Kargil war of 1999 to enlist with the Maratha Light infantry, serving 60 days and earning a promotion to the rank of major.
Back on civvy street, he landed a signature role as Inspector Sadhu, the dirty cop who becomes the hero of Ab Tak Chhappan (2004), and swept India’s best villain prizes as the underworld don Tabrez Alam in Apaharan (2005). He then switched into a lighter mode for the knockabout comedies Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015).
Elder statesman status beckoned: he played Mumbai’s police commissioner in The Attacks of 26/11 (2013), voiced Shere Khan in the Hindi dub of Disney’s The Jungle Book (2016) and enjoyed a major success with the Marathi film Natsamrat (2016), playing an acclaimed actor unravelling in retirement. He was awarded the Padma Shri and the Raj Kapoor special contribution award in 2013; in 2015, he set up the Naam Foundation with fellow actor Makarand Anaspure to help drought-hit farmers.
Then came Dutta’s 2018 interview with the Hindu , where she repeated an earlier accusation that Patekar had first sexually harassed her while shooting a dance sequence for Horn “OK” Pleassss (2009), then, when she fled the set, sent hired thugs after her. Footage of the incident aired on Indian TV showed a mob surrounding her car, her windscreen smashed and tyres being flattened. Patekar denied the allegations. The Mumbai police opened an investigation; while no formal charges were brought, the incident sparked renewed concern about the treatment of women in Bollywood.
After a spell in industry purdah, Patekar recently attempted a comeback. There were supporting turns in the propagandistic The Vaccine War (2023), limp comedy Housefull 5 (2025) and the streaming-bound Subedaar (2026), though the actor did lend a wry centre to Vishal Bhardwaj’s Shakespeare riff O’Romeo (2026).
He married Neelakanti in 1978, and they had two sons, the first of whom, Durvasa, died in 1980, aged two. Patekar is survived by his wife and his second son, Malhar.

title: Fifa increases preparation money for Women’s World Cup to match men’s teams
description: Preparation money for the 2027 Women’s World Cup will match the men’s for the 2026 World Cup and players will be provided with improved flights and individual hotel rooms
content:
Funds for 2027 will match men’s World Cup in 2026
Players given better flights and individual hotel rooms
Teams in the 2027’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil will receive the same preparation money from Fifa as those that played at the 2026 men’s tournament, the world’s governing body has announced.
The preparation money for the 32 teams has been more than doubled to $2.5m (£1.86m) each. In 2023, the total preparation money for the tournament was $31m; it will now be $80m.
Every player will be guaranteed business class or chartered flights, as well as their own hotel room rather than having to share. Fifa says this will bring the provisions for the women’s players in line with the men’s World Cup. That is likely be welcomed after the topic caused controversy at previous tournaments.
A survey conducted by the players’ union Fifpro in 2023, after the most recent Women’s World Cup, co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand, found 80% of players’ return flight had been in business class. Ninety-four per cent flew in business class on their outbound flights.
The total prize fund for the tournament is yet to be decided. Fifa has named the United States as the host of the inaugural Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028. The Guardian revealed this month the US was lined up to stage the event, with Los Angeles and San Diego among the favoured host cities.
The competition will feature 19 teams, with seven already qualified: Arsenal, Club América Femenil, Barcelona, Gotham FC, Naegohyang from North Korea, Corinthians and Wuhan Jiangda. Six European teams will take part, with the AFC, CAF, Concacaf and Conmebol being represented by three clubs each, plus one team from Oceania.
Fifa’s chief women’s football officer, Sarai Bareman, said: “We undertook a detailed assessment to identify the most suitable host for the inaugural edition of the Women’s Club World Cup. Ultimately, the United States’ recent excellence in staging top Fifa tournaments, combined with the significant interest in women’s football there plus its elite sporting infrastructure, made the country the standout option.
“Alongside the vibrant and passionate women’s football ecosystem in the United States, the qualified clubs, government, host cities, our commercial and media partners and more, our mission will be to set an impressive standard for global women’s club football and a benchmark for the future.”

title: Tommy Robinson tells court he had photos taken of journalists’ homes to pressure them
description: Far-right activist says he used private investigators to track down journalists but denies trying to intimidate them
content:
Far-right activist says he used private investigators to track down journalists but denies trying to intimidate them
The far-right activist Tommy Robinson has told his harassment trial that he used private investigators to track down journalists who had written about his alleged role in the 2024 riots, and had photographs taken of their homes “to put pressure” on them.
Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, denied in court that his actions, which included sharing photos of the wife and daughter of one of the journalists, were designed to intimidate and bully.
“I’m not coming to beat [them] up … they know that,” he said, referring to messages and telephone calls, including a voicemail message left for the editor of the Daily Mail after Robinson had paid to get his personal number.
Robinson is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, in 2024. He denies the charges.
Robinson, 43, gave evidence and was cross-examined on Thursday, when he claimed he “felt it was totally reasonable” to publish a photo of Dirnhuber at his home because he was “in a race against time” to get the Mail to remove a photo of his ex-wife, which the Mail published in a story about him being in Cyprus, with the headline: “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.
However, he conceded that when he sent messages to the journalists, spoke to one on the phone, and left a message on the voicemail of the Mail’s editor-in-chief, Ted Verity, he had not asked for the Mail to remove the image.
Robinson said he believed he was “restrained” in the voicemail he left for Verity, in which he said he would make him and his family famous, and went on to say he told the journalists involved that he would get their addresses because he was “using it as a play card”.
The prosecutor Ben Holt asked him about Dirnhuber and his partner having to leave their home as a result of threatening emails he allegedly received, and about Young’s family having also considered leaving their home.
“The entire situation, I wish didn’t happen, I wish that none of that had happened,” said Robinson. “I was unfortunately in a situation where I was panicked.”
Referring to the journalists and how they felt about messages he sent to them, he told Southwark crown court: “They know I’m not going to come and beat them up. They know that.”
Holt continued: “They are scared of you, Mr Lennon,” to which came the reply: “They are not scared of physical violence from me.”
Robinson was also asked about messages and online posts directed at the journalists by others after he had started using his own X account to tweet about them, including one post from an X user who told Dirnhuber they would beat the “fuck” out of him.
Asked by Holt if he appreciated that messages such as this had been “generated” by his own output, Robinson said: “I don’t agree with any of these messages … I don’t know who sent these messages. I don’t know, I don’t know, I don’t know.”
Robinson had been in Cyprus in early August 2024. At the time, violence was breaking out across England in the wake of the murder of three girls in Southport. He told the jury he was with “my ex-wife, my three children and three other families and their children”.
In the witness stand, Robinson claimed he had not “stoked” the riots, but tried to calm things.
The first day of the trial was told on Monday that journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after Robinson deployed “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics”.

title: Dollar General agrees to nearly $1.9m settlement for overcharging New York customers
description: Inspections showed overcharges as high as 39% on some items. Discount store giant was subject of 2025 investigation by the Guardian
content:
Government inspections showed overcharges as high as 39% on some items. The discount store giant was the subject of a 2025 investigation by the Guardian
Dollar General, the nation’s largest dollar-store chain, has agreed to a $1.875m deal to settle allegations that it “repeatedly and persistently” overcharged customers across New York state.
The New York attorney general’s office found that Dollar General often charged customers higher prices at checkout than the prices it promised on shelf labels, signs, advertising circulars and its mobile app. The state agency said one check of 114 items across multiple stores revealed overcharges on individual items as high as 26%, 38% and 39%.
Under the settlement, Dollar General will donate $1.875m in food and personal items to a regional food bank in upstate New York . The agreement also requires that the company put in place comprehensive price-accuracy safeguards at its more than 600 stores statewide.
“When New Yorkers see a sale price advertised on the shelf, they should be able to trust that they’ll be charged that same price at the register,” the New York attorney general, Letitia James , said.
The pricing issues at the company – which promotes itself as “a lifeline for affordable, everyday essentials” – are not limited to the state of New York.
A Guardian investigation published in December reported that the chain frequently overcharged customers across the nation for such items as Flintstones vitamins, Peter Pan peanut butter and Prego pasta sauce. Dollar General stores flunked more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states between 2022 and 2025, the Guardian found.
An inspection at a Dollar General in Port Henry, New York, for example, flagged overcharges on 78% of the items checked.
Under the terms of the New York settlement, the company will be required to embrace a long list of policies and procedures – including scheduling staff to ensure shelf tags are updated for pricing accuracy and hiring independent auditors to conduct secret shopper tests.
The company will also be required to reformat its receipts. State investigators found Dollar General’s receipts included “various confusing formats” that made it difficult for consumers to figure out what they were really paying.
Dollar General neither admitted nor denied New York authorities’ findings.
In a statement in response to questions from the Guardian, it said: “Dollar General is committed to providing customers with accurate on-shelf prices on items purchased in our stores, and we are disappointed any time we fail to deliver on this commitment. When a pricing discrepancy is identified, our store teams are instructed, expected and empowered to correct the matter on the spot for our customers.”
It added that “we have in place a number of measures designed to promote pricing accuracy, and we continuously evaluate and evolve these measures”.

title: Bruno’s betrayal? ‘Toxic’ Fernandes is symptom of United’s culture of entitlement
description: Michael Carrick must now deal with more dressing-room unrest after Lisandro Martínez’s attack on the board
content:
Michael Carrick must now deal with more dressing-room unrest after Lisandro Martínez’s attack on the board
“Toxic”: this is the damning characterisation of Bruno Fernandes from one highly placed Manchester United source after the captain’s incendiary betrayal of Michael Carrick.
There has surely never been a greater anti-leadership act in United’s history than Fernandes questioning the man who trusts him to unify the dressing room and execute his on-field plan. The Portuguese has proved this faith wrong at the precise moment he was required to step up and exude a defiant togetherness.
Nothing could be more dysfunctional than civil war between United’s head coach and captain, featuring Carrick biting back at Fernandes for questioning his tactics as matters hit a new low in the aftermath of Wednesday’s pathetic 4-1 loss to Como .
A litmus test for any leader comes when the storm arrives. At the Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium, Fernandes failed miserably as he squealed about “the staff” deciding the best tactic was not to press Cesc Fàbregas’s bright, emerging team.
For “staff” read Carrick because he decides strategy and bears responsibility for performance. Fernandes is Carrick’s on-field proxy, so his behaviour is the dictionary definition of betrayal. His conduct is not expected to lead to an disciplinary action in the way Lisandro Martínez’s calling out last week of Jason Wilcox as, perhaps, this is a greyer area.
Discussing tactics may be more within Fernandes’s remit, as captain, than a defender suggesting the director of football’s recruitment failed. Provided there is no damage to the team. But even if Fernandes issues an apology, some acts are irreversible. There is a case for Carrick to strip the 32-year-old of the captaincy and appoint a senior man such as Youri Tielemans or Harry Maguire.
Carrick is expected to hold his pre-game media conference on Friday afternoon and be in charge for Bournemouth’s visit on Sunday, so when the team is announced whether Fernandes has the armband will intrigue. Could he even drop the playmaker? Whatever the decision, Fernandes can have zero excuse for his Como outburst.
Fernandes witnessed how Martínez’s criticism of Wilcox became an extra headache for Carrick, whose sole focus should have been on arresting the direst start to a campaign since 1986. Instead, Carrick had to thrash out the most prudent line of action – Martínez is understood to have been fined – then field questions about the episode.
Yet still Fernandes rounded on Carrick after one of United’s poorest displays in a European competition. It was a performance the player was part of, having been on the field until Carrick removed him on 67 minutes. Being replaced by Joshua Zirkzee, who United tried to offload in the last window, shows how ineffective Fernandes was, first as a false 9, then, after the interval, in his favoured No 10 role.
Fernandes’s comments indicate he is seriously disaffected with team strategy and his role within this. But is there, too, a frustration at still being at the club as his prime years – he was 32 last month – begin to expire? This is someone who voiced disquiet last December , during a jarring interview with Canal 11, the Portuguese Football Federation‑owned channel, at United’s desire to sell him.
Fernandes was asked whether there had been an offer from Paris Saint-Germain or Real Madrid. He said: “Nowadays, the issue of loyalty is no longer seen the way it used to be. I could have left in the last window and would have earned a lot more.
“At one point I was going to leave and I would have won many trophies that season. I decided to stay not only for family reasons, but because I genuinely like the club. The conversation with the coach [Ruben Amorim] also made me stay.
“But from the club’s side, I felt: ‘If you go, it’s not really that bad for us.’ More than hurting, it makes me sad, because I’m a player they have nothing to criticise me for.”
Now the club, and specifically Carrick, do feel let down by Fernandes. But, it is also relevant to ask how Fernandes (and Martínez) have come to feel so at ease with going off-message.
These are highly remunerated employees. Their job is to play and maintain a united front – whatever happens – and for Carrick to allow a culture of entitlement to fester shows up a serious fault in his management. For now, Carrick and Fernandes limp on – just like the team.
It will be some act for Carrick to save his job – even victory over Bournemouth may not do so – and for Fernandes to rehabilitate himself, before the head coach and fans. But this is football, a world that can be unpredictable and illogical.
The measure, though, of the debacle at Como, and the wider malaise at the club, can be found in Fàbregas’s post-victory words when he bemoaned allowing Zirkzee’s added-time strike for United.
“I regret the last 10 minutes because I was the one who told the team to slow down the tempo because there’s another match [Sassuolo, on Saturday] and at 4-0 we could manage things a little,” he said.
“Their goal hurt me because we dropped our intensity and dropped our defensive block, but it was my fault.”
How Carrick wishes this was what he had to contend with rather than a mutinous captain and a ship that seems to be sinking deeper on every matchday.

title: Haiti move Nations League home clash with USA to Miami amid gang violence crisis
description: Unable to play on home soil amid a worsening security crisis, Haiti will host the US in Miami, where a large Haitian community promises a warm welcome
content:
Concacaf approves exceptional hosting arrangement
Haiti to face US at Nu Stadium on 14 November
Miami’s Haitian community offers home advantage
Concacaf on Thursday announced it has approved Haiti’s request to relocate their Nations League quarter-final first leg against the United States on 14 November from Kingston, Jamaica, to Miami in an “exceptional hosting arrangement”. Haiti have been unable to play nominal “home” games within their borders since July 2021, with the United Nations estimating that 90% of the capital of Port-au-Prince – including the national stadium – is controlled by violent gangs.
Haiti’s match, the first leg of a home-and-away series against the US, had been booked for Kingston. The Grenadiers played their 2026 World Cup qualifiers in Curaçao, Aruba and Barbados. However, the Nations League format slated Curaçao and Jamaica to host their matches on the same night as Haiti’s, shunting Haiti to Sabina Park, the home of the Jamaica national team until their current venue opened in 1962. Now a cricket ground, Sabina Park hosted two of Haiti’s Nations League qualifiers.
While the shuffle sends Haiti within their opponents’ borders, they couldn’t have found a more hospitable home away from home. Miami boasts by far the largest population of Haitians and their descendants in the US, with nearly half a million concentrated predominantly in south Florida. They will play at Nu Stadium, where they played the venue’s first international friendly – a pre-World Cup clash with Peru – in June before a sold-out crowd of 26,700. That support dwarfed the crowds they drew at Sabina Park, where their two matches attracted an average of 297 fans.
The US have won four of their six clashes with Haiti this century, with the other two matches ending in draws.
This will be Haiti’s first trip back to the US since this summer’s World Cup, a hero-making turn for the Caribbean nation in their first tournament appearance since 1974. The Grenadiers were handed a difficult group, losing all three games against Morocco, Scotland and Brazil. Nonetheless, they enjoyed fantastic support from fans at their matches in Massachusetts, Philadelphia and Atlanta.
The second leg of the quarter-final is set to take place on 17 November at TQL Stadium in Cincinnati.
Concacaf added that “this flexibility will remain in place for as long as the security situation in Haiti persists”. Haiti, as well as clubs based in the country, will need to seek approval from Concacaf for each match they look to play in “the territory of its opponents”, a separate arrangement from the neutral sites they have previously booked. The confederation stipulated that the measure “may be amended or withdrawn by the Concacaf Council at any time”.

title: Reform snowflake Zia Yusuf demands safe space from ITV’s racism hunters
description: How can it be right that undercover reporters failed to ask permission to expose party’s racist and misogynist views?
content:
How can it be right that undercover reporters failed to ask permission to expose party’s racist and misogynist views?
T he world has gone mad. What has happened to the country when you can’t even have a bit of racist and sexist banter with your mates at work? Time was when up to 20 million viewers would settle down to watch Till Death Us Do Part, for 30 minutes of laughter with Alf Garnett moaning about black people while calling his wife “a silly old moo”. That was a Britain that was worth living in. These days the thought police are everywhere. The wokerati from London, Oxford and Cambridge who are out to ruin everyone’s lives. What’s wrong with letting sleeping racists lie?
Well, Zia Yusuf has had enough and he’s not going to take it any more. After the ITV exposé which revealed racist remarks by members of the party, he has posted a six-and-a-half-minute video on social media promising extreme retribution against the undercover journalists who posed as Reform-friendly.
You have to love the irony. Because for the past six months, Zia has been posing as something he isn’t: the shadow home secretary. Now he may be equally as half-witted as Chris Philp, but the last time I checked, they weren’t the same person. Maybe Zia has a crush on the Philpster. Longs for the gym bod and absence of brain. Zia isn’t even an MP. When the Gorton and Denton Reform association prefer the dislikable Matt Goodwin, you know how loathed you are.
Hoping to add some gravitas by sitting in front of a union jack in a wood-panelled room, Zia prepares to address the nation. And it turns out that he’s not the slightest bit bothered that some Reform members are racists and misogynists – it was probably as much of a surprise to him as it was to the rest of us. What really seems to bother him is that ITV didn’t ask permission to film colleagues being racist. Which is a bit like being annoyed that Pete Hegseth wanted to broadcast a live execution because it wasn’t being streamed on pay per view.
Zia has clearly never heard of undercover public interest journalism. And he’s crushingly disappointed by the deception. He had imagined that ITV would have taken the trouble to personally write to him, asking permission to film people being racist. And he would have happily let them do so. Because then everyone would have known exactly what was going on. I mean, think of the possible consequences of not doing it this way. It might turn out that there were dozens of other undercover journalists in Reform. All just hoping to catch each other out. No one at Reform HQ might be who they say they are.
