James Graham has written a shaming amount. I’ve listed below three
Dear England : about England’s football team
Sherwood : mentioned in the conversation, set in the village where James Graham grew up in the shadow of the miners’ strike
Quiz : set on the British quiz show, Who wants to be a millionaire, where a contestant wins a million quid
A lot of people say culture is stuck, although few sketch out the political consequences of that stagnation as well as James Graham does in our chat.
For ‘it was the algorithm that did it’, read Filterworld: How algorithms flattened culture by Kyle Chayka
For a wider ranging explanation look at ‘Blank Space: A Cultural History of the Twenty-First Century’ by W. David Marx
Those two are fairly recent. Much earlier and truly magnificent is the much-missed Mark Fisher on what he called the slow cancellation of the future
On the same theme this essay by Adam Mastroianni is great

title: More than third of post offices in TG Jones stores to shut by early 2027
description: Closures within chain formerly under the WH Smith brand raise fears of high streets becoming ‘postal deserts’ Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing. So far this year 36 branches within the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith have closed and a further 34 are set to close by early 2027, according to Post Office records analysed by the Guardian. Continue reading...
content:
Closures within chain formerly under the WH Smith brand raise fears of high streets becoming ‘postal deserts’
Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing.
So far this year 36 branches within the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith have closed and a further 34 are set to close by early 2027, according to Post Office records analysed by the Guardian.
TG Jones was bought and renamed by Modella last year. Before the private equity group’s restructure won approval from creditors in July , the chain operated 180 post offices and it had been feared that as many as 60 could be closed under the shake-up.
Up to 150 of the 450 stores acquired by Modella are expected to shut, about 65 of which have already closed and at least another 46 are to cease operating early next year. This total of 110 announced closures include the 70 containing post offices.
The larger-than-expected wave of TG Jones branch closures follows an announcement in the summer that 52 post offices will close within Morrisons Daily convenience stores this year, some of which are close to the TG Jones sites. The move forms part of a wider plan by Morrisons to close 100 loss-making small stores.
The raft of closures means that towns such as Stevenage in Hertfordshire, Bracknell in Berkshire and Orpington in Greater London, and some smaller cities including Hull and York are each losing two post offices in a matter of months. Telford’s last one is due to close in January.
The majority of these lost sites replaced former crown post offices, the now almost entirely closed network of more than 100 directly operated large branches, which offered a full suite of services such as identity and passport checks, driving licence and banking operations.
Some regions such as Essex, the West Midlands, Wales, Suffolk and Hertfordshire have been particularly hard hit. Six post offices in TG Jones stores in Essex are going, with Clacton-on-Sea and Brentwood shutting in January after the closure of ones in Basildon, Southend-on-Sea, Harlow and East Ham. Five are closing in the West Midlands and four in Wales.
The Post Office is trying to find new operators in these locations but so far only Stirling has reopened after a TG Jones closure, and a permanent replacement for Ipswich is set to open in November. Temporary branches are to operate after TG Jones closures in Maidenhead and Uxbridge.
Such losses can be devastating to the health of local economies. As the Post Office itself pointed out to a parliamentary inquiry into revitalising high streets, almost a third of small- and medium-sized businesses use their local branch at least once a week and more than half use the network at least once a month. Many small businesses report that losing this access would threaten their viability within months.
After the closure of more than 6,800 bank branches across the UK, the Post Office “plays a critical role in protecting this essential service”, according to thetstate-owned company’s evidence to the inquiry. Post office operators already run 250 banking hubs, which combine services for several banking brands, across the UK.
Mole Meade, a senior member at the CWU, the largest union for postal workers, said the closures would leave some areas as “postal deserts”.
Meade added: “What we are seeing with the TG Jones closures is the continuation of a long-term strategy of cutting costs and chasing profit, with little regard for the communities that depend on post office services.
“The CWU believes the Post Office should be focused on protecting and expanding access to services, not presiding over a continued reduction of the network.”
The Post Office said: “We fully recognise the challenging trading conditions that TG Jones and many other high street retailers are facing at the moment. We proactively sought expressions of interest from our postmasters and partners to take on post offices within TG Jones stores that may close as a result of their restructuring plan or any decisions taken by landlords.
“There is interest in taking on every location where it has been confirmed that a post office within a TG Jones store will close. In some locations there are over 40 applications from our postmasters who recognise the significant footfall operating a post office brings to their store … We’re committed to replacing every branch within a TG Jones store that closes and are working to progress applications as quickly as possible.”
The state-owned Post Office – which is still reeling from the Horizon IT scandal – announced the closure of more than 100 branches in late 2024 .
WH Smith travel stores in railway stations, hospitals and airports were not part of the Modella deal and remain owned by its original stock market-listed parent company.

title: Most levelling up projects still unfinished years after funding allocated
description: Data released under freedom of information laws reveals hundreds of projects unfinished despite Tory promises on regional equality • Can a £5.8bn scheme help revive Grimsby and other town centres? Most levelling up projects are not finished, years after funds were allocated, highlighting how ambitious Conservative promises of quick progress on regional equality have faltered. Data released under freedom of information laws and manually reviewed by the Guardian found 821 levelling up projects out of 1,347 were yet to be finalised as of May this year. Across the UK, 73 council areas that had a bid for a project accepted were yet to see a single one fully completed. The Guardian has identified 59 projects that were completed since the data was collected. Continue reading...
content:
Data released under freedom of information laws reveals hundreds of projects unfinished despite Tory promises on regional equality
Can a £5.8bn scheme help revive Grimsby and other town centres?
Most levelling up projects are not finished, years after funds were allocated, highlighting how ambitious Conservative promises of quick progress on regional equality have faltered.
Data released under freedom of information laws and manually reviewed by the Guardian found 821 levelling up projects out of 1,347 were yet to be finalised as of May this year. Across the UK, 73 council areas that had a bid for a project accepted were yet to see a single one fully completed. The Guardian has identified 59 projects that were completed since the data was collected.
Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have seen slower delivery in their levelling up projects, despite having fewer overall. North-west England and Yorkshire also had low project completion rates, but they were also the two regions allocated the most projects to begin with.
Boris Johnson’s government swept to power in 2019 after promising to revive left-behind towns and spread opportunity as part of a levelling up agenda headed by Michael Gove. With 57% of projects still unfinished, the figures show many communities are still waiting for those ambitions to become reality.
The figures cover three of the main funds associated with the levelling up agenda : the Future High Streets Fund (launched in 2018), Town Deals (2019) and the Levelling Up Fund (2021).
The Future High Streets Fund was supposed to complete in March 2024, and the official deadline for spending all of the Towns Fund and Levelling Up Fund money was March 2026. The Levelling Up Fund and Town Deals were consolidated into the Local Regeneration Fund under Labour, with a new deadline of March 2028.
Labour has since also launched the Pride in Place programme. It gives places longer-term funding, with local boards deciding how it is spent, rather than making councils compete for grants.
Jack Shaw, the director of Groundwork Research, which supplied the data to the Guardian, said it showed a large gap between the intentions of levelling up and what had been delivered. He said: “Despite significant funding, too many one-off commitments have failed to translate into substantive improvements in communities or local economies.
“The Pride in Place programme is a step forward because it provides communities with £2m a year over 10 years, giving places the certainty and time to deliver visible, lasting improvements.
“But in future the government also needs to look at how investment can reach communities more quickly, so that funding announced at this budget can improve neighbourhoods over the course of this parliament, whether that be through new social infrastructure or a better public realm.”
Blackburn with Darwen council had eight projects funded through the Local Regeneration Fund, none of which have been fully completed.
Similarly, all eight projects funded in Leeds are yet to close. Five are in Morley : a refurbishment of Morley town hall, the establishment of a learning and skills centre, the station gateway transport scheme, a project to make the area greener and better connected, and the Heritage Investment Programme (which has only partly been completed).
Two projects in Holbeck – a green housing retrofit and a local centre scheme – also remain incomplete, as does the St Matthew’s community centre and Old Box Office project.
Part of the reason for the delays across the UK has been inflation, which meant councils had to scale back or pause projects due to increased costs eating into their awarded pots.
Zoë Billingham, the director of the IPPR North thinktank, said the Tories’ Town Fund failed because it had created a “begging bowl culture” where councils would need to approach Whitehall mandarins to access centrally controlled funding pots.
She said: “The levelling up – the ‘hanging baskets strategy’ as it was called – was short-term pots of money that could help clean up high streets and make tangible and important improvements. But that’s different to long-term support for what high streets are and should be. No one would dismiss it [levelling up funding], but you have to have a long-term plan rather than pots of money that run out.”
Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist who has advised Burnham, said the levelling up fund was “better than nothing” despite problems with it. He said: “It was in some ways the kind of worst of Whitehall. Because all the decisions were centralised. There looked to be degrees of pork barrel politics rolled into which places got it.
“It was all a bit sort of unsightly and pork barrelly.”
The national figures exclude 69 projects that were either cancelled or merged into another existing project. Some of the projects are broader programmes of funding, parts of which may have been completed.
Sarah Longlands, the chief executive of the Centre for Local Economic Strategies, warned Labour’s Pride in Place programme could face similar pitfalls to the Tories’ towns fund. She said: “It doesn’t surprise me the [Towns Fund] projects are not finished. Capital money takes time – you just can’t throw stuff up. This is my worry with the current programme of neighbourhood boards. We’re dealing with a lot of capital money, and it can’t be done quickly sometimes.”
You can look at the projects in your area and whether they have been completed or not using the map below. The government data may be missing some recent project completions. The Guardian has attempted to correct for this using published online announcements, but it is possible some completed projects may be missing from the data.
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We are committed to driving good growth in every postcode, giving local leaders stability through long-term targeted funding.
“That’s why we introduced our £5.8bn Pride in Place programme, giving the power to local people to decide how to invest this money to regenerate their own communities.
“And thanks to our Local Regeneration Fund, we’re seeing more money from previous funding programmes being delivered quicker.”

title: John Healey pledges to use budget to harness power of AI to bolster Britain’s security
description: Chancellor says government to commit hundreds of millions to develop ‘distinctively British’ approach to AI John Healey has pledged to use Wednesday’s budget to harness the power of artificial intelligence to bolster Britain’s security and prosperity against the risks in the accelerating global technology arms race. As he prepares for his debut budget, the chancellor said that Andy Burnham’s government would commit hundreds of millions of pounds to develop a “distinctively British” approach to AI that would capitalise on the benefits of the frontier technology. Continue reading...
content:
Chancellor says government to commit hundreds of millions to develop ‘distinctively British’ approach to AI
John Healey has pledged to use Wednesday’s budget to harness the power of artificial intelligence to bolster Britain’s security and prosperity against the risks in the accelerating global technology arms race.
As he prepares for his debut budget, the chancellor said that Andy Burnham’s government would commit hundreds of millions of pounds to develop a “distinctively British” approach to AI that would capitalise on the benefits of the frontier technology.
At a fork in the road as AI developments pose both existential threats and transformative economic potential, Healey said he would be making the biggest ever investment to guard against cyber risks and the disruptive potential of the technology.
As part of the measures in his tax and spending statement, he promised fresh investment for Britain’s AI Security Institute and other critical institutions, alongside allocating public money to support the use of the technology for good.
“AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school and every aspect of our economy can benefit,” Healey said.
“I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI – one that doesn’t leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country.”
Three months into Burnham’s premiership, Healey is poised to deliver a budget against an increasingly volatile backdrop as the war in the Middle East sends shock waves through the global economy, putting pressure on public finances and reigniting the cost of living crisis.
The chancellor has vowed to use his first budget to provide households and businesses with “breathing space” as the global surge in energy costs triggered by the war hits millions of families this winter. On Friday, the latest tensions in the Gulf sent the oil price to its highest level for six months, rising above $117 a barrel at one point.
However he will also use the opportunity afforded by the critical speech to the Commons to flesh out Burnham’s policy priorities for government after he replaced Keir Starmer this summer, and to spell out a vision for Britain amid the increasingly turbulent global economic outlook.
Aiming to harness the opportunities of AI to raise living standards, back UK businesses and support economic growth, the chancellor said he wanted to seize the opportunities of the technology as a central plank of Labour’s plan for growth.
It comes after official figures show AI investment has helped the UK outperform gloomy economic forecasts as the Iran war pushes up inflation and drags down business confidence, powering the country to the strongest growth performance in the G7 in the first half of this year.
However, there are growing fears over the security of the nation and critical industries as the technology opens up the danger of cyber-attacks, IT systems turning rogue and devastating job losses as companies invest in machines rather than humans.
It comes as websites around the globe went dark this week after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web, in a development made possible by rapid AI advances. It also emerged this week that Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of cost-saving plans identified by bosses as the rollout of AI across the bank helps it make efficiency gains.
Healey said he wanted to use his budget to protect against risks while also nurturing homegrown businesses and talent, in order to cut Britain’s dependency on other countries that were also making strides in AI technology.
New investments would be made in AI chip design capability in Edinburgh, alongside a new AI Centre of Excellence in Manchester that it said would enable the UK to harness the technology’s benefits.
The government would also spend £10m a year to lead the UK’s work on understanding how AI will reshape jobs and industry, aiming to address concerns about potential job disruption.
As part of the plan the Treasury said it would back up to £300m in public-private investment in a new AI Biosecurity Lab, designed to serve as a world-leading institution bringing together scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats.
It comes after the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, warned on Thursday that UK households should make preparations against the mounting risks from weather, cyber or other serious emergencies.
The advice to stock up on supplies to last 72 hours, in a campaign called Be Ready , comes as Silicon Valley bosses sound the alarm over the increasingly existential threats AI could pose, and amid growing official concern over the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.
Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said: “I’m proud the UK has repeatedly been at the forefront of global efforts to use AI for the benefit of humankind.
“Today’s investment will help the UK seize the opportunities AI presents to strengthen our national security, while staying one step ahead of those who seek to use AI to do us harm.”

title: Democrat James Talarico targets Elon Musk at rally: ‘Texas is not for sale’
description: The Senate candidate denounced opponent Ken Paxton, calling out corruption allegations and support from Musk James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has taken aim at Elon Musk, warning that the tech mogul is trying to buy political influence and declaring: “Texas is not for sale.” Talarico held a campaign rally on Friday at the University of Texas at Austin, packing an auditorium at his alma mater with hundreds of students and other supporters, who cheered, whooped and waved campaign signs. Continue reading...
content:
The Senate candidate denounced opponent Ken Paxton, calling out corruption allegations and support from Musk
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has taken aim at Elon Musk , warning that the tech mogul is trying to buy political influence and declaring: “Texas is not for sale.”
Talarico held a campaign rally on Friday at the University of Texas at Austin, packing an auditorium at his alma mater with hundreds of students and other supporters, who cheered, whooped and waved campaign signs.
The Presbyterian seminarian’s insurgent run against Texas attorney general Ken Paxton – a staunch ally of Donald Trump – has become one of the most closely watched races in next month’s midterm elections to decide control of Congress. Democrats are seeking their first statewide win since 1994.
Talarico, 37, struck his usual upbeat message on Friday but also pulled no punches in denouncing Paxton – who was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and had a very public divorce – as the most corrupt politician in the state’s history.
“I have a legislative record; Ken Paxton has a criminal record,” said Talarico, a state representative, wearing a dark blue jacket, white open collar shirt and blue jeans. “This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or who puts money in their own. This election is about whether you want a senator who is for Texas or for himself. This election is about whether you want senator who serves you or serves their billionaire mega donors. ”
Paxton, he continued, has the ultimate mega donor . “Elon Musk is trying to buy the Senate seat. We just found out that the richest man in the world is almost single-handedly bankrolling this effort to install Ken Paxton in the US Senate and stop the movement that we are building in our state.
“In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your screens, that was Elon. If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you received a text message saying scary things about me with scary black and white photos, that was Elon too.”
Speaking against the backdrop of a giant Texan state flag and 40 young supporters holding “Talarico” signs, the Democrat said that, where his movement is funded by 1.3 million individuals, Paxton is funded by “one dude”.
In a state where data centres have become an incendiary issue, Talarico said: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas. But on November 3rd, we are going to deliver a crystal clear message to the world’s first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale.”
Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X and other businesses there, has contributed $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund, which in turn transferred the same amount to Texas PAC, a Republican super PAC supporting Paxton, according to federal filings.
Talarico has offset the outside-spending disadvantage with grassroots fundraising. His campaign says it raised $64m from July through September, more than triple Paxton’s total, with 97% of donations under $100 each.
Talarico told the crowd that super PACs and “billionaire mega-donors” are spending $200m in the most expensive Senate race in US history to defeat his grassroots campaign. “Big money is powerful, but it is nothing compared to people power,” he insisted, invoking biblical imagery comparing his supporters to “the slingshot” that David used to defeat Goliath
Talarico’s rally capped a turbulent month in what has emerged as America’s biggest battleground state. Talarico fell ill with the flu at the end of September and was not seen in public for nine days.
At a rally in San Antonio, Texas, Donald Trump claimed without evidence that “Tala-freako”, as he nicknames the Democrat, is vegan and had fallen ill because he tried eating meat for political purposes. That quickly metastasised into an online rumour that Talarico had checked into a mental health facility in Ohio. It was comprehensively debunked.
Meanwhile the Wall Street Journal published a video showing Paxton celebrating New Year’s Eve in Dubai with two US fugitives, Anosh Ahmed and Sameer Suhail, who were indicted in Illinois on healthcare-fraud charges. Ahmed donated $190,000 to Paxton, including $25,000 after his indictment.
Back on the campaign trail, Talarico set out on a “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts” tour of the state. He held a CNN town hall with sceptical Republicans and independent voters.
Paxton, meanwhile, launched an 18-day bus tour of Texas. His message was aimed at conservative voters with the slogan “Come and Take It”, an attack on what he called the far left. Republicans sought to tie Talarico with positions on transgender issues that have proved potent in conservative campaigning.
The campaign entered its final stretch with the Democrat holding a narrow polling advantage. The RealClearPolitics average for polls conducted from 6 to 19 October put Talarico ahead by 1.8 percentage points. An Emerson College Polling/ Nexstar Media survey released on Thursday found that 48% of voters support Talarico while 46% favour Paxton.
Early voting began on 19 October, giving both campaigns an immediate test of their ability to mobilise supporters. Talarico voted earlier on Friday.
Supporters at Friday’s rally expressed growing frustration with incumbent Republican officials such as Paxton along with optimism that Talarico’s message could signal a new political era for the Lone Star State.
Alina Anil, a 19-year-old student at the University of Texas, who had already cast her ballot, said she attended the event to see Talarico in person and demonstrate her support.
“We’ve been red for a long time and nothing has really come out of it,” Anil said. “As a student, I don’t think there’s been a lot of changes in Texas. We need some change and James Talarico seems promising. He was a teacher before, so I have faith in that and I have faith in him.”
Dakota Walker, 31, a pediatric physical therapist, arrived wearing a custom T-shirt reading “Talafrico: Talarico refreshing for Texas”, in the style of the Topo-Chico brand of sparkling mineral water.
“What’s not to like about him, what’s not to love about him, honestly?” Walker said. “He has morals, he has values, he’s an overall good human being and I think we need a drastic change.
“I have to spend so much of my time fighting for my kids, making sure that they get what they need when a family with a child with a disability or different abilities shouldn’t have to do that. I know we need healthcare reform and he is very big on that.”
Texas Democrats have had their hopes dashed before, notably when former congressman Beto O’Rourke lost a race to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018 by less than 3 percentage points.
Asked what a Democratic statewide victory would mean, Walker replied: “Oh man, I’ll probably cry, honestly. We need a lot of change and I feel like it’s time for a new era.”
Patrick Pearson, 46, an assistive technology professional, said he wanted to back Talarico because of his commitment to policy change. “From everything I’ve read about him and heard, I think he sounds really awesome,” Pearson said. “He’s actually trying to make a change and has a very positive message.”

title: Ramaswamy accuses Acton of ‘lying’ about attack ad, but court records contradict mother’s claim – as it happened
description: This live blog is now closed. Sign up for the Breaking News US email With less than two weeks until the midterms, my colleague Jonathan Freedland and Guardian US columnist Moira Donegan are answering your questions in this week’s episode of Politics Weekly America. They break down the final stretch ahead of these hugely consequential elections, that will decide control of Congress in Donald Trump’s final two years of office. Continue reading...
author_name: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat Marina Dunbar and Fran Lawther
content:
Vivek Ramaswamy , the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, accused his Democratic opponent, Dr Amy Acton , of “lying about lying” in her outraged response to an attack ad released by his campaign.
“We ran an ad about lying,” Ramaswamy argued on Friday , “it had nothing to do with childhood abuse”. Instead, the Republican claimed, his opponent was lying “about her history”.
The Ramaswamy campaign ad features Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur , accusing the daughter she lost custody of in 1978, after her second husband was charged with raping her then 12-year-old daughter, of lying about her childhood.
According to police and court documents obtained by the Associated Press, Arthur’s second husband, Cledith Arthur , was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter in July 1978, after Acton’s biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978, when Acton was between 10 and 12 years old.
Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty and was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. Donna Arthur fled the state with her husband, who later died.
Philip Stearns , Acton’s brother, said in a statement denouncing the ad that after his stepfather was arrested “and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.”
In the attack ad , Donna Arthur called her daughter “a liar” and said “she lies about her past; she says she grew up living in a tent, none of that is true.” That part of the ad uses stock video of a tent that had previously appeared in a biographical ad from Acton’s campaign , in which the candidate described her troubled upbringing. “I think it was somewhere off Route 7,” the candidate recalls. “I was 12, and we were living in a tent.”
A copy of the 1978 arrest warrant for Cledith Arthur, posted online on Friday by Nick Evans , a reporter for the Ohio Capital Journal, suggests that Acton was telling the truth. The warrant lists a campground off Ohio Route 7 in Rogers, Ohio as Cledith Arthur’s address.
“In 1982, after the Arthurs had skipped bail and fled Ohio, a deputy attempted to serve a warrant at” the same campground, Evans reports . “In a hand written note, the deputy relays that the park’s manager said Arthur ‘has not camped here for over two years.’”

title: California officials ordered by DoJ to set aside ‘likely’ noncitizen ballots
description: Letters from federal prosecutors represent latest escalation as Trump continues to make claims of voter fraud Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Department of Justice said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles county registrar and a letter obtained by the Associated Press. The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and Donald Trump’s Department of Justice, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Continue reading...
content:
Letters from federal prosecutors represent latest escalation as Trump continues to make claims of voter fraud
Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Department of Justice said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles county registrar and a letter obtained by the Associated Press.
The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and Donald Trump’s Department of Justice, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections.
Data shows illegal voting by people who are not US citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.
Earlier this month, the federal government targeted Los Angeles county and the California secretary of state’s office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of roughly 20,000 people who are “likely” noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday.
The Trump administration asked the ninth circuit court of appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday.
Now, according to the LA county registrar’s office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters.
They have been given a 48-hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified.
“Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy,” said first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli.
The justice department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including social security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more.
That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government’s list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland southern California county.
California’s secretary of state and the Los Angeles county registrar have opposed the federal government’s demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government’s data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens.
Voting is under way in California, with the state’s more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted.
The letters on Friday came on the heels of statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.

Defense secretary Pete Hegseth alleges Confucius Institutes operating in disguise on US university campuses
The ⁠US defense department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centers on university campuses ⁠known as Confucius ⁠Institutes ​as a threat to US national security, defense secretary Pete ⁠Hegseth said on Friday.
Washington has long accused Confucius Institutes of being Chinese propaganda ⁠tools and has taken steps to ​crack down on them.
Hegseth, ‌in a ‌video posted on social media, alleged that Confucius ‌Institutes were operating under disguise at US universities and that the Pentagon had added them to its list of institutions that threaten US national security.
“It turns ‌out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped ​up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds ⁠of American students,” Hegseth said.
The defense department over ​the ​past two months has “systematically ​dismantled every single one of ​these organizations”, he ‌said.
The Chinese ​embassy ​in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter speaks out for first time: ‘I have to go in’
description: Kaylub Giamanco recounts the day he confronted the Silver Rail elementary school shooter, who killed three boys and one teacher The Oregon father hailed as a hero for stopping a school shooting last week spoke for the first time about the incident, describing his experience and how he told a 911 operator: “I have to go in. People are going to die.” Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter, has received national attention and praise for stopping the bloodshed at Silver Rail elementary in Bend, Oregon, where his children attend school. Continue reading...
content:
Kaylub Giamanco recounts the day he confronted the Silver Rail elementary school shooter, who killed three boys and one teacher
The Oregon father hailed as a hero for stopping a school shooting last week spoke for the first time about the incident, describing his experience and how he told a 911 operator: “I have to go in. People are going to die.”
Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter, has received national attention and praise for stopping the bloodshed at Silver Rail elementary in Bend, Oregon, where his children attend school.
He fatally shot Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school, who broke in and shot six people , killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.
In an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB), his first since the 15 October shooting, he recounted that day. He told reporters that he was only in the area because he had decided to return home and eat lunch with his wife rather than the meal he brought to work that day.
For a moment, Giamanco, who lives near the school, thought it was a prank when he saw a man in black armed with a gun headed toward Silver Rail, he said. Then he saw the man fire the gun and climb over a school fence. Giamanco pulled out a .40 caliber handgun from his center console and headed into the school parking lot, calling 911, before himself hopping over a fence to pursue the shooter.
He quietly followed Griffin without the teenager seeing him, at one point crawling on his hands and knees when he heard “children pleading for their lives”.
“I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do,” he told OPB.
Giamanco crawled through a broken window and toward the special education class Griffin had entered, where a teacher was fighting with the shooter. He came into the classroom and fired his gun. Griffin fell and was reaching for his weapon before Giamanco, who said he “was afraid of him shooting anybody else”, shot him two more times.
He told OPB that he lies awake at night thinking of what he saw that day and the teenage perpetrator, and wonders if he could have done more.
“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” Giamanco told the outlet. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn’t save.”
Giamanco said he wants to see safer schools with school resource officers at every site, and that he would like to raise funding to support school safety efforts.

title: He wants to clean up the city and banish high prices. But who is ‘London’s Batman’?
description: The caped crusader is paying for hospital parking fines, giving out fuel to drivers – and sponsoring the return of cut-priced Freddo bars In the harsh light of day, a caped crusader storms the streets of London to tackle a crime that has long blighted the capital: littering. “When I said I wanted to save London, I meant it. I will not stop until every single bit of trash is off the streets,” he says in a viral video, narrated in his trademark deep, husky and (suspiciously) American voice, joined by a gang of hooded helpers clearing rubbish-strewn streets in Tower Hamlets. content:
The caped crusader is paying for hospital parking fines, giving out fuel to drivers – and sponsoring the return of cut-priced Freddo bars
In the harsh light of day, a caped crusader storms the streets of London to tackle a crime that has long blighted the capital: littering.
“When I said I wanted to save London, I meant it. I will not stop until every single bit of trash is off the streets,” he says in a viral video, narrated in his trademark deep, husky and (suspiciously) American voice, joined by a gang of hooded helpers clearing rubbish-strewn streets in Tower Hamlets.
This was Batman’s first good deed for the capital and, in the month since relocating from Gotham, he has carried out many more: paying parking fines for those visiting loved ones in hospital, giving out “free fuel” to motorists and bringing back £1 chicken and chips to those who once savoured this cheap and filling after-school meal.
But who is he really and what does he stand for? In a recent interview with a BBC reporter, who was only given a time and location before the masked figure emerged in an alleyway, he summed up his mission: “People are struggling and I want to help them.”
As for his identity, Niko Omilana – YouTuber, prankster and fifth-placed London 2021 mayoral candidate, who has pulled off similar stunts – is the most obvious guess, though he has denied it.
When asked by BBC London if he was the city’s masked mystery saviour, Omilana sent the team a voice note saying: “BBC, just to tell you, I’m not Batman.”
Count Binface, who has faced off against some of the nation’s most high-profile politicians in elections across the country, is another name in the mix, though he denied the rumours.
He told the Guardian: “I can see why a human might think that ‘London’s Batman’ is me, but it is actually a bit armour-ist of you. We’re not all the same.
“I’m happy to make the clarification and I would like to take the opportunity to wish London’s Batman well, including with his inevitable battle on the planet Copyright.”
Omilana remains the most likely suspect. His 2021 mayoral manifesto pledges included turning off all power in London once a year to “call it Londoff”, forcing then-prime minister Boris Johnson to “shush” and reducing the price of a Freddo chocolate bar to 5p.
Curiously, in one of his most viral stunts, London’s Batman set up a stall in Oxford Street where a Freddo could be exchanged for a tiny, silver 5p coin. (The frog-shaped chocolate bar was never officially sold for this sum, with 2p in the 1970s and 10p in the 1990s and early 2000s being the lowest retail prices documented.)
Ace Clvrk was in the area buying a guitar when he came across the stall. “I was lucky that day I had exactly 5p. It felt like fate,” said the 32-year-old musician.
He was approached on the street by some “hooded, masked youths” who “seemed really friendly”. They stopped him and asked: “Do you want to buy a Freddo?”
Clvrk was guided to a stall where he saw the caped crusader in the flesh. He told Clvrk he was “trying to bring attention to lowering the cost of Freddos”.
Like Gotham’s caped crusader, his London doppelganger appears to have significant resources behind him. His social media videos are slickly produced and the tasks he has carried out are hardly cheap.
For the “free fuel” stunt, one resident, speaking to the Times, estimated he gave away more than £3,500 to motorists throughout the day. The Guardian contacted several organisations that had benefited from London’s Batman’s good deeds who declined to speak citing confidentiality reasons.
Clvrk said it looked like a well-run stunt. “Everyone that I spoke to was really friendly and the actual content came out looking great too. I don’t remember actually seeing the camera,” he said.
In the video touting his bargain frog-shaped chocolates, London’s Batman featured a clip of Andy Burnham holding a Freddo while declaring it the “most talked about cost of living symbol in the UK” before going on to say he “might not be able to do anything to reduce the price of these”.
The caped crusader’s Freddo policy could suggest he’s vying for real power. “I’d vote for him, 100%,” said Clvrk. “5p Freddo, £1 chicken and chips and paying for fuel. What’s not to love?”
There could be some weight to this, especially if two-time political candidate Omilana, who also ran against Rishi Sunak in his Richmond and Northallerton seat in 2024, is behind the mask.
The message appears to be resonating. On TikTok, he has already amassed 315,000 followers in just over four weeks.
“I think everything he’s doing is amazing,” said Clvrk. “Politics and prime ministers are removed from the everyday Londoner and British person on the streets who used to be able to get a Freddo for 10p or cheap chicken and chips.
“With rising prices, it’s shining a light on things that seem small to those that are removed from it, but not for the everyday person.”

title: Trump drops some Canada tariffs in bid to boost embattled Susan Collins in Maine
description: Republican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged voters Donald Trump dropped some of the US’s tariffs on Canada on Friday to “better serve the public interest” the White House said, handing a win to Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, as she faces a tight re-election campaign that will help determine whether Democrats can flip control of Congress. Collins announced that the exemptions would apply to nine agricultural products, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed. content:
Republican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged voters
Donald Trump dropped some of the US’s tariffs on Canada on Friday to “better serve the public interest” the White House said, handing a win to Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, as she faces a tight re-election campaign that will help determine whether Democrats can flip control of Congress.
Collins announced that the exemptions would apply to nine agricultural products, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed. She added that many of the state’s farmers rely on specialized equipment and materials from across the border that are “unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense”.
“In my repeated conversations with Ambassador Greer, Secretary Lutnick, and other senior administration officials, I have asked for tariff relief for these important products, and I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner,” she wrote.
The White House also specified that certain processing equipment – such as plywood sheets, packing boxes, paper products, and certain machinery – would be removed from its tariffs. These materials can be crucial for Maine businesses operating close to the border.
“President Trump is further refining the scope of the July 20 and September 8 actions to better serve the public interest, and to ensure these measures continue to effectively offset the burden or disadvantage to US commerce from Canada’s discriminatory measures,” the White House said in a news release.
Collins, who has served in the Senate for nearly 30 years, is running for re-election against Troy Jackson, a Democrat who has served in the Maine state senate and is a former logger. The race is crucial for the Democratic party’s hopes of flipping control of the chamber, and is so far considered a toss-up.
The trade war between Canada and Maine has touched a nerve in the state, which relies heavily on commerce with Canada. Many of the industries most entrenched in the state’s history – such as logging, lobstering and fishing – were expected to take a hit after Trump’s tariff announcements this year.
Earlier this week, the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, said American tariffs hurt both American and Canadian households. He added that auto exports to the US had so far fallen 10%, and US exports to Canada have fallen by more than 20%.
“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”
After Trump placed a 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods, which began on 22 August, Canada announced its own retaliatory tariffs in response, ranging from 15% to 50% on $20bn worth of American goods. Canada later withdrew its tariffs on American seafood, which helped Maine’s fisheries in particular.
Maine is considered a purple state, and many within the state – including Collins – consider themselves to have an independent streak. Collins has frequently sought to distance herself from Trump, particularly when it comes to his trade policies, and has broken with her party more than any other Republican senator since Trump took office, according to a New York Times analysis of her voting record.
But her efforts to vote against Trump’s policies have rarely succeeded in his second term so far, the analysis found.
Jackson has frequently seized on this line of attack since replacing Graham Platner on the Democratic ticket. At a television debate earlier this month, Jackson also pointed to Collins’s crucial vote to confirm the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh. The court subsequently overturned Roe v Wade.
“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in his opening statement.
Democrats argued the decision to drop some Canadian tariffs was an admission by the White House that Trump’s policies were unpopular.
Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate finance committee, called the move a “desperate, 11th hour attempt to save Susan Collins’ political career”.
“The only way to get Trump to reverse course,” he said, “is for Americans to send a message that his sabotage of the American economy has got to go, along with any politician who has supported his agenda.”

title: UK government to make unprecedented intervention in setting of water bills
description: Exclusive: Angela Eagle tells utility bosses next price review ‘must focus on value for money for customers’ Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows. Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat. Continue reading...
content:
Exclusive: Angela Eagle tells utility bosses next price review ‘must focus on value for money for customers’
Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat.
Sources at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Andy Burnham’s 10-year plan, which will follow next week’s budget, would hand the government more robust powers to keep bills affordable and direct local investment. But sources close to Eagle said there also needed to be immediate action as companies began to make decisions before the next price-setting process, expected to conclude in 2029.
There has never been government intervention in the five-year review process. It is run by Ofwat, which analyses companies’ business plans and determines how much can be charged to customers in their bills to fund investment and running costs.
Eagle has written to regulators and water company chief executives, saying that the process must meet specific government priorities, including offering bill payers much better value for money – though stopping short of demanding bill cuts.
The letter to companies and regulators says they must be focused on investment in new technology to save money, and early intervention on leaks and sewage. It also called for far better communication and decision-making power handed to local communities and leaders.
The first priority must be affordable bills, the letter says, adding: “Affordability means a laser focus on value for money for customers.”
The letter says the public is clear about what the objectives for the industry should be. “They want clean rivers. They want reliable water services. They want to know that their money is being spent wisely, and that bills are kept affordable. And they want confidence that the system is working in their interests.”
The letter warns company bosses that it will “not be a business-as-usual price review … it is the beginning of a long-term transition to a different model for the water sector”.
Defra sources said Eagle intended it to be the first in a series of changes that will be announced in the coming months on the water industry, calling it “one of the clearest symbols of public frustration with Britain’s infrastructure”.
A Defra source said the intervention by Eagle was a down payment on bigger changes that would come in the 10-year plan. The source said: “Angela will take a much more bullish approach to telling water companies and regulators what is expected from them. This is the start of a journey to a very different water system and one that delivers for the public.
“There are also things we want regulators and companies to be doing now and so Angela is using the levers she’s got to influence their investment decisions at an early stage and make sure they’ve got no excuses. As well as looking at ownership structures, there are other ways we can go further than what came before.”
The new intervention from Eagle comes as the government continues to explore more radical options for the stricken company Thames Water. The Guardian reported earlier this week that Burnham had told officials to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that meant spending taxpayer money and going to court.
Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames Water – which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn – but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.
The outcome of the last price review process in 2024 led to highly controversial bill rises, after Ofwat authorised a £104bn modernisation programme, funded in large part through progressive annual rate increases that will see average water bills surge by 36% over the second half of the decade. The biggest increase was allowed for Southern Water, whose customers will pay 53% more by 2030, at an average of £642 per year.
Over the summer, several major suppliers requested permission to charge billions more to cover mounting capital costs and debt obligations, sparking fury from campaigners and from politicians, including Burnham.
The prime minister criticised the decision , warning that bill payers must no longer be treated as a “blank cheque” or a “bottomless source of funding for other people’s failures”, saying ordinary households were being forced to plug massive corporate balance-sheet deficits.
However, campaigners for public ownership have warned the move will do little in practice to reduce bills or the environmental impact of sewage or leaks. Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “These proposals are yet more reshuffling of the deckchairs on the Titanic, and fall far short of Burnham’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism.
“This government should be intervening on behalf of households to stop bill hikes. If water companies can’t function without siphoning more and more money out of our pockets, then this government should let them go bust.
“From there, we can bring water affordably into public hands. ⁠Under public ownership, we can put people and the environment ahead of the interests of faraway shareholders and hedge funds.”

title: ‘Comfort in a bowl’: porridge hotter than ever as fibremaxxers get their oats
description: Humble breakfast staple at heart of trend stirred up by health concerns and hearty spoonfuls of nostalgia The clocks may be going back in the UK this weekend, but the biggest sign winter is coming is a steaming bowl of porridge on a breakfast table.
