title: ‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providers
description: Our dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts say It happened again. A power outage hit a datacentre in London , and things cascaded from there: multiple banking services faltered, court hearings were put on hold and patients reported temporary glitches on the NHS app. The datacentre in question was in Google’s europe-west2-b zone, one of more than a dozen “zones” that the US search giant maintains in Europe to service its clients. Continue reading...
content:
Our dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts say
I t happened again. A power outage hit a datacentre in London , and things cascaded from there: multiple banking services faltered, court hearings were put on hold and patients reported temporary glitches on the NHS app.
The datacentre in question was in Google’s europe-west2-b zone, one of more than a dozen “zones” that the US search giant maintains in Europe to service its clients.
The outages – which have affected, according to the website Downdetector, Royal Mail, Revolut, HSBC and Lloyds bank, among others, are so far not of the scale of a similar cascade this time last year, when Amazon Web Services went down for nearly half a day.
That outage hit a far bigger node – Amazon’s us-east-1 – in a concentrated region of Virginia, which hosts the greatest density of datacentres on Earth. It saw cascading effects worldwide: taking out the Roblox game and Signal messaging app and causing smart mattresses worldwide to suddenly heat overnight and toast their occupants.
Today’s problems appeared to peak at about 9am, and by mid-afternoon were somewhat resolved, according to reports submitted to Downdetector. Because Google Cloud stores data and runs operations for a number of businesses, there were widespread knock-on effects – mostly confined to UK businesses.
Revolut confirmed “a service disruption affecting multiple services”, but added that “all our customers’ money and data are safe”. Lloyd’s said its app was working, but “we understand some [people] are having issues with certain online services this morning”.
HM Courts and Tribunal Service, which handles remote video hearings in courts across England and Wales, said it was “aware of an issue affecting Cloud Video Platform,” and was “working with our technology partners to restore service”.
Like the far bigger outage last year, it’s a reminder of the physical infrastructure – often creaking and provisional – that underpins most of the virtual world.
Michał “rysiek” Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said the outages were a reminder of the increasing concentration of the internet and vital services on the infrastructure of a few key companies – the “hyperscalers”.
“Hyperscalers have become too big to not fail. But worse, they’ve become so deeply ingrained into the very fabric of our digital lives that switching away from them seems unimaginable.”
The Guardian has reported that British police keep vital data on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, despite being apparently aware that this exposes sensitive information to US government insiders, hostile foreign actors and outages like today’s. Up to 60% of the UK government’s infrastructure is hosted on cloud services – mostly Amazon, Microsoft and Google.
“I am sure Google’s engineers are doing everything they can to mitigate them, but it is unreasonable to have a handful of gigantic companies whose outages time and again cause public institutions or large swaths of the digital economy to stop working en masse,” said Woźniak.
Last year’s AWS outage was later revealed to have been caused not by a power outage, but by a bug in automation software . A separate outage was caused by an AI tool that Amazon had adopted after laying off tens of thousands of staff last autumn.
Woźniak pointed at an announcement this year from Google indicating that it was also embracing AI, with 75% of all new code “now AI-generated and approved by engineers”.
“One can only wonder how that affects the reliability and quality of Google’s services. Multiple large outages at another hyperscaler, AWS, a year ago have been linked to internal AI tooling.”
A Google spokesperson said: “We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event. Services have been restored. We will update our public status dashboard with an analysis of the incident.”

title: ‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off
description: School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat. But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town. Continue reading...
content:
School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments
On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.
But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town.
The local comprehensive, King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC) , has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field – and it is likely houses will be built on it.
School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.
“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.
“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”
Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealing almost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.
Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”
Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign group Friends of Lower Field , said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”
Lewis Winks, a leading member of the Right to Roam group, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known for progressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate , about a century ago.
A key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.
Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”
The Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”
But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to them are unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.
Matthew Shanks, chief executive of Education South West , said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.
He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.
School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.
Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for 60 years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.
“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”

title: Stinky business: south London bike shop hit by ‘unbearable’ stench from Thames Water sewer
description: Owner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problem The leafy south London neighbourhood of Herne Hill is a haven for cyclists who can often be seen lapping the local parks and refuelling at the many cafes that line the suburban streets. content:
Owner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problem
T he leafy south London neighbourhood of Herne Hill is a haven for cyclists who can often be seen lapping the local parks and refuelling at the many cafes that line the suburban streets. But there is something foul in the air of this corner of the capital – and for once it’s not the traffic fumes hitting bicycle riders.
A toxic stench thought to be caused by untreated sewage stuck in Thames Water drains has been emanating from the subterranean depths for months, most likely caused by the summer’s lack of rain.
The stink is so acrid that the Bicyclenation shop has had to bar some customers and its mechanics have been forced to work on the pavement outside.
The owner of the shop, Tamas Polocz, has repeatedly complained to Thames Water since the smell first hit the shop in June and caused his colleague Nick to vomit.
Last week the troubled water company told Polocz it accepted that a mains sewer directly beneath the shop was to blame, but it has yet to offer him and his team of 11 any date for resolving the problem.
Polocz and his colleagues have been left fearing for their physical and mental health after repeated exposure to the gassy stench. And the outlook for the business is bleak.
The odour comes in putrid wafts that occur at least five times a day, according to a “smell chart” used to log the time and duration of each incident with a description. The words used include “cabbage”, “teargas”, “onions”, “spicy BBQ” and repeated references to “shit”.
When the Guardian first arrived at the shop there was a whiff of rotten eggs but not enough to stop mechanics working inside and customers milling about. But within minutes we were overpowered by a repulsive gas that hit the back of the throat and left us scurrying outside, gagging for air.
“It’s unbearable,” said Polocz. “You can’t be in the shop when it comes.”
He added: “It has a really strong physical presence. This is a smell you take home with you. It’s in your hair, on your skin, sometimes it feels it’s inside your skin. When you go home and cough, you taste it again.”
The ordeal comes after record-breaking temperatures and drought prompted calls for a radical overhaul of an outdated sewage system , just as the Great Stink ushered in new sanitation in the Victorian era.
Thames Water initially suggested the Herne Hill smell was due to a gas leak. But extensive tests by the local gas supplier ruled that out.
Polocz said he had been battling the company every week. “Thames Water have always tried to push me away, or blame others. When they finally accepted liability last week I just broke down. But we still don’t have a date for fixing it.”
The exact cause of the stench remains unknown, but a Thames Water engineer told Polocz it was likely to be linked to the lack of rain. The engineer also told him that a cast-iron ventilation pipe that had previously drawn odours away from the shop had not been replaced.
Experts warn that during dry periods, untreated sewage builds up in pipes with no rainwater to flush it out. Microbial activity in the sewage causes foul-smelling gas to be emitted in wafts , in a similar process to the one that causes flatulence in human digestion.
Prof Barbara Evans, the chair of public health engineering at Leeds University, said: “It sounds like methane and it’s probably unsafe working conditions. Biological processes are cyclical just like in your digestive system, which is why sewer smells come in wafts.”
When Polocz woke up to rainfall, he was hopeful it would flush away the stench. “I looked out through the window at home and thought, oh good, but it didn’t make any difference. Even after the rain there was still the smell. Maybe the rain will eventually clear it, but we don’t know. Something is happening down there that is pushing the smell up.”
Evans said: “The first flushes of rain will probably make things smell worse because it just stirs things up. It needs a lot of rain to clear. There might be some blockage there but it’s impossible to know without a proper inspection.”
Harriet Talbot, a board member of Bicyclenation, said: “You can’t run a business relying on the weather.” She helped set up a webpage asking for customers to sign up for a collect and repair service to help the shop survive.
Polocz said the shop was currently unsustainable because staff had to evacuate so frequently. “We have to do half a day in the shop and half outside on the pavement. But now the cold weather is coming, we can’t keep doing that.”
And the stress from the stink is taking its toll. Polocz said: “I’m 49, but today I feel 62-ish. We have guys calling in sick. It affects you both physically and mentally.”
Polocz said he laid in bed at night worrying how he would be able to keep the shop going. “The last thought of the day and the first thought of the day are now both the same,” he said. “And I wake up at night thinking: what are we going to do about it? I try to listen to a podcast, but I still keep thinking about the smell. Somehow I’m going to get through this and change back to normal.”
Polocz’s plight is likely to add to calls for an overhaul of London’s Victorian sewage system. Evans said: “This underlines the need for a rethink of our sewers. The system was designed for a climate that we just don’t currently have any more.”
The Guardian asked Thames Water when the problem would be fixed, why it had taken so long to resolve, and whether the company would apologise to Polocz.
A spokesperson replied: “Our teams are investigating the source of an odour reported at a bike shop. Initial investigations have confirmed there are no blockages in the sewers surrounding the property. Odour monitors are to be installed, which will enable engineers to detect, measure and track odorous gases in real time and help determine the exact cause.”

title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom
description: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say The David Attenborough -narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said. content:
BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
The David Attenborough -narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.
Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hit BBC series is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam.
Since the first Blue Planet, TVs and cameras have evolved to give viewers sharper, higher definition pictures. But the combination of the rise in AI and the extraordinary sequences and fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios’ natural history unit for this series led producers to include what they called more “organic” footage and less polished shots, to show that the animals were not AI-generated.
The executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI, “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real”.
She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’”
But now such things are being left in as “we’re really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage.
For the first time, the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It’s all real photography.”
Bootle added that as we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they’ve seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”.
That includes never-before-seen action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV – developed by the programme’s producer and director, Yoland Bosiger.
Over the four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton, creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, camera operators wearing leg-mounted scooters to create immersive TikTok-style diving footage and using lasers to film deep-sea creatures.
Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and footage involving penguins that echoes the Planet Earth II, ‘iguana v snakes’ sequence.
Threats to the ocean as well as its resilience are addressed in the series. Episodes show how the climatecrisis is killing off the sea where anemone clown fish live and what they do to try to fix their homes, and the issue of plastics raised in Blue Planet II continues with a story about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White.
Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts.
White added: “What’s wonderful is he hasn’t lost his curiosity … he’s still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.”
Asked if the BBC’s £500m cost-cutting drive would affect BBC Studios’ renowned natural history reputation, White said she could not comment on that but pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series.
Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1 November on BBC1 and iPlayer

title: Which is really England’s oldest pub? Tree-ring dating helps settle debate
description: Historic England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest is from 1430 With their low ceilings, timber beams and roaring fires, many of England’s inns lay claim to being the oldest in the land and to have been visited by Vikings and Saxons. But an archaeologist who worked on behalf of Historic England says not one of the more than two dozen pubs that make this claim is being accurate. Continue reading...
content:
Historic England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest is from 1430
With their low ceilings, timber beams and roaring fires, many of England’s inns lay claim to being the oldest in the land and to have been visited by Vikings and Saxons.
But an archaeologist who worked on behalf of Historic England says not one of the more than two dozen pubs that make this claim is being accurate.
While many claim origins dating back 1,000 years, Dr James Wright, a buildings archaeologist, said it was difficult to verify whether any pubs were built and used as inns or ale houses and kept in continuous use prior to the 1400s.
After painstaking investigation, including tree-ring dating on the wooden beams of pubs – a process known as dendrochronology – Wright named the George Inn, of Norton St Philip, Somerset, as the oldest pub in England. It has fabrics dating from the late 14th century.
He told the Guardian: “Not one of the claimants to be the oldest pub (and there are over two dozen of them) are even vaguely close to being so in reality.”
Of the George, he said: “The architectural history of the George Inn’s stone and timber suggests that this building has been in continuous service for over 600 years.” He said the pub was set up in the 14th century by the monks of nearby Hinton Priory.
Tree-ring dating had helped “to understand scientifically exactly how old the timbers are,” he said. “Because we know medieval carpenters didn’t muck around at all and they would fell the timber when it was green and build almost immediately afterwards, the actual date of felling gives us the near date of construction.”
Ye Olde Fighting Cocks in St Albans, Hertfordshire, claims to have been established around AD800, and the Bingley Arms in Bardsey, West Yorkshire, declares on its site: “It’s the original English pub – officially the oldest in Britain – dating back over 1,000 years to a time when Vikings were conquering parts of the country.” Similarly, the Royal Standard in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, boasts that it was a favoured watering hole of King Alfred the Great’s West Saxons in around AD880.
Wright said most of these claims seemed to be “modern marketing strategies”. “The Fighting Cocks is often said to date to AD793. This date was probably not arrived at until 1926 when it appeared on a postcard. Prior to that, it was speculated to date to 1030, 770 and 672,” he said. “There does not seem to be a basis in reality for any of those claims. Instead, the building started as a monastic dovecote, built around 1400. The earliest date when we can say for sure it was active as a public house is the first decade of the 19th century.”
Many of the pubs claiming to be the oldest say they were mentioned in the Domesday Book, but the historian said: “There are no pubs mentioned – at all – in the Domesday Book, so any pub claiming to be in it is having you on.”
Wright added: “The claims are likely to originate less in folklore and more in canny marketing strategies by landlords, tenants, breweries and pub companies. The claims potentially rely upon the public not being aware of how to accurately date historic buildings.”
He provided the Guardian with a list of the pubs he believes to be the oldest in the country. His methodology was to determine that it was purpose-built as a public house, that it had been in continuous service and that there was archaeological, archival or dendrochronological evidence for the existence of significant primary fabric remaining from the original construction.
“I did consider buildings which had been converted and others which had periodically changed in land use,” he said. “Even with those taken into consideration, there are only about 12 to 16 genuine contenders which have been doing trade since the medieval period. Of these, the oldest date to the 14th and 15th centuries.”
George Inn, Norton St Philip, Somerset: late 14th century and 1430-32.
Bull Hotel, Ludlow, Shropshire: 14th and 15th centuries.
King’s Head, Shrewsbury, Shropshire: 1426, 1430-31.
New Inn, Gloucester, Gloucestershire: 1432.
White Hart Inn, Hook, Hampshire: 1419-51.
George Hotel, Dorchester-on-Thames, Oxfordshire: mid 15th century.
Kings Head, Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire: 1445-55.
Angel, Grantham, Lincolnshire: circa 1450.
George and Pilgrims Inn, Glastonbury, Somerset: 1461-83.
Saracen’s Head, Southwell, Nottinghamshire: 1460s.
George Hotel, Odiham, Hampshire: 1486-87.

content:
Cate Blanchett and Hannah Waddingham join William on sofa for special edition to celebrate prince’s Earthshot prize
The Prince of Wales has braved the chatshow sofa, making a surprise appearance on The Graham Norton Show.
In the pre-recorded show, to be aired on Friday on BBC One, William made a surprise appearance in a special Earthshot prize edition to promote his environmental initiative, which has an annual awards ceremony due to be staged in Mumbai, India, next month.
The prince revealed his family’s love for The Celebrity Traitors show, saying: “I love it, the family love it. Charlotte and Louis are obsessed with it. It’s really good telly.”
Speaking of the EastEnders star Ross Kemp’s fear of being murdered by touch in plain sight on the Traitors show, he joked: “I saw Ross Kemp the day after the first episode and I couldn’t help but try – in the most appropriate way – to touch him to see what reaction I got from him. Turns out he was really jumpy!”
William, the first royal to appear on the chatshow, also revealed he switches off through music and film. “I love getting immersed in deep-thinking films. I like action films too, but I like something a bit different. I’m a big fan of everything Christopher Nolan does. His films are fantastic – The Dark Knight series is psychologically dark and deep and I absolutely love that.
“He takes concepts that are completely out there and makes them incredibly entertaining.”
Joining him on the sofa were the actors Cate Blanchett and Hannah Waddingham, and the environmentalist Robert Irwin, who are all connected to the Earthshot prize which was founded by William in 2020 to recognise and reward issues and ideas to help save the planet.
William told Norton and the other guests about the origins of the prize and its role in identifying and supporting innovators around the world. He said: “For many years I was hearing stories about environment issues, and one thing that struck me was the negativity and doom, which got me down.
“I thought we could do something more powerful and more optimistic and the idea of an awards’ ceremony came about and we could talk about urgency and optimism together.

title: Ohio man convicted of murder for running over officer after police killed his son
description: Rodney Hinton ran over Larry Henderson after he viewed body-cam footage of police shooting dead his son Ryan An Ohio man who killed a deputy with his car just hours after seeing video of his son killed by Cincinnati police was found guilty of murder and other charges on Friday, according to authorities . Rodney L Hinton , 40, faces between 15 years and life in prison after his convictions in the death of Hamilton county special deputy Larry Henderson. His sentencing is tentatively scheduled for 16 November. Continue reading...
content:
Rodney Hinton ran over Larry Henderson after he viewed body-cam footage of police shooting dead his son Ryan
An Ohio man who killed a deputy with his car just hours after seeing video of his son killed by Cincinnati police was found guilty of murder and other charges on Friday, according to authorities .
Rodney L Hinton , 40, faces between 15 years and life in prison after his convictions in the death of Hamilton county special deputy Larry Henderson. His sentencing is tentatively scheduled for 16 November.
During his 10-day trial, Hinton’s defense argued that he was so distressed over his son’s killing that he could not legally distinguish between right and wrong at the time of Henderson’s killing. But jurors rejected that defense after deliberations which began on Wednesday, finding him guilty of murder, reckless homicide and felonious assault.
“The senseless murder of Deputy Larry Henderson Jr shattered a family and left a community mourning the loss of a dedicated public servant” who had spent 33 years on the job, Ohio’s attorney general, Andy Wilson, said in a statement. “We are thankful to the jury for its verdict, which accurately reflects the evidence in this case.
Wilson’s statement added that Henderson’s “death is a painful reminder of the risks that law enforcement officers face every day while working to keep us safe”.
Hours before Henderson’s killing, the Cincinnati police department sat down with Hinton’s family and their attorneys to view body-worn camera footage of his son, Ryan Hinton, being shot and killed by the agency’s officers the previous day.
Ryan Hinton, 18, was killed after officers responded to a report of a stolen vehicle at an apartment complex. Two officers attempted to detain four people, including Ryan, in the reported stolen car – and all of those in the vehicle in question began to run, police said.
The body-worn camera footage , which was published by NBC News, showed an officer exiting his vehicle and aiming his gun at Ryan Hinton, who appeared to be running away. Another recording captured an officer saying, “He’s got a gun!” The firearm was reportedly recovered at the scene.
The officer who shot Ryan Hinton fired about four times. It is unclear from the footage if Hinton had aimed a firearm at officers.
After seeing that footage, Rodney Hinton left in his own car and took aim with it at Henderson, according to Cincinnati police. Officials say Henderson saw the car coming toward him but could not avoid being hit. Prosecutors contended that Hinton “tracked” Henderson.
“He turned his wheel the same direction that Larry moved, and the car struck Larry, throwing him, tossing him into the air, twisting him until he landed,” assistant prosecutor Kate Burroughs said in closing arguments on Wednesday.
Rodney Hinton’s attorney, Clyde Bennett II, had asked jurors to find the defendant not guilty of all charges by reason of insanity.
Bennett told reporters after the verdict that Hinton planned to pursue an appeal.
“The fight is not over,” Bennett said in remarks recorded by Cincinnati news station WLWT.

title: Trump says he ordered DoJ to file lawsuit to block Alaska Senate results certification
description: Trump justice department claims there could be ‘confusion’ about two Republicans on the ballot named Dan Sullivan Donald Trump said he ordered the justice department to file a lawsuit to block the certification of Alaska’s US Senate results if the Republican incumbent loses, a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance. “I’m the one that said do it,” the president told reporters as he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday. Continue reading...
author_name: Shrai Popat in Washington and Sam Levine
content:
Trump justice department claims there could be ‘confusion’ about two Republicans on the ballot named Dan Sullivan
Donald Trump said he ordered the justice department to file a lawsuit to block the certification of Alaska’s US Senate results if the Republican incumbent loses, a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.
“I’m the one that said do it,” the president told reporters as he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday.
The justice department argued in its lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before election day, that there could be “voter confusion” over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the November ballot, which Republicans fear could take away votes from the incumbent and influence the race’s outcome in favor of the Democratic nominee, Mary Peltola.
Experts saw the lawsuit as extremely weak and unlikely to succeed. “The legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” Derek Mueller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, wrote in a blogpost .
Control of the Senate could come down to Alaska, and polls suggest the Republican incumbent senator, Dan S Sullivan, is in a dead heat with Peltola, a former Democratic congresswoman. Another candidate named Daniel J Sullivan , a retired schoolteacher, is also running as a Republican and will appear on the November general election ballot.
The federal government argues in the complaint that “the sole purpose” of Dan J Sullivan’s candidacy is to “benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan”.
As a result, “there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity,” the complaint states.
The administration is asking for a pause in certifying the vote in Alaska “pending an investigation” to determine whether votes that are cast for Dan J Sullivan were actually meant to be for the Republican incumbent.
David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said the department’s lawsuit was “an unprecedented intervention by the federal government” and said the issue of two candidates with similar names appearing on the ballot had already been “ fully litigated by Alaska’s courts”.
He said the lawsuit “raises serious concerns about political interference”, adding that he could not recall an administration “ever attempting to stop the certification of an election – and certainly not 11 days before polls close”.
Trump and his allies have repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that Daniel J Sullivan – who is challenging the two-term incumbent – is an “impostor”.
Meanwhile, many Republicans across the country have accused the former teacher, who lives in Petersburg – a town of about 3,000 people in the southern part of Alaska – of being a Democratic plant in place to cannibalize votes from Dan S Sullivan.
Trump has targeted the state’s use of ranked-choice voting, adopted by voters in 2020, which he has attacked as a “scam”. At a recent rally in Wasilla, Trump encouraged Alaskans to support a state ballot measure to repeal it.
Under the state’s voting system, the top four candidates from an open primary advance to the general election. Voters then rank candidates in order of preference, and votes can transfer to their next-ranked candidate as lower-placed contenders are eliminated.
The incumbent senator will appear on the 3 November ballot in Alaska with the words “(Registered Republican) Incumbent” next to his name to make it clearer for voters.
Voting rights experts say the basis for the lawsuit is thin given the fact that any meaningful investigation into voters’ preferences after they have voted would be practically impossible to conduct since Americans vote on a secret ballot.
Experts were also skeptical of the language in federal law the justice department cited to justify its lawsuit. In the filing, the justice department pointed to broad language in the preamble of the 1993 National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) saying one of the purposes of the law “was to protect the integrity of the electoral process”. Such an argument was akin to “suing the government for money because the Declaration of Independence guarantees ‘life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness’”, Chris Shenton, a lawyer at the Southern Coalition for Social Justice, posted on X .
In June, the Alaska supreme court ruled that Dan J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, despite the frustration it has caused the Trump administration and national Republicans.
The Trump administration’s targeting of Alaska’s Senate race is particularly consequential as Democrats increasingly believe Peltola, a moderate Democrat who supports gun rights and oil development, is on the verge of flipping the red-leaning state.
Peltola would be the first Democrat to win the seat in nearly two decades if she is successful.
In an interview with MS Now on Friday, Peltola described the lawsuit as “a distraction” that amounted to “corruption”.
“This is clearly a very desperate attempt to cling to power, using his allies in Washington DC, to rig the system even further,” Peltola said, adding: “There’s no reason to have any doubt that Alaskans know exactly who they’re voting for.
Alaska’s other senator, Lisa Murkowski, a Republican who has frequently broken with her party, also condemned the lawsuit on Friday.
“Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the state of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” she wrote on social media. “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.”

title: Mysterious ‘black triangles’ spotted over sensitive US site, new Pentagon UFO files reveal
description: Unidentified object vanished suddenly and silently, anonymous senior military observers claim Two senior military observers say they watched a mysterious black triangular object flying at an extraordinarily high speed over a sensitive site in the western US earlier this year, in the latest tranche of reported UFO sightings released on Friday by the Trump administration. The unidentified object showed none of the characteristics of a conventional military aircraft, their report to the defense department said, and it vanished suddenly and silently within seconds, leaving no exhaust trail or other evidence of its existence. Continue reading...
content:
Unidentified object vanished suddenly and silently, anonymous senior military observers claim
Two senior military observers say they watched a mysterious black triangular object flying at an extraordinarily high speed over a sensitive site in the western US earlier this year, in the latest tranche of reported UFO sightings released on Friday by the Trump administration.
The unidentified object showed none of the characteristics of a conventional military aircraft, their report to the defense department said, and it vanished suddenly and silently within seconds, leaving no exhaust trail or other evidence of its existence.
The claimed sighting, by anonymous sources with “extensive operational experience working alongside government agencies”, occurred at a location that was redacted in the file made public on Friday.
The “unidentified anomalous phenomenon” (UAP), a term that has superseded UFO in military, governmental and scientific circles, resembled a delta-wing drone with a wingspan between nine and 15ft (2.75 to 4.5m), the observers recalled. They calculated its speed at 1,800mph.
Similar to hundreds of other reports released by the Pentagon since May as part of Donald Trump’s promise to bring transparency to decades of previously classified or secret documents relating to UFOs, many other details are vague, inconclusive or blacked out altogether.
While many previous accounts have been accompanied by real photographs or video footage of apparent sightings, the “black triangles” report features nine identical images of the same unidentified canyon with tiny, trilateral silhouettes crudely added to replicate the movement of the object the observers said they saw.
“This does indeed look like little more than a black triangle shape superimposed on a landscape background to illustrate the report. I don’t think it really adds anything substantive to the report itself,” said Greg Eghigian, professor of history and bioethics at Penn State University, and author of the 2024 book After the Flying Saucers Came: A Global History of the UFO Phenomenon.
After an early flurry, the Pentagon’s releases in the second Trump administration have become less frequent in recent months, and noticeably thinner since the US president declared in February that he was ordering full disclosure about the government’s knowledge of UFOs and the search for alien life beyond our planet.
The move followed allegations aired in Congress in 2023 by a former intelligence official that successive administrations engaged in a cover-up, and that the government had possession of crashed alien spacecraft .
Friday’s release contained fewer than 25 text documents, and no videos or images.

title: Trump again invokes claim he has the ‘right’ to run for third term as president
description: US constitution unequivocally states that he can’t campaign again, which the president also seems to acknowledge US politics live – latest updates Donald Trump joked with rally-goers on Thursday evening that he had “the right to run again” for president, invoking a claim he has repeatedly made that he may seek a third term despite it being unconstitutional . “I don’t know who is going to be your next president and I think the law said, I’m not 100% sure, but I think the law says I’m not allowed to run again,” Trump said in Sioux City, Iowa . content:
US constitution unequivocally states that he can’t campaign again, which the president also seems to acknowledge
Donald Trump joked with rally-goers on Thursday evening that he had “the right to run again” for president, invoking a claim he has repeatedly made that he may seek a third term despite it being unconstitutional .
“I don’t know who is going to be your next president and I think the law said, I’m not 100% sure, but I think the law says I’m not allowed to run again,” Trump said in Sioux City, Iowa .
Trump went on to seemingly acknowledge that the 22nd amendment prohibits presidents from seeking a third term but then invoked his familiar false claims that Democrats “stole” the 2020 presidential election from him.
“Well, the one thing is different: they cheated us on the second one because we won it three times. So I think I have the right to run again,” Trump said, laughing.
“I think I have the right to run again because they cheated,” Trump added with a coy smile, drawing applause from the crowd.
Trump has consistently teased that he will run again for president, which would be a direct violation of the US constitution.
In October 2025, Trump told reporters he “would love” to run for a third term. At a rally in Texas in February, the president told the crowd, “Maybe we should do one more term,” claiming he was “entitled” to it.
Last year, the Trump store started selling “Trump 2028” hats. The US president went as far as to wear one during the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in July.
His allies have dismissed the president’s claims as a joke.
Mike Johnson, the speaker of the House, told reporters last year that Trump “has a good time with that, trolling the Democrats” with claims of a third term. Johnson said he didn’t see a way to amend the constitution to allow Trump to run again.
But opponents have raised concerns that Trump is being serious.
Trump himself has recognized the restrictions imposed by the US constitution.
Even during Thursday night’s rally, he said, “I’ve studied that phrase for ever. Unfortunately, it’s quite concise. There’s not a lot of wiggle room. It says something to the effect that ‘under no circumstances and for any reason will you even consider thinking about running for president if you had – ’.”
The president, who enjoys wide support thanks to his loyal Maga base, has urged supporters to vote as though he is on the ballot in November’s US midterm elections to help Republicans pick up more seats. The impact of this unconventional strategy remains to be seen as Trump’s approval ratings fall to new lows .

title: Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis
description: People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive. content:
People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds
The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.
In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians.
Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.
Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.
The White House statement said the ceasefire was brokered by Melania Trump , and her representative worked directly with ​Russian and Ukrainian ‌leadership to define the ​terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said.
Despite the claim the ceasefire had been brokered by Melania Trump, there had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, with claims by Ukrainian officials that it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls.
Calls for a ceasefire had been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe . As recently as 18 October, Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had also said he thought agreement was close without any mention of the first lady’s involvement.
Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town.
Lubinets ⁠told Reuters on Friday that the mission to Oleshky would involve ⁠demining roads leading into the town, delivering food and evacuating civilians. “A sufficient ​quantity of ‌humanitarian ‌aid will be delivered to ‌meet the needs of everyone who requires it. What’s more, we are working to ensure ‌that this is not just a ​one-off event, and that it is not limited to Oleshky alone,” ⁠he said.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network , despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.
The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskyy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with Trump and Musk denying responsibility. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place.
“I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, “underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access” to Starlink in a phone call with Trump on Friday, Downing Street said.
Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.
“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.
“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.
The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.
The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.
Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel , as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday, and on Friday the Russian deputy prime minister, Alexander Novak, said three tankers were en route to the US and claimed Russian companies could supply 500,000 metric tonnes in October.
Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.
Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.
Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war. “The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.
The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

title: As Trump’s time runs out, this could be his most dangerous legacy: a world divided into three | Steve Bloomfield
description: We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise In the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world. In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. content:
We’ve heard much about the end of the west. At the proposed summit between Trump, Putin and Xi, those fears could crystallise
I n the final two years of a US presidency, when Congress has been lost, approval ratings have sunk like a stone and their party has started to think about who’s coming next, the person occupying the Oval Office can feel their power draining away. Domestic legislation, particularly in an era where bipartisan cooperation is almost nonexistent, grinds to a halt. But as the days tick by until the end, and as presidents begin to think about their legacy, there is one part of the job where they still have power: the rest of the world.
In the final weeks of his presidency in 1992 George HW Bush sent 28,000 American troops to Somalia to help end a famine. For Bill Clinton, it was a quixotic attempt to bring peace to the Middle East by ending the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Barack Obama restored diplomatic ties with Cuba, making a historic visit to Havana, as well as a final, successful push on the Iran nuclear deal.
In 10 days, Donald Trump will enter his own twilight zone. He is almost certain to lose control of the House and it’s not impossible he will face a Democratic Senate too. Any hopes of passing domestic policy – not that he’s bothered with that much during his first two years – will disappear. Instead, he will face a series of investigations that could lead, once again, to impeachment.
On the world stage, however, it will be a different story. And unlike Bush senior, Clinton and Obama, his ambitions won’t be peaceful. The first two years of his second term have been catastrophic; the final two could be even worse.
Once the midterms are over, the US is understood to be planning to restart its unwinnable war with Iran , already carrying out exercises with the Israeli military and withdrawing diplomats from the region. Trump’s sellout of Ukraine is well under way. In the past week he has argued that “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine”, while his envoy Steve Witkoff met with Vladimir Putin in Moscow, praising him in a televised meeting as a “humanitarian…and I salute that, I commend you and I thank you again.”
On top of a reckless war in the Middle East and appeasement in Europe, the shadow of a new world order is emerging, which Trump will relentlessly pursue in his final years. Putin has proposed a summit between himself, Trump and China’s Xi Jinping , to be held in China next month.
Such an unprecedented meeting, were it to take place, would have potentially devastating consequences for the rest of us. The three leaders have ambitions to transform the way the world is governed, essentially dividing it into spheres of influence. One summit wouldn’t turn an idea into reality, but it would send us down a very dangerous path. In Europe, it would have an impact beyond Ukraine if the US refused to help protect nations threatened by Russia . In east Asia, the withdrawal of the American security blanket would cause enormous problems for Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, as well as Australia.
We’ve talked a lot about the end of the west over the past two years – this feels like a moment when many of those fears will crystalise.
The Trump administration’s ambition to divide the world into spheres and side with dictators over democrats has long been evident. Last year’s National Security Strategy was deeply critical of the US’s traditional allies in Europe and east Asia. But it was what it didn’t say that was most shocking. Both Russia and China avoided direct criticism. In six paragraphs describing the threat to Taiwan, China was not mentioned once. Elsewhere in the document, China was actually praised as “rich and powerful … us[ing] its wealth and power to its considerable advantage.” The section on Russia’s war in Ukraine failed to mention how it started and did not suggest that Putin should be defeated; instead it focused on how the US could help Europe and Russia mend their relationship. The 33-page document discussed the importance of the US controlling the western hemisphere, but made clear that so long as the US still had economic dominance, it cared little whether other parts of the world are protected. “The affairs of other countries,” it stated, “are our concern only if their activities directly threaten our interests.” For too long, it argued, America’s allies had “suck[ed] us into conflicts and controversies central to their interests but peripheral or irrelevant to our own”.
For Putin, this is a success almost three decades in the making. He has long viewed American support for democracy in eastern Europe and central Asia as “interference” in Russia’s backyard. Now he has a US president who agrees. Trump has also placed Putin on a far higher pedestal than Russia’s economy and its technological prowess deserves.
Xi, too, has welcomed the US’s rhetorical retreat from east Asia, particularly if it allows China greater maritime control in the East China Sea and South China Sea. World opinion on China has dramatically improved as that of the US has slid. As Chrystia Freeland, a former Canadian foreign minister, put it this week, “there has not been a president who has been more beneficial for China than Donald Trump”.
At stake is not merely territorial control. All three governments see the possibility of increasing economic ties. For the US and China, the bigger issues are future control of economic supply chains and technology platforms, while Russia’s fossil fuel resources are also a factor. All three are key players in the next space race, both in terms of commercial and military control. If these three nations begin to work together, at the expense of Europe and the rest of the world, it will fundamentally change the nature of geopolitics. A decade ago, talk of a multipolar world was based around the idea of the US, China and the European Union as the three most powerful blocs. Somehow, Brussels has been replaced by Moscow.
Until now, the rest of the west has – on the whole – tried to muddle through. Nato still exists on paper, G7 and G20 summits may be chaotic but they still take place. Optimists in the Foreign Office point out that Trump turned up to the UN general assembly and his administration is still deeply involved in the UN’s day to day activities.
Mark Carney spoke of a “rupture” and warned the old post-cold war world was not coming back, but despite warm words from Emmanuel Macron, and renewed discussion about how Europe can protect itself without the US, there is still a sense that everyone is waiting for Trump’s time in office to end. A Great Powers summit makes this harder to ignore.
While US presidents seek foreign policy success in their final months, history suggests they rarely find it. Clinton’s Camp David talks collapsed after Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat were unable to reach an agreement. Bush would argue that his initial intervention in Somalia eased a famine, but it ended in humiliation. A botched raid on a warlord led to the deaths of 18 US soldiers and several hundred Somalis. Obama’s diplomacy in Cuba and Iran succeeded, but were both promptly ripped up by Donald Trump.
Trump will get his photoshoot – and maybe that’s all he wants – but there is no guarantee that this unsavoury troika becomes a permanent geopolitical fixture. Trump’s foreign policy has divided his Maga movement and has shocked traditional conservatives. The Wall Street Journal editorial board described the proposed summit as “arguably the worst idea of the second Trump term”. A President Vance or Rubio might be less willing to throw in their lot with dictators; a President Ossoff or Ocasio-Cortez certainly won’t.
But just because Trump won’t win, doesn’t mean that the US won’t lose. He will be arriving in Shenzhen at the weakest moment in his presidency. An 80-year-old lame duck leader fated to limp towards the finish line unable to pass any legislation and threatened by two chaotic years of investigations into his alleged corruption. Opposite him will be two authoritarian leaders in their early 70s who believe the only thing preventing them from ruling their nations for another two decades is death. Indeed, given their “hot mic” discussions about longevity drugs last year, perhaps they both believe they can rule for even longer.
If it goes ahead, this summit will bring Putin back in from the cold and reiterate Xi’s position as a global leader who cannot be ignored. The image of the three leaders will come to define this era when the rules-based international order was torn apart and a new, uncertain period began to form.
Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

content:
An electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, too
F rance sneezed, and Europe has again caught the cold. The wave of unrest which began with teenagers at a high school soon drew in hundreds of thousands of people nationwide and then spread across the continent . Protests have filled the streets in Lisbon and Madrid, and have ignited into violence in Milan , Brussels and Tirana as well as in French cities.
French authorities say they are deploying 70,000 officers on Saturday and are allowing only marches organised by unions. They blame hard-left militants as well as opportunistic young perpetrators for last weekend’s destruction and looting, when a minority hijacked largely peaceful protests . But with fuel prices set to rise further over the winter, the demands and participants broadening, and President Macron utterly failing to meet the moment , there is no sign of an end to the wider discontent and no speedy resolution in sight.
Europe is experiencing distinct movements, with distinct causes, demands and actors, which should not be elided. In France, crumbling and overcrowded schools were the touchpaper, with Greek protesters echoing their complaints about educational underfunding this week. In Spain and Portugal, housing is the central issue . German students are angered by the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service . But those involved see the commonalities, with some Italian demonstrators chanting in French.
Underlying all these is the breakdown of the social contract . A generation expect, with reason, to be worse off than their parents. They are understandably angry at inadequate education and job precarity, are struggling to rent places of their own well into their 20s, and are paying for pensions which they don’t believe that they will ever receive themselves, while the climate crisis haunts their futures. They see that governments worried about debt and fearful of the bond markets either cannot or will not offer them solutions. It might be more remarkable if they were happy with their lot, or confident that casting a vote at their next opportunity would fix it.
Meanwhile, increasing inequality means that they watch others grow wealthy, sometimes profiting directly from their misfortune, with flats and houses treated as financial instruments rather than homes.
This unrest also echoes the wave of gen Z protests seen around the world last year – with some of those on the streets in France, Italy and Germany even borrowing emblems used earlier from Morocco to Madagascar. The affordability crisis, heavy-handed security forces and the sense that ordinary people are being left behind while governments have no convincing answers for them were at work in those cases too.
In Europe, far-right parties, egged on by the Trump administration, are seeking to capitalise on the unrest through lies that immigrants and open borders are to blame, and that a strong hand is needed to restore order. Within the next year, four of the biggest states – Spain, France, Poland and Italy – will hold elections, threatening a radical rightwards shift that could fundamentally change the EU. Yet these parties do not have real answers to the questions raised by protesters, and a financial crisis in France might yet highlight Marine Le Pen’s economic weak spot and National Rally’s internal divisions . The future course of the continent is being shaped, for better or worse, on the streets as well as at the ballot box.

content:
The New York mayor’s passion for the Gunners and human rights presents an opportunity to push back on the club’s lucrative UAE sponsorship
L ike him or not, there is no doubt that New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s passion for certain issues is electric, and that passion played a large part in him getting elected. But today, two of his biggest passions are on a collision course.
On one hand, Mamdani is now arguably the US’s most high-profile supporter of English Premier League champions Arsenal. A superfan since he was a child , he has put the Gunners into the American spotlight more than anyone since becoming mayor. The Empire State Building gleamed in Arsenal’s red and white when they won the Premier League title. He wrote an essay about what Arsenal’s championship means to him, talks about Arsenal at press conferences and interviews and inaugurated Thierry Henry Way near Times Square in honor of the Arsenal legend.
But another of Mamdani’s passions – standing up against genocide and for human rights – is now presenting a problem for the mayor’s Arsenal fandom. One prominent part of Arsenal’s current image is deeply disturbing, and it presents a major opportunity for Mamdani.
Arsenal’s chief sponsor is Emirates Airlines, owned by the Emirates Group, a state-owned Dubai-based holding company. Emirates is on the front of every jersey, and the team plays at Emirates Stadium in London. The United Arab Emirates has spent more than $1bn sponsoring the team, including expanding its contract through 2033 to more than $100m per season. Arsenal is the UAE’s second biggest sports investment globally.
The trouble is the UAE is also sponsoring a genocidal militia in Sudan, where war has created the world’s largest displacement crisis, with 14 million people , or a quarter of the country’s population, forced to flee their homes, and 21 million people facing acute hunger. The UAE has provided the militia, known as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), with weapons and killer drones , according to numerous investigations . In fact, the UAE is the RSF’s biggest supplier of weapons and drones.
And therein lies the rub. The UAE is engaging in one of the world’s largest sportswashing campaigns in an attempt to clean up its image, including with Mamdani’s beloved Arsenal. The UAE’s sportswashing isn’t limited to the Gunners. We calculated that the UAE government has spent more than $5.2bn on sponsoring sports teams and leagues around the world, including Manchester City, the NBA champion New York Knicks (a team Mamdani also cheers for), the Emirates NBA Cup and Formula One . There are multiple other football, basketball, cycling, rugby, cricket and UAE-sponsored teams as well.
The good news is that Arsenal’s ownership isn’t blind to abusive sportswashing relationships. Last year, the club announced it was cutting its sleeve sponsor, Visit Rwanda, after the country’s invasion of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the humanitarian catastrophe that ensued as a result. More than 8 million people have been displaced from their homes, as Rwanda has invaded the DRC and commanded the deadly M23 militia that has tortured victims , engaged in extensive sexual violence and enlisted child soldiers . The Arsenal Supporters’ Trust weighed in on the issue, following campaign initiatives such as Gunners for Peace, and the owners changed course.
Now it’s time for Arsenal to tackle their bigger sportswashing sponsor, and Mamdani can play a key role. As one of the world’s most visible Arsenal fans, his voice would have an important impact on the club’s decision makers. The club’s owners are American, Josh and Stan Kroenke, and they have stood up in the past for human rights – for instance, calling for a lifetime ban on former Los Angeles Clippers owner Don Sterling for making racist remarks.
Mamdani could make the Kroenkes and the rest of the Arsenal board aware of the UAE’s sportswashing and call on them either publicly or privately to move on to another sponsor because of the genocidal militia the UAE is sponsoring in Sudan. The club is, after all, awash in cash after winning the league and reaching the final of the Champions League, earning $411m in total, a record for Arsenal. It is now reportedly the most profitable football club in England. So they don’t need the Emirati money.
Importantly, the UAE is not the only game in town for football sponsors – there are viable alternatives. Snapdragon, a Qualcomm tech company, pays approximately the same amount for sponsoring Manchester United as the Emirates pays Arsenal , and automaker Jeep and telecom company T-Mobile pay Juventus and Bayern Munich just a hair under.
Arsenal canceling the deal would also have a meaningful impact on the UAE and on the genocide unfolding in Sudan . The UAE is very sensitive to public image, and a cancelled Arsenal deal would be a major public relations blow. Mamdani’s intervention could have major human rights implications.
Mamdani is passionate about human rights, combating genocide and supporting his favorite team. Urging the club’s leadership to change its sponsor from the UAE would combine all three passions into one and potentially have a positive impact on the world’s deadliest humanitarian crisis. New Yorkers and Arsenal fans alike should encourage Mamdani to weigh in with the club on this important issue.
Sasha Lezhnev is Senior Policy Advisor at The Sentry , where John Prendergast is Co-Founder.

title: A Democratic win in Texas is a long shot – but Ken Paxton’s weakness is obvious | Moira Donegan
description: Republicans are resorting to childish taunts to defend an uncommonly dishonorable state attorney general It’s a bit like Lucy with the football. Every few years, Democrats convince themselves that a Texas Senate seat might finally switch from red to blue. On paper, it makes sense. Texas is a large and urbanizing state with an increasingly educated – and increasingly non-white – population. Other one-time Republican strongholds that have undergone similar demographic shifts have turned purple or even blueish – think Georgia, for example. The border counties along the Rio Grande valley, with their deep poverty and big Latino populations, were long thought to be fertile ground to nurture a kind of anti-Trump populism that could be converted into pro-Democratic sentiment. The state Democratic party is anemic there, but a few talented candidates have emerged. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist Continue reading...
content:
Republicans are resorting to childish taunts to defend an uncommonly dishonorable state attorney general
I t’s a bit like Lucy with the football. Every few years, Democrats convince themselves that a Texas Senate seat might finally switch from red to blue. On paper, it makes sense. Texas is a large and urbanizing state with an increasingly educated – and increasingly non-white – population.
Other one-time Republican strongholds that have undergone similar demographic shifts have turned purple or even blueish – think Georgia, for example. The border counties along the Rio Grande valley, with their deep poverty and big Latino populations, were long thought to be fertile ground to nurture a kind of anti-Trump populism that could be converted into pro-Democratic sentiment. The state Democratic party is anemic there, but a few talented candidates have emerged.
Who else remembers Beto O’Rourke, the former Texas Democratic congressman and onetime presidential hopeful, who appeared on a 2019 cover of Vanity Fair, photographed in muted Annie Leibovitz tones along a desert dirt road, promising to deliver his home state, and a crucial Senate vote, from the clutches of Republican control?
Does that hope seem naive now? Even almost childish? Given what we know of O’Rourke’s subsequent success – or of the voting trends in the Rio Grande valley – does the past hope of a blue Texas begin to seem at all arrogant?
Forgive me, then, for harboring doubts about whether Texas will vote, as some pollsters and many hopeful Democrats now say it will, for James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, over his Republican opponent, the odious state attorney general, Ken Paxton .
The excitement of Democrats in the Texas US Senate race this year carries with it the aftertaste of past disappointments. Lucy swears that this time, she’ll let Charlie Brown kick, and Charlie Brown – a slave to his own optimism – draws back his leg.
But if there was ever a cycle where optimism from Texas Democrats seemed reasonable, it might be this one. Polls have put Talarico, a former seminarian, at a steady, though narrowing, lead. And there is reason for his appeal: Talarico speaks in eloquently religious terms that are well-tailored to his Bible belt audience; at 37, his relative youth will probably appeal to voters fatigued by gerontocracy.
But the real deciding factor in the election may well be his opponent: Paxton is an uncommonly dishonorable man, even by the very low standards of a Republican Senate candidate. He’s been indicted on various fraud charges by Texas grand juries (he denied wrongdoing and eventually paid $300,000 in restitution).
He was sued over similar fraud claims, subjected to multiple whistleblower complaints, nearly disbarred, and impeached in his capacity as attorney general by members of his own Texas Republican party. (He was later acquitted.)
He is also going through a messy, public divorce after his wife of several decades, Angela, finally began proceedings against him after an alleged extramarital affair .
He subjects women to systematic mistreatment in public life, too: as Texas AG, he has presided over one of the most maximalist and sadistic abortion ban regimes, leading to one of the highest maternal and infant mortality rates in the country. He is unlikable, and unliked. Republican Texans who would have come out to vote for another candidate are more likely to stay home rather than vote for him.
If winning a Texas Senate seat has long been a pipe dream for Democrats, the possibility that they might do so seems to be frightening Republicans .
A loss in Texas would not just be a strategic defeat for the GOP, but a psychic one – a failure to hang on to unified power in a state that is supposed to be both the geographical center and the cultural linchpin of conservatism. It presents a risk to the emotions and morale of the Republican party much more than other potential losses in states such as, say, Maine, Michigan or Alaska.
In a word, it would be emasculating. And in characteristic fashion, Republican power players have sought to assert masculinity as their central line of attack in the race.
Over and over, Republicans have sought to keep Texas by insinuating that Talarico is gay, a woman or a pedophile – sometimes all three – and persistently linking him to the issue of gender transition treatment for minors. They have implied that he’s weak, that he’s either asexual or sexually threatening, depending on the occasion, and, weirdly, that he’s vegan.
JD Vance, who has used the midterm cycle to informally launch his 2028 bid for the Republican presidential nomination, has seemingly decided to imitate Trump in vulgarity even where he lags him in charisma and humor. Like many, he’s been trying to get a 2016-style nickname for the Democrat to stick: “Talafreako.” It doesn’t quite roll off the tongue.
But Vance has also suggested that Talarico is gay – and that he would somehow be disqualified from the Senate if he was. At a rally in Tyler, Texas , Vance told a male audience member that he loved him. “In a totally platonic way, to be clear. I’m the vice-president, not James Talarico.” He paused and waited for the crowd to laugh.
Before that, he had insinuated that Talarico was a pedophile. “A guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on transgender children, I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history ,” Vance said.
Elon Musk – nominally a resident of Texas, though billionaires don’t really “reside” anywhere – has looked to rescue Paxton’s candidacy with a massive infusion of cash, dumping $158m into the race late last month on the Republican’s behalf. On his social media platform, X, he has taken on a similar tone to Vance in attacking Talarico, alternating between casting vaguely sexual aspersions about Talarico’s character – Musk has repeatedly called him “creepy” – and making specific, incendiary and false claims about the Texas Democrat. “Talarico would vote to take away your kids and transition them,” Musk wrote. “Not just in Texas, but nationwide. Pure evil.”
These kinds of low-brow, sexualized smears are the kind of thing Republicans do to make themselves look tough. The name-calling is supposed to evoke the power of the schoolyard bully in the form of a man in a suit, to conjure the image of someone so powerful that rules, and decorum, don’t apply to him.
But I think that really, these kinds of juvenile taunts are a sign of the party’s weakness. Republicans have no answer to mainstream Americans’ economic pain; all they can offer are titillating little libidinal gratifications for their base.
They are betting that the grim satisfaction of dominance, of cruelty, will be more important to voters than $5 gasoline. They’re leaning into being mean, in short, because they don’t have anything else.
Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

title: The Trump-Putin love story’s next chapter: selling out Ukraine | Sidney Blumenthal
description: The US president is portraying Zelenskyy as the villain as he strives for Russia’s approval If Donald Trump could, he would fly to Munich to sign away Ukraine to Vladimir Putin, and return to wave the document as “peace in our time”, hoping to claim at least the second Fifa peace prize.
