content:
The US president is portraying Zelenskyy as the villain as he strives for Russia’s approval
If Donald Trump could, he would fly to Munich to sign away Ukraine to Vladimir Putin , and return to wave the document as “peace in our time”, hoping to claim at least the second Fifa peace prize.
Whatever the complicated motives of Neville Chamberlain, his well-grounded fear after the carnage of a world war of another apocalypse and his wishful thinking that Hitler would be satiated after carving up Czechoslovakia, Chamberlain had not sent his son-in-law and former golf partner and real estate partner in advance to cut back-end deals with the Nazis to profit for his family and cronies.
Though Chamberlain is judged as grievously misguided in history, Winston Churchill eulogized his “perfect sincerity according to his lights” and declared his mistaken gesture as rooted in the “noble and benevolent instincts of the human heart”.
Putin has proposed a meeting with Trump and Xi Jinping to settle the Ukraine war on Russian terms without the presence of the troublesome Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Wall Street Journal described such a meeting as “unprecedented”.
As a historical matter, that would be untrue. The Czechs were not present at Munich when their country was delivered to Hitler.
Part of Trump’s urgent reason for selling out Ukraine is to cast blame before the midterm elections for the inflation wrought by his tariffs and Iran war. Panicked by plunging polls, he has ramped up his rhetoric against Zelenskyy as the alleged source of the crisis that Trump himself has created.
Portraying Zelenskyy as the villain, Trump projects himself, as usual, as the victim. His perceived political need and irreducible pathological neediness dovetail with his longtime admiration of Putin as the unconstrained strongman he has always wished to be.
Since Trump’s first visit to Moscow in 1987, he has dreamed of the bonanza of Russian deals to be lavished on him from Putin. Upon his return, he paid for full-page ads in major newspapers calling for the US to stop funding the defense of countries capable of defending themselves and to cease defending the flow of oil through the Gulf. “The world is laughing at America’s politicians as we protect ships we don’t own, carrying oil we don’t need, destined for allies who won’t help,” the ad said.
From the start, the ideology has been a token of his greed, decades before he hawked his “America First Collection” of digital tokens . Putin has been the unwavering object of his aspiration, one of the few people he has not betrayed or sought to humiliate, but to whom he bends his knee.
“ Together, ” tweeted Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s head of the Russian sovereign wealth fund, over a graphic showing the Russian bear and the American eagle on the same side poised to fight against the British lion and a shattered European Union flag. He was celebrating on 16 October what he conceived as the new axis against the western allies the same day that Trump waived sanctions against Russia under the Lindsey Graham Act.
Graham, who died in Washington just hours upon returning from a visit of support to Ukraine, was hailed as Trump’s closest friend in the Congress, which passed the bill overwhelmingly, Democrats and Republicans in rare unity.
Graham’s sister, Darline Graham Nordone, whom Trump imposed on the South Carolina governor to be appointed as the martyr’s replacement, was prominently made the marquee sponsor, lending the novice senator a credential. In a Republican primary debate, she said : “National security is not my thing.”
When Trump tossed aside the Graham Act without bothering to consult her, she was left to sputter an ineffectual objection, leaving her vulnerable in an unexpectedly close race. Her prospect and dignity were shards of Trump’s collateral damage.
Trump vehemently blamed Zelenskyy for supposedly prolonging the war, called him “not a good guy for us to deal with”, and said that the Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries were a “ disgrace ” and had “ better damn well stop ”, and that Ukraine needed a “new leader who can make a deal”.
After an hour-and-a-half phone call with Putin on his 74th birthday, so friendly that neither wanted to hang up the phone first, according to Yuri Ushakov, Putin’s aide , Trump announced his sweetheart deal for 300,000 metric tons of diesel from Russia , followed in November by 500,000 and an additional million. For this, Trump waived sanctions.
The stunt gives Putin hard cash to continue operating his war machine, while the diesel will be statistically insignificant to the price in the US market. The US consumes 300,000 tons within 14 hours. Zelenskyy called this a “happy birthday gift to Putin”. The effect of Trump’s transaction could not help struggling American consumers, but is a practical help to sustain Putin’s aggression.
Trump’s giveaway was followed by the sudden restriction of Ukrainian access to the Starshield network, managed by Elon Musk for the Pentagon, that is indispensable to Ukraine’s defense. For a week, in an Abbott and Costello routine of “who’s on first”, Musk blamed the Pentagon, while Trump claimed to be out of the loop. “It wasn’t me and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said.
Ukraine’s frontline communications were immediately degraded. The outage directly preceded barrages of Russian missile strikes that knocked out energy infrastructure and left 600,000 Ukrainians without power. Slowly, after outraged reaction from the Europeans and Congress, connectivity was mostly but not completely restored.
Musk, whose businesses are dependent on federal contracts, is the largest donor to the Republican campaigns in the midterm elections, spending $366m so far, exceeding the $276m he spent to elect Trump in 2024.
The diesel deal was a successful ploy as part of Putin’s larger scheme to leverage Russian energy assets as bait to Trump in order to end US support for Ukraine. In early September, Putin pitched Trump’s self-interested envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, on the vast international assets of Lukoil, Russia’s second-largest oil company, requiring a treasury department waiver, thereby opening the door for a host of shadow agreements.
The Abu Dhabi royal family and the Qatari Al-Khayyat brothers would hold a large part of the equity, the New York Times reported. The Qatari investors are simultaneously partnered with Kushner on his luxury real estate project in Albania, which has provoked a popular uprising called “the Flamingo revolution”.
Another partner in the Lukoil consortium, Todd Boehly, CEO of Eldridge Industries, a holding company, and co-owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers and Lakers, has donated $2m to Trump’s political action committee, Maga Inc.
The negotiator on the Russian side, Kirill Dmitriev, is the one who enthusiastically tweeted: “ Together .” But the Lukoil deal is hardly the only one apparently in the pipeline; Trump laid the groundwork for an array of post-sanctions opportunities. “A classified report produced by a European intelligence agency states that Trump and people around him have discussed several potential contracts in Russia,” Dexter Filkins reported in the New Yorker. The document detailed 10 ventures after a “peace deal” – that is, after forcing a Ukrainian surrender on Russian terms.
Against this background of the Russian strategy, large and small movements of Trump and his family become clarified, from the Kushner-Witkoff-Dmitriev negotiations to Don Jr’s wedding party in the Bahamas paid for in part by a Putin thug, Umar Kremlev, head of the Olympic-banned International Boxing Association.
A “large” contingent of Russians was present at the intimate wedding party, according to ProPublica , but their identities remain unknown. Kushner was also present at the celebration.
Fiona Hill, who served as Trump’s director for Russian affairs on the national security council in his first term, has described Trump as awestruck in his relationship with Putin. Trump envied him as the “ ultimate badass ”. She observed how Trump’s pathetic need to be seen as a peer to the autocrat allowed him to be played like a fiddle .
At the 2018 Helsinki summit, she was horrified when Trump dismissed the findings of the US intelligence community that Russia had interfered in the presidential election of 2016 on his behalf, deferring to Putin by saying : “President Putin says it’s not Russia. I don’t see any reason why it would be.”
Hill thought she might stage a fake medical emergency or pull a fire alarm to stop Trump from humiliating himself and the US.
But that was during the first term, before Trump grasped how to use the presidency, with official immunity granted by the supreme court, to forge his own kleptocratic state to achieve his highest aspiration: attaining the exalted law-free status of Putin. Trump’s effort to become the full partner with Russia makes his pay-for-play ballroom seem a mere bauble by comparison.
Among Trump’s infinite abuses is his suborning of the Department of Justice to pursue his retribution snark hunt of a “grand conspiracy” of his alleged enemies of the “deep state” for perpetrating the “Russia hoax”, those national security officials who asserted the factual truth that Russia interfered in the 2016 election to benefit him.
In early October, however, the key man appointed to run this operation, the veteran Washington attorney deep into rightwing causes, Joe diGenova, resigned, “saying top department officials were pressuring the team to bring criminal cases before they were ready”, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Nobody now observing Trump’s relations with Putin is accusing him of “collusion”. There is no secrecy. Trump brazenly proclaims his aspiration to partner with Russia and to become the equal of Putin. “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much,” he said .
After Russia released an American schoolteacher imprisoned for four years on what the state department called false charges, a human chip to personify Putin’s gratitude to Trump, Witkoff praised Putin: “ You are a humanitarian .”
Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press that if Trump “will take the side of Russia”, it would be a “a historic mistake and big tragedy”. Dmitriev tweeted Trump’s remark: “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given us nothing.” Dmitriev added his comment: “Clarity.”
Nobody in retrospect will eulogize Trump for “noble and benevolent instincts of the human heart”.
Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man , Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth . He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

title: America must reverse Trump’s moral squalor | Robert Reich
description: The president shows a unique disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation – and, for that matter, humanity The Democrats’ focus on affordability seems to be a winning strategy (we’ll know for sure in a little over two weeks). But we mustn’t lose sight of the moral squalor at the core of the Trump regime and the necessity of ending it. It’s that moral squalor – the utter disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation and, for that matter, of humanity – that uniquely marks Trump and the reprobates he has attracted to Washington. It has also poisoned much of the Republican party, including the billionaires and tech bros who finance it. Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK Continue reading...
content:
The president shows a unique disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation – and, for that matter, humanity
T he Democrats’ focus on affordability seems to be a winning strategy (we’ll know for sure in a little over two weeks). But we mustn’t lose sight of the moral squalor at the core of the Trump regime and the necessity of ending it.
It’s that moral squalor – the utter disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation and, for that matter, of humanity – that uniquely marks Trump and the reprobates he has attracted to Washington. It has also poisoned much of the Republican party, including the billionaires and tech bros who finance it.
To put this despicable era behind us, we’ll need to renounce and reverse this squalor.
What are loosely described as Trump’s “conflicts of interest”, for example, extend way beyond enriching himself from his presidency. He has violated the norms of presidential decency.
He recently decided to host the Group of 20 annual summit of world leaders at his private golf club in Miami in December. When he sought to do this during his first term, it was viewed as a blatant violation of the emoluments clause of the constitution. Now, after America’s moral sensibilities have been numbed by Trump’s appetite for foreign gifts – such as Qatar’s “donation” of a $400m jumbo jet – it barely merits a mention.
Trump’s social media platform Truth Social could reportedly charge up to $100,000 a month for access to “Truth API”, a service that gives subscribers access to potentially market-moving posts by high-profile users such as Trump “in milliseconds”. The service, in other words, enables subscribers to make lucrative stock market trades off market-moving information coming from the president.
A company linked to his family files a trademark application for “Trump TV” to control the name of a streaming service that the White House uses for official presidential communications, thereby pocketing the benefits from taxpayer funds used to create and run the channel.
His family-backed crypto firm introduces a stablecoin just months before he signs legislation promoting that type of cryptocurrency . His wife is paid tens of millions for a self-promotional film by Jeff Bezos’s Amazon, a federal contractor and major retailer subject to a myriad of regulations. His son has a Russian oligarch , close to Putin, pick up the tab for part of his wedding afterparty in the Bahamas.
He arranges for the justice department to grant him and his family immunity for any back taxes and penalties they might owe.
And so on. Trump has tossed away all constraints on making money off his presidency “because I got no credit in the first term” and “I found out that nobody cared”.
Credit? Someone who is entrusted with the highest office in the land must receive “credit” for doing what’s right, in order to continue doing what’s right? Nobody cares? A president can embrace corruption if the public doesn’t mind?
It’s not just the blatant self-dealing. His moral squalor extends to every aspect of governing.
He lies incessantly – a gushing firehose of deception.
His foreign policies make Henry Kissinger’s realpolitik seem principled by comparison. He orders the abduction of the president of another nation, installs a new president of his choosing, and announces he’s taking that nation’s oil – and doesn’t even account for what he does with the oil money.
He attacks Iran without consulting America’s traditional allies or even Congress.
He turns his back on Ukraine and sides with Putin, the aggressor in that conflict. He pursues diesel oil from Putin in violation of US sanctions on Russia and blames the Ukrainian president , Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for high oil prices rather than Trump’s war on Iran. He says Ukraine should get a new president.
The moral squalor extends to usurping the authority of Congress to decide on tariffs, wars and whether and how to spend taxpayer money.
It extends to his cynical defiance of supreme court orders. When the court invalidates his tariffs, he reimposes them under a different statute. When the court rules that he doesn’t have grounds to remove a member of the Fed board of governors, he concocts a means to do so anyway. When the court says he has to remove his name from the Kennedy Center, he closes the center and threatens to demolish it .
It extends to his using the justice department and the FBI to prosecute people who have stood up to him, including courageous officials.
It extends to his claims that Mexicans are “bringing drugs and crime”; calling Somali-Americans “ garbage ” and denouncing “what they’ve done to Minnesota, these people from Somalia”; and taunting Muslims, including by calling Dr Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, “ Mohammed ”.
It extends to giving a gigantic tax cut to America’s wealthiest people, financed by cutting nutrition assistance and healthcare to America’s most vulnerable people.
The moral squalor has turned much of America into a police state – terrorizing large numbers of people residing here, including many here legally.
Deploying ICE agents at schools, courthouses and hospitals. Forcibly taking parents away from their children. Allowing masked gunmen without identification to grab suspected undocumented immigrants off our streets, from their cars, and out of their homes – giving them no opportunity to defend themselves in front of third parties before putting them into often overcrowded and unhealthy prisons or sending them to other countries where they’re imprisoned. Killing people.
When asked if there are limits to his authority, Trump replies : “Yeah, there is one thing. My own morality. My own mind. It’s the only thing that can stop me.”
“My own” morality is no morality at all. Morality reflects collective judgments about right and wrong, shared values about what we owe one another as citizens of the same society. Morality refers to the ideals we seek to achieve together.
Trump is not guided by any sense of right and wrong. He is guided only by what enriches him or gives him more power and glory – a nihilistic might-makes-right in which the strong do whatever they want and the weak suffer what they must.
To be sure, Trump’s moral squalor could not have permeated America – he could not have been elected a second time – had our shared norms and ideals not already been compromised.
Vast inequalities of income and wealth, coupled with a growing sense that the social contract at the heart of the American system was coming undone and that those at the top have rigged the game, were already fueling anger and distrust. Trump ignited that fuel.
Without shared ideals or common moral values, there is nothing pushing back against this despicable president and regime – no countervailing moral force against the ongoing squalor.
Part of the project of ridding ourselves of Trump, therefore, must be to rekindle our understanding of the common good and appreciation of what we owe one another as members of the same society.
Of course we must make life more affordable; Democrats are wise to emphasize this in the midterms. But we also must demand common decency.
Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is at robertreich.substack.com . His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, is out now in the US and in the UK

content:
Former USA team doctor Larry Nassar’s 2018 conviction sparked a global reckoning in gymnastics, yet gymnasts say they are still being let down
I t has been 10 years since the Indianapolis Star published allegations of sexual abuse by Larry Nassar, the former team doctor for USA Gymnastics , setting off a chain of events that would lead to a reckoning for the sport. Hundreds of women came forward with their own allegations against Nassar, who also worked at Michigan State University, leading to his conviction and jailing.
The exposure of his crimes sparked a wider investigation into how gymnastics had allowed predators to abuse young athletes around the world. While Nassar was the worst recorded case, it emerged many other countries had questions to answer about the failure to protect victims from not only sexual but physical and emotional abuse. But a decade later, on a large houseboat moored in Rotterdam three tram stops away from the Ahoy Arena, where the World Gymnastics Championships are taking place this week, survivors and advocates raised fears about the slow pace of change.
The impact of the Nassar case was seismic, not least because of the decision of Judge Rosemarie Aquilina, on agreeing to Nassar’s plea deal, to allow his victims to have their say in her courtroom. People tuned into Aquilina’s courtroom from all over the world to watch as 169 people took to the stand across seven days, delivering blistering, emotionally charged and brave testimonies of Nassar’s abuse and the impact of that abuse. Aquilina sentenced him to up to 175 years in jail with other convictions, federal and state, making a total of 300 years to life.
“ I know, dealing with so many victims, that when they speak publicly you see them shed their pain and get taller. You see them have a relief, an automatic release ,” says Aquilina, perched on a seat in the helm of the boat. “The most interesting thing was that at first I had a list of maybe a dozen names who wanted to speak, then it was 20, then it was 30, and then it got up to 80, 100, etc.
“What happened was that one girl empowered the next, who empowered the next. It was the beginning of their healing because they felt finally heard and believed, in a safe space, and they got to tell him to his face, eyeball to eyeball: ‘You hurt me. I am not a number, I am a name, how dare you?’”
“Nassar constantly wanted control. He wanted to continue to control me, to control the girls, and to say: ‘Look what I’ve done. I took the plea for you’. That was constant … Did he deserve my respect? No. Did he give me respect? No. Did he give any of the victims respect? No. He never owned it. That infuriated me. It should infuriate everyone.”
Among the victims motivated to speak after hearing others’ statements was the Olympic gold medallist Aly Raisman, who was excoriating in blaming USA Gymnastics for enabling Nassar. She was joined by fellow gold medallist Jordyn Wieber, Olympic bronze medallist Jamie Dantzscher and former US national champion Mattie Larson. The mother of the athlete who first complained about Nassar, Maggie Nichols, read out a powerful statement on her behalf. Simone Biles, the most famous gymnast of her generation, revealed she was a victim on social media and later testified publicly in front of the US Senate Judiciary Committee.
Two years after Nassar’s sentencing, a documentary film named after Nichols, called Athlete A, was released, shining a spotlight on the traditional coaching system of compliance, fear and silence and how it allowed Nassar to operate. The documentary opened the global floodgates.
Kim Shore, who was a gymnast in Canada in the 1980s and “experienced all forms of abuse, but also all forms of joy”, was then on the board of directors of Gymnastics Canada, the national governing body, after stepping into governance when her own experiences and direct intervention had failed to prevent the cycle of mistreatment repeating with a family member.
“I absolutely love the sport. I love how it feels in my body. I love so many aspects of it. And yet I spent most of my time surviving it,” she says.
Shore, who is an independent safe sport advocate, says of the impact of the Nassar case: “I was floored, understanding: ‘OK, I wasn’t a bad kid, I wasn’t a bad gymnast, this is why I was treated that way, it’s endemic.’”
Yet the reaction from the organisation was “absolutely lacking”, says Shore. “I remember I sat and watched those girls tell their story in the courtroom and I just bawled. I encouraged the board members that I was associated with to watch it as well.” She does not believe any of them did.
Eloise Jotischky, 23, who at the end of last year won the first civil case against British Gymnastics for the abuses she suffered in the sport, says the impact of the film was being able “to articulate what you’ve been through and find the terms to understand and talk about your experience”.
“It’s very hard to explain it to people who are not within that culture, that sport,” she says. “The only way I can really describe it is that it’s sort of like a cult in a lot of ways. It’s a very closed system, you’re very isolated, in a lot of cases you’re pulled out of school, you’re removed from your friends, you’re travelling to competitions all the time and you’re deprived of a normal social life. I’d say it’s very similar to a coercively controlling relationship in a domestic setting, there’s a lot of parallels there, but you’re a child, so there’s the duty of care issue as well.”
Jotischky stopped training at 14. “By the end, it wasn’t joyous. I think I hated it. You just blame yourself and you think that you’re the problem, until Athlete A comes out. That was about sexual abuse, but the underlying themes of Athlete A are about the physical and emotional abuse, the non-contact physical abuse, which made it get to that point. That’s what all resonated.”
At the same time, the life of former British gymnast and athlete Claire Heafford was in transition. She was splitting from her husband, leaving her dream job and taking up wrestling. “Those major changes were partly taking place because I hadn’t yet realised I’d been so badly abused and that I had some psychiatric issues,” she says.
“I got into professional wrestling when I saw it and felt very drawn to it. I didn’t really understand why, but it’s a performance art that is largely about the performance of masculinity and the violence is clear and obvious. I was really attracted to that being the inverse of my own experiences. I couldn’t understand that at the time. I was like: ‘I’ve gone mad, I’m 36, I’m learning to be a Mexican wrestler. I’m splitting up with my husband. What the fuck’s gone wrong in my life?’
“It was only when Athlete A came out that the penny dropped.”
The documentary made Heafford want to act; she decided to set up Gymnasts for Change, an alliance to bring about safer sport. As the head of Gymnasts for Change International, she brought together the advocates and survivors in Rotterdam.
“Athlete A was seismic. It came out just as Me Too had started,” she says. “On the one hand, Athlete A showed how awful the sexual abuse was and on the other it demonstrated to everybody in the world that gymnastics was a coercively controlling environment built on control and power. It showed that was just what the sport was, that everybody in it had experienced it and that they almost believed that it was necessary.”
The Nassar case triggered a series of reports and new measures in the US including the FBI acknowledging its handling of the case was “inexcusable” and Congress establishing the US Center for SafeSport. That organisation has since faced heavy criticism. USAG went through four presidents in less than two years, said it would adopt 70 of the recommendations in an independent report into preventing sexual abuse and set up an Athlete Bill of Rights. USAG now says athlete safety has been its “top priority since establishing a new board of directors and leadership team in 2018-2019”. It emphasises that “a culture of safety is something that has to be worked on every day, at every level”, requiring all adult USAG members to be trained in safeguarding. Eight members of the board are former elite athletes and one seat is dedicated to that of a survivor.
The case also inspired athletes around the world to speak up about their own experiences of abuse, including in Australia, Brazil and Britain. In Britain, an independent review led by Anne Whyte QC found that physical and emotional abuse were systemic, leading British Gymnastics to launch a 40-point plan aimed at changing the sport. That included a zero tolerance approach to abuse and a gymnast-coach led environment where “both feel empowered to create safe, positive and fair experiences at every level”.
Such an environment is something Aimee Boorman, who is Simone Biles’ former coach, has spent her career advocating for. Boorman channelled her anger at her own experience of negative coaching as a child gymnast into her coaching philosophy. “I knew that I never wanted to make another child feel the way that I felt as a child. So, that was the basis of everything,” she says. “So many times I was told that I wouldn’t be successful because I was too nice. I was like: ‘Well, then I guess I’m not going to be successful by your metrics, your standard, your qualifier for success’. For me, success is having happy, healthy athletes who want to put their children in gymnastics because they have such a good experience.
“Then, I went from being too nice to just being lucky that I had Simone, she’s successful and I’m successful because I was lucky that I had her. No, the reality is that Simone never would have gotten to where Simone is without the training she had from me and the other coaches that she had growing up. So, I’ve just had to hold on to my core beliefs.”
Across Europe, too, gymnasts have spoken out to force change. Former Dutch gymnast Petra Witjes and Germany’s Adina Hausch document falling out of love with the sport because of their experiences.
“At the elite club in the city I moved to it wasn’t fun anymore,” says Witjes, whose book, Silenced for Gold, is a memoir about the systemic abuses within sport and her battle to expose it. “My dad taught me to let my voice be heard but in the gym it was the opposite.”
Witjes was terrified of speaking to her parents, she was taught not to trust them. “I didn’t feel safe at first, because my coach always said that parents don’t understand elite gymnastics,” she says. “They push your parents away from you. We were in total isolation.”
Hausch says an injury that forced her from the sport was a relief. “I was on beam and I slipped with one leg and fell with the other on to the beam and then crashed down,” she says. “The leg was pushed sideways so much that it broke. From the age of 13 I don’t think there was a week without training through pain. When I left after the injury, the worst injury I’ve ever had, I was really happy that I didn’t have to go to the gym anymore.”
In Rotterdam, survivors vary in age from their 50s to their teens; it is hard not to view the issues as systemic and global. And ongoing. Charlotte Jacobs, who is only 18, quit the sport after suffering emotional abuse when training in the UK.
“It got to a point where I was like: ‘I can’t do it anymore’,” she says. “My experience was strange because it wasn’t physical, it wasn’t sexual, but it was emotional. You were ridiculed all the time, constantly. You weren’t allowed to cry, you weren’t allowed to talk, you weren’t allowed to sit down, if you were caught leaning on anything you’d have to run, you needed permission to go to the toilet, you needed permission to drink, and it’s that sort of really controlling, consistent and dismissive behaviour so that no one really felt safe that was prevalent.”
Shore, who is a member of G4C Canada, argues that if a big list of cultural reforms comes from the top, that is then normalised within the national federations and then the clubs “all the way down to grassroots, then I think we would see faster reform and less resistance”.
“The more I learn that the stories are consistent internationally the more it says something about the need for World Gymnastics to take a leadership role,” she says “The treatment across the world is pervasive and coaches are moving from space to space, country to country, more frequently now or they’re not even staying in this sport, they’re moving into other sports, especially if they’ve come into trouble.”
World Gymnastics has moved to address the cross-border issue within the sport at least, publishing a new safeguarding policy last week which notes that the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation, which it launched in 2019 and has handled nearly 500 reports, has the power to extend sanctions imposed by member federations providing they are compatible with the rules of the governing body and general principles of law.
Among the efforts of World Gymnastics to address safeguarding concerns was the launch of the 10 Golden Rules of Gymnastics in 2021, the establishment of a s afeguarding commission in 2022 and, this year, the launch of a safeguarding newsletter and the appointment of a full-time Safeguarding Manager.
Shore believes the pace of governing bodies fully engaging with the change needed has been slow, however, “because to admit that there is harm going on in the sport puts organisations into a liability risk. Also, they have been able to deflect responsibility for so long. They don’t know how to solve it and they are getting pressure from all sides. By putting their head in the sand for literally 50 years we’ve now got to a crisis.”
A statement from World Gymnastics said: “Creating a safe environment for current and future generations of gymnasts is a responsibility that World Gymnastics takes extremely seriously and shares with all stakeholders across the sport. The priority for World Gymnastics is not only to strengthen safeguarding rules and policies, but to ensure that they lead to meaningful changes in everyday practice.”
Heafford alleges that British Gymnastics isn’t entering into meaningful engagement and collaboration with Gymnasts for Change and other survivors in the sport and says that she finds that “extremely frustrating”. She is also hugely critical of the processes gymnasts have to go through in raising a complaint against a coach or gym and what resolution looks like, saying: “In six years, we haven’t had one outcome that we can stand by and say that was a good outcome.”
British Gymnastics, however, insists it has engaged with the organisation regularly which has “helped shape its approach”, including a meeting with G4CI and others in Rotterdam as well as introducting a new complaints and disciplinary process “ to improve transparency and fairness” .
Minky Worden, of Human Rights Watch, fears the situation could worsen. “Sport is getting younger. There’s a youth Olympics about to launch in Senegal. There’s going to be thousands of athletes, every one of them 18 or younger. They’re all children and they’re at a very elite level,” she says. “These children are being monetised and they are not protected because we know the systems are not in place to protect them.”
Hausch wants to see “measurable boundaries, for example increasing the competition age to 18,” she says. “I would root for Germany not to join youth international competitions. Having a 13-year-old do youth European championships is the same as doing it as an adult, it’s the same amount of work you have to put in, the same amount of pressure, it’s not a softer version, it’s the full version, and it doesn’t make sense.”
All agree there needs to be more done to help athletes advocate for themselves and others. Jacobs says: “There needs to be a sort of package of what to look out for. I think there needs to be more training for coaches in terms of mental wellbeing, disability, neurodiversity, all that, alongside what are and are not best practices.
“We need more regulation,” she adds of the British landscape. “Look at the new guidance that’s come out about keeping children safe in education. That’s all been updated. Where’s the guidance for anything sports-wise, extracurriculars, whether it’s swimming, gymnastics, dancing, anything like that?”
British Gymnastics says that it “recognises there is always more to do” but that prevention is “at the heart of our work. We have overhauled learning and development … and set clearer policies and guidance to drive meaningful change.” It says a coach developer network, regional teams and safeguarding and welfare officers in every club support communities.
Jotischky, who is now studying law off the back of her experience, says there are changes needed there too. “The legislative gap that exists is astonishing. You have the 2015 Serious Crime Act section 76, which talks about coercive control, but it’s limited to domestic and familial relationships. Then you have the 2021 Domestic Abuse Act which lists personally connected individuals as only being family members. In a coach-to-athlete relationship where you spend 30 hours a week in the gym with your coach, and some gymnasts even go and live with their coach because they’ve formed such a close relationship, of course coercive control and emotional abuse can happen but it’s not recognised within the law. So, we have very little legislative ground to deal with the most serious cases in particular.”
Listening to this group of women in Rotterdam, what becomes clearer is that while federations, to differing degrees, make changes in the name of athlete safety, survivors are still being failed. Meanwhile, these survivors and knowledgeable advocates remain isolated from the very structures that should be embracing them and channelling their knowledge and understanding of their experiences into the changes necessary to ensure the future health of the sport.
Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: Brewers survive chaotic ninth-inning replay drama to beat Rays in World Series opener
description: Brewers claim 3-2 victory in Game 1 of World Series Yelich triples home a run and scores in first inning Misiorowski and Megill hold off late Rays fightback Trevor Megill struck out Jonny DeLuca with runners on second and third to escape a ninth-inning jam as the Milwaukee Brewers held on for a 3-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night. DeLuca’s strikeout came after Tampa Bay’s Liam Hicks had grounded into an apparent game-ending double play that was overturned after a video review. Replays showed that Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang. Continue reading...
content:
Brewers claim 3-2 victory in Game 1 of World Series
Yelich triples home a run and scores in first inning
Misiorowski and Megill hold off late Rays fightback
Trevor Megill struck out Jonny DeLuca with runners on second and third to escape a ninth-inning jam as the Milwaukee Brewers held on for a 3-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.
DeLuca’s strikeout came after Tampa Bay’s Liam Hicks had grounded into an apparent game-ending double play that was overturned after a video review. Replays showed that Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.
“You have a big range of emotions,” Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich said. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it.”
Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to earn the victory.
“Not perfect, but good enough to get a win,” he said.
Yelich hit a run-scoring triple to spark a two-run rally in the first inning that put the Brewers ahead for good and delighted a sellout crowd reveling in Milwaukee’s first World Series game since 1982. Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.
It was the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.
The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.
Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and had not put a runner on base since the sixth inning until mounting a comeback attempt in the ninth.
Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles off Megill. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put the potential tying run in scoring position with Rays slugger Junior Caminero at the plate. Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.
Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what was initially ruled a game-ending double play.
Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared – before the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.
A replay review determined Pratt’s right foot came off the bag as he caught Turang’s throw. Hicks was still out at first, but the Rays now had runners at second and third with the score 3-2.
“I thought Coop had him, and obviously I was wrong,” Misiorowski said.
Megill finally sealed the win as DeLuca struck out swinging.
“You just have to lock it back in,” Yelich said. “It’s the World Series – you have to do what you have to do to make things happen.”
By sweeping the two-time defending World Series champions, the Los Angeles Dodgers, in the National League Championship Series, the Brewers had time to set up their rotation the way they wanted by handing the Game 1 start to Misiorowski, the hard-throwing NL Cy Young Award favorite.
Misiorowski opened the game by throwing the fastest pitch ever delivered in a World Series, a 103.5mph ball to Yandy Díaz. The right-hander finished with a season-low three strikeouts.
While Milwaukee started with their ace, Tampa Bay countered with Nick Martinez to give two-time All-Star pitchers Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta an extra day of rest. Martinez struck out five and allowed two runs over five innings, but a slow start proved costly.
Chourio lined a single to right field on Martinez’s first pitch, and Yelich drove him home with a one-out triple to centre. DeLuca covered 85ft to track down Yelich’s drive but just missed making a diving catch as the ball glanced off his glove.
Yelich was batting third in the lineup for the first time since 3 August. The three-time All-Star and 2018 NL MVP posted the lowest on-base percentage (.315) and OPS (.692) of his career, but he has stepped up his game since being named the first team captain in franchise history during the final week of the regular season.
He was the seventh player to triple in his first World Series plate appearance, and the first since Kansas City’s Lynn Jones in 1985, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
Contreras knocked home Yelich with a line-drive single to left that was deflected by shortstop Taylor Walls with the infield playing in.
Aranda drew a leadoff walk and advanced to third when Caminero doubled on a one-out liner with a 112.7mph exit velocity that sailed over centre fielder Garrett Mitchell and off his outstretched glove. Aranda came home on Hicks’ groundout to the right side.
Milwaukee extended their lead to 3-1 in the seventh. Pratt drew a leadoff walk from Steven Matz and scored from second when Chourio greeted Kevin Kelly with a two-out single.
“The guys settled in right away and did a great job,” Yelich said. “We still have a ways to go, but it’s nice to get that first one.”

title: Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders unionize after years of fighting for fair pay
description: Team elects to voluntarily recognize union Squad members have advocated for better wages The Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders have unionized, in a watershed labor victory that comes after years of fighting for fair pay. The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association (DCCA) was voluntarily recognized by the Cowboys as the collective bargaining representative for the cheerleading squad, according to a Friday news release. The recognition came after “meaningful discussion” between the Cowboys organization and the DCCA, and the parties are set to begin collective bargaining. Continue reading...
content:
Team elects to voluntarily recognize union
Squad members have advocated for better wages
The Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders have unionized, in a watershed labor victory that comes after years of fighting for fair pay.
The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association (DCCA) was voluntarily recognized by the Cowboys as the collective bargaining representative for the cheerleading squad, according to a Friday news release. The recognition came after “meaningful discussion” between the Cowboys organization and the DCCA, and the parties are set to begin collective bargaining.
“The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders are an esteemed part of the Cowboys organization, deeply respected for the talent and dedication they exhibit,” the DCCA said in a statement. “They remain one of the most sought-after opportunities for talented dancers worldwide.”
Established in 1961, one year after the football team played its inaugural season in the NFL , the Cowboys cheerleaders are among the most recognizable dance groups in the world. The squad’s national profile rose as they were chronicled in a Netflix series, America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, which released its third season in June.
For decades, the franchise has faced scrutiny over the cheerleaders’ low salaries, despite their enduring pop culture relevance.
The squad’s compensation was largely shrouded in mystery until details spilled into the public view in 2018, when cheerleader Erica Wilkins filed a federal fair wage lawsuit against the Cowboys. Wilkins claimed she averaged $15,000 during her seasons with Dallas and said she made less money than the team’s male mascot. The Cowboys are the NFL’s most valuable franchise at $17bn, per Forbes.
The second season of America’s Sweethearts followed oft-tense contract negotiations – including threats of a walkout – involving the 36-member team. Several squad members spoke of holding full-time jobs in addition to their demanding DCC schedule so they could pay their bills.
By the end of the season, the dancers received a 400% pay raise, increasing the hourly rate for some members from $15 per hour for the 2024 season to $75 per hour. One squad member told the New York Times that while the new contract increased wages for game day appearances, it did not provide health insurance.
The Cowboys cheerleaders are not the first in the NFL to form a union. In 1995, the National Labor Relations Board ruled that the Buffalo Bills cheerleaders could unionize. The Buffalo Jills, as they were known, joined the National Football League Cheerleaders Association. The union was short-lived and the Jills squad disbanded in 2014.

title: F1 crown in reach for Kimi Antonelli at bumpy Austin circuit drivers insist is ‘unacceptable’
description: Mercedes youngster could become youngest title winner Max Verstappen says bumpy track makes drivers ‘suffer’ The Formula One world championship is within reach for Kimi Antonelli at the US Grand Prix in Austin this weekend. content:
Mercedes youngster could become youngest title winner
Max Verstappen says bumpy track makes drivers ‘suffer’
The Formula One world championship is within reach for Kimi Antonelli at the US Grand Prix in Austin this weekend. But while the young Italian approaches the race ­intending simply to have fun, there is disquiet among other ­drivers about the potential long-term health ­dangers posed by the state of the Texas circuit.
The 20-year-old Antonelli will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he claims the title at the Circuit of the Americas on Sunday, eclipsing Sebastian Vettel’s record from 2010, when the German driver was 23 and Antonelli was four. It is an outside chance, as the Italian has acknowledged. He must win while needing his rivals to endure a poor day. His Mercedes teammate George Russell would have to finish outside the top eight and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton outside the top four.
Nonetheless, while Antonelli knows the title race is in effect over, he is keeping the cool head that has brought him to this point with such alacrity. The Mercedes ship, helmed by his race engineer Pete Bonnington, who was alongside Hamilton for his six titles with the team, is steady as she goes.
“We had a meeting with Bono this morning and we said: ‘Just have fun,’” Antonelli said. “It’s the same mindset I’ve had all year. One race at a time. Just try to do the best I can every race weekend, and then we’ll see.”
After a tricky rookie season last year, Antonelli has adapted remarkably quickly to competing at the front of the grid. But as he seeks to close out the title, he feels able to draw on previous experience.
“Formula One is different because the pressure is a lot bigger than in anything else,” he added. “The competition is a little bit higher as well because you’re racing with 21 of the best drivers in the world. But when you fight for championships in karting and junior series, the mindset is very similar in the way you approach races and the way you think.”
Going into the weekend, however, the circuit has drawn unusually severe criticism from drivers. The race was first held in 2012 and the circuit has a contract until 2034. It has become hugely popular, with sold-out crowds, but the track has come under intense scrutiny.
It is built on marshland and the bumps caused by the ground beneath the track have been condemned as potentially harmful, with the uneven surface forcing impacts into the base of the drivers’ spines.
Max Verstappen, Red Bull’s four-time world champion, said: “The bumps are unacceptable. Over time they’ve been grinding a little bit here and there but it’s just putting a plaster on the big problem. You need to really fully open up the track. That costs a lot of money and time but that’s the only way to get rid of it because these bumps are not natural and they are out of control.
“From the checks that I’ve done from my spine, the bottom end doesn’t look that great. I know that’s part of racing. I know that can be part of sport, but it’s also further damage from the cars that we had the last few years. If we continue with finding this acceptable to drive on, then you are going to suffer with that much more.”
Verstappen’s opinion was echoed by the defending world champion, Lando Norris, who is frustrated that drivers’ concerns are not being ­listened to. “It’s pretty bad,” he said. “There’s a lot of places I need to take headache tablets before I go out simply because it’s so bumpy and you’re hitting your head pretty hard against the headrest because of the bumps. So it’s certainly not a nice thing. There’s not much we can do. I mean, we complain about it, it’s stuff we’ve brought up many, many times but there’s only so much we can ­complain about things.”
In first practice at the Circuit of the Americas, Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc topped the timesheets from Verstappen, with Lando Norris third for McLaren and Russell and Antonelli in fourth and fifth. Ferrari had brought their final swathe of upgrades to the race and on the early showing they had found some extra pace.
In the afternoon running Leclerc was once more on top, four hundredths clear of Antonelli in second. Verstappen was in third, from Hamilton in fourth.

title: United Airlines CEO faces rightwing backlash after calling for US wealth tax
description: Scott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interview Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview. Talking to the New York Times , Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust. Continue reading...
content:
Scott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interview
Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines , is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview.
Talking to the New York Times , Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust.
“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”
In response, headlines from Fox Business and the New York Post decried that Kirby made $32m in 2025. In response to Kirby’s comments, Glenn Beck, a former Fox News host, and other users on X called for a boycott of United Airlines. Jeff Landry, Louisiana’s governor, said the statement was “audacious”.
“How audacious from a guy that didn’t even build @united and makes $32 million a year,” he wrote on X, adding a link to a government website to donate money to the government. “Better yet, he should distribute his salary to the employees at the bottom of the ladder @united!”
“Let’s see you step up and place your money where your mouth is!” Landry added.
The comment comes just two weeks before voters in California will decide on a so-called “billionaire’s tax”, which would put a 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, that the wealthy have been spending millions fighting against.
Kirby was also asked about the rising cost of flying and said that high prices this year were being compared to the “artificial low” prices from the pandemic, which largely halted travel and highly disrupted the airline industry.
“We have to charge enough that it covers the cost of flying, and it’s expensive to fly airplanes,” he said.
When asked about the $70 passengers must pay to sit in an aisle or window seat if they aren’t a frequent flyer with United, Kirby responded that “the way to give everyone what they want is to charge for the services and products that those customers want,” adding: “There are customers that pay more that get more.”
Kirby also maintained that fares were still lower than in 2019 after adjusting for inflation. According to data from the labor department, the index for airline fares increased by about 20% from September 2019 to September 2026, while overall consumer prices increased by 31%.

title: HelloFresh workers claim physical abuse and denied bathroom breaks in class-action suit
description: The meal kit delivery service denies the allegations, saying it found claims to be ‘entirely without merit’ Workers at a HelloFresh facility in Newark, New Jersey , have claimed in court documents that they were verbally and physically abused and denied regular bathroom breaks, with one former worker telling the Guardian he experienced incontinence issues as a result. The newly proposed amended complaint comes in a class-action lawsuit first filed in August 2024 against the food prep service giant and staffing agencies. A New Jersey state court judge is expected to review the amended complaint in a hearing scheduled for 23 October. Continue reading...
content:
The meal kit delivery service denies the allegations, saying it found claims to be ‘entirely without merit’
Workers at a HelloFresh facility in Newark, New Jersey , have claimed in court documents that they were verbally and physically abused and denied regular bathroom breaks, with one former worker telling the Guardian he experienced incontinence issues as a result.
The newly proposed amended complaint comes in a class-action lawsuit first filed in August 2024 against the food prep service giant and staffing agencies. A New Jersey state court judge is expected to review the amended complaint in a hearing scheduled for 23 October.
In the civil lawsuit, workers allege HelloFresh and temp staff managers took ID badges from temp workers that are required to be able to leave the facility, repeatedly threatened to call ICE and immigration authorities on workers, subjected workers to physical and verbal abuse, sexually harassed Hispanic female employees, and discriminated against the temp workforce that consisted primarily of Hispanic workers in violation of New Jersey’s anti-discrimination laws.
A spokesperson for HelloFresh denied all allegations in the lawsuit.
“Upon learning of these allegations, which date from 2023 and years prior, we conducted a thorough internal investigation and found these claims to be entirely without merit. We vehemently denied these allegations when this lawsuit was filed over two years ago, and we continue to vehemently deny them today,” the spokesperson said in an email.
In a reply to the lawsuit filed by HelloFresh in April 2025, the subscription-based meal kit delivery service denied the allegations in the lawsuit.
Action Staffing, On Target Staffing and ProStaff Workforce Solutions did not respond to multiple requests for comment but have moved to dismiss the lawsuit.
The lawsuit alleges HelloFresh assigned its Hispanic workers “the hardest work”, and that supervisors consistently made racist, abusive remarks to workers and berated them for speaking Spanish rather than English. The suit claims supervisors enforced a no-cellphone policy for Hispanic workers, while not enforcing it for others.
Luis Penafiel, a former temp worker at the HelloFresh distribution center in Newark, New Jersey, from November 2021 to August 2023, and a plaintiff in the lawsuit claims that the working conditions began to deteriorate shortly after he was hired. “We started to realize that because we were Latinos, we were being forced to do all these kinds of duties. We started noting the discrimination,” he said.
“We were afraid of punishment for complaining,” said Penafiel. “We want the authorities to listen to us and to realize the conditions that people are working under at these places.”
According to the complaint, workers also alleged Hispanic workers were required to use a sign-out system in order to use the bathroom and that management policed the time they spent in the bathroom.
“There were many times I had to hold it for hours because they would note down the time you went in,” Penafiel said. “I had to go to the clinic to a urologist because I started experiencing incontinence, as I had to hold it for a long time and ended up getting infections.”
The lawsuit claimed non-Hispanic workers were allowed to use the bathroom whenever they wanted and for however long, often with the temp workers expected to fill in on work lines for direct hires when they took longer breaks or were using the bathroom.
“On several occasions, a HelloFresh manager menaced Hispanic workers with a baseball bat to limit their time in the bathroom and force them to return to work on HelloFresh’s production line,” the complaint alleges. “HelloFresh’s bathroom policy was so restrictive that several Hispanic workers were forced to urinate on themselves and continue to work because their supervisors denied them permission to use the bathroom.”
It added, “defendants’ bathroom policies were so restrictive that at least one member of the Hispanic Employee Class brought multiple pairs of underwear and fresh clothes to work because she was forced to urinate on herself on several occasions.”
The complaint alleges instances of workers grabbing female employees’ body parts, having managers show workers pornography and photos of their genitalia, using loaves of bread and cucumbers to simulate sex acts, and regularly propositioning female workers for sex.
“HelloFresh supervisors physically assaulted and battered several Hispanic employees during their employment at HelloFresh,” the lawsuit alleges, arguing the alleged assaults were done in view of other Hispanic employees with the intent of inducing fear of not following supervisors’ directives.
The lawsuit described the alleged assaults as managers “physically beating workers”, “putting their hands around workers’ necks” and “screaming in workers’ ears”. The lawsuit also claimed workers were denied medical treatment for injuries sustained on the job.
“When people would raise complaints about what they were suffering, what supervisors were doing, they were bounced back and forth between HelloFresh and the staffing agencies with very little resolution, so there was really no place for people to go with these complaints,” said Lauren Herman, an attorney with Make the Road New Jersey and one of the plaintiff’s attorneys in the lawsuit.
“I think this lawsuit really illustrates what happens when you have effectively a two-tier labor force in the economy where we have the kind of aggressive immigration enforcement that’s happening right now that leaves people feeling so vulnerable that employers can hold their immigration status over their heads in this way and use that as a tool to exploit them,” said Michael Scimone, a partner at Outten and Golden representing the workers in the lawsuit.
In court filings, the staffing agencies claimed HelloFresh offered direct employment to all workers, which the plaintiffs’ lawsuit disputes.
Target Staffing’s attorneys argued in its motion to dismiss that the workers falsified their immigration documents and would not clear HelloFresh’s verification system. They also claimed no workers ever complained about the work environment at HelloFresh.
The requests from each staffing agency to dismiss claims alleging violation of the New Jersey Human Trafficking Prevention, Protection, and Treatment Act were granted, though the judge allowed the plaintiffs to file an amended complaint to specify individually named plaintiffs or defendants.
In December 2024, the US Department of Labor announced an investigation into a different staffing agency at a HelloFresh facility in Illinois over allegations that migrant children were working at the facility. HelloFresh noted it terminated its relationship with the agency upon learning about the allegations.
“Our frontline workforce is the foundation of our company, and ensuring a safe, fair, and respectful workplace is our highest priority,” HelloFresh said in an email. “HelloFresh maintains robust anti-discrimination and anti-harassment policies governed by our Employee Handbook and Global Code of Ethics . They are backed by mandatory training and multiple reporting channels, including a 24/7 confidential hotline for anonymous complaints. We take every concern seriously and remain fully dedicated to upholding a culture of integrity and accountability.”

title: Small business owners are doing OK – but will that help Trump overcome his low approval ratings?
description: Overall, economic sentiment for Trump is poor, but small businesses seem fairly confident, according to several surveys There are 34m small businesses in the United States. They employ approximately half of the country’s workers and generate about half of the country’s GDP. They’re an important voting block. So how are they feeling about the economy as we head into November’s midterm elections? Overall, economic sentiment for Donald Trump is poor but small business – admittedly a diverse demographic that’s hard to poll – seems fairly confident. A number of recently published surveys and reports can help understand their mood. Confidence is generally stable. Continue reading...
content:
Overall, economic sentiment for Trump is poor, but small businesses seem fairly confident, according to several surveys
T here are 34m small businesses in the United States. They employ approximately half of the country’s workers and generate about half of the country’s GDP. They’re an important voting block. So how are they feeling about the economy as we head into November’s midterm elections? Overall, economic sentiment for Donald Trump is poor but small business – admittedly a diverse demographic that’s hard to poll – seems fairly confident. A number of recently published surveys and reports can help understand their mood.
This week, the National Federation of Independent Businesses said that its Small Business Optimism Index fell to just below its long-term average, while uncertainty rose slightly. Labor quality was the top concern for 26% of owners and inflation for 20%. Expansion plans weakened, though 17% still plan to add jobs during the next three months.
However, small-business confidence improved significantly in the third quarter, according to the recently published Justworks/US Chamber Small Business Index . Some 72% of the 750 small businesses surveyed say they are comfortable with their current cash flow, but only 27% believe the US economy is in good health. Inflation remains the biggest problem, cited by 54% of owners.
Hiring is not strong, but not weak either.
HR platform Gusto estimated that small businesses added 28,000 jobs in September, making it the eighth consecutive month of employment gains following a decline in January. According to the company’s data, hiring accelerated from August’s revised gain of 18,500 jobs and growth was broad across industries, regions and company sizes, with healthcare and social assistance among the strongest sectors. Particularly notable is that some of the smallest employers continue to participate in the expansion, rather than job growth being concentrated solely among larger companies.
In its latest Small Business Employment Watch report, Paychex, another large HR and payroll processing service (and a client of my company), said that hiring in September essentially matched its 2026 year-to-date average with overall employment among companies with fewer than 50 employees appearing “stable”.
ADP , the country’s largest HR and payroll processing service, reported that US private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, with hiring accelerating for the first time since May following three months of slowing growth. Education and healthcare and leisure and hospitality led the gains, while financial activities and professional and business services were weaker. Importantly for small businesses, establishments employing one to 19 workers added 18,000 jobs. According to ADP, private-sector employers have not shifted into recession mode and although hiring has cooled from earlier periods, businesses are still adding employees.
Intuit painted a slightly different jobs picture. Its Intuit QuickBooks Small Business Index , which is based on data it gathers from its millions of QuickBooks customers, found that employment at US businesses with one to nine employees fell by 7,000 jobs in September and that jobs declined across most sectors and regions.
Intuit’s QuickBooks data shows that revenues moved sharply up this past month as inflation-adjusted average monthly revenue increased 1.68% and growth occurring in 11 of 12 industries, every region and 19 of 20 states.
Fiserv , a payment-processing service, said that its September data showed improving sales among US small businesses. However, the company reports that consumer behavior remains selective and that traffic has been weaker even as customers spend more when they do shop.
Economic growth continued in the third quarter.
Overall, US manufacturing remained firmly in expansion territory in September. The Institute for Supply Management’s Manufacturing Purchasing Manager’s Index marked its ninth consecutive month of growth after years of contraction. Despite rising prices, new orders, production and employment all remained expansionary and order backlogs increased. As usual, the ISM reported yet another month of expansion in the service sector (it’s been 27 consecutive months) with new orders remaining “particularly strong”.
The Wall Street Journal and other media sources reported recently that first-quarter annualized growth was revised to 2.5% from 2.1%, and second-quarter growth was increased to 2.2% from 1.5%, which, its editors argued , shows that the “US economy is performing considerably better than pessimistic headlines imply”.
My business is based in Philadelphia, a heavily Democratic area in a swing state. My clients appear to mostly be doing well so far this year but, like most small businesses around the country, continue to struggle navigating higher costs and a tight labor market.
This anecdotal evidence is somewhat supported by a May survey by WSFS Bank that found “surprisingly strong confidence among Philadelphia-area businesses” despite inflation and economic uncertainty. In that study, 92% of owners and business decision-makers say their companies are meeting or exceeding expectations, while 66% anticipate growth during the next year.
Philadelphia, however, has its own unique problems, particularly adding fewer small businesses per capita than other large cities. A recent study from Pew Research found that the number of Black-, Hispanic- and female-owned small businesses increased 39% between 2012 and 2022, showing meaningful entrepreneurial growth, but barriers including access to capital, regulatory requirements, taxes, commercial space and the difficulty of scaling companies continued to restrain business formation in the city.
The Democratic strategist James Carville once said that when it comes to electing candidates, “it’s the economy, stupid”. The good news for the Republicans is that the economy is resilient and the overall mood of the country’s small businesses is generally optimistic, despite the many challenges they face. But will that overcome the president’s low approval ratings?

content:
Electrifying your block of flats could cut emissions and save money. Don’t wait to plan the change
Change by degrees offers life hacks and sustainable living tips each Saturday to help reduce your household’s carbon footprint
Got a question or tip for reducing household emissions? Email us at changebydegrees@theguardian.com
Around Australia, homes are getting off gas. Gas cooktops are being swapped for induction stoves , gas hot water replaced by heat pumps , and gas space heating with reverse cycle air conditioners .
In combination with solar panels, batteries and better insulation, electrification saves money, cuts emissions and makes homes healthier to live in .
Electrifying a freestanding house is often straightforward. Apartments are more challenging because you generally need your neighbours’ cooperation.
“It’s relatively easy for an individual apartment owner to replace a gas cooktop with an induction stove,” says Luke Barry, an engineer at GHD.
But if every apartment owner in a building does the same thing, he warns, then the extra electrical load could overwhelm the main switchboard.
Piecemeal replacement of gas appliances with electric devices and uncoordinated installation of electrical vehicle chargers may even require an expensive upgrade of the building’s connection to the grid.
Extra load can be offset by installing solar panels, and it’s now possible to fairly distribute the power they generate with technology like SolShare, which won top honours in the 2026 Australian Good Design Awards.
But many apartments also have centralised gas-fired facilities like hot water heaters, swimming pool heaters, or HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) systems that provide building-wide heating, ventilation and cooling and rely on gas boilers to generate warmth.
Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads
Replacing this equipment requires action by the organisation that manages common property in a building, known in some states as the owners corporation and in others as the strata corporation or body corporate.
“Usually in energy efficiency you are dealing either with owner-occupiers or with tenants and their landlords,” says Trent Jones, founder and managing director of All Electric Homes. “But in an apartment complex you also have a third actor to contend with – the owners corporation and its elected committee.”
While all apartment owners are automatic members of the owners corporation, many pay little attention to committee meetings and decisions, making it hard to get everyone on board with big changes like electrification.
Sometimes, everything goes smoothly. At the recent High Life Living expo , Jones presented a case study of a block of 18 flats in Brunswick in Melbourne’s inner north. The owners contracted All Electric Homes to replace their building’s failing gas hot water system with a bank of heat pumps backed by solar panels. The work took four days and wiped out the building’s $19,000 annual gas bill. The investment paid for itself in less than two years.
In a larger apartment building, the issues can be more complex.
It’s technically difficult, for example, to replace the gas boilers in HVAC systems with heat pumps. First, the boilers need to generate much higher temperatures than can easily be achieved with heat pumps. Second, it can be hard to find enough room for banks of heat pumps, especially in towers that have lots of apartments and limited roof space.
As GHD’s senior sustainability consultant, Barry is leading a City of Melbourne program to assess the feasibility of electrifying 13 medium- and high-rise apartment buildings. He hopes that these case studies will chart new ways forward for retrofitting existing apartment blocks.
“The technical solutions are often quite easy,” says Jones. “The difficulty is getting everyone to agree on what needs to be done.”
“The larger the building, the more likely it is that there’ll be dissent,” says Dr Janette Corcoran, board director of the not-for-profit Owners Corporation Network that advocates for people who own and live in strata titled apartments.
Presenting electrification as an environmental initiative can complicate the issue by polarising neighbours into pro- and anti-groups, she cautions.
“Lowering emissions appeals to some people but not to everyone. Once people feel you’ve got an agenda, they start getting their backs up.”
To defuse this risk, Corcoran recommends treating electrification like any other major work to maintain a property in good condition.
“There are always a lot of infrastructure needs to be looked at in an apartment building. For example, a lot of buildings may need facade replacement or lift upgrades.”
She recommends that owners committees include the replacement of gas equipment in their plans for long-term maintenance and capital works.
With a horizon of a decade or so, these plans don’t just consider what upgrades are needed and when, but also enable owners to smooth costs by gradually accumulating funds to pay for major works without blowing the budget.
This reduces the risk of being caught out when gas equipment fails and the owners corporation is forced into emergency mode to replace it quickly.
“People hate special levies,” Corcoran says, referring to extra charges when apartment owners must cough up for sudden unforeseen expenses. “If you have a plan and the plan is approved by the owners, then you can act in a planned and sequenced manner.”
As a first step, she recommends a holistic energy audit to determine how much energy a building consumes, for what purposes, from what sources and at what times.
“There are many moving parts, and the best approach is to have rock solid information.”
It’s imperative for all residential buildings to get off gas over the next two-and-a-half decades for Australia to achieve net zero by 2050.
“If you are looking to rent or buy an apartment, consider an apartment that is already electrified or can be electrified relatively easily,” Corcoran suggests.
She urges residents in existing apartments to start “tilling the soil” for electrification by asking their owners corporation committee how they are preparing to replace gas assets before they age out.
While electrification can be complex, kicking the can down the road poses huge financial risks. As fewer households use gas, those remaining on the network will face escalating bills as they carry a bigger share of network costs. Apartment residents still reliant on gas in the 2030s and 2040s could find themselves stuck with an expensive, stranded asset.
“You don’t want to be left holding the baby,” says Corcoran. “You’ve got to have a plan, you’ve got to have a strategy, and they’ve got to be approved.”
