content:
As glaciers melt and permafrost thaws, Longyearbyen, on the remote Arctic islands of Svalbard, faces climate-induced problems from tap water to housebuilding to landslides
Heavy metals make Norwegian village’s tap water toxic
O n a rugged mountain plateau of snow-dusted rocks, in the remote archipelago of Svalbard, a glaciologist, Andy Hodson, points out the “ears” of ice, white against the rock, that gave Foxfonna glacier its name, after the arctic fox.
The small glacier, on a mountain 8 miles (15km) outside the Norwegian village of Longyearbyen, is a popular summer hike for tourists who come here seeking the Arctic experience.
But in Svalbard, where glaciers cover 57% of the land and temperatures are rising up to seven times faster than the global average, making it one of the fastest-warming places on Earth, Foxfonna is changing rapidly.
“It is slowly dying,” says Hodson, a professor at the University Centre in Svalbard (UNIS). The telltale signs include a concave profile: Foxfonna is no longer accumulating snow. Precipitation here is increasingly falling as rain. Its thinning rate is between 1 and 4 metres a year, making it unrecognisable from when Hodson was last here a few years ago.
Out in the fjords, on the other side of the coastal village, the large glacial fronts extending into the sea that are characteristic of the islands are melting at an even faster rate: over the past two years, 10 have retreated entirely on to land .
In 2024, “things went crazy”, Hodson says, after record-high summer temperatures led to a big ice loss, of 1% , across the archipelago. It is affected by Arctic amplification – a feedback loop in which sea-ice retreat and atmospheric warming make each other worse.
“Pretty much the whole island is losing ice now,” says Hodson.
Longyearbyen, a scatter of brightly coloured houses, research institutes and tourist hotels at the bottom of a steep valley, lies at a latitude of 78 degrees north, the last stop in the high Arctic before the north pole. An important outpost of Arctic science, it attracts explorers, adventurers and nature lovers.
The village’s 2,600 inhabitants are used to extremes: winter temperatures can drop as low as -20C (-4F) and, from late October to early March, the sun does not rise, plunging the valley into more than 100 days of darkness.
But they are now facing new and unsettling challenges – things that many point out should serve as a warning for other Arctic regions. Not only is snow melting faster but now the permafrost – ground that once remained frozen all year – is thawing.
This is having unexpected but significant consequences. People have recently been warned not to drink from their taps due to heavy metals contained in the bedrock leaching into the village’s water supply. Instead, they now have to fill up containers from a central tank of filtered water in the village’s supermarket, while the municipality investigates and works out what to do in the long term.
The thaw has also caused landslides, damaged foundations and cracked walls, rendering some homes uninhabitable and threatening the long-term stability of other buildings. As a consequence, there are no longer enough homes for the number of people who need them.
The authorities in Longyearbyen have been forced to learn lessons, acclimatise and try to adapt to the changing conditions.
On the rooftop of the Svalbard Science Centre, which featured in the opening scenes of Vigil, the recent BBC thriller set in Svalbard, Gunhild B Sætren points out the scene of the most devastating avalanche in the archipelago’s history. The avalanche, in December 2015 , buried nine people, killing one man and an infant in their homes in the shadow of Mount Sukkertoppen.
“It was terrible,” says Sætren, a professor of safety psychology, who manages the Unis Arctic Safety Centre (ASC), established after the tragedy to focus on hazard management and climate adaptation. “Climate change is impacting us in very many ways. The greatest risk is avalanches. The area used to be an Arctic desert, but now there is more rain.”
The tragedy, which was followed by another, non-fatal avalanche that damaged two houses in 2017, happened as the result of warming strong easterly winds and drifting snow. At the time, the avalanche danger from Sukkertoppen was known about, but no avalanche warning system was in place .
Since then, snow fences to reduce drift and a wall of avalanche traps have been installed on the mountain and some houses pulled down, including Sætren’s own. The centre now provides weekly snow observations for the municipality’s avalanche warning system.
Sætren also works on a programme with other high Arctic remote settlements in Iceland and Greenland, to look at common problems, such as evacuation procedures for avalanches. A new tour guide approval system, introduced by the governor of Svalbard to better assess climate and other risks, is expected to be in force by 2027.
Arctic geology is complex and changing fast, with tour operators saying the changes are curtailing certain activities. At the Husky cafe, Matilda Weihs, 30, a guide for Svalbard Wildlife Expeditions who was trained by the ASC, says that this year they had to move the snowmobiles seven miles out of the village to find enough snow cover for tours.
“We are losing snow earlier and the melt is starting earlier,” says Weihs. “There are big changes in the fjords. You need to stay away from glacier fronts due to the danger of glaciers calving into the sea.”
T he loss of drinking water has been a huge shock to people, says Terje Aunevik, mayor of Longyearbyen and a former husky musher. “In Norway , where we have always taken for granted that we can drink the water from the tap, it’s challenging to start thinking that we need to carry our water. People get angry, wondering ‘why don’t we have control over it?’”
It has forced a rethink about how to tackle the problem longer term, says Aunevik.
“Now we are using a lot of resources to clean our tap water, when we use maybe 1-2% of that for drinking. That’s crazy energy use. We could have two different water-supply systems into our households, one for drinking and one for grey water.”
Aunevik says the challenges of thawing permafrost are also forcing a rethink of the way the village is built.
The construction of new homes to tackle the housing crisis was held up while the village grappled with a transition to a new energy system (a former mining camp, it previously used waste hot water from the mines for heating). And then, in 2025, scientists discovered the heavy metals were contaminating the water supply.
“I sometimes say that we are in the beginning of building a completely new town,” Aunevik says. “We need to change everything.
“There is a saying that wood does not rot in the Arctic, but now it does. It challenges how we construct our buildings.”
Ingvild Sæbu Vatn, a partner at the Longyearbyen architecture firm LPO Arkitekter, says one solution to the problem of melting permafrost affecting wooden foundations has been to drill into the bedrock. Another settlement in Svalbard, Ny-Ålesund, tried this, but Sæbu Vatn says some buildings began to be pushed up by the movement in the ground .
“They thought, ‘we’ll put the foundations in the bedrock and then we’ll be fine’ but they were wrong,” says Sæbu Vatn, who adds that this needs to be done with care. “If you put foundations in bedrock but you don’t do it properly, the buildings will still jack up. We need to look again at how we are building foundations.”
Those working on solutions have also not ruled out the extraordinary. “One solution being explored [to stabilise building foundations] is to freeze the ground by blowing cold air under the buildings in winter,” says Sæbu Vatn.
She says that while Longyearbyen is undoubtedly struggling, her hope is that in finding a way to survive they can offer hope to other Arctic regions, such as those with Inuit populations in Greenland and Canada.
“The big resource that Longyearbyen has is its population,” she says. “People are adventurous and resourceful, and a lot of companies are very innovative. Maybe we can build knowledge from this strange little place that is rapidly warming. That would be a nice goal.”

title: Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian village as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals
description: Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the world’s fastest-warming places Residents of a remote village in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond. Continue reading...
content:
Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the world’s fastest-warming places
Residents of a remote village in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost.
Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard , gets its main drinking water supply from a 1.5 mile-long (2.5km) dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond”. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond.
Longyearbyen, 800 miles from the north pole, is warming at between five and seven times the world’s average rate , with autumn temperatures rising at up to 4C a decade.
Heavy metal contamination of the water supply is likely to be linked to two factors, researchers say: the thawing of permafrost – rock-hard ground that remains frozen all year apart from a so-called “active layer” that thaws in summer – and the geology of the former mining settlement.
“The combination of the thawing permafrost and the shale bedrock, which contains a mineral called pyrite, or fool’s gold, is causing contamination of its water supply,” said Marjolaine Verret, a permafrost expert and associate professor in Arctic geology at the University Centre in Svalbard.
When pyrite came into contact with water and oxygen, it oxidised and generated acidity, she explained. “The acid produced can now leach heavy metals from these rocks into the waterways. The issue we’ve been having here in Longyearbyen is manganese, but other contaminants can be leached out from the rocks.”
The municipality, Longyearbyen lokalstyre, first alerted its 2,600 residents after manganese levels in the water supply were found to be 25 times higher than the 50 micrograms per litre recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, in September last year. The mayor of Longyearbyen, Terje Aunevik, said that while drinking water quality had never been good, due to sediment, the manganese levels had “gone ballistic”.
Prolonged exposure to high levels of manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants.
Emergency, temporary measures were rolled out, including the installation of a central tank of free purified water, filtered by the local brewery, for residents to refill containers at the local supermarket, and an investigation was launched.
Manganese levels have since dropped, but earlier this year sulphate and nickel levels were found to exceed recommended drinking water limits. As a result, the ban remains in place.
Aunevik said that while manganese levels were “not dangerous”, government guidelines had to be followed. The drinking water crisis had created a lot of “noise”, he admitted, with some residents angry at the inconvenience.
The mayor, who has commissioned an investigation into water quality, said a “completely new water mains supply” may be needed. Potential solutions being considered were installing a filtration system to Isdammen and having a desalination plant as a backup, or the other way around. Either way was “extremely expensive” and, due to the extreme temperatures of Svalbard, with water temperatures often below zero, would include technical challenges, Aunevik said.
“ In Norway , where we have always taken for granted that we can drink the water from the tap, it is challenging to start thinking that we need to carry our water like we do now. Other small communities should be precautious and start thinking of what to do if it happens to their sources.”
Verret and other scientists have warned that the contamination of water sources in Longyearbyen could be a foretaste of what is to come for Arctic communities.
“These ingredients [bedrock rich in pyrite and heavy metals] and thawing permafrost are present in other parts of the Arctic so this could be a first example of how climate change can impact freshwater, for example in northern Canada and Alaska,” Verret said.

title: ‘Like selling wolves from Yellowstone’: how protected US sharks are being sold off to foreign aquariums

content:
While anglers cannot take endangered sand tiger sharks, a loophole lets private firms catch the fish to sell abroad, profiting from Delaware Bay’s conservation success
S hortly after 12.45pm, what remains of a 300-metre line goes taut. Somewhere beneath the murky green surface of Delaware Bay, on the eastern US coast, a sand tiger shark has taken the bait of a mackerel chunk. Marine researchers at the University of Delaware haul the line towards a small boat as the shark’s grey-brown outline emerges.
It is a large animal: 225cm (7ft) long with a 90cm girth. Its mouth hangs open, revealing rows of jagged teeth. The researchers work quickly, measuring the shark, recording its sex, and taking blood and muscle samples. A tag is then fastened beneath its dorsal fin, through its thick sandpapery skin.
The mature male seems to watch them as they work. Then it is lowered back into the bay. With a powerful flick of its tail, it disappears almost as quickly as it arrived.
Several thousand miles away, sand tiger sharks collected from these same waters circle tanks in Abu Dhabi, moving among artificial reefs and through blue-lit tunnels in the desert city’s aquariums, where visitors pay up to $100 (£75) for day passes. They will never return to Delaware Bay.
Tagging sand tigers – a species of concern that is prohibited from being caught in US waters – offers clues about the lives of these fish, which are critically endangered globally.
However, in recent years, the bay – a US habitat of particular concern between the states of Delaware and New Jersey – has become a hotspot for private collection of specimens for the global aquarium trade.
A recent study by marine researchers from the University of Delaware, Delaware State University and the University of Rhode Island shows that, since 2018, the number of sand tiger sharks collected from Delaware Bay for public display has risen sharply, from two that year to 40 in 2023. In total, 80 of the sharks were taken from Delaware waters for aquariums between 2018 and 2024.
The study, citing data from Delaware’s Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control (DNREC) shows that nearly all the sand tiger sharks collected from Delaware Bay were sent overseas: the highest numbers went to China and the United Arab Emirates, while others went to South Korea and Thailand. Some were sent to other countries – including Turkey, Scotland, Israel, Italy, France and Uzbekistan – with a few remaining in the US.
“This [private collecting of sand tiger sharks] is like going into Yellowstone [national park] and catching wolves and then selling them to zoos in France or in the Middle East,” says Brad Wetherbee, a shark researcher at University of Rhode Island who co-wrote the study.
“[These countries] used to have sand tigers. They could just go out in their own waters and catch them and collect them, but their populations are so low they can’t do that any more.”
The US has spent decades restricting the killing of sand tiger sharks, yet in recent years, through a regulatory maze of federal and state permits, private collecting companies can legally remove these protected sharks from the wild for public display. A shark that an angler would be required to release after catching can instead be transported thousands of miles and placed in a foreign aquarium, with private companies profiting from the trade.
“How can we say these people [private collectors] can remove them and functionally harvest them, whereas these ones [recreational anglers] can’t?” says Aaron Carlisle, an associate professor from the University of Delaware’s school of marine science and another of the study’s authors. “If our concern is sustainability, we need to know what is the impact of removal.”
Sand tigers, despite their fearsome appearance, are non-aggressive and docile. They have one of the lowest reproductive rates of any shark species, reaching sexual maturity at about six to 10 years old, depending on sex, and producing just one or two pups every two to three years.
Once widespread across subtropical and temperate coastal waters, the species has declined across much of its range. Populations in parts of south-east Asia, west Africa and the Arabian Sea have fallen to critically low levels , largely because of overfishing , including bycatch, and habitat degradation . In some regions, they are believed to have been wiped out entirely.
The north-west Atlantic is one of the few regions where the species’ populations are not critically endangered, largely due to federal and state protections. Yet the population has never had a formal assessment, and how healthy it actually is remains difficult to determine.
One private company has accounted for most of the recent collection in Delaware Bay. Dynasty Marine, a Florida-based supplier of live marine animals to aquariums and research institutions worldwide that drew bipartisan outrage in Florida in 2025 after legally netting a manta ray for SeaWorld Abu Dhabi, began collecting sand tigers in Delaware in 2021.
A spokesperson for Delaware state’s department of natural resources and environmental control (DNREC) says the company has “ramped up collection in the following years”.
Records reviewed by the Guardian show that Dynasty Marine collected 71 sharks between 2022 and 2024. The study also records 35 sand tiger harvest requests in 2025, with most destined for China.
Recipients of the sharks caught between 2022 and 2024 included SeaWorld Abu Dhabi, Dubai Aquarium and Underwater Zoo, Sea Life Busan in South Korea, Aquaria Phuket in Thailand and Guangzhou Ocean World in China.
Dynasty Marine was asked to comment on the number of sand tigers it collects a year but did not respond. In a statement to the Guardian, it said: “Every collection we conduct is done in full compliance with all applicable federal and state permits and regulations.
“The animals we collect are cared for to the highest standards and go on to live in human care, where they play a vital role in educating millions of people each year about marine life and the importance of ocean conservation.”
The company says it supports “numerous marine conservation, science and education initiatives”, including shark research, manatee rehabilitation and coral restoration efforts.
Private companies seeking to collect sand tigers for public display must first obtain an exempted fishing permit from the US National Marine Fisheries Service (known as Noaa Fisheries). If the collection takes place in Delaware waters, the permit holder must then obtain a scientific collecting permit from DNREC.
Noaa Fisheries says it reviews applications for capture of the sharks on a “case-by-case basis”.
“We have an overall scientifically based annual quota for all shark research and public display,” says John Chu, a Noaa Fisheries spokesperson. “We consider that overall quota when issuing public display permits.”
The state follows the federal lead in granting permits. The DNREC says Noaa Fisheries’ approval is “evidence enough for the state to believe that removal of the permitted number of individual sharks is sustainable”.
However, scientists argue that, without knowing the population’s size or trend, it is difficult to determine what impact removing sharks for display in an aquarium may have.
The concern is heightened by the size of many sand tigers collected in Delaware. Many are large juveniles or near-mature adults that could soon reproduce if left in the wild.
The DNREC says the recent increase in collections is “an emerging concern”, but says it would be up to the federal government to act on that. It says an assessment on the number of sand tiger sharks in the area would “lend context” to a permit request from a private collection company.
This uncertainty extends to what happens to the sharks after they leave Delaware Bay. Neither the DNREC or Noaa Fisheries record the sharks’ final status, including whether those animals become sick or die, though the DNREC says it intends to change this.
Dewayne Fox, an assistant fisheries professor at Delaware State University who also worked on the study, says the issue is not just whether the collections are sustainable, but also who benefits from a population protected in US waters.
“We have protected the habitat and yet we are going to allow some out-of-state company to come in, catch these animals and then ship them all the way around the world and make money,” he says. “Everybody else is benefiting from our conservation success.”

title: This is one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. So why is it being used as a dumping site for mine waste?
description: The Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord despite a 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against it Shortly after the Norwegian stock market closed on 17 June 2026, a few dozen local people from the small west coast town of Vevring crowded around a laptop in a school. The moment marked the end of a 17-year fight, one of Norway’s most protracted environmental battles in living memory. In Oslo, Ingvild Fonn Asmervik, the project leader for Naturvernforbundet (Friends of the Earth Norway), compared the joy she felt to giving birth to her child. For Anne-Line Thingnes Førsund, a third-generation fisher living on the banks of the fjord in Vevring and a volunteer for the charity’s local branch, it was more of a relief. Like a mountain lifting off her shoulders, she said. Continue reading...
content:
The Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord despite a 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against it
S hortly after the Norwegian stock market closed on 17 June 2026, a few dozen local people from the small west coast town of Vevring crowded around a laptop in a school. Surrounded by children’s drawings and windows looking out over Førde fjord, they listened as news arrived from Oslo. Norway’s supreme court had ruled against its government: a permit to release mining waste directly into the fjord two miles upstream was illegal, the court said.
The moment marked the end of a 17-year fight, one of Norway’s most protracted environmental battles in living memory. In Oslo, Ingvild Fonn Asmervik, the project leader for Naturvernforbundet (Friends of the Earth Norway), compared the joy she felt to giving birth to her child. For Anne-Line Thingnes Førsund, a third-generation fisher living on the banks of the fjord in Vevring and a volunteer for the charity’s local branch, it was more of a relief. Like a mountain lifting off her shoulders, she said.
These feelings of elation were short-lived. While Førsund and others celebrated, a government lawyer appeared on a television debate show to set out plans for a new temporary permit, and to allow the mine to continue to release waste directly into the fjord in the meantime. Four days later, the mine applied for fresh permission, and in late September, it was granted by Norway’s climate and environment ministry.
“When we heard the pollution would continue, it was like they snatched the carpet from under us,” says Førsund. “We have answered every letter, commented on every consultation, complained whenever we could. We have been knocked down so many times and this could have been the opportunity for change.”
While the government insists that it is acting lawfully, critics say the dumping threatens to foul one of Norway’s most pristine fjords . Others worry that the decision heralds a new wave of permits to pollute Norway’s fjords in the race to secure critical minerals.
“This is not only about the fjord and us and our lives,” says Førsund. “This is about principles. When you have a government that doesn’t respect the supreme court you’re changing the system itself.”
The move comes just as a wider spotlight is being shone on the issue of polluted waters in Norway. A recent report showed that Norwegian fish farms are filling fjords and other coastal waters with nutrient pollution equivalent to the raw sewage of tens of millions of people each year.
Meanwhile, populations of Atlantic salmon are at a historic low in the country – 155 of Norway’s 450 or so salmon rivers were closed to fishing at the start of the season this year.
Submarine tailings deposition (STD) – known colloquially by Norwegian critics as “fjord dumping” – is the process of pumping crushed rocks and chemical waste into the sea through pipelines hundreds of metres underwater. Proposed as an alternative to disposing of waste on land, the Norwegian government’s own Institute of Marine Research (IMR) warns that STD releases fine particles of toxic waste that can accumulate in smaller sea life and disrupt ecosystems at large.
STD is outlawed in all of North America, Australia, Russia, Brazil, China and most of Europe . The few countries that still permit the practice include Papua New Guinea, Indonesia and Turkey.
The Engebø titanium mine, on Førde fjord near Vevring, was first proposed by Nordic Mining in 2006 and the government awarded a permit to release waste into the fjord less than 10 years later. In response, Friends of the Earth Norway launched legal challenges that worked their way up the country’s legal system, arriving at a week-long supreme court hearing in spring 2026. Meanwhile, the mine came online and began releasing waste late in 2024.
Nordic Mining is financed by investors including Japan’s Iwatani Corporation and the British offices of the international banks Morgan Stanley, UBS and Goldman Sachs. Other banks, including Standard Chartered and Citigroup, explicitly ban financing projects using STD.
Nordic Mining did not respond to repeated requests for comment from the Guardian, but said in a social media post shortly after the supreme court decision that it would continue with how it disposed of waste, with the encouragement of Norwegian officials.
“It has been said that our operation is illegal, that we have to close, that our work must stop. That is not the situation,” Nordic Mining said, adding that it was continuing “with the ambition to act responsibly, with respect for the fjords and mountains, and for the local community around us”.
Legal wrangling over the permit came to focus on the EU’s water framework directive (WFD), which applies to Norway as a member of the European Economic Area. The WFD allows industrial activities to pollute water bodies only when there is an “ overriding public interest ”.
The supreme court ruled that the reasons given when the permit was first awarded were not strong enough. However, the government argues they have grown stronger since the EU added titanium to its list of “critical minerals” in 2020.
“The Norwegian government considers the Engebø project to be of significant importance for Norway and Europe,” a ministry spokesperson said, because “the Engebø mountain contains one of the world’s largest known deposits of rutile, a titanium-bearing mineral. Within Europe, Norway and Ukraine are the only countries with significant resources of this kind.”
Legal scholars have questioned this logic. “That’s wrong. A permit exists or it doesn’t, and the supreme court decision is quite clear: the permit is illegal,” says Tarjei Ellingsen Røsvoll, associate professor of administrative and constitutional law at the University of Inland Norway.
“The government is then openly allowing a company to dump a bunch of stuff in a fjord illegally. That is unprecedented; it damages trust and undermines a fundamental structure of constitutional and administrative law. They should take responsibility for having made an invalid and illegal decision, morally and legally.”
While Nordic Mining awaited its new three-year permit, it continued to dispose of waste into Førde fjord. Økokrim, Norway’s central office for white collar and environmental crime, is now considering whether to investigate the dumping for illegality.
While there have been few comprehensive studies of the impact of STD on marine ecosystems, scientists have linked heavy metal pollution now present in some fjords to STD decades earlier.
The impact is particularly damaging when the waste is milled into small pieces, according to Terje van der Meeren, a research professor at the IMR, who co-authored the institute’s response to the Engebø mine application and testified during the supreme court hearings.
“It’s like flour,” says Van der Meeren, adding that waste from Engebø includes a chemical that degrades into carbon disulphide, a neurotoxin. “Our concern is that this fine dust will pass into the rest of the fjord. What will happen with the [fish] spawning in this fjord? We don’t know.”
In 2016, Van der Meeren and other IMR researchers travelled to the Arctic Repparfjord, in Hammerfest in the far north of the country, where a copper mine dumped waste for six years in the 1970s. Decades later, they found haddock with higher levels of lead, arsenic and chromium in their muscles than those in nearby waters, according to research published this year . Other Norwegian studies have found historic STD contamination in plankton , crabs and fish eggs .
Back in Vevring, Førsund and other campaigners are now preparing for a fresh legal battle over the temporary waste permit – though dumping is likely to continue for as long as it takes for a new decision to be reached.
She looks back on the first protests against the mine with nostalgia. In one photograph, taken more than a decade ago, protesters gathered for a meal on the banks of the fjord; Førsund’s daughter, now an architect, was only a child. “So many of these people are dead now,” she says.
“The fjord is bigger than us. It has given us food and income and meaning and music and fish and birds for thousands of years. Now it gives us the energy to keep fighting.”

title: Colin Sherriff obituary
description: My friend and former colleague Colin Sherriff, who has died aged 75, worked in social housing for half a century, including as a director at three housing associations, Circle 33, Thames Valley Housing and English Churches Housing Group. He then became chief executive of Windsor and District housing association, which was set up to receive housing stock transferred out of local authority ownership. He was their first (and initially only) employee, and from 1994 to 2006 added 450 people to his team, creating a positive tenant-focused culture. Continue reading...
content:
My friend and former colleague Colin Sherriff, who has died aged 75, worked in social housing for half a century, including as a director at three housing associations, Circle 33, Thames Valley Housing and English Churches Housing Group.
He then became chief executive of Windsor and District housing association, which was set up to receive housing stock transferred out of local authority ownership. He was their first (and initially only) employee, and from 1994 to 2006 added 450 people to his team, creating a positive tenant-focused culture.
Later he was a troubleshooting interim CEO for various associations, and ran his own trading company, Broadreach Strategies, through which he delivered coaching and mentoring to people in the housing world. In addition he had a wide range of non-executive portfolios, starting as chair of Origin Housing in London . At his death he was still chair of Grainger Trust, a rapidly growing for-profit social landlord.
Colin was born in Glasgow to Iain, a clerk at the Coop, and May (nee Forsyth), a draughtswoman at the North British Locomotive Works. He went to Dunfermline high school and then to Sidcup and Chislehurst grammar school in Kent when his parents moved south.
At Christ Church, Oxford, he studied engineering, but due to ill health was unable to take his finals. Afterwards he found his way into housing, initially in a junior role at Circle 33 (now Clarion Housing Group) from 1976 onwards. Over the years he gained a number of promotions, and when he left in 1990 he was director of housing.
Following his time at Circle 33, Colin moved on to Thames Valley Housing (1990-91) and English Churches Housing Group (1992-94) before accepting the post of chief executive of Windsor and District.
After taking 2007 off to sail in the Clipper Round the World Yacht Race, he returned to the UK to run Broadreach Strategies and to work as an interim CEO for various housing associations, roles which he partly picked up through my consultancy, Campbell Tickell.
Parallel to his housing career, Colin had also been involved in local politics. Elected in 1978 as a Labour councillor in Haringey, north London, he became one of the country’s youngest chairs of housing, and held elected office until 1986.
He was widely admired for his strong personal values, his kindness, his generous support for colleagues and friends, and his mischievous sense of humour.
Colin married Ingrid Reynolds, who also worked in housing, in 1986. She survives him, as do their two children, Anna and Alex, two grandchildren and his younger brother, Gavin.

title: ‘We were not going to let this rapist destroy our lives’: how one couple came to terms with a devastating attack
description: After Susan Brison was raped and left for dead, her husband, Thomas, did his best to support her. They are still together, while many relationships collapse after a sexual assault. What did he get right – and wrong? On a hot, still, silent noon, at a junction of dirt roads in rural France, Thomas Trezise stood scanning the horizon, looking and listening for his wife. He tried to soothe a deep foreboding. Susan Brison had headed out for a morning walk two hours ago. How could she be gone so long? This was 4 July 1990, the start of what was meant to be a busy summer. Trezise and Brison were both assistant professors in the US – he in French at Princeton and Brison in philosophy at Dartmouth – and had just arrived at the remote farmhouse of Trezise’s French colleague. Life seemed packed with promise. “I’d found someone with whom I really wanted to spend my life and I just felt very, very lucky,” says Trezise. “Susan and I had fallen quickly and deeply in love – it was magical – and at that point, we were also trying to conceive a child. We loved being in France. I kind of felt I’d found my way. It was a good place … until it happened.” Continue reading...
content:
After Susan Brison was raped and left for dead, her husband, Thomas, did his best to support her. They are still together, while many relationships collapse after a sexual assault. What did he get right – and wrong?
O n a hot, still, silent noon, at a junction of dirt roads in rural France , Thomas Trezise stood scanning the horizon, looking and listening for his wife. He tried to soothe a deep foreboding. Susan Brison had headed out for a morning walk two hours ago. How could she be gone so long?
This was 4 July 1990, the start of what was meant to be a busy summer. Trezise and Brison were both assistant professors in the US – he in French at Princeton and Brison in philosophy at Dartmouth – and had just arrived at the remote farmhouse of Trezise’s French colleague. Life seemed packed with promise. “I’d found someone with whom I really wanted to spend my life and I just felt very, very lucky,” says Trezise. “Susan and I had fallen quickly and deeply in love – it was magical – and at that point, we were also trying to conceive a child. We loved being in France. I kind of felt I’d found my way. It was a good place … until it happened.”
By 1pm, Trezise was still trying to push back a rising panic when, from the corner of his eye, he saw his colleague running towards him, yelling. “That’s the moment I remember,” says Trezise. “I just thought: ‘OK. I wasn’t wrong about something happening.’ It was terrifying.”
An ambulance was at the gate, but Trezise could not recognise the figure inside. She was bandaged, bruised and bloodied, her cheeks hugely swollen, her eyes slits, an enormous bulge on her forehead. Seeing his reaction, Brison slowly lifted her oxygen mask and said in a hoarse voice: “I’ll be OK.”
Outside on the driveway, Trezise allowed himself one scream to the skies, fists clenched. Though it would be days before he would learn exactly what had happened, it was instantly clear to him that a man had done this to her. Back in the ambulance, en route to hospital in Grenoble, it took Trezise every ounce of will to contain his anger, fear and frenzied emotion, and to instead project calm. It was, he remembers, like “an actor taking the stage”. He became, or tried to become, “the strong, supportive spouse”.
This is the starting point of Trezise’s memoir, Beginning Again, which gives a powerful account of the days, weeks and years ahead. It’s a voice we rarely hear, especially in such depth – a man’s experience of his wife’s rape and attempted murder.
Trezise and Brison are in their seventies now, tenured professors, with an adult son. Within months of the assault, Brison had begun speaking publicly about sexual violence. Before long writing about it too. In 1993, her account was published in the New York Times and later, her book, Aftermath, was an exploration of finding sense and meaning when you have landed far beyond the moral universe. It was Brison who suggested that Trezise write about it too. “I knew he had it in him to write this book,” she says, “and I was always encouraging him.”
For Trezise, there were many layers of difficulty in doing so. “One was this feeling of complicity,” says Trezise. “It’s impossible not to know that the vast majority of sex crimes are committed by men. A simple way of putting it is that, if I’d gone on that same walk that day, I would have been safe.” Entitlement was another barrier. “What voice do I say this in? I do not want to claim ‘victimhood’ when Susan’s victimisation was so much worse. But I did want to say that this has very dire effects and it’s not just my story, it’s the story of millions of people.” When men stay silent, sexual violence gets filed under ‘woman’s problems’, when of course, says Trezise, it’s “a problem for humanity”.
During their first 11 days in hospital, Trezise slept beside his wife, with the help of sedatives prescribed to both of them. Brison could barely speak – she had been so badly strangled, she had a fractured trachea – and Trezise was her voice, her support, her advocate and also her guard, because Brison was terrified that her assailant might appear in the hospital. Trezise was on high alert too. They refused to be separated, even during treatments and examinations. His book describes helping with her first bath – just the two of them, locked in the bathroom, him washing her, then taking a shower himself, sticking his head out every 15 seconds to check she was still safe.
The account of the attack itself is given by Brison, through the unedited deposition that she wrote with a detective in the hospital, a painstaking procedure that took eight hours to complete. It’s a horrifying, harrowing read that tells how Brison was grabbed from behind by the throat while walking, and taken to a muddy ravine. She was punched, assaulted, strangled, smashed by a rock; she came in and out of consciousness, and bargained and begged for her life. The ordeal only ended when she pretended to be dead.
Brison had barely looked at the deposition since giving it – and had no intention of doing so until Trezise asked permission to include it in his book. “It was important, as wrenching as it is, for the readers to know exactly what she went through,” says Trezise. “If I had paraphrased it, I would have felt like I was appropriating her voice.” For Brison, reading it within her husband’s narrative gave her a different perspective. “I was very moved,” she says. “I had never stopped to think how he felt as I was giving it. It’s important for people to know the effect on him.” At one point in the deposition, Brison describes being in so much pain that she thinks it would be better to die – but then imagines her husband finding her body in a ravine and being “alone in the world”. This gives her the strength to carry on. “It left me speechless,” says Trezise. “Just like in the ambulance, when she said: ‘I’ll be OK.’ She didn’t say that for her own sake. She said that for my sake.”
Still, through all this and back in the US, Trezise contained his emotions to be the “supportive spouse” he thought Brison needed. At Princeton, Brison at home on disability leave, doors and windows locked, it was Trezise who stepped back out into “normal life” – going to work, buying the groceries, performing all life’s admin. “The question for me was, ‘How can I help her? What should I do?’ – and those are the things I knew how to do,” he says. “The trouble is, I feel like at times, they were done to the exclusion of me being emotionally accessible, because that was more disorienting. I knew I needed to be there, that I needed to listen, but – this is a masculine thing too – I wanted to fix it and I knew I couldn’t. And that was a source of great frustration and, at times, anger and depression.”
Many couples do not survive trauma like this and Brison can see why. “My trust in the world was so shattered, I didn’t feel viscerally that I could walk out the front door and not get killed or the ground would fall beneath me,” she says. “Tom was so strong, he was a rock. I know that’s what he thought I needed, but I needed to be accompanied. He hadn’t cried. He hadn’t shown that he was hurt. For a while, our ability to understand each other was shot.” Brison resented his ability to pick up his former life, and imagined him out there, doing fine. In truth, Trezise was barely coping. “It was hard to get through the day,” he says. “Before I taught my class, I lay on the floor of my study and just dreamed about being somewhere else. The most banal, everyday exchange like, ‘How was your summer?’ or ‘How are you doing?’, was so difficult to answer, and 99% of the time, I said nothing, which meant I was like a ghost.” Though he’d received a fellowship to write a book on Samuel Beckett, he’d lost all interest. (He never wrote it.) Having built a career around his love of France – the country and the language – Trezise had no wish to ever return and could hardly bear to hear French.
Every aspect of their life and marriage had been profoundly changed. “It’s partly because the attack was of a sexual nature,” says Trezise. “We’d been trying to conceive a child before the attack, but physical intimacy – any intimacy, emotional, psychological – becomes really fraught. In one sense, you’re asking: ‘Am I entitled to feel attracted to Susan?’ ‘Am I entitled to cry?’ I didn’t feel entitled to my own feelings a lot of the time. It’s as though I couldn’t be myself. I had to walk on eggshells. Susan was angry – and I did not blame her in the least. But it can be hard to be in the presence of someone who’s angry, even if the person’s not angry at you.”
What helped? For Brison, finding her own community, especially a survivors’ self-help group, was hugely important. Though there were no support groups for partners at that time, Trezise also began therapy. “It was absolutely essential,” he says. “It was a revelation to have one hour a week with someone who knew a great deal about trauma and whose job it was to listen so I didn’t feel like I was imposing.” He advises anyone in a similar position to seek support. “Just because you’re a carer doesn’t mean you don’t need care,” he says. “You need to find it, whether that’s family, friends, a group, a therapist. If you don’t have the support yourself, you’re not going to be a good care-giver.”
Though there is no linear path to recovery, Trezise found comfort in the passing of time. “Even when things seemed to be absolutely impossible, somehow we kept going the next minute or the next hour,” he says. “And I think the other side of it was that we were not going to let this rapist destroy our lives. As Susan put it in her book, we were not going to finish his job for him.” (The assailant, a local man, had been quickly identified and was later sentenced to 10 years for rape and attempted murder.)
Perhaps most healing of all was the arrival of their son, Gabriel, four years after the assault almost to the day. “Having a child was terrifically important,” says Trezise. “It’s magical. Here comes this creature who’s absolutely unprecedented, he’s new, and guess what? It’s not a bad thing to be a boy. He knows nothing about this, and that was gratifying to me. Also, this is the start of a new story. It’s a story that’s going to be his but we can help him and he’s helping create a new story for us by showing, ‘Look, this chapter you’ve been going through, it’s not the only one you’re going to have in your book.’ It was a way for us to love each other too, through him.”
The cover of Beginning Again depicts the Japanese art of kintsugi, where pottery is repaired with the breaks left visible, lined and lacquered in gold and silver. For Trezise, it seems apt. “Things got radically changed but they can be put back together in a very beautiful way,” he says. Decades on, there is still PTSD remaining for both of them. Brison will always turn around if she hears someone walking behind her, and, though they now live in a beautiful part of Vermont, she would never take a country walk alone. In Trezise’s case, he struggles to contain deep panic if he has arranged to meet his wife and she isn’t there. (She has learned to let him know when she’s running late.) And they both have a strong startle response. “He’s worse than I am!” says Brison. “When we’re in the house together and one of us is about to appear in the room, we whistle or say, ‘I’m coming!’”
But, trite as it may sound, they are closer for having survived this. “I said it in the dedication in my book and it still brings tears to my eyes,” says Brison. “‘For Gabriel, who arrived, and Tom, who stayed.’ He stayed. It wasn’t easy, and lots of men don’t stay. I knew, even when we were having the hardest of times, that he would stand by me.
“I always knew that he was a good human being,” she continues. “He has always been incredibly kind and generous and thoughtful. What has changed enormously is that he has become so much more aware of his feelings and able to articulate them. He has overcome decades of being socialised as a boy and man so that I don’t have to read his mind any more.”
Trezise has learned more about Brison too. “The depth of her strength is just incredible,” he says. “She’s so incredibly brave. Her resilience is amazing. I already knew she was a wonderful person – she’s loving, she’s a terrific friend to her friends – but if one thing comes out of this, it’s that this is a person I can trust with everything. And I’m just so lucky.”
Beginning Again by Thomas Trezise (University of California Press, £23) is published on 27 October. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.
Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland , or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland . In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: I was abused as a child – and thought I had healed. Then I began drinking in lockdown
description: Decades after being sexually abused, the author and doctor Frank Spinelli believed he had moved on emotionally. But alcohol destroyed his sense of security. content:
Decades after being sexually abused, the author and doctor Frank Spinelli believed he had moved on emotionally. But alcohol destroyed his sense of security. He describes how he confronted his shame
N ot so long ago, Frank Spinelli seemed to have sorted out his life. He was happily married, working as a doctor and had a sideline writing medical thrillers. He thought he had dealt with the sexual abuse he had suffered as a child – not only had he helped bring the man who groomed and abused him to justice, but also he had written a memoir about it. “I felt that I had closure,” he says. “I had the good fortune of working with some amazing therapists and I believed I had done the work and moved past it and I was a healed person.”
Little did he know that his recovery was fragile. The Covid pandemic took away his routine and structure: “All the external pillars that were tightly holding me together – the engagements at the office, the work trips.” Two years earlier, he and his husband had moved from Manhattan to a leafy suburb, from where he is speaking to me over a video call today. He was dealing with uncertainty and felt isolated. “We know one thing about shame: shame breeds in isolation.”
Spinelli had never had a problem with alcohol before. In the lockdowns, though, he found himself drinking more and more . A glass of wine while cooking dinner turned into two; a bottle shared with his husband turned into another. Drinking was no longer something that mainly happened at the weekend, but had blurred into the week. Three months into lockdown, Spinelli’s husband realised it wasn’t doing him any good and decided to stop drinking, but Spinelli continued.
“You make all these qualifying statements to yourself – you’re home, you’re not bothering anybody, I’m not driving,” he says. He convinced himself that if he drank in secret, it didn’t really count, so he started to take long dog walks, sipping from a water bottle filled with vodka; he hid empty bottles in the garage. When his husband confronted him about it, Spinelli promised to stop, but it lasted less than a week. He found better hiding spots: old bags in the wardrobe, empty cleaning-product bottles, the recycling bin.
At this time, a class-action lawsuit against the Boy Scouts of America was going through the courts. Spinelli was one of 95,000 alleged survivors of sexual abuse within the organisation. The man who had abused him from the age of 11, from 1978 to 1980, was his scoutmaster, William Fox. In September 2022, a $2.5bn (£2.2bn) compensation fund for victims was established. In order to work out how much he would be entitled to, Spinelli was sent a 47-page questionnaire to fill out, in which he was asked to detail the abuse and its impact on him.
He read this piece of brutal bureaucracy, relying on alcohol to get him through. It wasn’t the “dramatic rock bottom I’d expected from movies and recovery narratives”, he writes in his new book, The Shame Compass. “There was no car accident, no lost job, no intervention from concerned family members. I was alone in my home office, staring at a legal document that reduced my childhood sexual trauma to data points.” It felt like another violation, “documenting my own rape for a legal system that would assign it a dollar value”, he writes.
The shame came flooding back – not just about the abuse, but also shame that he hadn’t got over it and shame that he was having to drink to cope with it. “You think you’re healed, you think you’ve moved on, and that is one of the myths,” he says. “The shame is still with you.”
Spinelli grew up in Staten Island, New York, the youngest of three children of Italian parents. “It was a very traditional background,” he says. His mother raised the children and sometimes worked in a supermarket; his father was a labourer. Neither had much education, but they expected big things of their children. “You really only get two choices: doctor or lawyer,” he says. Spinelli was already interested in science and wanted to become a doctor.
He was a sensitive boy. “Joining the Boy Scouts was my parents’ way of perhaps toughening me up a little bit. Unfortunately, that’s where we were introduced to a man who would change all our lives,” he says. As a scout leader, Fox, who was also a police officer, was commanding and authoritative. Otherwise, “he was sort of jovial and there was a lot of camaraderie. And then the sexual abuse began.”
In Spinelli’s previous book, his memoir Pee-Shy, “I wrote that the most insidious thing about child molestation is that it creates a desire in the child to want to please the molester, so I constantly was feeling: what am I doing wrong? How can I make him happy?” The psychological and physical bullying from other boys Fox had groomed was also extremely damaging. “There was this hierarchy that he established – if you got to ride in the front seat, you were one of Bill’s favourites that day. If not, you got to ride in the back. That is the type of psychological manipulation he employed as a tactic to keep you under his thumb.”
When Spinelli was 13, he told his parents about the abuse. “They went to the senior leaders and, in a sense, they were shamed into secrecy,” he says. “They were told: ‘You do not want this to get out – think of your son, think of your family,’ and I think they saw some truth in that. They agreed that Bill Fox could step down quietly, no charges pressed, and that would take care of matters. Now, unfortunately, we know many boys suffered after that fact.”
Spinelli’s takeaway was: “This was how you handled matters – with secrecy.” He had begun to realise around this time that he was gay, another source of shame in his traditional Catholic community. He imagines his parents’ thought process: “A young boy who might be gay, or we’re not really sure, is involved in a sexual relationship with an adult man. While we know child molestation is not a consensual relationship, looking at it from the outside, they probably said: ‘Do we really want to shine a light on this? Think of the scrutiny.’” His parents also took advice from their priest, says Spinelli. “I think my parents thought they were protecting me. I was already being bullied at school; this would only add to it.”
Spinelli struggled in his teenage years and dropped out of college. “This was not how I envisioned my life,” he says. “By accident, I came into contact with a therapist who happened to be an art therapist and she saved my life. I painted, she taught me to write, and I used that creative outlet to heal, to move beyond the trauma.” Other than his immediate family, she was the first person he told about the abuse. “I went into very specific details about what had happened and what made it so painful was to hear it out loud.” He was still blaming himself, thinking he was complicit. “But that’s what grooming is – making you believe that these actions are coming from you, when they’re being installed in your mind.”
Spinelli went back to college, then to medical school. He became a doctor, specialising in treating people living with HIV. The workload of being a doctor was a good distraction, although he was also being treated for anxiety and depression. “There was an undercurrent of unhappiness. Certainly, that was reflected in the relationships I had – perhaps dating people who weren’t always the nicest to me, or didn’t treat me as kindly as they should have.”
In 2008, he published a book on men’s health. While he was promoting it, he got back in contact with two old friends from Staten Island. His childhood felt closer to him again. “That night, I had a dream about Bill Fox, me waiting by the screen door for his red truck to pull up.” Spinelli looked up Fox online – and what he found shocked him. “I discovered that the year after he stepped down [from the Boy Scouts], he talked a suicidal teenage boy off a ledge and adopted him.”
Shortly afterwards, Fox was feted in TV appearances, won a “father of the year” award and published a book called The Cop and the Kid. He would go on to adopt about 15 boys – many, according to Spinelli, with special needs.
Spinelli was astonished and appalled and knew he had to do something. “It was horrifying to me that we allowed this man to step down from the Boy Scouts of America and one year later he adopts a boy, but doesn’t stop there.” When Fox was finally arrested, in 2011, he still had some boys in his care, Spinelli says. “I found that story shocking, that this could have happened even after I came forward, and so I felt it was my obligation to finally see this to the end. What motivated me was a sense of blinding justice. All I saw was the end goal of bringing him to justice because that would be the only thing that would make sense.”
Spinelli went to the police soon afterwards. Although his abuse was past the statute of limitations, he helped keep the pressure on the investigation, even wearing a wiretap in a phone call with Fox. Three young men, two of whom had been adopted by Fox as children, came forward. In August 2011, Fox pleaded no contest – by which he did not admit guilt, but accepted the conviction – and was sentenced to at least 35 years in prison. He died in prison not long afterwards.
Spinelli’s memoir about the case was published in 2013. The act of writing everything down, along with securing Fox’s conviction, had felt like closure. And then came the pandemic and that questionnaire. “That’s when I thought: I really don’t have all of this managed. And that’s common: people who experience trauma will find that at different points in their lives it will re-emerge because something happens – life happens. It’s not as if you’re going to just be level for the rest of your life.” After completing the questionnaire, he woke up the next morning: “I looked myself in the mirror and I said: ‘This is not how the story ends.’”
He turned his attention to the feelings of shame, which would become his Compass framework: confront, observe, map, process, accept and sustain, plus a final “S” for service, sharing your experience to help others. What if he could dismiss the inner voice that had told him he was “bad” all his life and instead see if shame was trying to tell him something important?
“That inspired me to think about shame in a way that I hadn’t before. Shame is something we think is negative, but there’s also a way of looking at it where perhaps the shame is showing you that you are just out of alignment with your core values. My core values are kindness, compassion, loyalty.” His shame around drinking was reminding him not that he was a “broken” person, but that he had become someone who was lying to his husband and hurting him.
In Spinelli’s framework, once he had confronted and observed his shame, he mapped the source of its inner voice – it was, unsurprisingly, his scout leader. Looking back over his life, he could see all the moments he was triggered by other authoritative men. “I had this wonderful professor, who was brilliant, but he would talk to me in a condescending tone and it would make me freeze,” he says. The voice reminded him of his scoutmaster. “But I’m not 11 years old. I’m an adult man. That’s how I utilise the framework to help get through those situations. It was important for me to go back to all those different times and to map out my reaction to that situation and what I could have done differently.”
Learning to deal with his shame didn’t magically cure his alcohol dependency, but it helped, as did learning about the neuroscience of problem drinking: “It wasn’t necessarily a moral failing on my part. It was the fact that I had created these dopamine loops and the loop was encouraging me to drink more.”
He is no longer ashamed of shame. “I feel those scars are battle wounds and I’m proud of them; they’ve developed who I am as a person. If we try to understand shame, we might be able to move through it, not run away from it.” Some days are still a struggle, but others are not. Daily practices, including journalling, help. “It goes back to being as honest as I can with my partner and my family. But understanding that, again, I’m not infallible – things are going to happen. I’m just more resilient.”

title: Gen Z and millennials have it far worse than my generation. Here's why | Opinion
description: 'I know my age group has called the young lazy, entitled snowflakes,' says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee, who has been writing for the Guardian for nearly 50 years. Polly believes that the social contract between younger and older generations has been broken, with gen Z and millennials set to be worse off than their parents in the face of soaring unemployment, stagnating wages and ballooning house prices. title: ‘It’s rare to hear: I’m black and middle class’ – Symeon Brown on black Britain’s enduring ‘taboo’

content:
Black people are more prominent than ever in the UK’s politics and culture. But are they overwhelmingly from the middle class, as Brown argues in his new book? And if so, why isn’t anyone talking about it?
S ymeon Brown and David Lammy went to the same primary school in Tottenham, north London. One went on to a selective secondary school, and became the second black person to hold one of Britain’s great offices of state. The other became a journalist who would go on to survey the country’s black professional class more thoroughly than anyone ever had – and who remembers being told by Lammy that he could “never become prime minister, because you sound like where you come from”.
It was 2010, and Brown, interested in politics, was interning for the then Labour backbencher. “And he was right, certainly at the time,” Brown says now.
It’s a small exchange, but it sits at the centre of everything Brown’s new book, The Good, the Black and the Boujee, is trying to work out. What separated the two boys from the same Tottenham streets was class. And class, Brown argues, is the elephant in the room in almost every British conversation about race.
“In the book, I was trying to reconcile two of what seem to be contrary events,” he says, as we chat over Zoom. “On the one hand, Britain’s black population has never had more cultural stature and economic capital – in politics, music, film, publishing – but those same years produced the Black Lives Matter protests and the toppling of Edward Colston ’s statue into Bristol harbour, and black people saying that it is harder than ever to succeed.”
Kemi Badenoch, Stormzy , Daniel Kaluuya , Olivia Dean : are these a reflection of a more equal Britain, or are we simply more comfortable looking at elite black faces while nothing structural changes underneath them? Their success is real, but a handful of people crossing class boundaries is not the same as collective progress.
“Black people in Britain are hyper-visible, but also, in many cases, disenfranchised,” Brown says. “And that creates a tension – class has been missing from conversations about race.”
To get underneath that tension, Brown interviewed about 1,500 members of Britain’s black middle class about their education, employment, families, aspirations, spending, social values and, of course, class. He touches on some questions that feel taboo within this community, such as why middle-class black Britons tend to date white people. What his findings reveal is something Brown thinks Britain has never quite reckoned with: the fact that, as he says, “to be black in Britain is so often to be assumed to be working class”, and that assumption has masked how the black Britons who come closest to power are actually, disproportionately, middle class.
Not everyone was pleased that he went looking. “Bona fide black elites don’t like the idea of this book,” Brown tells me matter-of-factly. Some people, once they heard what he was working on, stopped returning his calls. “People felt it was going to be an exposé.”
The objection, as he understood it, came from the idea that to be black and middle class doesn’t mean you are anywhere near as privileged as if you were white and middle class. “That may be true,” Brown says, “but it doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t interrogate it.”
Britain is a nation obsessed with talking about class and allergic to admitting it has any issue with it. Everyone wants their success to look like the product of hard work and nothing else; nobody wants to concede they had a head start. Black Britons, it turns out, are no exception. “It is very rare to hear someone say, ‘I’m black and middle class,’ in Britain,” Brown says. “The most common response I got from interview requests was: ‘Thanks, but I’m not middle class.’”
Part of the reason is that class itself refuses to sit still long enough to be defined. It is nebulous and mercurial, with economic and cultural dimensions that don’t always point the same way. “The middle class itself has always been quite fragmented,” Brown says. “There’s always been variety in terms of social, economic and political capital.”
Perhaps the most visible example of the changing face of Britain is in politics. Britain has had its first black leader of a major political party; it has had a black chancellor and foreign secretary. And yet, for all that representation has grown, Brown thinks it has brought remarkably little benefit. “Ultimately, these people are representing their class interests,” he says. He runs through the roll call: “David Lammy, educated at a school founded by Henry VIII; Kwasi Kwarteng, Eton and Oxbridge; Miatta Fahnbulleh, the current cabinet’s only black minister, privately educated, Oxbridge … Black politicians actually have to have more elite credentials than white candidates,” he says.
Brown’s point is less that every politician on his list was born privileged than that advancement often depends on acquiring the educational and cultural credentials prized by the establishment. Lammy, for example, was raised by a single mother in Tottenham after his father left the family; he attended the sought-after state-funded King’s School in Peterborough, which paved his way to university in London, then Harvard Law School.
School turns out to be one of the clearest mirrors of class that black Britain has. Among black professionals Brown surveyed, almost one in four had attended a fee-paying school at some point – and, contrary to the popular image of the scholarship kid, 72% of them had their fees paid outright by their parents.
“Representation has been the end goal, and I think people have found it unsatisfying,” Brown continues. For him, the muted response among some black and leftwing voters to Lammy’s departure from government illustrated the limits of symbolic progress.
Brown sees this as part of a wider pattern of a black British elite that increasingly lacks political imagination, or a model of success without assimilation and establishment acceptance. “I was a child of the 90s; it was a very radical period,” he says. “People were critical of corporate behaviour; my parents and their friends had been galvanised by the anti-apartheid movement. There was a kind of radicalism to black sensibility. But black Britain has now been co-opted by corporate and individualist ideals.”
Outside politics, Brown argues that often conversations that are putatively about race are actually about class. He remembers, for example, the debates that used to dominate the heyday of “Black Twitter”, about issues such as “proximity to whiteness” – the notion that lighter skin brought you closer to acceptance. “Completely missing from this is the notion of class,” Brown says. “Because then who has greater proximity to whiteness, Eton-educated Kwasi Kwarteng, or mixed-race Mark Duggan from Tottenham ?”
The arguments over black dating patterns – who is dating outside their race and why – tend to present themselves in the same way. “People primarily date class before race,” he says. “It’s the most visceral discourse that is happening online, and I thought it was useful to add a data intervention.” Brown found that black women, for example, are more likely to be middle-class professionals than their black male counterparts. “What many women were saying was: ‘I’ve got this level of professional success, I’ve hit these particular class markers, but I can’t find a man who also equals this on the terms that I want,’” he says.
Brown grew up in the 90s, in a terraced house on the edge of Tottenham’s once notorious Broadwater Farm estate, an area he describes as “a hub of grime, street life and black radicalism”. His parents were both second-generation British-Jamaicans – his father a “career criminal” and his mother a childcare worker. He describes early years in social housing, when his mother delivered the Yellow Pages for extra cash. He started his professional life as an assistant archivist at the Black Cultural Archives before joining the Guardian as a researcher on a Scott Trust bursary, and later moved to Channel 4 News, where he is now home affairs correspondent. All of which is to say that he now operates in a decidedly middle-class milieu.
When I ask him how he would describe his class status, he laughs. “Everyone always wants to ask me that!” He describes himself, in the end, not as middle class but as “multi-class”, adding: “I’ll never really be read as middle class, because of my accent and other things.”
Whatever the terms, Brown is part of an emerging, often young, black professional class that hasn’t assimilated into the frameworks of white cultural sensibilities. He can be found at book launches populated by the “black literati”, and festivals such as Detty December in Nigeria, or Paris’s Fête de la Musique – as Brown puts it, a “middle-class cultural life driven by black cultural products”.
The Cambridge sociologist Ali Meghji, whose research on Britain’s black middle class predates Brown’s, argues that black middle-class identity in Britain tends to take one of three forms: those who don’t see racism as a significant issue and feel a stronger affinity with people of the same class; those who strategically code-switch to match white middle-class taste; and those who deliberately steer their cultural life towards black diasporic culture.
Brown himself, and many of his subjects, fit firmly into the third category. Like the traditional white middle class, it’s a sort of “if you know, you know” crowd. And like any middle class, it is also full of gossip, drama and internecine fighting. (“There’s so much beef within the black literati, you wouldn’t believe,” Brown laughs.) “When I go to a book launch, I don’t want to drink warm wine and eat cheese,” he continues. “I want to turn up, hear some bashment, dancehall and soca.”
Yet the flourishing of this confident black professional culture is only one half of the story Brown tells. “We’ve never had a greater cohort of black people with this level of cultural or economic capital, but we still have a huge working class that is also, in some cases, disenfranchised from citizenship,” he says. He points to unresolved Windrush cases as an example. Black Britain, Brown argues, has become more stratified – even as the country continues to talk about it as though it were a single, undifferentiated group.
That flattening also shapes the way Britain talks about the working class. Political debate routinely treats the “white working class” as a uniquely left-behind constituency, even though black and other minority-ethnic working-class people face the same pressures, often compounded by racial discrimination. The label can turn shared material problems into a racial contest, inviting struggling groups to see one another as rivals rather than people with common interests.
And for all the pleasures, rivalries and contradictions of black professional life, the economic foundations of middle-classness are shifting beneath everyone’s feet. Three decades of wage stagnation and rising costs have made the category less secure – and membership of it worth considerably less than it once was. “If we think about what it means to be middle class, whatever your race, at this moment in time,” Brown says, “it means to be poorer, less influential, and doing work of lesser stature than 30 years ago.”
The irony, then, is that just as black Britain has developed a sizable middle class – and a culture distinctly its own – the middle-class bargain itself is beginning to fall apart.
The Good, the Black and the Boujee: How Black Britain Became Middle Class by Symeon Brown is published by Dialogue (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

title: We’re teenage girls fighting to ban the use of school uniform in porn. Why have you left it up to us? | Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow

content:
No one should have to feel nervous about walking to school in clothes designed for children. It’s time for UK law to end the disgusting sexualisation of minors
I n the Little Feminist Book Club, we don’t read a lot of books. The group, set up by former students at our school, is more about reading poems and articles, analysing song lyrics, discussing the issues that matter to us and, most importantly, campaigning.
Our current campaign – the one you might have heard of – is to ban school uniform from pornographic content. Simply put, we want to end the depiction of school uniform in pornography to ensure that minors are not viewed as anything other than what they are: children. We were shocked when we realised that this content is currently legal – most of the adults we’ve spoken to agree that it is wrong. But apparently it falls to us – students aged 14 and 15 – to take action.
A new law , due to come into force on 6 November, will ban pornography that shows sexual activity involving anyone pretending to be under 16. But it won’t outlaw the depiction of adults dressed as older schoolchildren. We want to remove this grey area in order to stop normalising the sexualisation of school uniforms. We believe children and children’s clothing should not be associated with sexual acts. Therefore, we believe that school uniform should not be shown as something “sexy”, regardless of the actual age of the person wearing it.
Previous members of the Little Feminist Book Club, working with Tools for Change , successfully campaigned for better access to period products in our school. We then heard about another school feminist group who had campaigned to get school uniforms banned from sex shops. We were appalled that they were being sold in that context, yet somehow not surprised. From an early age, some of us had noticed that school uniforms are depicted in ways that sexualise women wearing them. Mae recalls: “For me it started when I was 12, watching TV with my mother. A female character put on a school uniform to turn on a man and I thought, ‘I’m going to have to wear a uniform like that tomorrow.’”
No 12-year-old should feel uncomfortable about going to school in a uniform that is designed to promote unity and community and safety. Yet we did. It made us question how we would be perceived when we left the house in our uniforms. These were women dressing up in school uniform specifically to turn on a man. The only people who should be wearing school uniform are children.
This issue has affected us personally. Members of our group feel too uncomfortable to wear their uniform out of school. One no longer wears skirts at all. When we were asked to speak at a Tools for Change event in parliament in July we unanimously agreed not to wear our uniform. In a world of AI, we were well aware of the dangers of being photographed in uniform while being associated with this campaign. Before we sent our first letters to MPs and charities, we discussed what it might mean if anyone actually paid attention to what we were saying. Would we be prepared to take this on, given all that it might mean? We were, and so we did.
Since starting this campaign, we have been flooded with support. Sadly, this has included other women and girls sharing their experiences of the same issue – dating back generations. Surveys show that one in three girls has been sexually harassed while wearing school uniform, and we have seen comments from many of them. Older women said that they have never been catcalled more than when they wore school uniform as children; others have shared with us their feelings of disgust and horror. One recalled being assaulted by a group of men in the 2000s “explicitly because of my school uniform”. A teenager said that the number of older men who sexually harass her almost every day is “uncountable”.
Getting to hear people’s own personal experiences fuels our passion and drives us forward. The overwhelmingly positive response truly gives us hope that we can make a difference. We want to protect children now and in the future.
As the campaign continues to gain attention, we have received support from important figures including our local MP and an MSP. One has agreed to directly pass our handwritten letter to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and to table an early day motion. We now also have a meeting scheduled with Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims, and another with Jess Asato MP and the peer Gabby Bertin, who was instrumental in the amendments to the crime and policing bill. Our MP is helping us turn our campaign into a law. He suggested that, instead of creating an entirely new law banning school uniform in pornography, it would be quicker and easier to amend existing legislation – meaning that it would take less time for children to be taken out of this harmful and dangerous position that perverted people have placed us in. But these are not decisions we can make. Everyone has a responsibility to end this cycle of sexualisation and objectification of children. We can’t do that as a few kids in the middle of our GCSEs.
We have made a start by launching this petition. Now, we need the adults who vowed to protect us to get behind it. We need the politicians who pledged to halve violence against women and girls to change the law. It’s all well and good to read this article by a group of kids explaining how we’re trying to keep ourselves safe and think this is a fantastic campaign. But that’s not enough. Things will only change when adults take responsibility for ending the disgusting practice of sexualising clothes made for children. Then perhaps one day young people can go to school knowing the only thing our uniforms signify is that it’s time to learn.
Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow are students aged 14 and 15

content:
Ollie Whitehouse, chief technology officer at the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre , told Radio 4’s the World at One that incidents like today’s computer system shutdowns because of a coding problem were likely to re-occur. He explained:
double quotation mark [This] highlights to a lot of organisations that technology is not a one-time purchase now, that it needs that continuous investment throughout its operational lifetime.
