title: What gets in the way of prisoners’ rehabilitation | Letters
description: Anthony Goodman argues that probation officers have increasingly lost their autonomy, while Joe Sim says rehabilitation will not work in a society divided by brutal social divisions. Plus letters from Chris Parsons and Tracey Burley Your editorial on overcrowded prisons and probation ( 13 October ) was most welcome as it highlights a crisis in community justice that shows little sign of abating. You say that problems date back to the failed part-privatisation of the probation service, but in reality political interference has been happening for far longer than that. Having worked for years as a prison probation officer and then in an aftercare and resettlement unit for ex-offenders, I saw good practice and ongoing practical and emotional support that demonstrated all the important points raised by Enver Solomon in his recent Guardian article. Continue reading...
content:
Anthony Goodman argues that probation officers have increasingly lost their autonomy, while Joe Sim says rehabilitation will not work in a society divided by brutal social divisions. Plus letters from Chris Parsons and Tracey Burley
Your editorial on overcrowded prisons and probation ( 13 October ) was most welcome as it highlights a crisis in community justice that shows little sign of abating. You say that problems date back to the failed part-privatisation of the probation service, but in reality political interference has been happening for far longer than that.
Having worked for years as a prison probation officer and then in an aftercare and resettlement unit for ex-offenders, I saw good practice and ongoing practical and emotional support that demonstrated all the important points raised by Enver Solomon in his recent Guardian article.
Staff visited prisons and got to know inmates before they were released, which involved in-depth discussions of their offending history and what was needed for successful resettlement. Staff visited wet day centres for problem drinkers and established links with community organisations. They did not see themselves as the exclusive purveyors of rehabilitation.
In 1984 the government produced a “statement of national objectives and priorities” that made work with prisoners low-profile, and the aftercare unit closed a few years later. When I tried, as part of my doctoral research, to interview probation staff in the 1990s about their role in prison resettlement, I found that such work had stopped.
Since then, probation officers have increasingly lost their autonomy – and the opportunity and permission to get to know the people they supervise. Risk has become the driving force, resulting in an incredible rate of offenders breaching their licence conditions and being returned to prison.
Probation staff are told to be more professionally curious and to give hope to offenders. The service has struggled to hit its targets, but has surely lost the point of its work, which is not the fault of its hard‑working staff. Action is required, now. Anthony Goodman Professor of community justice, Middlesex University
Your editorial on rehabilitation in prison makes some important points. It is also worth noting the political hypocrisy around this issue. The Barlinnie Special Unit, which did change people in prison, was closed in 1994, while the rehabilitation policies pursued in Grendon Underwood, which opened in 1962, have rarely been extended into the main system.
Why? Because these places challenged the decades‑long political obsession with punishment and deterrence. Whether or not the “Scandi” units at Wandsworth and Pentonville in London, which pursue a similar philosophy to Barlinnie and Grendon, will also be marginalised and ignored remains to be seen.
More broadly, rehabilitation will not work in a society divided by brutal social divisions, a point made by Victoria Law in her book “Prisons Make Us Safer”: And 20 Other Myths About Mass Incarceration : “What does it mean to rehabilitate a person to their former state if that state involves poverty, racism, unemployment, unstable housing, and/or violence? Can a person be rehabilitated if they have never been habilitated (or made fit or capable for society)?”
We must address these issues, stop prison building, redirect the billions wasted on prisons towards probation and other radical alternatives, and reduce sentence lengths, or the devastating cycle of crisis/reform/crisis will only continue and intensify inside. Joe Sim Emeritus professor of criminology, Liverpool John Moores University
Your editorial rightly highlights that the government must prove community supervision works to win support for early releases, while calling for a “person-centred” approach and noting the value of “purposeful activity”.
At LandWorks, a charity providing intensive placements for people on licence or serving community sentences , we see every day that community projects can deliver powerful results. By providing person-centred support wrapped around meaningful, purposeful work and the building of trust, real change can and does happen.
There are many men and women in the system who want to change their lives but face huge hurdles – addiction issues, chaotic home lives, little or no employment history and failed relationships. Providing consistent support can transform lives and reduce the likelihood of further offending. Our independently analysed reoffending rates can attest to that.
The voluntary sector already holds blueprints for breaking the cycles of prison overcrowding, recall and reoffending. A commitment from the government to learn from these existing successful models could transform our criminal justice system and improve public confidence. Rehabilitation and resettlement support makes a huge difference when delivered effectively. Chris Parsons Project director, LandWorks
The debate over early release from prison masks a deeper issue. The underlying problem is a failure to invest properly in early intervention and prevention.
The prison governor Polly Toynbee spoke with was right to highlight the need for early-years support ( Britain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t work, 16 October ). School exclusion, episodes of going missing and disruption in childhood are often warning signs of the harm and offending that may follow.
Trusted-adult mentoring can make a decisive difference. Giving a young person someone to turn to in a moment of stress can help prevent that moment from ending with a weapon being picked up.
St Giles and other like-minded organisations provide this support in schools, with positive results: a 21% reduction in violence and a 14% decrease in offending, according to the Youth Endowment Fund .
The same approach can support people serving sentences in the community, helping them to access services that address the root causes of offending while strengthening the effectiveness of community sentences.
But investment alone is not enough. We must also rethink our justice system and ask who genuinely needs to be in prison. Effective community-based solutions already exist; expanding them would tackle the causes of offending, while easing the intense pressure on prisons and probation staff. Tracey Burley Chief executive, St Giles

title: Wes Streeting in US for Hegseth meeting as Ukraine tensions escalate – as it happened
description: This live blog is now closed, you can read more of our UK political coverage here Labour says it’s told all of its local councils who share power with the Green Party to review their agreements after the Greens passed a “Zionism is Racism” motion at their autumn conference earlier this month. If Green coalition partners don’t agree to condemn the policy, the Labour council groups have been instructed to terminate existing power deals. We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds [the] position that has recently been adopted. “Now is the time to step up pressure on Putin and step up support for Ukraine.” “I’m working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine, military, diplomatic, and economic, and you know, if anybody needed any reminder of that, it’s what we see coming out of Ukraine, with Putin targeting these energy systems , leaving thousands without power, as we’ve got a harsh winter approaching. The future of Ukraine is the future of European security, and that’s that’s why it’s so crucial that Putin doesn’t prevail.”d Continue reading...
content:
Wes Streeting’s meeting with his US counterpart Peter Hegseth at the Pentagon later today will be his first since becoming Defence Secretary in July.
As my colleague Dan Sabbagh noted above – there are lots of issues on the agenda, Iran, Ukraine, and not least the growing US-Nato rift and Washington removing bombers from a UK air base earlier this month amid reports of a possible Iranian plot. Hegseth has also been heavily criticised for his annoucement that he is planning to livestream a public execution by military firing squad on December 3. Streeting was asked on the weekend’s political shows his thoughts on such barbarity. He steered clear of any personal criticism of Hegseth saying only that the UK does not support the death penalty, and as such did not support such an event. PM Andy Burnham has described Hegseth’s proposed event as “abhorrent”.
UPDATE: The US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of the Fort Hood killer Nidal Hasan. Trump had previously said he approved of his secretary’s plan but there has been so much backlash this week to Hegseth’s bloodlust including protest by former military chiefs. Trump’s retreated from the idea, saying just now: “many very good and well meaing people would rather not watch him die.”

title: Nigel Farage says charities that help asylum seekers reach UK should be prosecuted
description: Reform leader did not say who should be targeted but party figures have been critical of small boat rescues by RNLI Charities and volunteers who help asylum seekers get to the UK should face potential criminal prosecution, Nigel Farage has said in an interview with a rightwing US podcaster. While the Reform UK leader did not specify which organisations should be targeted, he and other senior Reform figures have been heavily critical of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), which has faced a campaign of intimidation for its work in rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel. Continue reading...
content:
Reform leader did not say who should be targeted but party figures have been critical of small boat rescues by RNLI
Charities and volunteers who help asylum seekers get to the UK should face potential criminal prosecution, Nigel Farage has said in an interview with a rightwing US podcaster.
While the Reform UK leader did not specify which organisations should be targeted, he and other senior Reform figures have been heavily critical of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), which has faced a campaign of intimidation for its work in rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel.
Speaking to Benny Johnson , a podcaster who has previously written for a series of rightwing US outlets, including Breitbart News, Farage discussed the arrival of asylum seekers on small boats, calling it “literally an invasion of people who could cause us enormous harm”.
Johnson asked him: “Do you believe in criminal penalties for those who facilitated this invasion of the English Isles?”
Farage replied: “Totally, totally. The role of the NGOs, the role of those that are sponsored by taxpayers’ money, because they’re nice, they’re good, they’re kind. They have actually aided and abetted criminality in absolutely every way.
“These are people [who are] are deluded – deluded, hard-left socialist Marxists, who don’t believe in countries, don’t believe in borders, don’t believe in identities, are intent on destroying everything that exists.”
Farage has previously described the RNLI, which rescues some asylum seekers, a small proportion of its lifesaving work, as a “migrant taxi service”, while other Reform figures have criticised the charity, including sharing footage of far-right protesters abusing RNLI crews bringing people ashore.
Calling for charities and campaign groups to be prosecuted for their work has echoes of the efforts by the former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán to try to cement his grip on power.
A Reform spokesperson said Farage’s comments “speak for themselves”.
In his conversation with Johnson, Farage repeatedly raised what he said was the issue of Muslim asylum seekers arriving in the UK, citing what the example of Michigan, the US state where rightwing agitators have sought to whip up anti-Muslim feeling.
Farage said: “We are importing into our countries … people who will do us enormous harm, who will change, disrupt our lives in every way, in fact make our way of life potentially unrecognisable.”
Saying that European countries such as the UK and France had a greater problem with migration than the US, Farage said if Donald Trump was followed in office by a “weak politician” who did not tackle migration and stand up for “American, English-speaking Christian values” then the consequences would be dire.
Farage told Johnson: “If we don’t, this show of yours will be illegal in five or 10 years’ time. Literally, you’ll be banned for hate speech.”
Elsewhere in the interview, Farage speculated that five UK nationals arrested near RAF Fairford late last month before being bailed had been undertaking “a dummy run for a proper terrorist attack on UK forces”.
He added: “I’m deeply, deeply shocked that they’re out on bail whilst there are other people in this country who have said things that the establishment now thinks are racist, who are held inside behind bars without, frankly, proper charge. So it’s what we call here two-tier policing.”
Farage has a habit of sometimes making his message more robust for rightwing US audiences.
He has appeared several times on the web TV show hosted by the disgraced far-right pundit Alex Jones, who was sued by bereaved parents of the 2012 Sandy Hook school shooting , which Jones said had been a hoax.
Farage was criticised by some Jewish groups for using these and other US interviews to discuss tropes and conspiracy theories associated with the far right and antisemitism.

title: Is the modern economic system broken? These urban beekeepers think so – and this is their solution
description: At Bybi in Copenhagen, a dedicated group of staff and volunteers have built a community for all centred on the production of honey – much of which is given away for nothing. Could it be replicated elsewhere? The bees at Bybi, a collective of beekeepers in Copenhagen , live on the roof. Their home is a complex of Victorian buildings, right in the centre of the city, that looks like an idealised vision of the modern social enterprise, ennobled by the architecture of the past. It’s a place of cottage industry in concert with nature, where the marginalised are brought in from the fringes and corporations stand waiting to help, where jobs happen but a lot of the work is done by volunteers, and where – this bit is important – a lot of time is spent discussing ideas. Oliver Maxwell, Bybi’s 48-year-old founder, encourages me to examine the buildings more closely. They were once a prison, a workhouse and a hospital; their functions today – a homeless shelter, a young offender institution and, until recently, a job centre – are not so different. Denmark’s Victorian transformation, from “agricultural backwater to industrialised agriculture”, was reflected in how they treated people, Maxwell says. Continue reading...
content:
At Bybi in Copenhagen, a dedicated group of staff and volunteers have built a community for all centred on the production of honey – much of which is given away for nothing. Could it be replicated elsewhere?
T he bees at Bybi, a collective of beekeepers in Copenhagen , live on the roof. Their home is a complex of Victorian buildings, right in the centre of the city, that looks like an idealised vision of the modern social enterprise, ennobled by the architecture of the past. It’s a place of cottage industry in concert with nature, where the marginalised are brought in from the fringes and corporations stand waiting to help, where jobs happen but a lot of the work is done by volunteers, and where – this bit is important – a lot of time is spent discussing ideas.
Oliver Maxwell, Bybi’s 48-year-old founder, encourages me to examine the buildings more closely. They were once a prison, a workhouse and a hospital; their functions today – a homeless shelter, a young offender institution and, until recently, a job centre – are not so different. Denmark’s Victorian transformation, from “agricultural backwater to industrialised agriculture”, was reflected in how they treated people, Maxwell says.
In the middle of it all is the collective, which looks like a lot of things – a commune, a kitchen-table business, an art space. Everything smells of honey. Long drapes in earthy colours frame the entrance to a space where volunteers jar honey by hand. Small pots are stacked against a window in what appears to be a random formation, but this turns out to be a stylistic map of the city: each jar is from a particular street, with its own shade and its own taste, thanks to “the flowers people planted, the weather, the bees’ own decisions and choices”, as Maxwell puts it.
“Bybi is a constellation of time, work, money, community and connection, a place asking an open question: what would it take for bees, people and communities to thrive?” he says. Between 40 and 50 volunteers come in and out throughout the year, with a core team of 15 undertaking practical, honey-related tasks and events.
They have 80 to 100 colonies, not just on this rooftop, but all over the city, on businesses and conference centres, schools, municipal buildings, restaurants. They produce between four and six tonnes of honey every year. How that turns into money really depends.
Sometimes they give it away, at weddings and festivals. “Honey is an invitation,” Maxwell says. “It wants you to come in as a co-creator, with a joint responsibility for its health. We ask that you share it with someone you care for. And you plant a flower to help the bees.”
Sometimes they sell it in the old-fashioned way, at a couple of boutique delicatessens around the city. Sometimes they ask people how much they want to pay; some are generous, some are not. Sometimes they discuss it in a reverse haggle, sitting in a group where they, as sellers, start low; the bidders tend to drive the price higher by thinking deeply about what went into the honey.
Maxwell, an anthropologist, is originally from the UK. He spent time in Vietnam doing forest protection, some more in Brighton training social enterprises, then arrived in Denmark in 2007, setting up Bybi along similar lines in 2010. The plan was to employ homeless and other marginalised people, who would then be absorbed back into society. Honey would be made at the same time. Bybi also employed a social worker, “who was always a really nice person”.
The problem is, “it just doesn’t work”, he says. “The bottom half of the jobs market has fallen out and everyone else has to run faster and faster. The moment you make contact with the market economy, everyone just melts. We’re sitting here with a crisis of community, a loneliness crisis , a crisis in the meaning and purpose of work. People need to do stuff – we’ll find stuff to do. But the labour theory of value, where you create worth with your time, your boss takes it and gives you some back that you can live on? That does not work.”
They abandoned the “giving homeless people jobs” agenda. Now, people come because they want to, not because they’ve been forced to by the job centre. Five or so people are employed, with more in the summer; there are scores of volunteers, including disabled people who pack flower seeds. “They do it as slowly as they like and we give most of the seeds away for free,” Maxwell says. “It’s outside the logic of work.”
And yet jobs are found. Maybe that, like the honey, is a byproduct of the bees. Back on the roof, 53-year-old Aref Haboo, the principal beekeeper, is looking for the queen amid sheets of honeycomb. The Syrian Kurd, who came to Denmark in 2014, finds her first time with an instinct gleaned from 18 years doing this job in the Afrin province of northern Syria, before he was displaced by Islamic State. Bees can recognise faces , apparently; they can also count and maybe even dream.
Anne-Louise Krogh Hornbech Jensen, 34, who wrote her dissertation on Bybi and now works here, says she always sticks by Haboo around the bees because then she doesn’t get stung, which is as much proof as a bee could give you that they recognise faces. Haboo says Danish honeybees are less aggressive and more productive than Syrian bees.
This haphazard income stream isn’t the only thing keeping Bybi afloat. Its partners include universities, architects and corporations such as L’Oréal, which took some bees for the land at the back of a distribution centre. “The director became fascinated and stopped cutting the grass,” says Maxwell. “He got bat boxes, bird boxes, hedgehog boxes. They sponsored our work with schools. Employees collected the seeds and took them home, so the biodiversity of the field was spreading through the city. The director discovered a kestrel was nesting there when he found a dismembered rabbit.”
When rewilding, says Nicolas Hansen, a 27-year-old volunteer and nature management student, “you have to be OK with saying: ‘Our primary interest is not humans.’ You have to give nature its space.”
Those various sponsorships support schools programmes at Bybi, plus they collaborate with a lot of artists. People sometimes write messages to the bees, just catching them up with the news, recalling a preindustrialised era when many households would keep a hive or two and talk to the bees.
Refugees also work here, while people on incapacity benefits volunteer, but no one would call this a project for employing refugees or refurbishing the economically inactive. “We also have corporate refugees volunteering,” Maxwell says breezily, describing the volunteers burnt out by their high-flying jobs. Andrew Japp, a 52-year-old from Scotland, says: “I’d call myself more of a transient.”
Every society projects their image on to honeybees. Ancient Egyptians said they were the tears of the sun god Ra, to reinforce the divine right of the pharaoh, who was given the title Nesut-Bity, “he of the sedge and the bee”. To Aristotle, bees were the first “political animals”, organised in city states. In Manchester, the birthplace of modern capitalism, there is a bee on every lamp-post. All the language we use about them – hives, colonies, workers, queens – makes them not just capitalism’s mascot, but an attempt to reconcile the contradictions of the new, self-correcting market economy into a coherent picture, modelled in the natural world.
“We layer this industrious language on them, but it’s completely wrong,” Maxwell says. “The relationship they have with a flower isn’t toil – it’s sexual. It’s the reproduction of life in a language of touch, taste, smell, dance, colour; the hair they have on their eyeballs, the way they can hear through their feet. It’s an intense sensory experience and it can only be understood as pleasure. They’re not obeying an order. They’re obeying their senses telling them it’s gorgeous.”
Bybi’s mission is sometimes described as “degrowth” or “regeneration”. Both apply, but neither captures the sense of urgency, that “we’re all living with this cognitive dissonance all the time, that everything bad is being hyperscaled, from AI to El Niño , yet we’re meant to exist as if everything works and nothing has changed,” says Maxwell. “The problem here is that we need to change metaphors.”
Often, when it makes a decision, Bybi will deploy what the philosopher Bruno Latour called the “parliament of things”– a bid to expand democracy to take in nonhuman agents such as animals, rivers and plants. “Stay with the trouble,” is Maxwell’s watch‑phrase, or one of them, referencing Donna Haraway’s 2016 book, in which she argues that, in the face of ecological crisis, we shouldn’t wait in despair to be rescued: instead, form bonds of care and fight like hell.
Madeline Pugh, 26, is a student volunteer from the US. She says Denmark is the perfect sandbox for this experiment: “As a culture, it really appreciates and finds beauty in slow processes, taking time to build something with good intentions.” But it’s not a sweet story of easy integration and togetherness. Haboo’s life outside the bees is precarious – he got a speeding ticket the other day that could have jeopardised his citizenship application, even though he has been in Denmark for 12 years and his wife and children are here, too.
“Danish society makes out it’s all about sourdough and pretty girls on bicycles, but it’s incredibly racist. It wins all the prizes for being livable, but not if you’re brown,” Maxwell says.
There is a raging debate about honeybees in Denmark, which is a kind of nativism with the sting removed (ironically): there are 293 species of bee in the country, but only one makes honey; all the others are, to varying degrees, endangered. People make the argument that honeybees aren’t properly Danish, that they are taking work from wild bees, that they are sexually promiscuous, that they spread diseases and that they are a conspiracy of the EU and industrial agriculture. Honeybees are so connected with industrial agriculture that they have become a lightning rod for rural communities who feel trampled by it, who see themselves as the disenfranchised wild bee in this equation.
As much as honey is all around, Bybi isn’t taking the honeybee’s side in this culture war – it wants to introduce a relationship with bees that enriches conditions for all pollinating insects. That means more flowers planted and more spaces left to be rewilded, but also, on a deeper level, more people engaging with the interdependence between our activities and the ecosystems that sustain us.
But there is pushback to what Bybi does. Some say it shouldn’t be getting into bed with corporations, although Japp says the relationship with businesses is more: “We don’t subscribe to your bullshit, but you should subscribe to ours.” People say it’s not scalable: they ask how it’s going to feed the world and point to the reliance on volunteers as a sign that it’s not a viable concern that could stand on its own two feet. “As if there’s a spot on Earth where capitalism doesn’t exist,” Maxwell says, exasperated. “We have to start in the conditions that exist today, which are messy and compromised, but also full of possibilities for improbable collaborations across people, plants and animals.”
As part of an internship at Gehl, a design consultancy that specialises in urban transformation and community-building, Pugh is doing a project on the eight components of awe, as defined in Dacher Keltner’s 2023 book, Awe. These are moral beauty (other people’s kindness or courage); collective effervescence (bees are good at this); nature; music; art; spiritual and religious experience; life and death (being present at one); and epiphanies. “A lot of people here are keepers of awe,” she says.
There is no blueprint that could replicate the precise alchemy of people, place and nature found at Bybi. But an experiment in cooperating across species and within our own – to bring in everyone from the suits to the left-behind – to foster a sense of common purpose and imagine a post-industrial future? That must be scalable.

title: ‘Big business’: little-known court system in Louisiana churns out thousands of evictions – and millions in fees for judges
description: Guardian investigation: Louisiana’s justice of the peace court system may violate tenants’ constitutional rights as eviction fees boost judges’ incomes Continue reading...
author_name: Oliver Laughland and Will Craft with photography by Annie Flanagan
content:
Guardian investigation: Louisiana’s justice of the peace court system may violate tenants’ constitutional rights as eviction fees boost judges’ incomes
When she arrived at the justice of the peace court on a rain-soaked morning, Marchana Watts hoped she could fight off her landlord’s push to evict her and her five children from their trailer home on the outskirts of Baton Rouge.
Watts, a careful record keeper who earned $20 an hour as an insurance analyst, came to Justice Tracy Batieste’s small courtroom with receipts. They showed she had paid her $950 monthly rent for the past year and a half, she said.
But when her case was called, Watts said in a complaint to the state judiciary commission, her evidence was “COMPLETELY IGNORED by the ‘judge’. She did not print out all of my documents and didn’t allow me to properly present them.”
Within a few minutes, Watts recalled in a later interview, Batieste moved to the issue of a court fee, instructing the manager of her trailer park to pay up.
He handed the justice a folded bundle of cash with a hundred-dollar bill on top, Watts said. “She stuck it in her robe … And then she was like: ‘You have 24 hours to move.’”
Watts had been evicted from her home by a little-noticed judicial system that orders thousands of evictions in Louisiana each year.
Inside Louisiana’s justice of the peace courts, evictions often move swiftly, landlords rack up wins, some judges earn outsized incomes – and housing advocates say tenants’ fundamental rights are at risk.
The state’s 390 justices of the peace work part-time – ruling on evictions, small claims and wage garnishments as well as, in happier moments, performing weddings. They are required to have only a high school diploma and their courts do not need to keep detailed records or follow standard rules of evidence. They are paid directly by the fees their court charges, including court costs in eviction cases that can total $150 or more.
In court documents and interviews, tenant advocates and legal experts say the interplay between fees and justices’ personal income creates conflicts of interest that can incentivize them to evict tenants and win the favor of landlords who bring in cases and fees.
“Why would landlords prefer to go to a justice of the peace court?” said Bradley Benton, a former legal aid attorney who has defended Louisiana tenants in eviction cases. “It’s faster. It’s cheaper. And it’s easier to evict.”
Eviction fees helped the justice of the peace in one part-time suburban court earn more compensation last year – over $400,000 – than the chief justice of the US supreme court earns.
That justice of the peace is one of five who earned more than $220,000 in a single year from filing fees, much of it derived from eviction cases. Renters are frequently compelled by their leases to pay court costs back to a landlord following evictions.
One longtime justice of the peace calls some of these courts “big business”. A clerk for another justice told a tenant’s lawyer that “we are a for-profit court”. A legal expert described a justice of the peace court in a New Orleans suburb as an “eviction mill”.
The Guardian’s nine-month investigation draws on analysis of more than 11,000 pages of eviction records and 3,400 financial disclosure forms as well as deposition testimony, recently unsealed investigative evidence and documents released under public records requests. The reporting also draws on dozens of interviews with justices, tenants and housing attorneys, and the observation of eviction hearings at five justice of the peace courts in the Baton Rouge and New Orleans metro areas and in St Tammany parish.
“I believe this system is blatantly unconstitutional,” said Lisa Foster, a retired California superior court judge and the former director of the office for access to justice at the US Department of Justice. She pointed to a more than century-old US supreme court precedent , which found that a defendant’s rights were violated if their case was heard before a judge with a direct financial interest in the outcome. “Without question, the Louisiana justice of the peace system has failed its citizens, yet no one seems to be taking action.”
This scrutiny comes as Louisiana’s state government has quietly backed this court system with new laws that expand these justices’ authority, while at the same time passing a law that carries possible jail sentences for homeless people .
In Louisiana and across the US, millions of tenants are struggling as the overall cost of living continues to soar – and rents and junk fees charged on top of rents have surged amid shortages of affordable housing . Roughly one out of every 13 renter households faced eviction filings in 2025, according to research by Princeton University’s eviction lab covering 10 states and dozens of metro areas.
When landlords seek eviction, renters are often at a disadvantage because of their limited finances, lack of understanding of the eviction system and, frequently, lack of legal representation. Studies around the country often show that less than 5% of tenants have lawyers to fight for them in eviction cases, while more than 80% of landlords typically have attorneys on their side .
Uneven playing fields in the eviction process can put additional strains on renters already struggling to get by – piling on court fees, moving charges and other costs and, studies show, harming families’ mental and physical health .
Louisiana, one of the poorest states in the US, offers some of the weakest legal protection for renters in the nation. A first-of-its-kind data analysis conducted by the Guardian found that the eviction filing rate within the jurisdiction of the busiest justice of the peace court was nearly three times the national average. The rate of legal representation for tenants in this court, according to documents reviewed by the Guardian, could be as low as 1%.
The Louisiana Justices of the Peace & Constables Association and the state attorney general’s office did not answer a series of detailed questions from the Guardian for this story.
In a recent public statement, the Louisiana attorney general, Liz Murrill, said the state’s justices of the peace “play a vital role in serving our communities and upholding the rule of law” and “providing access to justice close to home”.
After the short hearing in Justice Batieste’s court concluded in July 2024, Watts left in tears.
She had moved into the three-bedroom trailer home after the death of her sister to be closer to her only remaining sibling. It was cramped and damp. But it was a stable place to live.
The eviction order, tacked to her door earlier in the month, had come as a shock. She had tried to find free legal representation, but Louisiana’s eviction process – which generally requires just 72 hours’ notice before an eviction case can be heard in court – was so fast she did not have enough time.
Black women, like Watts and the majority of renters interviewed for this series, face greater risk of eviction than any other demographic group, according to numerous studies .
Watts said she suspected her eviction was an act of retaliation. Her property manager, who had stood before her in court that day, had made continued, unwanted sexual advances via explicit images sent over text message and knocks at the door past midnight, according to Watts and records seen by the Guardian. In her written complaint – which was part of a tranche of recently unsealed records obtained by the Guardian – she told the state judiciary commission that the manager had “emotionally and mentally abused me”.
There was no chance to discuss that in court.
Batieste did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the Guardian. In an interview with the judiciary commission in February 2025, she asserted that when she ruled on Watts’s case there were “some materials that were missing that kind of had a question mark on them”.
Under state law, Watts had 24 hours to vacate her home. She borrowed money to book a removal van and rent a storage unit to keep her possessions. She found a place for her boys to stay, moving 50 miles south to the rural town of Donaldsonville, which sits on a stretch of the Mississippi River and is surrounded by chemical plants.
For the next four weeks she slept in her car, parked nearby in the driveway of her late grandmother’s abandoned home. She prayed for strength each night before falling asleep in the back seat.
“It was a lot,” she recalled. “But I had to stay strong for my sons.”
Justice Chuck Cusimano II’s courtroom sits off a tight corridor on the sixth floor of a tall government building in the New Orleans suburb of Harahan. A slight man with wavy gray hair, he has been the elected justice of the peace for Jefferson parish’s fifth district for almost 20 years . He previously served as a district court judge and a state legislator.
Eviction hearings begin promptly at 9.30am on Tuesdays and Thursdays, usually wrapping up before midday. A large clock adorns the left-side wall of the courtroom and wooden public benches are separated by sheets of hard plastic.
On a recent June morning, as the clock ticked a few minutes before 9.30am, a cluster of landlords and property managers lined the benches, waiting to appear before the judge.
“He’ll be done with this whole docket in 30 minutes,” quipped one representative for a local leasing company. “He’s fast!”
“I love that!” replied a property manager, also awaiting her turn.
The Guardian observed five separate eviction dockets at Cusimano’s court throughout June and July, witnessing the speed with which cases were heard, almost always resulting in a judgment ordering a tenant to vacate their home within 24 hours.
On that morning in June, Cusimano ran through 11 cases in 14 minutes. Two days later, on 18 June, the morning after a tropical storm hit New Orleans, flooding parts of the city and downing trees across roadways, he heard 86 cases in 36 minutes. All but one resulted in a judgment of eviction.
Over the sessions observed by the Guardian, the tenants ordered to leave their homes included single moms, cashiers, healthcare workers and law enforcement professionals. Some had fallen behind on rent because they had been laid off from their job or missed time from work because of illness.
The majority of the cases, though, resulted in default rulings in favor of the landlord after a tenant did not appear in court. Louisiana, like nine other states, allows landlords to issue leases that waive a tenant’s right to a notice period following a missed rent payment, meaning an eviction summons can be filed almost as soon as someone falls behind. In contrast, Washington DC requires 30 days’ notice and Vermont 14 days – providing tenants more time to find legal representation, scrape together additional funds or negotiate payment plans with their landlords.
After Cusimano had issued several judgments at a hearing on 2 June, he joked with the landlords in the public benches: “No more tenants? Then we’re winning!”
The small group of renters who showed up at Cusimano’s court on the morning of 18 June included Leroyalnika Pierre, a 24-year-old single mother who works at a Waffle House and as a part-time hairstylist. She sat in the waiting area, holding her two-year-old son, waiting for Cusimano to call her name. It was her first time facing eviction and she did not know what to expect.
As she heard her name called, amid the flurry of activity, the case began before she had even made it to the judge’s bench.
“Did you pay your rent?” Cusimano asked, after the court heard from a property manager at a rental company named 1st Lake Properties, who said she owed $1,395.
“No,” she replied, her voice barely audible. “I was waiting on them to fix my place.”
Justice Cusimano immediately ordered the eviction, informing Pierre she could not withhold payment over the conditions of her apartment, but could sue 1st Lake, one of Louisiana’s largest rental firms , separately over the issue. Pierre, like almost all others that day, had no attorney. Her hearing lasted less than a minute.
“He wasn’t even trying to hear the reason why I hadn’t paid,” she said later. Her apartment was infested with termites, she claimed in a brief interview after the hearing.
During an interview, Cusimano acknowledged the speed of his hearings but said he always allowed tenants to articulate a defense.
“I don’t think I’ve ever told anyone they couldn’t be heard,” Cusimano said. “I do stop them when the stories go off on a tangent that has nothing to with the eviction, including … when they start to tell me that they were laid off. I’m not trying to be rude to them, but being laid off has nothing to do with their contract.”
He added that Louisiana law does not allow a tenant to simply stop paying rent if they have a termite infestation or other maintenance problems. If the landlord doesn’t fix things after they have been informed in writing, he noted, the renter can hire someone to make the repairs and withhold part of the rent to cover those costs.
When Louisiana’s current governor, Jeff Landry, was attorney general in 2020, his office released a document that lauded justice of the peace courts for “providing constituents with an often faster and less expensive avenue to justice”.
The volume and speed of eviction cases heard by Cusimano help explain how, in 2025, his court raised revenue of just under $1m in fees, of which Cusimano directly retained $380,929, records show . That amounted to over $63,000 more than the US chief justice, John Roberts, earned in salary last year . Cusimano has earned more money in fees alone than the nation’s chief justice in six of the last 10 years. He is also paid an additional $21,600 in parish salary, taking his earnings to more than $400,000 in 2025.
“I made a very good living last year,” Cusimano, whose court’s jurisdiction spans just over 25 sq miles, acknowledged in a recent interview.
“I am not embarrassed for the work I do,” he said. “And I think that I do the exact same work as every other justice of the peace in this state for each case. I happen to have more.
“It’s my location. It’s the numbers,” he explained. “… I have a lot of apartments in this district.”
Cusimano’s court charges at least $150 for filing an eviction – the maximum allowed by statute for justice of the peace courts that employ a clerk. Like other justices of the peace, he is entitled to keep roughly half of that amount. In some cases the court also charges an additional $60 fee for a writ of ejection, a separate order allowing the court’s constable to physically evict a tenant and their belongings from premises. A justice and their constable – an elected official who enforces the court’s decisions and also keeps a portion of filing fees – are entitled to an even split of the ejection fee.
Because justice of the peace courts are not courts of record, there is no digital record of case dockets or proceedings, making the sheer volume of eviction cases, their outcomes and who brings them almost impossible to track.
To do so, the Guardian spent three weeks inside his courtroom, and manually scanned more than 11,000 pages of eviction records from June 2025 to May 2026, to understand how these cases are handled. The records were kept individually stapled inside stacked document boxes at the side of the justice’s bench.
Data analysis by the Guardian revealed that Cusimano’s district had an eviction filing rate of almost one in five renter households per year, which would rank third out of the states and cities tracked by Princeton’s eviction lab. In the 12-month period ending this May, Cusimano’s court ruled on nearly 3,300 eviction cases. Some were handled by his son and daughter, who occasionally serve as “ad hoc” justices , records show.
The analysis also found that eviction fees were responsible for the majority of Cusimano’s salary and that 98% of the eviction filings in his court were for non-payment of rent.
The data showed that one landlord – 1st Lake Properties – was responsible for over 60% of Justice Cusimano’s entire eviction docket. 1st Lake won 1,974 eviction judgments in Cusimano’s court from June 2025 to May 2026. Nineteen eviction orders were denied because 1st Lake representatives failed to show in court. Just three evictions filed by 1st Lake were denied for other reasons.
The company, which has “developed, acquired and managed” more than 10,000 rental units in Louisiana, also charges its tenants “any and all fees, including attorneys fees, and costs associated with eviction”, according to a review of 1st Lake leases and interviews with attorneys who have represented their tenants in court.
Foster, the former US justice department official, said the Guardian’s findings indicated the court was functioning as “an eviction mill and a ‘company court’”.
“When a single landlord accounts for the majority of cases in the court, when virtually all of the cases result in judgments for the landlord, when the tenants are paying for the cost of their own evictions, there is something fundamentally wrong,” said Foster, who is a co-founder of the Fines and Fees Justice Center, a non-profit group that fights against what it sees as unfair fees and fines.
During an interview, Cusimano forcefully denied that landlords repeatedly paying fees to file eviction cases in his court might represent a built-in conflict of interest.
“I don’t see a conflict at all,” he said. “It’s fee based, and they pay upfront to us, irrespective of the outcome.”
Asked about any appearance of a conflict of interest, Cusimano responded: “I don’t know. I can’t do anything about appearance.”
1st Lake was co-founded by Henry Shane Jr, a local businessman and Republican party donor. According to a 2015 media profile , Shane had used his fortune to collect more than 160 vintage cars and personally commission a recreation of the Nottoway mansion, one of the largest plantation homes built during the era of slavery.
The Guardian’s analysis of a year of Justice Cusimano’s eviction records found that 1st Lake filed an eviction claim against one out of every 10 renter households in the district, nearly all of which were for unpaid rent.
1st Lake Properties did not respond to repeated requests for comment.
Cusimano’s court has consistently yielded the highest revenue from fees among Louisiana’s justice of the peace courts, according to a Guardian analysis of more than 3,400 annual financial filings, which are mostly handwritten and document the self-reported earnings of each justice of the peace over the past decade. The analysis revealed that the 10 justice of the peace courts in the state with the highest revenue brought in nearly $31m in fees over the past 10 years.
It also revealed that the justices in those 10 courts earned nearly $12m from their court fees over that decade and received an additional $1.2m in salaries paid by their parishes. The rest of the fees were used to compensate their constables and other staff as well as pay for office expenses and training.
Hannah Adams, a senior attorney at the National Housing Law Project, said the findings highlighted the “massive amount of money that is flowing through the system”. The non-profit, alongside the Southern Poverty Law Center, is pursuing a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Louisiana that claims the state’s justice of the peace system is unconstitutional.
“The fact that it is flowing directly into the pockets of independent judges, combined with a lack of oversight over these courts, means it is like the wild west,” she said. “There is no other state in the country that retains a system like this.”
Justice Steven Sanders, in the fifth district of East Baton Rouge, is the state’s second-highest-paid justice. His small courtroom sits on the south-eastern outskirts of the state’s capital, surrounded by low-rise housing units and next to a moving company. He holds court on a foldout table draped in black cloth.
In 2024, his court generated more than $753,000 in fees. Roughly 90% of that came from evictions, Sanders has said.
Combined with his parish salary, the part-time justice earned more than $299,000, a salary that is almost equal to what an associate justice of the US supreme court earns. Sanders, like other justices in high-revenue courts, hires a part-time clerk funded by an additional filing fee. She was paid more than $145,000 in 2024. She is also his wife.
Sanders estimated during deposition testimony in August that his court hears 300 to 400 evictions a month.
Sanders, who has served in the same role for 30 years , is the defendant in the class-action lawsuit, which was filed last year .
“Like all justices of the peace in Louisiana, Defendant Sanders’s dependence on filing fees to pay his salary and the court’s operating expenses creates an incentive for him to maximize the number of eviction cases filed in his court by ruling in favor of landlords, who select where to file a petition for eviction,” the suit claims, adding that the charging of additional fees for ejection writs “creates an incentive for him to enter judgments of eviction against tenants”.
In September, a federal judge rejected the Louisiana attorney general’s office’s attempt to have the case thrown out of court, marking a significant victory in the case.
Sanders declined to respond to written questions from the Guardian, citing ongoing litigation.
Landlords in Louisiana typically have a choice of which type of court to file eviction cases in. The state’s district and city courts also have the authority to handle eviction claims. Judges in these two more formal court systems must hold law licenses.
Litigants in justice of the peace courts also have more limited appeal rights. If tenants want to challenge a justice of the peace’s ruling, they must seek an entirely new trial in a district court. These appeals generally must be filed within 24 hours to avoid eviction, and probably mean payment of a security bond that can equal one month’s rent. They are nearly impossible to navigate without an attorney.
Established during the era of colonization, justice of the peace courts were once a mainstay of the American legal landscape.
By the 20th century, they faced closer scrutiny. In a groundbreaking 1919 American legal text, Justice and the Poor , Reginald Heber Smith argued that justice of the peace courts had formed “unholy alliances with collection agencies” and “very generally became actually corrupt”. Thanks to lack of oversight and justices’ dependence on fees, he wrote, “JP came to mean ‘judgement for the plaintiff’”.
During the last decades of the 20th century, many states moved to abolish justice of the peace courts or limit their powers. In Mississippi, the justice court was reformed following a federal appeals court decision in 1981 that found the fee system to be unconstitutional and “ a malignancy weakening the administration of justice ”. Now, only seven states grant these courts judicial powers, and even fewer allow their justices of the peace to handle eviction hearings, according to a review of state laws . Louisiana is the only state where justices of the peace reap income directly from the court fees they charge.
A century after Justice and the Poor was published, concerns about the system’s vulnerability to misconduct remain.
In 2019, a justice of the peace in Jefferson parish was sentenced to three years in prison for diverting money from his court to satiate a gambling addiction. In 2020, a justice of the peace in rural Morehouse parish was removed from office over a series of allegations including overcharging eviction fees. In 2021, a justice of the peace in Ascension parish resigned after local news revealed he had heard cases outside his territorial jurisdiction, which was described as a “money grab”.
In December 2025, Justice Tracy Batieste, the East Baton Rouge justice who evicted Marchana Watts, resigned from office after being temporarily disqualified by the state’s supreme court subsequent to the judiciary commission finding “substantial, credible evidence” establishing probable cause that she was charging unlawful and excessive court fees during eviction proceedings.
Batieste’s court raised more than $120,000 in revenue in 2024, according to her latest self-declared financial disclosure, ranking 10th in fees gathered by the state’s justice of the peace courts.
Recently unsealed evidence reviewed by the Guardian revealed that the justice faced sustained complaints from landlords who came before her court. One told the judiciary commission that there seemed to be “an incredible increase in fees over the past few months”.
Another indicated to the commission that Batieste’s preferred method of receiving payment was via the mobile payment service Cash App. A photograph obtained by the Guardian shows a large printout of the Cash App account pinned to a noticeboard in her courtroom.
Batieste acknowledged some of these unlawful charges, which included a “Covid fee” and additional service fees and copying fees, in unsealed sworn testimony. She also acknowledged owing her constable thousands of dollars in fees.
Tyja Jackson fell behind on rent after tragedy enveloped her life.
In March, her son Kyion, a seven-year-old with dimples and a deep smile, was killed in a car crash.
Four months later, Jackson, 27, found herself before the justice of the peace Mark Miley in East Baton Rouge, facing an eviction summons from her landlord. Jackson, who had no attorney, explained to Miley, who holds court in the boardroom of his private law office, that she had been unable to return to her job as a cashier at a local Wendy’s due to overwhelming grief.
“I attempted to go back. I just couldn’t,” she told the court. “It’s all just falling apart.”
Kyion’s funeral had cost $12,000, she later told the Guardian. Along with her overdue rent, Jackson said, she was now being charged $360 in late fees and court costs. The company was not responding to messages or maintenance requests, she said, meaning she was living without air conditioning. She had to send her infant daughter to live with relatives due to the sweltering heat.
Miley has held office since 2009. In 2025, his court, which hears eviction cases only once a week, generated $524,726 in fees, of which he retained $296,215 in compensation. At multiple instances during the Guardian’s visit he referred to the “big business” of justice of the peace courts around the parish. On a separate visit later in July, Miley offered a photographer for the Guardian a payment of two folded $20 bills alongside a small note that contained his phone number, telling them that they could spend it on “coffee”. He expressed surprise when they said they could not accept the payment.
In February of this year, Miley signed a deferred discipline agreement with the state judiciary commission after admitting that he had “ regularly and knowingly ” ruled over eviction cases that fell outside the geographical boundaries of his jurisdiction.
The agreement acknowledged that Miley’s conduct “gave the appearance that he was improperly presiding over the matters due to the direct financial benefit he received from the filing fees” and bound him to stop the practice.
Benton, the former legal aid attorney, said he defended about 100 eviction cases in Miley’s court between 2022 and 2024. He estimated that all but three had been improperly filed.
Less than a month after Miley signed his reprimand, the state legislature took action.
A Republican lawmaker introduced a bill to expand the borders of Miley’s district along with other justices in East Baton Rouge, across the entire territory of city court. It had the wholesale support of local landlords.
“Essentially, the way my court operates is if you file an eviction by Friday, we have court the following Thursday,” Miley told lawmakers during a legislative hearing, describing the value of expanding the boundaries of his power. “You can pull up to my office and you can get in and get out. It’s easy to access. It’s good for tenants and good for landlords, in my opinion.”
The bill was quietly passed by the state legislature – with no media coverage – and became law in June .
It had been in effect for nine days by the time Jackson appeared in Miley’s court. He listened as she told her story. She had just been able to return to work, and had taken on two jobs: one at an Amazon delivery warehouse and another for an events security company. But still, she was behind on rent.
Miley granted her an extra couple of days to find the funds, but issued a judgment of eviction nonetheless. He counseled her to contact a charity to look for financial support, and suggested his judgment against her might actually help.
“Sometimes, I’ve heard if you let a charity know you’ve got a judgment against you, it helps expedite” them offering funds, he told Jackson as he handed her a copy of the ruling against her. She appreciated the suggestion, Jackson said after the hearing.
The eviction judgment, later reviewed by the Guardian, revealed that despite the judiciary commission’s reprimand and the new law expanding his jurisdiction, Miley had still unlawfully evicted Jackson. Her rental unit was located outside his newly enlarged legal domain.
“Unlike in other states where these judges would have to remit all of their filing fees, and then be paid by fixed salary, either set by the county or the state, these justices have a literal financial incentive to break the rules,” said Adams, the National Housing Law Project attorney. “The more cases they take, if they stretch the boundaries of their jurisdiction just a few blocks further, they’re going to make more money.”
Miley did not respond to detailed questions from the Guardian.
Justice Mark Spears of Jefferson parish’s second justice of the peace court holds his eviction hearings in a small office suite next to a noisy highway in the New Orleans suburb of Marrero. A crinkled US flag is tacked to the wall behind his desk.
A notice stuck to the clerk’s window reads:
YOU ARE RESPONSIBLE OR [sic] MAKING SURE YOU ARE FILING IN THE RIGHT COURT
In May this year he appeared at a rare public hearing in front of the state judiciary commission, accused of engaging in “willful misconduct” by lending “the prestige of your judicial office to advance your private interest”. Specifically, the commission admonished him for using an Instagram account named “judge.markspears” to promote himself not only as a justice but also as a private practice attorney and an NFL sports agent.
He apologized multiple times during the hearing. He acknowledged to the commissioners that he now understood that “I can’t put out to the public that I’m a justice of the peace and that I have private stuff, that I’m an attorney also. Because people would think of the prestigiousness of a judge and maybe, you know, use me as an attorney.”
Two weeks later, before an eviction docket hearing on 4 June, the court’s constable, Kendall Bussey, touted Spears’s work as a private attorney and a justice in a speech to landlords and tenants waiting for their eviction cases to be heard.
“Judge Spears is very good at what he does. He’s not only a judge, he’s also a lawyer,” Bussey said during a mass swearing-in, which took place in a cramped corridor out of the justice’s earshot. “Part of what he do is tenant-eviction law. He understands the law.”
Bussey acknowledged that tenants have a right to appeal the judge’s decisions, but added: “I will be open and honest, if Judge Spears gives you an order, 99.9% it’s not going to be overturned.” He then claimed that due to Spears’s expertise “the higher judges actually call him for advice when it comes to Louisiana tenant law”.
In response to questions from the Guardian, Spears distanced himself from Bussey’s remarks. “Constable Bussey is an independently elected constitutional officer. He is not my employee, I do not supervise him, and he does not speak for me or for this court.” The justice said he had never instructed Bussey or anyone else to make those kinds of statements.
“I do not hold myself out as a housing attorney,” he said. “In 20 years of practicing law, I have handled two eviction matters, and I handled both pro bono.” He added that he had never received calls from “higher judges” for advice on housing law and that he always informed litigants of their right to seek a new trial in parish court.
Spears, a former parish councilman, was first elected justice of the peace in 2019 and is running unopposed this November. His court – which is located on the West Bank of the Mississippi River across from New Orleans – has brought in more than $600,000 in fee revenue since 2020, according to his financial statements.
A 2022 recording obtained by the Guardian documents a clerk in Spears’s court explaining to an attorney why it would not be possible to waive court fees for a low-income tenant: “We are a for-profit court and we have to collect those fees.”
Spears said he “will not respond to a characterization of a four-year-old conversation to which I was not a party”.
“My court is not a ‘for-profit court’,” he said. “… If a clerk used the phrase you attribute, that was that clerk’s phrasing, not the policy of this court, and I repudiate it.”
Louisiana’s supreme court is currently considering the judiciary commission’s recommendation that Spears be suspended for six months without pay, with all but 30 days suspended. Its recommendation of discipline stated his actions had “harmed the public’s confidence in and respect for the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary”.
Spears declined to comment on the disciplinary case.
Marchana Watts is still fighting to recover from eviction two years on.
She lost her job about a year ago and started taking antidepressants. She developed diabetes and Cushing’s disease, she said, a hormonal condition which can be triggered by stress.
She found shelter at a relative’s home but was sleeping with four of her sons in a single bedroom. Her eldest was forced to move out.
The cost of a storage unit became unmanageable and so she sold almost all her possessions.
“Everything is still about my children,” she said. “I didn’t want them to see me go through it. That was the hardest part for me.” Over the summer she launched a GoFundMe drive to help pay for school supplies for her sons. To date, it has received no funds.
At the Jefferson parish fifth justice of the peace court one recent morning, Justice Cusimano showed journalists from the Guardian a small wad of cash, held together by a clip, that he kept inside the back of a drawer in his private office. It was about $120, he later said, adding it was held in reserve for especially “sad” eviction cases where he might offer to personally help.
But he added: “You can’t change the law with your compassion.”
In August, as the Guardian was reporting this story, Justice Cusimano announced his retirement at the end of this year, leaving the bench as perhaps the highest-paid judge in the nation.
The position will be filled without a competitive election because just one candidate is running to replace him. His name is Chuck Cusimano III.
He is the son of the justice of the peace.

title: Key findings from the Guardian’s investigation of Louisiana’s justice of the peace courts
description: The system allows judges to boost their modest salaries, with one judge earning more than $400,000 in 2025 Continue reading...
author_name: Oliver Laughland and Will Craft with Tom Richards
content:
The system allows judges to boost their modest salaries, with one judge earning more than $400,000 in 2025
The highest-paid judge in the United States does not sit on the US supreme court.
The jurist who is probably the country’s highest-paid judge holds a part-time position as a justice of the peace in the suburbs of New Orleans, hearing cases in a small courtroom twice a week and presiding over a jurisdiction of just 25 sq miles.
In 2025, Justice Chuck Cusimano II earned more than $400,000 – over $80,000 more than the chief justice of the United States, John Roberts. Cusimano was able to earn that much because – under the rules of Louisiana’s justice of the peace system – most of his compensation is taken directly from the court fees he charges on eviction cases and other matters that come before him.
The system allows a handful of the state’s roughly 390 justices of the peace – who also hear small claims cases and perform marriages – to boost their income well beyond the modest salaries they are paid by local governments.
Although most US states use fines and fees to help fund their justice systems, legal experts and housing advocates say Louisiana is the only state where the total amount of fees justices of the peace charge directly determines how much money they earn. They argue that it is unconstitutional because it creates potential conflicts of interest that put tenants at a disadvantage when they square off against landlords who bring in cases and fees.
A class-action lawsuit being pursued in federal court in Baton Rouge alleges that these fee arrangements encourage justices of the peace to “maximize” the number of eviction cases filed in their courts “by ruling in favor of landlords, who select where to file a petition for eviction”.
Because landlords frequently include provisions in their leases that require tenants to reimburse them for court costs, tenants often end up paying the costs of their own evictions on top of late fees, moving expenses and other charges.
Most of the cases heard in Justice Cusimano’s court were eviction proceedings, according to a nine-month investigation by the Guardian, which has examined the operation of Louisiana’s unique justice of the peace system and how it presides over thousands of eviction cases throughout the state each year.
The investigation included an analysis of more than 11,000 pages of eviction records and 3,400 financial disclosure forms filed over a 10-year period. The Guardian has observed eviction proceedings at five justice of the peace courts throughout the state, and interviewed a dozen individuals who have faced eviction and 10 lawyers who have operated within the system.
The investigation has also examined repeated allegations of misconduct and uncovered widespread failures by justices to observe state training standards. It has identified five justices of the peace who earned more than $220,000 in income from filing fees in at least one year from 2023 to 2025.
Lisa Foster, a former California superior court judge and former director of the office for access to justice at the US Department of Justice, said the Guardian’s findings indicated Louisiana’s justice of the peace system was “blatantly unconstitutional”.
“Courts are supposed to serve the entire community: they are supposed to resolve disputes fairly, they are supposed to enforce rights and responsibilities, they are supposed to keep communities safe,” said Foster, who is co-founder of a non-profit group, the Fines and Fees Justice Center. “And because they serve the entire community, they should be paid for by the entire community out of general tax revenue.”
In an interview with the Guardian, Cusimano denied that there was any conflict of interest in the way court fees paid by landlords seeking evictions help elevate justices’ compensation. “I don’t see a conflict at all,” he said. “It’s fee based, and they pay upfront to us, irrespective of the outcome.”
He said his court handles a large number of evictions because there are “a lot of apartments in this district”.
The state attorney general’s office and the Louisiana Justices of the Peace & Constables Association did not answer detailed questions from the Guardian for this story.
In a recent public statement, the attorney general, Liz Murrill, said Louisiana’s justices of the peace “play a vital role in serving our communities and upholding the rule of law”.
Justice of the peace courts operate in all of Louisiana’s parishes except for the city of New Orleans, which abolished the system in 1879. In almost all jurisdictions in the state, landlords have a choice of where to file their eviction petitions, which can also be heard in city courts and district courts.
Justice of the peace courts generally charge less money for evictions, they process these cases faster, and their judges, unlike other judges in Louisiana, do not need to hold law licenses. Instead, according to state law , they must be of “good moral character”, have graduated high school and “write the English language correctly”.
Louisiana is among 17 states that allow judges, including magistrates, with no law license to preside over eviction hearings, according to research . While prevalent during the era of colonization, justice of the peace courts have been reformed or abolished in most states, with only seven states now granting them judicial power.
The rules of evidence are also relaxed in these courts. Hearsay is admissible under state law . They are not required to maintain digital dockets or employ court transcribers. The Guardian has obtained documents under public records revealing that a quarter of all the state’s justices failed to complete their training requirements over the last two years.
Justices are permitted to use informal venues – including their own living rooms, pool houses, businesses or even an old jailhouse – to hold court.
The Guardian conducted two first-of-their-kind data analyses on the system. The first involved sifting through a decade of annual financial disclosure forms, which each justice of the peace is required to submit to the state’s legislative auditor to report their yearly income.
This analysis, which covers 2016 through 2025, revealed:
The system has generated $45m in fees alone over that decade, with at least an estimated $31m kept as personal salary for the justices. The rest goes to expenses and staff, including elected constables who serve court orders.
The top 10 highest-earning justice of the peace courts in the state, mostly concentrated in the urban centers of Jefferson parish and East Baton Rouge, collected more than $30m in fees over this time period, and were paid nearly $12m out of that amount. Over half of the courts in this system declared less than $10,000 in fee revenue within the decade.
Jefferson parish’s fifth justice of the peace court, presided over by Justice Chuck Cusimano II, generated more than $7m in fees over 10 years, representing 16% of the entire revenue generated by this court system in that time.
“Having a court system that is funded by filing fees is a really bad idea,” said Davida Finger, associate dean at Loyola University’s law clinic. “It creates perverse incentives. It is an old system that needs to be revised in the interest of justice.”
The Guardian conducted a deeper examination of evictions in Justice Cusimano’s court by manually scanning and analyzing 12 months of recent eviction records from his courtroom. This revealed:
The court, which is one of eight separate jurisdictions within the parish, processed more than 5,500 eviction cases from June 2025 to May 2026. This is a higher total than the whole of Orleans parish in 2025 and represents one of the highest eviction filing rates recorded in the United States, according to data held by Princeton University’s eviction lab.
Almost one in five renter households faced eviction in this district.
The court ordered 3,276 evictions during this time – and ruled in favor of tenants in only 141 cases, mostly because landlords failed to show up to court.
“I am not embarrassed for the work I do,” Cusimano told the Guardian. “And I think that I do the exact same work as every other justice of the peace in this state for each case. I happen to have more” cases.
The Guardian’s reporting comes as the US experiences an affordable housing crisis, which is particularly pronounced in Louisiana , one of the poorest states in the nation. There are few protections for renters in the state, which allows fast-turnaround evictions and does not permit rent control. The Republican-dominated state government recently passed anti-homelessness legislation that criminalizes unauthorized outdoor sleeping.
Additional reporting – Rachel Shur, Sophie Sullivan , Cameron Armstrong, Mahesh Makani, Georges Lebreton, Izzy Kiff, Frederick O’Brien and Aliya Uteuova

content:
Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor are rumoured to be the final candidates taking screentests this weekend. So how can they best prepare? And who is likely to triumph?
T his weekend, the identity of the next James Bond is finally expected to be known – to the insiders, at least. According to reports, a number of youngish British actors – definitely three, possibly five – will have their final screen tests.
To say it has been a long time coming is an understatement. It is five years since Daniel Craig was killed in a hail of missiles at the end of No Time to Die, and in that time – even long before it – a swarm of actors have been tipped to replace him, only to age out of the role due to a combination of indecisiveness and cutthroat backstage corporate shenanigans. Whoever is declared to be 007 will be joining the franchise after what is likely to be the longest fallow period in the franchise’s 64-year history.
As such, this is kind of a big weekend. Let’s run through what we know so far.
If three actors are to screen test for Bond this weekend, then they are Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. If there are more – some outlets state that one other actor might be participating, others two – then they won’t include Jack O’Connell or Jacob Elordi , who are both out of the race for one reason or another.
The identity of the other actors are not yet known. Let’s take an uneducated guess and assume that one of them is a Beatle (the best fit is Harris Dickinson) and another one is more famous but less suitable (like Tom Cruise).
Outlets are reporting that the screen test will encompass three main elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. These are all equally important for a modern Bond. Remove stunts from the equation and your film will be boring. Remove camera presence and you’re likely to end up with a George Lazenby type, who has the potential to fluff what would otherwise be an all-timer. Remove dialogue and you’re left with Quantum of Solace, and God knows we don’t need another one of those.
You could argue that Jack Lowden is the frontrunner, if only because the first scene of the first episode of Slow Horses was a pretty good Bond audition in itself. It was, you’ll remember, a race against time sprint through an airport and train station, on foot and in a car, complete with hand-to-hand combat and gun play. And it was very good indeed. Working against him is the sense that he’s a bit too much of a teddy bear for a sociopath like Bond. Plus the fact that he has spent every subsequent scene of Slow Horses doing a pretty good Simon Pegg impression.
Callum Turner would seem to make a sexier Bond, partly because he was able to conjure chemistry from the very silly sex purge movie One Night Only , and partly because he’s married to Dua Lipa, who would almost certainly get the role of Bond Girl Who Dies First if he were cast.
I still think Josh O’Connor would be the best fit, though. He looks good in a tux, as anyone who has seen The Crown will testify. He is very good at convincingly delivering absolute nonsense, as anyone who has seen Disclosure Day will testify. However, his best-known stunt work must be the long scene in The Mastermind in which he slowly climbs up and down a ladder several times in a row.
Now, this is all well and good for a traditional Bond film. But we’re talking about an Amazon Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve . This means that more will be asked of whoever gets the role, and the screen tests are the perfect way to see if they can pull it off.
For example, which of the finalists will best be able to carry their voice in such a way that it isn’t drowned out by all the seat-rumbling full-volume honking noises that Villeneuve will almost certainly use instead of a traditional soundtrack? Which of the actors will most convincingly be able to interact with a side character created with the express purpose of carrying their own spin-off series, to better sustain cross-media IP synergy? Which of them will least overtly die on the inside during the scene in which an Amazon drone delivers them a gun? That is the stuff that will really make or break James Bond going forward.
