content:
Celia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet. The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owl
I t all began on a Dutch trading ship in 1628. No, really. When the Batavia set sail from Amsterdam, it crashed and the shipwrecked survivors were left stranded on a tiny island off the coast of Western Australia. As mutineers eyed the Batavia’s stash of silver, shipmates, friends and families turned on each other. About 100 people were brutally murdered, making it one of the most violent chapters in maritime history.
Nearly 400 years later, in 2015, creative entrepreneur Marc Pos had a lightbulb moment while reading about this “adult Lord of the Flies” atrocity. It gave him the idea for a reality TV show – the game of trust and treachery we now know as The Traitors . It was originally envisaged to take place on a boat, with banished players jumping overboard into the sea.
Co-creator Jasper Hoogendoorn joined Pos to develop the idea, The Mutineers. After 20 rejections, they fine-tuned the game further. Filming it on a boat was too limiting, so they shifted the action on to dry land – and looked for more aesthetic inspiration. Pos was once a choirboy in a 14th-century cathedral, gazing up at its spooky gothic architecture. This became the template for the show’s setting: cue cloak-clad figures walking silently down torch-lit corridors to a secret tower. The Traitors was finally born in 2021, now known as De Verraders.
UK production company Studio Lambert – maker of superior reality TV from Gogglebox to Race Across the World – soon clocked this new Dutch show. “We watched it in the office and couldn’t stop talking about it,” says creative director Mike Cotton. “Reality TV goes in cycles. At the time, it was in a phase of dating shows. This felt totally different. It wasn’t about love, it was about trust.” He and executive producer Sarah Fay visited the Netherlands to witness the phenomenon first-hand. “We went straight to the set,” says Cotton. “All these people in a castle were discussing how someone had been murdered and taking it very seriously. Even unedited, it was fascinating to watch.”
Snapping up the UK and US rights, Studio Lambert began adapting it. “The Dutch version was smaller, so we supersized it,” says Cotton. “We tweaked the format. Changed the endgame. We decided to film the British and American shows at the same castle in the Scottish Highlands.” Each episode is estimated to cost £1m, almost double a normal reality show, enabling it to splash out on cinematic flourishes such as exploding pirate ships and creepy cabins.
Now all it needed was a worthy host. Enter Claudia Winkleman, clad in covetable knitwear. “[BBC One controller] Kate Phillips said she had a show for me,” recalls Winkleman. “It was in Scotland for four weeks. But I don’t leave the kids or my bed, so I said no thanks and forgot all about it. Then Kate said: ‘You should rethink. I’m going to send you the original series they made in Holland.’ I watched two episodes and called back to say I was booking my train to Inverness.”
“Once we had Ardross Castle and Claudia, everything fell into place,” says Cotton. “The UK version quickly became its own thing.” Launching in 2022, it pulled in ratings of about 4 million. As buzz spread and punters caught up on iPlayer, audience figures grew exponentially. The second series leapt to 7 million, the third to 9 million, the fourth to 11.5 million. The inaugural celebrity edition last autumn peaked at 14.9 million, making it the year’s most-watched show.
Did Winkleman ever imagine such stratospheric numbers? “Not a chance,” she laughs. “But I don’t like knowing about ratings. My BBC boss Ed [Havard, director of entertainment] called me a couple of weeks ago to say ‘10 million’. I told him it was a clerical error and never to call me again.”
Fay believes Winkleman is key to the show’s success. “As much as possible, we wanted The Traitors to feel like a drama,” she says. “That was our approach in every department, be it set design, music or Claudia’s wardrobe. It needed to feel like a premium show. Claudia’s integral to that. It’s not your usual reality host role, where they’re slightly removed from the action. She’s embedded as queen of the castle and obsessed with the game. Right from the start, she begged to have screens in her dressing room so she could watch the footage.”
Ever modest, Winkleman plays down her importance. “I disagree with that quite viciously,” she says. “At first, I couldn’t bear being mean or cold. I loathed not smiling and telling everyone they were amazing. But under Sarah’s guidance, I learned to trust that I could be a bit strict. It’s hard because I feel protective and maternal – is that weird? – towards all our players. I want them to know they’re smashing it. Then again, I’m dressed like Chewbacca and throwing portraits on the floor, so I’m hard to take seriously.”
Now airing in more than 40 countries, The Traitors has officially become the most successful TV show on the planet. It has won Baftas and Emmys, while spawning board games, stage shows, escape rooms, even a Prom. Did TV insiders expect the show to strike global gold?
“Nobody saw it coming,” says Deadline’s TV expert Jake Kanter. “Viewing figures growing steadily is always a good sign because it means word of mouth is strong. The best definition of a hit is that you don’t need to tell anyone how well it’s performing, they just know. Your friends, family and colleagues are talking about it.”
When Pos and Hoogendoorn shopped the show around, they resisted pressure to compromise and dug their heels in over certain core principles. One was that gameplay should take place in a self-contained bubble with minimal interference.
“The Dutch always talked about it as a game, not a TV show,” says Cotton. “This is the game, these are the rules. After that, they’re very hands-off. That’s something we’ve adopted. We set up the game and just let it go. That’s rare nowadays. We never want producers to come up at the round table or be the reason someone’s suspected as a Traitor. If you interfere, they’ll latch on to it. We plan certain elements but have no way of controlling what happens.”
Another cardinal rule was that the identity of the Traitors isn’t hidden from the audience. Wouldn’t it be better if viewers played detective, too? “We did dabble with the audience not knowing with the Secret Traitor twist in series four,” says Fay. “But what’s delicious for the viewer is that they’re in on it all. They see the strategies and paranoia on both sides. Imagine if you didn’t know Alan Carr was a Traitor last year. You’d have missed out on the hilarity of him sweating, panicking and going: ‘What am I doing?’”
Winkleman finds the psychology of the game endlessly fascinating. “It’s about gut instinct,” she says. “Turns out it doesn’t exist. It’s about what happens when we try and ‘read’ people. It’s about trust, betrayal, friendship, all of it.” It’s no coincidence that The Traitors was conceived during the era of fake news and social media manipulation. In a post-truth world, it offers insights into conspiracy theories, herd mentality and groupthink.
“What still wows me is that every series is completely different,” says Fay. “That’s the beauty of a murder mystery. We’re just back from filming the seventh UK series and, again, there are things coming up that you’ve never seen before.”
When did the makers realise they had a smash hit on their hands? “For me, it was episode four of the first series,” says Fay. “The Red Breakfast, when Tom stood up and went: ‘Alex isn’t a Traitor, she’s my girlfriend!’ We were watching the rushes with our mouths wide open.”
“It’s rare to find a format that’s multi-generational,” says Fay. “Remember when we walked down the street and pubs were showing the series one final on big screens, like a football match?” grins Cotton. “That blew our minds.”
What have been Winkleman’s highlights? “There are so many I could bore you for 18 months straight. I often have to stop myself gasping out loud at the round table. When the Faithful catch a Traitor, it’s electric. If Traitors turn on Traitors, I always think my head is going to fall off. And I still get a total buzz from going into the turret. It feels very special to be allowed in there.”
For its award-garlanded host, The Traitors has been transformative. “It’s the greatest job I’ve ever been given,” says Winkleman. “It has changed my life and my career, no question. I’ll be there with Barry the owl long after they’ve fired me. I’ve also told the peacock to make room in the shed where he roosts.”
The Traitors has overtaken Strictly Come Dancing as the BBC’s crown jewel but it’s a mutually beneficial relationship. From Celia Imrie’s guff to Richard E Grant’s gaffe, from Ross Kemp’s twitching paranoia to James Acaster’s trembling terror, the franchise thrives on communal talking points. It wouldn’t work nearly as well being binged on a streamer. “The Traitors demonstrates the power of television to bring people together,” says Kanter. “At a time when there’s lots of existential hand-wringing about the health of the broadcast industry – and the BBC particularly – it’s a reminder that when terrestrial TV is good, it’s something to treasure.”
The chaotic second celebrity series reaches its climax this week, with 17 million expected to tune in. What can they reveal about Friday’s final? Fay laughs. “I’m trying to work out what we can tell you without ruining anything.” “It’s stressful and unpredictable,” says Cotton. “Genuinely surprising, even for us,” adds Fay. “With real heart-in-mouth moments.”
“I always cry at the endgame, regardless of who wins,” concludes Winkleman. “Whoever is left standing has played the best game. I feel incredibly proud of them. This series is no different. It feels momentous.”
The Celebrity Traitors climaxes at 8pm on Thursday 29 October and Friday 30 October on BBC One and iPlayer.

title: The Narco Hack review – an epic tale of how detectives’ tech wizardry smashed a billion-euro drugs ring
description: Human heroism is celebrated in profoundly personal ways in this extraordinary tale of a mind-boggling investigation into massive criminal organisations. It’s part The Wire, part The Imitation Game We begin with the audio of a horrifying call made to the French police in 2020. Two men are driving home when their car is attacked. The police ask for the caller’s name as bullets ricochet around the vehicle. “Who cares what we’re called?” the man shouts. “I’m going to die!” Seconds later, his companion is dead. This killing (of a mechanic called Houcine Hakkar) was planned and discussed in detail on an app called Sky ECC. The police were at the tip of an enormous iceberg. Showing modern law enforcement on screen can be a challenge: in the online era, it’s less cops and robbers; more zeros and ones. So it’s a surprise to be confronted with something as thrilling as The Narco Hack. This three-part documentary explores an extraordinary investigation by French, Belgian and Dutch police, during which they undermined several massive criminal organisations via methods at once impressively logical and completely mind-boggling by compromising Sky ECC’s encryption software. content:
Human heroism is celebrated in profoundly personal ways in this extraordinary tale of a mind-boggling investigation into massive criminal organisations. It’s part The Wire, part The Imitation Game
W e begin with the audio of a horrifying call made to the French police in 2020. Two men are driving home when their car is attacked. The police ask for the caller’s name as bullets ricochet around the vehicle. “Who cares what we’re called?” the man shouts. “I’m going to die!” Seconds later, his companion is dead. This killing (of a mechanic called Houcine Hakkar) was planned and discussed in detail on an app called Sky ECC. The police were at the tip of an enormous iceberg.
Showing modern law enforcement on screen can be a challenge: in the online era, it’s less cops and robbers; more zeros and ones. So it’s a surprise to be confronted with something as thrilling as The Narco Hack. This three-part documentary explores an extraordinary investigation by French, Belgian and Dutch police, during which they undermined several massive criminal organisations via methods at once impressively logical and completely mind-boggling by compromising Sky ECC’s encryption software.
Sky ECC was developed by a company called Sky Global, apparently with lawyers and journalists in mind. The app was designed to strip phones of all their normal features, leaving just itself. When the app was shut down, the phones deactivated. Oh, and the phones could be wiped remotely, which was a handy feature. “At Sky, they knew very well that it wasn’t going to be choirboys buying it,” says “Albert”, a drug dealer. “You weren’t going to be talking to your mum on Sky.” Thomas Herdman, who worked for the company, is interviewed and offers an unconvincing defence constructed around the idea that a luxury hotelier wouldn’t ask their guests how they could afford to stay at the hotel.
And so begins an epic tale of brave detective work and tech wizardry. This kind of material is undeniably hard to render visually – but while The Narco Hack does feature an awful lot of scrolling computer text and close-ups of smartphones being turned on, it also hears at length from the cops involved. From shrewd, single-minded prosecutor Johanna Brousse to eccentric cybercrime whiz “Bertillon” (his name is protected and he appears via a series of AI-rendered face-swaps), they’re an engaging bunch.
Furthermore, the investigation grips hard, and the stakes are extremely high. As Bertillon walks us through the decryption process (server locations, cryptographic keys: you’re glazing over already, aren’t you?), most viewers almost certainly won’t fully understand. However, what unfolds on the ground is approximately The Wire meets The Imitation Game. The various police jurisdictions involved aren’t singing from the same charge sheet – the Belgians want to stop the drugs and guns moving, while the French want to identify suspects and follow them.
Then there’s the issue of how much to reveal to their quarries. As the detectives realise they’re looking over the shoulders of drug kingpins, they also understand that if they act hastily, they’ll only land small fry. How much further could access take them? This dilemma is sharpened by the sheer horror of what is being revealed as indigestible chunks of gibberish text become comprehensible. Sexual torture. Skin flayed with scorching hot skillets. An innocuous-looking pink house in Serbia which turns out to contain meat grinders into which informants are fed. Surely, at some point, the police have to stop intelligence-gathering and start smashing down front doors?
Soon enough, they do. They uncover billions of euros (mainly laundered via cryptocurrency) and Dubai-resident drug lords calling themselves things like Saddam Hussein, Putin and Hitler. It’s hugely satisfying to witness but feels like a sisyphean task all the same. Underpinning everything is perhaps the crucial conversation of our era. About the thin line between innovation and crime. About who polices tech companies and how. And about where responsibility ultimately lies.
This documentary is specific in its field of interest but it’s more widely thought-provoking, prompting consideration of everything from social media companies that enable the creation of child sexual abuse material to AI companies and their laissez-faire attitude to intellectual and creative theft. Sky ECC is what happens when tech finds its ideal users and, for reasons of commercial expediency, simply shrugs its shoulders.
Still, there’s a very human heroism being celebrated here. The consequences of the hack were significant in all sorts of smaller, more profoundly personal ways too. In the wake of Houcine Hakkar’s horrible fate, there were mutterings about the unlikeliness of smoke without fire. In revealing the conversations around his killing, the hack unequivocally cleared his name. His murder had been a terrible mistake. The look on his sister’s face as she talks about her brother suggests that’s no small consolation.

title: ‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender

content:
The auteur’s new film – a study of labour, capital and the fallout of redundancy – won the grand jury prize at Venice. Telling tales of the disenfranchised is ‘our moral responsibility’, he says
A quintessential 21st-century horror story: a private equity firm has set its sights on your company. That’s the premise behind director Lee Chang-dong’s new film, Possible Love, and the idea for it first came more than a decade ago, when mass layoffs resulted in a standoff that “fundamentally changed the Korean labour movement”.
In 2009, workers at Ssangyong Motors company protested against plans to lay off between 37 and 43% of the workforce, staging a historic 77-day strike and occupation of the factory that was eventually broken up by riot police. “Until that point in time in Korea, labourers’ rights were widely accepted,” Lee says, speaking through an interpreter in a central London hotel; “however, afterwards, the basic rights of labourers changed; to the public, they couldn’t be seen as more important than market profitability or corporate competitiveness.”
At the time, Lee shelved the project. “The more I examined the pain of these individuals” – after the violent crackdown on the Ssangyong Motors strike, there were several suicides, and reports of long-term mental health issues – “I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story? And if I am, how do I tell it? Do I stand close to the workers, or keep my distance?” Later he and his co-writer Oh Jung-mi, wrote “many different” scripts, including one with post-apocalyptic elements, before Oh suggested introducing a character who is a documentary film-maker, thereby finding a way to work in Lee’s ambivalence about his intentions.
The result is a sharply observed Russian doll of a film that places a narrative about “labour and its relationship to capital” within a broader story about the ethics of film-making, and the tensions and desires that emerge when a working-class couple collide with an astronomically wealthy one. It has, like many of Lee’s previous films, been received to great acclaim: it recently won the grand jury prize at Venice film festival , and has been hailed by critics as one of the best films of the year.
The film’s opening title shows the 10th commandment, “Thou shalt not covet”. You can already guess that it will be swiftly broken. Soon we see the depressed Ho-seok, who has been fired from his job at a metal factory, reprimanding his free-spirited wife Mi-ok for caring about her clothes. They’re on their way to a funeral of Ho-seok’s former colleague, who killed himself after being made redundant, and meet the ambitious film-maker Lee Ye-ji and her financier husband Sang-woo. They radiate the kind of glow afforded by wealth. After a stay at a luxury resort in Qatar made Ye-ji reflect on the nature of hidden labour, she’s making a film about the state of labour in Korea, and believes she’s found her ideal subjects; if only Ho-seok, who refuses to go to therapy let alone talk about his experiences in front of a camera, would agree.
Since his first feature in 1997, Lee, now 72, has made luminous yet unsparing films about disempowered people swept up in brutal economic and political circumstances: his protagonists include blue-collar workers, ex-prisoners, people with disabilities. In his previous film Burning, an adaptation of a Haruki Murakami short story, a poor writer battles for a woman’s affections with a wealthier rival. (Possible Love brings together two lead actors from Lee’s most acclaimed films; Secret Sunshine’s Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu who starred Peppermint Candy and Oasis.) Class tensions bristle throughout his work: now, however, he’s wondering whether we’ve outstripped the usefulness of the term.
“It’s difficult to use the word ‘class’ because it is so vast,” he says of the difference between the couples in Possible Love. He describes Sang-woo, who moves about the world with possessive ease, an allure and emptiness, as a “symbol of capital … It’s not even that Sang-woo is a wealthy man. It’s about how he is capable of moving and controlling a huge amount of capital. And that capital creates further wealth. It’s almost as if you can’t really grasp how much wealth it creates. It’s just something of a different dimension.” At the same time, “I didn’t want to show that the two couples belong to completely different worlds, because they do live in the same world.” It is, after all, the abstract financial machinations of people like Sang-woo that materially overturn the lives of people like Ho-seok. Making the characters interact together at restaurants, their homes, and on a charged summer holiday “was going to naturally bring out the tension, the hidden power difference between them. There is a gap that just cannot be crossed.”
The film exposes the audience to many different kinds of looking: we are shown Ye-ji’s documentary footage; a CCTV feed; newsreel-style clips of a violent police crackdown on a workers’ strike. Lee wanted to study the “issue of the gaze”; “the ethics of capturing and observing the lives and pain of others”. Ye-ji has a habit of holding her camera up at inappropriate moments, often to the discomfort of Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s young son, Cheol. I wonder if she’s supposed to be a sympathetic character. “Anyone who’s really hardworking, they tend to overdo it,” Lee says. He feels a “closeness” to her, “and cameras by their nature search for drama.” Can there ever be equality between a film-maker and their subject? “It’s very hard to be equal because the person holding the camera without even realising it is given power. And it’s a one-sided relationship.”
In his telling, Lee became a film-maker almost by accident. He was a writer in 1980s South Korea , then under a military government, feeling called to draw attention to human suffering: “That was our moral responsibility.” As the country moved towards democracy and into the new century, he felt that although the suffering still remained, “that moral responsibility among people in literature began to disappear. Literature that dealt with the close pains of reality were treated as if they were expired goods. I was disappointed with that change.” He took up screenwriting to try something new, before working as an assistant director, “because I almost wanted to punish myself in a way, make myself go through something very tough. I worked so hard at it that people around me were moved, and they said: ‘Oh, you should be a film-maker.’”
South Korean films today are known globally for their confronting depictions of capitalism, though unlike, say, Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite (which also features a class divide between two families) or Park Chan-wook’s No Other Choice (also about the misery of corporate layoffs), Lee’s characters are not schemers who attain pyrrhic, depraved victory against the system. We instead are often left to observe how they are marginalised by the world around them; we witness their small disappointments, the cruelties they endure, and how they strain to hold on to their hopes.
Yet his films also reveal the small but significant moments of solace and grace these characters find: in nature, other people, or their own willpower. Lee has previously described his films as stories about people taking on impossible fights against large, impenetrable entities. “However, despite that, I think the fight itself has meaning. I think these fights the individuals take on against the world is quite possibly the only way they are able to reclaim dignity. Regardless of your chances of winning, I think the fight itself is significant and meaningful.”
You could say that his latest film was made after a fight of sorts. Lee struggled to find domestic funding for the film, given the “structural crisis” facing the Korean industry, caused by the economic losses from a strict Covid 19 lockdown, and the rise of streaming services. Netflix stepped in to fund it, granting the film a theatrical release in some countries worldwide. “The character Ye-ji has a wealthy husband. She lives with someone who holds that capital but still tries her best to be independent,” Lee says. (Her husband, Sang-woo, somewhat disparagingly describes an independent film as a “film independent of capital”; “I thought it would be very amusing to have him say that line,” says Lee.) “I feel like she and I are in the same shoes. I am also dependent on capital to get my films made. You could say that I am also someone who is married to capital, but trying to protect my own voice, which I almost think is the fate of all film-makers.”
After its victory at Venice, there are already whispers about the Oscars; it is South Korea’s submission for best international feature. I ask what success means to him. “I’ve always made films wanting to connect with audiences. It’s always meaningful for me when my audiences accept the questions that I ask through my films and try to find their own answers. And hopefully that leads to a very small change in their lives.” It’s a fitting answer for a film-maker who has long portrayed the subtle acts of resistance people can mount against a hostile world; who finds in small changes, causes for hope.
Possible Love is in cinemas now, and on Netflix November 6.

content:
The bestselling writer, known as Japan’s enfant terrible, explored the dark underbelly of Japanese society in more than 40 works of subversive fiction including Audition, later made into a landmark indie horror movie
Ryu Murakami, the cult Japanese author and film-maker whose subversive, blackly comic novels found millions of readers, has died aged 74. He died on 17 October at home, according to his Japanese publisher Gentosha.
Described as the enfant terrible of contemporary Japanese literature, Murakami incorporated violence, explicit drug use and sex into stories that offered a sharp-eyed critique of Japanese and American culture.
“It has been a huge privilege to bring many of Ryu Murakami’s strange, original and cinematic novels to an English-speaking audience,” said Adam Freudenheim, publisher and managing director at Pushkin Press, which, along with Bloomsbury, publishes Murakami’s works in translation in the UK.
Murakami was the son of two teachers, born in Sasebo, Nagasaki prefecture, in 1952. During high school, he joined a rock band as a drummer, and after participating in a rooftop protest was placed under a three-month house arrest. He published his first novel, Almost Transparent Blue, in 1976. The book, written while he was still a student, is narrated by a character called Ryū, and depicts the hedonistic lifestyle of a group of disillusioned, nihilistic young people. It won the Gunzo prize for new writers along with the Akutagawa prize, Japan’s most prestigious literary award.
Murakami was not related to his better-known namesake, Haruki. Ryu Murakami’s books are “edgier and angrier” wrote the journalist David Pilling in 2013. “If Haruki is the Beatles of Japanese literature, Ryu is its Rolling Stones”.
Murakami went on to write more than 40 novels and short story collections, including Coin Locker Babies, In the Miso Soup, Audition, Piercing and Popular Hits of the Showa Era. Most of his books have not yet been translated into English.
Many of his works have been adapted for screen, either by himself or other film-makers. The best-known is Audition, a 1999 feature film directed by Takashi Miike. The story follows a widower holding fake movie auditions in order to find a new girlfriend. Writing about the novel in the Guardian in 2009, Irvine Welsh described its prose as “elegiac and affecting, but it has the sharp, visceral feel of the butcher’s knife or surgeon’s scalpel”.
Murakami’s third novel, Coin Locker Babies, about children abandoned in storage lockers, won the Noma literary new face prize. The novel is “a surreal coming-of-age horror story that runs wildly through the heights of love and superstardom, and the lows of insanity and murder”, wrote Russell Thomas in the Guardian in 2020, selecting the novel as one of the best books set in Japan. “Murakami’s stories never shy away from shining a light on the darkest corners of society,” he added.
“All at Pushkin Press are saddened to hear of his death and extend our sympathies to his many readers around the world,” said Freudenheim.

title: Nobody Wants This creator says she disagrees with Adam Brody’s ‘free Palestine’ comments
description: After Brody called out the ‘death and misery’ in Palestine, the Netflix hit’s Jewish creator said they don’t see eye to eye The creator of the hit Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This has responded to star Adam Brody’s recent support of Palestine amid the Israel-Gaza war . “Everyone is entitled to a different opinion,” Erin Foster said in an interview with the Not Skinny Not Fat podcast when asked about Brody calling for a free Palestine. Continue reading...
content:
After Brody called out the ‘death and misery’ in Palestine, the Netflix hit’s Jewish creator said they don’t see eye to eye
The creator of the hit Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This has responded to star Adam Brody’s recent support of Palestine amid the Israel-Gaza war .
“Everyone is entitled to a different opinion,” Erin Foster said in an interview with the Not Skinny Not Fat podcast when asked about Brody calling for a free Palestine.
“You know, it’s complicated,” said Foster, who also has an acting role in the new season. “I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing.
“While I love Adam, I also disagree with him. And that’s OK.”
Nobody Wants This, which returns for its third season this week, chronicles the unexpected love story between agnostic podcast host Joanne Williams (Kristen Bell) and rabbi Noah Roklov (Brody).
The story was inspired by Foster’s own real-life love story after she converted to Judaism after meeting her husband.
“As the creator of the show, all I can say is that I want our Jewish fans to know that I see you and I hear you and I understand how you feel,” Foster said. “The show has always been and always will be a love letter to Judaism. That is why I made this show. It’s because of how beautiful of an experience I’ve had becoming Jewish and being a Jewish person.
“Sitting here right now at this time in the world where there is almost zero positive representation of Jewish people, I think it’s so important to have that.”
Last month, Brody opened up about his political views for the first time. “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” he told GQ . “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”
Nobody Wants This’s third season sees Joanne and Noah move in together while their siblings continue to look for love. In a four-star review , the Guardian’s Jack Seale said the new episodes will make fans of the show “fall in love with it all over again”.
Foster has often posted about the Israel-Gaza war on social media.
“Nothing that is happening in Israel/Palestine is acceptable or comfortable to look at,” she wrote in 2021. “Innocent lives lost as casualties of war, as well as the atrocious lack of human rights that exist under a Hamas run government.
“There is a chance for peace here, and it involves a two state resolution where both exist next to each other, respecting each other’s beliefs, and sharing the holy land that all three major religions call sacred. Palestinians deserve to live in peace without fear. So do Jews.”
An independent UN inquiry in June found that Israel continues to commit genocide by targeting children in Gaza.
The Guardian has reached out to representatives for Foster, Netflix and Brody for comment.

8pm, Channel 4 In 2008, the remains of a boatload of Vikings were discovered on an Estonian island. Graeme Virtue

9.20pm, BBC One “A $200m deal with Netflix or the death of a sick, elderly woman 20 years ago. Which matters more?” asks Jonathan (Rupert Penry-Jones) in the penultimate episode. But that shouldn’t eclipse the rest of Ingmar Bergman’s 1957 classic, worth seeing in full for its allegorical depiction of plague-ravaged medieval Europe, the austere black and white cinematography of Gunnar Fischer, and a climatic rendering of the Danse Macabre, performed before slowly dissolving dark clouds. Ellen E Jones

content:
This rehash of the notorious study in which volunteers role-play as prisoners and guards pretends to be science. It isn’t – it’s patronising reality television
T elevision has rerun the Stanford prison experiment before, most notably in 2002 when the BBC aired The Experiment, which advertised itself as a more rigorous version of the stunt where volunteers role-play as prison guards and prisoners. The creator of the original 1971 experiment, Philip Zimbardo, would probably have criticised the new versions to preserve his own status, but the main point he made was valid. These people all know they’re on TV, he said. They’re playing to the cameras.
Whether the participants in a behavioural study forget they’re part of a study is an eternal debate point. One of the strengths of the other notorious American people-are-awful research project, the Milgram experiment , was that it made the artifice part of the process, telling the volunteers that they’d spoil the science if they didn’t keep giving strangers electric shocks: “The experiment requires that you continue.” Without that, the stooges may never act naturally; if they know the experiment is also a TV show, they definitely won’t.
Reality TV has a similar credibility problem: although a show might say it’s found a group of ordinary people and put them in such-and-such a situation, the obvious answer is always that they’re not ordinary people. They applied to be on reality TV, which ordinary people don’t do.
The two issues combine in Netflix’s The New Stanford Prison Experiment, which has hired part of a real county correctional facility in Georgia and filled it with 30 people divided into two factions: eight guards, three of whom are women, and 22 prisoners, all male. The haves wear sleek grey uniforms, set the rules and retire to their hotel between shifts; the have-nots are given bright yellow jumpsuits and scratchy bunk beds, and eat tasteless slop under harsh strip-lighting.
It keeps pretending to be a study of whether power corrupts in an institutional environment, but it is undeniably reality TV to its core, starting with how it’s presented to us. As well as seeing what the prisoners and guards have done, we’re told about it by them in the obligatory to-camera interviews, filmed afterwards. Also informing us about events we have just witnessed for ourselves are a trio of experts – a behavioural psychologist, a former federal correctional officer and, er, a journalist – watching a bank of screens. The series runs to six episodes, which could have been four if the patronising recaps had been edited out.
Inside the jail, any hope that the TV prisoners and guards might forget where they are and start behaving like actual prisoners and guards is soon lost. Everyone constantly references the “experiment”, and the show refuses to sit still for more than half an episode before drawing on textbook reality TV tricks to engineer discord: the guards are split into night and day teams, which undermine each other by approaching the task differently; they are asked to elect a head guard, which irks those not picked; at the halfway point in the series, some prisoners and guards switch roles.
None of it is real, and nobody thinks it is. The show doesn’t create any moments where the contestants suspend their disbelief – as in The Traitors , where the faithfuls sometimes start genuinely seeing the traitors as duplicitous villains. There is no game to win, no goal to work towards and, apart from the unspoken potential reward of a media career in every reality show, no prize. There’s nothing incentivising anyone to continue. More than one participant realises this and simply walks off the show.
What is interesting – not enough to make The New Stanford Prison Experiment worth nearly six hours of your time, but it’s something – is how reality TV contestants, with their unusually high self-regard and their tendency to use a lot of loud, confident words to say very little, behave when they know what and where they are. The most fertile conflict here springs up between prisoners who want to disobey the guards to see what happens, and those who’d rather stick to the current dynamic. It’s not an illustration of how a carceral institution restricts free will and removes individuality. It’s people who know they’re co-authors of a piece of entertainment and disagree on how the story should develop. Who know they’re characters in a story and have ideas for their own narcissistic reality “journeys” that clash with those of the others.
There is, however, one group that does fall for the conjuring trick. Up in the gallery, the three superfluous experts rather adorably persist in analysing hierarchies and interpersonal power struggles and the rest of it, as if any of those things are meaningfully occurring. They seem to have bought into The New Stanford Prison Experiment – watching at home, that’s impossible.

title: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV
description: Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy When Dan had had enough of his television, he threw a rock straight through the screen. The offence? His smart TV was downloading its third update in three days. “It drove me crazy with what seemed like daily software updates that never fixed anything and ‘features’ that never seemed to work,” says the 71-year-old from Illinois. “And of course, constantly trying to push me to subscribe to paid-for services when all I wanted to do was watch over-the-air TV, play a DVD or stream something from my computer.” Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasingly enshittified .” Continue reading...
content:
Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy
W hen Dan had had enough of his television, he threw a rock straight through the screen. The offence? His smart TV was downloading its third update in three days. “It drove me crazy with what seemed like daily software updates that never fixed anything and ‘features’ that never seemed to work,” says the 71-year-old from Illinois. “And of course, constantly trying to push me to subscribe to paid-for services when all I wanted to do was watch over-the-air TV, play a DVD or stream something from my computer.”
Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasingly enshittified .”
The first smart TVs entered the market in the late 2000s, when companies introduced operating systems, media players and apps to screens that were becoming wider and thinner. In recent years, the luxury status of smart TVs has waned and increasingly affordable options are widely available. Tom Parsons, TV and audiovisual editor at the electronics magazine What Hi-Fi?, explains that these cheaper models can struggle under more advanced features. “They’re not necessarily super-fast and responsive out of the box,” he says. “And then two, three, four years down the line, they can end up slowing down quite a lot under the weight of all that processing.”
Dan is just one of a growing number of tech-savvy watchers wishing their TVs weren’t so smart. Erin McQuiston and Matthew Schroyer, a couple from Connecticut, share his smart-screen scepticism.
“I don’t think we’ve ever used [our TV] as anything other than just a giant display,” says McQuiston. “There was a period where we were running it through an Xbox. And that was a constant battle because that was constantly being updated and patched and then you’d have to redownload all the apps for it.”
Meanwhile, Schroyer says his job as a software engineer has influenced his decision to “intentionally keep it very dumb” by keeping their TV disconnected from the internet. “A rule of the house is: don’t give things the wifi password,” he says. “It concerns me that folks increasingly have to be IT experts to get the bare minimum enjoyable experience out of this stuff.”
Instead, the 41-year-old connects his screen to an Apple TV box as a streaming workaround, and cites privacy as well as “highly invasive” advertisements for doing so. “Our living room is not a billboard for sale,” he says.
When asked how the couple might cope in a future where TVs may have mandatory internet, McQuiston says her husband is “handy enough to break every terms of service known to man and get in there and unsolder something to manually disconnect it”.
For Helen Northmore, a 51-year-old from Wales who works in AI delivery for the UK Health Security Agency, privacy is also a worry. Her grudge against smart screens began four years ago, when her faithful dumb TV broke without warning and she had to quickly find a replacement.
“We had already decided that we didn’t want the smart functionality, but it became really clear that it was very hard to find one that didn’t have any,” she says. Northmore, whose partner works in cybersecurity, says the couple wanted to “keep control” over their devices, which cost them a premium. “We were willing to pay more. One of the boundaries in how we live our lives is we want to minimise the smart element. We don’t have smart speakers. We don’t enable or connect to the internet.”
Today, she watches entertainment through a Sky box connected to her dumb TV, and dreads that when her current telly breaks there won’t be any option but to get a smart model and offer up her data.
More consumers are becoming worried about how their information is being used by manufacturers. “There are increasing privacy concerns around to what degree TVs are essentially scraping your data,” says Parsons. “TVs these days are full of sensors, including microphones, and that can make people nervous.”
But according to Parsons, despite interest in “dumber” models from some buyers, most shoppers want their TVs to be catch-all entertainment systems. The result is that the dumb TV market is almost nonexistent. “You can buy cheap monitors for signage,” he says, “but from a features point of view, you wouldn’t get the same performance that you would from a consumer TV.”
Paul, a public servant from Australia, knows just how hard finding a traditional TV can be. “When my last telly – a glorious 32-inch dumb TV – died recently, aged approximately 10 years old, I spent about three weeks scouring the city looking for something comparable. What I found is that they do not exist any more.”
After much searching, Paul discovered a single 40-inch TV without any smart functionality in the back of a shop. “It had zero ways to connect to the internet – just a couple of plugs on the back for making it work with the aerial on the roof and my VHS player, and that was it.” He remembers that it “was very dusty and cost about 200 dollars. Naturally, we fell instantly in love.”
“My friends all laugh at it when they come over,” he admits, “but secretly I know the joke is on them. My little telly doesn’t spy on me, and has a DVD player built in.”
The punchline may eventually land on Paul, however. In September, the Australian government launched a consultation into the future of the country’s free-to-air broadcasting , asking citizens for feedback on how TV should be accessed. One of the proposed scenarios would see traditional broadcast services cut in favour of streaming services and video on-demand apps.
In the same month, the UK government released a media green paper outlining its plan to fully move away from digital terrestrial television to services provided over a broadband connection by 2034 at the earliest. Such a situation would mean viewers having to rely on broadcaster apps and streaming services.
If a similar fate befell North America, James certainly wouldn’t care. He is originally from the US but now lives in British Columbia, Canada, and says traditional broadcast TV is “dead to him” and that he prefers to watch shows on streaming services or on YouTube. For the father and husband, privacy is a top priority.
“No one expects an end-user licence agreement to include giving up autonomy,” he says. “Having my TV listen to any conversation and use that for monetary or any form of gain is above and beyond expectations on the loss of privacy.”
In September, the YouTube channel Gamers Nexus released a two-hour investigation into LG Electronics’ smart televisions, saying that the devices record audio – even when they are offline or powered down. The South Korean company denied the allegations . In the fallout, some have taken measures to modify their smart TVs, regardless of brand or model. Some videos online show users replacing motherboards , cutting out Bluetooth and wifi modules and removing microphones from their TV remote controls.
Amid the controversy, James read online advice that modifying a TV remote microphone was a simple procedure. So he surgically removed the sensor himself. “Removing the mic was literally as easy as using a [craft] knife to scrape it off the top,” he says, “and the remote continued to work fine.”
James’s willingness to dissect his tech comes from fears for his children. “My kids are not teenagers and they have no agency to protect their private information,” he says. “Someone listening in on a TV gets to find out about my daughter’s first period without her knowing. And that is a level of invasion no one should have without explicit consent.”
Frustration and controversies have sparked a DIY interest in opening up and neutering the black rectangles in our living rooms. Though the desire in the first place may lead consumers to ask themselves an important question: have our TVs become too smart for their own good?
Gutting any piece of electronic equipment should be left to professionals. However, some may find that, for a complex problem, the simplest solutions are the most elegant. As Dan recalls: “It was enormously satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen.”

content:
She got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis. But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequel
‘T he first time I had the tooth in my hand,” says Linda Cardellini, “I thought, ‘Oh my God, this is what I’m doing.’” The star of Freaks and Geeks, ER, Dead to Me, Mad Men and DTF St Louis (for which she recently won an Emmy) is talking about her pivot towards full-blown horror. In Crystal Lake, the prequel to the Friday the 13th movies, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original slasher of the 1980 film. The tooth, by the way, is human and gets embedded in Pam’s knuckle – until she yanks it out with a gruesome, revolting slurping sound.
Casual filmgoers may associate Friday the 13th with Jason, the hockey-mask-wearing serial killer. But aficionados will know that Pam, Jason’s mother, is the villain of the first movie. “He didn’t even have the mask until the third movie,” says Cardellini, who has clearly done her homework. “Pam is the original killer, in vengeance of his death.” (There is some massaging of previous storylines in Crystal Lake, such as moving Jason’s drowning from the 1950s to the early 70s, but since the franchise is flexible enough to have sent Jason into space at one point, a bit of timeline tweaking feels fair game.)
The Friday the 13th franchise has a devoted audience – and Crystal Lake’s showrunner, Brad Caleb Kane, is among them. “He’s such a fan,” says Cardellini. “I felt he would have an idea of what fans were wanting.” Kane wrote the part specifically for her, after seeing her in Netflix thriller Dead to Me, which came as a surprise. “My biggest question was, ‘How did I become the person at the front of your mind for this?’” she laughs. Did they feel any pressure in taking Friday the 13th on? “It’s daunting, but hopefully it’s an opportunity to see more of something that didn’t really get its own avenue.”
Anyone who grew up in the 1980s and 90s, as Cardellini did (she is 51), will remember sleepovers with rented VHS tapes and a lot of screaming whenever Freddy Krueger, Michael Myers or Jason Voorhees appeared on screen. “It was forbidden fruit, almost,” she says. “You weren’t supposed to be able to watch it, but you would. And not only the gore but the sexuality – all the things you’re not supposed to be watching. I think it is part of the allure when you’re young. It seems off-limits and rebellious.”
She liked the jump scares and the gore, which is handy, because Crystal Lake is full of them. One vivid sequence involves an astronomical amount of blood. “We reserved a whole week for that,” she says, which is highly unusual for TV, as it tends to move quickly. It had to be precisely planned and choreographed, not least because Cardellini’s hair in the show is lighter, and they soon found that the fake blood stained it pink.
“Even the guy’s face coming off is done on the day with prosthetics, instead of CGI. It’s what you’re actually looking at, which helps with your reaction.” So that wasn’t done in post-production? “No! They pulled it off with fishing wire. So I saw it for the first time as it came off. It stuck with me for a while, because it’s disgusting .” It proved to be one of her highlights. “That’s actually one of my favourite parts of the show. It’s like a blood opera.”
Crystal Lake arrives on a new wave of mainstream horror, from films such as Obsession and Backrooms to Carrie and Widow’s Bay on TV. Why does Cardellini think horror is having a moment? “It’s a great question. I can imagine there’s something about the experience of it that is very present – and it’s a controlled fear, because you know that in a few hours, you will have a resolution. Maybe that is digestible.”
Recently, Cardellini was backstage at a screening of the show at New York Comic Con. “There was some gasping and yelling and cheers – and afterwards, a laugh. That’s when you’re like, ‘OK, this is great, because that’s what the movies did.’ They made you afraid, then you laughed out loud. That is what we were going for. That felt good.”
Cardellini grew up in California and started acting in the mid-1990s. Her breakout was Freaks and Geeks , the Paul Feig/Judd Apatow teen comedy in which she played good girl gone bad Lindsay Weir. The early 80s-set series, a fond, witty look at teenage rebellion, burned bright and fast and was promptly cancelled by NBC in 2000, before its first season had finished airing. As well as Cardellini, it rocket-launched the careers of Seth Rogen, Jason Segel and Busy Philipps.
“If you got cancelled, you were just gone ,” she says now. “You didn’t even know where it went. The idea that it would live on, once we weren’t going to make any more, just didn’t seem possible.” Through DVDs and word of mouth, though, Freaks and Geeks slowly became a classic of the high school TV genre. “That it had a life afterwards was a shock – and that it still has a life is amazing.”
On the subject of all-time-greatest TV series, Cardellini joined Mad Men in its sixth season, playing Sylvia Rosen, who has an affair with Don Draper. There was such secrecy around this that when she auditioned, names and details were changed. “I had no idea what I would be doing and [creator] Matt Weiner said, ‘Just trust me, it’s gonna get great.’ I think it was the first two scripts I got – I had one line. I thought, ‘What am I doing? What is this?’” But Weiner had told her it would be a great part and he was not lying. Not only does her character go on to remind Don of a sex worker from his youth, she also gets to leave him, triggering an obsession. “It unfolded like a surprise for me,” she says.
In September, Cardellini won her first Emmy for her role as Carol Love-Smernitch in HBO’s DTF St Louis. “I’ve been nominated before, but winning is a very different feeling,” she says. “It was a wonderful moment.” DTF St Louis is a singular series: Carol is married to American Sign Language interpreter Floyd, but is having an affair with his best friend Clark, a TV weatherman who rides a weird bike and likes to pretend to be a robot during sex. When Cardellini first heard about the show, she thought she knew how the story would go. “A love triangle between a married couple and a best friend, and somebody turns up dead,” she recalls. “But when I read it, I thought, ‘I’ve never read anything like this.’ Every time I thought I knew where it was going, it went somewhere else, in this beautiful, nuanced, very human way.”
The show is a strange, sweet meditation on loneliness, with an offbeat streak. Carol, for instance, is a part-time baseball umpire. “Since I’ve played an umpire, I’ve met so many people who have told me they are also umpires, and it’s people you don’t expect. Also, the parent attacks that they have to weather are pretty funny.” Could she still umpire a game? “Maybe Little League. I don’t know if I can handle the parents!”
That Emmy award now lives on the mantel of her fireplace. Her first appearance on TV was in 1994, when she was a contestant on the quizshow The Price Is Right. You can see it on YouTube – she won a fireplace. Hang on, it’s not the same fireplace is it? “I wish! I don’t have that fireplace any more because, oddly enough, I lost it in a fire.” You lost a fireplace in a fire? “I was working and put a lot of stuff in storage. The storage facility caught fire.” But she had kept it for a long time? “Oh, for years and years and years.”
Earlier this year, Cardellini filmed They Know, a psychological horror movie written and directed by Bill Hader, who also stars. “It’s definitely his incredibly extraordinary point of view,” she says, reluctant to give too much away beyond the fact she plays his ex-wife. The fact that it’s another horror does not mean, however, that Cardellini is in her scream queen era. “I like to change it up,” she says. “I went from DTF to Crystal Lake with one week in between. That seemed like a big left turn. So we’ll see what comes up.” She pauses and adds: “But you never know.”

title: Children’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novels
description: A sumptuous collection of fairytales; a dreamy Minotaur retelling; the explosive finale of the YA Torch Trilogy and more Dogs, Dogs, Dogs by John Devolle, Pushkin, £12.99 “Old dogs, young dogs, dogs on wheels, dogs that want to eat your meals” – this “very silly book about dogs” is a polychromatic picture-book treat for little canine fans, full of bold graphic artwork and audacious rhymes. More! by Ged Adamson, Moon and Bird, £12.99 Best friends Squirrel and Mouse are on a blissful walk together, but Squirrel keeps wanting more – a hat, a tie, a boingy stick! – until he realises it’s all pointless without Mouse to share it. A slyly hilarious anti-consumerist picture book that encourages small readers to pore over its delightful background details. Continue reading...
content:
A sumptuous collection of fairytales; a dreamy Minotaur retelling; the explosive finale of the YA Torch Trilogy and more
Dogs, Dogs, Dogs by John Devolle, Pushkin, £12.99 “Old dogs, young dogs, dogs on wheels, dogs that want to eat your meals” – this “very silly book about dogs” is a polychromatic picture-book treat for little canine fans, full of bold graphic artwork and audacious rhymes.
More! by Ged Adamson, Moon and Bird, £12.99 Best friends Squirrel and Mouse are on a blissful walk together, but Squirrel keeps wanting more – a hat, a tie, a boingy stick! – until he realises it’s all pointless without Mouse to share it. A slyly hilarious anti-consumerist picture book that encourages small readers to pore over its delightful background details.
The Tale That Time Sews by Sita Brahmachari, illustrated by Jane Ray, Templar, £12.99 A little girl waits for her new sibling to be born while Nana stitches together family stories in a quilt that will wrap them both in this 5+ picture book; a lyrical, beautiful account of displacement, migration and learning to flourish in new places while remembering your roots.
Little Minotaur by Gaia Alessi, Walker, £14.99 In ancient Crete, a boy with a bull head is cherished by his sister Ariadne and mother Pasiphaë. Though he struggles to form words, he rejoices in the natural world. But when fearful rumours rise up, he must find his place – and a better ending to his story – in this dreamy, beguiling picturebook Minotaur retelling for 5+.
Pomona: Stories of the Cat Witch by Tor Freeman, Guppy, £14.99 Pomona the cat witch lives in the forest, surrounded by pals including Ratso, Elfis and Prince Frog. It’s here that she discovers empathy while dusting her house, finds a friend for a lonely caterpillar and helps Ratso break an annoying curse. These daft, whimsical, highly illustrated stories are perfect for 5+ readers with a taste for thoughtful silliness.
A Year of Fairy Tales by Sophie Anderson, illustrated by Elisa Paganelli, Usborne, £25 This sumptuous hardback collection – one story for every month – features retellings of classic fairytales like Jack and the Beanstalk as well as original tales rooted in world folklore. Anderson’s lively, adventurous writing marries with Paganelli’s swirling, soaring artwork to create a treasure trove for 7+ readers to share at bedtime or explore solo.
Lumi and the Wolf by Lottie Saahko, Hachette, £14.99 Sent to stay with relatives in Lapland, autistic Lumi struggles to adapt, and her family warns her that a dangerous white wolf is lurking. When she befriends the wolf, Lumi and local boy Oskár set out on a perilous journey to the national park where Wolf can be safe – though she will have to use all her sharp senses and stored knowledge to get him there. Atmospheric and fast-paced, with intricately drawn illustrations, this tense, heartfelt 9+ animal adventure deals both with the impact of climate change on traditional Sami ways of life, and the deep human need to find where you belong.
The Rambler’s Curse by Mikey Please, HarperCollins, £14.99 Things are going well for the magical Café at the Edge of the Woods until a terrifying customer arrives: a human. His appearance sets off a chaotic chain reaction, involving a temperamental wizard’s staff, a red motorbike, a stolen gold hoard and a blanket of carnivorous moss. Can chef Rene and waiter Glumfoot defend the Woods from catastrophe in this laugh-out-loud, shaggy-dog spiral of purposes mistook? Developing the world and characters of Please’s Waterstones prize-winning picture book, this is the first in a trilogy for 8+.
Girl With a Sabretooth Tiger by Jasbinder Bilan, Chicken House, £7.99 In prehistoric England, 11-year-old Swallow, afraid her baby sister will die, undertakes a dangerous quest: to fetch a piece of green jadeite from the heart of a mountain god. Ishi, a village boy, insists on coming too – but it’s the spirit of the great tiger whose tooth she wears that will guide and protect her in this poetic, powerful, pared-back 9+ story of love, determination, courage and shared resource.
Anger Is Only a Shadow by Elizabeth Acevedo, Hot Key, £8.99 Lil is on probation. She needs to be New Lil – staying head down and out of trouble until her next court hearing – but Old Lil, barely contained, is desperate to make bad, impulsive decisions. Then her brother Aldwin, hundreds of miles away at college, starts talking about hearing voices, and Lil realises she’s the only one who can help. But can she get to him without sacrificing her freedom? A poignant, complex, thought-provoking YA novel by a Carnegie-winning author.
Nightcurse by Emma Hinds, Usborne, £9.99 Revenant Emrys Swift has been 17 for 157 years, living a cloistered life in a secret magical library and trying to remember his own death. When three important books go missing, he must collaborate with his nemesis, charismatic shapeshifter Aubrey Vale, to figure out where and why, but as spectral warnings rise around them, and the secrets of Emrys’s death and Aubrey’s life are laid bare, could their antipathy be changing to attraction? A gorgeously readable queer enemies-to-lovers romantasy, set in a richly realised magical world.
Flarestorm by Moira Buffini, Faber, £9.99 In a world where telepaths called Torches are either oppressed or exalted, an uprising is under way, seeking equality for all. The rebels are marching on the Capital, but Torches Elsa and Kaira are struggling to break out of their underground prison, while Rye, in captivity, is being forced to track powerful Torch Petra as she flies into the unknown. And where will conniving Zara Swan decide her ultimate loyalty lies? Messy, explosive, bloody and brutal, the concluding volume of the bestselling YA Torch Trilogy resolves multiple storylines and perspectives in a blaze of pain, fear, loss and glory.

The author of the global sensation on being inspired by Harper Lee, the craft of Joan Didion, and the joys of rereading Louisa May Alcott
My earliest reading memory I have a very clear memory of reading Fun With Dick and Jane. I was four years old, and my dad wrote each word on a chalkboard. I memorised them, then opened the book and read them back to him. I couldn’t believe it. It felt like magic! When I was older, I stumbled across the book and was surprised to find Dick and Jane didn’t really have all that much fun.
My favourite book growing up Harriet the Spy by Louise Fitzhugh. Eleven-year-old Harriet Welch wants to be a writer, and her nanny encourages her to keepa notebook so she can practise writing every day. But when the other kids at school find her book (which is filled with her meanest, most vulnerable thoughts), she quickly becomes the school pariah. I must have read this story a hundred times. Harriet Welch was the reason I started writing stuff down. She was also the reason I understood that no matter how hard it feels, it is imperative to own and apologise for your mistakes.
The book that changed me as a teenager To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee. Scout’s voice grabbed me from the start. It was a deep dive into racism, poverty, hatred and social justice, and it had a direct impact on how I saw the world.
The writer who changed my mind Henry David Thoreau. “I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately,” he wrote in Walden, “to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.” I was 18, loved the outdoors, craved adventure, and desperately wanted to see what I was made of. But it’s hard to get work from a mountaintop, so I settled for living deliberately in my tiny, overpriced, noisy, too-hot apartment. Survival comes in many forms.
The book that made me want to be a writer Fun With Dick and Jane! Seriously. I was in love with reading from the very beginning, and writing a story seemed like the obvious next step. At age five I wrote my first book. It was a page long and included an illustration. It has not yet been picked up by a publisher. I also wrote an entire novel by 12. For some reason, that, too, remains unsigned. All offers considered.
The book I came back to Little Women by Louisa May Alcott. I was supposed to love it (I was nine; I fitted the demographic), but it didn’t speak to me. Fast forward 15 years. I was trekking in Nepal’s Annapurna range and found it on a hikers’ bookshelf. I reread it in my tent by candlelight. I couldn’t believe how great it was. Jo is amazing!
The book I reread The Virgin Suicides by Jeffrey Eugenides. The writing is extraordinary, and the point of view is one of a kind. There isn’t a wasted word in the entire book. I also love to read essays and often return to The White Album by Joan Didion to study the way she crafts sentences. She has an amazing ability to capture the energy of an age, a movement, a fad, just as it begins to slide.
The book I could never read again The Gormenghast Trilogy by Mervyn Peake. I loved this when I was a teenager and maybe I would love it again, but I don’t want to run the risk of spoiling my good memories.
The book I discovered later in life So Long, See You Tomorrow by William Maxwell. It’s told from the point of view of a man in his 60s looking back on a childhood upended by murder and the loss of his mother. It’s a brilliant study of how impossible it is to make sense of our memories, because they have a bad habit of rewriting themselves.
The book I am currently reading May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry.

title: The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch by Thure Erik Lund review – is this the greatest living Norwegian writer?
description: Translated into English at last, this portrait of a man appalled by modernity and desperate to get back to nature is brimming with Nordic weltschmerz T-O-M. The initials of Tomas Olsen Myrbråten, the narrator in Thure Erik Lund’s The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch, spell out the Norwegian word for “empty”. Approaching 38, he’s already a relic. He spends his days slumped at the kitchen table or staring out of the window, convinced that the ceiling is about to fall and crush him. He sobs about the state he’s in and the state of society around him. Of one thing he’s sure: “It is no longer me who cries, but the world, the world crying, in me.” Nordic weltschmerz: you’d have to be a saint not to giggle. Lund has been described by Karl Ove Knausgård as the “greatest Norwegian contemporary writer”; this novel, originally published in 1999, is his first to be translated into English. In it, Tomas describes himself, over and over and over again, as a “life-of-the-mind individual”. Cursed as much as blessed, life-of-the mind individuals have a keen and unconsoling sense of how things are (“one is a wretched, contemptible, and unworthy being”) and how things will end for them (“in the sewers of society, at nature’s nadir, incessantly ground down into the mud and the mire so that one day, millions of years from now, they become oil, life-of-the-mind oil, at the very bottom of life itself”). Is he making fun of himself? In 2026, he seems closer to an eco-prophet. Continue reading...
content:
Translated into English at last, this portrait of a man appalled by modernity and desperate to get back to nature is brimming with Nordic weltschmerz
T -O-M. The initials of Tomas Olsen Myrbråten, the narrator in Thure Erik Lund’s The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch, spell out the Norwegian word for “empty”. Approaching 38, he’s already a relic. He spends his days slumped at the kitchen table or staring out of the window, convinced that the ceiling is about to fall and crush him. He sobs about the state he’s in and the state of society around him. Of one thing he’s sure: “It is no longer me who cries, but the world, the world crying, in me.” Nordic weltschmerz: you’d have to be a saint not to giggle.
Lund has been described by Karl Ove Knausgård as the “greatest Norwegian contemporary writer”; this novel, originally published in 1999, is his first to be translated into English. In it, Tomas describes himself, over and over and over again, as a “life-of-the-mind individual”. Cursed as much as blessed, life-of-the mind individuals have a keen and unconsoling sense of how things are (“one is a wretched, contemptible, and unworthy being”) and how things will end for them (“in the sewers of society, at nature’s nadir, incessantly ground down into the mud and the mire so that one day, millions of years from now, they become oil, life-of-the-mind oil, at the very bottom of life itself”). Is he making fun of himself? In 2026, he seems closer to an eco-prophet.
Perhaps it was always meant to be this way. His family line consisted of poor, mostly illiterate farmworkers in eastern Norway and, after he moved away to university, he learned to speak about his upbringing in casual, almost condescending fashion. Over time though, especially as he travels across the country, he begins to question his snobbery. He’s aghast at how history is being turned into heritage, ancient folk traditions repackaged for tourists, culture seen as being not so much about lived experiences and relations as a commodity. Wildness is disappearing. Even mountain roads no longer wind like they used to. There are echoes of Thoreau in his invocations of “children getting lost in the woods, in a world without human signifiers, without signage or trails, only celestial bodies and natural forms”. Echoes too of John Berger’s Pig Earth, as he charts the impact of machinery on how peasants speak and engage with each other.
This is a universal story of modernity and its discontents, but Lund is at pains to give it a specifically Norwegian dimension. Like one of Thomas Bernhard’s grumpus narrators railing against Austrian idiocracy, Tomas lays into his country’s governing class (“a gang of boasting sanctimonious humanistoid individuals”) which has ushered in “a thoroughly criminal, narcotised shopping-mall world”, a “Norwegian global hell” full of “pale, withered souls who seek solace in cinemas and fitness studios”. Listing his present-day false prophets – “computer engineers, course facilitators, business commissioners” – he sounds like someone who’s read the Unabomber Manifesto.
What’s funniest – or maybe funny-tragic – is that Tomas thinks he can express all this not only in a think piece commissioned by the Royal Norwegian Ministry of Culture, but to the face of the culture minister herself. She is not amused, especially when he blurts out a four-letter word. Dragged out of her office by security guards, his reputation and social standing are destroyed. He’s assumed to be a nationalist, a Nazi even, is unable to get work, and becomes homeless.
Then things get even worse: in a nightmarish middle section, somewhere between Hieronymus Bosch and Lars von Trier, he returns to his parents’ farm. He’s hoping to turn his back on decadent city ways, but there’s nothing Arcadian here. In this perverted pastoral Tomas digs ditches, lives with his drunken wife Helena, whose gaze is a “pustulated mongrel-eyed leer”, cages his mentally defective brother and dumps him in a remote Swedish village. Is this the authentic Norway he’s been hankering for? It’s in a state of decomposition and liquefaction – all slime, moonshine, blood, vomit, grease.
Language is a key actor throughout. Paragraphs are often long, larded with clauses that repeat, with sententious neologisms that David M Smith translates as “enfletted”, “enhammered”, “vocabulation”. At other times, when Tomas lets go his urban sensibilities, the sentences are slangy and pungent.
The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch is prescient about the “language forms” that digital capitalism requires – the data and information, the “demonic and inhuman” scientism, the fear of allegory. Its astonishing final section sees Tomas, alone in a forest, all ears. He can hear himself, his surroundings, the past, the future. He’s attuned to what connects him to shit, steel wire, dead plant tissue, bacterial cultures. Eureka! “That’s what I was. A kind of pulverised form of language which, by chance, had been imbued with natural substances, here and there.” Nordic weltschmerz: what a wonder it is.

content:
Published four months after her death, the poet’s reflections on mortality are both agonising and profoundly life-affirming
T here are no atheists in foxholes, goes the saying, and indeed social scientists and evolutionary biologists have argued that the experience of war or conflict drives religious belief; in 2019, Joseph Henrich and others surveyed almost 2,000 people in three post-conflict societies – Uganda, Sierra Leone and Tajikistan – and concluded that their experience of conflict had prompted them to participate in Christian and Muslim rituals and groups. Atheism, it seems, may be as fragile as faith.
“No matter how attached you are to your own rational worldview, your rationality won’t survive long under the threat of imminent death,” writes the former Dutch poet laureate Lieke Marsman in her book On Another Planet They Can Save Me. Part scream, part song, it charts the gradual dissolution of her own rational assumptions, which govern everything from her views on God to extra­terrestrial life. It is a brilliant, playful, layered and humane plea for openness and hope in the face of her own foxhole of intolerable suffering.
Marsman was not a soldier, but she knew a thing or two about living with constant reminders of her own mortality. In 2018, at the age of 27, the poet was diagnosed with a rare and incurable form of cartilage cancer. “There are little balls of failed cartilage in my lungs, balls that will slowly, agonisingly, take over until, at last, I suffocate,” she writes. When a doctor informs her that her illness is terminal, she lets out a scream. “[H]ow else are you supposed to behave when handed a death sentence?” she asks. Desperate to live, Marsman undergoes a barrage of treatments, including an operation to remove her arm and shoulder.
However grim her situation, there is remarkably little about her body in this book, and the trials of her cancer treatment, from surgery to immunotherapy. “After all, isn’t a disease only really interesting to the one who has it?” she wonders. “The temperature of my anus doesn’t affect the temperature of the world.” Instead, she writes about her relationship with certainty, gradually unpicking her own materialism and positivism. She opens herself to God, reads about the supernatural, and wonders whether aliens may come down and take her away. “Sometimes I think I’m going crazy, at other moments I think how crazy I was not to have allowed myself to broaden my perspective until now.”
This is well-trodden ground, but Marsman’s language is so beautiful (her translator, Sophie Collins, has done a fine job), and her textual references so original, that it feels as if we are walking on fresh turf. Her range is wild: she cites Leopardi, Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Robert Musil, Spinoza, Euripides, Wittgenstein and William James. The most interesting sections, for me, related not to artists’ or writers’ reflections on mortality or rationalism, but those of scientists who expressed doubts about the solidity of the scientific framework that they themselves constructed. “To speak in terms of Plato’s well-known simile,” wrote cosmologist James Jeans, “we are still imprisoned in our cave, with our backs to the light, and can only watch the shadows on the wall.”
Side by side with these reflections are Marsman’s poignant memories of the quotidian reality of a terminal cancer diagnosis, which form a strange blend of the mundane with the otherworldly. She writes that she and her girlfriend spent hundreds of euros on empanadas. “[E]ven when you’re dying, you have to eat, and those things only need a blast in the oven.” When she wakes up from an operation without her arm, she recalls that the first thing she craved was … a croissant. If the narrative vibrates with pain, there are also releases of humour; at one point she considers all the absurd things she could do to spice up her obituary, such as crashing in a paraglider or go-kart.
Any reviewer knows that the author may read what you have written; a review is intended for potential readers of a book, yes, but I also think of it as a dialogue with its author. Here there is no right of reply: Marsman died in June of this year, aged 35, and this book, more than a memoir, is a testament; to review it almost feels like a sacrilegious act, and perhaps it is best to let the author speak. “[D]ying with hope, however far-fetched and unrealistic that might be, is always better than continuing to live without it. And in those moments when everything in the here and now turns out to be utterly hopeless, I allow myself to think: on another planet they can save me.” I hope that that other planet exists, and somewhere, somehow, Marsman is still writing.

title: Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser review – the deep roots of a contemporary movement
description: A biographer’s affecting account of prominent critics of Zionism, from Hannah Arendt to Nan Goldin “Everyone in America – at least as far as I knew – was a Zionist,” recalls Benjamin Moser, “especially but not only if you were Jewish.” A Pulitzer-winning biographer of Susan Sontag, he remembers being brought up short in his 20s, when a friend described Israel as “a bunch of foreigners who had no business in the Middle East” and Zionism as a “terrible mistake”.
