content:
A biographer’s affecting account of prominent critics of Zionism, from Hannah Arendt to Nan Goldin
“E veryone in America – at least as far as I knew – was a Zionist,” recalls Benjamin Moser, “especially but not only if you were Jewish.” A Pulitzer-winning biographer of Susan Sontag, he remembers being brought up short in his 20s, when a friend described Israel as “a bunch of foreigners who had no business in the Middle East” and Zionism as a “terrible mistake”. Moser, who recently turned 50, admits: “I was not even aware that Zionism was controversial.” The shift in perspective culminated in a visit to the occupied territories in 2016, during which he found “the reality of the occupation of Palestine … deranging”.
His new book includes 12 portraits of Jewish figures who have opposed Zionism, a movement formed in the late 19th century to advocate for the creation of a homeland for Jewish people in Palestine. It is contentious to oppose Zionism today, but Moser wants contemporary Jewish activists to “feel less alone” by showing that debates about Zionism were once mainstream in Jewish communal life. While around 90% of American Jews now support Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state (although fewer identify as Zionists), fewer than 1% belonged to the largest American Zionist organisation in 1914. The first character study is of Rabbi Aaron Samuel Tamares, who thought that Judaism offered a vision of a world beyond the devastating nationalism of the first world war. The book closes with a moving account of the photographer Nan Goldin, who spoke out, at considerable cost, as the assault on Gaza began in 2023 following the October 7th attacks.
Many of the protagonists, like Moser, were once committed Zionists. When he was 10, Ronnie Kasrils set up a stall in front of his home in South Africa to sell toys and raise funds for Israel. He was later an anti-apartheid leader who became an ardent anti-Zionist during 27 years living abroad in exile: “Ronnie drives them crazy,” a friend of his tells Moser. “And a lot of it is because he’s so Jewish .”
Jacob Israël de Haan, an influential Dutch poet, wrote in 1912: “We want our own Land, our own Language, our own Art.” He was horrified after he relocated to Mandatory Palestine: “Zionism is a beautiful ideal,” he lamented, but it had “fallen into the hands of hustlers”. He was murdered in 1924 by Avraham Tehomi, a 21-year-old member of the Haganah paramilitary organisation, after his increasingly outspoken opposition to the Zionist leadership.
Hannah Arendt worked for Youth Aliyah in Paris, supporting refugee children to immigrate to Palestine, after fleeing from Germany herself in 1933. Her orientation changed after the Biltmore Conference in 1942, when some 600 delegates from Zionist organisations gathered in New York. Before Biltmore, some in the movement still imagined a single state rooted in the historically strong relations between Jews, Muslims and Christians in Palestine. The Holocaust sharpened the urgency of the argument for a Jewish state instead, but Arendt warned that this would leave the Arabs with “the choice between voluntary emigration or second-class citizenship”. She foresaw, Moser writes, that “a victory [in the fight for a state] would bring the Jews of Palestine neither peace nor security”.
Moser’s study includes many instances of despair. The scale of the devastation wreaked on the Palestinians disturbs each of Moser’s subjects, many of whom are demonised or accused of antisemitism “so promiscuously that the word would eventually become meaningless”. After the Occupation of Gaza and the West Bank began in 1967, the lawyer Felicia Langer dedicated her life to representing Palestinians. Her first clients, Sheikh Musa al-Bukhari and his wife, knew their son was in prison: “Nobody would tell them why, but when he had picked up his son’s clothes to wash them, he had found a shirt covered with blood.” Langer came to see “the State of Israel as a criminal enterprise” and emigrated in 1990 because she no longer believed it could be reformed.
The Arab-Israeli historian Avi Shlaim, who was born in Iraq, was at the forefront of revising the established Israeli histories of 1948 and describes being “radicalised in the [Israeli State] archives … I didn’t have any revisionist ideas. It was the material I was reading which completely, flatly contradicted the official line.” Shlaim describes the situation today as “utterly bleak”. In 2023 he argued: “For all its sins, Israel has not engaged in genocide.” In 2025 he published a book called Genocide in Gaza.
Moser’s focus on individual lives is affecting. He makes no claims to be writing a definitive history and is aware of the Palestinian lives that shadow those of his protagonists but fall outside the scope of this study. There are nonetheless gaps. For example, there is no mention of the Satmar Hasidic movement, an ultra-Orthodox Jewish group that believes it is forbidden to establish a Jewish state before the Messiah’s arrival, showing that anti-Zionism can also be theological and conservative.
Early in Anti-Zionism, Moser reads his grandfather’s copy of Theodor Herzl’s founding Zionist text, Der Judenstaat, and finds it “disquieting”, at best a fairytale and at worst a profoundly disturbing vision. Moser wonders how his own life might have been different “if I had grown up with the Palestinian story” instead. This beautifully written cri de coeur is inspired by an “exilic vision” of equality, an alternative Jewish tradition, resistant to nationalism and rooted in solidarity with others.
Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser is published by 4th Estate. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

content:
Waititi joins a long list of movie-makers who were expected to bring a new direction to the franchise, before the studio appeared to get cold feet
M ovie-making these days is a very expensive endeavour. In 1977, George Lucas’s Star Wars cost $11m to make, which would be approximately $60m in today’s money, and has since amassed $775m at the global box office, including rereleases. Fast forward to 2026 and the most recent film in the long-running space saga, The Mandalorian and Grogu , cost a reported $165m and brought in $346m worldwide. If there was ever a Hollywood gold rush, the mines ran dry long ago.
Perhaps this is one of the reasons why Disney-owned Lucasfilm seems to be so terrified of making new Star Wars movies. Since 2019’s The Rise of Skywalker, only one Star Wars film, the aforementioned Mando and Grogu movie, has actually made it into cinemas. But that has not stopped the studio announcing a small armada of other projects – sometimes via press release, more often at various high-profile celebrations, conferences or other corporate jamborees – that have so far failed to reach multiplexes.
This week, Taika Waititi revealed in an interview with Inverse that his proposed Star Wars film, announced six years ago , has been “put on ice”. No clear explanation was offered, but frankly nobody should be surprised. It now joins mooted projects from Patty Jenkins, Kevin Feige and Game of Thrones creators David Benioff and DB Weiss on the list of Star Wars movies that we were once told we were definitely (probably) getting, but that we never actually did. Some, such as Rian Johnson’s proposed trilogy, have spent years receding into the distance, while others – Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy’s film about Rey’s new Jedi order, anyone? – have never been officially cancelled.
The failure of Waititi’s project may be the most damaging of the lot. Why hire a film-maker with such distinctive, punky sensibilities, only to leave them announcing to the world that their movie is now frozen in carbonite? Surely Lucasfilm teed up this film in the first place because it thought it might be an idea to shift away from dynastic daddy issues and planet-sized weapons with inexplicable design flaws, towards something whose plot couldn’t be guessed halfway through the opening crawl?
There is every chance that Waititi’s movie would have focused on an annoyingly genial Kiwi stormtrooper who insists on interrupting vital lightsaber duels to ask whether anyone fancies a sandwich. Johnson might have delivered 500 minutes of space opera in which the Jedi council are eventually forced to admit that the feeling of a disturbance in the Force is usually just trapped wind. But at least nobody watching the opening crawl would have known what kind of Star Wars movie they were about to witness – and that alone would have been worth the price of entry.
At some point, Lucasfilm has to let somebody make one of these films that might go wrong. Familiar faces and established audiences did not guarantee Mando and Grogu the kind of triumphant return we all wanted to see, and bringing back the saga’s big bad, Emperor Palpatine, more than three decades after he fell down an Imperial reactor shaft, was very far from a smart move. The forthcoming Star Wars: Starfighter , starring Ryan Gosling, may yet surprise us, but any film that already has Star Wars in its title and still needs one of Hollywood’s most famous faces to get us through the door isn’t exactly venturing into the Outer Rim.
Surely somewhere out there in a galaxy far, far away is a film-maker who can bring something fresh to this venerable old saga. Disney needs to find them, commission them to make a movie, and then actually let them get on and do it.

title: Junk review – David Schwimmer is lost in Mubi’s frustrating LA-set misstep

content:
The Friends alum makes up half of a messy and pretentious comedy drama that boasts some visual panache but is dragged down by a confused tone
Y ou could be forgiven, upon watching the first scene of Junk, for believing that this debut feature will boldly, perhaps ill-advisedly, dare to satirize the industry it’s purporting to join. At a swanky restaurant in LA, four people aglow with self-importance embark on the time-honored ritual of discussing the screenplays they’re working on – specifically, the screenplay Martin (David Schwimmer), is “working on”. It’s classic industry navel-gazing, underscored by a tight focus on Martin’s clammy face as he sputters poorly through a confidence game.
Schwimmer, of course, is still best known for playing a perpetually and comedically exasperated sitcom character; it’s hard to square that extremely familiar voice with Martin’s dark bluster on how “drug-addled gen Zers” have “no respect for the communal aspect of the cinema”, an off-putting rant that is also a tad intriguing – who is more pretentious here, the sweaty character or the picture starkly sending him up?
But Junk, directed by Jack Begert from a script co-written with Dani Goffstein, swerves quickly and, for too long, inexplicably to a different stratum of Hollywood. Somewhere else in the city, two burnouts, played by Dominic Fike and Talia Ryder, find themselves without their car, pills or plans once a house robbery goes awry. The sharp pivot is confusing, though not unwelcome; Begert, a prolific director of surrealist music videos for artists such as Olivia Rodrigo , Doja Cat and Kendrick Lamar, has an eye for LA’s seedy beauty, the way a night can unwind like the city’s endless roads. You could, like the chihuahua nicked from the house and hot potatoed while the thieves flee to the scene to the modest synths of Caroline Polachek’s So Hot You’re Hurting My Feelings, just be along for the ride.
Alas, it’s a bumpy and unsatisfying one. Junk is molded from another feature by a different name, Little Death, that premiered at the Sundance film festival back in 2024. According to press notes, that earlier movie was “a different shape entirely” from the new picture released by Mubi , though “at heart it’s the same movie.” I unfortunately missed Little Death on its festival run, where it picked up a Sundance innovator award, so I cannot speak to what, exactly, has changed, though the new shape is an odd one: two loosely connected stories of addiction and desperation in LA, one far more compelling and visually stimulating than the other, and only one deserving the film’s billing as a “slacker odyssey” across the city.
That section, as AJ (Fike) and Karla (Ryder) struggle to score and strive in nearly equal measure, beguilingly conveys, for a too brief stretch, the feeling of an unplanned evening in LA, hazy and sprawling and peopled by unpredictable characters who are at once assertive and stoned. There’s something appealing, if derivative, to lurking with two kids as they hurdle roadblock after roadblock of their own making. The appearance of Euphoria alum Fike, as another optimistic addict endearing even as he’s lying through his teeth, recalls the audacity of that now-cursed show – an impression unfortunately underscored by a visit to an antiseptic, sinister apartment owned by a drug dealer with “school shooter vibes” (an off-putting Karl Glusman) that undercuts the film’s woozy naturalism.
Unfortunate, too, that the 110-minute film’s middle section returns to Schwimmer’s screenwriter, sweatily withdrawing into fantasy with a molten core of self-loathing. The title card, presented 35 minutes in, presents an art exhibit that teases Junk as “a search for meaning in the post-post-modern dilemma” – a line surely meant as a joke, though it more or less describes the film’s grating meta ambitions, as Martin maybe or maybe not writes the other half of the story. It is, I assume, supposed to be ironic that Martin, stymied by a male protagonist deemed too “unlikable” by broadly drawn film executives, resorts to increasingly repellant behavior and flights of fancy. But whatever the intentions (and impressive flourishes of surrealist animation), it is certainly a slog to witness. The fact that, in taking the exec’s notes that he switch his protagonist to a woman in order to get made, Martin is played, for a time, by Gaby Hoffman, scans as unduly cynical. (And the less that is said about a recurring fantasy sequence involving a beautiful woman, played by Angela Sarafyan, in a barn described by his therapist as his “mother’s womb”, the better.) That Jena Malone, as Martin’s beleaguered fiancee, gets a well-earned tirade puncturing his absorption is only fair, though of little comfort.
If this sounds like the review of two entirely different movies – well, though connections between the two are eventually revealed, Junk never coheres into one picture. There’s admirable ambition here, and plenty of sumptuous visuals to spare, but the clash between one section’s biting cynicism and another’s ragged heart proves too discordant to overcome. Which is a shame; as a whole, the film may be a mess, but there are little treasures within this Junk to perhaps be reimagined down the road.
Junk is now available globally on Mubi now

title: Making Marie Antoinette review – sweet Coppola home movie reveals the family business
description: Shot by Sofia’s mother Eleanor this documentary shows something of the strain of shooting a period piece, but is a far cry from the tumultuous portrait of her husband in Hearts of Darkness It is 20 years since the release of Sofia Coppola’s Marie Antoinette starring Kirsten Dunst; it is a supportively unjudging, unironised study of the queen’s early years before the 1789 revolution, lavishly and accurately costumed, shot on location at Versailles and based on the Antonia Fraser biography – but also subversively and amusingly using pop tracks from the 70s and 80s on the soundtrack. It got a storm of booing from French critics, reportedly annoyed at the way their history had been reduced to a music video and fashion shoot with no French actors involved. Or hardly any. In fact, for all the lack of political grit, the film was interesting and accomplished, and deservedly has a fanbase – and it is to that constituency that this making-of documentary from the director’s mother Eleanor Coppola is really addressed. It is basically a sweet family home movie on digital video which shows something of the strain and the longueurs of shooting a demanding period picture, but tactfully not seeing anything really explosive or bad-tempered. It is very far from Eleanor Coppola’s sensational behind-the-scenes film Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse about the tumultuous creation of Apocalypse Now, directed by her husband Francis Ford Coppola. content:
Shot by Sofia’s mother Eleanor this documentary shows something of the strain of shooting a period piece, but is a far cry from the tumultuous portrait of her husband in Hearts of Darkness
I t is 20 years since the release of Sofia Coppola’s Marie Antoinette starring Kirsten Dunst; it is a supportively unjudging, unironised study of the queen’s early years before the 1789 revolution, lavishly and accurately costumed, shot on location at Versailles and based on the Antonia Fraser biography – but also subversively and amusingly using pop tracks from the 70s and 80s on the soundtrack. It got a storm of booing from French critics, reportedly annoyed at the way their history had been reduced to a music video and fashion shoot with no French actors involved. Or hardly any.
In fact, for all the lack of political grit, the film was interesting and accomplished, and deservedly has a fanbase – and it is to that constituency that this making-of documentary from the director’s mother Eleanor Coppola is really addressed. It is basically a sweet family home movie on digital video which shows something of the strain and the longueurs of shooting a demanding period picture, but tactfully not seeing anything really explosive or bad-tempered. It is very far from Eleanor Coppola’s sensational behind-the-scenes film Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse about the tumultuous creation of Apocalypse Now, directed by her husband Francis Ford Coppola.
Eleanor and Sofia edited the footage together during the Covid lockdown and diary entries by Eleanor Coppola, who died in 2024, are sensitively read by Diane Lane. There are innumerable shots of Sofia smiling at her mother’s camera, yet sometimes looking a little tired and ill. Jason Schwartzman, playing Louis XVI, grins cheerfully, while Marianne Faithfull, as Empress Maria Theresa, cheerfully banters with Sofia in a very naughty English way. Francis Ford Coppola arrives at one stage and says that his advice to Sofia had been to “throw a Marie Antoinette party and invite everyone to come to it…” A good description of the film, actually.
Elsewhere, in Lane’s diary voiceover, Eleanor talks about the pain involved for her personally when Sofia all but broke off contact with her in her teen years, but Eleanor recognised that this was a process she had to go through before they became close again. Yet there is of course no hint of anything problematic here; this in effect is a very indulgent bonus feature, which in a DVD would come in at about 15 minutes, tops. But it does give what looks like a pretty faithful account of the patient slog needed to shoot a feature film.

content:
As the haunters of Button House hit the big screen with a plot about an escaped phantom, we hear how the team just missed each other too much – and why grunting Robin may get his own show
W hen the final episode of Ghosts was aired in December 2023, the sitcom felt as if it had reached a definitive conclusion. The show’s central relationships, between Charlotte Ritchie’s Alison and the ghosts who haunt her tumbledown inherited manor house, were neatly tied up, as they encouraged her to sell the place to a hotel developer. It was a tearjerker of an episode for the millions of people who watched it, as well as for the cast and crew behind the scenes.
“We had stopped the series with genuinely no intention of coming back,” explains the show’s co-creator Mathew Baynton, who also stars as the callow romantic poet Thomas. “We were all in tears on the last day of filming,” he says, now perched on the uncomfortable end of a chaise lounge in a London hotel suite.
“I was so upset that it finished,” adds Lolly Adefope , who plays the excitable Kitty, from the better structured end of the chaise. “It was like being at a party and you guys were leaving.”
“It was a clear ending, and the guys felt like they had fully explored all of the characters,” says director Simon Hynd, “but I did notice a look of regret in some of their eyes.”
All of which is to say that Ghosts is now back. Although the television series remains over, the story will continue in the new film Ghosts: The Possession of Button House. So the question is, who blinked first?
“Alison Carpenter, our executive at Monumental, had started to say, ‘We could get the funding for a film if you guys want to do that,’” explains Baynton. “But we just batted it away.”
“The fear was that you’d end up making a 90-minute episode of a TV show, and it would feel like, Please Sir! The Movie,” says co-creator and star Laurence Rickard, who plays both caveman Robin and decapitated nobleman Sir Humphrey Bone. “Which I love, by the way.”
Eventually Carpenter convinced the show’s six creators and stars (the others being Simon Farnaby, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick and Ben Willbond, not present) to at least get into a room and discuss the prospect. “We all talked through what we didn’t want it to be, and what it sort of had to be to be a film,” explains Baynton. “That led us very quickly to the concept of possession, which would allow one of the ghosts to get out of the grounds.”
“It was the fastest turnaround ever,” laughs Rickard. “We went in at 9:30am going ‘I mean, it’s nice to see everyone, but I think the answer is probably no’ – and then by 11 o’clock, we were going, ‘We have to do this.’”
The resulting film is still very much Ghosts, with its unique mix of sharp absurdity (at one point a Ouija board spells out ‘Leave’ to make a point about Brexit) and near-debilitating emotional notes (you may never again look at a scotch egg without crying). But it is undoubtedly a movie, with stakes and a ticking clock and big set pieces.
“The possession idea immediately invites a body swap sort of thing, which reminded us of Big,” says Baynton. “Then we were talking about, what if the possession doesn’t last and his spirit is fading, which reminded us of Back to the Future. The group of kids breaking into the house felt like The Goonies. All our touchstones for this were films we loved in our youth.”
The film is an astonishing feat, not just because of its quick turnaround – Hynd only learned of the film late last year – but because every member of its ensemble has a vital part to play in the plot.
“With the series, we got so used to writing multi-thread narratives,” explains Baynton. “In any episode, the actual stories are told in two or three brief moments, so that had become our mode of writing anyway.”
This approach meant that, despite no longer living in Button House, Alison and her husband Mike, played by Kiell Smith-Bynoe, find themselves swept up in the action. Smith-Bynoe seems especially pleased with his arc. “Mike gets to prove himself in this one,” he explains, “which felt good after spending a few years not getting to do that.”
Smith-Bynoe has arguably always had the hardest acting job on Ghosts, as Mike is often the only person on screen who isn’t a ghost and can’t interact with them. This challenge was doubled for the film’s climax when, without giving too much away, a roomful of characters old and new flit in and out of tangibility. “It took me a minute,” he says. “I had to keep asking Simon who I was supposed to be able to see.”
Much of the cast this time around are new, in the form of the aforementioned kids. It takes a lot to steal a film out from underneath a cast as talented as this, but Scott Ellis Watson, who played the young John Davidson in I Swear, is phenomenal here, largely because he spends a lot of time doing a bang-on impersonation of a dead middle-aged Tory MP.
The new additions were something that Adefope in particular appreciated. “It was so fun having Scott around,” she says. “I was sort of the Gen Z member of the cast, so we talked a lot about memes and TikTok.”
“You were the child whisperer, weren’t you?” says Rickard.
“Yes, exactly. I was translating for you,” she smiles back.
With the show, the six creators were able to break off and write individual episodes in various permutations of their troupe. But the film is credited to all six of them. Was that a hard thing to accomplish? “It was just a process of who was around at what time,” says Baynton. “So sometimes it was two of us, sometimes three or four. What is lovely about that is that the person who’s absent for a little period of time then becomes your fresh pair of eyes when they return. You get to a point at times where all you can see is A or B and both of them are problematic, but then someone who’s been away for a couple of weeks comes in and goes, ‘Well, what about C?’ And you go, ‘Oh yeah!’”
A lot of this is simply muscle memory. The Ghosts team are now veterans, having met while making the Horrible Histories TV show almost two decades ago, and continued with the sitcom Yonderland and the 2015 Shakespeare comedy film Bill. It’s hard to think of any writing and performing group this large who have managed to stay intact for so long. Even Monty Python ran out of films and shows in less time, their work together now largely consisting of tweeting hatred at each other.
“Oh, we’ve got that phase to look forward to,” laughs Rickard. “I’ve been drafting some of that stuff.”
Rickard is the one who seems to have most keenly felt the absence of Ghosts: “The first year after the series stopped was the first time that we hadn’t done something together in 18 years.” You get the sense that this film exists in part because its creators missed hanging out with each other.
So why stop the party now? Will there be anything else to look forward to from the gang? “There isn’t something secretly being developed,” insists Baynton. “But we’ve always had the same feeling, which is that we love working together and we’ll keep doing it if people will pay us to do it.”
Does that mean more Ghosts films? That prompts a slightly more uneasy response. “This does sort of feel like, you know, the big swan song,” replies Rickard.
“Yes, but we said that before, so no one can take our word for it,” adds Baynton. “But there’s no intention. Also, ghosts can’t age, and I’m rapidly getting way too old to play Thomas.”
“But Robin could definitely have a spinoff, and that wouldn’t be a problem,” cracks Rickard, noting that he’s looking more and more like a long-dead caveman with every passing year. “It would be great. My makeup call would get shaved right down.”

content:
Bristol Old Vic A family are just getting used to their new home in this haunting drama when a parallel world emerges
O verheard in the auditorium during the interval: it’s like Tales of the Unexpected meets Jackanory. But if those references are dated by several decades, they go some way to summing up the strange mix of elements in this drama about a boy who goes missing from a village, and the ancient myth of a “green man” who might have something to do with it.
But then, Max Porter’s novel , on which it is based, weaves so many seemingly incongruent parts together to create its own beautiful brand of rural noir. It might be better described as The Missing meets This Country meets Stranger Things, except the Upside Down here is English countryside.
The story follows townie couple Robert (Raj Bajaj) and Jolie (Hanora Kamen), who move to the sticks and are just settling in when their otherworldly son, Lanny (Lucian Thomas on press night), goes missing. A local artist (Richard Cant), dubbed “Mad Pete” – for his bohemianism or, as a gay man in these parts, for his sexuality? – had formed a friendship with Lanny and is now considered prime suspect. The myth of a pagan figure, Dead Papa Toothwort, looms over the human drama as the police procedural unfolds.
It is a lot to transpose to the stage, alongside Porter’s multi-voiced portrait of a village and satirical social observations of country life. Bea Roberts does a deft job of adapting the mixer-blend of reality, imagination and hallucinatory bucolic lore. The production is full of pace and creepiness when it could so easily slide into the ridiculous.
It is much helped by Rebecca Jane Wood’s haunted set design, incorporating the village and its woodland. Screens show scratchy images of bare branched trees and antler-figured silhouettes, reminiscent of a Brothers Grimm storybook. Together with Zeynep Kepekli’s contrasting of warm/cold lighting design, the optics capture the chilling magic of Dead Papa Toothwort’s parallel world.
It is smartly directed by Nancy Medina too. Horror and humour squat at close quarters although the story is heavy on green man mythology at first and it does not give enough space to domestic realism. But there is an accomplished bridging of the dark and scary with the satirical and light. The book lends itself to dialogue and the many voices of the village and the babble of modern life criss-cross in disembodied audio, sometimes accompanied by floating sentences written across the set.
This seems, ultimately to be a story about the pain, responsibility and sometimes the emotional disconnect in parenthood. As Robert reflects, “who can have children and not go completely mad?” In this production he is not an emotionally numbed dad but seems a little generic. Jolie is excellently played by Kamen as a mother left broken and furious by her loss, while Thomas does a great job of bringing Lanny to life.
Village homophobia is made more emphatic and there is an added racial element: Lanny is a brown boy, we are told, but this does not feel fully developed. Some of the underlying anxieties of the book are lost among the many strands: the sense of dislocation for these urban folk in a village environment and its spikier, more judgmental neighbours; the question of who belongs here, and whom the land itself belongs to, ultimately. Some of these inquires are subsumed by the fever and gothicism of the plot.
It swings into the surreally hallucinatory in its final scene. The happy ending might be a story, a song or a miracle – a pagan god showing mercy to the humans that occupy his land.

title: Standup Jon Richardson on turning his dark teenage diaries into a tearjerking memoir: ‘I couldn’t sugarcoat those years’

content:
While facing grief, illness and a very public breakup, the comic reached for his diaries – and found a happy kid who spiralled into despair. Inspired by a Nobel laureate, he wrote a frank, funny book about that boy and what he grew into
I t begins on Christmas Day, 1996: “It’s been a lovely day … I realised how much I love my family.” It ends three years later: “I’m lying on the floor in floods of tears and all I want to do is die.” Say what you like about adolescence but it is nothing if not an emotional tumult. “If I’d known as a teenager,” says the comedian Jon Richardson ruefully, “that I’d one day write a book about them, I couldn’t have bookended my teenage diaries with better quotes to show what a storm of shit those years can be.”
The book is The Teenage Diaries of a Stand-Up Comedian, and it has been two years in the making. Two years that, if not quite the hormonal rollercoaster the book itself records, have been quite the ride. The project is borne of a crossroads moment in the Lancashire man’s midlife, after he experienced bereavement, serious illness among family and friends, and the breakdown of his marriage to fellow comic Lucy Beaumont. The last was an inevitably very public ending, splayed across the tabloids, to a relationship which itself played out in public, courtesy of the couple’s acclaimed mockumentary about their domestic arrangements, Meet the Richardsons .
“There was a lot going on,” he recalls, “some of which called for self-reflection, and some that was completely beyond my control – to do with getting to a certain age, when the people around you get frailer, and you start looking differently at your relationships with your parents and your own childhood. So I was in quite a reflective period anyway.” But in Richardson’s case, there was a specific focus for that reflection. “I have genuinely accumulated a horrific amount of paraphernalia from my own back story,” he says. An inveterate hoarder, the 44-year-old had cupboards full of detritus (ticket stubs, photos, certificates, VHS videos, letters and emails – and of course, his teenage diaries) salvaged from the early years of his life.
“I felt like there must be a reason I’ve kept it,” says Richardson. “And perhaps the reason is that, one day, if you’re lucky enough to have the time, you can work out: what is of meaning, why did you keep certain things, what can you afford to get rid of? That’s the journey of the book really. It’s in the present tense because it documents me doing the reflecting and the clearing out. But it’s about those first 20 years and how much of them you carry over.”
While writing, the comic deep-dived into teenage memoirs from Rae Earl’s My Fat, Mad Teenage Diary , via the works of Nobel prize winner Annie Ernaux (thanked by Richardson in the acknowledgements), to the recent Coming of Age: How Adolescence Shapes Us by psychologist Lucy Foulkes. The resulting book may not be the one you’d expect from the neurotic standup once branded “the nation’s favourite worrier”, or from the team captain on Channel 4’s 8 Out of 10 Cats, or even from the presenter of popular documentaries about OCD. This is not a book to nestle snugly in the humour section of Waterstones, nor one that jauntily glosses the anxieties of adolescence.
“I’m always very aware my job is to make people laugh,” says Richardson, “and I hope there is plenty of humour in the book.” There is. Its structure – diary extracts followed by grownup Jon reflecting ruthlessly thereupon – offers Richardson endless opportunities for entertaining self-abasement. And there is nostalgic delight to be had in the period detail: “Blockbuster video, Tupperware parties and Ann Summers.” And there is droll dramatic irony too, as per Richardson’s favourite entry, aged 14, apropos of nothing: “I’ve decided that although I’ll probably end up being a teacher, I’d love to be a comedian.”
He says now: “But in terms of the emotions, I couldn’t sugarcoat what those years were. Very few people become comedians because they’re well-adjusted and just want to spread joy in the world. Going back to the 60s and 70s, and those people who now have BBC Four documentaries made about them, people tend to come to comedy through having unscratched itches, or to make amends for some shortcoming in themselves. And I’m no different.”
In the book, we follow Richardson’s teenage self from 14 to 17. “I think I watched Zack Morris on [the sitcom] Saved By the Bell ,” he recalls, “and thought, ‘Oh, teenagers are supposed to keep secret diaries.’ But those early entries don’t have anything to say. I’m in my room playing Mario Kart most of the time.” At first, teenage Jon comes across as kind, bright, tentatively happy. But as time passes, his diary increasingly records a sense of isolation, frustration and low self-worth. He goes to a single-sex school. He feels ugly. He is growing up in a town – Morecambe, Lancashire – that seems to him like the dead-end back of beyond. His parents are separated and, in a book that is eloquent on poverty and class, money is tight.
These are all factors in Richardson’s spiral into a dark place. “There were an awful lot of happy times that I never wrote about,” he insists. But “very quickly the diary becomes a place to put the emotions that you don’t want to burden other people with, a place where you only talk about the struggle. It can become quite unhealthy.” In the book’s final chapter – ring-fenced from the earlier material, says Richardson, because it’s hard to be funny about – diary entries show teenage Jon considering suicide.
In 2023, alongside the former athlete Jessica Ennis-Hill and broadcaster Dan Walker, Richardson launched Bright Young Dreams , a fundraising campaign to support youth mental health – into which he will “put more of my energy over the next few years than anything else”. When I ask what might have made life more bearable for junior Jon, he would not, he replies, have changed any of the material circumstances of that boy’s life. What would have helped, he says, is “some understanding that it’s OK to be struggling and to be sad. A lot of kids just need to be told that, yes, it is really hard, these are difficult years”.
As the parent myself of a boy on the precipice of his teens, the book terrified me about what’s in store – while rallying my resolve to care for him through it. “If nothing else,” says the comic, “consider this a handbook for parents to make sure their kids don’t turn into Jon Richardson! That is a great gift I bestow on the nation.” But if his book offers a sobering reminder of the trials of teenagedom, it is also very affecting on family love. Its heroes, alongside the foundering teen centre-stage, are Richardson’s mum, dad and sister.
“You can’t talk about those years without bringing other people’s lives into it,” he says. “My main concern was protecting the privacy of people who haven’t chosen to write a book.” But his loved ones, off the page as on it, have been unstintingly supportive. “I write about my dad’s depression in the book, and I had to say to him, ‘Do you mind if I tell that story?’ And he said: ‘You do what you want to do.’” That conversation, says Richardson, was easy. Far harder for this working-class northern male was having to address his family about – ugh – their love for one another. Towards the end of the book, he reprints an email from his sister, sent at a fragile time of Jon’s life, that is so trenchant and loving in its support of her wee brother, that I couldn’t read it without welling up.
“It had the same impact on me,” says Richardson. “But my sister doesn’t know yet that it’s in the book. I haven’t been able to have that conversation. It’s easier to just put it in and not talk about it. ‘I love you. It’s in a book, so it’s a fact. Bye!’”
Now living a life his teenaged self could scarcely have dreamed of, is Richardson still keeping a diary? He is not – give or take the purely factual records he keeps, in an array of journals behind his head on our Zoom call, of his every gig since taking up standup in 2003. Grownup friendships and counselling have all supplanted the role diaries once played in his life. “They ended,” he says, because “I started going to the pub and hanging out with people.” And then he discovered standup, which was “transformative”.
“My approach to standup has always been: ‘How do I feel at this moment, and how do I package it in a way that’s interesting and amusing?’ It’s like a house conversion, like walking into a dilapidated wreck and turning it into something presentable. I take a difficult emotion and, instead of blurting it out on a page, I get to talk to people every night who’ve had similar experiences, and convert it into punchlines. And I can see people laughing and having a good night because I’ve confronted this emotion. And that,” says the tormented teenager, the teacher manqué turned comic and now memoirist, “has done wonders for my wellbeing.”
The Teenage Diaries of a Stand-Up Comedian by Jon Richardson (Little, Brown Book Group, £25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

title: ‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joy
description: Hailed as a prodigy at 16, the Saddleworth singer-songwriter was patronised in the press and lost his musical path. Now courted by imaginative new bands, he explains his route back Kiran Leonard presses the tips of his fingers together and looks at me solemnly across the table. “I don’t know if I’m doing a very good job,” he says, “But I’m trying really, really hard not to swear.” A decade ago, he explains, he was interviewed by the Guardian , got too drunk, and “swore all the way through the interview”. content:
Hailed as a prodigy at 16, the Saddleworth singer-songwriter was patronised in the press and lost his musical path. Now courted by imaginative new bands, he explains his route back
K iran Leonard presses the tips of his fingers together and looks at me solemnly across the table. “I don’t know if I’m doing a very good job,” he says, “But I’m trying really, really hard not to swear.”
A decade ago, he explains, he was interviewed by the Guardian , got too drunk, and “swore all the way through the interview”. When the piece came out, his grandfather was thrilled. “But he couldn’t show any of his friends because I just sounded really aggressive,” he tells me sheepishly.
It’s true that, the last time Leonard had a profile in this paper, he sounded a lot like a twentysomething trying hard to shed the preciousness of his former status as a teenage wunderkind. Hailed as a prodigy at age 16, upon the release of baroque, bonkers 2012 debut Bowler Hat Soup, a lot of Leonard’s early press plays up his age in a way that now reads as embarrassingly trite. “I think, unconsciously, I was probably quite defensive about how I was written about,” he says. “It’s not nice for journalists to fetishise the density or the ambitiousness of the music – it [was] obviously meant in a slightly patronising way.”
The Leonard sitting across from me at a pub near his home in south-east London speaks calmly and carefully, like someone with nothing to prove – because, perhaps, he has so thoroughly proved himself over the interceding decade. In the past five or so years, Leonard has emerged as one of Britain’s most consistently fascinating experimental musicians. His recent slate includes 2024’s Real Home, a rangy pop record that touches on ramshackle country, menacing prog and Jonathan Richman-esque romanticism; last year’s Small Brown Bed/With You Waltz, a surrealist album of live takes recorded at notable DIY venues such as the Golden Lion in Todmorden and Delicious Clam in Sheffield with a group of musicians he calls No Tailgate; and credits on acclaimed records by Eli Winter, Caroline and My New Band Believe.
His music is certainly far less wordy these days, far less likely to garner comparisons to Captain Beefheart or Joanna Newsom. But that’s because at this point, he says, he’s searching more for a sense of pure feeling: “I’m strongly driven by a very physical thing – which might seem quite broad, but it’s what distinguishes what I’m interested in and what I’m not.”
Leonard was born and raised in Saddleworth, near Manchester, the son of a community midwife and John Leonard, a folk musician who worked for BBC Radio 1 and 2 in Manchester in the 80s and 90s. Although it’s clear he was making music from a young age, it’s less clear how he ended up signed, with a manager and booking agent, before he could legally drink. “The short answer is: I don’t know,” he says. “I was very ignorant and sheltered from a lot of it. I made Bowler Hat Soup and put it on Bandcamp. I think I sent it to a load of blogs, and a blog wrote about it, which was then read by [the people who ran the label] Hand of Glory. I didn’t really come up through like, gigging.”
From there, Leonard was set up with that dreaded industry mechanism: a team. He got a publicist and a radio plugger and, through his management, a band, thankfully comprised of Manchester musicians who were at least making music that felt aligned with Leonard’s own. “I was fortunate to work with really good people and great musicians and have all this support, but the context was wrong,” he says.
During that period, he made and released four albums, but increasingly felt as if he wasn’t in the right zone. Enamoured by fuck-the-industry icons such as Steve Albini, he began tanking his commitments because the music was the one thing he had control over. He moved to London and then, one day, ditched his entire team. “It was a disaster – just total scorched earth,” he says with a sheepish smile. “I had no plan, had no idea what I was doing.”
Leonard found London “really alienating and difficult”, a feeling that was compounded by the fact that, he soon realised, he didn’t really know how much his team had sheltered him. “I couldn’t really find another manager – never have since, actually. And couldn’t get gigs,” he says.
Leonard “gradually found a groove in London, found a way to find it really stimulating and engaging”. That came through booking more shows and from befriending the post-rock band Caroline, who are the nexus of some of the country’s most vital experimental music. “I’m sure many people in this community would say the same thing,” he says. The band have become “a centre of activity in a lot of the work that I do because there’s so many of them, the quality of what they do is such a high standard and they’re operating at a level that everyone is very proud of and impressed by.”
Leonard quickly realised that his work could comprise “different investigations” – that he didn’t have to feel pinned down by one style, and that he didn’t have to be haunted by the music he made as a teenager. “I wanted to articulate myself more clearly and with less pomposity, less adolescent over-the-top-ness,” he says. “With the teenagery records, a lot of them were coming out much later than they’d been made. The difference between 15 and 18 is really massive, so playing those songs, I’d feel a bit of a dissonance, which made me more conscious of wanting to move past [them].”
Leonard says that most of his work now is extremely solitary, although he occasionally plays in Caroline, and enjoys playing in a project where he doesn’t have to add his own compositional voice to the mix. An exception to that solitary work is Or Sobre Blau, Leonard’s duo with Catalan guitarist Andreu G Serra. Their remarkable second album, Making Friends, released earlier this year, is a heady mix of ambient guitar primitivism, oddball samples and scratched-up found sound. “Or Sobre Blau is really thrilling because it’s in a totally different voice,” he says. “It’s the voice of that friendship, which is really thrilling because for my stuff, I’m just in my head, which is sometimes horrible.”
If there’s a common link between all Leonard’s work now, it’s that it often comes from a desire to make sounds that conjure full-body sensations. He often gets there. “I remember having a conversation with someone about the Caroline song Total Euphoria,” says Leonard. “They were like, I don’t know how often I feel total euphoria. I’m like: ‘I feel it quite a lot.’”

content:
Sohmen Concert Hall, Schwarzman Centre, Oxford Six performers navigate a disjointed world of online slang, loneliness and absurdity in the UK premiere of Jennifer Walshe and Philip Venables’ thrillingly original collaboration
A s we found our seats, a druidic figure wearing a string of vapes as a necklace sat on stage swathed in white fabric and smoke, emitting close-miked mouth noises amid a rising chorus of percussive hisses and rattles. Then dancing flashlights, reverb and thunderous drum rolls. Later came monologues delivered with quiet, skin-crawling sincerity or pounded out as a kind of manic rap and comically dysfunctional text chats projected on the backcloth. Not to mention the dance breaks. There was an angular, hyper-controlled trio fluent in the language of modern ballet and a hands-on-hips traditional number as faux-folk lyrics scrolled in gothic script and a hefty synthetic beat throbbed below.
The first collaboration between Jennifer Walshe and Philip Venables – two of the most distinctive creators in music theatre today – The Alonetimes was never likely to adhere to the conventional playbook of opera. The programme for its UK premiere describes the work as “a fragmented archaeology of personal stories”. Alternatively: there is no single linear plot but instead six performers, who step constantly in and out of unnamed roles, switch between playing instruments and singing, form a taut Greek chorus and stand alone in the spotlights.
The text is at once very online (hello, “soft looksmaxxing”) and very sweary – “super-fucking awkward!” intones the Greek chorus in one scene – but also fleetingly poetic in its observations on life, love and loneliness. The music obsesses over short loops (frantic violin lines, for instance, that might have escaped from one of Bartók’s folksier scores) and hammers away rhythmically like a sonic answer to strobe lighting. There are moments of ethereal beauty, too: quiet drones, gentle humming, disjointed suspensions on the accordion, timpani sliding in unison with a single voice, a brief six-part chorale.
Above all, though, The Alonetimes is funny. Not because of the contemporary references and the jokes about dating apps – but because these six performers brought to life people we’ve all been or met with absolute care and conviction. Oskar McCarthy’s turn as the instructor of an over-65s aerobics class – “hi everyone”, he murmured, the swerve into slippers-and-Ovaltine provoking gales of laughter – was one comic highlight. But Andreas Borregaard, Diamanda La Berge Dramm, Loré Lixenberg, Vanessa Porter and Adam Starkie were every bit as virtuosic as they negotiated the work’s hyperactive tragicomedy. Sometimes baffling and often bonkers, this was also an exhilaratingly enjoyable piece of contemporary music theatre.

title: The CO2-absorbing building made of old sinks, windscreens and toilets: Ghent’s £17m design museum is a green marvel
description: Inspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festival Museums often try to reflect the world around them, but rarely are they made so literally of their surroundings as the new design museum in Ghent . content:
Inspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festival
M useums often try to reflect the world around them, but rarely are they made so literally of their surroundings as the new design museum in Ghent . Rising above the Belgian city’s medieval tiled rooftops like an angular white watchtower, the new building has vacuumed up the city’s condemned concrete frames, windows, car windscreens, sinks and old toilets, and transformed them, phoenix-like, into a gleaming monument to recycling.
“There’s nothing new about reuse,” says Andy Groarke, co-founder of Carmody Groarke , the London-based architects who designed the €20m (£17m) project with local firms Atama and Re-st . “We’ve just forgotten how to do it.”
He says the team drew inspiration from Ghent’s 16th-century gothic cathedral, Saint Bavo’s, which was partly built using the white limestone blocks of the 10th-century romanesque basilica that had stood on the same site (recent renovations also ghoulishly uncovered walls made of human bones , femurs and tibias apparently having particularly useful structural properties, with crushed skulls for infill).
The new design museum doesn’t quite go that far in its nose-to-tail approach, but almost. The toilet cubicles are a smorgasbord of “biomaterials”, each featuring different tiles made of seaweed, flax, wood terrazzo and volcanic ash (you can scan a QR code for more info while you’re sitting on the loo). Some walls are plastered with local clay, while a chunky column in the entrance hall revels in its earthy layers of rubble dug straight from the building site.
But the real innovation is the brick , which was specially developed, tested and certified for the project (funded by a grant from Circular Flanders and Sogent, the city’s development agency). Each brick is made of 63% construction waste, sourced from within 8km of the museum, pulverised and compressed with hydrated lime, saving two-thirds of the embodied carbon of a regular fired clay brick. And the lime will continue to absorb CO2 from the atmosphere as it cures over the coming months and years.
“We’re not claiming this is a panacea, or a solution to the climate crisis,” says architect Sian Ricketts, Carmody Groarke’s sustainability lead. “But it is a sort of 82,000-brick proof of concept that you can do something different, with the right collaborators and the right clients.” Developed by East Sussex firm Local Works Studio and Brussels group BC Materials , the bricks were made in a former railway depot nearby, with the public invited to mix the ingredients and press their own blocks during a two-day festival of brickmaking. For €10, you can take one home from the museum shop.
Public participation extended to defining the very essence of the museum, too. In keeping with Belgium’s democratic traditions, a “citizens’ panel” of 40 people, drawn from a wide variety of Ghent residents, was established to inform what the museum should be. Their 100+ recommendations ranged from incorporating unticketed areas, to being able to see work-in-progress, and having plenty of seating, as well as ensuring that the “chic” building didn’t put people off. The result is as locally sourced and collaboratively created as big civic buildings come. “This expansion and renovation are not about creating more museum,” says the outgoing director, Katrien Laporte, “but about creating more than a museum: a community sense-making museum with real social relevance.”
The extension fills a leftover plot on the museum’s site, uniting the galleries that were previously spread between an 18th-century rococo mansion, called the Hotel de Coninck, and a troublesome 1990s addition – designed with a moving glass floor that rarely moved, now thankfully banished. The new building stands with the presence of a grand Ghent house, rising in five large storeys, and turning as it climbs to face the city centre, with big picture windows looking out in different directions on each floor. “We wanted it to feel domestic, industrial and civic at once,” says Groarke. It certainly has a bold presence.
Not everyone has welcomed its industrial bulk. Concerns have been raised about how the boxy white mass lumbers into view from the city’s quaint historical centre, and there is something slightly clumsy about the form on the skyline, topped with multiple roofs angled in different directions. Silicone joints between stretches of brick don’t help either, reading as unsightly seams from a distance. The museum defended the height as providing never-before-seen views of the city, and it’s true: when you’re on the top floor – a freely accessible public loft – or the roof terrace below, the panoramic vistas of Ghent’s castle and church spires are a treat.
Skyline concerns also fade away as you approach the museum at street level. A gate in the form of a billowing metallic curtain , frozen in motion, signals the new entrance in a delightfully surreal touch. Designed by Antwerp studio Unfold and 3D-printed in aluminium, it is a welcome change from the previously off-putting carriage entrance of the historical hotel down the sidestreet. The striking gate is one of a series of special projects commissioned by curator Siegrid Demyttenaere that have been dotted throughout the building, from a cast street number to a reception desk and lockers, making functional parts of the museum exhibits in themselves.
A lobby lined with timber salvaged from a tobacco factory in Brussels leads into the stadskamer , or city room, opening through big sliding windows on to the museum courtyard on one side, and the street on the other. It was thronging with visitors during the opening weekend, with the feeling of a true public square. The chubby earthen column (a commission by Grond Studio ) rises to support an intersection of the deep wooden beams that crisscross the ceiling, the first glimpse of the building’s sculptural timber frame. The architects say it is the biggest mass timber public building in Belgium, featuring walls and floors of spruce CLT (cross-laminated timber) and chunky beams of beech LVL (laminated veneer lumber), imported from Austria. A beautiful oak staircase connects the floors, with joinery details in darker walnut, its angular geometries lending a Piranesian air.
The new building is “a stack of five rooms”, says Groarke, “each with a particular identity”. The stairs lead to the Forum, for lectures and events; the Atelier, a light-flooded studio for education workshops; and the Vitrine for temporary exhibitions – before arriving at the Loft, a grand event space with spectacular views. Its balcony became an urban-scale DJ booth for the opening party, when local duo 2manydjs performed above the rooftops to 5,000 revellers dancing in the streets below.
Spectacle aside, one of the building’s most useful achievements is connecting the museum’s pre-existing wings in a continuous, accessible loop for the first time. Visitors can now move from the chandelier-bedecked suites of the Hotel de Coninck, through to the 90s wing – from which 60% of the columns have been removed and voids filled in to create more display space for the permanent collection – to the light, woody world of the new tower. It was made possible by a wise use of funds: while competing architects proposed taller towers and deeper basement levels, the winning team suggested a better use of some of the tight budget would be to refurbish and renew what was already there.
“The competition was such a great process,” says Groarke, singing the praises of the renowned Flemish Open Call run by the Vlaams Bouwmeester (the government architect), with a jury that included five international museum directors alongside architects and planners. You can still see all the entries online . “Architecture is in the public consciousness here in a way that it’s not in the UK,” Groarke continues. “Back home, it’s seen as an extension of the property industry, with a pyramid scheme of mediocrity in the way.”
He’s got a point. It would be hard to imagine a building of such quality and imagination being realised on British shores, where contractors rule all and architects are forced to compete on fees in a self-sabotaging race to the bottom. Public procurement rules also mean architects generally have to have built several buildings of the type they are bidding for before they can even qualify to compete, meaning few opportunities for young practices.
Our bureaucrats might do well to spend some time in the museum’s opening exhibition, Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy . Curated by Amelie Klein and Vera Sacchetti, it is a fascinating exploration of the design of democratic decision-making, examining everything from ballot papers to the layout of parliament buildings, to how nature might be given a seat at the table. One particularly revealing project, The Flemish Scrollers by artist Dries Depoorter, uses AI to track distracted politicians scrolling on their phones during parliamentary sessions, and automatically posts screenshots of the live stream to social media, asking the elected officials to do better.
Perhaps a similar algorithm could be used to name and shame each time a public tender is awarded to the same old suspects, with dismal results for our built environment. Once again, the Flems are leading the way.

title: ‘If the lion does not tell its story, the hunter will’: a century of thrilling Cameroonian art

content:
Key players in the country’s art history feature in a hefty new tome that covers everything from royal-carvers to bronze-smiths to work inspired by a horrific video smuggled out of a torture chamber
One Sunday last year, the Cameroonian-Guadeloupean-French artist Roxane Mbanga was relaxing in bed when she received a message that made her sit up. It was about working on an art history project.
Growing up in Paris, she had been a regular at Maasai Mara, the now defunct restaurant owned by her father, where Africans in the diaspora, including the artists whom he helped organise exhibitions, convened to eat and chat. Thus the concept of a book, attempting for the first time to comprehensively compile and document key players in Cameroon’s vast visual art history, made obvious sense to her.
“It’s a magical reconnaissance, being recognised by my peers and being in the same book as people I look up to,” says the 30-year-old artist. “This idea of creating spaces, as with the book, is incredibly important because it allows us to build from there and leave traces for people that will come after. I really lacked that growing up … spaces like books, podcasts or whatever, where I could really see people that resemble me, that do things similar to me.”
She is one of 180 artists who appear in Ô Cameroon! , a 424-page volume that launches at the 1-54 Contemporary African Art Fair in London in October, with planned stops in Côte d’Ivoire’s Abidjan, Paris and the Cameroonian cities of Douala and Yaoundé. Posthumous additions include the painter-sculptor Koko Komégné , who died three weeks after submitting his contribution to the book, and the first African woman to curate the Venice Biennale, Koyo Kouoh who died of cancer last year.
The book was curated and conceived by Cameroonian national Ozong Agborsangaya-Fiteu, an Abidjan-based collector and development finance executive. During her travels, she kept encountering artists from her homeland of different generations and in different places, and realised that there was also no single archive or directory to find out more about them.
“There was a sense of absence or loss … I became increasingly conscious that if we did not document these artists’ works, some could just simply disappear,” she says. “At some point, my own curiosity became a feeling of urgent responsibility. I began to feel that if we did not gather these histories right away, we might lose them for ever.”
In 1919 , a year after Germany was defeated in the first world war, its former colony of Kamerun was split into two unequal halves between the French and British. Despite the profound transformation – and as European colonial administrators looted thousands of artefacts from the country – societies of artists continued their intellectual and cultural work underground. Royal carvers and bronze-smiths in the ancient walled city of Foumban, for example, thrived under the reign of Sultan Njoya, famed for his promotion of the arts.
Ô Cameroon! covers from then until 2025, a century of diverse art from east to west and between anglophone and francophone regions, presented in non-chronological order. “The book is an act of cultural recovery and restitution,” says Agborsangaya-Fiteu. “Art for Cameroon is not a new story. Before Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso and Constantin Brâncuși, there were big sculptors like Ateu Atsa , who is Cameroonian” – from the 19th century. “Many of these artists influenced European modernism.
“If the lion does not tell its story, the hunter will,” she adds. “This is an attempt for the lion to tell its own story, and given that Cameroon is so complex, it was very important that the story be told by multiple voices so that there could be multiple interpretations and perspectives shaping the book.”
In 1961, a UN plebiscite led to English-speaking Southern Cameroons rejoining the country after almost four decades as part of neighbouring Nigeria, while Northern Cameroons voted to remain in Nigeria. That reunion laid the foundation for a civil war between the anglophones and the state security apparatus, while deepening regional tensions. In that time, some on the art scene who didn’t leave earlier under the repressive, four-decade rule of Paul Biya, who remains the world’s oldest head of state , emigrated.
The most recent chapter of Cameroon’s art history has been tough to document. Among those included in the book is Em’kal Eyongakpa , an Amsterdam-based botanist turned artist, who has worked on subjects focusing on the Cameroon volcanic line. He had plans for building a physical art space in his native south-west Cameroon, but they were disrupted by the anglophone conflict.
“I think [the book is] mainly for historicity and because there is a need for accuracy, especially with respect to people from my side of the Cameroons, as Cameroon is two colonial entities that came together,” says Eyongakpa, who now runs creative spaces in camp settlements in southern Nigeria hosting refugees who fled Cameroon.
One of his projects documented in the book is s ǒbàtú “to cleanse one’s ears” (in the Kenyang language), inspired by a horrific video smuggled out of a torture chamber as the crisis intensified. He hopes it can fill a gap. “There had not been any discussions within the academia that really looks at this conflict that has taken the lives of so many people and it really felt like kind of a big betrayal,” he says.
For Agborsangaya-Fiteu, this book is only a start. She wants to inspire more exhibitions and research including elsewhere in Africa. “This was a very emotional project and I’m getting goosebumps as I reflect,” she says, sobbing quietly. “It’s a love story since we are all immigrants. We all left to go out to find things to do, to find our dignity and get education, to find our purpose. But I was born in Cameroon, so you cannot [but] love where you’re from.”
Mbanga, who has been on a lifetime quest for identity, believes that the book can help broaden the scope for young artists like her in the diaspora: “I think it can allow people to dream bigger.”

title: Hokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji review – sublime wonders from the Great Wave to that heroic, eternal peak

content:
Dulwich Picture Gallery, London With its helpless rowers, naked river-crossers and snowbound tea-drinkers, this magnificent series is a warning to put your faith in the essential and enduring
T he giant wave’s foaming white summit spreads high over the heads of the helpless souls huddled in their long thin boats, crackling into what look like many sharp claws. It is a monster, hungry to swallow human flesh. But beyond it, over the wild water, soothing the terror of those in peril on the sea, is Mount Fuji – a solid cone of hope and solace. The mountain, not the wave, is the hero of this masterpiece, as it is the hero of all the prints in Dulwich Picture Gallery’s stunning exhibition – the first in Britain – of the complete Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.
When you look closely here at three different, superb impressions of Katsushika Hokusai’s Under the Wave off Kanagawa – widely known today as the Great Wave – your mental picture of this icon is shattered by the violent onrush of water. In reproductions the wave just seems beautiful, an elegant curl of blue and white. But here, to paraphrase Tennyson, it is nature, blue in tooth and claw. The wretched people are the emotional heart of the picture, their imminent risk of drowning its whole point.
The wave is out of control, murderous, yet it is also a passing moment, shows Hokusai, a devout Buddhist. He offers this consolation: the wave looks as vast as a mountain but soon it will break and be gone. Meanwhile the sacred peak of Mount Fuji endures eternally. It can’t be hurt by the ephemeral dragon of saltwater. Put your faith in the essential, enduring things beyond the nightmare of mutable appearances and you will find inner peace. The wave is an illusion. Mount Fuji is the truth.
Yet that colossal truth is easy to forget as we move around it, pass it by, catch sight of it in the everyday rush – a distant peak on the horizon. On a city bridge people swarm without looking up from under their round hats at the mountain in the distance. A man working bare-chested, wiry and worn, has no time to study the far-off peak as he concentrates on making a barrel.
Hokusai delights in epic shifts of perspective, seeing Mount Fuji as an apparently small insignificant object while filling the foreground with distracting action. You do a double take at Fuji from Kanaya on the Tōkaidō Highway. Dressed people sit on the shoulders of nude men who are almost completely submerged in turbulent blue and white water, while others are sealed inside boxlike palanquins to be carried too over the water by crushed bearers gasping for air. It is no illusion. This crossing point over the Ōi River was a key military point for the city of Edo, so no bridges were allowed to be built there. Travellers had to be borne across.
No one in this strange scene looks at Mount Fuji. And yet not to notice the mountain is to miss out on something very big indeed. In another image a ferryman does pay attention to it, set against a golden evening sky under a layer of deep blue, as he rows people across another river: some passengers also look, while others do not. Other people – tourists as well as pilgrims – seek out the views, like Hokusai himself, delighting in nature and its mystery, even in extreme conditions: one group has trekked to a country teahouse in winter to view Mount Fuji in the snow. They’re rewarded with an icy scene of devastating beauty, picked out in golden white and intense deep blue.
Hokusai’s miracle colour, Prussian blue, came from Europe, where it was first used in the early 18th century. His knowledge of perspective is also coloured by European art. But the traffic of influence went both ways. It is impossible to overstate the centrality of Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji to the birth of modernism. It is the first global masterpiece. When Hokusai created this series of closely linked prints in the early 1830s he reinvented landscape art as a conceptual and symbolic meditation that would thrill and inspire artists across the world.
It’s no secret that Van Gogh, Whistler and other members of the European avant garde collected and emulated Japanese woodblock prints. But I hadn’t realised how deeply Cézanne was in his debt: the French painter’s repeated efforts to paint Mont Sainte-Victoire in Provence, fragmenting its rocky mass into shards of perception to see its true nature and discover its secret, echo Hokusai’s journey around Mount Fuji. So do Monet’s obsessive paintings of Rouen Cathedral, a haystack and his (very Zen) waterlily garden. Hokusai taught these Frenchmen to see landscape as metaphysical.
That we make icons of separate images from this series – and not just the wave – is understandable. Here is Ejiri Station, Province of Suruga, Hokusai’s depiction of people holding on to their hats as the sky fills with blown paper in an unexpected turn in the weather. Jeff Wall famously restaged it in his photograph A Sudden Gust of Wind (After Hokusai) .
What a timeless artist Hokusai is, influencing Monet and Cézanne and still inspiring remakes today. But it distorts his meaning if we focus on his separate images without seeing them as part of one long meditation on Mount Fuji. By itself, Hokusai’s gust of wind may seem an image of crisis and impermanence. But Mount Fuji is in the background: the godlike summit that shows us there’s a serenity beyond the chaos.

title: Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography review – a rhapsodic show to stop you in your tracks
description: Tate Modern, London From a Singapore construction worker to a loincloth-wearing Sri Lankan, this awe-inspiring and truly global exhibition finds epic beauty in the everyday I don’t remember the last time I saw such a well-researched and truly globally representative exhibition that doesn’t patronise but quietly makes its case unapologetically, fearlessly and through sheer quality. Apart from being the first retelling of the international, pluralistic pictorialism movement, Tate’s new show allows for some refreshing encounters with unknown works for British audiences – around half of the works included here have never been shown in the UK. The effect is to radically deepen and widen our understanding not only of art history but the human impulses that drive us to make images in the first place. We move seamlessly from the sudden shock of colour in three-colour carbon prints of flowers in a London garden in the 1920s to works born of the photographic salons, circles and clubs of Sydney, Hong Kong and Brazil. Historical moments collide; the epic emerges from the everyday. A man rows home across the Norfolk Broads, another works on a construction site in Singapore. None of it feels out of place. It all belongs. It is all extremely, almost ecclesiastically, beautiful. Continue reading...
content:
Tate Modern, London From a Singapore construction worker to a loincloth-wearing Sri Lankan, this awe-inspiring and truly global exhibition finds epic beauty in the everyday
I don’t remember the last time I saw such a well-researched and truly globally representative exhibition that doesn’t patronise but quietly makes its case unapologetically, fearlessly and through sheer quality. Apart from being the first retelling of the international, pluralistic pictorialism movement, Tate’s new show allows for some refreshing encounters with unknown works for British audiences – around half of the works included here have never been shown in the UK. The effect is to radically deepen and widen our understanding not only of art history but the human impulses that drive us to make images in the first place.
We move seamlessly from the sudden shock of colour in three-colour carbon prints of flowers in a London garden in the 1920s to works born of the photographic salons, circles and clubs of Sydney, Hong Kong and Brazil. Historical moments collide; the epic emerges from the everyday. A man rows home across the Norfolk Broads, another works on a construction site in Singapore. None of it feels out of place. It all belongs. It is all extremely, almost ecclesiastically, beautiful.
More than a few times, I stopped in my tracks. I could spend hours with Yip Cheong Fun’s 1940 Father’s Care, a cinematic image of a man holding one child with his hand extended to another, helping them down from the rocky crag they are walking over, on a journey across an open rural landscape somewhere. It’s a touching image of parenthood and the passage of time. Like this show overall, it’s about gestures rather than flashy declarations of feeling.
From this purist vision of love, we find a more ambiguous exploration in Lionel Wendt’s excruciatingly charged study of a young Sri Lankan man’s loincloth-clad body in the private intimacy of his Colombo studio, revealing hidden desires and truths the camera can’t conceal. It’s beauty as a kind of torture: the same medium that can expose the body to anthropological scrutiny transforms looking into something far more complicated.
I’m equally intrigued by a 1955 series by Han Youngsoo: small, noirish works of Korean street scenes that beg for narration from the viewer. Two 1925 bromide prints by Kate Smith show a woman in a flowing pre-Raphaelite style, pausing in a field dense with vegetation and foliage. Its title draws me closer: The Listener. What is she listening to, and what does this photograph want us to hear? It leaves me hovering between the visible and the imagined, its silence and stillness charged with the possibility.
Limb Eung-sik’s Feet 2 has a similarly ethereal atmosphere: flowing, diaphanous material folds around a dancer’s feet so that they dissolve into light and shadows. Nostalgia and sentimentality are dialled up, but it’s irresistible. If you’re attuned to it, these images suggest that anything – shells, shadows, a faucet, a wilting flower, a fishing net – can become magic, and these pictorialists teach us how to see the world that way.
This is not by any means a critical look at pictorialism. Mysteries are left intact, politics are largely left at the door. There’s no attempt to unravel the reductionist pitfalls of pursuing the fantasy of beauty. Some of the educational intrusions feel unnecessary – a timeline of photographic techniques is helpful and interesting but risks putting “art photography” back in the realm of craft, as does a full-scale recreation of a darkroom that you cannot enter. The magic of the darkroom is not that it is a dark room with a bunch of dirty aprons hanging outside. It is the transformation that happens within it: the strange alchemy of chemistry and light, which is already accounted for in abundance in the photographs.
But I can forgive these things. There’s genuine care and awe here. It’s a reminder that seeking moments of magic and breathtaking beauty is a human instinct, and we have a right to it. This is an exhibition about things that are universally shared and eternally human, that cannot be destroyed by the politics of a time or place, that survive and thrive. Light and Magic is as intelligent as it is beautiful, as whimsical as it is informative, as rhapsodic as it is real.

title: The fascinating tale of a heart that died twice: best podcasts of the week
description: How did two men who shared the same heart and the same wife end up dying the same way?
