content:
How did two men who shared the same heart and the same wife end up dying the same way? Plus, inside the beef between ‘the Kennedys of Italy’
This fascinating series opens with the death of a man from a gunshot wound – and the revelation that this isn’t the first time his heart has stopped beating. It previously belonged to another man who died the same way, and who also had the same wife. Hosted by Karen Kilgariff, what follows is an intriguing eight-part tale that veers between a scientific exploration and a gripping true-crime saga. Alexi Duggins Apple, from Monday 19 October
Another series of the slick podcast about powerful business dynasties, and the beef behind the scenes of some of the world’s best-known brands. This time, Sofia Bettiza investigates the Agnelli family, sometimes called “the Kennedys of Italy”, who founded the car giant Fiat and were rocked by the death of their powerful patriarch Gianni. Hannah J Davies BBC Sounds, all episodes out from Monday 19 October
Colin Norris was a Leeds nurse who became known as “the angel of death”, convicted for murdering four elderly patients and attempting to kill two more. But new evidence suggests they weren’t murdered. Louise Shorter investigates, starting with the insulin poisoning of Ethel Hall. Hollie Richardson Widely available, episodes weekly
Journalist Audrey Gillan takes an appropriately delicate approach to the story of a 16-year-old girl murdered by a classmate. Diane Watson died in Glasgow in 1991, but the pain for those who knew her continues. In this six-part BBC Scotland series, Gillan looks not only at the consequences for her killer, but also Diane’s family’s fight to stop the press from defaming their late daughter. HJD BBC Sounds, all episodes out from Monday 19 October
After the first season of this podcast’s reporting on the US educational system, 26 states changed the way they teach reading. Now, education journalist Emily Hanford offers a colourful tale of a US maths experiment that left four-year-olds fluent in algebra – only for it to be shunned. AD Widely available, episodes weekly

title: Another taste of honey: Shelagh Delaney’s long-lost play about a teenage truant is a little gem
description: The playwright’s daughter found Catch Me Who Can after her mother’s death. Now it has become a compelling audio drama with Toby Jones and Rita Tushingham Was Shelagh Delaney a one-hit wonder? Absolutely not. Aside from A Taste of Honey which, in the words of Dominic Dromgoole, “has a rock-solid heart and the gleam of the natural”, she wrote the screenplays for the films Charlie Bubbles and Dance With a Stranger, TV series including The House That Jack Built and several radio plays. But now a 30-minute piece, Catch Me Who Can , has come to light, been released as an audio drama and turns out to be a little gem. Its origins are fascinating. It deals with a teenage truant and was discovered by Delaney’s daughter, Charlotte, after her mother’s death in 2011. But why did it lay hidden for so long? According to Charlotte, who has adapted it for audio: “It imagines my last few hours on the lam having run away from home and school when I was 14 in 1978. I was gone for three days and two nights. content:
The playwright’s daughter found Catch Me Who Can after her mother’s death. Now it has become a compelling audio drama with Toby Jones and Rita Tushingham
W as Shelagh Delaney a one-hit wonder? Absolutely not. Aside from A Taste of Honey which, in the words of Dominic Dromgoole, “has a rock-solid heart and the gleam of the natural”, she wrote the screenplays for the films Charlie Bubbles and Dance With a Stranger, TV series including The House That Jack Built and several radio plays. But now a 30-minute piece, Catch Me Who Can , has come to light, been released as an audio drama and turns out to be a little gem.
Its origins are fascinating. It deals with a teenage truant and was discovered by Delaney’s daughter, Charlotte, after her mother’s death in 2011. But why did it lay hidden for so long? According to Charlotte, who has adapted it for audio: “It imagines my last few hours on the lam having run away from home and school when I was 14 in 1978. I was gone for three days and two nights. I’d suggest it’s a racing certainty that the reason nothing has ever been heard of it is that it’s about me and my mum had rules about that kind of thing.”
The bulk of the play consists of a testy confrontation between the runaway Hattie (Ivy Sheehan) and her maths teacher (Toby Jones) who tries to persuade her to return home. Although the teacher is only out jogging in a park because he is on strike, he stands for a world of order, discipline and control; Hattie, on the other hand, embodies the need for freedom, anarchy and self-expression. But Delaney imbues the situation with its own ironies. The teacher argues for the sanctity of family life but is himself a conspicuous loner; Hattie’s urge for self-discovery conceals a total disregard for other people including her anxious parents.
Several things make the play worth listening to. One is the ease and naturalness of the dialogue. Hattie, not unlike the teenage Jo in A Taste of Honey, asks endless questions. At one point she taxes the teacher as to whether he ever did anything to find out what it was like just for the sake of it since “you once told us curiosity was divine”. Delaney also introduces an itinerant bag lady – played by none other than Rita Tushingham who was Jo in Tony Richardson’s film of A Taste of Honey – who says of a relative: “They took him into hospital and took his leg off – just like President Tito.”
As well as a collision between self-restraint and teenage truancy, the play offers – in Charlotte Delaney’s words – a snapshot of London life in 1978, with oblique references to the IRA, the Vietnamese “boat people” and Rock Against Racism: a reminder of the turbulence of the times.
Deftly produced by Polly Thomas, the piece is very well acted by Jones as the audibly repressed teacher and by Sheehan as the experience-hungry Hattie. What you come away with is a reminder of Delaney’s remarkable gift for dialogue and her equal understanding of the value of education and the exuberance of youth.

content:
In this week’s newsletter: As platforms chase ​s​ubscribers, podcasts are losing their off‑screen charm​, leaving listeners to wonder whether the intimacy of audio can survive the studio lights
Don’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
T his has been the year that podcasting properly, unapologetically “ pivoted to video ”. Yes, it’s been a progression that has been in the making for quite a while, arguably ever since Joe Rogan first trained a webcam at himself and whichever guest he was smoking weed with in his studio back in 2009 – but in 2026 the medium’s transformation from purely aural to audio/visual (often with more of an emphasis on the visual) is truly complete.
In January, Netflix started broadcasting video versions of popular podcasts from The Ringer, iHeartMedia, Barstool and more, as well as continuing to make video pods of their own. That landgrab was a slightly desperate response to YouTube’s phenomenal success with visualised pods; after becoming the preferred podcast platform for most Americans in 2024, it managed the same feat in the UK in 2026 , overtaking Spotify. No wonder, then, that Spotify has – as part of a wider push to get people sticking to its platform for pods – continued to bolster viewing capabilities for its own pods too.
Meanwhile, more and more podcast creators are running into the arms of video, wheeling cameras into studios that often resemble an Ikea showroom circa 2008, with their felt throw cushions and chairs that are absurdly poorly suited to facing someone and having an actual conversation with them. (I’m concerned about what all this pivoting to video is doing to these poor podcasters’ backs; they all seem to be sitting so uncomfortably, swivelling between guest and camera.)
You might have guessed from the slightly sniffy tone that I’m not entirely on board with podcasting’s video pivot. Podcasts have long had a clearly defined role in my life: they are there for when I’m ironing, on my commute, at the gym or the ever-shrinking bit of time not glued to a screen. Adding video complicates that. If people are performing to camera as much as to microphone, you start to feel like watching them is the only way to get the whole picture. And some podcasters are just not suited to camera: I don’t want their true gift for audio to be diluted by them having to constantly think about the lens pointed squarely at their face. Let podcasts be podcasts, I say!
But lately I’ve realised that my King Canute stance against this tide is futile. I need to learn to stop worrying and love – well, tolerate at least – the video pod. This is a permanent revolution – and one that does have its advantages. Making a show visual as well as aural allows podcasters to clip up their best bits and share them for potential new fans on social media, a crucial arrow in the quiver of smaller podcasts that lack the marketing budgets of their bigger competitors. It feels a bit churlish of me to deny them that out of sheer podcast purism.
Worse still for my militant anti-video pod stance, I have to shamefully concede that some of them work pretty well visually. Who would have thunk it, but it turns out that comedians, in particular, are good with a camera pointed at them: I’ll regularly try to catch a good moment from Elis James and John Robins that I enjoyed in audio form on video later on – just to see the redness of John’s face (pictured above), and the reality of his contempt as he embarks on a white-hot rage at having a less than perfect credit score rating, say.
Other podcasts, for example some of the Ringer stable, are starting to skilfully knit in clips and stills from the shows and films they are talking about, which is definitely an improvement over watching two people talk at each other over a desk for an hour. (The Rest is History’s own attempts – flashing up the odd picture of a historical figure mid chat – is a little less slick but just about does the job.)
I still have quibbles. Many of these video podcasts will never look to me like anything other than bargain-basement daytime chatshows, causing them to shed the aura of their audio form. And I will never stop being infuriated by podcasters who forget that they have a listening audience as well as one watching on a screen. Gesticulations are completely useless to those who can’t see them, and please, if something funny happens in the studio, explain it to listeners rather than just bursting into guffaws and moving on. Maddening!
What I’m trying to say is: I still want most podcasts to stay podcasts, nattering away amiably in my ear while I’m at the supermarket. But I will concede that the video podcast isn’t a totally terrible idea, particularly when set against, say, AI-generated podcasts . But that’s a rant for another newsletter …

content:
At barely 20 minutes, this satire on strongman politics serves to jolt audiences out of their complacency
“I s this theatre for the TikTok generation?” one critic asked of the latest play by 88-year-old Caryl Churchill, lauded as Britain’s greatest living playwright. Triumph , her blistering satire on contemporary strongman politics, is barely 20 minutes long.
Cleverly spliced with Suetonius’s The Twelve Caesars, the play takes the form of a press conference given by a blond-wigged apparatchik, who smilingly extols the barbarities of an unnamed narcissistic emperor. If “Triumph” were a crossword answer, the clue might be “To greet a populist US leader in confusion – a win (7)”. Even given Churchill’s reputation for prescience, the play was uncannily timely. It premiered in London and New York on the same day that President Trump’s short-lived press officer Katie Zacharia was forced to resign. As the American comedian Robin Williams quipped of an earlier administration, “People say satire is dead. It’s not dead; it’s alive and living in the White House.”
Churchill is a playwright of ideas who, throughout her long career, has played with structure. Her 2012 play Love and Information depicted the fragmentation of modern life through 57 scenes and more than 100 characters. With just three actors, this new play is a triumph of form and content: as short and direct as a press conference, its purpose is to alert us to a global crisis. This is the theatrical equivalent of a political sketch.
A story arc in one act, it is not a highbrow version of the 60- to 90-second schlocky microdrama episodes for mobile phones, which have become so popular that Channel 4 is launching its own series. Short plays go back to Suetonius’s time. Chekhov, Beckett and Albee were all masters of the dramatic sprint. Churchill started out writing short radio plays, and in later years her work has become an increasing feat of compression.
But this brevity goes against a trend for theatrical maximalism. To persuade audiences back to theatres and cinemas after the pandemic, plays and films have been getting longer, perhaps to justify the price of a ticket. The Oscar-winning movie The Brutalist required a 15-minute interval in 2024. A two-part RSC dramatisation of Middlemarch has just opened at Stratford, where an epic Game of Thrones ended last month. However, a reducio spell has been cast on the six-hour, two-part Harry Potter and the Cursed Child juggernaut, which has reopened at half its original length.
A play in your lunch break or after a night out is not practical for many. And while mini dramas make use of empty theatre hours and fit around evening performances, only a playwright of Churchill’s stature could guarantee a sellout, weeklong run for a show briefer than an interval without audiences feeling short-changed. Triumph could be seen as a curtain raiser for a revival of her 1979 classic Cloud 9 at the National Theatre next month, and Three and a Bit , a new collection of “biting short plays” at the Almeida in January.
The Guardian’s Michael Billington called Churchill “ theatre’s great disruptor ”. With Triumph she is disrupting the conventions of theatregoing itself: a play isn’t always something to be enjoyed between an early supper, interval drinks and the last train home. She has turned the attention economy on its head. Like a Covid-era emergency press conference, Triumph interrupts its audience’s day to make them listen. It jolts us out of our complacency.

title: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
description: For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam. Aditya’s suggested reading: To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair. For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books. To learn more about what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the Guardian. Phil Burton-Cartledge examines why Britain's most successful political party is now failing in his book The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak . Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshal a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch. Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory Party For more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper examines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers. Two of its authors will join us for a podcast later in the series. And if you want to read how Brexit may have cost the UK 8% of GDP, read this paper based on data from the Bank of England. Finally, on the Spectator, read Nesrine Malik’s recent column in the Guardian: Why has Britain’s oldest political magazine become such a rabid cheerleader for Islamophobia? Continue reading...

title: From strife-torn France to the UK, rightwing populists win when they stir chaos while promising order | Rafael Behr
description: Marine Le Pen and Donald Trump are arsonists who play at being firefighters. Nigel Farage is finding that act harder to pull off in Andy Burnham’s Britain An election where one side represents chaos will nearly always be won by the party that promises order instead. Public fatigue after years of turbulent Tory rule accounted for Labour’s 2024 landslide victory more than any policy in Keir Starmer’s manifesto. Across the Channel, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally (RN), is currently on course to win next year’s presidential poll with a pledge of “restored authority and security” for a country that has spent years cycling between enervating stasis and explosive crisis. Le Pen has been boosted in recent days by scenes of city centres ablaze and shops being looted as student demonstrations mutated into riots. Street confrontation is a more standard feature of the political repertoire in France than in most settled democracies, but the destruction was disturbing by any measure. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...
content:
Marine Le Pen and Donald Trump are arsonists who play at being firefighters. Nigel Farage is finding that act harder to pull off in Andy Burnham’s Britain
A n election where one side represents chaos will nearly always be won by the party that promises order instead. Public fatigue after years of turbulent Tory rule accounted for Labour’s 2024 landslide victory more than any policy in Keir Starmer’s manifesto. Across the Channel, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally (RN), is currently on course to win next year’s presidential poll with a pledge of “restored authority and security” for a country that has spent years cycling between enervating stasis and explosive crisis.
Le Pen has been boosted in recent days by scenes of city centres ablaze and shops being looted as student demonstrations mutated into riots. Street confrontation is a more standard feature of the political repertoire in France than in most settled democracies, but the destruction was disturbing by any measure.
President Emmanuel Macron’s government, debilitated by the lack of a parliamentary majority, looked unprepared for the scale of the unrest. There was ample indication that something big was brewing. What began with high school students despairing at the neglected state of secondary education evolved into a general mobilisation of anger at high living costs and a lack of economic opportunities. Aggressive police tactics radicalised the crowd. As night followed day, and just as predictably, political fury gave way to opportunistic pillaging.
Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu accused “ultra-left” provocateurs of stirring disorder as part of a strategy to render the country ungovernable in the run-up to next year’s elections. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the populist left’s presidential candidate, countered that violence was the natural byproduct of a degenerate repressive state that conspires to discredit resistance, and that the protests channelled the heroic spirit of May 1968.
At 75, Mélenchon is old enough to remember that Paris spring of revolutionary fervour. He has a keen following in the current generation of activist students, but the insurrectionary rhetoric unsettles swathes of conservative France . His pungency could put Le Pen in the Élysée Palace.
In the past she has been locked out of the presidency by coalitions of moderate and left voters rallying , often without enthusiasm, behind the candidate best placed to stop her. RN’s advances in parliament have been checked in the same way, although it is currently the biggest party.
Macron has twice been the beneficiary of that dynamic, but he can’t run again, has no obvious successor and is so radioactively unpopular that the whole liberal centre ground is contaminated by his standing on it.
Current polling indicates that the “republican front” would unravel if the only names in a second-round run-off were Mélenchon and Le Pen. The centre-right would break for the RN leader. It probably wouldn’t even be close.
France’s crisis has not escaped notice across the Atlantic, where it is viewed through the warped lens of Maga ideology. Donald Trump explained that “France is burning” because the country has been overrun by immigrants “with hatred in their hearts”. JD Vance agreed that “western liberals” were to blame for opening European borders to “the third world” and advised American voters to view French misfortune as a premonition of the future if Congress is captured by Democrats in midterm elections next month.
Republican efforts to cast their rivals as catalysts of national ruin have limited traction when Trump is the obvious engine of chaos. Democrats didn’t start the war in Iran. Nor did they author a deranged trade policy that alienated the US’s friends, turning even Canada into a foe.
This is a common problem for incumbent demagogues. In opposition, simple solutions are proposed for complex problems: tariffs as the remedy for industrial decline; expelling illegal immigrants as the answer to every social and economic grievance; trusting in the leader’s judgment as the answer to everything else.
In office, those mechanisms fail to deliver the promised benefits. Someone needs to be blamed. The categories of undesirable element grow. Media, universities, courts and opposition parties are called crooked or treasonous. But purges disrupt the smooth running of a country. They are bad for the economy. This is how the insecure leader goes through the gears of tyranny. A craving for control generates dissent, which is attacked as a menace to society, requiring more draconian law enforcement. When that provokes more determined opposition, the dissenters are denounced as extremists who jeopardise public safety.
Trump has travelled some way down that road already. He might accelerate a lot further after the midterms. One option is to make bogus claims of election fraud, denying the validity of results that, if allowed to stand, would empower Democrats to hold a rogue president to account. His despotic temperament and his record of refusal to admit any electoral weakness suggest he would rather trigger a constitutional crisis of existential dimensions for American democracy than acquiesce to cohabitation with an unfriendly Congress. He will plunge the country deeper into chaos and insist that the nation rally around him as the only one capable of restoring order.
That is standard authoritarian operating procedure. The arsonists affect dismay at the conflagrations they ignite. They cavort in firefighter costumes and hose the flames with petrol.
This is the role Le Pen is readying herself for now in France. If she wins next year’s election, the backlash from the left will be ferocious. That challenge will be eagerly confronted by an incoming president likely to be looking for pretexts to declare a national emergency and remake the republic as a vehicle for her personal authority.
Britain’s radical right parties dream of an equivalent opportunity. They revel in lurid imagery of societal breakdown. Sometimes the fantasy is camouflaged as a warning about the dangers of unchecked immigration, but impatience for a violent reckoning is never far from the surface. For Rupert Lowe , leader of Restore Britain, there is seemingly no effort to conceal the relish. He told his followers on X last week that his agenda would certainly trigger “civil unrest and rioting,” and that “what needs to happen will be incredibly painful”.
Lowe is still a relatively fringe figure but he exerts disproportionate influence in the conservative digital ecosystem thanks to amplification on X by Elon Musk , the platform’s oligarch proprietor. Lowe’s candidate beat the Tories and Liberal Democrats in Manchester’s mayoral byelection earlier this year. By competing for votes with Reform UK, Restore Britain has drawn Nigel Farage into an arms race in fanatical anti-migrant rhetoric.
Farage’s status as a more serious contender in the electoral arena allows him to launder ideas that were once self-evidently extreme – mass deportations, for example – as mainstream policy. That doesn’t automatically make them popular. There is an audience for ethnically selective nationalism but it has a ceiling. The voters who are motivated by determination to thwart Farage outnumber those who want him installed in Downing Street.
That tactical coalition is easily galvanised because prominent figures on the British right wear their arsonist intent so brazenly. Also, a stable Labour government isn’t giving them opportunities to play at being firefighters.
To advance on power, Reform UK has to win over the kinds of voters that Le Pen sees heading her way through the smouldering rubble of French politics: people exhausted and bewildered by the system unravelling, without hope that incumbent authorities can get the country back on track, and amenable to the argument that fanatical leftists are the more menacing agents of chaos. Thankfully, those are not the conditions of British politics. Andy Burnham’s every step should be guided by the need to keep it that way.

title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff
description: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. content:
The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost
A nother morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway.
In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back.
And therein lies the challenge to the government’s hopes of AI helping to transform the machinery of the state on the cheap, saving not only time but billions of pounds in public money. It’s early days, but AI seems not so much to be streamlining public service delivery as gumming it up – partly because, as was once the case with email, the public is using it right back at them.
In a Substack post last week, the former civil servant Sam Freedman noted that governments around the world seem to be experiencing unusual surges in complaints, requests and responses to regulatory and official bodies since the adoption of ChatGPT. It’s the same story in the courts , with employment tribunal cases in England, Scotland and Wales reportedly rising by 39% in a year thanks in part to claimants using AI to draft claims, while magistrates and judges face a wave of people who can’t afford lawyers using ChatGPT to build cases that often don’t make sense. And all of this needs patient disentangling by a human, on the grounds that just because a defendant is citing precedents that don’t exist, it doesn’t mean there isn’t a genuine grievance buried in there somewhere.
Whitehall special advisers complain of departments drowning in AI-generated freedom of information requests, an abuse of a system originally intended to empower individuals. MPs’ offices are similarly swamped by AI-generated letters, all of which need to be read by humans for fear of missing something important from a constituent.
How long before public consultations on changing the law become so spammed by slop that they are in essence useless as a measure of what the country actually thinks? There’s a fine line between the noble aim of making it easier for individuals to interact with an otherwise remote state, and making it so easy that the result is an uncontrollable firehose of meaningless machine-generated guff.
The obvious answer to this kind of AI flooding is getting AI tools to detect or sift it, but that doesn’t always work when dealing with potentially vulnerable human beings. Constituents who use AI to express themselves in more fancy-sounding language when writing to their MP, for example, still have the right to expect a personal response from a human being.
Employers who thought they were being smart by getting AI to sift job applications, meanwhile, are reaping what they sowed, as resentful applicants automate their end of things too and spray-gun applications across the board, rather than concentrating on the jobs they really want. Now neither side can separate the wheat from an avalanche of chaff.
The risk of paralysis is likely only to increase if the public starts adopting agentic AI in the kind of numbers big tech fondly imagines. Early adopters might well find agents save them time and hassle. But shortcuts stop being shortcuts once everyone else is using them too, and risk turning into bottlenecks instead. Think of cars, which have vastly shortened journey times compared with travelling by horseback, except in cities at rush hour when too many other people are also trying to shorten theirs. By 2018, central London daytime traffic was moving on average at just over 7mph – about the same speed as a trotting pony.
Historically, humans have always learned to develop ways around problems of our own making. We have spam filters for email, congestion charges to keep cars out of cities, and in the long term we could well figure out what kind of frictions we need to put back in the system to make it possible to live with the impact of AI.
But for now a useful rule of thumb, if improbable claims start to be made for savings due to AI, will be that more isn’t always better; faster and easier isn’t always more convenient; and time saved in one section of public services has a horrible habit of popping up in another one. Let the Whac-A-Mole begin.

title: Shall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet | Polly Toynbee
description: We saw last time what reckless reliance on close polling led to. The horror! No, never again, not another referendum. But the idea is back in play as Andy Burnham looks for ways to reverse a decade of economic stagnation. content:
We saw last time what reckless reliance on close polling led to. The omertà on rejoining has now been broken, but it would be folly to move too soon
W hen I hear that word again, a shudder runs down my spine. I want to groan, hold my head in my hands and wail. The horror! No, never again, not another referendum. But the idea is back in play as Andy Burnham looks for ways to reverse a decade of economic stagnation.
As the prime minister dared to unlock the door to a Brussels reunion, you could hear Ode to Joy burst out from all remainers. But the prospect of a re-run of the most self-destructive vote in our history is dismaying.
Remember that morning a decade ago. First came Sunderland’s 12.20am result, a 61.3% vote to leave, but there was still hope for remainers … until the BBC’s 4.40am verdict that leave had won. In that second a great rift tore across the country. Remainers, dubbed remoaners, never recovered. UK politics became a circus: we who paraded as the west’s strong and stable “mother of parliaments” ran wildly through seven prime ministers in 10 years. Both Labour and Tory parties were wrecked by the most shattering event of our political lifetime. It is a wound neither has dared to reopen.
Only now Burnham has finally broken the spell of Brexit silence, aiming to rejoin, while the Tories will stay in the wilderness until they repent the Brexit disaster they inflicted on the country.
As Burnham sets out to explore all the options, outriders scout the way back in. Making the strong case for full EU membership, IPPR, the thinktank closest to Labour, has published a weighty report this week on how it can happen and why it must: we need it for prosperity, security and democracy. It has left us dangerously alone and friendless in a world of great power blocs. Our once reliable ally, the US, is never to be fully trusted again now we know what its people are capable of voting for. And so the warmth of familiar democracies across the Channel looks welcoming (at least for now). Make this bid to rejoin about who we are, bonding with where we belong, emotionally and historically. We have discovered “sovereignty” is a mirage: every treaty and trade deal requires sharing it with allies.
Within a year, a majority of people in the UK thought Brexit was a mistake (not quite the same as regretting their own vote). Now we know that Brexit has robbed us of a walloping 8% of GDP. IPPR and Persuasion UK polling finds 52% want to rejoin , 29% to stay out. Support grows by the year, partly as older people drop off their perches and young pro-Europeans join the electoral roll. As the IPPR tested every option from Keir Starmer’s slight reset to full membership, the least popular was leaving things as they are. The current Boris Johnson/Lord Frost deal is so dysfunctional that Burnham says keeping it would be a “dereliction of duty” . As ever ignoring the public mood, last year Kemi Badenoch wrote to the EU ambassador warning that, if elected, she would repeal any change , an act of near-treason that could sabotage negotiations in Brussels that start next month. Watch Michael Gove, arch-Brexit manipulator, telling the Guardian’s Aditya Chakrabortty he regrets nothing , blaming others for failing to capitalise on those illusory Brexit benefits. Would that bleating work? I think not.
But is this shift to 52% v 29% strong enough to dare throw the dice and risk everything? No, not quite yet. The IPPR admits it is still “soft”, and there are familiar echoes of what happened last time. After years in which it felt as if we could talk about nothing else, the EU now has reassuringly low salience. But that’s just as it was until Ukip and Tory Brexiters turbocharged what had been a non-issue. As before, polling figures that encouraged David Cameron to breeze arrogantly into a referendum looked sufficient to someone who assumed he would win. This time we know better. Prepare for Dominic Cummings et al rising from their coffins with Brexit defibrillators to shock new life into the issue. Nigel Farage was at it on Sunday, claiming the EU would charge Britain £42bn a year to rejoin .
Testing arguments for both sides, this report reveals traps to avoid and what people like about rejoining. Red lights flash over joining the euro, scrapping our other trade deals, giving up fishing rights and high contributions to the EU budget. Top of the most effective reasons for rejoining is passport queues. Second comes security : Ukraine has exposed this dangerous Trump/Putin world. Third is the need to bring lost foreign investment back to Britain.
But reasoned, fact-based focus groups in a calm and rational atmosphere can’t begin to replicate the monstrous lies, fabrications and devilry of a TikTok, Instagram and X referendum campaign. Remember the £350m-a-week bus, the Turks are coming, immigration will end and, best of all, “take back control”. Of what? Everything! That’s what referendums do.
So not yet. The case for joining has to be powerfully made, the argument won overwhelmingly for allied EU forces to circle the wagons against what Peter Ricketts, ex-national security adviser, along with the head of MI5, warns are “more reckless, more dangerous” cyber-attacks on vital services, such as energy, water, transport, banking or air traffic control. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, meeting with the EU home affairs commissioner today to restore data cooperation on crime and migration is a reminder of how insanely self-destructive Brexit was.
In a decade, Britain has changed. Though Brexiters will threaten floods of migrants storming the border on joining the EU, IPPR polling shows freedom of movement no longer alarms voters as it once did. The cost of living is now the top national concern, not immigration. Look how poorer countries have caught up to us: per capita income in Bucharest, Romania’s capital, is far higher than Sunderland’s.
But the EU has changed too. The question is what kind of Europe we would join if Marine Le Pen and the Alternative für Deutschland became its new axis of power. Here’s the answer: that would make joining even more urgent, to be inside to influence what we can, bolstering the democrats. Staying out leaves us powerless.
This report sets to work on the campaign Burnham ignited when he proposed going “all the way” . The goal is clear and the need is growing urgent. As the EU ambassador told the Guardian’s Patrick Wintour, the ball is in our court. Brussels, he said , is “ready to engage”, once Britain decides what it wants.
Let’s decide, but proceed with extreme caution. Would you risk the next general election by putting this into Labour’s manifesto, certain to become the right’s battle-flag? Yes, when a strong pro-EU campaign makes it winnable. But there should be no referendum until public opinion is so solid that it would be a mere rubber-stamping of the overwhelming public will.

title: After the ITV exposé, see Reform’s fixation with ‘hate preachers’ as the stinking hypocrisy it really is | Owen Jones
description: Far-right extremism and rhetoric is coming from activists and unvetted councillors, but party leaders who peddle fear and rage can’t escape blame Who are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists? As the head of MI5 warns that anti-migrant haters are increasingly considering terrorist attacks, it is surely a question we must ask. After all, the role of hate preachers in Islamist terrorism has long been debated. After the London Bridge Islamist terrorist attack in 2017, Nigel Farage demanded that Sadiq Khan – “as the first Muslim mayor of London” – declare that he would do all he could “to work with the Muslim community to drive out the extremist preachers from our mosques” and to fight radicalisation in schools and prisons. More recently, he suggested that Muslim parents in the United Arab Emirates feared sending their children to study in British universities “given the risk of radicalisation here”. His colleague Suella Braverman agrees. “There should be zero tolerance for hate preachers in mosques or radicalising imams in prisons,” she says. Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West, is out now. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply. Continue reading...
content:
Far-right extremism and rhetoric is coming from activists and unvetted councillors, but party leaders who peddle fear and rage can’t escape blame
W ho are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists? As the head of MI5 warns that anti-migrant haters are increasingly considering terrorist attacks, it is surely a question we must ask. After all, the role of hate preachers in Islamist terrorism has long been debated.
After the London Bridge Islamist terrorist attack in 2017, Nigel Farage demanded that Sadiq Khan – “as the first Muslim mayor of London” – declare that he would do all he could “to work with the Muslim community to drive out the extremist preachers from our mosques” and to fight radicalisation in schools and prisons. More recently, he suggested that Muslim parents in the United Arab Emirates feared sending their children to study in British universities “given the risk of radicalisation here”. His colleague Suella Braverman agrees. “There should be zero tolerance for hate preachers in mosques or radicalising imams in prisons,” she says.
And what of Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s self-styled shadow chancellor, who warns of “terrorist influencers and radicalising inmates” in prisons and demands “complete zero tolerance on hate preachers”?
Yet on the very day of MI5’s warning, Jenrick declared that Royal Marines would be deployed to turn back migrants in the Channel – and that “if they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so”. Here was one of Britain’s most prominent politicians injecting violence into our already deeply toxic debate about immigration.
Farage sought to backtrack on Jenrick’s behalf, claiming force “would be used only if soldiers were fired at” and insisting that Jenrick had been “utterly misconstrued”. This made little sense: the Home Office said last year that it had no record of firearms being brought in via small boats over the previous seven years.
Not that long ago, there was supposed to be a strict demarcation between the mainstream right and extremists. No longer. Consider the ITV investigation , screened last night, that exposed Reform councillors describing Asian families as “parasites” and Black children as “animals”. Another spoke of training young men to round up migrants “street by street, house by house”. One spoke of holding asylum seekers in “concentration camps” . Another Reform figure spoke of criminals facing “Sunday morning rose garden executions” . Some of these individuals have since stood down. But while the leaders of Reform have not yet plunged to such extreme depths, what effect might their own words have on impressionable people?
Consider that last week, Jenrick appeared on the YouTube channel of former GB News presenter Dan Wootton, a supporter of both Tommy Robinson and the anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, the latter of whom he calls “a British hero”.
Take the anti-migrant protests outside hotels housing asylum seekers. Last August, Jenrick turned up to such a demonstration in Epping, Essex, where far-right activists were also present, praising the “peaceful, patriotic protesters”. A month earlier, following clashes which left eight police officers injured, Braverman insisted the protests had been “largely … peaceful”. Farage, meanwhile, warned that Britain was close to “civil disobedience on a vast scale” and said he understood the anger in Epping: “You bet your life I do.”
Asked about Thomas’s group, Patriot Platform, Jenrick sympathised with masked protesters, arguing that, without a face covering, “you can lose your job, you can be cancelled”. When he was pushed on whether he would accept Robinson supporters into Reform, Jenrick’s response was telling. “Ultimately [it’s] not my call who comes into the party, that’s for Nigel and others in the party to determine,” he said . “But look, I want to build as broad a coalition as possible of people who share my values, who want us to fix this country.” How to square this with Jenrick’s denunciation of Islamist hate preachers?
In the recent past, Reform politicians – Farage , Jenrick and Braverman among them – have described migrants arriving in small boats as an “invasion”. It is the language of war: a nation under siege, an enemy to be repelled. It is hardly a leap for fearful people to conclude that those who resort to violence are not really dangerous extremists, but patriots defending their country.
We can hardly forget that Farage called for “pure, cold rage” in response to alleged police failings over the murder of Henry Nowak. Hours later, violence erupted on the streets of Southampton. He increasingly embraces the language of white resentment, claiming that “anti-whiteness is institutionalised into every aspect of public life”, calling diversity policies a form of “social cleansing” and warning of white Britons becoming a minority by the end of the century. Such rhetoric echoes the “great replacement” conspiracy theory, which argues that white people are being deliberately displaced by mass immigration.
Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, meanwhile, describes Conservative and Labour politicians as “traitors to their country”, warning – without elaboration – that a “reckoning is coming”.
None of these statements constitute a direct incitement to violence. But taken together, they can conjure up a terrifying picture in impressionable minds: a nation and a people under attack, its own political leaders conspiring in its destruction and time running out to save it.
This can’t be divorced from rightwing media outlets echoing and amplifying such rhetoric. We’ve already had the far-right uprising of August 2024, when racist mobs assaulted people of colour in the streets, attacked mosques and migrant-owned businesses, and tried to burn down hotels housing asylum seekers. We’ve had far-right terrorist attacks, such as the neo-Nazi attempted murder of an Eritrean man in 2024, the firebombing of an immigration centre in Dover in 2022, the attack on the Finsbury Park mosque in 2017 and the murder of Jo Cox a year earlier.
None made a dent on the national discourse. It has only become cruder, more toxic and more inflammatory. So, with all we know, time to ask again. Who are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists?
Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West, is out now. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

title: Britain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t work | Polly Toynbee
description: The current system is unable to quench the public thirst for locking people up – and certainly doesn’t ensure proper care once they are released Public services need more investment across the board. Every day, another wretched story. Look at the Institute for Government’s (IFG) Public Services Performance Tracker for a plain assessment of A&E corridor care, councils struggling to meet the demands of social care and the Send system, the courts backlog, GP caseloads or families lost in temporary accommodation. A chancellor approaching a budget is besieged by need. It’s easy for us journalists to pick out shock stories and claim each one is an absolute priority, but how should a chancellor choose? Today it’s the probation officers, whose conference in Newcastle is launching a ballot for industrial action. Their caseloads overflowed long ago, but now thousands of prisoners released early – 2,000 this month – have been thrust upon them. The responsibility is overwhelming, with officers blamed for crimes their clients commit. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist The headline on this article was amended on 19 October 2026 to reflect the fact that the reports it mentions refer to the prison system of England and Wales, rather than Britain as a whole. Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate prison systems. Continue reading...
content:
The current system is unable to quench the public thirst for locking people up – and certainly doesn’t ensure proper care once they are released
P ublic services need more investment across the board. Every day, another wretched story. Look at the Institute for Government’s (IFG) Public Services Performance Tracker for a plain assessment of A&E corridor care, councils struggling to meet the demands of social care and the Send system, the courts backlog, GP caseloads or families lost in temporary accommodation. A chancellor approaching a budget is besieged by need. It’s easy for us journalists to pick out shock stories and claim each one is an absolute priority, but how should a chancellor choose?
Today it’s the probation officers, whose conference in Newcastle is launching a ballot for industrial action. Their caseloads overflowed long ago, but now thousands of prisoners released early – 2,000 this month – have been thrust upon them. The responsibility is overwhelming, with officers blamed for crimes their clients commit.
The probation story is told in scores of reports: the National Audit Office found the service running on half the staff needed to cover released prisoners. It also reported failures in electronic tagging , echoed by the IFG reporting only 55% of tags were fitted in time . Napo, the probation officers’ union, blames the problems on awarding contracts to the lowest bidders at prices that mean the job isn’t done properly.
The number of offenders charged with serious further offences while on probation has increased, with the public accounts committee blaming staff shortages. Vacancies leave probation services 25%-30% below target levels . The government is training another 1,300, but that’s not enough, says Napo, considering the high dropout rate once recruits discover the abuse, threats and stress of the work, alongside the fact that the most common cause of staff sickness is mental ill health .
The sheer impossibility of their caseloads caused the government to abandon any attempt to say what their caseload should be, so the “workload measurement tool” was abruptly ditched in September just before the October raft of new prisoner releases. There is no point in stating an official workload standard that can’t be met.
Eleven hostels and seven halfway houses, places that help probation officers supervise released prisoners, have just closed for repairs and because of a lack of staff . Drug addiction and mental health problems untreated in prisons, coupled with cuts to education, training and rehabilitation, make prisoners even less prepared for release.
The probation system was broken by a disastrous privatisation when Chris Grayling (who banned the sending of books to prisoners ) split it apart into 21 private companies, with the workforce organisationally divided in two. Private companies only handled offenders judged low to medium risk, while the most serious offenders remained under the control of the state. Companies under-invested, experienced staff left, and none of the innovation promised was delivered. After this ideological privatisation was abandoned in 2021, the probation service never recovered.
The lord chancellor is set to address the probation officer’s conference. “But please,” says Napo chair Ben Cockburn, “no bullshit. Don’t tell us how well we do an exceptionally difficult job. We know that.”. Napo rejected a 5% pay offer on the grounds it falls far behind equivalent offers to workers in local government, police and social work. Under planned industrial action, Cockburn says probation officers will work to contract and refuse unpaid overtime. That, he says, will cause collapse.
What probation officers need immediately is reduced workloads, pruned to the riskiest cases, leaving less serious cases unallocated. “Put the service into special measures,” Cockburn says. He also wants the courts to stop piling on more cases until there are enough staff to cope. “We are firefighting from one emergency to another,” he says – or called away to someone in a police cell, or to a paedophile found dating a woman with a child, or a domestic violence case.
Cutting workloads for probation officers is only a short-term solution, one that avoids the real question. Why is there an ever-rising prison population, despite the sustained, multi-decade fall in crime rates?
“We are addicted to prison,” Cockburn says. In his view, probation works when officers have time for long-term working relationships with offenders. “It’s the best job in the world,” he says, recalling the journey of one prisoner who had committed a terrible crime as a young man. “I saw him in prison, knew him for 15 years, with time for therapeutic work.” But, these days, that’s so rare. “Someone now might see eight different officers, retelling their story over and over, creating no trust.”
Why build more prison cells? An inspection of a brand new private prison, HMP Millsike in East Yorkshire, found it unsafe due to a lack of experienced staff, as well as chronic staff shortages. Even at its opening, it was “chaotic” , lacking basic processes for important things like locking doors and counting prisoners. Hundreds of cells are still empty because of a lack of officers.
Public pressure to lock up more prisoners and supervise them when released will never be matched by a willingness to pay the taxes needed to cover the cost of attracting people to work in this sector. That’s the truth Cockburn wants politicians to be brave enough to tell. This country is not alone in wrongly believing crime is ever-rising when all across Europe it has fallen for decades . But no one believes it. A news and drama fixation on horrific crime stirs primal fears that belie these facts. Politicians everywhere score points with a frightened public by clamouring for more punishment.
When I last visited a hard-pressed prison, I asked the governor what she most needed, and was astonished when she said she wouldn’t invest here, but “right at the start, before the damage is done, in early years”.
Asking where every pound spent does most good is the kind of mega-question budgets don’t answer. But a brave chancellor would cut prison funding down to housing only the most dangerous, and spending better on what works, such as well-funded probation officers.
Keep telling this fact: all crime is horrible – sex crime is at last reported more often – but the overall drop in neighbourhood-level crime in England and Wales has been about 80% since its peak in 1995. Meanwhile, prison numbers have risen significantly . In his upcoming speech at the probation officer’s conference, it would take unprecedented political bravery for the lord chancellor to dare end the pretence that prison works.
The headline on this article was amended on 19 October 2026 to reflect the fact that the reports it mentions refer to the prison system of England and Wales, rather than Britain as a whole. Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate prison systems.

title: We are reclaiming real life after getting rid of Instagram | Letters
description: Readers on taking back their lives – and brains – from social media algorithms I couldn’t agree more with Georgina McNamara ( The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life, 19 October ). Reading about the sheer relief of stepping away from Instagram resonates deeply with my own feelings over the last few years. There is an incredible quiet joy in reclaiming a truly private life, entirely free from the pressure to document, curate and perform our daily routines for an invisible audience. Continue reading...
content:
Readers on taking back their lives – and brains – from social media algorithms
I couldn’t agree more with Georgina McNamara ( The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life, 19 October ).
Reading about the sheer relief of stepping away from Instagram resonates deeply with my own feelings over the last few years. There is an incredible quiet joy in reclaiming a truly private life, entirely free from the pressure to document, curate and perform our daily routines for an invisible audience.
This shift immediately brings to mind Jaron Lanier’s compelling points in his 2018 book Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now . Lanier warned us that these platforms aren’t just neutral tools; they are behaviour-modification engines designed to hijack our attention and slowly erode our autonomy.
His argument that social media algorithms inherently reward outrage, tribalism and comparison to drive engagement feels truer today than ever. By participating, we unwittingly allow algorithms to alter our moods and warp our sense of reality, stripping away the simple contentment of just being.
In my own life, stepping back from that digital noise has been incredibly grounding. I’ve found that my most meaningful moments – whether I’m spending a few focused hours woodworking in my workshop, sitting down to figure out a new arrangement on the guitar, or just out walking the spaniels – are vastly richer when they exist solely in the present, without the impulse to photograph or share them.
Getting back to tangible, analogue realities has felt like taking a long, deep breath. Even organising a recent social evening at the local pub in Hipperholme reminded me how much more genuine our connections are when we are physically present, sharing a pint and a conversation rather than a screen.
A private life is not a smaller life; it is an unmediated one. As Lanier suggests, opting out isn’t just rejecting technology; it’s reclaiming our free will and our peace of mind. Guy Edmondson Hipperholme, West Yorkshire
Georgina McNamara’s article really resonated with me. I haven’t deleted Instagram, but I check it very infrequently now. While I didn’t post all that often, the compulsion to document experiences and turn moments into posts or stories, rather than being in the moment, was always there – and with it, the eventual anxiety about whether anyone had liked what I had posted.
I also realised that comparing my day-to-day life with others’ carefully curated highlights was making me unhappy: an endless stream of holiday photos made me keenly aware of how long it would be until I would next have a break, while other fitness instructors posting photos taken from strategic angles made me worry that I wasn’t as flexible as them in comparison, or that my technique was poor.
After reading some books and articles on cutting back on smartphone use, I took a number of steps to reduce my phone use, and used the One Sec app to trigger a breathing exercise whenever I opened Instagram.
It made me realise how often I checked Instagram as a reflex, and that I could be devoting this time to other activities that I found more fulfilling. The few occasions that I do check it these days, I find it a bit overwhelming.
I find that my mind is a lot quieter now and that I pay more attention to what is around me, appreciating what I see as a moment that doesn’t have to become a post or a story. And if I take a photograph of something, it’s because I like it, not because I’m concerned about whether someone else will. Laura Dobie Glasgow
I deleted my Instagram account after getting pregnant with my second child. At first, I muted it; when I returned, the algorithm had decided that, with all the information it had gathered on me, I must have taken a break due to baby loss. It bombarded me with images and messages about baby loss, until it realised this wasn’t the reason and started to fill my algorithm with “two under two” narratives. The juxtaposition was stark and insensitive. It felt awful.
I realised I didn’t want this platform having information about not just me but my family as well, and I hated that by feeding into it (with likes on obsessed-over images and funny captions), I was allowing it to dictate some of my parenting decisions through algorithms and advertised content. Since leaving it, my motherhood journey has been much happier, simpler and in my control. I completely agree that it’s the change that works! Stefanie Withey-Jones London
I enjoyed Georgina McNamara’s account of leaving Instagram, particularly her observations about the time spent checking reactions and seeking validation.
However, there is an important distinction to be made between sharing our lives and seeking approval for them. I use social media to share photographs with friends and family because I enjoy letting people I know see what I have been doing. For me, that is about connection, not validation.
There is another pleasure too that is rarely mentioned: unexpected reminders of photographs posted one, five or even 10 years ago. A holiday, a familiar face or an ordinary moment that I had forgotten suddenly reappears, bringing back the feelings associated with it.
It’s not just the memories themselves I treasure, but the unexpected joy of being reminded of them, often when they’re furthest from my mind.
The problem, perhaps, is not posting our lives online, but allowing other people’s reactions to determine how much we value those experiences. Nicky Atkinson Shoreham-by-Sea, West Sussex
I lasted only six weeks on Instagram. Unlike Georgina McNamara, I came to the party late, in my 60s. Almost immediately, I resented the way that posts were pushed into my feed. In no time at all I was spending hours watching posts of horse sanctuaries in the US and feeling depressed and resentful at whole sections of society. So I deleted my account – no small feat in itself, as the process is determined to keep you there.
Afterwards, I felt relief at getting back hours of my own brain time, but for months, I would think: “I could just pop on and look at x, y, z.” I’m glad that I’m off, and scared at how quickly I became addicted. Now when I look around I see that I am the only person on the bus or train who is not looking at a screen but at the outside world, and thinking for myself. Dr Hilary Redden Aberdeen
The one change that worked? I deleted all social media from my phone and instead installed the Guardian app with a subscription to news and well-curated content. No more time-wasting, bottomless doomscrolling for me. Do it, kids! Cecilia Scott Woking, Surrey

Paul Mitchell recalls snooker champion Alex Higgins tearfully celebrating his win with his young daughter

Paul Mitchell Belfast

title: Crowded nest? How parents and their adult kids can live together in peace
description: With record numbers of adult children living at home with their parents, how can this arrangement work for everyone? Set ground rules from the off, respect each other’s privacy, and don’t revert to type, say the experts Whether they are fresh out of university and looking for a job, have recently been made redundant, are saving to buy a home or newly divorced, it’s becoming increasingly common for adult children to live at home with their parents. According to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), 35% of men and 22% of women aged between 20 and 34 were living with their parents in 2025. I speak from experience: my younger sister lived at home with my mother for two years while she did her PhD, and I moved home for almost three years after becoming a single mother postpartum. content:
With record numbers of adult children living at home with their parents, how can this arrangement work for everyone? Set ground rules from the off, respect each other’s privacy, and don’t revert to type, say the experts
W hether they are fresh out of university and looking for a job, have recently been made redundant, are saving to buy a home or newly divorced, it’s becoming increasingly common for adult children to live at home with their parents. According to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), 35% of men and 22% of women aged between 20 and 34 were living with their parents in 2025.
I speak from experience: my younger sister lived at home with my mother for two years while she did her PhD, and I moved home for almost three years after becoming a single mother postpartum. In both of our situations, it would have been good to have some practical advice to make it work, with tensions sometimes running high and arguments inevitable.
If parents and their adult children are going to coexist successfully, honest communication is essential from the outset. How long do children expect to stay? Will they contribute financially? Will they do any housework? Are guests allowed? Difficulties will arise if you aren’t clear about these boundaries from the off.
“You won’t be able to anticipate every point of tension in advance, but you might want to discuss typical frictions like noise and overnight guests,” says Anita Cleare , a parenting expert and author of How to Get Your Teenager Out of Their Bedroom . “Parents should aim for a balance between making adult children feel welcome and maintaining their own mental and financial wellbeing.”
Parenting expert Sue Atkins , whose grownup children have both lived with her for periods, recommends writing down everything you want to say first, so that you can stay focused – and, crucially, to pick your moment. “It’s all about your tone of voice and your attitude,” she says. “If you do it when you’re angry or frustrated, that’s the wrong time. I always say: ‘Strike when the iron is cold.’”
Both parents and adult children can fall into the trap of reverting to childhood dynamics. Parents find children annoying and untidy, and feel free to comment on their lifestyles (“You’re not going out in that?” “What time will you be back?” “That’s a waste of money,” etc), while children regress into teenagers, expecting Mum and Dad to do the laundry, housework and cooking.
“The biggest trap adult children fall into when returning to live with parents is to demand the rights of adulthood while still expecting to enjoy the privileges of a child,” says Cleare. “For example, expecting their parents to provide household comforts while insisting on sticking to their own separate daily schedule. Vice versa: now that your child is an adult, you don’t have the right to know where they are at all times, what they are doing or what they are thinking. Voicing your opinion on how they should be going about life differently will send you right back into parent-teenager dynamics.”
Instead, conceive of it as more of a housemate situation. “It can help to think of your adult child as a friend who is staying with you, rather than as your child,” says Cleare. “Parent-child dynamics have a power imbalance – parents tell children what to do (and children assert their power by not cooperating). Friendships tend to be more equal. Aim for discussion and collaboration rather than rigid rule-setting. Set your parameters, but then treat your adult child as a problem-solver by inviting their views and ideas.” For the adult child, they can also consider what being a good housemate means: chiefly, pulling their weight by doing chores without being asked.
If an adult child is moving back home after living away for some time – perhaps even in their own home – then they will have accumulated a lot of “stuff”.
Kate Edmondson, the founder of Home Edited , a professional organisation service, recommends first agreeing on where belongings will be stored and how much space is realistically available. “Ask them to go through their belongings and make decisions about what is genuinely worth storing,” she says. “Make sure they know what they have and where it is. Clearly labelled, categorised boxes make belongings much easier for them to access without having to pull apart an entire storage area. If you’re storing a larger volume, encourage them to keep their own simple inventory on their phone.”
While you might not agree on politics, what to watch on TV, or other hot topics, see this as an opportunity to spend quality time together.
“Build some new family traditions,” suggests Cleare. “Families are glued together by spending time together – whether that’s eating or cooking, watching TV or sport, or shopping. So try to find new ways to spend time doing things you all enjoy.”
There’s no reason you can’t view the experience as a positive one. “I think you have to see living together as a springboard, not a destination,” advises Atkins. “When you come through the other side, you may realise you gained a lot from it and are closer.”
Whether you are already in a relationship, or looking to date, there’s no denying that living with your parents puts a dampener on romance. Elinor Harvey, a psychotherapist at The Relationship Therapy Practice, says communication and boundaries are key.
“A family might agree that Friday night is the adult child’s night to go out and date, and that they can bring someone home afterwards,” she says. “Another family might be more flexible, but simply want advance notice if someone is coming back. There doesn’t have to be one set of ground rules that works for everyone. What matters is agreeing to the rules early and making sure everyone understands them.” It’s also important to remember that if the adult child’s parents are in a couple – whether with each other or a new partner – then they will want time alone for their relationship too.
If parents don’t want their child to bring anybody back, and that’s a deal-breaker for the adult child, the arrangement is simply not going to work.
If there’s one thing that adult children and parents are likely to fall out over, it’s privacy. After all, many have been living away from home – whether at university halls, in shared housing, or with an ex-partner – and won’t appreciate parents walking into their room without knocking. The same goes for asking about their whereabouts or who they are seeing – though it is always considerate for adult children to check in and offer a little reassurance, rather than turning up half-cut at 3am after a night out and waking everyone up.
“They’re adults now,” says Atkins. “You don’t just walk into their bedroom because they’re your children. You have to respect their personal space and remember that they may have been independent for years.”
As tempting as it is to try to swoop in and save adult children living at home in less than ideal circumstances, Cleare advises against playing the hero. “When adults move back home, it is often because something isn’t going right in their lives,” she says. “They might have lost their job or relationship, or be struggling to cope in some way. The temptation is for parents to see these issues as something their adult child needs our advice on and to overstep the mark.”
Instead, parents can try to boost their child’s confidence by taking an interest without meddling. “Be mindful not to rescue them – empower them,” says Atkins. “If it’s budgeting and money, you might say: ‘Can I give you a hand? This is how we do it.’ You’re helping them develop the skills to move forward rather than taking over. Don’t judge them or patronise them. Ask open-ended questions: ‘What can we do to support you?’ And use ‘I’ statements. Say: ‘I’m feeling … ’ rather than: ‘You always … ’”
When an adult child moves back in with a parent, it can cause undue pressure on household budgets, particularly for single parents. And as more than 38% of people who married in England and Wales in 1995 had divorced by 2015, according to the ONS , this is clearly an issue for many families.
Beverley Sayers, a mediator who works with the Family Mediation Council, has encountered parents who are struggling to support an adult child after a separation or divorce. “There’s an unrealistic idea that you don’t have to continue paying for children once they reach 18,” she says. “I often advise the young person to have a conversation with the parent they don’t live with and ask: ‘Can I have some funds to help with this situation so I can contribute to the household?’”

It literally arrived this morning – a medieval instrument called a psaltery. It’s a bit like a dulcimer or zither, a kind of V shape you hold and pluck. That’s the sort of thing that I buy.
Some of it online, but we’re lucky where we are in west London, with a great greengrocer, butcher, fishmonger, a little Korean store and a Thai shop called Sriracha supermarket, where I can get spices from.
A Gibson Les Paul guitar to my godson. It was brilliant seeing someone really immerse themselves in playing it. I think giving a musical instrument is a great present generally.
That was a guitar as well, from my wife as a birthday present. I was doing a standup residency in the West End, and there was a bit in the show where I would pick up an electric guitar and start playing it. Unbeknown to me, in the interval, she colluded with the crew to switch the standard guitar for a rare vintage white Gibson. I went [to pick it up] in the second half and thought: “Wait, what’s this?” Then I noticed there was a bow tied around the neck. I was completely overwhelmed; it was a brilliant way to have it delivered. It almost completely derailed the gig.
A music store called Thomann. They sell all kinds of interesting instruments, but also accessories, guitar leads and all the extra stuff you need when you’re playing or writing music at home.
I buy a lot of outdoor stuff – boots, camping equipment – from Cotswold Outdoor in Kensington. I recently bought a LifeStraw, which apparently you can stick in almost any water source and it will filter it into drinking water. I haven’t tested it in rivers, but it might be a life-saver in an apocalypse.
A Chemex coffee system, a simple glass flask and filters. It makes the best-tasting coffee.
It was a semi-computerised accordion. It weighed an absolute ton, so it was impractical to play on stage because I could only hold it for very short periods, and it was festooned with cables and things trailing from it. In the end, it sat in the cupboard and gathered dust until I bought a much lighter one.
Big hiking socks – I do a lot of walking, so you work your way through them.
The last lot I bought was from TK Maxx – a bargain.
£20: I would probably buy a multipack of socks. For £200, art materials for my dad because he paints a lot and brushes, oils, acrylics and paper are not cheap – we go to Chiswick Arts & Crafts.
I don’t have one, but I buy secondhand furniture from eBay.
A Turkish saz, a long-necked lute. I love those instruments that, on the face of it, seem pretty simple and limited, but then you get to know them, and you realise you can play all kinds of things.
Day to day, I love a decent coffee. It’s become something of a ritual.
I bought a little Krups coffee grinder a few years ago, which I use with the Chemex.
I drink more coffee, so probably teabags. I get a big multipack from the Co-op or cash-and-carry, because we have lots of people coming around all the time; you can’t be too precious about the teabags in our house.
