content:
They claim to fix fine lines, blemishes, and redness – but which stand up to scrutiny? After consulting dermatologists and putting them to the test, we have crowned a brand new number one
The best anti-ageing creams, serums and treatments
L ED face masks are booming in popularity – despite being one of the most expensive at-home beauty products to hit the market. They claim to either reduce the appearance of fine lines, stop spots or calm redness, with some even combining different types of light to enhance the benefits.
However, it’s wise to be sceptical about new treatments that are costly and non-invasive, and to do your research before you buy. With this in mind, I interviewed doctors and dermatologists to find out whether these light therapy devices work.
They’re not a miracle cure for deep-set wrinkles, but experts say the best light therapy masks can promote collagen production, improve elasticity and help smooth skin with sustained use. And while it may seem like a new technology, research from the 1990s shows the efficacy of light therapy in wound healing, acne treatment and skin rejuvenation.
Red and infrared light are safe to use on all skin types, but be warned that blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones.
I’ve tested some of the most popular devices on the market – including infrared masks – to narrow down my favourite LED face masks for treating a range of skin concerns.
Best LED mask overall: CurrentBody Multi Light Therapy LED mask
Best budget LED face mask: Silk’n LED face mask 100
Best LED mask for fine lines and blemishes: Shark CryoGlow
Best LED device for acne-prone skin: Lustre Solo
Best LED mask for quick treatments: Dr Dennis Gross SpectraLite FaceWare Pro
Best LED mask for travel: Silk’n LED face mask Pro
I’ve been reviewing health and beauty tech for the past four years. During this time I’ve witnessed many beauty fads come and go. Naturally tight-fisted and a sceptic, I was initially struck by the cost of these masks. How on earth can an elaborate LED light strip set you back more than £300?
But after testing multiple light therapy masks, I’ve come to understand the technology behind them – and, sadly, you won’t be able to engineer your own light therapy system with a costume mask and a set of LED string lights.
I don’t have many fine lines or wrinkles to test on, but I can comment on how blue light treatment affects acne because I’ve suffered from it since I was a teenager – despite my mum’s assurances that it would clear up after puberty. The experts I spoke to agreed on the efficacy of red and infrared light for anti-ageing.
Light therapy masks are fantastic additions to a skincare routine, helping to smooth, firm and reduce blemishes. Since I started using one more than a year ago, my skin is calmer, less prone to redness, and has a more even tone.
However, LED masks can be expensive, and if you’re not disciplined enough to use one regularly, you won’t see results. Before you splash up to £500, keep in mind that light therapy masks are most effective when paired with a good skincare routine. It’s crucial to make sure skin is properly cleansed before treatment and protected from sun damage afterwards.
If you don’t already have a skincare routine nailed down, don’t buy a light therapy mask just yet. Consider starting out using a gentle cleanser and moisturiser, with an SPF for daytime. You could also incorporate targeted skincare serums, such as retinol and vitamin C , to help firm and brighten the skin without the need for an expensive light therapy mask.
Since LED treatments take a while to show visible results, it’s difficult to test multiple light therapy masks at once (at least, without spending a few years testing them), so I enlisted the help of dermatologists who were familiar with light therapy treatments long before they were commercially available.
I spoke to Dr Barbara Kubicka, an expert in aesthetic medicine; Dr Derrick Phillips, a consultant dermatologist and spokesperson for the British Skin Foundation; and aesthetic doctor Dr Priya Verma, an authority on the science of skin ageing.
I asked these experts to identify which features of a light therapy mask – such as bulb quality and quantity, light wavelength and treatment time – matter the most, to inform my choices. They also outlined the suitability of light therapy for different skin types and its associated risks.
Armed with their advice, I tested the fit, comfort levels and usability of 15 of the most popular light therapy masks and other targeted LED devices. Getting hands on with the masks allowed me to pinpoint any of the key features the experts recommended, as well as features I found helpful as a consumer.
I’ve been using a light therapy mask regularly for the past 18 months, so I can identify a good mask from a bad one. My tests also included monitoring results after four nightly sessions, with the obvious caveat that only very minimal changes could be observed after such a short-term treatment. I then tested my favourite masks over several months, too, helping me to verify any unique treatment claims – as well as giving me plenty of opportunities to scare my boyfriend by sneaking up on him wearing each one.
Only masks that use the brightest, flicker-free bulbs, fit comfortably and are easy to use made the final cut. After testing, I returned the masks sourced for this article to the manufacturers. Where that wasn’t possible, I cleaned the masks and donated them to the Redbridge Reach Out service, a charity that supports anyone experiencing domestic abuse.
I ’ve tested many more LED devices than can fit on this page, and while I don’t usually draw attention to bad products, I came across so many poorly designed models that I feel it necessary to shed light on the LED masks that overpromise and underdeliver.
First, we have the Revolution Pro Miracle LED face mask , which costs just £59.99 at full price. Believe me, I wanted this mask to be a winner, but its solid plastic structure, with no eye shielding or padding, made it so wildly uncomfortable to wear that it was an almost instant write-off. The straps are another problem; they come together around the bottom part of your head, causing the mask to constantly fall. It also seems built for very small faces, so it constantly slipped down my face, pinching my nose and making it difficult to breathe properly – even if I used it without the straps and lay flat during treatment. Throw in fewer LED bulbs than average and dim lights, and this mask is impossible to recommend.
A high price tag doesn’t guarantee how good the mask is either, as evidenced by the £719 Foreo FAQ 202 LED mask . Its lightweight and comfort level, along with an array of treatment options via its app-based controls, meant it impressed initially. However, its silicone design felt incredibly flimsy, and after a week of use, it had already started peeling away from the central battery pack.
This might be forgivable if Foreo offered a full warranty and repair service. There’s a two-year warranty covering defects and faulty workmanship, but this does not cover “cosmetic deterioration caused by fair wear and tear, or damage caused by accident, misuse or neglect”. To access accidental damage coverage, you have to pay Foreo’s £9.99/month subscription. Even if you’re happy to risk it, you still have to shell out £4.99/month to access the mask’s full suite of preset treatments. Add to this the scale of advertising you’re bombarded with in the app – some of it unskippable. When you consider its price, this brazen money-grabbing leaves a very bad taste.
Through testing this family of devices, I had also been hoping to find an undereye brightening LED patch to usurp the Peep Club wand, which requires constant movement across the eye area. I had hoped that the Lustre GoGlow brightening and de-puffing patches would fit the bill. They come in a handy headphone-like charging case and have a clever wireless design. However, when positioned under the eyes as advertised, the light was incredibly bright, which made it tricky to see. The sticky pads, although small, were uncomfortable to remove, and my skin was left feeling irritated for a day afterwards. The search for the perfect undereye LED patch continues …
“LED (light-emitting diode) therapy is a non-invasive treatment that uses specific wavelengths of light to stimulate various cellular processes in the skin,” says aesthetic medicine expert Kubicka. “Depending on the colour or wavelength, LED light can target inflammation, promote collagen production, accelerate healing and even kill bacteria.”
Light therapy is a great addition to your skincare routine – for me, it’s helped reduce breakouts, improve healing and reduce the appearance of my acne scars. LED face masks are quick, gentle and non-invasive, and suitable for most skin types (although as mentioned above, blue light can worsen hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones, according to the experts I spoke with). The masks are effective and foolproof to use, and the daily treatments also force you to take a little time for yourself – perfect for a morning pick-me-up or an evening wind-down.
“Red-light therapy can reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles through a process called photobiomodulation,” says consultant dermatologist Phillips. “It energises mitochondria, which are the batteries of the cells, powering the production of collagen and elastin by fibroblasts, the factories of the skin.”
Elastin and collagen are “the building blocks of firm, youthful skin”, says Kubicka. Stimulating the production of these molecules can “improve skin density, elasticity and overall smoothness” as long as you complete treatments regularly.
I have yet to develop fine lines or wrinkles, but I’m keen to avoid them by using red-light therapy for “preventive ageing”. However, “most of the clinical evidence focuses on treating visible signs of ageing or repairing damaged skin, rather than long-term prevention in younger skin,” as aesthetic doctor Verma explains.
Still, Verma reassured me my efforts wouldn’t be in vain. “Using LED light consistently and appropriately may help support overall skin health […] especially when combined with sun protection and a good skincare routine.”
For more, read do you really need an LED face mask ?
Several colours are available, with each wavelength claiming to target a different skin concern. These colours correlate to the visible light spectrum, and each can have a different effect on the skin.
Red light has a wavelength of between 630 and 700nm and is the most widely known form of light therapy, loved for its non-invasive potential anti-ageing benefits. Near-infrared light above 700nm “penetrates the skin more deeply to support tissue repair and reduce inflammation”, according to Kubicka. Blue light therapy (415nm), on the other hand, has been proven to target acne-causing bacteria, leading to a reduction in breakouts over time. Kubicka also says blue light can help regulate oil production – another common problem for those with acne.
The effects of some types of light on the skin are better researched than others. Near-infrared , red light and blue light are backed by scientific studies that identify the biological processes that each type of light triggers in the body.
Meanwhile, research into green and yellow light is more limited. One study questions the efficacy of yellow light therapy and claims that a previous study may have been influenced by the placebo effect. Similarly, a study on green light therapy suggests that more research is needed to provide a solid recommendation for use as an anti-ageing treatment.
The “how” is simple: always use light therapy masks on freshly washed, dry skin, before applying serums and creams. This will give the light the most direct access to the skin.
Despite what some instruction manuals advise, don’t jump into daily treatments straight away – you may end up with slightly irritated skin. Start by introducing treatments two to three times a week, and monitoring the impact on your skin. If you don’t notice any sensitivity, you can incorporate more treatments, if permitted by the manufacturer’s guidelines.
Once your skin is used to the treatment, “home devices should be used three to five times a week, for 10-20 minutes a session,” says Phillips. Don’t expect instant results, though. If you’re hoping to treat breakouts, you should “see a reduction in redness and the frequency of acne breakouts within two to four weeks”. Those using red light for anti-ageing benefits will need to wait a little longer: “It typically takes six to eight weeks to see visible changes.”
“LED light therapy is generally very safe when used correctly,” says Verma. This is because, unlike laser hair removal, it only uses low-level, non-thermal light. “The most common side effects are mild and temporary, such as slight redness, dryness or irritation.”
“People with known photosensitive disorders or taking medications that make them more sensitive to light (eg certain antibiotics) should consult their doctor,” says Phillips. He also warns that those with darker skin tones should exercise caution when using blue light, since “some blue wavelengths have been associated with hyperpigmentation”. The Lustre Solo patches recommended above offer exclusively blue light, but the other masks on this roundup have blue-light-free settings if you do find that it causes sensitivity.
There are hundreds of light therapy masks available at different prices, but the quality varies wildly. You may see results from a budget-friendly mask, such as the £119 Silk’n mask , but spending more will generally get you a larger quantity of bulbs that offer a greater range of wavelengths. You’re also more likely to get a mask with a better fit and coverage.
The best mask for you will depend on your skin concerns and budget. Those hoping to invest in a mask with anti-acne properties will be able to spend less, since blue light is more widely available, but if you’re looking for the best anti-ageing deep near-infrared light therapy, you will need to part with more cash.
High-end red light therapy masks can cost up to £500; if you spend that much, just make sure you use it regularly, or you won’t see results.
Cleaning instructions for LED masks will differ slightly from brand to brand, based on the different materials used. As a general rule, you want to steer clear of using chemical or alcohol-based cleansers since these can damage a mask’s delicate silicone and padded components. Always check the instructions for your specific mask before jumping into cleaning.
The usual best practice is to use a non-abrasive cloth, such as microfibre , dampened with water to wipe down your mask after every use. Try not to use too much water and never submerge the mask, as doing so will damage the electrical components. Always make sure your mask is unplugged and switched off before cleaning, and wait for the mask to dry completely before storing, charging or switching it on.

Sarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, and can sniff out a fad from a game changer (that doesn’t mean she’s disciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)

content:
Christmas is getting closer, and this year’s calendars are already on sale. We tested the biggest releases to find the ones worth buying, including cruelty-free picks
Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
C hristmas might feel like an age away, but the festive season has already begun for fans of beauty Advent calendars. Most of this year’s calendars are now on sale or available to preorder, and many of the most popular could sell out long before Whamageddon claims its first victim.
So, much as it pains me to say it, now might be a good time to buy one. Below, you’ll find my favourites, from bargain beauty Advent calendars under £50 to three-figure luxuries. I’ve tested 20 to find calendars packed with cult-favourite products suitable for a whole spectrum of skin types and preferences. I also looked at the packaging and broad appeal of each calendar to help minimise waste.
If nothing tickles your fancy just yet, don’t panic. More calendars get released in the lead-up to December, and I’ll keep updating this article as they drop.
I test beauty products for a living, which means I’ve worked my way through more skincare, makeup, hair care, perfume and nail care products than I dare to count. Working in this industry has shown me the very best and absolute worst of what’s out there. I know how to spot a good product when I see one, even if it’s tucked away in the corner of a beauty Advent calendar.
I also have a certification in cosmetic science, so I know how to identify products suited to different skin and hair types. I’ve struggled with sensitive skin for years, so I keep a close eye out for ingredients that might irritate. The calendars below are all full of products suitable for most people to minimise waste.
Heaps of Advent calendars are released every year. To help find the best, I longlisted 30 before testing the 20 that offer the best range of products and value for money. I’ll continue to update this page with new options in the run-up to Christmas .
Testing them lets me assess the quality of each calendar and its contents, as well as the packaging it arrives in. If the calendar itself is recyclable but arrives shrouded in plastic bags and polystyrene, it’s a non-starter. I also check that each calendar is made from packaging that is recyclable at home or genuinely reusable.
It’s impossible to test every product inside every calendar – I only have one face, after all – but I judge each calendar based on the range, quality and usefulness of the products inside. Broad appeal is key to avoiding wasted products, and luckily, this is how most Advent calendars are designed.
I look for a good mix of skincare, makeup, body care, hair care and nail care, unless a calendar is specifically dedicated to a certain product type. I also check how easy it is to incorporate each product into a typical routine. Too many harsh treatments or bold makeup shades would be less appealing than a calendar with a more approachable lineup.
This helps me assess how broadly usable the contents are and how much is likely to go to waste. While beauty Advent calendars can’t be considered eco-friendly, it’s important to minimise waste where possible.
Each year I end up with far more products than one woman can reasonably use. This year, I donated the contents of the calendars to the Redbridge Reach Out service, which supports anyone experiencing domestic abuse.
For more, read Sali Hughes’s guide to the best anti-ageing creams, serums and treatments
This depends entirely on your beauty routine and how much you enjoy experimenting with new products. If you like high-end, luxury beauty, then beauty Advent calendars can be a great way to get expensive products bundled together for a lower cost. It’s also an opportunity to try luxe brands without committing to buying full-size products.
The first risk is you end up spending a lot of money on products you won’t use. To avoid this, think about the elements of your beauty routine that you like to switch up. If there’s anything you’re staunchly loyal to, for example your skincare, think twice before buying a skincare Advent calendar.
There’s also the environmental impact of any products you don’t use, so it’s worth considering either donating them unopened to charity or giving them to any other beauty lovers in your circle.
There is a huge range of beauty Advent calendars available, from below £20 to over £500. That chasmic difference in cost makes a big difference to the products inside. Entry-level calendars offer mostly mini-size products from high-street beauty brands. Some more affordable calendars also offer 12 doors, for the 12 days of Christmas, rather than 24.
With the £20-£60 bracket covered by budget brands, the mid-range contenders sit somewhere between £61 and £150. These calendars tend to offer more full-size products than lower-priced calendars from mid-range brands. Unless you’re a big fan of one particular brand, the best way to try lots of new skincare, makeup and hair care is to choose a calendar from a beauty retailer such as Anthropologie, which offers curated calendars with a selection of brands. Most beauty fans will find something suitable in this price bracket.
Spend between £151 and £250, and you can expect to find calendars filled with mainly full-size products, whether from mid-range or luxury brands or higher-end beauty retailers such as Cult Beauty and Space NK .
If you’re hoping for full-fat luxury at full-fat prices, you can spend over £250 and grab a calendar from super-high-end retailers such as Selfridges and Liberty , or premium brands such as Diptyque . These tend to contain higher-value products, with some brands claiming a total value of more than £1,000. Just be sure to triple-check the contents all appeal to you before spending this much.
Unlike edible Advent calendars, which can be packed up and filled with the same chocolates year after year, beauty Advent calendars take months of planning and coordination. As you’re opening the 2026 calendar, most brands will already be deep in planning what to include in 2027.
By opening waiting lists early, brands are able to better plan the number of calendars they need to make, and ensure they have enough time to send them out before 1 December.

description: From luxury Simba and Otty mattresses to brilliant budget buys, here’s what we recommend – and how to know if you’ve found a good deal • The best mattresses for back pain • The best mattresses for side sleepers • The best mattress toppers, tested A good mattress improves your sleep, say mattress makers – and they would, wouldn’t they? content:
From luxury Simba and Otty mattresses to brilliant budget buys, here’s what we recommend – and how to know if you’ve found a good deal
The best mattresses for back pain The best mattresses for side sleepers The best mattress toppers, tested
A good mattress improves your sleep, say mattress makers – and they would, wouldn’t they? But they’re right. The older I get, the more I know it. When I was 20, I could sleep anywhere: a friend’s floor, a sofa – even a phone box one night. These days, I won’t get a single one of 40 winks if I’m not lying on a decent mattress. Comfy but firm, cosy but breathable, and with lots of cool spots for my feet.
Today’s best mattresses promise all this and more. Pocket springs are still around, but they face stiff – well, medium-firm – competition from hybrid mattresses that combine springs and memory foam for the ideal balance of comfort and support.
Many of today’s trendiest brands don’t have showrooms, so you can’t usually try before you buy. Instead, these bed-in-a-box models come with generous trial periods – but you’re still buying blind. That’s why I’ve tested them myself to help you separate the dream buys from the nightmares.
I, along with a panel of family members, tested 18 bestselling bed-in-a-box mattresses – including four in this latest update. The full rundown now includes six pocket-sprung models, three all-foam models and several bed-in-a-box hybrids (which combine springs with layers of memory foam), covering various degrees of firmness, features and price. Here’s how we got on with our top picks, including the one my dad gave up on and the one my niece didn’t want to give back.
I’ve spent three decades testing products, from mattress toppers to heated clothes airers , so I’m professionally sceptical of manufacturers’ claims to magically improve our lives by buying their stuff. I also have a solid background in napping, insomnia and swearing at alarm clocks, so I welcomed the chance to sleep on the job.
First, I needed some sleepers. I wanted a broad range of feedback from people of varying sizes who sleep in various positions. I asked my dad (85), my niece (24), my sister and our husbands to join my mattress panel. We each spent at least a fortnight (and sometimes months) sleeping on an allocated mattress.
Before we divvied them up, my panel assembled to offer their first impressions. I asked them to sit, bounce and lie down on every test sample, alone and together. This enabled us to compare the mattresses side by side. I collected scores out of 10 for everyone’s assessment of firmness and other factors such as breathability, motion isolation and overall comfort, then worked out our average score for each mattress.
We then began the sleeping tests. To quantify sleep quality, I used the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index , which uses a questionnaire to assess factors such as how long it takes to nod off. I then added questions such as whether they experienced back pain or woke up in the night. Some of us also used our smartwatches to gather sleep-tracking stats.
I tested other factors on my own. I used dumbbells to measure how far each mattress sank under various weights, while an infrared thermometer and heat pad revealed how fast they could cool under a warm body. A glass of water on the surface gave an idea of how well a mattress would absorb the movement of a restless partner (motion isolation).
Environmental credentials were also a consideration. I gathered what information I could about each model’s materials, manufacturing processes, and its potential for recycling. I also checked verified reviews from paying customers and excluded any mattresses that received significant negative feedback for delivery and customer service.
The mattresses sourced for this article are being donated to two charities: Southampton-based poverty support group Scratch and Hampshire-based survivors’ advocacy organisation Stop Domestic Abuse .
To dive deeper in to my testing process, read how I tested mattresses for comfort, cost and sustainability
If you’re an average-size person who sleeps mostly on your side and occasionally on your back, then your ideal mattress is medium-firm. The upper layers of such mattresses – the Otty Original Hybrid and Simba Hybrid Pro , for example – are soft enough for immediate comfort and pressure relief, while the lower layers make you feel supported.
This balance of cushioning and support is important for spine alignment, as explained in our guide to the best mattress for back pain . “Medium-firm mattresses consistently come out on top in research into back pain,” says osteopath and sports coach Ian Greaves of Southampton Physio . “Comfort matters as much as support, and medium-firm beds strike a better balance than firm or soft types.”
However, there’s every chance you’re not average, so you may need something firmer or softer. Depending on your size, sleeping position, and propensity to aches and pains, you may feel more comfortable (and do your back more long-term good) on a mattress with a lower or higher firmness score than a standard medium-firm.
Generally speaking, the bigger you are, the firmer your mattress should be. A robust, relatively unyielding mattress such as the Sealy Elevate Emin Firm or Origin Hybrid Pro will give your back the extra support it needs.
Conversely, if you’re small, like me, you need cushioning for your pressure points (hips, knees, shoulders). This is especially important if you experience joint pain, which may be relieved by the soft, cradling sensation of a memory foam mattress such as the Tempur Pro Plus SmartCool or the Eve Wunderflip Premium Hybrid .
Side sleepers need cushioning, too, for the same reason. When you lie on your side on a too-firm mattress, your hips don’t sit low enough, and your lower spine curves up: a recipe for back pain. People who sleep on their back or front, though, may find that a firmer sleeping surface is just right.
The bed-in-a-box industry has upgraded mattress delivery for the era of apartment living, with companies such as Otty, Eve and Simba vacuum-shrinking their models for transport.
As a house-dweller who goes through mattresses as frequently as a normal person goes through tubes of toothpaste, I can confirm that getting a mattress up a flight of stairs is significantly easier when it’s shrunk into a box.
Not all mattresses can be delivered this way, however. The more conventionally constructed mattresses I’ve reviewed, including the Woolroom Standen Wool and the Millbrook Wool Luxury 4000, were delivered full-size. Mattresses that contain foam seem more likely to be delivered in bed-in-a-box format, but this isn’t always the case: the all-foam Tempur Pro Plus SmartCool was delivered full-size.
Vacuum-shrinking a mattress is essentially the same idea as squeezing winter duvets into vacuum storage bags – but on a bigger scale. It’s convenient, but it leaves you with a huge amount of plastic packaging that’s unlikely to be picked up with your recycling collection, which means a trip to the tip – unless you repurpose it as a dust sheet.
On the upside, vacuum-packing allows a single lorry to carry many more mattresses than traditional deliveries. Bed-in-a-box brands also tend not to have showrooms, so they offer lengthy home trials to help you decide whether your new mattress is truly right for you. My experience of this process has been fairly smooth, with Otty and Emma collecting mattresses and issuing refunds quickly.
Note that no delivery team took away my old mattress. Most will offer a recycling service for a fee of about £50, but this has to be organised at the time of ordering your new mattress. It also seems expensive given that my local council’s recycling team collects mattresses for £20.
Ultimately, when it comes to environmental considerations, the worst mattresses are those that are thrown out the fastest. Bed-in-a-box warranties typically cover 10 years, which is excellent. Just don’t void your guarantee by, for example, standing on the mattress or using an electric blanket (as foam can soften and even crack under too much heat).
It’s Black Friday all year round in mattress world. Bed-in-a-box companies seem to regard “sale” prices as the rule rather than the exception, and Simba , Emma and Dormeo have all been sanctioned by the Advertising Standards Authority for misleading marketing tactics.
There are genuine deals to be found, however. Search PriceRunner to view the price history of a model, while the free AnyTracker app is less quick but gives richer results, including alerts when your desired mattress meets your desired price.
Here are a few stats to help you sleep at night: the average mattress contains between 1.5 million and 10 million dust mites, depending on whom you believe. These mites feast on dead skin cells, of which you shed up to 40,000 a minute, and thrive on moisture, of which you leak about a pint a night. “Up to 10% of the weight of an old pillow could be made up of dust mite faeces,” say researchers from UCL . Sweet dreams.
To keep your mattress in as good a shape as possible, start with a good mattress protector and clean sheets, which you should change about once a week. A zip-off washable cover, as featured on many of our best mattresses, including the Otty Original Hybrid and Simba Hybrid Pro , is another key line of defence against grossness. Just make sure all covers are fully dry after washing, because any remaining moisture will lead to mould – and you really don’t want to share your bed with mould spores .
While all the covers are removed, get out the vacuum cleaner . Vacuum every surface of the mattress, including the bottom if it’s one-sided, and into any nooks and crannies. Now let it air for a while, with an open window if the weather allows. You could also hang your duvet out to air for a few hours. Just remember that while fresh air can help dissipate smells, it also lets in allergens, so it’s worth vacuuming your mattress again before you put all the freshly cleaned elements back together.
If there are no stains, a vacuum will be fine. For spills or accidents, blot up as much liquid as possible to stop moisture from soaking in. Fresh stains can be dabbed with a little cold water and washing-up liquid – avoid rubbing, as this can spread the stain. Upholstery cleaner is safe in small doses, but don’t use carpet cleaner, as it may damage your mattress. For odours, sprinkle baking soda over the surface, leave for several hours, then vacuum thoroughly.
For more, read our guide on how to clean your mattress
The Sleep Foundation and Bed Advice UK suggest that your mattress will need replacing every seven to eight years. “After that time, your mattress will have had around four bathtubs of sweat applied to it,” says Hannah Shore, head of sleep science at Mattress Online . “Dust, dead skin cells and other matter will also collect in the mattress, making it unhygienic.”
That may be true, but most of the mattresses we reviewed come with 10-year warranties, and two – the Woolroom Standen Wool and Origin Hybrid Pro – even stretch to 15 years. So what’s the deal? Surely it’s more environmentally and financially responsible to hang on to a mattress until it’s falling apart? Maybe, but studies suggest it’s not good for your health or your sleep quality.
The cocktail of bacterial goo that leaches into a mattress under the weight of at least one human every night eats away at its springs, fillings and foam. The result is a lumpy surface that loses its comfort and support. Support is key when choosing a mattress – without it, you’ll suffer all manner of maladies, including back pain, aching shoulders and poor sleep. One US study tracked a cohort of men and women with minor sleep-related pain, and whose beds were an average of nine-and-a-half years old. Switching to new, medium-firm mattresses resulted in “significant improvements” in their back pain and sleep quality.
The seven-year switch is not an exact science, though. Mattress durability varies widely, and some mattresses made using high-quality materials such as natural latex can have a lifespan of up to 20 years, according to UK mattress company Latex Sense. Rather than assume your mattress will need replacing in seven years, look out for some tell-tale signs.
Sagging and failing springs are the most obvious. Others are that you wake up sneezing, feel your partner moving in bed more than you used to, and feel the bed giving way when you sit on the side. “One of the best signs is that you sleep better elsewhere,” says Shore. “If you sleep significantly better in a hotel bed, it’s probably a sign that your mattress at home needs replacing.”
A few provisos, though. One thing I’ve learned from sleep-testing more than a dozen mattresses over the years is that a new bed can mess up your sleep for the first couple of nights, especially if you’re used to a much softer surface. Your body needs to adjust. Bear in mind that even the firmest foam layers soften over the first few months, so give your new bed a chance – and take advantage of free trials if you don’t get on with it.
The road to environmental hell is paved with old mattresses. According to the latest fly-tipping action plan from Keep Britain Tidy , we throw away more than 5m mattresses annually, with only a quarter being recycled. The Furniture Recycling Group is even more gloomy, claiming that 8.5m mattresses go to landfill every year.
Most councils run a bulky waste collection service, but it’ll cost you (about £20 a mattress outside London; perhaps more than double that in London), and you may have to book well in advance. What’s more, your council-collected mattress will probably end up in landfill.
There are ways to keep your old mattress out of the waste mountain, though. Here are a few to try.
Have it recycled by a mattress brand Most bed brands will collect and recycle your old mattress, although this service is often only available if you buy a new mattress from them. It gets pricey, too – a problem that the Keep Britain Tidy report blames on a widespread “lack of specialist equipment”.
Here’s a quick guide to prices at the time of writing, with links for more details:
We’d like to see more companies following the lead of Panda , which doesn’t charge a penny to recycle your old mattress if you buy a new one from it (otherwise, it costs £50).
If you can squeeze your old mattress into (or on top of) your car, it’s worth checking the Recycle Now website to find a local recycling facility that’ll take it. You could also investigate Dunelm’s mattress and furniture recycling scheme , which works with Clearabee to recycle mattresses, although collection prices are significantly higher than those from mattress brands.
Give it away If – and this is really important – your mattress is in good condition, you could give it to charity. Dunelm’s mattress and furniture recycling scheme also works with the British Heart Foundation to collect unsoiled mattresses and other furniture for free. Look for local organisations, too: my test mattresses go to hardship charity Scratch in Southampton. You may also be able to find a taker via platforms such as Freecycle and Buy Nothing .
Find a waste-to-energy skip Waste-to-energy skips convert rubbish, including mattresses, into electricity or heat through incineration. You may have to pay a fair amount to hire one, but if you’re having a household clearout or renovation, it’d be well worth finding.

Jane Hoskyn is a consumer journalist and WFH pioneer with three decades of experience in rearranging bookshelves and “testing” coffee machines while deadlines loom. Her work has made her a low-key expert in all manner of consumables, from sports watches to solar panels. She would always rather be in the woods

title: ‘No influencers’: the hotels, restaurants and beauty spots restricting photoshoots
description: Backlash against content creators includes restricted hours for filming and even outright bans Stand in any vaguely photogenic spot these days on holiday and the chances are you will come across people posing with raised phones and even ring lights. Some may be influencers with huge audiences on social media, others just overkeen Instagram users. With hotels and beauty spots now so overrun, however, bans on photography are coming into place. The five-star Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes, known for its glamorous clientele, views of the Côte d’Azur and a stunning infinity pool, has brought in rules against photoshoots: no longer allowed without prior permission. Continue reading...
content:
Backlash against content creators includes restricted hours for filming and even outright bans
S tand in any vaguely photogenic spot these days on holiday and the chances are you will come across people posing with raised phones and even ring lights. Some may be influencers with huge audiences on social media, others just overkeen Instagram users. With hotels and beauty spots now so overrun, however, bans on photography are coming into place.
The five-star Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes, known for its glamorous clientele, views of the Côte d’Azur and a stunning infinity pool, has brought in rules against photoshoots: no longer allowed without prior permission.
According to reports , this has been prompted by people booking lunch reservations and bringing bags of clothing and jewellery. Instead of sitting down to eat, they have used their time at the hotel for photoshoots of themselves in different outfits, creating images to post to their social media accounts.
Less glamorous spots are also clamping down. The Hollies, a Cheshire farm shop which has become a popular content stop thanks to the Love Island star Molly-Mae Hague posting images from there, has banned photography and filming between 10am and 4pm.
Meanwhile Jeremy King, the London restaurateur behind places such as Simpson’s in the Strand and the Park , wrote an article in the Evening Standard earlier this year titled: “I’m fed up with influencers over-running my restaurant – enough is enough.”
In the US, a shop on Nantucket, an island off Cape Cod, Massachusetts, went viral earlier this year for a sign reading “no influencers”, while the town of Pomfret in Vermont has banned influencers taking pictures in front of foliage in autumn. In Fujikawaguchiko in Japan , a screen has been put up near a convenience store to stop people taking pictures there in front of Mount Fuji.
Part of the argument from venues is that these photoshoots jeopardise privacy and discretion, especially as expected at expensive hotels. Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc’s manager, Sophie Volant, told Travel Weekly : “As much as [guests] appreciate having people in the restaurants and in the bars, they also want their summer home to remain private. We had to think about a solution.”
Anna Fedou, the chief marketing officer at the Beaumier hotel group, says it sometimes works with influencers to capture content to promote its luxury hotels, which include Les Roches Rouges near Marseille, loved for its photogenic pool. The group does not have specific rules around photography, Fedou says, but stays mindful of its primary purpose.
“We’re in the business of hospitality, not running photo studios,” she says. “People travel from all over the world to experience the atmosphere, sense of space and feeling that make a hotel unique. It’s our responsibility to protect that.”
Rules around photography at hotels and restaurants mirror a trend away from capturing the moment and towards being in it. Alex Goat, the founder of the youth culture agency Livity, compares these rules to clubs asking visitors to put stickers over their phones’ cameras. “They want to signify that they’re here for people who love music. There’s something potentially similar [here],” she says. “It’s ‘I’m here because I want to enjoy the space’ rather than ‘I’m here to document something to other people’.”
Part of the disapproval towards influencers is a common misconception is that they are paid well for such content. Sometimes, as with Beaumier hotels, influencers will produce posts in exchange for a free room, but the idea is that brands will want to make deals with influencers due to their association with glamorous locations. “The majority are creating most of their content for their audiences for free,” explains Nicole Ocran, an influencer who set up the Creator Union to represent those in the industry. “They create content in the hope of courting brands and seeing who will bite.”
There has been previous outrage around influencers’ behaviour, as in 2021 when Love Island stars travelled to Dubai during lockdown, for example. And if there is an underlying snobbery to a luxury hotel instigating anti-photoshoot policies, there may be sexism, too. “Influencer culture has always been vilified in popular culture,” says Sophie Bishop, the author of Influencer Creep . “It’s a very feminised form of media, that’s bound up in promotional culture.”
Ocran agrees. “Most people have a particular stereotype in mind,” she says. “That isn’t to say that influencers and content creators can’t overstep or be insufferable when getting their shots and filming in public.”
Fedou believes that the key is to walk a balance that engages with social media content while keeping a restful experience at hotels. “Influencers will generally choose quieter moments for shooting content, to capture the space without disturbing others,” she says. “Les Roches Rouges has a relaxed atmosphere, but guest experience always comes first.”
While the backlash might be aimed at influencers with lots of followers, over 5.4 billion people use social media every day .
Ocran hopes that rules around photography might promote a more balanced attitude to social media in general. “[It’s] pushing back against the idea that not every space is meant for public consumption, and not every experience should be turned into content,” she says. “And as a creator, that’s quite a healthy message to send to us all.”

title: How to dress a tech oligarch: The Social Reckoning’s costume designer on Zuckerberg’s style evolution
description: Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters The first Aaron Sorkin Facebook movie, 2010’s The Social Network, helped cement the early aughts image of Mark Zuckerberg rebelling against corporate norms in rumpled hoodies and T-shirts. content:
Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters
The first Aaron Sorkin Facebook movie, 2010’s The Social Network, helped cement the early aughts image of Mark Zuckerberg rebelling against corporate norms in rumpled hoodies and T-shirts.
The follow-up, The Social Reckoning, is carbon-dated from 2019 to 2021. This is “post-hoodie”, as the movie’s costume designer, Susan Lyall, describes it, “post-thumbing his nose” to formality. It is also peak robot. Zuckerberg’s reserved wardrobe of suits or interchangeable long-sleeved shirts echo his chilling composure throughout, even as fury simmers under the surface.
The costume was based on deep research by Lyall and also by actor Jeremy Strong who, she says, is “very into costume”. Having worked together before, on the Sorkin movies Molly’s Game and The Trial of the Chicago 7, they would text a lot during the preparation process.
“He reaches out before I even get to reach out to him. It’s my third movie with him, so I’m pretty used to it. He’s very proactive. He’s one of my favourite actors because of that. He would know exactly where [Zuckerberg] wore what. He wanted the exact Nike shoe – the footwear was very important to him – and the exact Brunello Cucinelli T-shirt and sweater, and so on,” she says.
Strong has become notorious for method acting, and method dressing, too, seems to be part of his process. “It’s sort of the first step in the performance. That and the haircut,” says Lyall.
The conversations went deep. “It’s actually kind of nerdy, you know, to sit there and talk about the color of the shoelaces. There aren’t that many people who want to talk about that. I always joke with him, if the acting thing doesn’t work out, you can have a position in my department!” she says.
Lyall found those Nikes – to be specific, the 2018 Nike Flyknit trainer in black anthracite – on Grailed. For the sweaters, it was Strong, she says, who worked out how to reach the eye-wateringly expensive Italian luxury brand Brunello Cucinelli, in order to buy specific pieces, “because we don’t want the latest. We want stuff from five or six years ago, and they were very helpful at procuring it. And that was because of him. He was really proactive.”
Lyall has spent a lot of hours thinking about how tech oligarchs dress. Not only Zuckerberg but Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and others too, who were partial inspiration for another of her recent credits, the 2025 Jesse Armstrong movie Mountainhead about four devilish plutocrats.
They, too, wore a lot of Brunello Cucinelli. That brand sells cashmere cardigans for $16,500 and ribbed sweaters for $4,600. Amusingly, it currently has the Immanuel Kant quote “beauty is the symbol of the morally good” in prime place on its website homepage.
In Lyall’s view, Brunello Cucinelli is a “safety net for people like Mark Zuckerberg. If they’re not sure about what they’re wearing, if they pay a lot for it, they feel a little better about it. You know, if this little sweater is $2,000, it must be good. It’s kind of a security blanket, or just an affirmation of your own success. You’re going to be OK if you’re wearing this tasteful thing.”
The Zuckerberg of The Social Reckoning had moved on from the earlier antifashion stance that prompted him to declare, in 2014, that he was “not a cool person”, and only wore grey T-shirts because he wanted to make “as few decisions as possible … I feel like I’m not doing my job if I spend any of my energy on things that are silly or frivolous.”
By the period captured in the movie, says Lyall, “I believe Zuckerberg was trying to be relatable, but also starting to understand Silicon Valley’s obsession with taste and the cost of things.” He was also more buff than he had been. In her interpretation, he seemed to be thinking: “My fit physique looks very nice in this clingy but expensive sweater. And ‘if you know, you know’ – I think there’s a bit of that. But I also think, he’s nouveau riche without being gaudy. It’s not without taste.”
Since then, Zuckerberg’s outward presentation has graduated to outright peacocking.
For the tech billionaires, in general, says Lyall: “I think something happened. I think they have discovered a new way to flex. And it’s not quiet luxury. It’s loud.”
For Zuckerberg specifically – whose makeover came suddenly with ostentatious gold chains, Loewe shorts and Alexander McQueen suits embellished with dragonflies in around 2024 – it could not feel much more strategic.
Dabbling with fashion allows Zuckerberg to look like a different guy from the one we have seen so many times sweating in a suit in front of Congress. It also provides a distraction from the reality of his products and work, giving him something soft and harmless to talk about.
Zuckerberg has even used the classic fiction writer’s trick of embedding backstory within his jewellery. In 2024, when he started wearing a large, gold pendant necklace over his T-shirt, he claimed it wasn’t just because he wanted to look like a hip-hop star, as the internet understandably concluded.
When finally asked about his pendant in an interview (“oh this?” he said, with an approximation of spontaneity) he explained that it was embossed with a Jewish prayer he sings to his kids every night at bedtime, thus reminding the public of his humanity – his faith, and the importance he places on being there for his children.
This year, as Meta has recruited fashion stars such as Kylie Jenner to market its smart glasses, he has spent yet more time courting fashion, attending Prada shows and the Met Gala.
Last month, he gave the New York Times an interview purely about clothing, claiming that he buys almost all of his wardrobe on Instagram himself – which sounds extremely decision-requiring and time-consuming for a person of his workload.
Many of the labels he mentioned were more contemporary, less oligarch-coded, among them Mike Amiri, a purveyor of $400-ish T-shirts, with whom he has worked on bespoke items including the “Building is my love language” he wore to present Muse at a Facebook conference. Online, too, when he buys something of the $200-ish, rather than $2000-ish price tag, he may even pop into the comments, when complimented on that item, to draw users’ attention towards it (“It’s @johnelliottco – I’m loving their stuff recently”).
Just as the new personal AI assistant Muse has been fashioned to look utterly adorable – surely such a cute fluffy Labubu-like creature could never spark an apocalypse! – Zuckerberg’s own continuing makeover appears conceived to make him a more friendly and, ideally, more human.
In fashion, though, it’s not as simple as ticking the box to confirm you are not a robot. When he explained his interest in style to the New York Times , for example, he said, “I think the company is an instantiation of my values” and claimed he wanted to “be intentional about how I program that”.
A turn of phrase that suggests that, under his vibrant new clothing, the cashmere-clad machine depicted in Sorkin’s movie may not have been properly deactivated.

title: Jackson Boxer’s vegetarian recipe for brown butter pumpkin soup
description: The base of this easy roast pumpkin soup is rich, nutty, Halloween heaven – you can go wild with the garnishes A lot of my early life in professional kitchens was spent making vegetable purees, which I find rather tiresome, not least because they can often lapse into baby food: creamy, bland and flattened by a cosseting blanket of dairy. With a judicious and considered approach, however, they can also be incredibly vivid, explosive and concentrated expressions of the very essence of the vegetable in question. I love this seasonal (not to mention Halloween-appropriate) soup for its simplicity of approach – essentially, you just roast a beautiful pumpkin with caramelised butter – and the remarkable complexity of its result. Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House , Vesper and Dove , all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London Continue reading...
content:
The base of this easy roast pumpkin soup is rich, nutty, Halloween heaven – you can go wild with the garnishes
A lot of my early life in professional kitchens was spent making vegetable purees, which I find rather tiresome, not least because they can often lapse into baby food: creamy, bland and flattened by a cosseting blanket of dairy. With a judicious and considered approach, however, they can also be incredibly vivid, explosive and concentrated expressions of the very essence of the vegetable in question. I love this seasonal (not to mention Halloween-appropriate) soup for its simplicity of approach – essentially, you just roast a beautiful pumpkin with caramelised butter – and the remarkable complexity of its result.
When browning butter, always bear in mind that it has a high water content, and that the initial seething cook is done to evaporate this – until all the water has cooked out, you won’t get the butter high enough above 100C for the milk solids and sugars to caramelise. That’s why browning butter happens two ways, like Hemingway’s bankruptcy – gradually, then suddenly. And pay close attention, or it will burn and you’ll have to start again.
250ml vegetable bouillon (homemade, ideally; see my recipe last week ) 1 delica pumpkin (800g), cut in half, deseeded and peeled (I don’t bother peeling it, but cooked pumpkin skin is an acquired taste) 250g butter 10g flaky sea salt (about 2 tsp) Sherry vinegar , to taste
To finish Creme fraiche Chilli oil Toasted pumpkin seeds Ground black pepper A squeeze of lemon
Heat the oven to 195C (175C fan)/385F/gas 5½. Pour the bouillon into a roasting tray large enough to hold both pumpkin halves, then put them cut side up in the tray.
In a frying pan, simmer the butter on a high heat until it stops foaming, then turn down the heat and cook until it’s rich, brown and nutty. Immediately pour the scalding butter evenly into the pumpkin halves, then lay a sheet of greaseproof paper over the top of the pumpkins and tightly cover the whole tray in foil. Bake for 45 minutes, until the tip of a sharp knife meets no resistance and comes out clean.
Cut the cooked pumpkin into chunks, put these and the bouillon from the tray in a food processor and blitz to a smooth puree. Add the salt and vinegar, then taste and adjust the seasoning. If the puree is too tight, add more vegetable broth just to loosen – it will depend on the water content of the pumpkin and how airtight the seal was on the foil tray.
Transfer the mix to a large saucepan and reheat gently without boiling. Check and adjust for seasoning and acidity, then ladle into bowls – I serve this soup topped with creme fraiche, chilli oil, toasted pumpkin seeds, black pepper and a squeeze of lemon; other nice garnishes might include toasted croutons, fried sage leaves, chilli and garlic butter, and salsa verde, any and all of which would be very fine additions.
Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House , Vesper and Dove , all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London

content:
A lively tequila sour shaken up with an injection of tamarind and star anise
Rich tamarind chutney gives this vibrant tequila sour a sweet-sour depth that pairs brilliantly with crisp apple juice.
45ml blanco tequila – we use Olmeca Altos Plata 25ml apple juice 25ml fresh lime juice 20ml sugar syrup ½ tsp tamarind chutney – any decent brand will do 1 egg white , or 3 drops cocktail foamer 1 star anise , to garnish
Put everything bar the star anise in a shaker and shake vigorously without ice to set the egg white and build a smooth foam. Add a good handful of ice, shake again until well chilled, then strain into a tumbler filled with fresh ice. Garnish with a star anise.

title: Something crunchy, something sharp, something sweet: Sam and Sam Clark’s autumn meze recipes
description: Tabbouleh, apple, beetroot, minty yoghurt, oyster mushrooms … a riot of colour and autumnal flavours with every forkful Autumn is a time of year when our meze plate becomes more comforting and generous, with earthy beetroot, sweet squash and woody mushrooms. The cooking is simple, but the flavours and textures are layered and kept lively with sharp vinegars and citrus. Each one of today’s dishes is considered individually, but also in the context of the plate as a whole, and how each element relates to the others to achieve balance and harmony. And, of course, always serve with pitta or flatbread to scoop up every last morsel. Served together, this meze selection should feed four generously. Continue reading...
content:
Tabbouleh, apple, beetroot, minty yoghurt, oyster mushrooms … a riot of colour and autumnal flavours with every forkful
A utumn is a time of year when our meze plate becomes more comforting and generous, with earthy beetroot, sweet squash and woody mushrooms. The cooking is simple, but the flavours and textures are layered and kept lively with sharp vinegars and citrus. Each one of today’s dishes is considered individually, but also in the context of the plate as a whole, and how each element relates to the others to achieve balance and harmony. And, of course, always serve with pitta or flatbread to scoop up every last morsel.
Served together, this meze selection should feed four generously.
Raw beetroot has an earthy sweetness and plenty of crunch that works particularly well with the acidic sharpness of a granny smith. Mint lifts and toasted walnuts bring richness. A good, sweet-sharp vinegar and olive oil are really all the dressing this needs. Serve at room temperature.
1½ tbsp sweet aged red-wine vinegar (we use Forum’s cabernet sauvignon vinegar ), or good red-wine vinegar sweetened with a pinch of sugar 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil Salt and black pepper 250g raw beetroot , peeled and coarsely grated 1 large granny smith apple , unpeeled, quartered, cored and cut into very thin matchsticks 2 tbsp thinly shredded mint leaves 50g lightly toasted walnuts , sliced
In a small bowl, whisk the vinegar and olive oil, season to taste and set aside.
Mix the beetroot and apple in a large bowl with half the shredded mint and half the walnuts, pour on the dressing and toss gently. Check for seasoning, then serve with the remaining mint and walnuts scattered on top.
We tend to think of tabbouleh as a summer dish (cucumbers, tomatoes, lemon, parsley, mint), as something fresh and light for when the weather is warm. But the idea of tabbouleh lends itself well to the changing seasons. What matters most is the balance of herbs, grain, fruit or vegetables, something crunchy and something sharp, and all those things can change to suit whatever’s around. This is a celebration of autumn in one dish. Serve at room temperature.
40g medium bulgur wheat 100g white muscat or sultana grapes , halved 2 fresh figs , peeled and cut into thin wedges 75g lightly toasted almonds , roughly chopped 2 spring onions , cut into thin rounds 1 small bunch flat-leaf parsley , finely shredded 1 small bunch mint , finely shredded Salt and black pepper
For the dressing ½ small garlic clove , crushed to a paste with a little salt 1 pinch ground cinnamon 1 tbsp orange juice 1 tbsp lemon juice 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
Put the bulgur in a bowl, add cold water just to cover and leave to sit for 10-15 minutes. Meanwhile, put all the dressing ingredients in a jar, season and shake well.
When the bulgur has absorbed all the water and is soft (if it’s still al dente, stir in another tablespoon of water and leave for a couple of minutes), gently rub it between your palms to fluff it up. Put all the remaining ingredients in a large bowl, then pour the dressing on top. Add the bulgur to the bowl, toss to mix, check the seasoning and serve.
The seared and nicely caramelised mushrooms give this dish a great complexity of flavour and texture. Serve at room temperature.
8 large oyster mushrooms , thicker ends of stalks cut off and discarded 3 tbsp olive oil Salt and black pepper 2 garlic cloves , peeled and finely chopped 2 tbsp roughly chopped dill
Put a large, heavy-based frying pan on a medium to high heat. Toss the mushrooms with a tablespoon of the oil and season. When the pan is hot, lay in the mushrooms gill side down and leave to fry until caramelised and a rich golden colour. Turn over, cook for 30 seconds, then spread out on a platter. Evenly scatter over the raw garlic and dill, drizzle over the remaining two tablespoons of oil, check the seasoning and serve.
A classic Moro recipe that’s also great with salted anchovies. Serve at room temperature.
1 large aubergine , cut into 1½cm-thick rounds Salt and black pepper 100ml olive oil , plus 1 tbsp extra for frying the garlic 100ml sunflower oil 1 large garlic clove, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks 4 tsp sweet aged red-wine vinegar (we use Forum’s cabernet sauvignon vinegar ), or a good aged red-wine vinegar sweetened with a pinch of sugar 1 heaped tbsp finely shredded mint , plus extra to serve 1 long green chilli , cut in half lengthways, deseeded and finely chopped 4 dssp Greek yoghurt 1 pinch black onion seeds , to finish
Put the aubergine slices in a colander, toss with half a teaspoon of fine salt, then leave for 20 minutes to drain off any excess water and to get rid of any bitterness. Dry the slices on kitchen paper.
Heat both oils in a wide frying pan until hot but not smoking. Lay in the aubergine slices in a single layer (if need be, cook them in batches) and fry, turning as required, until deep golden brown and crisp on both sides. Transfer to a plate lined with kitchen paper to absorb any excess oil. Meanwhile, fry the garlic matchsticks in the extra tablespoon of olive oil, until golden, then drain.
Put the drained aubergine slices on a platter, sprinkle over the fried garlic, vinegar and mint, then leave to sit for five minutes.
Stir the chopped chilli into the yoghurt and season with a little salt. Spoon a small dollop of the yoghurt on top of each aubergine slice, scatter over a little extra shredded mint and the black onion seeds, season and serve.
The keys to this dish are to toast the cumin, to fry the garlic to the darkened side of golden, and to use the coriander stalks as well as the leaves. Serve warm or at room temperature.
4 tbsp olive oil 2-3 garlic cloves , peeled and finely chopped 1 rounded tsp cumin seeds , roughly ground 250g cooked small brown or puy lentils (from a tin or pouch) 1 small bunch coriander , stalks and leaves separated and roughly chopped 50g caramelised crispy onions (shop-bought or homemade) Salt and black pepper
Put three tablespoons of the oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. When it’s hot but not smoking, add the garlic and cumin, and fry until light brown. Stir in the lentils, chopped coriander stalks, half the crispy onions and enough water to loosen the mix to the consistency of a thick soup. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for five minutes, until the lentils are soft. Take off the heat, stir in the chopped coriander leaves, then season. Scatter the rest of the crispy onions on top and serve.
Kaboucha squash has an excellent sweetness and dense texture, although its knobbly skin is tougher than other squashes and therefore harder to peel. Make this dish last, because it’s the only one here that needs to be served warm.
1 small-medium kabo cha squash (about 450g), or butternut squash, peeled, deseeded and cut into 3cm chunks 3 tbsp olive oil ½ tsp ground cinnamon ½ garlic clove , crushed to a paste with a pinch of salt Salt and black pepper 4 tbsp tinned chickpeas , drained 1 tsp finely chopped red chilli ¼ tsp nigella seeds
For the tahini sauce 1 small garlic clove , peeled and crushed 1½ tbsp tahini 1 good squeeze of lemon 1½ tbsp olive oil
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Put the squash in a roasting tray, add the oil, cinnamon and garlic, season generously, then toss to coat. Spread out into an even layer, then roast for 20 minutes, until the pumpkin is soft and caramelised.
Scatter over the chickpeas and bake for another five minutes, until they’re slightly crisp.
Meanwhile, make the sauce. Mix the garlic, tahini and lemon juice in a small bowl, whisk in two and a half tablespoons of water, then whisk in the oil. Check the seasoning.
Transfer the pumpkin mix to a platter, drizzle over the sauce and finish with the chilli and nigella seeds.
Sam and Sam Clark are chefs/owners of Moro and Morito in London EC1

title: My longterm boyfriend died last year. Is it too soon to date someone new? | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
description: Only you can know when you are ready, but a year is not long to process grief, and you seem to have doubts about this man My long term boyfriend died of cancer last year. We’d been together for 16 years , since I was 21 and he was 23. I had given birth to our only child three weeks before his diagnosis. My son was just shy of 10 months old when his dad died, and he’s now turned two. I loved my late partner deeply and had planned to stay with him for ever. We were embarking on an 18-year project together, raising our son. Now I think, how can I ever be happy again ? Continue reading...
content:
Only you can know when you are ready, but a year is not long to process grief, and you seem to have doubts about this man
My long term boyfriend died of cancer last year. We’d been together for 16 years , since I was 21 and he was 23. I had given birth to our only child three weeks before his diagnosis. My son was just shy of 10 months old when his dad died, and he’s now turned two.
I loved my late partner deeply and had planned to stay with him for ever. We were embarking on an 18-year project together, raising our son. Now I think, how can I ever be happy again ?
Before he died, my partner told me to find a single dad to go out with . When I returned to work, a colleague I had considered a flirt was away – getting chemo. Now he’s in remission. He’s also a single parent. Lately, I’ve realised I have a crush on him. His life has been touched by tragedy and he knows what’s important to him. He’s very kind, like my late partner, and I think we click.
What gives me a lot of pause is that I find him to blow hot and cold. Also, because I’m a solo mum I don’t really have time for someone else. But he has recently left the company, so I wouldn’t be dating a co-worker.
I s it remarkable to meet a single dad you genuinely like? Or are there more out there than I think? Please tell me what you think I should do.
What a devastating loss you’ve experienced, and at such a tender time of motherhood. I’m so sorry.
I spoke to UKCP-registered psychotherapist Stephanie White, who wondered, given that you were with your partner almost your entire adult life, “if you have learned to trust your gut and made ‘good enough’ decisions on your own”. You seem to look outside yourself to validate what you’re doing: your partner “told you” to find a single dad to go out with. You ask me to tell you what you “should do”. Ultimately, we all need our own internal guide, and I’d like you to think about yours.
I wouldn’t want to stop you having fun – you deserve it – but you have “a lot of pause” about this new man. This could be because he has a lot going on in his life, but it could also be because something doesn’t feel right for you. Also, are you in a place to potentially take on his issues?
White said: “There seems to be something here about an expected narrative thread getting cut: you were ‘embarking on an 18-year project together’, but reality is not panning out as expected. This can lead to feeling stuck.”
She also felt there could be a “trauma bond” between you and this other man – his life has been “touched by tragedy” too – and wondered if there was “something about wanting to skip, perhaps unconsciously, the phases of the grieving process by substituting a ‘facsimile’ for your former partner”.
“But grieving is a long process,” White warned, “and one of the most important parts is accepting that the death has occurred and, in your case, that the expected narrative arc of your lives has now ended. At some level, you seem to know this new man is not ideal. You’re not a widow years out of bereavement who finds love; you’re a year in, and that’s no time at all.”
You have a young son to care for. We wondered about your support network. Lean into it, maybe look into some therapy or support groups such as Widowed and Young . Take it slowly, and put yourself and your son first. Don’t rush into a new caring role beyond this just yet. But that doesn’t mean you can’t – or shouldn’t – love and have fun again.
Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem to ask.annalisa@theguardian.com . Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject to our terms and conditions . The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is available here .

title: Blind date: ‘We overstayed our welcome – the waiters were shaking the cutlery drawer really loudly’
description: Alexandrea, 32, a lawyer, meets Pardis, 32, a doctor Continue reading...
content:
Alexandrea, 32, a lawyer, meets Pardis, 32, a doctor
What were you hoping for? A fun date and to hopefully meet the one!
First impressions? Handsome and relaxed.
What did you talk about? The sports we do. Books. Family. Friends. Our jobs. Travelling and travelling mishaps. Vermin infestations. Stocks and shares. ISAs.
Most awkward moment? We both arrived at the restaurant on time but there was a big queue which resulted in me sitting at the table alone for about 10 minutes – I got a bit nervous.
Good table manners? No faux pas so all good.
Best thing about Pardis? He is very sincere. He asked lots of questions, seemed interested in what I was saying and was a great listener. I also loved how laid-back he was – he went with the flow when I proposed the tasting menu.
Would you introduce Pardis to your friends? Of course – he’s interesting and really good company.
Describe Pardis in three words Easygoing, kind, engaging.
What do you think Pardis made of you? A ray of sunshine, akin to what everyone else thinks of me!
Did you go on somewhere? No, but we did overstay our welcome at the restaurant, to the point where the waiters were shaking the cutlery drawer really loudly.
And … did you kiss? A lady never tells … But no.
If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I would have loved it to be in Paris. Pardis in Paris!
Would you meet again? Pardis is a lovely guy but I think we’re better suited as friends.
What were you hoping for? The scene in About Time where the protagonist meets Rachel McAdams in that dark dining restaurant. (I appreciate that isn’t quite the same concept as a blind date.)
First impressions? I was a few places behind her in the queue to get in the restaurant. I could only see the back of her head but thought: nice hair, good fashion sense.
What did you talk about? There was a healthy amount of chat on the life cycle of a fly and the declining quality of mousetraps. We’ve both had minor pest issues recently – a perk of living in London.
Most awkward moment? Probably mistaking her Irish accent for a Scottish one. Not my finest hour.
Good table manners? Excellent, a picture of sophistication.
Best thing about Alexandrea? Very down to earth, clearly adventurous and a great dinner party guest.
Would you introduce Alexandrea to your friends? I wouldn’t put the poor girl through the trauma of meeting my rabble …
Describe Alexandrea in three words Adventurous, kind, intelligent.
What do you think she made of you? I think she enjoyed my chat. Either that or she’s great at acting entertained (or I’m completely oblivious).
Did you go on somewhere? No, I was on early morning uncle duty the next day, so had to call it a night.
And … did you kiss? No, a good wholesome hug.
If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I’d brush up on my accent recognition beforehand.
Marks out of 10? 8 (for a friendship connection, otherwise it would have been higher).
Would you meet again? Sure, as friends I’d be happy to.
Alexandrea and Pardis ate at Mildreds , London W1 . Fancy a blind date? Email blind.date@theguardian.com

title: This is how we do it: ‘After marriage counselling, she no longer wants the lights off and the covers on’
description: Financial, work and child-rearing pressures had killed off their sex life, but therapy gave Henry and Kelly an insight into each other’s perspective • How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously I stopped trying to initiate sex. If it passed the six-month mark, she would initiate. Like she wanted to be a dutiful wife Continue reading...
content:
Financial, work and child-rearing pressures had killed off their sex life, but therapy gave Henry and Kelly an insight into each other’s perspective
How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously
double quotation mark I stopped trying to initiate sex. If it passed the six-month mark, she would initiate. Like she wanted to be a dutiful wife
Kelly and I met in our early 20s in a gym-slash-nightclub – she was an aerobics teacher and I was a bartender. I remember spying her incredible figure from afar, through all the chrome decor and disco balls. A year after marrying, we became parents and the sexiness got squeezed by screaming children, bills and responsibilities.
During these fraught years, I would frequently initiate sex, but I was often met with “my hair is a mess” or “the dishes are not done” – and eventually, I stopped trying. If it passed the six-month mark Kelly would initiate, but I got the sense she was just playing the dutiful wife. She would want to do it with the lights off and the covers up to her chin.
When our kids left the nest, all of our tensions around child-rearing went away, but so many issues remained around how much I was spending and socialising. I suggested we try marriage counselling, and I learned that she wasn’t nagging at me to stop spending money on golf because she was being selfish; and she realised I wasn’t being selfish for wanting to spend time with friends. It helped me to see that Kelly worries about money, and her to see that I’m just desperate for a bit of me time amid the chaos of everyday life.
It was on a trip visiting family, three months into therapy, when something changed in Kelly. This time she didn’t care about having the lights off or the covers on. It was like the floodgates opened, and ever since we’ve started having sex weekly. In the past, when I would ask her what she wanted during sex, she would respond: “Nothing. I don’t have anything to tell you.” Now, she gives me specific directions. We are much better at communicating – even if it’s not working. We might say let’s watch TV instead.
I think not giving up on our marriage has brought us closer together. We hold hands now when we walk down the street. I feel as if I have my girlfriend back from when we first started dating – although she wears less neon spandex, her body is still as incredible as it was when we first met.
double quotation mark I realised our two dogs were the glue holding us together. It shocked me
A couple of years ago, I asked Henry: “What would our relationship be like if we hadn’t got dogs?” He replied: “I think we’d be divorced.” I realised in that moment that our two dogs were the glue holding us together since our kids had left home. It shocked me. As we approached retirement age, Henry felt as though we were coexisting roommates, rather than husband and wife. He wanted more of a relationship and more intimacy. I realised I needed to step up and move in that direction.
At the time, our sex life was typical of a couple who had been together for ever. It was a big deal for Henry that we’d spend such long stretches of time without having sex, but it wasn’t a big deal for me. From the beginning of our marriage, we had a lot of financial stress. As a nurse, I worked night shifts and at home I was busy attending to three children. I was tired all the time. Sex started to feel like a chore. I’ve never had a hard time orgasming, so I would come first and then count down until he finished.
Last year, we started counselling and became more intentional about our relationship. I realised I could hold off my orgasm and enjoy being together. It shifted my perspective, from thinking of sex as a chore to something fun. Another important shift is feeling more confident in my body. I always thought I needed to be thinner, but seeing this recent craze of women my age getting very thin, it strikes me that they look frail and older. It’s helped me embrace my body.
The newfound intimacy has reminded me why I started dating Henry in the first place. When we met, Henry would wine and dine me, even though we were 20 and at university. No other guy had done that for me. He was fun to be around and open to new experiences – and we’ve rekindled that sense of fun together.
