author_name: Will Huxley, as told to Doosie Morris
content:
Will Huxley thought Garrett looked like a Heathcliff type. They bonded over their shared love of Kate Bush. Then one day Garrett handed over an ornate gift box
Find more stories from the moment I knew series
I n 2006 I’d just graduated film school at the Victorian College of the Arts and was working at the ABC in Melbourne. It was a pretty tumultuous time of my life. I had just broken up with my best friend and high school sweetheart – whom I adored – and was in the process of coming out.
I was drinking too much and in breaks from the chaos I’d find myself drawn to the local video store. That’s where I first saw Garrett behind the counter. I had an instant crush on him and spent a lot of time perusing the art house section, so he would see how creative and cultured I was.
I never had the guts to talk to him but one night in spring we ran into each other at a party. We hit it off and arranged a date at a cafe in the city.
I was obsessed with Kate Bush and Wuthering Heights, and Garrett struck me as this sort of Heathcliff type; he was a dark, handsome artist with very dramatic, gothic vibes. That day we talked about art and the things that we love. I was so excited that he shared my passion for Kate Bush, and listening to Hounds of Love on repeat. We talked about John Waters and Cindy Sherman and all these artists that were really formative for us.
But that coming-out period was really intense for me. Growing up, my father had enforced this notion that being gay was this dark, shameful, lonely experience. I was so scared of my truth and deep down I felt as if I didn’t deserve to be loved because of it.
Garrett is nine years older than me, and was comfortable with himself in a way I thought was so brave and found so inspiring. Still, my coming-out summer was messy.
I’d get hideously drunk and perform these outrageous stripteases to Tina Turner’s Private Dancer, or Sade’s Smooth Operator for him. They were ridiculous and borderline grotesque – usually involving me tearing my underwear and wearing an assortment of cheap wigs. Instead of running away in fear – like most people would – Garrett would just sit there and smile and enjoy it. He encouraged the wildness.
His patience and kindness during that time is something I will never forget and always be grateful for. It undid years of self-loathing and made me see that having a beautiful, loving relationship with a man was possible.
By February we were celebrating our first Valentine’s Day together. As a gift, Garrett presented me with an ornate box. Inside I was shocked to discover a real life cow’s heart he’d procured from a butcher, covered in fake blood. It was so dramatic and macabre. I couldn’t believe the audacity! I felt like Divine, in the John Waters film Pink Flamingoes when she receives a bowel movement in the mail – simultaneously appalled and thrilled. We both love John Waters – but we’re also lifelong vegetarians and huge animal lovers – which made it all the more potent.
He told me later it was a test to see if I could deal. If this really overly wrought gesture of romance would spook me. If I was horrified, he said, he’d have known I wasn’t the right person for him.
Garrett’s artwork at the time was drenched in this sort of visceral imagery of hearts beating and bodies coming together. This gruesome offering was outrageous but it perfectly captured Garrett’s theatricality, which I loved, and the intensity of that time for me. After that we began to connect even more through our art.
For two decades we’ve been working, living and creating together. Our life’s work is conjuring our own queer utopia, as we call it. It’s all about queer romance and joy, because for both of us growing up, we didn’t have access to that.
Learning about his First Nations heritage and the pride it brings him has also been a real honour. Sharing that, along with the queerness that I hid for so long, through our art is so healing and so beautiful.
Like any couple we have our moments, but our fights are more likely to be about which heels are suitable for traversing our inflatable vulva sculptures and the best way to attach fake eyelashes in a windstorm than who’s doing the dishes.
The Huxleys’ Bloodlines exhibition will show at the Brisbane Powerhouse from 21 October to 8 November as part of Melt festival

content:
For skiers looking to reduce their carbon footprint, rail travel from the UK to the Alps has never been quicker or easier. Here’s how to get there
S peeding effortlessly towards the slopes by train, you might wonder why you ever flew to a ski resort. On paper, it seems a short hop by plane; in reality, airport queues, cramped flights and long transfers can mean the journey eats up a whole day.
Measured door-to-door, daytime rail travel from London can be as fast as flying, while taking a sleeper train gets you extra time on the slopes. And with Alpine glaciers suffering significant loss of snow cover as global temperatures rise, rail travel constitutes the biggest emissions saving a skier can make.
An exciting recent development is the arrival of a dedicated sleeper train for skiers, the Travelski Night Express (TNE), launched last winter and with an additional new route for the coming one. Each carriage has couchette berths, but the train’s crowning glory is its large, speakeasy-cafe-bar-restaurant, with retro decor, soft lighting and music – you get the romance of overnight rail travel with the potential for two extra days’ skiing thrown in.
The TNE has two routes: one from Paris, the other from Amsterdam and Brussels, going out on Fridays and returning on Saturdays. Both routes access Moûtiers, Aime-la-Plagne and Bourg-Saint-Maurice – stations in the popular Tarentaise region of the French Alps. UK-based skiers can connect to the TNE by Eurostar to Paris or Brussels.
Overnight journeys to Austria are also possible, with a Eurostar to Paris or Brussels and then a Nightjet sleeper train to the Salzburgerland region; or, for Innsbruck and the Tirol, a Nightjet from Amsterdam and Cologne.
An array of resorts in France and beyond can be reached every day of the week by taking the Eurostar to Paris Nord, getting a taxi or the RER for the short transfer to Gare de Lyon, and from there catching a fast TGV train south.
The most direct daytime option is Eurostar’s flagship ski service, Eurostar Snow , which carries snowboards and skis free of charge on top of the usual luggage allowance. Skiers take it from London to Lille, then switch to an adjacent platform for the onward train to Bourg-Saint-Maurice.
Unfortunately, the final outbound departure for this coming season is on 20 February, leaving the ski industry frustrated. Eurostar’s explanation is that it needs to “deploy rolling stock to where it best meets customer demand. Historically, March has not always been the strongest period for Eurostar Snow.”
Iain Martin, founder of sustainable ski-travel campaign Ski Flight Free , says: “It’s ridiculous for Eurostar to curtail their flagship service and blame lack of demand. If Eurostar worked effectively with the ski industry and ski tour operators to market the train, they could sell it out many times over.”
Ski tour operators are certainly hungry for more train seats. “We’re keen on promoting rail travel to the French Alps and we know clients want this,” says Alison Willis, managing director of French ski specialist Peak Retreats . “While changing in Paris is straightforward, we know that direct services are an even more compelling alternative for those who usually fly. March ski holidays, with longer days and excellent conditions, are really popular. So, we’d welcome more direct rail options across as much of the ski season as possible.”
It’s a view echoed by ski tour operator Inghams , which has increased its range of rail-inclusive packages to include 75% of its French destinations, as well as some in Switzerland, Italy and Austria. “There’s a genuine appetite among skiers to travel to the mountains by train,” says head of sustainability Krissy Roe.
Here are 12 resorts you can reach easily by rail.
“The cradle of skiing”, St Anton is consistently ranked among the best resorts in the world. While its slopes are known for being challenging and exhilarating (the mighty Valluga being the pinnacle), there are plenty of gentler areas, too. St Anton isn’t just about skiing, either: this delightful village offers a host of activities, including swimming, bowling, indoor rock climbing and some of the best toboggan runs in the Alps. Completing its ski-hard, party-hard image, the resort is renowned for its après-ski, with a long list of celebrated terraces where visitors can dance to live music while knocking back schnapps.
By train: 10h 30min Depart London St Pancras on the 07.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 12.22 TGV to Zurich; then the 16.40 Railjet to St Anton, arriving at 19.01.
Where to stay Ski Solutions offers seven nights at the Hotel Post from £1,870pp half-board, including return rail travel.
Comprising antique, chocolate-box chalets, Alpbach is perhaps the prettiest village on this list, with fantastic skiing to boot. Despite its low altitude, the resort’s north-facing slopes protect fresh powder, with the best off-piste and snowboarding terrain being on the far side of the Wiedersbergerhorn. Alpbach has gone to great lengths to preserve its rustic character. The main lifts are a short shuttle ride away from the village, and you’ll find gorgeous Tyrolean dishes at mountain hut restaurants such as Böglalm , torchlit walking trails, horse-drawn carriage rides and an Alpine coaster. Pick up a free Alpbachtal Card for access to local activities.
By train: 16h 49min Depart London St Pancras on the 15.04 Eurostar to Brussels-Midi; then catch the 18.25 ICE to Cologne; get on the 21.45 Nightjet to Jenbach, arriving at 08.53. From there, it’s 20 minutes by bus or taxi.
Where to stay STC Ski offers the four-star Hotel Alphof , with doubles from £955pp for seven nights’ half-board.
Sainte-Foy, the smallest resort on this list, is highly regarded among ski writers as a “hidden gem” . Just 25 minutes from Bourg-Saint-Maurice station, it has retained its cosy, quiet ambience, thanks to bigger nearby names drawing the crowds. Yet Sainte-Foy has truly excellent skiing: powder that lasts on its untracked, north-facing slopes, and fantastic provisions for children and beginners. Despite some development, the village has remained rustic, with traditional dishes served in 16th-century farmhouses and glasses of local rosé downed on sunny terraces. The quiet pine woods are perfect for snowshoeing, while adrenaline junkies can try their hand at paragliding high above the Tarentaise.
By train: 7h 58min Eurostar Snow departs London St Pancras at 09.01 to Lille Europe; switch to the 11.35 Eurostar Snow continental train to Bourg-Saint-Maurice, arriving at 17.45. From there, it’s 25 minutes by bus or taxi.
Where to stay Premiere Neige offers seven nights’ self-catering in the three-bedroom Panorama apartment from €600pp, based on six people sharing.
Commanding spectacular views of the Tarentaise valley, La Rosière is as beautiful as it is convenient. Its position on the Franco-Italian border allows skiers to choose between south- and north-facing slopes (in neighbouring La Thuile), while its two core villages are relaxed and compact, in classic chalet style. La Rosière has kept up an excellent pace of development, exemplified by the new high-speed Petit-Bois chair, ensuring a high-quality experience all-round. Sledging is popular, including the new sunset toboggan run from the top of the Les Eucherts lift. While fairly quiet, you’ll find some decent après-ski and DJ sets at Le Comptoir , too.
By train: 7h 44m in Eurostar Snow departs London St Pancras at 09.01 to Lille Europe; switch to the 11.35 Eurostar Snow continental train to Bourg-Saint-Maurice, arriving at 17.45. From there, it’s 40 minutes by bus or taxi to the resort centre.
Where to stay Traditional chalet-hotel L’Accroche-Cœur has double rooms from €240 a night B&B.
Part of the famous Three Valleys, Les Menuires is one of the best value-for-money resorts in the Alps: 600km of piste but without the high price tag of Méribel or Courchevel. Unsurprisingly, it’s very popular with families who love the resort’s early-access ski patrol lessons with ESF Club Piou-Piou . Dining is similarly family-oriented: expect hearty, locally sourced Savoyard meals at restaurants such as Chez Pépé Nicolas . Finally, in March, Les Menuires hosts a seasonal silly slalom, Complètement à la Masse , open to all ages.
By train: 13h 5min Depart London St Pancras on the 17.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 22.52 Travelski Night Express to Moûtiers, arriving at 07.36. From there it’s 45 minutes by bus or taxi.
Where to stay Travelski offers seven nights at Hôtel Les Menuires Les Bruyères from £1,356pp B&B, including rail travel from Paris, transfers and seven-day ski pass. The Eurostar to Paris needs to be booked independently.
France’s oldest ski resort, Montgenèvre was the stomping ground of the Parisian set before British skiers started arriving in the 90s, attracted by its bargain prices and easy access to Italy. Pleasantly old world and fully pedestrianised, “Monty” is the ideal family resort, with an extensive beginners’ zone and affordable accommodation. Intermediates will enjoy the network of red and blue runs, while experts can plough through off-piste powder in the Gondrans bowl and off the Col de l’Alpet. Over the past year, the resort has extensively redeveloped its lift system to dramatically improve speed and ease – in time for hosting the 2030 Winter Olympics.
By train: 8h 20min Depart London St Pancras on the 08.01 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 12.46 TGV to arrive at Oulx at 17.21. From there it’s 35 minutes by bus or taxi.
Where to stay Peak Retreats offers seven nights B&B in a suite in Hôtel Anova from £1,046pp, including rail travel, based on four sharing.
Peisey-Vallandry occupies a prime position between Les Arcs and La Plagne, connecting to both via the immense Paradiski domain. Its sunny, west-facing piste offers something for everyone: a high-altitude beginners’ area, picturesque intermediate tree runs to the Chapelle Notre-Dame, and two challenging blacks (plus some fairly gnarly freeriding and all 425km of Paradiski). Thanks to its golden child, Olympic champion Éric Perrot , the resort has a strong reputation for cross-country, including a new Nordic centre, shooting range and 43km of high-quality trails (open for ages 3+). For something more unusual, try Summit Bike ’s electric snow-biking sessions or skijoring (putting on skis and being pulled across the snow by a horse).
By train: 7h 47min Eurostar Snow departs London St Pancras at 09.01 to Lille Europe; switch to the 11.35 Eurostar Snow continental train to Landry, arriving at 17.34. From there, it’s 25-35 minutes by bus or taxi.
Where to stay The ski-in-ski-out, fully renovated Hotel Émeraude has doubles from €130 B&B.
Saint-Gervais has been a popular tourist destination since the middle ages, owing to its natural hot springs. Today, the resort’s state-of-the-art thermal baths are still a huge draw for skiers seeking the ultimate wellness holiday. Combined with more than 455km of quiet piste and the best views of Mont Blanc in France, Saint-Gervais is a must-visit. In 2022, the resort opened a world-class indoor climbing facility, Le Topo . Dining, meanwhile, remains suitably traditional, including Savoyard platters, fondue and local craft beer. It’s also perfect for holidaying by rail, with a station-to-village gondola, Le Valléen , plus the Mont-Blanc tramway, one of the highest in Europe.
By train: 8h 45min Depart London St Pancras on the 09.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 14.18 TGV to Bellegarde; then the 17.15 TER to Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, arriving at 19.16. From there, it’s five minutes by the Valléen gondola to the village centre.
Where to stay Seven nights’ self-catering in a two-bedroom apartment in Les Sources de Canopée in Saint-Gervais, with Peak Retreats , costs from £645pp, including rail travel, based on four sharing.
Val Cenis recently invested €25m in sustainable development and infrastructure, and the results are showing. The resort has successfully created a second “recycled” chairlift, Combe de l’Ours, using secondhand seats, pylons and cables to reduce new materials tenfold. A new panoramic treetop walkway and energy-efficient gondola will greet guests this winter, giving easy access to its 125km of high-quality, north-facing piste. As a year-round working community, the resort comprises several well-stocked villages with a wide variety of shops, restaurants and bars, as well as a bowling alley. Off-piste snowshoeing in the spectacular Vanoise national park is a popular activity; locals Thierry Bardagi and Hélène Degano offer a combined snowshoeing and mountain refuge package , with a cooked breakfast overlooking the mountain sunrise.
By train: 7h 47min Depart London St Pancras on the 08.01 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; change to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 12.46 TGV to arrive at Modane at 16.48. From there, it’s 30 minutes by bus or taxi.
Where to stay Erna Low offers seven nights’ self-catering in a one-bedroom apartment in Les Balcons de Val Cenis Village, from £132pp, based on four sharing, travel not included.
Villars is one of French-speaking Switzerland’s quieter and (relatively) affordable resorts, perfect for an active holiday. Its respectable 130km of piste spreads across neighbouring Les Diablerets and Gryon, providing something for all ages and abilities, as well as cross-country, touring and toboggan trails. Plus, there’s a spectacular 1,500-metre off-piste descent from Les Diablerets glacier to the village. After a long day’s skiing, book in for a spa massage at Les Bains de Villars or a dip in the hot springs at Lavey , before a night of music and malt whisky in the bar at Les Mazots du Clos .
By train: 8h 49min Depart London St Pancras on the 09.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 14.18 TGV to Geneva; then the 18.05 InterRegio train to Aigle, arriving at 19.20. From there, it’s 20 minutes by bus or taxi.
Where to stay Alpe Fleurie Hotel & Residence has double rooms from £193 B&B.
Andorra’s duty-free status makes Grandvalira particularly attractive to visitors looking for shopping and high-quality, low-cost accommodation. Spread across three high-altitude villages, the resort is by far the largest in the Pyrenees, with 215km of piste best suited to intermediates. The village of Pas de la Casa has garnered a reputation for its après-ski, while further along, Soldeu is home to some swanky four- and five-star hotels. The ace up Grandvalira’s sleeve, however, is its unique Catalan cuisine, quite unlike traditional Alpine fare, with an emphasis on flame-grilled meats and hearty vegetable stews.
By train: 15h 12min Depart London St Pancras on the 17.31 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare d’Austerlitz and take the 22.14 Intercités de Nuit to Andorre-L’Hospitalet, arriving at 09.43. From there, it’s 35-55 minutes by bus or taxi.
Where to stay Alpine Answers offers seven nights in a double room (with balcony) at the four-star Sport Hotel Village, from £1,030pp B&B.
Europe’s first purpose-built ski resort remains cheap and cheerful, catering best to families and young adults on a budget. Sestriere’s slopes are some of the best in the Via Lattea domain (which includes France’s Montgenèvre and neighbouring Sauze d’Oulx), ranging from sprawling nursery meadows to the steep Col de Sises Olympic giant slalom. Local amenities are well-organised and non-ski activities abundant, including a sizable leisure centre and swimming pool, open-air ice rink and dog-sledding. Après-ski is also surprisingly lively for a family-focused resort, with several popular pubs in the centre of town, alongside a good, old-fashioned discoteca , Tabata .
By train: 8h 20min Depart London St Pancras on the 08.01 Eurostar to Paris Gare du Nord; transfer to Paris Gare de Lyon and take the 12.46 TGV to arrive at Oulx at 17.21. From there, it’s 35 minutes by bus or taxi.
Where to stay Inghams offers seven nights at Grand Hotel Sestriere, from £1,134pp, including rail travel and transfers.
Accommodation prices are for the 2026/27 season and were correct at the time of publication

title: I closed my eyes and stuck my finger on a map of western Europe: ‘This is where we’re going on holiday!’
description: Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance. Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central France An unruly rabble bursts on to the street: a noisy eruption, bubbling towards us. content:
Sick of relying on internet recommendations, I left my next destination to chance. Luckily, it led to me discovering a magical hamlet in the Cévennes mountains of south-central France
A n unruly rabble bursts on to the street: a noisy eruption, bubbling towards us. This isn’t closing time on the Croisette in Cannes. A flock of sheep bustles past our cottage towards the shade of a huge chestnut tree, driven by three generations of herders and their dogs. The waterlike cacophony of their bells slows until only the odd tink tink punctuates the cicadas’ hum. The sheep graze, the shepherds doze off, and the mountain hamlet is still again.
My partner and I had set off by Eurostar less than 24 hours before, yet this place felt a world away from the ad agency where I work.
We’d booked cheap tickets to Paris months ago, intending to plan a trip on from there by train. As our departure approached, Instagram seemed to be full of aspirational, yet similar, holiday photos, and almost every other TikTok post I flicked past offered the promise of a hidden destination … discovered.
I find ratings, reviews and recommendations just as reassuring as the next person, especially when faced with a limited holiday allowance. The safety of the search bar helps to give me the confidence that I’m spending my hard earned money as wisely as possible. I work in a world that runs on data and optimisation and I love it, but I wondered whether I’d optimised the adventure out of my own holidays.
So, we tried a simple experiment. We closed down the tabs and opened a map of western Europe. Embracing a bit of low-tech randomness, we chose to let chance decide our trip.
I shut my eyes and we promised to go wherever my finger landed. I waved my hand like a magic wand and pointed, then took a deep breath, eyes still closed. What if we ended up in some industrial wasteland? But we were in luck. My finger landed upon the commune of Saint-Hilaire-de-Lavit in Cévennes, a place we’d never heard of and almost certainly would never have found by searching “places to go in France”.
After overnighting in Paris, a three-hour fast train zipped us down to Montpellier, where we hired a car. We stopped for provisions in a Lidl on the edge of town, stocking up for the whole trip – we weren’t expecting to find any shops at our journey’s end. A short drive inland, and the roads began to get narrower and more sparsely populated. As they climbed and zigzagged into this south-east corner of the Massif Central, we entered a south of France far removed from the honeypots served up by algorithms.
We pulled into a grassy layby on a high mountain pass where there was one other car parked. Had we arrived? We’d followed the cottage owner’s directions as there was no signal here for Google Maps, so it was hard to tell. Stretching our legs in the fresh, cool air, the first thing we noticed was the quiet. No traffic, no tourists. Just stillness. But the languid buzz of big insects flying by and the whirring chorus of cicadas told us this place was alive.
Squinting into the low sun, we saw someone waving. Our host, Guilaine, had appeared as if by magic and was beckoning us to the cottage a little farther down the road. We had found the hamlet of Les Ayres: a cluster of maybe 10 stone buildings, 800 metres above sea level. The rough-walled dwellings huddled either side of the narrow road, making the most of the tiny strand of level ground before the mountain’s spine fell away into steep forest. A long wooden awning and some outdoor tables suggested a cafe opposite our cottage, but the building was shuttered, and Les Ayres’ only potential customers seemed to be ourselves and Guilaine. She took us to the back of our accommodation, to a veranda that looked out over chestnut and pine-clad mountains rolling into the horizon. It’s a landscape that appears wild but has actually been shaped by farming, forestry and the seasonal movement of livestock for thousands of years.
The next morning, as I watched the sheep and their guardians settle down in the shade, I felt the ancientness of the place. Shepherds must have moved their flocks along the same path and most likely slept under the same chestnut trees for centuries. Traditional farming practices endure here in part because the area is veined with crystal-clear mountain streams, meaning animals traversing the paths are never too far from a drink. So rather than opening the internet, we let these ancient tracks, known as drailles , guide our hikes.
We took sweaty, daylong expeditions without seeing another human or hearing the sound of cars. The forests protected us from the worst of the sun’s blaze but, on our first trek, the real treat came when we rounded a corner to find that what we thought was the sound of wind in the pines was actually water gushing through a narrow gorge below us. Another couple of switchbacks and we arrived at a deep, clear pool created as the stream carved a corner into the rock. Dappled sunlight filtered down through trees clinging to the steep-sided valley, creating spotlights for damselflies to dart through. We stopped for a picnic and a swim in the freezing mountain water, picking wild strawberries from the bank for dessert.
We discovered that these shady, secluded river pools were waiting for us on all the paths that led down from our cottage. As well as being the ultimate pit stops for mid-hike refreshment, they were teeming with wildlife – tadpoles wriggled in the shallows, fish flickered in the depths and a huge variety of butterflies, dragonflies and other insects skimmed the surface. We even saw a snake swimming across water we’d been submerged in just minutes before.
We spent our last afternoon reading on a rock, summoning the energy to walk back up the mountain (one drawback of staying high up on a pass). We watched the sun swing over the water and the light change as the day wore on. When the air began to cool, we worked our way back towards the cottage. As the path turned into an empty, single-track road, a car approached – a big event after so much seclusion. It was Guilaine – the only person apart from the shepherds we’d encountered.
In the evening, as the light faded, the sound of brass band practice drifted towards our veranda. Later, owls called to each other and a distant wild boar screeched into the quiet night. None of this had appeared in my search results. There was no review promising unexpected trumpeting, no listicle recommending the best pool for swimming among tadpoles, and no algorithm that could have told me where the sheep would pass on that first morning. We hadn’t looked at our phones for days – maybe that was the real discovery.

content:
The first stage of an ambitious new hiking route that will link woodlands across Wales takes walkers into the wild hills above the valleys’ old mining villages
B racken and heather ripple across the plateau. I exhale into the chill autumn air and my breath mists a view that reaches all the way to Gower and the ochre peaks of Bannau Brycheiniog (formerly the Brecon Beacons). Far below, the Ogmore valley’s terrace houses look like tiny constellations but up here on Tarren y Fforch, it’s just me and a few sheep taking springy steps between tufts of bilberries. If this corner of the south Wales valleys feels a long way from its coal mining past, that is, partly, the point.
I’m hiking the new Llwybr Coedwig Cymru Trail , or Wales Forest Trail. Running from Porthkerry Park, near Barry, to Pont Walby, close to Glynneath, this 50-mile (80km) pilot route is the first section of what the National Forest for Wales hopes will eventually be a trail linking woodlands across the length and breadth of Wales: a sylvan counterpart to the Wales Coast Path .
My father grew up in one of the valleys’ mining villages and, when I visited relatives there as a child, the disconnection of those post-industrial communities from the wild hills that loomed above them was striking. Mountain bikers have long discovered the region’s potential, but walkers still tend to head for the more obvious trails that wind through the national parks or along the coast. This pilot trail seems a good excuse to explore untapped footpaths.
With the sea behind me, I set off from the oak leaf sculpture that marks the trail’s start. The viaduct ahead once carried coal to Barry docks, but today it stands over Caffe Matteo , busy with dog walkers sipping cappuccinos. Leaving them behind, I cross the park between the soft greens of birch and oak trees.
I swerve on to a fern-fringed path and follow a stream to the outskirts of Barry. The next section is less lovely – a long stretch of roadside pavement until I enter Hensol Forest . The sunshine splinters through ancient pine trees and their needles cushion the ground. Weaving in and out of forest and fields, I soak up all the calm this long-distance forest-bathing exercise can offer until the Vale Resort comes into sight.
This vast hotel is popular with golfers, but also holds two trump cards for walkers: a spa where weary hikers can swim, sauna and steam their muscles limber again, and a bar serving energy-boosting Welsh rarebit spiked with ale mustard, Dragon cheddar and charred leeks.
Restored, I rejoin the trail the next morning, dipping along leafy lanes and footpaths as the roar of the M4 gets louder. I cross beneath it to enter Coedwig Gellihir, a small broadleaf woodland, then continue north into Pontyclun, before clambering down to the river at Ynysmaerdy Forest to pick up an old railway path to Coedely.
The trail has been designed to offer stretches for cyclists, pushchair users and horse riders, with more pavement-pounding and, in Thomastown, a reminder of the challenges faced by post-industrial communities. Leaving the village behind, the trail opens out again on to a little rocky path with soaring views of Ogwr Fach Valley.
One of the National Forest for Wales’s aims is to help communities connect with nearby woodlands. In Blackmill, the next village I come to, the trail passes Coed Bach Dimbath, a small community woodland where local groups have come together to build an otter hide, outdoor classroom and accessible paths.
“The woodland there had been inaccessible for decades, and now people can access it,” says Rhodri Hewitt of Natural Resources Wales, the trail’s project lead. “The valleys can feel desperately poor in places, but the River Ogmore is another world entirely.”
Continuing north to Nant-y-Moel, I come to Blaenogwr Farm, a Georgian farmstead marooned in the village, where I’m staying in a homely holiday cottage . I drop off my backpack and head across the road for fish with buttery potatoes and laverbread (made from edible seaweed) and cockle sauce at the Blaenogwr Hotel .
My final day’s walking starts with a climb up to that extraordinary plateau on Tarren y Fforch. Hewitt tells me that parts of the trail follow the paths miners took across these hills to work in pits in neighbouring valleys. I’m glad they had this antidote to the darkness and danger underground. Today’s route feels uplifting. I slip through an ancient gate on to open moorland and pick my way up the escarpment, meadow pipits chirruping around me.
Crossing the plateau, I enter Afan Forest park , a large commercial woodland that’s also home to a forest of wind turbines, a peat restoration project and a network of mountain-biking trails . I have an urge to be inside the forest rather than tracing its edges and detour on to a footpath leading up to the trig point at Craig y Llyn, the highest point of the valleys at 600m.
Continuing beneath branches dripping velvety lichen, I come to another spectacular viewpoint, as the land drops away to the waters of Llyn Fach and Llyn Fawr, with the peaks of Corn Du and Pen y Fan shrouded in soft-focus drizzle behind them. Soon I dip into the loveliest stretch of forest along the whole trail.
The valley of Cwm Gwrelych is a designated geological site of special scientific interest because of the near complete 300m-year-old strata exposed here. But it’s also rainforest-like, cut through with waterfalls, a dark, glossy river and dense, broadleaf woodland. I feel completely enveloped in green as I hike the last couple of miles to the trail’s current end, the Isambard Kingdom Brunel-designed viaduct at Pont Walby. As I continue to Sgwd Gwladys pub with rooms in nearby Pontneddfechan, I remind myself that this is not a finished trail but the beginning of one.
The next morning, I pull on my boots one last time and set out in search of the waterfall the pub is named after. Mist rises from the river, shafts of sunlight turn the leaves amber and a heron glides past in cinematic slow-mo. When we spoke about the trail, Hewitt mentioned an old Welsh proverb: Dod yn ôl at fy nghoed , meaning “To return to my trees”, or finding your way back to a balanced state of mind. As I sit and admire Sgwd Gwladys’ thundering cascade, I realise this leafy trail has delivered exactly that.
The trip was provided by the National Forest for Wales and Natural Resources Wales . Vale Resort has doubles from £104 room-only. The Airbnb cottage costs from £87 a night . Sgwd Gwladys has doubles from £65.55 , room only. For trail information , visit gov.wales/llwybr-coedwig-cymru-trail and for region information Visitwales.com

title: A perfect weekend in the Lincolnshire Wolds: wide skies and gentle walks
description: The landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break. content:
The landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break. Here’s where to eat, where to stay and what not to miss
W ide skies, gentle footpaths through gold and copper wooded hills, thatched cottages, cosy pubs and quirky shops: the Lincolnshire Wolds have all the ingredients for the perfect autumnal mini break. Victorian poet Alfred Tennyson lived in the village of Somersby for most of his first three decades and the local landscapes echo through his verses. In The Lady of Shalott: “Long fields of barley and of rye / That clothe the wold and meet the sky …”
The Lincolnshire Wolds National Landscape covers an area of 216 sq miles. On its southern boundary, halfway between Lincoln and the coast, the friendly market town of Horncastle bills itself as the “gateway to the Wolds”. With handsome brick houses, great cafes, a market on Thursdays and Saturdays and decent public transport links, it’s a perfect base for exploring the area.
Horncastle overflows with antique shops. Laurence Shaw , with half a century’s knowledge of the trade, runs an elegant wholesaler on the corner of East Street. In an old chapel across the road, the Trinity Centre has all kinds of ancient treasures piled in fantastical heaps under lancets of Victorian glass: porcelain milkmaids, jelly moulds, cotton reels, teetering piles of teacups and thick vines of jewellery. Round the corner in Stanhope Antique Centre you may find anything from a wooden decoy duck to a roulette wheel between chandeliers and grandfather clocks.
By the “Ducks Crossing!” sign opposite Tesco, mallards gather on the reedy River Bain. And in the 13th-century St Mary’s church there are gold angels in the rafters and lines from Tennyson’s poem Ring out, wild bells in stained glass. The new Riverscape Walk , launched last year, will take you past the canal basin, watermill and former leather tanning warehouses.
There are plenty of rewarding walks nearby and you don’t always need a car to reach them. The hourly 56 bus from Lincoln to Skegness stops in Horncastle and, 10 minutes later, in Hagworthingham, a peaceful Wold-edge village. From here, a six-mile loop of undulating lanes and footpaths takes in tiny Somersby, Tennyson’s birthplace, and Bag Enderby (which sounds straight out of Tolkien), where St Margaret’s church has an intricate 15th-century font, carved with religious symbols and medieval scenes. Bag Enderby’s -by suffix comes from an Old Norse word for village.
From Hagworthingham, you can also stroll through Snipe Dales nature reserve, where a 3-metre (10ft) wooden snipe, carved by local sculptor Nigel Sardeson, has just been installed on a wooded bank. The valleys here are fragrant with late meadowsweet and water mint and the trees are full of birdsong, from tiny goldcrests in the conifers to huge buzzards over the oaks. If you have time and energy to spare, the Viking Way long-distance walk – waymarked with horned Viking helmets – runs through Horncastle and the Wolds on its 149-mile journey from Rutland Water to the Humber.
In Horncastle, the Joseph Banks Centre multitasks as a tourist info point, local museum and natural history hub. Banks , a botanist and Horncastle’s most famous inhabitant, sailed with Captain Cook and oversaw the creation of Kew Gardens. The museum courtyard is bright with hydrangeas, which Banks helped introduce into Britain.
The Edwardian village of Woodhall Spa , six miles from Horncastle, has wide leafy avenues and smart black-and-white buildings; even the public loos next to the Tory club are half timbered. Nineteenth-century entrepreneurs, digging for coal, found instead a source of mineral-rich water, a magnet for the era’s wellness-seekers. I meander past the Dambusters memorial and mural, the thriving Kinema in the Woods , opened in 1922, the nearby Tea House and Cottage Museum , then back to Horncastle along the sculpture-dotted Viking Way.
Horncastle’s top lunch spots include the cafe at Myers Bakery , fragrant with spice and yeast, where you can buy Lincolnshire plum loaf. Round the corner, the spacious and welcoming bike-themed Pedal and Paws serves pizzas, salads and cakes. No 8 Coffee Shop , which opened in March 2026, is already popular for inventive hot drinks such as cinnamon-bun matcha and pistachio hot chocolate.
Montebello , in the former Angel Inn, serves home-cooked Italian food, while Magpies offers refined white linen and candlelight dining, with dishes such as Grimsby crab linguine or loin of Lincolnshire lamb. Magpies also has rooms, in cottages next to a Tardis-like guitar shop .
The cheerful, timeworn Admiral Rodney Hotel is right in the middle of Horncastle, with affordable rooms and details you might see in pricier places: speedy wifi, retro radio, Twinings teabags. It offers great veggie breakfast options, fresh fruit and pastries, served in a big glass-walled conservatory with peacock fanlights. Dinner dishes such as pan-fried sea bass with pickled fennel, or sticky date pudding with butterscotch sauce, chicly garnished with edible flowers and micro-herbs, make a celebratory end to days spent hiking through the Wolds.
The 56 bus heads to Horncastle from Lincoln bus station hourly and takes 50 minutes. The less frequent 30 bus takes 10 minutes longer and winds through warm-stoned villages. Local buses include the new B617 from Horncastle to Woodhall Spa. The coast is 20 miles away, on a bus with top-deck views across the Wolds.
Accommodation was provided by the Admiral Rodney , doubles from around £100, room only . Train travel was provided by LNER

title: ‘Wrong’ type of credit card wrecked my Enterprise car hire pickup
description: Not having the right kind when picking up a vehicle can leave travellers scrambling to find alternative transport If your children are on half-term holiday soon and you are planning to collect a hire car, make sure you have the right kind of credit card. These cautionary tales show the costly consequences if yours does not pass muster. I hired a car for a family holiday from Enterprise Rent-A-Car in France. The collection desk at Carcassonne airport refused to hand over the keys when I presented the Visa credit card used for the booking because it was issued by First Direct. It told me it did not accept cards from online banks. Continue reading...
content:
Not having the right kind when picking up a vehicle can leave travellers scrambling to find alternative transport
I f your children are on half-term holiday soon and you are planning to collect a hire car, make sure you have the right kind of credit card. These cautionary tales show the costly consequences if yours does not pass muster.
I hired a car for a family holiday from Enterprise Rent-A-Car in France. The collection desk at Carcassonne airport refused to hand over the keys when I presented the Visa credit card used for the booking because it was issued by First Direct. It told me it did not accept cards from online banks.
The rental branch subsequently confirmed this in writing. Enterprise’s terms and conditions state that Visa, Mastercard and American Express are accepted, while virtual, single-use and prepaid cards are not. We were forced to arrange alternative rail and taxi transport for our group of 10, costing us €440 [£370] and causing considerable stress.
The booking agent has refunded the £388.44 rental cost, but Enterprise first ignored, then refused, my requests for my expenses to be refunded. JM , Oxford
This is an extraordinary stance on the part of Enterprise, given that First Direct is part of HSBC and that terms and conditions not explicitly stated in a contract are unenforceable.
You have been battling vainly for redress since May, so it’s provoking that Enterprise instantly rolled over when I waded in. It admitted that First Direct Visa cards were accepted and that branch staff blundered.
Apparently, it says, staff are now “very apologetic” three months after the event despite the company having doubled down in writing when you complained.
It has now refunded your expenses, though not a penny more to reflect the impact of its error.
It says: “On this occasion, the customer did not receive the high level of service and support that we aim to provide. We sincerely regret the inconvenience caused in this situation.”
VD of London was also caught out by unexpected credit card rules when she tried to collect a prepaid car from Warsaw airport that had been booked through Holiday Autos. The provider, Flex To Go, refused to release it because her credit card bore her initials instead of her forename.
“The Holiday Autos confirmation did say ‘no abbreviations’, but I took that to mean shortened names rather than initials, and I have had no problems with my card over many years of hiring cars,” she says. “In the end, we had to get a Polish friend to call the car hire desk and pay over £145 for their comprehensive insurance – when we already had our own – so we could have the car.”
Although it is common for UK credit cards to replace a customer’s forename with initials, it is not unusual for car rental companies to refuse them as security guarantees. Instead, they insist the name on the card matches the name on the lead driver’s licence.
However, I agree that Holiday Autos’ warning about this was open to misinterpretation. Flex To Go’s Ts & Cs did specify it, but these were not given to you until you had completed the transaction at the collection desk. Those Ts & Cs conceal other nasty surprises.
Buried in the small print are clauses stating that the company charges customers for “minor expenses for ordinary use of the vehicle, ie refilling screen washer liquid and washing the vehicle”.
Customers are also required to carry out “daily inspections” of brake fluid, oil and liquid coolant control, regardless of any dashboard warnings.
These terms strike me as onerous and unusual, and were neither highlighted by Flex To Go as “onerous and unusual” terms must be, nor were they mentioned by Holiday Autos.
Flex To Go did not respond to any of these points. Holiday Autos ignored the point about the ambiguity of “abbreviations” and its supplier’s maintenance demands.
It told me that names on cards and driver licences must match for identity verification and fraud prevention, and that customers should review terms and conditions before travel. “We appreciate how frustrating this situation must have been,” it says.
Always read reviews of car rental firms before booking to discover which ones to avoid. Looking at the Ts & Cs of Flex To Go, which operates on three continents, I will not be using them. And don’t be caught out by hire firms’ rules on credit cards that are designed not only for identity verification, but to ensure deductions from a customer’s bank account are possible if a vehicle is damaged.
Hire companies tend to accept physical credit cards only, not Apple Pay, as one reader found to his cost. If the firms can’t reliably match the card to the licence and booking name, they are likely to insist that you pay for their comprehensive insurance, which can be expensive.

title: BT charged me for more than a year despite landline being dead
description: It is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital Voice I’ve had no landline since May 2025 when BT switched it to Digital Voice. Weeks passed, and each call to BT involved at least an hour waiting on hold and answering security questions before being passed between departments. Eventually, last December, two engineers were sent and discovered that a wire had been severed during the upgrade. They said they needed a cherry picker to reconnect it to its original location and would return. They did not. Continue reading...
content:
It is billing £32.99 a month but I have had no functioning phone line since it switched me to Digital Voice
I’ve had no landline since May 2025 when BT switched it to Digital Voice. Weeks passed, and each call to BT involved at least an hour waiting on hold and answering security questions before being passed between departments.
Eventually, last December, two engineers were sent and discovered that a wire had been severed during the upgrade. They said they needed a cherry picker to reconnect it to its original location and would return. They did not.
Since then, I’ve called BT to no avail, and all the while I’ve been paying for a landline that doesn’t work.
I am on the priority register due to serious illness and am reduced to tears of helplessness.
You have been paying £32.99 a month for a dead landline and broadband, which was unaffected. BT claims it was unaware of the problem until you complained last December. You insist you had reported it before then, but do not have records of when. It turns out the case was closed in December after the engineers’ abortive visit.
You next complained in January, but BT admits it again closed the case because, by then, your landline had been removed from your account, though you were still being charged.
It says it did not hear from you again until I intervened in July.
You said that you had believed promises that a fix was under way.
A complaints manager rang you after my contact, and you were offered an extraordinary £6.46 to “make up” for its failings. Your line was eventually activated in September.
The telecoms regulator Ofcom requires providers to pay £10.34 compensation a day if a reported fault is not corrected within two working days, which means you are, in theory, entitled to more than £4,600.
I’ve put this to BT, but it is digging in because, it claims, you waited months to report the problems. Since you can’t provide proof to contradict it, I can’t argue the toss.
You have the option of a complaint to the Communications Ombudsman but have now accepted £689 for the 60 days without service which BT acknowledges fall within the compensation rules, and for its mishandling of the two complaints it has on record.
Always keep a timeline of interactions with a company and follow up unaddressed complaints promptly and in writing.

title: Father was asked for DNA test to get a passport for his daughter
description: New post-Brexit rules mean that dual nationals cannot enter the UK unless they have a British passport My teenage daughter is unable to see her grandparents because of the UK’s new requirement for dual nationals to hold a UK passport. I’m a UK citizen, married to a French national, and we live in France. Our two older children have both French and UK passports. Our third child was born while we were living in Zimbabwe and only has a French passport. Continue reading...
content:
New post-Brexit rules mean that dual nationals cannot enter the UK unless they have a British passport
My teenage daughter is unable to see her grandparents because of the UK’s new requirement for dual nationals to hold a UK passport.
I’m a UK citizen, married to a French national, and we live in France. Our two older children have both French and UK passports. Our third child was born while we were living in Zimbabwe and only has a French passport.
I began her application for a British passport in February. I had to submit photos of my wife when pregnant, family photos from the birth to the present day, hospital records and official translations of French marriage and birth certificates.
During an official interview I was asked about my job, commute and the layout of my house, but very little about my relationship with my daughter.
I was then told that there was insufficient evidence to prove my paternity and was invited to consider a DNA test, which will cost £600 and take yet more time.
We need to visit my elderly father who is unwell in the UK but cannot risk it in case our daughter is denied boarding.
Your daughter is a victim of new rules that came into force in February and effectively deny entry to the UK to dual national Britons who do not have a British passport.
Foreign nationals can enter freely on passports issued by their country of residence, but expats cannot unless they stump up £589 for a certificate of entitlement. The law has caused chaos, with children being stranded abroad or arbitrarily denied a passport granted to their siblings.
Since the UK government is not accepting that your daughter is a UK national, you asked if she could travel on her French passport. No one could answer the question.
As a result, you face Christmas apart from your parents. Home Office rules state that officials must consider a passport application on the “balance of probability” if an applicant refuses a DNA test. They must also explain why an application is refused. You have never been told why your copious proofs of paternity have been deemed inadequate.
The Home Office will not comment on individual cases, but it did tell me that additional evidence, such as the layout of a home, may be requested to add “credible authenticity”.
Soon afterwards, you were informed that the application had been accepted after all, despite no new paperwork having been sought since April. I can only assume that press scrutiny prompted the realisation that your domestic floorplan is credibly authentic.

title: Holiday cottage company insisted on a death certificate to amend our break
description: Sykes Holiday Cottages showed no empathy and insisted on paperwork we didn’t have so soon after my husband’s death We booked a break with Sykes Holiday Cottages for 11 of us to celebrate my mum’s 80th birthday last February. The cost was £2,400, paid for by my 87-year-old dad, but it was my husband who made the booking. In January, my husband was diagnosed with aggressive lymphoma, and he died 10 days before the trip. My parents and some other members of the party still planned to take the holiday, and my dad informed Sykes of the death, since my husband was their point of contact. Continue reading...
content:
Sykes Holiday Cottages showed no empathy and insisted on paperwork we didn’t have so soon after my husband’s death
W e booked a break with Sykes Holiday Cottages for 11 of us to celebrate my mum’s 80th birthday last February. The cost was £2,400, paid for by my 87-year-old dad, but it was my husband who made the booking.
In January, my husband was diagnosed with aggressive lymphoma, and he died 10 days before the trip. My parents and some other members of the party still planned to take the holiday, and my dad informed Sykes of the death, since my husband was their point of contact.
Sykes declared that the booking could not be honoured in my late husband’s name and that they would need a copy of his death certificate to move it into my name. We did not have one since an inquest into the death had been ordered.
Sykes said a copy of my marriage certificate would suffice. I submitted this, only to be told that “an official document recognised by the state that confirms the passing of the deceased” was required.
We provided a screenshot of the inquest listing from the coroner’s court website but were advised that this was not sufficient evidence.
My GP wrote a letter confirming the death, but Sykes did not reply, and by then we were all too distressed to continue.
Later, Sykes sent numerous emails to my late husband’s email address asking whether he had enjoyed the stay. We never received a refund, and I have not felt emotionally strong enough to do anything further before now.
I could hardly believe what I was reading as I trawled through Sykes’s correspondence. Its response, on being informed of your husband’s untimely death, was to send him an email asking for information.
When Sykes received the requested marriage certificate, the company simultaneously stated in an email that this provided sufficient proof for the booking to be transferred to your name, and that the booking could not be transferred without an official confirmation of death.
The GP letter confirming the death merely elicited an email saying Sykes would be in touch. By then, the trip was two days away. Sykes still did not amend the booking name, nor did it acknowledge the link to the coroner’s inquest listing.
The next you heard from them was the first of several emails addressed to your late husband hoping that he had enjoyed the holiday. When you asked them to stop using his email address, Sykes apologised for the “inconvenience”.
Four days later, when you had to complain about another such email to him, you were told unapologetically that feedback forms are sent automatically. By then, Sykes had been informed multiple times over a fortnight that your husband had died.
Sykes, I discover, does not have an official bereavement policy which, given the size of the business, is poor enough. But empathy does not require an official mandate and you received none.
Its onerous name change requirements are more suitable for a visa application than checking into a Cumbrian cottage. It refunded the £2,400 pronto when I got in touch and added £150 in “goodwill”. I think that’s a paltry sum for the distress it caused, but you have accepted it so you can put the ordeal behind you.
A spokesperson said: “We have contacted the family directly to apologise and resolve the matter, and are reviewing our processes to ensure situations like this are always handled with the care and sensitivity they deserve.”
Our spirits need some good news, so here are some tales of how customer service ought to be.
“We bought a secondhand Scandibørn bed from a third-party seller and found four screws were missing,” writes CC . “They were so specialist that no shop even knew what they were called. We contacted Scandibørn with low expectations of help, but they immediately offered to send us the missing screws for free. Exemplary customer service, which has earned a customer for life.”
MS , meanwhile, raises his revamped hat to Tilley. “Thirty years ago I bought a Tilley hat, which became a constant companion on walks and holidays. It was beginning to show its age and, since the label promised a lifetime guarantee, I contacted Tilley. I was asked to submit photographs and was promptly invited to choose from three designs. The replacement was dispatched within days, with a handling charge of £20. Sadly, this one will outlast me.”

title: LV= insurance is ignoring us while our house literally falls apart
description: We are living in a collapsing property because of cost-cutting and delays over our subsidence claim LV= General Insurance is forcing a family with three young children to live in a collapsing home because of cost-cutting and delays. We lodged a claim for subsidence damage to our extension and conservatory in 2023. content:
We are living in a collapsing property because of cost-cutting and delays over our subsidence claim
LV= General Insurance is forcing a family with three young children to live in a collapsing home because of cost-cutting and delays.
We lodged a claim for subsidence damage to our extension and conservatory in 2023. Instead of authorising the repairs recommended by independent experts, LV= has spent years stalling and proposing inadequate, superficial patching methods.
Three years on, significant cracking in the interior walls has caused a radiator to shear away. We have provided proof to LV= but are being ignored while our home literally falls apart around us.
Meanwhile, the company has hiked our annual premium from £400 to £2,500. I feel they are penalising us for a claim.
Subsidence claims are soaring as repeated droughts cause soil to shrink. Nearby trees accelerate the problem, and you have, on LV=’s advice, had several removed, but to no avail.
An independent surveyor, commissioned by you in May – when you had reached an impasse with the company – concluded that the damaged extension needed underpinning or rebuilding. There was no obvious progress in the case, however.
LV= now tells me that it obtained a quote for underpinning last February, although the work wasn’t carried out. It has since acknowledged that the cracks have worsened and a full rebuild is required.
It says repairs will begin as soon as the designs and council bureaucracy are complete. The company blames the subsidence and the delay on an eucalyptus tree owned by a neighbour who refuses to remove it.
A spokesperson said: “LV= General Insurance takes this claim extremely seriously and we understand and appreciate the frustration at the time it has taken to resolve it. Subsidence claims can be protracted because the most important step is to address the cause of movement, in this case tree removal, before permanent repairs can be undertaken.”
LV= says it is reviewing your premium price rise under its complaints procedure.

content:
In search of autumn festivals, good food and islands where it still feels like summer? We asked you to recommend your best off-season breaks
Tell us about a spooky spot in the UK – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher
Last October, while I was cycling around south-west France, near the Spanish border, a tip from a local waiter led me to Collioure , near Perpignan. The town was like a Mediterranean dream, where the summer crowds had faded, leaving behind a peaceful, artistic haven of soft light, warm sunshine, cobbled streets, sandy beaches – and the Pyrenees as a backdrop. In the early evening, the still balmy autumn air was perfect for wandering through the quiet, pastel-coloured alleyways of the Le Mouré district to enjoy €5 off-season happy hour wine with fish tapas. I had planned to stay a weekend but ended up staying a week, seduced by Collioure’s perfect autumn cocktail of chilled Catalan culture and sunkissed seaside sensuality. April
Sitting outside in T-shirt and shorts on the deck of a boat gliding along the Tagus River in Lisbon, sipping a glass of crisp Portuguese wine as the setting autumn sun illuminated the pastel-coloured hills, is a lasting travel memory for me. October temperatures were still in the mid-20s, perfect for exploring fascinating areas on foot, or hanging out of trams as they rattled up and down the cobbled streets. In the evenings, I joined local people basking in the remaining warmth of the year at outdoor cafes or waterside tavernas like Ponto Final, enjoying coffee and pastries, or anchovies and beer, while watching magnificent sunsets without the summer masses. Nicoletta
My autumn escape is St Davids on the Pembrokeshire coast. Once the summer crowds disappear, it feels wonderfully wild and tranquil. We walk the coast path towards Whitesands , stopping to watch for seals below the cliffs, before heading back into tiny St Davids for something warm to eat. The beaches are often almost empty and, even when the weather turns, the dramatic sea and windswept coastline are part of the charm. My tip is to visit in early autumn; pack proper walking boots and layers, and embrace the weather – you get one of Britain’s loveliest coastlines almost to yourself. Tess
Görlitz makes for a fascinating autumnal base, with its location on the German-Polish border to the east of Dresden. The highlights were day excursions to Bad Muskau, where there is a wonderful baroque palace, and the Rakotzbrücke (Devil’s Bridge), reached by a narrow-gauge forest railway ( waldeisenbahn.de ). It’s a part of Germany rarely visited, but those who go there will be rewarded with amazing photographs. Martin
The Canary Islands are well-trodden choices for autumn sun, but the island of El Hierro remains a wilder alternative to Tenerife or Lanzarote. The scenery is beautiful and bizarrely varied: from pine forests to black volcanic lava flows – most of which you’ll have to yourself. You can pass hours exploring the rugged coastlines, where volcanic swimming holes such as Charco Azul can be found. We spent a blissful few hours there, relaxing on the rocks and looking out at the Atlantic. There are no big resorts but plenty of guest houses and smaller hotels, and sunshine is almost guaranteed into November. Leo Mark
We stayed in Woolacombe , north Devon, with our three-year-old in October 2023 and the off-season suited us well. The three-mile beach gave us room for proper sandcastle engineering, and the Atlantic offered drama rather than deckchair weather. We watched the sunset turn the sea orange and purple from the hill above the bay. We could walk into the village, then use Woolacombe as a base for Mortehoe and the South West Coast Path . Pack waterproofs as well as sunglasses: north Devon makes no promises. But on a bright autumn day, those enormous sands feel almost privately hired. Katharina Parsons
Funchal on Madeira is my pick for an autumn escape because it still feels properly alive after summer. The seafront is made for slow walks in the sunshine, with cafes and gardens open year-round. You can browse the colourful Mercado dos Lavradores , ride the cable car for views over the terracotta rooftops and Atlantic, then cool off at one of the city’s lidos. The weather is pleasantly warm rather than overpowering, while the mountains and levada (aqueduct) walks are within easy reach. It combines coast, culture and dramatic scenery without feeling like a resort that closes down for winter. Bernice
If you’re looking for a cracking wee coastal escape, head straight to St Abbs in the Scottish Borders. My wife and I absolutely fell in love with its rugged charm and bonny views. First off, Marvel fans will know it as New Asgard from Avengers: Endgame, and taking a selfie by the official sign set the right tone. Beyond the film fame, the dramatic clifftop walk up to St Abb’s Head is brilliant, packed with seabirds and proper fresh sea air. Afterwards, grab a fresh crab roll down at the harbour cafe – nae hassle, just proper good cheer. Craig
Autumn came brutal and early to Crete this month. But the ferocious northerly that drenched the northern coast got stuck on the White Mountains. And on just one tiny south-west speck of the island, the sun shone all and every day. Palaiochora is a year-round magic place anyway. No big hotels. Still proudly Greek. A place where the town’s rhythms are set by the comings and goings of the Loutro ferry. But this past week, while thunder stalked the mountains, we swam and walked every day. “We’re unique,” said the man at the cafe. “Please don’t tell anyone.” What have I done? Kay Jones
For an autumn city break, Zaragoza comes alive during the Fiestas del Pilar in October. We spent a week there, wandering bustling streets lined with people, many in traditional dress, queueing to lay flowers at the vast floral tribute to the Virgin Mary in Plaza del Pilar. Along the river, food stalls served Aragonese specialities, from chistorra (sausage) and stews to roast chestnuts and sweet wine. Between festivities, we explored the stunning Aljafería Palace and discovered tiny tapas bars tucked down side streets. The city felt wonderfully local, lively and full of surprises. Carrie

title: ‘A candlelit spa, followed by an ice-cold plunge and a nightcap’: readers’ favourite European wellbeing breaks
description: From a historic bathhouse in Sweden to forest bathing in Croatia, readers share their favourite places to relax and recharge • Tell us about a small European ski resort – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher Tucked away off a pretty shopping street in a beautiful art nouveau building is one of Stockholm’s oldest spas, Centralbadet where a day ticket costs from £23. content:
From a historic bathhouse in Sweden to forest bathing in Croatia, readers share their favourite places to relax and recharge Tell us about a small European ski resort – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher
Tucked away off a pretty shopping street in a beautiful art nouveau building is one of Stockholm’s oldest spas, Centralbadet where a day ticket costs from £23. As winter darkness descends, candles are lit around the pool and a quiet calm envelops you. Swimming by candlelight is a treat. Next a sauna followed by an ice-cold plunge. Afterwards a nightcap is in order so it’s a brisk walk in the cold crisp air to Fotografiska restaurant. It’s a great spot to savour one of Stockholm’s best views; the old town Gamla Stan and the twinkling lights on Lake Mälaren. Sarah Rochfort
Birdwatching at the Cley and Salthouse marshes in Cley-next-the-sea, Norfolk. The two bird hides are meditative and relaxed spaces. The windows open directly on to the pools of saltwater where many different species of birds obliviously wander around. It’s a place that is completely timeless and immersive. Your only job is to gaze out at the birds. It’s a very popular spot for birdwatching but the atmosphere is friendly and quiet. Someone even let us have a go with their binoculars. We particularly enjoyed watching a nest of baby swallows huddled in the corner of the hide. The marshes cover a wide area and are so important for biodiversity, providing an essential resting place for resident and migratory birds. You might even spot a spoonbill, which have returned to the UK from 2010 after being absent for hundreds of years. Well worth a wellness visit, even if you don’t really know anything about birds (like me). Petra
A fresh ginger concoction, orange slices and a friendly sauna master greeted us at the Hello Outdoors shepherd’s hut sauna , which has a picture window overlooking the historic Lymington Sea Water Baths . The deep blue of the sky and water, Swedish sauna hats, the calming scent of our chosen essential oil, a soothing soundtrack and the option to ease the sauna heat with an exhilarating plunge in an ice-cold tub or more genial dip in the sun-warmed sea baths made for a very enjoyable and restorative couple of hours away from real life. We didn’t want to leave. Claire Edwards
For five days in Radoboj, northern Croatia, we forest-bathed beneath the trees, walked slowly, practised breathing and meditation and ate simple local food. No luxury spa, no expensive treatments – just nature and time. I wore an Oura smart ring throughout. My resting heart rate fell markedly and, by day four, the ring recorded four and a half hours of restorative time. More importantly, I felt profoundly different. It completely overturned what I thought wellness travel was. Sometimes the most restorative place isn’t a spa. It’s a forest. Bex Hamilton
The natural mineral springs in Sofia mean bathhouses are a way of life. Bankya is on the outskirts of the city, so I travelled by bus to visit the Central Mineral Bath Bankya . This opulent bathhouse is owned by the Sofia municipality, meaning the atmosphere is a mix of the everyday council baths and extraordinary architecture from the early 20th century. You can visit from under €10 and, as well as the promised health benefits of the natural spring water, there is a thermal zone, a salt room, aromatherapy, saunas and steam rooms with an array of massages too. Sarah Collings
While skiing in Zakopane, Poland, we made a lot of use of Terma Bania , an incredible pool and spa centre right in the heart of the ski resort. There is something magical about watching the sun go down in blissfully warm water and surrounded by snow. There is an astonishing array of saunas, pools and steam rooms, surrounded by mountain views. We discovered there are also several thermal pool and spa complexes in the surrounding area, and ended up spending as much of our holiday in the spas as we did on the slopes! Frances
The Lochside Sauna at West Coast Wellness (£17 for 2.5 hours) in Evanachan sits on the shore of Loch Fyne. Hidden away from the single track road, a 10-minute walk takes you to one of the most peaceful saunas in the UK. From the giant window, sit back and watch the water of the loch (keep an eye out for dolphins), slowly preparing yourself to make the short walk down and take a dip in between the heat. Alternatively there is a cold water plunge which if anything is colder than the loch! The centre also offers yoga and pilates sessions and there’s the delicious Inver restaurant just around the corner. Lewis
Wild swimming at Pool Bridge Farm guarantees a wholesome retreat from the vibrant bustle of neighbouring York. Transformed from old fishing ponds, the sprawling site comprises four lakes and ample space for lounging and lunching. A revitalising dip is best paired with a stop in the sauna (£16.50), priming those brave enough for the raw, heady thrill of the next plunge. To top it off, head to nearby Wheldrake Ings nature reserve , one of North Yorkshire’s top wildlife destinations, especially for waterfowl. As the flood waters rise from autumn, so does the abundance of migratory birds. A serene natural scene to soothe the soul. Fin
My two teenagers and I stumbled on a wellness experience for the mind, body and soul while we were wandering around the Black Forest near our holiday base of Freiburg last summer. A friendly German walker with a tree branch for a stick and a large husky for a companion told us to try a barefoot sensory trail at Park mit Allen Sinnen (park of all the senses) as we walked along together through the forest. So we followed his advice. It involved walking barefoot over grass, sand, woodchips, stone, mud and more while trying to tune into our five senses. We began by putting our hands into hollowed-out trees with our eyes closed to guess what objects were placed there. There were bright, colourful flowers, natural scents to imagine and huts to relax and sit in full of sounds and smells to immerse ourselves in with eyes closed. We repeated these walks for three days, heightening our contact with our own senses – and treating ourselves to rye bread and cheese sandwiches with forest fruits berry juice from simple forest cafe cabins as a reward. Helen
If you find yourself on the wild coast of south County Donegal, head to the Sliabh Liag Sauna at Teelin pier. After a day of hiking (and maybe one or two pints of porter the evening before), the small wood-fired sauna right on the pier was the perfect unwind. We followed it up by taking a sea dip in the bay just steps away. If you have plenty of time, combine the sauna with a nearby boat trip to the unforgettable Sliabh Liag sea cliffs towering 601 metres (1,972ft) above the sea. Peter Henry

title: I travelled all over the country on a €63 monthly rail pass: readers’ favourite holidays in Germany
description: From cycling in Berlin and the Black Forest to world-class cocktail bars in Cologne and magical North Sea beaches, readers share their travel tips • Tell us about a sunny autumn break – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher In an often overlooked corner of Germany, near the Dutch border, Münster is an absolute gem. Covered porticos will convince you you’re in northern Italy, gothic churches will remind you you’re in Mitteleuropa and the buns from Zeit für Brot will insist you’re in heaven. Nature-lovers can take in the Botanical Gardens and relax by the Münstersche Aa river. Those of a historical bent can peek into the room where the Treaty of Westphalia was signed in 1648 and mull the report card of nation states in the nearly 400 years since. But really, it’s a great place just to drop-anchor and lose a few days. Jeremy Continue reading...
content:
From cycling in Berlin and the Black Forest to world-class cocktail bars in Cologne and magical North Sea beaches, readers share their travel tips Tell us about a sunny autumn break – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher
In an often overlooked corner of Germany, near the Dutch border, Münster is an absolute gem. Covered porticos will convince you you’re in northern Italy, gothic churches will remind you you’re in Mitteleuropa and the buns from Zeit für Brot will insist you’re in heaven. Nature-lovers can take in the Botanical Gardens and relax by the Münstersche Aa river. Those of a historical bent can peek into the room where the Treaty of Westphalia was signed in 1648 and mull the report card of nation states in the nearly 400 years since. But really, it’s a great place just to drop-anchor and lose a few days. Jeremy
In the verdant countryside near Düsseldorf, the 129-year-old Müngsten Bridge, the country’s highest railway bridge, rises 107 metres above the River Wupper. The impressive iron and steel structure is billed as Germany’s answer to the Eiffel Tower (yes, really!) and if you’ve got a head for heights, you can don a harness and make the exhilarating climb to the highest point. You’ll be rewarded with incredible views across the valley, especially if you steel yourself (!) for the nerve-racking walk across the narrow beam that spans the top of the bridge. Eat your heart out, Sydney Harbour Bridge. Bex
Sylt is more than a North Sea island to us. My German grandmother met my British army grandfather, and Sylt became my mother’s childhood island. It feels made for cycling, with peaceful paths winding between grassy dunes, sweeping beaches and little villages. Spend the day riding, watching the surfers and eating warm Nutella crepes by the sea, before settling into a traditional hooded Strandkorb (hooded beach chair) to listen to the waves. Bike hire costs €8-€10 per day . It is wild, windswept and magical, somewhere our family history becomes real every time we return. Fay
Get the Deutschlandticket ! An entire month of public transport for €63 – buses, trains, trams, ferries ... The only thing that isn’t included is faster long-distance trains, but you can figure out how to get from A to B using the Deutsche Bahn website, which has a special “Deutschlandticket only” filter; the need to change trains means you’ll end up discovering places you wouldn’t otherwise visit. It’s worth it just for a week, or, if you do want to travel long distances quickly, just for inner-city transport. Use the German public transport app Mopla to buy one at any time. Joseph
Cologne’s famous cathedral dominates the skyline and tops most travel itineraries. But having visited for a day on a previous trip, we returned for a city break with one thing in mind: cocktails. The mixology scene here is world-class. The jewel in the crown is Seiberts (pictured), which often and rightly features in lists of the world’s best bars, but Little Link , Woods and Ona Mor all contend and offer different vibes. While not sat at the bar, you’ll find excellent 20th-century art, street art and a lifesized Milka cow at the chocolate museum. John
On a warm autumn afternoon in Berlin, a friend and I rented classic Dutch bikes to explore the city. As the golden hour approached we discovered Tempelhofer Feld . Used as an airfield during a darker era, today it’s a vast recreational green space. Biking on the disused runway was enjoyably bizarre. Berliners and visitors alike were picnicking, kite flying, inline skating, lolling about on bales of hay, skateboarding, tightrope walking, birding … you name it. It is also an important site for rare flora and fauna and grazing animals. Sarah
Ebikes are the perfect way to explore the beauty and vastness of the Black Forest. Powering up gravel tracks that would be impossible on a push bike was so fun and a real hit with the teenager. Setting off from the astonishingly well preserved town of Gengenbach, we headed to the viewpoint at Moosturm observation tower and the Lothar Monument (pictured), where we were rewarded with a glorious 360-degree view of hills patterned with colour and wisps of cloud. On the way down it seemed churlish not to stop at the Naturfreundehaus Kornebene mountain hut and restaurant for possibly the best sausages of my life. A thoroughly deserved reward: ebiking counts as exercise, right? Alex
Görlitz, near the Polish border, merited more than just the day trip I had planned from Dresden so I returned later in my holiday to explore its delights. It’s chock-a-block with charming, colourful buildings, making it beloved of German and international film-makers. Strolling through the cobbled streets of the old town is like leafing through a lavish picture book of 500 years of German architecture, from gothic through the renaissance to art nouveau – don’t miss St Peter’s Church . Eat hearty Silesian sausages at beer houses and if you feel like a swim head out by bus to Lake Berzdorf, with views of the mountains from the sandy beach – or even the middle of the lake where I ventured to. April
When my son turned 16 we drove to Munich so he could buy his first beer legally. Breaking up the journey we stopped overnight near the Nürburgring racetrack, to take the family estate car around the Nordschleife circuit. You turn up, pay €30-€35, and get in the queue. We were overtaken by everything apart from a coach full of Italian tourists and an ice cream van. Tim
The unexpected highlight of our German road trip was Kassel’s extraordinary Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe , a Unesco world heritage site. On water feature days, park below Wilhelmshöhe Palace (€8.50 per car, including bus travel for up to seven), ride to the Hercules monument, then follow the water downhill on foot. The free spectacle sends 750,000 litres tumbling without pumps through baroque cascades, waterfalls and a Roman-style ruined aqueduct, culminating in a soaring 52 metre fountain. Following the rushing water from one dramatic stage to the next was an adventure, and after the 2.3km descent, your car is waiting at the bottom. Mary
