content:
I love exploring Poland by rail. When I heard about a new back-to-the-80s service, I booked a retro seat …
T rainspotters jostled on platform 2 as sunshine lit up the polished olive-green carriages of the 11:07 from Warszawa Główna (Warsaw main station) to Poznań. As I was readying to board, a man, sporting bow tie and braces, zipped past me, making it to the steps first. Excitement was palpable. But then this was no ordinary train, but rather an event. A throwback in time.
The Polish parliament had declared 2026 as the Year of Polish Railways, and there is a double jubilee under way: the 25th anniversary of the long-distance operator PKP Intercity and the centenary of Polish state railways. To celebrate, a series of retro rail journeys called Nieśpieszny (“Unhurried”) has been launched.
Every weekend over the spring and summer (at least until the end of August, with more departures likely), a fully refurbished train from the 1980s, with livery matching the era, departs from a different region in Poland, from the mountainous south to the Baltic coast in the north. When my friend Mariusz mentioned this to me, knowing that I take an annual railway trip to his country, I jumped at the chance, booking my ticket to Poznań the day they went on sale.
On board, settling into a marmalade-coloured six-seater compartment furnished with armchair-like seats, I sensed a sociable air; after all, nobody was commuting or in a rush. Our “unhurried” journey would take about five hours compared with just over two on a faster service.
Ready for an early lunch, I stowed my bag and headed off, following the smell of fried sausages to the dining car. The WARS catering company has been feeding passengers on Polish trains since 1948, and our menus and plates for this journey were pleasingly vintage. Having ordered, I squeezed on to a stool next to fellow passenger Anita and her son – who I later worked out was the concert pianist Jan Lisiecki – visiting from Calgary, but with family roots in Gdańsk. “In the 1980s, trains were packed. You’d even have people standing in the toilet. This is nothing,” Anita said.
Tucking into fried eggs, potatoes speckled with dill and a cool cup of kefir, I thought how easy it would be to dismiss the thought of communist-era food, such as we were served, but it was freshly cooked and excellent. I asked another man at our shared table about his soup. “This is flaki , made with tripe,” he said, taking a spoonful.
The landscape we trundled through – wind turbines, Scots pine forests and cabbage fields – was unremarkable. It was the train itself, and its handsome interior, for which we had all signed up. That, and the novelty. Even the windows opened fully, as they once did, allowing us to poke our heads out.
Getting to know Poland by train has provided umpteen enjoyable experiences over the years. I’ve crossed the country by rail, from the industrial but fast-changing city of Katowice in the south to the Baltic port city of Gdynia in the far north, but there is still so much more I want to see: Lublin in the east for its underground brewery and Zakopane for its access to hiking in the Tatra Mountains. I know the trains will get me there. Now, with my phone battery thoroughly dead – in keeping with the theme, there were no obvious sockets to be found – I recalled some highlights.
Sometimes in Poland, the pleasure is all about the railway station itself. Neogothic and completed in 1857, Wrocław Główny, for example, with its stained glass, neon signs from the 1950s and wood-panelled ticket counters, is worth a visit alone.
Joy also comes from stopping somewhere purely because doing so works with certain routes and timetables. That was the case when I visited Toruń in north-central Poland. After disembarking the train, and crossing a bridge by foot over the Vistula River, a gloriously panoramic view of the medieval old town began to open up. Shortly after, I wandered into a small museum dedicated to the city’s globetrotting son, Tony Halik, a celebrated adventurer and reporter. Old photographs showed him driving his Jeep from Argentina to Alaska between 1957 and 1961.
The next day on that previous trip, after taking the train from Toruń north to Gdańsk Główny – another photogenic station with its clock tower and copper-clad turrets – I switched trains again for a 20-minute hop to Sopot, a small resort city on the Baltic Sea. A walk by sea buckthorn bushes took me to Bar Przystań and its famous fisherman’s soup featuring halibut, salmon and herbs. It was there, too, I bought my first jagodziank a , Poland’s famous blueberry-filled bun, the taste of summer and very delicious, before boarding the train to Katowice.
Back on the current retro train, and with just 45 minutes to go before our arrival at Poznań, I returned once more to the lively dining car. The queue was just as long as before but the staff were friendly as ever. The apple pie was generously fruity. As I winced at sipping the harsh grainy coffee, my neighbour said: “That’s the old, traditional stuff – still the only coffee my grandma drinks.” Another nod to the past, and thus forgivable.
I was not keen for the journey to end, but eagerly anticipating my return to Poznań. A train had delivered me to the city a couple of years ago, when I had fallen for its general buzz and energy, its Palm House – one of Europe’s biggest greenhouses – and the atmospheric milk bar Pod Arkadami, but I had run out of time for the Croissant Museum . A trademark of the city, Poznań’s St Martin’s croissants, AKA rogale świętomarcińskie , are iced and have a white poppy seed filling, and the museum has baking classes.
Our unhurried train contrasts sharply with the rapid development of modern rail services in Poland. To keep up with demand, disused carriages are being revamped and others are being sourced from abroad. Plus, in February, Poland won the 2026 Rail Champion award in Brussels for its contribution to the development of rail transport in Europe. When the future is this promising, surely there is nothing wrong with indulging in some good-natured nostalgia, bitter coffee and all.
Nieśpieszny journeys cost from £20. Koleo , a mobile app and website, is useful for navigating Poland’s railway system

content:
The reopened Train de Merveilles route takes passengers from the glamour of Nice to a grandiose alpine landscape
N ine-thirty on a sunny Tuesday morning, and the platforms at Nice-Ville station are buzzing. Office workers nudge their way past backpackers, passengers clamber on to trains heading east to Monaco and Italy, or west to Antibes and Cannes. My husband and I, however, are heading away from the glittering coastline and boarding the Train des Merveilles (Train of Wonders) into the Alpes-Azur mountains .
Back on track last December after a programme of major works closed the line for a year, it’s one of the most spectacular train routes in Europe, a two-hour journey that climbs 1,000 metres in 100km, linking Nice with the medieval town of Tende, surrounded by the soaring peaks of the Mercantour national park .
It’s barely 10 minutes before the suburbs of Nice begin to melt into low hills, scattered with auburn-roofed villas and copses of chestnut trees. Once the ascent begins, it’s easy to see why maintaining the line, begun in 1883, is a serious task. More than 100 bridges and viaducts – and almost as many tunnels and retaining walls – stitch the track together, along with ingenious helical loop tunnels, which gain altitude by following a series of bends inside the mountain itself.
It’s a breathtaking ride, the hills gaining height and heft, until a great mountainscape begins to unfold before us; jagged peaks that make the valley road below seem little more than a thin sliver of ribbon.
Many passengers ride straight up to Tende and set off to hike the mountain trails that lead off from the town. But we want to see a little more, and disembark first at Sospel, a medieval town where the 13th-century Pont-Vieux straddles the Bévéra River. It’s market day and, even in such a small town, there are flower and vegetable stalls, great wheels of cheese and delicious looking breads. We stroll the quiet streets, past crumbling baroque churches and gothic-style houses. It’s amazing to think we are barely an hour from Nice – it feels like we’ve been transported to an entirely different region of France.
The higher we go, the more the feeling of stepping back in time grows. At La Brigue, the gateway to the Mercantour national park, the tangle of medieval streets feel barely raised from their winter sleep; the town only really comes alive in summer, when the hikers arrive. La Brigue’s claim to fame is the Chapel of our Lady of Fountains , a couple of miles outside the town. Named for the seven springs that trickle through the rocks nearby, parts of the church date back to the 13th century, when, legend has it, villagers built it as a sign of gratitude to the Virgin Mary after prayers for a new water source for La Brigue were answered. While the facade is unassuming, the interior is truly extraordinary; its walls and ceiling are covered in 15th-century frescoes by Giovanni Canavesio that are so vivid the church is sometimes called the Sistine Chapel of the Southern Alps.
By the time we arrive in Tende, where the houses cling to the mountainside, we are 800 metres above sea level and there is nothing but wooded slopes leading to high peaks and a crisp, clear silence. We follow the modern main street through the clustered, medieval houses of the old town up to the ruins of Chateau Lascaris , where the views stretch to the distant peaks of the Marguareis massif, the last mountains before Italy. It’s quite a pull, and afterwards we reward ourselves with mammoth croque monsieurs at Stella Alpina – part outdoor equipment shop, part rustic eaterie. Around us, hearty looking chaps in Lycra cycling tops are tucking into pints of lager and platters of local cheese and cured meats.
Much restored, we dip into the Musée des Merveilles , where we learn (through our fractured French) that the area is home to one of Europe’s largest Neolithic and Bronze Age rock-engraving sites. The town’s more recent (relatively speaking) history is tied to the Salt Road, a mule train route between the Piedmontese Alps and the Ligurian coast, used from the middle ages until the 18th century. Built as the last French stop-off along the trade route, it partly explains why a town of such a size was located in such an isolated, mountainous location.
Next morning, we’re back in Nice, from where we head along the coast to Antibes. It’s such a bonus, being able to explore so easily; 40 minutes later, we’re strolling past gleaming yachts in the marina and on to the 16th-century ramparts, to sit in the sunshine and watch the kitesurfers whisk across the bay. We head to a restaurant on the Place Nationale, where I eat crispy fritto misto (mixed fried seafood) and try to ignore my husband tucking into buttery, garlicky snails. The following day we take the 10-minute hop east for lunch in Beaulieu-sur-Mer, where the streets ooze belle epoque glamour, and the Plage de la Petite Afrique makes the perfect spot for a paddle and a pile of mussels, thick with cream and garlic.
Food, inevitably, plays a big part in our time in Nice too. As touristy as the old town is, we find two absolute gems; a recommendation sends us to Acchiardo (on Facebook ), where the fourth generation of the Acchiardo family serves up classic local dishes such as daube Nicoise – a rich, slow-cooked beef stew and duck breast with fig sauce. The second, Les Bar Des Oiseaux (on Instagram ), we simply stumble across. It’s a classic bistro, with wood panelling painted with flawless reproductions of artworks by everyone from Joan Miró to Paul Klee and Roy Lichtenstein. My bourride (a traditional Provençal fish stew) was one of the most delicious things I’ve ever eaten.
And that’s the beauty of Nice. It’s both a destination itself and a gateway to very different worlds, all of them just a train ride away. The Train des Merveilles is unarguably the highlight; those extraordinary twists and turns, the grandiose scenery, wild and untouched, so different from the busy streets of Nice. But to pack all of it into one short trip is to make the very most of this diversely beautiful region; a trip des merveilles indeed.
The trip was provided by Mama Shelter hotels and the Nice Côte d’Azur tourist board . Doubles at Mama Shelter Nice from £114 B&B . The Train des Merveilles runs daily from June-September, with an onboard guide on the 9.30 departure . A regional rail day pass with Ter Zou! , including the Train des Merveilles, is €20

title: £3,500 and no work done: the offer to help that’s really a roofing scam
description: Citizens Advice warns of its No 1 scam as growing number of people are targeted by criminals posing as roofers The builder who calls at your door says they are doing some work in the area and has spotted a loose tile on your roof. They offer to fix it for a good price that you agree to. But when they go up on their ladder to inspect the problem, they see another problem. Rain has been splashing out of the gutters and the wood around them is getting damaged. The only solution, the builder says, is to have rigid PVC trays installed to divert the water. content:
Citizens Advice warns of its No 1 scam as growing number of people are targeted by criminals posing as roofers
The builder who calls at your door says they are doing some work in the area and has spotted a loose tile on your roof. They offer to fix it for a good price that you agree to.
But when they go up on their ladder to inspect the problem, they see another problem. Rain has been splashing out of the gutters and the wood around them is getting damaged. The only solution, the builder says, is to have rigid PVC trays installed to divert the water.
More rain is forecast and you are worried about what damage could be done so you pay the builder via bank transfer to get the job done there and then. They are gone within an hour, having apparently completed the work.
But nothing was done because there was no problem with your guttering. Instead you were one of a growing number of people who have been targeted by criminals posing as roofers, only to make off with payment after doing unnecessary or no work.
The charity Citizens Advice says suspected roofing frauds were the top scam it heard from consumers about in the last year. It received more than 2,200 complaints of suspected roofing scams in the year to August in England and Wales, about 10% more than the previous year.
“The vast majority of cases is … somebody just knocking on your door saying that they’ve noticed that there’s something wrong with your roof and they’re in a position to help you,” says Ruwani Purcell, the director of external affairs at Citizens Advice.
“The difficulty is [that] your roof is out of sight and out of reach. You can’t fully see what’s going on.”
Purcell says the fraudsters use really persuasive tactics to offer you confidence and reassurance that they know what they’re talking about. “And you might not be familiar with [the] terms,” she says. “In the worst case scenarios, they’ve been quite intimidating to compel people to hand over money there and then.”
While more than three-quarters of the roofing scams reported to Citizens Advice start with someone knocking at the door, some criminals look online for potential victims.
In one case dealt with by Citizens Advice, a 65-year-old woman posted on an online platform that she needed someone to fix a dripping sound in her gutters. A builder phoned her to say that it would cost £250 but when he and another man came and examined her roof they said they had discovered more problems and the price quickly grew. At one point they showed her a bucket of cement and said it was crumbling from under the tiles.
The woman said the man and his accomplice said the work needed to be done immediately and once they claimed to have finished they wanted the payment straightaway.
“I was afraid, two men in front of me in the dark, demanding money and making it clear they weren’t moving,” the victim told Citizens Advice. “They knew I was alone, I didn’t feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500.”
She paid it using bank transfer. “The next day there was no trace that any work was done,” she said. “I felt stupid, and tried to contact them, but couldn’t get through.”
Be wary of anyone offering unsolicited work by cold calling and demanding confirmation of a job and payment there and then. No reputable builder will do that, says Purcell.
To check the roofer’s authenticity, ask for references and for all proposed work to be confirmed in writing. Treat it as a red flag if they refuse this or if they insist on being paid in cash.
To see if a trader is reputable, you can check your local council’s website as it often lists trusted traders. The government runs the TrustMark scheme which lists approved tradespeople.
Citizens Advice says that if a trader has done a poor job without reasonable care and skill, the victim is entitled to ask for the problem to be fixed or get a refund under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Keep any paperwork and receipts, take photos and document what happened to make your case.

Unfortunately, this was not a failure of your memory but a calendar phishing scam. You have handed your name and password to fraudsters who will sell it on in a batch with other people’s details, use it to break into your work email, or to persuade you that they are contacting you from your bank , or another institution.
Luke Wescott, a threat detection engineer at Sublime Security, says calendar phishing is still relatively new but the company has seen “exponential growth”.
The scam takes several forms, including a fake meeting, or a prompt to renew a service you pay for. In all, an entry appears in your electronic calendar.
It ends up there after scammers send an email to your work, or personal address, with a calendar request. It doesn’t matter if you miss it, or it ends up in your spam folder.
“Calendar apps, such as Google Calendar, can add invitations automatically without users even accepting them,” Wescott says. “So scammers don’t even need you to open an email.”
And while you may not look twice at one from someone whose name you do not recognise, when something turns up in your calendar you may treat it differently. “It can create a borrowed credibility by showing up in the same place as your dentist appointment or a weekly 1:1 with your boss,” he says.
Max Gannon, an intelligence analysis manager at the cybersecurity company Cofense, says some scammers are using legitimate platforms such as Zoom to send the invitations, making them look more convincing to the recipients, and to security software.
“That makes it really hard to block,” he says. “Even AI-backed blockers struggle.”
If you set up something to filter out invitations from these platforms, he says “that would also block any legitimate meeting invitations”.
You will receive an email and see an entry in your calendar. The titles vary: examples seen by the Guardian include fake meetings, notifications of voicemail messages, and software renewals.
Wescott says this is standard. “We typically see stuff like ‘New voicemail received’, ‘Payment receipt confirmation – $298.99’, ‘PayPal unusual activity’ warnings, ‘Your auto-payment will be processed within 24 hours’, and invitations to bid on a contract,” he says.
Gannon says the invitation could look like it has come from within your company. “If they want to they could make it look like an internal invitation,” he says. “They can customise the content, may be adding the logo of your company.”
The event description will typically contain a link, or a phone number.
Wescott adds: “Either they want you to click a link to a fake login page like Microsoft, Google or PayPal, and enter your password, or to call a ‘support’ number to cancel a charge that never actually happened.”
Until you click on this, or make a call, you are not compromised. The scammers do not have access to everything in your calendar – they are just trying to lure you to a place where you will hand over your details.
As Wescott says, “it sounds familiar to typical phishing, it’s the same technique, just using a different delivery method”.
Don’t panic if you see an unexpected meeting or reminder in your calendar. Treat it as you would an unexpected email and don’t click on the link.
“My number one advice is people just need to be paranoid,” Gannon says. “It doesn’t matter if the invitation has come from someone two desks down, you’ve got to be suspicious of everything.”
Wescott advises turning off automatic accepting. In Google Calendar you can go into settings and opt to only accept invitations from known senders, or when you have accepted.
He adds: “Don’t click ‘decline’ on suspicious invites as it can tell the sender that your address is ‘live’. Instead, delete or report it as spam/junk.”

title: ‘They call every week’: the phishing attacks targeting past victims
description: Scammers reuse personal details harvested from fake Esta websites – and texts and calls can keep arriving for months When the British actor Lisa Riley was preparing to travel to the US last year, she applied online for an Esta so she would not need a visa. After finding the site through a Google search she filled in her passport, bank and personal details and waited for the confirmation, which normally takes just under an hour. When it failed to arrive, she emailed an address from the site where she had paid and got back a message unlike any she had seen before, with a link to a website that displayed a jumble of words and letters. Continue reading...
content:
Scammers reuse personal details harvested from fake Esta websites – and texts and calls can keep arriving for months
W hen the British actor Lisa Riley was preparing to travel to the US last year, she applied online for an Esta so she would not need a visa. After finding the site through a Google search she filled in her passport, bank and personal details and waited for the confirmation, which normally takes just under an hour.
When it failed to arrive, she emailed an address from the site where she had paid and got back a message unlike any she had seen before, with a link to a website that displayed a jumble of words and letters.
It was then she realised she had been scammed. But that was just the start of her problems, which persist to this day. She has been repeatedly targeted by criminals, receiving text messages and calls many times every week.
Riley was the victim of a fraud where criminals create websites similar to the legitimate one run by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). After fooling unsuspecting applicants they pocket a fee and use the personal details of victims for later scams.
Riley lost £16 – the cost of an Esta back then – but says there has been a huge increase in the number of scam calls and texts she has received in the 17 months since the fraud happened.
Often the person claims to be from her bank with queries about a money transfer. “Calls are once a week, easy – sometimes twice a week,” she says. “And the texts even more often.”
Research from Nationwide building society suggests that 15% of people have given personal information to something who later turned out not to be genuine, leaving them open to future frauds.
“Criminals do sadly retarget people after an initial scam,” says Annya Burskys, head of fraud operations at Nationwide. “They take the personal information they have gained and either sell it on to other scammers or use them to make follow-up bank impersonation calls , texts and emails appear more convincing.”
The fake Esta site that stole Riley’s personal details looked very similar to the official one and showed up high in search results, she says.
“The webpage was absolutely identical so there was nothing that would remotely make me fearful up until [I realised],” she says.
Criminals can use AI to recreate legitimate government sites and will frequently use key words such as “Esta”, in the domain name to try to portray legitimacy.
A spokesperson for the US CBP says some sites may demand action by the applicant quickly, a common tactic by criminals to try to get people to act without thinking something through.
Only use the official Esta website, which has a .gov address, or the mobile app.
“Applicants should protect their Esta confirmation number and payment details, retain application records, and review financial statements for unauthorised charges,” says the CBP spokesperson.
“Suspected fraud should be documented and reported promptly to the applicant’s financial institution and appropriate local government reporting channels.”
In the UK that means telling your bank and Report Fraud .
If you have inadvertently handed over your personal details you are at risk of future scams, so be alert to unexpected calls, texts or emails, says Burskys.
“Don’t feel pressured to act. A genuine call or message from your bank will never ask you to move money, never ask you to share codes, and will never tell you what to say to your bank or friends, family,” she says.
“Take a moment to verify who you’re speaking to and contact your bank directly using trusted contact information from your bank card or search for the official website if you’re unsure.”

title: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children
description: Criminals are trying to glean login details to harvest players’ in-game currency and personal data Your 10-year-old son has started playing Roblox, when he realises all of his in-game currency, Robux, is gone. When you try to find out what happened, he says he was recently promised extra Robux if he followed a link on YouTube. When he signed on at the site link, he was taken to the Roblox site as usual but there was no sign of the extra currency. Continue reading...
content:
Criminals are trying to glean login details to harvest players’ in-game currency and personal data
Your 10-year-old son has started playing Roblox , when he realises all of his in-game currency, Robux, is gone.
When you try to find out what happened, he says he was recently promised extra Robux if he followed a link on YouTube. When he signed on at the site link, he was taken to the Roblox site as usual but there was no sign of the extra currency.
He has fallen victim to a fraud where Roblox users – many of whom are children – are being targeted for their login details. With those details criminals can steal the virtual currency and players’ personal data.
Within Roblox, players use Robux to buy virtual items, such as skins or animations for their avatar. You can earn the currency within the game, but it can also be bought. At Roblox’s online store you can buy packages costing up to £199.99 .
Using ready-made kits bought on the dark web, fraudsters create a fake login page that is identical in appearance to the legitimate Roblox site.
“The kid will enter their details and the fake website will actually redirect them to a legitimate Roblox page,” says Gerald Kasulis, the vice-president of global affairs at the cybersecurity company NordVPN. “So ultimately, the kid will get to where they want to go.”
By that stage, however, the criminals will have the details they need for defrauding.
Researchers from NordVPN say that over a seven-day period they found almost 200 addresses selling ready-made phishing pages that provided the tools to defraud Roblox users.
Often the links to the phishing sites are in comments on YouTube or TikTok videos or in chats on Discord, the chat app for gamers.
The message might say there are free Robux available if a player clicks on the link provided. Like many scams, there will often be an element of urgency attached, such as the offer apparently only being valid for a few hours, to encourage the victim to act without fully thinking through the consequences.
From that link, the child will be taken to a fake sign-in page that will probably be identical to a legitimate Roblox site in appearance. The address will usually contain the name Roblox, for example “Roblox-verify” or “login-Roblox”.
When they are on the scam site, the child will be asked for their username and password but may also be told to put in two-factor identification codes, says NordVPN. But then the child is taken to the legitimate Roblox site so they can play their games as normal, leaving little indication that anything is amiss.
Once they have the login details, the fraudster may sell them on or use them to transfer Robux to another account.
“One of the simplest habits is to encourage children to open Roblox directly through the official app or website rather than logging in through links they are sent,” says Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN.
“Two-factor authentication remains an important protection, but authentication codes and backup codes should be treated just like passwords and never handed over to somebody else.”
If your player has lost their Robux to a hacker, it seems unlikely that they will get it back. Roblox says that it is under “no obligation” to assist people whose accounts have been compromised, unless it is required to do so by law.
“Roblox does not guarantee that an individual’s account will be restored to its previous state, or that Roblox will be able to recover lost virtual items or virtual currency,” it says.
In “very limited circumstances”, Roblox says it may recover lost items or the value of them.
A spokesperson for Roblox says there are security measures in place to prevent phishing, such as two-factor authentication and a feature that stops criminals logging into your account from elsewhere.
“We continue to work on new ways to minimise the risk of account theft and actively encourage Roblox users to follow security best practices, including not clicking on links or downloading anything from unknown senders or websites,” the spokesperson adds.

title: UK politics: Reform UK claims racism exposé has left some members ‘psychologically damaged’ as it reports ITV to police – as it happened
description: Zia Yusuf claims undercover investigation broke the law as broadcaster stands by its journalism Here is an explainer by Jill Ambrose about the Jackdaw decision. But environmental groups have condemned the decision. Ami McCarthy, head of politics for Greenpeace UK , said: Approving Jackdaw shows the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy. Andy Burnham promised pragmatism [see 8.40am ] , but there is nothing pragmatic about rubber-stamping a project that won’t lower energy bills, won’t boost energy security and will create just 27 full-time jobs … True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates. Is the prime minister living in a parallel universe? One where we haven’t just endured our hottest summer on record, with droughts, wildfires and, in all likelihood, the most heat-related deaths on record? And where the UN hasn’t warned that we’re on the brink of breaching the all-important 1.5 degree warming limit? Shell will be cheering this decision but it won’t knock a penny off our energy bills, which is what’s keeping people up at night, or make a meaningful difference to our gas supply. Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly ten years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely. Continue reading...
content:
Reform UK says it has reported “multiple” ITV journalists, and the company’s board of directors, to the police on the grounds that their undercover reporters working on the exposé of racism in the party broke the law. The party says it will also be suing them for damages.
Zia Yusuf , the party’s home affairs spokesperson, posted this on social media summarising his party’s allegations.
double quotation mark Reform UK has reported ITV, its board, and its undercover reporters to the police.
Some of the crimes carry up to 10 years in prison.
They directly interfered in elections and almost certainly altered the results. Being paid to “canvass” for Reform in crucial wards we lost by a few dozen votes.
They lied to a veteran about their service and left him “violated”.
Scrutiny of political parties is one thing.
But anyone breaking the law to try and ruin the lives of Reform’s staff, members or volunteers will be reported to the police and pursued relentlessly in the courts.
In a video setting out his case against ITV at greater length, Yusuf claimed ITV “psychologically damaged innocent and decent Reform staff and members who were not featured in any documentary”.
As an example of this, Yusuf said that one of the undercover reporters met a Reform UK member in Portsmouth who had served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He said:
double quotation mark One of the undercover reporters told him that they shared the same military background. That was a lie. The marine, believing him, took him for a drink. They spent hours talking about their service, and the marine shared deeply personal stories from the front line because he believed he was talking to a friend and a fellow soldier. He has told us he feels violated.
Yusuf also explained why he was alleging electoral interference. In Portsmouth two undercover reporters were tasked with delivering leaflets in one ward where Reform UK lost in the local elections by 24 votes, and in another ward where Reform UK lost by just 85 votes. Yusuf said these margins were smaller than the number of leaflets the undercover reporters were supposed to deliver.
But he did not assert in the video that they failed to deliver the leaflets, and he offered no evidence that they had done anything to suppress the Reform UK vote at the time.
Asked about the legal threats, an ITV spokesperson said:
double quotation mark ITV stands by its journalism. The programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest. All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme’s producers. Should the police get in touch we would fully cooperate.
People tend to assume that a public interest defence will protect journalists from allegations of minor law-breaking if they are investigating wrongdoing. In fact, the law is more complicated than that, a public interest defence applies in some instances and not in others, and there are probably enough allegations in the Yusuf video to keep a media lawyer busy for days assessing the evidence.
But, in practice, it is rare for the criminal law to be used successfully against legitimate journalists. When the Crown Prosecution Service prosecuted police officers who had taken bribes, and the journalists who had paid them, under Operation Elveden , the officers were largely convicted but the journalists were largely acquitted. Juries seemed to accept they were operating in the public interest.
In the ITV case, the public interest case for the programme is particularly strong. Reform UK has accepted that some of the people exposed making racist comments should not be in the party – although it has also claimed they were not representative of the membership as a whole.

title: Schools in England must recognise antisemitism as distinct category of harm, report says
description: Government expected to accept recommendations of review, which found three in five Jewish students had experienced prejudice Schools and colleges in England will be expected to take a tougher stance against antisemitism after a report found that three out of five Jewish students said they had been affected. Sir David Bell, the former chief inspector of Ofsted who was commissioned by the government to lead the independent review, said he found many cases of antisemitism going unreported or unchallenged by students and teachers. Continue reading...
content:
Government expected to accept recommendations of review, which found three in five Jewish students had experienced prejudice
Schools and colleges in England will be expected to take a tougher stance against antisemitism after a report found that three out of five Jewish students said they had been affected.
Sir David Bell, the former chief inspector of Ofsted who was commissioned by the government to lead the independent review, said he found many cases of antisemitism going unreported or unchallenged by students and teachers.
Bell told Sky News that “a general commitment to tackling racism or prejudice or hate has not properly identified antisemitism as a particular kind of hate”, with the review, to be published on Wednesday, recommending increased awareness and teaching.
“We do need to name antisemitism as a particular kind of prejudice and hate, because I think if you don’t name it, you don’t actually know what you’re tackling or what you’re going to be able to do to respond to it,” Bell said.
The review’s conclusions would require schools and colleges in England to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it.
The government is expected to accept the review’s 27 recommendations, including provision of resources to tackle antisemitism in schools, dedicated teacher training in antisemitism awareness and a national hotline where school leaders can quickly get advice on tackling antisemitism.
Other recommendations include encouraging schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism, as well as strengthening teaching of the Holocaust to ensure that antisemitism is seen as a central theme of the genocide.
Policies on staff behaviour should also make clear that antisemitism is not acceptable, and that all schools and colleges should have “robust” reporting and response procedures.
“This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries,” Bell told the BBC.
Bell added there needs to be stronger guidance on political impartiality for schools so that students can “debate topical and difficult issues without feeling that teachers are imposing their own views on students”.
A survey conducted for the review found that one in five students said they had witnessed antisemitism, and three in five Jewish students had experienced it. However, fewer than half of those surveyed felt it would be addressed if reported.
The review was launched by the government in March, after antisemitic episodes including the attack at Manchester’s Heaton Park synagogue in October last year.
The Community Security Trust (CST), which provides security and support to the Jewish community and schools, has published figures showing rising numbers of antisemitic incidents at schools this year.
In the first half of 2026 the CST found that reports of antisemitism in schools had reached the highest levels it had ever recorded, from 112 incidents in the first half of 2025 to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026.
A spokesperson from the Board of Deputies of British Jews said: “Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children’s safety, and will strengthen accountability.”
Bell’s review will be presented to MPs in parliament on Wednesday.

title: Foamy war? St Andrews students play out modern take on ancient ritual
description: Scottish university’s annual tradition once involved giving out raisins but fancy dress and shaving cream now in vogue Nobody at the University of St Andrews in Scotland seems to remember how Raisin Monday became a giant foam fight. For 600 years, first-year students have taken part in the ritual of thanking older students for mentoring them through their first few weeks of university life. Traditionally, freshers would give their elders a pound of raisins – hence the name. This Monday however, hundreds wore fancy dress as they streamed on to St Salvator’s lower college lawn at 11am armed with cans of shaving foam, covering one another in soapy clouds as they have for the past few decades. Groups of students dress as Smurfs, mice, bananas, grandmas, sunflowers and chefs to participate in the annual rite of passage. Continue reading...
content:
Scottish university’s annual tradition once involved giving out raisins but fancy dress and shaving cream now in vogue
Nobody at the University of St Andrews in Scotland seems to remember how Raisin Monday became a giant foam fight. For 600 years, first-year students have taken part in the ritual of thanking older students for mentoring them through their first few weeks of university life.
Traditionally, freshers would give their elders a pound of raisins – hence the name. This Monday however, hundreds wore fancy dress as they streamed on to St Salvator’s lower college lawn at 11am armed with cans of shaving foam, covering one another in soapy clouds as they have for the past few decades. Groups of students dress as Smurfs, mice, bananas, grandmas, sunflowers and chefs to participate in the annual rite of passage.
The theme for each group is chosen by second- and third-year students, known as “mums” and “dads”, who have been matched with the first years. The proud “parents” stand on the edge of lawn screaming and waving to their “children”. Within minutes, the smell of shaving foam fills the square as cans are emptied over other students. It quickly becomes impossible to distinguish between costumes.
“Traditions like this are much more important because people are less connected face to face than they were before. Getting to do something like this brings everyone together,” says Freya, a first year whose group has been dressed as periodic table elements by their chemistry student parents.
Simon, who is part of the same family, says: “When you are covering each other in shaving foam, how much more bonded can you get?”
Everyone involved recognises that this activity is particularly strange in a crowded field of unusual university rituals. At Merton College, Oxford, students walk backwards around Fellows’ Quadrangle when the clocks go back in October. In Aberdeen, each new rector is carried around campus on the back of a stuffed bull by students.
There is a serious point to the St Andrews ritual at this isolated university on the east coast of Fife, the third oldest in the English-speaking world. More than half of the small town is made up of students – who come from all over the world – and the tradition helps break down barriers between students.
Deborah, an American medical student, is looking out at her academic children in the crowd. Her group has dressed as the blue-skinned supervillain, Megamind, from the animated DreamWorks film. “Because it’s such a small university, we get to have these sort of events. It wouldn’t be feasible at a bigger place. It brings people together. We do not have as many things going on because we are so small, so it helps create community and people you wouldn’t usually meet,” she says.
Sunday has always been a crucial part of the weekend tradition, when first years are woken early, “kidnapped”, and made to take a dip in the North Sea. But in 2026, that is optional. For the Monday foam fight, students are encouraged to donate to a local food bank before they start spraying from their canisters – and appears to be far less alcohol-fuelled than it has in previous years.
After about half an hour, the excited students running around the green begin to slow. The cans of shaving foam are empty and the first years head to the exit to be hosed down despite the single digit temperature. Away from the green, foam-covered students greet their parents with bear hugs, covering them with foam, before heading home for a shower.
“It’s amazing,” says Henry, an American student whose camouflage face paint has been completely covered in foam. “I only really know Americans, so getting to meet people from Singapore, England, South America, Africa and the Middle East through this is great. It’s rare to find a place where you can meet such a diverse group of people.”

title: Youth services in parts of England in state of emergency, children’s commissioner says
description: Rachel de Souza names Middlesbrough and Hounslow among hardest places in which to grow up and says some children are being ‘radically failed’ Services for children in parts of England are in a “state of emergency”, according to a report that identifies what it claims to be the hardest places in the country for young people to grow up in. The children’s commissioner, Rachel de Souza, said in some local authorities individual service failures or systemic problems meant “no child could reasonably be expected to thrive and those that do thrive do so against the odds”. Continue reading...
content:
Rachel de Souza names Middlesbrough and Hounslow among hardest places in which to grow up and says some children are being ‘radically failed’
Services for children in parts of England are in a “state of emergency”, according to a report that identifies what it claims to be the hardest places in the country for young people to grow up in.
The children’s commissioner, Rachel de Souza, said in some local authorities individual service failures or systemic problems meant “no child could reasonably be expected to thrive and those that do thrive do so against the odds”.
She said she had spoken to children on recent visits to schools, youth clubs and young offender institutions around the country and some of the things she had heard and seen had “utterly disgusted” her.
On a recent visit to Middlesbrough, a 14-year-old-girl had informed her of the crime statistics in her area. “Children should not have to know those statistics,” De Souza said.
She added: “Their parents should not have to talk about them over dinner to explain why children cannot play outside. Schools should not have administrative staff dealing with drug overdoses and racist thugs. Nowhere in England should ‘a chase from the police’ be a primary source of entertainment.”
De Souza said she wanted to shine a light on areas where childhood was hardest. “We cannot shy away from the fact that indicators such as poor education outcomes, long health waiting lists or simply feeling unsafe converge in particular places,” she said.
“In some communities, these challenges amount to nothing less than a state of emergency. Not for every child. Not everywhere. But what we see here is a litany of failure. In so many areas of the country, children are being radically failed.”
Her analysis is based on official data covering more than 160 measures, including child poverty, educational outcomes, community safety, NHS waiting times and access to playgrounds.
It names a clutch of relatively deprived areas – Middlesbrough, Hounslow, Bradford, Nottingham, Halton, Peterborough, Leicester, Liverpool, Sunderland and Medway as the hardest places in which to grow up in England.
By contrast, a series of relatively wealthy areas – Cheshire East, Merton, Surrey, Richmond upon Thames, Hertfordshire, Cheshire West and Chester, Haringey, Leicestershire, Central Bedfordshire and Wokingham – are identified as the least challenging places in which to be a child.
“What children across the country feel to be true is in fact true. That it simply is harder to be a child in Middlesbrough than it is in Cheshire … the outcomes are shocking … an unacceptable failure,” the report says.
It adds: “When areas are unsafe, that is not a point on a dashboard, it is children being the subject of racist abuse and violence on the way to school. When local services fail, it is not a failure to hit KPIs [key performance indicators], it is a child on the phone to their school with their parents dead in the other room.”
The report, called The Childhood Lottery , says a north-south divide exists, with authorities in the south more likely to score higher across the metrics, and those in the north more likely to score lower, with the Midlands in between.
De Souza said children should be a priority in the government’s devolution agenda and she urged the government to draw up a series of minimum standards for education, policing, health and youth services. A national fund should be created to invest in areas that fail to hit the benchmarks.
She recommended that every strategic authority should have a deputy mayor for children, accountable for delivering on a “children’s test” ensuring that local policies bring benefits and improvements to young people’s services.
The Department for Education said it was working to improve childcare support and school standards, and it was giving more power to “local leaders” to shape the future of their education.

title: ‘I didn’t know what to do’: collapse of providers of high-end digs leaves students in shock
description: Cost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodation “It was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust. “I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved. Continue reading...
content:
Cost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodation
“I t was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust.
“I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved.
Her sudden upheaval was emblematic of the wider crisis in student housing. While UK universities face a financial crisis , providers of accommodation are grappling with falling international student numbers , a cost of living squeeze and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties.
A string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA), targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty.
It had been touted as the ultimate student living: smart city centre blocks with gyms, cinemas and rooftop terraces have sprung up across the UK. A world away from the traditional image of dirty and dingy shared digs , the flats have offered a spacious alternative for their relatively affluent residents – often international students. Now, some sit half empty, and several schemes have gone bust .
Sriwiboonrattan was among nearly 70 students in Dundee who were left scrambling to find accommodation in late July after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a 116-room city centre block that had a concierge and a shared games lounge with a pool table.
Despite the boom in housing developed by financial institutions in recent years, many students heading off to university this term faced a different dilemma. Rents at the tower blocks have grown much faster than maintenance loans for British students, leaving PBSAs financially out of reach.
Meanwhile, the cost of living crisis has put financial pressure on students seeking university-owned or managed accommodation, while rising rents have hit those wanting to live in shared private rentals. Underlining the scale of the shortage of affordable housing, the students’ union in Bristol included an emergency support number for the housing charity Shelter in an email to new students.
At PBSAs, the national average rent, excluding London, is £191 a week including bills, according to the website StuRents.
At the top end, en suite rooms in Manchester command a weekly rent of £170 to £320 , whereas in London, en suite rooms are £250 to £650 a week , and studio apartments in Bloomsbury cost between £550 and £800 plus.
“I wasn’t able to get into PBSA because it is very expensive in Birmingham,” says Soham Chougale, 23, a student at University College Birmingham. “I am an international student, so my working hours are capped at 20 hours [a week in term time], which means I can’t afford to live in PBSA,” says Chougale, the education officer at UCB Guild of Students .
He lived in university-owned dorms for the first two years of his aviation management degree and now shares a two-bedroom privately rented flat with a friend. On campus, he paid £660 rent including bills a month during the first year, which rose by 10% in his second year; now he pays £700 rent a month, excluding bills.
While living on campus “gave me the best feeling of community” and “I still have those friends that I met on the first day”, the wifi was patchy, some facilities were broken and there was a mouse infestation, he recounts.
“PBSA can be quite pricey,” says Matthew Pointon, a real estate analyst at Capital Economics, but adds: “Normally professionally managed buildings are better in terms of quality.”
In London, which attracts the richest students, there is still demand for upmarket accommodation, but outside the capital, there is an oversupply in some cities, such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham.
This week, university staff began strikes in Dundee, Edinburgh and Nottingham over budget cuts, with the industrial action threatening to wipe out a term of teaching for many students.
In Nottingham, demand has fallen from a pandemic peak of 46,295 beds in 2022-23 to 42,290 beds in 2025-26, while 7,700 more PBSA beds came on to the market, the student housing charity Unipol calculated.
The number of students arriving from China has stagnated, and those from the new growth countries India, Pakistan and Nigeria are much more cost-conscious than the pre-Covid students from China , says Martin Blakey, an adviser on student living and the former chief executive of Unipol.
Deniz Yalçın, the chair of the Newington-Meadows branch of the Living Rent union in Edinburgh, says: “In Edinburgh, we’re seeing an explosion of PBSA despite the fact that this type of development is not needed and actually fuels the housing affordability crisis here.
“Many of them lie empty during most of the year, using the Fringe [festival] to bolster profits. Some have even been bought by the council to become temporary housing.”
Richard Ward, the head of research at StuRents, says the key issue is the big gap between maintenance loans and rents, after double-digit rental growth at PBSA blocks and shared houses in recent years.
Maintenance loans have declined in real terms because of below-inflation increases and frozen parental income thresholds. “And what have we seen? More students commuting ,” Ward says. “Outside of London, you’re talking about £300 rent a week to make a new PBSA scheme viable. Well, your average British student is paying about £160 a week.”
Occupancy rates at the tower blocks range between 71.3% in Glasgow, 69.9% in Coventry, 89.7% in Bristol and 95.3% in Exeter, as of August, according to StuRents.
Student housing providers are increasingly focusing on the cities with the best universities. Unite Group, the UK’s largest developer and manager of student accommodation, has stepped up sales of unwanted sites.
The loss-making group aims to slim down its portfolio to 55,000-60,000 beds in 20 cities compared with 72,000 beds in 29 cities at present, “to increase alignment to the UK’s strongest universities, where student demand is robust and growing”. Unite reduced rents and tenancy lengths in Nottingham, Leicester and Sheffield, the “most challenging” cities, earlier this year, and rooms start from £99 a week in Coventry.
About 95% of new student beds are being built in cities with Russell Group universities, up from 81% last year, according to the property agency Knight Frank, by investors such as Blackstone, KKR and Greystar. The Russell Group is an association of 24 established UK universities including Cambridge, Oxford, Durham, Edinburgh, Manchester and King’s College London.
Smaller PBSA operators are struggling, with average occupancy levels of 85% across the sector, Unipol estimates. The housing association Sanctuary has been trying to sell student assets of more than 5,600 beds, across 21 properties in eight locations across the UK, for nearly two years, and in July said the buyer had “sought to revisit pricing assumptions” citing changes in economic and market conditions.
Investors poured £164m into the PBSA sector between April and June, one of the lowest quarterly levels on record, although total investment of £2.3bn in the first half was ahead of 2025, according to Knight Frank research. Only 13 deals were completed during the second quarter.
In response to the sector’s headwinds, several PBSA owners plan to rent some floors to young professionals, while one block in Leeds that is only 50% full could partly be used for short-term hotel stays .
In Dundee, Sriwiboonrattan has found alternative accommodation – a studio in the nearby Parklands block – which has a sky lounge with city views, gym and rooftop terrace – where she is paying weekly rent of £240, with financial support from her family. At Marketgait, she says the “walls were thin” with noise coming in from neighbours and lifts unreliable, so she prefers her new surroundings now the initial shock has dissipated.
Others still face a bleak picture, with the freshers’ week parties fading into the memory and the academic year now in full swing. Lewis Wilson, the vice-president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says: “The whole system is broken around student finance and student loans. Some students are going homeless, some students are relying on food banks.” A quarter of student unions now provide a food bank or food pantry.
Wilson, who graduated from the University of Sussex two years ago with a law degree, argues that PBSAs need to be better regulated, and become more affordable. “For the students on lower incomes like I was, I would never have been able to afford a PBSA,” he says.
The government says : “We expect higher education providers to consider the supply, and affordability of student accommodation in relation to their anticipated student intakes and across all years of study at least five years ahead.
“Recognising the inherent uncertainties in student demand and housing delivery timelines, providers should engage with the local planning authority on need.”

title: From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schools
description: Ten years after full extent of problem was revealed, Guardian investigation finds schools facing uphill battle amid rapid societal changes Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales It is 10 years since a report first revealed the epic scale of sexual bullying, harassment and abuse girls faced in England’s schools on a daily basis. content:
Ten years after full extent of problem was revealed, Guardian investigation finds schools facing uphill battle amid rapid societal changes
Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales
It is 10 years since a report first revealed the epic scale of sexual bullying, harassment and abuse girls faced in England’s schools on a daily basis.
The report , by MPs on the women and equalities committee, showed the horrifying normality of child-on-child abuse in schools. The need for government action was “overwhelming”, said the committee chair, Maria Miller. Ofsted duly investigated, recommendations were written, promises were made and a new sex education curriculum was rolled out.
A decade later, and six years after the Everyone’s Invited movement began to collect anonymous testimonies from victims, a Guardian investigation has shown the problem persists unabated at schools in England and Wales. In many ways it may be more pernicious as a result of the rise of social media, misogyny and the mass consumption of online pornography by teenage boys.
The freedom of information investigation captures only the most serious incidents; those reported to and recorded by police. Interviews with experts, lawyers and campaigners suggest many more cases never get reported, often because the children involved are under the age of criminal responsibility and the assault is dismissed as “age-related exploration”.
Andrew Lord, a partner with Leigh Day solicitors and a specialist in abuse claims, has dealt with cases of child-on-child sexual abuse in private and state schools, inner-city schools, rural schools, primary, secondary and boarding schools for more than a decade. He says the impact on victims can endure for years and many suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder.
“From my own cases I can see it’s happening up and down the country to children of all ages,” he said. In many instances, however, schools were still struggling to deal with it appropriately. “If you have children in a physical fight, schools know exactly how to react. When you are talking about sexual assault, it’s a different matter.”
Lord is currently representing a secondary school pupil who reported being subjected to a number of sexual and physical assaults by fellow pupils in a changing room. The family is seeking a claim for negligence and breach of human rights against the school for its failure to protect the child.
“Schools do have a duty to ensure that both children [involved in an incident] receive their education, but I am aware of situations where the children continue at the same school and the victim has felt that they have not received adequate support to enable them to engage safely with their studies after disclosing incidents of sexual violence.
“Victims can find themselves being ostracised, which may represent a breach of the Human Rights Act,” he added.
Lord also represents a number of primary school children, including a boy who reported being seriously sexually assaulted by another child on school premises. He was scared he would be hit if he did not comply.
“The biggest issue for me with primary-age cases, when children are below the age of criminal responsibility, is there is often no real statutory investigation and there’s an overreliance on ‘age-related exploration’.”
What typically happens on primary school premises, Lord said, is that a child is taken to a more hidden area by fellow pupils – behind a shed, climbing frame or bushes – is forced to undress and is assaulted, often under threat of being excluded from play and friendship groups.
While most victims of sexual abuse in schools are girls, boys are also targeted. Bethany’s* eight-year-old son was sexually abused on three occasions by a classmate during play dates at her home.
She only discovered what had happened when he began crying at bedtime. She reported it to the school but claims it tried to dismiss what happened as relationship difficulties. “This was not a relationship difficulty. This was sexual assault,” she said. “No one was taking it seriously.”
Her son was never interviewed. There was no proper investigation into what happened and no appropriate safety plan was drawn up to protect her son. “They wanted to sweep it all under the carpet, and that’s not good enough. It was like he was not believed.” In the end, he moved to another school. The other boy remained.
“My son was never treated as a victim in any sense. They offered him no real support. What was worse than the incident itself was how the school dealt with it. It was just appalling. We both felt very, very let down,” said Bethany.
Richard Scorer is another lawyer who deals with civil claims arising from sexual abuse and receives regular approaches from parents, and in some cases teenagers who have suffered child-on-child sexual abuse of various kinds in school.
“We see a lot more of it now than we would have done even a few years ago. As well as a greater awareness, it’s also possible there’s a greater underlying level of abuse and that may have something to do with the pervasiveness of online pornography, particularly in the lives of teenage boys.
“It’s the full range of sexual assault, ranging from unwanted touching to rape. Some of that will take place on school premises, some of it will be off-site. Boys are overwhelmingly the perpetrators. There’s obviously all of the issues around revenge porn and the sharing of intimate photographs – that’s a big issue as well.
“My sense is that schools in some instances are struggling to know how to respond because of the extent of what’s going on and because safeguarding is quite resource intensive. Schools are forced into a bit of a social work role, picking up the pieces from things that are going wrong in society at large.”
Tony Hartney, a school improvement consultant and former headteacher, said awareness around child-on-child sexual abuse was much better in schools and there was a greater willingness to tackle such issues, but they remained “tricky” to handle.
“When there are allegations made like this, schools are very sensitive to the needs of both young people involved to try and make it as viable as possible for them to continue with their education in schools.
“The difficulty of course is things take time. Whilst investigations are going on, you ideally want them to be in schools and to have as normal an education as they can. It’s tricky for schools to manage these situations.”
When she became children’s commissioner for England in 2021, Rachel de Souza knew from her time as a headteacher about sexual harassment and abuse in schools.
“But what I heard as I listened to young people shocked me. Children were viewing violent pornography, it was changing behaviour and peer-on-peer abuse was widespread, normalised and too often brushed under the carpet.
“We have taken important steps in the last few years – from work to bring highly skilled professionals together under one roof to care for child victims of abuse, to action to prevent children from accessing pornography, and a focus on evidence-based relationships education that addresses the realities of teenagers’ lives.
“But as these figures show, we have a long way to go. This is not simply a school or college issue, it is a societal one. We need to address the causes – harmful sexual behaviours are increasingly shaped by the content and cultures that children are exposed to online.
“And we need to urgently improve what happens when young victims of sexual assault speak out and their experience of the justice system, and make sure they get the support they need.”
* Name has been changed for reasons of anonymity

title: ‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technology
description: Patrick McCabe’s herculean feat shows limits and possibilities of special educational needs and disabilities system Patrick McCabe is instantly recognisable in the early autumn sunshine, his wheelchair surrounded by fellow pupils at Fallibroome Academy in Macclesfield, Cheshire as they move from lesson to lesson, chatting, laughing and joking around. His extraordinary GCSE success this summer has become the stuff of legend. The 16-year-old has cerebral palsy and it took four months for him to complete his exams using eye-tracking technology. Now Patrick has started his A-levels – French, business and media studies – and fresh challenges lie ahead. Continue reading...
content:
Patrick McCabe’s herculean feat shows limits and possibilities of special educational needs and disabilities system
P atrick McCabe is instantly recognisable in the early autumn sunshine, his wheelchair surrounded by fellow pupils at Fallibroome Academy in Macclesfield, Cheshire as they move from lesson to lesson, chatting, laughing and joking around.
His extraordinary GCSE success this summer has become the stuff of legend. The 16-year-old has cerebral palsy and it took four months for him to complete his exams using eye-tracking technology. Now Patrick has started his A-levels – French, business and media studies – and fresh challenges lie ahead.
In person, Patrick is impish, thoughtful, articulate, witty, intelligent and honest. Using his augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) device, he tells the Guardian school has been a good experience overall. Born in Switzerland, his family moved back to England when he was six. Since then, he has gone to local mainstream schools, where he wanted to learn like everyone else.
“The best thing has been that, just like my big brothers, I’ve been able to learn and develop skills and gain knowledge of the world around me,” he said. “Even if some days I didn’t always want to go [to school], I think the opportunity to learn has helped me to grow and develop an independent mind.”
It has not been easy. “The most difficult things have been building meaningful relationships, and communication barriers do exist,” said Patrick. “People are not always familiar with Eyegaze technology and are not always willing or able to give it a chance in terms of friendships.”
In many ways, Patrick epitomises the Labour government’s ambitions for students with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). Forthcoming reforms are built on an inclusive approach , keeping children and young people in local – rather than special – schools with all the necessary expertise and support on hand.
But Patrick’s story also illustrates the scale of change required if education and assessment in England are to be truly inclusive. His experience shows that exams are far from accessible to all, his family and school say vital expertise is not always available and – crucially – funding is never enough.
“All we wanted was for Patrick to have the opportunity to demonstrate his knowledge and be given something resembling a level playing field compared to other students,” said the headteacher, Ross Martland. The school and Patrick’s mother, Jo, battled with the exam boards to try to ensure he was given a fair chance.
In the end, it doesn’t sound very fair at all. While his peers spent the first part of the year revising, Patrick’s exams got under way on 2 February and went on every morning until 5 June. It required a herculean effort from him, which left him exhausted, frustrated and sometimes ill.
A 30-mark question that might form just one element of an exam could take up to six hours. Patrick was supported throughout by CandLE, an organisation that helps students using AAC technology to access education across the UK. That he passed all seven GCSEs and achieved the grades he needed to continue into sixth form is testament to his determination.
“Revising for my GCSEs was very exhausting because it took extra time and effort to revise in the first place,” said Patrick. “I felt I had to work harder to express what I know, even when I understand the subject. This was tiring, both physically and mentally. I needed extra breaks to rest, but I still wanted to do my best to show what I had learned.”
Martland is fully supportive of the government’s Send ambitions. “I think the plans are right. Morally and values-wise, it’s absolutely right.” The issue is funding, he said, adding: “I’m concerned it will add significant pressures to schools if it’s not resourced properly.”
Throughout his time at Fallibroome, Patrick has worked with a devoted team of teaching assistants who support him not only with his learning in class but also his personal care. “We are incredibly proud of Patrick and all of our Send students,” said Rachel Crew, one of the teaching assistants working with him.
Patrick says the transition to sixth form is going well. He’s shed the bottle green uniform in favour of a smart blue suit and he says the school is doing everything it can to support him.
He says his mum has been “amazing” and he thinks students with physical disabilities who use eye-tracking technology should be assessed in a more appropriate way, so they don’t face additional barriers. But it is not only exams that worry him. “My concerns remain around friendships, if I’m honest,” he says.
So what’s Patrick planning next? After A-levels, he wants to study media at university. “I find it interesting and I’d like to go into the industry.” His mum tentatively suggests nearby Salford. Patrick’s looking at Bournemouth, 200 miles away. Is he daunted? No chance. “I feel excited about the experience.”
