content:
Online comments reflect class tensions at Scottish university between those from lower-income families and wealthier US undergraduates
W hen Sophie Rose Jenkins announced she would not return to St Andrews University this academic year because of her experiences of classism on campus, she did not expect much of a response. But in the two weeks since she published her story on LinkedIn, it has resonated with hundreds of others.
“Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” the former comparative literature and classical studies student wrote in a lengthy post . “Arriving at a university ranked first in the UK at the time from a background like mine, I thought I was doing everything right.
“I don’t mean for this to be a sob story but an explanation. I recognise the privilege of access to higher education, however I am also brutally aware of the hidden privilege of having unobstructed access to studying for a degree. There is a deep gap between the two, and it is never addressed.”
For many responding, her comments touched on a growing tension at St Andrews, driven by the funding model of Scotland’s cash-strapped universities. Places for Scottish students, who study for free, are capped by the Scottish government and account for about 30% of students at St Andrews. Maintenance loans and bursaries cover basic costs, but those from lower-income families are still often left with less disposable income than their contemporaries – including wealthy international students who pay much higher fees.
St Andrews, ranked second in the Guardian’s university league table for 2026, accepts one of the highest percentages in the UK of privately educated students. The British aristocracy has long adored the medieval town’s cobbled streets, wind-swept beach and grand stone buildings: Prince William and the Princess of Wales met there.
But the recent influx of wealthy US students has changed the dynamic on campus, students say. Americans account for around a fifth of undergraduates at St Andrews, the highest proportion in the UK, with each paying £33,250 for this academic year, more than three times what British students pay.
“My parents were worried about me coming here. They didn’t want me to be left out,” said one Scottish fresher who is on a scholarship to study classics. “Most of the people I have met are international students. I didn’t grow up with tons of money. Maybe they can be a bit ignorant to the cost of things.”
Another said: “There’s a Pret here. You have to ask yourself why that is in such a small town.”
Aspects of fraternity and sorority culture have started to blend with the upper-class experience of British university, some students say. Regular black-tie dinners and balls are now rivalled by fashion shows and exclusive societies. A short walk from the student union bar, an interior design shop advertises luxury bed linen for students, while a popular coffee shop sells designer clothes and candles alongside speciality matchas.
“I totally see her [Jenkins’s] perspective,” said one privately educated student from Edinburgh, who was returning from hockey practice with friends. “It can be quite segregated: the English hang out with the English, the Americans with the Americans. We knew lots of people from hockey already so it’s easy to feel left out if you’re not from that environment.
“The American culture is coming in and it massively influences everything at the moment. They compete with each other. If you look at how they dress, people arrive in lectures as if they are going on a night out.”
One student referenced a well-known student newspaper article published last year about how St Andrews had turned into the Scottish Upper East Side, which said: “Our beloved Scottish town is day by day turning into a microcosm of Manhattan’s elite world; complete with intrigue, privilege, and secrets that spread like wildfire.”
Underlining the point, an American student walks past the student union loudly explaining to a friend: “Everyone is going to think you’re rich if you have a Ralph Lauren bag. But that doesn’t make you rich.”
St Andrews said it had reached out to Jenkins to better understand her experience, but she had decided not to engage for now. It said it had a robust system for reporting complaints from students, and only a handful of complaints had been made in the last five years.
“Yes, some students do arrive here in St Andrews, and at every other university, with immature, offensive and classist views. But they tend not to leave with them,” said the vice-principal Niall Scott.
“This isn’t a St Andrews issue – it’s a societal issue. Classism begins in the home or at school, not at university. Universities like St Andrews have a crucial role to play in challenging these attitudes by bringing together people from different backgrounds, cultures and perspectives, encouraging understanding, respect and inclusion.”
The debate around classism at Scottish universities is not new. In 2024, Edinburgh University offered guidance on how students should treat one another after rising claims of discrimination and classism. “Don’t be a snob!” read the advice given out to students. At St Andrews, some students said the issue of classism was not only linked to the rise in American students.
“It is generally an attitude thing. There is an idea that working-class students can’t speak about issues that are going on elsewhere in the world because they are not as well travelled,” said one science student. “At St Andrews, even for moderately wealthy people, it feels like there is an old money level above that you don’t even get to speak to.”
Rasmus, a Danish student, said he was bemused by the social dynamics at the university.
“It took two weeks for me to meet a Scottish person. They are surrounded by people here who have the money for international tuition, which is quite narrow. I can imagine that being quite a difficult experience,” he said.

title: My critics think speaking fluently is vital for fee-paying pupils, but not for anyone else. Here’s why I reject that | Lucy Powell
description: We are accused of dumbing down, but that’s nonsense: this is levelling up. All the evidence shows helping children articulate improves their life chances Lucy Powell is UK education secretary and deputy leader of the Labour party Private schools don’t leave confident communication to chance. They teach it. Debating, public speaking, presentations, interview preparation. It’s all part of the deal. And parents paying the fees would soon have something to say if it wasn’t. They know that being able to speak up, make your case and hold your own can open doors. I want that for every young person, wherever they grow up and whichever school they go to. This matters now more than ever. Young people are more connected than they’ve ever been, yet too many feel isolated and unheard. Social media is transforming their friendships and relationships. Artificial intelligence is changing the world they will work in. And in an age dominated by screens and algorithms, the human ability to connect, communicate and make yourself heard has never been more important. But the ability to find your voice should never depend on your parents’ income or the school you attend. Lucy Powell is education secretary and deputy leader of the Labour party Continue reading...
content:
We are accused of dumbing down, but that’s nonsense: this is levelling up. All the evidence shows helping children articulate improves their life chances
Lucy Powell is UK education secretary and deputy leader of the Labour party
P rivate schools don’t leave confident communication to chance. They teach it. Debating, public speaking, presentations, interview preparation. It’s all part of the deal. And parents paying the fees would soon have something to say if it wasn’t. They know that being able to speak up, make your case and hold your own can open doors. I want that for every young person, wherever they grow up and whichever school they go to.
This matters now more than ever. Young people are more connected than they’ve ever been, yet too many feel isolated and unheard. Social media is transforming their friendships and relationships. Artificial intelligence is changing the world they will work in. And in an age dominated by screens and algorithms, the human ability to connect, communicate and make yourself heard has never been more important. But the ability to find your voice should never depend on your parents’ income or the school you attend.
Spoken communication is not a soft skill or a bolt on. That is why we are strengthening oracy across the curriculum, from primary to post-16, in all types of lessons and subjects. Being good or not good at these skills affects whether a young person can get ahead. Yet critics have called our proposals a sign of “ dumbing down ” and a departure from high standards. This is hypocrisy. Support for developing these skills has stretched across political divides for years. It’s what we want, but also the wish of Conservatives, such as ex schools minister Nick Gibb and former culture minister Lucy Frazer .
I do not accept a two-tier system where confident communication is seen as essential for children whose parents can afford school fees, but optional for everyone else.
Raising standards means giving children knowledge, and the confidence to use it, hold their own, make their case, seize opportunities and succeed in work and life. And the evidence supports this. The Education Endowment Foundation identifies oral language approaches as among the most effective interventions available , with particularly strong benefits for disadvantaged pupils, delivering six months’ worth of additional progress in primary school and five months in secondary school.
Earlier this week, author Michael Rosen welcomed a rebalancing towards speaking as a key component of how we use language, calling it “a great bridge between the mind and the page”, and the basis of our thinking.
And former general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, Geoff Barton, now chair of the Oracy Education Commission , pointed to high-performing systems in Japan, Singapore and the Netherlands, where pupils in maths, for example, are expected to explain their reasoning, listen to others and defend their approach. Far from lowering standards, he said it makes them better mathematicians.
Employers understand this too. When they talk about work readiness, they mean being able to articulate yourself, work with others, respond to feedback and deal confidently with customers and clients. A recent Chartered Management Institute survey found managers concerned about gaps in workplace readiness, specifically highlighting gaps in communication skills.
The evidence has not changed, the politics has. Because this was never really about standards. It was about who gets the chance to succeed. And if we’re serious about social mobility, raising standards and tackling the fact that one in eight young people are not in education, employment or training, we cannot pretend that the ability to communicate, persuade, present ideas and work with others does not matter.
In a fast-changing world, every young person deserves the confidence to speak up, the skills to be heard and the power to shape their own future.
Lucy Powell is education secretary and deputy leader of the Labour party

title: The Guardian view on schools: the hardest questions for Lucy Powell are about priorities | Editorial
description: The education secretary is right that her job is not to ‘polish the status quo’. Next, she must decide what to change first There is a good case to be made for the increased importance of speaking skills in our new age of machines. With the UK economy’s stronger-than-expected recent performance widely linked to AI investment, it is vital that people are equipped for the kinds of in-person, public-facing jobs that are least likely to be automated. A concerning decline in children’s language development, both in the UK and internationally, has been linked to high screen use. There is a grim irony in a situation where tech companies both compete with humans for contracts and undermine our ability to talk to one other . The Guardian has previously backed efforts to more strongly embed speaking skills, or oracy, in British schools. In a speech on Thursday, Lucy Powell promised to give them equal status to reading and writing in English (education is devolved, so her main responsibility is for England, but there are parallel initiatives in the other nations). Yet with promised updates to the national curriculum postponed, and plans for special educational needs reform causing deep anxiety to families, schools and councils, the hardest questions for the education secretary are about priorities. Following negative feedback from schools, she has also asked Ofsted to look again at its new inspection framework. Continue reading...
content:
The education secretary is right that her job is not to ‘polish the status quo’. Next, she must decide what to change first
T here is a good case to be made for the increased importance of speaking skills in our new age of machines. With the UK economy’s stronger-than-expected recent performance widely linked to AI investment, it is vital that people are equipped for the kinds of in-person, public-facing jobs that are least likely to be automated. A concerning decline in children’s language development, both in the UK and internationally, has been linked to high screen use. There is a grim irony in a situation where tech companies both compete with humans for contracts and undermine our ability to talk to one other .
The Guardian has previously backed efforts to more strongly embed speaking skills, or oracy, in British schools. In a speech on Thursday, Lucy Powell promised to give them equal status to reading and writing in English (education is devolved, so her main responsibility is for England, but there are parallel initiatives in the other nations). Yet with promised updates to the national curriculum postponed, and plans for special educational needs reform causing deep anxiety to families, schools and councils, the hardest questions for the education secretary are about priorities. Following negative feedback from schools, she has also asked Ofsted to look again at its new inspection framework.
The curriculum review completed last year was deliberately cautious, reflecting the Starmer administration’s overall tone. Since then, England’s high scores in maths and science, in international tests, have shown that standards in some subjects have risen. But in English, an overly prescriptive and grammar-obsessed curriculum is putting pupils off. This is the obvious place to start with new speaking skills. The delayed curriculum revisions should set out how it is going to be done.
The energy that Ms Powell brings to the education brief is welcome. She is right to refuse to “sit still and polish the status quo”, especially as the Conservative party seeks to take credit for improvements to English schools that were a legacy of New Labour . The decline of the arts in schools must also be tackled. An improved vocational offer is arguably most urgent of all.
But there is no point denying the challenges around implementation. The government is already committed to the introduction of new maths and English qualifications, to replace demoralising GCSE resits. Reform of the special educational needs system will need to be carefully monitored. Many experts in the college sector believe that the scrapping of BTec qualifications , in favour of T-levels and V-levels, is a mistake. This too needs to be closely watched. A stronger steer from government on universities is also needed. Bridget Phillipson’s decision to unfreeze fees after eight years has only slightly eased their funding difficulties. Reform of unfair student loan terms must come sooner rather than later.
Ms Powell is not unique, among Andy Burnham’s new brooms, in facing a daunting set of challenges. Her pledge to go “further and deeper on curriculum reform” is welcome; the world is changing fast and schools need help to keep up. A strengthened emphasis on the spoken word is just one part of this. But in the coming months, she will need to make decisions about where to put her energies. There are only so many changes, on top of special educational needs reforms, that schools can be expected to cope with.

title: We are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently? | Simon Jenkins
description: The education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculator At last the fourth R is born. Articulation – speaking – is to join reading, writing and arithmetic in the education canon. What has become the mighty struggle against the dictatorship of the screen can begin in earnest. The spoken word, human-to-human communication, must finally be recognised by the gods of reactionary schooling. The pundits call it oracy. On Thursday, the education secretary, Lucy Powell, called the academics’ bluff. She wants a radical reform of the national curriculum in England to reduce “desktop” working in favour of verbal fluency and practical skills . This will take courage. For decades, education’s senior leaders have been ramming easily forgotten “subjects”, such as maths and French, into children’s brains so they can be judged and measured in league tables. These tables have grown ever more dominant as ministers seek to climb “ global rankings ”. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...
content:
The education secretary is right to focus on what students need most: the ability to express themselves. As for maths, grab a calculator
A t last the fourth R is born. Articulation – speaking – is to join reading, writing and arithmetic in the education canon. What has become the mighty struggle against the dictatorship of the screen can begin in earnest. The spoken word, human-to-human communication, must finally be recognised by the gods of reactionary schooling. The pundits call it oracy.
On Thursday, the education secretary, Lucy Powell, called the academics’ bluff. She wants a radical reform of the national curriculum in England to reduce “desktop” working in favour of verbal fluency and practical skills . This will take courage. For decades, education’s senior leaders have been ramming easily forgotten “subjects”, such as maths and French, into children’s brains so they can be judged and measured in league tables. These tables have grown ever more dominant as ministers seek to climb “ global rankings ”.
After the second world war, an “academic” secondary education was shaped by the increased demand for a university-educated workforce. Higher education was expanded, but Britain’s technical and vocational schools and colleges were relegated out of sight . Teaching became enslaved to exam quantification and lost contact with the real world.
But the act of excluding communication skills from this academic orthodoxy has come home to roost. Artificial intelligence and mobile phones are progressively distancing young people from adults and each other. I notice gatherings of young people who used to chatter, laugh and banter. They now stand gazing at their screens or they just shout at each other. Conversation – sharing, informing, discussing, sympathising – seems on the way out.
Speaking itself is going out of fashion. Research suggests that in the past two decades the number of words people say each day has shrunk by nearly a third . They prefer texting. A quarter of young people now say they never even answer the phone unless pre-arranged. They fear a phone call means bad news.
Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage. It is about conveying what one means clearly; listening, debating and handling disagreement. Speaking well means using eye contact and appropriately adjusting your tone of voice. It means politeness and tolerance. Above all, it enables young people to present themselves to others effectively, whether in work, play, argument or friendship.
To the Greeks and Romans, oracy was the towering skill of rhetoric. It was central to citizenship. The New Education movement of Steiner and Montessori in early 20th-century Europe stressed building on the qualities of the individual child rather than imposing rote learning from above. It is significant that the movement has seen a revival in the Waldorf schools now favoured by California’s AI executives in Silicon Valley.
That such ideals of progressive education have long been drummed out of the English curriculum is outrageous. The aversion to the spoken word has corresponded with the increasing prominence of maths in the curriculum, its skills beyond foundational arithmetic irrelevant to all but a tiny minority of adults. Children need to master elementary maths in primary school. But after that they only need to know how to use a calculator. I wonder how many readers remember being able to answer this question from last year’s GCSE paper : “The volume of a sphere is 4/3πr³ where r is the radius. Work out the volume of a sphere with diameter 20cm in terms of π .”
It is extraordinary that passing this exam is still required for most apprenticeships . Yet while he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak wanted maths to be compulsory until the age of 18. Small wonder it has long headed the list of “most hated” school subjects .
Quite how the teaching profession will react to Powell is not clear. The hyper-centralisation of British government has meant ever more school time spent on exams. This has led to cutting back on individualised learning and creativity, which typically flourishes in teaching of the arts. Teachers are pressed to “teach to the test”, at peril of damnation from Ofsted. These days, only the private sector dares resist. Winchester college devotes an hour a day to its form of oracy: “div” and “forum” sessions, when pupils discuss contemporary topics not covered by the examination syllabus: scientific ideas, philosophy, politics, music, critical thinking and the acceptance of others’ opinions.
Such speech-centred concepts as group learning and peer tutoring are being pursued in some universities, and the cause was taken forward in the 2024 oracy commission report . But the catch is always resources. The essence of teaching people how to speak must lie in personal contact. It is in the human relationship of tutor and pupil, which was once the essence of teaching as a profession, not a mechanical skill.
One key might lie in killing maths. Leave it to its enthusiasts. For the rest, school should be about the world outside, a world of other human beings. It is about how to go about handling them that young people have most to learn.

title: ‘This petrol station is my home now’: Malawi’s fuel crisis forces desperate drivers to queue for days

content:
Shortages caused by the country’s lack of hard currency have escalated into a national emergency, with drivers waiting for a fuel tanker that may never arrive
F rom the driver’s seat of his rusted minibus, Sido Sombeja stares out at a stationary sea of rear lights stretching for almost a mile down the road. It is 3am in Zomba, the old capital of Malawi , and cold night air comes through the cracked windscreen. For eight consecutive days and nights, the 40-year-old father of four has lived out of this vehicle, waiting for a fuel tanker that may never arrive.
Sombeja chews on a cold piece of fried mandazi – a doughy snack that has been the only food available. The Meru petrol station is no longer just a place of transit; it has transformed into a makeshift village of drivers in parked vehicles. In these queues, strangers form uneasy alliances. Motorists group together to guard one another’s vehicles during rare bathroom breaks, and coordinate to aggressively block any queue-jumpers. Men sleep under the bellies of trucks. They wash their faces with bottled water on the kerbside and gather around charcoal braziers ( mbaula ) at night.
“This is not a petrol station any more,” Sombeja says, gesturing at the hundreds of dark chassis surrounding him. “It is my home now. It is like I have two families – the one back home waiting for me to bring back money, and this second family of strangers on the road where I must buy snacks just to survive the night.”
Malawi has experienced intermittent shortages since late 2022 but in the past four weeks the problem has escalated into a national emergency. Urban hubs are adjusting to a new reality: a queue economy where the boundaries of labour, community and patience are pushed to their limits.
The roots of this societal paralysis lie in an economic bottleneck. The National Oil Company of Malawi attributes the persistent shortages directly to the country’s lack of hard currency. In briefings before the parliamentary committee on budget on 2 October, oil officials revealed that a surge in domestic vehicle usage meant Malawi now burned through 2m litres of fuel daily, requiring $49m (£37.5m) every month in foreign exchange.
It is a financial burden that the impoverished nation cannot sustain as agricultural exports have collapsed . According to Joan Thaundi, a spokesperson for Malawi’s energy ministry, the petroleum sector must compete with other goods for limited US dollars. As a result, international banks repeatedly leave local letters of credit unhonoured, halting fuel tankers at regional African ports before they can even cross into Malawi.
To manage the escalating panic, the state is taking extraordinary measures. Fitina Khonje, a public relations manager at the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority, says that while fuel procurement is heavily prioritised by the government, the national cash deficit remains an obstacle. The government has liquidated millions in gold reserves to secure short-term credit from international lenders, while withdrawing non-essential state vehicles from the roads to preserve what little fuel remains for core operations.
At the petrol stations, such explanations do little to soothe a frustrated public. The crisis is turning patience into hostility.
At the Petroda petrol station in the capital, Lilongwe, WillKens Chimwaza, a 26-year-old attendant, says that the station’s normal daily operating capacity of 30,000 litres has dropped to 5,000. When that runs dry, usually within an hour of a tanker’s arrival, the mood among waiting drivers turns ugly.
Chimwaza describes being routinely surrounded and threatened by angry motorists, facing a barrage of verbal abuse for a national shortage he has no power to fix. To keep the peace, attendants are told to ration the amount each customer can buy. “It is terrifying,” Chimwaza says. “People are desperate, and they look at us as the gatekeepers who are actively denying them their livelihoods.”
Gift Ngala, a 34-year-old taxi driver operating out of the business district of Mzuzu city, says the scarcity has hit him hard. Ngala has to buy illicit fuel from roadside dealers at inflated prices to keep his vehicle on the road. “The shortages are hitting us hard, and our customers are paying far more than the normal fare because we are forced to source fuel from the black market just to remain in business,” he says. For low-income commuters, fare increases drain household budgets meant for food and basic necessities.
Back in Zomba, the psychological toll of the prolonged crisis weighs on drivers such as Sombeja. His daily minibus routes used to provide a modest but steady income for his family. Now, his earning capacity is frozen.
He urges the authorities to stop politicising the distribution of resources and to stabilise the supply chain. “We are struggling to meet our basic needs,” he says. “They must ensure the fuel is stabilised so we can go back to work.”
As the sun rises over Meru petrol station, it casts an unforgiving light on the exhausted faces of hundreds of drivers stepping out of their vehicles to stretch. No tanker has arrived. Sombeja turns his key, checking his empty dashboard gauge one more time, before settling back into the driver’s seat to begin his ninth day of queueing.

title: The ‘Finger cutter’ and the ‘Brazilian Escobar’: the men accused of bringing cocaine cartels to Europe
description: A Belgian criminal organisation’s links with a Brazilian cocaine gang have been the focus of a major trial in Brussels, where smuggling links have been alleged between European players and the drug cartels of Latin America In the early hours of 7 September, a convoy of heavily armed police swept through the sleeping streets of central Brussels towards the Haren district, on the city’s north-eastern outskirts. author_name: Andrei Netto in Brussels and Paris
content:
A Belgian criminal organisation’s links with a Brazilian cocaine gang have been the focus of a major trial in Brussels, where smuggling links have been alleged between European players and the drug cartels of Latin America
I n the early hours of 7 September, a convoy of heavily armed police swept through the sleeping streets of central Brussels towards the Haren district, on the city’s north-eastern outskirts. They made their way to 22 Avenue du Bourget, a militarised bunker-like complex that was the former headquarters of Nato.
The modernist complex, with its austere and functional architecture, was hastily built in 1967 and houses the Justitia courtroom, where Belgium’s federal trials are now held. It was here that the perpetrators and accomplices of the 2015 Paris terrorist attacks and the 2016 Brussels attacks were tried in 2022.
Last month, officers armed with assault rifles patrolled the building’s wide corridors, protecting those involved in this decade’s most high-profile trial: the Bressers-Carvalho case .
For a month, judges and a legion of lawyers shared the main courtroom with journalists and the public on one side of a large armoured-glass partition. On the other side were the defendants, 31 in number, flanked by officers with their faces masked to protect them from possible reprisals. It was a scene more typical of countries ravaged by mafias.
During the lengthy hearings throughout the month, two among the many defendants stood out. The first was Flor Bressers, a 40-year-old Belgian born in Lommel, a town of 35,000 in the province of Limburg. Bressers has an unusual profile for criminal circles. A criminology graduate of the Free University of Brussels (VUB), he was often known to his peers as “the professor” or “the academic”.
Yet his most commonly used nickname contradicts the image of a refined and scrupulous man: Bressers is best known as “the Finger cutter ”.
Arrested in 2022 at a wine tasting with his wife in a penthouse of the luxury Renaissance Zurich Tower Hotel, Bressers has been facing charges of kidnapping, unlawful detention, extortion involving firearms, and leading a criminal organisation.
The other key figure alleged to be in the criminal organisation is a 68-year-old Brazilian: Sérgio Roberto de Carvalho. In a joint operation involving Interpol, Europol, the Brazilian federal police and the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Carvalho was arrested on 21 June 2022 at a luxury hotel overlooking the Danube in the Hungarian capital, Budapest.
Based in Mato Grosso do Sul, a Brazilian state in the tri-border region of Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay, which is one of the continent’s centres of organised crime, Carvalho became known in his own country by the nickname “Major” , from his rank when he was a military police officer, a past life in which he blended corruption and crime. In Europe, his moniker was more revealing: “the Brazilian Escobar”.
Together, the Finger cutter and the Brazilian Escobar are the main defendants in a Belgian courtroom bristling with security as the international cocaine trafficking network between Latin America and Europe is put under the spotlight.
Bressers and Carvalho are alleged to have been behind an organisation suspected of transporting up to 45 tonnes of cocaine to Europe .
Prosecutors said they led a lawless multinational operation that moved hundreds of millions of dollars through front companies, one of which, the Antwerp water treatment firm Kriva Rochem , has given the case its alternative name.
The money – allegedly laundered through cryptocurrencies, financial markets and property – financed the complex logistics involved in transporting cocaine produced in Peru and Bolivia along illegal, dusty routes in Brazil , before crossing the Atlantic and being distributed in an unknown number of countries in Europe and beyond.
B ressers had been on Europol’s list of most wanted fugitives since 2021. According to the agency’s notice, he was wanted for kidnapping and unlawful deprivation of liberty, extortion involving a firearm and participation in a criminal organisation.
An earlier case from 2010, in which he was eventually acquitted in 2015 for lack of evidence, alleged that he had ordered a settling of scores, in which the victim had a finger cut off with pruning shears – giving rise to Bressers’ nickname.
In 2020, five years later, he was convicted in relation to another revenge case: kidnapping a Dutch drug dealer who was beaten, threatened with death and cut with a razor blade after being blamed for a missing cocaine shipment. Bressers then became a fugitive, spending two years on the run.
Bressers also appeared as a suspect in at least one other violent case, this time in Guyana, involving the death of a rice wholesaler in the South American country whose seized consignment contained cocaine. His death is believed to have been a cover-up to prevent the gang’s network being dismantled. That case also never went to trial.
Bressers’ partner, Carvalho, is perhaps better known in Europe than in Brazil. According to Brazilian court documents, he led the group that acquired dozens of tonnes of cocaine produced in Peru and Bolivia and transported it through the Brazilian midwest to the ports of Paranaguá and Natal, from where the drugs were shipped to Europe.
Born in 1958 in Ibiporã, in southern Brazil’s Paraná state, Carvalho grew up in Mato Grosso do Sul and became engaged in criminal activity while a police officer in the state. First sentenced to 15 years in prison for drug trafficking in 1998, he was not dismissed from the police until 2010 . Rather than continue running his operations from Latin America, the Brazilian Escobar moved to Europe, first hiding in Portugal and then in Spain.
There, according to Spanish police, he took up residence in a €2m mansion in Marbella on the Costa del Sol, using the identity of Paul Wouter, a wealthy Surinamese citizen. From this base in Spain, a known hub of international cocaine trafficking, prosecutors say he coordinated, between 2017 and 2020, an organised crime network spanning Portugal and Spain, specialising in drug smuggling through ports such as Setúbal, near Lisbon, and Leixões in northern Portugal, and through Lisbon airport, as well as the ports of Rotterdam and Antwerp.
Portuguese police suspected that Carvalho had links to the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command), Brazil’s leading criminal organisation.
Carvalho was cornered – but not arrested – in November 2020 in coordinated raids involving more than 1,000 police officers police from Portugal, Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands, Romania and the United Arab Emirates, as well as Europol. The operation led to 45 arrests and the seizure of more than €13m (£11m) in cash, 70 luxury cars, 37 aircraft and 136 properties.
The court heard that Carvalho is said to have staged his own death in the same year by obtaining a death certificate for Wouter, who was allegedly the victim of Covid-related complications.
He then moved to Budapest, where he was arrested in 2022 while using the identity of Guillermo Díaz Flores, a Mexican national. Carvalho is alleged to have used at least 10 false identities before being detained in Budapest. Extradited to Belgium in June 2023, he was sent to a high-security prison.
I n court, he was reunited with the Finger cutter, his alleged accomplice, as they faced charges of orchestrating a transnational criminal organisation. In his trial evidence, Bressers did not admit any of the charges and claimed to be the victim of a media witch-hunt. “I have a strong feeling that all of this was orchestrated by the authorities,” he says.
Bresser’s defence team is contesting the admissibility of the evidence and has requested the case be dismissed. When approached, Bressers’ lead solicitor, Hans Rieder, had not commented by the time of publication. During the trial, the defence accused the press of “painting an absolutely monstrous picture of our client”.
Carvalho, who did not attend all of the proceedings due to health problems, maintained his innocence and claimed to be the victim of persecution by the Brazilian federal authorities. “I have been in prison for five years and nobody is listening to me,” he said at the hearing. “It was a namesake who committed these crimes, not me.”
Carvalho’s lawyers, Frédéric Thiebaut and Renaat Landuyt, were approached for comment but did not respond. The Belgian federal prosecutor handling the case also declined to comment.
The trial hearings wrapped up on 9 October, with a verdict anticipated on 15 December. Bressers could receive up to 20 years in prison, while Carvalho could be handed up to 15 years.
O ver the past decade, cases such as the Bressers-Carvalho one have multiplied. During this period, cells of Latin American drug-trafficking groups have been identified by national police forces, Europol and intelligence services in Portugal, Spain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Italy, the Nordic countries, eastern Europe and the Balkans, as well as north Africa.
These criminal offshoots have become embedded in Europe through “brokers” or members of drug cartels that “provide specialised services related to cocaine production in Europe, including extracting cocaine from various carrier materials or the processing of trafficked coca paste”, according to Europol’s Andy Kraag , head of its serious and organised crime centre.
“Latin American criminals are heavily involved in this. We see the presence of Latin American criminals in Europe growing, their activities becoming more and more relevant.
“It used to be the other way around – it’s a two-way street now. We already saw, for decades, European high-level criminals embedded in Latin America, settling down there. And now you see more and more Latin American criminals permanently or semi-permanently active in Europe too,” Kraag says.
High-level sources across Europe and Latin America indicate that these groups are expanding their operations and influence in the real and digital economies, fuelled by cryptocurrencies, gambling companies, and the financial and property sectors.
According to Juan Gabriel Tokatlian, a professor of international relations at Universidad Di Tella in Buenos Aires, and an expert on Latin American organised crime, the “war on drugs”, as waged in Colombia – where he lived for 20 years – made cartels more resilient and dynamic, which explains their ability to adapt and expand internationally.
“Europe has become, in recent years, a place where drug consumption has increased in particular. If you look at the UN reports, it is an important market – in the 1980s, particularly as regards cocaine, it was not relevant,” he says.
“In that context of European demand and an erratic anti-drug policy that militarises but then coexists, we find a series of situations that end up empowering organised crime,” says Tokatlian.
Like Carvalho, dozens of alleged leaders of criminal organisations such as the PCC, Tren de Aragua, the Sinaloa cartel, Clan del Golfo or Los Lobos are being held in prisons across Europe, wanted by national police forces or Europol, or listed on Interpol’s red list of most wanted individuals.
They are sought for links to trafficking cocaine to Europe, trafficking arms and synthetic drugs to Latin America, and ties to European organisations in the Balkans or the Italian ’Ndrangheta mafia.
Gabriel Feltran, a sociologist at Sciences Po university in Paris and director of research at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), say groups such as the PCC or Sinaloa are partnering with European crime organisations such as those in Albania or the ’Ndrangheta in “joint ventures”.
He says they buy coca directly from Latin American producers and are capable of delivering directly at the end – so drug ownership no longer passes from hand to hand along the chain.
It is what Feltran calls the “platformisation” of organised crime, in which, like multinational digital platforms such as Amazon, Google and Meta , the cartels integrate their infrastructure and economic models with the aim of controlling the entire drug-trafficking chain, from production deep in Latin America to sale on the streets of Europe.
It means that everything from communications, payments, precursors (chemicals needed to manufacture drugs) and laboratories to logistics is concentrated at the top, with carriers and local operators often unwittingly hired as paid service providers, such as Uber drivers.
Feltran says that, before this platformisation, trafficking was based on routes and several intermediaries who were drug owners in each step of the chain. Now, he says, such “joint ventures get together at the top, buy directly from the producer and deliver directly at the end. They no longer go through intermediaries.”
“Ownership of the drug no longer changes hands. They concentrate everything, optimise a lot and grow very quickly. The more people use their services, the more dependent they become – that’s a network effect.”

title: As King Charles heads to the Caribbean, he should know that Winston Churchill admitted to imperial plunder 90 years ago | Kenneth Mohammed

content:
Modern politicians play on tales of empire to exaggerate what Britain left behind, but the monarch should consider a historical speech on imperial plunder
F or us in the Caribbean, there is something surreal about Britain’s renewed nostalgia over empire. As Britain’s monarch prepares to visit the Caribbean , and at a time when we in the former colonies are demanding to have a serious reckoning with slavery and reparations , UK politicians are invoking a dumbed-down distortion of history.
Rewriting the facts: the Reform MP Robert Jenrick has argued that colonies owed Britain a “ debt of gratitude ” for the institutions empire bequeathed them. Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former minister in a Conservative government, has described British colonialism as “one of the greatest civilising, prosperity-creating forces the world has ever seen”. The opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, has disputed colonialism’s contribution to Britain’s prosperity. Then there is Suella Braverman. The Reform MP suggested in July that rather than Britain paying reparations, former colonies should repay Britain for the investment and infrastructure provided under empire. This prompted Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, to call that proposition “asinine”. At best it is historical amnesia. At its worse it is an insidious misrepresentation of facts.
The question from a global development perspective is: who developed whom? We can ask Eric Williams , Walter Rodney , George Padmore or generations of African, Caribbean and Indian scholars. But there is one inconvenient witness that stands as a testimony to the truth. Winston Churchill.
On 20 July 1937, Churchill addressed the West India committee dinner at London’s Dorchester Hotel. Peter Hulme, emeritus professor of literature at the University of Essex, painstakingly reconstructed the provenance of that speech .
In it, Churchill reflected on how Britain became a global economic power. His words seem stark when placed alongside today’s politically sanitised recounts of empire. Britain’s possession of the West Indies and India, Churchill explained, provided “the strength, the support, but especially the capital, the wealth” that allowed Britain to survive its wars, dominate international commerce and establish its global commercial and financial leadership. Churchill was acknowledging that colonial wealth had financed the development of Britain.
Churchill’s surviving notes contained an even more revealing phrase: Britain’s Caribbean possessions had provided “that unexpected margin of capital”, an advantage Hulme describes as arising from two centuries of Caribbean slavery.
The conventional imperial story begins with what Britain left behind: railways, ports, courts, schools, parliamentary institutions, the English language and Christianity. It rarely begins with what Britain and Europe took away, or rather extracted, through exploitation and genocide. Railways and ports were integral to transporting colonial commodities to overseas markets. Colonialism was an exploitative and violent system designed solely for the benefit of the coloniser.
The Caribbean provides the clearest illustration. For generations, extraordinary wealth was produced through sugar by enslaved Africans and their descendants. Yet when slavery was abolished, Britain compensated not the enslaved but the enslavers.
Hulme’s reconstruction of Churchill’s dinner provides an almost grotesquely appropriate snapshot of that political economy. Among those present was Lord Hailsham, whose family fortune was connected to Caribbean sugar and enslavement; his ancestor Charles McGarel received £129,464 in compensation following abolition for 2,489 enslaved people. About £101m in today’s money, by Hulme’s calculation. The Register of British Slave Traders presents data on the 13,000 investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. It reveals the impact on Britain’s development during its formative era. So, while the slave trade built generational wealth in Europe, it kidnapped and displaced about 13 million Africans, stealing and destroying their generational wealth.
While Churchill celebrated imperial achievement at the Dorchester, Caribbean workers were rebelling against their economic conditions. The 1930s saw strikes and disturbances across the British Caribbean. Movements demanding political representation and self-government were gathering strength. These must seem strange expressions of gratitude to the rehabilitators of colonialism. They ask what Britain built rather than what Britain extracted. They count railways but not resources. They celebrate institutions while ignoring who those institutions were originally designed to govern and whose interests they protected. That is the part of the “gratitude” argument that is so troubling. It asks us to judge colonialism through the eyes of the coloniser.
Most importantly, they treat development as something Britain bestowed upon the rest of humanity rather than a global historical process in which the labour, resources and markets of colonised peoples contributed heavily to Britain’s transformation. That is why the question of who developed who is consequential.
Which brings us to King Charles. From 27 October to 4 November, he will visit the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, culminating in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting. Buckingham Palace describes the visit in terms of community and a shared future. But is this royal diplomacy an attempt to contain or dissuade Caribbean demands for reparatory justice and constitutional independence?
Britain faces growing demands to confront its colonial responsibilities. Jamaica is pursuing a legal route now. However, in 2014, several Caribbean countries attempted to sue the British government for reparations. Britain then used jurisdiction issues arising from the Commonwealth to block the claim . Caribbean and some African governments continue to press for dialogue yet several, seemingly suffering from Stockholm syndrome, persist in retaining the British monarch as head of state: Antigua and Barbuda, Bahamas, Belize, Grenada, Jamaica, St Kitts and Nevis, St Lucia, and St Vincent and the Grenadines.
Buckingham Palace has already confirmed that Charles will not formally apologise for Britain’s involvement in slavery. Apparently, apologies and reparations are matters for government, which opposes paying reparations. Charles has expressed personal sorrow over slavery and described it as an atrocity. But sorrow without accountability is a meaningless attempt at appeasing the “natives”.
The Commonwealth presents itself as an association of equal, independent nations, committed to democracy, development and cooperation. Its supporters point to diplomatic access, technical assistance, educational opportunities, election observation and collective influence on the climate crisis, debt and development. But membership must be judged by outcomes, not colonial sentiment.
If Commonwealth countries cannot secure meaningful engagement from Britain on one of their most consequential historical grievances, how equal is the relationship in practice? What influence do smaller members genuinely exercise over the priorities of the organisation’s wealthiest and most powerful states? And does membership provide sufficient economic and diplomatic benefits to justify its continued symbolic association with an empire whose historical injustices remain unresolved?
These questions are particularly relevant to Caribbean states confronting climate vulnerability, high debt burdens and persistent structural economic disadvantage. The Commonwealth cannot remain an instrument of British soft power, where royal receptions and appeals to shared history substitute for substantive economic justice. Therefore, proposals on reparations warrant serious negotiation, even where governments disagree about legal liability and historical responsibility.
As King Charles arrives in the Caribbean, there will be welcoming ceremonies and speeches about friendship and solidarity. But these crucial questions remain unanswered.
Churchill concluded, on that now-forgotten evening in London: “We could never forget the patriotism and loyalty of the West Indies in those historic times to the mother country.”
The Caribbean should welcome genuine partnership. It need not accept neocolonialism and historical amnesia as its price.

title: Attacked from the sky: Sudanese goldminers count deadly cost of eking out a living on the Egypt border
description: As civil war has left their country in ruins, many young Sudanese have turned to artisanal mining.
