content:
As civil war has left their country in ruins, many young Sudanese have turned to artisanal mining. An airstrike on a mine last week killed more than 100 and has provoked anger against Egypt, seen as the most likely suspect
T orches still fixed on their heads but tools cast aside, the Sudanese goldminers of the North Valley had already mounted an impromptu rescue operation by the time Ammar* arrived at the site of a suspected Egyptian airstrike.
At least 114 were killed, according to the Sudanese rights group Emergency Lawyers, in the strike on Saturday 10 October on an artisanal goldmine brimming with young Sudanese trying to eke out a living in a country where the economy has been shattered by three years of war.
There has been anger in Sudan among those who accuse Egypt of being behind the strike, furious at what they see as aggression by their northern neighbour against workers who produce much of the gold consumed regionally and at the country’s inability to defend itself.
“These are people who have just come here to earn a living, through their own hard work,” says Ammar, a gold trader who worked at a different site and responded to calls to help the survivors.
“Their families are scattered by the war and they send them what they earn,” he says. “Sudan doesn’t have jobs, so they go to the mountains and dig with their hands to live.”
When Ammar arrived, he found chaos at the scene after the strike. The green bags used by the miners to carry excavated materials littered the ground as they abandoned their work to rescue the injured. They made stretchers from blankets, loaded the wounded into pickup trucks to be rushed to nearby towns, and began digging graves for the dead.
The strike was immediately attributed to Egypt by the miners, whose military later confirmed they had carried out operations as part of their push to end “illegal goldmining in the eastern desert”, though they did not address the airstrike.
Egypt reportedly struck the same site in June, killing at least 15 people, according to Sudanese media , and has carried out raids, arresting miners and confiscating equipment .
Egypt said it had distributed leaflets warning civilians to leave before launching the operation. Photos on social media appear to show a leaflet stating: “Surrender yourselves and your equipment. Your lives are more important than any equipment.”
Mohamed Salah, director of Emergency Lawyers, said there were scuffles before the bombing between miners and Egyptian security forces trying to force them out of the area.
“While Egyptian authorities have sought to curb illegal border trade for a long time, locals did not anticipate an escalation involving military aircraft,” says Salah.
He says most of the miners have dispersed since the attack but does not expect them to stay away.
“The miners say they will return – artisanal goldmining in these border areas is the only source of income for them,” he says.
Many come from conflict-hit parts of the country, such as the Darfur and Kordofan regions, he adds, and have slowly made their way through the country’s interior until finding themselves try to make a living prospecting for gold on the Egyptian border.
While Egypt has framed its operations as an attempt to curtail illegal mining, it has been a beneficiary of the informal mining sector, receiving an estimated 60% of the gold produced and smuggled from parts of northern Sudan that border Egypt.
Despite a three-year war between the Sudanese military and rebel paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, gold production has continued in areas controlled by both sides, with artisanal mines proliferating because of rising poverty in the country.
The mines rely on manual labour and expose workers to health risks because of the chemicals used to process the gold, such as mercury and cyanide.
The human rights campaigner Hala al-Karib says the airstrike reveals the vulnerability of the prospectors.
“They are blocked from any other means of livelihood with the collapse of the education system [and] the high rates of unemployment. What other options do they have to survive?” says Karib, who leads the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa network.
“They are at the bottom of the chain because they are subject to the exploitation of big traders. So it is quite painful that on top of that they are exposed to this terror, being killed randomly. It’s a crime and there is nothing to justify it.”

title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
description: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report . More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network , an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status. Continue reading...
content:
At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports
Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report .
More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network , an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.
The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.
The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.
Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”
Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations , framing the issue as a national priority.
Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones , third-party allegations or raids on private premises.
The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.
While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.
Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.
“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”
She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.
The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.
LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.
The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.
The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.
There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “ sexual relations with a person of the same sex ” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.
In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities” . The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021 . In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

title: From black soldier flies to mealworms: farming insects for food, fodder and fertiliser in Uganda
description: Cultivating the nutritious bugs means families can raise livestock and enrich their own food, while lowering pressures on the land Just a few minutes’ walk from his home in the Kyaka II refugee settlement, Kanane Bikanyale keeps a small flock of chickens. From a modified jerrycan, he pours out black soldier fly larvae into the coup where they disappear in a scrum of pecking chickens. Kanane Bikanyale tends to his black soldier fly larvae in a rearing unit in the Kyaka II refugee camp in Uganda Continue reading...
content:
Cultivating the nutritious bugs means families can raise livestock and enrich their own food, while lowering pressures on the land
Just a few minutes’ walk from his home in the Kyaka II refugee settlement, Kanane Bikanyale keeps a small flock of chickens.
From a modified jerrycan, he pours out black soldier fly larvae into the coup where they disappear in a scrum of pecking chickens.
Bikanyale kept chickens before he arrived in Uganda from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). But rising feed costs made things difficult – a pressure felt by millions of smallholder farmers whose margins are tight.
In 2019, he began farming black soldier flies, giving the larvae to his chickens and the tilapia in his small fishpond. The debris and excrement, known as frass, made fertiliser. The flies feed on organic material, from household food scraps to crop residues.
Kavira Musabingo came to the settlement in 2018 with her husband, daughter and five grandchildren. Also refugees from conflict in the DRC, the family arrived with nothing.
She joined a women’s group learning to raise black soldier flies. She initially sold her share of the larvae then later, began rearing insects at home.
Now she provides chicken, eggs and vegetables for her family and earns an income from selling what is left over.
Uganda hosts a large refugee population; Kyaka II alone, in the west, is home to nearly 140,000 people , most, like Bikanyale and Musabingo, displaced by years of conflict and instability in DRC. Women and children make up 78% of people in the camp. As the settlement expanded, land allocations got smaller: by 2018, new arrivals received plots of 30 by 30 metres. Split between a home and crops, and with humanitarian support declining, families had to grow enough food from less and less space.
About 500 people here now work in 32 insect-farming groups. Insect rearing requires little space or water – trays of insects can be stacked vertically.
Alongside the flies, they raise crickets and mealworms, both eaten in many parts of the world. In Uganda, insects have been traditionally gathered from the wild, making supply seasonal. Urbanisation and western food habits have also changed perceptions: dismissed as rural or backward, insects disappeared from diets.
“Their nutritional potential is particularly relevant for vulnerable groups such as women of reproductive age and children under five, since some species are particularly rich in proteins and micronutrients such as iron and zinc,” says Dorothy Nakimbugwe, an associate professor in the food and technology department at Makerere University in Kampala.
Nakimbugwe has also led Refugee Insect Production for Food and Feed (RefIPro) , a project organised by the Danish non-profit Raise, which has worked locally to train and support farmers in Kyaka II since 2018.
More than 10 schools have got involved. Among them are Bukere and Kako primary schools, which now run their own insect farms and were involved in a randomised trial involving 342 children testing the effects of mealworm-enriched porridge. The University of Copenhagen, another partner in the project, reports that children grew taller and showed improved body composition.
But first, the insect rearing system has to work. Edward Ssebbombo, working on RefIPro in Kyaka II, has provided technical support over the years, designing farm equipment, including a pedal-powered sieve, sorters made of recycled motorcycle-wheel spokes and Bikanyale’s rail-mounted shelter, which protects the breeding unit from the weather.
There remain challenges. “In a food-insecure setting such as a refugee settlement, households produce very little food waste,” Ssebbombo says.
“Farming black soldier flies therefore often requires collecting organic material from markets or other sources,” he says, noting that even when the waste itself is free, “sorting, collecting and transporting it can still be costly for small-scale producers.”
Mealworm production faces similar constraints: larvae are fed maize and wheat bran. At Bukere, families contribute banana and sweet-potato peels, but dry feed is expensive.
Violet Gwokyalya leads Mothers Against Malnutrition and Hunger (Mamah), coordinating RefIPro’s work.
She hopes to involve families through a model in which “parents can rear mealworms at household or community level and supply them to schools, helping sustain school feeding while creating an income opportunity for themselves”.
Outside Kampala, the Kollekt Village, a recycling centre run by a local environmental organisation, works with food markets and waste pickers to separate organic material before it reaches dumpsites, integrating insect farming into a zero-waste system.
In Jinja, Bioconvision turns organic waste from food processors and markets into black soldier fly larvae for animal feed and frass-based fertiliser for farmers, including those farming fish on Lake Victoria. In 2025, the company processed nearly 1,000 tonnes of organic waste, producing about 60 tonnes of fresh larvae and 83 tonnes of fertiliser. Both are connected to Bugs-Africa, a project that promotes black soldier fly waste processing.
Uganda is also Africa’s second-largest coffee producer , after Ethiopia, an industry with large amounts of plant waste. In Kasese in western Uganda, Proteen, a Ugandan social enterprise, turns coffee pulp into feed protein and frass-based fertiliser.
Insect farming is a rapidly growing market – estimated to be worth up to $8bn (£6bn) by 2030 . Increased investment has led to industrial-scale ventures in Europe, Asia and North America but the practice is also spreading across rural tropical regions, where the climate favours insect growth.
The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), says animal feed can account for up to 70% of the cost of keeping livestock , leaving farmers exposed.
Enthusiasts believe that insect farming, in scale from a single cut-open jerrycan to industrial facilities, has the potential to reduce the use of soya and fishmeal in animal feed, lowering demand for land and pressure on marine ecosystems.
In Uganda, a recent conference on insect farming brought together Ssebbombo, Gwokyalya, researchers such as Nakimbugwe and members of refugee communities, alongside representatives from Bugs-Africa, FAO Uganda and public institutions.
At the conference, Ronald Kaggwa, of Uganda’s National Planning Authority called for insect farming to be seen as part of a broader system linking waste management, livestock, aquaculture, income generation and food security, and to be integrated into Uganda’s farming system.
“For this sector to contribute meaningfully to Uganda’s development, we must understand the entire value chain,” he said. “It’s about transforming innovation into productive enterprises, turning research into practical solutions, creating opportunities for communities and contributing to more nutritious, resilient, circular and competitive food systems.”
Umberto Diecinove’s INSCTS project documents the growing role of insect farming around the world

title: Iranian woman handed death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media post
description: Rights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year Human rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death sentences and executions in Iran, after reports that a 23-year-old woman, Najmeh Amini, has been sentenced to death for blasphemy over a social-media post. Amini, an accounting student, is being held in Vakilabad prison in the north-east city of Mashhad. She has been sentenced to more than 12 years in prison and death in separate cases heard by a revolutionary and a criminal court. Continue reading...
content:
Rights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year
Human rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death sentences and executions in Iran, after reports that a 23-year-old woman, Najmeh Amini, has been sentenced to death for blasphemy over a social-media post.
Amini, an accounting student, is being held in Vakilabad prison in the north-east city of Mashhad. She has been sentenced to more than 12 years in prison and death in separate cases heard by a revolutionary and a criminal court.
A source close to Amini’s family told the US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRAI) that Amini was sentenced to death on charges of “ sab ol-nabi ” (insulting the prophet). She was reportedly arrested following online monitoring by Iran’s Cyber Police (Fata). The exact content of her posts has not been publicly disclosed.
In the second case, Amini was sentenced to 12 years, six months and one day on charges including acting against national security and spreading propaganda against the regime.
Amini was arrested by security forces during January’s nationwide protests , which were suppressed with a deadly crackdown. Thousands were reported killed, while the HRAI news agency, Hrana, said more than 50,000 people were arrested.
In an audio recording released last month and attributed to Amini, she appealed for international intervention, calling on the UN, lawyers and rights groups to investigate her case.
“I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice,” she said.
“I am an innocent young girl with so many hopes and dreams,” Amini said. “I have parents who are waiting for me. A family that every night, with the fear of losing me, turns their night into morning.”
Rights groups warn that the Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to instil fear and suppress dissent. According to the Oslo-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), more than 600 executions have already been carried out this year.
Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of IHRNGO, said Amini’s case should be seen as a serious warning.
“Sentencing a young woman to death for what she posted on social media risks normalising the use of the death penalty against peaceful expression and pushing the boundaries of the death penalty even further,” he said.
Amiry-Moghaddam added that the Iranian authorities were testing the international community’s “tolerance” towards capital punishment. “If the international community does not respond firmly now, cases like this could become far more common,” he said.
Under article 262 of Iran’s Islamic penal code, insulting the prophet Muhammad or revered Shia figures is punishable by death. However, article 263 provides exemptions for statements made while intoxicated or without deliberate intent, although offenders may still face up to 74 lashes in certain circumstances.
According to the Iranian newspaper Khorasan, which confirmed the judicial proceedings, Amini told the court she had posted the remarks while hallucinating after taking psychedelic mushrooms with friends and her defence argued it was a “slip of the tongue”.
The presiding judge rejected her defence, reportedly asking: “Why, in that same hallucinatory state, did you not insult other individuals or opponents of the regime, such as America and Israel?”
Amini’s death sentence is not final and remains subject to appeal before Iran’s supreme court.
The student’s sentencing comes at a time when Iranian lawmakers are seeking to criminalise contact with all foreign media, including posts on social media deemed to be financed by another country.
Elnaz*, 24, who took part in the protests in Tehran in January and was arrested over social-media posts at the height of the war in March, said she lived in constant fear of surveillance.
“I was arrested even though my social-media account was private. So it’s not just the regime’s cyber-police we have to worry about. There’s also this constant mistrust, this feeling that someone is watching me all the time, even when I’m alone in my room.
“I’m scared to post anything on social media … but after everything they’ve put us through, do we really have anything left to lose? They can kill us even if we don’t post anything on social media.”
Although executions in Iran have surged in recent years , reaching their highest level in three decades, death sentences for blasphemy remain relatively rare. The last documented case was on 8 May 2023, when Yousef Mehrad and Sadrollah Fazeli-Zare were executed after being convicted of blasphemy-related offences tied to social-media activity.
* Name has been changed to protect her identity

title: Nuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessment
description: Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists Humans could become extinct by the year 2100 due to malicious use of AI or nuclear conflict, according to a new global risk assessment. They top a list of 17 major threats to human health over the next 75 years, which also includes cuts to aid spending by wealthy countries, the climate crisis and childhood malnutrition. Continue reading...
content:
Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists
Humans could become extinct by the year 2100 due to malicious use of AI or nuclear conflict, according to a new global risk assessment.
They top a list of 17 major threats to human health over the next 75 years, which also includes cuts to aid spending by wealthy countries, the climate crisis and childhood malnutrition.
The experts behind The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health said all the threats interact, meaning they must be addressed together – but stressed that there was “a realistic route to act” on each.
“Decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation,” said Prof Christopher Murray, commission co-chair and the director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington.
To create its list, the commission modelled how many years in good health might be lost due to sickness, disability or early deaths due to each threat, based on current trajectories – a measure known as disability-adjusted life years (Dalys).
“Malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the report said, adding that while their likelihood remained low, they had the potential to end humanity in the case of nuclear conflict by injecting enough particles into the upper atmosphere to block sunlight and cause famine, or via AI-created biological weapons. An accompanying Lancet editorial, published alongside the report, warned: “The scale of harm, should they be realised, would inflict an apocalypse on humanity.”
Other risks that could cause more than 1bn cumulative Dalys, and therefore deemed “major catastrophic threats”, included air pollution , antimicrobial resistance , childhood malnutrition and climate breakdown, as well as conventional conflict, declining overseas aid , high alcohol use , high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics , obesity , poor mental health , smoking and unhealthy ageing .
To be included on the list, threats not only had to potentially cause a high number of lost healthy years, but also to have potential solutions.
Ibrahim Abubakar, commission member and professor of infectious disease epidemiology at UCL, said: “We are not starting from a point of view of ‘oh look, we want to scare you – we’ve got X many threats facing humanity’. We’re starting from the premise that if you are a policymaker today, whether at the global multilateral level or at the national level, these are the potential threats that you could face, and this is the magnitude by which, if you act, you can actually make a difference.”
Action to limit global heating to about 1.8C (3.2F) rather than letting it reach 4.4C could prevent 1.89bn years of healthy life being lost, according to the report, which modelled best and worst case scenarios for each threat.
In higher income regions, non-communicable diseases such as obesity and poor mental health were the dominant threats, while in lower income regions health loss was driven by issues such as low educational attainment.
Many major donor nations, including the US and UK, have announced large cuts to aid spending over the past year. The potential collapse of, or steep reduction in, international health aid could cause up to 1.5bn Dalys before 2100, the commission found, nearly 70% of which would be in sub-Saharan Africa. The region also bears the brunt of child malnutrition.
The commission was made up of 35 experts, and its findings will be shared on Sunday at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany. Their assessment will be updated annually to re-evaluate the 17 threats identified, incorporating new data and any emerging hazards.
The authors urged leaders to address the risks before they escalated into crises, including via investment in technological innovations and by strengthening health systems.
“We started this process three years ago, thinking that there were three big threats: conflict, climate, and pandemics,” said Murray. “There’s a much larger number of threats that we need to worry about, and governments really need to dedicate some money and staff to the task of anticipation, prevention and preparation for this more diverse set of threats.”

title: ‘Defend our men!’: fears for women’s rights in Latin America over plans to counter gender violence laws
description: Women ‘set back by 50 years’ as Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Peru debate tougher penalties for false reports of sexual assaults, despite such cases being rare The Chilean senator Vanessa Kaiser is on a mission. In her view, men are under attack and need to be protected from the wrongs that feminism has brought about, including a barrage of false accusations of gender-based and sexual violence. “I want to be the first minister in the history of the west to defend men,” she says. “I want to defend you against the idea that, simply for being born male, you are guilty,” she said in July, speaking about a proposed bill that would create sanctions for falsely reporting domestic violence and sexual assaults. “Because now, on top of all the burdens we already had, thanks to those horrible ideologies called feminism and the gender perspective, we have to defend our men.” Continue reading...
content:
Women ‘set back by 50 years’ as Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Peru debate tougher penalties for false reports of sexual assaults, despite such cases being rare
T he Chilean senator Vanessa Kaiser is on a mission. In her view, men are under attack and need to be protected from the wrongs that feminism has brought about, including a barrage of false accusations of gender-based and sexual violence. “I want to be the first minister in the history of the west to defend men,” she says.
“I want to defend you against the idea that, simply for being born male, you are guilty,” she said in July, speaking about a proposed bill that would create sanctions for falsely reporting domestic violence and sexual assaults. “Because now, on top of all the burdens we already had, thanks to those horrible ideologies called feminism and the gender perspective, we have to defend our men.”
Kaiser’s comments capture a belief gaining ground across Latin America: that laws introduced to protect women from violence have gone too far, leaving men vulnerable to malicious accusations. Now, politicians across the region are beginning to turn that argument into legislation.
In Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Peru, lawmakers have proposed bills that would toughen punishments and, in some cases, create new procedures for people found to have made false reports, with a particular focus on cases involving domestic, sexual or gender-based violence.
Individually, the measures are presented as safeguards against fabricated allegations. Taken together, women’s rights groups say they reflect a growing – and disturbing – narrative that women routinely misuse laws intended to protect them, one they say risks making victims too afraid to report abuse in the first place.
That the bills have been presented almost in “parallel” suggests that conservative groups campaigning against women’s rights are pursuing a broader and coordinated regional strategy, according to Paula Ávila-Guillén, director of the US-based Women’s Equality Centre. “The likelihood of it being a coincidence is very low.”
And the proposals are advancing despite scant evidence that such cases of false accusations are widespread – and that false reporting already exists as a criminal offence in each of the countries concerned.
In Bolivia, MPs have proposed an amendment to Law 348 , the country’s legislation on violence against women, which would introduce prison sentences of up to six years for falsely reporting gender-based violence.
Another bill, approved in general terms by senators in July , would toughen penalties for false criminal accusations more broadly, while creating aggravated penalties for allegations involving gender-based violence and sexual offences.
In Argentina, a bill pending before the senate would also significantly increase penalties for false accusations . A version approved by a senate committee in April would raise the current maximum sentence from one to three years, and to as much as six years for allegations involving gender-based violence, sexual offences or violence against children . A newer version removes the explicit reference to gender-based violence, replacing it with “serious intentional crimes” – an undefined category that lawyers warn could still encompass many of the same cases.
Chile has gone further, proposing a special procedure for alleged false complaints arising from family court proceedings, which include cases of domestic violence – and sexual offences. The procedure could be triggered after an acquittal, dismissal or other decision rejecting an allegation, with a finding against the complainant potentially leading to compensation, public retraction and criminal proceedings.
In Peru, lawmakers have proposed harsher penalties specifically for false allegations involving violence against women or the family, with sentences of up to six years in prison.
In Bolivia, supporters of a similar bill say the measures are necessary to protect people wrongly accused of serious crimes and reinforce the presumption of innocence. Defending the proposal in the legislative assembly, the senator José Manuel Ormachea, from the right-wing Alianza Libre party, said: “We need regulations that counterbalance Law 348 [outlawing violence against women].”
In Chile, Kaiser presented the bill as a response to what she describes as widespread abuse of the justice system. “Today, false accusations are a tumour in our society, spreading like cancer, claiming more and more victims,” she said on the senate television programme Profundidad de Campos.
But researchers say there is little evidence that false accusations are a serious problem.
Official national statistics on false accusations do not exist in Chile. In Bolivia, false-accusation claims accounted for 0.13% of all the cases filed in 2024, according to the public prosecutor’s office . In Argentina, a report from the public prosecutor’s office found that false-report investigations represented about one in every 1,000 criminal cases examined between 2023 and 2025 – just 0.09% . In jurisdictions able to break the cases down further, only 8% of all false-report cases related to gender-based or intrafamilial violence.
The far greater problem, critics say, is that violence often goes unreported. In Chile, data shows that most gender-based or sexual violence is never reported at all. In a 2024 government survey , just 12.1% of women who had experienced sexual violence said they had reported their most recent experience.
Meanwhile, only 15% of women who were victims of femicide in Argentina in 2025 had previously reported violence, according to the country’s national femicide register. Another survey found that among women who had experienced violence from their partner, 77% had not filed a complaint.
“For years women have been afraid to report because nobody believed them,” says Ávila-Guillén. “This risks sending us backwards, even to before the #MeToo movement, where women are not only discouraged from reporting sexual violence and harassment, but now also risk being sent to prison if the accusation is not successful.”
In Bolivia , Martín Vidaurre, a policy coordinator for Ipas, an international non-profit organisation specialising in reproductive health, says women already face significant barriers when reporting violence, from an overstretched justice system to economic obstacles and institutional prejudice. Yet a powerful counter-narrative has taken hold: that women routinely abuse the system through false reports.
“There’s a narrative that when you report a case, a man can immediately go to jail. There’s a narrative that women use this law against men when they are bad to them, when they want to divorce them,” he says. “They’re saying that this law, 348, against the violence against women, is actually a law against men.”
Vidaurre says that in practice women may report abuse but later abandon proceedings because they cannot afford legal costs, while overstretched prosecutors, police and judges struggle with heavy caseloads.
Similar conditions exist in Peru . Susana Chávez, a prominent women’s rights advocate and director of Promsex, which defends reproductive rights, says victims often report only repeated or extreme violence, and can then face scepticism from police, lengthy court proceedings and a large backlog of cases when they do so. Some abandon their cases because an abusive partner makes continuing to support their children conditional on dropping proceedings. “It’s very difficult, already, to confront the issue or speak out against it,” she says.
It is against such a backdrop that campaigners see the growing focus on false allegations as part of a much larger political battle.
Chávez described the proposals as part of “a very organised, very large packet” pushed by an anti-women’s rights faction that has also sought to dismantle sexuality education, remove references to gender and eliminate inclusive language. “It’s a very coordinated, orchestrated agenda,” she says.
Over the past decade, women’s movements have become an increasingly powerful force across Latin America. Ni Una Menos (Not One [woman] Less), which began in Argentina in 2015 as a protest against femicide, spread rapidly across the region, while the “green wave” for abortion rights helped propel important reforms in Argentina, Mexico and Colombia.
At the same time, conservative movements have increasingly mobilised against what they describe as “gender ideology” – a label used to challenge policies ranging from abortion and sexuality education to LGBTQ+ rights and protections against violence against women.
“We have a very strong presence of the ultra-conservative sector in the [Peruvian] congress,” says Chávez. “These policies put at risk the entire spectrum of sexual justice and reproductive justice. It is a very complex amalgam that sets women back by at least 50 years.”
In Argentina, Natalia Gherardi, lawyer and director of the feminist organisation Latin American Team for Justice and Gender, sees the proposed bills as part of the same ideological fight. Since taking office, the government of the far-right president, Javier Milei, has abolished the ministry of women, gender and diversity and later shut down its successor office for protection against gender-based violence, while cutting or scrapping a series of programmes aimed at supporting women and LGBTQ+ people. It has also sought to remove femicide from the penal code as a specific category.
“The government in Argentina has built a cultural battle around the idea that feminism has gone too far, and that women should be put back in their place, and that all gender-based violence allegations are an invention of feminism,” she says.
The series of false accusation bills has now attracted the attention of the regional body responsible for monitoring countries’ compliance with the Belém do Pará convention, the inter-American treaty on violence against women.
In August, the committee of experts of Mesecvi, the convention’s monitoring mechanism, issued a strong warning over the initiatives in Argentina and Bolivia. It said the proposed legislation could create an additional legislative barrier to justice, increase fears of retaliation and deepen the re-victimisation of women.
“It is very serious,” says Mónica Maureira, vice-president of Mesecvi. “There is a concerted strategy at the regional level; that is, there are multiple countries in the region that are imposing laws with similar characteristics.”
The committee has also been monitoring similar proposals in Guatemala, Uruguay and Paraguay, Maureira adds.
For Gherardi, the danger lies in the effect such laws could have on women considering whether to report abuse at all. “It will prevent women from looking for protection,” she says.
“If you can’t turn to the judiciary for protection then who will you turn to?”

title: Tigray rebel groups ‘forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15’ as fighting spreads

content:
Civilians try to flee as men and boys rounded up on streets by new alliance as Ethiopia conflict erupts again
As renewed fighting has threatened a fresh humanitarian crisis in the northern region of Ethiopia , reports are emerging that a new alliance of armed groups in Tigray has been forcibly recruiting men and boys to its ranks.
Renewed conflict erupted on 23 September between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which rules the region, shattering the fragile Pretoria peace agreement signed between the two sides in November 2022.
The latest fighting started after months of escalating tensions when the TPLF launched an attack in what it claims was a response to drone strikes by the federal government.
Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian described a broad campaign of forced recruitment in Tigray, targeting men and boys between the ages of 15 and 65.
The Eritrean Defence Forces and Amhara militias, which committed war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 2020-22 conflict, have switched allegiance and are now fighting in support of the TPLF.
Along with this new alliance, testimonies of forced recruitment, child soldiers and fresh humanitarian crises are emerging out of the already battered region.
Gezu*, 34, who fought with the Tigrayan forces in the 2020-22 war, lost many of his friends on the battlefield and was grateful to survive the deadly conflict. He was planning to start a family when he received a call from the TPLF authorities to join their armed group after the latest outbreak of hostilities.
“I refused to join the war,” he said. “I responded to them to kill me rather than ever force me back to the horrors of the battlefield.
“When they saw no one would join their army willingly, and people fleeing to the capital city, they started rounding up people from the streets. I didn’t want to leave my home town until things started getting worse.”
In the past few months, Tigrayans with the means to leave have been heading for the capital, Addis Ababa, fearing that war was coming. But on 23 September, Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to and from the Tigray region, stranding many people, after Tigrayan forces seized the airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray region.
Solomon*, a 52-year-old man who was able to flee to Addis Ababa, said: “The main targets are those between the ages of 15 and 40. I have seen the armed group of the TPLF rounding up people as young as 15 and 16 at gunpoint from the streets and public transportation areas.
“I know parents who tried to save their children by showing medical certificates. The officers don’t care whatever internal disease you have; they forcefully recruit anyone whose hands, eyes and feet work.”
Ephrem, 40, is a father of three who, fearing conscription, was planning to leave the region weeks before the fresh fighting erupted. “Every time I go outside the house, my wife and the kids are anxious. The kids cry fearing that I will be rounded up from the street.
“People who have money protect themselves and their children from the forced recruitment by bribing the officers. It is devastating; no one wants to join the war,” he said.
The Tigray region has been under siege for the past week, when citizens’ bank accounts were abruptly frozen by the federal government, leaving people unable to withdraw their money. The banks have since reopened with a daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr (£9) and with long queues forming outside.
Negus*, an elderly man in Mekelle, said: “We don’t know for how long the siege and the war are going to stay. A daily withdrawal limit of 2,000 birr can hardly afford to buy the skyrocketing food prices. It is impossible to leave this embattled region. There is no way for relatives outside to send medicine or cash. I am just hoping it all ends soon.”
Internet and phone communications were also cut off on the orders of the TPLF until this week, leaving families desperate for news of relatives in the region.
Meanwhile, the Ethiopian government has been accused of carrying out indiscriminate drone airstrikes and there have been reports of attacks by the opposition forces coming close to Addis Ababa.
An estimated 300,000 to 800,000 civilians died during the Tigray conflict, according to the British government. The Ethiopian army, Eritrean forces and Amhara nationalist “fano” militias , have previously committed grave atrocities against the Tigrayan population that amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, according to the UN International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia . Tigrayan forces were also accused in an Amnesty report of committing atrocities during the war .
* Names have been changed to protect their identities

title: Shortages of crucial HIV medicines due to aid cuts are a ‘warning’, say experts
description: More than half of organisations providing HIV care surveyed by International Planned Parenthood Federation said they had run out of stock at some point during past 12 months Aid cuts have affected HIV drug and test supplies across the world, with some providers reporting they are out of stock of key medicines, according to a survey of 40 countries. content:
More than half of organisations providing HIV care surveyed by International Planned Parenthood Federation said they had run out of stock at some point during past 12 months
Aid cuts have affected HIV drug and test supplies across the world, with some providers reporting they are out of stock of key medicines, according to a survey of 40 countries.
Organisations providing HIV care revealed that more than half (55%) had run out of stock within the past year, with a critical scarcity of HIV tests and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – a prescription medicine that people take to reduce the risk of getting HIV.
The survey by the International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF), a network of organisations in more than 170 countries dedicated to sexual and reproductive health, rights and justice, showed that at the time of questioning, 40% of its members reported they had run out of all stock of a product and 60% had at least one product at low stock levels.
Mallah Tabot, a senior adviser at IPPF Africa’s regional office, said: “These shortages are a warning of what happens when funding becomes uncertain and the supply systems communities depend on grow fragile.
“We cannot let decades of progress against HIV be undone simply because products aren’t available. This is not a distant risk – it is already happening.
“HIV infections are rising in a number of countries around the world and lives are being lost,” she added.
Findings from the 40 member associations that responded to the survey revealed that HIV rapid diagnostic tests were the most critically affected product across all respondents.
Testing is provided by almost every responding member association, yet 17 reported low stock and a further five reported no availability, meaning that more than half cannot offer sustained HIV testing at the point of care.
Oral and injectable PrEP were also scarce, with 12 member associations reporting low stock or none at all. Without reliable access to these basic commodities, there will be gaps and interruptions in care for people seeking healthcare from IPPF member associations.
In general, respondents from the Arab world, Asia and Oceania, Europe, the Americas and the Caribbean said supplies, including condoms and antiretroviral therapy, were unreliable.
An estimated 40.9 million people were living with HIV worldwide last year, when there were 570,000 Aids-related deaths recorded, alongside 1.2 million new HIV infections.
In 2025, HIV responses around the world were disrupted by cuts that threatened to stall years of progress. That year, there was a fall in aid spending of about 23% compared with 2024, leading the UN to warn in June of the risk of a resurgence of the HIV epidemic .

title: One green shoot at a time: the women restoring mangrove forests in the oil-ravaged Niger delta

content:
In a region of Nigeria blighted by decades of pollution, Martha Agbani and her team are not just replanting trees but regaining ownership of their lost lands and livelihoods
A toxic landscape was familiar to Martha Agbani when she was growing up – the smell of crude oil in the air, rivers running black and trees dying on the banks. In Ogoniland, in Nigeria’s oil-exploited Niger delta, Agbani saw the spills rot away the mangrove forests and destroy the livelihoods of communities around her.
Now, she is training women to plant them back – one fragile green shoot at a time.
Agbani saw first-hand the toll on Nigerians who protested against the damage inflicted in the delta by big oil companies.
Her mother, Theresa Terabiewaa Agbani, was an activist and, when Agbani was in college, they were devastated by the state’s execution of Ogoni activist and playwright Ken Saro-Wiwa , who, along with eight other environmental campaigners, was hanged in 1995.
“The execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and the other Ogoni land defenders decades ago opened my eyes to what really lay behind the destruction of my home town,” she says.
Agbani has adopted a different kind of activism – planting trees. In 2003, soon after the death of her mother, she established the Lokiaka Community Development Centre, to support female Ogoni farmers in caring for the environment and helping to restore the mangroves, devastated by more than five decades of oil pollution.
Her aim isn’t just to put trees back in the ground but to heal the wetlands, restore livelihoods and peace, and rebuild the sense of ownership Ogoni communities lost along with their mangroves.
In the swamp flats at Teenama, Joy Lebewi is ankle-deep in mud, holding a sapling in one hand. Trained at Agbani’s centre, Lebewi works alongside a dozen other women, all planting while keeping an eye out for crabs and periwinkles worth collecting. In the wetland of Teenama they have planted more than 150,000 mangrove saplings.
“We want to space the mangroves right,” says Lebewi, her brow furrowed with concentration. “This is our forest.” She knows that restoring a forest is about more than putting a bunch of seedlings into the ground. When the women started restoring mangroves in 2018, they planted them too close together, and the trees’ canopies crowded each other out. Now, they use a stick – 2 metres long, with one end pressed into the swampy ground to mark where the next seedling will be planted. It is a simple tool in a landscape of widespread losses, but each mark is a small act of reconstruction.
Teenama sits between the Kwawa and Kpean oil settlements in the Yorla oilfields of Ogoniland, a region ravaged by decades of oil production and spills.
The ecological damage has been felt across the region – people who relied on mangrove-lined creeks to fish and gather shellfish have lost a valuable food source and income.
In Bodo, where Shell was ordered to pay £55m in compensation to local people after two big oil spills in 2008 and 2009 , Dr Ferdinand Giadom is deputy project director of the Bodo Mediation Initiative, a stakeholder group overseeing oil cleanups around the region.
About 1,000 hectares (2,500 acres) of mangroves were directly destroyed in the 2008 Ogoniland spill and Giadom estimates that more than 500,000 barrels of crude oil have been spilt into the environment in under 20 years, an impact felt across generations.
“Two decades have been lost,” Giadom says. “Livelihoods over that span of time have been lost.”
The wetlands are also being encroached on by the nipa palm, also called mangrove palm, an invasive species from south-east Asia that has spread through disturbed areas of the Niger delta. Thick clusters of nipa crowd out native species and make it difficult for local people to access the wetlands.
Clearing nipa is demanding work. In Teenama, men from surrounding communities are clearing the land to prepare it for the women who will plant the native mangrove saplings. The mangrove ecosystem in the Niger delta region is the largest in Africa and the third-largest globally, covering about 1m hectares.
These forests provide habitat for fish, shrimps and molluscs and act as nurseries for other aquatic life. They help protect coastlines, store carbon and support communities whose food and incomes depend on the wetlands.
“Millions of people’s livelihoods depend on healthy mangroves,” says Oluwakemi Odufuye, a coastal ecologist at the Nigerian Institute of Oceanography and Marine Research.
For Agbani, that connection between environmental destruction and human lives is deeply personal. She watched pollution alter her childhood landscape, and saw women losing access to vital forests and waterways.
Inspired by her mother’s activism and the risks faced by Ogoni activists such as Saro-Wiwa, she chose her path in restoration. Her Lokiaka Community Development Centre merges environmental justice, gender inclusion and biodiversity.
Instead of classrooms, women are taken into swamp forests, supervised by experienced restorers.
Her goal is to empower women in the Niger delta to restore their wetlands independently. She has trained more than 400 women from various communities, many of whom have replicated the training locally.
Since 2018, Lokiaka’s teams have restored 3m mangroves and reclaimed 190 hectares of swamp forest in Ogoniland.
For Agbani, the return of fish and crabs demonstrates progress. “Life is returning,” she says.
Erabanabari Kobah, an environmental scientist and campaigner from Ogoniland, says one measure of success is what happens to a forest over time, not just how many trees are planted. “Planting in unsuitable areas won’t ensure long-term success,” he says.
For the planters, that means understanding how the forest behaves – where the water moves, where the mangroves can survive, how the forest can eventually support marine life again.
Collins Lebeteh, an environmentalist who works in community-led conservation, says a different way of measuring success is needed.
“What is really important is who is doing the planting. Many women who rely on and are affected by the degraded environment are often left out of decisions around the restoration of ecosystems,” he says.
Agbani wants to change that. Her organisation also works with local fishers, training them in species identification and managing mangrove buds.
Her hope is for restoration to become a process communities own and control, rather than another “top down” intervention.
Back in Teenama, Lebewi pushes her spacing stick into the mud again. It is a mark almost invisible in the vastness of the wetland but here another sapling will be planted – and spread its roots.

title: Murdered for their eyes: people with albinism living in terror in Madagascar
description: The country is struggling to address a rise in attacks, with a record 13 people – mostly children – killed this year for body parts, which some believe can bring good fortune Not long after midnight in late May this year, three men barged through the door of the small room where Nicole Soalala lived with her family on the outskirts of Toliara, a coastal city in the south of Madagascar. Her eldest daughter, 15, hid under the table with her other two children, aged six and three. Continue reading...
content:
The country is struggling to address a rise in attacks, with a record 13 people – mostly children – killed this year for body parts, which some believe can bring good fortune
Not long after midnight in late May this year, three men barged through the door of the small room where Nicole Soalala lived with her family on the outskirts of Toliara, a coastal city in the south of Madagascar . Her husband got up to ask what they wanted, but they attacked him with a piece of wood and an axe.
Soalala, 32, grabbed her youngest child, Landricia – an 18-month-old girl with albinism – and hoisted her on to her back, holding her there with a piece of fabric she started to wrap around herself. Her eldest daughter, 15, hid under the table with her other two children, aged six and three.
As Soalala’s husband lay on the floor on the verge of losing consciousness, the attackers turned their attention to her. “I felt that I was the one they were coming for and I waited to die,” she says. “But then the one with the axe suddenly started trying to pull my child away from me.”
Soalala tugged on the fabric, pressing her daughter closer to her body. “Let the child go,” said the man. Soalala pulled tighter still. “Let the child go, or we will kill you,” he repeated. Losing patience, the men wrenched away the little girl and ran.
She chased after them, screaming for help and crying. “My heart hurt me so much that I couldn’t stand it and my legs gave up on me,” she says. She collapsed about 100 metres down the dirt road, outside the large faded red gates of a school.
Days later, Landricia’s decapitated body was discovered at the home of a witch-doctor. Her head was found wrapped in plastic bags in a suitcase at another property a couple of kilometres away from where she was taken.
Landricia is among 13 people with albinism who have been killed in the country this year, according to Albinos Madagascar , an organisation set up in 2022 to advocate for people with the condition. Every one of them was beheaded. All but three of the victims were children, ranging from nine months old to 14 years. According to the association, this is already the worst year on record for killings of people with albinism in Madagascar.
“The situation is very critical, very cruel.” says Fulgence Soja, the association’s president, who lives with albinism himself. “There are a lot of big problems facing us, and we feel really unsafe.”
Albinism is an inherited genetic condition that reduces the amount of melanin pigment formed in the skin, hair and eyes and occurs in all ethnic groups. It often leads to poor vision and heightens the risk of skin cancer.
In sub-Saharan Africa, the prevalence of albinism is the highest worldwide, affecting more than one in 4,000 people in some countries, according to the World Health Organization.
People living with the condition face severe threats, including ritual killings, rape and mutilation, in several African countries. These attacks are driven by harmful superstitions that their body parts bring wealth, political success and good luck.
In Madagascar, the eyes of a person with albinism are particularly sought after. Children are targeted because of beliefs suggesting their innocence will make any potion made from their body parts more powerful. They are also vulnerable and easier to kidnap.
Nobody will talk openly about what goes on, but everyone is aware. Witch-doctors the Guardian spoke to denied all knowledge of any beliefs surrounding people with albinism, or what they might be “used for”. They, and others, say these beliefs must come from “outside”.
This level of brutality against people with albinism is said to be a recent phenomenon in Madagascar. Soja remembers first hearing about a beheading of someone with albinism in 2017. Muluka-Anne Mitti-Drummond, the UN independent expert on albinism, started receiving reports of killings in Madagascar in 2021.
“We had recorded more than 28 cases of attacks between late 2020 and 2022; the majority were against children. I was very concerned,” she says. She visited the following year and compiled a report on what was happening .
Mitti-Drummond found that profiles of attackers varied, and included relatives of victims, community members, people who travelled from other regions, and dahalos (cattle raiders). “Most perpetrators are acting with the intent of selling body parts or exploiting a person with albinism for financial means,” she wrote. “In many cases, only the middleperson is caught, while the masterminds of the attacks remain unknown.”
Life-altering sums of money are paid to those willing to kill a child with albinism and procure their eyes. Often entire networks are involved, and violence is said to increase in the run-up to elections. Sources told the Guardian that, because of this and the expense, high-powered people, including senior politicians and business people, were probably ordering some of the killings.
Madagascar is one of the poorest nations on Earth with about 80% of its population living on less than $2.15 (£1.60) a day. Since it gained independence from France in 1958, the country has experienced bouts of political instability, disputed elections and violent coups. In October 2025, youth-led protests toppled president Andry Rajoelina , and Col Michael Randrianirina declared himself head of a transitional government for what he said would last 18 to 24 months.
The country is also among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis , with drought, floods and cyclones causing death, displacement, and damage to crops and infrastructure. A lean season and El Niño threaten to push the south into emergency conditions this year, with high levels of food insecurity and malnutrition.
Sabina Lauber, a senior human rights adviser to the UN in Madagascar, believes it is this that is driving people to target individuals with albinism. “Madagascar is one of the very few countries in the world where every development and wellbeing indicator has decreased over the last 10 years ,” she says. “At the same time, the population has dramatically increased and so there is a level of desperation for survival. People are turning to harmful practices to address the problem.”
In the hours after Soalala’s daughter was taken, a phone and a flip-flop were found in the courtyard outside. They had been left behind by the attackers and were taken away by the police for investigation.
Soalala divided her time between searching for Landricia alone and with members of the police and her wider family and visiting her husband, Mario William Solovenin, in hospital. It was a few days before she remembered where she had seen one of the attackers before.
About three months earlier, she says she and Solovenin had taken Landricia to hospital to treat sunburn on her shoulders. On the way they met a man that Solovenin knew through his work as a rickshaw driver. That man later came by the house, which the family now believe was to scout out their home.
Soalala told this to the police, who went to arrest him. He gave up the names of his accomplices. Chantal Rasoavahininoro, Soalala’s cousin who also lives in Toliara and acted as an intermediary between authorities and the family, says the men were tortured to extract confessions and information as to where Landricia’s body was.
When Soalala was told her daughter had been beheaded, she was inconsolable, says Rasoavahininoro. “Her first question was, ‘Are the eyes there?’” she says. “She almost went mad, she lost her mind.”
Four months on, a team of lawyers representing the family is in the preliminary stages of putting a case together. According to one of the team, Arlette Rafanomadio, 18 people, including two women, have now been arrested and are being held in custody.
One is a Sri Lankan national involved in mining.
Madagascar has a wealth of natural resources, including gold, manganese and copper. The island produces at least 40% of the world’s sapphires , alongside rubies, emeralds and semi-precious quartz. Tohovery Razakamanana, a UN human rights officer, says a significant proportion of attacks against people with albinism have occurred in or near mining areas, particularly mines for precious stones and gold. He also notes that while these attacks used to be concentrated in certain areas of the south, widely seen to be poorer and with higher levels of food insecurity, they are now happening all over Madagascar.
“To get back to the very beginning,” he says, “it all started in the deep south. Then we observed some cases in the south-east, south-west, midwest, and then in the north. But rarely in the capital and surrounding districts.”
While data collection has been poor, making it difficult to determine the origins and extent of attacks against people with albinism, human rights organisations say the situation this year is particularly worrying because of the geographical spread and grisly nature of the killings. People in cities are now being targeted rather than just those in remote rural areas.
An atmosphere of terror now exists for people with albinism and their families. Odette, 20, lives in a city in northern Madagascar where it is hot year round. She doesn’t understand why she is a varira (the Malagasy word for someone with albinism), but she knows her eyesight is blurry and that she burns easily. She squints as she struggles to see, there are sores all over her arms and legs and her lips are cracked and swollen from the sun.
In February, her cousin Marcellin, 14, who also had albinism, was murdered. She remembers him as a cheerful and talkative boy, who used to come round asking for soap.
Marcellin was beheaded and his body left under a mango tree across the dirt track from the wooden property where he lived with his older sister and her family. His head has never been found.
When the Guardian visited, two young girls sat behind a table under the same mango tree selling vegetables. The tyre Marcellin was sitting on outside his front door when he was snatched is still there. According to Soja, four people linked to a local politician have been arrested.
Odette has a three-year-old son and struggles to make money; she earns about 3,000 ariary (50p) a day from working in the fields and doing odd jobs. She is not with the father of her child. When she told him she was pregnant he didn’t stick around. She says: “He told me, ‘I love the colour of your skin, but I’m not going to be with you, because you’re varira .’”
One evening about a month ago, she was at the home she rented with her son when she heard a group of men approach and bang on the door. She ran to her mother’s house. After that, she decided to move in with her wider family and now sleeps sharing a mattress with about a dozen people in a small mud hut with a straw roof overlooking a patch of water not far from the city centre.
“I am a varira like Marcellin, so I’m really scared,” she says. “The house is not a good one, it’s not secure. I worry that there aren’t enough people here and that if someone comes, they will murder me.”
About 90 miles (150km) west, nine-year-old Veroline and her younger brother play outside the mayor’s house in a village near a Unesco-recognised national park where tourists go to see lemurs and other wildlife.
Both children have albinism. Three members of the armed forces watch over them; one carries a shotgun, another wears a handgun at his side.
They are here, living under the mayor’s protection, because in May, their older brother, Rakotombelo, 14, was killed. Veroline was sleeping in the same room when some men crashed through the wooden door. It remains broken to this day. She has very few memories of that night, other than her aunt telling her to run. Her father, who lives in a nearby town, says she told him she hid under a cart parked outside, against the wall of the house. “Some people came and I found out they were enemies,” she says. “I saw them carrying my brother. I told them, ‘Why are you doing that? Is he a child you gave birth to that you can do that to him?’”
Her aunt, Rasoa, and her husband were held hostage by two men in the next room. “They carried knives and said ‘Don’t move, or we will kill you’,” says Rasoa. When they left, she screamed until neighbours came. It was then that she realised her nephew’s head had been cut off. His body had been left, and the wall was covered in blood. “What happened was scandalous,” she says. “I was so sad because he was like my child. Even now, I’m devastated that a child I raised was violated like that.”
While she was at Rakotombelo’s funeral a couple of days later, there was a secret ballot held among the villagers to determine who they suspected had committed the murder. Fourteen people were arrested and are being detained, according to Francois Xavier Zaranaina, the mayor. Rasoa’s husband is one of them. “We don’t have any proof, but all I can say is that some of them might have done it, some of them probably didn’t do it, but because of various rumours and conflicts, those people were arrested,” says Zaranaina.
He has heard the superstitions about the eyes of people with albinism and suspects that is why Rakotombelo, who he says was good at football, was killed. He is eager for Veroline and her brother to no longer be his responsibility, particularly as the killers may come back. “They are burdens,” he says.
The killings have become an issue of national concern. The president has deployed his personal guard to hunt down perpetrators, and the first lady has promised to open a centre in the south where people with albinism can seek refuge.
On 4 August, a video was posted on the president’s Facebook page showing the alleged perpetrators behind the murder of a child with albinism who were caught in a sting operation; among the accomplices were the child’s grandfather and police officers. Two days later, the president wrote in a post accompanied by photos: “Because I heard that there are still people threatening to kill this albino child and her mother, I have decided that the family will be brought up to [the capital] Antananarivo immediately, and I will personally take full responsibility for their lives!” The Guardian could not independently verify the information in the posts, or the videos.
UN experts and local advocates emphasise that addressing the crisis facing people with albinism in Madagascar requires collaboration. Soja, who is now advising the president on the issue, wants a national action plan that addresses security, education and health “so that we can live like everyone else”.
Before that, he says: “The priority is to stop [the killings] because any solution for people of albinism to be able to educate themselves and go to work, depends on that.”
Razakamanana at the UN says a lack of accurate data remains a stumbling block. He is urging the government to conduct a census to determine how many people with albinism there are in the country.
Much needs to be done in terms of raising awareness, he adds. “Even educated people in the capital are not aware [that albinism is a genetic condition]. We have to start with awareness-raising campaigns and education.”
Four months on from the murder of baby Landricia in Toliara, Soalala and her husband’s grief is still raw. They look broken, weary and like every last drop of joy has been drained from them. Tears form in Soalala’s eyes as she talks about what her daughter was like. Landricia had a reddish tint to her hair with chocolate-coloured eyes. “She took after her father, and was a calm and happy child,” she says.
Soalala still cries often and so does her eldest daughter. Her youngest remaining child, Patricia, who also has albinism, often asks where nanke (an affectionate Malagasy term for a younger sibling) is. “I tell her she is dead, I don’t want to lie. I also tell her I don’t want to talk about it,” says Soalala.
When Patricia was born, Soalala says people in the community warned her: “The child has albinism. Be careful, protect her because she might get stolen.” For that reason, Soalala doesn’t work and rarely goes out, preferring to keep her children hidden. The family relies on her husband’s daily income of about 6,000 ariary (£1) from driving a rickshaw.
The family lives in a constant state of anxiety and terror. As Patricia starts to cry and demands attention from her mother, Soalala says: “I can’t sleep at night because I’m so scared and anxious. The evil people might still be seeking this child.”
Translation and additional research by Holifeno Hantarinoro

title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin
description: Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about pharaohs’ origins On the eve of the Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight. Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by a group of young volunteers, Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square. content:
Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about pharaohs’ origins
On the eve of the Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.
Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by a group of young volunteers, Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.
But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the 14th-century BCE pharaoh’s origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.
Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.
The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.
Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.
“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.
“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”
Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.
One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.
Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.
“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.
“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.
This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.
Monica Hanna, a prominent Egyptologist and assistant professor of archaeology at the American University of Iraq–Baghdad, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.
“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”
Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.
They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.
“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.
Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.
“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.
This article is published in collaboration with Egab

title: ‘Africa hasn’t decolonised education enough’: how world’s youngest continent can unlock potential
