content:
Dr John Nkengasong, a former WHO adviser who worked with Biden administration on Aids policy, says innovation and investment are key to unlocking potential of continent’s graduates
A frican governments need to shake off the legacy of colonialism and underfunding if their education systems are ever to harness the vast potential of the continent’s young talent, says the public health expert Dr John Nkengasong.
Africa’s young demographic – it is the world’s youngest continent with 70% of people aged under 30 – is seen as its greatest asset . But a lack of cohesion between education institutions and employers means graduates in Africa, whose number is rising, are not well prepared when they start work, Nkengasong says. In an interview with the Guardian, he says students should be primed to address the continent’s socioeconomic problems, whether through influencing public health policy or technological innovation.
He adds that the continent needs to immediately prioritise investment and leadership that will create universities that not only catch up with the rest of the world but leapfrog ahead.
“No modern or ancient country has developed without a strong higher education system driving research, innovation and critical thinking,” says Nkengasong, an executive director for education at the Mastercard Foundation, which works primarily in Africa trying to ensure young people have access to work and business opportunities.
“We need to actually look at our problems and see what higher education can contribute to [fixing] that.”
Nkengasong says the solution is revitalising an outdated, theory-based education system, for example, by ensuring science-based degrees also include teaching students how to influence policymaking.
The Cameroonian virologist has spent three decades in public health policy for Africa, working at the World Health Organization in the early 1990s and leading the public health institution the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention through Covid-19. He also worked on Aids policy with the US under former president Joe Biden.
Nkengasong says that by looking to countries such as Singapore and South Korea, the continent could find examples of governments that had overhauled their systems to become leading forces in innovation and business.
He says the Africa Higher Education for Transformation prize awarded to five universities for the first time this week was an example of how to incentivise institutions to encourage innovation, better pathways to employment and research focused more on local needs.
The award aims to provide $500m (£380m) to 150 universities over the next decade.
Political will and investment from the continent’s governments is also required to connect what is taught in universities to the requirements of employers, he adds.
“My ask to countries is that we should see higher education as a national interest and an investment, not just a social sector that you want to pour money into. There hasn’t been the political recognition that this is an investment and that you do not develop without doing research, innovation and ethical leadership,” he says.
“There is no country that can construct roads, electrical grids, railways, dams, manufacturing or industrialisation without the human capital that is required. Investment in higher education is investment in your human capital.”
While the proportion of graduates from higher education is still much lower in Africa than the global average, it doubled between 2000 and 2021 to 9% and is expected to continue growing at a similar rate.
According to the Africa Workforce Readiness Survey 2025 , which surveys students across the continent, only about half of employers rated recent graduates’ employability as very good or excellent.
A study from South Africa’s Human Sciences Research Council, tracking more than 500 African tertiary education graduates over five years, found that only 16% moved smoothly from education into work and were able to hold a job during the period of the study.
However, the study also highlighted that there was untapped potential, with many of the graduates juggling further studies with seeking income, building businesses or running family farms.
The study suggested that degrees did not directly prepare students for livelihoods and they needed to be prepared for work with more skills, and taught how to adapt better and think in more entrepreneurial ways.
Nkengasong says the causes of the disconnect between education and employment are deep-rooted. In part, they come from a reliance on colonial-era education systems that have not adapted to the modern world, but also because of the impositions made on governments receiving loans in the 1980s.
He points out that organisations such as the International Monetary Fund made governments deprioritise spending on higher education and focus only on primary and secondary education. Even now, sub-Saharan African countries are spending 3.6 times more on debt than education.
This, he says, turned universities into a “high school-plus”, which provide students with education but do not produce research or scientists prepared to have a public impact.
“The history of higher education on the continent is shaped by its past, which is the colonial past, where these curricula were designed many, many years ago. Africa hasn’t decolonised its educational system enough,” he says.
Nkengasong says the public health sector is an example of where Africa could benefit from new talent equipped to deal with the continent’s problems, and believes the continent needs its own research and development hubs creating vaccines and diagnostic tools in order to ensure its health sovereignty.
He added that the Ebola crisis in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which has killed almost 3,500 people , was an example of a localised crisis where a quicker response could have taken place if talent and resources were more available.
“Why would a pharmaceutical company in Canada or the United States be investing millions in R&D to develop a diagnostic test or a vaccine for Ebola, when there’s no Ebola in Canada and North America? We should be doing that in Africa,” he says.
He believes this would require public health officials, not only trained in the science of epidemiology, but also equipped by universities to deal with the diplomacy required in shaping policy.
He says they should be able to talk to governments often lumbered with large debts and explain to them why prioritising health investment also ensured security and economic health.
This kind of overhaul of the education system will take time and requires immediate action, but urging governments to prioritise improving higher education and provide leadership and finance will ensure it happens, he says.
“It takes a generation to build anything meaningful,” he says. “I’ve been in global public health for 35 years, and it always takes you 25 years to 30 years to do anything impactful.”

title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
description: Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes. Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. content:
Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups
A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.
Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.
The charity Reprieve says Manasif was tortured and coerced into signing a false confession and only met his state-appointed lawyer for the first time in 2022 – five years after his arrest.
Manasif’s death sentence has now reportedly been upheld by the Saudi supreme court, which was likely to be his last hope of avoiding execution.
His family have not spoken in public about the case and could face harassment or arrest if they do so. “There is nothing they can do now but wait,” said Duaa Dhainy, a consultant for Reprieve and the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights.
Saudi Arabia has seen what activists describe as a “horrifying” surge in executions under the rule of the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. Last year saw a record 356 people put to death in the country. Most of those executed are foreigners convicted of minor and non-violent drug crimes .
At least 17 people, who were children at the time of their alleged offences, have been executed in Saudi Arabia since 2015, according to Reprieve.
Saudi Arabia issued a royal decree abolishing the death penalty for children in 2020, stating that individuals would not be sentenced to death for crimes committed when they were minors.
However, it has since upheld the death penalty in a number of cases involving child defendants. In April, it executed Ali al-Subaiti , along with his uncle, Mustafa al-Subaiti, for non-lethal “terrorist” offences committed when he was 12 years old.
The UN’s independent human rights experts have previously expressed concerns about Manasif’s case. It said Saudi Arabia should immediately halt planned executions of people convicted of offences allegedly committed when they were under 18. “They are using execution as a tool to show how powerful they are and how they can threaten anyone who does not follow their rules,” Dhainy said of the Saudi regime. “We think he should be treated as a minor and not sentenced to death as his charges relate to when he was under 18.”
Human Rights Watch said executing Manasif for a non-violent crime committed as a minor would be “an unconscionable new low”.

title: ‘I am still a child, it cannot be good to be married’: how drought forces Afghan families to sell girls as brides
description: As climate breakdown pushes families to starvation, many feel forced to ‘sacrifice’ daughters to save siblings. Photographer Elise Blanchard travelled the country speaking to girls as young as eight, 10 and 14 who have been engaged or married to repay debts or pay for food ‘I’m not happy about this,” says 11-year-old Khatira, who was sold into marriage to repay debts, sitting in her home in Qala-e-Naw, capital of Badghis province in north-west Afghanistan. “She was healthy before her engagement, now she is worried and cries a lot,” says her 40-year-old mother, Noor Bibi. When her 20-year-old husband-to-be comes to her home, Khatira runs away. Since her engagement, she has stopped going outside because she “is ashamed of having a husband in front of the other girls”, says her mother. Continue reading...
content:
As climate breakdown pushes families to starvation, many feel forced to ‘sacrifice’ daughters to save siblings. Photographer Elise Blanchard travelled the country speaking to girls as young as eight, 10 and 14 who have been engaged or married to repay debts or pay for food
‘I ’m not happy about this,” says 11-year-old Khatira, who was sold into marriage to repay debts, sitting in her home in Qala-e-Naw, capital of Badghis province in north-west Afghanistan . “She was healthy before her engagement, now she is worried and cries a lot,” says her 40-year-old mother, Noor Bibi.
When her 20-year-old husband-to-be comes to her home, Khatira runs away. Since her engagement, she has stopped going outside because she “is ashamed of having a husband in front of the other girls”, says her mother.
Khatira’s father grew wheat and herded cattle before the family was displaced from its rural village by drought.
In Badghis, 95% of the population relies on rain-fed agriculture and livestock to live. But droughts, made more frequent and extreme by climate breakdown, have robbed people of their incomes.
As a result, selling young daughters into marriage to repay debts, feed the family or pay for medical treatment has become a common way to cope.
“As a mother, I cried a lot, but I knew my husband had no choice,” says Gul Bobo, who does not know her own age, regarding her daughters, aged two and five, at her home in Tayz Nāwah, a village 12 hours’ drive from Qala-e-Naw. Both girls are engaged to be married.
Like many there, Gul Bobo’s husband used to buy seeds each year and rent a tractor or donkey to cultivate a wealthier man’s plot of land.
“I know they are too young to be engaged but we had no choice – otherwise we would have waited until after 18,” says Gul Bobo.
“I expect them to be beaten, but there is nothing I can do about it. And at 14, they will be pregnant.”
Underage brides are often expected to have children when they reach puberty, leading to well-documented health problems – in a country where maternal mortality is among the highest in the world .
They are also expected to know how to run a household. When they are unable to do so like adults would, domestic violence from in-laws is not unusual.
Five-year-old Nazila’s husband-to-be is 15. According to Gul Bobo, she could leave to live with her in-laws in two or three years.
‘I would have preferred for her to be dead rather than be married off to such an old man,” says Bana, the mother of Gulalai, 11, who is engaged to a shopkeeper in his late 40s. Her parents owed him money.
The story is always much the same. Gulalai’s father was a farmer and the family were displaced by crop failure from their remote village in Qadis, Badghis province.
“We have to sacrifice a family member to save the others,” says Gulalai’s father, Niaz Mohammad, who says he would have preferred to wait until his daughters turned 20 to marry them off – instead, four were married as children.
The family only eat homemade bread, tea and wild mallow leaves they gather and boil, using rubbish to make a fire.
When asked about climate change, most people in Badghis do not know what it means. In villages, most live in mud homes, with no electricity besides the occasional solar-powered battery, and little transport aside from an occasional motorcycle. The population relies on so little to live that notions of overconsumption or greenhouse gas emissions are completely alien.
In a desperate attempt to survive droughts over the past nine years, thousands have abandoned their ancestral villages to try to find work in Qala-e-Naw, often in vain.
To feed his family, Mohammad Yawaz, 55, sells ice-cream on the roadside for 100 afghanis (£1.20) a day, after spending his mornings with his six-year-old daughter Zubaida, collecting cans and bottles. They make, at best, 500 to 1,000 afghanis a month reselling them.
Yawaz eventually felt he had no choice but to marry off his first daughter, now 15, who has already left for her husband’s home, and Zubaida, who was engaged last year to a 12-year-old boy.
His neighbour, Surgul, is in the same situation. In the morning, he collects rubbish with his daughters Zartila, 10, and Bibi Aisha, seven, who are both engaged. The decision to sell Zartila into marriage was taken after the family had to endure “three days and three nights with nothing to eat”.
Recently, Surgul sold the only battery he had for lighting in his mud home to buy medications for one of his daughters. A few years ago, he and his wife lost an infant to illness.
But this was not always their life. Surgul once had cattle in his village. As droughts hit the area, he sold them.
Cattle markets in Badghis are full of men selling their precious animals because they cannot afford to buy fodder to compensate for the lack of grass. In some areas, villages have become ghost towns.
Some families go to Herat, the third-biggest city in Afghanistan, where the Shahrak-e-Sabz camp houses tens of thousands of displaced people. They come here in the hope of finding humanitarian aid – but it has dried up. Then they resort to selling their daughters into marriage to repay debts.
Darellah, 15, lives with her 30-year-old husband, Mollah. Her family was displaced from their village in 2018.
That year, Badghis suffered a historic drought , and since 2021, droughts have ruined harvests and starved livestock every year.
Now pregnant, Darellah is visiting her family. “I am still a child … it cannot be a good decision to be married at that age,” she says. Her sisters, Bibi Zat, nine, and Rahimah, 11, are both engaged but still live with their parents.
Their neighbours were all displaced by the drought as well. Bahahuddin, 40, had to sell his land.
When he found himself unable to feed his family by collecting rubbish and begging, he sold his 10-year-old son Ziauddin’s kidney for 100,000 afghanis. He wanted to sell his own but said he was not healthy enough for people to buy it.
In the camp, stories like these do not raise an eyebrow. Residents say children have often died from not being able to access health services.
Khomakha, 30, is another neighbour displaced by the droughts. Her husband made a deal to marry off their two-year-old daughter Fatemah only three months after the girl was born.
The urgency came as they could not afford the small fee for shared transport to take their eight-year-old son, Ehsanullah, who has blood cancer, to the hospital for a transfusion each week.
Khomakha may not see Fatemah ever again after she marries and moves to a village 15 hours’ drive away. “I will not be able to afford transport to visit my daughter once she leaves,” Khomakha says.
B ut life is not much easier for families who stay in their villages. In Khoshkian, Abdul Aziz’s wheat harvest failed seven times in eight years. Over the years of drought, he sold five of his daughters into marriage, for between 90,000 and 150,000 afghanis (£1,000-£1,750), to repay debts.
Mazari, one of Abdul Aziz’s daughters, left home at about 12 or 13. Now 16 or 17, she lives with her husband in his 40s, their two-year-old son, and a baby born just one day ago.
“Getting married at 12 was really hard; when I came to his home, I wasn’t able to cook, but my husband and in-laws have been really kind,” she says.
Her younger sisters, aged between three and 13, will live at home until their bride prices are paid. While they weed a field, they remember the years of war when soldiers from the previous government used to shoot from the mountains behind them.
“There was no difference – the previous government’s army shot whether we were Taliban or civilians,” says Shamael, Mazari’s 13-year-old sister. “We feel better now because we are not woken up by fighting.”
Sitting in the field, Shamael’s sisters nod as they continue weeding.
“People cultivate their land for several years. People invested a lot to do so, and there is no harvest, so they are in debt,” Shamael says. “Then some people sell their lands, some sell their daughters – to survive.”
There is no law regarding the age at which girls can leave home for marriage. Bride prices range from hundreds to a few thousand pounds and are paid in instalments. Once the dowry is paid in full, the in-laws are free to claim the bride. In many cases, it happens at the beginning of puberty.
“Everything that is happening to us is because of poverty,” Shamael says.
O n her wedding day, in the village of Nookhil, Bibi Samia, 14, at first appears calm. She had cried a lot the night before, says her mother. She has remained stoical for hours but, just before she has to leave her home, bursts into tears. “I am not happy because I am very small,” she says.
As foreign aid dries up, programmes that should provide support for these girls are disappearing.
Mark Calder, advocacy director for Afghanistan at the aid organisation World Vision International, says: “Early marriage exposes girls to potentially deadly health risks, but the clinics treating them are disappearing as aid is cut.”
The psychological toll for child brides is immense. Despite her crushing poverty, Sara brings her daughter, Aisha, 12, to primary school every morning, walking from the same slum Khatira lives in, bordering Qala-e-Naw, since they fled droughts in 2021.
Still, Sara’s husband sold Aisha into marriage to a 20-year-old to repay debts; when it is paid, she will have to go.
The bride price has done little to alleviate the family’s poverty: their rent of 1,000 afghanis has not been paid for two months and the landlord has told the family to leave. When her last baby was born, Sara had to walk to the hospital, unable to pay for a lift.
Despite this, Sara says: “I try not to contact the in-laws to ask them for the rest of the bride price, so that Aisha will not have to leave.”
Sara cannot speak about her daughter’s impending marriage in front of her, as it makes Aisha cry. She prefers to let her continue quietly doing her homework while she still can.

title: Curse of the Nile’s gold: how Sudan is losing its fertile fields and ability to produce food
description: An artisanal mining boom driven by war and poverty is causing a public health emergency, as chemicals poison soil, water and society In Abu Hamad, on the banks of the Nile, verdant orchards, gardens and fields once produced a bounty of dates, citrus fruits, winter grains and cereals for the towns and cities of eastern Sudan, including Khartoum and Port Sudan. Dotted around the town and its outskirts, more than 700 mounds of grey waste are poisoning the soil, water and air. The mounds are the toxic remnants of artisanal gold mining, a practice that began in about 2008 and has intensified over the past six years. Continue reading...
author_name: Samira Hassan Khalifa in Abu Hamad
content:
An artisanal mining boom driven by war and poverty is causing a public health emergency, as chemicals poison soil, water and society
I n Abu Hamad, on the banks of the Nile, verdant orchards, gardens and fields once produced a bounty of dates, citrus fruits, winter grains and cereals for the towns and cities of eastern Sudan , including Khartoum and Port Sudan.
Today, the land looks drastically different. Trees have been cut down, agricultural areas cleared, and farms have been replaced by shops and commercial sites. Dotted around the town and its outskirts, more than 700 mounds of grey waste are poisoning the soil, water and air. The mounds are the toxic remnants of artisanal gold mining, a practice that began in about 2008 and has intensified over the past six years.
In 2024, artisanal operations accounted for more than 90% of Sudan’s gold production . And Abu Hamad in River Nile state has become one of the largest gold-mining and trade towns in the country .
Desperate for income, locals process tailings, the byproduct of artisanal mining, which contains about 70% of gold and is extracted using chemicals such as cyanide, mercury or thiourea, a compound that was initially thought to be relatively safe.
The creeping toxicity has decimated the agricultural foundation of Abu Hamad, transforming the town’s tranquil way of life into a daily battle against pollution and disease. Flood waters carrying runoff from mining sites have caused massive spikes in soil salinity, leading to a catastrophic decline in food production. Mohamed Fathi al-Rahman al-Khalifa, a local farmer, has watched the soil turn hostile.
“When the trees were still very young, the first harvest produced nearly four truckloads of oranges. Today, production does not exceed half a truckload,” Al-Khalifa says, highlighting the unnatural stunting of his orchards.
The agricultural collapse across all major staples is staggering, say farmers. A single acre (0.4 hectares) of wheat that historically yielded between 40 and 60 sacks now produces 12 to 18 sacks.
Similarly, fava bean yields have plummeted from an average of 40 to 50 sacks per feddan (a unit of land equivalent to about an acre, 0.4 hectares) to just three or four, according to local farmers. Even fully mature orange groves that should easily produce 10 truckloads of fruit now yield less than half a truckload, they say, with much of the harvest arriving misshapen and thick-peeled.
Al-Khalifa warns of a looming catastrophe that extends far beyond the borders of River Nile state. “Food security is no longer merely a local issue affecting Abu Hamad. It has become a national issue that concerns Sudan as a whole.
“Sudan possesses enormous agricultural potential and is crossed by the Nile River, [meaning] agricultural products should be abundant and affordable, yet the reality is quite different. Today, we see rising prices for vegetables and farm products across different states and cities,” he says.
The tragedy of Abu Hamad is not isolated. It is deeply entangled in Sudan’s war, now in its fourth year. The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) rely heavily on the gold sector. Since the war started in April 2023, both sides have been involved in controlling mining, says researcher Suliman Baldo of the thinktank Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker.
Last year, the mining sector generated approximately $1.8bn (£1.3bn) in revenue from production and exports, producing roughly 75 tonnes of gold over the year and exceeding the SAF-controlled government’s target by 13%. This gold accounted for 58% of Sudan’s total export value in the SAF-controlled areas. The actual profit margin, however, may prove much higher, given the high level of gold smuggling across the border into Egypt . Production and trade levels among the RSF-controlled mines remain undocumented.
For the most part, Sudan’s war has allowed mining operations and gold trading to take place unabated and unregulated. According to Mubarak al-Fadil al-Mahdi, the head of the Umma party, a former investment minister and a businessman with ties to the gold sector, there is very little incentive for the warring parties to stop these practices.
“This is one of the Sudanese army’s most important incentives to perpetuate the war and prevent it from ending so that it can benefit from the corruption of these funds,” al-Mahdi says. “These funds are not subject to any oversight and are solely managed by the army commander and the governor of the central bank.”
The devastating impact of this unregulated mining is equally visible in the region’s pastures. Abu al-Qasim al-Khazin, a livestock herder from the Al-Sharik locality within the district of Abu Hamad, paints a grim picture of the toll the chemical runoff is taking on local fauna.
“We have seen numerous cases of animals born completely without hair [and] extremely unusual cases in which animals were born without eyes,” Al-Khazin explains.
The toxins affect more than just physical development. “In some cases, the animals appeared to have completely lost their normal behaviour – some people described their condition as resembling madness.”
The environmental disaster has inevitably become a public health emergency. Analysis in 2022 revealed that 20% of drinking water samples contained mercury.
A local doctor and medical activist, who asked to remain anonymous for security reasons, says that health issues previously rare in the area are now everyday realities. “Among these concerns is the rising rate of miscarriages among pregnant women, as well as cases of congenital abnormalities in foetuses,” they say.
The strain on local healthcare is immense, with the dialysis centre in Abu Hamad now serving close to 100 patients – far beyond its original intended capacity – after a rise in kidney failure.
The danger peaks during the rainy season, when the lethal grey mounds are disturbed. “During the rainy season two years ago, we witnessed mining waste and tailings being washed away by flood waters and carried into residential neighbourhoods,” the doctor says.
Hashim Abdelazim al-Mahi, an engineer and local environmental activist, has tracked the devastating reality of the pollution . He points to the introduction of thiourea, as an alternative to cyanide in the gold extraction process.
“When thiourea was first introduced into Sudan [ in 2017 ] it was promoted as an environmentally friendly material. However, reality has shown otherwise,” Abdelazim says.
According to recent local medical records, approximately one out of every 50 children is born with some form of serious congenital abnormality, including cleft lip conditions and complex cases such as skull deformities.
Despite the risks, Abdelazim is not demanding a complete end to the industry but rather an end to the negligence. “Of course [gold] mining will continue. We cannot expect the industry to stop completely,” he says. “Mining should not stop, but the state must stop these harmful practices linked to the industry and address them seriously; human health should remain a priority for the state and should never be compromised or bargained away.”
As the land dies, the social fabric of Abu Hamad is unravelling. Driven by soaring poverty and the allure of quick profits, young men are abandoning their education to enter high-risk mining operations.
Mohamed Ahmed Abdelaziz, the headteacher of the Northern Boys’ School in Ghariya, has watched his classrooms empty. Primary school classes have dropped from 75 pupils to 20, and secondary classes show identical attrition. “A student may see someone working in mining who has bought a vehicle or earned a substantial income within a short period and begin to ask himself, ‘Why should I continue studying?’” he says.
The long-term consequences of this shift in community priorities is deeply troubling to the veteran educator. “If large numbers of students continue to abandon their studies, society will lose the teachers, doctors, engineers, university professors and other professionals it needs for development.”
For the young men in the pits, survival, not greed, drives their decision. Al-Daw Adam Jibril Mohammed, a high-achieving student, dropped out of university when he could no longer afford the tuition.
“I felt that education required many years of study, while mining offered immediate and direct financial returns,” Adam says. However, the reality of the work is gruelling and far from a guaranteed payday. “A person may work an entire day and find nothing whatsoever; income from mining is uncertain and depends largely on luck.”
In July, the prime minister, Kamil Idris, who is part of the army-controlled government, ordered the immediate removal of all gold-processing mills from residential and military areas. The directive will also introduce mandatory ID cards for miners and increased security in mining regions. In 2024, authorities also tried to ban the use of mixers such as mercury and cyanide in Wadi Halfa, Northern state, and South Kordofan state. But these piecemeal efforts have proved too little, too late.
In Abu Hamad, the contaminated mounds of toxic soil and gravel remain exposed and untreated. As the rainy season approaches, the risk of these toxins seeping into the Nile River increases.While the war rages on, the residents of Abu Hamad must navigate a landscape permanently altered by human greed. Until state authorities intervene to regulate the informal sector and enforce safe processing methods, the grey mounds will continue to multiply. For the farmers, herders, doctors and children of Abu Hamad, the gold rush has yielded little wealth – only a slow, relentless poison.
This story by independent Sudanese outlet Ayin Network is supported by the Impact Reporting programme of the Institute for War & Peace Reporting ( iwpr.net )

author_name: Zeinab Mohammed Salih in Korsi refugee camp, Central African Republic
content:
Since civil war first reached her village in 2003, Samira has been displaced seven times, enduring devastating losses and injuries along the way
E very morning, she spreads small piles of rice and spices on an aluminium tray in the market of Korsi refugee camp. Some of it comes from her monthly food ration, already meagre, distributed by the UN’s World Food Programme; some she buys when she can and resells for a small profit.
Samira crouches quietly behind her modest display, greeting customers as they pass. Her loose red toub cloth frames her thin face and falls across one side of it, hiding her injured right eye. Every so often she adjusts the long cloth to cover the empty sleeve where her right arm would have been. It is a habit the 33-year-old has developed since the war, but her injuries are only part of the terrible damage it has inflicted.
Samira has been displaced seven times since war first reached her village in 2003, when she was 10 years old. She has fled one conflict after another across Sudan and now beyond its borders. The journey eventually brought her, by minibus, motorbike, taxi and on foot, to Central African Republic , where she now lives among thousands of refugees who have escaped Sudan’s latest civil war, which erupted in 2023.
Around her, rows of small thatched shelters line a dusty path that cuts through the heart of Korsi camp. This is the market, where traders arrange handfuls of tomatoes, dried fish, onions, soap and secondhand clothes on wooden tables or plastic sheets spread on the ground.
Children weave through the crowd, between people carrying jerrycans and bags of charcoal, while women wrapped in colourful toubs bargain for handfuls of spices and vegetables.
This is a settlement built almost entirely from wood, straw and plastic. The refugees have fashioned their homes from branches and thatch, covering them with white tarpaulins distributed by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR. From a distance, the structures look fragile against the vast sky of north-east CAR.
Over the past week, dark clouds have begun gathering overhead as the rainy season approaches. Soon, heavy downpours will drum against the fragile shelters, built for survival rather than permanence.
Samira’s life once followed the rhythm of the seasons in a village on the outskirts of Tine, on the Sudanese side of the border with Chad. Her family farmed during the rainy months and moved with their livestock when drier conditions demanded it, combining agriculture and pastoralism in a way that had sustained generations.
There was a school – and she loved studying. Samira dreamed of one day travelling to Khartoum to study law at university and becoming a judge. “I wanted to help people find justice,” she says.
But in 2003, rebel groups drawn largely from communities in Darfur that complained of decades of political and economic marginalisation took up arms against the Sudanese government. Khartoum responded with a brutal counterinsurgency campaign, deploying its military and arming Arab militias that gained notoriety as the Janjaweed.
For villages such as Samira’s, the consequences were devastating. She remembers hearing warplanes overhead before attacks reached the ground. Villages were bombed, burned and looted. Families fled with whatever they could carry; some never returned, others disappeared altogether.
The violence uprooted her family and ended the life she had imagined for herself. After moving repeatedly across Darfur, she eventually married a man from her Zaghawa community and settled in El Geneina, capital of Sudan’s West Darfur state. Life felt stable for the first time in many years, she says.
Her husband traded goods between Sudan and Chad, where many Zaghawa families maintained close social and commercial ties across the border. Business was good. The family acquired vehicles, expanded their trade and raised five children.
For Samira, El Geneina became home. The memories of flight and loss never disappeared, but they no longer defined every day of her life.
Then, in April 2023, war returned to Sudan when two generals in the military government fell out once again – Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti , led his Rapid Support Forces paramilitaries against the Sudanese government army soldiers of Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. Other smaller militias have joined in the conflict.
West Darfur once again became a battleground. Ethnic tensions that had smouldered for years exploded into open violence.
By June, the city was descending into chaos. On the day that West Darfur’s governor, Khamis Abbakar, was abducted and killed, armed men arrived at Samira’s home. They came for her husband’s vehicles, money and property.
According to Samira, he refused to surrender what the couple had spent two decades building. “They killed him in front of me,” she says. “My husband spent all his life working for his family. They killed him and my two daughters on the same day.”
Everything was destroyed in a few hours.
In accordance with a tradition practised by some families, relatives then wanted her to marry her late husband’s younger brother. “I had to run away,” she says. “The boy was younger than I was. I couldn’t do it.”
She gathered her three surviving children and travelled again, this time to Nyala, a city in south-west Sudan, where relatives agreed to shelter them. But the war found them again there.
Artillery shells began falling on residential districts, with one striking the house where Samira was staying. The blast killed two people instantly. The explosion tore off Samira’s right arm and destroyed her eye. After her wounds were treated, she was on the move again.
In the market at Korsi refugee camp, her scars visible even as she pulls her toub to cover them, Samira follows the news from Darfur, now hundreds of miles away. At the siege of El Fasher , many of the fighters defending the city belonged to armed groups rooted in her Zaghawa community giving her a sense of connection to the city.
Some of her relatives were forced to flee as fighting intensified; others died in the massacre of civilians in October 2025 when the city fell to RSF militiamen. Some scattered across Chad and neighbouring countries. With each phone call to a relative, another familiar place disappeared from the map of her life.
“There is nowhere left for us,” she says. Her eldest son left Korsi a month ago to take the dangerous migrant trail to Morocco with other young Sudanese refugees, hoping to make it to Europe and find work. She has not heard from him since.
In the afternoon heat, Samira gathers the rice and spices she has not sold and folds the aluminium tray beneath her arm. She still has two children to feed and care for. Around her, traders close their stalls and families disappear into their shelters of thatch and white plastic sheeting.
Many of these shelters and stalls will not stand up to the wet conditions when the rains arrive.
Samira is thinking of leaving Korsi for Cameroon. Other refugees have told her life there might be easier, although she knows only too well that feelings of safety can be fleeting.
But when asked where she wants to live, she does not hesitate. “I love every corner of Darfur,” she says. “I dream of living there, but I can’t. The war took everything from me. It took my eye, my arm, my mother, my children and my husband.”
But if peace returned, she says: “Even with one eye and one arm, I would go back.”
More than two decades after she first had to leave her home as a 10-year-old girl dreaming of becoming a judge, Samira is preparing for yet another uncertain journey.

title: UK prioritised ties with UAE over averting mass atrocities in Sudan, MPs to be told
description: Foreign Office failed to act on warnings of genocide due to ‘pressure’ from emirates, Yale human rights investigator will tell a parliamentary select committee The British government had received intelligence that Ethiopia appeared to be supporting a genocidal militia in Sudan’s civil war as far back as 2024 but did not go public with the news for fear of upsetting the United Arab Emirates (UAE), a parliamentary committee will hear. In May 2024, officials from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) told Nathaniel Raymond , an American human rights investigator at Yale University, that “significant private pressure” from the UAE meant the UK would not publicly divulge information linking Ethiopia and the emirates to their support for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. Continue reading...
content:
Foreign Office failed to act on warnings of genocide due to ‘pressure’ from emirates, Yale human rights investigator will tell a parliamentary select committee
The British government had received intelligence that Ethiopia appeared to be supporting a genocidal militia in Sudan’s civil war as far back as 2024 but did not go public with the news for fear of upsetting the United Arab Emirates (UAE), a parliamentary committee will hear.
In May 2024, officials from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) told Nathaniel Raymond , an American human rights investigator at Yale University, that “significant private pressure” from the UAE meant the UK would not publicly divulge information linking Ethiopia and the emirates to their support for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
Ethiopia’s role in Sudan’s civil war did not become public until early this year. It continues to deny involvement.
In testimony to a parliamentary select committee on Tuesday, Raymond will allege that the UK government was more interested in preserving relations with the Emiratis than averting mass atrocities in Sudan .
The Commons international development committee is investigating the UK’s response to atrocity prevention after reports in the Guardian about the FCDO’s response to the RSF seizing the city of El Fasher, last year.
Raymond will also focus on what he describes as the UK’s “failed efforts to prevent the mass killing” of tens of thousands of people during the RSF’s genocidal massacre in El Fasher.
His testimony will include details of how a senior FCDO official attempted to downplay the huge death toll in El Fasher for “political” reasons.
After El Fasher fell to the RSF, following an 18-month siege, Raymond, director of Yale’s Humanitarian Research Lab (HRL), privately briefed the international development committee that at least 60,000 civilians had been killed .
An FCDO atrocity-prevention official contacted Raymond to ask if the figure was too high.
Raymond responded that his number did not include deaths from famine or the RSF’s bombardment of the city during its siege.
“I explained the math. I stated that, in reality, the number of people that the RSF systematically killed after capturing the city could have been higher,” said Raymond in written testimony to be presented to the commitee.
“The FCDO official and I discussed numbers further. I came to believe that this estimate of at least 60,000 people killed by the RSF was a political problem for the FCDO.”
Based on three years of encrypted messages, internal meeting notes, memos and phone records between the HRL and FCDO, Raymond’s testimony will also reveal how on 26 September 2025, a British UN official “expressed despair about the lack of any possible action by the Starmer government as the city was about to fall” – amid intelligence indicating that mass atrocities were inevitable .
Raymond’s revelations of longstanding Ethiopian involvement in Sudan’s war relate to 15 May 2024, when he met FCDO officials in London and shared collated data from mobile phones inside RSF headquarters during discussions on El Fasher’s worsening predicament.
HRL had tracked handsets moving between Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, to RSF-held territory in Sudan.
Some phones, Raymond will tell the committee, moved from RSF locations to addresses in the emirates, which HRL believes were shell companies linked to the RSF’s deputy commander, Abdul Rahim Dagalo.
One phone moved to Abu Dhabi from Addis Ababa in four hours, despite no official air traffic data or scheduled commercial flights matching the route, indicating deliberate attempts to evade detection.
FCDO officials requested Raymond to publicly release the phone data analysis linking UAE-based facilities to the RSF because the UK government could not.
Raymond will tell the committee: “They told me that the UK was facing significant private pressure behind the scenes from the UAE, limiting its ability to affect the situation.
“FCDO personnel suggested that HRL releasing this information could help neutralise these efforts by UAE to prevent the UK from linking them to the armament of the RSF.”
At the time, HRL could not share the telecommunications data publicly because it would compromise sources and operational methods.
However, HRL secretly shared the data with the US to support sanctions against Dagalo-linked shell companies.
Details of Ethiopia’s involvement in the Sudanese conflict became public in February after Reuters reported that Addis Ababa was hosting a camp to train RSF fighters .
Reuters said the move was backed by Ethiopia’s close ally, the UAE.
Ethiopia rebutted the reports, as did the UAE, which has also denied repeated accusations that it funds and arms the RSF.
Raymond will tell the MPs that he believes the FCDO prioritised the UK government’s “economic, security and diplomatic relationships with the UAE above preventing the intentional starvation and genocidal slaughter of tens of thousands of civilians living in El Fasher”.
He will add the UK’s position as “penholder”, or lead country, on Sudan at the UN security council meant its role was vital.
“The UK was our best hope at that time for stopping what we believed would become one of the single largest mass-casualty events of the 21st century.”
Referring to Raymond’s evidence, Jennifer Chapman, minister for development, said: “I would be surprised if it was as simple as that, and I think there are many countries playing games in Sudan.”
She also referenced the lack of media coverage of the Sudanese conflict. “It’s an outrage. It gets nowhere near the visibility that it needs until something like El Fasher happens, and then suddenly there’s momentarily some interest.
“One of the things we should be doing and [former Cabinbet minister] Anneleise Dodds has been brilliant on this, is really trying to get this into the press, really shine a spotlight on it.
“The invisibility of this conflict is creating a permissive culture for those external actors, shall we say, to feel that they can do this and that there is no consequence.”

title: Sudan paramilitary leaders acquired £17.7m property portfolio in Dubai, investigation reveals
description: The RSF leadership, accused of committing genocide, used UAE as a ‘safe haven’ for family members and their wealth, records show A network linked to the leadership of a militia accused of genocide has amassed a vast property portfolio in Dubai as part of a sprawling “paramilitary-industrial complex” across Africa and the Middle East, an investigation has revealed. Family members, individuals under sanctions, and entities linked to the leader of Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti , have acquired more than 20 luxury properties, worth £17.7m, in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), according to the Sentry, a US investigative group. Continue reading...
content:
The RSF leadership, accused of committing genocide, used UAE as a ‘safe haven’ for family members and their wealth, records show
A network linked to the leadership of a militia accused of genocide has amassed a vast property portfolio in Dubai as part of a sprawling “paramilitary-industrial complex” across Africa and the Middle East, an investigation has revealed.
Family members, individuals under sanctions, and entities linked to the leader of Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti , have acquired more than 20 luxury properties, worth £17.7m, in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), according to the Sentry, a US investigative group.
Sudan’s ruinous war between the RSF and the Sudanese armed forces has caused the world’s largest humanitarian crisis with 33 million of the country’s 50 million population requiring aid, and at least 19 million facing acute hunger.
The Sentry’s findings revealed the (UAE) provides a “safe haven” for the RSF leadership’s family and wealth, much of which is believed to come from gold smuggled out of Sudan.
Hemedti seized control of Darfur’s largest goldmine in 2017 , with exports enabling him and his family to accumulate significant assets.
A network of firms based in the UAE has allowed the RSF leadership to turn smuggled gold into hard currency, with Dubai a major hub for the precious metal, which is trading at near record highs .
Nick Donovan, senior investigator at the Sentry , said: “In addition to arming the militia, the UAE allows the RSF to base part of its paramilitary-industrial complex in Dubai.
“Our investigation shows the Dagalo family has also found a safe haven for its wealth in the Emirates.”
The Gulf state – the RSF’s chief foreign backer – is widely accused of supporting the militia with weapons and mercenaries, something it denies.
Analysis by the Sentry of leaked real estate records revealed that properties owned by a company linked to the RSF and members of Hemedti’s family were worth approximately £7.4m, with real estate owned by individuals under sanctions who are linked to the RSF worth another £10.3m.
Relatives of Hemedti acquired luxury six-bedroom villas in a small gated community near Dubai’s Meydan racecourse, close to the city centre.
The villas were brought by the UAE-registered firm Prodigious Real Estate Management Supervision Services, whose owner is also linked to Dubai’s gold trade, and who had sanctions imposed on them by the US for running other companies that provided funding and military equipment to the RSF.
Further analysis of other data, including phone records and passport data, revealed that relatives of the Dagalo family have congregated within the gated community.
Farther afield, the investigation found that Hemedti’s wife bought a plot of land for £627,000, six months into Sudan’s war , in a yet-to-be-completed luxury development near Dubai’s Trump International Golf Club.
Individuals with ties to the RSF were also named including Mustafa Ibrahim Abdel Nabi Mohamed – sanctioned by the EU and the UK for his role as a financial adviser to the RSF and the Dagalo family – who is said to own an apartment worth £516,000 in the Burj Khalifa skyscraper in Dubai.
According to the Sentry, the Dagalo family declined to comment on whether its members still owned specific properties, and said that any private residences or assets had been properly obtained.
Ownership of property by Dagalo family members does not constitute or imply wrongdoing. The family also stressed that members had been engaged in legitimate commercial activity such as livestock trading, for generations.
The Sentry could not reach Prodigious for comment but said its owner had previously declined to answer questions regarding his role in other companies under sanctions for links to the RSF, stating that matters were subject to legal proceedings.
Mohamed told the Sentry that he is not a financial adviser to the RSF but has been the “financial director seconded to the Rapid Support Forces” since 2017, during a period when the RSF was a properly constituted entity governed by Sudanese law. He added that since the war began, he has not engaged in any activities that hinder peace and stability in Sudan .
The UAE has previously stated that it “categorically rejects” claims that it has provided “weapons, funding, trainers or logistical support to the RSF”. Spokespeople have been contacted for comment.
The RSF is commanded by Hemedti and his brothers Abdelrahim and Algoney, all of whom have had sanctions imposed on them.
Recently, the UN said the RSF’s attack on the western city of El Fasher last year bore the “ hallmarks of genocide ”, while the US has accused the group of committing genocide.
A separate report last week found a network of Colombian mercenaries, backed by the UAE, provided crucial support to the RSF during the fall of El Fasher.

title: I was tortured because I’m a Somali woman who dared to speak out | Sadia Moalim Ali

content:
I was sentenced to three years in jail for insulting government institutions. Now I am free, I will carry on fighting for the women I met in prison
‘W hy don’t you just drive your tuk-tuk and do your work?” the judge asked me after videos from my social media accounts were shown during my court hearing. I had spoken on TikTok and Facebook about issues in Somalia that concerned me: forced evictions in the capital, Mogadishu, high fuel prices and nepotism in government.
I had described how, when I applied for work in hospitals and government departments, I was told on three occasions that I’d have to give a sexual favour in return.
In Somalia, women have no right to be part of society or to express themselves. They are not respected. Those who do dare to speak out are subjected to violence – or even disappeared.
Two days earlier, I had been abducted by two police officers and forced into a vehicle. At the police station, I was slapped and my head was hit against a wall. I had no access to a lawyer and no formal charges were made.
In court, the judge said I would be held in custody pending investigation. I was taken to Mogadishu Central prison. The female wing of the prison held about 120 women, and there were about 30 in my cell. The prison was built in colonial times and has never been renovated. There were no windows or lights, and there was a terrible smell. The only toilet had no door and there was no privacy.
The first night was horrible. I was imprisoned with members of [jihadist militant group] al-Shabaab and they were talking about killings, explosions and targeting well-known individuals. I was too afraid to sleep.
Every day we’d get tea and one slice of stale bread for breakfast, and then half a plate of rice about three hours later. To go outside for sunshine, you had to bribe the guards.
A lot of the women were depressed and had health issues. I developed skin problems, lost a lot of weight and my period stopped.
As time went on, I started hearing other women’s stories. One woman had been imprisoned while pregnant. Her ex-husband was thought to be a member of al-Shabaab and their joint bank account was found to have some irregular payments.
She gave birth to her now 18-month-old daughter inside her cell with the help of the other women. I found that heartbreaking – the baby hadn’t committed any crime and deserved a better life.
Every time I saw her, I was reminded of my own daughter who I was breastfeeding when I was taken. I was incarcerated alongside two girls aged 13 and 17. Women were imprisoned for debt or for non-payment of fines. Many had no access to a lawyer and had been sentenced to years in prison without understanding what crime they had committed.
I noticed that many of the imprisoned women had never received an education and had been exploited. I started teaching some of them how to read and write.
I managed to get a phone in prison and decided to speak to a local radio station. I did the interview for my safety and protection, and to let people know about my situation.
An hour after it was released, a group of men came to my cell and took me to a room used for torture and punishment. The prison commander started stripping me, removing my headscarf and dress, and beating me. My hands were tied behind my back, and they told me to crawl on my chest while they threw water on me. There were CCTV cameras in the room.
After that, I spoke to the media again – this time to the Guardian . I wanted to show that I was not going to back down and that this punishment would not stop me from speaking out. Even if you torture me, I will continue to rise up and speak.
After that interview was published, I was threatened with rape. The prison authorities said they would record it and release the video.
Three men forced me to the floor and removed my headscarf. They sexually assaulted me. All this was recorded on a mobile phone.
I eventually got access to a lawyer and, after a month in jail, I had the first of three court hearings. At court, the prosecution produced the Guardian article about me being tortured, alleging that I was spreading anti-government propaganda. I knew then that the story had hit a nerve.
On 25 June, I was convicted of insulting government institutions and sentenced to three years in prison . It was like a shot to the head. I was shaking and my vision went blurry.
My lawyer filed an appeal. That, along with the knowledge that people were campaigning for my freedom, gave me hope. On 12 August, the Banadir [region] court of appeal overturned my conviction and three-year prison sentence, leading to my release on the same day.
When I reunited with my daughter, she did not recognise me. Her punishment was much worse than what I had been subjected to.
I kept receiving threats and was being pressured to stop talking. Members of al-Shabaab had seen how my case had played out and wanted me to join them. I became scared for my safety, so I left the country.
Now, I am recovering from my ordeal. I want to get mental health support because I still have flashbacks to my time in prison. I am writing a book about my experiences.
And I am using my social media channels to advocate for some of the women I came across in prison. They are invisible – I want to help them get their freedom.

title: Exile has not broken young Rohingya people. But survival cost us more than our homes | Ajas Khan
description: Nine years growing up in a tent robbed me of my freedom and childhood. But my generation is determined to fight for a better future – one that we must be involved in shaping Nine years ago, I was forced to flee my home in Maungdaw township, Rakhine state, Myanmar. I was 13 years old. I remember how quickly an average day turned into a day when life felt extinguished, leaving behind the place where I grew up with my family. Even now, when I go to sleep, what comes into my mind is the memory of that journey, the fear of not knowing what awaited me. It took three days to reach refuge. Continue reading...
content:
Nine years growing up in a tent robbed me of my freedom and childhood. But my generation is determined to fight for a better future – one that we must be involved in shaping
N ine years ago, I was forced to flee my home in Maungdaw township, Rakhine state, Myanmar . I was 13 years old. I remember how quickly an average day turned into a day when life felt extinguished, leaving behind the place where I grew up with my family.
Even now, when I go to sleep, what comes into my mind is the memory of that journey, the fear of not knowing what awaited me. It took three days to reach refuge.
With so many others, my family and I crossed the Naf River into Bangladesh . But survival came at a high price: the price of my home, my liberty, my life.
I am Ajas Khan, a climate activist, youth leader and Rohingya genocide survivor.
Nine years is a long time for a child to grow up, to feel at home, or not to feel at home if the place you are staying in is not your country.
It is a long time for the whole family to wait, in exile, seeing another generation grow up in the camps. The people of Bangladesh have given us a safe place to stay, which we are incredibly grateful for and can never forget. Humanitarian organisations have saved many lives. However, a plastic shelter is not a permanent solution. It can provide a place to sleep, but little else in the way of home, citizenship, freedom or dignity.
But the exile has not broken us. Young Rohingya people are studying, caring for each other, and survivors are telling their stories. We are not just victims; we have a history, a culture, a home and dreams for the future.
When we speak of justice, we do not seek revenge. Survivors want the truth to come out about those who have committed genocide against the Rohingya people, and for the international community to continue to provide all possible support. Those responsible for these crimes must be brought to justice, which will allow us a future away from the brutality of the past.
It makes no difference if the perpetrators are soldiers or politicians , state actors or non-state actors . If they destroy homes, expel people, take away their lives and nothing happens to them, they will do the same again.
Nine years is more than enough. Time must never become an excuse for impunity.
I’ve never for one second let go of the hope of returning to my home. Going home doesn’t mean just crossing back over the Naf River. It means going home with full human rights in our motherland, without fear, with our citizenship, security, equality, land and livelihood restored. Our healthcare and education.
There is no choice between being rendered stateless and living in the camps, or repatriation without rights. Return without citizenship is no solution at all.
On this ninth anniversary, I would like to raise the point that decisions over the fate of the Rohingya people must no longer be made by any entity other than the Rohingya themselves.
The government of Bangladesh and NGOs have made immense sacrifices to care for Rohingya refugees, navigating the immense humanitarian and economic implications of hosting more than a million Rohingya in Bangladesh. It is understandable that the government of Bangladesh might want to make concessions in its negotiations to ensure solutions can be brokered, and to engage with anyone claiming authority in Myanmar who could contribute to this goal. But such concessions should not come at our expense.
The Rohingya are not a footnote; we are a people with a history, and our future can no longer be dictated either by governments or armed groups. Should the governments of Bangladesh or Myanmar, or the Arakan Army in Rakhine, or any other interlocutor, make decisions, then Rohingya representatives must be at the table.
We give our breath to our future. And through all these years of fighting, our identity is still there and our dreams have not gone away, despite the pain.
I remember all the people who were lost during the 2017 massacres , and those who survived but are still being chased and hated. I think about the people whose families are broken, who have injuries, and those whose childhood was taken away.
Rohingya children should grow up with different stories – not of loss, but tales of returning home. We need justice; we need to be recognised as humans; we need our citizenship; we need accountability. And we need to go home.
I want our next generation to hold their lives in their own hands and not in those of strangers. I want them to see our land, not just hear stories.
For me, I have spent nine years in a foreign refugee camp without a future, in an open jail, and I’m still waiting for hope to return.

title: As president of Botswana, I know how we can make malaria a memory in Africa | Duma Gideon Boko
description: The disease is soaring as funding is cut. African nations are plugging the gap but they need help with the transition Botswana nearly defeated malaria. Then, as is unfortunately the nature of malaria, it came back. In the first 23 weeks of 2025 we recorded 2,223 cases and 11 deaths . The disease reached places where previously there was no malaria. content:
The disease is soaring as funding is cut. African nations are plugging the gap but they need help with the transition
B otswana nearly defeated malaria. In 2024, we recorded just 290 cases and one death. Through our elimination efforts, many of our districts had seen no local malaria cases since 2010. Then, as is unfortunately the nature of malaria, it came back.
In the first 23 weeks of 2025 we recorded 2,223 cases and 11 deaths . The disease reached places where previously there was no malaria. We were not alone. Namibia recorded more than 95,000 cases in 2025, and Zimbabwe more than 156,000 , according to government figures.
Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe were all affected by a perfect storm of threats. External resources fell rapidly and are continuing to fall. The mosquito is evolving and becoming resistant to the traditional insecticides used on our nets and for spraying. In addition, partial resistance to our frontline medicines has been confirmed or suspected in eight African countries . Severe weather events, including flooding and higher temperatures, are increasing malaria mosquito populations and malaria cases.
I begin with my own country and our neighbours because they offer a clear demonstration of the results of these combined threats. Malaria is a disease of poverty and persists in those countries with the least financial capacity and resources to mount an effective response. African Union (AU) member states suffered 96% of the world’s malaria cases and 97% of malaria deaths in 2024.
As we have seen time and time again, malaria does not wait for a funding cycle to conclude and can resurge in just one season. One missed spraying round, or one mosquito net campaign that slips a season, is enough for the malaria mosquito and parasite to destroy progress that took decades to win. Most diseases give a country years of warning, while malaria may only give it months. That is why, when the financing tightens, malaria is the first disease to come back.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention records a fall of about 70% in health assistance to Africa since 2021, and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, which tracks what donor governments spend, projects a further fall of between 29% and 46% in aid for health by the end of 2026. The Global Fund’s latest replenishment raised $12.64bn (£9.45bn) against an $18bn target , and as a direct result allocations to countries have reduced.
Modelling by the African Leaders Malaria Alliance and Malaria No More UK predicts that a 30% cut in malaria funding could lead to 146m additional cases and 397,000 deaths across sub-Saharan Africa by 2030, three-quarters of them children under five. Additionally, it would cost the continent as much as $37bn in lost economic output.
Africa’s leaders have already decided what needs to be done. In Accra in July, our heads of state and government adopted the Accra declaration on the implementation of the AU roadmap to 2030 and beyond , committing us to finance our own health systems and for our performance against its targets to be measured every year. It elevates the roadmap as our continental framework for health sovereignty, resilience and self-reliance, and commits us to reduce dependence on external funding. It reaffirms the earlier Abuja declaration , in which we undertook to spend 15% of our national budgets on health. Leaders also committed to accelerate the Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Plan for Africa and the African Pooled Procurement Mechanism , to make the African Medicines Agency fully operational , and to press for the transfer of technology, scientific knowledge and manufacturing processes to facilitate the development of innovative tools and commodities in Africa.
Several African countries are already leading the way. Benin took its malaria budget from $1.7m to $6.3m in the three years to 2025 . Ghana has uncapped its National Health Insurance Levy, releasing about $300m for health this year, and expects domestic funds to cover 72% of its health spending in 2026. End Malaria councils and funds now operate in 14 countries and have raised more than $245m from business, faith leaders and philanthropy, demonstrating the value of public-private partnerships and the economic benefits of malaria control and elimination.
A full transition to domestic financing of health is the solution. But the lack of financial capacity in many of our countries means that bridge financing will be required during this transition phase to reduce the risk of malaria resurgences across the continent. As we transition to this new model, support from global partners will still play an important and valued role in keeping two decades of hard-fought gains alive long enough for the transition to be completed.
This has been done before, at exactly this point in the cycle. Twenty years ago, the World Bank’s Malaria Booster Programme committed more than $1bn to supplement existing resources and support achievement of the UN’s millennium development goals . And it worked. For example, malaria cases among Zambian children under five fell by 29% and deaths by a third.
African countries had ambitious plans, and the political will was there, but unfortunately financial resources ultimately fell short of what was needed. Most of Africa faces a similar situation today. The political will and technical knowhow are there, but the financial resources remain insufficient. Africa therefore urges the World Bank to deliver a second Malaria Booster Programme to bridge the gap and support countries to transition to sustainable domestic financing. Countries should also include malaria within their health compacts.
The destination is not in doubt. African countries are determined to pay for their own malaria and health programmes, and a growing number are already doing this. Collectively, we must get this transition right so that the children born in Africa this year become the first generation to grow up on a continent where malaria is a memory. That is within reach, and the decisions needed to make this vision a reality are being taken now.
Duma Gideon Boko is president of the republic of Botswana and chair of the African Leaders Malaria Alliance

title: Nine women in South Africa have been murdered since July. We are being told to be vigilant – but where are the warnings to men? | Nolethu Ndude
description: The country has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, and women are yet again being asked to remove themselves from public life to counter it When I heard the authorities advising women in and around Kempton Park, the site of a recent spate of femicides, not to walk or run alone, to avoid isolated places and to “remain vigilant”, my immediate response was anger. Remain vigilant. How groundbreaking. Women are already vigilant. We photograph number plates before entering vehicles. We share Uber details with friends. We phone one another while walking. We watch the driver’s route and notice every unexpected turn. We avoid certain roads, certain times and certain conversations. We scan parking areas before getting out of our cars. We check the back seat. We listen for footsteps. We carry pepper spray where we can. We hold our keys in a way that makes us feel slightly less defenceless. Continue reading...
content:
The country has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, and women are yet again being asked to remove themselves from public life to counter it
W hen I heard the authorities advising women in and around Kempton Park, the site of a recent spate of femicides, not to walk or run alone, to avoid isolated places and to “remain vigilant”, my immediate response was anger. Remain vigilant. How groundbreaking.
Women are already vigilant. We photograph number plates before entering vehicles. We share Uber details with friends. We phone one another while walking. We watch the driver’s route and notice every unexpected turn. We avoid certain roads, certain times and certain conversations. We scan parking areas before getting out of our cars. We check the back seat. We listen for footsteps. We carry pepper spray where we can. We hold our keys in a way that makes us feel slightly less defenceless.
Women have informal safety systems built into our friendships. “Please let me know when you get home” is not simply a polite farewell. It is a survival protocol.
Police are investigating the deaths of nine women whose bodies have been found across the Ekurhuleni district, east of Johannesburg, since July. Some were found naked or partially clothed, and several had visible injuries.
One of the women was Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo , a 38-year-old who disappeared after leaving her home in Kempton Park for an afternoon run on 9 September. Her body was found three days later.
Now running must be approached like a security operation. Choose a group. Share your route. Check the time. Avoid quiet roads. Stay where people can see you. Keep one earphone out. Carry your phone. Remain visible. Remain alert. Remain vigilant.
But women cannot “vigilance” themselves out of gender-based violence and femicide.
Where are the instructions to men? Where is the urgent public warning telling them not to harm women? Where is the nationwide mobilisation asking men to confront their friends, brothers and colleagues? Where are the campaigns teaching men that affection does not create ownership and that rejection is not humiliation?
Where is the same relentless attention on perpetrators, effective policing, prosecution and prevention?
The truth is, women are not safe anywhere.
In 2019, 19-year-old University of Cape Town student Uyinene Mrwetyana went to collect a parcel from a post office in Cape Town. She was raped and murdered inside that post office by an employee. Her murder shattered the idea that danger is limited to badly lit streets and isolated fields.
If we must avoid every place where another woman has been attacked or killed, where are we allowed to exist?
We are told to stay indoors, although many women are abused in their homes. We are told not to trust strangers, although women are killed by husbands, boyfriends, relatives and former partners. We are told to choose better, as though abusive men introduce themselves honestly and arrive carrying warning labels.
South African women were killed at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 in 2022 , nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. That figure should stop the country in its tracks. Instead, it becomes another statistic repeated during interviews, marches and annual campaigns.
After protests ahead of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis. Women had already spent years explaining that it was one.
The issue is not whether government has heard us. It has. The issue is what actually changes after gender-based violence is declared a national crisis?
Which institutions become accountable? What additional resources are committed? Are police stations properly equipped to act when a woman is reported missing? Are officers trained to respond to survivors with care rather than suspicion? Are investigations adequately resourced? Are protection orders enforced? Are shelters funded? Are survivors protected while cases move through courts?
Who answers when commitments are not fulfilled?
The Commission for Gender Equality has called for an urgent safety audit of the affected areas. It wants attention given to lighting, surveillance, public transport routes, neglected spaces, police visibility and access to emergency assistance. That is necessary.
But the response cannot end at Ekurhuleni’s borders. Women are being killed nationally, therefore prevention strategies must implemented at a national level.
We also need to stop treating every killing as an isolated tragedy with no relationship to the culture around it. Femicide does not begin when a body is discovered. It develops along a continuum.
Through my work with young people, I see why intervention must begin long before violence reaches the criminal justice system. We need sustained education about consent, bodily autonomy, healthy relationships, emotional regulation and positive masculinity.
That is not an excuse for violence. It is part of preventing it.
Men must confront misogyny in their own circles. They must challenge the jokes, controlling behaviour, coercion and entitlement before somebody is dead. Silence is not neutrality. It protects the conditions in which violence thrives.
This responsibility does not belong only to activists, police or women’s organisations. It belongs in homes, schools, churches, workplaces, sports clubs, taxis, universities and friendship groups. It belongs wherever boys learn what manhood means.
I am not arguing that women should ignore immediate safety warnings. I am arguing that those warnings cannot be presented as the solution. There is a difference between sharing information about a specific risk and building an entire response around women limiting their lives.
The state’s responsibility is not to teach women how to stay alive around violent men. Its responsibility is to prevent violence, investigate cases properly, pursue perpetrators and build a country in which women can collect a parcel, go for a run, leave a relationship, take a ride home and simply live.
We have restricted ourselves. We have changed our behaviour. We have remained vigilant. We are still being killed. It is time the authorities, and men, tried something different. Accountability would be a good place to start.

title: ‘There’s always been a belittling of African women’: honouring history’s invisible heroines
description: Congolese photographer Pamela Tulizo uses costume and vivid scenery to celebrate women’s strength and give a new perspective on slavery Pamela Tulizo’s latest series of photographs started with a question. “I asked myself, why are women in my community in particular, and African women in general, so strong?” says Tulizo, an artist and photographer from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. “Where does this strength come from?” Growing up in Goma in eastern DRC, Tulizo was informed and inspired by the women she was surrounded by, including her mother, her sisters, her mother’s friends and her neighbours.
