content:
Congolese photographer Pamela Tulizo uses costume and vivid scenery to celebrate women’s strength and give a new perspective on slavery
P amela Tulizo’s latest series of photographs started with a question. “I asked myself, why are women in my community in particular, and African women in general, so strong?” says Tulizo, an artist and photographer from the Democratic Republic of the Congo . “Where does this strength come from?”
Growing up in Goma in eastern DRC, Tulizo was informed and inspired by the women she was surrounded by, including her mother, her sisters, her mother’s friends and her neighbours.
Years later, when she began to look into the role of women throughout African history, she says: “I realised that perhaps women have been forced to be strong since the dawn of time, forced by circumstance to build that resilience.”
Her research brought her to slavery, the “cruellest period in human history”, which is often just associated with the men who were forced across oceans to form workforces abroad. Women, she noticed, were largely invisible, their stories untold.
With that in mind, Tulizo placed women at the centre of her series of 23 staged photographs called Mababu (“ancestors” in Swahili). In it, she portrays figures such as Kimpa Vita and Queen Nzinga , who were both renowned for resisting the European colonisation of Africa in the 17th and early 18th century.
“Because of racism, there’s always been this belittling of African women that portrays them as vulnerable, as victims, and suggests they lack strength or intelligence,” says Tulizo.
“I wanted to end that narrative by showing that despite everything they endured, they remained strong and fought for freedom.”
Tulizo’s path to photography has not been easy – in part, she believes, because she is a woman. She started her career as a reporter but decided to focus on photography when she felt she could not write about everything she wanted to cover.
There was nowhere to train as a photographer in Goma so she took photos whenever she could, and became one of a handful of female photographers in the city.
“It wasn’t easy at first because I didn’t have a role model to follow, or anyone to guide me in my early days,” she says. “The community didn’t accept me right away – whether it was my parents, or even other photographers – since it was very much a male-dominated world.
“But facing so many obstacles motivated me to stick it out to the end and prove that I could be a woman and a photographer,” she says.
In 2020, her work Double Identity won the Dior photography and visual arts award for young talents, a series that contrasted the media portrayal of Congolese women as victims with their true identities. This allowed her to finance the creation in 2021 of a cultural centre in Goma for women and girls, Tulizo Elle Space . When renewed violence broke out in the region in early 2025, she fled and now lives in France.
She approached her latest series of work, Mababu, as if she were making a film, using cinematic staging with actors, costumes, makeup and outdoor sets to create vivid scenes.
In one set, a woman stands in Lake Kivu holding a basket of either cotton, tobacco or sugar cane, and surrounded by other women bound in bandages (wrapping the body being a common practice in funeral rituals). The images, which were shot in Goma and Belgium, are defiant, and do not gloss over past suffering.
Fashion is a crucial element of the series and Tulizo uses it to elevate and pay tribute to women. She uses colour, accessories and styling to express hope, courage and strength. In some images, where a woman is bound or suffering, she is still elevated through a hat, dress or gloves, says Tulizo.
“To me, she remains a heroine, and fashion allows me to honour her, giving her the strength and power she deserves,” she says.
Some of the photos incorporate images of natural resources. The titles of the opening works – Tumbako , Miwa and Pamba – refer to tobacco, sugar cane and cotton, three commodities that played a central role in fuelling the transatlantic slave trade. “Slavery did not happen in a vacuum,” says Tulizo. “It was driven by the pursuit of natural resources.”
The photos echo what is going on today in eastern DRC, where devastating conflict and sexual violence have been driven by decades of competition over rich mineral resources.
“Regrettably, today we are experiencing a modern form of slavery driven by technology, development and global progress,” says Tulizo. “Back then it was tobacco, sugar and coffee. Today it is war and sexual violence over lithium, gold and minerals.
“Everyone wants to conquer the world, to be the first to produce electric cars, or to be the leading global power with nuclear weapons. None of that is possible without these raw materials.
“Unfortunately,” Tulizo adds, “humanity has not learned its lesson, and we are repeating the same mistakes in a modern form.”
M ababu – Spirit of the Ancestors by Pamela Tulizo is at GC De Markten , Brussels, as part of the Vrije Universiteit Brussel cultural diplomacy initiative, from 8 to 31 October

content:
Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive
T he cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.
In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama ’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.
Delgado’s milk production has fallen by half. As the dry season approaches, he is selling off cattle for fear of what is to come. He says: “I and other producers have had to slaughter or sell animals of high genetic value simply to avoid the heartbreaking prospect of watching them die of thirst or starvation. The lack of water has greatly affected us, and it is going to continue to do so.”
Panama is gripped by a water crisis. A rainy season punctuated by drought, exacerbated by the climate crisis, has ravaged large swathes of the country. El Niño threatens to continue the havoc. In August, the government declared a national state of emergency that will remain in place until June 2027. Authorities forecast rainfall deficits of more than 50% in some regions until December.
“The situation is dramatic,” says Panama’s environment minister, Juan Navarro. “Climate change has undoubtedly increased the frequency and also the gravity of El Niño, as well as other climate extremes; we used to get an El Niño every 10 or 20 years. The last, in 2023, cost the Panama canal almost a billion dollars in revenue.”
And this latest El Niño, Navarro says, citing scientists, is pointing towards being the worst in history . He says: “We are already starting to feel the impact, but we have seen nothing yet. For Panama, this is life or death. The canal is life and death for our economy, and for our drinking water supply.”
Panama’s economy relies heavily on the Panama canal – and the canal is acutely vulnerable to the climate crisis. The 50-mile (80km) waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, through which about 5% of global maritime trade flows , accounts for up to 7.7% of Panama’s GDP . The freshwater lakes that supply the canal’s locks, Gatún and Alajuela, also provide drinking water for about 2 million people – nearly half of Panama’s population . A sizeable chunk of the country’s hydroelectricity generation also depends on the watershed.
In September, low water levels twice triggered restrictions on daily vessel transits. While some have been lifted, officials are braced for worse when the El Niño-intensified dry season begins in December.
The government is funnelling $80m (£60m) towards “resilience actions” to prepare for El Niño, Navarro says. In the long term, it is investing about $1.5bn in a reservoir on the Indio River intended to supply Lake Gatún and meet demand for the next five decades.
The new reservoir is, in Navarro’s words, “the most important investment we are making – Indio is the ultimate bet on resilience”.
Yet the project has not come without controversy and fierce resistance. Damming the Indio River will flood the lands of 550 families in 38 rural communities , about 2,500 people in total, who live in the basin. Cropland will be swept away, graves exhumed and reburied elsewhere, and whole communities – homes, schools, churches – will be dismantled.
In response, people have held street protests, taken legal action and set up blockades. Yet the project is steaming ahead; authorities forecast completion in two to three years.
“For us, this isn’t merely a matter of changing homes,” says Florentino Chirú, vice-president of the Coordinadora Campesina por la Vida Contra los Embalses (Peasant Coordinating Committee for Life Against Dams). “It means leaving behind the history of entire generations. Furthermore, we would lose fertile land.”
According to Chirú, farmers rely on small-scale livestock farming for their livelihoods, meaning they would lose their only means of feeding themselves and generating income.
“The impact would be absolutely devastating. There are no words to describe it. I’ve lived on this land for 63 years; my whole life is here,” he says. “If we were to be displaced, well, this is our life insurance. We would be left with nothing.”
The Panama Canal Authority says the resettlement will include compensation for homes, land, crops and livelihoods, along with support to restore families’ income sources. It says residents can choose from different relocation options, including moving together to preserve community ties.
A greater supply will not solve all of Panama’s water management and storage problems, though. Experts say the current crisis has exposed structural failings in the country’s relationship with water.
Despite living in one of the wettest countries on Earth, hundreds of thousands of people still lack access to reliable drinking water. In places such as Azuero, drought is compounding a chronic lack of potable water. By the government’s own estimates, in some areas about 50% of water is lost through ageing, leaky pipes.
A recent El País investigation found that 240,000 Panamanians lack regular access to drinking water, and even communities within the canal watershed rely on rainwater, tanks and informal deliveries.
“We have a challenge with water,” Navarro acknowledges. “The number-one challenge is the watersheds. Number two: our water purification and treatment facilities to produce potable water are inadequate. Three, we have a horrendous problem with loss. Because we have such abundant water, we haven’t taken adequate care of it in the past.”
Along with legislation to pave the way for public-private partnerships and infrastructure investments, the government has announced an $8.2m emergency package , including funding for livestock feed, irrigation equipment and the like.
But for Azuero farmers, rice growers in Coclé, and others already grappling with drought’s effects, long-term investments will do little to ease the immediate crisis.
“If there is no regrowth during the rainy season, how are we going to sustain the animals during the dry season when there is absolutely nothing?” asks Delgado. “What we lose today, we sorely need in the future.”
Delgado fears that the cattle population will drop drastically, and rebuilding those breeding herds, whether for milk or meat, will take a long time. “This combination of problems, compounded by the climate crisis has made the agricultural sector’s situation so dire that we risk disappearing altogether,” he says.

title: The hidden costs of fracking: boom in Argentina linked to trail of sickness

author_name: Elena Basso in Allen, Neuquén and Añelo, Argentina
content:
Families in Vaca Muerta, the centre of Patagonia’s shale operation, report cancers, miscarriages and pollution
I n Allen, a small town in Argentine Patagonia, many people living on the same street ended up falling ill. For some, it was severe migraines, nausea or skin irritation. For others, cancers, congenital abnormalities, miscarriages or stillbirth seemed to affect foetuses or children. People say it all started 13 years ago – when a well was drilled near their homes to extract gas and oil.
Calle Ciega 10 [Dead-end Street 10] lies on the eastern edge of Vaca Muerta, a vital area for Argentina ’s economy, home to the world’s second-largest reserve of shale gas and fourth-largest reserve of shale oil. The region has more than 2,600 active wells , including one on this small street where about 20 families live, most of them seasonal workers on fruit farms.
“There have been cases of cancer, and several women had to move away because they could not carry their pregnancies to term. They kept losing their babies. Some were born with illnesses, or died shortly after birth,” says Roxana Valverde, who has lived in the area for nearly 30 years. “Before the well, we didn’t experience these illnesses, or if we did, they were much less common.”
Valverde adds that, during medical appointments, doctors say the illnesses could be caused by pollution from fracking, while acknowledging that, without in-depth studies, it is hard to establish with 100% certainty.
Vaca Muerta covers more than 11,500 sq miles and spans four Argentine provinces. Since 2012, under the government led by Cristina Kirchner, the area has been extracting gas and oil using fracking, a technique that injects water, sand and chemicals at high pressure to fracture rock and release trapped hydrocarbons.
Now, under Javier Milei, the Argentine government is heavily reliant on Vaca Muerta’s gas and oil resources to help the country recover from years of economic crisis, and has opened the door to foreign companies to extract and export hydrocarbons.
By the end of 2025, the all-time production record had been broken . For the first time in the country’s history, crude oil overtook soya bean meal as its leading export , partly driven by European companies that invested in the Vaca Muerta region to find another option as well as Russian gas.
According to a report from the NGO OpSur , 33% of the unconventional gas and 39% of the unconventional oil extracted in Vaca Muerta are controlled by the state-owned energy company YPF, while the rest is handled by foreign companies, including the US company Chevron, France’s TotalEnergies and the UK’s Shell.
F racking is a highly invasive technique that poses environmental risks and has been linked by numerous scientific studies to ecological harm and health issues for people living nearby, such as respiratory and skin conditions, cancer, congenital disabilities, miscarriages and pregnancy complications .
Calle Ciega 10 is in the countryside, and the families living there come from low-income backgrounds. The houses are small and dilapidated. Children play and ride bikes just a few metres from the well, while workers and a crane operate nearby.
According to those who live in Calle Ciega 10, the well ceased operations in 2019, but work resumed in May this year. They have repeatedly tried to file complaints, but the courts have never heard their pleas. They suspect that several incidents at the well could have contaminated a pond from which they draw water for their daily needs.
The family of Analía Celeste Saldías has faced numerous health issues. In 2023, while pregnant with her youngest daughter, Bianca, Saldías faced complications, including what she described as the beginning of a stroke.
Her son Joel was born in 2020 with three lungs and had surgery as a baby to correct a severe congenital malformation. In 2019, her eldest daughter, Michelle, experienced serious skin problems, with painful patches on her back, arms and torso.
Since fracking operations began, health concerns have spread beyond Calle Ciega 10. Lef and Jorge Nawel are members of the Zonal Xawvn Ko Mapuche confederation , an organisation that brings together 14 Indigenous communities from different parts of Vaca Muerta.
The Mapuche people, the largest Indigenous group in Argentina, are frequently among those most affected in the region due to the widespread construction of wells on their ancestral lands.
The Nawels say that the community has seen numerous cases of miscarriage and nervous and respiratory system disorders, particularly among children.
In Añelo, a small town considered the operational core of Vaca Muerta, Lorena Bravo Maripe, the ancestral leader of the Añelo Lof Campo Maripe Mapuche community with 106 members, also reports numerous health issues in her group. That includes several cancer cases – such as her mother’s breast cancer and her own cervical cancer – as well as numerous respiratory and skin ailments.
“This is a polluting industry and, instead of monitoring it, the state is completely absent,” she says, adding that the community raises livestock and has noticed that animals are often born disfigured or experience complications during birth.
The rise in serious illnesses is raising concerns among doctors working in Vaca Muerta. Silvia Ávila, dean of the faculty of medicine at the National University of Comahue, says the government must monitor citizens’ health, ensure transparency and publish results.
“The entire population, including healthcare workers, should be informed about the public policies and monitoring carried out by the state and companies regarding people’s health – but we are not,” she says.
“We lack medical and scientific research ,” says Alan Rocha Varsanyi, a researcher at OpSur. “It is highly possible that we are already paying the health costs of this today, but we lack the tools to determine whether or to what extent this is the case.”
When approached for interviews, health ministers in Neuquén and Río Negro provinces declined to comment. YPF, Chevron, TotalEnergies and Shell were approached for comment.
A ñelo is surrounded by hundreds of active wells, yet hydrocarbon extraction is not the only threat to the health of people living in Vaca Muerta. The region also hosts numerous open-air toxic waste dumps, and hundreds of lorries pass through daily.
People’s wellbeing is at the heart of Vaca Muerta’s most critical environmental lawsuit: the Comarsa case , initiated after complaints from local people, environmental groups and civic organisations.
Comarsa, a waste management company, is accused of storing rather than properly handling and disposing of more than 300,000 cubic metres of toxic waste , now in a dump in Neuquén , a city with more than 300,000 inhabitants.
If the courts have not yet considered the allegations, prosecutor Maximiliano Breide Obeid, the head of the environmental offences and special laws unit in Neuquén, leads the new case and has no doubt about the dangers posed by toxic waste such as that found at the Comarsa dump.
“We have established that the nearest homes are just 200 metres from the toxic waste,” he says. “We believe there is an immediate danger to people’s health, and that there will be a future danger if the situation is not resolved.”
A crucial piece of evidence for the prosecution is a report by the forensic medical corps, where doctors state that contact with the toxic waste from the dump – polluting soil, water and air – can lead to severe health issues such as respiratory, skin, neurological, stomach and kidney problems, as well as cancer and miscarriages.
According to the doctors, the waste contains barium, cadmium, lead, copper, mercury and arsenic – heavy metals that can be toxic to humans. Comarsa has been approached for comment.
The prosecution says that the company stored toxic waste on the surface and underground without properly sealing the soil, violating safety regulations and risking contamination of water and soil. The air around the dump emits a very strong odour, making it unbearable to breathe, and within minutes, people’s eyes start to water.
Yet new plots for residential building are being developed around the dump, just a few dozen metres away.

title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
description: Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations. The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. content:
Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift
A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.
The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.
The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.
The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisations ELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.
These organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.
Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.
“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southern France , north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”
Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, partly based on data from the Brazilian intelligence agency (Abin) – which the Guardian reviewed – shows, for example, that the PCC, now Brazil’s biggest criminal group, operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.
The suspicion that Latin American cartels and factions are seeking to become established in Europe is not new. Since at least the 1980s, Colombian criminal organisations such as the Cali and Medellín cartels had footholds in regions of Spain such as Galicia. In 2013, a Europol report in 2103 warned of their rise. But what authorities are witnessing now is on an another level.
A Europol report this year states that “Latin American MTCNs [most threatening criminal networks] have also settled in the EU, from where they direct operations that affect the EU. This is particularly the case for mobile criminal networks involved in organised property crime.”
Interpol , led by the Brazilian federal police officer Valdecy Urquiza, has been approached, but has not commented.
The problem has become more visible over the past decade. Drug production in Latin America in that time has increased roughly fourfold to reach a record of about 4,100 tonnes in 2024. This comes after growth of up to 35% at the beginning of the decade . More cocaine is now produced in Colombia than during the era of the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar . Nearly all the world’s cocaine and many related substances originate from Latin America, particularly Colombia.
Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, an academic at the Autonomous University of Coahuila in Mexico who is an expert on organised crime, says: “The main ones are the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco cartel [CJNG] in Mexico; the Comando Vermelho and the PCC of Brazil; the Gulf Clan and different factions of the Colombian Farc; the Lobos and the Choneros of Ecuador; and Tren de Aragua of Venezuela.”
He believes that the Latin American presence in Europe is even more widespread than is generally recognised. “Sinaloa cartel and the CJNG have a presence in more than 20 European countries. Obviously, that does not mean they dominate or have large cells,” he says. “Rather, they are business emissaries.”
The UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2026 World Drug Report on illicit crimes states that global cocaine production in 2024 was between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes – more than four times higher than it was in 2014. South America remains the main production hub, with coca cultivation covering a record 385,000 hectares over the past decade – three times the 2014 figure.
Europe has emerged as a key market because it offers organisations higher profit margins than the US. Since the beginning of the decade, European police have confiscated more drugs than American forces, and data indicates that Europe now represents about a quarter of global consumption.
Europol recently reported that out of 731 MTCNs operating across Europe, 149 are connected to Latin American organisations. Of these, 67 have Latin American members, and 22 mainly consist of Latin Americans.

title: What is state capture and why does it matter?
description: Different forms are distinguished by who exercises control and which institutions they target Read more: How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state Two crypto-billionaires pour millions into a political party and its wannabe prime minister in return for legislation that favours their businesses. A drug trafficker’s bribe to a senior official buys a cocaine shipment safe passage across a border. Human traffickers installing loyalists in the agencies mandated to stop them. A foreign power uses evidence of a president’s sexual abuse of children to dictate government policy. An influential lobby group donates to both a ruling party and opposition members to hedge their bets on influence. All are routes to state capture. The Dictionary of Corruption defines state capture as systematic corruption whereby narrow interest groups take control of the institutions and processes through which public policy is made, directing it away from the common good and towards their own interests. Continue reading...
content:
Different forms are distinguished by who exercises control and which institutions they target
Read more: How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state
Two crypto-billionaires pour millions into a political party and its wannabe prime minister in return for legislation that favours their businesses. A drug trafficker’s bribe to a senior official buys a cocaine shipment safe passage across a border. Human traffickers installing loyalists in the agencies mandated to stop them. A foreign power uses evidence of a president’s sexual abuse of children to dictate government policy. An influential lobby group donates to both a ruling party and opposition members to hedge their bets on influence. All are routes to state capture.
The Dictionary of Corruption defines state capture as systematic corruption whereby narrow interest groups take control of the institutions and processes through which public policy is made, directing it away from the common good and towards their own interests.
It can create systems that allow access to power where corruption can be repeated and protected . Laws are structured to favour particular businesses. Contracts are designed so only a preferred supplier qualifies. Loyalists are appointed to public companies, regulatory agencies or the judiciary. Public resources are allocated in ways that can keep a party in power, reward supporters and undermine opponents. That political advantage then protects the network’s ability to keep benefiting from the state.
Different forms of capture are distinguished by who exercises control, why they seek it, and which institutions they target.
Involves business interests controlling public institutions. One example is South Africa’s Gupta scandal , which illustrates how corruption can function between private and political elites. During Jacob Zuma’s presidency, the Gupta brothers developed relationships at the highest levels of government to win lucrative state contracts and influence political appointments.
Centres on personal enrichment. Kleptocracy describes a government in which individuals rule on the basis of extensive self-enrichment rather than the public interest, expropriating the wealth and resources of the state and of private citizens.
Peru under Alberto Fujimori offers a clear example of accountability being bought off. Researchers examined how the regime undermined checks on its power as the intelligence service chief Vladimiro Montesinos bribed politicians, judges and the news media during the 1990s.
Includes narco capture, where drug traffickers gain influence over public authority to protect their operations, but covers too other illicit enterprises, but both include financing politicians, corrupting senior security officials and using threats against those who resist.
The former British Virgin Islands premier Andrew Fahie was sentenced in 2024 for cocaine-trafficking and money-laundering after a US undercover operation. He facilitated shipments through the territory’s ports and protected them through his official influence, placing public powers at drug traffickers’ service.
Narrower, and occurs when a watchdog becomes excessively aligned with the businesses or industries it oversees, for example in food, pharmaceuticals, oil or crypto: favouring their interests or overlooking violations. This can contribute to wider state capture.
A compromised regulator does not by itself establish that an entire state has been captured; neither does every successful lobbying campaign amount to capture. Businesses, trade unions and campaign groups can legitimately seek to influence policy; the concern is when it becomes sustained.
Improper advantage that redirects favour towards a narrow group undermines accountability. The OECD has identified how capture is achieved through legal channels, including lobbying and political finance.
Breaking corrupt relationships requires more than change at the top. Public appointments need safeguards against patronage; contracts and their beneficiaries need scrutiny. Investigators need the independence to follow evidence into powerful circles, while political finance and lobbying require transparency. Whistleblowers must be able to act without retaliation. Courts, auditors, journalists and civic organisations need freedom to challenge decisions.
The questions for any government accused of capture is simple: who controls its decisions, who repeatedly benefits, and who can investigate them effectively?

Almost 100 days ago, Africa’s public health watchdog reported an outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo .

title: ‘They showed no mercy’: mapping the Rohingya villages being erased by rebel forces
description: Nearly a decade after the ethnic cleansing of Rohingya people by Myanmar forces, satellite images show the insurgent Arakan Army is now emulating the killings and land grabs There are at least 10 camps like the one on the paddy fields at Hnget Thay, built after the insurgent Arakan Army (AA) took control of most of northern Rakhine state in 2024. Continue reading...
author_name: Kaamil Ahmed, Yassin Abdumonab, Anna Leach, Prina Shah and Pablo Gutiérrez
content:
Nearly a decade after the ethnic cleansing of Rohingya people by Myanmar forces, satellite images show the insurgent Arakan Army is now emulating the killings and land grabs
There are at least 10 camps like the one on the paddy fields at Hnget Thay, built after the insurgent Arakan Army (AA) took control of most of northern Rakhine state in 2024. These are where many Rohingya people in the state now have to live. Others hide in the mountains, or flee abroad to the refugee camps of Bangladesh or make deadly boat journeys to Malaysia .
The arrival of more than 155,000 Rohingya in Bangladesh since 2024 , which amounts to 25% of the 600,000 estimated to still be in Myanmar , has raised concerns about the very survival of a people who now mostly live abroad as refugees.
The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority group from western Myanmar who have faced decades of persecution and clashes with Buddhist nationalists. The word translates as from Rohang – the district that is now Rakhine State. Speaking a language similar to the Bengali dialect of Chattogram (formerly Chittagong) in Bangladesh, they are reviled by many in Myanmar as a foreign people and are denied citizenship by the regime.
In a military crackdown from 2016 to 2017 that led to Myanmar being accused of orchestrating ethnic cleansing, most of the Rohingya population, about 700,000 people, sought refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh. The campaign of massacres unleashed against the Rohingya then is being investigated as possible genocide at the international court of justice (ICJ).
There are now 1.2 million Rohingya in Bangladeshi refugee camps . Since Myanmar’s civil war erupted in 2021, Rohingya remaining in the country have been caught in violence, forced displacement and oppression from both sides – the insurgent AA and government forces, which are fighting each other for control of Rakhine state.
Testimony received by the Guardian and reflected in recent UN reporting provides an insight into the “catastrophic” conditions that the UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, says Rohingya are facing, including torture, gender-based violence, arbitrary arrests, confiscation of land, displacement, forced labour and conscription.
Many of the Rohingya are confined to a makeshift camp, Hnget Thay, to which the AA forced some survivors to relocate after a massacre at Hoyyar Siri. Human Rights Watch documented hundreds of unarmed Rohingya being killed at the village by AA forces.
“This is the end of the Rohingya in northern Rakhine, there is no question about that. It might take time, but the Arakan Army is working quietly to ensure the community has no future there,” says a UN specialist on Myanmar, who requested anonymity as they were not authorised to speak.
“The Rohingya can stay in prison-like camps in appalling conditions for as long as they can bear it, but they will not be permitted to return home,” they say.
An internal UN report has identified at least 800 hectares (2,000 acres) in 23 Rohingya villages that have been seized and repurposed as camps, settlements for other communities or for military infrastructure since 2024, describing this dynamic as linked to the AA’s consolidation of territory under its control.
Muhammad Ares, 18, a Rohingya who now lives in Bangladesh , says: “They used bulldozers to clear out entire residential areas, turning our villages into completely flat, empty fields.
“They cut down all the trees and cleared away every trace of our community, leaving nothing but barren ground. In the areas where they demolished our houses, they cleared the debris and set up their own military camps and outposts.”
The changes in the Buthidaung area of Rakhine happened after the AA took control of much of the region and active fighting abated. Data from the independent conflict monitor Acled shows 12 battles in Buthidaung in 2025, compared with 103 in 2024.
Mohammed Sadik, 26, from Ywet Nyo Taung, says: “They ordered us to stop farming and declared that the land no longer belonged to us; they confiscated the agricultural fields entirely.”
“They forced us to clear roads, dig trenches, and perform heavy labour inside their camps,” he says. “They forced us to work continuously. If anyone collapsed from exhaustion, they were left in the sun.”
All of their farm tools and land were confiscated and the AA authorities refused to return them, Sadik says, even when they explained they needed to grow food to survive.
Video shared with the Guardian by people from Ywet Nyo Taung appears to show the destruction wreaked on the area during this period. The footage was filmed by two locals riding on a motorbike southwards from the main school to the village of U Hla Hpay, which was completely destroyed.
In the footage, they point out landmarks such as schools, mosques, ferry docks, shops and homes. Towards the end of the footage, the person filming points out his own home. Scorched earth is visible and the structures are almost entirely demolished apart from a former bathroom that is partially intact.
Throughout the footage, bricks are seen lined up, often in neat piles, along the side of the road.
In multiple testimonies from Rohingya who were made to work by the AA, they said the forced labour included dismantling Rohingya property to use the materials to build new buildings for the insurgents, including the construction of military barracks, locally known as the AP Battalion , in Ywet Nyo Taung, for housing forcibly recruited Rohingya.
The AA claims to fight in the interests of all Rakhine state’s ethnic groups, and since 2024 has seized control of most of the region. Outwardly, it has proclaimed sympathy for the Rohingya’s suffering but conversely stands accused of emulating the policies of the Myanmar military when it destroyed and confiscated Rohingya land and subjected people to forced labour and conscription, including in the fight against the AA.
Last year, the UN-backed Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) released a report listing seven villages the Myanmar military had destroyed in 2017 and then built bases on. The ICJ, which is expected to deliver a decision in October on whether Rohingya were subjected to genocide in 2017 , has previously considered the “systematic expulsion from and destruction of homes” to be an element of genocide.
The report highlighted that land in Myanmar is owned through a leasehold system and that the military exploited laws designed for natural disasters that allowed burned land to revert to the state, stripping away Rohingya ownership. Another law passed in 2018, after the Rohingya exodus, allowed uncultivated land to be taken by the state.
It was under these conditions that 250,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in the early 1990s, first creating the refugee camps that became the world’s largest in 2017.
The IIMM’s head, Nicholas Koumjian, says: “Clearly, those that orchestrated the attacks on the Rohingya had the objective to create ‘facts on the ground’.” However, he adds that they have not confirmed the AA is responsible for the destruction of Rohingya land. “The Rohingya still inside Myanmar seem to be targeted by all sides of the ongoing conflict and caught in the middle of that conflict.”
Aung Kyaw Moe, who was until recently the only Rohingya member of Myanmar’s “national unity government”, a pro-democracy body in opposition to the 2021 military coup leaders that operates in exile, says the Rohingya are facing a “dangerous new phase” for those inside the country and for refugees hoping to return.
“The central issue is no longer whether Rohingya can survive in Myanmar,” he says. “It is whether conditions are being created that will make their permanent displacement and the erasure of their physical, political and historical presence irreversible.
“If villages are erased and land is being transformed while refugees remain outside of the country, then return becomes progressively more difficult.”
The UN report and testimony shared with the Guardian describe how Rohingya were not only displaced from their land but forced to provide men and women to work for, and to train for, the AA.
“I was forced to undergo military training against my will. I never volunteered to join any armed group,” says a 32-year-old Rohingya man conscripted by the insurgents. He described being initially held for a month, during which time he was repeatedly beaten.
“Throughout my detention, I endured constant physical abuse, psychological intimidation and forced labour.”
Another man said his 22-year-old daughter was taken by AA militia, who subjected her to physical and sexual abuse and made her carry out housekeeping duties for them. She also had to undergo military training.
As well as being forced to provide labour and conscripts, testimony from Rohingya who escaped to Bangladesh from Rakhine describe coercion to make regular payments of “taxes” to the AA, confiscation of land and livestock, and restrictions on their free movement. All of these were tactics enforced previously by the Myanmar military.
Tom Dannenbaum, a professor of international law at Stanford University in the US, says a combination of coercion and the dislocation of Rohingya, either internally or abroad, could amount to the war crime of population transfer .
“It’s devastating for any group to be socially dislocated, inflicted with destructive conditions of life, have their property destroyed and seized,” he says. “All of that is part of making the viability of that group socially, as well as physically, ultimately [impossible]. It clearly creates conditions for that group that make it very difficult to sustain.”
Salamat Khan fled from Rakhine state to Bangladesh in 2024. He feels it is impossible to return to Myanmar, as AA fighters ordered him to leave after attacking his village: “The fighters said to us: ‘go to Bangladesh, your homes are gone, go to the [refugee] camps’.”
This independent journalism was supported by theguardian.org
UN research identified land and property confiscation sites and camps created to confine displaced Rohingya. Interviews and additional testimony also provided information on where Rohingya villages were destroyed. Satellite imagery was used to analyse changes in these areas from before the Arakan Army’s takeover of these areas in April 2024 and after.
The photo and video of Ywet Nyo Taung were verified through the use of landmarks, notably the large school near the May u River, and the shape of the mountains behind the village. Nasa Fire Information for Resource Management (Firms) data was used to confirm the timing of fires in the area.

title: ‘Extraordinary cruelty’: images show longterm ‘starvation strategy’ in Sudan
description: Experts argue sensor and satellite data reveal targeted attacks on farming communities by the Rapid Support Forces were intended to prevent villages producing food There is strong evidence that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) committed a war crime by depriving the villagers of north Darfur of the means to produce food, legal experts argue in a new analysis published today calling for the Humanitarian Research Lab’s (HRL) revelations to be used in international courts. Continue reading...
content:
Experts argue sensor and satellite data reveal targeted attacks on farming communities by the Rapid Support Forces were intended to prevent villages producing food
There is strong evidence that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) committed a war crime by depriving the villagers of north Darfur of the means to produce food, legal experts argue in a new analysis published today calling for the Humanitarian Research Lab’s (HRL) revelations to be used in international courts.
The destruction of the villages, farming equipment and infrastructure all provide strong evidence of a “starvation strategy” against a population already struggling with food insecurity because of the war, says Tom Dannenbaum, a professor at Stanford Law School and a leading expert on the use of starvation in war.
“People were at the brink of starvation and objects indispensable to their survival were being destroyed,” says Dannenbaum, who co-authored the analysis alongside Yale Law School professor Oona Hathaway.
He says it was not merely the fact the villages had been attacked but the targeted destruction of livestock enclosures, as well as the forced displacement of the farmers, that led to reduced farming activity that suggested a deliberate attempt to prevent the villages from being able to produce food.
Dannenbaum and Hathaway believe the HRL research is a breakthrough in attempts to prove how a starvation strategy was imposed because of the way it uses remote sensing technologies. They also think there is potential for the same techniques to be used to investigate war crimes in places such as Gaza and Ethiopia.
“It’s evidence of extraordinary cruelty and the real horrors people have been facing,” says Hathaway. “The report provides a unique level of fine-grained, over-time analysis documenting exactly what was attacked, going far beyond our general knowledge of the fighting … [it] is of a quality that could be submitted in a court for criminal prosecution.”
The international criminal court has been investigating genocide in Darfur since the 2000s, and has issued calls for evidence related to recent violence including the takeover of El Geneina in West Darfur in June 2023, when RSF fighters imposed a months-long siege that killed tens of thousands and displaced hundreds of thousands more people from the Masalit community .
The UN human rights council has also been documenting rights violations throughout the war and last month published a report saying the RSF’s attack on El Fasher last year bore the “hallmarks of genocide” , including a siege that imposed conditions designed to destroy non-Arab communities including the Zaghawa and Fur.
There have also been investigations into the “genocidal attack” on Zamzam in April 2025, which at the time was Sudan’s largest displacement camp , hosting about 700,000 people just south of El Fasher.
HRL’s researchers used sensors that can remotely detect the presence of fires, together with satellite imagery to monitor the locations of the attacks on these 41 villages, where it found there was a 2040% increase in fires during the period studied.
A quarter of the villages were attacked more than once, and after being attacked 68% of them show no signs of normal life. The researchers found that vehicles consistent with those used by the RSF could be identified near the scenes of the violence.
Yasser Abdul Latif, a teacher from the village of Jughmar, two miles (3km) south of Ammar Jadid, is among those who cannot return home.
Before the war he had been studying in El Fasher but returned home to help his family farm and wait out the fighting.
Men on camels would often come to raid the village and, not far behind them, there were always armed men on trucks to intimidate anyone who considered resisting.
Then, one day in March 2024, the situation escalated. Abdul Latif saw smoke rising from neighbouring villages; reports arrived that the people of Ammar Jadid had fled. By the afternoon, the RSF fighters had arrived in Jughmar.
“We heard gunshots and everyone started running, no one understood what was happening,” he says.
He saw the fighters kill two people – one who had tried to defend his house and another who had been running to find his family. The raid continued until sunset when the fighters moved on to the next village.
But they returned later that night as the villagers were burying their dead, forcing them to flee to Golo, a village where the displaced from Ammar Jadid and other nearby communities were already gathering.
“The next day they started to burn Ammar Jadid, Jughmar and so many villages,” says Abdul Latif.
The attacks on villages began just months before the siege of El Fasher. HRL researchers believe this was part of a plan to cut the city off from the areas that fed it.
“They ripped out the breadbasket of El-Fasher as an intentional strategy to starve the city,” says Nathaniel Raymond, HRL’s executive director.
During the subsequent 18-month siege of El Fasher the RSF prevented food, water and medicine from entering the city, and constructed an earthen berm at least 19 miles long to physically prevent civilians from leaving.
Throughout the war the RSF have imposed long sieges on cities with large non-Arab communities such as El Geneina and El Fasher, before militarily taking them over.
The RSF now controls all of Darfur’s main cities but its use of siege tactics has continued in its fighting against the Sudanese army elsewhere, which has most recently been focused on the neighbouring Kordofan region.
Like Darfur, Kordofan is resource-rich with supplies of gold, oil and gum arabic , a key ingredient in cosmetics and soft drinks – Sudan provides 80% of the world’s supply . It is also the location of Kadugli, a city which alongside El Fasher, has been declared as suffering famine and where the price of staple foods such as sorghum are 1,000% higher than before the war.
In February, the Sudanese army announced that it had broken a siege on Kadugli that prevented aid trucks from arriving, but violence has continued and concerns remain that the RSF will try to reimpose siege conditions. On 20 February, a convoy of aid trucks that had waited weeks to reach the city was hit by a drone strike, killing four people.
Hunger is also growing in eastern Sudan’s Blue Nile state where farmers have not been able to access their land because of RSF attacks, leaving crops unharvested according to campaign group Avaaz, which reported that the price of flour rose 43% in January.
Raymond says that HRL’s work is evidence that the RSF is using hunger as a means of war and that unless they are investigated and held accountable, there is a threat of the same fate facing other communities.
“This report is quantitative proof of RSF’s intent, which is to prevent those they perceive as enemies from being able to feed themselves,” says Raymond. “What this means for Sudan is clear: what happened here can happen again.”

In this week’s newsletter: drones in Somalia, robots in India and smartphones in Afghanistan
In this Global Dispatch, I’d really like to highlight the goodness of strangers, inspired by Guardian readers.
It was unexpected this week when readers reacted to our story about the US drone attack on civilians in Somalia by raising money to help one of the surviving victims. Seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah (pictured above) was left with shrapnel injuries in the attack , which also wounded his brother and sister.
The operation that would help him recover cost more than his mother could possibly raise – a story reported on by Mohamed Gabobe on the ground in Somalia in collaboration with Mark Townsend in London. We are all hoping Abdiqadir makes a good recovery now the equivalent of £750 is on its way to the family.
“What’s worse than being a mother who can’t do anything for her wounded children?” his mother, Marian Haji Abdi Guled, had said at the time she talked to Mohamed.
It is no surprise that the US did nothing to help. After all, our leaders – not just Trump but others across Europe and Africa – continue to be mealy-mouthed in calling out some of the terrible suffering of children in entirely avoidable conflicts.
See Mark’s story this week about the UK’s continuing “diplomatic” response to the utter horror being unleashed on the people of Sudan and the UN’s report on Israeli targeting children in Gaza – two genocidal conflicts which it seems to be beyond the international community to even decisively condemn, never mind to act on.
Putting politics before people and warmongering before peacemaking are exactly why inhumanity thrives in parts of our world, where children like Abdiqadir become merely collateral damage.
Tracy McVeigh, editor, Global development
Global health | African and Asian midwives were denied visas to attend a conference in Portugal on preventing deaths in childbirth. As politicians, donors and UN agencies gathered for the International Confederation of Midwives congress in Lisbon, eminent midwives were excluded from countries including Nigeria, Ghana, Rwanda, Ethiopia, Bangladesh and Indonesia.
Kabul | The Taliban began destroying smartphones after the Islamist regime ordered a sweeping ban on their use by government officials. Analysts say the move could lead to broader restrictions with civilians including women, medical workers, schoolteachers and students targeted in some provinces.
FGM | The first lady of Sierra Leone was forced to deny reports that she supported female genital mutilation amid rising anger around her perceived approval of the practice. However, Fatima Maada Bio said she would not condemn FGM until she saw “reliable data” that the practice was harmful, prompting concern among medics, survivors and human rights activists.
Education | Violent attacks on schools, pupils and staff rose around the world by 40% , according to the Global Coalition to Protect Education from Attack. Cases were reported in 83 countries, with at least 10,600 students and staff killed, injured, abducted or arrested, the report found.
The family were sitting down for breakfast when the drones struck. A grandfather rushed to the wreckage of their home in Jamaame to find his pregnant daughter-in-law and her two small children dead. The most deadly US attack in the east African country for 18 years killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children. Washington has never acknowledged their deaths. The Guardian has pieced together what happened that day.

content:
In this week’s newsletter: can the Melbourne declaration help women affected by injustice?; plus the artist chronicling the DRC’s blood-soaked history in embroidery
I first spoke to Shazia Khanum for a report on informal jobs. The 16-year-old’s fingers moved swiftly as she talked, rolling bidis – tendu leaves tied around tobacco. She rolls about 300-500 of the cigarettes daily, earning about £1. In the cramped workshop in Karnataka’s Yarab Nagar, India , where she works, there are no toilets or sanitary facilities. Asked how she manages her period, Khanum pointed to a makeshift curtained space where she changes and reuses cloth rags.
Last week, about 6,000 miles away, world leaders and advocates came together in Australia to launch the Melbourne declaration for gender equality , a framework for gender-responsive funding, policy reform, and a fundamental shift in how power and resources flow. In the conference, the mood was one of urgency but also solidarity. Women and queer leaders spoke about power and rights with an openness that felt both overdue and fragile. The document itself is, by any measure, ambitious. But for girls like Khanum working in India’s informal sector, its promise is a distant one.
That is not a criticism but rather a diagnosis of the problem we face. The Melbourne Declaration points to governments’ obligation to “ensure local civil society is adequately resourced, politically protected, globally connected, and locally rooted”.
It calls for the “those most affected by injustice” to be central to the work across the gender-equality ecosystem.
Khanum is not an outlier but a statistic that the system has chosen not to count. One of the 61% of female workers in India’s non-agriculture sector employed informally, she is among the 80% of south Asian women who work outside formal protections. She has no contract, payslips or access to welfare schemes. As far as the state is concerned, she does not work at all.
India’s government has made moves in the right direction. The e-Shram portal has registered more than 300 million informal workers, and pension schemes now exist. But there is no outreach, and Khanum remains invisible to the system. Even though India acknowledges that about 45% of its GDP comes from this informal sector, that has yet to translate into ground-level engagement.
This is the distance between commitment and reach. Maliha Khan, president of Women Deliver, architects of the declaration, says holding leaders accountable must also mean ensuring that public systems recognise and respond to everyone’s reality.
The only way Khanum will benefit from the declaration is through direct access to cash and healthcare. The best way to do that is either through funding from on-the-ground NGOs or by funding community health workers and bringing informal workers into policy consultations.
To paraphrase Khan, at the end of the day the declaration will be measured by whether it translates into policy, financing and practice, and whether it delivers change for women whose work has too often been invisible, undervalued and unprotected.
As applause filled the conference halls in Melbourne, I knew Khanum would be at her workbench, rolling her bidi, without knowing that people are debating whether systems like the one that has failed her can be fixed. Her ambitions lie in getting better pay and a proper toilet.
Cheena Kapoor is a journalist and documentary photographer based in Delhi. Read the full article here

In September 2022, as revolution spread across Iran, I witnessed it from Dubai through the unstable glow of phone screens. Raw videos surfaced daily before disappearing into internet blackouts: women burning their hijabs, young men wounded by metal pellets, teenagers dragged into unmarked vans.
Unable to return safely to Iran, where I had spent six years documenting life under repression, I felt helpless. This work emerged from that pain and is both testimony and absence: the public violence of the state and my private, long-distance bearing witness.
Using open-source protest footage, I began isolating frames from videos circulating on social media and photographing them directly from my computer with a Fujifilm instax camera, which can produce prints immediately. I wanted to interrupt the relentless flow of digital images – to arrest their movement.
This image comes from a protest video in Tehran: crowds circle a fire burning in the street, holding hands and chanting, “You’re the pervert. You’re the whore. I’m a free woman” – transforming misogynistic insults into defiance against the state.
I photographed the silhouette of a young woman with a high ponytail moving against smoke and fluorescent light. Its grainy, pixelated surface carries the urgency of testimony over perfection.
The photograph is part of a wider body of work drawn from protest fragments. In January 2026, after state massacres and executions, I began burning the instax prints as an act of mourning. Fire scarred their surfaces, echoing the violence they depict. This was not erasure, but a way to push against the stillness of the image, allowing it to convey and to carry rage, grief and refusal.
For me, this photograph holds revolt and transformation. It speaks to rebellions public and private and belongs to an unfinished, unfolding story of resistance.

title: Telegraph cuts up to 100 jobs as new owner promises to turn paper into ‘AI-powered’ global business
description: Redundancies come after paper was bought in June by European media group Axel Springer The new owners of the Daily Telegraph have made large numbers of staff redundant, telling them the title will be transformed from a newspaper “into a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”. content:
Redundancies come after paper was bought in June by European media group Axel Springer
The new owners of the Daily Telegraph have made large numbers of staff redundant, telling them the title will be transformed from a newspaper “into a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”.
In an all-company briefing and email on Friday morning, staff were told the title would rely increasingly on technology, data and AI to “reinvent the reader experience”. Newsroom insiders said they expected as many as 100 people to lose their jobs.
The “next chapter” of the Telegraph will focus on new revenue streams including “video, audio, puzzles, events, B2B, licensing, commerce and new products”, the CEO, Carolin Hulshoff Pol , wrote.
It will also focus on growing its audience internationally, “particularly in foreign affairs, defence and business”, she said.
Some staff were told on Thursday they were being fired, while others received calls and emails on Friday morning. Some senior staff were said to be in tears as they told colleagues their fate.
The culture and sports departments have been particularly hard hit, according to insiders. A source from inside the Telegraph said the atmosphere in the newsroom was “like a morgue”.
The Telegraph was bought in June by the European media group Axel Springer for £575m, ending three tortuous years for the title and its staff, during which potential owners were blocked, fell through or faced fierce internal opposition.
The paper joined a stable of media brands including the German titles Bild and Die Welt, as well as the digital outlets Politico and Business Insider. Mathias Döpfner, Axel Springer’s chief executive and controlling shareholder, said he intended to invest in the Telegraph to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.
However, heavy job cuts have been expected at the paper amid an internal staff consultation in recent weeks into the future of the business.
Pol said that during the lengthy sale process, “the Telegraph had limited ability to invest, adapt and move at the pace the market demanded”, adding that “the media world and technology have changed at extraordinary speed”.
“Our ambition is to transform the Telegraph from a leading British newspaper into a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business – built on trusted journalism, direct relationships with our audiences and expertise that sets us apart.
“To deliver on this ambition, we need to change how we are organised, how decisions are made, where we focus our resources and create efficiencies. We need clearer accountability, faster decision-making and a simpler, more effective organisation.”
She said the organisation would “use AI confidently while enhancing what technology cannot replace: judgment, originality, courage and trust”.
A spokesperson for the Telegraph Media Group reiterated Pol’s remarks, adding: “Today marks the start of a formal consultation process. These are difficult choices that we believe are necessary for the future of the business.”
TMG would not confirm the number of redundancies.

title: Being pro-Trump has been ‘easy radio’ for conservative hosts like Jesse Kelly. Those days are ending.
description: Conservative media personalities who have long benefited from boosting the president will be forced to wrestle with the likely fallout of Republican losses in next month’s US midterm elections Nothing lasts forever. content:
Conservative media personalities who have long benefited from boosting the president will be forced to wrestle with the likely fallout of Republican losses in next month’s US midterm elections
Nothing lasts forever. Jesse Kelly knows his meteoric rise through conservative radio will end one day – just like Donald Trump ’s power over the Republican party.
Every day, the 6ft 8in Kelly walks a tightrope between sycophancy and criticism of the US president: the same fine line many rightwing hosts have attempted to tread throughout Trump’s rise, fall, and then resurrection from the political graveyard after his 2020 presidential election defeat.
What Kelly, 45, does next will be telling. Conservative media hosts have achieved untold fame and fortune riding the Trump train. Yet as Trump enters the final two years of his presidency, these hosts must prepare for life after the train pulls into the station. More imminently, they will wrestle with the likely fallout of Republican losses in next month’s US midterm elections – and the question of how much blame to put on an unpopular president.
With a daily show syndicated by radio powerhouse Premiere Networks across more than 200 stations across the country, between 6pm and 9pm, Kelly is one of the most influential players in the medium. His broadcast follows a three-hour block by Fox News host Sean Hannity, long an eminence grise in conservative media.
“When he was the bee’s knees there for a while on the right, honestly, it was easy radio, easy podcasting, easy TV to just sit down and just powder Trump’s butt all day long,” Kelly said over lunch recently at a suburban Red Lobster in Webster, Texas, approximately 20 miles south-east of downtown Houston. “That’s what the audience wanted to hear.
“For a while, that was the case. But like any other politician, same for all of them, you don’t stay hot forever. It’s not possible. No matter what, we’re nearing the end of the Trump era because his last term’s almost over and people are going to start looking around for the next guy.”
In recent months, Kelly has gained even more attention for his willingness to criticize Trump for starting a war with Iran just months before an election he reckons will be “rough” for Republicans. “I think if you told Donald Trump that he’d still be stuck over there with $4-a-gallon gas a month before the election, I think he probably would’ve made a different call,” he said.
But these days, any criticism of Trump from a conservative media figure leads to questions like the one he got from a Twitter user named @Swanso45003Kyle recently: “Are you anti Trump now?”
Kelly is not anti-Trump. But he is prepared to upset those who are slavishly devoted to praising the president and ignoring his missteps.
“When Trump does something I don’t like, I’ll say it. And I’ll say it when he does stuff I like,” he said. Make no mistake: Kelly still spends most of his time bashing “commie” Democrats, referring to them on a recent show as “sick, evil and demonic”.
While Kelly said “a lot of people” in conservative media care about securing an invite to the White House, he claims to be uninterested in such an offer. Unless he approaches his daily show with candor and honesty, he worries listeners will think he’s a phony and turn the dial.
“I think a huge percentage of Trump’s supporters have always understood that Trump has flaws like any other human being has flaws,” said Kelly. There is “a tiny percentage who worship everything he says and does”, he added. “Those are just generally ridiculous and stupid human beings. But the large percentage of Trump supporters are not sheep.”
Michael Harrison, the founder of the talk radio-focused publication Talkers magazine, said the art of “positioning” is an extremely important skill in the industry – and one that conservative hosts will need to lean on when pondering a post-Trump political world. “Anybody who is in radio and who plans to be in radio for a very long time has got to – or eventually learns – that the carpet is going to be pulled out from you eventually, with switching circumstances and public opinion,” he said in an interview.
Talkshow hosts on the right are “all competing with each other”, added Harrison. “It’s a game of musical chairs, and right now that’s what the conservative element of news talk radio is facing. All of a sudden the game is changing, and it’s changing very rapidly, and they’ve got to figure out what their position is.
“And it’s got to be somewhere between their own deeply held beliefs or what the audience wants. It ultimately comes down to business. It ultimately comes down to what will get ratings, what will get clicks, what will get views and what will get advertising.”
Kelly was an unlikely candidate to host a nationally syndicated radio show. Born in Ohio, he went to high school – and a little bit of college – in Montana before joining the marines in 2000, serving in Iraq before being honorably discharged in 2004.
He lived in Arizona for a time and worked for a family-owned construction company. Then, fully embracing the Tea Party movement , he ran for Congress in Arizona in 2010 and nearly ousted incumbent Democratic representative Gabrielle Giffords.
“I just got out of the Marine Corps and got mad and decided to run for Congress,” he recalled. He tried again in a special election two years later, but lost again to a Democrat – something he says he is now thankful for. “It would suck to be in Congress.”
Not giving up on politics, he moved to Washington DC and worked in development for the conservative advocacy group Citizens United , but hated living there and left the job after a year. He says he then drove around the country looking for work, getting close to running out of money before eventually finding a job through Craigslist selling RVs in Texas.
After one of his tweets went viral, Kelly did a guest appearance on Houston-based conservative radio host Michael Berry’s show, and it was Berry who called him up – while he was in a Taco Bell drive-through – to introduce himself before ultimately suggesting he pursue radio as a career.
In 2018, he began hosting a one-hour, late-at-night show on KPRC 950 AM: an entry-level “prove it” gig in the radio business. Only three years later, in 2021, he got “the phone call everybody who does what I do wants” from Premiere Networks president Julie Talbott offering him a job.
“I don’t think it’s supposed to work out that way,” Kelly said of his quick rise in an interview.
Talbott suggested in a statement that Kelly’s non-traditional background “gives him a fresh perspective and an unfiltered style that stands out in today’s media landscape.” She added: “Over the past five years, we’ve had the opportunity to watch his audience and influence grow significantly, and that success is rooted in the trust he’s earned with listeners.”
For several years, he also hosted a nightly streaming show for rightwing online platform the First, though that arrangement recently ended. Kelly said he wants to focus fully on radio moving forward.
On a recent Monday afternoon, Kelly settled into his desk chair and prepared for his show. On the front of his large desk, he placed his car keys and his gun. “Unless I’ve gone through a metal detector, I have a weapon on me,” he said.
While Kelly has been encouraged to use a “show sheet”, listing segments and topics for the day, he feels better off the cuff, detecting a certain stiffness in his presentation when working from prepared lines. The same was true when campaign consultants told him to script speeches during his two runs for Congress. “I just would rather do it off the top of my head.”
Kelly doesn’t take the current success of his radio show for granted. “I’ll probably never fully understand why people love it the way they love it,” he said. But while he believes “the safest thing you can possibly do is everything Maga, all the time”, at least for the past decade, he has made the calculation that his market value depends on ideological consistency without predictability, as well as a heavy dose of personality and banter.
“In a lot of ways, in a lot of different places in life, you completely eliminate your voice as having any importance if you’re a given on anything,” he said. “You just get dismissed. You’re banked already.”
He hopes his audience – at least those who have not dropped him in favor of a more reliably pro-Trump host, or because they dislike one of his food opinions – will keep listening, even when they disagree. “Look, you’re never going to get 100% of a rightwing media audience,” said Kelly. “That’s not possible. But if there are 40%, and you can grab them and keep them, then you can have a long career that way.”
During a late September radio segment comparing Trump to a once-elite baseball player who has lost his home run power, Kelly acknowledged that his day, too, will come – possibly sooner rather than later.
“There will come when I don’t deliver for you when you tune in,” he told his listeners. “And that sucks. And when you think about that, especially when you’re doing OK – right now, the show is growing, doing great – when you think about that, you think, ‘No, it’s going to last forever!’ No, it won’t.”

content:
Show features live chat sessions with breeders, a podcast and updates on dogs’ progress from birth to weigh-ins
A 24-hour Finnish TV show dedicated entirely to the live progress of a dog and her six newborn puppies is drawing millions of viewers.
As well as a 24-hour webcam, Pentulive (Puppy Live) includes live evening chat sessions with the dogs’ breeder, a podcast and an instant notification service that updates followers on the puppies’ progress – from their birth to weigh-ins and first nail trims – for eight weeks.
This is the sixth season of the hit show by the broadcaster Yle, and the latest contribution to the growing Nordic cultural phenomenon of “slow TV”.
The trend started in Norway in 2009 with Bergensbanen, a seven-hour train journey broadcast on NRK , and was followed in Sweden by SVT’s Den stora älgvandringen (The Great Moose Migration), which features unnarrated glimpses of moose from the north of the country making their annual journey to summer grazing grounds.
Pentulive has long attracted interest from outside Finland, but this year it is also being broadcast in Sweden (under the name Valparna live ). Yle recently announced that it had also sold the format to a broadcaster in the Netherlands.
Ville Alijoki, the editorial manager of Yle’s factual journalism, said: “There’s a certain magic to it, something that people miss when this world is sometimes quite dark.”
On Saturday, the lagotto romagnolo puppies – four male and two female – will mark their two-week birthday by being officially named after a vote by viewers. Among the nominations are Martha, Timo, Ronja and Dante.
In mid-December, the puppies will leave their mother, Hilkka, and be adopted by new families.
Yle said the current season of Pentulive was on a path to break previous viewing records. Across its first two weeks, the stream has been watched for more than 1m hours, and the show has attracted 1.85 million unique viewers across all related content.
Fans say the puppies offer a relaxing break from work, and comfort from stress, loneliness and illness.
Pirjo Koskinen, a science journalist who came up with the Pentulive concept with the aim of educating viewers on the latest dog research and the importance of the first few weeks of a dog’s life, said the show provided “relief from the terrible things happening in the world”.
She said: “Wars, bombing, climate change, habitat loss etc make us anxious and you can escape, for at least a moment, by watching the canine family.”
Watching the mother and breeder take care of the puppies was like watching “a loop of love and caring”, she said.
“It’s real and we are in the basics of life: the miracle of birth, growth and development. It’s so heartwarming to see eyes opening and first clumsy steps, and it’s happening right now. That brings us joy, but also many funny moments during eight weeks.”
