content:
Once Bobby Robson’s translator at the Camp Nou, Mourinho is tasked with bringing down Barcelona on Sunday
J osé Mourinho has done the por que?, the printout and the press conference no-show, and he’s been here only three months. The Real Madrid manager has played the classics without even playing a clásico. Not yet anyway, but it’s time: on Sunday night he returns to the stadium he first arrived at 30 transformative years ago as Bobby Robson’s talented young translator, and last visited in 2013 as the most famous manager in football.
The coach who once declared “today, tomorrow and always, Barcelona in my heart,” and claimed he would only ever go to Real Madrid to destroy them, has been entrusted with attempting to bring about the destruction of Barcelona. It is not the first time: if his return is about nostalgia, which it is, that’s wrapped up in their rivals too.
“The clásico is just another game in the championship but to say it’s a game like any other would be to lie, totally unreal,” Mourinho said on Wednesday, and he knows. As for Barcelona’s latest star, he’s looking forward to seeing Mourinho again. “I love the needle,” Lamine Yamal says. “The Mourinho-Guardiola era, I loved all that. That’s football. Sport is serious but I want a show and we have more fun.”
There are bigger things, sure; life beyond Barcelona. Madrid’s astonishing Champions League record since Mourinho was last here – following up the elusive decima , the 10th title which had evaded them for 12 years, with the 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th and 15th in 10 years – played out without Barcelona. There has not been a European clásico since the 2011 Champions League semi-final when the man Pep Guardiola had just called the puto amo , the fucking master, produced his por que speech, asking why Barcelona were favoured by the continent’s referees and accusing Uefa of fixing it for them.
Yet right now it doesn’t feel as if anything is bigger, this week’s Champions League matches framed around what they meant for the game that really matters, even with Barcelona going to Paris . The rivalry is always there; in Mourinho’s case it is at the heart of it. The day he got the Madrid job in 2010 was the day he won the Champions League with Inter but its genesis lay in the semi-final, when he had sprinted across the Camp Nou pitch , finger raised, celebrating. Madrid were relieved and grateful, spared the sight of Barcelona lifting the European Cup in their stadium and shown how to stop a team that appeared unbeatable. Mourinho, leaving the Santiago Bernabéu in Florentino Pérez’s car while his joyful players returned to Milan, was asked to repeat that with Madrid.
Pérez, who had presided over the galácticos’ failure and walked away, had returned in 2009 but won nothing. Instead, Barcelona dominated. They had the core of Spain’s World Cup 2010 winners: six starters in the final. Madrid needed a culture shift, to go to war, a manager to rule over the dressing room. “This year’s galáctico is José Mourinho,” the president said .
By the time Mourinho left , it had turned nasty, his enemies internal too. They had been, Mourinho later said, “three intense, almost violent years”. Yet Pérez had always felt drawn towards the only manager he has truly liked. Including when Mourinho was belligerent; especially when he was belligerent. Mourinho had, Pérez said, returned Madrid to their rightful place. After every subsequent success the president called to tell him he started this. And if Mourinho’s first clásico brought a 5-0 defeat , Barcelona going on to win the league and Champions League; if his final season had ended trophyless; and if Guardiola had won twice as many trophies, it was also true that of the four competitions Guardiola failed to win at Barcelona, three were taken from him by Mourinho.
Time has passed, things have changed, but the parallels are clear. Madrid have gone two years without a trophy. In the first of those, Barcelona won the league with two weeks to spare, completing a domestic treble. They had defeated Madrid four times, scoring 16 goals. Last season they wrapped it up with three weeks to spare via a clásico victory as incontestable as their superiority throughout a season when Madrid’s splits played out in public. Then Spain won the World Cup with eight Barcelona players in the squad. Madrid’s only representative, Marc Cucurella, joined the club after the tournament started.
If this was a crisis, it was time for Mourinho. A man whose flaws had been forgotten over time, nostalgia eclipsing all else. A man with the authority – a man afforded the authority – to impose on the dressing room. One with the personality to fight, go to war again. With just about everyone, and Barcelona especially. When you listened to Pérez’s extraordinary rant in May, the quiet part said out loud, all campaigning and conspiracy, politics and paranoia, it made sense.
When it comes to the still unresolved Negreira case , in which Barcelona paid the vice-president of the referees’ committee, José María Enríquez Negreira, more than €7m between 2001 and 2018, there is substance to Madrid’s complaints. Barcelona have denied corruption, saying Negreira worked as an adviser, but that case has become the centrepiece of Madrid’s discourse, unlike when the two clubs were still holding out in the Super League. It doesn’t help when the league president likens your TV channel to Joseph Goebbels’ propaganda .
Whether those complaints have validity now is a different question; whether the discourse of conspiracy does is another step again, even when decisions go against you. Every mistake – and decisions that are not even mistakes – is framed as a machiavellian plan, the insinuations constant – when they are not said outright.
When Mourinho arrived he said he was older, calmer, but here he is. In defeat, perhaps he was always likely to be. After losing to Betis, he asked por que? (Why? Because that’s the rule, the decision correct.) After losing to Atlético, he turned up with a printout. And then he didn’t turn up to the press conference after he had run on to the pitch to embrace Vinícius Júnior after the Brazilian scored against Villarreal only for the goal to be ruled out and Vinícius sent off for pulling Nathan Saliba’s hair. That led to a four-game suspension, the forward ruled out of the clásico .
The reason for the no-show was that Mourinho didn’t want to risk saying something that would earn him a suspension for the clásico, the game . And he is happier now, if only for a little while, something shifting. When last Saturday Barcelona made it 11 wins from 11, averaging more than four goals a game, most agreed they would win the clásico and the title would be done: they were flying, led by Lamine Yamal , while Madrid, beaten twice, hadn’t taken off. Mourinho’s team had not been very good, familiar problems still there. In short, there was not much football.
The previous Wednesday Madrid had delivered another of their seemingly inexplicable comebacks, from 3-1 down at Roma, to win 4-3 in the final seven minutes, but was there really anything to build on? It turned out there was something of an explanation. In those minutes Arda Güler played, Yan Diomande played, Fede Valverde played at right-back, and Vinícius didn’t play.
It seemed so obvious to everyone, including the manager. So he did it again, and Madrid scored four against Sevilla – three of them glorious – last Sunday and four more against Leipzig on Wednesday, Diomande belting in a wonderful volley once Vinícius had gone off. The night before, Barcelona conceded four at the Parc des Princes.
Hansi Flick admitted he prioritised the clásico over PSG, leaving out Rodri and withdrawing Pedri and Raphinha early to keep them fresh for a game that could be decisive and tends to shape a season. But he has injury concerns at the back and warned his players that 15 goals conceded is too many. Mourinho couldn’t resist complaining that Madrid have a day less rest for the clásico – something perhaps mitigated, much like any analysis, by playing at home against Leipzig rather than away at Paris Saint-Germain – which got the excuse in early, more evidence of how “they” have it in for his side.
“We need to cut the gap and we can only do that by winning,” said the Real Madrid goalkeeper, Thibaut Courtois, of the six-point deficit. “We’re going with confidence.” Yet things do feel a little better now, defeat for Madrid not inevitable, a title still there to played for and something like a team taking shape. “I had to get to know them,” Mourinho said on Wednesday night. “I’ve only been here 105 days; it’s not long.”

title: Enciso rescues point in storm for Ipswich to deny Nottingham Forest

content:
Amid a Suffolk squall, winds whipping, a constant drum of rain, an encounter full of half-chances, mistakes, the obligatory refereeing controversy and searching questions. Do Ipswich possess the stones to deal with the big league? Perhaps so. How long can Nottingham Forest’s dip sustain before their president, Evangelos Marinakis, takes his usual course of action. Perhaps not much longer.
Ipswich’s Gary O’Neil was the happier manager, Forest had created the cleaner opportunities, only for familiar failings to cost them. “We were never quite good enough with the ball to turn it into a football match,” said O’Neil. Further adding to Forest’s disappointment, Ipswich’s Issa Diop escaped what looked, on first glance, a red card for a last-man foul. A first-half exchange of goals, both owing much to defensive laxness, determined the result.
Ipswich’s aim is to establish themselves as Forest have in the Premier League. Though Forest and their manager cannot be presumptive of their statuses. “The result doesn’t reflect the performance but I don’t see another solution other than to keep going,” said Oliver Glasner. Forest have six points from eight matches , just a single win.
Glasner admitted he is still “waiting for this click” while saying: “I see great togetherness. The spirit I start to feel … I loved everything I saw today, just not the result.” A record of starting slow only to flourish at previous clubs offers partial protection, though Forest’s ownership is not like other clubs’. Wednesday was the anniversary of Sean Dyche’s appointment. That tenure lasted just 100 days.
Liam Delap’s presence in the Forest ranks, the striker barracked at every touch by home fans, served as a reminder of Ipswich’s failed mission two seasons ago. Unloved in Ipswich for decamping to Chelsea, Delap continues to be short of the confidence he showed back then.
Forest kicked off as lowest scorers in the division; no side had drawn a blank more often. Their drought did not take long to break but no flood followed. Neco Williams’s goal came via an overlap and then a looping cross from Daniel Muñoz. Williams glided in unmarked, his finish low and true beyond Christian Walton.
Another Forest goal appeared likely before home fans, previously exasperated, were lifted by Jaden Philogene forcing a save from Matz Sels and Julio Enciso dancing through red shirts to force another.
The equaliser came via a collective loss of concentration characteristic of Forest’s season so far, echoing defeat at Crystal Palace, and at home to Coventry. Jair Cunha gallivanted forward and, adrenaline coursing, lost possession. Dara O’Shea’s punted clearance was poorly dealt with by Nikola Milenkovic, an under-amped back-pass allowed Enciso to show admirable calm when others had surrendered theirs.
Forest’s failure to claim the rewards on offer from the first half told a familiar story. So too do repeated refereeing controversies, and howls of conspiracy among their supporters. How the officials, led by Thomas Bramall, the referee, did not view Diop’s clattering of James McAtee as a foul defied belief. Play was waved on. More understandable, if still highly debatable, was the verdict via video assistant that McAtee had conceded possession with a heavy touch as the collision came. “Leif [Davis] was there to cover,” said Diop, shown a yellow card. “I don’t think it’s a red.”
“I think they came to the right conclusion, a good process,” O’Neil said. As well he might. “It looks like the VAR was not from the East Midlands today,” said Glasner. “It felt like it was a red card.”
Injustice fuelled Forest though did not make them any more clinical, the best of their second-half flurry of chances involved Murillo missing a free header from a corner. That asked for staying power from Ipswich. So far this season, they have not been the soft touch under O’Neil they became in Kieran McKenna’s survival attempt. “We had to show another side to get something,” said O’Neil. “We can play better but if we think we’re going to be dominant in every game … we’ll be fighting for scraps a lot of the time.”
Luck was definitely ridden. Callum Hudson-Odoi, as eight messy minutes of injury time were being added, received more than enough time and space to do far better than drag beyond the far post. The story of the night encapsulated for Forest. And of their season.

title: Change captain? Play the kids? How to solve the problems at Manchester United

content:
The beleaguered Michael Carrick’s job is on the line, but there are steps he can take to revive the stricken club
The big question as Bournemouth arrive for Sunday’s 2pm kick-off at Old Trafford is whether Michael Carrick will show his authority by stripping the captaincy from Bruno Fernandes and/or dropping Manchester United’s five-times player of the year. On Friday, Carrick refused to deny he may do so, but the bigger picture concerns whether cashing in on the Portuguese and his fellow mutineer, Lisandro Martínez, in the winter window would be prescient to initiate a new era. Fernandes and Martínez are out of contract in the close season (the club has an extra year’s option in both cases) and, judging by recent behaviour, intend to leave. So yielding, say, £40m and £25m respectively for them in January would allow investment as the rebuild begins. Even a few days on, Fernandes’s words in Como seem incredible: “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” he said after Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation. Fernandes’s open questioning of the tactics is a challenge to the head coach’s authority and we wait to see how/if Carrick will face it down. If Carrick acts and proves he is not a lame duck then even if he is removed a favour is done for his successor.
Seven hundred United supporters made the trip to Lombardy and witnessed a horror show in incessant rain as their team folded against Cesc Fàbregas’s side. Yet, as always, the faithful will be there on Sunday desperate to cheer their men on against Bournemouth and beyond. Carrick constantly talks of how fans are the club’s lifeblood but do all of the players feel this? Performances such as that at Como will surely be averted if a base creed citing how fundamental supporters are to United is laid down to the squad by the manager.
Sir Alex Ferguson’s flying wingers, Sir Matt Busby’s holy trinity of Best, Law, Charlton, the “attack, attack, attack” mentality: none of this is evident currently on the field; part of what Carrick admitted on Friday had been “lost”. What is needed is a return to this tradition, and this team are capable as was evident in the spirit of Carrick’s first game of his second tenure. Then, on 17 January 2026 at Old Trafford, he sent out an XI that went at Manchester City from the opening whistle, gave Pep Guardiola’s men zero time to breathe, and a rousing 2-0 victory sent all of a United stripe home jubilant. This, basically, was Carrick’s side last season, a proposition that played with a bounce that landed in third place. This term the smile has vanished and a prevailing sense of doom has settled over the club – precisely what Carrick had vanquished after the gloom of Ruben Amorim’s final days. Time to restore the cavalier edge.
United have suffered, in part, this term owing to Carrick’s drive to move to a more possession-based proposition. The problem is one of the key midfielders recruited to execute this, Youri Tielemans, does not have the legs for a central role, and so has been fielded at 10, while Kobbie Mainoo, who can run an engine room, is injured, and Fernandes’ penchant for running about, out of position, means gaps appear where a ball receiver should be.
In Fernandes, Luke Shaw, Harry Maguire, Diogo Dalot, Marcus Rashford, Amad Diallo and Martínez there is a core of long-serving senior players who are not performing. To wake this cadre and freshen the mood from what feels a pervasive staleness, why not blood, more regularly, the younger players? The “play the kids instead” trope can be a cliche but it is a truism for a reason: youth has zero to lose, should run around with a smile and can brighten the darkest of times. Shea Lacey, a nippy wide man, Harry Amass, a promising left-back, and the Fletcher twins, Jack, a clever No 10, and Tyler, a defensive midfielder, are 19 and have 22 appearances between them. None could do worse than those senior players ahead of them.
In seven of their 11 games this season United have scored either a solitary goal or none, a shocking statistic that shows up how dysfunctional the attack is and, as part of the creative collective, the midfield too. United have only 10 goals in seven league outings and in three Champions League games have managed five – four of these against the minnows Sabah. At Como there was, again, zero pattern of play, control and a paucity of chances that has to be a serious concern. This has to change or a relegation fight could be United’s. A more off-the-cuff style, allied to an attacking outlook, would suit Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and others and start menacing teams again as United did when beating City, Arsenal, Chelsea and Liverpool last year.

content:
Arteta: ‘We need to understand how to manage his load’
Max Dowman could play against Everton on Saturday
Mikel Arteta has expressed concern over Bukayo Saka’s robustness after a series of injuries to the forward in the past year and as he awaits further news on how long he will be out for with a thigh issue.
Saka is set for an MRI scan after limping off in the 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League, with Arteta revealing the 25-year-old had “quite a lot of fluid in the area so it was difficult to understand the extent of the injury”. Saka will definitely miss Saturday’s game against Evertonand, it is understood, Arsenal fear it could be a grade-two tear that could potentially keep him out for up to six weeks.
Saka missed a large portion of last season due to hamstring, hip and achilles tendon injuries having also been sidelined by another hamstring issue in 2024-25. In total, he has had 11 different injuries since September 2023 and Arteta insisted that he has been trying to ease his workload as a result. “It’s certainly been different in the last year or so,” the Spaniard said when asked if Saka remains robust enough to start every match. “The demands that we are putting on every player are immense. The amount of games, the intensity of those matches, the international competitions, the times as well between games are getting narrower.
“Bukayo against Lille [in the Champions League last week] didn’t start the game because we knew what was happening. We have to play three times in less than six days. And especially when the games are so demanding, until the last minute you are there, you are chasing the game, you want to win. The necessity is to win every game, so we know that. So we are preparing the players for those scenarios and we do the best that we possibly can.”
Saka missed only three Premier League matches in three seasons between 2021 and 2024 and broke the Arsenal club record by playing in 83 consecutive top-flight games. He is already approaching 300 appearances for the club he joined as a seven-year-old and was rewarded with a lucrative new contract in February that made him one of the highest-paid players in the club’s history.
Asked whether he feared Saka could suffer from burnout having made his Arsenal debut three months after his 17th birthday, Arteta said: “I don’t have that feeling at all but something we have to be very mindful of is to create the right ecosystem around the player to fulfil his qualities. We really need to understand, whenever he comes back, how we are going to manage his load, what he is capable of to sustain having an impact in the team.”
Saka had only three weeks off after the World Cup but Arteta rejected suggestions that he should have been given more We want to pick on something, we will find it, but we won’t know whether it is for that or not. Maybe we needed to load those tendons more during those three weeks? Because if you don’t load the tendons, it becomes a problem. Who knows? I don’t know.”
Saka’s absence could hand an opportunity to Max Dowman on Saturday. The 16-year-old has played only nine minutes in the league this season and Arteta feels sure he is ready to make an impact after he became the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history , against David Moyes’s side in March.
“There is something inevitable to go back to that memory and the feeling of the moment. That’s with us, that’s going to stay in that stadium for a long, long time,” said Arteta. “He’s training and every time he’s got a moment to play, he’s showing that he’s a player that is going to impact the game. For sure he’s going to have minutes.”

content:
Bayern Munich head coach had been nursing a virus
Coach ‘undergoing thorough examinations’, club say
Vincent Kompany has been ⁠taken ⁠to ​hospital after the Bayern Munich coach felt unwell during training ⁠on Friday.
The Belgian, ​who ‌had been ‌nursing a virus in ‌recent days, was coaching his team before feeling unwell and being taken to ‌hospital.
The Bundesliga leaders, who drew 2-2 ​at home against Arsenal in the Champions League on Wednesday, are due ​to ​travel to ​Freiburg on Sunday. Kompany was on the bench for the Arsenal game despite the viral infection.
Bayern said on their website: “Vincent Kompany required medical ⁠attention after collapsing during a training session for ​Bayern’s reserve team. The ‌head coach of the professional squad had been observing ‌the second team’s session.
“Kompany is currently undergoing a thorough examination in the hospital and will remain under medical care. For the time being, his coaching staff will manage all training ‌and match-related operations.“
Max Eberl, Bayern’s sporting director, said: “Vincent Kompany’s health is our top priority. At Bayern, we will do everything ​we ​can to ensure he ​makes a speedy recovery.
“Vinnie is receiving ​all the ‌necessary medical care ​and ​support, and he will be given as much time as he needs. Everyone at FC Bayern wishes Vinnie a quick recovery.”

content:
Pierre Sage and Matthias Jaissle face some key questions: both were appointed this summer yet form, and results, have proved elusive
Conceding 17 goals in seven Premier League matches is not exactly the start Pierre Sage or Crystal Palace’s hierarchy would have hoped for. The transition from Oliver Glasner’s counterattacking 3-4-2-1 formation to the Frenchman’s more aggressive approach has exposed massive weaknesses in defence, culminating with last week’s humiliating defeat at Brighton. Palace fans became used to success under Glasner and they are already looking nervously over their shoulders at the bottom three. Even their league wins under Sage so far – against Fulham and Nottingham Forest – could have ended in defeat. Something doesn’t seem right in south London. EA
There have been so many arrivals and departures on Tyneside in recent months that it’s too early to say. Any team that sold their three best players – Sandro Tonali, Anthony Gordon and Bruno Guimarães in Newcastle’s case – during the summer would expect a degree of disruption. Eight signings were made, with four aged 20 and under and the others aged 24 and under, and only one (Nico González) had Premier League experience. Throw in a change of manager and an almost entirely new backroom staff and playing style three weeks before the season and teething troubles seem almost inevitable. LT
Sage is sailing extremely close to the wind and was warned after the Brighton game that things must improve quickly or he will be shown the door. It is understood that the Palace chair, Steve Parish, has yet to be convinced by the manager who led Lens to the French Cup last season and has demanded improvements in defence. After the creditable Europa League draw with Besiktas in midweek, Sunday’s meeting with Newcastle is crucial to his future. Thomas Frank and Kieran McKenna are likely candidates should Sage get sacked. Ipswich would be due substantial compensation for McKenna despite him leaving Portman Road in the summer, which could be a major hurdle. EA
Very little internally but, externally, the honeymoon is over. Newcastle paid Saudi Arabia’s Al-Ahli £9.5m compensation for Matthias Jaissle, convinced that the 38-year-old German and his “vertical football” were ideal fits. David Hopkinson, the chief executive, and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, are very impressed by Jaissle’s management style, particularly his collaborative approach. They appreciate that Eddie Howe’s successor is new to the Premier League , did not have a proper pre-season and is coping with a raft of injuries. All parties remain sufficiently realistic to predict a season of “ups and downs” but Newcastle’s Saudi Arabian owners crave a return to Europe. Many fans believe Jaissle’s football is old-school, rudimentary long ball with a fancy name, and believe his system and team selections have been flawed. They fear he may be a slave to philosophy. LT
Palace have looked a shadow of the side that won three trophies in the space of 12 months under Glasner and Sage must take some of the blame. He fell out with Parish after failing to sign several of his preferred targets in the summer, but it was his decision to break up the Adam Wharton-Daichi Kamada axis in central midfield having brought in Quinten Timber on deadline day. While the Dutchman, who missed the game in Turkey due to injury, has provided extra energy and Kamada has excelled in a more advanced role, Wharton has been struggling defensively. Palace looked much more solid when Wharton and Kamada started together against Besiktas – surely Sage will now stick with the partnership that served Glasner so well. EA
Jaissle’s belief in a gung-ho 4-2-3-1 featuring a classic No 10 is serving him badly at Newcastle, where he does not possess a natural attacking playmaker. It is also leaving González, a holding midfielder, frequently overrun and in need of additional support. With Malick Thiaw and, particularly, Sven Botman struggling in central defence, a switch to a more stable 3-5-2 may be sensible. More importantly, changing the philosophy to a more contain-and-counterattack approach would help camouflage the flaws and make the most of the team’s blistering attacking pace. Jaissle’s high-pressing, attack-minded tactics often appear overly high-risk. His critics fear he may prove to be another Ruben Amorim but Newcastle insiders insist Howe’s successor will prove more flexible than he may seem. Newcastle have not kept a league clean sheet for 13 games, equalling a club record, but six of those came under Howe. LT
A typically chaotic end to the transfer window left Sage with a bloated squad but insufficient leadership at the back after selling Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea. Axel Disasi’s three-match ban due to a reckless red card against Ipswich, after he arrived on loan from Stamford Bridge along with the promising Italian teenager Honest Ahanor, hasn’t helped. Parish and the sporting director, Matt Hobbs, deserve criticism for not bringing in more experienced replacements, with the latter’s position also thought to be under heavy scrutiny. Sage has also had to deal with unhappy attackers in Ismaïla Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta, who made no secret of their desire to leave Selhurst Park in the summer. EA
Quite a lot. Given his late arrival, Jaissle had limited influence over Wilson’s eight summer signings. He has, though, apparently swiftly decided that Aladji Bamba (£34m from Monaco) and Bazoumana Touré (£43m from Hoffenheim) are not ready to be thrown into Premier League combat. Similarly, the fleet-footed £51m former Lille forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo looks as if he is going to need time to adjust. Newcastle’s policy of generally recruiting players under 25 dictates the dressing room is a little light on leadership. Meanwhile iIt is hard to say whether the manager’s high-intensity training bears any responsibility for a lengthy injury list, with Anthony Elanga, Tino Livramento and Jacob Ramsey notable absentees. LT
After seeing positive signs against Besiktas, as Mateta scored on his first start since the opening day, three points on Sunday will be crucial for Sage. Yet while Palace haven’t lost to Newcastle at home since November 2020, Jaissle’s side have had extra time to prepare and will present a difficult challenge. EA
Given that Newcastle are 11th it is far from imperative. And yet after a demoralising 4-1 defeat at Coventry and a 1-0 home reverse against Aston Villa, victory would offer much-needed reassurance regarding the team’s potential and boost player confidence, not to mention quieten the social-media noise surrounding Jaissle and his tactics. LT
Palace’s summer net spend of almost £40m in profit was the second lowest in the Premier League behind Aston Villa. They also have American owners who are estimated to be worth a combined £10bn. But Parish revealed last month that he is still looking for extra funding for the new main stand at Selhurst Park, with Woody Johnson, Josh Harris and David Blitzer thought to be open to selling their shares after Palace enlisted Raine Group to seek fresh investment in the club. So there is plenty riding on making sure there is no prospect of being relegated. Sage showed at Lens that he is capable of building a winning team and needs time to do that. EA
Yes, quite a few. Jaissle, understandably, does not want to overplay the 18-year-old central midfielder Sean Steur but the summer signing from Ajax is a joy to watch, has a wonderful passing range and looks capable of reaching the top. Lewis Hall, the England left-back, looks to be going from strength to strength and is capable of elevating standards. Despite an undoubted dogmatic streak, Jaissle appears intelligent – and humble – enough to learn from his mistakes and make necessary adjustments. Club insiders cite his refreshing willingness to listen. Newcastle also possess several extremely quick attacking players – and, as coaches rarely tire of pointing out: “If you’ve got pace, you’ve got a chance.” LT

title: Pascal Gross: the obsessive runner keeping Brighton ‘one step ahead’ after fast start
description: Midfielder ‘who can never stand still’ has brought renewed energy to Seagulls since return to the club in January Most footballers like to spend their summers unwinding after a long season but not Pascal Gross. content:
Midfielder ‘who can never stand still’ has brought renewed energy to Seagulls since return to the club in January
M ost footballers like to spend their summers unwinding after a long season but not Pascal Gross. Having been part of the Germany squad eliminated in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024 , the midfielder entered – and won – a running race.
Gross completed the 8.4km course on Juist, in the East Frisian islands, in 31 minutes and 35 seconds. He is not known as someone who courts attention, and his victory by more than a minute came to light only when a video was posted on social media by a competitor.
Gross was moving from Brighton to Borussia Dortmund after seven years in the Premier League and reported to his boyhood club for pre-season training days later. Running is an obsession for Gross, as it is for his former teammate James Milner, who revealed last month he was training for a marathon after finally hanging up his boots, and that has shown since he returned for a second spell at the Amex in January for a bargain £1.2m.
“I think he’s looking in his free time now: ‘Where can I run a race?’ Because he will never stand still,” joked Brighton’s head coach, Fabian Hürzeler, after the 35-year-old scored the opening goal in a 3-0 victory over Arsenal last month . “ During the off-season he’s never the person who can lay on the beach for several hours and do nothing. He always needs to do something.”
Given that Gross has this season racked up an average distance of more than 11.5km per match and has covered the third-most ground of any player in the Premier League, it is no surprise Hürzeler has compared his compatriot to a good wine: “The older the wine gets, the better it gets.”
That analysis is borne out by the rest of his statistics this season as Brighton have emerged as challengers for Champions League qualification, at the very least, before Sunday’s game at Liverpool. Not only has Gross, the Premier League’s player of the month for September, contributed a combined seven goals and assists, he is in the top five for several other metrics such as big chances created (six), chances created from open play (14) and line-breaking passes leading to a goal (three). In a team that have scored the fourth-most goals (23) in Premier League history after seven games, Gross has been the standout performer.
“Sometimes he’s just one step ahead than his opponent,” said Hürzeler, who is understood to have been instrumental in bringing back Gross. “He might not be the quickest player, but he can be the quickest in the head and sometimes being the quickest in the head is very helpful. No one expected that it would be this good. But it also shows that he still has this capacity in his body.”
At a club where experience is valued despite Hürzeler being the youngest permanent manager in the Premier League’s history, insiders describe Gross as the perfect role model for some of Brighton’s younger players. Charalampos Kostoulas has scored three goals in his past four league matches and the 19-year-old Greece striker is clearly thriving alongside the man who is approaching 300 appearances for the club. Diego Gómez, the dynamic Paraguayan who scored a goal-of-the-season contender against Crystal Palace that will go down in Brighton folklore, the homegrown talent Jack Hinshelwood and the midfield linchpin Yasin Ayari are others benefiting from his vast experience, as is Hürzeler.
Gross managed 75 Brighton goals and assists after joining from Ingolstadt in 2017 in the summer when Brighton were promoted. His departure for Dortmund, a year after his first Germany cap, was to fulfil a boyhood dream but there was always something drawing Gross – who wears a long-sleeve shirt owing to a grass allergy – back to the club where he is known as the Kaiser .
“It was really difficult,” Gross said of his Brighton exit. “Only something really special got me out of here. There were a couple of other options [before returning], but Brighton was always the priority. I just stayed in touch with all the lads over the time away. Maybe you watch less of the games or you don’t stay in touch as much any more, it gets less and less. But it never really did.”
Gross retiring from international football after the World Cup has also been to Brighton’s benefit. His status as a club legend was augmented by delivering the free-kick that Palace’s Jaydee Canvot headed into his own net during the 5-0 humiliation on Sunday. That was the third game in a row in which Gross has provided an assist and he has an opportunity to become the oldest player to make it four since Chelsea’s Gianfranco Zola in December 2002.
The trip to Anfield continues a gruelling run of five away fixtures in a row. Brighton drew at the Czech club Jablonec on Thursday in the Conference League and after Sunday they go to Manchester City twice in four days – the first in the Carabao Cup – before heading to Spain to play Getafe. It will test Brighton’s mettle after their spectacular start. Hürzeler can count on Gross – who has started every game in all competitions – to last the course.

title: NWSL drops controversial criteria around ‘Rodman Rule’ in settlement with NWSLPA
description: Any player will be eligible for High Impact Player status Requirements had included top 100, marketability lists Sides also resolve grievance on Rodman contract refusal The NWSL and the NWSL Players Association have reached a settlement to drop the restrictive criteria around the controversial High Impact Player (HIP) rule, allowing any player to earn the league’s highest salaries. The NWSL introduced the rule late last year, allowing teams to spend an additional $1m above the salary cap to sign star players. Continue reading...
content:
Any player will be eligible for High Impact Player status
Requirements had included top 100, marketability lists
Sides also resolve grievance on Rodman contract refusal
The NWSL and the NWSL Players Association have reached a settlement to drop the restrictive criteria around the controversial High Impact Player (HIP) rule, allowing any player to earn the league’s highest salaries.
The NWSL introduced the rule late last year, allowing teams to spend an additional $1m above the salary cap to sign star players. Players with the designation had to meet one of eight criteria, ranging from US national team minutes and Ballon d’Or recognition to NWSL Best XI honors to media lists, including the Guardian’s Top 100 and a ranking that ordered athletes by marketability.
The NWSLPA opposed the mechanism and filed a grievance, arguing that the classification of players was a violation of federal labor law and the existing collective bargaining agreement. About 100 players had qualified for the designation based on the criteria – a total that, at the time the rule was introduced, included the likes of Trinity Rodman and Sophia Wilson but would have excluded such players as two-time NWSL MVP Sam Kerr and US star Catarina Macario.
Under the settlement, which was announced Friday, the eligibility criteria were eliminated. Beginning 1 January 2027, clubs will be able to designate any player as a High Impact Player, so long as their salary equals at least 12% of the base salary cap. The league can also set a limit on the number of HIP players per club.
The two sides settled six grievances in total, including one over the rejection of a contract proposal between the Washington Spirit and Rodman. Another involved the league’s footwear policy, which had dictated what brands players could wear during games.
“This settlement is certainly evidence of the NWSLPA’s strength and commitment to enforcing the terms of the Collective Bargaining Agreement,” NWSLPA director Meghann Burke told ESPN , which was the first to report news of the settlement.
“Disagreements are a natural part of any mature labor relationship, particularly in a league that is growing and evolving as quickly as ours,” NWSL executive vice-president Bill Ordower said in a statement. “What matters is how you work through them. This agreement gives the players, clubs and league greater clarity and certainty moving forward, while protecting the integrity and competitive balance that is fundamental to the NWSL.”
The initial version of the HIP Rule was introduced by the league last December. It allowed teams to spend $1m above the salary cap – for the 2026 season, set at $3.7m – to keep star players amid a wave of talent departing for Europe, where teams are not bound by salary caps.
The rule was ratified by the league’s board of governors and went into effect on 1 July. It became known informally as the “Rodman Rule” because its introduction coincided with the Washington Spirit star’s prolonged contract saga this past offseason.
Rodman had received lucrative offers from teams in Europe that the Spirit could not have matched under the NWSL’s salary cap rules. In November, before the HIP rule was introduced, the Spirit attempted to re-sign Rodman to a deal that would have averaged more than $1m annually, but NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman blocked the offer and said it violated the league’s rules because of its backloaded structure. The NWSLPA filed a grievance on Rodman’s behalf, calling the refusal a “flagrant violation” of player free agency rights.
Weeks later, the league introduced the HIP rule. Rodman re-signed with the Spirit in January on a record deal worth more than $2m annually.
The union grievance over the initial refusal of Rodman’s contract remained open after she signed the new contract. While teams are not required to disclose who is signed using the HIP mechanism, several players who would have been eligible under the criteria have since been signed or re-signed by teams in the league, including Denver’s Lindsey Heaps, Orlando’s Barbra Banda and Gotham’s Rose Lavelle.
The league will still have the ability to reject contracts for salary cap circumvention, but it must notify the union of the decision and provide an explanation within 72 hours. The league will also be required to provide salary cap and revenue updates to its clubs throughout the year.
The settlement also addressed the league’s footwear policy. Throughout this season, some players have received warnings and fines for wearing cleats from brands that were not official sponsors. The league will now honor pre-existing endorsement deals for most players and withdraw previous fines.

title: A-Leagues look past Manchester City distraction to ‘showpiece’ Melbourne derby
description: The Premier League scandal may have gripped English football but the A-League club is ‘critical’ to football’s presence and new strategy in Australia Sign up for Football Desk Australia: our newsletter from Jonathan Wilson In Australia’s most populous city, the A-Leagues derby between Melbourne Victory and Melbourne City will have more than a tinge of Manchester on Saturday night. Former United player Juan Mata, now a part-owner at Victory, will be farewelled after he chose not to play on with the A-League foundation club this season. The match is also City’s first at home since their parent club was found to have breached the Premier League’s financial rules . Continue reading...
content:
The Premier League scandal may have gripped English football but the A-League club is ‘critical’ to football’s presence and new strategy in Australia
Sign up for Football Desk Australia: our newsletter from Jonathan Wilson
In Australia’s most populous city, the A-Leagues derby between Melbourne Victory and Melbourne City will have more than a tinge of Manchester on Saturday night.
Former United player Juan Mata, now a part-owner at Victory, will be farewelled after he chose not to play on with the A-League foundation club this season. The match is also City’s first at home since their parent club was found to have breached the Premier League’s financial rules .
These storylines are both peripheral to the main event, however. The marquee fixture is both a “shop window” for the A-League Men and the competition’s footballing “showpiece”, according to Melbourne Victory chief executive Caroline Carnegie, who is not shy about her ambitions to sell out the derby. “Anything less than full will be less than what we would like to see,” she says.
Melbourne derby attendances peaked at more than 50,000 for Victory’s 2015 semi-final win, in the first year their opponents swapped the red of Melbourne Heart for the sky blue of City. Since Covid, crowds have been strong but not as they once were, with only one sellout at the 2025 grand final. “This is a really good opportunity for us to get people in to see what we’re all about, and then hopefully, we can convert them into people who are coming to other games,” Carnegie says.
Under new coach Giovanni Savarese, Victory are reeling after a shock loss to semi-professional South Melbourne in the sold-out Australia Cup final, and a first round league defeat in Wellington. A-League officials have not been generous to the Venezuelan, handing Victory a schedule with their earliest derby since 2022.
Veteran City attacker Mat Leckie has recovered from a hamstring injury suffered at the World Cup in time to play a part, and he will be joined by Socceroos teammates Aziz Behich and Awer Mabil. The experienced trio will complement emerging talents such as Medin Memeti, Quinn MacNicol and Kavian Rahmani, emphasising the club’s status of one of Australia’s most important talent factories. “The young boys that we have are some of the best in the country,” Leckie says. “So the expectation on them to go on and do good things is there.”
The City model mixes proven internationals with opportunity for youth. Three of the A-League Men’s four most valuable players according to Transfer Room are at the club, with Memeti, Rahmani and forward Max Caputo all said to be roughly worth $1.5m. “You look at our team and everyone’s age, I think when the club’s looking for talent and new players to bring in, they’re obviously looking for the young talents of Australia,” Leckie says.
City’s approach reflects a broader shift of the A-Leagues towards development, from its initial promise as a mass entertainment product competing alongside major players like the AFL and NRL. Annual transfer revenue for Australian clubs more than trebled in 2023-24, and has stabilised at between $10m and $20m per year, softening the economic strain for owners faced with declining broadcast revenue.
That dynamic happens to be aligned with the motivations of City’s network – City Football Group. Socceroos goalkeeper Patrick Beach moved to another CFG club, Troyes, in the off-season, and his World Cup teammate Kai Trewin joined New York City FC at the start of the year. Melbourne City has set multiple outgoing A-League Women’s transfer records amid the global women’s football boom, most recently Leticia McKenna to Nottingham Forest for close to $200,000 .
Sign up for Football Desk Australia: our newsletter from Jonathan Wilson
Melbourne City’s investment is focused on development. The owners splashed out $2m for a training pitch when they first bought into Australia, and a new academy worth close to $20m was unveiled in 2024 (with roughly half local government funding).
Steve Rosich, chief executive of A-Leagues operator APL , said City were a “significant” club in the competition and “critical” to football’s presence in Melbourne. “City continue to produce a number of Socceroos and Matildas, and we commend them in particular on their investment in the women’s program,” he says. “They have state of the art infrastructure, they’ve invested in the region. They’ve got an academy that’s produced well over 50 A-League players, which is a market leader.”
Melbourne and New York were the first stops in City’s multi-club ownership rollout and CFG connections ripple throughout Australian football. One of Rosich’s bosses, APL board member Simon Pearce, was an architect of the separation of the A-Leagues from governing body Football Australia in 2021 and is also vice-chair of Melbourne City. The PR executive was born in England but lived in Australia prior to moving to Abu Dhabi. There he found work with Khaldoon Al Mubarak before the well-connected Emirati became Manchester City chair. Pearce has since returned to live in Sydney.
FA chief executive at the time of the A-Leagues’ “unbundling”, James Johnson, spent time within the City family, as did several current and former executives. CFG minority owner Silver Lake also invested $140m in the A-Leagues in 2021.
While the Manchester City scandal may have gripped English football, across the other side of the world there are more pressing concerns. Leckie says the matter has been raised but not discussed at length in the Melbourne City dressing room. “Whatever happens, there’s nothing we can do,” he says. “It’s just play on.”
The outlook is similar for Rosich, who deflected questions about City at the season launch and already has his hands full. An arrangement with FA headed off a dispute with referees earlier this month, and a new player pay deal is close. Clubs have begun transferring increases agreed during negotiations, even before the final deal has been signed.
The work in the off-season has cleared a backlog – largely outstanding items dating back to the APL’s separation with FA – that has afforded oxygen to the start of the season, including this week’s clash in Melbourne. The “reach” for the round one broadcast on Network Ten, featuring the Sydney derby, was the highest since 2021 according to Rosich. The five matches recorded the highest average attendance for an opening round since 2019, even with Macarthur’s crowd of 3,441.
But there is clear appetite to do more to grow the league, and urgently. City coach Aurelio Vidmar called for an expansion of the competition on Friday by adding four clubs as soon as possible to lengthen the season. Rosich has had a “near term” strategy signed off by Pearce and his board colleagues, that will now be taken to clubs. The document will home in on the A-Leagues’ popularity among fans under 35, the potential of the A-League Women , football’s large participation base, and how these components can deliver immediate gains, especially around fan growth.
In that context, the Melbourne derby will be instructive. Carnegie says investors like Victory’s minority owners Mata and Tony Bloom from Brighton, QPR – whose owners Total Soccer Holdings hold the Central Coast Mariners licence – and Auckland FC’s American billionaire Bill Foley, show the “underlying foundations” of the A-Leagues already exist. “What we need is for people to come along and support, and then it will snowball from there.”

title: Is el clásico still the world’s biggest match? Three questions before Barcelona v Real Madrid
description: The fixture’s relevance waned as the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded. Can Lamine Yamal and Mbappé lift it into a new era? For the best part of a decade, el clásico was more than just soccer’s biggest fixture. It was the defining narrative. At the peak of the Lionel Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo era, there were clásicos everywhere. Yes, when the two historic rivals clashed on the pitch, but also in the voting for the Ballon d’Or every year and in so much of the discourse around the sport. As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico ’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico ’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture? Continue reading...
content:
The fixture’s relevance waned as the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded. Can Lamine Yamal and Mbappé lift it into a new era?
F or the best part of a decade, el clásico was more than just soccer’s biggest fixture. It was the defining narrative. At the peak of the Lionel Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo era, there were clásicos everywhere. Yes, when the two historic rivals clashed on the pitch, but also in the voting for the Ballon d’Or every year and in so much of the discourse around the sport.
As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico ’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico ’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture?
Sunday’s match at Camp Nou will be watched by hundreds of millions of viewers all over the world. A clásico always carries significance, but this weekend’s edition will be especially significant. A Barça win would move them nine points clear of their rivals at the top of La Liga . A Real Madrid victory could be a catalyst for the rest of their season.
Lamine Yamal may be the best player in the world right now, and he could have the Ballon d’Or trophy to prove it by Monday. Kylian Mbappé is up there too. The Clásico doesn’t lack for star power, but the framing of the fixture has changed in recent times. Not so long ago, the world stopped to watch it. Now, the world doesn’t seem so bothered.
Unless Manchester City’s financial rule-breaking has a tangible effect on the Premier League’s reputation, the English top flight remains soccer’s dominant league. The league with more fans around the world than any other. A behemoth so omnipresent that even the uninterested are at least aware.
April’s title clash between Manchester City and Arsenal set a new record as the most-watched Premier League match in US TV history, nearly doubling the mark for the most-watched clásico in US TV history set in October 2025. Audience trends point towards the Premier League being European soccer’s most compelling product.
The packaging of the division is possibly part of this. While La Liga has bounced between different broadcasters, the Premier League made a long-term commitment to Sky Sports in the UK and NBC in the USA to properly broadcast and promote matches. Premier League matches are filmed with more cameras. They look better. More vibrant. It also helps that fans know where to consistently find games in their TV guide.
La Liga has tried to broaden its global appeal, setting up an office in New York and even floating the idea of playing a competitive match in Miami. Past clásico encounters have been scheduled for a primetime audience in Asia. The Premier League, however, has the advantage of being an English language-first league which appears to be an advantage in the modern media market.
At the peak of the clásico ’s relevance, there was an unavoidable sense that the fixture was a showcase for the very best that the sport had to offer. That, however, is no longer the case. Barcelona are Europe’s most exhilarating team to watch, but the inherent chaos of their playing style under Hansi Flick comes with problems (primarily their high defensive line) that have prevented them from truly challenging for the Champions League.
It’s been a full decade since Barça last won the Champions League. While Real Madrid have enjoyed continental glory more recently, winning a 14th European Cup in 2024, they are a long way from being the team who dominated Europe under Carlo Ancelotti and Zinedine Zidane.
Real Madrid find themselves behind the curve of the modern game and the appointment of José Mourinho in the summer didn’t change that. If anything, the Special One’s not-so-special return to the Santiago Bernabéu has highlighted the club’s stagnancy. Xabi Alonso dared to introduce new ideas and was hounded out for it.
Instead, Paris Saint-Germain are setting the standard at the top of the game – and doing so with a former Barcelona player and manager at the helm. And with a former Barcelona forward performing a false-nine role pioneered by Messi.
Lamine Yamal has 20 goal contributions in just 12 games for Barcelona this season. Mbappé has 15 in the same number of games for Real Madrid. Both players represent a new direction for their respective teams and could dominate the clásico as individuals for years in the way Messi and Ronaldo did.
Perhaps Sunday’s encounter will be the first truly memorable clash between the two. Vinícius Júnior is suspended while Raphinha is only just returning to fitness after a minor muscle injury, meaning there will be even more focus on Mbappé and Lamine Yamal.
Messi scored 26 clásico goals, the most of any player in the fixture’s history. Ronaldo had the second most (18), tied with Alfredo Di Stéfano. Mbappé and Lamine Yamal have a long way to go to reach such heights as the two new faces of Spain’s Big Two, but with every meeting their personal rivalry will grow. The narrative will build.
Meaning comes out of history. Shared experience. A consensus that something matters can take time to be reached and while the consensus is that Mbappé and Lamine Yamal are two of the best players in the world, their careers have yet to be intertwined as two rivals whose story can only be told as one. When that happens, the clásico may reclaim its status as soccer’s most meaningful game.

title: Slegers and misfiring Arsenal badly need a result in WSL north London derby
description: Gunners’ title hopes have seemingly evaporated and their under-pressure head coach faces her latest test against Spurs on Saturday It says much about Arsenal’s predicament that the team who have conceded 12 goals in two games are not the side whose head coach is under most pressure before a north London derby. Tottenham, four points above their neighbours before Saturday’s meeting, may have been humbled in consecutive Women’s Super League matches but all eyes are on Renée Slegers. Arsenal are winless in five WSL matches for the first time, and the most decorated club in English women’s football desperately need a turning point. Their failure to beat Birmingham at home last Saturday, dropping points against a promoted side for the second time this season, again demonstrated the team’s inability to convert possession into goals. They increasingly look like a team stuck in Groundhog Day. Continue reading...
content:
Gunners’ title hopes have seemingly evaporated and their under-pressure head coach faces her latest test against Spurs on Saturday
I t says much about Arsenal’s predicament that the team who have conceded 12 goals in two games are not the side whose head coach is under most pressure before a north London derby. Tottenham, four points above their neighbours before Saturday’s meeting, may have been humbled in consecutive Women’s Super League matches but all eyes are on Renée Slegers.
Arsenal are winless in five WSL matches for the first time, and the most decorated club in English women’s football desperately need a turning point. Their failure to beat Birmingham at home last Saturday, dropping points against a promoted side for the second time this season, again demonstrated the team’s inability to convert possession into goals. They increasingly look like a team stuck in Groundhog Day.
The Arsenal hierarchy are understood to remain behind Slegers, but for how long? The answer may hinge on Saturday lunchtime’s result. However much goodwill the Dutchwoman gained for guiding Arsenal to Champions League glory in May 2025 , the simple truth is, it is unacceptable for a club with one of the biggest budgets in the world to be 12 points behind the leaders after six games.
That gap is why the draw with Birmingham not only pretty much extinguished Arsenal’s title hopes but also burned a hole in their secondary domestic objective – Champions League qualification. The unthinkable prospect of failure appears a genuine possibility: they are nine points adrift of third-placed London City. Arsenal need a derby win on Saturday but also a winning run to reverse the slide, and there is little evidence to suggest such a turnaround is close.
Arsenal have the worst shot conversion rate in the league (4.1%) and, according to Stats Perform, the third-worst shooting accuracy (30.6%) and third-lowest average xG per shot (0.09) despite averaging over 60% possession. Slegers’s persistence in deploying Alessia Russo – widely regarded as one of Europe’s best No 9s – in the No 10 role has baffled supporters and commentators alike. Russo has scored more WSL goals against Tottenham (eight) than any other player so Saturday’s game may be the perfect moment for that to change.
Arsenal have struggled against low blocks for a number of seasons, though, so not all fault lies at Slegers’s door. Nonetheless, the 37-year-old was substantially backed in the summer, with Arsenal enjoying perhaps their strongest transfer window in recent memory. So far though they have looked confounded tactically, bruised mentally and lacking the self-belief to grab a game by the scruff of its neck.
Asked if she was surprised to still be in her job, Slegers said: “That’s not something I think about. It’s about, ‘where are we as a group?’ and ‘what are we working towards?’ It’s absolutely not what we expected [our recent results] or what we wanted. But I’m in the here and now, and we are preparing for the north London derby. We have the group together. Everyone is going in the same direction and the fuel and motivation is sky high, because of the fans that will be there for us. That’s where my focus will be.”
Asked how imperative it is that Arsenal climb back up into a Champions League place this season, Slegers added: “Of course that’s in the back of our heads, but what we need right now is to get back to winning ways. We can only do that with the next game in front of us so that’s why the next game in front of us is the most important right now.”
Slegers has maintained after last weekend’s draw that Arsenal will recover when they fix some “details and margins”. Perhaps taking on a Tottenham side who have become only the second team in history to concede six or more goals in consecutive WSL games is the perfect opportunity.
“It is a little bit of game intelligence and smartness in moments,” said the Spurs head coach, Martin Ho, insisting he is not worried about his team’s defending in the long-term. “There have been certain aspects that, collectively, players and staff, we were not happy with in certain moments, and we have to make sure we correct them. At the moment we’re getting heavily punished for some small errors with the ball that we’re making.”
The Englishman also only had praise for Arsenal’s qualities when speaking on Friday morning. “If you try and underestimate a team with Arsenal’s quality you’re in for trouble,” he said. Asked about Arsenal’s poor run, Ho added: “Arsenal aren’t a bad side. Their possession stats are probably the highest in the league, alongside Manchester City. Their goalscoring chances and touches in the opposition box are very, very high. They have world-class players.”
Last season’s runners-up do have world-class players but it is high time for them to play like a cohesive team.

title: Too much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no bounds

content:
The Overlap has gone daily, with Steven Gerrard and Joe Hart among the latest additions to an ever-growing family
V iewed in 2026, Nathan Barley, Chris Morris’s 2005 sitcom, shows remarkable prescience about the last two decades of metropolitan life, from smartphone addiction and digital derangement to sheer existential vapidity. When Barley’s character referred to his occupation as “self-facilitating media node”, Morris and co-writer Charlie Brooker were way ahead on the creator economy. What the pair failed to predict was ex-footballers joining the sector in droves. These days, if you are a former footballer without a podcast or YouTube channel, then did you ever really play the game?
Setting aside the Gary Lineker Goalhanger empire, manspreading its centrist-dad agenda into issues way beyond guffaws with Micah Richards and Alan Shearer, there is Gary Neville to rule them all. Manchesterism’s second-most influential practitioner has been on heavy manoeuvres. Unlike Lineker’s productions, the Overlap’s output continues to stick largely to football; a rugby podcast was mothballed in February, though its cricket equivalent continues.
Having snatched Wayne Rooney from the BBC in the summer for a Manchester United-based two-hander with the YouTuber Mark Goldbridge, last week the Overlap went daily, extending the output to 4pm Monday to Friday. An online launch had Jamie Carragher baiting Goldbridge, real name Brent Di Cesare. The former policeman shunned a “no comment” approach during his interrogation, biting back during an exchange that had Neville choking on his Huel in laughter. Clipped up, the send button pressed, job done.
The Overlap has gained a TV family dynamic, a chorus line of familiar characters. Neville and Carragher are mummy and daddy bear, football’s Richard and Judy. Jill Scott is the dotty aunt, Roy Keane the irascible uncle, smirking along with Ian Wright in picking over the latest gossip. It has been highly popular, occasionally agenda-setting, softening Keane’s image, even making a cultish figure of production hand Kiaran Saunders, supplier of biscuits and blueberries. Neville’s empire-building, though, is boundless, his tanks bulldozing into the already packed football podcast space, with newsletters to follow. The Overkill, anyone?
The family has been extended. Mondays have Steven Gerrard reviewing the weekend’s action with Becky Ives, this week offering a defence of Florian Wirtz: “Don’t give up on him.” Tuesdays have Kelly Cates and Ashley Young in tandem. Tim Sherwood and Jamie Redknapp are Wednesday’s pairing. Not the first time the Sky mainstays, one-time Tottenham midfield partners, have diversified. In the mid-2000s, they ran Icon, a lifestyle magazine initially only available to professional players. A combination of high-end advertising, onanistic photography and Redknapp’s purring interviews with A-list sportspeople fell flat, even after it became available in airport first-class lounges.
Two decades on, such cologne-fragrant exclusivity has been swapped for the ubiquity of Bury’s most famous son piling it high. The quarter-zipped ex-Spurs duo are not alone as 1990s footballers taking the Neville shilling. Mark Crossley and Duncan Ferguson make an unlikely – but promising – pairing. Previously most famous for being the only goalkeeper to save a Matthew Le Tissier penalty, Crossley has made a successful after-dinner speaking career of Brian Clough anecdotes and “young man” impressions. “Big Dunc” completely refused to speak to the media when a player but he was a hit within ITV’s World Cup 2026 coverage.
On last week’s edition Ferguson suggested Gianluigi Donnarumma might be over the hill. “He’s 27, actually,” said Crossley before a classic game’s gone discussion of video assistant referees ruining the sacred art of smashing into the opposition at goal-kicks. Just what the listener came for, eating perhaps into the Under The Cosh’s market share of real football man podcasts. Whether Ferguson’s appointment as Glentoran manager breaks up the band is unclear, though management never halted Robbie Savage’s many media ventures.
Two further goalkeepers have signed up. Last week’s Friday edition had Joe Hart and Peter Schmeichel entering the Manchester City charges chat. While admitting to mistakenly burying the lead when Lisandro Martínez was willingly dishing the dirt on Manchester United while serving as CBS’s Champions League interviewer in Madrid last Tuesday, Schmeichel gave Hart a far harder ride. “It’s tough to be a Manchester City person,” Hart said. “I love the club … we’re in it together.” Schmeichel stayed insistent on City’s owners: “They’re letting Manchester down, they don’t understand what this place is. They have built a lot of towers and homes and all that but they don’t get this place.”
“I’ve worked closely with Khaldoon [al-Mubarak] and he does get this place, that’s my reference point,” said a hesitant Hart. “He’s an incredible person.” More good, strong, clip-up content.
The City affair will ask former players to intersect with uncomfortable issues for some while yet. That Neville’s further business interests include building projects running parallel to the Abu Dhabi-funded developments in Manchester is another example. Overlaps have become unavoidable in more ways than one.

title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run?
