content:
Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success
Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here
I n 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series .
We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).
Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:
double quotation mark The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.
It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:
double quotation mark The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.
Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here .
Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.
These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.
Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.
Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.
Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”
Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.
From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.
The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025 . “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”
Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.
The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

title: Dwight Yorke: ‘I’m not a kid trying to get into management – I’m a manager’
description: Ghana may soon come calling for Trinidad and Tobago’s former captain and manager, who is proud of his CV since his days as a Premier League striker Dwight Yorke wants you to stop calling him a former player. “I’m not a kid trying to get into management for the first time,” he says from his home in Dubai. “I’ve done that and I want that message to come across clearly.” The message has a deadline. Carlos Queiroz left his job as Ghana head coach on 1 October and the Ghana Football Association is searching for his successor. Yorke is among the names under consideration, along with Pape Thiaw, Aliou Cissé and Walid Regragui, the former Morocco head coach, according to Ghanaian media. Continue reading...
content:
Ghana may soon come calling for Trinidad and Tobago’s former captain and manager, who is proud of his CV since his days as a Premier League striker
D wight Yorke wants you to stop calling him a former player. “I’m not a kid trying to get into management for the first time,” he says from his home in Dubai. “I’ve done that and I want that message to come across clearly.”
The message has a deadline. Carlos Queiroz left his job as Ghana head coach on 1 October and the Ghana Football Association is searching for his successor. Yorke is among the names under consideration, along with Pape Thiaw, Aliou Cissé and Walid Regragui, the former Morocco head coach, according to Ghanaian media.
He is tired of the shorthand way he is described during these high‑profile job hunts. People focus on his playing accolades, including calling him the treble winner, a label he says belongs to one season in a run of three Premier League titles at Manchester United from 1999-2001. “I’m a manager,” he says.
Over the past four years, Yorke has quietly built a coaching résumé far removed from Old Trafford. His first taste of management came in May 2022, taking charge of Australia’s A-League All Stars against Barcelona in front of more than 70,000 people in Sydney. They lost 3-2. “I realised then that I enjoyed it,” he says.
Macarthur, based in Sydney, followed that July . “We went to a relatively unknown team in the A‑League and managed to win the cup.” The Australia Cup success, three months into his spell, was the club’s first trophy.
It did not last. Macarthur sacked him in January 2023, with the club sixth, after a post-match address when he reportedly called the club a “pub team” run by “muppets”.
A Fifa chamber found Macarthur had dismissed him without just cause. The court of arbitration for sport upheld that in 2024 and ordered the club to pay AU$212,500 (£111,300 at current exchange rates).
“I wish I’d had the opportunity to finish what I started,” Yorke says. The job taught him communication and the importance of being transparent. “There was a disagreement. It was resolved amicably and I’ve moved on.”
Between Macarthur and his next role, he kept his hand in. He worked as a pundit for beIN Sports and on the Saudi Pro League and travelled the world watching coaches at work.
In November 2024, Trinidad and Tobago came calling . The Soca Warriors finished third in their World Cup qualifying group behind Curaçao and Jamaica, missing out on the finals tournament, and Yorke’s tenure ended soon after. The Trinidad and Tobago Football Association said talks over revised terms had not produced an agreement and the contract was ended by mutual consent, announced in March. “The decision to end things was out of my control,” Yorke says.
He does not accept that missing the World Cup defines his time in charge. “People can be blind to success because they focus on whether you qualified.”
He lost once in six qualifiers, 2-0 in Jamaica in September 2025. He had been handed a brief: make people care about Trinidad and Tobago again, boost recruitment and qualify. “I was given three tasks and completed two,” he says.
With Yorke as the head coach, crowds came back and a number of US-born players with Trinidadian and Tobagonian heritage, such as the CF Montréal winger Dante Sealy and Real Salt Lake’s Kobi Henry, opted in and made their debuts. Yorke gave a new generation a fighting chance to emulate the team he captained to the finals in 2006. “I left Trinidadian football in a far better place than I found it,” he says.
The TTFA president at the time described Yorke’s mandate as qualification alone. The team were ranked 102nd by Fifa when Yorke was hired, behind Curaçao (91st) and Jamaica (62nd). “I miss management,” Yorke says. “I miss what we were creating.”
The players are understood to want him back because his successor, Derek King, is struggling with two draws and eight defeats from his 10 games. Ghana, though, is the live opportunity. “It’s a job I’d be interested in, given Ghana’s history and the players available.”
The Ghanaian FA has not confirmed any approach. The team are bottom of their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying group with no points, after a 2-0 defeat in Côte d’Ivoire and a 4-2 home loss against the Gambia in which they led by two goals. It is a sharp decline for a side that reached the last 32 of the World Cup this summer, losing 1-0 against Colombia .
“You look at the squad and your eyes open even wider,” Yorke says. He says an agent called to tell him Ghana were interested. “The conversation started there and then reached the media before I really knew it.”
From the outside, he says, Ghana “sometimes looks disjointed”. The GFA has said its women’s head coach, Kim Björkegren, will take temporary charge of the men’s qualifying double-header against Somalia next month. In Yorke’s view, outside noise unbalances things, from the administration to the players. So how would he fix it? Organisation, transparency and everyone speaking the same language. “The talent is there. Build the culture and get the players to buy in and the football will follow.”
He has considered the effect that diaspora players could have in the role, pointing to Ghana’s Antoine Semenyo and Brandon Thomas-Asante as proof that countries can benefit immensely from UK-born talent. It reflects a broader trend: at the World Cup, 23.6% of the 1,248 squad players represented countries outside their place of birth. For Yorke, the approach is simple: identify the players, establish their heritage and quality and sell them a vision. “I’d make sure that what I say is what I do.”
Older managers might have screamed and shouted to get messages across, but he says: “I’m not sure that approach can last in the current environment.” He would not berate a player in public. “That can be done behind closed doors, while still being assertive.” Respect and punctuality are non‑negotiable. He has sat in dressing rooms with big egos and says nobody gets special treatment. “Everyone starts equally.”
He borrows, but he does not copy. Sir Alex Ferguson, who managed him at United, is the shadow over any such comparison. Among contemporary managers, Pep Guardiola offered him the best advice. “He said, in effect, that I can’t be him or any other manager. I have to be myself.”
Other labels have stuck anyway. “People still call me a ‘party boy’. That stigma has been overused and has followed me since I retired from football. I’m not saying I didn’t enjoy myself as a player.” But he says: “You never hear that I didn’t turn up for training or wasn’t fit.”
In Dubai, he tends to fast for nearly 20 hours a day and eats one meal. “I’m a fitness fanatic who trains every day.”
Ask Yorke how he wants to be remembered as a coach and he sits up and answers with a list. Committed. Transparent with players. Decisions made for the team, never for an individual. “I’m straightforward. I don’t mess around, take shortcuts or do the job halfway.”
Yorke has the interest and, by his own account, the answers. “If anyone doubts me, I can prove them wrong.”

title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...
content:
The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career
“T he perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.”
McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.”
But there’s sadness, too, in the way his life and career were scarred by his refusal to wear the poppy when playing games around Remembrance Sunday in England. “It’s completely changed me as a person,” McClean says. “It’s made me a bit of a recluse because I don’t trust a lot of people now. I’ve been stung bad.”
McClean’s autobiography, The Walls , is one of the best sports books of the year. It’s a powerful and sometimes disturbing read elevated by McClean’s willingness to show himself in an unflattering light.
I have written a lot about Derry and boxing, and Bloody Sunday , but it helps to be back here to understand how McClean can respect the millions of soldiers who died in two world wars while refusing to forget how the British army killed so many Irish people in this city.
He comes from Creggan, the estate affected most on Bloody Sunday in 1972 when 14 unarmed civilians were killed by the British army in Derry. Six of the fatalities were from Creggan. In 2010, after the Saville report finally concluded that all the victims posed no threat, the British prime minister David Cameron apologised for the “unjustified and unjustifiable” massacre.
McClean was born in Derry in 1989 and he writes that “learning how to make a petrol bomb was one of my first life lessons. I was 11 before I’d properly mastered it.”
He pauses when asked how he would feel if any of his three daughters or his son, who is 11, ended up making petrol bombs. “I’m very thankful they don’t have to. It’s a different era now. I just want them to be proud to be Irish.”
The 37-year-old spells out the contrast with his youth. “I grew up in a very Republican community still dealing with the effects of the Troubles. You would see gunmen on the street. People got shot, kneecapped. To get access to my street you had to go through a lane where you sometimes saw masked men doing punishment beatings. But you weren’t scared. You knew you’d done nothing wrong. That was the norm … but it’s not normal.”
His biological father, Joe Kelly, was an alcoholic in Creggan and McClean spoke to him only once – when he shouted at him in the street to stay away. But he remembers a happy childhood and, when his professional career began with Derry City, “I was very carefree”.
McClean was 22 when Steve Bruce signed him for Sunderland in August 2011. He made his Premier League debut that December after Bruce was replaced by Martin O’Neill. McClean soon became a regular starter and that first season in English football was full of joy and praise. He was fast, skilful and disciplined. Apart from wasting money his biggest vice was typing his name on Twitter where he would revel in glowing reports of his play.
“It was amazing,” McClean says. “I never thought about the politics when I first got to England so up until November 2012, when the poppy thing started, I never experienced any bother.”
Everything changed when he told Sunderland he wouldn’t wear the poppy because it also represented the British army which had occupied Derry for so long. “There was never a decision for me to make,” he says. “Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen. It was a very difficult year and I felt a lot of that could have been handled better by the club. But Sunderland came out with a statement before the game which drew all eyes on me. It was there to protect the club. They basically said this is James’s personal decision but we, as a club, wholeheartedly support the poppy appeal.
“I wanted to make my own statement but I was constantly told by the club that: ‘No, no, it’ll die over. Just leave it.’ I’d just turned 23 and I thought the club had a duty of care to look after me and that’s what they were doing. I’d won the player of the year the previous season but I felt they hung me out to dry.”
McClean recalls that: “The next game was away to Fulham on a Sunday, on Sky. A threat was made that I would be shot if I came on to the pitch. I remember [his wife] Erin panicking. It sounds extreme and people might say: ‘Oh, wise up, you’re not going to be shot on TV.’ But the night before the game I was assigned two police officers to stand outside my door. So the Met police took it seriously and that made it more real.”
O’Neill brought him on in the second half and his every touch was booed – by the Fulham and Sunderland supporters. The vitriol poisoned his world but McClean kept searching for his name on Twitter. He became furious whenever, after a mutually respectful encounter with a member of the public, the person would go online to abuse him.
Sometimes McClean would track the person down and demand an apology. “Maybe that madness was always there, but it got stronger,” he notes.
McClean moved to Wigan before joining West Brom where, in “the best kind of madness” he earned £42,000 a week while he had his best spell in the Premier League. But as one poppy season blurred into another , the death threats kept coming, as did the warnings that Erin would be raped. McClean says: “My reaction was always to fight fire with fire. I went into some games in the wrong frame of mind. It wasn’t: ‘Can I help the team?’ It was: ‘I hope I score today so I can shush them up.’”
McClean admits: “There were days where I went looking for the conflict.” He posted a photograph of himself listening to his favourite Wolfe Tones song, The Broad Black Brimmer. “I knew exactly what I was doing,” McClean writes. “It was an IRA song – and I was sure it would rile a certain type of person up.”
By the time he reached Stoke, for whom he played 111 games between 2018 and 2021, his problems in English football reached a new low . “Brexit made the idiots louder” and “the poppy season seemed to be getting longer every year”. He had also made a stupid mistake during lockdown when he posted a photograph of himself, wearing a balaclava, with his two eldest children below a caption which read: ‘Today’s school lesson – History.’”
McClean thought he was being funny but his choice not to wear the poppy, in contrast, was heartfelt. “I thought others might have followed suit but it never turned out to be the case.”
Did he feel that a more rounded understating of his stance had emerged by the time he enjoyed his happiest seasons in English football, while playing for a Hollywood-tinged Wrexham from 2023 to earlier this year? “A wee bit, aye. When you explain it to footballers you’ve played with, and to people on a personal level, it opens their eyes and they say: ‘Oh, I understand that.’ But the overall British population? I don’t think so.”
Reflecting on his Premier League years, McClean marvels at the brilliance of Kevin De Bruyne and Eden Hazard. “You had to accept there were lads capable of doing things that were beyond you,” McClean writes. “But there were also games where I thought I was coming up against a physical strength that I found suspicious. Coming back into the Premier League after a break convinced me that some players had to be benefiting from some kind of performance-enhancing support.
“I remember coming up against one player that I’d encountered at Sunderland who I always felt that I’d been able to match in terms of his speed and power. While I’d been away from the Premier League, he’d gone to a bigger club, and now he was a different animal completely.”
These are startling allegations and, while McClean has no concrete evidence to support his doubts, he trusts his gut reaction. “I’ve always been very fanatical about my fitness,” he says. “But when you come against the top Premier League clubs, no matter what height, what size, they’re just faster, they’re stronger, and you’re thinking: ‘How is that possible?’”
After their daughter Willow was diagnosed with global development delay and autism, Erin persuaded him to be tested for autism . He was found to be “at the high-functioning end of the spectrum” but he still struggles with the fact that “I’ve probably got body dysmorphia or some kind of bulimia. Maybe it’s the autism thing, because I’m so strict with my diet 95% of the time. But when I can’t work out I binge. So if I’m travelling and flying, I’ll just eat that much shite to the point where I have to make myself sick. I still feel really guilty, because the next day I’ll punish myself in the gym – which is not healthy.”
Life has become even more complicated since he returned to Derry City in January. “I was meant to be coming home for the fairytale ending. But you quickly realise the promises are just bullshit.”
McClean has not played for the club since July and, asked about the situation, he says: “It’s not good. It’s a player against owner and there’s only one winner. I think that’s it in terms of Derry City. You never think you’ll be betrayed by your own so it’s painful.”
When contacted by the Guardian, a spokesman for Derry City said: “The club cannot speak to, or comment on, how James feels.” He also rejected the suggestion that Derry City had failed to fulfil any promises made to McClean.
Earlier this month, McClean said he couldn’t “understand or accept” the way he was being treated by the club and that he was fit to play despite being left out of the squad by interim manager Mark Connolly. Derry City then released a statement in which they said: “The club has sought to resolve this internal matter privately. Out of respect for confidentiality and the fact that this dispute involves sensitive medical details regarding James’ hip condition, the club have previously refrained from making any public statement on the matter.”
McClean insists he could play football elsewhere but how does he feel if this is the end of his career? “It doesn’t unsettle me because I’ve been boxing off and on for 10 years and in the past 18 months I’ve really thrown myself into it. I’m not going to start a pro boxing career because it’s just not feasible at my age. But I’ve been in contact with Misfits and they want me to fight.”
Misfits Boxing was set up by KSI and the Sauerland brothers, who made their name in the traditional fight game, and it features YouTubers and former athletes who want to become boxers. It is dismissed by boxing purists but McClean sounds enthusiastic about making his debut in the ring once his contract with Derry expires: “Boxing is giving me that purpose to wake up and train hard.”
What kind of boxer would he like to become? “I’m a pressure fighter. I like to be constantly in someone’s face because I’ve got the fitness to maintain that. I’m not saying I’m by any stretch of the imagination a [Gennady] Golovkin or a Canelo [Álvarez], but I love watching them. I’m not looking to have a career in boxing but three or four fights a year is perfect. The dream was always to be a footballer but this is a new excitement, a new challenge.”
As we prepare to step out into a rain-sodden Derry, there seems little chance of any reconciliation for him on the football field. But he looks up and his taut fighter’s face suddenly relaxes into a smile. “It could be a blessing,” McClean says softly. “It could end up a blessing in disguise.”

author_name: Dominic Booth at the Brick Community Stadium
content:
Gary Caldwell, club captain in 2013 and now manager, needs much more than the weekend win against Reading to disperse the clouds
I f the 2013 FA Cup final represented a blip for the Sheikh Mansour-era Manchester City in their quest for total domination of English football, it was a historic moment for their conquerors, Wigan Athletic .
Memories of that famous day at Wembley still endure for Latics supporters despite the relegation from the Premier League that followed. Yet watching the modern‑day Wigan, who remain bottom of League One despite a 1-0 win against Reading on Saturday, makes the toppling of City in a Cup final seem an epoch ago.
The club, perhaps understandably, continue to hark back to their halcyon days. Last season they brought back Gary Caldwell – club captain in 2013 – for his second stint as manager, having led the club to promotion from this division in 2015-16. Choosing to swap Exeter for a return to the Latics was seen as a risky move by Caldwell, considering the shoestring budget imposed upon him by Mike Danson, the owner who is keen to sell.
Finances are ultra-tight at the Greater Manchester club amid dwindling crowds and losses on the pitch and on the balance sheet. The local businessman Danson and his family saved Wigan from liquidation in June 2023 after mismanagement from previous owners brought a points deduction and relegation from the Championship . Three successive mid-table finishes in League One under their stewardship have brought a semblance of stability, but this season they have plummeted.
The problem is the Dansons have been unable to find an ambitious buyer to take the club to the next level. Now the prospect of a first season in the fourth tier since 1996‑97 is a distinct possibility, although victory against Reading – the Latics’ second league win of the campaign, sealed by Scott Hogan’s 71st-minute strike – made the picture a little rosier.
“Some of our play was tremendous,” Caldwell said. “Our spirit, our character, our determination not to let the ball go in the net was fantastic. It was pretty stressful towards the end. We need to try and build on this. You have to keep the players believing and committing. There’s still so many aspects of our game that need to be better, but a result makes you feel better about yourself psychologically.”
The presence of Leam Richardson in the opposition dugout at the Brick Community Stadium gave fans more reason to reminisce about better days. Richardson, who claimed the League One title as Wigan manager in April 2022, was sacked in November of the same year just 16 days after signing a three-year contract.
Caldwell has also found himself under pressure. The former centre‑back has been criticised by fans for his team’s uninspiring style of play, which has produced just six goals in nine games, the fewest in League One. They went 447 minutes without a league goal until Hogan, the veteran forward, converted after Christian Saydee’s cross was parried out by the Reading goalkeeper, Joel Pereira.
And while Wigan’s keeper, Joe Whitworth, was regularly called into action to see out the win, the home team were still good value for three points, allowing Caldwell and his squad to breathe. The manager’s backers will rightly point to the lack of spending by the club in the summer, with the £1.5m generated by the sale of Sam Tickle to Bristol City not yet reinvested on players and an overreliance on young loanees to prop up the squad.
Danson and the club’s hierarchy have issued rallying cries to supporters to return to the stadium in an effort to generate more revenue, thus making the club more appealing to new owners, but why should fans part with hard‑earned cash to watch such insipid football?
Before the game, Caldwell said: “We also recognise the need for points is big, for our supporters to have that feelgood factor, and be able to leave the stadium in a much better frame of mind than they have been.”
The Scot got what he needed against Reading, yet the sense of chaos above Caldwell was evidenced by the abrupt departure of Sarah Guilfoyle from her role as managing director on the eve of the new season, after a 10-year stay at the club. And there are plenty who feel the owners ought to bear the brunt of criticism.
The Wigan Athletic Supporters Action Group is demanding answers from Danson on why selling the club has been such a struggle and the lack of investment. Other fans are more resigned to the idea that some short-term pain may be necessary for long-term gain; most agree a sale would be transformative.
For now, despite a rare victory against a hitherto in-form Reading, the short-term struggles look likely to continue. The hope is that a hero of 2013 can perform miracles on the pitch, despite the constraints off it.

content:
The former Palace chair seeming very angry indeed about others’ opinions is just par for the course as football’s age of rage ramps up another level
Yet again the mainstream wokealorium is preachifying from its pulpitrex. It’s egregious. It’s sanctiforial. It’s a wangitude of complete retardifaction.
This has not been an easy column to write. It has been difficult, gruelling in parts, but also warm, exhilarating and at times deeply erotic. Yes. I was SAVAGED by Simon Jordan. And I’ve never felt so alive.
You know who Simon Jordan is. Used to own Crystal Palace. Now a very good and listenable pundit on TalkSport , where he does the grown-up topics. Simon Jordan has strong opinions. This is his thing. His worldview says: the world is bad. The world is in need of correction. And he’s right about that, as he often is about things.
That’s what makes this all a bit surprising because I like Simon Jordan! I listen to his morning show with Jim White and it’s often really good. I respect the fact he has industry knowledge because he ran a football club. And yes that involved lots of dealings with Steve Bruce, Iain Dowie or similar, but it’s still basically the same thing.
I like the way he pops up in clips looking like an exquisitely powdered 17th-century Umbrian count, some gorgeous little angry blond glove-puppet I want to sit on my knee and pet and cosset and whisper in his ear about granditudinous hypocralism, in a way that’s just warm and fond and not, for me, in any way sexual, but which definitely is for him.
I like the way he talks. It reminds me of Jackie Chiles, the lawyer in Seinfeld, saying it’s outrageous, egregious, preposterous . Sometimes this can have a Mrs Malaprop edge. But that’s also fun and even then you get his point, which is usually good, even if you didn’t expect to agree, or can only agree secretly. When you’re right you’re right. When you’re veritudinously superfactual you’re veritudinously superfactual.
By now you’re probably wondering what happened. Well, I was definitely savaged. No one can take that away from me. And yes this was a week ago, but other stuff happened in between and I forgot about it for a while. I also haven’t fully listened to the savaging. It’s two minutes long and life is short.
In fact I only know about it because my friend and colleague Barry Glendenning is very reliable in this respect. If you’re ever cancelled, owned, or significantly beasted on the internet then Barry will let you know, as an act of love and kindness, and not, repeat not, because he enjoys it and is killing time in the pub on his phone. It’s like having a faithful and attentive online Lassie. What’s that? Slow down boy. Wait, you’re saying Michaela Strachan has called me a nonce? On LinkedIn? Good boy. Easy. There you go. Here’s a lovely bowl of vape oil and Guinness.
I have to admit I am also amplifying this, promoting myself as genuinely savage-worthy. In reality I was savaged in a minor, offhand way that I still don’t really get. I was at Croatia versus England in Rijeka . The game was meant to be played without fans as punishment for some Croatia-related disorder in Paris last year, which included accusations of people making Nazi salutes.
In the event the Croatian FA filled the ground with children, which is allowed under a loophole in the rules. It felt a bit weird in the moment . At the very least it didn’t seem to fit the spirit of the offence. Nazism, yes, bad. But also: a lovely day out for Year 8.
I still don’t really get why anyone would strongly disagree with this. It seems obvious enough. Yeah, everyone likes happy jolly children. Personally I believe the children are our future. I’ve always said that. But they’re not some kind of smart bomb that disintegrates the capacity for logic.
The counter-argument seems to be that this is joyless liberal Guardian stuff. It’s the woke mind-virus. It’s being too interested in not promoting nazism, when you should simply enjoy the laughter of little boys.
And yes Simon Jordan is right. It is annoying to be preached at. But we’re not talking libtard snowflake stuff here. We’re talking actual Nazis, people who just like and enjoy swastikas, who talk fondly about the Ustase, arguably the most vicious sect of the Third Reich war machine. I don’t know, man. The more I hear about the Nazis, the less I like the sound of them.
Plus we now have the sight of Hajduk Split fans this week walking behind an actual coffin and chanting “Auschwitz”. Does this seem like the message is being hammered home? At the very least we’re going to need more children. How many is this one going to take? Ten thousand? Maybe if we can get children to carry a coffin through Amsterdam then it’s fine and just a heartwarming event that shows lessons are being learned.
This is how it goes you see. You are supposed to LASH BACK in these situations. But it’s all a bit weird. Suddenly Simon Jordan is attacking me with children. He’s barging me out of the way in Starbucks with his mega-buggy, one hand clutched to his pearl-draped throat, saying, what about the children, the children, the children?
You see? I’m being sucked in. Because this is what the internet will do to you. I wasn’t even the main savaging that day. I was a side-beef, an afterthought. By now the algorithm is already filling my feed with fresh SJ face-offs, the latest a “heated exchange” with Dale Vince about Robbie Savage, in itself a mouthwatering trio, perpetual savaging motion in action.
In the end this is the only real point of interest here. This stuff is utterly addictive. And with good reason: it’s designed to be. Vast amounts of expertise and resources have been poured into this irresistible machinery. David Squires did a brilliant cartoon this week about the rise of the celebrity football chat-cast , the industrial-scale, seed-funded waffle that must now justify its space by shouting above the noise, and which will always tend towards beef-culture and a narrative of opposition.
I’ve tried really hard to stay out of this. I don’t do radio or TV stuff, because, well, what’s the point, but more because nobody’s clean, nobody escapes, suddenly you’re having a charity boxing grudge-match with Stephen Warnock.
But it is worth logging for the record that we are at fever pitch. The level of rage around football right now is genuinely astonishing. The story of the Manchester City verdict is, in part, a regulatory ruling over a breach of financial rules. But really it’s the astonishing post-truth online response, the urge to assail and objectify and dehumanise over a tribunal’s interpretation of accountancy practices.
Just going to report on a game at the Etihad this week involved BRAVELY DEFYING assorted threats of violence in response to articles written in these pages. And yes, these are clearly the work of a 77-year-old hunchback in Jakarta, or a drunk and bored corporate lawyer taking a break from surfing porn on the family computer.
But it is all part of the design too. This is meant to happen. A new book called Our Minds Under Siege by Bruno Giussani, a former global curator of TED, describes the way algorithm life is actively changing human behaviour . This is not a secret. Marketing has wanted to do this since the early 20th century.
Walter Dill Scott’s Theory of Suggestion. The Drive Theory of Motivation. The deliberate creation of want and anxiety into the way we sell things. And now we have a new and commercially irresistible language. Dopamine craving. Variable social validation. The feedback loop.
The way even random scrolling is controlled and metered, designed to create a craving that’s always there inside your head, and controlled by tech platforms that openly define humans as eyeballs, want, need, hunger.
In the end, this is why Simon Jordan seems to care so violently about someone else’s opinions on the children-washing of Uefa sanctions. It’s why I’m just incredibly excited by this as an outcome, why I want more not less. Savage me again. Make me feel something. Let me exist inside the machine with you, egregious, preposterous, vibramoniously alive.

Football Daily has never had much time for conspiracy theories. Lee Harvey Oswald dunnit, Stanley Kubrick didn’t fake the moon landing, Vinícius Jr doesn’t have a body double and Miranda isn’t a secret traitor. But our Spidey senses picked up when the UK government announced their Be Ready campaign on Thursday night. In case you missed it, or live outside the UK and couldn’t care less about this weird little island, we’ve lifted this from our news story :
“Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. The Be Ready campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.”
War’s a comin’, in other words, so you’d better buy some tomato soup (10 tins of), mushroom soup (eight tins of, for consumption cold) and ice cream (vanilla, one large tub of). Here’s where it gets interesting. The government released their three-day survival plan on Thursday afternoon, three days before the event most likely to cause World War III: José Mourinho’s first Clásico since 2013. Barcelona meet Real Madrid at the Camp Nou on Sunday and suddenly the government are telling us we may need to hunker down. Coincidence? We think not!
OK, OK. Coincidence? We think so! José may be the most charismatic baddie since Dirty Den’s most recent death, but not even he is capable of starting the geopolitical answer to El Clásico. Sunday’s match will spark a form of global conflict, even if it’s just a load of strangers caterwauling at each other on the internet rather than talking to their children, reading a book or practising any of the gazillion behaviours that would make their lives and the world a better place.
Mourinho’s relationship with Barcelona could fill a book, never mind a teatime email. There is love lost, but it’s decades since it went missing. These days they can’t stand the thought of each other, never mind the sight. There is an argument (NB: Football Daily doesn’t actually want to argue) that Mourinho’s greatest achievement in football, apart from finishing second with Manchester United in 2017-18, was to take a La Liga title off probably the greatest club side of all time. He also drove Pep Guardiola into a sabbatical – but that, and the Realpolitik of the Bernabéu dressing-room, took so much out of Mourinho that he has never been the same since that triumphant 2011-12 season.
The Camp Nou was the venue for Mourinho’s “most beautiful defeat” ( you know the one , when not even a good hosing could douse his celebrations) and his most humiliating defeat a few months later. He can’t afford any kind of defeat on Sunday: Madrid are six points behind Barcelona, who have won all nine league games, scoring 39 goals in the process. But Mourinho’s team have scored four goals in each of their last three matches and, even in the absence of the suspended Vinícius Jr , have attacking threats galore. And whatever the result, Mourinho’s post-match press conference will be must-see TV.
The match kicks off on Sunday evening, but only if you take these things literally. For Mourinho, it began the moment he was asked a question about it. He has had the face on all week because, well, wouldn’t you if you were treated like this? Barcelona played 24 hours earlier than Madrid in Bigger Cup, an open goal for conspiracy theorists and performative underdogs. “We’re pushing ahead,” he said. “At the moment, we’re missing out on 24 hours of rest, but we’re moving forward.” So is Football Daily, to the supermarket to get some urgent shopping. We’ll Be Ready for Sunday – not with 72 hours of essential supplies, but with a month’s worth of popcorn.

title: Brighton are the apex B club – their next target should be a Champions League place | Jonathan Wilson
description: Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team Sign up for our free newsletter here For two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes. This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. content:
Diego Gómez’s wondergoal in a five-star demolition is just the latest in an impressive run of results for the south coast team
F or two or three years now, it’s been standard to nod approvingly at how well-run Brighton, Brentford and Bournemouth are, and to move on. What else is there to say? It’s true, of course – these are sides who have made the most of relatively limited resources. But there’s also an underlying assumption in the designation: that these are clubs who have no higher aspiration, that their limit is earning praise for upper mid-table finishes.
This season, perhaps, offers an opportunity to change that. Other than Arsenal, every major club is undergoing significant transition. Manchester City may have started the season with seven straight wins, but there’s every chance the punishment for their multiple breaches of Premier League regulations takes them out of the race for the top five. In that context, why shouldn’t one of those efficient smaller sides qualify for the Champions League?
Brentford began the weekend in third and with, perhaps, a slight sense of frustration that they had drawn four games. Again, they will feel they might have done rather better on Saturday; they were leading Liverpool 1-0 when Yehor Yarmolyuk foolishly flicked his head towards Jérémy Jacquet and was sent off just before half-time. The result was a 2-1 defeat and a sense of an opportunity missed. Bournemouth have not had the easiest start under Marco Rose, but Sunday’s 2-0 win over Sunderland perhaps hints at a brighter future.
Which left Brighton to carry the charge of the B clubs, which they did in emphatic style, ending a run of four derbies without success with a crushing 5-0 win . Crystal Palace had been extremely fortunate to survive a first-half battering from Nottingham Forest last week. They were thoroughly outplayed in the early stages again, and this time found themselves 3-0 down inside 10 minutes. Perhaps the opening goal, a cross headed into his own net by Jaydee Canvot, was fortunate, but it was an error induced by the intensity of Brighton’s start. The second goal, a perfectly weighted drive from just inside the Palace half from Diego Gómez, spoke of a side playing with immense confidence. Already this season, 11 different players have scored for Brighton in the league. They have become the image of a side without stars, the whole far greater than the individuals who comprise it.
The difference from February, when Brighton last played Palace, is stark. They lost that game 1-0, meaning they had won just one of their previous 12 Premier League games. Generalised grumbling had begun to curdle into calls for Fabian Hürzeler to be sacked. When they lost Carlos Baleba, Jan Paul van Hecke, Danny Welbeck and James Milner over the summer, there were reasons to wonder whether they could keep going with the process of continuous renewal.
There were the usual assorted signings, the usual mix of Premier League experience and exotic unknowns. The 19-year-old centre-back Luka Vušković, who spent last season on loan at Hamburg from Tottenham, already looks at home (and who really thought, when Spurs and Brighton effectively swapped centre-backs, with Van Hecke moving to London, that Brighton would not end up with the better of the deal?). The 21-year-old Spanish midfielder Chema Andrés, who arrived from Stuttgart, sparkled from the bench against Arsenal and has excelled in the two games since.
But the stand-out performer this season has been a far more familiar name: Pascal Gross, who returned in January after a season and a half at Borussia Dortmund. No player in the Premier League has registered more than his four assists this season. Nobody has run further. He has three goals. He averages a league-high 3.0 key passes a game. To bring back a player who is now 35 has been a masterstroke.
The victory over Arsenal before the international break suggested a team capable not merely of accumulating points against the league’s lesser lights, or even of challenging the elite, but of overwhelming them. Arsenal were suffocated by the Brighton press and, while a couple of low-xG long-range finishes in the first half helped, the fact is that Brighton dominated the match to a remarkable extent.
The question is whether they can keep it going. Just as their transfer policy is now an accepted feature of the Premier League, so too is Brighton’s mid-season slump. They haven’t won a game in December since 2023. Is this squad strong enough to sustain the challenge? Europe seems not to be unsettling Brighton as it did on their first foray, or as it appears to be draining Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Sunderland – which may be a reflection on the relative quality of the Conference League.
They are doing this without Kaoru Mitoma, Yankuba Minteh and Mats Wieffer, all of whom should be back at some point over the next month. That suggests the depth of this Brighton squad. It’s always a major step for a club unfamiliar with the Champions League to haul themselves into the top five. At times it often feels a mental barrier as much as anything.
But if any of those B clubs are ever going to break into the Champions League, they may never have a better opportunity than Brighton do this season.

title: WSL talking points: pressure mounts on Slegers as Hemp closes on record
description: Another round of games and another disappointing draw for Arsenal while Manchester City sit top of the table with a 100% record There would have been hope that the international break could offer the Arsenal players and staff a reset but the same problems reared their head at the Emirates on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Birmingham. author_name: Suzanne Wrack, Sophie Downey, Emillia Hawkins and Réshma Rao
content:
Another round of games and another disappointing draw for Arsenal while Manchester City sit top of the table with a 100% record
There would have been hope that the international break could offer the Arsenal players and staff a reset but the same problems reared their head at the Emirates on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Birmingham. As they have done so often this season, the Gunners dominated most attacking and possession-based metrics – they registered 76% possession, a 2.73 xG and 43 touches in the opposition box – but their profligacy in front of goal and lack of urgency in their play once again came to the fore. Of their 27 chances, they managed just four on target as they toiled against a resilient opposition who understood the playbook. Birmingham set up in a strong defensive structure, protecting their box admirably with numbers to frustrate Renée Slegers’s side, who famously struggle to break down low blocks. In contrast, Birmingham scored with their one shot on target as Océane Hurtré took her impressive tally to six in six. Sophie Downey
London City’s impressive start to the season continued as they extended their winning run to four games with a 2-1 victory against Everton. If the match against Tottenham before the break had been an illustration of their attacking power, this was a much grittier performance. The Toffees, who have the joint second-meanest defence in the league (shared with Eder Maestre’s team), proved tough to break down with London City managing just five shots on target despite creating 16 opportunities. Their two first-half goals, however, once again came on transition and were a sign of the deep quality they possess. Plenty has been made of London City’s attack this season but it was their out-of-possession work that shone through. They have now faced the fewest shots on target in the division (12) and the way they handled the slight change of momentum in the second half when Everton switched things up and gained belief was an indication of their growing defensive mettle. SD
Charlton may still be pointless six games in, but their second-half performance against Manchester United impressed their manager, Karen Hills. After a rough first half an hour, in which the final score of 3-1 to United was established, the home team held firm. “When we talk about bravery, I thought we took the second half to Manchester United,” said Hills. “If we can do that against a very, very top team like United, then I’m hoping that we can continue on that run. I think you saw that in the first half as well, when we actually got the ball we played some really nice football. It’s a team that’s very aggressive and on the front foot. It was just the moments when we didn’t have the ball that probably cost us today.” Given Charlton only had 23.8% possession in the match, those moments without the ball were many, but finding silver linings when you’re down is important. Suzanne Wrack
The 6-2 scoreline looked an unlikely one when Tottenham went into their dressing room at Stamford Bridge at half-time with the score level at 1-1. It had been an assertive first half from the visiting team against an increasingly impressive Chelsea. The Blues did put their foot on the gas in the second half but the Tottenham head coach, Martin Ho, said his team had to do better to not collapse after conceding. “We conceded three goals in nine minutes and then two in six. We can’t completely collapse in those moments. That’s individual responsibility and accountability to defend,” he said. Tottenham have not won in 20 games against top-four opponents. “You can see that, as a young team, we lack a little bit of maturity in these big games. That will come with time.” SW
Lauren Hemp closed in on the WSL all-time assist record after setting up two goals in Sunday’s 3-2 win against Brighton. The 26-year-old recorded numbers 50 and 51 within the opening 16 minutes of the game by setting up Khadija Shaw twice. She now sits just three assists behind record holder and teammate Beth Mead, who has 54 in total. Hemp, who has eight goal contributions for the season, said: “I want to keep improving and I want my whole performance across the game to be good and I thought I lost the ball too many times today. So I want to keep pushing for more, keep striving and I still think my best is yet to come. But I’m happy with the contributions I’ve done in games recently.” Emillia Hawkins
Aston Villa finally got their first win of the season after a second-half comeback for a 2-1 victory against Liverpool. Villa had managed just three draws from their opening five games before the international break, but doubled their points tally thanks to a second-half strike from Chasity Grant and an own goal from the Reds defender Grace Fisk. It was a positive result for Brian Sørensen, who took over from Natalia Arroyo last month and was this week confirmed as the interim head coach until the end of the season. Sørensen said: “Incredible. Also the manner that we did it in, we were really struggling in that first half and Liverpool were so good, but we made changes tactically but also personnel at half-time and that flipped the game around. Credit to the girls … best day ever!” EH
Kelly Gago’s second league goal of the season secured West Ham a 1-0 victory over Crystal Palace and their first away win of the campaign. The French international’s goal came from an assist from Oona Siren who capitalised on a defensive error, and Gago fired home a left-footed finish, proving the difference in the contest. Gago joined the Hammers from Everton at the start of the season and is beginning to make her mark in east London. Her contribution offers a boost for a West Ham side looking to build momentum and move away from the bottom end of the table following three consecutive losses prior to the international break. Réshma Rao

content:
Plus: the longest kit supply partnerships, more own goals (part II) and consecutive goalless draws
Mail us with all of your questions and answers
“Harry Kane is now Bayern’s seventh-highest scorer of all time, as well as being Tottenham’s highest scorer. The man he overtook at the top of that list, Jimmy Greaves, is also Chelsea’s seventh-highest scorer of all time. Do any other players feature on two (or more) clubs’ all-time top- 10 scoring charts?” asks Owen Powell.
A trawl through the Knowledge archive reminded us that we have previously looked at players who are the record goalscorer for more than one club . This question is slightly different, as we’re focusing on goalscorers who are in the all-time top 10 for the most different clubs. There are dozens of players who appear for two clubs, including Sergio Ag üero (Atlético Madrid and Manchester City), Kenny Dalglish (Celtic and Liverpool), Jimmy Greaves (Chelsea and Tottenham) , Lionel Messi (Barcelona and Inter Miami), Cristiano Ronaldo (Real Madrid and Al-Nassr) and Alan Shearer (Blackburn and Newcastle).
There’s one more worthy of mention. “ Harry Johnson is all-time top scorer for both Sheffield United and Mansfield,” writes Darren White. “He played for the Blades between 1919 and 1931, scoring 201 league goals. At the age of 32, he left for Mansfield, scoring 104 goals for them over three seasons. He didn’t play for anyone else, so he has the possibly unique record (for someone with more than one club) of being top scorer for every team he represented.”
And so to those who are among the top 10 goalscorers for more than two clubs: “ Romário (Vasco da Gama, Flamengo and PSV) and Delio Onnis (Monaco, Tours FC and Gimnasia) feature on at least three clubs’ all time top-10 scoring charts,” writes Dirk Maas. “Onnis also played for Toulon, but I could not find an official source to confirm that Onnis is in their top 10 as well.”
Elsewhere, Rhys Shakeshaft suggests Robbie Keane , who is among the top 10 goalscorers for three of his clubs (Tottenham, LA Galaxy, ATK), and André-Pierre Gignac (Marseille, Toulouse, Tigres UANL). And Tom Stuart was among those who nominated John Aldridge (Newport County, Oxford United, Tranmere Rovers). The striker is also the Republic of Ireland’s fourth-highest goalscorer.
As well as being Cameroon’s all-time leading goalscorer, Samuel Eto’o is potentially in the top 10 for four clubs: Mallorca, Barcelona, Anzhi Makhachkala and Antalyaspor. “I’m not 100% sure if I can trust the Antalyaspor record,” writes Rhys Shakeshaft, who sent in the answer, “but I’m happy with the other three.”
Historical goalscoring data isn’t always 100% reliable, but we think Sam Kerr is among the top 10 leading scorers for five teams: Perth Glory FC, Western New York Flash, Gotham FC, Chicago Red Stars and Chelsea.
Even five clubs wouldn’t be a record. “I’ve managed to find one male footballer who, amazingly, is in the top 10 for six different clubs!” writes Ben. “Morocco’s Abderrazak Hamdallah is the all-time top scorer for OC Safi (Morocco), second for El-Jaish (Qatar), fourth for Guangzhou R&F/Guangzhou City (China), fourth for Al-Nassr, seventh for Al-Ittihad and 10 for Al-Shabab (all Saudi Arabia). He’s 35 years old and has just joined Al-Taawoun, so it’s entirely possible he’ll add another club to that list.”
“The German national kit is not going to be made by Adidas any more, going to Nike after 70 years. Is this the longest kit supply partnership in history, and what’s the longest current run in club football?” asks Paul Savage.
Dirk Maas has unearthed a couple of club sponsorships that have lasted more than 60 years. “Adidas has been Bayern Munich ’s kit sponsor since 1965 ,” writes Dirk, “but the first time the Adidas trefoil was visible on the shirt was 17 October 1973. HJK (from Helsinki) also started a partnership with Adidas in 1965, one that has continued uninterrupted ever since. The first HJK shirt with the Adidas trefoil I could find was in 1976.”
We can’t find anything to beat the 70-year relationship between Germany and Adidas. We think that, when that deal officially ends, the longest partnership in international football will be between Austria and Puma. That goes back to 1977 and includes some memorable kits – most of them for the right reasons.
In the Knowledge last week we looked at players who scored more own-goals than goals during their career. A number of you pointed out the omission of Des Walker , a magnificent defender for Nottingham Forest and England in particular, but one who wasn’t renowned for his goalscoring exploits.
Walker famously scored only once in more than 800 games, an improbable belter for Forest against Luton in 1992 . But he scored at least seven own goals – four for Forest and three for Sheffield Wednesday. The Forest collection included the winner for Spurs in the dramatic 1991 FA Cup final. He also scored at the wrong end when Sheffield United came from 2-0 down to beat Forest in a First Division playoff semi-final in 2003. His other own goals came in the League Cup: against Crystal Palace in January 1992 (a week after he scored against Luton) and Portsmouth in 2003.
He also managed at least three own goals during his time at Sheffield Wednesday, against Liverpool (1994-95), Tottenham (1995-96) and Preston (2000-01). That gives him a career balance of -6 goals: an unbecoming legacy for one of England’s greatest central defenders.
“After Lahti’s fourth consecutive 0-0 draw last night, does anyone know of a similar run?” tweeted Finnish Football Show back in 2017 .
This question was made for George Graham, and he hasn’t let us down. His Arsenal team played four league games in October 1993 and drew the lot 0-0. In Arsenal’s defence (or should that be attack?) they did score some goals in cup matches during the month. Still, four consecutive 0-0s in the league is pretty impressive.
Surprisingly enough, Arsène Wenger’s Arsenal also managed a quartet of 0-0s in the league during the 2008-09 season – though they also scored and conceded in cup games during that period.
Goalless George did it again at Spurs, with four consecutive 0-0 draws in January and February 2001. They were all in the league but as no cup games were played in that period it counts as four consecutive 0-0s in all competitions. Serhiy Rebrov was guilty of appalling statisticide when, in the next league match at Manchester City, he scored the only goal in the 90th minute.
Wolves tested the will of season-ticket holders with four consecutive 0-0s at Molineux at the back end of the 2015-16 season. Udinese managed four in a row in the 1982-83 Serie A season, a campaign in which – and you’ll like this – they drew 20 of their 30 games. Como matched that feat in Serie A in 1986-87. That season, they played 30 games, scored 16 goals and conceded 20.
Best of all, earlier this year [in 2017 – ed] FC Rostov followed a 6-0 win at Tom Tomsk with five consecutive 0-0 draws in the Russian Premier League , though they were punctuated by a Europa League goalfest at Old Trafford: Rostov lost 1-0.
“Burnley have gone a calendar year without a home league win. What is the longest home drought, in the league or in all competitions?” asks our own Niall McVeigh.
“Last week, Justin Seven-Seven came on in the 75th minute and then scored in the 77th minute for West Brom Under-21s against Sutton United in the National League Cup. You have probably already guessed my question, but has anyone else ever scored in the same minute as their name?” wonders Peter Skilton.
“Since the advent of squad numbers, has any club used every number from 1 to 99? Which British club comes closest to using all 99 one and two-digit numbers?” asks Vasko Wackrill.
“With the constant talk of the golden boot and how unstoppable Erling Haaland is for Manchester City, wouldn’t a team be more dangerous if all of the outfield players, including substitutes, scored at least once or perhaps a few times during a season? Have there been any teams in which all of their outfield players have scored at least once in a particular season? If not, which group has had the most players score in a season?” asks Bob Zoellner.
“In the third round of the Portuguese Cup, played last weekend, six clubs from the Primeira Liga were eliminated by teams from lower divisions ,” begins Cláudio Gameiro. “Is this a record for a European league? And has a national cup final ever been contested by two teams from lower divisions? I’m betting France.”
“By my reckoning, Ross County have already scored 81 goals this season: 38 in 10 league games (including beating poor Queen of the South 8-0 and 7-1), 30 in six Challenge Cup group games, 13 in six League Cup games. They may well have scored a century of goals by the end of October! Surely that cannot be bettered. What is the earliest a team has hit a century of goals in a season?” asks Stephen James.
Mail us with all of your questions and answers

content:
The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals
W hat makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.
After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.
Based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.
Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?
One lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.
Around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.
The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).
B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).
C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.
But the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona , who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde ; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool , when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0 ). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail , it felt like a relief for all parties.
There is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.
At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s plan was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.
I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

content:
The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes
They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.
Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.
Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.
In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.
It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges .
Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.
In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland , Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.
The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.
Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.
In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.
Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.
Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.
Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.
Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.
The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.
The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.
But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.
