content:
England beaten in Ottawa for third loss in past 74 matches
History-makers, era-enders, giant-slayers. Breaking England’s unbeaten run was a statement for Canada last Friday but they backed it up in a 31-22 win to deal the Red Roses their first consecutive loss in a decade, sending a formidable message to the rest of world rugby. Some may view it as too early to call but Canada are serious contenders for the World Cup trophy in 2029, especially if they progress at the same rate that their performances have improved in just a year from that World Cup final loss to England in 2025.
On a cold Ottawa night, Canada played with freedom and pace to down England once again. The captain Sophie de Goede laid bare why she is the reigning world player of the year with a hat-trick and some excellent defensive work, and Julie Omokhuale also stood out among a good team performance.
For England, well they were looking for a response to that record-ending defeat but it never came. A strong and confident start ebbed into a scrappy and hesitant overall outing which they will want to put right for their final WXV Global Series match against the USA next Friday. But there were some positives for the visitors, namely the skipper Meg Jones. The captain, who turned 30 on Friday, was imperious in defence and Maddie Feaunati had another good game in the hour she was given.
An Owellian atmosphere was created for those watching from home with the pitch having a grey tinge to it, a dystopian world isn’t usually compared to that of the vibrant and action-packed women’s rugby sphere but it may have felt like another world for England players losing back-to-back games. It was their third loss in 74 matches, so the panic won’t set in, but this result will unsettle them.
Jones said she told the team in the post-match huddle that they are “not broken, we just need to grow”. The captain added: “We’re a high performing team in a high performance situation. Our mindset is our biggest asset and it always will be. I genuinely believe we have the best players in the world and when we are firing we are genuinely unstoppable.”
The Tests between these two this autumn have been ferocious and it was an utterly brutal start. A key part of Canada’s win last week was their defensive set and keeping England from scoring for a long time but that was a different story with Feaunati over in the seventh minute. Canada put England’s defence under its first proper stress test next and the white wall was impressive with a particular focus on double tackles but it eventually buckled as Omokhuale dotted down. But the second Canadian try came all from England’s scrappy attack. A bouncing ball didn’t sit well for Zoe Harrison, who knocked on as a result and Gabrielle Senft pounced. De Goede tracked her run and was on her shoulder to receive the ball to finish it off with Canada’s secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, who announced new funding for Rugby Canada during the match, in the commentary box to celebrate the score and add: “I love it!” Several knock-ons and a try being held up stifled England from hitting back and so it was Canada who held a 12-7 lead at the break. The Red Roses’ need for points was made very clear when they opted to kick a penalty to start the second 40.
England reverted to their deadly rolling maul from the 22 in an impressive score by Amy Cokayne. However, captain fantastic De Goede struck twice in quick succession for her hat-trick, with Savannah Bauder putting England out of sight despite a consolation score by Emma Sing.
Head coach John Mitchell was critical post-match and said the referee Aurélie Groizeleau did not have a connection to the television match official. “I think the game potentially needs an improved standard with TMO, there was no TMO connection tonight,” he said. “I think we have got to improve that. These games are so meaningful and there are going to be situations where there are going to be major turning points and I think the girls deserve quality decision making.” Canada can ride the high of this victory into 2027 where their next games are slated to be in the Pacific Four tournament, while England have one more WXV match against the USA. The Americans are in form but they should heed a warning: this England team are not used to losing and they will be pursuing a big response.

content:
With first drivers’ title all but secure, a friendlier champion would be hard to find, but Italian’s eight wins this season speak to his focus
E ven as Kimi Antonelli may be world champion-elect, it is sometimes hard to equate the young man who has driven with such exceptional skill and no little verve to touching distance of an historic first Formula One title with the smiling, wide-eyed kid with tousled hair who still almost looks out of place in the F1 paddock. Yet what has become clear in this extraordinary season is that Antonelli’s talent and his personable, endearing character are inextricably entwined.
Whether the Italian seals his place as F1’s youngest world champion, at 20 years old, at this Sunday’s US Grand Prix in Austin or the next round in Mexico or even beyond that is moot – that he will do so is all but assured and for all that he is still in only his second season in the sport, a more rounded, well-liked champion than the Mercedes driver would be hard to find.
Engage with Antonelli and it is almost impossible not to still see the three-year-old child who insisted on taking to his father Marco’s knee to try out the racing simulator the former driver had brought home. Marco would control the pedals and his son the wheel with an irrepressible enthusiasm that could barely be contained and is still there in every dart, feint and incisive pass he makes today.
Pictures from his childhood in Bologna, a couple of hours’ drive from where his father runs a racing team in San Marino, show whenever Antonelli has a wheel in his hands there is a smile on his face and his eyes alight. His joy is clear and it is a passion that has run clearly through his career. From going karting at the age of five, a meteoric rise through the ranks, being taken on as a Mercedes junior driver aged 12, then making his debut for the team in 2025 after a whirlwind of three years moving from F4, to Formula Regional and then F2.
The faith Mercedes placed in him, not least in that he was stepping into the shoes of the departing seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, was huge, yet the team principal Toto Wolff had no doubts as to his talent and his character.
“In the past, there was the opinion in F1 that in order to be winning, you need to be an asshole, you need to be ruthless and opportunistic,” he observed this season as Antonelli made a stunning start with five wins on the trot and the entire world was paying attention to the kid who, for many, had come from nowhere. “I don’t think that Kimi is that. It’s just down to driving faster than the others, and being a nice person also.” It is an opinion often echoed by those close to the young Italian. Gwen Lagrue, the talent scout who led Mercedes’ junior driver programme, remembers more than just his remarkable talent from their early encounters.
“With Kimi, I saw almost from day one that I was dealing with a different kid,” Lagrue said. “First, what impressed me, well, amazed me, was his natural presence. He was already having such an impact on everyone in the paddock, you noticed this kid has something different than the others. Everyone liked Kimi, everyone was hugging him. He was like the Kimi you see today when he was 11. He was so passionate about what he was doing, about racing, about F1, everything.”
At the heart of this engaging character it seems is a grounded and emotionally rich relationship with his family. While he was supported in following his racing dreams, he was told unequivocally that if he was to kart on a weekend, school must follow on a Monday until he graduated. He duly did so, completing his maturità school exams just after coming third – his first podium – at the Canadian GP last year .
“Which driver has done the A-levels or the baccalaureate? Name me one that has finished school. No one,” Wolff observed pointedly of his prodigy. The role of his family has clearly been crucial. His father as guide, mentor and, both have admitted, stern taskmaster at times, whom Antonelli has described as his “rock”. But there is also clearly a hugely important relationship with his mother, Veronica, and younger sister Maggie.
“My dad is always going to give me his point of view, he’s going to give me advice and then if I decide to listen, good, but if I don’t decide to listen, it’s OK as well,” he said. “We always have a strong relationship but this is the same with my mum and my sister. The way I am I don’t think I could cope with having a bad relationship with my family member, it’s something that I would really struggle to cope with, that’s why I couldn’t see myself, you know, just taking distance from them.”
Intriguingly, racing was not a direction his father had initially wanted him to go in. Marco had been a quick sportscar driver and almost signed as works driver for two German touring car teams but was unlucky in not getting a shot. “I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation,” he said. “At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport.”
However, having decided to let him pursue the dream, Marco has been there ever since. He is at the track on many weekends and clearly the pair share an easy, close bond with echoes of the one Hamilton shared with his father, Anthony, in his early years. In Hungary, the race after he had risked receiving a penalty for exceeding track limits on his way to a brilliant win in Belgium, Antonelli laughingly recalled his father’s reaction: “He said: ‘Congrats, but …’ Always a but … ‘If I see you doing another track limit for nothing, I’m gonna stretch your neck like a chicken.’”
Antonelli’s boyish honesty has been as engaging as his talent. Wolff has noted his ability to switch into a “race mode”, a zone where he is wholly focused on the task, where he has a daring, aggressive driving style, pushing to the limit and past it, on occasion, but which he always learns from. “We had to teach him instead of always being at 110%, just be at 100%,” Lagrue said which, as Wolff has remarked, is a trait he would rather indulge than having to “take a stick to a donkey”.
Yet alongside that verve Antonelli has shown a maturity beyond his years belied by his character when out of the “zone”. He has displayed the judgment of a veteran while being able to manage the endless adjustments of touch and feel of the car and its balance – especially of these fiendishly complex modern rides – such that he, like many of the greats, has made it look easy.
Watching him do so this season has been a pleasure not least because he is a driver who has taken such untrammelled and infectious joy in doing so. A feeling perhaps summed up by his father, who told La Gazzetta dello Sport just after his son turned 20: “I hope he remains who he is, sweet and generous, and continues to do what he loves for as long as possible.”
Before his extraordinary victory from 19th on the grid at the Italian GP, Antonelli said he wanted to win the championship but that it was important for him to do so by being himself. The latter he can consider a job most admirably well done. The former is only a matter of time.

content:
T20 franchise cricket is trash sport and killing the five-day game is cultural vandalism. What would Orwell have made of this?
H ave you read George Orwell’s review of Mein Kampf? This might not sound like a grabby reference, or a killer hook for the algorithm. But Hitler is always hot. Hitler is legacy brand. Hitler is eyeballs. Also, it’s just a great review, even more so because it was written at a time when the world didn’t quite know what Hitler was “all about”.
True, you get a vibe off people. The invasion of France. The ranting, visceral hatred. There were signs, clues, indications that this guy, this guy is not my kind of guy .
But the full Hitler-verse had yet to reveal itself. And for a while you worry Orwell’s going to get it wrong, not go hard enough, misread the full history as we now know it. He writes about how much he likes Hitler’s face because he looks pained and sad, like a wounded dog, giving off that sense of eternal injustice the German people really went for.
By this point you’re trying to catch his eye, coughing loudly, saying “Holocaust” into your fist. No, George. Don’t start talking about charisma.
Luckily, it all turns out fine. Orwell says that he would definitely kill Hitler if he got within arm’s reach of him. Then he describes, better than anyone before or since, the terrifying nature of the world Mein Kampf is proposing, above all its utter boredom, the eternal grey repetitions, same struggle, same triumph, same boot stamping on same face, same pitch of willed and empty hysteria.
And yeah … you’re thinking about T20 franchise cricket, aren’t you? I didn’t say it. You did. It’s fine. The mind goes where the mind goes.
You’re picturing a year-round cycle of brain-flooding noise. An endless will to power. The Kansas City CheeseSteaks v the Reykjavik Unmentionables live from the Jakarta T5 Megascream, injected straight into your eyeballs by a robot replicant Danny Morrison.
It’s fine that you want to make this connection. It’s even deeply fitting given the greatest story of the sporting week by an absolute mile, a story so big, so sweeping, so viscerally personal, that most people seem to have completely ignored it, comes from the polar opposite place.
This is of course Temba Bavuma’s match-winning nine-hour hundred in the second Test against Australia in Gqeberha, one of those episodes where sport and the life of the nation seem to cross, blend and become indistinguishable.
Mainly Bavuma in Gqeberha was an incredible feat of skill, resilience and constant adaptive intelligence, in the way only Test Cricket can deliver. Bavuma walked out to bat with the summer running away from him. Thrashed in the first Test, South Africa were 12 for two, faced with one of the great bowling attacks.
Bavuma has been a transformative Test captain, with 12 wins in 14 matches, four hundreds, a world championship mace , all stretched over three broken years. But he is still always, always chasing legitimacy and affirmation, in a way that is unique to cricket, but also unique to this man in this role in this sporting nation. First black middle order batsman. First black captain. How is this going to fall? How strong is that ice underfoot?
Two days later Bavuma was last man out for 179 in a total of 425 for nine, sprinting off with a kind of light around him, waving his bat giddily, 36 years old, wife and kid in the crowd, the greatest moment of his sporting life.
There were so many parts to this. First, the survival period, with that endearing tic of gently jutting his chin out at the bowler, mixed in with the odd deliciously clean whip or push or clump. Bavuma has really quick hands. I remember seeing him in east London in a white-ball game against dark skies and low stands, and all you could really see was his hands whizzing with thrilling speed, like fireflies in the night.
In Gqeberha he was all poise and measured severity. When he plays a cover drive he seems to lean at 45 degrees, knees bent, entire body easing into the oblique, perfectly contained in his own little square of time and space.
The game changed with the partnership of 106 with Marco Jansen before lunch on the third day, brilliant counterattacking Test cricket, but also an amazing tableau. At one end the gangling Dutch farmer with the easy, guileless stride, a cricketer who always seems to be running in with a bushel of radishes over one shoulder and a bolt-action rabbit gun in his waistband. At the other the tiny, super-smart black captain. It’s no more than an optic, unrelated to the nation’s real-world struggles. But it’s also real. Sport is, as ever, saying: how about this version of things?
Bavuma got to his hundred with a release of pent-up power, swivel-pulling Pat Cummins through midwicket, holding the shot, one of those moments where the batter feels what has happened a second before anyone else, allowed in that microsecond to exist all alone inside his own little pocket of private triumph.
But then Bavuma has always had to be aware, to hold himself a certain way. There was surprise in some corners that he turned out to be such an unflappable captain. Try being Temba Bavuma for a bit. You think this stuff is going to faze you?
Bavuma is a child of the transition period, born three months after Nelson Mandela left Victor Verster Prison, the same day (get this) the government finally opened up all its public hospitals to black citizens. He grew up a township boy in Langa, playing in the street, learning which strips of local tarmac had the most carry and bounce.
Plucked out aged 10 on a scholarship to one of South Africa’s top schools, he struggled. Ten is relatively late to start trying to become an elite batter. How about still perfecting your English, learning how to act, what to put on your plate at dinner? Even his height, which we must always talk about, is a thing. Bavuma is the 10th shortest man ever to play Test cricket. Yeah, pour it on. What else have you got?
There was the slow-burn start to his career. For years the quota talk circled, the weird dual burden of innate outsiderdom and suspicions of favour. Then suddenly you’re the first township captain of what has always been an anglophone, military-elite kind of sport.
It sounds overwhelming. Right up until you hear him speak, at which point you just want him to talk about all the stuff in that soft voice, gentle but deliciously insistent. It’s no surprise to learn Bavuma has a normal life away from this, that his wife is founder of a luxury real estate firm, he takes his kid to school, doesn’t do celebrity, that he’s never really made a point of making a point, but made it all the same by being relentlessly himself.
Why talk about this here? Why bring endless grey, smothering repetition into it? First because even without the Bavuma story this was just an epic piece of sport, one of those occasions where every detail feels meaningful.
Steve Smith getting actual whiplash, literally wearing a foam neck-brace after whirling around to see if an edge had carried. Marnus Labuschagne whirling at the crease, acting out his own thoughts in the air like a tortured pantomime horse, while his career self-suffocates in real time. Here is Anrich Nortje, the perfect composite of shoulders, glower and vengeful moustache, looking on like the hand of fate from a deserted balcony, groin-knacked but somehow still profoundly present.
The whole thing heads on to Newlands on Tuesday and the sandpaper reunion game, an impossibly fine piece of narrative work, slow-cooked over eight years, the kind of storytelling the human brain just thirsts for.
Although now it is also time to zoom out and feel the whiplash. On the fifth day of the first Test in Durban, as Australia wrapped up their own victory the TV commentator talked about the fine sporting spirit of the contest and how “it’s credit to the people of South Africa”, at which point the camera panned back with perfect comic timing to show: a completely empty stadium.
So, back to Orwell and being on the right side of history. Because a great thing, a carefully woven cultural exhibit, is being overtly encouraged to die here. South Africa hadn’t played a Test before this series for 11 months. They played eight last year, two a second-string trip to Zimbabwe.
The hard game, the actual game that still produces the short-form TV offshoot, is being sacrificed mercilessly. And the thing that is replacing it is not just demonstrably inferior, but self-dooming in its basic inanity.
In the intervals of the Test, South African TV showed a mouthwatering banter-table chat-along featuring all of South Africa’s craggy modern greats, Polly, Makhaya, AB, the Steyn Gun, sat around just telling stories, doing everything but hug each other, conjuring up moments of beauty, gold, legend.
This will not be allowed to happen in the future. T20 cricket can’t produce these stories. It’s throwaway content, parasocial celebrity fawning. What are we going to have 20 years from now? Lhuan-dre Pretorius telling bardically embroidered tales about the time he slash-hoicked 37 off 12 balls in the now defunct North American Mega-Lurch?
There is still a fear of saying this out loud, of making the unarguable observation that a form of sporting hyper-capitalism is dictating that nothing can matter if it’s not monetisable right here and now. Half-understood arguments about demand and supply will justify an act of cultural vandalism. Well, yeah, but look at the way this entity in a state of managed decline appears, believe it or not, to be in a state of managed decline.
The reality is something beautiful is being extinguished. It feels like the sporting arm of a process that has been called the enshittification of modern life, where the bottom line is the only line, where everything must be reduced to stupidity and profitable chaff.
Orwell was also good on the “machine worship” of the early 20th century. He was, in the best way, a luddite. Inefficient, human-scale elements have a right to exist too. The mechanised loom made a few things better. But mainly it made a few people quite a lot richer.
We can resist this, and not just in the realm of trash sport, but trash life generally. Humans still know what’s good. We crave these things, still hunger for stories like the Bavuma supremacy, which may never happen again, not in the current timeline, because its structures are being peeled away even as it plays out.

content:
Outsider Kingofthefrontier wins Sharp Novices’ Hurdle
Trainer John Dawson gets better of Dan Skelton
The jumping game increasingly resembles the Flat when it comes to the concentration of racing power in ever fewer trainers’ hands, but the opening day of Cheltenham’s new season – the first, in fact, since Gold Cup day in March – brought a reminder that romance has not been drained entirely from the winter code.
Dan Skelton, who dethroned Willie Mullins to become the new champion over jumps last season, had already trained 115 winners in the current campaign before racing on Friday, nearly halfway towards Martin Pipe’s all-time record of 243. John Dawson, by contrast, had sent out a total of six winners from his yard in North Yorkshire since May 2023.
However, it was Dawson’s Kingofthefrontier, a 20-1 outsider and only the trainer’s third runner at the home of jumping, who led the field home in the Grade Two Sharp Novices’ Hurdle, with Skelton’s Cooltobecareless, the 13-8 favourite, only third. The winner was nearer last than first turning in but showed an impressive turn of foot to run out a two-and-a-quarter length winner from Nicky Henderson’s Planters Punch.
Dawson rode into the famous winner’s enclosure aboard Sine Nomine after the Hunters’ Chase at the festival meeting here in March 2024, but his first Cheltenham winner as a trainer was an even better moment in what is still a young racing career.
“We’ve always loved him since the word go,” Dawson said. “I just felt we had a horse to come and have a go with.
He’s still got a lot to learn and the way he went through the race, Conor [O’Farrell, his jockey] said he was a bit stumbly and he had to balance him a couple of times. But speed wasn’t a problem for me, he was always going to have enough boot to get there, and he picked up really well.
“He’s actually a little bit horse-shy and when that big horse of Dan Skelton’s came running towards him, I think he was edging away from him, but he’ll learn a lot from that and he could still be anything.”
Dawson and Kingofthefrontier’s owner, George Critchley, opted to run in Friday’s Grade Two feature event in preference to a novice handicap hurdle at Carlisle.
“He’d never disappointed us,” Dawson said. “George puts a lot into the game, I wanted to bring him here and I thought he had a horse good enough to do it. I just can’t believe it came off.
We’re ambitious [but] we only want the horses to have a go with and hopefully we’ve showcased ourselves [today] to do that. I don’t want to be a massive Dan Skelton in numbers, but I just want real quality.”
Irish stables have been dominant at the festival meeting in March in recent seasons and Gordon Elliott is already looking ahead to a possible run in the Grand Annual Handicap Chase for Bowensonfire after the six-year-old’s win in the card’s two-mile novice chase.
Bowensonfire was the first leg of a double for Elliott, completed when Cosmos D’Ainay took a novice hurdle later on the card, while Cian Collins sent out a third winner for Ireland on the day when Brandt, at 10-1, took the final race on the card.
Aidan O’Brien and Andrew Balding field four of the seven runners in Saturday’s Futurity Trophy at Doncaster, the final Group One of the British season, but the focus on their neck-and-neck tussle for the trainers’ title could mean that the improving Breacher (1.30) sets off at a value price on ground that promises to suit.
William Muir and Chris Grassick’s colt has progressed by the run in three starts to date over seven furlongs, while also looking sure to thrive at middle-distances next season.
Cracksman, his sire, was at his best with some cut in the ground and a demanding mile on heavy going could well see Breacher outrun his early odds of around 10-1.
Doncaster 12.55: Ancient State seems to save his best form for this track and trip and has been dropped 1lb since finishing around one-and-a-half lengths behind the winner at Ascot last time.
Cheltenham 1.10: Ben Pauling has his string in excellent form and the returning As Legends Have It is an interesting contender at around 8-1. He has gone well fresh in the past, remains fairly weighted on his winning form at the end of last season and his prominent run-style is ideal for this track and trip.
Cheltenham 1.45: Olly Murphy’s Road To Wembley – part-owned by Sir Alex Ferguson – was better than the bare result when fourth on his handicap debut at Worcester in September and should appreciate this move up to three miles.
Doncaster 2.05: Bengal Tiger ’s 12-length win in a maiden at Naas last time was backed up by an excellent time and he should handle this step up to Listed company without too much fuss.
Cheltenham 2.20: James Owen’s string remains in strong form whatever the season or code and Idaho Fire posted a new career best at Uttoxeter last time out – a performance that suggests he could cope with a subsequent 10lb hike in the weights.
Cheltenham 2.55: With further rain expected before Saturday’s card, Katate Dori ’s form when second over track and trip off a 3lb higher mark in January looks as strong as anything on offer.
Cheltenham 3.30: Four of the seven runners in this four-year-old event were in the field for the Triumph Hurdle at the festival and while Indian River was only 10th, he finished third in the equivalent event at Aintree. A recent run in a handicap at Market Rasen should have him spot on for this.

title: Will Borthwick’s autumn England squad embrace Prem chaos or prioritise prudence? | Gerard Meagher
description: Scoring spree will be forgotten at the Rugby World Cup, and a return for Courtney Lawes may hint at coach’s thinking It says much about Steve Borthwick’s approach to England’s coming autumn campaign that he is due to name his training squad within minutes of the full-time whistle at Harlequins on Sunday. Simply put, there is no time to waste. Borthwick will have his squad for only a couple of days after the Prem’s derby weekend before they return to their clubs for a domestic fixture. In years gone by there was an extra week with the players but this time, as 12 months ago, Borthwick’s preparations are truncated. Continue reading...
content:
Scoring spree will be forgotten at the Rugby World Cup, and a return for Courtney Lawes may hint at coach’s thinking
It says much about Steve Borthwick’s approach to England’s coming autumn campaign that he is due to name his training squad within minutes of the full-time whistle at Harlequins on Sunday. Simply put, there is no time to waste.
Borthwick will have his squad for only a couple of days after the Prem’s derby weekend before they return to their clubs for a domestic fixture. In years gone by there was an extra week with the players but this time, as 12 months ago, Borthwick’s preparations are truncated.
When it comes to naming squads he does not spring too many surprises. But what fascinates is how he may interpret what he has seen in the Prem and the solitary round of Champions Cup matches. Feasts at domestic level, famine on the continent.
Will Borthwick look to employ the attacking abandon that has taken hold of the Prem or write it off as bubblegum sport, unsuited to the Test stage and, with only 12 matches left before England’s World Cup opener, rely on players he knows can perform on the international stage? Without getting too reductive, Sunday’s squad will give a clue. If players such as George Hendy, Will Joseph and Fitz Harding are included, it would suggest Borthwick is embracing the chaos. A recall for Courtney Lawes, meanwhile, would hint at a more prudent approach.
He may do both or neither. But whether he sees the try-fests as something to harness, or a hindrance, will be revealing. It calls to mind Thomas Tuchel’s insistence before the summer’s World Cup that he wanted England to play like a Premier League side. Does Borthwick want his England team to play like a Prem side? According to Rassie Erasmus he is a coach who “chases trends”.
This cuts to the heart of something Borthwick has never really mastered. What is England’s identity? Does Borthwick pick players who best fit his vision for England, or the best players available, creating a gameplan around them? “Your identity comes from the pool of players you have and what it looks like and over time,” the England assistant coach, Richard Wigglesworth, said last month.
“The style of English rugby has changed and the profile of player has changed considerably. We’re dynamic, skilful, we want to play fast. When someone mentions identity, they’re incorrect because there’s playing well and there’s not. You can have an identity and lose, who is bothered about that? It’s about playing well and then you’ll see an identity. I think there’s a bit too much made of that.”
The dilemma facing Borthwick is all the more acute because the suspicion is the coming month of Nations Championship fixtures will be high-scoring if the weather holds. While the international game is not all-singing, all-dancing in the way that the Prem is, there is evidently a trend towards attacking dominance. And as much as the Nations Championship title is coveted, the stakes are nowhere near as high as they will be in Australia next year.
Borthwick will be aware that in the knockout stages of the World Cup, tries do not come for free. South Africa became champions in 2023 without scoring more than 16 points in either the semi-final or final. Of eight knockout matches, only New Zealand scored more than 40 – in a mismatched semi-final against a poor Argentina. The next highest was England with 30 against Fiji, but no one else made it out of the 20s. At the 2019 World Cup in Japan both semi-finals were won with 19 points. The expectation is a significant drop-off in scoring in Australia, once the pool stage – which will witness numerous blowouts – is out of the way. It is all the more relevant next year because the new format means an extra knockout round.
“It’s set-piece and defence when the stakes are so high,” says Saracens’ Brendan Venter, who won the World Cup with South Africa in 1995. “You end up having two teams with the best set-piece and defence. The All Blacks often play some cracking stuff but when you go through to the knockouts it’s just low-scoring games.”
Borthwick is under pressure. Do not be fooled by his recent contract extension, if England are beaten by Australia in their opener, the heat will get more intense. Playing in a manner that excites supporters would help his cause and the best international sides tend to have a strong spine from the dominant domestic club.
It is hard to argue against Northampton’s hegemony in England and in Alex Mitchell, Fin Smith, Tommy Freeman and George Furbank – even if he is no longer at Saints – Borthwick has the players to showcase the best of the Prem. “Lots of those skills are relevant,” says Northampton’s director of rugby Phil Dowson. “Are international players better decision-makers in defence? Yeah, I think they probably are but that’s international level isn’t it? Everything is going to be a little better. We always talk about Prem being slightly differently refereed but the ability to run at a defender, sit him down and make him make a decision because I’ve got the ball in two hands is still going to be relevant.”
Borthwick sought to bring officiating in the Prem closer to the international game this season but judging by the first few weeks, it is yet to bear fruit. It is a concern that seven of the eight Prem sides failed to win in the opening weekend of the Champions Cup and the manner in which they were outgunned at the breakdown is all the more reason to worry. Again, that is one of Lawes’s strengths, and it felt significant that Borthwick watched Sale’s rearguard action in victory over Saracens earlier this month.
Borthwick must sift through the sediment. Find the nuggets that he can employ both in the autumn and next year’s World Cup.Cherrypick the best bits but ignore the bells and whistles. As George Skivington, whose Gloucester side went into the weekend’s fixtures top of the table, puts it: “Steve’s job is to take from what we’re doing well what he thinks can translate … that’s the challenge of being an international coach.”

title: Daniel Stewart, former Port Adelaide AFL player, dies aged 37
description: Key forward played 36 games and kicked 31 goals between 2010 and 2013 Power will wear black armbands at first home game of 2027 season Former Port Adelaide player Daniel Stewart has died suddenly at the age of 37. The Power confirmed Stewart’s death on Saturday as the club said it was “deeply saddened” by the news that had come as a “shock”. Continue reading...
content:
Key forward played 36 games and kicked 31 goals between 2010 and 2013
Power will wear black armbands at first home game of 2027 season
Former Port Adelaide player Daniel Stewart has died suddenly at the age of 37.
The Power confirmed Stewart’s death on Saturday as the club said it was “deeply saddened” by the news that had come as a “shock”.
Stewart played 36 AFL matches and kicked 31 goals for the Power between 2010 and 2013 after being selected with pick No 35 in the 2009 rookie draft.
The 200cm key forward was recruited from North Adelaide in the Sanfl, after coming through the Eastern Ranges and Queensland club Labrador.
Stewart was promoted to the Power’s senior list at the end of the 2009 season and the next year made his debut in round four against Geelong.
He booted a career-high four goals, including two in the final term, to help the Power hold on for a tense victory against Richmond in the last round of 2010.
“On behalf of everyone at the Port Adelaide Football Club, I extend our deepest condolences to Daniel’s family including his mum Donna, dad Byron, wife Laura, his two sons Bernie and Lando and his brother Leigh,” Port Adelaide chief executive, Matthew Richardson, said.
“We also extend our thoughts to his friends, including his close friend and former teammate Matt Thomas, and to all those at North Adelaide and Labrador who knew him.
“Daniel was part of the Port Adelaide football family, and he always will be. A sudden passing like this is devastating and our thoughts are with everyone who loved him, and with the teammates, coaches and staff who shared the journey with him here at Alberton.
“The club will provide support to those affected by Daniel’s passing, including his former teammates and the people who worked alongside him. We will honour Daniel by wearing black armbands in our first home game at Adelaide Oval in 2027.”
Former Port Adelaide teammate and current AFL analyst Kane Cornes joined the messages of condolence sent to Stewart and his family.
“A true tragedy. A brilliant and caring teammate who always had a smile on his face,” Cornes said in a post on X.
“I loved watching him and his beautiful family from afar. He built a thriving business and shared a special friendship with Matty Thomas. Heart goes out to his family.”

title: World and Olympic marathon champion Jepchirchir suspended after positive doping test
description: AIU investigates after sample tested positive for EPO 33-year-old won Olympic marathon in 2021 In a fresh blow for Kenyan athletics, the women’s world marathon champion, Peres Jepchirchir, has been provisionally suspended for doping, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced on Friday. The highly decorated 33-year-old, who won Olympic gold in the Covid-delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, was suspended after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for the banned blood booster EPO. content:
AIU investigates after sample tested positive for EPO
33-year-old won Olympic marathon in 2021
In a fresh blow for Kenyan athletics, the women’s world marathon champion, Peres Jepchirchir, has been provisionally suspended for doping, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced on Friday.
The highly decorated 33-year-old, who won Olympic gold in the Covid-delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, was suspended after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for the banned blood booster EPO.
The athlete is provisionally suspended while the case is investigated, while the AIU said Jepchirchir’s out-of-competition sample had been collected in Kenya before her recent Sydney Marathon victory.
More than 140 Kenyan athletes, including the women’s marathon world record-holder, Ruth Chepngetich , have been suspended or banned by the AIU since 2017.
Jepchirchir’s lauded career includes a world record in the half-marathon, while she is a four-time World Marathon major winner, having captured the 2026 Sydney Marathon, the 2024 London Marathon, the 2022 Boston Marathon and the 2021 New York Marathon.
The decision of World Athletics to award Nairobi the 2029 world championships is likely to increase the scrutiny of the east African nation’s anti-doping policies.
Barnabas Korir, Athletics Kenya’s youth development director and vice-president of the national Olympic committee, said he was left feeling shocked by the news of the suspension. “It’s a big disappointment coming soon after we were awarded the World Athletics Championship in 2029,” Korir told AFP. “We are in shock, especially in the calibre of Peres Jepchirchir after a stellar career. We don’t know what is happening with our athletes.”
Jepchirchir’s manager, Gianni Demadona, said she had tarnished her reputation. “When I learned from the AIU three days ago that she had been tested positive for EPO, I was confused and shocked,” Demadona said. “I can’t say anything because I was trusting her after 13 years working together that she was one of the most trustable athletes around. I was completely wrong. She spoiled her long and amazing career and she closes her career in the worst way.”
Kenya played host to a three-day visit from the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) this month, with the body’s president, Witold Banka, telling the country that it had to strive for zero tolerance on doping.
“Kenya proudly calls itself the home of champions. But for that home to remain respected and credible, it must also be clean,” Banka said. “That is why Kenya needs a strong culture of clean sport, zero tolerance for doping, and a more determined approach to preventing and fighting doping.”
Banka said that joint cooperation with Kenyan authorities would help lay the foundations for a cleaner sport. “Wada or Adak [Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya] alone cannot achieve its vision if we do not cooperate with those who have the power to go against those who are producing, smuggling and trafficking dangerous steroids to your athletes,” he said.
“We’ve found a common understanding and we are on the same track and there’s a clear goal within Kenya for zero tolerance for doping policy and it has to be established immediately with joint actions and a more aggressive approach to those who are destroying the image of the country and the reputation of the athletes.”

title: Molly Picklum claims lead in WSL title race with ‘dream’ win in Portugal
description: Australian defeats Cailtin Simmers in World Surf League women’s final Griffin Colapinto scores near-perfect barrel to beat ⁠Gabriel Medina Australia’s reigning world champion Molly Picklum won the Portugal Pro in thumping tubes on Friday, claiming her first victory of the year and ⁠jumping to the top of the rankings with just two events of surfing’s world tour remaining. California’s Griffin Colapinto scored a near-perfect barrel to come from behind and ⁠claim the win over Brazil’s ⁠Gabriel Medina in ​the men’s final, notching up his third victory at the powerful Portuguese beach break of Supertubos. content:
Australian defeats Cailtin Simmers in World Surf League women’s final
Griffin Colapinto scores near-perfect barrel to beat ⁠Gabriel Medina
Australia’s reigning world champion Molly Picklum won the Portugal Pro in thumping tubes on Friday, claiming her first victory of the year and ⁠jumping to the top of the rankings with just two events of surfing’s world tour remaining.
California’s Griffin Colapinto scored a near-perfect barrel to come from behind and ⁠claim the win over Brazil’s ⁠Gabriel Medina in ​the men’s final, notching up his third victory at the powerful Portuguese beach break of Supertubos.
Picklum has had a strong if not spectacular season after winning ⁠her first world title in Fiji last year, but had made only one final and set her sights on securing a win in Portugal ahead of the season finale in Hawaii ⁠in December.
“It was a dream of mine to win here,” the 23-year-old said. “Portugal is like the cross between the ​Brazilian energy and Pipeline. Those are two of ‌my favourite things.
“I’m really happy to ‌hit my stride at the right time. We work so hard and not many people get to win, but ‌I’m so stoked to get my win this year.”
Up against California’s 2024 world champion Caitlin Simmers in the final, Picklum slipped behind in the early exchanges before locking into a deep, overhead tube on her backhand that scored 7.83 out of 10 and gave her the lead. Simmers threaded some nice tubes of her own but ended with a two-wave total of 12.84 to Picklum’s 13.33.
Colapinto, 28, has developed a special relationship ‌with the powerful, punchy tubes around the seaside town of Peniche, securing event wins in 2022, 2024 and now 2026.
He started strongly in the final, hustling Medina for the first ​wave, pulling into a deep barrel on his forehand and finishing it strongly. He scored an excellent 8.17 and backed it up quickly with a similar wave to pile the pressure on Medina.
But Brazil’s three-time world champion responded with an incredible barrel of his own on his backhand, squeezing out when all hope seemed lost, then took the lead with ⁠another long tube.
Needing something special, Colapinto found a gem on his backhand, disappearing behind ​the curtain for the entire wave ​and emerging near the packed crowd on ​the beach for a 9.43 out of a possible 10 and a lead he held ​until the clock ran ‌out.
“That’s the dream. How ​good were the waves ​out there?” said Colapinto, who climbed to third in the rankings after his win. “The battle with Gabriel was unreal … Portugal has a big place in my heart.“
The tour heads next to a new stop in the Philippines before the last event of the year at Pipeline, where 1.5 times points will be on offer.

title: Golden bat or ball: does cricket need an equivalent to the Ballon d’Or? | Taha Hashim
description: Football is obsessed by its annual award, but cricket seems less enthusiastic about crowning its own best player in the world It’s time for the Ballon d’Or because it’s always time for the Ballon d’Or. Once the golden ball is presented at the London Palladium this month to Harry Kane/Lamine Yamal/Lionel Messi (let us know in the comments!), the debate will quickly switch to next year’s contenders, continuing football’s unhealthy relationship with an individual trophy. “How World Cup final could be pivotal in Ballon d’Or race”, read a BBC headline in July, though the real jump-the-shark moment was when Real Madrid boycotted the ceremony in 2024 because Vinícius Júnior had to settle for silver. Perversely, quite the team move. Cricket celebrates the individual with greater range. The sport lauds hundreds, five-wicket hauls and averages, making for games within games, prompting forensic analysis of when Joe Root will overtake Sachin Tendulkar as the leading run-scorer in Test history. The International Cricket Council has its rankings for the best batters, bowlers and all-rounders in the world, across formats for men and women. My Instagram feed has recently been hijacked by: 1) AI bunnies breakdancing; 2) adverts for hair loss pills; and 3) Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler ranking the best Test batters of the century. Continue reading...
content:
Football is obsessed by its annual award, but cricket seems less enthusiastic about crowning its own best player in the world
I t’s time for the Ballon d’Or because it’s always time for the Ballon d’Or. Once the golden ball is presented at the London Palladium this month to Harry Kane/Lamine Yamal/Lionel Messi (let us know in the comments!), the debate will quickly switch to next year’s contenders, continuing football’s unhealthy relationship with an individual trophy. “How World Cup final could be pivotal in Ballon d’Or race”, read a BBC headline in July, though the real jump-the-shark moment was when Real Madrid boycotted the ceremony in 2024 because Vinícius Júnior had to settle for silver. Perversely, quite the team move.
Cricket celebrates the individual with greater range. The sport lauds hundreds, five-wicket hauls and averages, making for games within games, prompting forensic analysis of when Joe Root will overtake Sachin Tendulkar as the leading run-scorer in Test history. The International Cricket Council has its rankings for the best batters, bowlers and all-rounders in the world, across formats for men and women. My Instagram feed has recently been hijacked by: 1) AI bunnies breakdancing; 2) adverts for hair loss pills; and 3) Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler ranking the best Test batters of the century.
But there’s also something missing here, something by which the sport is less consumed – the question football asks itself constantly. Who is the best player in the world? Yes, there’ll be talk of the best batter, bowler or all-rounder, but what about ignoring the subcategories? For better or worse, there doesn’t seem to be a desperate push to celebrate the ultimate crown.
The ICC does have its own annual awards, launched in 2004, with the Sir Garfield Sobers Trophy given to the men’s cricketer of the year and the Rachael Heyhoe Flint Trophy for the women’s equivalent. But the last declared winners were Jasprit Bumrah and Melie Kerr for their international performances in 2024. Even the most ardent followers of the game will have failed to notice the absence of any awards for 2025.
An ICC spokesperson said: “The ICC has presented its annual awards digitally for a number of years, but we deliberately held back the 2025 edition to rethink what that platform can, and should, look like.
“As a result of that rethink, we are now in the process of developing a new approach to the ICC awards, which will return in 2027 and treat 2025-26 as a single season, as we look to create a broader, more meaningful way for cricket to celebrate its leading players, teams and achievements.”
The spokesperson said that as the ICC tries to “refine” its plan for the awards, “there is a real opportunity for the awards to become a significant global occasion for cricket that generates genuine excitement on the calendar”. An acknowledgment, then, that the old model didn’t make much of a splash.
Then there are the annual titles bestowed by the Wisden almanack, including the five Cricketers of the Year, an honour with its own terms and conditions. Chosen by the editor, the picks are based on performances in the previous English summer and it can be won only once.
To go for something more global and resembling the Ballon d’Or, though, there is the Leading Cricketer in the World. The men’s version was introduced in the 2004 almanack, and the women’s award came 11 years later. Mitchell Starc, lethal in the Ashes, and Deepti Sharma, central to India’s World Cup win , are the current holders. And the fun goes back, with the almanack having declared retrospective winners for the 20th century, too. Don Bradman, in case you’re wondering, had his own Messi-like run, victorious on 10 occasions from 1930 to 1948.
But, according to Lawrence Booth, the almanack’s editor, being one of the five is still “the plum prize”, having been around since 1889. “That’s the prize that most people talk about,” Booth says. “That has a resonance in a way that the Leading Cricketer doesn’t quite yet.
“The Leading Cricketer in the World is our chance to point out that we’re not just Anglocentric and that we take into account all kinds of cricket throughout the year and all nationalities. It’s similar to the ICC awards – you could predict in a way who’s going to win those awards because it’s generally the leading run-scorer or wicket-taker, whereas the five is a bit more quirky. The five is the one that most people ask about.”
There’s no glitzy trophy on offer for the leading cricketers, nor a real crowning image on stage like the Ballon d’Or has every year, backed by the institutional might of Uefa. Then again, is this really a problem for cricket? While the ICC ponders how to jazz up its own awards, there’s plenty of issues that should be higher on the priority list for the governing body.
A prestigious award celebrating the best of the best is certainly worth having and if an updated version gains some heft it should make for a good story during a bland white-ball series. Greater exposure is always welcome and it’s undoubtedly fun to speculate: survey the current international landscape and you’ll probably find Harry Brook, Beth Mooney, Shai Hope and Shree Charani among the contenders for 2026’s major gongs.
But it’s also worth appreciating that the game, as it stands, isn’t consumed by a solo prize. While Rio Ferdinand cried: “Ballon d’Or, Ballon d’Or, Ballon d’Or!” as Vinícius sealed Real Madrid’s Champions League triumph two years ago , we don’t need Michael Atherton screaming: “Wisden, Wisden, Wisden!” as Brook reaches three figures in a World Cup final. Football can keep that to itself.

title: ‘My time, my era’: Dubois sends out warning to rivals with Wardley demolition
description: WBO heavyweight champion targets big paydays against Hrgovic, Kabayel and Itauma after second round win Thirty minutes after Daniel Dubois had dismantled Fabio Wardley in less than two rounds on Saturday night, his promoter Frank Warren shook his head in slight awe as he described the intensity before the annihilation: “I went in the dressing room beforehand like I normally do and I couldn’t have a conversation with Daniel because he was so zoned in and focused. It showed when he got in the ring. He went out there on a seek-and-destroy mission.” Dubois resembled a much bigger and heavier version of a young Mike Tyson as, wearing black trunks and a black cape, he walked to the ring with intense purpose. There was not a flicker of emotion as he marched quickly towards Wardley for their WBO world title rematch. Continue reading...
content:
WBO heavyweight champion targets big paydays against Hrgovic, Kabayel and Itauma after second round win
T hirty minutes after Daniel Dubois had dismantled Fabio Wardley in less than two rounds on Saturday night, his promoter Frank Warren shook his head in slight awe as he described the intensity before the annihilation: “I went in the dressing room beforehand like I normally do and I couldn’t have a conversation with Daniel because he was so zoned in and focused. It showed when he got in the ring. He went out there on a seek-and-destroy mission.”
Dubois resembled a much bigger and heavier version of a young Mike Tyson as, wearing black trunks and a black cape, he walked to the ring with intense purpose. There was not a flicker of emotion as he marched quickly towards Wardley for their WBO world title rematch.
In the first fight , five months ago, Dubois was knocked down after just 16 seconds. He was dropped again in the third round, before he went to work behind his jolting jab and proceeded to beat up a valiant Wardley who refused to surrender until rescued by the referee in the 11th round.
The clear consensus was that Wardley would be a reduced figure in the rematch and that his only real hope boiled down to the fact that he still hits like a mule and that Dubois is regarded as a slow starter. But the champion was ready. “I was more focused than I was in May, big-time,” Dubois said. “It was go-time from the minute I put my gear on. Maybe the warm-up was more extensive than usual but I was in the zone quicker. Everyone was saying Fabio was going to start fast so I was ready for him.”
Had he expected such a brutally quick stoppage? “I can’t say I did,” Dubois said. “I was prepared for a war. I wasn’t going to be denied. I refused to lose.”
Dubois insisted that no heavyweight in the world could have withstood the ferocious blows he rained down on Wardley. His certainty was understandable as he looked formidable – even if Wardley’s famed punch resistance has dissipated. “Fabio has got a great chin,” Dubois pointed out and it’s true that Wardley has never been dropped. Even in Saturday’s dark whirlwind he took a standing count after just 17 seconds when a monstrous right hand left him crumpled against the ropes. Wardley was also still on his feet, while hunched over in a corner, when his trainer Ben Davison threw in the towel.
After his victory, Dubois proclaimed that “this is my time, my era.”
Only three men currently have the movement and skill to hold off a rampaging Dubois. Oleksandr Usyk remains the best heavyweight in the world and he has already defeated Dubois twice . But the unbeaten Ukrainian master will turn 40 in January and he wants just one more fight in America. As he had appeared keen on facing a washed-up Deontay Wilder, it is likely that Usyk is in the mood for an easy last dance.
Tyson Fury, who should beat Anthony Joshua in December, could be tempted by the riches of another lucrative all-British showdown against Dubois. In his prime, Fury would have dazzled Dubois with his awkward mobility and slippery skills. But Fury is 38 and a waning force.
Moses Itauma is the third boxer with the speed and dexterity to trouble Dubois – but the 21-year-old prodigy suffered a severe setback when, having won every round against Filip Hrgovic, he ran out of steam and was overwhelmed in the ninth . It was a sobering reminder that Itauma has much to learn about the harsh realities of boxing.
“I just want to know who’s next Frank,” Dubois said cheerfully.
Warren explained that Hrgovic, the IBF champion, has a mandatory defence against Frank Sánchez in Croatia. The WBC version of the world title belongs to Agit Kabayel, a decent heavyweight who is a huge ticket-seller in Germany.
Hrgovic, Kabayel, Fury and Itauma are all promoted by Warren, who said: “The good thing is that everyone wants to fight. They’re fighting men. There will be great fights and, this will be music to Daniel’s ears, great money.”
Dubois laughed in delight before he was asked who he would like to fight most. “I’ve heard talk about Kabayel but I’ll fight whoever’s next in line … whoever pays the most cash.”
Hrgovic had been ringside and he suggested he had struggled with illness when losing a bruising battle to Dubois in 2024. The confident Croat promised to “smash” his rival next time.
“Did he really say that?” Dubois asked in amusement before turning to the unlikely prospect of fighting Usyk for a third time. “Definitely. I’d love that. We’re coming out on top this time. We’ve made our mistakes but I’m a different fighter now.”
Warren confirmed that he could easily imagine Fury accepting the challenge of facing Dubois while Itauma’s name was mentioned next.
Itauma is the most naturally gifted heavyweight in Britain but Warren reminded us of his age. He also stressed that a future clash between Dubois and a more experienced Itauma would be “a gun fight” to fill a stadium.
Dubois smiled with the look of a man who knows he could dominate heavyweight boxing for years. When asked if he would like to fight Itauma one day, Dubois nodded intently. “I hope so because I need dance partners.”

content:
A first defeat in four years could be liberating for England after so long fighting to preserve their historic unbeaten run
E ngland’s glittering unbeaten era is over. Canada defeated the Red Roses to deal them a first defeat in four years after 40 wins and one draw. It was a landmark result for the Canadians, who will look to replicate the outcome this weekend when the two nations meet again. England must reset but they won’t panic; the Red Roses have been the standard bearers for the past seven years, which is why they have lost only twice in 73 matches. But while no team would ever aim to lose, falling to defeat is a good thing for England and the wider sport.
Losing could actually make England a deadlier team to face. That is because they now need to find another level to their game with teams beginning to figure out ways to beat them. They have been pushed over the past few years by teams such as Canada, New Zealand and France, but they always had just enough to get the result over the line. Now they have been presented with a new challenge and John Mitchell, who lost his first game as Red Roses head coach, said post-defeat when his side “gets a setback, it generally learns quicker”.
It is not just tactically and physically that the Red Roses may grow, but the mentality of the group may also shift. A defeat was inevitable at some stage, with everyone watching and waiting for the game in which it would come. Mitchell said his players may feel “freer” now that the unbeaten run is over.
“The important thing is winning after winning is harder than before,” he said. “I guess what it does to everyone is it frees us up, which is cool. It allows us all to find more. I know this group has definitely got more in it but sometimes it requires the context that we have just received to dig deeper and push for something more.”
Losing an international rugby game is a new experience for some of the players in the squad. Abi Burton and Maddie Feaunati are among those who have never tasted defeat for England. Jess Breach’s record is an incredible 59 wins and one loss. The defeat may make those players more versatile and adaptable, too.
The England captain, Meg Jones, said of the initial reaction from the squad: “For us the biggest thing is that we stick together. Games are built on moments, it is not one individual moment, it is multiple. That is the beauty of it and we get to review it, we get to go again next weekend, we get to stick together.
“I think it is good for us to reassess this and see where we are at. I think togetherness is the main message to come out of that because it’s how you respond when you have had a loss, I think that is the biggest test of character.
“They are lessons at the end of the day, I don’t think a loss necessarily changes the way we approach things. You genuinely do learn from it. I spoke to Burts [Abi Burton] and we said: ‘How many games have we lost in our career?’ And we had a little chuckle, those are the ones that shape you the most at times. It’s the biggest lesson for sure. Teams are coming out to beat us, they are going to put their best foot forward. We need to make sure we have got our best foot forward as well.”
The fact that England ended their unbeaten run away from home is also significant. Had the Red Roses lost one of their home games, which they almost did against the same opposition with that draw in Exeter, it would still have been a good thing for the team but the benefits would have been less impactful.
It is rare for the Red Roses to play non-Six Nations teams away from home and the revamped WXV gives them more of those experiences, perfect preparation for the 2029 World Cup in Australia. England won’t have the cushion of home support and stadiums they are used to playing in when they attempt to defend their title in three years’ time, which is the ultimate goal of this cycle.
If England get into a potentially similar situation in 2029 they won’t be in unfamiliar territory. They have now been away from home, in front of a hostile crowd and lost for the first time since the 2022 World Cup final . In three years they may be able to weather the storm better and have more contingency plans.
Mitchell had said before WXV began that the away part of these series of matches would be an “audition for 2029”. After the defeat against Canada, he was asked if this outcome and experience is what the team needed. “Definitely [it is],” he said. “I think even before that message we said: ‘Come and get us.’ We have been asking for someone to come and get us and they have done that. Not that we designed that to happen, far from it. We have to respond.”
For the sport more generally, this defeat may attract more fans or encourage those already watching to stick around and attend more matches. Rugby needs jeopardy and the thrill of a game comes when fans do not know who will be the winner on matchday. Of course this one loss won’t mean England’s dominance will disappear but when they play other top-five nations there will be more doubt over whether they will be the ones to come out on top.
England’s unbeaten ticker may now stand at zero but no one will forget the run of 41 games. The Red Roses are written into history and their world record may never be beaten. They have forced other teams to raise their game and made many take notice of women’s rugby with millions now following. England are entering a new era and they have a chance for immediate revenge this weekend as they play Canada once again. They will see it as an opportunity to start a new unbeaten run.
This is an extract from our weekly rugby union email, the Breakdown. To subscribe just visit this page and follow the instructions.

title: Cheltenham jumps into action after fixing its troublesome hole
description: Home of National Hunt racing has undergone extensive work on its drainage system in preparation for new season There is little chance to catch your breath as the racing seasons turn and six days on from Ascot’s exhilarating Champions Day Cheltenham will open its gates on Friday for the first card of the 2026-27 campaign.
