title: Jane Brown obituary
description: Garden historian whose books on figures such as Gertrude Jekyll and Edwin Lutyens helped revive interest in the subject
content:
Garden historian whose books on figures such as Gertrude Jekyll and Edwin Lutyens helped revive interest in the subject
Jane Brown, who has died aged 87, once described her relationship with garden history as that of “a spectator, only occasionally drawn into the fray”, but to anyone who has read her books this seems almost laughably modest. Brown led a resurgence of interest from the 1980s onwards in figures such as Sir Edwin Lutyens, Gertrude Jekyll and the American landscape architect Lanning Roper from the earlier part of the century, and she deserves at least some of the credit for the growing enthusiasm for garden history during the past 50 years, both as an academic discipline and as an area of interest to garden designers and casual garden visitors alike.
What was groundbreaking about her approach, however, was the determination to avoid what she called the “overly aristocratic” approach to garden history, which she felt made it seem “as if only the great and the good had gardens”. In the foreword to her book The Pursuit of Paradise (1999), she declared it was an attempt “to redress the balance, to outline a history of gardens that is also popular and nostalgic”.
This egalitarian approach assumed that cottage gardeners who grew Fat Hen and Good Henry among wild roses and flowers for bees, or the provincial florists’ societies that bred flowers such as carnations, polyanthus and tulips, could be just as interesting as princes and parterres.
Brown pointed out that Roper’s book Successful Town Gardening (1957) and John Brookes’s Room Outside (1969) were talking to a new generation of gardeners who did not possess ancestral acres; neither did they want to be reminded of wartime gloom and digging for victory. They preferred to create a small, preferably lawned oasis where they could sit and relax with family and friends.
Brown’s readable yet authoritative style occasionally ventures into the acerbic. A chapter ironically entitled Science Lends a Hand takes aim at the pesticide and fertiliser industry and their wartime advocates Sir Frederick Keeble and Professor Geoffrey Blackman. These two embodied what Brown calls “the scientist’s well-intentioned but disastrous role as friendly gardener-uncle” and between them introduced a generation of gardeners to the idea that chemistry was their ally. (Blackman later came to regret the fact that his work had resulted in the disappearance of poppies from cornfields.)
Those who knew her well describe Brown as friendly but unassuming; someone who did not want to talk about herself. Dr Catherine Horwood got to know her in 1999, while writing her own book, Gardening Women , and recalled her as “enormously helpful. There was never a hint of competitiveness. She was always so generous with her huge knowledge. I thought she might have been rather terrifying but she was the most modest, gentle person.”
Christopher Woodward, director of the Garden Museum , considered her “the most eloquent garden historian of her generation. She applied the approach of a top literary biographer – a Hermione Lee, say, or a Victoria Glendinning, whom she reminded me of in manner – to her subjects.”
Modest she may have been, but one can find little personal flashes in Brown’s writing that illuminate her life. In her forewords, she often explained why she took on the subject of the book, and very often it was her own experience that fuelled her interest. As she once admitted: “My books increasingly reflect my life.”
She also believed it was people rather than plants who were the catalysts for change in the gardening world. “Ten years of writing about gardening people – Gertrude Jekyll and Edwin Lutyens, Vita Sackville-West and Lanning Roper – have left me firmly convinced that gardeners are the chief inspiration of other gardeners, and that the more personable and distinguished the gardener is, or was, the greater the fund of inspiration.”
Brown was born shortly before the outbreak of the second world war, at the tea rooms run by her aunts at Picket Post, near Ringwood, in the New Forest. An advertisement placed in an RAC brochure from around the same time describes the Kettle Tea House as having two acres of “lovely old gardens” and names the proprietors as the Misses Taylor – these were Jane’s mother’s sisters.
One of her earliest memories, which later inspired her book about rhododendrons, Tales of the Rose Tree (2004), was of “the green ghosts that guarded a miniature cottage in a New Forest garden, where my favourite aunt once sat sewing petticoats out of parachute silk, guarded by a giant yellow teddy bear, all fascinating to an under-five”. In 1963, Jane married Peter Brown, an airline pilot, and in 1970 they moved to Abinger in Surrey, “in the greensand hills with rhododendrons in every garden”. However, it was what Brown called “the strong Lutyens inspiration of the house” that inspired her initial interest in the architect, and his partnership with Jekyll, which lasted until her death in 1932.
At the time, despite having two young sons, Brown was studying landscape architecture at Thames Polytechnic (now the University of Greenwich). Her father had disapproved of the idea of university when she left Winchester county high school for girls, and she had taken a secretarial course, followed by a job at the Royal Institute of British Architects in London.
There is no record of Brown’s reaction to her father’s attitude. However, in the foreword to My Darling Heriott (2006), Brown confessed that the subject of the book, the 18th-century gardener Henrietta Luxborough, “typifies a species that I find especially fascinating; a sister equally as talented as a brilliant brother, but with nowhere to go”.
In Gardens of a Golden Afternoon (1982), an account of the partnership between Jekyll and Lutyens, she described how she used the gardens at Orchards, a wonderful example of Lutyens’s work in Bramley, Surrey, for a measured drawing project and “was rewarded by the amazing patterns of the geometry”.
Investigating Lutyens and Jekyll became a passion and many Lutyens gardens were visited en route to family holidays in the north of England. Peter Brown took most of the colour photographs, but by the time the book was published, the couple had divorced. The dedication seems a poignant epitaph to the marriage – “To Peter, as promised”.
The book led to an exhibition at the Hayward Gallery in London in 1981 and the setting up in 1984 of the Lutyens Trust, for which Brown served as a trustee until 2008. She also became a patron of the Hestercombe Gardens Trust established in 1986 to oversee the restoration of the Somerset gardens laid out by Lutyens and Jekyll. Other books followed; 23 in total, including The Omnipotent Magician (2011), a biography of Lancelot “Capability” Brown.
This was critically well received, but the weighty subject – so many landscapes, so many clients – seemed to reduce what Woodward describes as Brown’s ability to “skip lightly through history” to a more dogged trot, a bit like Brown himself on his endless horseback peregrinations around the UK.
Her biographies of Roper and – less well-known to a British audience – Beatrix Farrand, who created the garden at Dumbarton Oaks in Washington DC, are more typical of Brown’s approach, which was to try to convey to the reader the passion she felt for her subject.
This was particularly true of Farrand, whom Brown admired for having had the foresight to rescue what remained of Jekyll’s drawings and donate them to the University of California, Berkeley.
Brown’s last book was Angel Dorothy (2017), a biography of Dorothy Elmhirst, founder of the trust that runs the Dartington Hall estate in Devon, where Farrand created the gardens. She had difficulty finding a publisher for it, which seems extraordinary for a writer with such a body of work behind her, but somehow the book got published, a tribute to Brown’s determination, as ever, to tell a story that had seized her by the arm and compelled her to put it down on paper.

title: Chris Wickham obituary
description: Historian who explored the nature of change in the creative and dynamic world that followed the fall of the Roman empire
content:
Historian who explored the nature of change in the creative and dynamic world that followed the fall of the Roman empire
Chris Wickham, who has died aged 76, transformed how we understand the millennium after the fall of the Roman empire. He did so not by focusing on religious or political elites, but on the other “85 to 95%” of the population, thus adopting the “history from below” approach.
Originally a historian of medieval Italy, Chris became known for his comparative approach and refusal to study societies in isolation from one another. But the broad syntheses for which he was celebrated were first built upwards from ordinary lives, thus placing his work alongside many other great Marxist-inspired historians.
In an essay in 1998 he showed that gossip in a 12th-century Tuscan village was not just malicious, but essential. “Talking about other people behind their backs” created an “agreed truth” among the peasantry that gave them a voice in local politics and enabled them to resist lordly power. Likewise, his 1992 book, Social Memory, written with his friend James Fentress, rejected static or passive notions of memory or concepts of a “collective unconscious”. It is individuals who do the remembering, not only on their own but by “talking about it” with others. Memories were made socially, and continuously remade, by groups – peasants, the working class, even nations – recreating usable pasts together to suit new politics and ways of life.
The books Early Medieval Italy (1981) and The Mountains and the City (1988) presented detailed social histories of rural communities and situated them within wider structures of power and the economy. From his beloved Rome, where he stayed every year, his historical imagination then stretched outwards.
His geographical and chronological range was vast. Chris’s Mediterranean was one synonymous with Europe as a whole and included the Byzantine and Islamic worlds. At times, as with Eric Hobsbawm for the modern period, one wondered whether he had a whole team of historians working for him across multiple languages.
Framing the Early Middle Ages: Europe and the Mediterranean, 400-800 won the 2006 Wolfson prize for history. It fulfilled the promise of his comparative approach by presenting a bold new analysis of the nature of change after the fall of the Roman empire, for regions from Denmark to Egypt. Reviewers acknowledged it to be the most significant work of its kind for a century.
Chris argued that the Roman empire did not simply collapse into the so-called “Dark Ages”. Instead, as he showed once more in The Inheritance of Rome (2009), the world that followed the Roman empire was creative and dynamic, and for the majority of people less oppressive. That world was built by peasants and by local communities.
These themes were brought to a wider audience in Medieval Europe (2016). They also lay behind Chris’s reinterpretation of the commercial revolution of the 10th to 12th centuries in The Donkey and the Boat (2023). Local and regional trade patterns, shaped by peasant production and feudal lords, were more responsible for economic growth than the maritime luxury trade of city states.
The study of economic relations expanded his geographical range. In a 2026 paper he used the trade in pepper from Kerala between 800 and 1600 to show again that internal regional economies drove economic growth, this time across the Indian Ocean. Likewise, northern Italy was comparable with Jiangnan China because of the commonalities of their economic systems. Chris was able to demonstrate the extended feudal logic of medieval societies across Europe, Africa and Asia.
Born in Rossett, near Wrexham, on the Welsh side of the border with England, Chris was the elder son of Cyril, a patent agent, and Brenda (Moss), later a Conservative councillor. The family moved to Chalfont St Peter in Buckinghamshire and Chris obtained a scholarship to go as a boarder to Millfield school, in Somerset. He was pushed three years ahead and completed 14 O-levels by the age of 15. Then he went to Oxford University early, to Keble College, committed to becoming a medievalist.
In the early 1970s he embraced a non-doctrinaire Marxism that shaped his historical thinking (he edited Marxist History-writing for the Twenty-first Century in 2007). But ever the pragmatist, he joined the Communist party because it demanded only one night a week of his time instead of the three or four the Trotskyist Socialist Workers required.
In 1977 he went to the University of Birmingham , where he remained for three decades, progressing from lecturer to senior lecturer, reader and, in 1993, professor of early medieval history. There, at a conference in 1987, he met the Byzantine art historian Leslie Brubaker. A transatlantic relationship (and marriage in 1990) was made easier with Leslie’s appointment at Birmingham in 1994. In 2005, Chris took up the Chichele professorship of medieval history at All Souls, Oxford.
As well as writing and editing two dozen books, plus countless articles, Chris found time to serve the discipline of history. He had an extraordinary capacity for work and an ability to get things done. In life, as in history, he was fascinated by institutions. This was as true in his role as branch leader of his trade union at Birmingham as when chair of the history faculty (2009-12) and head of humanities (2015-16) at Oxford.
He was a powerful advocate for the humanities, be it from the journal he edited, Past and Present, or as a chair of one of the national bodies set up to measure the “excellence” of research in UK universities, through the British Academy (he was granted a fellowship in 1998 and awarded the Serena medal in 2014), and as head of the advisory council for the government’s research funding body for the arts and humanities. Chris’s sensible negotiations helped ensure that the drive to make the books and articles deriving from publicly funded research free to read, or “open access”, did not have the unintended consequence of destroying the commercial logic of humanities publishing in Britain. No wonder that in retirement he was parachuted into the British School in Rome in 2020 to steady and guide its demoralised staff out of a crisis arising from the Covid pandemic.
Chris was generous with his time and expertise. He was a mentor to countless medievalists, historians of all periods, and scholars in other disciplines too, especially archaeology. He listened and he heard, and made real conversation happen.
He was also tremendous fun. When Chris chaired a committee, business was brisk and light-hearted. The raising of a valid but unconstructive point was met with a trademark shrug and raised palms. Dinners were always memorable. He could talk about any subject. It seemed he had read everything and forgotten nothing. This was not just academic. His passion and knowledge of Buffy the Vampire Slayer initially came as a surprise. Eventually one gave up speculating on whether Chris’s knowledge and interests had any limit.
He died after a short illness from complications following a cancer diagnosis, and is survived by Leslie.

title: Let’s go nuts in the garden – and the cobnut is a great place to start
description: It’s high time we rediscovered these delicious nuts, but be warned: like the Victorians, squirrels can’t get enough of them
content:
It’s high time we rediscovered these delicious nuts, but be warned: like the Victorians, squirrels can’t get enough of them
W hen I think of the crops I’m eager to grow, my mind rarely goes to nuts. But when I spotted the last of the season’s cobnuts at the greengrocer’s, it occurred to me that this could be one to consider. The nuts that come from the hazel – a tree that grows in many a woodland and also my front garden – have been foraged for millennia and cultivated versions have existed since Roman times.
It’s the cultivated varieties you want to plant for a decent crop of cobnuts, as wild hazel produces smaller yields. This is a tree that prefers mild conditions, hence their connection to Kent, where they were grown abundantly during the Victorian era (one of the most popular varieties is called the Kentish cob.) They prefer a sunny spot, in free-draining earth – a challenge for me with my clay soil – in a sheltered position where they’ll be protected from frosts that would affect pollination.
As cobnut trees are monoecious – meaning that the pollen-bearing catkins and the fruit-bearing flowers grow separately but on the same tree – pollination is a key consideration. Some cultivars will not self-pollinate and so rely on the presence of another tree (as well as the wind) for successful pollination. Fortunately, wild hazel can pollinate most cultivars, so if you have some in your garden, as I do, you may well be fine.
As with most trees, the best time to plant them is when they are dormant, so from November through to late winter works for cobnuts, which are generally sold as one- to two-year-old trees. While it is possible to get a crop of nuts from an unpruned tree, making the effort to prune should result in larger, better quality nuts. Aim for an open structured tree with about 10 leaders growing outwards. Once established, prune to prevent overcrowding in winter. If you do this after the catkins have arrived, this can help distribute pollen for better pollination. Additionally, brutting is a traditional pruning technique that encourages heavier cropping and involves bending that season’s side shoots in late summer, but leaving the broken section still attached.
Cobnuts are ready to harvest from August if you like the taste of them when fresh, before they start to ripen. In any case, this might be your only opportunity if you share your garden with squirrels. Green cobnuts have a delicate nutty flavour and a juicy texture, but for those who prefer the more typical nut experience, wait until the husks start to turn yellow a month or so later. Cracking, shelling and then lightly roasting your cobnuts serves to enhance their nutty flavour.

title: Billionaire tax and trans rights: what are key state ballot initiatives in midterms?

Voters in 39 states will face an array of referendum issues – including Alabama’s on the national anthem in schools
Americans heading to the polls for next month’s midterm elections are not just choosing whom to send to Washington, or their state capitols. There are also 145 statewide measures on ballots across 39 states, polling voters on actions from a novel wealth tax on California’s billionaires to requiring Alabama’s public schools to broadcast or perform the first stanza of the national anthem each week.
Voters in Idaho, Nevada and Virginia are asked to protect abortion rights; voters in Missouri are asked to give those rights back. Property tax issues appear on dozens of state ballots. Several state referendums ask voters to bar trans athletes from competing in women’s sports, or bar gender-affirming medical care for minors.
Voters like referendums, in principle, as a tool of direct democracy. “Polls in every state show at least 2-to-1 support for having an initiative process,” said John Matsusaka, a business professor at the University of Southern California (USC) and executive director of the Initiative and Referendum Institute.
In practice, however, they often do not like the measures put forward in referendums. The long-run average rate for passage is about 41%.

title: Detective raped by fellow officer David Carrick calls on Met chief to resign
description: Linda Williams, who was attacked in 2004, says force’s handling of her case was ‘like being raped all over again’
content:
Linda Williams, who was attacked in 2004, says force’s handling of her case was ‘like being raped all over again’
A detective who was raped by the former Scotland Yard officer David Carrick has called for the head of the Metropolitan police to resign, saying the handling of her case was “like being raped all over again”.
Linda Williams, 60, who has waived her right to anonymity, was attacked by Carrick in 2004. She launched a legal case against the Met for failing to protect her against the serial rapist, and has now settled for an undisclosed six-figure sum without the force admitting liability.
Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is one of the country’s worst sex offenders and is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.
Williams, from Hertfordshire, has said the way she was treated by the force throughout her legal claim was “devastating” and that it drove her to contemplate suicide.
“The whole process has taken me right back to how I felt when I was raped by Carrick: controlled, abused and powerless,” she said. “If I was raped tomorrow, I wouldn’t report it. Both the criminal justice process and the civil process have been so traumatic.
“I say that as someone who was once a sexual offences officer, supporting victims myself. Despite that experience and my understanding of the system, I still wouldn’t report it, because of the complete lack of empathy and support I have experienced from the police.
“At no point did I feel they sincerely acknowledged that I had been through a horrific sexual attack and that the trauma of that had deeply scarred me, or their role in it all.”
Williams brought a civil case against the Met seeking damages on the basis that the force failed to protect her from Carrick and that she felt she had been unable to report the rape. She said the Met’s legal team in the case questioned the severity of her post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) diagnosis.
“They used the fact that I just got on with my life as best I could after the rape against me,” she said. “I was an exemplary officer and continued to perform well at work, and they relied on that to suggest I had shown no signs of psychological trauma.
“As far as I am concerned, it is Mark Rowley , the [Met] commissioner, saying these terrible things, as he was the defendant in the case.”
She said the Met needed to set up a unit overseen by victims like herself who understood what it was like to be raped.
“For this to happen Rowley needs to go and we need a new commissioner,” she said.
Williams alleged it was the “Met’s fault” that she could not report the rape in 2004, and that “little had changed” in the culture since then. She added that the force was “like an episode of Life On Mars”, the 2000s TV drama set in a fictional 1970s police station.
She said: “I wouldn’t have had the backup of my colleagues in dangerous situations and ultimately, I doubt anything would have been done about Carrick.”
Williams reported the rape in 2021, and said she had had no relationships since the attack, 22 years ago. “After the attack, I couldn’t face the thought of being with a man or even having somebody in my home. That makes for a lonely Christmas and no holidays.
“It’s my choice, but the reason behind it wasn’t my choice. That’s down to the attack. Carrick stole the future that I wanted.”
Williams told the BBC the PTSD she had experienced after the attack was “90% down to the Met police, 10% to Carrick”.
In 2022 and 2023, Carrick pleaded guilty to 71 sexual offences , including 48 rapes against 12 other women over 17 years. In November last year, he was convicted of molesting a 12-year-old child in the late 1980s and repeatedly raping and abusing a female ex-partner.
A Met spokesperson said: “Serious flaws in the way we approached such investigations at the time meant we did not spot his pattern of abusive behaviour.
“As a result, we missed opportunities to pursue him through the misconduct process. We deeply regret this. We recognise the unique and additional impact on DC Linda Williams, whose exposure to Carrick came as a result of her being a Met officer.
“Her continued commitment to public service, in spite of the trauma she experienced, is commendable. Throughout subsequent legal proceedings, the Met has tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams’ welfare and has aimed to deal with her claims as quickly and compassionately as possible.
“The commissioner has previously met with DC Williams in person as well as spoken to her via email on multiple occasions. He has repeatedly acknowledged that she has shown courage in speaking out about her experience in an effort to drive forward necessary change and in now waiving her anonymity to continue to do so.
“He has contacted DC Williams to ask whether she would be willing to meet again and further discuss these issues in person.”

title: ‘We can’t let the far right take power again’: Lula voters in final push before Brazil runoff
description: In bellwether Minais Gerais, with polls about even, president’s supporters are striving to win over those who abstained or voted for Flavio Bolsonaro
content:
In bellwether Minais Gerais, with polls about even, president’s supporters are striving to win over those who abstained or voted for Flavio Bolsonaro
N aiara Boroni, Nikolas Domingues and Jodersson Diego live in the same city and do not know one another, but said they had done the same thing in recent days: persuaded at least one person who had not voted for the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round to choose him in this Sunday’s runoff.
In Boroni’s case, it was her grandmother who had not turned out; in Domingues’s, a cousin who had chosen a candidate who finished fourth. But Diego achieved what to many sounds almost impossible in such a polarised country: he said he had persuaded a woman who voted for the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro to switch sides.
“She’s a student of mine and didn’t vote for Lula because of her evangelical church. I didn’t argue; I tried to explain that he wasn’t everything they said he was, and she said she had changed her mind,” said Diego, 33, a dance teacher from Belo Horizonte, the capital of the state of Minas Gerais.
Winning over voters who abstained or cast null votes, and flipping as many others as possible, is at the heart of Lula’s strategy as he tries to do what no presidential candidate has ever managed in Brazil: overturn a first-round defeat like the one he suffered to Bolsonaro on 5 October.
Lula received 3.8 million fewer votes than in 2022, when he ran against the senator’s father, then president Jair Bolsonaro – who would go on to lose the runoff and try to stage a coup , which failed after the heads of two of the three armed forces refused to join him .
Serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest, he chose his eldest son to stand in his place. Flávio Bolsonaro has said that, if elected, he will pardon his father and receive the presidential sash from him.
The senator won 5 million more votes than his father and saw his party sweep elections for congress, state governments and state legislatures, which made him the clear favourite for many analysts.
In the three weeks of campaigning since then, however, polls have shown the gap steadily narrowing, and the two are now about even , with Bolsonaro still slightly ahead, but only by fractions of a percentage point.
“The scenario is one of a very tight tie, but with Lula’s campaign performing markedly better in the runoff,” said political scientist Manoel Leonardo Santos, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais.
The incumbent’s hopes rest on the narrowest-ever gap between first and second place, at less than 2% of the vote, while abstention reached a record 21%, which tends to hurt Lula more because it is more common among groups that favour him, such as lower-income and less-educated voters and older people.
Of the 10 cities with the highest abstention rates, eight are in Minas Gerais, the country’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo and a historical bellwether in presidential elections. No candidate has ever won nationally without carrying the state, where Lula now finished almost five percentage points behind Bolsonaro.
“If Lula’s voters turn out, he can win, but there is absolutely no guarantee that he will manage to make that happen,” said political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles, also a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais.
Bolsonaro supporters are also trying to keep mobilisation high.
Last Tuesday, at an event with local politicians that included an appearance by the senator via video call on a big screen, as well as a 23ft inflatable figure of his father, Minas Gerais governor-elect Cleitinho Azevedo urged the dozens of people present “not to think that we have already won the election and keep asking for votes”.
Pharmacist Magda Aparecida Araújo, 44, lives in the working-class neighbourhood next to the exhibition centre and was sitting in the back row. “I’m not going to belittle Lula’s governments, because I went to university thanks to a scholarship, but I now vote for Bolsonaro because he defends the family and I support traditional values,” said Araújo.
Given its electoral importance, both Lula and Bolsonaro chose the state capital for some of their final rallies: the senator’s was scheduled for this morning, while the incumbent held his last Wednesday.
“I’m here because we can’t let the far right take power again and destroy all of our rights,” said student Ester Nascimento, 17, who was with friends her own age, a symbol of what many see as perhaps the main catalyst behind Lula’s hopes of a comeback: young people who organically took to the streets in large protests all across Brazil.
“I think everyone felt obliged to make their voice heard,” said Nascimento.
Following advice from young, digitally native politicians , Lula’s team overhauled his online communications, and the 81-year-old incumbent, who does not even own a mobile phone, began recording selfie videos . Millions of his supporters joined a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where congressman André Janones sent dozens of daily instructions on how to make pro-Lula content go viral, and for the first time, the president’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s.
Lula also approved a “package of benefits” at the limits of what electoral law allows, including increasing and bringing forward payments from the main cash-transfer programme for poor families, while also securing a major political victory by getting congress to approve a shorter working week that could affect 30 million workers.
Even so, many analysts see much of the narrowing gap in the polls as driven more by Bolsonaro losing support , with his rejection rate having risen while Lula’s has fallen slightly.
Experts say some of Bolsonaro’s recent moves may have alienated the indecisive voters , including what was seen as an aggressive performance in the first presidential debate and a controversial speech in which he said he would use the new highly conservative congress to “change the constitution and re-democratise this country ”.
That was the first warning sign that led administrative assistant Douglas Pereira Melo, 25, who voted for far-right influencer Renan Santos three weeks ago, to now choose Lula.
“It’s very dangerous for him to say that he’ll change the constitution. His father tried to stage a coup, and I’m afraid he’ll follow in his footsteps,” said Melo, adding that “the Bolsonaro scandals” had also weighed on his decision.
The senator is under investigation in two federal police inquiries, one into what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father, and another into alleged money laundering and a possible business partnership with a close friend, the betting-sector businessman and lawyer Willer Tomaz.
The senator is also embroiled in a dispute with the footballer Richarlison , who accuses Bolsonaro and Tomaz of conspiring to strip him of a mansion on an island , while Piauí magazine revealed last Thursday that, at the height of the Covid pandemic in 2020, the senator attended a barbecue on a boat with sex workers and lobbyists who were negotiating vaccine purchases with his father’s administration.
Political scientist Manoel Leonardo Santos said he has “no doubt” that Lula will enter the runoff with better chances than he did immediately after Bolsonaro’s first-round victory.
“Whether it will be enough for him to turn it around, we can’t say. But Lula has gained ground while Bolsonaro appears to have stopped growing,” he added.

title: The Guide #266: The knives are out at Netflix – maybe now it will make something worth watching
description: In this week’s newsletter: Stalling subscriber numbers have led to a corporate bloodbath, but the streaming giant has an inherent quality problem that will be a lot harder to fix
content:
In this week’s newsletter: Stalling subscriber numbers have led to a corporate bloodbath, but the streaming giant has an inherent quality problem that will be a lot harder to fix
I n all the fevered hype around a certain three-hour, form-breaking documentary portrait of a disgraced tech CEO , another big Hollywood story this week has been relatively sidelined: the drama at Netflix, where sluggish subscriber numbers and a general lack of Wall Street enthusiasm has led to a remarkable spree of sackings. A thousand employees, or 6% of its entire workforce, have been laid off – including some very big names. Among a clutch of other execs, chief content officer Bela Bajaria – the figure most synonymous with Netflix’s tone and ethos over the past decade – has been fired. The company’s head of film, Dan Lin, has gone too. That shade of red on the streamer’s logo has never looked more bloody. You Can See Everything getting very messy indeed.
We’ve been here before, of course. Netflix – giant, controversial, inescapable – is the sort of company people love to make grand speculations about. Pencils were sharpened in 2022 when Netflix lost subscribers for the first time and saw its share price plummet as a result, before the company enjoyed a notable resurgence. Just as the obituaries written for the streamer were premature then, writing it off now would be foolish too.
But a cull of this magnitude is still telling, indicating that Netflix itself thinks something has gone badly awry – particularly in terms of the actual stuff it’s been pumping out. Bajaria was the exec who famously likened the streamer’s programming to a “gourmet cheeseburger”; a premium product that was also highly snackable. Her exit suggests that recipe isn’t as appealing to viewers as it once was.
It’s a question that gets asked more often than the streamer would like: when was the last time you watched a truly great new show on Netflix? Adolescence tends to be a popular answer, but that series (a limited run of only four episodes, let’s remember) was released 18 months ago. This year the cupboard has been extraordinarily bare. You might make a case for How to Get to Heaven from Belfast, or East of Eden at a push, but neither feel unmissably brilliant. And the streamer’s record with returning series is strikingly shaky, with precipitous audience drop-offs for shows’ second seasons .
Netflix’s quality issue is baked into its very model. The limitations of the company’s all-at-once, binge-friendly release strategy have been obvious for some time, resulting in shows that burn brightly but briefly for a week or two, before disappearing from the cultural conversation. But just as damaging, I’d argue, is a complete disinterest in cultivating shows with the potential for real staying power. Shows are often cancelled right as they are finding their voice, and flashy limited series with big names are prioritised over ones that could run and run. (Name-led series tend to take longer to return too, due to their stars’ many other commitments.) With the exception of cosy heartlands romantic drama Virgin River and Black Mirror (a bit of an outlier given it is an anthology series and debuted on another platform, Channel 4), no current Netflix drama has been airing for more than four seasons.
Netflix isn’t alone in its aversion to lasting, sprawling TV: in this era, post-the golden age of The Sopranos, Breaking Bad and the like, shows have tended to get shorter both in season and episode counts, with bigger gaps between seasons. TV as a whole feels less ambitious and substantial – not to mention reliably delivered – than it once did. But it is Netflix, as the chief disruptor of the old TV model, that bears the most responsibility for this shift – and that is perhaps most vulnerable as a result. It has become, for many, a platform that is clicked on to out of habit, rather than rushed to in fevered anticipation of the latest episode of a great show.
Perhaps that will change in the wake of all the corporate bloodletting; the new chief content officer, British industry veteran Peter Rice, has been talked up for his excellent taste, having overseen a dynamite run of films (28 Days Later, Sideways, Juno) when he was head of the Fox Searchlight studio. Or perhaps it doesn’t really matter either way: habit is a strong drug, and Netflix equals TV for many people. Indeed, its primary rival, in its own estimation, is not the BBC or Disney+ or the like, but YouTube, which is why it has been trying to hoover up many of the same things that are popular on that platform: influencer videos, podcasts, live sport.
Netflix has long dreamed of being the “everything store”, a place that has all the content you could ever need – which is a fine ambition. I just wish there was something good to watch on it once in a while.
