title: A Course Called Ireland: Bill Murray clearly hated making his new golfing show – but it’s extremely fun to binge
description: In his rogue new travelogue, the Hollywood star tees off, has drunken pub singalongs – but mostly just proves how tired he is of fame
content:
In his rogue new travelogue, the Hollywood star tees off, has drunken pub singalongs – but mostly just proves how tired he is of fame
I ’m suspicious of travelogues, which often feature celebrities in contrived situations, serving up a sentimental postcard of a place that is tantamount to a lie. I also hate how famous people are inexorably drawn to golf: a boring game historically predicated on a rancid mix of social exclusivity and extensive land ownership. So it was perverse of me to watch a show in which author Tom Coyne drives around Ireland playing various courses with his friend, actor Bill Murray . It’s the perfect intersection of none of my interests.
I was, however, hooked by a strange promise in A Course Called Ireland’s introductory sequence. “This is not a show about golf,” it says. “It’s not even a show about Bill Murray.” This was immediately followed by a scene in which an Irish woman standing by the roadside misidentified the actor as Bill Cosby. OK, I thought. What are they teeing up here?
There’s a hole in at least one of those promises. A Course Called Ireland (Sunday 25 October, 9.30pm, BBC Two) is intended to be a jocular road trip, in which the two friends meet colourful characters and reflect on their own Irish heritage, between spectacular rounds on the rugged links. It’s based on a journey Coyne documented in his book of the same name, in which he played every course in the country. Which again, sounds like a marriage in crisis to me – but the book is very popular.
What we get is a fascinating, existential snapshot of fame. A camera crew trailing a Hollywood legend around a series of Irish villages is, unavoidably, the story. Murray can’t stop for a wee without being mobbed. The director wants as much Murray on screen as possible. The 76-year-old Ghostbuster wants to give the spotlight to anyone else who’ll take it. The wheels quickly start to come off. He rips up the itinerary, digs in his heels, grouches. He cringes at the artifice of making TV, such as pretending to meet people for the first time. He’s been famous for 50 years – and it shows.
He also embodies the paradox of the reluctant celebrity, which is that most of them can’t stop doing things that perpetuate their myth. They hate the fame, they need the fame. The oddball actor is known for giving regular people “a Bill Murray story”, crashing graduation ceremonies or stepping behind the bar to pull pints. We see that here, as he hoists a groomsman on his shoulders, or gently pushes an ice-cream in a woman’s face. As he jokes, “If I wasn’t famous, I’d probably have a few more cuts and bruises to the face.”
In one sequence, Murray refuses to attend a pub as scripted, and disappears to a nearby evening of folk music instead. Later, once filming has been aborted, he returns to the pub to lead the room in a drunken singalong. It’s exactly what the producers would have wanted; for Murray, such larks only have meaning if they aren’t being manufactured for the cameras. There is something heroic in his stubbornness. (Of course, someone films the whole thing on their mobile phone.)
The show bends many of the format rules, by necessity or design. The BTS feeling of a crew working around a recalcitrant star is juicy. Each episode also boasts a voiceover from a supporting character – the proprietor of a tweed shop, a junior runner, Ireland’s former minister of the arts. The best is Margaret, an elderly woman outside a sweet shop who tells Murray he was the best thing in “Gorseboosters”. “Bill is 98% Irish if you look at his DNA, which I haven’t, but it says so here in the script,” she lilts. These unexpected and charming turns ground a show that otherwise feels like Lost in La Mancha set in Ballybunion.
If the show fails by its own marker, it succeeds at being funny, peculiar and melancholy: a much higher bar. It’s as unconventional and highly watchable as its impish star, the one it pretends not to be hopelessly in thrall to. What’s more, I finally understand why celebrities love golf so much. They want to be as far away from other people as possible.

title: ‘It annoys people when I eat’: Siobhán McSweeney on perfect snacks, parental pressure – and the power of being ‘a delicious fatty’
description: The Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast?
content:
The Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast?
S iobhán McSweeney is teaching me her preferred way to enjoy a packet of cheese and onion crisps. She has arranged two matching slabs of Cadbury’s Dairy Milk chocolate, two piles of Tayto crisps and two cans of Guinness on the table in front of us – and is issuing strict instructions. “Don’t swallow!” she booms theatrically, and I freeze, my mouth full of Taytos. The trick, McSweeney explains, is to get the crisps, chocolate and Guinness into your mouth at the same time, and then swill it all around a bit to make a kind of boozy, oniony soup. “See?” McSweeney is watching me carefully to check I am putting all the ingredients into my mouth in the correct order. “It’s delicious! Just delicious!”
McSweeney burst into the public consciousness back in 2018 with Derry Girls , a comedy series about a group of Catholic schoolgirls, set against the background of the Troubles in 1990s Northern Ireland. McSweeney won a Bafta playing the girls’ headmistress, Sister Michael – a potty-mouthed, judo-loving nun – and can count Martin Scorsese as a fan. Asked for a TV recommendation during a panel discussion in 2022, the director name-checked Derry Girls and then lifted his fist in the air in a kind of salute, exclaiming rapturously, “Those nuns!”
I have spent so many hours watching McSweeney in character as Sister Michael that it is almost a shock to see her without a nun’s habit. We are meeting today, in a conference room in London, because McSweeney is taking over from Grace Dent as the new host of the Guardian’s food podcast, Comfort Eating . I arrived at the interview with a multipack of Taytos, a family‑size Dairy Milk and two cans of Guinness in my bike bag, because McSweeney chose this concoction as her favourite snack when she appeared on the podcast as a guest, back in 2021. She also told a story about eating a caterpillar that had fallen from her moth-infested ceiling into her stir‑fry, purely because she couldn’t be bothered to fish it out. “Listen: protein,” she says today, remembering that caterpillar. “Free protein where you can.”
Since Derry Girls, the actor has made a habit of portraying slightly intimidating women. She plays the achingly sarcastic celebrity chef Della Fry in Amandaland , and hosts the Irish version of The Traitors, in which she commands a pack of wolfhounds and wears a lot of ruffs. But today, McSweeney’s short, silver‑grey hair is brushed back from her face and she is dressed casually, in trousers and a simple top. Sister Michael is always lolling back in her chair and surveying you sardonically across a desk – but the real McSweeney leans forward and asks a lot of questions.
It is lunchtime, so I have brought a takeaway from the Indian restaurant Dishoom with me, as well as the Taytos. “I love doing this podcast because it annoys people when I eat,” McSweeney says, tucking into a fish curry. Part of the reason why she accepted the job as host of Comfort Eating, she explains, is because visibly enjoying her food – as a woman who is not stick-thin – is a kind of provocation. “They’ve been told that somebody like me should not feel good about themselves,” she says, grinning toothily at me. “Being a delicious fatty.”
Ever since she first arrived at drama school, in the early 2000s, people have been telling McSweeney to lose weight. “Agents, casting directors, teachers” – McSweeney checks the list off for me now, almost breezily. “I have been different sizes but it’s never been an acceptable size,” she says. “‘Unruly’ I call it – there’s sort of an unruliness that has been forced upon my body that I don’t feel about it, but other people feel it’s unruly and it doesn’t behave.” All the other girls at her drama college were starving themselves, McSweeney remembers now. “They were starving in secondary school as well – it was the 90s! I don’t know how I managed to escape it.” She is grinning at me again. “I don’t think I have the willpower to not eat. I don’t really have much discipline.”
It strikes me that continuing to like yourself and your body, in the face of such vicious scrutiny, is not so much a failure of will as its opposite – proof that McSweeney has a will of absolute iron. Responding to a particularly poisonous bout of online criticism of her looks back in 2023, McSweeney delivered a kind of masterclass in the art of self-worth, tweeting: “I’m really lovely. I like my hair. And I like food. And I’m not sorry I’m loud. I thought feminism fights for me to be loud. And my accent is gorgeous. My teeth are yellow and wonky that’s true. But I sorta don’t care. And sure are you perfect?”
McSweeney says she wouldn’t even bother to respond to online abuse like that these days, because “it’s so insane now on social media. There is no honesty to it because we don’t know if they are bots or not.” But when I push her on the willpower point, and suggest that there is something inherently political about refusing to lose weight in her industry, she agrees with me. “I do get perverse pleasure in [responding to those] people who expect me to feel bad – by insulting me, by calling me ‘fat’ – by going, ‘And?’”
McSweeney also credits her mother, who she describes as “the kind of mam who would be round the back having a cigarette reading Dostoevsky”, with teaching her to aspire to a version of womanhood that wasn’t about appealing to men. “She wasn’t interested in me having boyfriends that much – she was, like, men will come, men will go; it’s fine.”
“She just instilled this utter independence in me that didn’t centre in any way on a romantic relationship.” McSweeney pauses for a moment here, and seems to reconsider. “I mean … she wasn’t completely immune to all that. No one is strong enough to combat that, you know? And there would be a bit of, ‘Would you not brush your hair?” McSweeney is putting on her mother’s voice now and making pleading motions. “Please, just briefly! Just give it a quick brush!”
S iobhán McSweeney grew up in County Cork, Ireland. Her father was a civil servant and her mother ran a cottage industry baking bread and cakes to sell to local shops, so the young Siobhán woke up every day to the smell of fresh soda bread. But, like any teenager worth their salt, McSweeney only wanted what she couldn’t have. “I went to the neighbours at one point because they had white sliced pan and red jam, and I thought, they’re so lucky, I have to go home now and have my freshly baked brown soda bread and my local butter,” she says. Her mother would make her school lunch every day with bread so fresh it was still warm. McSweeney remembers looking at her lunchbox and thinking “no one suffers more than me”.
McSweeney knew from an early age that she wanted to act. She says that as a child she would wish on a star every night that she would become an actor, and tells me that she once spent an entire day at school pretending she was in a sitcom, pausing every now and again to play the laugh track in her head. “Or I’d look to the camera” – she mimes whirling her head around to lock eyes with an imaginary film crew. “How obnoxious! What a pest to be around.”
McSweeney’s parents, however, had other plans for her. “We didn’t know anyone who was an actor. People on the telly didn’t look like me, didn’t sound like me,” she says. “My parents were, like, so what would that mean? You would do the panto once a year? You’re meant to work!”
Speaking to the Irish Times in August, McSweeney said that anybody in the creative industries has “an angel and a devil on your shoulder, and the devil quite often is your parents going, ‘Don’t embarrass us.’” Did she feel as if her parents were embarrassed about her? “Yeah, absolutely yeah – it’s embarrassing to have your child standing up there making a tit of themselves,” she says. “Also, Ireland in the 80s, you blend in – the idea of standing out is quite … ” she tails off thoughtfully. “I think it was a protective idea – when you are in the open you are open to abuse and people taking advantage. All these things are true and I understand fully why any parent wouldn’t want that for their child.”
M cSweeney was virtually unknown before the release of Derry Girls , which came out after her 40th birthday. She tells me that in a strange way she is pleased that fame came later in life for her, because she knows people “who have achieved success very early on in their career and their heads are turned”. But the years she spent trying and failing to get parts were gruelling. “I taught, I waitressed, I pulled pints, I went on the dole, I worked at music festivals,” she says. “And I was shit at every single one of them.”
She remembers being particularly “shit” at the waitressing. “Sure, I didn’t know anything about food. I was pouring the wine the way my parents would drink wine, which would be wine right up to the top of the glass, and I didn’t know about al dente,” she says. “I thought, who is this Al Dente?”
There was a point in the 2010s when she considered giving up acting completely. “I hadn’t worked in over a year and I had just got a litany of nos,” she remembers. “And now it’s getting harder and harder for not-rich people to be an actor.” McSweeney had received grants from the EU and a scholarship to study drama at the Central School of Speech and Drama – and that kind of funding literally doesn’t exist any more. “I get really panicky thinking about the other Siobháns who don’t get what they’re meant to do,” she says, and her face is unusually serious for a moment – but then she looks at me and her eyes begin to twinkle. “I mean it should be better, it should be a bit more useful than being a clown – but, you know, it’s what I’m meant to do.”
Part of the struggle when she was being rejected at auditions was the lack of decent roles available for women. In previous interviews, McSweeney has said that casting directors explicitly told her that even though she was the funniest person in the audition room, they were going to give the part to a “prettier, younger, less funny” woman. “I graduated into a world where I really hoped somebody had a girlfriend because there was no way on earth a programme was going to centre on a woman,” she says to me now. But she wouldn’t even be in the running for the girlfriend part because “they wanted somebody who was more ‘girlfriend material’, ie, more acceptable – so, bland and pretty”.
McSweeney says she would never be considered for the main character, “always the satellite”. She rolls her eyes. “And now I’m the mother.”
McSweeney tells me that she is deliberately taking on more presenting work because properly meaty, complex acting roles for women on TV are still so rare. As well as The Traitors Ireland, McSweeney hosts The Great Pottery Throw Down . She landed the job after an appearance on a Great British Bake Off festive special in which she had a meltdown over making a trifle and ended up sitting on a bench with Sandi Toksvig, drinking champagne (“They went, that’s who we want”).
McSweeney is also an acclaimed theatre actor. She played opposite her Derry Girls co-star Nicola Coughlan last year in The Playboy of the Western World at the National Theatre, and says that being onstage is what she has always enjoyed the most (she remembers being a child and “seeing red curtains on the telly and having a funny feeling in my belly”). But presenting is “work I find interesting – and it also pays more than the theatre”, she says, with characteristic honesty.
Presenting jobs pay better than TV shows do, too – even the most successful ones. McSweeney has said publicly “I think I got 40 quid” in residuals when Derry Girls sold to Netflix. The programme has been viewed for a total of 17.3m hours on the platform. Can that figure possibly be true? McSweeney nods enthusiastically. “When Netflix bought it we got fuck all!”
W hen she was 27, McSweeney lost her mother, who never saw her daughter succeed as an actor. In her Bafta acceptance speech , which has been viewed 467,000 times on YouTube, McSweeney told a story about how, as her mother lay dying, she pleaded with her to retrain as a teacher. “If she could see me now, winning a Bafta for playing a teacher,” she said, wearing a red vinyl dress and laughing, lifting her bare arm above her head to punch the air with her award: “Joke’s on you, Mam!”
Would her mother feel pride, if she could see her daughter now? Or relief? “Er, relief,” says McSweeney, quick as a flash. Then she pauses for a second. “And I think she would like … I have a lot of opinions and she would like the way I speak about certain opinions.” In the same Bafta speech, McSweeney thanked the people of Derry, calling out the “ignorance and stupidity” of their political leadership, and she is a vocal critic of both English and Irish policy. Last year she was among those who campaigned successfully for the thousands of UK-based survivors of the work camps for “fallen women” that were in operation until the 90s in Ireland – known as the Magdalene laundries – to be given compensation without losing their rights to benefits.
Would her mother have been proud of her feminism? “I think she would have been as close to proud as I would allow her to be,” says McSweeney, almost shyly. “And my dad, too … He was a natural feminist rather than a learned one – couldn’t think of anything I couldn’t do because of my gender, that would make no sense to him.”
Her father died in 2018. McSweeney moved back into the family home to live with him during his final illness. She drew on those experiences to make Spud in 2024, a beautiful, surprisingly funny short film about a middle-aged woman caring for her dying father (McSweeney summarises the plot, with fabulous bluntness, as being about “an unfuckable woman who is rural and who cleans her daddy in a bath”).
In one particularly tender scene, the father and the daughter, who is played by McSweeney herself, sit eating rice pudding together in front of the telly. Was that drawn from life? Was food a comfort for them both during that time? “The really sad thing about illness is that it often takes your appetite away,” she says. “I found it with my mum, too: her appetite went towards the end.” She tells me a story about sneaking a carbonara into the hospital to give to her mother, and the sadness of her not being able to eat it. “She was so beautiful and everybody’s mam is beautiful, but she ended up with a flat belly – and I was, like, what use is a flat belly? I want a lovely big belly.”
Right at the end of Spud, McSweeney’s character finds out her father has died, and the camera closes in on her face. There is pain there but there is also something else: she is smiling slightly. It’s a great moment because it is so unexpected – and so honest. You can see in the daughter’s expression that, on some level, her father’s death has come as a relief. “I remember when my dad died, I was sort of manic for about six months because I suddenly was free, and I was grieving, but I was also free,” McSweeney says. In the immediate aftermath of her father’s death, McSweeney was bursting with ideas for new projects. “With no parents, you don’t feel like you’re letting the entire family down if you say or do something.”
Between 2018 and 2021, McSweeney went through a period that she has described – in a moment of understatement worthy of Sister Michael herself – as containing lots of “life stuff”. Her aunt, who had been a kind of surrogate mother to her, died the year after she lost her father. In 2019, her London flat burned down because of a faulty plug adaptor. Then, in 2021, in the middle of filming a Kathy Burke-directed crime drama, Holding , she broke her leg so badly that at one point the doctors thought they would have to amputate it.
How did she cope? “We place romantic and biological relationships at the heart of our sort of experience,” says McSweeney, but it was her friends who got her through it. She tells me that when she was struggling the most, she became furious with one of her friends and accused him of talking about her behind her back with the rest of the group. “I was, like, ‘Are you all talking about me?’” She puts her hands on her hips here and mimes outrage, and then she switches characters so she can play her friend’s role: “And he was, like, ‘Yeah! We’re meant to do that! We care about you! We’re making sure you’re OK, we’re asking each other, how do you think she’s doing?’”
McSweeney talks about this being a moment of realisation. She saw that friendship has an elasticity and a resilience that no romantic relationship can ever really have. “You have a fight with your boyfriend and that could destroy the relationship, right?” she says. “You have a fight with your friend, you go into your respective corners, you sulk. You call other friends. You bitch about each other. Then you go back, you have a coffee, you get drunk!”
M cSweeney’s friends are annoyed with her at the moment, because she is getting her kitchen redone in her new flat, and she is refusing to install a dishwasher – as a way of preventing them from popping in for meals. “I don’t want you coming over and eating my food,” she says. She has described herself as a “sociable misanthrope” in previous interviews. As much as she loves her friends, she is not that fond of cooking and cleaning for them. I tell her I like going to other people’s homes and letting them cook for me, and then leaving without doing any washing up at all. “I bet you do!” she says. “It’s horrible for the other person – get out of my house!”
So who does she cook for? “Myself!” she says, looking me right in the eye – and for the first time there is a kind of challenge in her voice. She doesn’t like to talk about any romantic partners.
She lives alone in a flat she recently bought in London. What does she cook for herself? “It’s so boring, but I’ve been working so hard for the last five years that all my food is comfort food and I try to make it as healthy as possible,” she says. She makes a lot of bone broth and a lot of ramen. “Also, I like white bread toasted till it’s nearly black, with Kerrygold butter” – but the butter has to be sliced extremely thickly, she specifies. It has to be “sliced like cheese”.
We’re nearly out of time – and Dair y Milk. McSweeney has been hospitably breaking off slabs of chocolate and handing them to me every few minutes for the last half hour, so I can keep making Guinness-crisp soup in my mouth. I’ve got time for just one final question, so I ask McSweeney what she is looking forward to. “I’ve got my first day off for 26 days tomorrow,” she says, “but I’ve got nothing in the fridge.” She plans to go to a bakery round the corner and buy some freshly made soda bread. Ironically, after all that teenage rebellion, she likes it now. Would her mother be pleased to look down on her doing that? “Yes,” she says. “And I’m going to buy it with the money I earned being a clown.”

title: Violence, intimidation and fear: 10 years on from the ‘Jungle’, life in Calais migrant camps is harsher than ever
description: People living in tents in northern France hoping to find asylum in England face increasing intimidation from police and far-right agitators
content:
People living in tents in northern France hoping to find asylum in England face increasing intimidation from police and far-right agitators
I n the decade since the demolition of the “Jungle ”, an area of Calais where thousands of asylum seekers set up makeshift shelters before embarking on Channel crossings to the UK, everything and nothing has changed.
This week, in a woodland clearing not far from one of Calais’s busy main roads, several brightly coloured tents are pitched. A jacket hanging from a tree branch blows in the brisk autumnal breeze alongside a belt decorated with union flags. It is only October but the wind makes the temperature feel several degrees chillier.
“I live in a tent,” says Adam*, at a nearby charity-run phone charging session. He is an electrical engineering student from Sudan who fled his country when the war started. “We have been evicted so many times. It is not worth having any possessions because the police take everything. I only have the clothes you can see me wearing now.”
Successive UK governments have spent hundreds of millions of pounds on numerous initiatives to curb illegal migration via northern France , including paying the French for police enforcement along the coast. On Wednesday Rob Jones, the director general of operations at the National Crime Agency, told MPs that thanks to UK-France efforts the business model of the people smugglers enabling small boat crossings was “starting to shake”.
Nonetheless more than 200,000 asylum seekers have made the journey from Calais to the UK since the “Jungle” – one of the largest of its kind in Europe – ceased to exist. On the 10th anniversary of it being torn down, about 4,000 people remain in smaller camps in Calais, Dunkirk and Boulogne, waiting to cross the sea.
The predominant nationalities hoping to reach the UK are almost the same as they were in 2016 – Eritreans, Sudanese, Somalis, Iranians and Afghans. Their resolve to reach the UK, where they believe they will be safe, has not weakened. Living conditions continue to be harsh and basic.
While the number of people arriving in the UK illegally on small boats has been steadily dropping, from more than 41,000 in 2025 to about 21,000 so far this year, this can in part be attributed to an overall reduction of irregular migration to Europe, as well as a large number of windy days – making Channel crossings more difficult.
In 2016 almost nobody crossed the Channel in small boats. But from 2018 onwards, small boat crossings began to rise. A policy of “zero point de fixation” was introduced in France to prevent the establishment of another large encampment. As a result, small living sites in wooded areas – particularly in Calais – are evicted on average once every 48 hours, with asylum seekers having tents, clothing and other possessions destroyed or confiscated by police in the process. Most will set up a new camp nearby, often with donations of tents from charities.
Human Rights Observers, an organisation set up to document the treatment of asylum seekers in northern France by authorities, described this cycle as the “border spectacle”.
Far-right agitators have travelled from the UK to harass people in the makeshift camps, leading French authorities to ban 10 people from entering the country. But more continue to arrive. Recently two agitators from Belgium and a third from Poland also travelled to northern France to harass and intimidate the asylum seekers.
Many at the phone charging session have attempted to cross the Channel to the UK several times. This week’s home affairs committee heard evidence that the average number of crossing attempts a person has increased from three to seven.
Treatment by police is a much-discussed topic among those charging their phones. The French charity Utopia 56, which supports displaced and homeless people, says it has documented a 40% increase in violence by police towards asylum seekers between April and August 2026 compared with the same period last year.
“I understand that the police are doing their work but why do they have to be so aggressive?” says one boy at the session, who does not wish to be named. “They stop me so often in Calais even when I am not trying to cross. Life in Calais is too difficult, everyone wants to leave as quickly as possible. I’m 16, I’m too young for this life but I don’t have a choice.”
Human Rights Observers counted 539 evictions of 3,792 people in Calais last year. They say firewood used for warmth and cooking is seized during evictions.
Project Play, which supports displaced children and families in northern France, also says they have observed an increase in aggressive behaviour by police.
“In recent years, we have seen an escalation in violence against everyone at the border – including children and families,” Katie Hall, advocacy lead at Project Play, said. “This year, we have also seen the police forcibly separating families, including by preventing parents from reaching children already on boats by taking hold of their other children.
“This is catastrophic for human rights, and reflects a politics devoid of empathy and humanity.”
With his phone fully charged, Adam leaves the session with a cheerful wave, carrying several takeaway containers of food provided by the charity to share with friends in neighbouring tents.
“I don’t know if I will ever find a way of continuing my degree but for now I am just trying to find somewhere I won’t be evicted from every two days,” he says. “I would like to reach the UK because I can speak English. But I am scared of the water so don’t want to get into a dinghy. I am trying to claim asylum in France. There is no straight road to safety.”

title: Tim Dowling: why did I buy an electric car? Because I wanted a medal
description: Lunch with my agent is going nowhere, so I decide to share my latest motoring anecdote
content:
Lunch with my agent is going nowhere, so I decide to share my latest motoring anecdote
I’m having lunch with my agent – an infrequent occurrence, because neither of us ever has any good news for the other. This lunch is no different.
“Sorry to make you come all this way,” she says, “but I had to be near the office today.” She hints at some complex contractual negotiations involving an author for whom, I suspect, she always has good news.
“Did you come on the tube?” she says. “Did it take for ever?”
“I drove, actually,” I say. “Because I have an electric car.”
People sometimes ask why I bought an electric car. What did I want from it? To save money? To help the environment? To guard myself against future fuel shortages, or toxic emissions, or both?
The truth is: I wanted a medal. I wanted people to see the little green rectangle on my number plate and think: there goes a great guy, doing his best; let’s slow down and give him plenty of room to pull into our lane.
This does not happen. The official honours bestowed on electric car owners are actually pretty paltry: a discount on the London congestion charge and a slightly abbreviated MOT test. And you get no credit for being the green part of a traffic jam.
A few days earlier my wife and I had been invited to have lunch with the older one and his girlfriend, on the other side of town. In the morning, my wife declares that she will drive.
Traffic is light on the way, and we arrive ahead of schedule. There is, however, absolutely nowhere to park. Every available space is occupied.
On a second trawl through the neighbourhood a sudden gap appears ahead of us. “What about there?” my wife says, slowing down. I look up at the sign as we pass.
“It’s for electric cars only,” I say. “Hey, wait! That’s us!”
“But wait,” I say. “It’s actually a charging point. You have to be actively charging the car while you’re in it.”
“Fine, we’ll do that then,” she says. “It can’t be more expensive than parking.”
“But it’s broken,” I say. “The outlet thing is all taped up.”
“Well, it’s not our fault it doesn’t work, is it?” she says, pulling in.
I get out of the car and look at the sign and the broken plug, and my wife.
“I think that if I were a parking warden, I would love to give this car a ticket.”
“Oh, for fuck’s sake,” my wife says, choosing, on this occasion, to shoot the messenger.
We make two more wide circles of the area, varying the route slightly each time until we are a little lost.
“There!” my wife says, pointing. “What’s wrong with that one?”
Behind us a man in a car beeps, his impatience unmodulated by the green band on our number plate. My wife pulls over to let him pass. I have to open my door to examine the plug situation more closely.
“It appears to be operable,” I say, leaning out for a better look.
“Yeah, but our socket’s on the other side,” I say. “It won’t reach unless we’re facing the other way.”
“That’s fine, I can turn around,” she says.
“And also,” I say, craning my neck, “this particular charging point seems to be part of a local scheme. Like, you need a special parking permit from the borough to even use it.”
“Sorry, but I am just reading what it …”
I stand up and shut the door. My wife reverses down the road, leaving me on the pavement. So, I think. This is how it ends.
But it turns out my wife has noticed that the man who beeped at us had just vacated a parking space half a dozen car lengths back.
“That was lucky,” she says, all smiles now.
Two days later a waitress comes to the table, and my agent and I order.
“So,” I say. “If you get the right tariff and you only charge at night, it is a lot cheaper. But don’t expect special treatment. There’s no medal.”
“I think we’ve had enough about electric cars now,” my agent says.
A brief silence follows – neither of us willing, for the moment, to be the first bearer of bad news.

title: From Fatherland to Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back: the week in rave reviews
description: Sandra Hüller excels as Thomas Mann’s daughter in a fine historical drama, and a BBC documentary about the Welsh mining tragedy will enrage. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
content:
Sandra Hüller excels as Thomas Mann’s daughter in a fine historical drama, and a BBC documentary about the Welsh mining tragedy will enrage. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Summed up in a sentence Sixty years after the Welsh mining disaster, people tell their devastating stories – and their infuriatingly difficult fight to get justice.
What our reviewer said “Further indignities were caused to the stricken villagers, powerfully evoked in this restrained documentary by well-chosen memories from its interviewees. Gaynor remembers her father sitting puce with rage every evening in his chair as the NCB continued to fight liability for the deaths and deny the (expensive) need to remove the tips.” Lucy Mangan
Further reading I survived for a reason’: Aberfan fights to preserve memory of disaster 60 years on
Summed up in a sentence Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou are joined by a roster of brilliant comedy names in the second series of their hilariously weird sketch show.
What our reviewer said “There’s also a bit about a sack-wearing, trad wife-style content creator (White) who enjoys eating croissants, making collages and, er, keeping the woman her boyfriend cheated with locked up in her basement. So silly, so irresistible.” Hannah J Davies
Summed up in a sentence In a shocking experiment, members of the public tour a fake “residential home” for disabled people that’s riddled with Nazi ideology – and their reactions need to be seen to be believed.
What our reviewer said “This is a show so disturbing, timely and surreal that within 90 seconds of viewing it alone, I am looking around for confirmation from an empty room that any of this is happening.” Frances Ryan
Summed up in a sentence Comedian Leo Reich’s new sitcom, produced by A24, takes on gen Z houseshare life in London, with guest stars Lena Dunham and Andrew Scott.
What our reviewer said “It Gets Worse is, in many ways, a classic sitcom about surviving your 20s, complete with intensely awkward sex scenes (“Pull out!” “I’m not even in!”). And yet there’s a lot more going on here.” Hannah J Davies
Further reading ‘I’m lovingly making fun of everyone I’ve ever met’: on the set of Leo Reich’s gen Z sitcom
Summed up in a sentence Paul Bettany stars in a WandaVision spin-off that is visually striking and good fun – but it can’t help overdoing it on the dialogue and fight scenes.
What our reviewer said “VisionQuest is sometimes entertaining and always clever, yet if it does have anything to say about human nature, it is drowned out by dizzying plot particulars and the need for a big brawl every episode.” Rachel Aroesti
Summed up in a sentence Hanns Zischler stars as Thomas Mann on his 1949 tour of Germany along with his daughter Erika, played by an extraordinary Sandra Hüller.
What our reviewer said “An impossibly elegant, poised historical vignette whose brevity and control can hardly contain its characters’ personal and historical pain.” Peter Bradshaw
Further reading ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four – or, possibly, five – of the year’s biggest films
Summed up in a sentence Acclaimed Korean director Lee Chang-dong returns with an inspired account of an unhappy married couple befriended by a documentary-maker and her wealthy husband.
What our reviewer said “A finely judged, beautifully acted and rather novelistic work, in which a character at one point actually compares her surroundings to something from a novel.” Peter Bradshaw
Further reading ‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender
Summed up in a sentence Spin-off from the warm and comforting BBC TV sitcom, that picks up not long after the events of the final episode of the haunted house comedy.
What our reviewer said “Breaking out of the 30-minute episode structure seems to have freed up the writers to unleash new levels of giddiness with added spoonfuls of silliness.” Cath Clarke
Summed up in a sentence Thirtieth anniversary re-release of the Wes Craven meta horror with Neve Campbell and Courteney Cox – and a still alarming masked killer.
What our reviewer said “This film is brash and smart in that distinctive 90s way – and the title sounds like an order.” Peter Bradshaw
Further reading Scream: darkly funny, extremely meta horror and a 90s time capsule that never gets old
Summed up in a sentence Third cinematic adventure for Aardman’s resourceful ovine, in a spooky-season caper in which Shaun’s pumpkin-supersizing serum ends up in a balding farmer’s hair-growth bottle.
What our reviewer said “This is another excellent family film, crammed as ever with top visual gags, great throwaway references and, of course, a homemade Heath Robinson contraption, so often to be found in Aardman films.” Peter Bradshaw
Further reading ‘He goes to the dark side’: behind the scenes on the Shaun the Sheep horror movie
Summed up in a sentence The extraordinary posthumous memoir of a Dutch poet.
What our reviewer said “Marsman’s language is so beautiful … and her textual references so original … she cites Leopardi, Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Robert Musil, Spinoza, Euripides, Wittgenstein and William James.” Edward Posnett
Summed up in a sentence The poet laureate takes on the ancient Mesopotamian epic about the adventures of a demigod king.
What our reviewer said “Armitage’s tactile, visceral version is a tour de force, combining careful scholarship with poetic verve and deft linguistic meldings.” Philip Terry
Summed up in a sentence A long-thought-untranslatable portrait of a breakdown by the man Karl Ove Knausgård considers Norway’s best living writer.
What our reviewer said “This is a universal story of modernity and its discontents, but Lund is at pains to give it a specifically Norwegian dimension.” Sukhdev Sandhu
Summed up in a sentence The definitive biography of Seinfeld creator Larry David.
What our reviewer said “In 1992, just before it became the biggest show in America, [David] told friends: ‘Honestly, I would rather spend a year in prison than do another season of Seinfeld. It would be peaceful. Nobody would make me write anything.’ He was only half joking.” Dorian Lynskey
Summed up in a sentence The former Scottish first minister on his family’s Gaza ordeal.
What our reviewer said “Under Fire is most powerful when Yousaf gives full vent to his anger at the unfolding genocide in Gaza and articulates not just the plight of his in-laws … but the barbarity of Israel’s actions.” Fiona Sturges
Summed up in a sentence This follow-up to the cult horror-satire Bunny has been shortlisted for the Wodehouse prize for comic fiction.
What our reviewer said “Awad is here to show us that romantasy can be serious literature, and nothing can really be too camp.” Sandra Newman
Summed up in a sentence The nine-piece London-based group take a radically fresh approach to traditional music, sounding raging, lo-fi and joyful as they link Britain’s violent past to its present.
What our reviewer said “The most immediate pleasure of Everything in Readiness lies in the head-spinning sonic surprises it delivers. As it lurches wildly around, you find yourself struggling to keep up, a sure sign that you’re in the presence of music that feels entirely fresh and different.” Alexis Petridis
Summed up in a sentence Its release delayed by ill health, Kiwanuka’s latest was made in tandem with 2024’s Small Changes – but it’s much more than a mere companion album.
What our reviewer said “It may have had experimental beginnings, but it sounds remarkably like the work of a man who knows exactly what he wants to do. You leave it hoping that he’s able to continue doing it at some point in the not-too-distant future.” Alexis Petridis
Further reading ‘Everyone can relate to pain and struggle. So I’m sharing mine’: Michael Kiwanuka on life after his devastating stroke
Summed up in a sentence Edward Gardner and the LPO are taut and dramatically alert in fine performances of these two theatrical works.
What our reviewer said “As for The Miraculous Mandarin Suite, this is as fine a performance as any, sleek and sinister in its evocation of the honeytrap antics of the sex worker and her thuggish pimps, swaggering or shy in her encounters with the old rake and the young man.” Clive Paget
Summed up in a sentence Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tension.
What our reviewer said “On Ana Jaya, where the experimentalism peaks, the line between instruments and vocals blurs as the sound dissipates. The effect is bodily: tension you can feel, but can’t quite pin down. It’s a brilliant, heady formula.” Safi Bugel

title: From Wildwood to John Legend: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead
description: Anination studio Laika takes flight with a grownup stop-motion tale, while the Grammy-, Oscar- and everything-winner returns with a Pharell-produced 11th album
content:
Anination studio Laika takes flight with a grownup stop-motion tale, while the Grammy-, Oscar- and everything-winner returns with a Pharell-produced 11th album
Wildwood Out now If Pixar was a chocolate bar, it would be a Mars, while Laika – whose new film Wildwood incorporates themes of war and child abduction – would be something like Green & Blacks. Darker and with more esoteric flavours, this stop-motion animation is not so much for the nursery school crowd, but for discerning pre-teens and adults alike. Ghosts: The Possession of Button House Out now The beloved BBC TV comedy gets a big-screen outing, with Simon Farnaby’s trouserless Tory MP ghost, Jim Howick’s dead scoutmaster, shot by a member of his own troop, Ben Willbond’s closeted second world war officer and the other regular cast members all returning. Fatherland Out now Joint winner of the best director prize at Cannes, Paweł Pawlikowski’s latest is set during the cold war, and sees an actor, writer and rally driver, Erika (Sandra Hüller), set off on a road trip across Germany with her dear old dad, the Nobel prize-winning writer Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler). Ali G: Who Iz I? Out now Twenty four years after Ali G Indahouse opened at No 1 at the UK box office, Sasha Baron Cohen revives his alter-ego for a followup, making his directorial debut in the process. Morgana Robinson also stars. Catherine Bray
Suede, Manic Street Preachers OVO Hydro, Glasgow, 28 October; First Direct Bank Arena Leeds, 30 October; touring to 12 November Christmas comes early for people of a certain vintage with a penchant for evergreen British rock bands in the shape of this co-headline tour. Expect a smattering of newer material – Antidepressants, the most recent opus by Suede is Mercury-nominated – and some undeniable classics from both. Michael Cragg
Jasmine Myra Norwich Arts Centre, 27 October; Earth, London, 28 October; St George’s, Bristol, 29 October Alto saxophonist-composer Jasmine Myra is on the rise within the cinematic spiritual jazz orbit of Manchester’s Gondwana Records, a visionary operation devoted to the soulful lyricism and storytelling she espouses. This tour will be a fascinating insight into just how far the very promising Myra is instrumentally ready to go. John Fordham
False Idols Halloween Drumsheds, London, 24 October Queer club night False Idols returns to London for a special Halloween blowout featuring Boo! Bitch! hitmaker Kim Petras. Other spooky banger merchants on the bill include Swedish alt-popper Cobrah, London’s Rose Gray and US rapper Cakes da Killa. MC
London Symphony Orchestra/Pappano Barbican Hall, London, 29 October The LSO is the latest major international institution to commission British composer Hannah Kendall, a distinctive, ambitious voice in contemporary classical music. Her new work I Have Discovered the Secret of Death features Grammy-winning mezzo Fleur Barron. Its world premiere is paired with Tchaikovsky’s impassioned Fifth Symphony. Antonio Pappano conducts. Flora Willson
Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Tate St Ives, to 3 May A big part of St Ives’s modernist boom in the early 2oth century, Barns-Graham (work pictured above) quietly became one of the UK’s most important artists of her era with an emotional take on abstraction, celebrated here with 170 works from throughout her career.
LS Lowry MK Gallery, Milton Keynes, to 28 February This big celebration of the life and work of one of England’s best-loved artists is the first institutional show of his grimy, gritty industrial painting for 13 years, and marks 50 years since his death.
The Rupture: No Condition Is Permanent Talbot Rice Gallery, Edinburgh, to 13 February Attempting to respond to a time of unprecedented political, social and economic change, this exhibition brings together a huge cast of international artists to reckon with our increasingly broken systems.
The Way We Live The Box, Plymouth, to 21 February This exhibition looks at the idea of the home, and what it means to a variety of artists including the likes of Do Ho Suh, Rachel Whiteread and recent Turner prize winner Jasleen Kaur. Eddy Frankel
The Lives of Others Adelphi theatre, London, to 9 January Director Robert Icke adapts the Academy award-winning film set in East Berlin, 1984. A writer and an actor are put under state surveillance – and a Stasi operative is inexorably drawn into their lives. Keira Knightley, Stephen Dillane and Luke Thompson star. Miriam Gillinson
Macbeth Liquid & Envy, Oldham, to 7 November While Oldham’s Coliseum theatre is being restored, it is staging work in imaginative locations around town. This site-specific take on Macbeth is set in a real-life nightclub, invoking a world of 70s gangsters, casinos and shifting social codes. MG
Hansel & Gretel and the Witch Northern Stage, Newcastle upon Tyne, 29 October to 1 November Choreographer Liv Lorent and her company BalletLorent have really cornered the market in fairytale family shows with a bit of edge and a lot of imagination. The latest is a new take on Hansel & Gretel that promises a brand new ending courtesy of its writer, the former poet laureate Carol Ann Duffy. Lyndsey Winship
Susan Calman Touring to 20 November The Glaswegian standup has presented a slew of TV programmes and done a Strictly shift in the decade since her last tour, but new show Tall Tales – which combines showbiz stories with meditations on grief and depression – proves this glam career pivot has done nothing to dent her twinkly misanthropy. Rachel Aroesti
Nocturne Apple TV, 30 October Stephen Graham is back in his most sinister role yet: a serial killer who is apparently able to murder from the confines of his underground cell. This psychological thriller (above) pits him against not one but two haunted detectives: Liev Schreiber’s ex-soldier Jonah and his protege Saga (Zazie Beetz).
A Course Called Ireland iPlayer & BBC Two, 25 October, 9.30pm As a genre, the celebrity travelogue has become tired and bloated, but this new series is fuelled by an unusual level of star power, as the one and only Bill Murrray embarks on a golf-based trip around Ireland. Extra craic comes courtesy of guests including Chris O’Dowd and Joanne McNally.
Minimum Wage Netflix, 25 October What started out as a micro-budget webseries about incompetent teens manning a pizzeria has been turned into a 28-part sitcom by Netflix, who will be hoping its cast – including newly recruited SNL cast member Grace Reiter – become comedy’s next big things.
Beat Luke Littler Netflix, 30 October Is darts really that hard? Find out this Friday, as 20 amateurs take on the 19-year-old world No 1 in Manchester in an attempt to win £501,000. The event will be streamed live, with Gary Lineker on hosting duties and Richard Osman contributing Pointless-style statistics. RA
Pardon My French Toast PC, Switch 2, out 29 October A brightly coloured 3D platformer, in which you’re a slice of anthropomorphic brioche toast able to cover himself in different spreads to gain a range of special abilities. Like a ZX Spectrum classic reheated for the 21st century.
Phantom Blade Zero PC, PS5, out 29 October An elite assassin is framed for murder and must prove his innocence while a fatal wound slowly kills him. Stylised martial arts in a dark fantasy realm? Hand me that sword. Keith Stuart
Michael Kiwanuka - Fudge Out now Originally due for release last autumn, this fifth album from the Brit-nominated Kiwanuka was delayed after he suffered a haemorrhagic stroke after returning home from a tour. While his recovery continues, the self-produced Fudge is a reminder of his immense talents, as showcased on opener Summer Clothes’ gospel-tinged swirl.
Sasha Alex Sloan – And the Crowd Goes Mild Out now The Boston-born singer-songwriter, who’s co-written songs for the likes of Olivia Rodrigo, Charli xcx and Karol G, returns with her fourth album. As the title suggests, Sloan’s own songs veer towards the doleful, with singles Glitter and Empty pairing rich melodies with soothing soft-rock flourishes.
Claud - Me and the Music Out now Co-produced alongside John Congleton (Alvvays, St Vincent), Brooklyn-based Claud’s third album marks a shift in their mindset. While 2023’s lauded Supermodel took things very seriously, Me and the Music finds a lightness in a heavy world, especially on She Doesn’t Love Me’s effervescent indie jangle.
John Legend - Muse Out now After dabbling in music for children with 2024’s lullaby-centric My Favourite Dream, the Egot winner returns to more grownup themes on this entirely Pharrell-produced 11th album. The soulful Daylight is an upbeat love song, while the more politically focused Fireflies fuses jazz and gospel. MC
The One About Matthew Perry Netflix, 27 October A moving film recounting the life and career of the late Friends actor charting his rise to TV stardom and lifelong battles with addiction, as well as the tabloid scandals that accompanied his fame.
How Houdini Made Magic Podcast TV’s favourite illusionist Derren Brown tells the story of one of magic’s most iconic figures, Harry Houdini, in this 10-part series. Brown builds a fascinating picture of how Houdini fashioned himself a modern celebrity image.
3ETV Somerset House Channel London cultural institution Somerset House is celebrating the 10th anniversary of its experimental interdisciplinary Studios space with this diverse online channel featuring archived performance pieces, documentary shorts and new commissions. Ammar Kalia

title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian diesel tankers headed for North America, says Moscow, as US tries to revive peace talks
description: Tankers part of US-Russia deal that could see 500,000 metric tonnes of fuel supplied to world market this month. What we know on day 1,704
content:
Tankers part of US-Russia deal that could see 500,000 metric tonnes of fuel supplied to world market this month. What we know on day 1,704
Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their ⁠way to North America, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak said ⁠on Friday . In ​a statement quoted by Russian news agencies, Novak said the cargoes were ⁠part of a deal that could see Russian companies supply 500,000 metric tonnes to US and world markets in October. “The first ⁠three fuel tankers are already on their ​way to the eastern ‌coast of ‌the Atlantic Ocean, with significant support from the ‌RDIF (Russian Direct Investment Fund),” Novak said. Under a deal announced this month by US president Donald Trump, Russia agreed ‌to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel ​prices in return for Trump temporarily lifting US sanctions on Russian fuel. Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged ⁠medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes, loaded with ultra-low sulphur diesel, is expected to arrive in ‌the US on 7 November.
The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky , where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians. Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations. Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.
The Oleshky ceasefire comes as the US is trying to organise new talks aimed at ending the war . Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US have agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three ⁠countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Zelenskyy said he hoped a meeting of the countries’ leaders would follow.
The peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by Trump seen as favouring Russia, including limitations being placed on the Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem accessing the system, he would straighten it out ​and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
As the UK government prepares next week for the first budget under Andy Burnham’s leadership, EU leaders have pressed the new prime minister at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort . EU officials say Canada and Japan also should do more to support Ukraine .
The UN nuclear watchdog IAEA said ⁠Fiday ​that repairs to key ⁠power infrastructure near Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power ​plant ‌had been completed ‌ under a ‌temporary ceasefire it brokered. The repairs strengthened the plant’s connection ‌to its sole remaining external power ​line, known as Ferosplavna-1, reducing the ⁠risk of another ​loss of ​off-site ​electricity at ​Europe’s largest ‌nuclear ​power ​station.

title: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?
description: Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons
content:
Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons
For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.
Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia.
The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.
It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border , named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.
“China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.
Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to support Vladimir Putin ’s war in Ukraine, and has held two summits with the Russian president in the past three years. In 2024, the leaders signed a mutual defence pact that includes a clause requiring the countries to come to each other’s aid if attacked.
In return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the opportunity to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional ally China .
North Korea stands to benefit from increased trade but for China, the bridge could be of more geopolitical value than economic given how little trade China does with its neighbour compared with its other partners.
However, the insular regime in Pyongyang is thought to be reluctant to increase its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing’s previous support for UN sanctions targeting the North’s nuclear weapons programme .
In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese support for UN sanctions has collapsed. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University. “However, because China’s enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).”
The North’s “open” border with China contrasts dramatically with the one it shares with South Korea. In 2024, the North said it would sever all rail and road links with its neighbour, months after Kim said he would abandon the goal of peaceful reunification and declared South Korea his country’s “ principal enemy ”.
But Fyodor Tertitskiy, a North Korea expert at Korea University in Seoul, believes neither China nor Russia can influence North Korea in any meaningful way, citing Kim’s refusal to surrender his nuclear weapons or moderate his iron grip on power – two changes that would be welcomed in Moscow and Beijing.
“Both countries understand that Kim Jong-un would rather accept a complete breakdown in relationships than submit,” he says. “So I doubt we are seeing a straightforward struggle for influence. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.”
Kim is more likely to turn to China improve his country’s struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. China may seek to recover lost influence by increasing trade and people-to-people exchanges, but the Kim regime prizes autonomy and wants to limit foreign ideological and cultural influences.”
The South Korean government said last year that at least 17 active road and rail links connect North Korea and China along their 1,400 km-long border.
Tertitskiy is “not particularly optimistic” that the increased contact the bridges will bring means improvements to the lives of ordinary North Koreans or lead to a more western-style economy. “I think it will make reform even less likely. Why pursue reforms and take risks when you can just get what you need from abroad?”
Analysts say the expected rise in trade across the Yalu bridge is likely to be modest at first. But it could become a bellwether for the state of Sino-North Korean ties, says Easley.
“China remains economically indispensable to North Korea in ways that Russia cannot replace,” he says, adding, “In that sense, the bridge may offer an inadvertent window into bilateral relations if flows are visibly interrupted in the future.”
