title: Woman who faked pregnancies, including with Bachelor star, sentenced to 30 days
description: Laura Owens, who also received seven years’ probation, fabricated medical records to prolong relationships
content:
Laura Owens, who also received seven years’ probation, fabricated medical records to prolong relationships
A woman who admitted to faking pregnancies and fabricating medical records while aiming to prolong relationships with men – including a star of the reality show The Bachelor – has been sentenced to 30 days in jail in Arizona as well as seven years’ probation.
Laura Owens, 36, received her punishment on Friday in Maricopa county superior court nearly two months after pleading guilty to felony counts of fraudulent schemes and artifices, perjury and identity theft in a case that has been the subject of multiple true-crime podcasts.
“I’ve thought about the choices that brought me here every moment of every day, and I wish more than anything I could go back to the moments that I still had the opportunity to make different choices,” Owens said to judge Jeffrey Rueter shortly before he sentenced her. “I genuinely wish I had made better choices and hadn’t panicked.”
She was thrust under authorities’ scrutiny amid a legal fight with Clayton Echard, who starred in the 26th season of The Bachelor in 2022 – and contested her claim that he had impregnated her with twins after an encounter at his suburban Phoenix home in 2023, as the Arizona Republic reported.
Owens eventually claimed that she had a miscarriage. But the family court judge presiding over that case, Julie Mata, in 2024 determined Owens had falsified sonograms and medical records and lied under oath, according to reporting by the Arizona Republic and the Phoenix news outlet KPNX .
Beside ordering her to pay Echard’s legal fees, Mata referred Owens to prosecutors.
Prosecutors filed formal criminal charges against Owens in May 2025 in connection with Echard, 33. They then criminally charged her in relation to claims of having become pregnant by another man whom she dated in Scottsdale in 2021, the Arizona Republic reported.
The outlet wrote that prosecutors charged Owens with using forged medical records and misappropriating other women’s identities to buttress her deceptive claims. Both Echard and the second man were represented by the same family law attorney, Gregg Woodnick, who was credited with helping authorities investigating Owens to link the two cases.
Owens pleaded guilty on 28 August, setting the stage for her sentencing on Friday, which the Phoenix news outlet KSAZ livestreamed .
“I know there are people who have suffered because of decisions that I’ve made, and I want to take accountability for that,” Owens – the daughter of National Radio Hall of Fame inductee Ronn Owens – said to Rueter. “I am profoundly, profoundly sorry for the pain, distress and expense I’ve caused them and for failing to meet the standard of honesty that this court had every right to [expect] from me.”
In his own remarks to Rueter, Echard asked the judge to incarcerate Owens, asserting: “She’s not sorry. She’s sorry she got caught.”
He also said: “If you don’t take her out of her environment, she’s going to come back.”
Rueter concluded Friday’s sentencing by ordering Owens to immediately be jailed until 22 November and then to complete seven years of probation.
The judge noted that Owens could technically be sentenced to up to 12.5 years in prison if she ultimately fails to complete probation and has it revoked.
Rueter said he acknowledged Owens had inflicted “emotional and financial harm” to multiple victims, but that he did not think it was “the right thing” to put “a potentially mentally ill person who has committed a non-violent offense, with no prior criminal history, in prison”.
“I’m not going to do that,” Rueter said.

title: Five Great Reads: The fallout from French riots, supersized wealth and throwing rocks at the telly
description: The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert
content:
The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert
Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here
H ello and welcome to the weekend. The last seven days have been punctuated by political unrest in Europe with groups angry over the state of schools, the cost of living, and housing. Elsewhere, otherwise peaceful residents are throwing rocks at their tellies in their own personal revolt at omnipotent technology. You might want to hold off the coffee until after reading this one.
The protests gripping a string of European countries this month have largely been told through shocking pictures of violence – particularly on the streets of Paris. The riots in France have prompted questions over police tactics, as Emmanuel Macron’s government tries to get a handle on the civil unrest. Politicians are calling for ruthless sentencing, but lawyers blame the politicians for the poverty , and anger, behind their clients’ behaviour.
Fast-tracked fallout: Of the 2,500 people arrested during last weekend’s rioting and looting across the country , more than 900 are being fast-tracked through the courts using a procedure called comparution immédiate (immediate appearance). It sends them to trial straight or shortly after being taken into custody, or within three days if they are held in pretrial detention.
As Kim Willsher uncovers, most were young and unemployed, others in work with families. A 19-year-old student with no previous criminal record who was caught on his way home with several stolen black pullovers from a looted clothing store was fined and given a 14-month suspended prison term. “It was just a question of opportunity,” he said. “I thought: everyone else is doing it, why not me? I regret it.”
How long will it take to read: Two and a half minutes.
Further reading: What’s next for France after a weekend of riots ? And pro-Trump Maga media is in a froth over the protests .
The midterm elections are fast approaching, and Donald Trump is “ barnstorming the country ” before Americans head to the polls on 3 November. With his approval rating collapsing, and polls showing Democrats could wrest back control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, some have called Trump’s midterm push a “desperation tour”. But can he rescue the Republicans, or is the increasingly authoritarian president making life harder for his Maga mates?
Could the democrats take Kansas? Washington DC bureau chief David Smith was in Park City, Kansas for a rally in support of Senator Roger Marshall, who is facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. The state has been red since 1932, with no Democrat winning a Senate seat since “ Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic and the Nazis became the biggest party in the German Reichstag”. Smith was on the ground for what was Trump’s first campaign rally in the state for eight years, but Smith writes his presence could nationalise this local election, drawing attention to the consequences the Iran war has had on the heavily agricultural state.
Testing the old playbook: With the cost of living, foreign wars and government corruption at the forefront of voters’ minds, will Trump’s old tricks – “hurling insults, stirring bigotry and telling lies” – still work among a weary electorate? Notable quote: Largely dismissive of opinion polls, Darrell Claphan, a retired sales worker, echoed the sentiments of the Maga merch-wearing Trump crowd: “He’s doing fantastic. He’ll go down in history being the number one president at what he’s done for the country in my lifetime.”
How long will it take to read: Three minutes and some change.
Further reading: Is the blue wave real ?
In the last decade, the rise of political violence has – tragically – been a worldwide phenomenon. And in Australia, federal politicians have had a growing sense that something was shifting in the country’s national life. This week’s alleged attack on MP Helen Haines, which made global headlines, saw that tide turn into reality.
From the global to the local: Those responsible for protecting politicians in Australia often take their cues from overseas, Guardian Australia’s political editor Tom McIlroy writes . When a gunman opened fire at the Canadian parliament in 2014, the government built a fence around Parliament House. Amid threats stemming from Covid-19 lockdowns, the Asio director general cautioned the warning light for political violence was “already flashing red”.
A turning point? “The alleged attack on Helen Haines shows something rapidly being lost in our politics,” Tom writes. “The shift in sentiment can no longer be dismissed as social media noise or harmless comment.”
How long will it take to read: Just over a minute.
Further reading: Politicians say more security would “let bad people win” ; and Brendan Cox writes that the alleged attack on Helen Haines is a punch to the gut .
Feature writer Sam Wollaston dropped in on the world of the uber-rich in Monaco at Europe’s biggest superyacht show . After committing a few fashion faux pas, and despite the boats on offer being out of his price range, Wollaston took a tour and got a feel for a few of the aquatic behemoths up for sale. You can’t escape their sheer size, Wollaston writes, but there is also “no escaping the truth”. The recreational boating industry produces about 16m tonnes of CO2 annually , and they are a “monstrous” symbol of global inequality.
‘Turds of the sea’: Superyachts are growing more and more popular among the world’s richest, and owners include Mark Zuckerberg, Roman Abramovich, and Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi. A 2024 study looked at 23 superyachts owned by 18 billionaires, and it showed the average annual carbon footprint of each of these yachts to be 5,672 tonnes. It would take an average citizen more than 800 years to produce the same carbon footprint. The supersized boats’ anchors and chains also “act like the grim reaper’s scythe”, damaging the Posidonia seagrass which thrives throughout the Mediterranean.
Notable quote: “They just want something that’s big and flashy and comfortable, they don’t care about anything else.” – A yacht broker on what his clients are looking for
How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.
Further reading: Can you enjoy a life on the ocean waves when it’s costing you £1,000 an hour?
It stands to reason that, as a growing number of people look for dumbphones over smartphones, in a bid to combat screen addictions and worries over privacy, their consumer habits might spill over to other tech too. The Guardian’s George Francis Lee spoke to people around the world who are fed up with their televisions .
‘The joke is on them’: We’re not talking luddites here. Among those now on the hunt for a “traditional” TV are a 71-year-old Illinois resident with a master’s degree in computer science, a Welsh woman who works in AI delivery and a public servant from Australia. Some are worried about privacy, others are frustrated at how quickly their devices slow down or need updating. “My friends all laugh at it when they come over,” Paul, who has a traditional telly admits, “but secretly I know the joke is on them. My little telly doesn’t spy on me, and has a DVD player built in.”
Notable quote: “It was enormously satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen.”
How long will it take to read: Three minutes.
Further reading: Can these dumbphone evangelists convince you to dump smartphones?
If you would like to receive these Five Great Reads to your email inbox every weekend, sign up here . And check out out the full list of our local and international newsletters .

title: Indiana police officer arrested for using Flock cameras to search wife’s details
description: Justin Craig charged with official misconduct and fraud, after searching plates of wife and ‘previous acquaintance’
content:
Justin Craig charged with official misconduct and fraud, after searching plates of wife and ‘previous acquaintance’
An Indiana police officer has been arrested on allegations that he misused Flock cameras hundreds of times in a case involving his wife and a previous acquaintance of hers.
Justin Craig of Georgetown police department, was charged with official misconduct and two counts of fraud. Documents show that he searched his wife’s license plate more than 80 times and that of a “previous acquaintance” of hers nearly 250 times, the news outlet WLKY reported.
The documents say Craig’s searches started in January and continued up to July.
A reporter from the Washington Post triggered the investigation, the documents show, after he called the Georgetown police chief with the tip.
An internal review by the Georgetown police found that the searches Craig conducted on the Flock system were unrelated to any police investigations, and he had intentionally mislabeled those searches to make them appear justified.
The searches had been labeled with subjects including traffic infractions, narcotics, assault/battery, theft and stolen vehicles.
Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans monthly.
Flock, the company behind the tech, provides cameras and software to more than 4,800 law enforcement agencies and nearly 1,000 businesses. Flock says it intends for its technology to aid criminal investigations, but it has come under increasing bipartisan backlash over alleged privacy violations and data-sharing.
There have been multiple reports of police officers across several US states who have allegedly misused or abused the technology. That includes officers who have been accused of using the cameras to stalk former romantic partners and to track down individuals seeking abortions.
The network the cameras feed in to is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ), whose aggressive tactics under the second Trump administration have drawn nationwide criticism.
After Craig’s arrest, his attorney, Matthew Lemme, released the following statement to multiple news outlets: “Flock sells this same technology to cities, homeowners associations, and shopping malls. When public criticism of it came, the response was to put it on the shoulders of individual police officers. The conduct alleged does not violate any law or department policy.”
The statement continued: “If the public or police agencies believe it should, the answer is to write that law or policy. Having that public conversation about privacy and practice is appropriate. Charging officers before it has even started is not. Officer Craig will file a motion to dismiss the charges against him.”
In August, Flock’s CEO announced the company would be taking steps to curb police abuses of its tech by mandating that law enforcement agencies switch on features that could help audit the way individual officers use its tracking capabilities.

title: Skye Blakely caps remarkable injury comeback with world gymnastics all-around title
description: The 21-year-old American claimed the world all-around title in Rotterdam, two years after a devastating injury ended her hopes of reaching the Paris Olympics
content:
American, 21, wins world all-around title in Rotterdam
Blakely ruptured achilles before 2024 Olympic trials
First US champion since Simone Biles three years ago
Skye Blakely completed a sensational comeback from a ruptured achilles tendon to win the women’s all-around title at the world gymnastics championships in Rotterdam on Friday, claiming the biggest individual prize in the sport outside the Olympics.
The 21-year-old American scored 55.733 points across four apparatus to finish ahead of Russia’s Liudmila Roshchina (55.199), with China’s Ke Qinqin taking bronze (55.032).
Blakely’s triumph came little more than two years after her Olympic ambitions were shattered when she ruptured her right achilles during floor exercise training, just two days before the US trials for the 2024 Paris Games. The injury required surgery and ended a season in which she had finished runner-up to Simone Biles at the national championships.
It was the second major setback of her career after she tore an elbow ligament while warming up for the Tokyo Olympic trials.
“Throughout the meet, I was telling myself ‘Do it for the girl in 2021 and the girl in 2024 who couldn’t do everything, just fight for her,’” Blakely told reporters. “That’s what I kept telling myself: ‘I am capable, I am ready’ and I made every version of myself extremely proud.”
“I already cried, but it just means the world to me,” Blakely said after qualifying at the Rotterdam Ahoy arena. “Knowing how much I’ve been through – two major surgeries, a lot of hardships, ups and downs.”
Blakely, a Dallas native, entered Friday’s final as the second-ranked qualifier and delivered under pressure, producing assured routines on uneven bars and balance beam before protecting a lead of more than a point on floor exercise.
Her 14.200 on beam, an apparatus that had caused problems during the Americans’ silver-medal finish behind China in Wednesday’s team competition, gave her a commanding advantage heading into the final rotation. A misty-eyed Blakely became overwhelmed by emotion after completing her floor routine, then wrapped herself in an American flag once the result was confirmed.
“It truly means the world to me, knowing how much I have overcome, all of the hardship that I faced and the days that I wanted to give up or didn’t think it was possible,” Blakely said. “To see it really come to be tonight, is just, it makes me so proud of myself and makes me reflect on little me who would dream of this.”
Algeria’s Kaylia Nemour, the leading qualifier, finished fourth after a mistake on her opening vault forced her to perform a less difficult attempt. She recovered with an outstanding performance on uneven bars but missed bronze by just 0.034 points. Fellow American Claire Pease finished seventh after falling from the balance beam.
Blakely, a University of Florida junior, became the first American to win the world all-around crown since Biles in 2023 , extending a US streak of podium finishes at every Olympics and world championships since 2003.
Competition continues on Saturday with the first apparatus finals. Blakely and Pease are set to compete in the women’s vault and uneven bars finals, while Fred Richard will contest the men’s floor exercise and Patrick Hoopes the pommel horse.

title: Corrections and clarifications

title: Mediator to decide whether Nick Reiner can use trust to pay for murder defense
description: Son of Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, who is accused of killing parents, says funds have been withheld
content:
Son of Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, who is accused of killing parents, says funds have been withheld
The legal dispute over whether Nick Reiner, who is accused of killing his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, can access a trust fund established for him by the couple decades ago will go to a mediator.
Reiner’s attorneys announced in court on Friday to a Los Angeles judge that all parties involved in the matter had scheduled “a global mediation” for December.
The 33-year-old Reiner has said he needs the funds in order to pay for his defense in the case, and that funding has been withheld for years, before their deaths, without legal justification.
“Nick loved his parents, and he is devastated by their deaths. But the facts about what did and did not happen to them are not at issue in this trust litigation,” his attorneys stated in a petition filed earlier this year. “Like anyone accused of a crime, Nick is presumed innocent, and he is entitled to mount his defense with the resources that are lawfully his own.”
Reiner is accused of first-degree murder in the deaths of his parents, Rob Reiner, an acclaimed director and actor, and photographer Michele Singer Reiner. Prosecutors allege that he fatally stabbed the couple in their Brentwood home last December, and fled the scene. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder.
The high-profile private attorney Alan Jackson briefly represented him, but left the case because Reiner could not pay attorney fees, according to court documents. Reiner has indicated that he plans to rehire Jackson if he can access the trust.
Rob and Michele Singer Reiner set up individual trusts for each of their children with “unambiguous instructions” that Nick Reiner was supposed to receive half its money when he turned 30 and the remainder at 35, according to a court filing. Reiner never received funds and his attorneys allege that a trustee who oversaw the trust gave “a shifting series of excuses and justifications” to deny Reiner the money.
During Friday’s hearing, an attorney for a trustee asked the judge to allow payments from the trust to Reiner’s commissary account, Rolling Stone reported.
If the parties reach a settlement, it must be approved by a judge.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Aaron Rodgers says NFL’s Paris game is safe despite PSG cancellation amid unrest
description: The Steelers quarterback says he trusts the NFL’s security assessment as civil unrest and severe weather disrupt preparations for Sunday’s game
content:
Steelers, Saints still on for NFL’s Paris debut on Sunday
Violent protests prompt US security warning for fans
PSG cancel Sunday match amid escalating Paris unrest
The NFL would have cancelled its first regular-season game in Paris, scheduled for Sunday, if the situation were unsafe, Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said on Friday, referring to the recent protests in the French capital.
France experienced some of its worst urban unrest in years last weekend, prompting President Emmanuel Macron to tighten restrictions on protests on Thursday amid fears that demonstrations planned for Saturday could turn violent.
The unrest has already forced the postponement of Sunday’s Ligue 1 match between Paris Saint-Germain and Lyon, which has been moved to Monday night at the request of local police. Authorities cited security concerns and the strain on police resources over a weekend that will also see the NFL stage its first regular-season game in France.
The demonstrations have been driven by anger over the rising cost of living, deteriorating conditions in public schools and teacher shortages. Some estimates put the number of protesters who marched last weekend at 800,000.
The Steelers face the New Orleans Saints at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis on Sunday, around 10km from central Paris.
The four-time NFL MVP said he was confident the game would go ahead as planned.
“I definitely think that the NFL is alert to what’s going on,” he told a press conference on Friday.
“This game means a lot to the NFL. If it was unsafe, then I’m sure we wouldn’t be here.”
The NFL said last week that preparations were continuing as scheduled despite the unrest. “We continue to work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters,” the league said, adding that there had been “no disruption or impact at league sites”.
The game in Paris has been largely overshadowed by the nationwide protests, with new demonstrations planned for Saturday. The Steelers informed fans on Thursday that a “Steelers House” fan event in the Bastille neighbourhood would not go ahead.
The US state department issued a security alert on Thursday night, calling on its citizens to “avoid demonstrations and areas of unrest”.
“Americans in Paris for the NFL game on Sunday, October 25 should also exercise caution and be aware of their surroundings,” the state department added.
Many Americans and other foreign visitors have travelled to France to watch Sunday’s game despite the protests.
Fred Zelt, a 67-year-old Steelers fan at the NFL House set up in Paris, arrived in the French capital a week ago.
“We saw [last Saturday] a march of probably several hundred students. It was completely peaceful,” he told Reuters.
“Every place we’ve been seemed calm and normal to us. We now see shops boarding up windows.
“There are lots of people out. People are having a good time and we’re not overly worried.”
Fabian Bauer, a 28-year-old Saints fan, travelled from Germany with his parents.
“We had a long discussion about whether we should come here or not,” he said. “In the end, I informed myself, and most of the fans said it’s likely to be safe, especially on Sunday.
“It’s not as bad as one might have thought. The shop windows are a bit damaged.”
The NFL pop-up store in Paris will be closed on Saturday, the league said on Friday.
Monika Allen, a 56-year-old Steelers fan, was on her way to the shop on Friday to buy “more Steelers clothes”, saying she “didn’t prepare for the cold and the wind”.
The unrest is not the only thing that has disrupted the build-up to the game, with Storm Austen hitting parts of the country. Météo-France, the national weather agency, has issued orange alerts for much of the country’s north-west, including the Paris region.
The Steelers landed in France on Friday morning. They were due to practise at the Stade de France before holding a press conference.
They eventually cancelled their training session because of bad weather, and the press conference was moved to their hotel in Paris.
The Saints have been practising this week in Versailles after arriving in France on Monday.
“Due to elevated wind and rain conditions, in accordance with local authorities, there will not be a media viewing portion during today’s Saints practice,” the Saints said in a statement.
The NFL also cancelled a fan event on Friday.
“NFL Experience Paris presented by Wilson is closed for the rest of today due to adverse weather. Please do not attend the site,” the NFL said in a statement.

title: Swoon! London City Ballet are positively glowing in a night of dreams – and ghosts from dance history
description: Alina Cojocaru astonishes in John Neumeier’s Ghost Light, an ethereal meditation on time, while Glen Tetley’s Firebird has much to cherish
content:
Sadler’s Wells, London Alina Cojocaru astonishes in John Neumeier’s Ghost Light, an ethereal meditation on time, while Glen Tetley’s Firebird has much to cherish
A ghost light is the name for a single lamp left on stage when a theatre is dark, and one glows throughout John Neumeier’s ballet Ghost Light. Also never not glowing is Alina Cojocaru , superlative ballerina and guest dancer with London City Ballet, who has a longtime working relationship with Neumeier and his Hamburg Ballet – with whom this work was originally created in 2020.
When Cojocaru materialises onstage in silence, so ethereal it’s almost mystical, she is like a ghost of Swan Lake’s Odette, wings fluttering, eyes half closed, lost in a memory. Cojocaru’s divine delicacy embodies all of the romance of ballet, until suddenly her steps glitch, she stumbles over a chair and comes to. The stage is a place of dreams, for all the dancers who have crossed its boards and will continue to do so (superstition says that ghost lamps also allow spirits of former dancers to return to the stage). Neumeier evokes some of these dances in this piece, from a stray sylph upstage, to earnest solos, sparky allegro and two young men in a tender duet, passing each other sometimes in parallel worlds, sometimes in moments of connection.
The parts of this ballet were created separately during Covid with bubbles of dancers, a practical measure. But the result is actually a beautiful rendering of the passage of time and its circularity – of dance’s, and dancers’, evolution. Neumeier, at 87, has seen his fair share of stages – likewise Cojocaru, now 45, who always brings real poignancy.
It’s only three years since this new version of London City Ballet formed and the company is looking very fine. A major strand of its USP is piecing back together forgotten ballets and tonight that’s the late Glen Tetley’s Firebird (1981), celebrating Tetley’s centenary. An impressive Ellie Young dances the Firebird character, in this case a young woman ostracised from her austere family, who finds a partner in Joseph Taylor – and what a great partner he is: strong, lyrical and so attentive.
Tetley was a bridge between ballet and modern dance and the company pays exacting attention to form, in swift, clean steps and emotive expression. The narrative may be fuzzy, and the final scene – with its glorious Stravinsky score – nowhere near as majestic as in Michel Fokine’s (and designer Natalia Goncharova’s) version, but there is much to cherish here.
At Sadler’s Wells, London , until 24 October. Touring until 6 December

title: Why did an Epstein-linked billionaire step down from one of America’s most famous hospitals?
description: The board change is the latest development for Mount Sinai hospital which features prominently in the Epstein files
content:
The board change is the latest development for Mount Sinai hospital which features prominently in the Epstein files
The hedge fund billionaire Glenn Dubin, one of several Wall Street figures whose relationship with Jeffrey Epstein is facing scrutiny, has stepped down from the board of Mount Sinai hospital, according to sources close to the renowned New York institution.
The revelation follows news earlier this year that Mount Sinai, which has long ranked as a top medical provider in New York City, had reportedly formed a committee to review its longstanding ties to the late accused sex trafficker. The hospital features prominently in the Epstein files released by the Department of Justice, including an incident in which a Mount Sinai doctor appears to have operated on a young Russian woman inside Epstein’s Upper East Side townhouse after she got hurt during a stay on his Caribbean island.
Dubin, a founder of Highbridge Capital Management, who had financial connections to Epstein and previously referred to Epstein as a friend, served on Mount Sinai’s board of trustees since 2007 and was a vice-chair. His wife, Dr Eva Andersson-Dubin, who had once dated Epstein before her marriage, also stepped down earlier this year from the board of Mount Sinai’s Icahn School of Medicine.
The circumstances surrounding the Dubins’ departure from these Mount Sinai boards are not clear.
In a statement, Mount Sinai said: “The Dubins’ terms on the board of trustees ended this past spring, and they did not seek re-election.”
The hospital did not respond to questions about whether it had concluded its Epstein-related review or about the findings of the review, or about whether there was a link between the review and the Dubins’ decision.
A spokesperson for the Dubins did not respond to questions about their departure from the boards. In a statement, their spokesperson said: “Had they been aware of Epstein’s vile and unspeakable conduct, they would have cut off all ties long ago and certainly never allowed him to be in the presence of their children.”
The couple were still listed as members of the hospital’s “boards of trustees” in May 2025, in a journal marking the hospital’s 40th anniversary Crystal Party, a major fundraiser. In the journal marking the 41st annual Crystal Party, held this past May, neither of the Dubins’ names appeared on the “boards of trustees” list, which included those who were members as of 31 March 2026.
A 2019 report in the New York Times, published after Epstein’s arrest on sex-trafficking charges but before his death, said Dubin first met Epstein through his wife and had provided Epstein with financial advice earlier in their decades-long relationship. The newspaper also reported that Epstein had invested $10m in Dubin’s hedge fund, and that the two men continued to socialize in Palm Beach even after they “parted professional ways”.
At the time, a spokesperson for the Dubins said that they were “horrified” by allegations of Epstein’s sex trafficking. “The Dubins were loyal friends and mistakenly believed Mr Epstein, a person they had known for decades, had rehabilitated himself after his 2008 plea and deserved a second chance,” the spokesperson told the newspaper in July 2019.
Last month, Thomas Massie, a Republican congressman from Kentucky, alleged on the floor of the House of Representatives that Glenn Dubin was one of 14 “Epstein co-conspirators” who ought to face investigation and possible prosecution. A spokesperson for Glenn Dubin did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment about Massie’s statement.
Massie also named Leon Black, another Wall Street billionaire tied to Epstein who also served on the board of Mount Sinai hospital.
“Perhaps hearing these names,” said Massie, “will shame the Department of Justice into delivering justice.”
Black has said he is the target of a political witch-hunt. Last month, Congress voted unanimously to hold Black in contempt for refusing to comply with subpoenas issued by the House committee on oversight, which demanded that he appear for a deposition and provide the committee with all his nondisclosure agreements. Black, who has denied having any knowledge of Epstein’s alleged crimes and has sued the House committee for allegedly overstepping its authority, served on Mount Sinai’s board of trustees from 2001 to 2012. He also served on the board of its Icahn School of Medicine through 2024. In 2000 Black and his wife endowed the Debra and Leon Black professor of pediatrics chair at Icahn; in 2005, they established Mount Sinai’s Black Family Stem Cell Institute.
Attorney Brad Karp has served on the Mount Sinai board since 2019. He was the longtime chairman of the Paul, Weiss law firm until he resigned from that position earlier this year after emails released in the Epstein files revealed extensive personal and business communications with Epstein. Paul, Weiss has said that Karp “regrets” his interactions with Epstein. Karp remains on Mount Sinai’s board.
According to the justice department files released in January, Epstein donated hundreds of thousands of dollars to Mount Sinai and its medical school in the years following his 2008 conviction on state charges. In 2019, in the wake of Epstein’s death in jail by suicide, the hospital said it was “contributing a sum equal to the donations we received from Mr Epstein and his foundation to a charity focused on preventing human trafficking and exploitation”.
Mount Sinai declined to answer questions about how much money it donated, and to whom.
The Epstein files indicate that Epstein’s donations to Mount Sinai gave him “VIP” status at the hospital. According to a report in the New York Times, Dr Jess Ting, an assistant professor of surgery at Mount Sinai, sewed 35 stitches into the forehead of a young Russian woman inside Epstein’s townhouse on Manhattan’s Upper East Side after the woman injured herself, in October 2012, while riding an ATV on Epstein’s private island in the Caribbean. Alongside its article, the New York Times published an undated color photograph that appeared to show the surgeon performing the procedure in Epstein’s dining room.
In February 2013, four months after the procedure in his dining room, Epstein directed his accountant, Richard Kahn, to make out a check to Mount Sinai for $50,000 which, according to an email written by Ting, was “earmarked” for his research. When, four years later, Ting co-authored an article about an experiment related to “aggressive sporadic breast cancer” in Clinical Cancer Research, a peer-reviewed medical journal, the article’s acknowledgments noted that the research was supported by donations from, among others, “Jeffrey Epstein to JT”.
Tax records for the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai show Ting received $4.6m in compensation in 2019.
Mount Sinai did not respond to questions about whether Ting faced any consequences from the hospital for having apparently performed the procedure in Epstein’s home. Ting did not respond to questions from the Guardian.
The New York state department of health was asked to comment about the medical procedure apparently being performed in Epstein’s dining room and whether it was investigating the matter. In a statement, the department of health said:“While the department cannot discuss or provide details pertaining to active investigations, the allegations in recent media reports are deeply troubling and clearly warrant review. As regulator of New York state hospitals and diagnostic and treatment centers, the Department of Health holds all facilities accountable for the quality of care they provide to ensure the safety and wellbeing of all patients. The New York State Department of Health condemns any abuse that undermines patient trust and safety, including any predatory or unlawful behavior, and takes its responsibility to investigate allegations like this very seriously. We extend our support to all victims and survivors of medical misconduct, physical abuse, or sexual abuse and encourage any patient who believes they are a victim of misconduct to file a complaint.”
In 2010, the Dubins established Mount Sinai’s Dubin Breast Center, which is now a 15,000 sq ft facility inside Mount Sinai’s main campus on the Upper East Side. The center’s entrance on Fifth Avenue is marked by a large hot-pink awning with the words “Dubin Breast Center” imprinted on it in white.
The Epstein files reveal that Andersson-Dubin and Epstein communicated frequently about many topics, and that she reportedly served as Epstein’s “conduit” to Mount Sinai. In April 2012, according to emails released by the justice department, Andersson-Dubin, at Epstein’s request, sought to help a young Russian woman obtain a volunteer position at the Dubin Breast Center.
When Mount Sinai’s director of international personnel stated that the “volunteer tasks” that the “foreign national” was seeking to perform “potentially conflict with the duties designated for the union”, Andersson-Dubin wrote to Epstein that the young woman could “sit there and just look pretty … if that makes it better!! This woman … has something against Russian girls I think … ,” to which Epstein replied simply: “socialism.” Ultimately, after Andersson-Dubin made an appeal to the hospital, the volunteer position was approved.
A spokesperson for the Dubins did not respond to questions about the alleged incident. Mount Sinai declined to comment.
Celina Dubin, the Dubins’ daughter, was a student at the Icahn School of Medicine and is now an assistant professor of dermatology at Mount Sinai.
The daughters of two other billionaires linked to Epstein, both of whom have testified in Congress about their relationships with him, have also attended Mount Sinai’s medical school: Bill Gates’s daughter, who graduated in 2024 and is now a pediatric resident at the hospital, and US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick’s daughter, who is currently enrolled there.
Last month, the US district judge Jed Rakoff, who has presided over all the Epstein-victim class-action lawsuits filed against banking institutions – suits which, to date, have yielded $438m in settlements – ruled that the newest of these, brought against FirstBank Puerto Rico by Boies Schiller Flexner and Edwards Henderson, could proceed.
According to that lawsuit, Epstein’s donations to Mount Sinai, which included at least $50,000 drawn from his Enhanced Education account at FirstBank Puerto Rico in June 2014, were “directly used to fund” his illegal activities. In addition, the lawsuit alleges, Mount Sinai was “linked to individuals known to have recruited for him”. The lawsuit does not specify the names of those linked to Mount Sinai who it alleges “recruited” for Epstein.
Mount Sinai declined to comment on the lawsuit.
FirstBank said in a legal filing that while it provided “routine banking services” to Epstein, it did not violate anti-trafficking laws or knowingly facilitate his alleged crimes. The bank also said it filed a suspicious activity report (SAR) shortly after Epstein’s 2019 arrest.
A group of Mount Sinai employees, including female doctors, filed a separate federal employment discrimination lawsuit against Mount Sinai Health System, its Icahn School of Medicine, and various current and former male Mount Sinai officials in April 2019.
The lawsuit alleges, among other things, that one of the defendants, a Mount Sinai employee, “regularly called women ‘bitches’ and ‘cunts’”. The case now awaits a ruling on a motion for summary judgment brought by Mount Sinai before the US district judge Vernon Broderick.
In a legal filing, Mount Sinai called the complaint “nothing less than a malicious instrument of character assassination” that was “rife with allegations that are immaterial and/or scandalous”.
“The Epstein connection is what gets attention, but that kind of culture never has just one victim or kind of victim. When powerful institutions let their men mistreat women, it’s usually a feature, not a bug,” said Ann Olivarius, head of the McAllister Olivarius law firm, which filed the 2019 suit against Mount Sinai.
Mount Sinai did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the lawsuit.
This past summer, outside Mount Sinai’s annual Crystal Party fundraiser held at Chelsea Piers downtown, volunteers supporting Equity Now, an organization formed by the former Mount Sinai employees who sued the hospital, handed out flyers that featured photographs of its current and former Epstein-linked board members: Glenn Dubin, Brad Karp and Leon Black.
“WOULD YOU LET THESE MEN RUN YOUR PTA?” asked the text above the pictures. “SO WHY WERE THEY RUNNING MOUNT SINAI?”

title: Severe flooding in US west triggers rooftop rescues and evacuation orders
description: At least one injured after flooding in Four Corners region – which includes Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah
content:
At least one injured after flooding in Four Corners region – which includes Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah
Severe flooding in the Four Corners region on Friday led to water rescues – some from rooftops – and impassable roads, with some residents being told to evacuate low-lying areas of Colorado and New Mexico and others advised to shelter in place until water levels go down.
It followed several busy days of flooding in the region that swamped dozens of homes in Utah. Earlier in the week, tornadoes blew off roofs, knocked trees on to houses and downed power lines in Arizona . At least one person was injured.
An unknown number of people were rescued overnight and continued to be rescued on Friday by New Mexico guard boats, helicopters and amphibious vehicles, Devin Neeley, a San Juan county spokesperson, said.
“We’re picking people off of roofs and pulling people out of houses that have 3 or 4ft (1-1.5 metres) of water in them, and there’s more water coming,” Neeley said.
Skies were clearing but the rivers continued to rise, with forecast crests surpassed, he added.
“This is serious. We’re still sending deputies as I speak to get people out of their homes right now. In fact, our sheriff is damn near going to lose his home today,” Neeley said.
About 600 households were told to evacuate in Farmington, where areas along the San Juan River were closed off, city spokesperson Gina Intoppa said.
“We are kind of all hands on deck,” Intoppa said.
In a Facebook post on Friday morning, Farmington police said: “Agencies have been working through the night and are doing everything they can to respond as quickly as possible.”
Additionally, a flood warning in Rio Chama said : “The current extent of the flooding along the San Juan River in New Mexico has not been observed since before the completion of Navajo dam in 1962.”
On Friday, the National Weather Service issued a flood warning across west central Montezuma county in southwestern Colorado
Farmington is the biggest city in the Four Corners, the only place in the US where four states – Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah – come together.
National guard members also were deployed to assist with flooding in south-west Colorado. Rising waters prompted mandatory evacuations along four rivers, including the San Juan River through Pagosa Springs. The resort town famous for its riverside hot springs suffered flooding from a similar weather pattern a year ago.
“Please shelter in place, water levels are beginning to recede, but many roads are impassable and unsafe for travel,” the Archuleta county sheriff’s office posted online on Friday.
In nearby Rio Grande county, trailers at a campground were surrounded by high water and trucks were partially submerged in other areas.
Some homes along the Conejos River in the San Juan Mountains experienced up to 7ft of interior flooding, while homes in the South Fork area saw water levels reach 4-5ft, the Colorado Sun reported.
The small mountain town of South Fork reported a missing bridge that extended over Forest Service Road 380, the outlet added.
Meanwhile, the sheriff’s office of Archuleta county warned residents on Friday to shelter in place, saying: “Water levels are beginning to recede but many roads are impassable and unsafe for travel.
“The evacuation check-in center is not currently accessible, if you need an evacuation location the PLPOA Clubhouse at 230 Port Ave, Pagosa Springs CO is open and available,” it added.
Photos posted online by the Colorado Department of transportation showed a road washout near Silverton on Highway 550, where brown floodwaters surged across a large section of the damaged roadway, Colorado Public Radio reported.
Jared Polis, Colorado’s governor, had declared a disaster emergency in 11 counties in response to heavy rain and flooding in the south-west part of the state.
The city of Hurricane in far south-western Utah was cleaning up after declaring a state of emergency on Thursday. Reddish-brown flood water lapped into and about 80 homes in a neighborhood and 50 recreational vehicles in an RV park.
Surreal scenes included a shipping container drifting slowly down a street.
An evacuation order was issued for the Willow Wind RV Park in Hurricane.
Other videos posted online showed people in Hurricane leading horses to safety through murky floodwaters.
“The full extent and severity of the damage, as well as the potential displacement of residents, remain under assessment,” Hurricane officials said , adding that the floods have damaged or affected bridges, culverts, public roads and electrical power boxes.
The flooding was not unexpected, just the latest from two months of heavy rain that ended a summer of drought. While parts of the south-west are rocky with little vegetation and are naturally prone to flash flooding, the recent rains have made flooding everywhere more likely, said Kate Abbott, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Grand Junction, Colorado.
“At this point we’re saturated and can’t take too much more without flooding,” Abbott said. “This is the third or fourth round of this kind of moisture we’ve seen in as many weeks.”
The severe flooding follows weeks of extreme weather across the south-west, including Thursday’s storms in Arizona, which brought golf ball-size hail and tornadoes, and a prolonged heat dome that pushed temperatures across the region into the triple digits.
Meanwhile, California was gripped by an unprecedented heatwave last week, with downtown Los Angeles reaching a record 104F, surpassing the previous high of 101F set in 1953.

title: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
description: Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis
content:
Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany , represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

title: Paddy Donnelly obituary
description: Other lives: Photographer who documented apartheid South Africa and helped to maintain archival records of the era
content:
My husband, Paddy Donnelly, who has died aged 70, was a South African who moved in the early 1980s to London. There he worked for the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa (IDAF), which funded the legal costs of people tried or imprisoned for anti-apartheid activity.
In addition to its legal work, the IDAF had a large archive of photographs relating to apartheid, and Paddy ran that side of the operation, processing and distributing photos of ongoing state violence to media outlets, campaigning groups and many other organisations. He was an accomplished photographer himself, and many of his photos were held in the archive.
He had begun by taking pictures of townships and displaced people’s camps, and when he came to the UK he photographed anti-apartheid political meetings as well as visiting or exiled South African singers, musicians and activists.
Paddy was born in Germiston, south-east of Johannesburg, to parents of Irish descent: John, a bottle store manager, and Peggy (nee Sheridan), a yoga teacher. After attending the Christian Brothers school in Boksburg, near Germiston, he did national service in the Defence Force, where he avoided any serious soldiering by becoming a photographer. Afterwards he studied journalism and music at Rhodes University, Eastern Cape, before moving on to teach photography at Mafikeng College (now Mahikeng City College) in North West Province.
In his early 20s, over a two-year period, his father, mother and sister Marge all died of cancer, and after their deaths he decided to emigrate to the British Isles, first to be a photographer in Dublin and then to London, where in 1983 he joined the IDAF. We met when I visited the IDAF to source some photos for the publications section of World University Service, where I worked, and after many years together we married in 2016.
After four years at the IDAF, Paddy moved to the Catholic Agency for Overseas Development (Cafod) in London, where for more than a decade he was their media officer, also briefing photographers who were sent to record projects that the agency supported around the world. During his time with Cafod he was invited to photograph Nelson Mandela on his July 1996 visit to London as president of South Africa.
In 2006 Paddy returned to his homeland to join Africa Media Matrix, a training department for investigative journalists and documentary film-makers based at Rhodes University. He worked there until he retired in 2021, and then returned to the UK to live in York.
There he sung in the Yorkshire Bach Choir, having previously been a member of the Barts and Highbury chamber choirs in London and the Byrdsongs choir in the Eastern Cape.
He donated some of his photos and archival material to the Legacy Centre in London, a history and education hub located in the former offices of the African National Congress.

title: As midterms loom, Trump and his allies try to change the subject
description: Despite distraction and distortion, voters know what issues will be informing their votes in this election
content:
Despite distraction and distortion, voters know what issues will be informing their votes in this election
This was originally published in The Stakes 2026, a newsletter about the midterm elections. Sign up to get it in your inbox
Elections too often get pigeonholed. The hot take, or simplistic analysis, would have it that just one issue – often the issue the source so happens to be most animated about – will decide the entire result.
Tens of millions of Americans will go to the polls next month. Will they be galvanized by affordability? Maybe it’s Iran. Or healthcare? Taxes, perhaps. Or crime.
It depends, of course, on whom you ask. The US electorate is not a monolith. Just as different voters are grappling with different pressures and realities, they have different priorities and concerns.
Take a look at our voter panel . For Justin Daniels, 45, in Detroit, Michigan, the most significant issue in this election is economic malaise. For Yajaira Martinez, 43, in Pharr, Texas, it’s labor. For Scott Akridge, 60, in Marietta, Georgia, it’s the administration’s brutal crackdown on immigration.
The challenge for any one party trying to win over such a sprawling country is whether it can address enough of these concerns, and obtain the trust of enough voters, to build a coalition.
Which makes the latest polling all the more disconcerting for Republicans , less than two weeks before election day.
The headline takeaways from the most recent Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos survey were damning enough: as my colleague Shrai Popat reported , most Americans think Donald Trump is using the US presidency to enrich himself, and his approval rating has fallen to a new low.
Beneath the surface, though, the numbers are yet more dismal for Republicans.
Presented with a dozen issues, from affordability and corruption to taxes and transgender issues, respondents were asked which of the two main parties they trust to do a better job of handling them. On all but one – crime – a greater share picked Democrats than Republicans.
On the economy, as the White House continues to hail a “new golden age”, Republicans have lost ground significantly over the past six months. While they commanded a one-point lead over Democrats in April, they are now nine points behind on the issue voters consistently rank as a top concern.
And on immigration, which Trump and his officials have put at the heart of his second presidency, the five-point Republican lead in April has reversed. Almost two years into the administration’s deadly and controversial crackdown, Democrats are now ahead by two points.
In Kansas, where voters have not sent a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932, the party’s candidate, Adam Hamilton, has been pledging to turn down the heat , and ignore partisan battles, amid rising political polarization. Some recent polls have put him ahead.
Midterm elections are almost always tough for Washington’s governing party. There is a conventional playbook for navigating this: senior figures fan out nationwide to reassure the people who backed them two years prior that they get it. They hear them. They’re on it. They just need more time.
The president is indeed fanning out across the country. This week alone, he was in Kansas on Monday and North Carolina on Tuesday, before South Carolina on Wednesday, Iowa on Thursday and Florida on Friday. Georgia and Michigan follow this weekend. JD Vance is on a cross-country tour of his own.
But this is where Trump and his allies depart from convention. Rather than acknowledge the golden age has yet to shine for much of the country – let alone concede that some of his priorities since taking office, like the beautification of Washington, or adding his name to the Kennedy Center, were not among the campaign promises his base had found so appealing in 2024 – Trump has opted for an altogether different response.
This summer, as questions over Iran, the cost of living and hardline anti-immigration policies loomed large, the most powerful elected officials in the US tried to stoke fears that communism was rife inside the Democratic party.
In September, the president dangled a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen, a proposal that was widely criticized as a pre-election bribe.
Now, in the final stretch of the campaign, those questions very much remain. Rather than address them, Republicans appear to be resorting to a volatile mix of distraction and distortion.
Having spent much of the Iran war, which he launched in February, claiming it was about to end, the president is now pivoting to Ukraine – striking a stunning deal to buy Russian diesel , pausing some sanctions on Moscow and suggesting the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, should quit.
And as France was gripped by fresh unrest this weekend, Vance entered the chat. Demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living were, in fact, evidence of “western liberals” having “imported the third world” into their countries, according to the vice-president.
“And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” added Vance. Not to be outdone, Trump himself has used public appearances to echo such warnings in recent days, as my colleagues Joseph Gedeon and David Smith reported.
Many Americans are paying close attention – not to France, necessarily, but to the issues that dominate their daily lives. In November, we’ll find out whom Americans trust to address them.
The US politics team hosted a series of reader Q&As leading up to the midterms. In our final session, Guardian immigration reporters answered your questions about how ICE and Trump’s mass deportation agenda could shape election results. See our other conversations here:
The makeup of the Democratic party, plus key races to watch
Who are the groups financially backing the candidates in the midterms?
Will the Iran war cost Trump in the US midterm elections? Your questions answered
Will Trump’s economy sink Republicans in the US midterm elections? Our reporters answered your questions
Mary Peltola’s campaign to represent Alaska in the US Senate has taken her to parts of the huge state’s interior that are inaccessible by road and on the frontlines of the cost-of-living crisis she hopes will make her the first Democrat to win the seat in nearly two decades.
She has been to towns where paper towels retail for $40, a half gallon of oat milk goes for $21 and the cost of a new freezer can be quadruple what it is in the state’s largest city, Anchorage, simply because it’s so complicated to get there. She’s heard of communities along the Arctic Ocean where power bills have climbed to $1,500 a month because they rely on generators for power and the Iran war has pushed the cost of diesel to new heights.
“Nobody can afford that,” Peltola said in an interview.

title: Wallaroos complete Scotland sweep as retiring Smith gets standing ovation despite red
description: Australia completed a three-game sweep over Scotland with a 38-31 win in a spicy contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards
content:
Women’s rugby union: Australia 38-31 Scotland
Cecilia Smith ‘sorry’ for red card on final Wallaroos game
The Wallaroos completed their three-game sweep over Scotland with a 38-31 win on Friday in a spicy contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards.
Australia produced plenty of classy moments in Canberrabut again lacked discipline in tackles and around the ruck to keep the tourists in it. The hosts received four yellow cards, with the retiring centre Cecilia Smith earning two of those to finish her 34-Test career on a red.
Scotland had two players sent to the sin bin and it could have been far uglier if the Wallaroos centre Georgina Friedrichs’ accusations of biting had been verified on review. But the officials saw no evidence and there were no bite marks on Friedrich’s forearm, so the referee waved the complaints away.
The Australian prop Eva Karpani was shown a yellow card for a high shot in her milestone game on her 50th cap, while the impressive teenage fly-half Waiaria Ellis was also sent to the sin bin for slowing down a Scottish charge late in the first half.
The win came as a relief for the retiring pair Emily Chancellor and Smith, with the latter smiling as she received a standing ovation despite being sent off. “I’m really sorry about that, just wanted to go out with a bang I guess,” Smith said as she embraced her daughter, Ruby, after the match. “She’s been there since day one,” said Smith of her daughter. “Having her there at trainings, camps, on the sideline, means so much and I just want to be that role model and show you can do anything if you put your mind to it and put the hard work in.”
A teary Chancellor, former captain and two-time World Cup member, signed off with a win in her 42nd Test after making her debut in 2018. “It’s created so much opportunity for me, so much purpose in my life. I love these girls and what we play for,” she said. “I love what this game has given us: travel the world with great people and create opportunity. You can’t be what you can’t see.”
Victory for Australia followed wins in Sydney and Edinburgh against Scotland. The Wallaroos are now out of action until the side transitions to a full-time operation next year under their new coach, Sione Fukofuka, who has previously coached Scotland.
Australia led 14-0 early but trailed 17-14 at half-time after a string of penalties led to three successive Scottish tries. The Wallaroos regained the ascendancy and surged back ahead 38-24 when the captain, Siokapesi Palu, finished a long-range effort. But after losing Karpani and then Smith, Scotland surged back into the match, although they were unable to find the match-tying converted try on the final play.

title: Connor Hellebuyck traded to New Jersey as Winnipeg Jets end bitter standoff with US Olympic hero
description: The three-time Vezina winner joins Olympic teammate Jack Hughes in New Jersey after a months-long standoff with Winnipeg that included a suspension
content:
Three-time Vezina winner leaves Winnipeg after 11 years
Devils send four players and two draft picks to Jets
Olympic gold medalist joins US teammate Jack Hughes
Connor Hellebuyck finally has a new home after the Winnipeg Jets granted the three-time Vezina Trophy-winning goaltender’s trade request in a deal that sent him to the New Jersey Devils on Friday.
The Devils sent center Dawson Mercer, goalie Nico Daws, prospect Alexander Command, forward Nick Bjugstad, a 2029 second-round pick and a 2027 seventh-rounder to Winnipeg for Hellebuyck.
The long-awaited blockbuster trade ends months of speculation, a failed bid in June to move the US Olympic gold medal-winner and 2024-25 NHL MVP, and the Jets’ suspension of Hellebuyck for failing to report to training camp in a standoff that required the involvement of the league and the NHL Players’ Association.
The 33-year-old Hellebuyck, who backstopped the US to Olympic gold at the Milan-Cortina Games in February, leaves Winnipeg after spending his entire 11-year career there. Hellebuyck joins Jack Hughes, who scored in overtime of the final to defeat Canada, with the Devils and immediately puts them closer to being Stanley Cup contenders.
When training camp opened, new Devils general manager Sunny Mehta said he was very comfortable with the team’s goaltending situation. Since then, Daws and Jake Allen have combined for an .880 save percentage, which ranks 23rd among 32 teams.
It was not immediately clear how soon Hellebuyck may be ready to play for his new team. He had been skating in his home state of Michigan while trade talks were ongoing.
Hellebuyck has five seasons left on a seven-year contract with an annual salary cap hit of $8.5m.
He becomes the latest high-profile American to leave Canada for the United States . In June, Ottawa dealt captain Brady Tkachuk to the Florida Panthers, where he joined his brother Matthew. Last December, the Vancouver Canucks traded star defenseman Quinn Hughes, a brother of Jack and teammate Luke, to the Minnesota Wild.
The process to trade Hellebuyck became messy, especially after the goalie went public with his request to leave Winnipeg in September. The Jets suspended the goalie for failing to report for camp in a disciplinary move that extended into the season, with Hellebuyck not getting paid.
The length of the suspension became an issue, with the league and union determining Hellebuyck would be allowed to rejoin the Jets on Friday. Instead, a move to New Jersey materialized ahead of Winnipeg hosting the outdoor Heritage Classic this weekend.
The post-Hellebuyck plans went into motion over the summer, with the Jets signing Stuart Skinner in free agency. Winnipeg claimed Clay Stevenson off waivers before the season began, and their combined .907 save percentage is seventh-best in the NHL .
The Jets were second-guessed for not dealing Hellebuyck in June, when teams had more options to prioritize salary cap space to make room to acquire the goalie. The Sabres were among the teams expressing interest in Hellebuyck and were preparing to package a deal that included swapping first-round draft picks – Buffalo had the No 4 selection and Winnipeg had the eighth.
The challenge for Winnipeg became finding a willing trade partner to acquire a goalie with a high price tag and a lengthy contract well after most teams had set their rosters and had little salary cap space to work with. Another question mark involved Hellebuyck’s age and track record of following regular-season success with a spotty playoff record.
After Hellebuyck went 9-8 in leading the Jets to the Western Conference finals in his playoff debut in 2018, he has gone 15-26 since, with the Jets advancing to the second round just twice in their next six playoff appearances. In four first-round exits, Hellebuyck had a combined 5-15 record.
The disparity between regular-season and postseason success was evident in 2024-25. Leading Winnipeg to the Presidents’ Trophy and winning the Hart Trophy as MVP, Hellebuyck recorded a career-best 47 wins, then went 6-7 in the playoffs as the Jets were eliminated by Dallas in the second round.
With a 345-208-55 regular-season record, Hellebuyck ranks 27th in career wins on the NHL list and fifth among US-born players. Among US-born goalies with 300 or more career starts, his .916 save percentage ranks fourth and his 2.58 goals-against average ranks sixth.

title: Officer who shot and killed Black toddler in Mississippi resigns from police force
description: Hunter Foster fired at vehicle during a shoplifting call at a Walmart, killing one-year-old Kohen Wiley
content:
Hunter Foster fired at vehicle during a shoplifting call at a Walmart, killing one-year-old Kohen Wiley
Hunter Foster, the Mississippi police officer who shot into a vehicle and killed one-year-old Kohen Wiley, has resigned from the Senatobia police department. Earlier this week, Mississippi’s attorney general, Lynn Fitch, announced that the shooting was “justified”.
The Senatobia board of aldermen accepted Foster’s resignation on 21 October and the resignation took effect immediately. Foster was placed on leave on 16 June, days after the 14 June shooting. Yesterday, the Mississippi department of public safety released body-camera and surveillance footage from the shooting, at a Walmart in Senatobia, during which the toddler died in his mother’s arms after being shot.
In the footage, Foster is seen running out of a Walmart with other officers after an employee said shoplifters were fleeing. Officials have alleged that Kohen’s mother and a friend stole diapers from the Walmart; neither woman has been charged.
Within seconds of leaving the store, Foster aimed his gun at a vehicle in which Kohen, his mother and another woman were. Three shots were fired, all from Foster’s gun, though several officers drew their guns. Foster hit and injured the driver of the vehicle, and killed Kohen.
At a press conference on Thursday, the prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who is representing Kohen’s family, called for a federal investigation into the shooting. He is also calling for Foster to be decertified, which would prevent him from serving as a police officer anywhere else.
“The bullet that killed Kohen Wiley was not justified,” Crump said. “This decision sends a message that a Black baby boy, his life, is not as valuable as the white diapers that he is wrapped in.”
Kohen would have turned two on 1 November.

title: Two ex-FBI officials charged with lying about investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop
description: Contents of laptop of Joe Biden’s son were part of a bizarre saga in the final weeks of 2020 presidential election
content:
Contents of laptop of Joe Biden’s son were part of a bizarre saga in the final weeks of 2020 presidential election
Two former FBI intelligence officials who specialized in foreign election interference were charged on Friday with making false statements about their roles in investigating the origins of Hunter Biden ’s laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election .
Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides surrendered on Friday and made their first appearance in federal court in Washington DC. Floris’s legal team expressed outrage at the development coming from the US Department of Justice, the parent agency of the FBI .
“Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the [justice department] has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election,” her attorneys said in a statement.
The case was filed 10 days before the 3 November midterm elections and marks the latest in a series of high-profile and politically charged investigative actions the justice department has undertaken in the run-up during the height of campaigning ahead of the vote.
The prosecution, a rare justice department criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and bizarre saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race, in which Joe Biden, Hunter Biden’s father, beat Donald Trump but Trump refused to accept the result and tried numerous ways to overturn it – which ended up in his second impeachment , accused of inciting an insurrection attempt on 6 January 2021 , and criminal charges that were ultimately dismissed after Trump’s 2024 election victory.
Friday’s court proceedings also came amid a broader, backward-looking effort by the FBI director, Kash Patel , who before taking over the nation’s premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it, to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau’s recent past that for years have animated Trump’s conservative base.
The revelation of the laptop’s existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump and Biden.
The laptop’s contents were publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop. The laptop contained emails that appeared to show discussions of the younger Biden’s foreign business dealings.
The peculiar circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian disinformation, particularly when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community was assessing that Russia was attempting to interfere on Trump’s behalf in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens.

title: Life and love, shaped by the Guardian

content:
The newspaper has played an important part in the family life of Lucy Biggs
I used to work for the Guardian as a designer (2008 to 2010 or thereabouts), I met my husband, Stephen, through Guardian Soulmates (2012), I wrote a piece for the Guardian’s Weekend magazine when our first baby, Reuben, sadly died ( ‘Please find some words for me’: the conversations that helped after our son’s stillbirth, 17 August 2019 ), and now our next baby, Juno, aged six, has featured in your Saturday magazine ( The kids’ quiz, 19 September ). By chance, her question appeared a couple of days after our 10th wedding anniversary.
So now there is just our five-year-old, Toby, to go (he is very active in his submission of questions to the kids’ quiz), after which my Guardian life will be complete. Until I die, that is (hopefully not soon), at which point someone really should submit an obituary of my Guardian life’s work! Lucy Biggs Macclesfield, Cheshire
