title: Carrick delivers 5min 27sec monologue and says he will hold brolly to keep everyone dry
description: Manchester United’s head coach said he would hold an umbrella for ‘everyone else to stay dry’ while he got wet as he underlined the importance of humility
content:
Manchester United coach wants ‘humility’ and ‘resilience’
He does not rule out stripping Fernandes of captaincy
Michael Carrick began his Friday media conference with an extraordinary 5min 27sec monologue that cited Manchester United’s values of “humility”, “resilience” and “earning the right to win”, in what could be read as a public address to his players after the season’s dismal start.
The head coach, whose job is under threat , later stated “100%” he could turn United’s form around and sought to underline his selfless attitude by saying he would hold an umbrella for “everyone else to stay dry” while he got wet.
The downpour on Carrick intensified on Wednesday when Bruno Fernandes questioned his tactics after United’s 4-1 Champions League loss at Como and the coach did not rule out dropping the midfielder or stripping him of the captaincy when Bournemouth visit on Sunday. “I’ll always do what’s best for the football club,” he said. “The most important thing for me is the team, first and foremost – the squad, the dynamics in the squad.”
Carrick decided to make his speech, delivered without being asked a question, after events in Como and Lisandro Martínez’s criticism a week earlier of Jason Wilcox for the signings by the director of football.
United have won only two of 11 games and started the current round of fixtures in 13th. Carrick said: “We need to respect what it takes to be here, respect what it takes to win, what you have to do to win. I’m not entitled to be here. Entitlement cannot be at this football club. We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.”
Carrick, a highly decorated United player for 12 years until 2018, cited two of his former teammates. “Ryan Giggs, arguably one of the greatest to play for this club, it was never about Ryan Giggs, it was about Manchester United. Wayne Rooney was top goalscorer of this football club. His biggest thing was playing for the team, sacrificing for the team, and what was good for Manchester United.
“Sir Alex Ferguson, the best manager of all time, the greatest for me … his main priority was Manchester United. Going back to Sir Matt [Busby], Sir Bobby [Charlton], the resilience was beyond belief of what they showed and the way they rebuilt this football club,” referring to the aftermath of the Munich disaster. Carrick insisted he could embody these values and transform United’s campaign. “One hundred per cent, yeah,” he said, before confirming he had spoken to the hierarchy and players about the crisis.
“There’s always conversations going on. It’s pretty obvious how we’re all feeling. The responsibility for me to be in this position is to lead.” Warming to his theme, he said: “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry. That’s the position I’m in and it’s a privileged position.”
Carrick believes all of his squad share his determination – “If you don’t, this is not the place for you,” he said – and insisted there were no factions. “It’s not divided. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

title: US supreme court sides with Republicans on rejecting student IDs in New Hampshire midterms
description: Voting rights advocates say directive would disenfranchise young and low-income voters, but Republicans say it’s needed to combat voter fraud
content:
Voting rights advocates say directive would disenfranchise young and low-income voters, but Republicans say it’s needed to combat voter fraud
The US supreme court has cleared the way for New Hampshire to prohibit student IDs as a form of voter identification ahead of November’s midterm elections.
In a brief unsigned order , justices sided with a Republican National Committee (RNC)-backed appeal on the matter. They cited a longstanding rule that lower federal courts should not “alter election rules” too close to election day.
The challenge stemmed from a directive that New Hampshire state officials made earlier this year, which stated student IDs could not be used as a form of identification when voting at the polls, even as a backup under what is known as “safety valve” identification.
New Hampshire has required voters to present an ID to vote since 2012, but earlier this year the state’s Republican governor, Kelly Ayotte, signed a law tightening the rules by removing student IDs from the list of standard forms of voter ID.
Voting rights advocates had challenged the directive, arguing it would disenfranchise young voters, who may not have access to a driver’s license or passport. But Republicans insisted the directive was needed to combat voter fraud.
A lower court judge blocked the directive, leading state officials to ask the supreme court to intervene.
The dispute involving voter ID requirements highlights a national debate triggered by Donald Trump and other top Republicans who argue that voter ID laws are necessary to prevent mass voter fraud.
Despite there being little evidence that voter fraud affects the outcome of elections, the president and his allies have seized on the narrative to convince lawmakers and conservative voters to back initiatives that require ID at the polls.
Voting rights advocates argue that voter ID laws can disenfranchise low-income voters who may not be able to afford a government-issued ID, voters who may not have access to official documents, such as a birth certificate, to obtain an ID, rural voters who may not be able to go to a location with ID services and more.
While the supreme court justices did not disclose how they voted on the matter, Ketanji Brown Jackson , a member of the liberal wing of the court, dissented from the majority.
Jackson argued the lower court did not err when it blocked the directive because the lower court judge was asking state officials to correct guidance which “could mislead voters and local election workers”.

title: We asked real people what they’re wearing this fall – burgundy, secretly comfy pants and fierce boots
description: I chased down people on weekdays, interrupting their brisk walks and lunch breaks to ask them to share details of their fall outfits
content:
I chased down people on weekdays, interrupting their brisk walks and lunch breaks to ask them to share details of their fall outfits
‘Is nonstick cookware safe?’ Send us your food safety questions
I t’s October and New Yorkers have finally retired the breezy pants and linen button-downs required to brave stuffy subway stations. Like much of the US, we’re now tasked with expertly layering for autumn’s up-and-down weather while still looking put together for the workday.
You might also be staring down your closet’s sea of denim and bulky coats, wondering what to wear. Instead of consulting the runways or analyzing the latest fashion trends, I wandered through Manhattan’s financial district, which boasts millions of square feet in office space, to ask people about their outfits.
I chased down people on weekdays, interrupting their brisk walks and, most likely, their lunch breaks. Below, New Yorkers (and two visitors) share the details of their fall outfits. We couldn’t find exact matches for many of the items, so we linked to similar options, usually from the brands that they recommended.
“Comfort, mixed with a little professional.” Adele, court advocate
“A good leather jacket is regrettably worth it.” Ruth Baron, Guardian senior newsletter editor
“Technically in-office days require business formal but on days when I know I won’t see another soul in the office, I feel I can get away with a comfy sweater and dark jeans that could possible pass for slacks. Working in New York City requires comfy shoes en route, so I opted for my chunky Uggs.” Bridget, political communications (and friend)
“I love pants that are presentable yet feel like pajama bottoms (no one’s the wiser).” Karen Yuan, Filter commissioning editor
“I just like green.” T, children’s services
“I try to stick to neutrals.” Annalise, fashion PR
“I jokingly say I dress like an angsty teen.” Michelle, writer and publicist
“Comfortable, practical and also put together.” Nat, attorney
“Grown-up goth teen goes to the office (and maybe the tailor).” Jessica Machado, Guardian movement building and power editor
“I’m going for dark red, maroon, cherry (this fall).” Isabelle, Data scientist
“This fall, I’m leaning into basic silhouettes with pops of color.” Lauren Gould, Filter editorial coordinator
Flats (buyer beware: these may cause blisters)
“ I like to feel free and flowing, but I don’t like to look like I’m wearing a trash bag.” Lisa, UX researcher

title: Seth Meyers on Trump’s fixation on men’s bodies: ‘Why are you so weird?’
description: The late-night host discussed Trump’s ramblings at rallies and expressed disdain for a controversial Republican ad
content:
The late-night host discussed Trump’s ramblings at rallies and expressed disdain for a controversial Republican ad
Seth Meyers shared his horror at a much-criticised Republican campaign ad while also trying to understand why Donald Trump has become so fixated on men’s bodies of late.
The Late Night host said there had been “widespread bipartisan” outrage at a “despicable” new ad that has been causing controversy this week.
He started with footage of Trump at a rally, claiming the Democrats will undo all of the great work he has done if they were to triumph at next month’s midterms.
“All you’ve done is undo things!” Meyers responded, adding that “we had nice things” before Trump came in and ruined them.
Trump also claimed the midterms would be on 31 October before “a thing called November”, which Meyers said sounded like a book one would read to impress someone at a bar.
He also joked that if you said that after being pulled over by a cop, “they wouldn’t even give you a Breathalyser”.
Trump has been campaigning in deep red states but has been “unravelling” onstage, rambling again about not winning the Nobel peace prize while forgetting its name and calling it the Pulitzer.
“What other awards does this guy think he deserves?” Meyers asked before joking that he would expect a Tony as “I know so many Tonys.”
But on Wednesday he was “misfiring a lot” and made a bizarre sound that was “less like a president and more like a bullfrog”.
Trump has also seemingly developed “a bizarre fixation on men’s physiques” with Meyers playing a strange montage of the president describing men’s bodies. “The only issue he has left to campaign on is me likey what I see,” Meyers added.
Meyers said that Trump “sounds like a blindfolded bachelorette at a strip club” but he has “always valued surface over substance … he just knows marketing”.
There have been repeated references to men’s asses which Meyers shared with viewers before asking of Trump: “Why are you so weird?”
Meyers added: “No one cares if you can bounce a quarter off Jon Husted’s ass because thanks to inflation that quarter is worthless.”
Meyers joked that Trump sounds like “Samantha when she’s dating a new male model”, he said referencing the Sex and the City character. Yet with Texas candidate Ken Paxton, Trump has been “far less glowing”.
The Republicans are getting “desperate” and nowhere is that more obvious than in Ohio with candidate Vivek Ramaswamy , the “annoying tech billionaire that even Republicans hated when he ran in 2024”.
In his campaign for Ohio governor, he has been running “one of the slimiest and most disgusting ads in the history of politics” which uses the estranged mother of his opponent to claim she was lying about being sexually assaulted as a child.
“Have you ever seen a more insufferable prick in your life?” Meyers asked before saying the ad is “so clearly over the line” that even Republicans have been speaking out.
But instead, JD Vance has been attacking any Republicans who have called the ad out. “Is there no soul behind all that eyeliner?” Meyers asked.
Meyers added that the vice-president “revels in being an asshole but being an asshole has a cost”.

title: Authorities said Elizabeth Struhs was ‘safe’. So why did the eight-year-old die?
description: Opportunities to help the eight-year-old were missed well before she died in 2022 after her parents withdrew the insulin she needed for type 1 diabetes
content:
Opportunities to help the eight-year-old were missed well before she died in 2022 after her parents withdrew the insulin she needed for type 1 diabetes
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
The first time a Queensland government employee declared Elizabeth Struhs safe was two days after the six-year-old nearly died.
In July 2019, her father, Jason Struhs, had taken her to Toowoomba hospital in a coma. She was diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis, as a result of her previously undetected type 1 diabetes. She was intubated and ventilated; some doctors believed she was already dead. Both her parents were later convicted of child neglect for waiting until she was so sick to seek medical help.
But an officer from the department of child safety assessed Elizabeth as “safe” .
In December 2021, her mother, Kerrie, released after five months’ jail, told her parole officer she would do everything the same again.
A contemporaneous note presented to a court last week records Kerrie saying she “would keep that trust in God that he would heal”.
That officer assessed Kerrie as posing “no” risk to herself or others.
About a month later, on 6 or 7 January 2022, her daughter was dead.
Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard has heard nine days of evidence over the last fortnight about the adequacy and appropriateness of the actions of child safety, Children’s Health Queensland, Darling Downs hospital and health service, the Queensland Police Service, the department of education, and Queensland corrective services, and their management of risk to Elizabeth.
One child safety officer told the court she may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of Elizabeth’s “ upper class home ” and lack of obvious signs of neglect or abuse.
But another missed opportunity, Kirkegaard told the court this week, was simply a lack of curiosity by public servants about the extreme religious beliefs of her mother.
All 14 adult members of her mother’s church were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year.
Not everyone thought Elizabeth was safe, though.
Her specialist treating doctors, based at the Queensland children’s hospital in Brisbane, warned that Kerrie’s extreme religious beliefs could “sabotage” Elizabeth’s treatment.
Kerrie, like all members of the small sect known as the Saints, didn’t believe in medicine, and wouldn’t seek the assistance of doctors or paramedics. She repeatedly told police, healthcare workers, teachers, parole officers and child safety workers about her views.
During their criminal trial for murder and manslaughter, the court heard the group described as a “cult” . They believed the end times were near, that Elizabeth would be raised from the dead, and sang and prayed over her dead body. They spoke in tongues, didn’t celebrate Christmas, and didn’t believe in education. Kerrie had followed the Saints’ leader, Brendan Stevens , for 17 years, but Jason didn’t believe in God at all.
Multiple witnesses told the court they had little to no interest in the group and asked few questions about it. A key teacher in Elizabeth’s life thought the Struhs were Jehovah’s Witnesses. Child safety assessed Kerrie’s church as a form of support for her.
But Elizabeth’s Brisbane doctors saw it as a threat.
One doctor who spoke with Elizabeth’s mother, the inquest heard, described Kerrie’s attitude as “chilling” and recommended an involuntary mental health assessment .
That doctor barraged child safety officers tasked with assessing the case with emails, calls and other requests, emphasising that type 1 diabetes requires daily injections of insulin for life. But the doctor was “stonewalled”.
A 2019 email between doctors and child safety says Elizabeth would be at “extremely high risk of ongoing harm including death living in a household where her mother resides”.
Two days later, Elizabeth was discharged from hospital and sent home.
Child safety officers informed the Brisbane doctor of their decision in another email.
“That should send them in a panic on a Friday afternoon,” one child safety officer said in an email to another, about the decision to send Elizabeth home.
The doctor had asked to be included in future discussions about the case at a formal process known as a suspected child abuse and neglect (Scan) team meeting. They were not. Child safety officers emailed each other saying that the doctor didn’t “need” to be invited.
The inquest heard the second and last meeting to consider Elizabeth’s case went ahead without medical representation from the Queensland children’s hospital , in August 2019.
“I feel that removing her would be more detrimental and we currently have the father stepping up,” one child safety officer told the meeting, according to its minutes.
The Scan team determined that Elizabeth was a child in need of protection. Jason was deemed “able and willing” to provide it.
Elizabeth was discharged from Toowoomba into his sole care on 14 August 2019, subject to a voluntary child protection arrangement, known as an intervention with parental agreement (IPA), a less legalistic option than a formal order.
An IPA is supposed to be an intensive, short-term intervention. It should mean at least weekly visits to the Struhs’ home for about 12 weeks.
But the single child safety case worker dedicated to Elizabeth said she didn’t treat it that way.
She had a “big caseload” at the time, she said – approximately 25 to 28 children in 15 families on the same intervention – and didn’t attend weekly. Toowoomba is one off the busiest child safety districts in the state, the court heard.
Many of those other children appeared to be worse off.
“There wasn’t domestic violence,” Elizabeth’s child safety case worker told the court.
“There wasn’t drug use. To our knowledge, there was no sexual abuse.
“I believe that we may have prioritised other cases at the time for children who were presenting at more immediate risk.”
She also told the court that she may have had a bias because her own child had nearly died of type 1 diabetes at six years old. She had asked not to be assigned to the case, she said.
The court heard there was also “ organisational pressure to get a matter like this finalised quickly”.
After 17 weeks, a more senior child safety officer assessed Elizabeth as “safe” and the intervention ended.
“I did not examine the family dynamics closely enough,” that officer told the court. “I had faith that Mr Struhs would continue to care for Elizabeth and should Mrs Struhs stand in the way of that, he would leave the relationship.”
For two years, Jason did treat Elizabeth’s illness. But that changed when Kerrie went to prison in 2021.
What child safety officers, and other government agencies, did not know was that Jason had converted to his wife’s religion in August 2021. In December, he started withdrawing her insulin , as a result of his new beliefs. Elizabeth was dead days later.
During the nine-day hearing, most of the 92 seats at Brisbane’s magistrates court were empty, aside from the 19 lawyers representing nine parties, counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris and the coroner.
A smattering of media also attended, and often department figures. The mood was sombre. Several witnesses broke down on the stand; one child safety officer started sobbing once she was discharged by the coroner. Others had little to offer, saying they had forgotten about the case altogether despite being intimately involved in it, something coroner Kirkegaard said she struggled to understand given the case was “unique”.
None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.
As is routine for coroner’s court matters, part of the room is set aside for family. But Elizabeth’s sister Jayde Struhs never sat there. Most of the rest of Elizabeth’s immediate family are behind bars.
On the last day of the hearing on Thursday, fighting back tears, Jayde read out statements on behalf of Elizabeth’s uncle and aunt, another member of her family, and herself.
She said the family had never stopped grieving for a shy little girl who would now never grow into a woman.
“If Elizabeth’s life can do that for one other child, she will have done more in eight years than most of us do in 80,” Jayde said.
“I want the court to know Elizabeth as we knew her – a shy, clever, kind, funny girl with a beautiful smile, who was loved completely by us.”
Kirkegaard will hand down her findings next year.

title: The alleged attack on Helen Haines shocked the nation. It shouldn’t have
description: What happened in Wangaratta this week has horrified Australia. But around the world, politicians – and women in particular – face raised safety threats
content:
What happened in Wangaratta this week has horrified Australia. But around the world, politicians – and women in particular – face raised safety threats
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
“T houghts and prayers.” After each soul-destroying mass shooting in the United States, this is the platitude invariably trotted out by every impotent politician unable to confront the stranglehold reality of the country’s gun lobby.
“Turn the temperature down,” risks becoming Australia’s equivalent. The plaintive cry to hold back a rising tide of hatred and anger, incubated, amplified and legitimised online, now spilling into grotesque real-world violence.
Helen Haines, the independent member for Indi, remains in hospital. She has lost both legs after a driver allegedly deliberately drove into her twice, outside her electorate office. A man has been charged . The motivation for his alleged attack remains unclear. But the horrific incident has sparked an urgent national reckoning about the safety of public figures, especially women.
Haines’s life will never be the same. But what of political life? What of the lives of women who seek to claim their place in shaping the future of their country?
In the days since the alleged attack on Haines, politicians have detailed their own experiences of abuse and threats.
The minister for women, Katy Gallagher, has had her children threatened. A man told Pauline Hanson online he would “hunt her down and kill her”.
The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, received an anonymous note slipped under the door of her home, telling her they hoped her children “die of painful cancers”. The number of death and rape threats she has received over years in public life is beyond counting, she said.
Male politicians face threats too. ACT senator David Pocock has moved house several times because of safety concerns for himself and his young family. Barnaby Joyce says a driver performed a u-turn to drive directly at him.
But the attacks and threats are overwhelmingly gendered.
Last year, then AFP commissioner, Reece Kershaw, told senate estimates that “the nature of threats and comments directed at female parliamentarians and high office holders is particularly troubling, with a common feature being offensive material centred on derogatory language about their appearance”.
“Some of this material also contains extremely violent themes, including threats of graphic, sexual violence,” he said.
“These threats, which are being made online or are being sent in the post or over the phone, are sometimes also directed at their children.”
Kershaw said politicians were targeted because of their public profiles or policy positions. “However, in some cases, it appears male offenders are targeting women because they are women.”
A parliamentary report last year found 85% of surveyed parliamentarians and their staff reported dealing with constituents “behaving in a violent, threatening or volatile manner”.
Australia is not alone. The Inter-parliamentary Union (of more than 180 parliaments around the world) found “parliamentarians around the world are facing growing levels of intimidation, harassment and violence from members of the public ”. A global survey found the odds of a politician experiencing online violence were more than twice as high for women as for men.
While members of Australia’s political class are the victims of a rising hostility online erupting into the real world, they are part of establishing a baseline for the tenor and tone of political debate.
The week before Haines was allegedly attacked, the member for Moncrieff, Angie Bell, stood in the House of Representatives and said that the small business minister, Anne Aly, and the prime minister, should be “stoned in the square” for a decision made by the tax office.
That evening, Aly posted on Instagram a devastated, wearied, riposte.
“This is not just something that we should just turn away from.”
Aly then, almost as an afterthought, revealed: “this past week alone, I’ve had 19 death threats on my social media. And in the past I’ve had death threats that are couched in that exact same language: ‘stone her’.” Bell withdrew the comment and has since apologised.
There is a bleak irony that Aly took to social media – responsible for incubating and amplifying so much violent political rhetoric – to speak out against the attack made against her on the ostensibly more dignified floor of the parliament.
The chair of the Centre for Journalism & Democracy at City St George’s University of London, Prof Julie Posetti, is lead author of a series of UN Women reports, which began with last year’s publication, Tipping Point: The chilling escalation of online violence against women in the public sphere .
Surveying more than 600 women across 119 countries – with a particular focus on human rights defenders, activists and journalists – the report found more than 70% of respondents had experienced online abuse in the course of their work, and 41% had experienced real-world attacks, abuse, or harassment that they linked to online abuse.
British-Australian Posetti, familiar with the political culture of both countries, says attacks on politicians were both “entirely predictable and utterly shocking”.
“Women are being forced out of public-facing roles … including representative office, because of the serious threats that are being delivered at scale with virtual impunity.”
This pressure comes after years of hard-fought improvements for women in political power. While women’s representation in government has increased dramatically over the past decades, and in Australia women make up about half of federal parliament, globally women hold just 22% of cabinet level positions , and that proportion is now falling.
More than 100 countries have never had a female leader .
Posetti describes the online-to-offline trajectory of violence as a “vicious, self-perpetuating” cycle. Online threats beget offline attacks, and offline abuse – such as politicians attacking female journalists during press conferences – can trigger a tsunami of online harassment, further exacerbating the risk of offline attacks.
“It’s a fire where fuel is just continuously loaded into the mix. It elevates perpetually and it’s amplified online … through those algorithmic drivers, which are tuned to do what they do for profit, because we know that engagement is more likely to be driven by anger and rage than it is by support for some kind of positive action, for example.”
The rising tide of violent rhetoric and action is occurring alongside a broader democratic erosion, one being witnessed around the world.
Posetti said decades of progress on gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls were backsliding at an alarming rate under a rising tide of authoritarianism, in which “strong man” leaders decry everything from diversity, equity and inclusion, to low birthrates, and whose acolytes joke about male control over female bodies .
“An environment has been created where there is tolerance for slut-shaming women in politics who are routinely threatened with being ‘raped to death’, for threatening violence against women journalists, and for threatening the families of women human rights defenders with violence,” Posetti says.
“If you push women out of public life, you are less likely to get women’s issues represented effectively, you are less likely to see nuanced stories about women covered empathetically: there are real implications for women’s participation in democratic deliberation, not just in being elected to office, but women are being driven out of public debate entirely because there is no safe way to engage.”
Posetti argued misogynistic rhetoric “which just five or 10 years ago would have been viewed as repugnant and unpalatable” was being legitimised and reinforced online.
In the US, so often the grim indicator of the direction of Australian politics, in 2024 the president threatened a female political opponent with “nine barrels shooting at her … when the guns are trained on her face ”. Violence is celebrated: this week Donald Trump congratulated a supporter at a rally for punching a protester.
Law follows language. Rhetoric has real-world consequences.
The case that established abortion rights in the US, Roe v Wade – settled law of the land for nearly 50 years – was overturned in 2022. Even now, a decade-old tenacious right-wing movement has swung back into vogue in that country – #Repealthe19th – which overtly argues that women be banned from voting.
Fuelling so much is the isolating duality of the online world: the platforms that promise connection but offer only an ersatz counterfeit, while peddling invitations to the darkest corners and reinforcement of the basest of instincts.
Users are bombarded all by relentless “feeds” that feel public but are, in fact, uniquely private, carefully curated by deliberately arcane algorithms.
Violent memes are posted for all the world to see, but the algorithms hold each viewer in an individual self-reinforcing silo.
If those violent posts generate “engagement”, even a moment’s attention, more and more like it are offered, are imposed. Each feed is its own incubator, under constant singular refinement, making social media ever more isolated, more idiosyncratic, more dangerous to vulnerable people.
Posetti says there were two key elements to addressing the deepening crisis. The first is the human element: “There needs to be a commitment from organisations, from political and corporate leaders, and from others in public life, to treat other human beings with decency and dignity”.
The second is regulation of the technology platforms on which vitriol is allowed to flourish, amplify and spread. “No matter how effective the political leadership is, unless you address the technological drivers for the escalating hate towards women, minorities, other marginalised groups in society, then you are … sticking a used Band-Aid on a gaping wound, trying to address the aftermath.”
Australia, the global vanguard on social media bans for children, and the development of a proposed digital duty of care , “has a rare opportunity to take some global leadership on this”.
After the alleged attack on Haines, New Zealand MP Tamatha Paul saw parallels in the killings, 10 years apart, of female British politicians Jo Cox and Ann Widdecombe . (Male MP Sir David Amess was murdered in 2021 ).
“These were women in politics who were walking down the road, standing outside of their electorate offices, walking to their homes, being in their homes, when they have been attacked or murdered.”
Paul argued the well-meaning counsel from security agencies on how politicians could keep themself safe – don’t advertise social engagements, change routines and routes to work and home – undermined democratic engagement and missed the fundamental problem.
“Focus on the fact that misogyny and rape culture, and allowing it to manifest and fester in our society, is what normalises violence against women: either violence against high profile women in politics and all of the invisible violence that happens behind closed doors.
“Why do women have to pay with our lives?”
Paul said she had a message for men: “this is on you to call out your friends”.
“When they make jokes, when they say that politicians look like pigs, when they make comments that they would never make about another man, call them out.
“Call them out because this is what happens.”

title: Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote
description: Everything has become so frictionless and optimised that concerted efforts must be made to turn back towards beauty and individuality – even if it has no explicit market value
content:
Everything has become so frictionless and optimised that concerted efforts must be made to turn back towards beauty and individuality – even if it has no explicit market value
B y the time it’s 5pm on a Friday, the headache and dry eyes have well and truly settled in. Maybe it’s a long day in front of your four screens while funnelling white noise through a large pair of headphones to cancel out the calls of your co-workers. Or maybe it’s the almost chemical wash of white fluorescent lights that shine from the low ceiling in your open-plan office, or the feeling of enclosure as you look out the window on to the reflective walls of other towers.
To lift your spirits, you decide to treat yourself to a weekend at a beachside Airbnb.
But the town is not how you remember it as a kid. The farmland has been turned into identical housing estates broken up by highway-hugging shopping centres with the same Guzman, Woolies, Chemist Warehouse, Dan Murphy’s and Priceline as all the other shopping centres.
They’re not the only things that are samey. The cars in the car park are mostly white or grey, and stepping out of them, people are in near-identical athleisure or shorts and T-shirts.
The Airbnb is how it was depicted in the pictures (minimalist, fancy handwash in the bathroom, Anko soft furnishings) but there is something dispiriting about it. Just like the cars, the interior is grey and white, and it smells of surface cleaner. It’s a house devoid of colour, personality and character.
The beach itself is still beautiful, but coming out of the ocean you can’t remember where you left your towel. Every inch of sand is taken up with the same stripy Cool Cabana tents, rendering the visual landscape hectic and disorientating, as if you’d hit your head and were seeing double.
At the cafe (minimalist, blond wood, pot plants, $7 flat whites) you run into some people from school who you haven’t seen for ages. You can’t quite put your finger on it but they look different, weird almost. There’s something uncanny about their faces, with their foreheads smooth as a screen, their lips and cheeks plumped.
Looking around – with everyone wearing the same athleisure, staring into the same screens, drinking the same coffee, pouring it into the same-looking plastic faces – you wonder when did all this happen? Where did all the beauty go?
I t’s difficult to believe we are lucky enough to be born on a blue, watery planet that is covered in flowers. And that on this planet everyone is a completely unique individual, all 8.3 billion of us, with our own specific way of expressing ourselves, our unique faces and bodies, our idiosyncrasies, desires, aversions and tastes.
Because right now we are stuck in a sea of sameness. Whether it’s the design of our offices, the interior of our houses (major paint brands like Dulux and Sherwin-Williams say grey is a top-searched and frequently used colour, with the Financial Times reporting that grey is chosen because it may result in better resale value) or the cars we drive. Modern life is becoming drabber, uglier, more uniform and a lot less pleasing to look at.
But there are signs of a resistance – with one of the most fascinating being discussions around the need for beauty.
The left are reawakening to the fact that fighting for better material conditions for all people extends to what was previously thought of as a frivolous or optional extra. But beauty – and the elevation of beauty – is central to the project of flourishing.
This is an ancient ideal, and its suppression by the powerful is equally old.
The Greeks had a concept that bound beauty, goodness and truth together as kalos kagathos , literally “beautiful and good”. In The Symposium, Socrates describes beauty as the thing that draws the soul upward towards truth, justice and the divine. Ugliness, in this framework, was not merely unpleasant, it was a form of moral disorder.
Throughout history, there have been times when beauty has been elevated (the Renaissance) and suppressed (the factory districts in the Industrial Revolution). And in times of suppression, movements have emerged such as the Arts and Crafts movement in the 1860s, aimed at restoring dignity to working people through the elevation of beautiful objects in their homes such as wallpaper, textiles and furniture.
We are living in a time where originality and beauty have been suppressed, where everything has become so frictionless and optimised (such as the grey homes optimised for resale, not for living in) that concerted efforts must be made to turn back towards beauty and individuality, even if it has no explicit market value.
The tipping point for me is the very devaluation of the role of human-made art, writing, music and design by the rise of machine-made art in the form of AI slop.
I can live (I guess … ) with the grey houses and the bland homewares, but not with removing humans from the creation of writing, art and beauty in favour of AI.
Suffragists, unionists and workers have long fought under the banner of bread and roses – that is, having basic biological needs met while also having access to the things that elevate the spirit and please the eye.
Now the project has some new energy. You see it in Zohran Mamdani’s New York (he used the campaign slogan of “Roti and Roses”) where there was bread in the form of a promise of freezing rents, but roses too.
Everything from the way his campaign posters, font and videos were designed – with an eye for pleasing human-made (in contrast with the Truth Social slop, such as Trump as Jesus ) – to policy decisions such as releasing 70,000 free Metropolitan Opera tickets , has at its core the importance of flourishing on all levels.
Beauty can be something we vote for, but it is also something that right now we must fight for – whether we advocate for the natural world, or better-planned communities and housing.
It is also something we co-create with the world. Beauty is not slavishly following trends but working out what you like, what makes you happy – and going with that.
It could mean a maximalist apartment where the walls are pink. Or it could be wearing colour when everyone else is in black. Or it could be nurturing pot plants in your office or helping with a community garden. Or maybe it’s creating your own art, or employing an artist or writer, rather than using AI.
Beauty made by humans (and in the case of nature, protected and nurtured by humans) is not just pleasing to the eye and the spirit, but it is a form of protest. A pushback against dehumanisation of our current age.

title: The ABC’s internal politics can be toxic. But protecting Australia’s democracy is worth the pain
description: Some of its former executives (in my amateur opinion) have PTSD. And yet our public broadcaster remains a major cultural asset, making Australia resilient and livable
content:
Some of its former executives (in my amateur opinion) have PTSD. And yet our public broadcaster remains a major cultural asset, making Australia resilient and livable
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s free weekly media newsletter here
W hat the ABC does is reflected in almost every area of Australian life. In regional Australia, stories the ABC doesn’t report are likely to go unreported altogether. In the arts, books and events the ABC doesn’t cover are much less likely to reach audiences. If it stops commissioning drama and documentary, our creatives and their audiences suffer.
The existence of a well-funded public broadcaster, trusted by most, is one of the things that makes our politics different from that of the United States. It also, we can hope, makes our democracy more resilient.
Former managing director Mark Scott liked to describe the ABC as a town square. Kim Williams, who succeeded Ita Buttrose as chair in March 2024, adopted a similar idea, describing the organisation as a national campfire around which we gather. Media is both private and public. It is in our homes and in our cars and in our earbuds, the background noise to our lives.
The ABC is many things to many people, and the challenge in writing its story is this complexity. Many incidents are still the subject of hot dispute. Often, the interconnected disputes mean there are different perspectives on the same events. There are the politics, both internal and external, and endless small dramas within the larger narrative. The ABC’s internal politics are uniquely difficult. Sometimes they are positively toxic, despite near constant efforts by successive management teams to improve the internal culture. Both the ABC’s supporters and its critics tend to misunderstand this.
Those who love the public broadcaster and its personalities think of it as Aunty – cosy, well meaning and good. They are shocked when the internal toxicity occasionally emerges into public view. On the other hand, the ABC’s critics describe it as a sheltered workshop full of coddled lefties – the prisoners are running the asylum, these critics say, protected from the rigours of the commercial market.
Both sides misunderstand the dynamics that make the ABC both a tough and an extraordinary place to work and manage.
Sign up to get Guardian Australia’s weekly media diary as a free newsletter
ABC employees tend to be passionately attached to the cause of public broadcasting. It is not only a job but also a vocation and a privilege. As a result, the ABC runs on unpaid overtime and stress. There is no more potent drug than creative work attached to a sense of public purpose. Like all true lovers, ABC people tend to be constantly disappointed. Add to this a culture of scarcity: there is never enough money. Within this, some people have golden careers. But achieving good things within the public broadcaster generally takes very hard work, considerable sensibility and great fortitude.
It can also be nasty. When I checked a fact with a former ABC executive, they commented: “I see the hatchets are out as usual at the ABC.” If I had published even a small sample of the uncharitable things ABC people said about each other to me, I’d be buried in defamation writs. The ABC can break your heart and your spirit. I have met former executives who, in my amateur opinion, have post-traumatic stress disorder. Steering a fair path through this is not easy and does not always inspire love of the ABC culture, despite the many impressive people who inhabit it and the great work they do.
It is a constant at the ABC that for something new to start, something old must come to an end. At a time of transformational change, many things must end. But every program, every activity, has its passionate defenders both within and outside the organisation. The ABC staff are loyal not to management – and certainly not to the board – but to the content they produce and to their notion of their audience. Change is associated with loss and is therefore often resisted. Cliques, internally loyal, gather around particular programs or genres and work as tight teams. But these cliques frequently see themselves as embattled against external critics and against other cliques, their managers and the organisation. Added to all these pressures is the attitude of governments of both stripes. There has been active hostility, mostly from Coalition governments, as well as culpable carelessness and neglect from both sides of politics.
The second constant in the story of the ABC is the obsession of Rupert Murdoch’s News Corporation , which watches the ABC with a jaundiced eye. In its reporting, every error is amplified; every misstep, either real or imagined, becomes a story. Some of the reporting is inaccurate. Much of it is fevered. As Scott has put it, not all the ABC’s critics are fair-minded. Part of the motivation for this is commercial, and part of it is ideological.
The ABC is News Corporation’s main competitor as a national agenda-setter. So long as the ABC remains strong, the Murdoch organisation cannot claim to be the dominant organisation in Australian media and politics. As for ideology, many of News Corporation’s opinion writers and executives think that public broadcasting should not exist at all, and that taxpayers should not have to shell out for things the market can provide. Others want public broadcasting but think it should be different – more rightwing, more like News Corporation.
Like most mainstream media organisations, News Corporation has been losing influence. But the political culture has not yet caught up with the fact that News Corporation’s outlets no longer determine elections. As a result, a lot of people – politicians and journalists – care a great deal about what is said on Sky News or written in The Australian, even if it reaches a small audience. These outlets still influence and inform public discourse, of course, but people inside the ABC arguably care too much about what News Corporation outlets do, reacting to attacks or anticipated attacks.
It is understandable, given the accountability requirements that come with being taxpayer-funded. The Murdoch organisation’s criticism informs the cross-examination of ABC executives at Senate estimates hearings. Those encounters are reported prominently and unflatteringly by News Corporation outlets – and on it goes.
The problem with always reacting to a perceived powerful foe is that you unwittingly become its reverse image – you are moulded by it even while attempting to oppose it. News Corporation and the ABC shadow each other like warring siblings. The stories of the two organisations share characters and some plotlines. They love and hate each other, and News Corporation loves to hate the ABC.
But within this, there is a winner. The ABC is the more significant sibling. It has the most listened-to radio news and the third most watched television news. At the time of writing, in June 2026, ABC News is the country’s top news website, with almost 12.6 million unique visitors compared with News.com.au, which had 12.4 million unique visitors. The ABC and SBS are also, by a long way, the most trusted media organisations in the country. The Murdoch outlets are the least trusted. For all its faults, the ABC does the better job of reaching and reflecting the nation at a time when the influence of all mainstream media is in decline.
But this position cannot, and must not, be taken for granted. It could easily have been lost. Had the ABC been prevented from making huge technological changes during the Scott years, had it been differently led, had elections turned out differently, things could have panned out very badly indeed for the ABC. In the last decade or so, there have been several points at which the ABC could have been fatally weakened. Australia would be a different nation if that had happened.
The worst thing about all these battles is that debate about the ABC tends to be polarised – those who love it, those who hate it. This means that important issues, such as the role it should play in our culture and society – what we should expect of it, and what we are prepared to pay, through our taxes, to maintain it – are rarely sensibly discussed.
The ABC is a major cultural asset – part of what makes Australia resilient, and livable. It is one of the things which, if we are lucky, will make our cultural and political future better than that of the USA, or many countries in Europe. It deserves proper debate, and serious attention.
This is an edited extract from the forthcoming book Going Digital: The Transformation of the ABC by Margaret Simons (La Trobe University Press, $39.99, out 3 November)

title: Victorians can now see a home’s reserve price before auction. What does this mean for buyers and sellers?
description: State’s new transparency laws aim to make property sales fairer in what could be a test case for the rest of the country
content:
State’s new transparency laws aim to make property sales fairer in what could be a test case for the rest of the country
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Within days of Victoria requiring sellers to reveal their reserve prices before an auction, property agents started testing workarounds.
Market participants say there is already a pivot toward open-ended expressions of interest campaigns that allow sellers to keep their reserve price hidden. There is also a noticeable shift away from auctions to private sales.
By introducing stringent transparency laws to combat widespread underquoting , Victoria’s property reforms are shaping up as a test case for the rest of Australia.
Here’s what is happening in the early weeks of the new system.
The Victorian laws that took effect this month include three primary changes:
Publish the reserve – the lowest price a seller is willing to accept – at least one week before an auction or fixed-date sale. (If the sale process is open-ended, a reserve doesn’t need to be made public.)
Provide prospective buyers with additional market context, including nearby comparable sales.
Publish property sale prices after a transaction is completed.
The laws are some of the most progressive in the world, and aim to eliminate underquoting – sometimes known as “bait pricing” – which is the practice of marketing a property well below its expected sale price to artificially inflate buyer interest.
Nicole Jacobs from buyer’s agency Cohen Handler says she is seeing agents run expressions-of interest-campaigns with no fixed end date to avoid publishing a reserve.
“Selling agents at the moment are sitting down with their vendors saying, ‘OK, we can do an expression of interest campaign and not have an end date, and then we don’t have to disclose a reserve price’,” says Jacobs, Cohen Handler’s managing director for Victoria.
“They are also doing more private sales, and again, with no date, so therefore they don’t have to disclose a reserve. That’s what I’m seeing.”
Jacobs says that while underquoting needs to be confronted, she says it’s too soon to tell if the reforms will fix the problem.
“There’s so much going on that needs to be unpacked, and we probably need more time to see how it works,” she says.
Other jurisdictions have tried, with varying success, to combat underquoting and other poor practices, with the UK requiring the reserve price, which is private, to be capped within 10% of any single-figure guide price.
NSW policymakers have increased fines for so-called “dummy bidding” – an undisclosed bid to help the seller – and underquoting, while pushing for more realistic price guides.
Real estate agent representative bodies in Victoria have been highly critical of the state’s changes, arguing that they are confusing, add complexity and are suppressing an already dour market.
For example, given the Victorian system requires a published reserve at least seven days before an auction or fixed-date bids, a sale would need to be rescheduled if the seller changes their mind about the reserve in the final week.
There is some nuance in the reforms, given the seller retains control on auction day to reject a bid even if it is higher than the published reserve.
Veteran agent John Keating, a strong supporter of the reforms, warns that if sellers started to regularly reject the highest bid after a reserve is passed, it would show “agents and auctioneers are complicit in working with vendors to abuse the system”, requiring regulatory attention.
Keating says he has seen new examples of potential underquoting, with some agents using low price guides early in the campaign to generate interest, only to dramatically increase the figure when the reserve is finally published.
Victoria requires selling agents to include a “property price statement” (PPS) in online advertising that includes details of comparable nearby sales, an important tool for prospective buyers to value a property.
Unlike the reserve, which is the minimum amount a seller is willing to accept, a PPS is the initial estimate used by an agent to guide buyers.
Analysis by Guardian Australia has found numerous examples of selling agents claiming that no comparable sales exist over the past six months when, in many cases, there are many.
In one example in the suburb of Tarneit, a high-turnover outer-suburban commuter hub, one agent claims in a PPS that no comparable properties exist, despite an almost identical three-bedroom project home selling on the same street in late September.
There were also several other very similar homes recently sold on nearby streets, showing that even the best intentioned reforms require enforcement.
The changes come during a subdued period for the property market, with Melbourne prices down almost 7% from their December 2025 high, according to Domain.
While auctions are very popular in Melbourne and Sydney, most other parts of the country favour private sales.
During downturns, agents tend to favour private sales as bidding interest wanes even in states where auctions are usually preferred.
Data from Cotality shows that auction volumes in Melbourne fell sharply on the 17-18 October weekend, which represented the first auctions with published reserves, showing unease among sellers.
However, clearance rates – representing the percentage of properties successfully sold at auction – were higher than the prior week.
Cotality notes that the “fall in auction volumes could be a short-term disruption rather than a sustained retreat” with numbers bouncing back for the 24-25 October weekend.
Keating says there’s an “air of inevitability” that the Victorian reforms will be adopted elsewhere.
“This may take some time to settle down in Victoria, but when agents get their heads around the benefits of a transparent system, it’ll become very popular, and I believe will inevitably be picked up by the other states,” he says.

title: Counting crows (and cockatoos, and kookaburras): BirdLife Australia’s Aussie bird count takes flight for 2026
description: With more than 3.7 million birds counted already, the annual bird survey is on track to beat last year’s record by the time it closes on Sunday 25 October
content:
With more than 3.7 million birds counted already, the annual bird survey is on track to beat last year’s record by the time it closes on Sunday 25 October
Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here
Maths class looked more like owl-gebra for students at Cedars Christian College in Wollongong this week.
With BirdLife Australia’s Aussie bird count under way, teacher Karen Jooste has blended birdwatching into the curriculum for her year 2s, using the count to learn about data collection, along with avian-themed narrative writing and lessons on biodiversity and conservation.
It helps that there’s a tree-lined creek running through the school grounds, a gathering place for all manner of birds. There’s a resident family of tawny frogmouths with two fluffy chicks; nesting magpies and magpie larks; wood ducks; pacific black ducks; king parrots and rainbow lorikeets. There’s even a local bowerbird that has been known to build an astonishing bright blue bower in spring.
And, if her students catch the mournful cry of yellow-tailed black cockatoos in the distance, Jooste has been known to take the whole class outside to look for them.
“There’s never any shortage of birds,” she says. Jooste has a whole week of bird-based activities centred around the count. She’s made up her own tally sheet with pictures to help with identification, and even had some students doing counts during their lunch break.
“Today in our free reading time we all grabbed a bird book, we all grabbed a cushion and we went and sat under the trees and read with the birds around us. I try to make the most of it, and they actually love it,” she says.
“We really do have a very unique school environment, with the trees and the creek, so I want to make the most of it.”
With more than 3.7 million birds counted already and tens of thousands of Australians participating in the wholesome and unadulterated joy of counting birds, this year is already on track to beat 2025, according to BirdLife Australia’s Sean Dooley.
The annual snapshot runs until midnight Sunday. “We usually have a big flurry of people doing surveys over the weekend – it’s the six o’clock swill version of birding,” Dooley says.
Anyone who is outside for 20 minutes – whether waiting for a train, watching children’s sport, or on their lunch break – can wing it. The app makes it easy to record the data, with a built-in bird finder showing 30 of the most commonly recorded birds within 10km. If you spy one that’s not on the list, the app lets you search by characteristics like size, shape and colour, he says.
Dooley loves seeing people join in from cities, remote communities, outback properties and offshore islands. “The thing we want people to discover is that you don’t need to be in a remote national park to see birds,” he says.
Much like Jooste’s class, primary and even preschool children tend to get a kick out of it, he says. “ It’s great because they have to look up and look out and connect with something in the real world.”
“The advantage of doing it on the app is it’s still got that gamification aspect, they still get to enter something on a screen, and there is that competitive element; which bird species will you see the most of? Or, can we beat last year … can we beat Tuesday’s total?”
Speaking of competitiveness, Dooley hopes to top last year, when 64,000 Australians counted more than 5 million birds. The Australian magpie , rainbow lorikeet and noisy miner were among the most commonly spotted species.
He encourages everyone to “keep counting right up to the end”.
“We just want to spread the love. Know that you’re not the only birder in the village.”
Birdlife Australia’s Aussie bird count ends at midnight, Sunday 25 October

title: Met police searching for suspect after man shot near Royal Artillery barracks
description: Victim left with life-threatening injuries after incident in Frances Street, Woolwich, south-east London
content:
Victim left with life-threatening injuries after incident in Frances Street, Woolwich, south-east London
Police are searching for a suspect after a man was shot near the Royal Artillery barracks in south-east London.
The victim has been left with life-threatening injuries after the incident, which took place in Frances Street, Woolwich, located 600 metres from the barracks.
The Metropolitan police said they were called to the scene at 8.09pm on Thursday where they found a man in his 30s with gunshot wounds. He was taken to an east London hospital.
They said no arrests had been made and they were continuing inquiries to identify a suspect.
A Met police statement said: “Officers attended and found a man, aged in his 30s, suffering from gunshot wounds. They performed first aid until the London ambulance service and London’s air ambulance arrived.
“The man was taken to an east London hospital with life-threatening injuries. Firearms officers and specialist crime detectives attended the scene.”
