title: Minnesota officials say US government stopped sharing evidence on fatal ICE shootings
description: State authorities investigating killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti said federal officials paused transfer of evidence
content:
State authorities investigating killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti said federal officials paused transfer of evidence
The federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers during a violent anti-immigration, anti-protest crackdown in the state earlier this year, state officials said in recent court filings.
Minnesota officials sued the Trump administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings.
The family of Good, 37, earlier this month sued over her death when she was shot by a federal officer with Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) as she drove her car away during a protest in January.
Pretti, also 37 , was shot dead in the street by a border patrol agent as he went to the assistance of a fellow protester on the icy city streets during fierce demonstrations against the crackdown. Both Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and ICE are under the umbrella of the Department of Homeland Security.
The shootings of the two protesters, both US citizens, was a turning point in the government’s approach after weeks of violent action by ranks of militarized, masked federal immigration enforcement in Minneapolis, which local leaders called a siege , after months of similar mass operations in major cities.
There were immediate disputes over the investigations into Good’s and later Pretti’s killings between state and federal authorities.
The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don’t have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don’t trust the federal government to investigate itself.
The state is still seeking the cellphones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews.
State prosecutors announced in July that the federal government had begun turning over evidence in the cases, including police body-camera video and hard drives containing statements. The Hennepin county attorney, Mary Moriarty, said at the time that the state expected to receive “all the evidence”.
But Minnesota investigators said in October court filings that the transfer of evidence stopped soon after the July announcement. Moriarty said the US attorney’s office for Minnesota, the state outpost of federal prosecutors, told her on 10 September that evidence sharing would be on pause indefinitely “in light of challenges with DC”, according to the documents, referring to Washington and the federal authorities.
State prosecutors have again asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing they “have identified no legal authority or rational basis justifying their obstruction of state criminal investigations”.
In a reply filed on Tuesday, attorneys for the US justice department argued it was within their discretion to decline to share information with state authorities.
Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota bureau of criminal apprehension, said in a legal declaration that federal authorities still have Good’s clothing, the cellphone of the officer who killed her and interview recordings that state authorities have never been able to view. Bystanders captured footage of the shooting death of Good in her car and Pretti on the street , in each case contradicting key parts of what the administration said prompted the killings. No criminal charges have been filed.
Evans said the federal government also has not shared a recorded statement from an officer who shot Pretti, the firearms used by the officers, their phones, projectiles and casings.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Trump’s top border official defends Big Bend border wall plan despite mounting opposition
description: CBP commissioner Rodney Scott says $46bn Texas project is justified amid court-ordered pause on wall’s construction
content:
CBP commissioner Rodney Scott says $46bn Texas project is justified amid court-ordered pause on wall’s construction
The Trump administration’s top border official defended plans to build a wall and other infrastructure in the Big Bend of Texas despite mounting opposition against the project and a court-ordered pause on construction, saying his goal of fortifying the country’s borders was “non-negotiable”.
Rodney Scott, the commissioner of US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), said the $46bn wall project was justified despite a bipartisan coalition of landowners, local businesses and environmentalists who view it as a waste of taxpayer money that could be destructive to a region with historically low migrant crossings, in an exclusive interview with the Associated Press.
“Our number one goal right out the gate is we have to know who and what is coming into the United States,” Scott said on Thursday. If the Big Bend region were left without a wall or other border infrastructure while other areas along the border get those fortifications, he said, “I am 100% convinced it will be completely overrun and destroyed.”
The fight over the spectacular Big Bend area, close to the US-Mexico line , where the Rio Grande flows along a huge curve on its way to the Gulf of Mexico, has become a major test for how far the Republican administration is willing to go to shut off the border.
Scott, a former border patrol agent, was tapped by Trump to complete the border barrier.
His agency is responsible for executing a plan funded last summer by Republicans in Congress to line the roughly 2,000-mile (3,200km) border with Mexico with a mixture of steel fences 30ft (9 metre) high, vehicle barriers, new roads and surveillance technology to prevent irregular immigration – and smuggling of drugs and humans.
The Trump administration says it is building about 12 miles a week. Scott, who gets daily progress updates, said it would be complete by the end of Trump’s second term. The primary border wall – some areas also get a secondary layer – will be done by the end of December 2027.
“We’re actually ahead of schedule,” Scott said.
The wall plan has run into stiff – and bipartisan – resistance in some places, especially Big Bend. The Trump administration suffered a big setback earlier this month when a judge ordered a pause on border wall construction in the region, citing what could be a likelihood that plaintiffs “will suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction”. The administration has asked the supreme court to lift the order.
The ruling included any construction in Big Bend national park, an area that has seen a loud bipartisan outcry, including from some Republican lawmakers.
After bulldozers were spotted in the park tearing up ground in August, Scott ordered a pause on all construction-related activity there while he went to talk to people in the region. He said the agency was making other outreach to locals to discuss how to build projects so they don’t mar the park.
“We’re talking through and figuring out what is the right solution for that area,” he said. But he added that “protecting the country” with a barrier is “non-negotiable”. Scott added that the huge steel fences will not go up in the national park because of ongoing lawsuits.

title: EPA has failed to tackle cancer-linked pesticide pollution, lawsuit alleges
description: Suit alleges EPA has for decades failed under the Clean Water Act to address surface-water atrazine pollution
content:
Suit alleges EPA has for decades failed under the Clean Water Act to address surface-water atrazine pollution
A new lawsuit asks a federal judge to order the Trump administration to address widespread pollution from the hormone-disrupting pesticide atrazine – which has regularly been found at levels that threaten wildlife and human health.
The cancer-linked chemical is now contaminating nearly 25%, or about 860,000 miles, of all continental US rivers, according to a recent review of federal records . The waterways cover more than 20% of surface drinking water intakes across the country, and more than 675,000 private and commercial wells.
The suit alleges that the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has for decades failed under the Clean Water Act to address the surface-water pollution. It asks a federal court to order the EPA to develop quality standards for the chemicals.
The EPA was supposed to put a plan in place in 1999, but has not yet done so. Another plan it developed under the nation’s pesticide laws, instead of the water laws, would only address about 1% of atrazine pollution, according to a peer-reviewed study .
“It is absolutely insane that atrazine is one of the most widespread water contaminants and it isn’t even be properly regulated under the Clean Water Act,” said Nathan Donley, environmental health science director with the Center For Biological Diversity, a non-profit that is among the lead plaintiffs. “The fact that it doesn’t have any [limits] is bonkers and goes to show how little they’ve done.”
Atrazine is the second most widely used pesticide in the US, with about 70m pounds sprayed on cropland annually. It can have severe impacts on human and animal hormones, especially for developing children. The pesticide was found to “ chemically castrate ” frogs and cause some to change sex. It is so dangerous that it has been effectively banned in 60 countries, including the European Union, since 2003, and California this month proposed adding it to its carcinogen list.
The EPA’s plan to rein in pollution under the pesticide laws appears good on paper, but is “worthless” upon closer scrutiny, Donley said. It would require farmers who spray the maximum amount allowed under the law to reduce their use. But very few farmers spray the maximum amount, so the effect would be negligible, Donley said.
The EPA plan also offers a “menu” of about 30 actions from which farmers can choose to reduce the amount of atrazine runoff from farmland. But many of the options include actions like keeping a log of the amount of pesticide the farmer uses, which does not actually do anything to reduce runoff, Donley said.
“Where the rubber hits the road, the EPA plan does not do a damn thing,” Donley said. The chemical is such a problem because it is highly mobile and easily washes into waterways, and it is persistent, meaning it does not break down. The only real solution was a ban, Donley said.
“The rest of the world is banning this incredibly dangerous pesticide. Why is Trump’s EPA continuing to push this poison on people?” he added.

title: The US west has lost nearly 300 glaciers since the 1960s. Climate crisis is drastically shrinking what’s left
description: At the midpoint of the last century the region had 1,450 glaciers and a new study reveals the extent of losses
author_name: Oliver Milman, Andrew Witherspoon, Daniel Wolfe
content:
At the midpoint of the last century the region had 1,450 glaciers and a new study reveals the extent of losses
More than 11,000 years ago, the end of the last ice age left glaciers across North America.
The icepacks in the western US are vanishing in our lifetimes, accelerated by the climate crisis.
Researchers documented that hundreds of places like these are now lost to time.
Across the US west, rising temperatures are causing glaciers to retreat to the point of vanishing. About 300 glaciers have disappeared since the 1960s, with almost all of the rest set to drastically shrink as the climate crisis continues to escalate, a new study has found.
At the midpoint of the last century more than 1,450 glaciers – large tongues of ice, snow and rock that move under their own weight and gravity – were threaded throughout the mountains of the American west, providing cool water for ecosystems and agriculture as they gradually melted.
Some, in the Sierra Nevada of California, were formed a few thousand years ago while others, such as those in the Pacific north-west, are remnants from even further back in the last ice age, which ended about 11,700 years ago.
The long stories of these perennial masses of ice are coming to a rapid end, however, due to global heating caused by the burning of fossil fuels. The total area of glaciers in the US west has shrunk by a third since the 1960s, the new research found, with evidence this loss is speeding up as temperatures continue to rise.
About 300 of these glaciers have functionally disappeared, meaning they have reduced to the size of about two football fields and no longer move. After dominating mountaintops for thousands of years, hundreds of once regal glaciers have been reduced to tiny, sad scraps of ice just within the span of time since the Beatles released their first record.
“When I realized this it was like, ‘Yikes – that’s a lot more than I thought,’” said Andrew Fountain, a geographer at Portland State University and lead author of the new study.
The US’s largest glaciers are still found in Alaska but Fountain said he wanted to conduct the first proper inventory of the “unloved” glaciers that sit closest to where people live, in the lower 48 states. The new research, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , used satellite data and aerial photography to chart how glaciers across six western US states have receded.
Smaller, south-facing glaciers have experienced the greatest rates of shrinkage, particularly those at lower elevations of below 9,000ft in the Sierra Nevada and under 6,000ft in the Cascade range, which runs along the Pacific north-west.
But even many of the larger glaciers are set to disappear in the next half century, previous work by Fountain has found , with the end of the century likely to see them only existing, in a diminished state, atop the tallest mountains in the west such as Mount Hood and Mount Rainier.
“The sad conclusion is that we are seeing signs glacier change is accelerating and I’d say a lot of them will be gone by 2100,” Fountain said. “In the summertime they are melting more because it’s hotter and in winter they are getting rain instead of snow, which isn’t nourishing them. It’s a double whammy. There’s no good news on this.”
Glaciers are important components of alpine ecosystems and provide some water for agriculture and hydroelectric power in the US west, even if they are remote from where most people live. Still, their retreat has been fast enough to cause a sense of angst among locals, according to Fountain.
“People like knowing glaciers are around, they are close to their hearts and it’s worrying to see the mountains look bare,” he said. “The loss of glaciers is also tangible evidence of a shrinking snowpack, where a lot of drinking water is sourced from, so that is a concern when it comes to drought too.”
This problem is not confined to North America. In places such as Europe and the Himalayas , scientists have documented the decline of glaciers as global heating has intensified, imperiling crops and wildlife.
“We are turning up the heat in the refrigerator, so the ice is melting everywhere,” Fountain said. The loss of glaciers can be slowed by action to cut planet-heating emissions, he said, but the process of halting or even restoring them could take centuries, if at all.
Until then, glaciers will be at increasing risk of destabilizing in sudden, potentially disastrous ways, such as when a catastrophic glacier and bedrock collapse along the Tibet and Nepal border in August killed at least 1,400 people, with thousands more still missing .
“There is a whole suite of dangers we haven’t quite prepared for which is not just that the ice has gone but that the terrain isn’t stable any more,” said Eric Rignot, a glaciologist at the University of California, Irvine. “We have seen that in Nepal but also in the Alps, where the climbing season is getting shorter because it’s too dangerous. That is something I’m worried about.”
The rampant melting of glaciers at the great polar ice caps, meanwhile, is directly causing sea levels to rise. About 12.5tn tons of ice from glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica have melted away since 1979, a major study found last month .
This enormous amount of lost ice, enough that it could cover the entire continental US 5ft deep, has melted into three quadrillion gallons of water and raised global sea levels by about an inch over the past four decades.
Even a small sea level rise is enough to severely worsen the effect of storms and flooding on shores, with most of the world’s coastal cities now at risk of some level of inundation as the ice sheets lose mass.
“People have been shocked about the flooding in southern California but we have been telling you about this for 40 years, clearly no one is listening until their basement is flooded,” said Rignot, a co-author of the paper on the ice that has been lost at the poles.
“You get creeping sea level rise but then you have events like storms or king tides on top of that and then you are in trouble. It’s getting worse all the time but it’s not too late, any step in the right direction matters. People shouldn’t be overwhelmed by the task, we should think we want to change and we should change.”
Main photos of Hayden Glacier in Oregon. Photographs: IC Russel/US Geological Survey Photographic Library; Hassan Basagic/The Glacier RePhoto Project

title: ‘An orchestra being gassed should be an alarm signal’: the musical activists targeted in Paris
description: New World Orchestra’s musicians are shocked at French police targeting peaceful gathering with teargas
content:
New World Orchestra’s musicians are shocked at French police targeting peaceful gathering with teargas
A s riot police encircled Place de la République last week, lobbing teargas canisters to disperse demonstrators, the conductor Étienne Jarrier and his orchestra played on. They kept playing even after everyone else had disappeared and teargas was being fired into the central Paris square.
It was only when Jarrier noticed his musicians were being directly targeted that he ordered them to stop. “There were teargas canisters landing in the double bass and music stand cases, and starting fires the musicians had to stamp out,” he told the Guardian.
The Orchestre du Nouveau Monde (the ONM, or New World Orchestra) is used to accompanying protests. Co-founded by Jarrier in 2022, the Paris-based ensemble is made up of hundreds of young professional and amateur musicians, all volunteers and all committed to blend classical music and activism, particularly social and climate justice.
The orchestra describes itself as “anti-racist, anti-capitalist, feminist, environmentalist and committed to de-growth”, with the dual aim of linking artistic performance with activism and increasing awareness of classical music among the young rather than its traditional “white bourgeois and elderly” following.
In 2022, ONM played at the foot of a melting Alpine glacier; two years later it was outside the headquarters of the far-right Rassemblement National (RN), performing a parody of an anthem popular with Marshal Pétain’s Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis. Last year, it formed a welcoming committee outside a television station for the Eurosceptic RN leader Marine Le Pen, and played the EU anthem, Beethoven’s Ode to Joy.
“We’re very happy to play at demonstrations,” Jarrier, 25, said. “There are lots of anthems for social struggles in France , like the Marseillaise or the International or activist music of the last centuries, but it’s important to play music that appeals to new generations.”
For the recent protests, its repertoire has included The Hanging Tree from The Hunger Games, and the theme from Marvel’s The Avengers film. “Music from a superhero movie on a day of social struggle seemed appropriate” said the conductor.
Jarrier, whose late father was a photographer and whose mother is an archeologist, studied classical music and the clarinet until the age of 17, but is a self-taught conductor.
Photographs of last Saturday’s protests show Jarrier, baton raised, conducting the ONM against the backdrop of the 10-metre high bronze monument representing Marianne, symbol of the French republic, and a dense white cloud of teargas.
French security forces, including the CRS riot police, were unimpressed. The squadrons of police, often nicknamed Robocops, have been widely criticised for their aggressive policing of recent demonstrations, particularly their liberal use of stun grenades (that emit a deafening explosion), flash-balls, baton charges and teargas against protesters. Yet they seemed impotent to stop those looting shops and destroying public buildings.
On Saturday, Jarrier had invited musicians to join the orchestra at Place de la République, the starting point for the official demonstration by high-school students protesting a failing and unjust education system, and by unions angry with the government’s failure to address wider grievances.
“It was a day of what we call a convergence of struggles,” Jarrier said. “The orchestra is engaged politically in the fight, so our presence was necessary on such a day. We appealed to any musicians with an instrument who wanted to play to come to Place de la République before the official protest march starting at 1pm.
“We planned to make music when it set off,” he added.
As between 400 and 500 musicians gathered in the square, orchestra members alerted the CRS that they would be present and performing, Jarrier said. “We asked them to let us know if they plan to charge or gas the square, and they said they would warn us,” he said.
“While we were rehearsing, a very happy crowd of people of all ages gathered around us. Then the teargas canisters started being thrown around the orchestra. Not directly at us at that point. After a while there was almost nobody there except us.
“Clearly the aim was to clear a peaceful crowd from the place, which is quite serious and something we’ve not seen before. But even when the square was empty all around us, the CRS continued to gas the orchestra. After 20 minutes we had no choice but to stop playing.”
Jarrier said the musicians were “stunned” and “truly shocked”.
“It was quite scary,” he said. “We’d reassured the musicians before the protest saying: ‘Don’t worry – they’re not going to use teargas or charge us when we’re peaceful.’”
As the musicians packed away instruments, the orchestra’s security volunteers formed a human chain between the musicians and police.
“We are very angry about what happened,” Jarrier said. “It’s an extremely serious shift in maintaining order; the [government] is not listening to demands and is responding not with politics but police.
“It’s trying to divert attention from a legitimate movement that demands better public services, better lives. By making this about violent police repression they divert attention from the real concerns. We are not the martyrs, but the image of an orchestra being gassed should be an alarm signal,” he said.
The French Ministry of Defence and the Paris police prefecture were asked to comment on the use of teargas at Place de la République, but did not respond.
